questions.question: Why is the Royal Box always to one side of the auditorium? It's always on the right-hand side as you face the stage. And why isn't it bang in the middle? Because surely the best view would be right from the very middle of the gallery or something, rather than on the side.

answers.answer: One of the answers will be ease of ingress and egress, so they can get in and out without having to use the plebs entrances and exits.
If the royals are there, don't they want everyone to see them going down to the royal box and stuff? They get in and out. They wave at those plebs from the royal box.
Is it so that the performers can acknowledge them more easily? Because, you know, if you're sitting at the back in the middle, you'd be squished.
I'd be surprised if it didn't go back to George III.
It was on the other side (referring to John Wilkes Booth's position when he assassinated Lincoln).
Why you'd think that the most plumb seats in the place would be the ones with the best view? Yes. That's my question. Why aren't they the ones with the best view?

questions.question: Why is popcorn synonymous with going to the cinema? Where does that come from?

answers.answer: It's the biggest markup in the history of markups. Corn is practically free to make, then they charge you five quid for a bucket. They might as well give you loads so you don't wake up to what a massive rip-off it is.

Patrick worked in a cinema and made popcorn. He explains they only kept about 30% of ticket sales, so they had to make money through concessions. Popcorn is cheap to make - a kilo of corn kernels, half a kilo of sugar and some oil makes a bin bag's worth of popcorn.

questions.question: Why do we take our hats off when a hearse goes by? Why the hat, and where did it originate from?

answers.answer: Men have to take their hats off in church. And sometimes women are supposed to cover their heads. I think that holds true in more than Christianity, in other Abrahamic religions as well. Historically, a funeral would always have a religious dimension. So it may be just a translation of respect - it's a mark of respect for a man to take his hat off when he goes into church, and therefore a mark of respect for a man to take his hat off when a hearse on the way to the church or on the way from the church goes by.

questions.question: Is there any sort of linguistic or grammatical or underlying reason for the order of names in famous groups or pairs? Like Bonnie and Clyde and Tom and Jerry. Why is it Tom and Jerry? Not Jerry and Tom?

answers.answer: The answer's no. I think it's just about the way it feels on the tongue. It's like it trips off the tongue more neatly. But Jerry and Tom sounds nice actually.

In a double act, nobody thinks of Stan Laurel as being the senior partner in Laurel and Hardy. Or Gareth Hale being the senior partner in Hale and Pace. But if it's a business, I wonder if you would want your name to come first. So you have a chat about what sounds better. If it was James and Keith, Keith and James, what sounds better? Keith and James sounds better than James and Keith. So Keith would go first.
It's entirely subjective and arbitrary.

On Please Please Me, it was going to be McCartney, Lennon on the second, but they realized that Lennon and McCartney just sounds better. So they were going to alternate it but they left it as Lennon and McCartney because it's like Keith and James - it just sounds better than McCartney and Lennon.

We make unconscious rules about the order of language, all to do with the way the sounds roll off the tongue and the different shapes that we have to put our mouths in to make the words. It's prosody - the music of language. It's about the way sounds roll off the tongue.

questions.question: When an organ is playing in a cathedral and you get to the end of whatever they're playing, you've got this huge noise echoing through the cathedral. And then when the organ player stops, it carries on echoing for a millisecond and then it seems to go flat. It's almost like it's not like they've played the last note flat. Is it the echo that goes flat? It's not coming out of the organ. It's resonating around the building. And it's that resonance which drops down a half tone. Why does the echoing organ in a cathedral go flat right at the end?
Why is there a time delay between two televisions both playing LBC? She has the LBC app on both her upstairs and downstairs televisions, and there's always a delay between them.

answers.answer: Televisions are just computers these days. What you've got is some computer memory in there. Your internet's coming in as a stream of data. It goes into memory, then your processor dips into that memory and processes it and sends it out through the sound card to your speakers. The two televisions have just got a different size amount of memory - different capacity. That's why it's coming out at slightly different rates. It's because they are computers of different capacity.

questions.question: How can Mark paint his puppet theatres with coach enamel in hot weather without getting bugs landing on the wet paint? When he paints outside early evening when it's cooler, he gets bugs on it. If he paints inside with extraction fans, the theatres are too big to paint inside.

answers.answer: These days we tend towards using acrylic paints, which dry in a fraction of the time of solvent-based paints. These days acrylic paints are as good as oil-based paints because they had to get their act together due to VOC rules. The other thing you can do is put some terabin dryers in oil-based paints and that will dry it really quickly. But the biggest thing is you paint away from the wind. It's not the bugs landing on the paint, it's the wind blowing the bugs onto the paint. So you want the wind blowing towards you while you're painting the thing in front of you. Or paint when it's not windy at all.

questions.question: Why in music do we count 'one, two, three, four' and then play on four, but in dance we count 'one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight' and throw on eight?

answers.answer: In music, we count beats, and in dancing, we count bars. A bar is one, two, three in a Waltz - that's one bar. In dancing, we count bars and it's always eight bars that are counted in. In beginner's dance classes, they would count one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. But in advanced classes, you go one, two, three, four and then on five you get your body into the rhythm. Eight bars is usually the first repetition of the tune. You're getting your body into the rhythm for the big dance.

questions.question: What is the origin of 'something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue'?

answers.answer: It was printed in the St James magazine in Lancashire in the early 1870s by a writer at the time - just a little gimmicky rhyme. Lancashire at the time was still very heavily into folk tradition and magic and all of that belief. So it started that way and then spread through etiquette pamphlets and etiquette books throughout everybody. Everybody believed it because they loved a bit of superstition. They also added the sixpence to her shoe in the 1880s, but that got forgotten about. It was just for good luck.

questions.question: Do dogs have different blood types like humans do?

answers.answer: Yes, they categorically do. I asked a vet when my dog went in for an operation.

questions.question: Why do magpies like shiny things, why do they pick them up and fly away with them?
Why don't people ride zebras? They look like horses and donkeys, part of the same genus, but no one ever rides them.

answers.answer: From seeing this first hand, you won't be able to stay on a zebra more than about five seconds. According to the horse trainer, they're totally untrainable. You can't tame them. There was a Rothschild who had a carriage pulled by zebras, but that's different from riding them. Paul's friend has a safari park with a zorse (zebra-horse cross) that lived with horses and couldn't be trained despite being tame and raised in captivity - the natural temperament from evolution wouldn't allow it.

answers.caller: Gary (Calais) - Military historian, battlefield tours in France
answers.answer: The Germans seriously looked at riding zebras in the 1890s leading up to WWI as an alternative to horses due to the tsetse fly disease affecting horses in colonies. They did use zebras as pack/draft animals because tsetse fly didn't affect them, and they were good in the bush knowing predators. There are lots of photographs of German officers jumping zebras over obstacles and displaying them. But they were always too skittish - they couldn't breed out that characteristic. So they can be ridden, but were too unpredictable for military use. Horses have been domesticated for 2,000+ years, zebras are a standing start from the wild.

questions.question: Do flies get stressed? Do they feel anxiety? What is it that causes them to go faster (fly in circles under lampshades)?
Why do the Irish elm pipes have to be played while sitting down? What was the origin of that? Unlike Scottish Highland pipes which can be played standing or marching.

answers.caller: Ian (Stevenage) - Has been playing elm pipes since late 1970s, currently in UK visiting family
answers.answer: The elm pipes were a more complex instrument than Scottish pipes. To get the second octave you need to overblow the reed. With a bagpipe you don't have the physical contact with the reed like you do with an oboe where you use your lips. So they discovered that if you close the chanter up, you can compress the air and force it into the second octave. You put the end of the chanter on your thigh/knee to get that extra pressure, which is why you need to be sitting with your leg in the right position. It could be done standing if you propped your leg up but why would you when you could just sit down.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'screaming blue murder'?
Why do bouncers at nightclubs say 'one in, one out' when logically it should be 'one out, one in'? It doesn't make sense chronologically.
Why do different beaches have different granularities of sand? In Cornwall, different beaches within miles had radically different sand - fine powdery vs coarse sharp vs pebbles.

answers.answer: It's going to be a combination of rock type and tide/geology. Different rock washed in and out by the sea over time results in different sand granularity. Not just tide alone.

questions.question: How do World Cup commentating competitors know every name of every player? They can't see the names on the backs of shirts from the box.

answers.answer: Commentators have charts in front of them with player numbers, names, and notes about achievements. They do a lot of research, follow players around pre-game, and there used to be BBC pronunciation department for difficult names.

answers.caller: Ian (Wirral) - Commentated on 5 World Cups for BBC, hung up headphones in 2019
answers.answer: These days it's much easier because the Premier League, FA, FIFA and UEFA send all accredited commentators a video of all the players saying their own names properly and showing what they look like. They watch players warming up with binoculars to notice details like different coloured boots or strapping. They watch previous games of both teams (90 mins each) and learn about all the players, crowd figures, stadium layout, names of the ends. The job is often 3-4 days per match preparation.

answers.caller: Paul (Marlow) - Has John Motson's actual crib sheet
answers.answer: Paul has John Motson's original notes from a 2000 Newcastle vs Derby match - an A4 sheet with each player number, name, career stats (goals for each club), and 3-4 lines of notes per player. Ian Brown's preparation was even more thorough.

questions.question: When snooker players lean over the table to take shots, they rhythmically raise and lower their middle finger - what are they doing and why?

answers.answer: Maybe it's like sticking your tongue out when threading a needle - doing something not directly linked to concentrate, shifting focus, introducing rhythm subconsciously.

questions.question: In the show Legends (set in 1990), there's a kitchen scene with ketchup bottles and other period products. Do production companies make these items themselves or get the manufacturer to produce them?

answers.answer: There are specialist props companies who have warehouses full of period items. In the same way cars are sourced from suppliers, other companies store ketchup bottles and furniture for productions.

Some props are made specifically for a production, some are hired and some are bought in. It depends on the rarity and what someone specifically wants. There are props companies and agencies that supply these. If you can't find it, you make it.

questions.question: When a river meets the sea, you can often see a visible line where freshwater meets saltwater. Why does this happen and why doesn't it just homogenise immediately?

answers.answer: There must be a point where one stops and the other begins, and it must mix gradually. The line might be caused by the movement of the tide.

Saltwater and freshwater don't mix easily due to different densities. You can see very clear boundaries, particularly with larger rivers like the Congo, Orinoco, Amazon. The warm water from the Mediterranean mixes by a process called 'salt fingering.' The phenomenon is called a 'salt wedge' - saline water comes up a river with fresh water going over the top due to density difference. This can kill fish that aren't adapted.

questions.question: Where did the Mexican wave originate and why is it called Mexican?

answers.answer: It came to prominence all over the world at the 1970 World Cup in Germany.
It originated at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico.

It originated at a baseball stadium in California in the early 80s (81 or 82). His brother moved to LA in 82 and went to baseball games where people had to keep themselves entertained since not much happens. A super fan started it and it got picked up, becoming synonymous with football. It was adopted at the 1986 Mexican World Cup, which is why it's called the Mexican wave.

questions.question: Why are the metal zips on trousers called 'flies'?

answers.answer: Speculated about flaps moving, shiny like a fly, but wasn't confident.
It refers to the flap of fabric that covers the opening - like a flag that flaps, hence 'fly'. It comes from an old English word 'flown'.

questions.question: Does the heart of a caterpillar stay in it as it goes through the chrysalis stage to become a butterfly?

answers.answer: Speculated about whether insects have hearts at all.

Butterflies and caterpillars do not have hearts. They take in oxygen through passive diffusion via little tubes in their sides called spiracles. This is the limiting factor that limits the size of insects.

questions.question: Why does Europe have 100, 200, and 500 euro notes but the UK doesn't have equivalent high denomination sterling notes?

answers.answer: The high denomination notes were favoured by criminals moving money across borders. The Bank of England may be taking a stand against this in ways the European Central Bank has not.

answers.caller: Mark from Burgess Hill (worked in fintech, originally from EU)
answers.answer: High denomination notes were introduced, became popular with criminals and money launderers, so they tried to de-introduce them. Shops wouldn't accept them, banks wouldn't issue them, and they faded away. The 500 euro note hasn't been issued since 2019. UK anti-money laundering laws are among the strictest, which is why the Bank of England hasn't introduced higher denomination notes.

questions.question: Is there a word which is unique in each language - with no relationship to any equivalent word in other languages?

answers.answer: Dismissed as impossible to answer - would take decades to compare all words in all languages.

The word 'dog' in English is unique - it has no common root or derivation with words for dog in other languages (like German Hund, Latin canis). The earliest form is Old English 'docga' meaning mastiff. The etymology simply isn't known because it goes back to pre-written English. Many words have unknown etymology because languages weren't written for most of their history. Also noted that combination of sounds matters - Russian and Polish have 'szcz' (meaning soup) which is hard for native speakers of other languages to articulate.

questions.question: Does a cat's meow have an accent? Will a cat from Manchester sound different from a cat in Spain?

answers.answer: Recalled a previous Mystery Hour about pigeons having accents, where the caller did impressions of a Geordie pigeon. The short answer is he doesn't know whether cats have accents based on geography.

answers.caller: Ross from East Calder (owned by 10 cats)
answers.answer: Claims all 10 cats have different accents - some are gravelly, some soft. Devon cat has soft meow, Scottish cat has different meow. Russian Blues have completely different meow, Maine Coon has another distinct sound. Cats from same area can sound the same (one ginger, one black from same area).

questions.question: Why are slugs targeting my dishwasher specifically and not other appliances like the toaster or kettle? They've destroyed two dishwashers by getting into the electrics.

answers.answer: Slugs are attracted to food residue in dishwashers. People don't rinse plates properly before loading them. Slug trails affect sensors and block pipes. Advice: rinse plates properly and clean the filters regularly. Take away the temptation.

questions.question: Why do they weigh our luggage at the airport but not weigh the passengers? Surely we need to know the weight of passengers for fuel calculation and weight distribution.

answers.answer: Standard average weights are used for passengers - it's easier than weighing everyone. Luggage is weighed for financial reasons and to distribute it properly in the hold. On smaller aircraft, people are arranged for balance, but jumbo jets are so big that individual variation makes no difference.

questions.question: Why do I prefer to make tea in only five of our fifteen mugs, with a clear favourite? And why does my wife prefer the same mugs? Is it psychological?

answers.answer: The lip and shape of the cup dictates mouthfeel - the width and shape affects how volatile aromatic compounds reach you, which you perceive as taste. The colour creates a cross-modal effect in your brain. Pink/red cups make drinks taste more floral, yellow/green enhances certain qualities. This relates to the Booba Kiki effect - 95% of people, regardless of culture, agree chocolate is 'booba' and lemon is 'kiki'. Your brain fills in gaps based on visual cues. You and your wife likely have similar tastes and experiences, explaining why you prefer the same mugs.

questions.question: How do scientists know plastic takes 400 to 1000 years to decompose when plastic has only been around for about 80 years? They can't have observed this.

answers.answer: Scientists use accelerated aging tests. They expose plastics to extremes of heat, cold, and UV light to simulate what happens over years outdoors. By seeing how quickly plastics break down under these accelerated conditions, they can extrapolate and calculate how long it would take in natural environments over decades or centuries.

questions.question: How are cats able to eat an entire mouse while leaving the gallbladder completely intact? They don't touch it at all.

answers.answer: Cats use smell and taste, not vision. Their short-range vision is rubbish - they can't see things closer than about three inches. They sniff out the gallbladder (which is not firmly anchored inside the body cavity), nip it out with their teeth, and spit it out. Bile smells and tastes awful, which is why they avoid it. It's not that they eat around it deliberately - they detect it and remove it mid-meal.

questions.question: How does my new smartwatch know when I'm standing up versus sitting down? My hand position changes very little between sitting and standing.
How many unique jokes are there on Penguin bar packets? I count six or eight so far but get repeats.

answers.answer: A YouTuber tested this by buying multiple packs from a supermarket car park. He found about 9 different jokes across different multi-packs. Penguins also now have facts on them.

questions.question: The temperature outside is 16 degrees centigrade and warm, but my office air conditioning is set to 16 degrees and it's freezing, and my car is set to 16 degrees and it's also freezing. What's going on?

answers.caller: Kieran in Sligo (Building services expert, 40 years experience)
answers.answer: Comfort is subjective and affected by radiant heat from surfaces. When you're in a room with cold walls and surfaces, your body loses heat through radiation even if the air temperature is the same. Air conditioning is 'comfort cooling' that blows very cold air at you. The temperature reading is correct but the radiant effect of cold surfaces makes you feel cold. Also metabolism, clothing, and activity level affect perception. Instrument calibration and location also matter.

questions.question: If you're dyslexic, does the language you're reading affect how easy or difficult it is to manage? Is English and the Latin alphabet harder for a dyslexic person than Chinese or Arabic?

answers.answer: It's not about characters or language type. It's literally the black on white that causes issues - things move around on a page. Printing on different colored paper can alleviate difficulties. So it wouldn't make any difference if it was Chinese.

Her son is dyslexic but learned Hebrew (which is picture-based) in about six months. She also mentions Irlen syndrome as related but separate. The different colored pages/text is called Irlen syndrome.

It's about the orthography of a language - the relationship between letter shapes and sounds. In complex languages like French and English, they're harder to read, and dyslexia rates are higher. In simpler languages like Finnish or simplified Japanese, they're easier and dyslexia rates are lower.

questions.question: Is ticklishness genetic? His daughter who looks like him has extremely tickly feet, the other daughter has no feeling in her feet at all. His father has very tickly feet, his mother has none.

answers.caller: George in Rugby (final phase medical student)
answers.answer: Ticklishness is probably a very small genetic aspect plus a heavy evolutionary aspect. It's a response to threats to vulnerable parts of the body - shared mapping of where we're most ticklish. The actual individual response is more likely due to child psychology and early experiences, positive and negative associations, and learned behavior rather than biological genetics. A muted 'yes' to genetics.

questions.question: When towns like Southend were made cities during the Queen's Jubilee, would they have to rename their football team?

answers.answer: No, you don't have to change. Chelmsford City called itself that since the 1930s before becoming a city in 2012. Swansea used to be Swansea Town and changed to Swansea City when promoted. Some have changed, some haven't. The only rule is you can't call yourself United if you're just a town.

questions.question: Why does his nose not run when he sleeps, despite having terrible hay fever that makes it run all day?

answers.caller: Brett in Wigan (lifelong hay fever sufferer with sleep apnea)
answers.answer: It's gravity. When you're standing or sitting upright, gravity forces the fluid to drip out your nose. When you're lying down, the muscles relax and gravity allows the fluid to go back down the throat and disperse into the body.

questions.question: When looking at a star directly, it appears less clear than when looking slightly to one side. Why does looking indirectly at a star make it clearer?

answers.answer: In your retina you have rods and cones. When you look straight at something, you use the center of your retina with more cones which pick up color very well. Rods are more sensitive to light but only to the side and they work in monochrome. When you turn your head sideways, light hits the rods on the periphery of your retina which are more light-sensitive, making the star look brighter but more colorless.

questions.question: Why do we say we're 'scrambling' a fighter jet? We scramble eggs, so why use that verb for jets?

answers.caller: Paul in Inverness (RAF air traffic controller)
answers.answer: Two reasons. First, the technology used to code the alert message to pilots, air traffic controllers and surveillance was called a scrambler - it would scramble up words so if intercepted, enemies couldn't understand without the same scrambler (like the Enigma machine). Second, it became synonymous with the idea of scrambling to get to the jets and everyone getting to positions to get them airborne to intercept.

questions.question: Why do bagels have that hole in the middle where all the filling falls through?

answers.answer: The hole was a delivery system - bagels were stacked vertically on a stick/cane which would go on a doorknob, with a metal wedge keeping them from rolling away.

answers.caller: Avi in Mendelssohn (bagel maker, 3-5 thousand bagels per week in Suffolk)
answers.answer: The main reason for the hole is the cooking process - bagels are boiled/poached before baking. The hole allows air to flow through for an even bake because they're a very dense product. They can then be easily transported on sticks and were historically hung on strings at markets.

questions.question: When he yawns while listening to music, the pitch of the music drops slightly (about half a semitone). Why does this happen?

answers.caller: George in Rugby (final phase medical student)
answers.answer: There's a tube connecting the throat and the ear called the eustachian tube, which equalizes pressure between the two areas. When you yawn, you increase the pressure in that tube which equalizes the pressure in the middle ear and reduces the vibration felt through the tympanic membrane (eardrum). This reduced vibration alters the pitch of the sound.

questions.question: Why do we say '86 the chicken' when we have run out of chicken in hospitality? Where does 86 come from?

answers.answer: 86 is rhyming slang meaning 'nicks' - so 86 the chicken = 'nick's the chicken' (no chicken). It's an American thing from New York rhyming slang.

A story about someone falling out of a window on the 86th floor of a building - 'he's gone' (86). When he came back in, he came in on the 68th floor after a gust of wind. Heard this while working at TGI Fridays.
Corroborated Dan's story - heard the same thing working at TGI Fridays 25 years ago in Nottingham and Sutton Coalfield.

86 proof whiskey is 43% alcohol. In 19th century America, 86 became the legal maximum alcohol content for whiskey. In bars, to '86' someone meant to cut them off. Used as slang for running out or removing something.

questions.question: Why are magazines dated so far in the future? I subscribed in April and received the June edition. Why can't I get the April edition in April?

answers.answer: Circulation and readership figures are calculated from 'pass-on' - how many people read the magazine after the subscriber, including waiting rooms and dentists' offices. Putting future dates keeps the magazine relevant for weeks, so it stays in date longer and feels more up to date when passed on.

Originally from comic books in America in the 1930s - they were quarterly and would put the next quarter's date so they could stay on newsstands longer. It's about extending the shelf life and reading life of the magazine.

questions.question: When putting clothes you've worn once (but aren't yet dirty enough for washing) back in the wardrobe with the clean clothes, does it materially affect them?

answers.answer: No negative impact of putting worn clean clothes back with freshly laundered stuff. The only reason not to do it is probably laziness - not wanting to fold them again.

questions.question: What colour is an artificial testicle? I had an orchidectomy and didn't ask what colour the prosthetic was. I want to know if it's like a glow-in-the-dark LED or something.

answers.answer: Artificial testicles are normally translucent, like a little translucent egg. For children they can have a pink tinge to look more normal. For adults, it's a clear egg - like a marble but rubbery (silicone).

questions.question: When as a human race did we start laughing? What made us laugh for the first time? Was it a tickle?
Why do footballers always raise their arm before taking a corner kick?

answers.answer: Players give signals to teammates to indicate exactly where they're going to put the ball so teammates can go and attack it. They practice different corner routines in training and use arm signals to communicate which one they're taking.

questions.question: At Bexhill seafront near Hastings, when the tide goes out there are 4-5 dinosaur footprints. Why are there only those footprints? My son asked why there's no trail - like it walked in and walked away. Why are these preserved and not the others?
When sweating during exercise, is it better to constantly wipe away sweat to allow more moisture to evaporate and cool you down, or to let the natural process take over?

answers.answer: Leave the sweat on. The cooling effect comes from evaporation - your body gives up heat to evaporate the sweat, reducing your temperature. In humid conditions, sweat doesn't evaporate well so you don't get the cooling effect. Wiping sweat off doesn't help cooling - it just means less sweat to evaporate. If you want maximum cooling, don't wipe it off.

questions.question: Why does a microfibre disc cloth seem more effective when wet than when dry? When cleaning surfaces, it seems to absorb more moisture when damp than when bone dry.

answers.answer: Microfibre has split fibers that draw moisture in through capillary action. People often wash cloths with fabric softener, which creates a silicone layer that reduces absorption. Fresh cloths may not absorb well until that barrier is broken with washing up liquid. Also, fabric softener makes towels fluffy but less effective at drying - a bone-dry towel absorbs better than a fluffy softener-treated one.

questions.question: When did human beings start laughing? What made us laugh for the first time?

answers.answer: Laughter is first recorded about 4,000 years ago in the Bible. Abraham's wife Sarah laughed when she was told she would have a child at age 90. Her son was called Isaac, which means laughter in Hebrew.

questions.question: Why do cats like to sit on mats or mat-shaped things, even on uncomfortable surfaces like paper on top of Lego?
Why does luggage checked in at the same time arrive at completely different times on the carousel?

answers.answer: 20-25% of bags are flagged by x-ray machines for additional security screening. While one bag is being checked, others continue through processing, causing delays.
Luggage is loaded using 'visual compartmentalising' like Tetris - different shaped suitcases fit into different spaces on the aircraft, so even same-sized bags may not come out together.

questions.question: When senior Catholics like Cardinals move to the Vatican, do they have to go through normal immigration procedures or get work visas?
Why is the bottom buttonhole on men's dress shirts always horizontal when all the others are vertical?

answers.answer: It's a practical issue. The weakest point of a buttonhole is the end. With chest buttons, pressure is sideways. But at the bottom where shirts are tucked into trousers, pressure is upwards and downwards, so a horizontal buttonhole is less likely to tear or unpop.

questions.question: If walking along a path with a road on one side and a river on the other, where should her chivalrous husband Kurt stand to protect her?
Why do you never see yourself in mirrors or reflections when dreaming?

answers.answer: She dreams she's looking at herself in mirrors and often looks completely different - wrong hair (long when short, etc.), wrong clothes, ill-fitting or embarrassing outfits. Psychological reason involving subconscious and insecurity.

questions.question: How long does it take cobwebs to decompose?

answers.answer: [Answer in progress but cut off by phone issues]

questions.question: Are there any other types of geese that nest in trees?

answers.answer: Yes, loads of waterfowl nest in trees - Canadian geese, mallards, herons. They like the bowl in the middle of trees. Ducks and geese differ by: neck and beak size (geese are herbivores feeding on land, ducks are omnivores dabbling in water), and sound (geese honk, ducks quack). Egyptian goose is indeed technically a duck.

questions.question: Why are TV adverts louder than the programs they interrupt? Is there no technical control at the point of transmission?

answers.answer: It's about compression in digital audio. A compressor brings everything in an audio clip as loud as it can physically go, creating a 'wall of noise'. This relates to the 'loudness wars' in 90s music when CDs allowed louder recordings without vinyl limitations. Old films mixed on analog have peaks and troughs; modern digital content is compressed into one big block of volume. Adverts are deliberately mixed to maximum loudness as an attention-getter, though not technically intentional - it's commercial motivation.

questions.question: What's all that about? Where's that coming from? [Easter eggs, bunnies, chocolate eggs being delivered by bunnies]

answers.answer: Most festivals have been co-opted by Christianity from Druid or pagan festivals that went before. Easter - spell O-E-S-T-R-E - think of estrogen, something to do with eggs. Christian missionaries are very good at slotting into established traditions. Chocolate eggs definitely started with normal eggs and then became chocolate eggs.

questions.question: What would happen to a fly in zero gravity? If it went up in a space rocket into zero gravity, would it fly or would it float around?

In 1968 Richard Burton filmed Where Eagles Dare and in 1978 he filmed The Wild Geese - 10 years apart. In both movies when he's using the radio he uses the call sign 'Broad Sword to Danny Boy'. Why would he use that call sign in two movies years apart and not even the same era of war films?
In London there are lots of equestrian statues - people mounted on horseback. Some have their feet in stirrups and some don't. Why?
All the banks on the high street have gone. Every high street had two or three banks. What's happened to the bank vaults? Were the vaults always in the basement?

Is there a rise of the off-yellow, pale yellow kind of white daffodil in amongst the yellow daffodils? What determines the colour of the daffodil? Is it the bulb, the amount of water, or sunlight? Has there been an increase in the number of off-white, pale yellow daffodils?
Why does the date of Easter change each year?

answers.answer: It's the first Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox. The Christian missionaries accommodated older festivals when they arrived. It can't fall on a fixed calendar date because Easter Sunday has to be on a Sunday (for the resurrection) and Good Friday has to be on a Friday.

questions.question: Are we born with a fear of heights (wobbly knee feeling) or is it developed? Is it nature or nurture?
How can the Artemis astronauts be going further than any other astronauts have ever gone before when they're going to the moon - which everyone knows we've already visited?

answers.answer: Apollo 8 went around the moon (orbited). The Artemis is also going to orbit the moon, not land. The idea that it's going further could mean they're deliberately going further in mileage away from the dark side of the moon just to break the record.

questions.question: Why Easter falls on different days of the year?

answers.answer: It goes back to Judaism. We don't know when Jesus was born. Christmas is a guess. Easter is an accommodation of Passover. Passover falls on the evening of the first Friday after the first full moon after the vernal equinox. Christians changed it to the Christian Sabbath of Sunday. That's why Passover normally three times out of five falls on Good Friday. Occasionally if the first full moon is on Friday or Saturday, Easter falls after because it needs the first Sunday after the first full moon after the equinox.

questions.question: What have bunnies and eggs got to do with Easter given it commemorates the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus Christ?

answers.answer: Egg timeline: Pre-Christianity - egg was a universal symbol of fertility across many civilisations. Early Christianity - early Christians started dyeing eggs red to represent the blood of Christ. Medieval Europe - hare/rabbit becomes associated with Virgin Mary because it was associated with the blood of Christ. The Saxon goddess of fertility is Ostara. Hares and fertility go hand in hand because they reproduce fast and it's spring. The egg became more and more of a symbol through medieval Europe. By the 1400s-1500s, Lent forbids eggs and meat, making eggs a coveted treat for breaking Lent. The first chocolate egg was apparently around early 1700s by a widow in Turin - chocolate was a new luxury and breaking Lent a factor. Egg hunts started in Germany with Lutherans, allegedly by Martin Luther first. Chocolate eggs entered mass market in the 1970s.

questions.question: What happened to the bank vaults in former banks?

answers.answer: The main vault at the old Bank of Scotland on Union Street in Aberdeen has been turned into a restaurant called Glen House. You can book to sit in the vaults on the first floor. Ronnie mainly goes there for cocktails.

questions.question: What happened to the bank vaults in former banks?

answers.answer: They refurbished an old HSBC bank into a dental practice. The bank vault was kept - it's on the ground floor, not in the basement. When you buy the property, the vault comes with it. They had to get a specialist company to come in and cut it out and take it away. The walls are probably just under a foot thick. It cost around £25,000 to remove it.

questions.question: Are we born with a fear of heights or is it developed?

answers.answer: We're only born with two fears. Every other fear is learned. The two fears we're born with are fear of falling and fear of loud noises (you're pushed down the birth canal and out into a noisy room). The nurture part depends on upbringing - easygoing parents who let you fall off a climbing frame without freaking out versus parents who rush to pick you up. You can grow out of fears through upbringing, and grow back into them again if you experience something significant. Qualifications: Long-time neuro-linguistic programming student.

questions.question: What determines the colour of a daffodil? Why are there more pale/white daffodils appearing among yellow ones?

answers.answer: It relates to the Romans taking daffodils from the Iberian Peninsula. The originals would have been very small. As they've been spread across Europe with lots of gardeners cross-breeding, they've become bigger to maintain an ambient temperature eight degrees warmer than outside temperature inside the cup - this has evolved to attract early pollinators.

questions.question: Does being left or right-handed influence which shoe you put on first?
Why, when you're in the Wirral, are you referred to as 'on the Wirral' rather than 'in the Wirral'? What is the Wirral?

answers.answer: It's down to how you define the area. When you define a piece of land by its geographical features (moor, marsh, peninsula, mountain), you're 'on' it. When it's a city, country or county defined by administrative boundaries, you're 'in' it. The Wirral is a peninsula, so it uses 'on' historically from the geographical definition, though it was also a Norman Hundred (administrative). The peninsula definition came first.

questions.question: Why do we call Dutch people 'Dutch' when the country is called the Netherlands or Holland, which sounds nothing like 'Dutch'?

answers.answer: It goes back to the Romans when Western Europe was divided into Upper and Lower Germany (Germania Inferior). The Dutch/German said 'Deutsch'. For the English, it was hard to distinguish between Dutch and German, they all sounded the same, so they called them all 'Deutsch' which became 'Dutch'. It's a bit of laziness, slightly jingoistic laziness on the part of the English. The Netherlands should really be called Netherlanders.

questions.question: Why are there so many words for a bread roll in the UK? (muffin, barm, cob, bap, batch, stottie, etc.)

answers.caller: Mike (Cradley Heath/Boston British Fiddle - food historian)
answers.answer: It's down to three things: size, ingredients, and competition. A roll is smaller and more floury; a cob has a hard crust top while a bap has a soft top. Some are made with butter, some with bicarb of soda, some with different flours. Yorkshire's bread names came from competition with Lancashire. Before the 18th century, most people lived and died within 30 miles of where they were born, so regional names stuck because people didn't move enough.

Adding to the bread roll question - regional names stuck because people didn't move enough historically. Even with industrialization when people concentrated in urban centers for mining and building, it reinforced original differences rather than expanding them.

questions.question: What are the small hinged metal doors on some canal bridges in Birmingham (foot-squared, hinged, with a key slot, found on older bridges)?

answers.answer: Fire brigade access points from WWII. Firefighters used to open them to drop fire hoses down to the canal to use the water during the war. This was predominantly in urban areas where other canal access wasn't available. They're found mainly in Birmingham and other industrial urban areas. The River and Canal Trust would have the keys nowadays.

questions.question: Who invented the first paper aeroplane, and when? Did someone try to create one that looked like an old-fashioned monoplane?
Why in British Sign Language is the sign for clapping not a mime of clapping, but instead waving hands like 'jazz hands'?

answers.answer: Both his parents were deaf and he grew up going to deaf clubs. When hearing people clap, they keep hands close to their body or low. Deaf people can't hear that, so they raise their hands to about 90 degrees with the jazz hands gesture so everyone nearby can see they're giving applause.

questions.question: When and why did it become socially unacceptable for women to be hairy?

answers.answer: Sociologist who did her undergraduate thesis specifically on female body hair removal. The modern prohibition was pushed by Gillette and the fashion/hair removal industry about a hundred years ago to sell more razors. They persuaded women that body hair was unsightly and unattractive. As sleeves got shorter and skirts got shorter, there was more to remove. Prior to that in the 19th century, it wasn't even a thing. It was just another example of pampering and class division (like in ancient Egypt). The UK and Australia embraced this more enthusiastically than some European countries.

questions.question: Why can I cycle for two hours in Texas without getting sunburned, but if I stand outside for 10 minutes mowing the lawn, I get sunburned?

answers.answer: It's about movement. When cycling, the body parts are constantly moving so the sun isn't focused on one spot long enough to cause burn - like moving a magnifying glass over paper so it never burns. Wind also takes away the heat sensation so you don't feel it, but the UV damage still happens. He should definitely wear sunscreen.

questions.question: What speed would an airplane need to be going at before it falls out of the sky?

answers.answer: We're talking about stall speed, which is when air no longer flows over the wing properly to provide lift. It varies by aircraft - gliders can fly fine below 40 knots, while a huge aircraft like an A380 might be close to 200 knots. It depends on weight, wing size, and wing shape. For a normal jumbo jet, about 150 knots (roughly 130-140 mph).

questions.question: Why can one cat eat wasps and bees without getting stung, but the other cat won't go near them?

answers.answer: Cats are predators and have evolved to be insectivores. The cat that eats wasps knows how to rip out the sting before eating - some cats are very adept at this. The other cat either isn't as hungry, isn't as intelligent about it, or has had a negative experience with wasps before. It's like personal preference - some cats like tuna, others don't.

questions.question: What do angling shops do with the maggots they can't sell? Do they just turn into flies?

answers.answer: The second stage of a maggot's life is called a caster - the chrysalis stage. These are actually a huge carp bait. Tackle shops freeze casters in the freezer so they don't develop further. Most of the time, maggot-like things sold are actually frozen casters. The unsold ones either turn into casters and go in the freezer, or if they miss that window, they become flies and fly away. If they're going to throw them away, they do it before they turn into flies.

questions.question: Is the exercise benefit better than the damage from pollution when walking through town where I can taste the diesel from cars?
Why do I gag when I clean my tongue with my toothbrush some mornings but not others? I do exactly the same thing.

answers.answer: The gag reflex is controlled by the hindbrain - it's subconscious to protect your major airway. It will tolerate something in your mouth provided you are at optimum oxygen levels. If oxygen drops even a tiny bit, the hindbrain triggers the gag reflex. So some days you might be breathing more shallowly without realizing it, and that's when you gag. If you're stressed, you're more likely to gag because you're breathing more shallowly.

questions.question: Why do we stop enjoying the sensation of being dizzy as we get older, and when does this happen?

answers.answer: As you get older, there's a liquid in your ear that becomes more viscous. It doesn't happen at a particular age suddenly - it gradually gets more and more viscous over time. Eventually it reaches a point where it becomes really uncomfortable to be dizzy and harder for it to settle. Plus as you get older you're more aware of the dangers of falling over.

questions.question: Why does flat, previously carbonated water taste different from tap water even after all the bubbles have gone?

answers.answer: When you carbonate water, some of the carbon dioxide is in solution but some reacts with the water to make carbonic acid (H2CO3). That tangy taste is carbonic acid. Even when the CO2 in solution comes out and the water goes flat, the carbonic acid remains. Tap water never had carbonic acid in it, so that's why flat sparkling water tastes different from regular tap water.

questions.question: Why does your hair always feel cleaner and squeakier when you use a different shampoo for the first time, and then when you go back to your original shampoo, it feels cleaner and squeakier again?

answers.answer: It's going to have something to do with natural oils. It's going to have something to do with the relationship between oils and astringents. The basic answer is: if you change shampoo, your hair will feel squeakier regardless of what shampoo you're using.
The question was left unanswered for listeners to call in.

questions.question: Why is there no Aldi in Northern Ireland?

answers.answer: I have no idea.

Three main reasons: 1) Alcohol licensing laws in Northern Ireland operate a surrender license policy, meaning you can't open a new supermarket without a license to sell alcohol, and you can only get one by acquiring an existing license. 2) Land banking by existing supermarkets like Tesco. 3) Brexit has made it not worth the effort for Aldi.

questions.question: How do barnacles get on whales if whales don't stop moving and don't scrape around the ocean floor?

answers.answer: Barnacles are just floating around and then they land on a whale. There might not be any benefit to the whale - they might be parasitic or just neither parasitic nor symbiotic.

Barnacles are microscopic initially and are immature creatures floating around in the water like plankton. They attach themselves to anything - a whale, an oil rig, the bottom of a boat, any rock area. It's their life cycle. Once attached, they have a little feathery thing that comes up and feeds in the water - they don't need to expend energy moving around. A whale is just a platform to sit on, as good as a boat or a rock.

questions.question: When building tall structures like The Shard, how do they get the cranes down if the counterweighted concrete is still at the top?

answers.answer: They bring in a portable crane to help remove the permanent crane and the concrete. It's one crane bringing down another crane.

If the crane is really tall, it takes itself down using a jacking system because mobile cranes can't reach the top. It's like a climbing frame that wraps around the tower. The crane jacks the top up (the slewing and cab), takes the tower section out, and drops it down to a reasonable height for a mobile crane to reach.

questions.question: What is the difference between a pole and a post? Why do we say lamppost, signpost, but telegraph pole and flagpole?

answers.answer: It might just be random - someone decided at some point that's a post and that's a pole. James also noted the horizontal bar on old-fashioned lampposts was for resting your ladder on.
A post is 10 to 15 feet long and a poll is above 20 feet long. (James questioned this answer and suspected he was being 'yanked his chain' - no confirmation this was the correct answer.)

questions.question: Why did the letters of the alphabet come to be shaped the way they are? Why is an A like an A and not shaped differently?

answers.answer: This is about the invention of the written word - when we started writing things down, why did we choose the shapes we chose? James admitted he didn't fully understand the question.

All writing systems began with people drawing before they were writing. The letter A is based on an Egyptian hieroglyph originally representing a cow or bull. Imagine an upside-down semi-circle with a smaller semi-circle underneath - that's the horns and face of a cow. The symbol was pronounced 'aua'. In the Middle East, it was turned upside down and used to represent the sound 'R', eventually becoming the Greco-Roman capital A. All writing systems started as drawings or symbols of objects and nature, which is why different languages evolved differently.

questions.question: Why is the swanny whistle (penny whistle) funny?

answers.answer: Demonstrated the swanny whistle sound on air.

questions.question: What is the difference between a coat and a jacket?

answers.answer: A jacket stops at the waist and a coat goes below the waist. If you cup your hands over the bottom of the garment and it fits, it's a jacket. (James qualified this with five years at Aquascutum in Regent Street and six months at River Island in Worcester.)

questions.question: Why do mirrors give differing reflections? At home, Surrey looks slimmer in mirrors, but in Marks and Spencer's mirrors, he looks bigger.

answers.answer: Two answers: 1) Physical differences - tint, thickness of glass, how regularly it's cleaned, room lighting, all sorts of tiny distortions. 2) Psychological - your home mirror is the one you're most used to and your brain is kind to you in familiar settings. Shops wouldn't deliberately have less flattering mirrors - they're more likely to have tinted or slightly elongating mirrors. The home is where you're comfortable, and that comfort is reflected back at you.

questions.caller: Martin (security team/night manager at London hotel)
questions.answer: I knew when it was a full moon based entirely on guest behavior. (No question asked - just a contribution about full moon effects.)

questions.question: What is the behavior?

answers.answer: People just go a bit bonkers.

questions.question: Why does hot water from a tap sound different to cold water? It just sounds thicker, deeper.

answers.answer: It's physics. The water forcing through a pipe creates vibrations. As temperature changes, the stiffness of the pipe material changes, which changes the friction and resonance. The pressure might be the same, but the temperature changes the frequency you hear.

questions.question: Why does a brand new empty vinegar bottle smell of vinegar even though it's never had vinegar in it?

answers.answer: Psychological - your brain tells your nostrils to expect vinegar so you smell vinegar.

At the end of the manufacturing process, bottles are sterilized using peracetic acid (or acetic acid), which smells very similar to vinegar. That's why they smell of vinegar - nothing psychological about it.

questions.question: How do daffodils get planted in the middle of nowhere, miles from any houses or villages? If I want daffodils in my garden I have to buy and plant bulbs, so they're not spread by seed.

answers.answer: 95% of daffodils are planted by people. The Romans brought them from the Iberian Peninsula, thinking they had healing properties. They used them as grave markers for soldiers. Squirrels also plant bulbs by stealing them. Daffodils can propagate from seeds but very rarely.

questions.question: What determines someone's sense of humour? Why do I love Stuart Lee but hate Michael McIntyre? Similarly, why do some people love mature sitcoms while others prefer youthful comedies?

answers.answer: No direct answer provided. Discussion centered on Michael McIntyre having done holiday cover at LBC before becoming famous. James noted that McIntyre is objectively funny even if subjectively some don't find him so.

questions.question: Has birdsong changed over the centuries, or have birds always sung the same way since day one?

answers.answer: From David Byrne's book 'How Music Works' - birds in San Francisco were found to have raised the pitch of their songs over the last 40 years so they could be heard over traffic noise. Birdsong is mostly for bird benefit - they need to hear each other, not just for human enjoyment.

questions.question: Why do strawberries now require the hull to be cut out, whereas when we were younger, the stem/core would just pull straight out easily?

answers.answer: It's about ripeness and seasonality. Supermarket strawberries in spring/winter have white tops, no real strawberry flavour, they're forced. In summer, pick-your-own strawberries are coloured all the way through and the hull pops out easily. We've lost seasonality.

questions.caller: Sam (Great Lees, between Chelmsford and Braintree)
questions.question: How do they decide where to put post boxes? My small village of under 3,000 people has four post boxes on the main road, all within easy walking distance of each other.

answers.answer: Historically, when a property became a post office, they had to have a postbox attached. So village shops or PO premises would add one. The modern rule is that every house should be within half a mile of a postbox. They generally don't replace postboxes anymore since we don't use them as much.

questions.question: Who decides which direction satellites go in orbit when launched? How do they avoid all colliding with each other?

answers.answer: There's not enough in orbit for it to be a big problem. There's debris but mostly it's luck and physics given how much room is up there.

The International Telecommunications Union (ITU), an agency of the UN, governs this through radio regulations - it's a binding international treaty. You need permission and an assigned orbit to launch. It gets pretty heated in those meetings, especially with Musk's thousands of satellites in low orbit.

questions.question: Where are all the W's disappearing to? It used to be that you had to have a www. in front of every website, but one by one they're all disappearing. And I checked my own website and it's gone as well. Why?

answers.answer: It goes back to the history of the internet when different servers had different purposes - email server, web server, file server. You used to put a prefix to designate which one you were trying to reach. So www.lbc.co.uk was specifically for the website. Now people have introduced a shorthand - a redirect - so if you don't specify an explicit server, it sends you to the www one. It's just a shorthand that's been introduced.

questions.question: From old war films, I think it might just be Nazis but I'm not sure - in men's uniforms, the trousers have these weird kind of wings in their thighs. What are they called and why are they there?

answers.answer: These go back to the Prussian martial tradition. They're not actually trousers - they're what we would call jodhpurs. They're that shape because they're tight at the bottom so they can be tucked into boots, but they're baggy around the knees so when you sit on a saddle or move around, your trouser doesn't pull out the top of the boot. The cavalry became tank regiments and they carried on wearing the same trousers.

questions.question: Why when you kick a ball through someone's legs is it called a nutmeg?

answers.answer: Spices were very expensive back in the day. I wonder whether people would sell fake nutmeg in the 19th century and therefore being nutmegged became a byword for being swindled or bamboozled, and then it becomes the phrase used for knocking a football through someone's legs.

Nutmeg is a spice, but specifically they sold small pieces of wood fashioned into nutmeg shapes - dark wood. You could put a few wooden nuggets in a sack and charge a lot of money, making a lot of money for old rope. Bonus: in Norway they call it 'doing a window' - you can see straight through.

questions.question: Why are there no green mammals? It seems like a reasonably useful thing to be, evolutionary-wise. I just wonder why no green mammals have evolved ever.

answers.answer: As mammals we don't produce the necessary pigment to produce green hair. More interestingly, it depends on who you are as to whether mammals are green or not. If you are a small antelope or deer in the jungles of India, to you, tigers are green - they register that frequency of light as green. When is a mammal green? The answer is when it depends what mammal you are.

questions.question: My daughter had a hamster. Why does it spend its whole life trying to escape? You give it everything - happiness, joy, you cuddle it, stroke it, cook food. And it's constantly trying to find a way out. It would go round and round, bite the corner of the cage. Why are hamsters always trying to escape?

answers.answer: Hamsters have always had an instinct from their natural habitat of travelling at great distances at night time to search for food. They have a need to store food because they never know where they're next going to get it. Even if they've got a full bowl in their cage, they're genetically programmed whenever they find themselves wherever they find themselves to go look for more food. They have pouches to carry food at great distances.

questions.question: Threadworms come out at night. How do they know it's night? They're so simple they don't have a clock. How do they know?
What is the purpose of a bubble on a bubble hat?

answers.answer: It was for cushioning. Not miners - sailors. When they were going below decks, the likelihood of bumping their head on the beams was very likely. The bobble hat would keep your ears warm but also keep your bones safe. It would also warn you beforehand not to raise your head too soon because you'd feel it brush as you were passing under a beam.

Bobbles were also used as a signal from Scandinavian countries with big snow drifts. If you fell into a snow drift, you had a chance of being spotted with a nicely brightly coloured bobble against the snow if people were looking for you. Your whole body could be submerged but the little bobble would be poking out on top and that would help mountain rescue locate you.

questions.question: N/A - update about medieval knights book

answers.answer: Sandy Wainwright has written a book called 'The Life and Times of a Medieval Knight, Sir Geoffrey de Langley and Family'. A knighthood is an award of land and responsibility to the lord. You get given a knight's fee. Under feudal system you're responsible for people below you as well as those reporting above. You'd look after the land and the people for the lord and pass the money up.

questions.question: Why do they use little twigs of conifers on the ski jump landing area, but blue dye on other Winter Olympic events like big air?
Why don't crisp manufacturers use the same colour scheme for their flavours across all brands?

answers.answer: Walker's crisps launched in the 1970s. His late father John Langley ran an advertising agency and was tasked with choosing the colours. They went blue for cheese and onion because when you say 'cheese', people think of blue cheese, not green cheese. Walker's used green for salt and vinegar as that was already established in the market.

questions.question: When they built the canals back in the 1800s, where did they get the water from to fill them?

answers.answer: Most canals are fed by reservoirs, though some are fed by rivers. The reservoirs are often nearly 200 years old, same age as the canals. During last year's droughts, the Leeds and Liverpool Canal had issues filling up because of low reservoir levels.

questions.question: Why is Russia called Motherland and Germany called Fatherland? When was this decided?

answers.answer: It relates to the gender of the noun for 'land' in each language. In languages where the word for land is feminine (like Latin 'terra'), you get 'Motherland'. In Germanic languages where 'land' is neuter (like German 'das Land') or masculine, you get 'Fatherland'. Russia uses a feminine word for land (zemlya), hence Mother Russia. During the Napoleonic War, Germany tried 'Motherland' but it reverted to Fatherland once things settled down.

questions.question: Why is fresh ginger the only ingredient measured in 'thumb-sized' or 'thumbnail-sized' amounts? Why don't recipes give proper measurements like grams?

answers.answer: A chef he asked explained that it's because ginger is too knobbly to fit on a teaspoon, so they use thumb-sized as an approximation. It's basically the size of a teaspoon but too irregular to measure with one.

questions.question: How do bees communicate distances and locations through the waggle dance? Is it an innate ability they're born with, or is it learned?

answers.answer: It's social learning. Young bees, typically around eight days old, learn from watching experienced older forager bees who return from finding nectar. They observe the dancers to learn where to go, what quality the food is, and all that detailed information. It's learning through observation.

questions.question: Who used to wake up the knocker uppers - the people who used to knock on windows to wake workers up before alarm clocks existed?
How does the second flock of parakeets know what route the first flock has taken, even if it's 15 minutes later? The flocks consistently swoop through the same route between the same two trees.
What happens to the metal after you've been cremated? After a knee replacement with titanium, what happens to that metal?

answers.answer: Following cremation, titanium is recovered from the cremated remains, gathered together, and sold to a Dutch company who use it for second-grade medical titanium. The money given to the council is then given to charity. Alan is a funeral director. He also mentioned a case where a lady's mother had a metal plate in her head recovered and she polished it and put it on the mantelpiece.

questions.question: Why is it that we humans all have different enjoyments of taste? Why don't we all like the same foods? Is there an evolutionary explanation for our variation in tastes?
Do people know that they're going to die? Similar to the famous elephant's graveyard, do people have some kind of awareness that the end is near?

answers.answer: We can never truly determine this because for everyone who says they're going to die and it comes true, there will be hundreds who said it and it didn't. For those whom it did come true, they might have had subconscious knowledge of bodily decline or a sense of something being wrong without consciously acknowledging it. James mentioned a Scottish doctor story about prediction statistics.

questions.question: Why 12 people on a jury? Is there a religious or political reason? Why not 10, which would be the obvious number?

answers.answer: It goes back to the time of King Morgan, an 8th century Welsh king, who decided to base it on the 12 disciples of Jesus. This is because Judeo-Christian jurisprudence underpins so much of English law. Dinesh is a solicitor advocate.

questions.question: What is the actual origin of birthday cards? Is it something Hallmark pushed to sell more cards?
Why do spectacles never blow off in high winds when everything else gets damaged - wagons turning over, roofs blowing off?

answers.answer: Spectacles stay on because: A) they have hooks round the back of your ears, B) they're kind of wedged in place on the nose, and C) they may be heavier than objects the wind would lift off.

Many listeners reported that glasses DO blow off in the wind. Danny Wallace reported his glasses flew off at 82 miles an hour during an 80 mile per hour wind. Others confirmed similar experiences. Brian was apparently wrong in his premise.

questions.question: Why do certain nouns in languages like French and Spanish have a gender attached to them, when English doesn't? Who decides what gender a new word gets?

answers.answer: Grammatical gender exists in many Indo-European languages, not just Romance ones. English used to have three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter) like German, but lost them in the early Middle Ages when the language got 'pigeonized' alongside Norse - when languages share vocabulary but have different grammars, you get simplified compromised grammar without grammatical complexity. It seems to originate from animistic religious beliefs where people thought all things had gender or sex including rivers and trees. For new words in gendered languages, countries like France with language academies can make decisions, often based on word endings or meaning connections. New words in French generally become masculine. Mark is a professional linguist.

questions.question: Do people decide when they're going to die? (follow-up to Robert's question)
What happens to TV and film props that are thrown into water? Do they go and collect them? Let them sink? Are they made from something that disposes of itself in the water?

How come a cyclone is apparently lower than a gale on the shipping forecast? They list wind speeds from 1 to 12, 12 being the severest, but they say 'becoming cyclonic' which seems to refer to a cyclone - shouldn't that be higher than a gale?

answers.answer: What they say in the shipping forecast is the winds are cyclonic, which means there's a predictable change in the direction of the wind as a low pressure system passes over. A cyclone is a low pressure system - it's not a hurricane. Cyclonic winds are when the wind just changes direction because of a low pressure system passing over the area. The winds can be any speed from force 1 to force 8 depending on what kind of low pressure system it is.

questions.question: How does a tiny weed manage to push through tarmac on my driveway that was laid only 3-4 years ago? How do these small plants have the strength to break through thick and heavy tarmac?

answers.answer: The weeds don't grow through the tarmac - they grow on the tarmac. You need two things to make weeds: organic matter and moisture. The tarmac is really good at holding moisture and organic matter can come from dust, bird feces, animal feces - anything. The roots grow down and the plant comes up, making tiny cracks wider. Water gets in, freezes, and the crack gets even bigger. You can have organic matter growing on your freshly laid tarmac within days. The roots make their way through tiny gaps between the tarmac and that breaks it. Eventually your driveway fills with potholes.

questions.question: Why do eggs have a 'display until' date that is earlier than the actual 'use by' date? If eggs go out of date on the 30th, why are they taken off the shelf on the 24th or 25th? Why do eggs have their own rules for display dates when nothing else in the store is treated this way?

answers.answer: The display until is a recommendation to retailers to manage stock - you bring products with shorter dates to the front and put newer products at the back so customers pick them up first. However, the premise of the question was false - display until dates are not unique to eggs. They're also used on perishable foods like salads, meal deals, meats, and milk. Eggs are actually fine to eat past their best before date. To test if an egg is good, float it in water - if it floats, it's bad; if it sinks, it's okay. Anything with a best before date is edible as long as you use your common sense.

questions.question: Why do electric toothbrushes still require the same two minutes of brushing time as manual toothbrushes? What's the point of an electric toothbrush if you don't get a time saving? What's the actual advantage?

Is a helium canister heavier when it's full or when it's empty? If I put a full canister on scales and then empty it, will it weigh the same or will it be lighter? Is the canister filled with a vacuum?

answers.answer: As the canisters empty, they get lighter because the gas is escaping. Helium is compressed and forced into the canister under pressure. As it comes out, the canister gets lighter. Helium comes from the ground - it doesn't come from the air. It comes from the alpha decay of uranium and it's one of the few things that leaves the Earth because it's so light and fast that it radiates out into space. The walls aren't thick because of a vacuum - they're thick because the helium is under pressure. The canister walls are thick to withstand the pressure inside. We should be conserving helium because it's a finite resource needed for very cold temperatures in labs, CT scanners, MRI machines, and the Large Hadron Collider. There are only three or four mines in the world that produce it.

questions.question: Why does my strong German accent disappear when I sing, even though I sound very German when I speak? How come the accent goes away when I sing?

answers.answer: When people want to sing a song that they really like, they will inadvertently sing in the same accent as the music that they originally heard. Because Tom is singing in English, he will be subconsciously copying the singers - English language singers or American singers that he likes and admires. This explains why Mick Jagger from Dartford sings as if he came from the deep south states of the United States of America - he loves the blues from Louisiana. Most performers, 99.9%, sing in the accent they originally heard the song in. There are exceptions like the Proclaimers who sing with their Scottish accent, but most people copy the accent of the original artist.

questions.question: Why do humans settle in inhospitable places - like frozen north, deserts - when the world was big and the population was small?

answers.answer: When we were a hunter-gatherer society, we used to chase the food sources around. When it was summer, we focused on one food source; when it was winter, another. When seasons change and you don't have cities, you are forced to move around the globe and that's why we spread out. When you have an abundant food source like salmon in summer, people stay behind. Then winter comes, it's frozen, and people are forced to specialize - they dig holes in the ice to fish. When you've spent an entire season fishing and seen the weather patterns, you decide to stay. The population was small so being safe, even if it wasn't very nice, was more important than being comfortable. Very few populations are permanently peripatetic.

questions.question: Why isn't the medium wine glass size (175ml) exactly halfway between small (125ml) and large (250ml)? Why isn't it 187.5ml? Why do we have these weird uneven measurements?

answers.answer: I don't know why. It's just a nice round number. 250, 125, 175 are easy numbers to work with. Maybe because we were buying pints before metric.

It's historical. Only in last 30-40 years have there been set sizes. Previously pubs just poured a glass. Government looked at gin/vodka measures (25ml, 35ml) and came up with 125ml and 175ml as standards. 250ml is just a multiple of 125ml. Some pubs used to do 150ml.

questions.question: Is there an absolute hottest temperature like there is an absolute zero cold? Can something be so hot that it cannot get any hotter?

answers.answer: Yes, it's called the Planck temperature - the highest temperature our current physics can describe, around 10 to the power of 33 Kelvin. At those temperatures, quantum gravity dominates and we don't have a good understanding. Particles would collide with so much energy it would create black holes every time. Named after Max Planck.

questions.question: Why don't deer leave Richmond Park? There are no cattle grids on the gates, so they could just stroll out, but they don't. Why?

answers.answer: They can get out - there's nothing physically stopping them. But they're creatures of habit and prefer being in the park. It's a bit alien out there for them. They'd have to go on tarmac roads to get out, which they don't like on their little hooves. Once out, it's probably curtains for them because you can't herd a deer. Gamekeepers have to deal with it when they escape.

questions.question: Is there a physiological explanation for sensing when a room has a tense atmosphere? His blind grandmother can pick up on tension before anyone says a word.

answers.answer: It's called neuroception - part of Stephen Porges' polyvagal theory. The nervous system unconsciously scans for emotional shifts and relational threats. People who are very vigilant, often those who had childhood trauma, are really attuned to things like tone, pauses, and micro-expressions. That's probably why some blind people have a heightened sense - it keeps them safe, same as for children who had to attune to dangerous environments.

questions.question: What's the logic behind when football teams choose not to wear their first choice kit? Sometimes teams wear away kits even when there's no colour clash, and sometimes they don't when there is a clash. Is there a hard and fast rule or do they make it up as they go along?

answers.answer: It's a commercial decision. Clubs typically have three shirts, some have five. To get money back and make people buy shirts, you need to wear them. The commercial department contacts the kit manager and asks them to wear the third shirt. It has to be cleared with the referee beforehand. Goalkeeper shirts are the main issue - they have three different shirts too. Sometimes managers have superstitions and refuse to change a winning kit.

questions.question: Why is it incorrect etiquette to have your elbows on the table when dining?

answers.answer: It's naval. On ships, dinner was served on trestle tables that were put away the rest of the time. If you put your elbows on a trestle table, the whole thing could go up in the air, so it was frowned upon. It migrated from sea into domestic environments.
In big Saxon halls, tables weren't permanent either - they'd just pull them out at dinner time. So putting your elbows on could upset the whole shebang.

questions.question: With all the money we now spend on vets - pet clubs, hypoallergenic shampoo, pedicures - do dogs actually live longer than they did 25 years ago? If so, by how much?
Why are the fudge brownie pieces in chocolate fudge brownie ice cream not frozen solid? They're nice and soft and gooey straight from the tub - why don't they freeze like chocolate chips do?

answers.answer: Higher sugar content acts as a natural antifreeze. That's why root vegetables get sweeter in winter - they convert starches into sugars so they don't freeze. If you're making ice cream with brownie bits, you'd up the sugar content from what you'd have in a normal brownie to keep them softer.

questions.question: Why do they speak multiple languages in Asian countries? (e.g., China has Cantonese, Mandarin, Fukien; Pakistan has Urdu and Punjabi; Singapore has multiple languages)

answers.answer: It's simply because the country is so enormous that modern borders encompass many previous civilisations. Switzerland is a good example - they speak multiple languages and it's not very big because it includes parts of Italy, France, Germany.

There are about 6,000 languages in the world and only 200 countries. Chinese is actually a series of related languages sharing a script, not one language. India has different language families - Hindi came from the northwest, Tamil has been there much longer. It's a cultural and political decision - in Flanders some call their language Flemish, others Dutch. The English tried to outlaw Welsh. Most peoples try to suppress languages.

questions.question: When clearing bubbles from a bubble bath with the shower, why does cold water disperse bubbles much quicker than hot water?

answers.answer: Are bubbles melting? You're melting the bubble... a bubble's much thinner than a balloon.

Soap molecules are like tadpoles with an electrically charged head and a hydrophobic (water-fearing) tail. The charged head goes to the water, tail sticks up into the air. When you add hot water, the hydrophobic tails react more strongly - they flock together and become more water repellent. This creates a stronger barrier to the water. So hot water makes the soap more water-repellent, meaning it takes longer to wash away. It's the same principle as why a tea biscuit goes soggier quicker in cold tea than hot tea - hydrophobic attraction.

questions.question: How do they count the smallest creatures like beetles, ants, and penguins during the annual zoo stock take?

answers.answer: With penguins, all animals look the same - but you just get them all in a room and count them one by one. You might have six elephants and count seven because one moved from back to front... Penguins are birds, by the way.

answers.caller: James (the former zookeeper answering his own question)
answers.answer: Penguins have unique markings and are rung so you can just count them. Keepers know each penguin by name, how old they are, who they are, whether they're likely to murder you (penguins are pure evil and quite feisty). Zookeepers count their animals every single day - it's part of the zoo license. For insects and small creatures, we don't do individual counts - they're done on averages. For naked mole rats, which are colonial fast breeders, you know the queen because she breeds, but the rest are like workers in a beehive.

questions.question: Has any major composer ever written music that is actually unplayable - too fast or too complicated? Would they have to be able to play it themselves to compose it?
