answers.caller: Jack (in Bristol, piano teacher on lunch break)
answers.answer: Yes, for example Mozart wrote 'The Musical Joke' to make fun of bad composers (probably Salieri). It's unplayable because it doesn't follow the rules of music - you can't play it even though he could technically play it. Also some pieces have clusters of notes that are physically impossible to play without 11 fingers or a span wider than any known human. John Cage did 'As Slow As Possible' which is conceptually impossible to play at that speed - you'd be bored to death. '4 minutes 33 seconds' is silence that anyone can play.

questions.question: Who decides where bus stops should be placed in the countryside where there are no houses nearby? Why are they placed in random locations?

answers.answer: There probably is a requirement to have a bus stop within a certain distance of the last bus stop. So you have to put a bus stop within X metres or X miles of the last one, and if that area is empty, you still have to put a bus stop there. They only stop if someone's standing there waiting - they're request stops.

answers.caller: Stephen (in Ashington, long-distance hiker and endurance runner)
answers.answer: Bus stops are generally placed where hiking trails and bridleways crisscross main roads. For example, on the military road in Northumberland along Hadrian's Wall, there's nothing around but they put bus stops at key locations where the trail crosses the main road. Hikers use them to get to or out of remote areas. Though it's chicken and egg - are they there because of hikers or are hikers using them because they're there?

questions.question: Why do we clap when we applaud? Where did the tradition of clapping come from? Do all cultures clap?

answers.answer: It dates back to ancient Rome. When senators gave speeches, if people were impressed, on his way back to sitting down, people nearby would stand up and pat him on the back. People further away who couldn't reach started clapping their hands. Gradually over time it just grew until it became a round of applause. I read about it - I can't remember the book but it made complete sense.

questions.question: Why do paddle rackets have a wrist strap when other rackets like tennis, badminton, and squash don't?

answers.answer: It must be the likelihood of it slipping out of your hand and the likelihood of it doing you a mischief if it does. A badminton racket isn't going to hurt anyone. A tennis racket probably won't travel far enough to hurt anyone. But paddle rackets are about 350 grams - that's three whole nuts.

It's all to do with moment - the paddle racket is shorter and stubbier. When the ball hits the racket, the distance from that point to your hand is shorter than with a tennis racket. It's like Archimedes' lever - you feel more force on your hand with a paddle racket, so you're more likely to let go and it could fly out and hit someone. Table tennis bats are much lighter with lighter balls so less friction on impact. Squash rackets are longer so less force felt.

Two-thirds of a paddle court is surrounded by glass you can play the ball off. It's an enclosed area, so safety of other players is one reason. Also if the racket leaves your hand, it could damage the equipment. Plus, unlike tennis which is hard to get good at quickly, paddle is much more accessible - you can pick it up immediately and it's not as one-sided when a novice plays against someone more skilled.

questions.question: Why does the Air Mail sticker have French text 'Par Avion' on it when sending from England? Why not Spanish, Italian, German, or other languages?

answers.answer: It's probably something to do with French being a lingua franca or international language for post.

It relates back to a global framework signed in the 1874 Treaty of Bern. French was the internationally accepted legalese at the time - all international treaties were signed in French. All international mailing agreements are still tied back to that original 1874 Treaty.

questions.question: How was the exchange rate determined in Renaissance times? How did people exchange currencies when traveling? When did exchange rates become a thing?

answers.answer: Back in the day, money was made out of precious metals. You would have a set amount of grams of silver or gold in a coin, and you'd travel with that currency. When you arrived somewhere, they'd weigh your coins. Coins had stamps of the mint that were internationally understood. Pre-1920 coins from England and America had similar sizes in terms of precious metal content. The practice of 'clipping' coins was also common - people would clip tiny bits off coins because over time, clipping enough coins gave you valuable metal.

questions.question: How did it come about that outdoor workers wore donkey jackets? Why donkey jackets and not another type of jacket?

answers.answer: It would be a coat issued as uniform by your employer, probably.

When people used to work outside, like market traders and people like that, they used to carry goods on their shoulders and the shoulders of their jackets used to wear out. So they put a leather strap across the shoulders, like a donkey saddle, and that's why it's called a donkey jacket.

The word 'knight' is a modern term. In medieval times they were called 'milites' (Latin derivation of military). By about the 1200s, commoners or those not of noble birth could become knights. Under King Edward III in the 1350s, a professional army was created. The practice of aristocrats leading from the front continued much later - possibly 19th century, like the Crimea with Lord Cardigan.

questions.question: Why do washing machines have a window at the front? Dishwashers don't have them and top-loading ones in North America don't either.

answers.answer: If you open a top-loading washing machine when it isn't empty, no harm is done. In a dishwasher, even with a blockage, water is largely contained at the bottom when you open it. But if a front-loading washing machine hasn't drained properly and you open it, it would be flood central. So the window allows you to see the water level without opening it.

questions.question: Why is Molly, our rescue Border Collie, sprouting white hairs on the stump of her amputated tail? She's about eight years old, and it's only happened in the last year. She has no white hairs anywhere else except her face.

answers.answer: Border collies always have a white tip to their tail. So it might be that genetics is now showing what the end of the tail would have looked like.

questions.question: Was there one specific battle where they decided to let commoners fight in place of knights? In the Middle Ages, being a knight was almost an honour to fight in battle. At what point did aristocrats stop leading from the front?

answers.answer: Commoners always fought - they just didn't have horses. The Crusades were full of plebs led by knights. The knights would be like the generals with horses. The last time an English monarch led the army into battle was probably George II.

The knights of the realm were aristocrats who led into battle and got rewarded with castles. This practice continued much longer than medieval times - arguably into the 19th century (Crimea, Lord Cardigan). The Battle of Towton (War of the Roses, 1461) saw casualties equivalent to the first 15 minutes of the Somme. King Edward III in the 1350s created a professional army, changing how battles were fought.

questions.question: How does a kitten learn its name? I've been saying their names and they never respond - only about a third of the time.

answers.answer: Cats respond better to higher pitch sounds and baby language. Mango and Potato are very similar names with similar syllables, which might be confusing. He needs shorter names and a higher pitch. The cats need to associate the sound with reward. A clicker trainer once trained a cat named Leo to come when called using a clicker and snacks.

questions.question: Why do we write the pound sign before the number (£5.50)? Currencies always have the sign first, but units like kilograms, miles, metres come after the number. Why the inconsistency?
Why do we stand on the right side of travelators and walk on the left? Since we drive on the left and overtake on the right, why doesn't the same logic apply to escalators?

answers.answer: Because almost all people are right-handed, so you feel safer holding the handrail with your right hand while leaning to the right. Therefore you stand on the right.

The original escalator at Earl's Court was set up in Edwardian times with ladies' frocks at low level. There was a concern about dresses getting fed into the mechanism. When you came off the top, instead of coming straight off, there was a curve to the guide on the left. People moving on the left were coming off faster, so they didn't want them crossing stationary people. Thus: stand on the right, walk on the left.

questions.question: Why are eggs sold in sixes and twelves?

answers.answer: Prior to decimalization, 12 was the default number (12 inches in a foot, 12 pennies in a shilling). So eggs being sold in sixes and dozens is a throwback to that pre-decimal era.

questions.question: Why have humans evolved to enjoy music? Even when we were apes, we may have always liked music.

answers.answer: Speculated it might be connected to the heartbeat - the bass is the ground floor of music, an echo of the heartbeat, which is why we find it soothing.

answers.caller: Danny from Lewis (contribution to music question)
answers.answer: It's not just humans - fish also like music. Various studies show that fish grow faster if you play Mozart to them.

questions.question: How do shellfish breed? Do they crawl through the sand and find each other? Do they come out of their shells?

answers.answer: Most shellfish can't move, so the males release sperm and females release eggs directly into the water. It's a very well-synchronized event - they do it at exactly the same time. The sperm and eggs mix in the water, and the larvae develop in the water for about two weeks. If you're close to a mussel bed during this, you can see the milky appearance in the water.

questions.question: Why is it called 'mess' in the army? Why officer's mess, mess tin, mess kit?

answers.answer: It's an old French word meaning a portion of food or dish. It comes from a Latin word - 'messa' meaning table. They used to say 'eating mess mates' (a group of people eating together), then it became 'mess room', eventually shortened to officer's mess, NCO's mess, or sergeant's mess.

questions.question: Why does Mo sleep through his wife's alarm but not his own, and vice versa at weekends? They have the same ringtone on separate phones.

answers.answer: It's about timing - both of them turn off their alarms before they fully wake the other person. On weekdays, she turns hers off before it wakes him. At weekends, he turns his off before it wakes her. Their daughter remains asleep because she's in a 'sweet spot' between them.

It's the reticular activating system - a part of the brain that filters out sounds it doesn't deem important. The brain decides certain noises are relevant (your own alarm) and others aren't (your partner's alarm, even though it's the same sound). This is why you can sleep through a thunderstorm but wake instantly at your dog or cat being sick. The distance from the phone is also crucial.

questions.question: Why don't deer camouflage their smell when they can camouflage their appearance so well? Deer are perfectly camouflaged against dead bracken but you can smell them from far away.
Where does the saying 'coming out of your shell' come from? Is it linked to the shellfish question?

answers.answer: I don't know for certain. I think it probably comes from snails rather than razor clams. Being shy and 'coming out of your shell' like a snail coming out to say hello.

questions.question: Why do men lose hair where they want it (head) but grow hair where they don't want it (ears, nose, shoulders, back, knees, toes) around the same time in life?

answers.answer: Twofold - as men age, hormonal shifts occur. Testosterone becomes more influential and the body metabolizes it into DHT (dihydrotestosterone). The scalp is most sensitive to DHT, causing baldness, while hair follicles elsewhere (shoulders, chest, back) respond by growing more hair.

questions.question: How distantly related can you be to someone before you have no genetic link? When does a measurable genetic link to a shared ancestor disappear from DNA?

answers.answer: Approximately five generations away. Clare would share the same amount of genetic material as about a thousand people. You could tell someone is from a certain region or ethnicity, but you wouldn't be able to definitively say they are directly related because the genetic link is spread across so many people.

questions.question: What is the science behind shushing and white noise soothing babies? Why does it work for some people and not others?

answers.answer: Replicates the sound in the womb - like a heartbeat, a whooshing sound that babies hear when in utero.
It's taught in medical school that it simulates for unborn babies the noise of the mother's blood pumping around their body. It's a comfort recall for babies.

questions.question: Why was there a rainbow around the moon last night?

answers.answer: It's a moon bow - exactly a rainbow they're seeing. The reflected light off the moon comes back through the clouds and undergoes diffraction, bending the light and separating it into component parts in the same way a rainbow is made. The clouds can be anywhere up to about a thousand to two thousand feet away. It's quite rare and hard to photograph because there's so little other light - you're just getting that reflected light. All rainbows are actually circles but you only see half in normal times.

questions.question: Why do different ear piercing holes in the same earlobe react to different metals? Her daughter just had ears pierced with titanium. One of her own middle holes can only have cheap metals while another hole must have silver/gold.
Why did my leg cramps disappear when I started wearing socks in bed?

answers.answer: When you sleep, blood circulation in your legs changes. The air level between muscles, tissue and nerves changes. Because nerve endings are in your feet, if there's not enough air there, you automatically get cramp. When you wear socks, you warm up all that air so blood circulation can go back to normal. Terrycloth-lined or loose-fitting travel socks from M&S men's department work best. Avoid DVT socks as they restrict circulation.

questions.question: Can animals be allergic to humans? How would you know if an animal was allergic to you?
How does deja vu work?

answers.answer: I don't know the answer.

It's called conceptual cognitive metaphor theory or post-structuralist linguistics. Your brain stores everything - people, places, objects - in separate containers. When something happens, multiple containers collide in a 'momentary flash of hyperdrive' and create a feeling of familiarity from disparate memories combined. It's not actually a memory of something that happened before, but a 'memory recipe' made of real stored information that feels like a past experience even though it hasn't happened.

questions.question: Why does the UK still use miles per hour on road signs when we went metric in 1967/1969?

answers.answer: It's baked in. People are 'married to' imperial measures. You couldn't change the roads because there would still be cars with imperial speedometers. Cost of changing all the signs. Infrastructure is too embedded. We've had 58 years to do it and haven't.

Mainly government policy - lack of perceived need and cost of converting all the road signs. Public opinion and tradition play a role too. The government originally set a process in the early 70s but indefinitely put it on pause. As a landscape architect working on public road network infrastructure, there's no real downside to changing, but people are very used to miles and the older generations grew up with imperial.

questions.question: Do cats derive any direct benefit from purring?

answers.answer: I don't know. We've had why do they purr, but not this specific question.

Two primary benefits: 1) Social - kittens purr to signal contentment to their mother, and domesticated cats stay in 'arrested development' keeping kitten behaviors like purring. 2) Healing - research shows the vibration frequency at which cats purr helps accelerate bone and tissue healing. Injured cats will often hide and purr because those vibrations promote recovery. (Qualifications: volunteers at a cat shelter, works with rescue cats)

questions.question: Why can nobody ever scratch the right spot when you have an itch on your back?

answers.answer: I've never found anyone who's prepared to scratch my back. I feel I haven't lived.

Itch sensors are plumbed into demyelinated nerves (nerves without a protein coat) that go into various parts of the brain, not in a linear relationship. It's like phantom limb - you can feel sensation in a limb that's been chopped off. The itch doesn't actually move, you just don't know exactly where it is. (Qualifications: medically trained)

questions.question: Where do earthworms go during summer when the ground is dry and hard?

answers.answer: I bet they go to sleep. There must be another answer. Occam's razor - they can't have died out since they come back.

It's not hibernation, it's estivation (summer version). Worms prepare by creating U-bend tunnels so water can't get in. They detect weather changes and go deep underground out of hard soil. They cover themselves in mucus to stay dry. They do the same in winter for frost. Cats can still dig them up. At night they come to the surface and latch on at the top of their tunnel hole and breathe - nobody knows why. (She's writing a comedy novel about a displaced worm called 'Together in Electric Trees')

questions.question: Do animals actually get any enjoyment out of eating raw meat and leaves like we get dopamine from cake?

answers.answer: I don't know. I'm worried about asking this because people will believe their cat enjoys smoked salmon more than tin of whiskers.

Yes, animals have the same reward mechanism as humans evolutionarily. Food is scarce so we evolved good feelings when encountering high sugar, high fat sources. The difference is humans layer memories, comfort, and culture onto food that animals don't experience the same way. That's why animals in normal environments are unlikely to become overweight - but pets living close to humans can become overweight because they, like us, continue to tap on that reward part of the brain. Your dog turning up its nose at kibble but eating fancy food shows they recognize and seek high-reward food. (Qualifications: has a whippet that's a fussy eater, studied dog reward mechanisms for training)

questions.question: Are the swans in Skiathos, Greece owned by the British King like UK swans?

answers.answer: I can't see how that would be enforceable. We used to eat swans in Tudor times but Stavros seems to be yanking your chain. Given they're migratory, who owns the King's swans when they're not in his kingdom?

No, the crown only owns mute swans in England and Wales. Mute swans are non-migratory - they stay within 30-40 miles of where they hatch. So the Skiathos swans are migratory and not covered by crown ownership. Stavros was yanking your chains. (Qualifications: goes to local parks, watches breeding pair of swans. Recently watched swans nest and raise cygnets to maturity near a canal.)

questions.question: When tigers are shaved, why are stripe imprints still embedded on their skin, but zebras and dalmatians don't have this?
Who wins the Mystery Hour board game?
Why do police always press down on a suspect's head when putting them into the back of a police car, even when handcuffs are already on?

answers.answer: To prevent the prisoner from injuring themselves - whether they're doing it for the reason of pretending the police have injured them or whether they're doing it as a consequence of trying to escape and abscond. Also mentioned center of gravity point to make them less mobile.

questions.question: When you put your head under water in the bath, you can hear your own heartbeat. If a pregnant woman did the same, could she hear her baby's heartbeat?
Who invented the first suit and tie to make it acceptable? Why have we kept the same style of suits for so long?

answers.answer: Suggested Bo Brummel but acknowledged probably too long ago - he was Regency England dandy, still wearing roped great snoods. The modern matching jacket and trousers probably emerged early 20th century with city workers and bowler hats.

Bo Brummel did invent the trouser from breeches, but that was much earlier. What we'd recognize as a modern suit - jacket and trousers cut below the hip - emerged at the end of the Edwardian era, just pre-First World War. Waistcoats went out, jackets developed the breast pocket with buttonhole for fob watches before wristwatches came in. It was a style development, not one person taking credit.

questions.question: When people switch from summer weight duvets to winter weight duvets at home, what do hotels do? Do they change duvets seasonally?

answers.answer: Hotels don't change duvets seasonally because rooms are air-conditioned, so temperature remains the same all year. They use a mid-weight duvet that works year-round.

questions.question: Why do batteries have to go in opposite ends of each other? Why couldn't they all just go in the same direction to make life easier?

answers.answer: When batteries go in opposite directions, they're connected in series, which doubles the voltage (two 1.5V batteries make 3V). If you put them in the same direction (parallel), it doubles the capacity instead, meaning it would last twice as long. Some devices use either configuration for different purposes.

questions.question: Why does leaving the stone in guacamole keep it fresher for longer? How does the science work?

answers.answer: The stone only blocks air where it sits immediately below the pit - it has no magical properties to protect the entire guacamole. You'd get the same effect from a golf ball or any other object. The better method is to put a thin layer of cling film across the whole top, or add lime/lemon juice which slows oxidation.

questions.question: Last week there was a question about what makes someone good at singing. Does the same principle apply to artwork and painting? Why can some people draw well and others can't?
Why do flea bites itch? I understand the mechanism, but what's the evolutionary advantage for the flea of alerting its host to its presence? A silent biter would seem more effective.

answers.answer: Flea saliva has an anticoagulant so the blood won't scab over quickly and the flea can feed. Your body responds to this as an irritant/allergen, sending histamines and antibodies = the itch. Evolutionarily, one bite is enough for a flea to feed, so there's no evolutionary advantage to being silent.

It's actually your histamine reaction, not the flea itself. That's why some people say they never get bitten while others get eaten alive - they get bitten the same amount, but some people's bodies react more strongly. Same principle applies to mosquitoes. If you live where you're bitten a lot, you build up resistance and itch less.

questions.question: Is there actually a last person in line for the succession to the throne? If there's always someone at the end, it goes on forever, so there must be a thousandth person in line.

answers.answer: Probably nobody knows for certain, but the last person currently listed is Karen Vogel, approximately 4,973rd or 5,753rd depending on which list. Everyone in the succession is a direct descendant of Sophia of Brunswick under the Act of Settlement 1701. Some people have married Catholics and disqualified themselves. Some people don't even know they're descended from her.

questions.question: In bingo, number 10 is 'Downing Street', number 22 is 'Two Little Ducks'. But who's Kelly and what's her eye got to do with number 1?

answers.answer: Kelly's Eye refers to Ned Kelly's helmet, which had a slot for him to see through and that slot resembles the number 1.

questions.question: When and why did people from Newcastle start being referred to as Geordies?

answers.answer: Two main theories: 1) During the 1745 Jacobite Rebellion, 'Geordie' was used as a derogatory term for supporters of King George, and Newcastle supported King George. 2) The Geordie lamp was a safety lamp for mines created by local inventor George Stephenson, so Geordies could be miners who used those lamps. There isn't a definitive answer.

questions.question: Why do words like mutineer, domineer, engineer, auctioneer and Brexiteer all end in -eer?

answers.answer: The suffix -eer comes from French 'ier', which comes from the Latin suffix '-arius', which comes from the verb of doing something. So it's the noun for the person doing something. Musketeer = someone who works with muskets. Engineer = someone who works with engines. Mutineer = someone who does a mutiny. Brexiteer = someone who does Brexit.

questions.question: Why does nothing else boggle? Why is it only the mind that boggles?

answers.answer: Mentioned the geography teacher's catchphrase 'don't know, nobody knows, don't need to know' but acknowledged this may not be a proper answer.

A boggle is a northern spirit that lives in houses and confuses people. Similar to boggarts in Harry Potter. The word may be related to 'boggle' meaning to confuse or deceive. The term comes from folklore and fairy tales.

questions.question: What is the neurological or biological reason why some people can naturally sing in tune and others really, really can't?

answers.caller: Terry from Bournemouth (professional singer and vocal coach)
answers.answer: It's about the feedback loop between how your brain hears what's coming through your ears and how your brain interprets that and adjusts the vocal cords. It's not something you can see physically - you need to work with someone to understand this feedback loop. People who are deaf have odd voices because they can't hear what's coming back from their voice box. The three things (ears, brain interpretation, vocal cords) have to work together.

questions.question: Why do there seem to be no serial killers anymore compared to the 60s, 70s, 80s? Is it something to do with forensics and DNA technology meaning they get caught before they have a spate of killings?

answers.answer: DNA plus CCTV would almost certainly help catch serial killers faster. Peter Sutcliffe (Yorkshire Ripper) would have been caught sooner if they were swabbing people spotted in red light districts. The reduction in serial killers is probably a technological thing. Harold Shipman shows you could still have someone who gets under the wire because no one realised he was killing people.

questions.question: Why are all pills and tablets white when a lot of stuff is made from natural plant sources?

answers.answer: Kaolin (China clay) makes up a lot of tablets as an additive to make them pill-sized. The active ingredient is usually quite small, so they pack it with kaolin to make it big enough. Most tablets are mostly kaolin, which is the colour of China clay, ergo they're all white.

answers.caller: Lewis from Putney (20 years in pharmaceutical industry)
answers.answer: Not all medicines are white - there are coloured ones like certain blue pills. But most standard tablets are white because: 1) The active pharmaceutical ingredient usually comes from crystallised powders which lose colour in manufacturing. 2) They bind pills with inactive ingredients (excipients). 3) Historically, white is a very clean colour and you can easily pick up impurities and defects with the human eye. Now computers and cameras do this. Also, some are colour-coded so you don't take them by accident.

questions.question: When a man ascends to the throne, he gets a queen. When a woman ascends to the throne, her husband doesn't get the title king. Why?

answers.answer: A king outranks a queen. The consort cannot have a rank higher than the monarch. In playing cards, chess, everywhere, king trumps queen. So if you called the queen's husband a king, he'd look senior even though he technically wasn't. That's probably the answer - it's patriarchy.

The exception that proves the rule is William and Mary. Parliament and nobles don't want a foreign prince to marry the queen and take over. But with William and Mary, William said 'if you don't make me king, I'm going back to the Netherlands and taking my army with me.' They needed the army because James II would have come back. William had his own claim to the throne but it wasn't as good as Mary's, so they were made co-monarchs.

questions.question: At the very bottom of the ocean, deep down, is the water there thicker or more viscous than the water at the surface because of the pressure of all the water on top?

answers.caller: David from Putney (A stars at A level)
answers.answer: Liquids are incompressible. You can compress gases but not liquids. The amount you can compress liquids is negligible. The answer is no - viscosity won't change because viscosity is a measure of the cohesiveness of atoms, and pressure does not change that property.

questions.question: Why doesn't my smallest pot work on my induction hob when the larger pots do work?

answers.answer: Check whether the small pan is magnetic. Sometimes smaller milk pans don't have an encapsulated base needed for induction cooking.
The magnet DOES stick to the small pan, so it's magnetic. The pan is also flat enough when tested with spirit level.

Induction hobs have minimum size requirements for pans. If a pan is too small, the hob won't detect it's there and won't turn on. Different hobs have different size requirements. The small pan likely works on other hobs with smaller zones but not on his current hob.

questions.question: Why do we say 'the River Thames' but Americans say 'the Thames River'? Why do we put the river first and Americans put river second?
Why is our brain cross-wired so that the right side controls the left side of our body and vice versa?

answers.answer: The crossover is called 'decussation' (from Latin, meaning to form an X). It serves as a protective element - if one side of the brain is damaged (like in a stroke), you can still operate with the other side. It also helps the brain compute information more efficiently by splitting the processing into two halves.

questions.question: Why does putting the avocado stone in guacamole keep it greener for longer?
Why can we hear my grandson Theo's knuckle cracking from six feet away when cracking other joints like your neck can't be heard from one foot away? Is it harmful like people used to say?
Why do locals in sunny countries like Portugal not wear sunglasses when tourists do? Have they evolved differently - have their eyes adjusted to the brightness?

answers.answer: It's about the colour of their iris. People in very bright sunshine areas (Middle East, Africa) tend to have brown irises which block visible light from getting through. People of Irish/Scandinavian heritage tend to have blue or green eyes which don't block light as effectively. However, although darker irises protect against visible light, they don't protect against UV light, which can cause cataracts and retinal damage, so people in bright countries should still wear sunglasses.

questions.question: How does our brain remember that we've forgotten something but not remember what we've forgotten? You know you've forgotten to do something but you can't remember what it is.
Since the Christianization of Britain, why didn't the church change the names of the days of the week from their pagan origins (Tyr, Woden, Thor, Frigg, etc.)?

answers.answer: Alfred the Great DID try to Christianize the day names to move away from Germanic pagan gods (similar to Norse gods), partly to distinguish England from the Danes. However, it didn't take off - the common people weren't educated enough to change, and much of England was under Danish control at the time. The old names persisted. Saturday is named after Saturn (a Roman god) and nobody knows why. Sunday is Sunna's Day, day of the Sun. Sunna was actually a male sun god with a sister Mona (moon goddess), so they swapped the genders - we have feminine moon and masculine sun.

questions.caller: Bill from Newport, Isle of Wight
questions.question: Why is GMT so lopsided? We have 57 days from the clocks changing to the solstice, but 98 days until we put them forward again. Shouldn't it be equal? Also, why is sunset so early (half past four) in winter despite having less daylight?
If I'm cooking dinner and the potatoes are still hard, should I turn the heat up even though the water is already boiling at 100 degrees C?

answers.answer: If the water is genuinely at 100 degrees centigrade (boiling), it can't get any hotter, so turning the heat up won't make the potatoes cook faster.

Once water reaches boiling point, added energy changes the state from liquid to gas rather than increasing temperature. So turning the hob up increases the rate of boiling but not the temperature. The water stays at 100 degrees Celsius. A rolling boil indicates the whole pan has reached 100 degrees.

While the water stays at 100 degrees, turning up the heat creates more vigorous boiling and more turbulence in the water, which increases the rate of heat transfer into the potatoes. So it does make a secondary difference - maybe 30 seconds quicker on a 10-minute cook.

questions.question: Why don't bee colonies have genetic issues from what appears to be extreme inbreeding? The entire colony is siblings and cousins, and they've been doing this for hundreds of thousands of years.

answers.answer: Genetic problems in sibling/cousin scenarios are very rare even though documented. Royal families routinely married first cousins without widespread issues. Additionally, insect colonies might have genetic mutations we just don't notice because defective bees would be eaten by other bees.

answers.caller: Max from Sudbury (freelance ecologist and beekeeper)
answers.answer: The premise is flawed. When a virgin queen leaves to mate, she attracts drones from OTHER colonies via pheromones. She mates with multiple males (who die during mating - their sex organs explode). She stores sperm from multiple fathers for her entire life. The drones in her hive are NOT the ones who mated with her. While sister drones could theoretically be among the suitors, it's a numbers game. Beekeepers also practice selective breeding, and queens with bad temperaments get replaced.

questions.question: Why do people use the word 'Roger' to mean 'yes' or 'acknowledged' on VHF radio?

answers.answer: It's the R you're looking for. R in the NATO alphabet is Romeo. But R stands for received.

answers.caller: Steve from Basildon (qualified marine radio radar communications engineer)
answers.answer: It goes back to early Morse code days. R for received was 'did-a-dit' (dot dash dot). Later the alphabet was changed to Romeo for clarity - Roger was easily confused but Romeo has a harsher sibilance. The old timers still use Roger. Maritime safety concerns prevented a complete switch. Most airline pilots now use Romeo, but sea-going and amateur radio people often still use Roger.

questions.question: Why do mammals have milk teeth? Why don't adult teeth just come through straight away?

answers.answer: Baby teeth are small because the mouth is small. As the mouth grows, bigger teeth are needed. Otherwise there would be massive gaps. It's an evolutionary adaptation. Also, adult teeth are already sitting in the skull above the baby teeth.

questions.question: Why does it seem like posh people have more speech impediments (can't pronounce Rs properly), and why haven't they fixed it with speech therapy?

answers.answer: The central premise may be wrong - many posh people on radio can pronounce their Rs fine. Posh people might just be more represented on radio so you encounter them more. Or it could be related to Kate's inbreeding question.

answers.caller: Paul from Worcester Park (reader of social and military history)
answers.answer: According to George MacDonald Fraser (Flashman novels), it was a late Georgian/early Victorian affectation deliberately adopted by army officers to signal they were 'in the club.' It was an understated masculinity thing - officers could afford to sound a bit feminine because they were so tough. It then became associated with poshness through media portrayals like Jeeves and Wooster and P.G. Woodhouse adaptations where all the posh characters had speech impediments.

questions.question: Why doesn't a pedestrian crossing button change the traffic lights to red instantly, even when no other traffic lights are linked and stopping has no wider impact on traffic flow?
Why do some people get an aggressive impulse to squeeze or bite cute things, while others don't feel that at all?

answers.answer: You have to grab their little cheeks like that.

It's caused by three brain chemicals having a massive overload: dopamine, oxytocin, and vasopressin. Some people produce more than others, which is why husbands don't get it as much. The brain physically can't comprehend why something is so cute because of the chemical overload. The degree varies - some people spend their whole life squeezing cheeks. There's also a minor link to autism spectrum traits.

questions.question: Why were all the greatest British guitar players (Peter Green, Brian May, Eric Clapton, Jimmy Page, Jeff Beck) born within 20 miles of each other? Was there something in the water or particularly good teaching?
Does it make any difference whether you pour Guinness in one go or two goes? And if it doesn't make a difference, why do they do it? When did this two-stage pouring start?

answers.answer: It makes no difference anymore. But it used to matter historically - Guinness used to be a very flat beer, and they had a separate cask of frothy Guinness. They would pour most of the pint with the flat beer, then switch to the frothy pump. That tradition stuck for a couple hundred years until they introduced nitrogen in the mid-50s.

There IS a difference. The Guinness fonts are designed specifically. You need to fill to the bottom of the glass harp, let it settle, then push the handle backwards for the second pour. When you pull forward for the first pour, it releases much more gas. If you pour in one shot, you'd get about an inch and a half more head. You get about half an inch difference between one-pull and two-pull.

questions.question: Why do helicopter pilots sit on the right-hand side while airline captains sit on the left-hand side?

answers.answer: It depends on the manufacturer. American helicopters like Robinson have the main fuel tank on the left, so the sole pilot sits on the right to offset the weight. Some manufacturers like Eurocopter have pilots sitting on the left. In multi-crew operations, it doesn't matter who's in which seat - the pilot in command is still in command regardless of position.

It's about hand control. You have the cyclic stick (forward/backward/left/right control) and the collective stick (up/down control). If you're right-handed, you want your dominant hand on the more controlling cyclic stick. So pilots sit on the right to use their left hand on the collective. This gets reversed for left-handed pilots. On smaller helicopters that share a collective stick in the middle, the pilot in command would sit on the left.

For airline pilots sitting on the left - it goes back to the dawn of aviation. Early propellers created a leftward drift, making left turns easier. So pilots sit on the left to see the runway during left-hand turns when landing. This is also why boarding happens from the left side.

questions.question: Why don't we have court jesters anymore? When did they die out? Who was the last one?

answers.answer: The last named court jester was Dickie Pearce, who served the Earl of Suffolk and died in 1728. His gravestone inscription reads: 'Now here lies the Earl of Suffolk's fool. Men called him Dickie Pearce. His folly served to make men laugh when wit and mirth were scarce. Poor Dick, alas, is dead and gone. What signifies to cry? Dickies in earth are still behind to laugh at, by and by.' There was also an unnamed fool employed by the Bowes-Lyon family (the Queen Mother's family) who died in the late 1700s. Will Summers was Henry VIII's famous fool, and there's also a Jane fool who was Catherine of Aragon's fool. The profession died out essentially when courts disappeared. The Industrial Revolution made courts socially irrelevant, and new money came in. Although there was persecution of a man called Dummy in Norwich in the 1800s.

questions.question: Why do we instinctively fold our arms one way (one arm on top, one underneath), and why is it hard or uncomfortable to do it the other way round? Is it linked to handedness or is it learned behavior?

answers.answer: It's just genetic variation - there's no particular reason for it. Some of us come out folding one way, some the other. It's determined by alleles inherited, similar to eye colour or the ability to roll your tongue. It's not linked to handedness - it's just random natural variation.

questions.question: Why is it called 'corpsing' when actors break character and start laughing on stage?

answers.answer: You're 100% right. It's because the worst imaginable time to laugh inappropriately on stage is when you're playing a corpse. There's a modern metaphorical meaning (killing the character by laughing) that's American and more recent, but the origin is simply that playing dead is when you're most likely to get the giggles and most damaging if you do.

questions.question: Why do some animals' hair grow continuously and need cutting (like dogs, sheep), while most animals' hair grows to a certain length and stops? Is there a genetic benefit or is it due to domestication?

answers.answer: Two parts to the answer: 1) Evolutionary - for animals like tigers and wolves, hair length is genetically determined based on environmental factors like temperature. For humans, hair on the head and beard may have provided evolutionary advantage in attracting mates as we lost body hair. 2) For domesticated animals like dogs, it's about breeding - they were bred for primary characteristics, and the need for haircuts is often a byproduct of that selective breeding. Some is human intervention, some is evolution, some is just nature.

questions.question: Are High Court judges exempt from jury service? What if they're working on a years-long fraud case?

answers.answer: Judges were exempt, along with various civil servants, but they've lifted that exemption. It was quite some time ago when she was working at the Royal Court of Justice. Shortly after the exemption was removed, the Lord Chief Justice himself was called for jury service, which was quite amusing for the other jurors.

questions.question: Why do young children pick their noses and eat the results? Is there an evolutionary reason?

answers.answer: Initially believed it was good for your immune system - tiny doses of germs help build resistance. Later corrected - internet says it's not good for you and can transfer bad stuff to nostrils or scratch septum.
It tastes nice. Asked callers to ask their granddaughters why they do it and they'd say 'It's yummy, Grandma.'

questions.question: Why do we get two high tides every day when there's only one moon? I can't understand why the tide goes away from the moon on the far side.

answers.answer: Expressed discombobulation - admitted he couldn't figure out why you get two bulges when one goes away from the moon. Asked callers for help.

It's about average gravitational pull. The water closest to the moon has higher than average pull (creating one tide), but on the far side, gravity is less than average so water falls away (creating second tide). Also explained tidal locking between Earth and moon.

questions.question: Why do baby clothes labels say UK age 12-18 months but US/Canada age 24 months for the same size vest? Are babies in Canada and US that much smaller?

answers.answer: No theory - expressed genuine confusion and said he couldn't figure it out.
US and Canada uses 'up to 24 months' - meaning the label indicates the clothes fit up to 24 months, not that the baby is 24 months old. UK may be using different sizing conventions.

questions.question: Does sweeping up fallen leaves from my tree each autumn and putting them in the garden recycling bin damage the tree by depleting it of nutrients or carbon?

answers.answer: No - said he's 100% certain sweeping up leaves doesn't do any measurable harm to the tree. Said leaves have no evolutionary purpose once fallen.

DISAGREEMENT - In nature, leaves are taken back into soil by worms and break down, improving soil texture and being taken back up by tree as nutrients. If you continually remove them year after year, you deplete the soil and tree's nutrient base. Recommendation: sweep off lawn but sweep into planting beds around trees, leaving gap near trunk.

questions.question: When we borrow Italian words, why do we sometimes use plurals rather than singulars? Why does a coffee shop have 'cappuccino' on the drinks board but 'panini' on the food board? Why do we pluralise the plural?

answers.answer: When Italian immigrants like Rocco Forte arrived and opened milk bars, they put singulars on drinks board (cappuccino) and plurals on food board (panini). It's arbitrary - just how the mind worked when they set up their boards.

Italian masculine nouns end in O singular, E plural. Two theories: 1) Panini as singular started in US among non-Italian restaurateurs who mistook it for singular, then spread. 2) Panino was once used for half a panini (one folded bit) while two clamped together were a Panini. Also noted Chinese friend embarrassed Italian husband by asking for 'due a cappuccino' as Chinese has no singular/plural distinction.

questions.question: Why do tattoos hurt more on my right side than my left side? My chest, back and ribs all hurt more on the right.

answers.answer: Right-handed people have more developed muscles on their dominant side, meaning less fat and thinner skin (dermis). This means more pain on the right-hand side where the protective layer is thinner.

DISAGREEMENT - Body composition doesn't play much role. Pain is largely about perception. The dominant side receives more attention and fine motor skill use, making it more sensitive. You're more attentive to your right side, so you perceive more pain there. This also explains why non-dominant side is often stronger (gross motor movements).

questions.question: How big could a beard be before a boxer wouldn't be allowed to box? Would it act as a cushion, like WC Fields or Brian Blessed's beard? Tyson Fury occasionally has a beard.

answers.answer: Presumed a beard might act as some cushioning but wasn't sure if it would have measurable effect. Promised to find out from producer/boxer Elliot.

The reason for beard limits is NOT cushioning - it's because a large beard would cover up injuries. Ringside medic and referee wouldn't be able to see damage. So there is a limit on facial hair length, but for visibility reasons.

questions.question: How do all the trees know when to start dropping their acorns and how many to drop? Why is the acorn crop so wildly inconsistent year to year?

answers.answer: Oak trees have random mast years where oaks in sync produce overwhelming numbers of acorns to overwhelm predators - there's not enough acorns to feed all the acorn-eaters so some survive to grow. The years after have less of a crop which keeps predator numbers down. It's evolutionary - triggered by environmental factors like warm springs.

questions.question: If you take a multivitamin, paracetamol, and antihistamine all at the same time, how does your body know where to distribute what? How does it know what goes where and does what?

answers.caller: Callum (registered nurse, newly qualified cardiology HDU)
answers.answer: Anti-inflammatories reduce inflammation all around the body everywhere, but you only notice it in the places that were extraordinarily painful. So everywhere is affected, but you only notice it where it was really painful to start with.

answers.caller: Brian (Emeritus Professor of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, drug discoverer)
answers.answer: Drugs don't necessarily go all over the place - it depends on properties of the molecule. If it's more water soluble, it goes to watery areas of the body. If it's more greasy, it goes to fatty areas. Also, some vitamins are actively transported by mechanisms to get them to the right places. It's a complicated world.

questions.question: Why do TV reporters shout questions at politicians getting out of cars (like at Downing Street) when they never get answers? Is that the best they can come up with?

answers.answer: It makes for marginally more interesting footage for the evening bulletin than sitting in silence watching the car pull up and the politician walk through the door. It's content creation - a very early example of it. They could be doing the piece to camera from home, but being there makes it slightly more interesting.

questions.question: Why does my ridiculously loud snore never wake me up, but my girlfriend's much quieter snore can wake me up?

answers.caller: Simon from Reading (heavy snorer, investigates sleep)
answers.answer: The brain filters out auditory processing for constant background noises like traffic running down a street. If someone speaks to you or comes into your room, your hearing is waiting for that, so it would wake you up. Your own snore becomes absorbed into your normal existence.

questions.question: Where does the pound sign (£) actually come from? It's a fancy L with two lines through it - why that?

answers.answer: Italian lira used to be abbreviated with the same kind of pound sign. And 'pound' comes from Latin 'libra' - one libra equals one pound. It's the Roman imperial measurement for weight, and also the star sign. It's all about the Latin.

questions.question: How did we originally know which foods were safe to eat? Like who first decided to squeeze a cow's udders and drink what came out?

answers.answer: Trial and error. They'd try it, drop dead, and everyone else would think 'let's not have any of those berries.' The obvious answer is people would watch calves being suckled and then try it themselves. There's no other possible answer - you can't test everything scientifically in advance.

questions.question: If you boil an egg and put it back in the fridge, does it last longer than a fresh egg or the same time?

answers.caller: Tony (self-answer, but brought up in context)
answers.answer: Yes, boiled eggs stay fresh longer than fresh eggs. He ate one that had been there a 'rather long time' and it tasted really fresh.

questions.question: Why do women and girls put their hand over their mouth when surprised, but men and boys don't? I've noticed it on DIY reveal shows.
How can the nutritional value of supermarket milk be so uniform when cows' milk nutritional value changes based on their diet, the season, and pasture conditions? Why does it never change?

answers.answer: Every type of milk is standardized to whichever type they want to produce. It's done by machinists in the factory through homogenization and separation. They aim for certain levels - like 4% fat. The label says 'typical amounts' so there can be some deviation. Milk is produced to feed a calf and the nutritional content is standardized for consumer sale.

questions.question: Why is it that when you have an abandoned building, trees and things grow out of it over days and weeks, but this never happens when we inhabit a building?

answers.answer: Because we hoover up, sweep and clean up seeds that might potentially grow. The roads and pavements have plants growing out of them because we don't hoover them. But in our homes, unless you're observing extraordinary low standards of domestic hygiene, no seed is going to be able to get a green leaf. The seeds don't have the time and space to germinate and grow because we are there living there - if we saw anything sprouting we'd snatch it, snip it, get rid of it.

questions.question: Why can some dogs see what's on phone or TV and register what they're watching, while my dog doesn't register anything? I've tried showing her videos of other dogs, birds, and other films like Lion King but she doesn't react.

answers.answer: Show her the right stuff - maybe she's just not interested. Show her some football or dog videos. The question is what are you watching - if it's Summer I Turned Pretty that might explain it. Dogs want dogs, so show her dog content.

questions.question: Why was it less of a shock going back into the sea after 10 minutes in a sauna than it was going in fresh?

answers.answer: Was it less of a shock or was it just a more pleasant experience because you were uncomfortably hot and needed to cool down? If you're very hot and go into cold water, it should take your breath away even more than not being overly hot. The sauna makes your body think 'this is nice' rather than 'this is cold'.

questions.question: Old athletics tracks were 440 yards (one lap), 880 yards (two laps), and a mile (four laps). Why did tracks change to 400 meters, and why is the 1500 meters now 3.75 laps instead of 1600 meters (four laps)?

answers.answer: It stems from the metric system and the modern Olympic movement coming from France. As athletics went global, everything standardized to metric. The 1500m is called the 'metric mile'. Middle distance events follow metric progression: 400, 800, 1500. In America they run 1600m and call it the metric mile. The track design and metrication brought tracks from 440 yards to 400 meters. The distances also cater to specific energy systems - you don't want a 500m race because lactic acid would be crazy.

questions.question: What's the purpose of the patch/pocket thing inside my jacket? It's a piece of cloth sewn on both sides but open at the bottom - I've stitched them up on my old jackets including a ski jacket but I don't know what it's for.

answers.answer: It's an embroidery access point - to provide an opening for commercial embroiderers to get the machine in to put a logo on a jacket without sewing through to the lining.

It's a vestigial feature from when people wore waistcoats and had pocket watches chained to them with a fob. The open pockets allowed ribbons to be fed through to chain wallets. It's a holdover from that - to chain your wallet to you so you don't lose it.
It's an access point on a ski jacket - you put your hand in and access other items without having to take the whole jacket off.
It's the pocket bag - when making a jacket, you need a bag that your hand goes into. That pocket bag is attached to the outside with a zip but often looks like just a flap on the inside.

Lindsay was right. It's an embroidery access point - loads of jackets have a hidden zip on the inside that looks like a pocket. If you find this zip and open it, you can embroider or print on the jacket without going through the lining. Most people don't find them. Sometimes it's not a zip - just an open tube with nothing at the bottom.

questions.question: Is it more cost effective to heat a house from cold or to cool a house down when it's hot? I have air conditioning in Thailand where my mother-in-law lives and I'm curious whether it's more expensive to run than heating.

answers.answer: There would be variables - how high your heating is, how cold you set your AC. One unit of heat versus one unit of cooling. Central heating is like 10 radiators but AC is in each room. I don't know the answer.

questions.question: Why are some raindrops fat and some raindrops thin?

answers.answer: It depends on where the raindrops form and what the air mass is doing (going up or down). Raindrops form when there's a lot of water vapor in the air that gets colder and condenses. If that happens very high up with no updrafts, drops are small and fall slowly. Below them is warm air so they evaporate before reaching the ground - you get fine rain. If condensation happens lower down, even small drops reach the ground. If there's an updraft (upward wind), drops are kept in the condensing zone longer and get bigger. Very strong updrafts in thunderstorms create big drops. Below freezing altitude, drops become hail. In extreme weather like cyclones and tornadoes with monumental updrafts, you get golf ball size hailstones.

questions.question: Why does my face contort when I'm concentrating? When I'm doing up a screw or something, my jaw might tense and go to one side. If I'm thinking about something really intricate, I stick my tongue out. Is there an evolutionary reason for it?

How do they calculate use-by dates? What metric do they use and how regularly do they update that metric? Given that people will be storing things in a variety of different ways, what's the baseline for calculating a use-by date?

answers.answer: In cheese factories, they have in-house labs. They take samples of each batch and store some in a commercial fridge and some in the main warehouse fridge. They test the cheese at regular intervals to see how it progresses and when it starts chemical changes. This has to be agreed with the supermarkets. Some cheeses are signed off as lasting 63 days from manufacture date. They basically monitor it over time.

questions.question: Why are some horse chestnuts smooth and some spiky? Some of the shells have spikes all over but there's a few of them that are smooth on the same tree. What's the difference?

answers.answer: The spikiness of a conker is its defence mechanism against browsing animals. Above the height at which the seed or bud might be predated by a browsing animal, there is no requirement for the tree to develop the defensive mechanism. The same is true of holly leaves - above a certain height, holly trees will not produce spiky leaves. They're smooth. And beech hedges retain their brown crusty dry leaves throughout winter to protect new growth, but only up to a certain height.

questions.question: Why is a lazy Susan called a lazy Susan? I can understand why it's lazy - you can just spin the wheel rather than passing each individual dish. But why Susan? Who is Susan and why was she lazy?

answers.answer: Susan Jefferson, the youngest daughter of American president Thomas Jefferson. She was forever complaining that she was the last one to get past the salt or pepper. So he invented the spinning thing just to keep her quiet and called it a lazy Susan. Paul discovered this on a cruise ship pub quiz eight years ago.

questions.question: Where do novelty marathon runners (Spider-Man suits, fridges on backs) train? You never see them training in Warrington. You can't just rock up to a marathon with a fridge on your back and wing it. Do you have to train in the gear?

answers.answer: Dan Fairbrother from Stevenage Cricketers running club trained for his marathon with a full working fridge on his back. He also trained in Crocs. He ran the whole marathon with the fridge and proposed to his girlfriend halfway round.

You don't actually need to train with the actual costume or fridge. For example, you could wear a weighted vest or use an altitude mask which restricts breathing. When you actually do the real thing, you're substituting those. So you don't look ridiculous running in a costume while training.

questions.question: Why is it that we can find out exactly what people paid for a house, even over history, but you can't for virtually any other product? Why is that specific to houses?
Is it 'a nonsense' or just 'nonsense'? One sounds wrong to me. Saying 'a nonsense' doesn't feel right. Is 'a nonsense' wrong?

Why do we get fat rain and thin rain? Big water droplets that come on the windscreen and then the really fine stuff. What's happening in the clouds to make it fat rain or thin rain? Why aren't all droplets the same size?
Why are my thumbnails much thicker than my fingernails when I come to trim them? Same with my big toenail - it's like the mothership. Is it just me?

When I have a shower, I put shower gel on my loofah and it gets really soapy and bubbly. I don't rinse it before putting it back. But when I come back the next day, all the soap has disappeared. And when I re-wet it, it doesn't re-activate the soap. What's happened to the soap?

Why do some crow species live much longer than others? One species lives 3-5 years and another similar one lives up to 15 years. They live in the same habitat, look roughly the same. I know it's DNA, but what is the trigger that makes one live longer than another?

Why do trees planted by councils have hoses or spouts sticking out of the ground next to them? My mother suggested it might be to allow air to stop root rot, but I thought it was for watering directly to the root ball.

answers.answer: You put the water down the snorkel to get it directly to the root ball.

answers.caller: Lawrence from Blandford in Dorset (tree surgeon/tree consultant)
answers.answer: It's a solar pipe fitted at the time the tree is planted. It's corrugated with lots of small holes to allow water to flow down directly to the root ball of a newly planted tree.

questions.question: How do spiders know which web is theirs? My four-year-old son Sonny asked me this.
Does color affect our movement/mood? In the army, when running behind someone in a white top I enjoyed it, but when they wore a red top it really wound me up and made me frustrated.

answers.answer: Orange makes you feel better about things. When having fertility treatment they were told to fill the house with orange flowers. Orange calms you down. Krishna monks wear orange and are always very chilled out.

Color and light are inseparable and light is fundamental to our survival. Warmer colors generally mean more favorable conditions. When running and suffering in heat, red makes you feel worse and white makes you feel cooler. Orange is both warm and not extreme - it's optimum.

questions.question: Do the back pockets on jeans stay the same size regardless of waist size? I saw an American man pouring himself into a Porsche and noticed the distance between his back pockets was monstrous.

answers.caller: Sean from Long Melford (menswear shop owner)
answers.answer: They stay the same size. The actual pocket size varies between manufacturers but once you're in adult male jeans, the pockets are the same size on every waist size. It's down to cost - manufacturers have a standard design of pocket which is like a signature, with specific stitching. In a production line, pre-cut pockets are slapped onto the bum part.

answers.caller: Stephen from Nebworth (pattern cutter and grader for 30+ years)
answers.answer: He's incorrect. When you grade anything up, it's like blowing up a picture in proportion. You always grade pocket sizes. The back pockets of jeans do get bigger in proportion - hands get bigger so pockets have to get bigger. Front pockets as well. If you're doing it correctly, everything must be in proportion.

questions.question: When buying records online, if I use the packaging months later without crossing out the barcode, will that barcode be regenerated somewhere else? Do barcodes get reused?

answers.caller: Carl from Warrington (former Royal Mail director involved in QR codes rollout)
answers.answer: Barcodes are officially unique and cannot be reused. You apply to the UK barcode registry through GS1, a non-profit company, and get unique barcodes that become your property. You can theoretically reuse your own barcodes in different locations - like a jeans manufacturer could put a barcode on jeans and use the same one in a warehouse. But you can't stick a barcode from jeans on a tin of tuna years later - that would be complete misrepresentation. Technology is changing: QR codes are totally universal with billions of variations and will eventually replace barcodes.

questions.question: Why do oak trees drop so many acorns but there aren't millions of oak trees everywhere? What's happening to all the acorns?

answers.answer: Squirrels hoard acorns - that's a well-known fact. They collect a lot of them.

answers.caller: Caller with horses and oak trees
answers.answer: Squirrels do eat most of the acorns. In August, put temporary fencing around oak tree canopies and by October when you take it down, there are no acorns left to pick up because squirrels have eaten them all.

Squirrels damage most acorns, but the acorns that actually grow into trees are mostly planted by jays - Eurasian blue jays. Jays handle them delicately enough that they don't damage the acorn, unlike squirrels.

questions.question: Who names prescription pills and drugs and why are they so complicated and long?

answers.caller: Lewis from Putney (20 years in pharmaceutical industry)
answers.answer: Two-part answer: drugs under patent have a patented brand name by the drug company. When the patent expires and they become generic, they are named based on the molecule or API (active pharmaceutical ingredient). The complex long names are simply the molecular name - they cannot get away from it, it's the law. Like Nurofen is the brand name, ibuprofen is the generic molecular name.

questions.question: At a James concert at Colchester Castle, the band's daisy logo on the back screen went from 2D to 3D during a song - the tips of the petals were bigger than the screen. It can't be an optical illusion because they got bigger. How did they do that?

answers.caller: Chloe from Tunbridge, Wales (works in live visuals)
answers.answer: It's pixel mapping and LED screen expansion. They animate to a slightly smaller screen size first, then that screen size expands so it looks like it's popping out at you. The 2D image has been made to look smaller, then expands making your eyes think it's coming out towards you.

questions.question: Why can a piece of paper, no matter how big or small, only be folded eight times? It must be physics.
Why do prawns, lobster, and crayfish go orange when you cook them, but nothing else does?

answers.answer: Well that's because it's burnt (attempt at humor, not serious)

Prawns contain a pigment called astaxanthin, which is a type of carotenoid. Normally this pigment is bound to the protein called crustocyanin. Once prawns start to cook, the crustocyanin protein starts to denature and shrink, squeezing out the pigment which then colours the rest of the prawns.

questions.question: What percentage of hand sanitizer is alcohol, and does it enter the bloodstream and have detrimental effects on the liver like drink driving?

answers.answer: It's 70% alcohol. If you bathed in it... you'd just get a bit tipsy.

No, you won't get drunk from excessive use of alcohol hand gel. Most of the alcohol goes straight onto your hands, kills the bugs, and then evaporates off into the atmosphere. Studies with healthy volunteers repeatedly applying hand gel showed zero or negligible alcohol in blood. The only way it could absorb slightly is through cuts or abrasions, or theoretically very minor transdermal absorption.

questions.question: Why do people say 'O' instead of 'zero' when reading out telephone numbers? There's no such thing as an O in a telephone number.

answers.answer: Craig suggested 'nought nomenclature' - which was praised as a beautiful alliteration

In emergency services, armed forces, or radio communication, you never say 'O' when talking about a number - it's always zero because it's clearer. With background noise, zero is much more distinct. People substitute 'O' simply because it's shorter.

questions.question: What do you do with a lost homing pigeon in your garden? (Question 1 - crowdsourced)

answers.answer: Contact the racing pigeon organization. When you find the numbers on the leg tag, they can contact the owner. She found a pigeon on the A3 and returned it - the owner sent a courier box and got it back. The owner said all pigeons are called Beauty.

questions.question: If you keep homing pigeons and move from Cornwall to Glasgow, do the pigeons follow you to Glasgow or do they keep returning to Cornwall? (Question 2 - crowdsourced)

answers.answer: You can take your pigeons to Glasgow but you would have to retrain them. Homing pigeons are able to detect the Earth's magnetic field, navigate through smell, and use visual clues. You take them a mile away from their loft and let them fly back, building up to five miles and ten miles over time.

questions.question: Why are hay bales different shapes - some cylindrical and some cuboid - sometimes even in the same field?

answers.answer: It's about historical evolution of agricultural bales. Started with small rectangular bales for early tractors, then larger round bales came along because tractors got bigger - easy to put on a spike on the front of a tractor. Then large square bales were invented because they stack more efficiently in barns. Large round and square bales also suited being wrapped in plastic for silage. Different farms have different machinery and can't just switch - hence why adjacent fields have different shapes.

questions.question: Why do all dead flies lie with their legs up in the air?

answers.answer: It's about weight distribution

It's unstable equilibrium. The fly's body is top heavy - the head and thorax are heavy compared to the thin legs. When alive, the nervous system controls muscles to keep upright. When it dies, rigor mortis sets in. Imagine trying to balance a wobbly tripod upside down - it would constantly fall over. One in a million dead flies might end up the right way up.

questions.question: What starts a sneeze, and what stops the last sneeze when you've got a handkerchief ready?
Why do we call it a 'jackpot'?
Relative to its size, what is the loudest animal? If we were all the same size, what would make the most noise?

answers.answer: Hypothesized it could be crickets or cicadas - they're deafening for their size and you can barely see them

The water boatman - only a couple of millimetres long but produces around 90 decibels (like a lawnmower). If scaled to human size, it'd be like a human shouting at the volume of a space shuttle taking off. They make the noise through stridulation - rubbing its genitals against its abdomen. It's used to attract mates.

questions.question: When I use a fork in my left hand with a knife in my right hand, I have no problem. But when I'm just using a fork or spoon alone (like cereal), why can't I eat with my left hand? Why do I have to use my right hand?

answers.answer: Suggested it might be about the mechanics - when you use fork with knife, your knuckles point up. When using fork alone, knuckles point down. And the movement up to your mouth feels awkward and unsteady with your non-dominant hand, similar to how left-handed people have a different stance when writing.
When you eat with knife and fork, the fork is just loading food. Take the knife away and the fork has to do all the work with your weaker hand. Left-handed people eat the other way round.

questions.question: I put my son's smelly clothes in the freezer and the smell completely went - even before washing them. Does that mean nothing smells in the North Pole? Why does putting them in the freezer work?

answers.answer: In the cold, blood flow to the nerves reduces. Also, the molecules you need to smell need to be carried in moisture - when it's very cold, that transportation from particle to nerves is nearly blunted. So you can't smell much in extremely cold places.
Noted that Stanley answered from the wrong end (the North Pole) but correctly. Suggested that bacteria might also get killed in the freezer, which is why clothes don't smell when they defrost.

questions.question: Why is tagliatelle sold in nests while most other pastas like spaghetti, linguine, fettuccine, and lasagna are sold straight or in sheets?

answers.answer: Hypothesized there must be a 'golden ratio' point where putting pasta straight in water means it will stick together and not spread out. Tagliatelle must be on the other side of that mythical pasta line compared to spaghetti and linguine.

Tagliatelle is made with egg. When it dries, it's much more brittle than other pastas. Making it into a nest gives it structural integrity so it doesn't break up. When you make it at home, you hang it up to dry but then coil it into nests. It might also be custom and practice to make it look handmade.

questions.question: Who popularized the picture frame? Why do I need to spend £30 to put a £10 picture up on my wall?

answers.answer: Suggested the frame itself is aesthetic (to make unfinished canvas edges look nicer) while glass is for protection. Wondered if the invention of glass popularized the picture frame.

The origin of the picture frame was to disguise the edges of painted canvases. The addition of glass goes back to early photography when images were taken on glass plates - the emulsion was very fragile and needed something rigid and transparent to mount on. When images moved to paper, glass was still needed to protect the fragile surface.

questions.question: Why does starch aerosol have to have the nozzle aligned with a little mark on the rim when no other aerosols (spray paint, air freshener, furniture polish) require this?
In an emergency, could somebody with a taser do the same job as a defibrillator?

answers.caller: Andrew from Fulham (police officer, trained in defibrillators)
answers.answer: They are not interchangeable. A defibrillator scans the heart to see whether a shock is applicable in that situation. With a taser, you have no accuracy over where the two probes go, whereas defibrillator pads need to go in very specific places to send the charge through the body to connect the two pads.

questions.question: Why do different languages work asymmetrically? Spanish speakers understand more Italian and Portuguese than Italians and Portuguese understand Spanish. And Norwegians understand more Swedish than Swedes understand Norwegian?

answers.caller: John from Lisbon (tour guide, teaches languages, speaks 5 languages)
answers.answer: It's about exposure and cultural production. Portugal has more tradition of subtitling than dubbing, so people are more exposed to foreign languages. Spain produces more pop culture consumed in Portugal. Similarly, Egyptian and Syrian/Levantine Arabic are most understood because they were the main centers of cultural production for most of the 20th century. More traffic moves from the larger cultural exporter to the smaller one.

questions.question: Why are there so many Hotel Bristols around the world? Paris, Barcelona, Budapest, Asunción in Paraguay - they're normally older, not very expensive hotels.

answers.answer: Hypothesized there was probably an 18th or 19th century aristocrat - perhaps a Marquess or Earl of Bristol - who traveled the world and hotels were named after him for the association with luxury.

She stayed at the Hotel Bristol in Salzburg and asked after a few whiskeys. It's named after the 4th Earl of Bristol - a 19th century traveler who was thought to be a connoisseur and very rich. Hotels named themselves after him to be associated with that sense of luxury. They're not the same chain.

questions.question: Why do we use green as the fourth primary colour when red, yellow, blue are primaries and green, purple, orange are secondaries? Why not use orange or pink instead of green in games like Ludo?

answers.answer: Red, blue and yellow are primary colours in art. But red, green, blue are primary colours in science. When you look at old TVs and the sections of colour that would make up Technicolour, it was RGB, so red, green, blue. So the four colours in games would be an amalgamation of four primary colours from different systems - there are two double-powered primary colours depending on which lens you're looking through. We're talking about light.

questions.question: Why are chocolate bars always wrapped with the seal or fold on the bottom, making you flip them over to see the pre-cut scoring marks?

answers.answer: Every chocolate bar is put into a mould and the product settles or sets leaving a flat surface. When it's packaged, you cannot seal a Lion Bar or a Toffee Crisp on the bumpy side - it's impossible. So it's always put against the flat side. They use foil with two little up folds which seal and then fold flat against the flat surface of the chocolate bar. The fold leaves you the date, batch number and time it was packaged and by what machine. It's all to do with the seal - they fold it flat because it's able to fold it flat against the flat side, not the bumpy side.

questions.question: Why is 180 degrees Celsius the standard oven temperature for cooking almost everything? What happens at a molecular level that made 180 the default?

answers.answer: The browning reaction, called the Maillard reaction, starts at about 140 degrees C. 180 is the perfect sweet spot between cooking things through and browning - you're significantly above the Maillard point but not browning things hard at 200.

questions.question: Why does the national speed limit sign feature a white circle with a black diagonal stripe rather than a specific number like other speed signs?

answers.answer: Different vehicles are only allowed certain speeds depending on the road type. The national speed limit is the speed limit for a particular vehicle on that road, whereas the normal speed limit is the round sign with a number in it which applies to any vehicle. So the sign means 'your vehicle's national speed limit' - it encompasses all the different numbers for different vehicle types. It's incumbent on the driver to know what the national speed limit is for what they're driving, whether it's a caravan, lorry, bus, dual carriageway or single carriageway.

questions.question: Why doesn't the UK have time zones? When you cross the Channel to France, you gain light evenings, but the UK stays on one time.

answers.answer: Time zones were sorted out in the 1800s after an enormous train crash. Sir Sanford Fleming, born in Scotland and later Canadian, figured out there are 24 hours in a day, 360 degrees divided by 15 is 24. For every 15 degrees of longitude there's an hour time change. Canada has six time zones because it's so wide. The UK doesn't need time zones because it's not wide enough - we're long and thin, so our daylight doesn't change that much across the country.

In Europe, zero longitude goes through Greenwich because of the Greenwich Observatory. Paris tried to set it through Paris but we weren't having any of it and the rest of the world followed us. France could be in the same time zone as us because a large percentage of their country is in our zero to 15 degrees, but they don't do it for business purposes to stay in sync with Germany and Belgium. Spain does the same - all of Spain is in our time zone. Portugal doesn't because they're further west and it would give them problems with daylight.

questions.question: How do weather forecasters know exactly how many centimetres of rain we're going to get? My jug measured 3.5cm and the forecast said 3-5cm - how do they predict specific measurements?
