Why do satellites appear to bob and weave rather than flying in straight lines across the sky? I can watch them for 10 minutes and see 4-5 behaving in the same erratic way.
Is it a coincidence that a debit card is exactly the same size as a packet of cigarettes? What came first - did they design them to be the same size?
Why are tropical fish so colourful compared to fish in the UK waters which are brown and grey?

answers.answer: It's camouflage and an evolutionary survival technique. Coral reefs are very colourful so fish need to blend in. In the duller Mediterranean, duller fish survive better as they're less likely to be predated.

questions.question: Why do women's football shirts have first names on them rather than surnames? I noticed the Spanish players had first names like Alexia on their shirts.

answers.answer: Spanish surnames tend to be longer and may not fit on a shirt, so they use first names instead. If the surname fits, they use the surname.

Names became mandatory on the back of football shirts around 1994 for TV identification and commercial reasons. About 10 years later, rules changed to allow nicknames or first names. Some clubs used to charge per letter, which is why longer names got shortened to first names.

questions.question: If you massage your right foot properly with your right thumb, does your right arm end up two or three inches longer than your left arm?
Why is the place called 'Borehamwood' (one word) but the football team is 'Boreham Wood' (two words)?

answers.answer: Boreham Wood Football Club was founded in 1948 and was originally known by two separate words. Locals called it 'Boreham Stiff'. The railway station was called Elstree in Boreham Wood. Over the years, people got into the habit of writing it as one word. The council tried to change it to 'Elstree' about 10-15 years ago but the posh people in Elstree didn't like that, so they gave up and remained Boreham Wood.

questions.question: What is the evolutionary advantage of doing 'horse lips' (blowing air through pursed lips making a flapping sound) when we're cold?
When a fly dies on a vertical wall, does it immediately fall off or does its suction power remain for a certain amount of time?

answers.answer: I think it would stick because it's a substance that makes it stick. How long for? Unknown.

Spiders and insects stick to walls through electrostatic charge created by tiny hairs on their feet, not sticky substances. When they die, the muscles in their legs relax and the electrostatic tension is lost. On a dry surface, this happens within about an hour as rigor mortis sets in for such small creatures.

questions.question: Why do military pilots say 'pickle' when they press the button to release bombs? Where did this phrase come from?

answers.answer: The US Air Force had a 'pickle switch' - a transfer system to quickly switch between guns and bombs. The inventor boasted he could drop a bomb in a pickle jar from 20,000 feet. So when pilots pressed the button to switch to bombs, they announced 'pickle' to confirm the action was recorded.

questions.question: Why do your eyes water when you drink fizzy drinks too quickly?

answers.answer: The gas in sparkling drinks is carbon dioxide, which dissolves in water to make carbonic acid. When you drink quickly, pressurised CO2 goes through your Eustachian tubes (the tubes from throat to tear ducts), temporarily dropping the pH in your tears and making them more acidic. Your body then pumps more tears to readjust the pH - similar to what happens when slicing onions with sulphur compounds.

questions.question: Where have these bright pink fuchsia-coloured pigeons in Canning Town come from? Is it natural or have they been spray-painted?

answers.answer: Pink pigeons are part of the gender reveal trend. They use water-based vegetable dye which is harmless. Event companies release dyed pigeons for gender reveals (similar to doves). The two pigeons in Canning Town must have escaped from such an event - they normally retrieve them but sometimes they fly off in the wrong direction.

questions.question: If I lived in a hot country where mosquitoes bite me all the time, would they eventually stop finding me attractive? Would I become immune or less attractive to them over time?

answers.answer: Mosquitoes won't lose appetite for you - they'll continue to find you very tasty. However, over time your body will become tolerant to the particular anticoagulant they inject. Your histamine reaction to the bites will reduce, so you won't itch as much. But there won't be a reduction in the actual number of bites - you'll just notice them less.

questions.question: When did the Tour de France begin to evolve from being a contest between individuals to a team event?

answers.answer: In 1930, Henri de Grange (inventor of the Tour de France) introduced a team time trial. From 1903 it was individual, then became divided into international teams.

questions.question: Which is the earliest conspiracy theory known?
Why are some countries referred to as the motherland while some countries are called the fatherland? Which countries are the motherland?
If you drop a piece of eggshell into an egg white, nothing gets that piece of egg shell out. But the half egg shell itself will attract the little shard of shell - why is that?

answers.answer: Egg is made of calcium. When you drop shell into egg white, the calcium in the shell attracts the calcium in the egg white, moving the shell shard toward the larger shell piece like a magnet.

questions.question: Why is Hull in the East Riding called the Land of Green Ginger?

answers.answer: There's a street in Hull at the end of White Bridge, believed to date back to medieval spice trading through the port. The name of the road expanded to become the nickname for the whole city. There's also the world's smallest window there near the George Hotel.

questions.question: How does milk inside a human or animal not turn inside the body when the body is much higher temperature than outside? If we left it out at room temperature it would turn. Is it the oxygen?

answers.answer: Milk is made on demand, not stored. That's why regular feeding in early days helps build up milk supply. Also it's packed with white blood cells - if you put a drop under a microscope, an hour later it's even cleaner because the white blood cells have been eating anything and everything.

questions.question: With climate change, if Scotland continues to get hotter, how many generations would it take for his family to adapt like people in Turkey (dark hair)? How long would it take for evolutionary change to kick in for population coloring?

answers.answer: It took approximately 8,000 to 12,000 years to develop white skin and ginger hair. Originally all humans were dark-skinned. So logically it would take approximately the same amount of time to reverse if climate changed. But we travel and interbreed more now and aren't as susceptible to the environment anymore (sun cream, air conditioning).

questions.question: Why don't maggots drown? We tried to drown them with a kettle and they just reproduce.

answers.answer: Maggots have small hairs that trap air around them. They breathe through spiracles (little holes down the side of their body) and use that trapped air to survive underwater until it runs out, then they drown. That's why they look silvery when under water.

questions.question: How do spiders get into the bath and how do they get out? They come up through the pipe but they don't want to go down the plug.

answers.answer: Spiders fall in (often in autumn looking for mates). They can't get out without help - you need to drape a towel or toilet paper over the side as a 'spider ladder'. Jan cured her arachnophobia during COVID by joining the British Spider Identification Group on Facebook.

questions.question: My neighbor has copper rods for dowsing to find water in the garden. How can that work? There must be some form of truth to it.

answers.answer: I recently watched someone do it and it worked. I had a go and it worked too. It's about how lightly you hold the two bits of wire.

questions.question: I noticed at non-league games that away fans stand behind the goal their team is attacking and then swap ends at half-time. Is this legislated by the FA or is it just a natural occurrence?

answers.answer: It's not legislated for. At non-league level there's very little segregation so grounds are free to walk around. It depends on police advice and gate size.

questions.question: Why do American soldiers in Vietnam refer to the Vietnamese enemy as Charlie?

answers.answer: Victor Charlie from the NATO phonetic alphabet - shortened to Charlie. Dave was a professional soldier.

questions.question: How do train drivers get to and from their place of work? Do they always start and end shifts in the same location? What if their shift starts in Penzance?

answers.answer: Train drivers typically start and finish work at the same depot location. They can get the train to work or drive and park at local car parks. For distant routes, they do 'lodging turns' - drive the last train out, stay overnight in a hotel/lodging, then drive the first train back in the morning. There's also driver changeovers at terminal stations during a journey. All train drivers must live within one hour of a depot to help with fatigue management.

questions.question: Do all sports referees use the same type of whistle? Police whistles sound like train guard whistles, sports have P whistles, rugby refs seem to get different notes - are they all the same whistle?

answers.answer: No, sports whistles split into two categories: P-less (football) and with a P (Acme Thunderer - rugby). Football referees typically use P-less whistles. Rugby uses the Acme Thunderer with the pea, which allows referees to add musicality and expressiveness - short blasts for knock-ons, harder blows for more severe penalty decisions. Individual personality also plays a role. John is the archivist at Acme Whistle Company (J Hudson and Co) in Birmingham.

questions.question: Why do we emphasize the first word with 'Street' (Oxford Street, Sloane Street, Shrubbery Street) but emphasize the second word with every other thoroughfare type (Shaftesbury Avenue, Lordship Lane, Park Lane, Imperial Avenue)?

answers.answer: Three-part answer: 1) Street, crescent, terrace have a hard R followed by an aspirated vowel that naturally makes you push emphasis forward. Road has a glottal stop in the D. 2) Context matters - if giving directions you'd say 'take a left out of so-and-so ROAD' vs just mentioning it in conversation. 3) As English speakers, this is how we naturally use aspirated vowels, taught in school, and humans mimic more than they learn - it's a picked-up habit over time. Cecilia is a linguist.

questions.question: In tennis, why does a ball that clips the net and goes over count as a let on serve (requiring retake) but in normal play you simply continue the point?
How did people in the Arctic (Inuit) survive and flourish without vegetables, fruit, nuts, or any plant matter? They only had seals, whales, and fish.

answers.answer: No one ever lived on the ice completely year-round - they were also on land. They practiced nose-to-tail eating: ate the heart, liver, cooked bones for marrow to get all nutrients and B vitamins. In summer they had berries: cloudberries, lichen berries, blueberries. Even in winter at minus 20, they could preserve and freeze food outside naturally. Tonya was born in the north of Norway inside the Arctic Circle and grew up around the Sami indigenous people. She did a year's course on Arctic survival.

questions.question: Why haven't men's jumping records (long jump, high jump, triple jump) been broken for 30 years? Jonathan Edwards still holds the triple jump record, Mike Powell the long jump record.

answers.answer: Multiple factors: 1) Physical limitations - we're constrained by tendons, muscles, gravity and speed in how far we can propel ourselves. 2) Financial - unlike cycling where Sky poured in money and revolutionized the sport, jumping events don't attract similar investment. 3) Talent drain - athletes like Usain Bolt who could potentially break jumping records are incentivized to focus on 100m where the money is. 4) TV appeal - jumping events aren't prime-time material. Ned worked in a high-performance sports gym.

questions.question: Why doesn't his mole get nicked when shaving, even though he nicks other parts of his face?
Why do cyclists shout really loudly at each other when riding in groups? Can hear their entire conversations from across the path while cycling along the Amstel River.

answers.answer: It's a Dutch thing - Dutch people just shout. His wife's in-laws are Dutch and they shout relentlessly.

questions.question: Why does squash/cordial taste sweeter when it warms up? Same thing happens with flat Coke - it's fine when cold but becomes too sweet when flat/warm.

answers.answer: It's about the sweet spot around 60 degrees. When sweet molecules are most soluble, the drink tastes sweeter even though the sugar content is the same. More dissolved sugar equals sweeter taste.

questions.question: What happens to all the wood chips laid down at Glastonbury Festival? They must need to clear them before bringing the cows back to the working farm.

answers.answer: They use a rake attachment on the back of a tractor to rake up all the wood chips. It's piled up in a huge wood pile out of the way and left to rot down. They bring it back out when needed - it's constantly recycled.

questions.question: When and why did the media start referring to Wimbledon as SW19? You never hear people talk about rugby at TW2 or Silverstone at NN12.

answers.answer: Wimbledon is actually in Southfields, which shares the SW19 postcode with Wimbledon. Using SW19 avoids offending people in Southfields while also not offending people in Wimbledon. Similar to how you might get off at Waterloo for the Houses of Parliament.

questions.question: Why did men en masse stop wearing hats? Everyone wore them in pictures from 1900s-50s, it was classless, and even children copied their dads.

answers.answer: The invention of the car. In the 1930s-40s people wore fedoras with big brims, then in the 60s headrests in cars became common so trilbys were invented (shorter brims that fit better). But James wasn't persuaded this fully explains why hats stopped completely.

JFK's presidential campaign in 1960. His wife Jacqueline was a fashion pioneer who advised him not to wear a hat so his bouffant hair could be seen. Because JFK was so iconic, men around the world stopped wearing hats.

questions.question: Why is the Army called 'British Army' and not 'Royal Army' when we have the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force?

answers.answer: The British Army is made up of regiments and corps with specific roles. Some get the Royal Prefix as an honor bestowed by the monarchy, often for milestones like anniversaries. Newer regiments like the Parachute Regiment and SAS don't have it because they're too new.
The army historically doesn't belong to the King - it belongs to the nobility/Parliament. This dates back to after the Civil War when the New Model Army meant the army was not the King's personally.

questions.question: Why did his sliced bread go mouldy but his bakery baguette just went dry and hard? Both were left for 10 days.

answers.answer: Three things determine whether mould grows: temperature, humidity, and sugar levels. A baguette has less moisture and sugar. Supermarket bread is in plastic, very moist, and has additives to keep it soft - all conditions that encourage mould. The baguette was stored differently (paper bag lets it stay crispy).

questions.question: How do scientists accurately predict flying ant day? And why does it seem they always get it right?

answers.answer: Scientists can predict it based on temperature. When ambient temperature hits 25 degrees centigrade, it triggers the first swarm. There isn't one 'National Flying Ant Day' - there are several swarms over the summer. It's the black garden ant (Lassius niger) mating flight. James noted it usually happens late July but came early due to hot weather.

questions.question: Why do tennis balls come in pressurized cans? What's the point?

answers.answer: The pressure inside the ball diminishes over time through the container. If not in a pressurized tube, the ball would be measurably less bouncy by the time it reaches the shop or court. Pressurized tubes keep outside pressure equal to inside pressure so the ball doesn't lose bounce. That's why they change balls mid-game at Wimbledon - even 'new' balls lose pressure and pros can tell.

questions.question: Why do washing machines lie about their timings? It says 45 minutes but still has 10 minutes to go an hour later.

answers.answer: Washing machines estimate twice: at the start they assume a standard time (2.5 hours) but revise down if the load is half-filled. At the end, during the spin cycle, they measure how much water is coming out - if things need longer to dry, they keep spinning. So the time is always ballpark and gets revised based on actual progress. Newer machines lie more because they're more sophisticated at revising.

questions.question: If I'm a smoker and I get put in a coma for 12 weeks, when I wake up on that first day, am I craving as visceral as I would be on the first day of quitting?

answers.answer: Chris was a 30+ year smoker who had a cardiac arrest and spent weeks in a coma. When he woke up, his brother asked if he wanted a cigarette. Chris wrote 'I don't smoke' on a blackboard. From that day over 12 years ago, he has had no desire to smoke a cigarette. Being in a coma wiped out the difficult cravings bit.

questions.question: How do body weight scales actually tell you about visceral fat, body water content, and BMI?

answers.answer: The scales have four metal pads under the heel and sole of your feet. They send an electrical current around your body. Fat, water and muscle have different levels of resistance, which allows the scales to calculate different body composition metrics.

questions.question: Why do peas always come in 300g tins when everything else in the vegetable aisle is 400g?
How does anyone know how much a country has enriched their uranium to 60%? Do they have spies in there? How do they know they're not hiding something?

answers.answer: There are three isotopes of uranium. U-235 is the one needed for fissile material. They use centrifuges to separate uranium based on mass. The IAEA uses self-reporting and inspections, measuring the weight and radioactivity of uranium to determine enrichment levels. When you import uranium, you need import licenses and must reconcile everything. You couldn't hide a centrifuge needed for weapons-grade enrichment. Countries like Iran have to account for all their uranium.
Clarifies that in Back to the Future, it's actually Libyan plutonium, not Iranian uranium.

questions.question: How do they weigh a ship? And why did they tell everyone not to move around between midnight and 4am?

answers.answer: Suggested water displacement - the ship sits lower in water when heavier, so they measure how far it sinks.

They use a plimsoll line on the side of the ship. They know the weight of the ship when it was built. The depth the ship sits in the water tells them how much water is displaced, which tells them the weight. They told everyone to stay still so the ship wouldn't wobble and give an inaccurate reading.
Confirmation about weighing ships - the reading is based on displacement, so people moving would affect accuracy.

questions.question: Does the world get heavier? Has it always been the same weight? Sand turning into glass weighs more, children being born and growing weigh more, but all materials come from earth.

answers.answer: Everything is energy, so the world stays the same weight. A child gets bigger by eating things that also weigh stuff. You can't conjure matter out of nothing, you can only transfer energy. Things might actually get lighter rather than heavier. Meteorites might add a tiny bit, but rockets launched into space might reduce it. The numbers are negligible either way.

questions.question: Why don't they remove the silent letters from words in the dictionary? In German, words like Thema have a silent H. If they don't pronounce it and the T sounds the same, why keep the H?

answers.answer: Would take ages to change all dictionaries. People might continue pronouncing silent letters. Would create chaos with different spellings.

Spelling reflects etymology and history - it helps you understand where words came from. Written language lags behind spoken language. 100 years ago, Swedes pronounced things differently and there were more Hs. Some lingers. Language is fluid and constantly evolving.

questions.question: Why does it feel weird when you step off a broken escalator? I get a jolt like losing balance, even though I use them all the time when they're working fine.

answers.answer: Your eyes tell your brain you're on an escalator, so your brain expects the jolt. When you step off a working escalator, there's always a slight feeling. You're preparing for it. When the escalator is broken, you're still prepared for it but it doesn't happen. It's the moment of jarring when your expectation isn't met.

questions.question: Why does coffee seem to get stronger as you get towards the bottom of a jar of granules? You can't use the heat spoon anymore, have to use less.

answers.answer: Theory 1: Evaporation - once the seal is broken, water content leaves, leaving a stronger concentration of coffee. Theory 2: The oil in coffee sinks to the bottom, making it stronger at the bottom.
Could be smaller granules working their way to the bottom. Could be all three theories combined - smaller granules, oils, and water evaporation all contribute.

Called the 'Twiglet effect' - similar to the Doppler effect. When you dig your spoon in, small pieces flake off and fall to the bottom. Your final spoonful has more tiny granules with less air space, so it appears stronger even though the granules are the same concentration.

questions.question: If you get your fingers cut off and they reattach them, do you still have all the feeling that you had before?

answers.answer: It depends on blood supply. If you have a clean cut, they can reconnect blood vessels. But sometimes with circular saw injuries, the vessels can get pulled in what they call a 'ribbon effect' and can't be reconnected. If they do reconnect, they will try to re-establish blood flow using medical leeches. Patients can regain feeling over time as nerves grow back through the tubes, but it's not guaranteed. Full rehabilitation and desensitization exercises are needed.
answers.qualifications: Hand therapist - occupational therapist specializing in hand therapy at Wexham Park Hospital

answers.answer: From personal experience - the finger that was reattached regains all the feelings as it heals. The finger that wasn't reattached - in time the feeling goes away, but because the nerves of the fingers are all tied up at the base of the hand, you get a lot of phantom pain if you hit or bang your hand even where the finger isn't there.

I lost several fingers in a table saw accident. My colleague Dave drove me to hospital but forgot my fingers at the worksite, so had to go back. The surgeon performed a 10-hour operation to give me a semi-functional hand. My skin was grafted to my stomach to grow back over the fingers. After 7 months of hand therapy and ongoing neurological wave treatment to release nerves from scar tissue, I'm regaining feeling. The tingling is reducing and it's coming good.

questions.question: I've got a damson tree that grew long and thin with fruit at the top because it was overgrown. Now it's working better but I have a lot of trunk before branches start. Can I encourage branch growth from the trunk, or chop two feet off the bottom?
Why do rugs always migrate in the same direction, even if you are not walking in that direction more often than you're walking in the opposite direction?

answers.answer: It will always move in the direction of the nap of the carpet underneath. Every fabric has a directional nap that always lays in one direction. The motion of you walking on it pushes it in that direction. It never goes against the nap. So if you're walking against the nap, it resists and pushes back underneath you. It'll always travel with the nap.
answers.qualifications: 45 years in the carpet trade, 20 years fitting, now runs Hazelmere Carpet Company

answers.answer: The whole premise of the finger question is flawed - if you cut all your fingers off, you couldn't take them to the hospital to have them sewn back on because you wouldn't have been able to pick them up.

questions.question: How does a seagull know it's swooping down on chips and not just a bunch of plastic in a container?

answers.answer: It's learned behaviour. Gulls watch their parents when they grow up. They look at healthy gulls and see what they're doing - swooping down and grabbing chips. They develop foraging skills and have good enough eyesight to know what a chip is. If they swoop on plastic by mistake, they waste energy and that has a negative effect on their survival. Those traits that help them identify real food get passed on to future generations. It's natural selection - Darwinism.
answers.qualifications: Amateur ornithologist, birdwatcher for 50 years

questions.question: If you're an airline pilot, how difficult is it to fly between different destinations? What's the difference between flying to Rome, Barcelona or the Maldives? Does the actual mid-flight bit change according to the route? Does navigation change?

answers.answer: On all flights, pilots join the cruise stage, take weather for various airports, assess weather on the route in case of diversions, and always have a plan B - a suitable airport they can land at if needed. The altitude you fly at can vary. Different airports have different categories depending on difficulties and risks involved. Sometimes it's just a briefing between pilots before setting off. For more challenging airports, one pilot can only go if the other has been there a certain number of times. Very challenging airports require specific training in a flight simulator so you're aware of the specific challenges before you get there.
answers.qualifications: Airline pilot

answers.answer: Ladies and gentlemen, today we're cruising at 37,000 feet at a speed of 350 miles an hour, we'll be arriving 10 minutes early today.

questions.question: In Ireland they always refer to counties as 'County Dublin', 'County Wicklow'. In England, why is Durham the only county that has the word 'County' in front of it? Why not 'County Yorkshire'?

answers.answer: When counties were established in England, certain kingdoms became counties in their own right like Kent, Surrey, Essex. Others became shires named after the principal town governed by a sheriff - that's why you have Leicester Shire, York Shire, Lancashire. Durham, Cheshire and Lancashire were Palatines with more important powers issued by the monarch. Durham was never governed by a sheriff or shiree - it was controlled by the Bishops of Durham. So it was never a shire, it's never been a shire, which is why it's become County Durham as opposed to Durham Shire.
answers.qualifications: Deputy Mayor of Bath, interested in municipal and civic history

answers.answer: The answer just appeared while I was waffling - it's got something to do with Palatine...

questions.question: Why do different herbivores produce such different types of waste - some produce pellets (rabbits, sheep), some produce messy cow pats - if they all eat the same grass?

answers.answer: Most herbivores like rabbits and guinea pigs actually re-ingest their poo. There's a sort of fibrous aspect to it - they re-ingest it to make it easier to absorb nutrients. The re-digested one becomes the pellet. It forms into the ergonomically most precise way of getting it out again so it doesn't hurt. It's rectum-related. Also, wombats do square poo - that's true. Makes them easier to store. Different digestive systems and absorption methods lead to different waste products, plus different water consumption affects it too.
answers.qualifications: Illustrator who created 'Pooker Adventures, Journey to Pootopia' - a children's book about why poo doesn't stink and is the most important substance in the world

answers.answer: I think it's the digestive system - different animals have completely different means of absorbing nutrients, which means they produce measurably different waste.

questions.question: What's the 'seal' when people say 'don't break the seal'? Is breaking the seal a real thing and if so, why does urinating more frequently start after your first bathroom visit?

answers.answer: Breaking the seal absolutely exists and is a real thing. When you start drinking, your bladder is full of normal urine. As alcohol is processed, toxins get into your bladder. When you have that first pee, it gets rid of all the diluted stuff. Then from then on, all your body is doing is trying to get rid of the alcohol, which is toxic. So it doesn't matter how much you drink after that - as soon as toxins get into your bladder, your body goes 'need to get rid of that' and you're peeing all the time.
answers.qualifications: Ex operating department practitioner in the Royal Air Force, now a medical support officer in the Royal Air Force

questions.question: When did we start celebrating our birthdays annually?

answers.answer: Earliest documentation comes from ancient Egypt around 3000 BC - inscriptions on Ramesses II's tomb mark his birthday. Birthdays were originally for deities, then kings. Babylonians also had them, then Greece and Rome. Early Christians were against it initially because of pagan/deity associations, but later accepted it. Older cultures like the Dogon and Yoruba in West Africa had celebrations tied to time tracking using the solstice. There's the Isango bone in Belgium Museum dating back 20,000-30,000 years showing early calendar use.

questions.question: Why are UK cucumbers wrapped in plastic when French ones aren't?

answers.answer: English cucumbers have much thinner skin than other countries, which exacerbates dehydration. Since cucumbers dehydrate very quickly and UK supply chains are different (less fresh turnover than France), they wrap them in plastic to extend shelf life. In France, cucumbers turn over so quickly that dehydration isn't a problem.
English cucumbers have thinner skin than cucumbers in other countries, which exacerbates the dehydration issue. Might be the variety - they're grown in glasshouses rather than outdoors.

questions.question: Why do kids like spinning to make themselves dizzy but adults hate it? Is there any benefit to it?

answers.answer: When you're a kid, the fluid inside your ears is very thin - like water. So when you turn upside down and back, the fluid goes straight back down where it came from with no lasting impact. As an adult, the fluid in your ears is much thicker - like really thick honey or jam. When you spin, the thick fluid takes a long time to be displaced, and when you stop and turn back the right way up, it takes a long time to settle back. In those in-between times while the fluid is moving, you feel unsteady and out of sorts. (Source: friend who was a nurse told her about 10 years ago)

questions.question: Why do runner beans grow in a clockwise direction? And do they grow anti-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere like water going down a plug?
Why is the city called Liverpool when the famous building is the Liver Building and the birds are Liver Birds - why isn't it Liver-pool?

answers.answer: There are two different etymologies that aren't actually related. Liverpool's original name was something like a medieval term meaning 'pool' (wetland) and 'liver' comes from an old word meaning muddy - the area was very swampy. The Liver Building is named after the Liver Birds on top. The cormorant bird that the liver bird is based on looks identical to the liver bird image. The liver bird legend says one looks out to sea guiding ships and the other looks into the city to check when pubs are open.

questions.question: What is the contingency plan if Wimbledon gets rained out entirely for two weeks? Is there a point where they'd just abandon the tournament?
Why do we have milk teeth that fall out and get replaced by adult teeth, rather than being born with small adult teeth that grow like our fingernails do?

answers.answer: Teeth can't grow like fingernails because they're made of different material - enamel rather than keratin. You'd only be able to fit about two adult-sized molars and one canine in a baby's tiny mouth, so babies would look like gerbils and the species would die out.

Pictures of children's skulls show both layers of teeth - the baby teeth and the bank of adult teeth waiting to push through. Both sets of teeth are already present in the skull when born. Teeth aren't bone - they have enamel. This confirms the answer: adult teeth are there even when milk teeth are showing, but the mouth is too small for adult teeth, hence the temporary teeth.

questions.question: Why do most public bathroom doors push to enter but you have to pull the handle to leave?

answers.answer: If doors opened outward, you'd smack someone in the face without them knowing you were coming out. Same applies to cubicles - if someone pushes open while you're waiting, you get hit. Also, you need to be able to kick the door in if someone's hiding inside (smoking or something). You couldn't have doors that swing both ways either because you'd still have the same problem. Kitchens that do have swinging doors are very disciplined about which way staff go through.

questions.question: Why are cousins the only family relationship word that isn't gender-specific?

answers.answer: Our words come from different languages - Anglo-Saxon German roots or French roots (oncle/tante, Bruder/Schwester). The word 'cousin' comes from French, where the feminine form has an extra 'e' (cousine). But when it came into English, the pronunciation changed and we lost the distinction. You can't really say 'cousin' and 'cousine' distinctly in English, so we just use one word for both.

questions.question: Why do bottles of spirits on the continent have plastic flow restrictors in the neck but UK bottles don't?
What was the roller coaster James mentioned?

answers.answer: Confirmed it was indeed the Cobra. It did two circuits, the second was backwards. Still exported to an amusement park in the Philippines.

questions.question: How is the difficulty of a Sudoku determined? If you complete the nightmare level, is the number of starting clues the same as the expert level? And did Sudoku exist before computer algorithms?

answers.answer: I think it's the placement of numbers that delivers the difficulty, not the number of clues.
Patience.

questions.question: Why do I find myself listening to the same song over and over and over again?
Do animals favour their left or right side in the same way humans do?

answers.answer: Yes, dogs definitely can favour their left paw, and cats do too when you dangle string in front of them.

questions.question: Why do some birds hop and some birds walk?
Why do we bend over double after we've done some sort of exercise like running across the road or running for the bus?
Why don't we fall out of bed when we're sleeping? Why do we stay on the bed?
Why can't I hear my own accent when I'm speaking to you, but I hear it strongly when I listen to a recording of myself?

answers.answer: When you speak and listen to yourself, you're hearing your speech not just through the air but through your head, through the physiology of your head. You become accustomed to that all your life. Whereas when you hear yourself in a recording, that's coming through the air to your ears only and strikes you as different. There's also pitch and resonance. And some people unconsciously switch accents depending on their social environment.

questions.question: Why is toothache so excruciatingly sore? Is it the complexity of nerves in the face, or are facial nerves more sensitive?

answers.answer: Two key reasons. First, your cranial nerves - all the nerves in your face - go straight through your skull to the brain, they don't connect through the spinal cord. It's like cutting out the exchange from a phone call, simpler, straighter, fewer connections. The evolutionary benefit is you really want to know if something is harming your skull. Second, if you get an infection it will try to swell, but there is nowhere to swell inside a tooth. The nerve is in a box surrounded by calcium and the root is embedded in bone. That's why people say the toothache subsided after three days - the swelling has punctured through the bone.

questions.question: How can two little screws in the wall hold up a cupboard filled with heavy stuff like crockery or books without it falling down?

answers.answer: The reason the cupboard stays on the wall is the sheer strength of the screw. If you've got a screw in a good fixing in the wall, the screw in the horizontal plane needs enormous strength to break on the vertical plane. Andrew compared it to an RSJ holding up the side of a house held by four bolts - three would actually hold it up. The worse the fixing, the more important the length of the screw becomes.

You don't talk about screws, you talk about anchors. A screw needs to be anchored - you drill a hole, put a plug in, then the screw creates pressure and shear strength. The size and girth matters because of pressure, and the length matters because you need a 4-to-1 system - a 20mm board needs at least 80mm of screw going into the wall and plug.

questions.question: Why do so many churches have black and white square/diamond tiles on the floor, particularly in royal chapels like St George's and Savoy Chapel? I've found the same pattern in a church in Sweden.

answers.answer: The checkered pattern is one of the oldest symbols mankind has ever used, traced back to ancient Mesopotamia. It represents the eternal struggle between good and evil, or light and dark. The chessboard has been around in that form for over 5,000 years. Freemasons also use black and white checkered patterns as allegory to talk about life, death and our place in the universe. In front of the altar it represents that all that is created is within sight and controlled by the Almighty.

questions.question: Why do some people sneeze multiple times - like 10, 15 or even hundreds of times - while others just sneeze a couple of times?

questions.answer: Why do we bend forward after exercise?

answers.answer: Normally you breathe using the muscles between your ribs and your chest. If you bend forward and put your arms on your knees, your arms are fixed so the muscles between your arms and your chest contract and open your lungs even more, so you get more oxygen in. The ribs work like bucket handles swinging on your chest, whereas the muscles between your arms and your ribs pull the ribs up even further.

questions.answer: Do animals favour left or right like humans?

answers.answer: Yes, we see it almost entirely in bipedal animals. All red kangaroos are left-handed - that's why they box so much. We also see it in dogs and cats but not to statistical significance, they just have a preferred side they've learned. The evolutionary advantage comes from being better at fighting off rivals - left-handed people have a better win rate in MMA and boxing.

questions.question: What is the mechanism in the brain that makes us fall asleep and wakes us up in the morning? Is there a switch that gets flicked when you go from awake to asleep?

answers.answer: It's to do with a chemical in your body called adenosine. As your body does stuff throughout the day, it releases adenosine, and when it builds up to a critical mass on receptors in your brain, that makes you feel sleepy and eventually fall asleep. It's your body saying you need to rest.

[to Grant] You gave us some interesting information but it's not quite what the question was asking. What is the thing that flicks? You've told us about the build-up but not the actual trigger point where you go from awake to asleep.

questions.question: Why are they referred to as 'patient zero' not 'patient one'?
What is the most efficient way to peel a boiled egg?

answers.answer: Eggshells are easier to peel on older eggs. Fresh eggs stick to the shell because the albumen is more acidic and bonds with the membrane. When the egg ages, the pH changes and the air between the membrane and shell increases, making it easier to peel. Check the sell-by date - the closer you are to the eat-by date, the better.

questions.question: Why does orange juice taste horrible after brushing your teeth?

answers.answer: The toothpaste foams because of a surfactant called sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS). This chemical simultaneously suppresses your sweet taste receptors AND blocks the things that stop you tasting bitterness. So you can't taste the sweet but you're tasting all the bitter, which creates that weird taste. To avoid it, brush your teeth after orange juice, or if you brush first, wait a few minutes for the surfactant to break down.

questions.question: Is there a universal tempo for the spoken word? If you had the same conversation in English and then in another language, would you say it faster or slower?

answers.answer: [Commenting on Callum's suggestion] Shakespeare-era English was spoken quite a bit more quickly back then, so if that's true, there would be no universal tempo even 400 years ago.

The short answer is no - different types of languages have different characteristics. There are whistling languages and tonal languages like Mandarin, which has four different tones. People speak at different speeds depending on the language.

questions.question: Why do they use smoke to announce the new Pope? Why not a bell or a flag?
Where does the phrase 'hat trick' come from?

answers.answer: It's a cricketing term from Victorian era. A bowler took three consecutive wickets. There are different stories: some say he was presented with a hat by teammates (gentlemen wore hats back then), others say he passed his hat around collecting shillings and gifts. DV Wright was reportedly presented with a hat for bowling a hat trick.

questions.question: When a character in a film or TV show produces a photo of themselves as a child, is that actually the actor's real photo?

answers.answer: It's half and half. Sometimes they do use the actor's actual baby photos from their childhood. But if not, they'll create digital photos. Jay works as a cameraman and has seen this happen on several occasions where actual childhood photos were used.

questions.question: Why do people from Northern Ireland call themselves British?
Is toe shape genetic? Like eye color - do you get either ET toe (long and thin) or cherubic/pudgy toe as a trait?

answers.answer: It's called Morton's toe. It's not because the second toe is longer - it's because the big toe is shorter. The big toe stops growing prematurely. It happens in about 47% of men and is more common in people of Greek descent (explaining why flip-flops were invented in Greece).

questions.question: Who defined where the ocean ends and the sea begins? Who named them? How are seas and oceans distinguished when there's no land border between them?

answers.answer: Admiralty, cartographers and navies named most of them. It's a general consensus amongst seafarers that oceans are vast and uninterrupted while seas are bordered or surrounded by land.

questions.question: Can Peter delay the onset of pain by the power of thought? Is this a superpower? When he sees something coming (like walking into a desk), he can delay pain by 4-5 seconds by thinking 'stop it'. Is this unique to him or can everyone do it?

answers.answer: It's a type of self-hypnosis. Peter is engaging in low-level self-hypnosis whether he realizes it or not. Different people can do it to varying degrees with training and perception. (He was a hypnotherapist for 10 years)
She can stop pain in its tracks and everyone will be engaging in a form of hypnosis whether they realise it or not.

questions.question: Is there a scientific link between the colour and the smell of flowers?
Which device in the average household is most reliable for telling the time? How do you know which one to trust when different devices show different times?

answers.answer: Your mobile phone is most reliable. It's permanently connected to your mobile network which is constantly updating your phone every second. Somewhere along that chain, the network is connected to the world atomic clock.

questions.question: Why does a helium balloon in a car go in the opposite direction to the humans when accelerating or braking?

answers.answer: It's about fluid masses and densities. The air inside the car is much heavier than helium and carries a lot more inertia. When you brake, all the air is carried along with the car and sloshes towards the front, displacing the helium which then pushes backwards. When you accelerate, the air wants to stay where it is (high inertia) so it flies to the back and the helium gets pushed forwards as it's being displaced.

questions.question: Brendan got 11 out of 12 double yolkers in a box of Tesco eggs. Is there a super-duper laying chicken somewhere or is this just probability gone crazy?

answers.answer: Probability-wise, you're just as likely to get 11 double yolkers in a row as you are to get one in a row or nine in a row. It doesn't make any sense but it's true - everything resets after each egg so the odds of the second egg being a double yolker are exactly the same as the odds of the first egg. She can predict double yolkers by the size of the egg. It's possible they were selected for the box at the supermarket.

questions.question: Why does tea taste less sweet after dipping a biscuit in it and eating it?
What is the physiological threshold at which cats start to purr? Why do they purr - is it when they're happy, in pain, or sad?

answers.answer: Purring is a very complex behaviour. Cats purr when happy and contented, but also when in pain or anxious because it releases endorphins. They also purr when bonding (with humans and their kittens), when exploring, and for attention. It's a form of self-soothing and happiness.

questions.question: If people with really defined abs eat lots of food, does having strong stomach muscles push down on the stomach and make them digest more quickly?

answers.answer: No, it does not affect digestion at all. Even if you had the most perfect set of six-pack muscles, it would not affect your digestion by even a jot or an iota. The muscles on the outside have a completely different blood supply and the nerves are on a completely different circuit to the ones that supply the intestines. However, having strong abs might prevent you looking a bit pregnant after a big meal because the stomach walls would be tighter and thicker.

questions.question: Why don't ants get injured when they are flicked off desks? They land, think about it for a minute, then carry on wandering.

answers.answer: Terminal velocity. Ants are so light that they never achieve the speed humans would, which means the impact when they hit the ground is not damaging.

It's down to air resistance and surface area, not mass. It's the Reynolds number - as a body gets smaller, the effects of drag outweigh the effects of inertia. To an ant, air is more like water is to a human.

questions.question: Where did the famous 'da da da da da da da' football chant originate and what does it mean?

answers.answer: I don't know.
It's from a 1962 song by The Rooters called 'Let's Go'. One of the first versions was at Liverpool in the 60s for Ian St John. George Sefton, the DJ at Anfield, has told this story.

It's Algerie Francaise. Brought to Liverpool by French PSG Ultras in the European Cup in 1960. The first two beats are from hooting car horns to indicate support, then the last five beats are the chant.

questions.question: How do you explain caterpillars becoming butterflies from an evolutionary perspective? It's incredibly complex.

answers.answer: Metamorphosis is common across lots of insects - mantises, cicadas, mayflies. It's hyper evolution where the young don't compete for the same resources as adults. A caterpillar is a leaf-eating machine, while the adult butterfly focuses on nectar, mating and laying eggs. All insects shed their exoskeletons, and butterflies just evolved a bigger version where hormonal changes allow them to develop wings.

questions.question: How do we know we perceive colors the same as other people?

answers.answer: There's no color in the outside world - everything you see is your brain interpreting the environment. This is the 'hard problem of consciousness' - no one can know what other people's experience is. It's completely subjective.
If people perceive color differently between their own eyes (as 50% do), then they must perceive colors differently from other people. Taught color theory.

questions.question: If you put a candle in front of a mirror, do you have two candles' worth of light or still one?

answers.answer: No increase in total lumens produced - you can't conjure energy. But with a mirror behind, light going out 360 degrees is now concentrated to 180 degrees, giving twice as much light in that direction. Same amount of light, just redirected.

questions.question: What is the process for assembling a Terry's Chocolate Orange? Do they create segments then put them together, or create an orange and segment it?

answers.answer: They are done as individual segments held up in a mold, then chocolate is injected down the middle/spine to solder them together. Tiago worked as a production manager for cookery content and tried to reverse-engineer a giant chocolate orange.

questions.question: How do geese know when to return from Africa if the weather here is milder?

answers.answer: Wrong premise - no geese migrate between Britain and Africa. They winter in Britain but breed in the high Arctic (Iceland, Canada, Svalbard, Russia). They leave because it gets too cold and frozen there, not because of British weather. It's all about food availability. There's a migratory urge called Zogunru that triggers migration independent of conditions.

questions.question: When a bee sticks its head into a flower and collects pollen, how does it transfer the pollen from its head to the pollen sacs on its rear legs?

answers.answer: Bees have little combs on their legs. They cover themselves in pollen (it sticks due to positive charge), then brush it off into little pods/sacks on their back legs. They use a tiny bit of nectar to help it stick. Ex-beekeeper.

questions.question: Can my overseas rescue dog understand what British dogs are barking about?
Why are ferrets specifically included in legislation about travelling with pets to the continent, alongside dogs and cats?

answers.answer: Speculated it might be because ferrets were used for sporting purposes in country sports

Dogs, cats and ferrets are the same category when it comes to moving animals as property. Animal is very poorly defined in English law - a cat is not an animal according to the Road Traffic Act, but it is for cruelty laws. They specifically mention ferrets, dogs and cats in transport law because you need to be specific. Wealthy people with foreign houses often had ferrets and would take them for country pursuits.

questions.question: Has a snooker referee ever accidentally dropped the object ball into the middle of a pack of reds? And if so, what happened?

answers.answer: Said it's never happened on television as it would have been widely shared

Yes, it can happen. There's an official scorer who has a mirror image on a separate TV screen. He would put the balls back roughly where they were. Also, the referee can offer a re-rack and most players would accept if it happened early in the frame.

questions.question: When is the correct time to weigh a banana to figure out how many calories you are consuming? A banana loses about 20% of its weight after ripening because the water evaporates and starch turns to sugar - so does the calorie content change?

answers.answer: Admitted he couldn't understand the question initially, then reformulated it as: at what stage of ripeness is the calorific content calculated?

The green banana contains a great deal of starch and a little bit of sugar. As it ripens, the starch turns into sugar and the water evaporates. The glycemic load goes up because there's more sugar absorbed more quickly. But the question of when the powers that be calculate the average calorie content remains unanswered - it's essentially unanswerable because the values are changing all the time.

questions.question: When historical podcasts talk about events in AD 74, how do they know the exact month and day if the Gregorian calendar wasn't introduced until about 500 years ago?

answers.answer: Speculated it might be the Julian calendar that was used at the time, and they've just translated it into the Gregorian equivalent. The Julian calendar had 12 months, 365 days and leap years.

questions.question: Why do dragons in myths and medieval drawings look so much like dinosaurs, when dinosaurs were extinct millions of years before humans evolved? Isn't it extraordinary that our imagination created creatures that look exactly like what we later discovered?

answers.answer: Suggested Komodo dragons as the physical inspiration - just imagine a giant one that breathes fire

Paleontology has only been around a couple of hundred years, but for centuries people found fossilized remains of massive dinosaurs and called them dragons. Storytellers elaborated on this to terrify populations and get money. Combined with real animals like Komodo dragons, people had something physical to relate to.

All dragons around the world are actually very different from each other. It's a build-up process: snakes are scary, then make them fly, then make them house-sized, then add fire. It's the biggest scariest thing people could come up with, backed up by finds of big bones. Someone burned down a barn, you'd blame it on a dragon.

questions.question: My dad used to predict when a reel change was coming up during films - he'd say 'there's a dot coming in the top right corner' and he'd be right. He was a photographer so might have had inside information, but how did he know when it was coming?

answers.answer: Initially suggested it might be to do with timing - the reel length would be consistent so he'd know exactly when the next dot would appear. Then suggested there are actually two dots, with the first one warning the projectionist that the change is coming.

Correct! They're called cigarette burns. There are two dots - the first one tells you the next one's coming up, and the second one is the cue for the projectionist to pull the lever and change to the next reel. The length between the dots and from the second dot to the end of the reel is always the same. So the dad would spot the first dot and count down. Nicola used to be a projectionist in Sydney in arthouse cinemas.

questions.question: Why do film credits always follow the same structure regardless of whether it's a UK film, US film, or from any other country? Who decides the order?

answers.answer: Disputed Byron's premise - said credits are not always in the same order, sometimes cast appears right after 'a film by', sometimes there's lots of other content first. But agreed it was a good question.

The film credits do have a structure, starting with actors then crew. When the film industry moved from New York to California, the solicitors stayed in New York, and they needed credits to know who to pay - so credits became a payroll mechanism.

questions.question: Why is the numerical layout on a phone (1-2-3 going down) different from a calculator (7-8-9 going down)? This causes problems in our office.

answers.answer: Couldn't answer - speculated about rotary dial origins but said that doesn't work. Promised to find out.

questions.question: Where do space rocket boosters go after launch? When the Amazon pod lands, where are the boosters? Are they floating around in space?

answers.answer: Boosters either land in the sea or some self-land and steer themselves back to land safely. Elon Musk's rockets do this. They detach during take-off.

SpaceX and Blue Origin boosters return and land on land or floating platforms. NASA's SLS is still disposable - it's flown only once. Early rockets were disposable but companies are now moving toward reusability.

questions.question: Why do Scandinavian doors open outwards when most doors here open inwards?

answers.answer: Maybe because in Scandinavia everyone has a front garden, so doors don't open onto the street.
Snow - if there's a snow drift, an outward opening door means you're not pushing snow into your house.
Fire regulations - most buildings in Scandinavia are timber construction. Outward opening doors make it easier to escape during a fire. Same reason public buildings in the UK open outwards.

questions.question: Why don't milk floats have to obey cold chain rules? Milk is dropped at 4am and sits outside for hours unrefrigerated.

answers.answer: When the cold chain rules came in, milk floats were still buzzing around and it would have made their life impossible. They hadn't had problems in the past so were given an exemption.

questions.question: Do dogs have twins/identical twins?
Why don't we eat pigeons anymore? We used to - monasteries kept doves for food, pigeon pie was a thing.

answers.answer: Pigeons are still eaten - wood pigeons. Urban pigeons like Trafalgar Square pigeons are too polluted and filthy to eat. We get nice fat juicy wood pigeons fed from local woods or specific feed. They're shot and sold year round, especially in autumn during game season.

questions.question: Is sweating hereditary? I sweat a lot during combat sports, and my dad and brother also sweat a lot during sports.
When cats purr, is it voluntary or involuntary? Is my cat Finlay just manipulating me?

answers.answer: When comfortable, it's involuntary - it's an off-treative breathing mechanism. But cats can also choose to purr consciously for different purposes. When hungry or unwell, they'll purr differently and approach you. Different purring patterns communicate different needs along with their actions.

questions.question: Why don't woodpeckers get headaches when they're drilling into trees?

answers.answer: Their tongue acts as a shock absorber. The tongue is attached to the base of the beak/nostrils and goes up and around the brain, then out of the mouth. This also allows their tongue to be longer so they can get insects out of holes they've made.

questions.question: Why do rain clouds appear black when they're approaching but look lighter/grey when actually raining on you?

answers.answer: The darkness of a cloud depends on the density and size of water droplets within it. When rain starts falling from the cloud, it actually becomes less dense and therefore lighter in appearance.

questions.question: If a cat's whiskers are the right width for the cat so it knows which hole to go through, and they would grow as the cat grows, what if an adult cat puts on weight? Do the whiskers change?

answers.answer: I have seven cats and I've measured all of their whiskers. They are all between 2.5 and 3 inches long - no difference between them. The fattest cat has NOT got the longest whiskers. The thinnest cat's got the longest whiskers. I have a 3kg cat whose whiskers are almost the same length as a 6.5kg cat, and they are observably different widths and girths.
This could be an urban myth - if a cat puts on weight and its whiskers don't grow longer, then the whiskers wouldn't accurately indicate whether the cat would fit through a gap.

questions.question: Why do certain foods and drinks like limoncello or banana liqueurs taste better on holiday and not as good when you're back in drizzly UK?

answers.answer: When we're on holiday or having new experiences, our dopamine brain receptors are open and we have heightened sense of pleasure and adventure. We feel safe and are looking forward to enjoying ourselves. If you have your banana liqueur, things taste better. Food tastes better, cocktails taste better, wine is more exotic. It's emotional but also a physical connection to your environment and what you're experiencing. This is why even in a nice Italian restaurant after a lovely meal out, the limoncello goes down quite well - your dopamine levels are higher than sitting on your patio.

questions.question: Why are drinks sweet mostly and not savory? Why don't you get savory drinks?

answers.answer: The premise isn't true - it's a cultural norm. In Pakistan, salty lassi is a very common and popular drink. It's really good for replacing salts after exercise. We even put salt and spices on our fruit - we call it 'chat masala' - a mixture of spices and salts. It's activating your taste buds in exciting and unexpected ways.

questions.question: What determines the height a bird flies at? What stops a small bird like a pigeon from flying as high as a golden eagle?
Where does the wax go when you burn a candle? Some of it drips down, but where does the rest go?

answers.answer: Wax is a hydrocarbon - fundamentally a fuel no different to methane, petrol, or diesel. The only difference is the size of the molecule, which is why it presents as wax. When you burn it, oxygen in the atmosphere combines with the carbon and hydrogen in the wax to produce carbon dioxide and water. The water goes off as steam and the carbon dioxide goes off as gas. It's the conservation of matter - the amount of stuff before is the same as after the reaction, but it's different stuff. The energy in any substance is in the chemical bonds, and this reaction is exothermic so the excess energy is given off as heat.

questions.question: In Korea, one of the most popular surnames is Lee. However, Korean people don't say Lee, they say Ree. Why do we English-speaking folk believe they are trying to say Lee but it comes out as Ree?

answers.answer: In all languages, there are phonemes - sounds that change the meaning of a word. In English, 'i' and 'e' are phonemes so 'pin' and 'pen' are different words. In a lot of South Asian languages, the sounds 'r' and 'l' are not phonemes - they do not change the meaning of the surname. So it may be that they're saying Ree or Lee interchangeably, but because we have expectations around how Southeast Asian people speak, we hear it as Lee because in English, Lee is a surname. This is psychological prediction - we hear what we expect to hear. This applies in other languages too - Spanish speakers can't hear the difference between 'th' and 's', and Thai has aspiration we don't have.

Jenny was quite right about phonemes, but actually the surname in Korea is not Lee or Ree - it's simply 'E' (like Mc squared). To make the language easier for westerners, they use an anglicized version, so 'E' becomes 'Lee'. Korean people don't distinguish 'l' and 'r' - they also don't distinguish 'f' and 'p'. Someone could ask 'would you like a cup of coffee?' and it could sound like 'would you like a cup of pop?' because it's an entirely different language with entirely different phonemes. My wife is Korean and her surname is Lee - when she introduces herself to westerners, she says 'Lee' because they're all aware they use this anglicized version to make it comprehensible to westerners.

questions.question: Why is it that golden syrup tins always stick to the shelf?

Does SPF protection in suntan lotion gradually decrease over time (e.g., from SPF 30 to SPF 20 after an hour) or does it drop to zero instantly? Is the recommendation to reapply every 1-2 hours a marketing ploy to sell more product?

answers.answer: Sunscreen is made of organic and inorganic compounds. The organic compounds get absorbed into your skin and no longer reflect UVA/UVB light. The inorganic compounds stay on the surface and reflect it. Sweating dilutes the sun factor, creating an exponential curve of decreasing efficacy. Also, higher SPF numbers don't proportionally increase protection - SPF 30 gives around 97% protection, SPF 50 gives only 98%, SPF 80 gives 97%, SPF 100 gives 98%. Increasing the factor number doesn't give you the same relative increase of protection.

questions.question: After moving into a new house, I noticed a UK water filter pipe for 15 seconds without mentioning it to anyone or searching for it. The next morning, social media showed me adverts for water filters. How did this happen?

answers.answer: Possible explanations: 1) Complete coincidence (recency bias), 2) Algorithm knows he recently moved house and serves relevant ads, 3) Phones know they're near other phones and make demographic-based suggestions, 4) Previous owners had ordered one and the system knows someone has been there.

It's the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon or frequency illusion. Water filters have been on a rolling advertising campaign, and because he just saw one, he now notices them. When you click consent dialogue on websites, you're agreeing to share information about everyone in your household. If your phones use the same Wi-Fi hotspot, that's how it tracks you.

questions.question: How do we learn to stop ourselves from rolling out of bed while asleep? My 4-year-old daughter used to have bed rails but now sleeps without them and stays in the middle of the bed without falling out.

answers.answer: Possibly subconscious learning during dreams. We sometimes dream we've fallen over and jolt awake. A variation of that experience could teach us to recognise when we're about to fall and roll back without waking up.

questions.question: Do copper coins actually help keep cut flowers alive longer? I put 1p and 2p coins in roses from M&S and they've been alive for nearly two months.
What are ants communicating when they stop in columns and have a huddle? What are the reconnaissance ants looking for - predators or food?

answers.answer: Ants communicate using pheromones, similar to hormones. They leave scent trails marking where they've been and where they're going. When they stop to have a 'chat,' they're coming across a scent trail - possibly even from another colony - and recognising and relaying that information.

questions.question: What's happening in our brains when we watch a fictional drama on TV and forget within a couple of seconds that there's a camera crew and director present, and we become absorbed in the story?

answers.answer: It's called suspension of disbelief. We willingly put aside our critical thinking skills and knowledge that it's not real because we want to enjoy the narrative. If it was really bad acting, it would break that suspension. The phrase was coined by Samuel Coleridge. It's like a contract with the creator - there's no point watching unless on some level you believe it's real.

questions.question: Why do Yorkshire tea bags come attached together in pairs?

answers.answer: It's a cost-saving measure. The story goes that someone told a match factory they could make a fortune by only having the striking surface on one side of the matchbox. Similarly, tea bags are made as doubles on the production line, and having them sealed together saves the energy and cost of an extra cutting process to separate them.

It's not about cost saving - it's about the shape of the tea bags. The double bags can be stacked better, fit into boxes more efficiently, and don't topple over on the production line. The perforation suggests an extra production step to create the pairs for stacking purposes.

questions.question: Why can't type 1 diabetics drink insulin instead of having to inject it?

answers.answer: Insulin is made of peptides, which are building blocks of protein. If taken orally, it gets destroyed by digestive enzymes in the stomach and becomes completely ineffective. It would no longer be insulin and would have no desired effect. This is true of most injected drugs - they would be destroyed either by digestive enzymes or by the liver if taken orally.

questions.question: Why do we have to stay quiet at the snooker when we can be as loud as we want at the darts? Both require similar levels of concentration - darts players can get the yips just like snooker players.

answers.answer: It's about social context and origins. Darts is a pub game - people drink, smoke, it's noisy - that's the social convention that got transposed into professional venues. Snooker started as a drawing room game for the upper classes, then moved to temperance billiard halls (there was a big temperance movement 100+ years ago building these places where you'd play snooker instead of drinking). That atmosphere of quiet concentration stuck with the sport. It also explains the traditional dress - waistcoats, dickie bows - going back to the Joe Davis exhibition match days when you'd watch quietly and learn from the professionals.

questions.question: Why do gorse bushes flower every month of the year? I take photographs every month and can always find at least one bush in full flower.
Why do we call it a piggy bank?

answers.answer: The pig was associated with good luck over the years, and therefore it just became the basis for the vessel, the containers into which money would be put. They find them in archaeological digs going back a thousand years. It's not new and it's not British.

questions.question: Does music affect the mood of animals? Does it affect dogs?
Why do building sites have walls with small double-glazed windows that never get connected to anything?

answers.answer: They are called test panels. Bricklayers build them prior to the client and architect agreeing on the type of brick. They might have different coloured bricks or different types of pointing. Before any brick is laid on site, they come and check if they like the finish, the style, the pointing, and then they go ahead with the job. The window is there to show what the window looks like with a soldier course above it or an arch.

questions.question: Why are aircraft hangars called hangers when there's nothing hanging in them?

answers.answer: Hanger in English is spelled A-R (like coat hanger). Hangar in French is a basic building with pillars, posts and a roof used to shelter crops, equipment, vehicles or farm vehicles. We've adopted the French word for aircraft storage buildings.

questions.question: How come dreams always play out like a film or a story rather than being just a split second scene?

answers.answer: During the day we do things and when we dream we learn to properly compartmentalize those activities and integrate them into our physiology in a deeper sense. One theory is that you simulate the ways you would behave in situations in a risk-free environment. The narrative arc isn't just how we dream - it's how our brain works. It's how we think, it's how we learn. The fundamental link between conscious and subconscious is why dreams have narrative arcs - they are prolonged behaviors.

questions.question: Is it cost effective to make a 1 penny piece? Does it cost more to make than what it's actually worth?

answers.answer: Yes, it costs more to produce than it's worth. It costs about 20p to make a penny. This is why Donald Trump announced they're going to phase them out in America.

Copper coins used to cost a lot more to make than they were worth. People started shipping them out of the country in giant ship loads and melting them down in another country to make a profit. The Bank of England had a law requiring at least 95% copper content. They had to change the recipe in 1982, and now they're made of steel with just a bit of copper on the outside.

questions.question: Why do Scottish people call a hair parting a shed?
What is the scientific explanation for 'red sky at night, shepherd's delight, red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning'?

answers.answer: High pressure traps pollutants like dust and water in the upper atmosphere. This scatters the short wavelengths of light (blues and greens), leaving only the red light. In the UK with westerly weather patterns, when the sun is setting in the west under high pressure, that high pressure will be blowing over the country the next day with good weather. When it's a red sky in the morning in the east, the high pressure has already moved off over Scandinavia and it may be miserable the next day.

questions.question: In game shows, why is the backstage holding room called the green room?

answers.answer: The lights in the green room would be the least invasive light is green. When people come out of the green room into the wings, the green light won't spill out onto the stage.

questions.question: Why do sloths move so slowly?

answers.answer: Because they can. They have immediate access to infinite food supplies, they're built in a way that means they're never going to fall out of the tree, they digest very slowly, everything they do is very slow, and they've got no predators. If you had all that, you'd never get out of bed either.

They've got such a slow metabolism they don't actually really need to move very far. Sloths are at their most vulnerable when they're doing their toilet. When they're asleep or covered in algae, they're well camouflaged from eagles above.

questions.question: Answer to Peter's question: Does music affect dogs/animals?

answers.answer: Music does affect animals - they're sentient. Classical music is deemed the most popular in terms of responses from animals. Cows have been seen to produce more milk when music plays in dairies. There was a study done with monkeys where they were allowed to choose their own music and they preferred lullabies to techno music. She sings lullabies to her rescue pigs and when she starts singing, they come in and get into their beds. Pigs have higher intelligence than dogs - dogs are like a 2-3 year old child, pigs are like a 3-5 year old, and they watch cartoons.

questions.question: Where do international dialing codes come from and who decides what numbers countries get? Like if Scotland became independent tomorrow, who decides its code?

answers.answer: It's the International Telecommunications Union that issue dialing codes for international countries. They're a division of the United Nations based in Geneva. Netherlands is 31.

questions.question: Why, when you dip a rich tea biscuit in a very hot cup of tea, does it not soften as quickly as if you leave the tea for five minutes and then dip it? The cooler tea softens it faster.

answers.answer: Via osmosis, water wants to balance to the mean. In hot tea, water molecules escape via steam to the air, so less water goes into biscuit. In cold tea, no steam, so all the water piles into the biscuit and it gets soggier much quicker.

Starchy polymers have both hydrophobic and hydrophilic qualities. In hot water, the hydrophobic parts cluster together tightly (hydrophobic-hydrophobic attraction), making the biscuit less soluble. It's counterintuitive but true - the biscuit is less soluble in hot water than cold water. PhD in chemistry, teaches pharmaceuticals on hydrophobic colloids.

questions.question: When the weather gets warmer, flies seem to circle in the middle of rooms under light fittings. Why don't they land? Why do they expend energy circling and why only in the middle of the room?

answers.answer: Male flies establishing territory and warding off other males. They fly around lamps or lights marking out their patch. Sometimes they wrestle. They fly in zigzags or 90-degree angles to avoid predators and make it harder to catch. 24 years in pest control business.

questions.question: Why do all microwave ovens have the doors hung on the left-hand side?

answers.answer: Because we're almost all right-handed. Microwaves can't have reversible doors like fridges because of the safety interlock switches.

questions.question: Why do my sneezes smell of cinnamon?

answers.answer: Junior doctor. Two explanations: 1) Could be eating something with cinnamon flavoring in it (cinnamaldehyde is used in various flavorings), or 2) Ketosis from low blood sugar can cause sweet-smelling breath. Suggests Toff get checked for diabetes as a precaution but says if it were diabetic ketoacidosis he'd be much sicker and in hospital.

questions.question: Why don't deep sea creatures explode when they get dredged up or caught in nets and brought to the surface? You would imagine they'd expand quickly with the pressure change.

answers.answer: Water is incompressible, so a creature made almost entirely of water won't get compressed. Humans are also mostly water. Many fish have swim bladders they control to move up and down. A scientist called Richard Pyle discovered that bringing fish up too fast kills them because of swim bladder expansion. He started doing 'safety stops' and draining bladders with a syringe, which is now reflected in dive computer algorithms. He's a scuba diving instructor.

questions.question: What's the point of checking in online when travelling? In the old days it meant you'd arrived, proved documentation, and sent your bag on its journey. Now nothing changes except you don't queue.

answers.answer: They reduce staff by no longer having people queue for boarding passes. Passengers get opportunity to choose where they sit. Earlier check-in means more choice. Some airlines charge for seat selection. The earlier you check in, the more likely you are to get your preferred seat.

Three reasons: 1) Convenience - you can put boarding pass on your phone and avoid the check-in desk, 2) You can go straight to security without queuing, 3) You get to choose and confirm your seat in advance. Flies about three times a week for work.

questions.question: Do dogs have blood groups?

Can civilians play in military bands? A musician friend said his brother played in a British Army band in the household division but wasn't actually a soldier - just a musician in uniform to make up numbers.

answers.answer: Completely untrue. They might call in army reserve musicians, but not civilians just to fill numbers. More likely they'd borrow from another band, especially for household division. He spent over 20 years as a professional tuba player in the British Army.

questions.question: How do you determine top of the road? If the road is flat and connected to two main roads from each side, how do you know which is the top?

answers.answer: Roads are always numbered towards the centre of a town, so the top of the road is the highest numbered address.

Top of the road is the highest number. Number one is the nearest to town wherever you are. She lived at number 111 and friends always met her at the top of the road. Known this since she was about 7 years old in 1958.

questions.question: When did pubs introduce bells to call time and last orders?
If we wash our dishes and our clothes at hotter temperatures for stain removal, would it not be better or make more sense to brush our teeth with hotter water?
What happened to the rest of Downing Street? There's number 10, number 11, but there's no number 1 tonight.

answers.answer: Downing Street never actually existed as a numbered street - it was built as a cul-de-sac by George Downing, a shrewd man who made money during the Restoration.
