In the late 1860s, Sir Gilbert Scott knocked down the other half of the houses when merging Parliament Street with Whitehall to build the Foreign Office and Home Office. They didn't bother renumbering because number 10 already had a place in public consciousness. George II gave number 10 to Sir Robert Walpole, the first Prime Minister.

questions.question: Do we eat soup or do you drink soup?
Why is a top hat called a top hat?

answers.answer: There are a few reasons: First, because it goes atop your head. Second, it was also called a chimney pot hat, similar to chimney pots. Third, top hats took up the top shelf in hat shops - they were the biggest hats and got put at the top.

questions.question: Would a top racehorse trainer or breeder know if it was a boy or a girl if they could only see the front half of a horse?

answers.answer: You cannot tell the difference between a horse's gender just from the front half. Her daughter has had horses for nearly 30 years and confirmed you can't tell. You would need to see underneath.

You can often tell - but not always. It depends whether you're looking at a stallion, gelding, or mare. Stallions have thicker, cresty necks, and the way they arch their neck and their muscle tone down the shoulders and neck can indicate sex. But it's not 100% - she estimated she could identify correctly about 50-60% of the time. You can also tell by their mannerisms and attitude.

Mares have between 36 and 40 teeth, and geldings or stallions have between 40 and 44. Male horses often have extra canine teeth, which is a throwback from when they were wild horses and used them for fighting.

questions.question: Why is it known as Hull and not Kingston? Stoke-on-Trent is Stoke. Newcastle-on-Tyne is Newcastle. But Hull is just known as Hull. Why is it Hull and not Kingston?
On an aircraft manifesto, why do they say 'souls on board' rather than passengers on board?

answers.answer: It's just a way of describing the number of living humans on the airplane. Human remains might also be carried on an aircraft, so 'souls on board' specifically means living people - which is what air traffic control needs to know.

questions.question: Why don't fitted sheets have labels saying which is the top and which is the bottom?
When surgeons are all scrubbed up and they've got all the PPE on, how do they go to the toilet?

answers.answer: You just leave the operating theatre, walk down the corridor, do what you need to do, come back into theatre, wash your hands and put on a new gown and gloves again. It's as simple as that. If you're in a really long operation, you get quite dehydrated anyway so you need to pee less than you would anyway.

questions.question: Why do we grimace when we're picking up heavy objects or when we're in pain? Some people do and some people don't.

Why is tagliatelle and some other ribbon pasta sold in nests/bundles while spaghetti, linguine, capellini, bucatini and fettuccine are sold efficiently in straight flat packages? Why do some pasta types curl up when they could be sold flat?
Why does garlic turn bluey-greeny/turquoise coloured when left in a lemon, honey, ginger and garlic concoction for several hours?

answers.answer: Garlic contains pigments called anthocyanins and in an acidic solution they will change colour to bluey-green. It takes a while and depends on how strong the acid is and how old the garlic is. This is more prevalent in smaller, younger cloves of garlic.

questions.question: How do we know the perceived and published colourings of dinosaurs are accurate?

answers.caller: Sarah from Sheffield (Professor of Paleontology at University of Leicester)
answers.answer: The skin of dinosaurs is often preserved and we can put skin and feathers in a scanning electron microscope. We can see structures called melanosomes - tiny structures where you manufacture the pigment melanin. The shape of the melanosomes tells you about the colour. If they're little spheres, that equates to orange colour. If they're sausage-shaped, the colour was black. This is how we know Neanderthals had ginger hair - they've got sphere-shaped melanosomes.

questions.question: Why do static electric shocks seem to be getting worse as I'm getting older? They seem to be getting more frequent. Is it seasonal?
Why is there a layer of flint every meter in the White Cliffs of Dover? What is flint and where did it come from?

answers.caller: Thomas from Woodgreen (Geology lecturer at Open University)
answers.answer: The chalk formed under a shallow sea about 100 million years ago and is made of billions of microscopic organisms synthesizing shells from calcium carbonate. Living on the seabed were sponges made of silica. In an alkaline environment, silica dissolves, so when sponges died their skeletons just dissolved. But every so often there was a catastrophic event like a hurricane that killed all the sponges at once, overburdening the system with silica which couldn't dissolve. This created a mass of silica gel on the floor which hardened into flint - like the layer of ash in a delicious cheese.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'teaching your grandmother to suck eggs' come from? Who sucks eggs? Why would a grandmother be particularly good at it?
Is there a requirement for gravestones to face in a certain direction, or is each cemetery unique? Do they all face north, or northeast?

answers.answer: When her husband was a pastor and buried in a church-thinking graveyard, vicars and clergy are buried facing the opposite direction to the laity. She learned this because her husband was buried one way and three years later her son (who wasn't clergy) was buried in the same direction as his father, which meant a lot to her.
By tradition, Christians face east. The religion states that when Jesus comes again, everybody who's buried facing east will rise with him facing the same direction.

questions.question: How can beef-flavoured crisps be labelled 'no artificial flavours suitable for vegetarians'?

answers.answer: No artificial flavours means lab-created chemicals, as opposed to a powdered version of something else. They would have come from other vegetables. There's probably mushroom in there. It's about umami - something beefy that's not beef.
It's textured vegetable protein. They manipulate proteins from different vegetables to create the flavours. The explanation about mushroom and umami was right.

questions.question: Could you harness energy from the intense crushing pressure at the bottom of the sea?

answers.answer: Theoretically possible in principle - you could create a differential with a void chamber at the bottom and harness the pressure pushing for equilibrium. However, conservation of energy makes it cost-ineffective - you'd spend more energy pushing something to the bottom than you'd ever extract.

questions.question: Why do some animals do their toilet while moving (like birds and horses) while others have to stop (like cats and dogs)? Is there a biological reason?

answers.answer: Animals that stop to defecate are predators - they can do their business in peace knowing nothing will hurt them. Animals that have to keep moving are prey animals - horses and cows. Even rabbits can only do it on the run while in their burrows.

questions.question: When you have a pot on the stove (stew, bolognese, carbonade), you don't see much steam. As soon as you move the pot off the flame, all the steam suddenly comes off. Why?

answers.answer: Steam is actually an invisible gas. What you see coming above the water is steam condensing into tiny water droplets. When it's boiling hard, big bubbles of steam escape and disappear above you. When you take it off the heat, the boiling becomes less intense, smaller amounts of steam cool as they rise, and you see the little water droplets.

questions.question: If you're lying in the corner of a room breathing, would there be less oxygen in that corner after 12 hours? How does air circulate when there's no breeze or movement?

answers.answer: Air is like water but less dense. There are two concepts - diffusion (moving from high to low concentration) and convection (driven by pressure difference). Diffusion is slow but convection from body heat is also quite slow. The oxygen content might be measurably less after a very short time, but convection grows in the room over time.

Your body emits heat. That heat warms the air around you, which rises because it's less dense than surrounding air. Fresh air rushes in to replace it. So you're always getting fresh air through convection - there's no rising concentration of CO2.

No, the oxygen levels don't diminish significantly. It's the inhalation, not exhalation, that creates the air movement. When you breathe out, the changed air concentration diffuses into the rest of the room.

questions.question: When calculating calories for meat on the bone (like chicken wings), do they include the bones and cartilage that you don't eat?

answers.answer: There's a McCance and Widdowson database with all foods calculated. They've done separate calculations for meat with bone and meat only. It's up to the company or takeaway to decide which value to use. Generally, most places use the meat-only calorie count. The calculations are based on averages for each part of the animal.

questions.question: Dogs will happily jump into cold sea water or rivers, but absolutely hate being washed at home. Why do they love big bodies of water but hate small ones?

answers.answer: The key is surprise. When you hose a dog or put them in a bath without warning, they get shocked. But if they choose to enter water themselves or if you gradually build up (like starting at a back leg with warm water), they don't get scared. It's about being taken by surprise versus choosing to go in. Dogs who jump into the sea have chosen to do so - they know it's coming.

questions.question: Why is it called a cod piece? What's the origin of the term for those large decorated pieces heavy metal singers wear?

answers.answer: Cod means scrotum - that's where the name comes from. Medieval Tudors wore them because they hadn't invented trousers yet, just two stockings with the cod piece covering the middle.

questions.question: In deep space, there's no north, south, east, or west. How do spacecraft navigate without compasses or star charts?

answers.answer: Spacecraft use inertial navigation units - gyroscopic devices. Similar to those spinning toys that stay upright no matter how you move the plate beneath them. You set gyros in each direction and they measure movement from a reference point. You need at least one known reference point (a celestial body like the moon, Earth, or a star) to calibrate against, and ideally multiple for triangulation.

questions.question: How do they get cars into dealerships on the upper floors?

answers.answer: They use lifts. It's a big metal plate that is both the floor of a lift and also like a Lazy Susan in a Chinese restaurant - a rotating thing on it. They drive in and go into a big lift.

questions.question: Why don't Weetabix have the weight printed on them like other supermarket products?

answers.answer: Most foods are required by weights and measures legislation to have a quantity (volume or weight), but there are exceptions written into the legislation. Cereal biscuits are one of them - they only require the number. Also shell eggs don't have weight on them. Any foods where you're buying a single item don't require weight.

questions.question: Where did single A and B batteries go, and what did they look like?

answers.answer: A and B batteries still exist but are used in other parts of the world. An A is just a tiny bit longer and fatter than AA - about 17mm wide and 50mm long. A B is the even bigger brother - 21.5mm thick and 60mm long. You'd most likely need them in China or Russia. I use them for model radio-controlled aircraft.

questions.question: Why do moles like living by the roadside so much? There are molehills all along main roads but not in quieter fields.

answers.answer: It's not that moles favor roadsides - it's that roads get in the way of them expanding their territories. A single mole can have a territory of 2 to 2.5 acres. The road has concrete and hardcore underneath, so they can't burrow across. The hills look more prominent because they're burrowing down to try to circumnavigate. Moles are very active at this time of year.

Moles don't like being disturbed. By the roadside, other than the council mowing once a year, they have a quiet time. In a field, the owner will take action to get rid of them - using sonar devices and various methods. The reason they're by the roadside is they get much less hassle there. No one's going to come after the moles on a motorway verge.

The question may be wrong. Those aren't molehills - it's grit for the roads. I had the same question years ago and stopped the car to check. In Scotland during the Beast from the East, I wondered why Scotland was so popular with moles. I got out and picked up some of the soil and it was the same stuff in the grit box by the roadside. They put it there so someone can shovel it onto icy roads. Some are molehills but many are road grit deposits.

questions.question: Does catnip work on lions? If I threw a bale of catnip at a pride of lions on safari, would they roll around like cats do?

answers.answer: Catnip contains nepetalactone and it does affect felines, including big cats. I was a ranger tracking poachers in the Endangered Species Protection Unit in South Africa and studied big cats. We had to hand-rear orphan lion cubs. When we put catnip out, their eyes would just glaze over as if they were in love.

questions.question: Were all mountains formerly volcanoes? And which came first - volcanoes or mountains?

answers.answer: No, they're not all former volcanoes. There are three types of mountains: 1) Volcanic - formed by material erupting from below ground, 2) Tectonic - like the Himalayas where the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates ran into each other and pushed up, 3) Folded mountains - caused by folding further away from plate boundaries.

questions.question: What is the decision-making process for dogs when they sniff before they go to the toilet? Even on beaches where the tide has just gone out with no other animals around, they still sniff first.

answers.answer: They can't establish whether any animals have been there without sniffing. On a beach, they sniff, establish that no other animals are there, but they need a wee anyway. Just because they sniff doesn't mean what you think it means - they don't know no other animals have been there until they sniff.

It's a purely learned behavior about safety. It's natural for them to want to know what's been around because they make themselves very vulnerable when defecating. They need to check there aren't any big dogs that have recently deposited anything threatening. For urination, it's about letting everybody know they've been there - marking territory. So 20 sniffs before a wee is saying 'I've been here, I've been here' repeatedly. For number twos, they need to check for safety.

questions.question: Why do hospital gowns do up at the back instead of the front?

answers.answer: Maybe it's to protect modesty when someone else is putting the gown on you, coming at you from behind.
Surely they'd need emergency access to the front of your body for your airways or chest compressions rather than for an emergency colonoscopy.

I'm an operating department practitioner. When patients come to the anesthetic room, the first thing I do is ask them to sit forward and I do up the bows at the back of the gown. I need to put ECG dots on the patient - there's one on right shoulder, left shoulder, and left side. I can simply lift the gown and pop those on at the back because I don't want to expose the patient's front to do that. When the patient is transferred to the operating table, the gown is pulled completely out from the side so the patient's back is on the table because you don't want to create pressure areas from knots. Then the gown is pulled up to expose just where the operation is being done.

questions.question: Where did the urban myth about swimming pools having chemicals that would turn red if you urinated in them come from?

answers.answer: I think probably it was true at some point. We all heard it with those old signs - no petting, no bombing, no splashing.

It's an urban legend, unfortunately, drawn by parents 70 years ago. There's no chemical which can actually do that. Plus, if you did design a chemical, the chlorine in the swimming pool would kill it straight away. You'd also have false negatives for things like sweat, body motions, and a lot of swimming pools contain a lot of urine anyway, so it would change the colour of the water as well. The amount of chemical you'd need to use in the swimming pool would be a biteless amount, and you'd need to use pH neutralisers every day to counteract it. So it wouldn't be worth the effort. It's just an urban legend people use to stop children weeing in the swimming pool. It's extremely effective. I get asked this question so many times in schools and councils, and we say sorry, it doesn't exist. When they see a film and say they've seen it in the movie, they're doing it for effect - that's food dye.

questions.question: Why are we perfectly comfortable eating the same breakfast every day but would balk at the very notion of doing the same meal for dinner every day?

answers.answer: It might be something to do with not being up for very long and therefore your brain is kind of... I don't know. Breakfast, you start off absolutely fine with the same thing every single day. Then by the time you get to lunch, you can kind of get your head around someone having the same sandwich every day. But by dinner, it sounds insane - you'd be like, I can't have that, I had it last night.

questions.question: Why do choreographers and dancers start things with '5, 6, 7, 8' instead of '1, 2, 3, 4' like bands do?

answers.answer: If you don't want everyone starting at the same time... you've got the orchestra. Here's the band: '1, 2, 3, 4.' You don't want the dancers to start yet. The music's up and running and then it's time for the dancers - you go '5, 6, 7, 8' and then all the dancers start dancing while the music carries on.

You were wrong with your answer. It's not to do with coming at a different time. It's to do with how musicians and dancers divide their bar up - musicians divide into crotchets, which is what they're counting: 1, 2, 3, 4. Dancers tend to dance in groups of eight, so it's 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. But that's a bit too much to say, so they just say '5, 6, 7, 8' instead. It's when you reset. If a musician was playing in 3/4 time, they would go 1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3.

questions.question: What happens if you win a massive house in a competition but can't afford to upkeep it?

answers.answer: You could put it on Airbnb. Or sell it - you'd just have to pay the fee after you got the money for the house.

I buy an entry every month for one of these house competitions. They offer an extra cash prize on top if you win the house - currently £250,000. So in order to run the house, you can run it for as long as it takes before you want to sell. You're not going to be left with this enormous, expensive white elephant dangling around your neck.

questions.question: Is there an undisclosed weight limit on a flat? Can you put too much heavy stuff in a third floor flat?

answers.answer: These things are designed for houses. There's no way that an item of readily available furniture is going to be too heavy for an average flat.
If you were doing mechanics and taking a bit of car up the stairs and slowly putting a car together, would it reach a point where the floor collapsed?

I'm an architect. You were right - it is a building control thing. Inside buildings, there are things called uniformly distributed loads. You calculate the size of a floor joist on the basis of building regulations, depending on the size and how far apart they are. It depends on whether he's got a concrete floor. Engineers design based on reasonable UDLs so that you would not expect to have a car there. I've designed projects where we've put cars on office floors and had to reinforce the floor underneath specifically to take the weight of a vehicle. That would be abnormal. There's no specific limit on the resident - there's just an expectation that you won't be a bloody idiot. You'd have extra beams and supports underneath something like a bank safe. For things like pianos in old houses, you'd be better putting them on the edge than in the middle because you get more deflection in the middle of the span.

questions.question: Why don't commercial hand dryers exist for residential houses?

answers.answer: They're very expensive. You couldn't do it yourself - you'd need a sparky to wire it in. People spend like a grand, grand and a half on a TV these days, so it's possible. The reason you have hand dryers in public is because the idea of a communal towel is really unpleasant - but that's not an issue at home.

My husband purchased one. We had it in our downstairs bathroom. He purchased it from eBay - the notification said 'for sale, one unused chrome hand dryer.' We bought it because we didn't have a window in the downstairs toilet, so there were no towels to go down. It cost £100. We left it when we moved to Cardiff. If you really want one, you can get one on eBay cheap.

questions.question: Can deaf people who lip read detect regional dialect?

answers.answer: I'm deaf. I've been deaf since I was a toddler and taught myself to lip read. I can categorically state that yes, we can lip read regional accents and identify them. If I'm watching TV, I tend to watch with the sound down and subtitles on, and I can usually spot if it's someone with a Scottish accent or a Welsh accent. I don't know how I do it, but I can - it's because of the shape of their mouth. They do sort of form words differently.

questions.question: Are spaceships armed in case of alien attack?

answers.answer: I think on the first moon landing they probably were fairly confident there wasn't anything there. But they couldn't know for sure, so they might have had something on board. I'm oscillating between thinking this is a daft question and thinking it's a brilliant one.

I'm a little bit of a space history nerd. On Apollo 11, they had a machete because it was part of a survival kit. As part of their training, they went to various places on the planet to learn how to survive in jungles and barren places, because they weren't sure exactly what they were going to find on the moon. So they had a survival kit which included a machete, which can be used as a weapon. Cosmonauts used to carry a pistol. But the weapons they carried were more for quick death if something happened - if the engine failed, it's a slow death or a quick death.

questions.question: When do we stop closing our eyes when we fall asleep? Babies close their eyes and go straight to sleep, but adults close their eyes and wait. When does that change?
Why do Easter eggs now come in one piece instead of two halves with sweets in the middle like they used to?
Why do American male voices always sound much deeper than their equivalent English ones? They always seem to be about an octave lower.

answers.answer: I put it down to education starting around year eight, when you're eight years old, spelling bees. We are taught how to stand up, orate, speak from our diaphragm, not through our throats or our upper chest. You practice in the classroom, and when you're doing it in an auditorium with 300, 500, and thousands of people, you speak not only into a microphone but have to carry your voice throughout the entire room. You're taught that from a very early age, so by the time you're an adult man, you probably have that mastered.

questions.question: Why does my hair grow faster in Tenerife than in the UK? I shave every other day in the UK but have to shave morning and evening in Tenerife.

answers.answer: Hair does grow quicker in the summer than in the winter and in hotter climates than in colder climates. This is because your capillary blood vessels dilate in the heat, and therefore they carry more blood to the follicles, which carries oxygen and all the nutrients, and therefore it feeds the follicles and your hair grows quicker. There's also keratin involved.

questions.question: How do we define as humans the difference between a good smell and a bad smell? Is it universally acknowledged or is it chemical or preference?

answers.answer: Danger, surely. Things that are rotten - evolution has taught us to avoid certain smells because they could do us harm either by inhaling them or eating them. That makes the anomalies interesting because some people quite like the smell of petrol or bitumen.

questions.question: How long would a cable be on a 13-amp cable before the electric just wouldn't make it to the end? I noticed my drill wasn't as powerful using a long extension lead compared to plugging directly into the mains.

answers.answer: The longer the length, the more voltage drops. In electrical regulations, there's 3% and 5% for power and lighting voltage drop. The longer the cable, the more voltage it drops. If somebody's done their calculations correctly, it wouldn't go to zero, but theoretically with a long enough lead and no substations, voltage drop would mean nothing would happen at the other end. For an extension, 1.5 mil would usually be alright.

An electrical cable the longer it gets, the more electrical resistance you've got. The analogy is like a corridor full of people - to get from one end to the other you have to weave and push past people. Imagine the corridor is 10 times longer and it's 10 times harder. One and a half mil flex loses around 10 volts AC per 100 meters, so you would need a 1.5 mil extension lead to be about 2.4 kilometers long in order to reach nought volts at the end - about a mile and a half in old money.

questions.question: How do experts work out what sounds dinosaurs made when no one's ever heard one?

answers.answer: We don't know for certain, but there is some good news. In 2023, a paper was published on an ankylosaur fossil which contained a fossilized larynx - a voice box. Modern birds have similar voice boxes, which would be a good starting point. Some dinosaurs probably had something very similar and could have been quite squawky. If you found the right fossils, you could eventually reconstruct a larynx and pump air through it to see what happens. So we might be getting closer to the answer.

questions.question: Cow stomachs famously have four stomachs - are they sequential or parallel? If they chew the cud, how is it internally managed so that what needs to come back up does come back up?
If J.D. Vance decides to run for president, is Donald Trump allowed to run as his vice president? And if something happened to J.D. Vance, could Trump take over again?

answers.answer: The quick answer is yes, it's technically possible. The real answer is no one's ever tried it before. George Washington said no one should be president for more than 10 years, and that wasn't put into law until after FDR was elected four times. Now it's codified that you can't be president for more than 10 years. No one who's spent two consecutive terms has ever tried to run for vice president, so it's possible. If he became president because the VP retired, he would be caught in a two-year cycle. He could theoretically run for a third term but only serve two years of it because 10 years is the constitutional limit. There was a similar question about Obama being VP for Biden - he could have been vice president for all four years but only assumed the presidency for two years.

questions.question: Is there a name for people who love epic feats of engineering like bridges, cranes, viaducts, and aqueducts?

answers.answer: No definitive answer given. James mentioned the Scottish places Emma recommended including the Kelpies, Falkirk Wheel, and Queensferry Bridge. He suggested terms like 'feats of epic engineering' or 'majesty' but no established term was confirmed.

questions.question: Are the garden birds we see now (during RSPB Great Bird Watch) related to the ones we saw a few years ago? Do they stay local and pass on territory, or do they find partners elsewhere?

answers.answer: Small songbirds have high mortality rates. House sparrows are family orientated and nest together as a group. Robins live 2-3 years and are territorial. The grandchildren of birds counted years ago would be the current birds - if parents die, offspring can move back to the garden. Birds pass on territory to their offspring.

questions.question: When having brain surgery (with large scar on forehead where skull was removed), the surgeon photographed his ears beforehand. Was he just putting Jack at ease or was this actually necessary?
What happens to a pension fund (like British Coal mine workers) when all the beneficiaries die off? Do the last survivors get all the money, or does surplus go to government or Crown?

answers.answer: If it's a defined benefit scheme, the fund pays down. When only a few people are left, individual payments go up accordingly. Some funds with very few remaining members pay a lump sum to move into private pension pots. The multiplier is typically 30-40 times the final salary.

The mine workers pension scheme is defined benefit - members get a pension for life, possibly one for spouse/dependents. Once all members, spouses, partners and dependents are deceased, if there's surplus, the sponsoring employer (was British Coal, now government as guarantor) is entitled to claim it back subject to a tax charge. This differs from money purchase schemes where beneficiaries inherit.

questions.question: When opening a new jar of pickled gherkins, one or two always poke out of the vinegar at the top. Are they safe to eat or do they go bad since they're not submerged?

answers.answer: The jar is airtight and vacuum-sealed when you open it - that's what the popping sound is. The ones poking out above the liquid are perfectly fine to eat. If you're squeamish, you can store the jar upside down so the ones above the brine take turns being submerged.

questions.question: Is one blood group better than another? Is there a measurable health benefit to certain blood groups, like premium petrol vs standard?

answers.answer: Yes, there are advantages. Certain blood groups clot more frequently. O positive is arguably the best - it's one of the most common and useful for transfusions. Lewis has a degree in medical genetics.

questions.question: If a pink flamingo landed in my garden and I fed it cabbage and peas instead of its normal seafood, what colour would it become?

answers.answer: He worked at Dudley Zoo in the 1960s when flamingos arrived. They struggled to maintain the pink colouring and used carotene as a food additive. The flamingos looked scruffy when they arrived but looked much brighter the following year after being fed carotene. The pink comes from diet, not natural pigmentation.

questions.question: How do seagulls know when a farmer is ploughing a field miles inland? They appear from nowhere even when no seagulls were visible before.

answers.answer: Seagulls are scavengers - they're around, just not visible. They've learned that tractors ploughing fields means an easy meal of worms. They're highly adaptable and found inland near rubbish tips and farms. The 'misnomer' is that they're only found by the sea.

questions.question: What does 'Scott free' mean in the phrase 'got away Scott free'? Where does the word Scott come from?

answers.answer: It's Norse, not Scottish. 'Scott' comes from Old Norse 'skot,' which meant a tax. Getting away 'Scott free' originally meant you hadn't paid your tax - you got away without paying what you owed.

questions.question: How similar were prehistoric homo sapiens to us now? If you took a human from tens of thousands of years ago and raised them today, would there be any discernible differences? Would they be able to speak, learn, walk and talk like us?

answers.answer: Quarter of a million years is too far. 10,000 years is close enough - we were farming and doing human activities. The brain hasn't grown or changed in 10,000 years; evolution doesn't work on such short time periods. About 100,000 years ago, you had Homo erectus who would have been very different - much smaller brains and hairier than modern humans. The simple answer is no to the question of whether homo sapiens would be indistinguishable from us. If you trace your ancestry back far enough, every father looks like his son, and doing it a million times you'd end up with a fish. It would take about 500 million years to find a fish ancestor.

questions.question: Why does my stripy shirt make me feel ill when I iron it? When I move it too quickly on the ironing board, the pattern hurts my eyes and makes me feel dizzy and headachy. It only happens when I'm moving it.

answers.answer: It's called strobing. TV studios make presenters take different shirts because patterns on camera can strobe - the lines and patterns look like they're moving when they're not. However, this was about the naked eye rather than through a camera lens.

This could be something called visual vertigo. Humans balance three ways: vision, the vestibular system in the inner ear, and sensation in feet. Some people have deficits in their vestibular system - perhaps from infections or genetic weakness - and become more dominant with their visual system. These people often report dizziness or loss of balance when facing complex visual information such as stripy shirts or supermarket aisles. It's not the eyes that are the problem, it's the inner ear not doing its job.

I suffer from hyper photosensitivity - the kind where flashing lights can cause seizures. A byproduct is that certain patterns, especially straight lines, can make me feel extremely ill. It's possible Daniel has a mild case and it's only been triggered by this particular shirt.

questions.question: What happens on the Karakoram Highway between China and Pakistan when traffic from both countries meets, given that in China they drive on the right and in Pakistan they drive on the left?

answers.answer: The road was built for very low-powered, heavily-laden lorries following ancient Silk Road trade routes. The road was never steep - it was like a motorway steepness. At the border, there's no roundabout or special provision. There's just the passport stamp on the Chinese side, then 100 metres on is the Pakistani side. There may have been signs but it just naturally happens that drivers descend down the correct side. There's not enough traffic for it to be a problem.

questions.question: Why do worms come out when it rains? They live underground and can breathe underground, so why do they come out en masse when it rains?

answers.answer: There are a couple of theories. One is that if they stay in their holes and the holes fill up with rain, they'll drown. But the real reason is thought to be that it's easier for them to move around on the surface when it's wet - they can slither and migrate rather than having to stay underground. Qualifications: I live in Falmouth where we have an annual worm charming competition, which makes everyone a worm expert.
In response to James's theory about birds not being around in rain: actually, birds will stamp their feet, especially seagulls, to imitate rain and bring worms to the surface so they can eat them.

questions.question: When you get one of those really small spots or whiteheads on your face, why are they so painful? I'm not talking about acne-type spots that are inflamed or cyst-like, just the tiny little whitehead spots.
Where does the phrase 'how about them apples' come from?

answers.answer: The Mark II grenade used in the trenches looked like a pineapple and blasts into shrapnel. Mortars were nicknamed toffee apples because they had the stick coming out with the ordinance on the end. Because they were nicknamed pineapples and toffee apples, 'how do you like them apples' is what soldiers would shout when throwing grenades at the enemy. Qualifications: About 45 years ago I used to read a lot of comics like Action, Eagle and Commando where I read this in an action strip.

questions.question: How can cats find their way home over 800 or 900 miles? There are stories of cats travelling ridiculous distances and finding their way home. How do they do that?
In cricket, why are fast bowlers not getting faster? The fastest ball ever recorded was Shoaib Akhtar 20 years ago, and the great West Indians weren't really concerned with anything other than speed.

answers.answer: Possibly because batsmen now have armour/helmets, so fast bowlers aren't as intimidating. The answer might be that they're concentrating more on swing and accuracy. Also, they might be trying to prolong their careers - Jimmy Anderson would probably have had to retire 5-10 years ago if he'd been bowling hell for leather. Old cricketers from the 50s and 60s have broken knees and backs. The answer would be reprioritizing - going for consistency and more swing and accuracy.

I had a chat with Nick Knight (the batsman who faced Shoaib Akhtar's 100 mile an hour delivery). He told me the funny thing is the 100 mile an hour ball went up on the speed gun, everyone went 'yeah', but it wasn't even the fastest ball he bowled that day. So the theory is it's speed gun technology that's improved, not that bowlers have slowed down. I think it's that bowlers have more all-round fitness these days.

questions.question: Why don't babies reciprocate or mirror yawns? My youngest is nine months old. Babies can see that I'm yawning but they don't do it back. What changes between being a child and adult?

answers.answer: The reason yawning is contagious is because we're conveying to each other that we're safe. If I see you yawn, I know there's nothing coming up to hit me over the head because you're yawning. So I can relax too. It's very subconscious and evolutionary. Babies haven't developed a concept of risk or threat yet - they haven't developed the empathy or understanding that comes with recognizing how others are feeling.

Children start to be able to yawn reciprocally between the ages of four and five, once they develop the ability to recognize how other people are feeling - essentially, empathy develops around that age.

questions.question: When is the expansion pack for the Mystery Hour board game coming out?

answers.answer: They were hoping to get it out before Christmas but it didn't happen. It will come out this year. They'll be at the Kensington Olympia games fair later this month where they'll discuss and decide on it.

questions.question: Why are some beaches full of shells while others, like the Maldives, have absolutely no shells at all?

answers.answer: If you've got a rocky shore or rocky seabed, you get more mollusks living there, and when they die, their shells wash up onto the beach. On sandy beaches where there's nowhere for mollusks to live and thrive, there are no empty shells to wash back up onto the beach. Rocky shores covered in limpets will have limpet shells all over. Somewhere where it's just pure sand with no rocks, they don't wash up because there aren't any.

questions.question: Who are the drivers of the yellow gritter lorries? Where do they come from? Do they have day jobs? What do they do the rest of the year when gritters aren't needed?

answers.answer: Gritter driving is contracted to private companies that repair roads for the local council. Workers are volunteers from within the company - people like joiners by trade - who are asked to go out and drive the gritter wagons during cold spells. The gritters are owned by the company and parked up in the council yard for the rest of the year. It was great fun - cars follow behind the gritter to stay back because they don't want to be hit by the grit. The spread is calibrated on the back depending on weather severity. You drive solo.

questions.question: How do petrol stations change all their prices on the display? When do they do it? How does it work, especially at motorway service stations that are open 24 hours?

answers.answer: She witnessed a price change happen while she was paying at the pump. She drove in and chose the station based on price, then noticed a different message appeared during payment on the display. When she got her receipt, the price had changed - it had gone up by a couple of pence. She walked into the kiosk and got a refund.

A notification comes through from head office. The manager temporarily closes the pumps - if someone's currently filling up, they wait until they're finished, then tell anyone waiting to hold on for a minute due to a price change. The manager goes to the master till, inputs the new price, and there's a separate remote control to set the canopy price display visible from the road. It only takes a couple of minutes. Worked on a Tesco petrol forecourt for 21 years.

questions.question: Is the Earth's mass getting smaller? If you burn something like a 300kg shed, where does the mass go? Does it produce 300kg of waste, or where does the mass go?

answers.answer: The Earth gains mass from meteorite impacts - from micrometeorites up to really big ones. But the Earth also loses mass through the atmosphere - things that drift upwards eventually get lost into space. When you burn something, the gases go up but it's actually energy being transformed into light and heat. The interesting thing is that the loss from the atmosphere is actually slightly greater than the gain from meteorites, but not by very much. Both are negligible compared to the total mass of the Earth. Mark is chairperson of the Barrow Astronomy Society with a keen hobby interest in theoretical astronomy.

questions.question: Why do we say Napoleon had a 'short man complex' when he was actually of average height for his time (around 5'6")? At what point did we pin this on Napoleon?

answers.answer: Napoleon had his own imperial guard, all specified to be very tall people - around six foot plus. When he was out in public with his towering imperial guard, people would look and wonder which one was Napoleon - and it would be the little guy in the middle. Also, when he died, his measurements were sent from France to England, and there was confusion about the different measurement systems, leading to him appearing much smaller than he actually was. Napoleon wore a small tricorn hat while his guard wore tall bearskin hats, making him look even smaller by comparison.

questions.question: Is there a word that describes the feeling when a journey outbound feels longer than the return journey, especially the very first time you make a journey?

answers.answer: Yes, there's a name for it: the Return Trip Effect. On the way out, people tend to underestimate how long the journey will take because they're not familiar with it. On the way back, they see familiar landmarks and it doesn't take as long to process, so it feels quicker. This is from A-level psychology.

questions.question: Why are the laces on trainers always unreasonably too long?

answers.answer: It's the young people. The young people do fancy lacing on their trainers for which they need the longer ones.

questions.question: Why is there so much track-related stuff (sleepers, engineering bits, etc.) left on the actual railway line between tracks?

answers.answer: Most of it is preparations for engineering work that takes place over the weekend. You don't have time to transport or procure stuff on the day - it has to be prepared in advance. Steel needs to be seasoned - taken from the factory, laid on the ground outside in the elements where it oxidizes, shrinks and expands until it reaches a stable state, and that's when you can lay the tracks. Some old junk hasn't been collected but if it was worth money the privatized train companies would have sold it.

questions.question: Why is there only one species of people when other animals (dogs, cats, flies) have many different types?

answers.answer: Homo sapiens killed off all other types of humanoids, most obviously Neanderthals. It was an evolutionary success story - we were brutal and wiped out all potential rivals. We may have even engaged in cannibalism of Neanderthals.

We didn't kill them all off violently. The last surviving hominid was Homo neanderthalensis, and we out-competed them for available resources. They were more adapted to very cold environments like the last ice age, and we simply out-competed them - we ate all the pies. Genetically, any human of Indo-European/Caucasian origin has between 1.7-2.3% (average 2%) Neanderthal DNA, so interbreeding also played a role. Some scientists say circadian rhythm adaptation - people who become extremely morning people - is a Neanderthal trait. They were actually very intelligent and had very big brains compared to body size.

questions.question: How does the term 'millionaire' work across different currencies? In Japan, a million yen is only about £5,000, so when does someone become a millionaire and how is it calculated?

answers.answer: It might be an Anglo concept. The example of Zimbabwean millionaires proves the point - in countries with inflated currencies, the term doesn't really work. In countries like Japan where there's nothing above the yen, there can't really be a new unit.

In South Asia - India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Burma, and Sri Lanka (which comprise a quarter of humanity) - they have different terms. 'Lakhpati' is the millionaire equivalent (one lakh = 100,000, which was historically an enormous sum). 'Crorepati' is the billionaire equivalent (one crore = 10 million rupees). A hundred thousand rupees in old days was enormous money. Someone super rich with 100 lakhs (10 million) is a crorepati.

In Uruguay, Who Wants to Be a Millionaire has a prize of 2 million pesos (about £34,000), which is still considered a big win there, even though Uruguay is an expensive country for South America. Generally, people talk in US dollars instead of local currency.

questions.question: Why does her Standard Schnauzer go into a trance-like state when near bamboo - tail drops, rocks side to side, almost frozen for a couple of minutes?

answers.answer: Schnauzers were bred to hunt vermin and rats, and bamboo is notorious for housing rats - it's a perfect environment for both nesting and food. Gundogs when they get a scent get very busy with their tail going fast. The dog is probably scenting rats that are there or have been there. Like pointers, they point to where the scent is. The bamboo provides an ideal environment for vermin.

questions.question: How do they secure senior members of the Royal Family like Queen Camilla when they're out shopping privately, like at Fortnum Mason?

answers.answer: Close protection officers have different levels of security depending on the situation. Public engagements have much higher security because everyone knows where they're going to be (advance notice = higher risk). Private shopping trips are relatively run-of-the-mill operations with fewer officers. The Queen has to be somewhere, so it's just about risk management.

questions.question: How do they get cranes up and how are they constructed when they're so tall and look like they're touching the clouds?

answers.answer: A mobile crane builds the permanent crane piece by piece like Lego, starting with concrete because it's going to be properly routed. The mobile crane builds it up until it's finished, then it goes away. This is why it seems like a magic trick - if the mobile crane was still there, everyone would understand how it works.

questions.question: Why does sap or resin continue to drip from knots in wood even after the tree has been cut?

answers.caller: James (Taunton, chainsaw sculptor with 26+ years experience)
answers.answer: Timber from yards is usually seasoned or kiln-dried but not completely dry. As wood dries, it shrinks and compresses, and that's why resin slowly exudes from the wood, particularly around knots where most of the resin is and where the wood is much denser so it holds more water (known as 'bound water' within the cells). The knots take longer to dry even when the rest of the wood is pretty much dry. Cedar of Lebanon is particularly bad for this - it can carry on for years after it's supposed to be dried, which is why it smells so good.

questions.question: How does a guide dog know where to get you where you're asking? How does it work?

answers.answer: The owner knows where they're going and gives understated commands to the dog. The dog is assisting, not leading. The public gives all the credit to the dog and doesn't notice the owner is actually giving commands. Pedestrian crossings have tactile cones that the dog knows how to cope with. The dog isn't exercising some mysterious power.

questions.question: Why can't older people feel their nose dripping? I have a drip at the end of my nose but I can't feel it.

answers.answer: As people get older, the senses fade. Part of the brain that manages self-monitoring has to compensate for all the fading senses. Eventually we become less competent at self-management. The sense of touch fades as nerves age, but also the general managing of oneself. In our younger days, everything is sharp and doesn't need as much supervision. As we get older, all the other senses need more supervision, so the brain has more work to do and eventually our self-management falls off a bit.

questions.question: Why do I have to tick the box that says divorced when I'm essentially single? Who needs to know I was rubbish at being married and am not anymore?

answers.answer: It's a financial situation audit. On a finance application, if you're divorced, you could have a house and a car on paper but not be able to afford the loan once the divorce is finalised and your ex takes everything. If you were going through a divorce, they could loan you money and then you lose it all in the divorce settlement. Once your divorce is finalised with no financial ties, you're classified as single. But ticking divorced can put a negative factor on your credit application.

questions.question: Do the big TV companies for TV adverts talk about what background music they're going to use? How do they avoid ending up with the same Christmas song on two different Christmas adverts?

answers.answer: If you want to use a song or piece of recorded music, you have to apply for what is called a synchronisation licence. These can cost a lot of money. So you would want to protect yourself that the same song isn't used for a similar advertisement or any advertisement at all. A time limit is put on during what the rights owner can licence a song for another synchronisation licence.

questions.question: Are there any rules around what you're allowed to name a pub? Is there some sort of body you have to send your proposed name to?

answers.answer: There is a body which will vet your name. When you're filling out your form to start your business, you put your suggested name for the pub on the form and send it to the local council. They will say yes or no whether they want that name. It's definitely applied to pubs and I assume other premises as well. It applies when you're taking over the licence.

questions.question: Why do we describe it as having beef with people? My daughter uses this term at school.

answers.answer: It comes from Cockney rhyming slang. Hot beef is rhyming slang for stop thief. When you've got a problem with someone, you'd shout it on the streets, and it just became a slang term for having a problem with someone.

If it is rhyming slang, it's going to be grief, isn't it? Having grief with someone. It makes more sense than stop thief. The whole idea of rhyming slang was so police didn't understand conversations, which makes stop thief an absolutely meaningless intervention in this case.

questions.question: Kansas and Arkansas have identical spelling at the start but massively different pronunciation. Why is the S silent in Arkansas?

answers.answer: It's French pronunciation. Up until 1803, up until the Louisiana Purchase, these territories were French. If you were French, you would pronounce it Kansas, Arkansas. Kansas, Arkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Dakota, parts of Wyoming were all French territories.

questions.question: Two questions: 1) How likely is it that my insinkerator button is stuck vs something more serious? 2) Our work jumpers are 96% polyester but always get red blotchy marks even though they contain no red. Could it be flux or boss white?

answers.answer: The button is often made of plastic behind the back that splits. Try adjusting or changing the button. Also try those sucker darts from toy guns on the principle that there's a plastic mechanism that uses air to push through to the actual button to relieve it.

It's the flux. When you're applying flux on a pipe, you use it to make sure solder goes all the way around, it cleans all the dirt. When you get the brush and clean the pipe with a wet cloth, you get bits of flux on your jumper. It's a powerful acid or alkaline. It dyes the fabric - like bleach, but bleach doesn't turn clothes white, it does something that dyes.

questions.question: Why do some ships or boats have a bulky nose underneath the water at the front that goes out further than the above-water prow? Is it for ice?
If you are an amputee, does the human body account for the amount of blood in your body or do you still carry the same amount as someone who isn't missing limbs?

answers.answer: You still have the same amount of blood in your body after amputation. I met Billy Monga who had a horrible accident and he was told by a specialist. Your body doesn't know you've lost your limbs. It just keeps the same amount of blood as it had before.

questions.question: How does money work in the global postal service? When you post a letter to France and buy a stamp, where does the money go? How does the French postman get paid for delivering an English letter?

answers.answer: It's done by weights. If we send 20 bags of first class letters to France, they charge us for the weight of those 20 bags, and vice versa. That's how it works worldwide.

questions.question: Where do the babies come from on Call the Midwife Christmas specials? Are they real babies? Do pregnant women sign up to have their babies appear on the show?

answers.answer: The babies are real. I chaperone for them. The agent I work for gets the babies from birth. If she sees a pregnant woman walking past the office, she runs out and asks when it's due and if they want to be on TV. The youngest I've had on the show was a week old.

questions.question: Do doctors ever use stethoscopes to listen to other parts of the body like a creaky knee, or only heart and lungs?

answers.answer: The stethoscope has two parts - a diaphragm (flat bit) and a bell. The bell is used for listening to bowel sounds for abdominal pain. Also used for taking blood pressures with a stethoscope monitor - you pump up the cuff, listen to the pulse through the arm to pick up blood pressure readings.

A stethoscope can legitimately be used on the knee if you don't have a tendon hammer - you can use the edge to test the patella reflex which is an important part of the lower limb neurological examination. Also doctors use the stethoscope pretending to listen for bowel sounds but actually pressing gently into the abdomen to test for pain - patients don't flinch because they don't realize the doctor is assessing for pain.

questions.question: How do tulips continue to grow even after they've been cut? You buy them, put them in a vase and they keep growing upwards in height.

answers.answer: They do keep growing once cut - up to 6 inches. They have regenerative properties and are responsive to sunlight, looking for pollinators. That's why they keep growing in a vase.

questions.question: Why is London the only UK capital city with a nickname for its residents (Londoners)? Is there such a thing as Edinburghers, Cardiffians, Belfast people? Is it political?
If someone was sent to prison, escaped, proved their innocence and had the charges dropped, would they still be sent back to prison for escaping?

answers.answer: Yes - because you were a convicted criminal when you went to prison, and just because that conviction has subsequently been lifted, the new crime of breaking out of prison has nothing to do with the reasons why you were in there.

questions.question: As people get older they lose the higher pitch hearing range (like kids' whistles that adults can't hear). When they get hearing aids, can they recover that high pitch range or does it just make everything louder?

answers.answer: He lost the hurt frequencies (4000-6000 Hz) at age 54. Hearing aids cured everything - he can hear the upper register stuff again. Previously at the theater he couldn't hear the singer over the orchestra, now he can hear everything. The hearing aids brought back the high pitch hearing.

questions.question: Is positional vertigo (an inner ear problem) caused by a bad neck or by eyesight as he's been told? He suffers from it - when he lies in bed and turns over, the room starts going around.

Do all cultures regard rainbows as having seven colours? I was taught Roy G Biv at school, but rainbows actually contain all colours in the visible light spectrum. Is it arbitrary that we divide it into seven?

answers.answer: It's arbitrary that we've decided rainbows have seven colours. They have all the colours in the full spectrum of visible light. We could divide it into any number we chose.

Many cultures only see six colours in the rainbow. The idea that indigo is one of the colours is mainly due to Isaac Newton - before that it was just a dye for clothes. There's now a movement to abolish indigo as a colour of the rainbow. Languages divide the colour spectrum differently - some languages only have two basic colour terms (dark and light). Blue is rare as a colour term around the world. In Russian there are separate words for dark blue and light blue. In ancient Greek, colour terms related to luminosity rather than hue - that's why Homer described the sea as wine coloured (same luminosity as wine, not red).

questions.question: Are there any rules governing the speed or length of T&Cs at the end of radio advertisements? Some older people may not be able to hear them all.

answers.answer: I don't think there's a limit. We speed them up so we can fit them all in, and also because you'd have to pay for more airtime. There's no hard and fast rule - it's just people's intuition that at some point it becomes too quick and garbled.

No rules, at least not in the Irish ad industry. I recall during the Celtic Tiger a major bank had T&Cs running to 20 seconds in a 30-second advert. There's no limit on speed - it's decided on a session-by-session basis. If it sounds like the audience is being shouted at, a producer will reject that take.

questions.question: Regarding the pole star - in our heliocentric model, why does it remain fixed while everything else is moving? If the universe is expanding, shouldn't the pole star be moving too?

answers.answer: I don't know that it is fixed. How do you know it hasn't moved? You weren't here thousands of years ago. It might have moved further away, but if it was super bright, the human eye wouldn't detect that change.

answers.caller: Matt Zinskar (Master Mariner, Captain at Sea)
answers.answer: The North Star is currently observed above our axis of spin - the Earth's axis. So it appears steady in the sky. But it IS moving - it's so far away it's moving very slowly away from the axis. In a couple of thousand years time, it will be to one side and we won't have a pole star anymore.

questions.question: Why do countries have different names in different languages? For example, Anglia/Germany, and even road names stay the same but countries change. Why is it different for countries?

answers.answer: Part of it is translation - if I visited from France, I'd call it 'land of the angles' too, which becomes Angleterre in French. But that doesn't explain things like Anglia. The question of how much is simple translation vs. something else - I don't know.

questions.caller: Chris (Kingston) - question from his daughter Charlotte
questions.question: How do cats manage to communicate between themselves? They meow at humans but apparently not at each other.

answers.answer: Cats' meow is actually an imitation of a child - they evolved to make a sound similar to a child in need so humans are more likely to respond. But when cats interact with each other, it's all body language - visual signals, grooming, petting, friendly biting. They also communicate through urine (pheromones) to mark territory for cats who aren't there at the time. They can tell when another cat is relaxed through body language.

questions.question: Do animals know that they're pregnant? They just pop out babies and have to figure things out. Is this about consciousness or biology?

answers.answer: Some animals go and nest - create a little space under the table or bed when they're going to have kittens or puppies. So there must be some evolutionary impulse. Whether it would be knowledge in the human sense, I don't know. There's a state of discomfort that culminates in a 'just get the bloody thing out of me now' attitude, but I don't know if they'd have that awareness beforehand.

questions.question: I have a monstera adansonii (cheese plant) and the leaves have more holes than leaf. How did that evolve? Do plants evolve?

answers.answer: Plants do evolve - a mutation occurs that gives an advantage in the environment, therefore gets replicated. In the Amazon where there's not much light, having holes in leaves means less chlorophyll so you need less sunlight to thrive. A plant was born with a mutation for holes in leaves, and because of the Amazon environment where light is scarce, that was an evolutionary advantage.

The holes (called fenestrations, from Latin for window) allow sunlight to come through to reach the lower foliage. It's about light, not wind. I bought a cheese plant that arrived without holes and phoned to complain - they said the holes develop as it grows, which is correct.

questions.question: When a king is on the throne, his wife is a queen (Queen Camilla). But when a queen is on the throne (Elizabeth II), her husband is not a king - he's a Duke (Philip) or Prince (Albert). Why?

answers.answer: King outranks queen on a chessboard or pack of cards. If Prince Philip was King Philip, people would automatically think he outranked the queen. But you could introduce a new rule saying king doesn't outrank queen anymore. I don't really know.

It's about rank - a king is deemed higher ranked than a queen. If Prince Philip was King Philip, that would cause a constitutional crisis because people would think he outranked the king. You could pass an act of parliament to make them equals, but that would be a change in the constitution, and we don't have a written constitution, so it's more convention.

questions.question: Did Chloe get the job after quoting Mystery Hour as an example of keenness to learn at her interview?

answers.answer: Multiple theories: 1) She didn't get the job - was going for farmhand job on Charlie's farm (John's theory); 2) She was going for a job at Jacob Rees-Mogg's pieces; 3) Interview terminated when she mentioned James's name (pro-Brexit interviewer); 4) She did get the job with a creative answer (Marita's theory)
Confirming she didn't get the job - she was being interviewed for a farmhand position

questions.question: What is the point of some mugs being microwave safe and others not? What do you have to put into a mug to make it microwave safe or leave out?

answers.answer: It's to do with the temperature at which the ceramic is fired at. Earthenware is low-fired porous ceramics like flower pots which hold water. Stoneware-fired ceramics become what we call vitreous so the glass particles melt and seal the body so it can't absorb water, which is why it would be microwave safe. If you'd bought a mug from a craft fair, it may not have been fired at such a high temperature and it would not be microwave proof.

questions.question: Why is it that when the sun is setting, it appears to go faster than it does throughout the rest of the day?

answers.answer: It's about what our eyes are drawn to. If you're watching something move towards something, you're watching the space between the sun and the horizon shrink. Whereas otherwise you're just watching a ball on a big screen - you're not seeing it shrink.

The sun is a fixed point. We travel around the sun at the same speed and we spin on our axes at the same speed, so it's not actually quicker. It's all about perception. If you think about the film The Aviator, Howard Hughes noticed that planes without clouds in the sky appeared not to be moving. The clouds or the planes then appeared to move quicker and they weren't. So with the sun, as it reaches the horizon there are two contacts - one in the sky and one at the ground - and that makes it appear faster.

What Andy said about the relative position of the horizon and sun is completely correct. However, technically it appears to go slower now. As the sun gets lower in the sky and you're standing on the beach looking at the horizon, the further out to the horizon there is more atmosphere. As the sun passes into that light it gets refracted more - that's the same reason why the sky appears red at sunset - and as it passes into that apparent position because of the lights being refracted more, it will appear slightly higher in the sky. The effect of that is that it would appear slower. The higher it is, the slower it would appear as it gets to the horizon.

questions.question: Why is it that as an English person watching a film that's in English language, and if it has English subtitles, I'm still fixated on reading the subtitles?

answers.answer: Your eyes are naturally drawn to two key things - light and movement. Like hunting birds of prey or lions looking for a break in the pattern of the ground. Also in photographs and light areas in paintings, your eyes naturally go to the light. The subtitles are illuminated in a way that the rest of the action on the screen is not. They're scrolling and using white font so they're doing both - light and movement. That's why they're drawn to them.

questions.question: How come a raven can hop onto a live rail and nothing happens to it?

answers.answer: It's the same reason a bird can sit on a power line. Electricity will always take the path of least resistance to ground. A raven sitting on a live rail has no path to ground - they're just sitting on that rail, so they are essentially insulated from the ground. If they lifted one foot from the rail and put it on the ground they'd be toast. A human could also theoretically walk on a live rail as long as they didn't earth themselves, but that's absolutely not recommended.

questions.question: Why is it that when you heat up sparkling water, it loses its sparkles or bubbles?

answers.answer: The carbon dioxide in the fizzy water. As temperature increases in the water, the solubility of the carbon dioxide decreases, so therefore it leaves the bottle as bubbles. This is one of the examples of positive feedback - if you think about the oceans and global heating, the oceans have got lots of carbon dioxide in them. As the temperature has gone up because of the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, that heats the water so less carbon dioxide dissolves in the water, so it comes out. And as the temperature keeps increasing, the amount of carbon dioxide coming out of the oceans is just going to get more and more.

questions.question: Why is it when cats, particularly on ledges and tables, like to push things off?
Why is the bit that you put in mince pies called mince meat when it's not actually minced meat?

answers.answer: It used to have meat in it. Mince meat (no D) as opposed to minced meat that you might use to make a bolognese. The old usage would describe meat that was preserved by the addition of spices - you'd have beef with raisins and currants and spices like cinnamon. But as the years have passed, we took the meat out of it, and now it's fruit-based. There are also spirits like rum in traditional recipes preserved the meat.

questions.question: Why do hills look less steep in black and white photographs than they do in real life?

answers.answer: Black and white cameras are usually old cameras with fixed lenses, and they're usually wide-angle lenses, not telephoto. When you use a wide-angle lens, a hill looks much flatter on it than it does on a telephoto lens.

questions.question: What's the criteria for something to be classed as 'old school'? How old do you have to be to become old school?

answers.answer: The term 'old school' was first used to describe a musical genre. In the early 1980s, soul and funk DJs started looking back at obscure album tracks and rediscovering them. The original 'old school' anthem is Gwen McCulloch's 'All This Love That I'm Giving'. The DJs found these album tracks which were recorded in analog with poor recording levels. The term has since been used for anything that harks back to a preceding generation's sound or style. If one generation listened to something, the next generation calling something 'old school' for being influenced by that previous era would be accurate.

questions.question: When did we stop getting new surnames for people? For example, Barber, Gardner, Baker, Smith are common surnames that are occupations. But things like hairdresser or librarian aren't surnames.

Is there a word that defines the phenomenon of when you add a letter to a word, it changes the sound of the other letters in that word? For example, 'have' with an S added becomes 'shave' - adding the S changes the sound of A.

answers.answer: These are called digraphs. In many cases, the number of letters in an alphabet is not the same as the number of sounds (phonemes), so some sounds have to be represented by combinations of letters. For example, 'SH' normally stands for 'sh' as in ship - it doesn't have much to do with the sound of S on its own or H on its own. 'PH' is another example, representing the F sound, usually from Greek words. These are digraphs - one sound represented by two letters together. I'm not sure there's a specific technical word for the process that changes the sound when you add a letter. Some people call it a 'magic E' when there's a silent E that changes the vowel quality, but I don't think there's one technical word for the process.

questions.question: Why are there so many stories about statues of famous people that don't look anything like their subject?

Can you ever forget how to swim after you've learned? If you haven't swum for 30 or 40 years but you could swim, and then you fell in or dived in, would nature kick in? Or is there a chance you could just flail around?

answers.answer: I suspect there's a kind of genetic, a sense memory involved. Because the momentum that you need on a bicycle and the momentum that you need to swim are probably similar in some psychological way.
When Gareth said if you forget how to ride a bike, you just sit there, Steve pointed out no, you don't. You fall off.

I am living proof that you can forget how to swim. At primary school age I was able to swim after taking lessons - up to a length. But then for decades after that I've never had any occasion to swim. I've taken lessons as an adult - a year's worth of weekly lessons with additional practice time - and I know what to do but I cannot coordinate. I cannot swim. I swim like a brick.

You can forget something you've learned, although something of a skill that you mastered really well would go into your long-term memory and be harder to forget. She probably hadn't done it enough to imprint it on the long-term memory. It's called muscle memory. When people have neurological damage, like after a stroke, if it affects that area of the brain they also lose muscle function.

questions.question: Do fruit trees produce less or lower quality fruits as they get older? I see new plantations of trees and wonder if it's a new harvest or if they have to replant every so many years.

answers.answer: The short answer is I don't know.

They do diminish in yield and quality. But there's a trade-off - if you replant an orchard it takes quite a few years for the trees to get back up to full size. There are other reasons you might replant - tastes change, you might re-space the trees to allow for mechanical harvesters. There are lots of variables.

questions.caller: Nicola from Uxbridge (on behalf of 6-year-old daughter Keira)
questions.question: If somebody was to jump out of a window that's 100 floors up, would their parachute open in time?

answers.answer: I think the answer is yes. A base jump from 500 feet will only have a parachute ride of about 10 to 15 seconds. So we need to think of a parachute more as an emergency break that kicks in just before impact. But 500 feet wouldn't translate as 100 stories - it'd be higher than that.

answers.caller: Paul from Worcester Park (67-year-old former army paratrooper)
answers.answer: A hundred story billboard is a big deal. Using roughly eight feet per story you're talking about 800 feet. In the 1970s with old-fashioned army parachutes we would jump at 800 feet and land quite safely. Parachutes are so much better developed now. The answer is a definite yes for Keira.

I have literally jumped out of windows in buildings. I've jumped from as low as 122 feet. I've jumped from bridges, cranes, casinos. The lower you jump, the quicker you need to extract the canopy. Yes, categorically.

questions.question: Can someone explain why two people can hear the same word differently? His company made 500 meerkat toys with a sound chip inside them that said 'simples.' One lady rang up and said her meerkat says 'haggis.'

answers.answer: I've heard it before. That's a fairly comprehensive explanation.

answers.caller: Mike from Peter Lee (music nerd and 50-year-old musician)
answers.answer: If I tell you that you're hearing something, you will hear it. This has been proven in court in the US in the 1980s. Judas Priest were prosecuted for alleged backwards messages. The defence said pick any song randomly, wind it backwards and you'll hear what you want to hear. They won the case. So when Bruce said 'haggis', he put 'haggis' in all our brains. That's all it is.

Why do vinegar and brown vinegar have use-by dates if they're both preservatives?

answers.answer: Vinegar does go off. You get a really old bottle of vinegar out the back of your nan's cupboard and it's gone all cloudy with lots of sediment in it.

answers.caller: Pratap from Islington (chef and vinegar maker, member of the Fermenters Guild)
answers.answer: Technically vinegar won't actually go off, but if it is a live vinegar like a live apple cider vinegar, it can over-oxidize. Once the bacteria finishes converting the alcohol into acetic acid, it then starts converting the vinegar into water and carbon dioxide if not stored properly. The acetic acid content dilutes down and it's no longer viable for preservation. This only happens with live vinegars, not with normal malt vinegar or white vinegar.

What does a mental breakdown look like? Where on the spectrum from minor issue (putting socks on wrong feet) to psychosis (seeing wolves coming to eat them) is 'mental breakdown'? How do you know the difference? Does biology change? Do brainwaves change?

answers.answer: MRI scans show mental distress in the brain - traumatised brains light up differently. In distress, the emotional brain takes over in fight/flight/freeze mode first. For non-traumatised people, the rational brain kicks in afterward to assess if the reaction is appropriate. Traumatised people's rational brain shuts down during flashbacks.
