Sectioning happens when someone poses a danger to themselves - the safety point of whether they're safe in the community.

questions.question: CO2 is heavier than air, and in school experiments with a candle in a container, CO2 settles at the bottom and puts out the candle. Why doesn't CO2 sink to ground level in a valley and suffocate everyone?

answers.answer: Two reasons - microscopic and macroscopic. Microscopically, there's not much weight difference between CO2, oxygen and nitrogen molecules, and they're all travelling 1-2 miles per second, constantly colliding with each other so nothing can settle. Macroscopically, the atmosphere is constantly moving - if you imagine Frank's space as a tin can, it's being constantly shaken so nothing settles at the bottom. Even at very cold temperatures like minus 200 degrees you might see a slight effect, but not much. Like floating cream on coffee - it stays because it's lighter, but give it a stir and it mixes up and doesn't come back.

questions.question: Why are there so many Turkish barbers? Are they actually Turkish or is it just a style? Why that corner of the world produces so many barber shops?
If you go profoundly deaf, can you still suffer from tinnitus?

answers.answer: Tinnitus is actually within the brain, specifically in the auditory cortex, whereas deafness is in the cochlea. So tinnitus and deafness are linked but separate - you can be profoundly deaf and still have tinnitus because the sound is generated in the brain, not the ear. About 80% of profoundly deaf people have tinnitus as well. Robbie's qualifications: both his parents are profoundly deaf, his partner is deaf, and all of them have tinnitus.

questions.question: Why does the heating in my car go cold when I go around a roundabout? It happens halfway around, and it's happened in two different cars.

answers.answer: It's not that the heating goes cold - the air density in the car can't turn or stop as quickly as the car does. When you go around a roundabout, the cooler air in the back of the car moves forward and compresses, creating a draft against the vent and taking the warm air away from you. You feel the cooler air. David saw an experiment with helium balloons - a balloon filled with normal air pinned to the ceiling goes forward when braking, while a helium balloon pinned to the floor goes backward. So the hot air is still there, just no longer hitting Lauren. If you could colour the warm air, you'd see it just move to the front of the car.

questions.question: Is it Mystery Hour that has received a £100,000 fine from Ofcom for impartiality?

answers.answer: No. It's a platform popular among people who think everyone else is biased and impartial, but they are in receipt of the Real News. They've been hit with a £100,000 fine for one of the most egregious examples of political bias in broadcasting.

questions.question: Why are pumpkins associated with Halloween?

answers.answer: It goes back to an Irish tradition with turnips. There's a character called Stingy Jack who played a trick on the devil and was punished for it. The jack-o'-lanterns named after him were originally turnips. When Irish immigrants went over to America, the seasonal vegetable there were pumpkins, so they just used a different vegetable.

questions.question: Are voices unique like fingerprints? Could there be someone who sounds exactly like me?

answers.answer: Of course there are people who sound exactly like you. But the question is whether it's biologically identical to fingerprints.

questions.question: Why do some cheeses have holes in them?

answers.answer: Carbon dioxide from bacteria in the cheese creates the holes. The bacteria produce carbon dioxide during the curdling process, and in some cheeses the bubbles grow into holes.

questions.question: Why do footballers run to the corner to celebrate goals?

answers.answer: Because 50% of games are away, so they condition themselves to run to the corner for their fans. You could also factor in TV cameras.

questions.question: If Kamala Harris wins the presidential election, who will certify the results since the Vice President is the one who certifies?

answers.answer: I presume it's the Speaker of the House. They're next in the line of succession.

Actually, Kamala would preside over herself because she's also the Vice President of the Senate and it's a joint session. George H.W. Bush did this in 1989 when he ran for Reagan. Al Gore had to certify for Bush even though he'd lost.

questions.question: Why is the Deputy Speaker always the one who presides over the Budget?

answers.answer: The budget is a Ways and Means resolution. Anything that leads to the government raising taxes is always presided over by the senior deputy speaker, who is called the Chairman of Ways and Means. The Speaker can't do it. There are three deputy speakers all with similar titles.

questions.question: How do slugs get to the top of Munro mountains?

answers.answer: The same way they get anywhere - slowly.

questions.question: Why can the brain remember that it's forgot something but not remember what it's forgot?

answers.answer: When you keep trying to remember something, you set up a reverberation circuit that overloads the system. If you stop and pause, it calms down and allows the answer to pop in. Also, we remember that something is filed but are not sure where it's filed yet.

questions.question: Do they breed frogs specifically for frog's legs in France? And what do they do with the rest of the body?

answers.answer: Yes, they do farm them. There's quite a lot of frog farms in China as well.

They don't actually do anything with the body except throw it back. I used to import frog's legs. Compassion in World Farming sent me information showing frog carcasses floating down rivers. It was polluting the rivers. They just discard frog carcasses on an industrial scale. It stopped my business.

questions.question: Why do we say 'let's be frank' when we want to be straightforward? Who is Frank?

answers.answer: It's nothing to do with someone called Frank. It comes from 'lingua franca' - the language that both parties understand. To be frank means to be open and free in your talking with one another. That's where 'frankly' comes from too, from old French.

questions.question: Why does the moon always face the earth? Is it just luck that it turns precisely once every 28.2 days?

answers.answer: Tidal locking. The moon takes exactly the same time to complete one rotation on its axis as it does to orbit the Earth. The gravity pull causes this.

You were correct about tidal locking, but the moon doesn't actually go around the Earth - both the moon and Earth orbit around a point in space known as Lagrange points. That's the anchor that provides the locking.

questions.question: Where is the second world? We use the description first world and third world - what happened to the second?

answers.answer: The term Second World is a Cold War-era term to describe post-World War II countries like Russia and China that weren't Third World countries and weren't First World countries. In modern times it's been recategorised as emerging markets like India and Bangladesh.

Why is the sky darker blue above a rainbow and lighter blue below it?

answers.answer: The bit of the rainbow you see isn't all of it - it's actually a full circle. The brighter part is what's inside of that circle, where all the light rays that have been reflected by rain all meet in the middle. So the lighter part is inside the circle.

questions.question: Why do we sing in the shower?

answers.answer: The acoustics are really good in a shower.

It's about confidence. No one can hear you because the noise of the shower is drowning you out. You also can't hear yourself properly, so you think you're quiet when you're not. The soundproofing nature of the shower and the acoustics combined.

questions.question: Who awards hotel stars internationally? Are the ratings consistent between countries? In Dubai they have seven-star hotels - what makes something qualify?

answers.answer: In the UK it's either the AA or the RAC. As soon as you move outside the UK, it's the Wild West - you can just open a hotel and call it five stars. The Middle East particularly has self-awarded stars where someone invests in a big hotel and calls it seven stars, then someone else builds a bigger one and calls it eight stars.

questions.question: Why is a tea towel called a tea towel? Why not just a kitchen towel?

answers.answer: My grandma was a maid in a stately home. The tea towel was initially a towel to wrap the teapot in to keep it warm before the tea cosy was invented. It was for stately homes and posh people, and it was folded in a precise origami-style way to encompass the whole teapot.

questions.question: Why do people, even normally quiet people, erupt such a loud noise when they sneeze?

answers.answer: I think it's really enjoyable - maybe louder sneezing is more satisfying. People have thrown their backs out sneezing. But I think it just feels great to really clean the pipes.

questions.question: My mortgage has nearly doubled over four years to £2,000. Who's benefiting from that extra £1,000? Where does the money go?

answers.answer: Some people are earning interest on their deposits and some people are paying it. The lenders will have money on deposit too. The bank keeps some of it and some goes to people with large deposits.

Ultimately the money goes to the banks' trading P&L. But banks borrow money - they don't just match deposits to loans. There's fractional reserve banking, bank dealing desks borrowing overnight and lending for 30 years. So if his mortgage has doubled, it doesn't mean the banks' profits have doubled. The money may even be a loss if the bank borrowed at a higher rate than they're getting back.

questions.question: Why do we say 'Company and Sons' but almost never 'Company and Daughters'?

answers.answer: Companies with 'and sons' in their title are likely pre-1950s when sons would follow into family businesses. Daughters, even if they did join, would probably leave when they married and started families. questions.question: Why isn't there a law where motorists should never be allowed to touch alcohol when going to drive?
Why can I see the Northern Lights through my phone camera but not with my naked eye?

answers.answer: It depends on how bright the lights are. You have cone cells and rod cells in your eyes. Cone cells see colour but only work in light/daytime. Rod cells see in black and white and work at night. When you look at your phone screen, the light activates your cone cells so you can see colour. If you look away from the screen at the sky, your cone cells aren't activated so you can't see the colour.

A camera can record images over several seconds, seeing things the naked eye can't. The exposure is longer so it captures light you can't see with the naked eye. On a camera, photographers record over several seconds or even minutes to get the brightest images.

questions.question: Why do I get a stitch (pain in the side) after about a mile of running?

answers.answer: There's no single cause for a stitch - it's a global term for pain in the side while running. The most common cause is lack of blood supply to the diaphragm, which can lead to cramp of the diaphragm, usually caused by shallow breathing or breathing out of rhythm with your running stride. Marathon runners very rarely get it.

Niblings is the gender-neutral word for nieces and nephews. For aunts and uncles, it's 'pibblings' - your parent-sibling. It's even in use. My youngest non-binary child is a pibbling to my granddaughter.

questions.question: Why do we call them Steg and Hendos? What is the origin of 'stag' and 'hen' for stag and hen nights?
Why does the government form a 'cabinet' instead of any other piece of furniture?

answers.answer: In the early 18th century, landed gentlemen returning from the Grand Tour kept their curiosities in a piece of furniture with lots of compartments called a cabinet, kept in their most private quarters. After dinner they'd show guests their curiosities in the cabinet. By the 1730s under Walpole, the room where the collection was kept was called the Cabinet. Walpole took his ministers into that room to discuss government business because King George I couldn't speak English - it had to be kept secret and quiet. So the room became the Cabinet, and then the group of ministers became the Cabinet.

questions.question: Why is toothpaste always minty?

Colgate do a peaches and cream toothpaste and one with Asian lemon oil. There's also Willy Wonka chocolate toothpaste that probably has a hint of mint.

questions.question: How do you wash planes, especially jumbo jets? Do they wash the wings?

One person would go up in a cherry picker and spray, while others cleaned by hand with mops. They cleaned two planes a night and then got paid for the whole shift - quite cushy.

questions.question: How do they know a comet last passed Earth 80,000 years ago? How can they possibly know that?

answers.answer: You put the comet in an orrery, give it a spin, and spin it until you've reached 80,000 years worth of spins. Then the comet pops up again. It's maths.

It's because of Johannes Kepler, who made three rules of planetary motion. All orbits are ellipses. He did maths - you extrapolate from observable phenomena. You can predict the future because the laws of science and physics are constant. Kepler's laws explain orbital motion.

questions.question: Why do we never say 'whelmed'? We say 'overwhelmed' and 'underwhelmed' but never just 'whelmed'.

questions.question: What makes an English county a 'shire'? Why are some counties shires (Hampshire, Cambridgeshire, Devonshire, Shropshire, Worcestershire) and others aren't (Sussex, Surrey, Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex, County Durham)?

answers.answer: Anglo-Saxon origins. Originally spelled S-C-I-R; S-N-C in Old English is equivalent to modern S-H. The coin of the Shire was a shilling. A Shire was a measurement of land - Anglo-Saxons measured farmland in 'hides' (roughly 100-120 acres), and 10 hundreds make a Shire. County towns had a 'reeve' known as a Shire-reeve, which is where we get 'sheriff'. Sussex = South Saxon, Wessex = West Saxon, Essex = East Saxon. Counties that aren't shires were Angles, not Saxons. It's simply which areas were called Shires back in the day.

Who makes the decision about whether a tin has a ring pull or requires a tin opener? Is it the factory, the product, or something else? Why do some cans have ring pulls and others don't?

questions.question: Have deaf people created slang within sign language, or a secret language that only certain people can learn?

answers.answer: Yes, sign language has regional variations and slang. He's been signing for 20 years, having learned it through a girlfriend whose mother was a sign language teaching assistant. This is because transmission was limited before Skype and Zoom - people in Hull watched London-centric BSL and developed local variations. Within regions, people develop 'lazy' shorthands - he and his girlfriend only used their right hand for half-signs, a geographically specific contraction. Slang mainly involves strong contractions and disparaging words. The sign for 'fish' varies - some put thumb under chin and wiggle four fingers, others make a different sign. questions.question: Why does she sometimes forget English words while improving her German? Is there a relationship between learning a new language and forgetting some of the old one?

questions.question: If you step on a snail and break its shell but the snail is otherwise unharmed, can it survive without its shell?

answers.answer: The shell is supported by a mantle, which is like a muscular plug inside the shell. If the shell goes, the lungs can no longer be supported by the outside structure of the shell, and they suffocate. You cannot remove a snail from its shell—it would die. There are some examples where people have healed tiny holes with plaster of Paris, but it's very rare. The structure supports the lung organs, and without that, the snail has no chance.

questions.question: Why do Americans call a cup of coffee a cup of Joe?

answers.answer: In the early part of the 20th century, the Secretary of State for the United States Navy banned alcohol from ships. Therefore, the strongest thing you could have was a cup of joe. They actually called it 'a cup of uncle Joe.' The Secretary of State's first name was Joe, so in honour of the politician who denied them anything stronger, they called it a cup of Joe.

questions.question: When you're sitting on a plane on the runway accelerating before takeoff, you feel pushed back in your seat. But when you're up in the sky, the plane is going even faster and you don't feel that push. What's the reason for this?

answers.answer: It's to do with relativity. When you reach the same speed as the aeroplane, you don't feel it. It's conservation of momentum. Like standing on Earth at the equator, you don't feel you're moving at a thousand miles an hour. The Earth is spinning around the sun at thousands of miles an hour, the sun is spinning around our galaxy at hundreds of thousands of miles an hour, and the galaxy is rocketing through space—but we don't feel any of it because we're moving at the same speed.

Steve mentioned Newton, but it's Newton's second law—force equals mass times acceleration. When you're accelerating on a plane, you experience acceleration because you're a mass and hence you feel a force. When you're at a constant velocity or stationary, you're experiencing no acceleration, so you feel no force. When the plane is at cruise, you're not being accelerated. This is Newton's laws of motion, not Einsteinian relativity with space and time.

questions.question: What is the official dividing line between North and South London? Chelsea is north of the river but is SW postcode. Why isn't there an official dividing line?

answers.answer: Postcode areas roughly around the capital are N, E, W—and for our purposes, S and W. The directions are fairly clear: SW and SE are South London. N, E, and W are North London. And then in the middle there's EC and WC for East Central and West Central. Chelsea is an anomaly—it's SW3 north of the river while Brixton is SW2 south of the river. There is no official designation of where north stops and south begins. The Royal Mail would tell you it changes where the postcode line changes, which was based on where the head sorting offices were. Chelsea couldn't just be made W because W is further north (Bayswater, Chiswick, Acton). Each area was allocated a code based on where the sorting offices are located.

questions.question: Why do clothes moths attack cotton T-shirts almost always in the lower abdomen/navel area? Whether the T-shirts are folded or squished in a drawer, the holes are always in the same place. It's not belt buckles or contact damage.

answers.answer: The holes are caused by the T-shirt rubbing against the metal buttons on jeans and similar trousers. It's not moths at all. There's a product you can buy online—a little silicone rubber cover that goes over the buttons on jeans to stop this happening. The repeated incidence of holes in exactly the same place across a range of garments proves it, plus moths wouldn't burrow in the same location every time. The caller herself said it's not belt buckles or contact damage, but metal buttons on trousers would cause exactly this kind of gradual rubbing damage over time.

questions.question: St. Paul's Cathedral has two towers, one with a clock and one with a gaping hole that's never been filled. Why does one tower have a clock and the other have an empty aperture?

answers.answer: It's actually a bell chamber. The bells are just out of sight, below the level of the hole. There are actually four holes all around the tower, all the same size. The ringing room is halfway down where a little rectangular window is. The south tower contains the clock mechanism. It's a belfry—where the bells are housed.

questions.question: Why do you have to chase an itch? When you try to scratch a pinpoint itch on your back, you have to say 'go left, go right, go up, go down' to your wife, and the itch moves around until you never actually get to the bottom of it.
Why do seagulls stand on one leg? They look precarious and it doesn't seem like the most efficient or comfortable position.

answers.answer: It's about body heat. A bird's leg is one of the very few unfeathered parts of a bird, and they lose a lot of body heat through their legs. If you tuck one leg under in your feathers, it keeps warm, so you're only losing body heat through one leg rather than two. Flamingos do this too—and they're often in hot countries—but they're in water, so they'd lose heat through their legs in the water. They take one leg out, tuck it in among their feathers, and lose less body heat overall, staying warmer.

questions.question: Can we get an albino in all species? Humans, snakes, rats, any animals?

answers.answer: Any organism that produces melanin can be an albino. There is a gene that switches off the gene for melanin production. Whether it's a mammal or a reptile, if it produces melanin normally, it can theoretically produce an albino version. Anything that produces melanin can have albinism. Jellyfish are transparent, so that wouldn't apply to them—but any organism with the melanin production system could potentially have the albino variant.

questions.question: Why do we laugh? What is the evolutionary mechanism in our brains and bodies that makes us laugh at something?
What makes a beach more likely to have sea glass or ceramic in it than others?

answers.answer: It's about proximity to industry that used to dump waste into the sea. Glass factories and bottle works would dump waste directly into the sea. Seaham in the North East is world famous for sea glass because of the bottle works industry. The glass gets smoothed by salt and waves over time. It also depends on ocean currents washing stuff up on beaches. Same applies to ceramics (potteries dumped waste) and sea coal (slag dumped out to sea).

questions.question: Do animals (cats and dogs) suffer from shame or embarrassment?

answers.answer: It's debatable and largely anthropomorphism. Dogs can feel discomfort and slight self-shame but we project our embarrassment onto them. When dogs look 'sheepish' after destroying a sofa, they're actually just displaying pacifying behavior - picking up on their owner's anger and trying to appease them. It's the same face they pull when they want to be fed. It's an anatomical coincidence that we interpret as apologetic.

questions.question: When did people realize there were different time zones in the world?

answers.answer: Time zones were invented in the 1840s when railways opened in the UK. The railway between London and Bristol meant travellers with pocket watches noticed the time in London was different to the time in Bristol. This led to 'Railway Time' which later became British Standard Time, and this spread through British colonies. The telegraph later proved it in the United States.

questions.question: Is there a vernal equinox for the moon? Can the moon ever be directly overhead?

answers.answer: We live in the northern latitude so the moon will never be directly overhead. You need to be between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn to see the moon directly overhead. Both the sun and moon are at different angles to us (sun at about 15 degrees, moon at about 5 degrees) due to our orbital paths. Eratosthenes worked this out in ancient Egypt by measuring shadow angles at different locations to calculate the Earth's diameter.

questions.question: When we put sunglasses on, why doesn't the iris of the eye open up to accommodate the dark lens?

answers.answer: When you look in a mirror with sunglasses on, you're looking up close. Near vision triggers the accommodative reflex which includes slight constriction of the pupil. So you're seeing pupil constriction due to the near-vision focus, not because of the sunglasses. If someone looked at you from a distance, they'd see your pupils actually dilating with sunglasses on. This is the same reason older people need reading glasses - the lens-thickening process doesn't work as easily.

questions.question: How do generations get their names? Who names them? How did they decide the baby boomers ended in 1964 and Generation X began?

answers.answer: Generation names just catch on in common parlance. Baby boomers came from the post-war baby boom terminology. Douglas Coupland is credited with coining 'Generation X' in his 1991 novel 'Generation X: Tales for an Accelerated Culture.' After that, Generation Y, Z, and then Alpha followed. There's no official body naming them - it just catches on.

questions.question: When he loads his washing machine with a duvet cover plus socks, pants, and other items, why does everything end up inside the duvet cover by the end of the cycle?

answers.answer: It's about the aperture (the opening). A duvet cover has one hole - getting in is easy (one opportunity). Once inside, you get tangled and it's hard to get out. The sock has infinite chances to pass through the aperture as the drum rotates, but once it gets in and tangled, it's much harder to get out due to the physics of centrifugal force and entanglement. Steve confirmed by imagining himself trying to get out of a duvet cover after rolling around tangled.

questions.question: Why do some people get bitten more by mosquitoes than others? My daughters have different experiences - one gets riddled in bites, the other is fine. Is it something to do with blood?

answers.answer: Added to list - no answer given on air

Mosquitoes bite based on blood type, bacteria on skin, and clothing. Everyone has bacteria on skin naturally, but different bacteria can cause different reactions making you more attractive to mosquitoes. His teacher told him to study this in the library when he was young.

questions.question: Why is there shark liver oil in Preparation H (pile cream)? How would someone discover that shark liver oil is good for hemorrhoids?

answers.answer: Theorized it could be about dehydrating/shrinking effect - same reason some people use pile cream around eyes to reduce bags. If shark's liver is a known source of that chemical, it would be in the ingredients for shrinking effect.

questions.question: Why does tea change colour and taste worse after time? I use a flask when driving for 5 hours and the last cup looks grey. Same happens with tea left in microwave for 2 hours. Is it milk, tea, or oxidisation/enzymes?

answers.answer: Added to list - science is the answer but specific mechanism not discussed

questions.question: Is there science behind why couples end up looking like each other over time? My mum says my partner and I look alike after 12 years together but we don't have similar features.

answers.answer: Empathetic mimicry - subconscious mirroring of each other's mannerisms can impact how observers see you as similar. Also mentioned Chinese phrase Fu Qi Xiang (pronounced Fu Qi Xiang) meaning similarities in the face and appearance of old couples.

questions.question: Why does a car key fob work from far away when you put it to your head and look at your car, but not when you're at distance away normally? Is it conductivity?

answers.answer: Head acts as a bell/amplifier. Brain is mushy so doesn't interfere with amplifying qualities of skull. Best place is under your chin with mouth open.

It's height. Radio signals are line of sight and go in a straight line. If you hold it down low, it goes low. If you put it up high, it goes further. Tested it himself. Has degree in electrical and electronic engineering, worked in telecoms and defence.

questions.question: Why are there so many donkey sanctuaries in the UK if we don't use donkeys for work anymore? What do people use them for? Where are all these donkeys coming from?

answers.answer: Suggested if they don't work as much, they'd need sanctuaries, and then they breed. If they don't neuter them, a donkey sanctuary is a perfect business model. Keeps creating more product.

They import them from around the world, rescue them from places where they're still used for labour. Like Sidmouth Donkey Sanctuary - they literally extract them like military extractions. They come on a boat.

questions.question: What makes town pigeons look different from wood pigeons? Is it food, location, or something else that causes urban pigeons to change appearance? How long would it take a nice-looking wood pigeon to start looking rough in a town?

answers.answer: Suggested diet - city pigeons live on chips, what would you look like if you lived on chips? Also possibly stress.

Feral pigeons are result of thousands of years of human breeding. Wild progenitor is rock dove (Columba livia), bred selectively for 2000+ years for unique plumage. When pigeons escape and cross-breed, unique plumages cross and result in spectrum of different plumages. Some still look like wild type. Also bred for behavioural characteristics like tumblers. Is an ornithologist and environmental consultant.

questions.question: Can a recipe be copyrighted? If I take someone's recipe and change it slightly (like swapping Santa Lucia cheese for Cathedral City), can they sue me? Is this like music where even sampling a little bit gets you in trouble?

answers.answer: If it's in a published recipe book, there will be a form of copyright. But some recipes like carbonara can't be copyrighted since people have been making them forever. Wondered where the line is - in music you can't sample even a little bit.

questions.question: How do you get the letter of last resort to the nuclear submarine when a new prime minister takes over? And what happens in the gap between changes if something happens?

answers.answer: Thinks they wait until the submarine docks before changing the letter. Old letter stands until then.

Ex-Royal Navy warfare specialist on submarines. The letter is transmitted to the tech department (radar/sonar), then transferred via ship-to-ship rendezvous with the fleet along with supplies like food and fuel. There are 3-400 submarine warfare specialists in the whole Navy.

questions.question: Answer/correction: The Donkey Sanctuary in Sidmouth does NOT import donkeys from around the world. This is false information and should be corrected.

News agents or corner shops - those sort of places. How do they make money? You never see anyone doing a full shop in there. They're often right by a big supermarket. And people go in and buy a drink or a chocolate bar.

answers.answer: The short answer is they make a profit in the same way that everybody else does. They might be under threat from delivery services because the little things you need that you haven't got in your big weekly shop, you're going to pop to your local shop to get and pay a small premium for that. Also parcel pickup helps them.

One of the ways they deal with it is when supermarkets run promotions with half price or lower price compared to normal retail price, they buy and stock it and release it. Their margins are not high. Staying open all hours is really the secret - some days you're earning less than minimum wage hourly rate, but because you're open all the time, it evens out over the course of the year.

questions.question: If hot drinks keep you cool in the summer, would a cool drink sort of be better for you in the winter? So should we be drinking tea in the summer? And does it also apply to food? Should we be having currys and stews in the summer and salads in the winter? And perhaps that's why curry is such a big thing in Asia?

answers.answer: I just kind of doubt it [that cold drinks warm you up in winter]. But we'll see.

questions.question: In old movies and comics, prisoners would often be depicted as wearing uniforms with arrows on them. Did prisoners ever wear uniforms adorned with arrows? And if so, why did they put the arrows on them?

answers.answer: I think it's actually quite obvious when you think about it. If they escaped, they'd be quite easily recognizable. Until they managed to nick some clothes.

It was a symbol of government property. In the reign of William and Mary, they told the Earl of Romney, who is named Lord Sidney, that he must find a way of identifying government property to prevent theft. His family crest was a downward facing arrow, broad arrow. And so he used that. And all government property was stamped with the downward arrow.

questions.question: When I watch intricate operations on the telly and they make the incision with the scalpel, why doesn't it bleed a lot? If I cut myself, it bleeds. But when they cut into the skin, it never seems to bleed.

answers.answer: All tissues bleed when you cut them but some bleed more than others. Hands and fingers for example and the scalp have a much bigger blood supply than areas such as the skin on your abdomen or your back. There are also nuances: surgeons use blades called diathermy which actually seal off the blood vessels as they cut through the tissue layers. In some areas, surgeons will use local anesthetic infiltrated with adrenaline before they make the cut, which causes local constriction of blood vessels and prevents bleeding.

I would agree with everything Robin said. Different parts of the body bleed in different amounts. If you make a large incision on your abdomen, it's surprising you can cut through the very top layer of the skin and actually have relatively little bleeding. It's if you go deeper into the fat that's when you get more serious amounts of bleeding. What we tend to do is start to make a very superficial incision in the skin to begin with which often doesn't bleed that much, and then you use the cautery diathermy device to cut through the fat and get through the deeper layers.

questions.question: Royalty - royalty had a wardrobe of clothes. But where do they go? If you've got a relative that passed away, you normally bag up their bits and bobs and take them to a charity shop. But what happens to the amount of handbags, coats, shoes that the Queen had? There must have been hundreds of them. Where do they all go?

answers.answer: I don't know. I know she gave some to her servants - that was not unheard of for dressers to get some of the clothes. But you're talking about after she passed. What happened to her capacious wardrobe? It's a good question.
Queen Victoria's underwear often comes up for auction.

questions.question: How do electric toothbrushes charge? In order to charge it, it sits on a little plastic pedestal/nipple. But there's no metal contact. How do the electrons end up in the toothbrush?

answers.answer: It is magnets. It's magnetic fields transferring the power. It's called inductive charging - coils in the nipple and coils in the toothbrush create one circuit when you put them together that charges up the battery. You can do the same thing with wireless phone chargers.

questions.question: I'd like to know if local wildlife birds know the difference in branded food. I feed my local garden birds suet pellets and they love them. I've recently bought suet pellets from a different store and there's been no action in the last three weeks. The pellets look exactly the same - same color, same size - but it's just from a different shop.

answers.answer: They're not going to know the brand but they're going to know the recipe. There must be slightly different recipes between the two products.

My theory is that it's not so much about the brand of the suet pellets, but rather the seasonal instincts of the birds. Birds will naturally change their diet depending on the food that's available in the wild. The flowers that would produce seed and the plants that produce seed are now dying off. Suet pellets are high in fat and usually most satisfying for birds in winter and spring when they need the nutrients.

questions.question: What happened in a mobile phone call where he (Tim) and his wife kept repeating themselves in a 3-4 minute loop? They were both saying the same things and noticing each other repeat, and it turns out they had been cut off but somehow the conversation was being played back.

answers.answer: It sounds like your phone is being tapped and the conversation is being recorded. They are recording it and it just kept getting played back to you again and again.

What generally tends to happen is when doing overseas calls, the network jumps in and they repeat the conversation to keep you on the phone longer so that you're having to pay for the call more than what you should be.
Your calls are being recorded for training purposes - that's why your software repeats things back. That's what happened then.

questions.question: Have you ever heard of Caerphilly cheese? It's just disappeared. Like everywhere. Every supermarket, practically overnight, stopped selling it. Morrison's, Sainsbury's - you just cannot find it anywhere anymore. I wanted to know why.

answers.answer: Is it since Brexit? Could it have stopped with Brexit? It might have a constituent, an ingredient that has to come in from overseas and it's made it more expensive to make.

questions.question: Why do ambulance sirens have three different tones/sounds that all play in one go?

answers.answer: Ambulances have three different tones for different situations: short tone (neenaw neenaw) for junctions to alert people approaching; longer tone for driving along road; third tone for convoy driving so other drivers know there are two vehicles. Will likely heard two vehicles in convoy where the lead had long tones, then short at red lights, and the following vehicle had the third tone. Firefighters use a pedal to cycle through tones.

questions.question: Why do only some onions make you cry? Is it like Padron peppers where one in 20 or 30 is much more pungent? And have onions become less tear-inducing over time?

answers.answer: It's about the quality and freshness of the onions. When he grows his own onions and gives them to people, they cry a lot. Fresh onions are more tear-inducing. Store-bought onions have been sitting around in lorries for months in suspended animation and have lost their freshness. When you get them fresh from the allotment, they all make you cry. Suggestion: chop onion in half, leave one end attached until finished, or put in freezer to reduce chemicals released.

questions.question: Where did the X at the end of texts come from? When did an X or cross start representing a kiss?
Why does his blackbird Snowy wipe its food in the soil before eating it or taking it to the nest?

answers.answer: Blackbirds, particularly when feeding their young, often wipe earthworms through the soil for two reasons: either to take the slime off, or (as mentioned about the gizzard) to add grit. The grit helps break down and digest food, especially when feeding young. The pellets behave like earthworm - that's why the pellets get the treatment but not the raisins.

questions.question: Why do we call our children 'kids' which are baby goats? We don't call them kittens or puppies.
Why does the human brain make you feel like everything is in slow motion during car accidents and trauma?

answers.answer: David Eagleman researched this - threw people off towers 30 metres to test perception. The answer is about recollection vs perception. In the moment, it doesn't go in slow motion - that's proven. Time is an illusion. Different senses bring information at different times, brain integrates them into a narrative. When stressful events happen, there's so much going on, the brain needs longer to encode it all into high resolution memory. When you recall it later, it feels like slow motion because of the richness of the encoding. It's about memory, not actual perception. Every time we remember something, we're recreating and re-encoding it.

questions.question: Why do some surnames have colors (Black, White, Brown, Green, Gray) and others don't?

answers.answer: They're all descriptive of aspects of a person or the place they came from. There's Whitehead, Redhead, Green. Red might be read as in Brian Redhead. Black could come from blacksmith. Ball is a description of bald. Even names like Don come from old Celtic word for brown. They marked people out in tribal communities.

questions.question: Do pigeons have accents based on where they live, and how does that work if they're migratory?

answers.answer: He suspects George is describing two different species - a collared dove and a wood pigeon - which sound similar but not exactly the same. Later confirmed by Florence that birds can have different dialects depending on species.
Birds can have different dialects or accents depending on species. Some birds know how to sing innately when born but others are taught. This explains the variation George noticed.

questions.question: Why do chilli plants get hotter when you reduce watering frequency?

answers.answer: Explained through a thought experiment: Take a chilli, blend it with one cup of water, sip - mild. Then blend another with six cups of water, sip - much milder. The more waterdilution, the milder the taste. Less water means more concentrated capsaicin and sugars, making it hotter.Plants respond to stress by concentrating flavors.

questions.question: Why do coastal towns have a high proportion of bungalows?

answers.answer: Two reasons: 1) Seaside resorts are popular retirement destinations, and elderly people are less able to negotiate stairs, so bungalows are a clever commercial move for builders. 2) Views - everyone wants a sea view. If everyone is in a bungalow on gently rising land from the shore, everyone can see a bit of the sea instead of just the back of next door's house. Planning rules may also play a part.

questions.question: Why do we call children 'kids' when 'kid' also means baby goat? Why not puppies or kits (baby beavers)?

answers.answer: The word comes from Old English, Germanic in root, from 'Kin'. It only started being used about 300 years ago for humans in English, not for goats. The goat meaning is further back historically. The terms 'kith and kin' are related.

questions.question: Why do some of the best dramas from across the world insist on using empty takeaway coffee cups?

answers.answer: Discussed how the cup appears empty based on weight, heat, and absence of cardboard sleeve. Suggested directors prioritize convincing acting over realistic props, and proposed putting cold liquid in with a sleeve as a solution.
Health and safety - can't have water on set due to electrics. If someone spills, you wait for water to dry, causing continuity issues. Also technology reasons. He's an actor.

questions.question: Why do you get an incredible pain in your brain when you bite down on tinfoil with an amalgam filling, like when eating a Kit Kat?

answers.answer: It's hitting the nerve with a small amount of electricity caused by the electrolytic action between the silver paper and mercury amalgam fillings. Tony is a physicist.

questions.question: Why do I walk 10% faster backwards in a swimming pool than forwards? I tested this with myself and 10 others and got consistent results.

answers.answer: When walking forward, your leg is fully extended creating lots of resistance against the water. Walking backwards, you pick your foot up and push it backwards with less water resistance. Also, your hip flexor muscle is not as strong as your hamstring which moves your leg back. Steve is a retired aerobics instructor.

questions.question: When they're restoring black and white photos or video, how do they know the exact colour based on just grey? How can they find out what's there?

answers.answer: Explained that you use logic: buses are red, taxis are black, skin tones, and then match shades of grey accordingly. There are 257 shades of grey on the palette.

Light reflection off objects determines their shade in black and white - darker colours absorb more light, lighter colours reflect more. Restorers use human intelligence and assumptions (e.g., taxis are black, buses red) then technology to fill in matching shades. He's a keen amateur photographer who owns a camera shop.

Tonal differences used to be done by eye and guesswork. Now AI has got very good at recolouring photographs. He recoloured a photo earlier this week using modern AI after turning it back to black and white first. He restores photographs for funeral stationery.

questions.question: Beer and bread are cornerstones of early civilisation but you can't make those without yeast. How did they start putting yeast into stuff? Where does it come from?

answers.answer: Suggested humanity tried everything over millennia through trial and error, and fermentation was discovered by accident - someone saw a pig get happy eating rotten apples and tried it themselves.

In Africa, people buried food in sand to preserve it. They found it went bubbly, put reeds in to drink the liquid, got drunk, and kept doing it. For beer, yeast comes naturally from the air - pumped to top of brewery into a 'cool ship' with open windows, yeast inoculates naturally. The magic wand story: Egyptians didn't understand yeast, a stick worked because it had the right yeast on it, so they thought it was magic. Women were mostly brewers historically; when the church wanted to make money, they took brewing in-house and called the women witches. For bread, it was the same experimentation process. Bryn worked in beer and brewing industry for 12 years, now works in wine.

questions.question: Why don't we eat swans? And why do all the swans belong to the king?

answers.answer: Speculated they ate swans in Tudor times, mentioned the 'birds within birds' dish tradition.

The king's ownership only applies to swans on the Thames. His brother-in-law found a dead swan that had flown into pylons, contacted Defra (not the palace directly), got permission to eat it. It tasted like beef, not fishy, though not particularly nice. They had it at a medieval-themed family party. Swan is apparently still eaten in Denmark.

questions.question: How do indoor plants know what season it is? They follow the seasons even when kept at constant temperature indoors with no window access.

answers.answer: It's the quality of light, not temperature. In spring, when it's brighter for longer, plants absorb certain qualities of light which cause chemical conversions inside them, producing hormones that stimulate flowering and growth. You can fool plants with blue and red lights to simulate different seasons. This is how Iceland grows tomatoes year-round in greenhouses. Will is an A-level biology teacher.

questions.question: At what age do children or babies start becoming aware of others yawning around them and respond to it? Is yawning contagious from birth?

answers.answer: We have mirror neurons in the brain, specifically in the medial prefrontal cortex. We've had those from time immemorial because human beings are essentially a group species and to get on with the group it's very useful to pick up the expressions of people around you and then mirror them. So if someone yawns, you yawn. It's quite recent this discovery of the mirror neurons. People with autism or severe trauma have shut down mirror neurons which is why they withdraw and don't make eye contact.

questions.question: Why do automatic doors open extra slow if you approach them too fast? Is there a legitimate reason or is it psychological?

answers.answer: They actually do open slower when you approach fast. They have sensors to stop you getting too close and prevent you colliding with the door. If you're approaching too fast, the door's reaction is to stop rather than speed up. It works on sliding doors, swing doors, and every other type of automatic door. It's a safety feature.

questions.question: If you die in space and your body is floating, would it decompose like it would on Earth? What happens to a dead body in the vacuum of space?

answers.answer: No, we would not decompose. What would happen is our blood and bodily fluids would boil rapidly. Some of our organs would explode internally and we would freeze really, really rapidly because it's a little bit chilly in space. We would remain pretty much freeze-dried until somebody came along and brought us in and rehydrated us - then we would just rot away. Like space ice cream.

questions.question: Why can you go back to sleep after an alarm goes off on a work day, but if you wake up naturally minutes before your alarm on a weekend day, you can't get back to sleep even though you could sleep in?
Why do births, deaths and marriages have to be signed by a fountain pen? Is it the ink, tradition, or something else?

answers.answer: It's because they use a special ink called India ink - it's a solvent-based ink that cannot be removed by normal water-based ink. You can splash water on it and it will still be there. You can only apply that using a fountain pen because it's quite thick ink. So it's the ink that's specified, not the pen itself. The registrar offices used cheap Parker Vector pens and threw them away after a while because the ink would destroy them.

questions.question: Why can't pharmaceutical companies produce medication that doesn't have side effects? The technology must be there, surely?

answers.answer: It's largely a commercial imperative. Pharmaceutical companies get 25 years of patent and it takes about 10 years to develop the drug, so they want to bring it to market as quickly as possible. They also might not care about minor side effects if the medicine is effective for what it's treating. The biological reality is that you don't get something for nothing - there's always going to be some kind of side effect.

The body is a very complex system and a lot of what medicines target, whatever they're targeting, can also knock on to other areas of the body. For example, ibuprofen targets something called COX which is part of the inflammatory response, but COX is also involved in protection of the stomach lining and regulation of blood flow in the kidney, so you get knock-on effects in those systems.

questions.question: Why is it that we find certain sounds soothing like ocean waves and rainfall, while we find other sounds like construction sites not soothing (though the producer finds construction sites soothing)?
What were electric eels referred to before electricity was invented? Did they have a different name?

answers.answer: They're called 'perarchy' in the original language, which means something that numbs or stings. They're from the Amazon Basin and the original language is Rabacha. The first people to visit that area were Jesuit missionaries in the 1780s-1790s, which was after electricity had been generated for the first time. So we went in much later and said 'oh it's electricity' but it never was - we just gave it an electricity-related name.

questions.question: How far away is a rainbow? Is it 200 metres, a mile? When I see one from my house, how do I measure the distance?

answers.answer: The point of refraction is the raindrop itself. You've got a band of rain coming towards you, sunlight shining through it, and the eye sees millions and millions of points of light from the raindrop. It's like a physical magnifying glass - two people can look at the same magnifying glass from different angles and both see the image. So really, a rainbow is about as far away as the rain is. It depends on where you are.

questions.question: If you own land on a cliff and the cliff collapses into the sea due to coastal erosion, do you still own that land even though it's now at the bottom of the ocean or a beach below your house?

Why is it that you can go back to sleep when you have an alarm set for work, but on your days off when you wake up naturally, you can't get back to sleep even though you've got more time to sleep? Why do we always want to lie in when we can't but not when we can?
Why don't I like swedes and turnips? I've tried them prepared well but there's still something that repels me. Is it psychological or physiological?

answers.answer: There are studies on food dislikes. For coriander, there's the OR6A2 gene that makes it taste soapy. For spicy and fatty food, there's the TAS2R38 gene. Evolutionarily, sweet is good and bitter is bad, so some foods are growers (like beer - nobody likes it the first time). Some foods like swedes, turnips and parsnips can be a bit eggy/bitter so you learn to like them rather than having an innate preference.

Learning to like foods involves evolution, genetics, environment, exposure, learning, and association. It's very complex. Most babies need to taste something 15 times before deciding if they like it. We're born preferring sweet (breast milk is slightly sweet) and genetically averse to bitter (which in evolutionary days might have been poison). Turnips fall under bitter. You could train yourself to like them by cooking with something sweet, like adding sugar gradually. Also, psychologically it's hard to overcome association with disliking something.

questions.question: There are only so many chords you can play on a guitar and only so many keys on a piano. Are we going to eventually run out of original tunes? What about copyright cases like Ed Sheeran where the judge said combinations inevitably recur?

answers.answer: The number of possible combinations is so enormous that we're never going to run out of tunes. It's technically possible but practically impossible. Even by the time we approach running out, we'd have forgotten some of the earliest tunes like Greensleeves and could reinvent them.

Mathematically, yes, there are a finite number of tunes. About four years ago, a musician and programmer (Rubin) in America wrote an algorithm to store every possible tune on digital media. They filed these with the copyright office and made them public domain to help artists defend against copyright lawsuits. The number was 68.7 billion tunes.

questions.question: When did gift party etiquette in the UK collapse? At my birthday, I got a crate of real ale and by the end the fridge was full of other people's beer, not presents. At my partner's Indian birthday, people brought food they wanted to eat themselves. Have we stopped giving presents to adults?

Watching the Olympics, Rebecca and Sharon Davis mentioned 'slow pools' and 'fast pools' in swimming interviews. How can a pool be fast or slow? Surely all Olympic pools are the same length and full of water?

answers.answer: It's about the depth of the pool, not the length. In competitive swimming, times are adjusted based on pool depth. A deeper pool is slower because when water waves hit the bottom, they bounce back up and create resistance. In a deeper pool, the water takes longer to bounce back - it's like sonar. Shallower pools are faster.

questions.question: My daughter got tablets from the pharmacist - those torpedo-shaped ones that are half red and half white. Why are they half coloured and half white? Why are capsules two colours?

answers.answer: Pills are all different shapes, sizes and colours so they can be identified. Capsules are different for different dosages. Even though they're different companies, they're always the same for the same pill and dosage. It's for ease of identification - in case of overdose or if kids pick up a pill, you can identify what it is at the hospital.

questions.question: Why aren't people more creative at tying their shoelaces when there are hundreds of different knots? Like scouts and sailors use many different knots, but everyone ties their shoes the same way.

answers.answer: The knot you use is the most effective one. It's the same whether you lace your shoes normally or eccentrically.

The standard shoelace knot is the most simple and effective knot. People do have variations within the same knot type (like rabbit's ears). Some shoes now have different knotting options like pulley string systems or elasticated systems. For people with disabilities there are adaptations. But for able-bodied people, the same basic knot is used because it's by far the most effective.

questions.question: In track events that go round a bend, starting positions are staggered for fairness. But in long-distance events like the steeplechase, runners all start in a straight line and then run into the inside lane. How is that fair? Surely the person in the inside lane has an advantage if they finish only fractions of a second apart?
Why do some people read with no inflection or emphasis, like the King's speech? Is it possible to teach them to read with character?

answers.answer: When children learn to read, they use three cueing systems: graphophonic (letters and sounds), syntax (what word fits the sentence), and meaning (most important). People who read without inflection tend to be reading without picking up the meaning. You can teach for it by getting them to listen to their own voice while reading, but some people will never be great at it. The more you read, the easier it gets - you learn to read by reading.

questions.question: Why don't churches and cathedrals have chimneys, when other buildings built in the same era had fireplaces and chimneys?

answers.answer: Churches DID have chimneys. They all used to heat their spaces with coal, usually through great big cast-iron pipes under grids in the floor. But when the coal boilers became obsolete, they abandoned the chimneys, and a lot of them were taken down because they cost a lot of money to maintain.

questions.question: Can you hear the sun? If you got close enough to it, would there be a sound?

answers.answer: The sun is a big ball of nuclear reactions making a huge amount of sound. If the sound waves could travel to us, we would hear it all day every day and it would be very annoying. We can't hear it because space is a vacuum - sound waves can't travel through nothing. It is making a noise but we would never hear it. It's making a huge amount of sound.

questions.question: When Rishi Sunak handed in his resignation and there was a gap until Kier Starmer got told the nucleus, who was the prime minister to make big decisions? If the Russians invaded during that interregnum, who would be in charge of national security and the nuclear codes?

answers.answer: We do not use nuclear launch codes like the Americans. Each prime minister at the start of their term writes letters of last resort, which are given to the nuclear submarine. In the event that they are themselves incapacitated to give the order, the submarine commanders open these letters. The letter will be instructed on what to do - whether to surrender to a NATO country, retaliate on the enemy, etc. There's always a letter in place, so there's never a moment where neither letter is in position.

questions.question: All clowns have to have fully original clown makeup. How do they make sure theirs is completely individual? Is there some sort of clown trademark they have to get?

answers.answer: They paint the faces on eggs and register them at a place in London. A clown would come in and paint the egg to match his face paint, then they register it. There's the International Clowns Egg Registry in London with faces of all the clowns from the past to present. Whether they've updated it with digital technology now, I don't know.

questions.question: Was the color orange named after the fruit, or was the fruit named after the color?

answers.answer: The fruit definitely came first. It comes from the word naranga which means fragrant or fragrant fruit. When it came to France it was called naranja, then when it came to English-speaking countries it got corrupted to orange. Before that, if orange appeared in nature (which was rare), it was just called red or yellow-red. When pumpkins appeared around the same time, they started calling them orange-red and eventually dropped the 'red' part, making orange the color. This is why ginger people are called redheads - that name predates the color orange.

questions.question: Why does the Tupperware box dry but the lid stays wet in the dishwasher? We've tried different kinds - glass bottom with plastic lid, same issue. Is there a scientific reason?

answers.answer: It's the heat density. Thin plastic has what we call low heat density, which means it can't keep heat well. The item keeps heat to allow water to evaporate while it's cooling off. But thin plastic loses that heat quickly, so the water stays on the lid because it can't evaporate. The lid is physically thinner than the container, so it has lower heat density. Both might be made from polypropylene but the lid is thinner.

questions.question: Are some species more prone to albinism than others? Specifically, are squirrels more likely to be albino? I saw an albino squirrel, then met someone who said there was a whole family of them.

answers.answer: Those squirrels aren't actually albino - they're leucistic. Albino means devoid of all pigment with red eyes, while leucistic means they're washed out versions with pale markings but not completely devoid of pigment. You can get leucistic badgers, pheasants, squirrels, deer. Albinos don't do well in the wild because of predation and sun sensitivity. Leucistic animals can breed pretty much as normal if they don't get predated, which is why there's a little family in one area.

questions.question: How do noise-cancelling headphones work? They have 16 microphones in them apparently.

answers.answer: Sound cancellation works on the principle of one sound wave cancelling another. The headphones have microphones that record the noise around you that you don't want. When you press noise cancellation, it plays that sound back into the headphones, and the sound waves are identical so they collide and cancel each other out. This is why they need microphones. The better the headphones, the more and better quality microphones they have.
The previous caller forgot to mention that the sound wave played back has to be inverse to the one coming in, so they cancel each other out.

questions.question: Can young children see better in the dark than adults? When tucking my three-year-old in, I bash into everything but she navigates perfectly in the dark.

Why do tennis balls have seams/grooves instead of being completely covered in felt? It seems like the seam offers nothing in terms of spin or flight, and it looks like something from a bygone era when it was too difficult to cover them completely.

answers.answer: Tennis balls are made from two figure-of-eight shaped pieces of felt that are fused together. You can't have one continuous piece of felt because you wouldn't be able to fuse them together - it would be a messy gloopy mess around the surface. The seam is the rubber part where the two pieces meet.

You can't actually wrap a tennis ball in a single piece of felt because it will crease. The origins date back to real tennis in Henry VIII's day when all tennis balls were hand-sewn. Lawn tennis derived from real tennis only hundreds of years later. Real tennis balls are still handmade and last about two to three weeks before being remade.

questions.question: Why don't hospital toilets have lids? You'd think they'd help keep bacteria from spreading.

answers.answer: It's all to do with government regulations around something called Document M - Access to and use of buildings. Anything that requires extra movement or lifting, like a seat to lift up, would make access harder for people with disability or movement issues, which is why hospital toilets don't have lids.
As a hospital cleaner, I can tell you that toilets on almost all wards do have seats.

questions.question: Why in sport is a heat called a heat?
Where does the distinctive tune/sequence of whistles that referees blow at half-time and full-time come from? Why is it always the same?

answers.answer: There's no specific mentioning in the laws of the game about different whistle patterns, but usually you start the game with one whistle, do half-time with two whistles, and do full-time with three whistles. You can put your own spin on it as long as there are the required number of distinct whistles.

questions.question: Can you tell from a shell where it's from? If I gave it to somebody clever, could they identify the beach or region it came from?

answers.answer: Yes - there are geographically distinct isotopic signatures all over the world for certain elements, particularly carbon. When mollusks sequester carbon to create their shells, they draw in these isotopes which get captured in the shell material. By analyzing the isotopic composition, you can determine where a shell came from. It's even easier with mollusks because they don't move around much.

questions.question: Why does water get hotter when I lower my shower head from my head to my body? This happens in hotels and other places, not just my shower.

answers.answer: Water pressure with hot water is a lot lower than with cold water. When you bring the shower head off the holder and down closer to where the water is coming in from the pipework, it has less distance to travel up with that pressure, so more hot water comes out with the cold, making it feel hotter.

The temperature of water leaving the nozzle is X, but when you hold the shower head up high, the spray has a lot of surface area exposed to air and cools down by the time it reaches you (X minus Y). When you bring it closer to your body, there's less time to cool and less surface area exposed to air, so it arrives warmer.

questions.question: When you're on holiday on an island like Kos, how much of the money you spend stays on the island and how much goes back to mainland Greece? How does the economic arrangement work?
What happens to a spider's thread when it comes back up? The spider can't eat it because it would be like us having an eighth of an inch rope. Where does it go?

answers.answer: There are two different ways spiders recycle silk. Many species eat it, digest it, and resecrete it. But for spiders that drop down and speed back up quickly, they don't have time to eat it. Instead, they bundle it up with their back legs (legs six and seven) between their hind legs. This has been observed through macro photography. They can reuse it.

questions.question: I found army military food ration packs from 1992 when packing for a festival. They're dried in sealed bags with no best-before date. Can I eat them?

answers.answer: Technically it's safe to eat, but it will taste really bad and make you sick. I ate an MRE from the 60s - I tried the crackers and they were bad, and sniffing the beef was enough to make me feel sick. If it's not a matter of survival on a desert island, I'd say don't do it, especially when you can buy food at the festival.

questions.question: Why do you always get an itchy nose when your hands are covered in something like batter? I was making Dutch snacks (bitterballen and croquetas) and the moment my hands were covered in batter, my nose started itching.
If you cut a bar magnet in half repeatedly until it's very tiny, would it still be magnetic? Would the positive and negative poles cancel out because they're so close?

answers.answer: The laws of physics would still apply. Even if it was a micron thin and still had positive and negative poles, it would still create a magnetic field.

A magnet is just a moving charge. The smallest charge is an electron. In a bar magnet, all the atoms have electrons spinning around, which causes the magnetic field. The electrons are all aligned, so even the tiniest piece would still be magnetic because you can't cut an electron - it's fundamental.

questions.question: Why hasn't male baldness been cured by now? It's been around for ages, it's common, and the money you'd make from curing it would be enormous.

answers.answer: It might not be possible because something is dead in your head and cannot be resurrected. A living follicle cannot be brought back to life.

Baldness is genetic, inherited from grandparents and parents. Many genes are involved and the immune system can also be involved. To cure it you'd need gene therapy, but if you replace one gene you wouldn't be sure what side effects that could have. There's never going to be something that makes your hair grow back - the follicles are already dead. You can't resurrect them. All you can do is prevent it with gene therapy.

questions.question: Why do gangsters in movies always have toothpicks in their mouths? What's that about?

answers.answer: In the mid-19th century, Charles Forster from Boston invented the toothpick and hired people to go to upmarket restaurants asking for toothpicks and then complaining when they didn't have them. This created a trend. In those upmarket restaurants, chewing a toothpick became a sign that you'd been able to eat well, that you'd been dining in fancy restaurants. It spread from there as a status symbol.

questions.question: Why does muscle tissue burn more calories than fatty tissue? What's the scientific explanation for why more muscle improves your metabolism?

answers.answer: Fat cells are storage cells, so they only burn enough energy to keep the cell alive. Muscle cells need to burn more energy to make the muscle fibers contract, so they use far more calories doing that. They give off energy and heat, which is why you get hot when exercising.

questions.question: Do insects yawn? Her pet praying mantis did something that looked like yawning after breakfast.

answers.answer: Insects don't yawn. We yawn when carbon dioxide levels in our blood go up, the pH goes down, and we're programmed to yawn as a precursor to the pant reflex. Insects don't do that. They have spiracles down their bodies - holes that allow air in by passive diffusion. They don't breathe through their faces, so it's impossible for them to yawn. The reason many people listening probably yawned during this conversation is because yawning is contagious.

questions.question: Is it true that if your car goes into a river, you should wait until it sinks, fills with water, and when the pressure inside equals the pressure outside, you can just push the door open and swim to the surface?

answers.answer: If the car is full of water, the pressure inside equals the pressure outside, so you could theoretically open the door. But you wouldn't have a lot of time. You have a lungful of air. And these days cars have electric windows that won't work underwater, so you'd need to smash it with something like a seatbelt buckle.

The pressure differential between outside and inside must be equal, otherwise the outside pressure is too great to force the door open. Adam Savage on Mythbusters proved this works. You need to stay calm to conserve oxygen. You can break a window underwater using the headrest from the seat in front - it has two metal rods that concentrate pressure. A boot or flat shoe won't work because the surface is too flat.

questions.question: Why do humans still have canine teeth if we don't eat raw meat and bones anymore? We have cutlery now.

answers.answer: Evolution is a process that takes place over millions of years. If there was an evolutionary advantage to not having canines, and there clearly isn't, then maybe. But if you've ever eaten ribs, you strip them with your teeth. Without canines, you couldn't eat ribs properly. We have them because the evolutionary process that gave us canines was a massive advantage for diet, and therefore for procreation and gene replication.

questions.question: Why do private planes and helicopters always have serial numbers that start with the letter N?

answers.answer: Not all aircraft registrations start with N. Different countries have different prefixes - G for UK, F for France, D for Germany, N for USA.

The registration is allocated by the manufacturer, not the country. The first letters are allocated by the manufacturer, and the numbers indicate the sequence of aircraft built. So it depends on who made the aircraft.

questions.question: Why was the Battle of Bosworth fought at Bosworth Field specifically? Did they plan it or just happen to stumble across each other?
Indonesia has 17,000 islands. What constitutes an island? How big does it have to be? Does it have to be habitable or inhabited?
Why does your bladder relax when you get closer to home, and is there any medical reason for it?

answers.answer: This is called latch key syndrome. The doctor explained that the brain associates getting into the house with getting into the toilet. When you get your key out, your brain tells your bladder to relax because you're nearly there. A little bit of wee comes out.

questions.question: What's so alluring about alliteration? Why does it appeal to the psyche?

answers.answer: As a speech and language therapist, I can explain that when babies and toddlers learn to speak, we love babbling with the same sound - ga-ga-goo-goo, baba, mama, mimi. Our mouth and brain don't have to work quite so hard when we repeat sounds. We've got everything in place set up. So that repetition means not quite so much has to happen. It flows and it's much more natural. It's why we also like rhyme - hocus pocus, hubble bubble. It's just a real natural flowing sort of almost poetic movement. It sounds pleasant and it's easy to do.

questions.question: Is water ever as hard as concrete? At what height would hitting water be the same as hitting the ground?

answers.answer: There's no one universal speed at which water becomes like concrete. It's to do with the speed and the area that hits it. If you hit with your fingertips, you go in like a knife or spear, and you could be going faster than someone who hits differently. Water has strong bonds - hydrogen bonds. When you come in contact with water with a huge area, you're trying to break a lot of those bonds. According to Newton's third law, every action has an equal but opposite reaction. The force of you breaking those bonds has the equivalent force coming back to you. So if you're trying to break that, the amount of damage you're doing to the water trying to displace it - that force has come back to you as well.

questions.question: When does a boat become a ship? What is the difference between a boat, a ship and a yacht?

answers.answer: They used to say you can put a boat on a ship but you can't put a ship on a boat. But now massive salvage ships can put container ships on them, so that definition doesn't work anymore. The official definition now is: a boat leans into a turn; a ship leans out of a turn. This is decided by size and design. If you look at a picture of a big warship or ferry turning, it leans out of the circle in the direction opposite to where it's turning. A boat or sailboat like a yacht - the mast leans in the direction of the turn. The only exception is submarines which are always called boats. A yacht is a type of boat - it's a subcategory, like an estate car is a type of car.

questions.question: Is there a legal limit to how many times one can drive around a roundabout before you become a nuisance or before it becomes an offence?

answers.answer: As long as the driving around the roundabout is to the minimum required standard (test standard), you can go around as many times as you want without committing an offence. The caveat is that if you try it on a mini roundabout where you effectively block anybody from entering or exiting, you would commit Section 3 Road Traffic Act - careless and inconsiderate driving. On a bigger roundabout where that effect wouldn't take place, you could pop yourself in the lane next to the roundabout with a right-hand signal on and effectively go around all day without interfering with anybody else until you got bored. It's only when your standard of driving slipped below that expected of a safe and competent driver that the offence would be committed.

questions.question: How much energy or power is used to save an email in one of those data centers? How damaging is email storage to the environment in terms of carbon emissions?

answers.answer: Storage is already pre-built and pre-determined by any big company. The data centre is pre-built, the storage is already there, and each individual email that comes through subsequently doesn't take any more cost anymore. It's already storage that's pre-built and held in a data centre. It could run out technically, but they're upgradable and hot-swappable. The storage can be expanded. Data centres are like big libraries - one aisle is hot, one aisle is cold. They draw in cold air from the front and exhaust it at the back. They're very secure, sometimes hold government data. How much an email costs depends entirely on its size, which varies like asking how many animals you can keep in a zoo - you can't really say without knowing if it's chinchillas or elephants.

questions.question: Why do white keys on a piano have a lip or overhang beyond the black keys? What is the purpose of this design?

answers.answer: The official reason for the lip is twofold: First, to enable you to lift a sticking key easily - it gives you purchase. Second, the lip is a slight extension to the key for people with a larger size hand than the average, so it increases the playable surface area.

questions.question: Why does my hay fever not affect me when I'm asleep, but starts within five minutes of waking up?

answers.answer: It's to do with the temperature. At night, it's colder, so the pollen falls to the ground. When the sun comes up, the air warms up and the pollen rises again - called the pollen shower phenomenon. When you wake up, the pollen has also woken up and starts affecting you. Flowers and grass close at night, so there's less pollen in the atmosphere. If you stayed in bed until lunchtime, you'd be sneezing in bed.

questions.question: What is beagling?

answers.answer: Beagling is chasing hares across country on foot with hounds. But you don't ride horses. The hounds are different from foxhounds - they've got shorter legs and smaller bodies. You can sometimes see people having them as pets. It's when the country was overrun by hares. Her dad went to Radley near Oxford and helped set up a pack of beagles at the school. They took the beagles home in the holidays.

questions.question: Why do Tory politicians hold their hand in a closed fist with thumb on index finger at a right angle to their body when making points on news shows?

answers.answer: It's probably some form of media training - similar to the 'power stance' thing George Osborne and Theresa May were filmed doing about 10 years ago. James admits they look stupid doing it.

It's called 'the pointless point' - a way of emphasising a point you're making without pointing your finger because that's shown to be aggressive. Tony Blair did lots of it. Bill Clinton did as well. Qualifications: A-level in communication studies.

questions.question: Why is orange the only Smartie colour that has a flavour corresponding to its colour (tastes like orange) while all other colours don't taste of strawberry, lime, lemon etc?

answers.answer: He knows why the orange flavour in Smarties differs from Terry's Chocolate Orange - for Smarties the orange flavour is in the shell so they don't need a separate production line. But he doesn't know why only orange gets a flavour.

questions.question: How does a plant know when to stop growing? Garden centre labels say small/medium/large climber for the same plant type - why three different sizes?
