answers.answer: Plant labels give height and width at different timeframes - some are final size, some are 10-year estimates. Different books might say 5m or 10m for the same tree - both right at different stages. A tree company got sued for a tree growing bigger than stated, so now some inflate their estimates. Rootstock plays a role in controlling size. For James's elongated damson tree, fruit trees don't heal well (especially prunus), might be better to sacrifice and start fresh rather than try to reshape it.

questions.question: When clocks were invented in 1650, why did they only go up to 12 rather than 24 numbers?
Why do Y sperm swim faster than X sperm to reach the egg?

answers.answer: The Y sperm has a bit missing from its chromosome, making it ever so slightly lighter, so it moves faster. Timing sex close to ovulation suits Y sperm (boy), while earlier timing suits X sperm (girl). She was a biology teacher and researched this while trying to conceive a girl (daughter Evie).

questions.question: Why is the TB jab the only vaccine that leaves a lasting scar?

answers.answer: Most vaccines are given into the muscle, but the TB vaccine is given intradermally (under the skin, between skin layers). It bubbles up and blisters because it's a live dose, which is why it leaves a scar. Qualifications: Student nurse who just had TB vaccine herself.

questions.question: Will airships ever replace planes as a form of travel? Is the Airlander the future?
Why is there a 24-hour delay before muscle soreness kicks in after intense exercise like a long bike ride?

answers.answer: It's called DOMS (Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness). Doing intense activity without proper training causes micro-tears in the muscles. The pain hits 24-72 hours later when the body starts repairing. Qualifications: Chemistry and sport and exercise science degree.

questions.question: Why does the word 'penguin' come from a Welsh word meaning 'white head'? Who named the penguin?

answers.answer: It's probably Welsh. There was an island off Wales called Penguin (meaning white head) which was a colony of great auks. The great auk was an extinct Northern Hemisphere bird that died out in 1852, with Latin name penguinus. When European explorers saw Southern Hemisphere birds that looked like great auks, they named them penguins too.

questions.question: Does anyone else live on Downing Street? If Keir Starmer becomes Prime Minister, can he pop into number 12 for a cup of sugar?

answers.answer: No, the rest are offices. You would have to go through police cordon every time you wanted a pint of milk.
The Chief Whip lives at number 12 Downing Street.
The Chief Whip used to live at number 12 until the late 90s when Alistair Campbell kicked him out to use the office space.

questions.question: Why does honey not go moldy but my maple syrup went moldy after only two weeks?

answers.answer: It's about bacteria and water content. Honey doesn't have enough water in it to allow bacteria or mold to survive. The bacteria can't absorb enough water from the honey to survive due to osmosis.

questions.question: Why can I not buy blackberry jam in the supermarket?

answers.answer: Blackberries aren't a viable commercial crop because you can't harvest them efficiently - they're foraged rather than farmed.
You can buy blackberry jam - there are brands like Mackay's, Wilkinson and Sons, and even Diddly Squat Farm.

Two problems with blackberries: difficulty determining ripeness and they squish easily when picked. Since 2021, new machinery uses cameras to identify berries and suction cups to gently pick them, so commercial production is increasing.

questions.question: Has the bumblebee flying question been answered? Given modern computing and modelling, do we now know how bumblebees fly when we were taught their flight defied aerodynamics?

answers.answer: Scientists used very slow motion cameras (David Attenborough documentary) and discovered that at the very top of each wing flap, bumblebees do a little circular scoop. This rotation creates more uplift, which explains how they fly.

questions.question: Why is there no live video feed from an airplane cockpit back to the control tower? For safety reasons, wouldn't it be useful?

answers.answer: Aircraft already transmit data constantly - engine parameters and problems go to airlines and manufacturers via VHF radio or satellite. There simply isn't enough bandwidth to transmit CCTV footage. Security concerns exist too - keeping aircraft data separate from hackers. With thousands of flights in the sky at any time, no one could watch live anyway. Everything is already recorded in the data.

questions.question: How is it possible that a road can be underneath a canal? I was on an aero boat going to Little Venice and passed over the A406.

answers.answer: Aqueduct - canals are man-made waterways that can be elevated above roads using aqueducts. At Sloane Square tube station, there's a river in a pipe above your head. Viaducts carry roads over rivers, aqueducts carry water over roads. It's a river in the sky built by engineers.

questions.question: What is the difference between a violin and a fiddle? I saw a performer use different instruments for classical versus folk music and they sounded different.

answers.answer: Fundamentally the same instrument, but classically-trained players use strings made from more synthetic materials or gut, while fiddles often have slightly stronger strings. The sound difference comes from the string types used. A renowned expert still calls all violins fiddles regardless of their age or value.

questions.question: When I defrost sealed frozen meat in a zip-lock bag, blood always appears on the plate. How does that happen if the bag is fully sealed?

answers.answer: It's not blood - it's myoglobin. It's found in muscle tissue. Freezing damages the muscle tissue, so the myoglobin seeps out. Even chicken does this. If your bag truly had no holes, it would still happen because the myoglobin is inside the meat itself.

questions.question: How can I consciously switch between focusing on what's behind me in a reflection versus what's in front of me through a window? What allows me to do this?

answers.answer: The eye has suspensory ligaments that hold up the lens. These contract and relax depending on focal length - like adjusting a camera lens. Your brain sends messages to your eyes about what to focus on, and the suspensory ligaments adjust the lens accordingly.

questions.question: Iceland is covered in green and Greenland is covered in ice. Why are they named the wrong way round?

answers.answer: Viking propaganda - they wanted to repopulate Greenland, which had no permanent settlers. They called it 'Greenland' to attract people to move there, even though it was mostly ice. I heard this on Dan Snow's history podcast.

questions.question: Why is Earth represented on maps and globes orientated north-up? Why wouldn't it be south-up or east-up? It's all relative, isn't it? We were just floating through space. So who's decided that it's north-up?

answers.answer: It depends on where the map was made. In the Far East, they had maps east-up. Some of the earliest maps were south-up. The maps we see are from the Western world. It's geographical relativism - the UK is usually in the middle of a world map when we go to school, but it wouldn't be if you were at school in Ulaanbaatar.

Maps being north-up has more to do with the Greenwich Meridian than anything else. The Earth spins about its axis, so you want your equator in the middle. It was very nearly Paris as the prime meridian. Navigation goes degrees east or west. For a wall map, it makes sense to have the dateline in the middle of the Pacific, not cutting through major landmasses. Also, because we have a molten iron core, the Earth acts as a dynamo as we spin, making us like one gigantic magnet, which is why we get the aurorae at the poles.

questions.question: Why is it called D-Day? My daughter asked and I don't know.

answers.answer: The D stands for day. It's Day-Day.

The D does stand for day, but that's not the reason why it's called D-Day. When you're doing military planning for operations, you have to have something called a sync matrix, which queues up different units with different objectives to achieve certain things in time and space. The landings were going to happen on that day, the 6th of June, so that was D-Day. If they needed to leave the southern coast of UK a day before D-Day, that would be D-1. We also have H-Hours - if they needed to land on the beaches at 7 o'clock, that would be H-Hour. Every military operation has a D-Day. This one just became iconic and significant because of Operation Overlord - to put six divisions ashore with nothing more than a chalkboard is incredible.

questions.question: Why do we associate rabbits with eating carrots? In fictional stories, rabbits are quite like a carrot. But naturally, you don't see rabbits bouncing around in the wild with a bunch of carrots.

answers.answer: Probably Beatrix Potter. Peter Rabbit stealing Mr. McGregor's carrots. It's a story that was so popular that the behaviour in it became a trope, similar to how Long John Silver's speech pattern from one Charles Lawton performance became how we think pirates talk.

Beatrix Potter spent a long time observing nature, including her father's vegetable garden. For horticulturists, rabbits belong to the category of pests and diseases. Rabbits and rodents have a preferential taste for carrot tops, which is highly destructive because if they take the top off the carrot, it dies. So Beatrix Potter, being a great observer of nature, would have observed rabbits eating carrot tops and incorporated that into her story. The story became so popular that the relationship between rabbits and carrots fell into popular parlance.

questions.question: Have the Northern and Southern Lights ever met at the equator? There was such a big solar storm last Friday that the Northern Lights came very south, even to Lanzarote. I just wondered if there's ever been an event in history where the Northern and Southern Lights have met at the equator.
What's the origin of a deck of playing cards? Does it not all start with the tarot?

answers.answer: The current deck originated around the Middle Ages from France. The four suits were generally thought to represent the four different classes of society back then - clergy, military, farming, and trade/merchant class. Within that, the four suits also represent the four seasons, and within each suit, the 13 different ranks represent the lunar cycles in a year. There are 52 cards for 52 weeks. Tarot probably has something to do with it too.

questions.question: On Sunday, the last day of the Premier League season, Arsenal and Man City can only win. They're both playing at home, 200 miles apart. After the game, the trophy will be presented to the winning team. But where is the trophy during the game? What's the logistics of getting it to the right ground at the right time?

answers.answer: There can be up to three trophies - one real and two dummy trophies. They're all exactly the same. The real trophy at this present time will be at Man City in a nice big Louis Vuitton box. Another one will be at Arsenal in a nice big Louis Vuitton box. So there will be two trophies at each ground, and they know which one is real.

questions.question: How come a surgeon isn't a doctor? I had an appointment with who I thought was a doctor, but he was actually a surgeon. I asked for doctor and his name and was told it was mister. Why do surgeons go by mister instead of doctor?

answers.answer: Once you become a consultant, and in this case a surgeon and a consultant, you become known as mister. It's a respect thing - a more senior assignation. There are only two types of doctor in a hospital: the doctors and the misters. And the misters are senior to the doctors, even though they're doctors. It might go back to the 17th century when doctors were the learned ones who would analyze your urine and prescribe potions, while the surgeon was an inferior position - usually a barber would double up as a surgeon, called barber surgeons. So the roots go back to when the barber surgeon was inferior to the doctor. But because medicine has evolved, the surgeon has become a much more specialized practitioner, so the mister has overtaken the doctor.

The reason surgeons are called mister is extreme pretentiousness. Surgeons were developed separately from physicians, and the medics didn't think surgeons were proper doctors. This goes back to the barber surgeon era. In the late 19th century, when we became one profession, surgeons in the UK retained the title mister to keep themselves separate and to be pretentious about it - they turned the snobbery back on itself. But it's not hierarchical - it's just different branches. All registrars in surgery go by mister or miss, and then you have to pass the fellowship exam to become a consultant. Surgeons are hyper-qualified doctors, not less qualified - they've studied more.

questions.question: In Call the Midwife, when women are in the latter stages of labour, they're told not to push and to pant instead. I don't understand why panting stops your pushing. Even sitting here now, if I pant, it reduces my inclination to push. But why does panting prevent pushing? What medical thing happens in the body?

answers.answer: Pushing involves clenching. You take a breath and then you push. If you're doing panting, you can't push.

The difference between a voluntary and involuntary push. When you're giving birth and you're almost at the point of the baby being born, the baby will put pressure on parts of the body that will elicit an involuntary response. It's possible for women still to be pushing even though they don't think they are. When someone is directed to push, they take a deep breath and put their chin on their chest, which makes their pushes much more forceful. You're asked to pant because it stops the glottis in your body closing. When you pant, the part of your upper airway remains open and you can breathe through it rather than holding your breath and pushing down. It means the baby is descending under less pressure and less force and in a more gentle way, which is thought to be preferable unless there's a real emergency.

questions.question: Why is it that carrots take forever to cook in tomato sauce? If you simmer carrots in water, they're ready in 5-10 minutes, but if you put them in a tomato sauce for a curry, they take forever.

answers.answer: You should sweat your carrots and onions before adding tomato sauce. Keep them on low heat for about 10 minutes to get them soft without burning them - the Italians call it soffritto.

It's the acidic content in tomato sauce that prevents carrots from softening. You can boil carrots in water, milk and butter and they'll soften, but boil them for six hours in tomato sauce and they won't. The chefs I've worked with say it's about the acidity.

questions.question: Why is it when you go on an escalator that's not on, you still get the sensation of being pulled, even though it's not moving?

answers.answer: Your brain and eyes have a relationship that says prepare for movement. The message from your eyes to your brain is that you're getting onto a moving staircase, even if you're not moving. Your subconscious is saying we're getting onto that moving staircase even as your conscious says 'oh what a shame it's broken', and your brain sends the message to brace for action.

It's to do with Pavlov's dogs - operant conditioning. We go through a process where we touch an escalator and it takes our arm away. The next time we do it and it's not moving, we think it ought to be moving. We associate one thing with another, even if the second thing doesn't happen, you still do the first thing.

questions.question: In France they told me white wine winds you up (enerve). In Portugal they say white wine is bad for your joints - knees and hips. Are these rural myths or could the chemical constituents of white wine be so different from red that you'd have different effects?

answers.answer: From personal experience, white wine absolutely enervates me. Using myself as a case study, it's absolutely true. But you're interested in chemical composition - is it something special in the skin of the grapes? I don't know if making wine with or without skin makes a difference.

Red wines are fermented on skins whereas white wines are taken off skin straight away. The skins give anthocyanins (pigment) and tannins (bitterness). The only reason people might complain about white wine is that they generally have higher SO2 (sulphur dioxide) levels, which could cause worse hangovers. White wine also has lower alcohol content than red, so people drink it quicker. The lower pH makes the sulphur more abundant. Histamines - red wine has more of those.

questions.question: How do smelling salts work? What is the mechanism by which waving this magical fluid under someone's nose brings them back to consciousness?

answers.answer: Is it not just a really pungent smell that assaults your senses? But would that work with any really pungent smell? Could you use blue cheese? It must be something to do with the speed with which the liquid turns into gas - it turns into vapor so quickly it goes up your nose like a rat up a drain pipe. Is it something special about ammonia?

questions.question: How do groins work? Groins with a Y - the rows of plants that run vertically down the beach.

answers.answer: You'd think you'd build a wall across the bottom of the beach where the sea comes in, but all the water would wash out. Longshore drift moves sand horizontally along the beach, so you use groins to prevent sand being moved horizontally. You'll only find them on pleasure beaches where people have sandcastles and frolics.

It's not necessarily about pleasure beaches. Groins are also where we have coastal defences, to keep material in place to protect the toe of those defences. Visualise longshore drift as the teeth of a saw - the prevailing wind is usually oblique to the coast, so material is pushed up the beach on those waves, then dragged down vertically when water recedes, creating a zigzag pattern. Groins protect the loss of that material. You'll see a pile up of material on one side and a much lower level on the other. We gather and recycle that material back to the beach, especially after wind storms. It's environmental as well as recreational.

questions.question: A tulip has come up in the middle of my grass. I understand birds transfer seeds, but I thought tulips come from bulbs. If they can come from seeds, how does that work? I've lived here over six years and never had a tulip there before.

answers.answer: Tulips can come from seeds which then grow the bulb. But I don't know how long it takes for the seed to develop into a bulb before growing into a flower.

Tulips can be grown from seed but rarely are because they take such a long time to come to flower. The seed case grows behind the flower, and when the seed is ripe it can be blown away or picked up by a bird and nestle in a lawn. It would take many years for it to come to flower. The bulbs we buy from Dutch growers have been grown in a field for many years. The seed grows into a bulb and then the bulb produces a flower.

questions.question: Did the losing team on Pat Sharp's Funhouse ever get to have a go on the Funhouse after the cameras stopped rolling? My mum used to say the producer was her friend and they let the losing team have a play, but I'm almost certain she was just being kind.
Why do cobblers always also do key cutting and engraving? What common thread of skill training marries those three things together?

answers.answer: It might just be the machine - the same machine does all three. Or perhaps they just got the machine and it made commercial sense, and then it caught on.

questions.question: Why do towels in hotel rooms work so much better at drying me than the towels I have at home?

answers.answer: Maybe they wash them at a higher or lower temperature. The answer might be fluffiness - they wash towels with nothing else. Tennis balls in the tumble dryer fluff up towels. Possibly we don't tumble dry our towels normally; we hang them up to dry.

It's about GSM - grams per square meter. Hotel towels are around 400 GSM, which is much heavier and thicker than home towels. Higher GSM means better absorbency. They go in industrial drying machines which tumble dry them and add air to make them fluffy.

The previous answer is all true, but really the reason is that commercial items like hotel towels are simply better quality. Like catering ovens that cost three times more because they're built to last. They get washed so much more than normal towels so they must be made of better quality.

questions.question: I cooked turmeric rice and when I sprayed disinfectant into the sink, it turned the rice from bright yellow to bright red. What chemical reaction is happening?

answers.answer: Turmeric is a natural dye and many natural dyes respond to acids and alkalis like indicators. Turmeric goes red in the presence of alkalis. It's because of the alkaline in the detergent.

questions.question: How much hay would hay lorries actually lose over a journey? Would farmers be compensated for that loss?

answers.answer: The set weight of the bale is determined by the farmer who baled it. If you wanted to stop it shedding, you'd cover it in tarpaulin, but it's more cost in exertion and time than you'd make back from hanging onto it. Hay is worth about £220 a tonne and you can get about 40 tonnes on a lorry. Over an infinite journey, it would eventually have no hay bales left, especially on bumpy roads where the baled hay gets jigged.

questions.question: In the show Shogun, Japanese words like Shogun and Taika have accents over the O and I in the subtitles. Why do we have accents on English words when they're translated from Japanese?

answers.answer: I suggested it's because Japanese syllables change meaning based on inflection, and the marks help with pronunciation. The inflection changes the word meaning, unlike English where Solihull/Solihull are the same place.

The marks above characters determine how that particular phoneme is pronounced. In Japanese, the character う means it's a long O sound. Japanese shows long sounds using different characters. James was correct - it's about pronunciation guides for English speakers.

questions.question: If you were born blind, could you ever experience dizziness and get dizzy?

answers.answer: I think dizziness has more to do with your ears than your eyes. The inner ear, not hearing. Closing your eyes probably helps because you're sitting still, not because darkness removes dizziness.

questions.question: Why do railway tracks have thousands of stones on either side and in between the sleepers?

answers.answer: It's called ballast. The stones are for drainage - when water goes on them, it drains down and away from the tracks, stopping them from flooding and getting soggy and muddy.

questions.question: When cakes go stale they go hard, but when biscuits go stale they go soft. They've got the same basic ingredients. Why does the same stuff behave differently?

answers.answer: Biscuits are flat and thin. You bake out the moisture from them. Cakes are thicker and fatter - you don't bake out the moisture, it evaporates, which is why cakes go hard. Biscuits absorb moisture from the atmosphere because they're essentially very dry.

That's not osmosis. Osmosis is about the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane. What Mark described is hygroscopic - when water is simply absorbed from the atmosphere without any membrane involvement.

questions.question: If terminal velocity is around 122 miles per hour, how come an avalanche will drop at over 200 miles per hour? This question was asked in 2015 and never got answered.

answers.answer: Terminal velocity is determined by air resistance. In an avalanche, only the snow on the outside experiences air resistance to any degree. All the snow on the inside is pushing faster against the outside snow. When you see footage of an avalanche, it seems to be puffing over itself - the inside snow comes to the outside, gets slowed down, then gets pushed by more snow falling down the mountain.

questions.question: Why do we have England, Scotland, and Ireland all with 'land' in the name, but then we have Wales without 'Walesland'?

answers.answer: The word 'land' doesn't necessarily denote a kingdom or settlement - it's just a word the Anglo-Saxons sometimes applied. 'Wales' originally comes from 'Wealas' meaning foreigners. The English named the territories as they pushed the Welsh back into Wales and Cornwall, describing them as 'Welsh' which was quite an offensive term. But regions in England like Westmorland and Cumberland also have 'land' in them, so you don't necessarily need it to denote a country.

questions.question: Wind and snow can last all day or a couple of days, but why does hail only ever last 5-10 minutes and never longer than that?

answers.answer: I speculated that the meteorological conditions in which hailstones can be created are very rare and quick. Hail needs a very specific set of circumstances, and those conditions change very quickly, unlike for rain and snow.

Hail comes from convective, unstable clouds. The snow comes down, melts a little bit, gets water on the outside, then goes back up and refreezes, and repeats until it becomes too heavy for the updrafts to hold. This process has to go over and over again. That's why hailstorms are short - because they can only happen in unstable air. This is called the Bergeron process.

questions.question: How do air fresheners actually neutralize odors? Is it just masking the smell or doing something else?

answers.answer: It's about enzymes or enzyme cleaners. They speed up organic smell and decomposition - they make it die faster. If you leave food in a bin, eventually it stops smelling. The enzymes just speed up that process and stop the smell.

questions.question: Why do you have to turn a screw clockwise to drive it in? Is there a reason behind that?

answers.answer: I suggested it's because most of us are right-handed and we have more purchase turning clockwise. It's easier to screw stuff in than to screw it out again.

questions.question: How long have we been asking for autographs? Why did that tradition start and who started it?
How do fish know what species they are in order to congregate with other fish of the same species?
Has anybody actually ever died in the House of Commons or House of Lords chamber?

answers.answer: Spencer Perceval was assassinated but he was in the lobby of the House of Commons, not in the chamber itself. This is why Parliament is now guarded.

Michael Roberts died at the dispatch box in 1983. He was an undersecretary for Wales and had a massive heart attack while standing up answering questions. The Commons was suspended, they tried CPR, and he was pronounced dead at the hospital. He was already dead by the time they got him there. Carl was a junior civil servant in the Welsh Office at the time and remembers the conversation about whether you're allowed to die in the House of Commons (it's a myth that you're not).

questions.question: Where did the idea come from that fish guts could play a part in beer production?

answers.answer: Fish bladders were used to make gourds (containers). When villages went out hunting, they stored wine in fish bladder gourds, and the wine was clearer than wine from barrels. So they realized fish guts clarified wine and then applied it to beer. John runs pubs and won East Dorset Pub of the Year twice.

questions.question: Is there a scientific reason why petrol smells so good to many of us when it's toxic?

answers.answer: Petrol contains hydrocarbons like benzene and toluene, which are aromatic compounds. The same aromatic compounds are used in fragrances and deodorants. So the same chemicals in petrol are also found in expensive aftershaves and deodorants - that's why it smells attractive to us.

questions.question: When all analogue signals are turned off and we only have digital, what will be the nature of real exact time in broadcasts? How live will things be?

answers.answer: Light and radio waves travel at 186,000 miles per second (300,000 km/s). So radio signals reach you almost instantaneously - you wouldn't know the difference. However, digital signals go through fiber optics, satellites, and various servers which takes longer. If you were on Pluto, it would take 4 hours to get there. His son in New York likely gets the feed via faster routes like undersea cabling or satellites. Kerry is an amateur radio enthusiast and astronomer.

questions.question: What makes things sticky?

answers.answer: Sugar's stickiness comes from hydrogen bonding. Sugar molecules have lots of extensions that form weak bonds with each other and with water, which is why syrups are sticky - the hydrogen bonds make it stick to itself and to other surfaces. Leanne has a PhD in chemistry.

questions.question: Why do they say a company's 'in the black' when they're in profit but 'in the red' when in debt? Why not 'in the green'?

answers.answer: It's down to the color of ink used historically in accounting. The Romans used vermilion (red) for debts and black ink for credits - that's where the expressions come from. Rowan studied Roman taxation as part of a DPHC in accounting and learned this.

questions.caller: Jeremy from Bury St. Edmunds (formerly Belsize Park)
questions.question: If you order an expensive wine in a posh restaurant that supposedly needs to be decanted two days beforehand, what do they do? Do they ignore the decanting and serve it suboptimally, or keep you waiting for hours?

answers.answer: If the wine is older first growth Bordeaux that's already aged in the bottle, it may not need decanting beforehand. The advice Jeremy received may not be necessary or accurate for all wines. Victoria works in the wine trade and is studying for a degree equivalent in wine.

In restaurants, when someone orders a posh bottle of wine that needs decanting, they aerate it by pouring between jugs repeatedly, then put it in a decanter and serve immediately. This oxidizes it almost instantly. If you were at home, you could just pour it into a decanter and leave it to sit. Even a 5 pound supermarket bottle benefits from this aeration process. Richard was bar manager at a one star Michelin restaurant.

questions.question: Why is it that when long hair is tied up into a single piece, it's called a ponytail? Why is it that when it's tied into multiple pieces, it's called pigtail? Why is ponytail singular and pigtails plural?

answers.answer: Discussed that ponytails do look like horse tails but pigtails don't really look like pig tails. Questioned why one animal is singular and one is plural. Suggested pigtails look like two little pig's tails on a toddler's head.

Little toddlers with ringlet bunchies do look like pig's tails - the premise of the question was actually wrong. Once hair gets thicker and straighter as children get older, you say 'bunches' instead of 'pigtails'. Toddler hair does look like little pig's tails.

questions.question: Do cats retain memories of traumatic events? Does my cat have a form of feline PTSD?

answers.answer: Shared own experience of cat going missing for a week during Bonfire Night. Cats can go missing for up to a year and still find their way home. Cats' first instinct is safety - they'll hide from people even when their favorite treats are rattled.

Cats absolutely hold grudges and can be traumatized. It depends on the cat's experiences and whether they've learned to be chilled about challenges. Some are irrational about what they consider traumatic. Veterinary world focuses on making vet visits non-traumatic so cats tolerate going back. They learn through negative association - remembering not to trust someone with a net. Cats do most learning in first nine weeks of life and are hardwired then, but continue learning through negative experiences. Similar to pheasants being 'stupid' because they're bred for shooting and never learn about danger.

questions.question: What is the harshest, least vowel-y language in the world?

answers.answer: Didn't know the answer. Suggested linguists probably measure this. Mentioned Samoset, one of the Native Americans who could speak English, who had been taken as a slave and spent nine years in England.

Adige (Circassian language) only has three vowels and about 55 consonants. They have ejective consonants - for example where English speakers would pronounce a 'p' normally, Adige speakers use an ejective version. They also have click sounds like those in Welsh or Bedouin languages.

questions.question: When Rangers and Celtic play in Glasgow, why is it called the Old Firm Derby?

answers.answer: Admitted he didn't know the answer to this.

The term originated early in the 20th century from an early meeting of the two teams where commentators described the game as a meeting between two 'old firm friends' and the term stuck. Rangers went into liquidation in 2012 due to tax avoidance, and a phoenix club (Sevco plc) emerged. The Old Firm has basically died and been replaced by 'the Glasgow Derby' but the phrase persists.

questions.question: When the Bank of England increases interest rates and my mortgage payment goes up from £1,000 to £1,500, has the retail bank (Barclays, Bank of Scotland etc.) instantly made a windfall of £500 profit?

answers.answer: Expressed uncertainty about the answer. Noted that banks pay out more on savings when rates rise too, but they are slow to react on that. Still, there's a bigger differential between what they pay on savings vs what they charge on mortgages, so there is indeed a windfall somewhere.

It doesn't work that way directly. Banks go to other institutions and pay the interbank rate, which is directly related to the Bank of England rate. They borrow from markets at that rate and then lend it out. When base rates change, the rates they pay change too. It's not a direct relationship between rates and profits - there's a lag and it passes through the system. The money flows through markets, not directly to bank profits. The extra money goes into the ether through the markets where everyone gets their slice.

questions.question: How did sail-powered ships travel up the Thames to the docks on calm days when there was no wind?

answers.answer: Suggested they probably just waited for the wind. This is why it was very hard to give accurate arrival times for sailing ships - they'd wait for wind to come out.

answers.caller: Chris from Margate (Thames sailing barge trust member)
answers.answer: Large ships would use rowing boats called 'berthing boats' or old-style tugboats - strong crew members in small boats would row the enormous ships. Thames barges used a technique called 'drudging' - they'd wait for the tide going up the river, drop an anchor at the front that just bounces along the bottom (not enough to hold completely), and the force of the tide would push the barge backward while the rudder steered it. It's quite a difficult technique to master - knowing how much anchor to drop so it just bounces along the bottom.

questions.question: Is the white wig worn by judges a worldwide thing? Why only in some countries?

answers.answer: Suggested wigs go back to Charles II in the 17th century. Wigs were meant as a disguise so judges weren't recognized in the street. It's probably other Commonwealth countries too, but not the US where they don't wear wigs. It may extend beyond the reach of UK/British law.

Wigs in the Commonwealth come from Charles II in the 17th century when gentlemen wore wigs associated with aristocracy. Countries with wigs include Australia, New Zealand, some Canadian provinces, African countries (Kenya, Zimbabwe, Botswana), and Caribbean countries. The French abandoned wigs years ago - it contradicts the principles of legalité. The current situation in England is ridiculous: Court of Appeal judges wear only gowns while barristers wear full-bottom wigs and silk gowns.

questions.question: Why were Native Americans once known as 'Red Indians'?

answers.answer: Discussed the complexity - the question of what came first, naming the territory 'the Indies' or naming the people 'Indian'. It's possibly a complexion reference - a lazy language to describe exotic foreigners with brown skin. Those encountered in the New World had different complexions which were described as 'red'.

Christopher Columbus headed west to find a route to India, stumbled across Cuba, thought he was in India, so called all the people he met 'Indians'. They appeared tanned and red from sun exposure in the West Hemisphere. Some groups like those in Canada used red paint for war paint. Generally, Native Americans prefer to be called by their specific tribe name (Lakota, Navajo, Cheyenne, Cree, etc.). Some older generation are okay with 'Indian' because it's what they've always known. 'Native American' is curious - an old medicine man once told a YouTuber 'I'm a Lakota, you're a native American too'.

questions.question: Why have pheasants got a death wish? Why are they so stupid and can't get out of the way of cars?

answers.answer: Pheasants are bred in captivity. They don't learn off their parents. They're taken away when they're little chicks, bred by dealers, and 40 million are released each year for the shooting industry. They're unable to develop life skills. They're fat, have tiny brains, and predominantly lazy. If they actually knew what was going on, the last thing they'd do is take off in the vicinity of a shoot. As they manage to live out that game season into the next season, they actually get more wily. The pheasant that has managed to evade danger in one season and lives to fight another day is less likely to get hit by a car because they've managed to associate danger with cars.

questions.question: Why can my daughter's brother unlock her iPhone with his face using Face ID? They look similar but she's got blue eyes and long hair, he's got brown eyes and short hair.

answers.answer: When these pieces of software are calibrated, they need to keep the false match rate to an acceptable level because if they set it to 100% exact match, when people do their hair differently, wear makeup, glasses, have plastic surgery or disfigurement, they wouldn't be able to unlock the phone. So they build in a certain level of tolerance. Siblings have roughly similar facial and skeletal structure so they're edging in under that threshold. It wouldn't necessarily work the other way around. Also possible he has programmed his face into her phone settings as well - big brothers being big brothers.

questions.question: What's the texture of the smallest thing in the world? (bracket: I don't know what the smallest thing in the world is)
Why aren't you allowed to drink from the hot tap? My grandad was a plumber and said there's no reason you couldn't.

answers.answer: Back in the day, the hot water would come from the tank in the attic, into the immersion, then into your bath. That meant there could be something manky floating around in the tank in the attic, like a dead squirrel.

questions.question: Why do tins of tuna in spring water, brine and sunflower oil all cost the same? Surely the oil is much more expensive?

answers.answer: The cost is incurred in the canning process rather than the presentation. Any disparity in cost is so negligible that they even it out across the varieties. It makes life easier to sell at the same unit price. It's also easier for processing big shipments - you'd need three different sets of paperwork otherwise.

questions.question: If my cat grew bigger than me, would she see me as prey or does she actually love me?

How do they ensure on Mastermind that each person's specialist round questions are equally hard? If one person has Spice Girls and the next has Rhyme and Gods, how do they know the questions are as hard?

Why can't you cancel a button you've pressed on a lift? When your child presses other numbers or you accidentally press 102, you have to stop at every floor until you get to your destination. Why no cancel button?

answers.answer: Modern lifts have something called anti-nuisance setting. If 50% of the calls have been pressed, the system goes 'obviously there isn't 15 people in the lift' and cancels all of them. For some reason a lot of the time people don't turn it on. It would be cost - in a new lift someone has just got to spend the time writing the software. Most modern lifts probably have it on. Mitsubishi makes most of the high quality lifts so it exists in Japan and in some modern lift systems here.

questions.question: Why is horse racing measured in furlongs? Every other sport uses yards, metres, every other derivative, but you never hear 'Saka scored a screamer from half a furlong'. Why do we use furlongs only in horse racing?

answers.answer: Furlong comes from medieval times - it was one furrow long when ploughing a field. They had fields in strips and you'd pull your plough with your horse, and that was a furlong. It goes back to ploughing - one furrow long. It originated without a specific distance attached because it depended on field size. The question of why it's still used is immaterial because everyone knows what a furlong is in horse racing and everyone's happy with the system.

questions.question: Do total eclipses happen on other planets in our solar system? It's a bit of a coincidence that the moon is 400 times smaller than the sun and 400 times further away, giving us total eclipses. Does that happen elsewhere?

answers.answer: The Sun is 400 times bigger but 400 times further away, so it appears the same size. The Moon is moving away from Earth about 4cm per year. We can only see total eclipses for about 5% of Earth's history - we're quite lucky to be around at this time. For the rest of the solar system: there are hundreds of moons around gas giants like Saturn, Jupiter, Neptune and Uranus. They don't have solid surfaces themselves so their moons could blot out the Sun. You could probably see a total eclipse from the surface of one moon seeing another moon. The really rare thing is that our Moon is so big - all other moons are tiny compared to their planets, but our Moon is a quarter the size of Earth. We're effectively a double planet. Having that big Moon has been crucial for us - it stabilised Earth's spin like a top, kept the climate stable for life over billions of years, created tides which caused sea creatures to move onto land. This big Moon seems quite rare, which could have implications for how common life is in the Universe.

questions.question: Where does a fly/gnat go when it gets into your eye? I walked into a swarm, one ended up in my eye. I washed it out with eye wash but never saw the fly come out. Does it enter your body, get pushed out through your nose as a sneeze, or decompose within?

answers.answer: Your eye is like a bath. The water (eye wash) moves the fly to the side of your eye - the equivalent of it sticking to the side of the bath. It no longer irritates you because it's not on your eyeball. The next time you wiped your eye (which you would have done especially working outside), you got rid of it without noticing. That's what happened - it was washed to the side and then wiped off on your finger.

questions.question: Did gladiators in Roman times have names when they entered the arena? Like the modern TV gladiators who have names like Legend, Fury, Bionic, Electra - did they have stage names?

answers.answer: They did have names. There's graffiti in Pompeii with a Thracian gladiator called Hilarus. He was a famous gladiator and that's how he was known. David also mentioned he used to do gladiator reenactments and fought under the name Bulbus in the Roman amphitheatre at Caerleon in South Wales.

The vast majority of gladiators were slaves and their owners could call them whatever they wanted. They would probably get their name after they had fought a few times - you don't name a slave if they're going to die straight away. Some were named after members of the imperial family to get favour, or ones set up to die were named as enemies of Rome. You'd get gladiators called Thrax.

questions.question: Why is it that when you're bilingual, you seem to have a different speech or tone of voice between the languages that you speak? In one language you're usually higher, and in the other you're a lot lower. Chris goes higher in Portuguese than in English.

answers.answer: Each language is positioned in a different part of the body. Some languages are pitched quite forward near the top of the mouth and nose. Some are pitched at the back. Latin languages like Italian, Spanish and Portuguese tend to be pitched more forward and slightly higher. It's like singing - you can belt or have a head voice, and each language is positioned slightly differently. You have to be a native speaker or completely bilingual to switch properly. It's about thinking in two languages rather than translating in your head.

questions.question: Could you have a light so bright that you could see your entire skeleton? Like when he was a child with a new torch, he could see the bones in his fingers - could you scale that up to see your whole skeleton?

How specific is the training for sniffer dogs? If you take ones that detect drugs, do they only train them for the most obvious stuff rather than obscure drugs like LSD or ketamine? Can the same dogs do drugs AND explosives?

answers.answer: Dogs can be multi-disciplined but are usually single discipline for ease and accuracy. A dog would be trained on drugs OR cadaver OR currency OR medical OR arms AND explosives, but trained on specific substances. Any dog with a high drive for the ball can be trained to detect pretty much anything. Takes about 5-6 months to train a high specification dog. The first one is the hardest and then you can add to their palette. There's no theoretical limit on what a good dog can do.

questions.question: When a high street or residential road is created, how is it decided which end has the low numbers and which end has the high numbers?

answers.answer: Numbers start low near the centre of the city. The post office determines numbering. Odd numbers are always on the left side of the road, even numbers (2, 4, 6, 8) on the right as you look up the road from the low numbering area. The centre of London is near Charing Cross station and that's what the numbering is based on. For other cities, they would have their own catchment area focused on their own centre.

questions.question: Why do we use hand gestures when we speak? Why do we gesture when we're perfectly capable of explaining ourselves verbally?

Is it possible that our devices - Smart TVs, phones, Alexas - are actually listening to us? Had a conversation about halal meats with family and then started getting adverts for halal meats on Facebook, even though nobody searched for anything.

answers.answer: The reason is probably the smartphone. When you install apps, if you actually read the user agreement, some applications ask for permission to use your camera, listen to your microphone, or read some of your recent SMS messages. If you've sent an SMS about something and an app has access to read your SMS messages, they'll know what you're talking about. Everything is connected - smartphones, Wi-Fi routers, even fridges and coffee machines these days. It's the apps that have access, not necessarily the devices listening directly. When you install an application, have a quick skim through that agreement.

questions.question: When a person needs a blood transfusion they get blood from a blood bank. If an animal needs a blood transfusion, where do they get the blood from?

answers.answer: There definitely is a pet blood bank. His dog is registered on it. You need a big dog - there's a weight limit, his is about 28 kilos. They approach people with large dogs at events. You go to a big veterinary practice. First time they check if the dog's calm enough and send training materials. You get called back every so often. The dog gets a biscuit and a toy. The organisation is called something like Pet Blood Bank.

questions.question: All airports in Canada start with a Y (like Toronto being YYZ). Why is it only Canada that does this? Everywhere else you can usually work out the city from the airport code.

answers.answer: Before the three-letter codes were adopted worldwide, each country had its own system. Canada used two-letter codes based on the weather station each airport had (VR for Vancouver, etc.). When they needed to turn it into three letters, by that time most of the good three-letter combinations were already taken by other countries. So they just prefixed all Canadian airports with Y. They added Y to all their existing two-letter codes.

questions.question: How high is the average cloud?

answers.answer: In winter the minimum cloud base is 600 to 1,000 feet. In summer the lowest clouds are about 2,000 to 3,000 feet, maybe 5,000 in a really hot summer day. Clouds can go right up much higher.

questions.question: Why do we use the word 'Dutch' in so many different contexts - go Dutch, Dutch auction, Dutch courage, Dutch uncle? What's the origin of these expressions?
Why don't we recall smells from dreams? It's always auditory or mainly visual. Rarely, if ever, is it a smell.

answers.answer: I think you're right. I'm trying to think... I've not had a... I don't know. I think we don't smell in dreams.

I had a dream just last week that I was the doctor refused to treat me because I had incredibly smelly feet and I could smell how disgusting they were in my dream. I hasten to add my feet are not smelly.

questions.question: What do you call a female priest? A male priest is a father. What title is a female priest?

answers.answer: Reverend. Is that? I don't know. I'm just thinking out loud. I don't know. Well, it's not going to be mother, is it?

Reverend is a catch-all term. Depending on your tradition, a female priest can answer to father or mother or reverend. My wife is a priest. She's not too fussed on the tradition, so she'll answer to any of them.

questions.question: Why is arachnophobia commonly regarded as the most common phobia? Why are we largely afraid of spiders and not other very dangerous animals and organisms that we experience, possibly much more dangerous than a spider?

answers.answer: The most obvious answer is poison, isn't it? They're poison. There's an evolutionary response to poison, I think.

It is a learned behavior. The most common phobia is actually height. We're scared of spiders because of the way they move hydraulically. They move fast. The big, black, hairy ones are most scary, not the most venomous ones. We get bitten by snakes a lot more a year - 300,000 snake bites a year worldwide. Spiders can appear anywhere with their webs. If your mum was terrified of spiders, you probably are too.

questions.question: Why do we have two nostrils? We have two eyes for 3D vision, two ears to locate sound, but these two nostrils are so close together that... Do you know what I think? I think what you've done is you've focused entirely upon one function of the nasal passages, as opposed to the other one.

answers.answer: The hair in your nostrils filters the air. If you had one massive nostril instead of two little ones, how effective would that filtering process become? Also, if one gets blocked, the other one works. Whereas if your massive mononostral got blocked, you'd be in a lot more trouble.

questions.question: If fruit doesn't taste very good, even though it's ripe and in season, will it have the same nutritional value? I eat fruit every day in the evening. And even if the fruit doesn't taste very good, I will eat it, because I'm thinking that it's doing me good.

answers.answer: Give or take it will. But do you... unless you can qualify that with your qualifications, you know, I would like to have an answer from someone with the required knowledge.

If ripe but doesn't taste good, it could be high water content (less nutrients) or bad soil/sunlight/climate (less nutrients). Flavour IS a good indicator of nutrients. Expensive tomatoes have more nutrients than cheaper ones grown with high yield in the same amount of soil.

questions.question: Why are roses synonymous with romance? Why is it roses that are typically given for Valentine's Day?
Why do we say 'quid' when talking about pounds? Where did that come from?

answers.answer: I think it's just another word for a coin, 400 years or more. A type of coin would be a quid. And for some reason, it's stuck. Especially as a pound, for most of our lot.

questions.question: When I put watches in storage, if I pull the crown out, does the battery last longer?

answers.answer: Depends on the watch. When you pull the crown out, it engages a lever which acts as a brake on one of the wheels. The battery is still supplying power through the rotor, stator. It won't affect battery life. Two to three years is typical. Very few watches cut off electrical supply when crown pulled out. He should leave battery in, let them run, because oil flows around rather than seizing up. Change when it stops. After 2-3 years, cells can leak and destroy the watch.

questions.question: Why do you never, ever see baby pigeons?

answers.answer: They stay in the nest until they can fly, and as soon as they can fly they look like grown-ups. You don't see baby crows or baby seagulls either. If you wanted to see a baby pigeon, you'd just have to find a pigeon's nest full of pigeons that can't yet fly - an unfledged pigeon.

questions.question: Why is it that when you're looking at an island across water, on different days it can look closer or further away? I grew up opposite the Isle of May in Fife. And from Murano, Venice looked closer or further away.

answers.answer: Would it not just be the clarity? You know, the humidity. Or the... It could be the humidity, but I've got a strong feeling it's more complicated than that.

questions.question: Why is it that our moon doesn't have a nice fancy name like all the other moons in the solar system? It's just called the Moon.

answers.answer: Because it was the first moon. Because it was the only moon we could see. So they named it. They looked at it and said, what are we going to call that? And someone said, Luna. We'll call it Luna. So it became known as Luna. And it became known as the Moon. And then when interplanetary observation became more commonplace, after Copernicus and telescopes, they started discovering that other planets were orbited by bodies that fulfill similar purposes around other planets. So anything that orbits a planet becomes a moon, but there will only ever be one, the Moon.

questions.question: My dog can lie under my duvet for hours without coming out for air. But if I go under the duvet, I'll last about two minutes before grasping for oxygen. How can the dog survive under the duvet for that long?

answers.answer: I'm not sure that we've stumbled across a scientific phenomenon here. But on the off chance that we have, I'll put it on the board.

It's the nose. When you think of our nose, our nostrils go forward. If you look carefully at a dog's nose, they go forward and there's like a split to the side on each nostril. So we're taking air from the front, but dogs can take air from the front and the sides. Because of the olfactory system and how they send things, they have a much wider area to take in. They've got more suction, as it were. When they're under the duvet, they're taking it from different directions.

questions.question: Is it true that an egg can never be fertilized by more than one sperm? The teacher in sex education said the egg hardens after the first sperm penetrates it and no other sperm can get in. But what if two sperm get there at the same time?

answers.answer: It must take a certain amount of time for it to harden. That is an excellent question.

So rarely it happens, but when it does, the two nuclei of the sperm will cause the zygote to self-abort. It can happen, but it would never go to term. It would never even start developing. It's thought that in one percent of conceptions this happens. But on the massive majority, we're talking ninety nine point nine percent of the cases, the fertilized egg will self-abort. But sometimes it does go, and this is called a chimera. The hardening process is an instant process. When a sperm enters the egg, you imagine the egg being penetrated by a number of sperms at the same time, but yes, immediately as the single head of the sperm enters through the outer membrane of the egg, there's a sort of electrical change in the nature of the cell membrane, which causes no other sperm to enter.

The 1% that become a chimera that gets fertilized and carries on is also known as a hydatidiform mole. It is a type of pregnancy. And the way you discover that you've had it is when you go for your scan, because you have all the normal symptoms and you do your test and you have your pregnancy hormones, but when you go for a scan, there's no baby. When they take it away and test it, they see that it is this type of tumor that is really, really rare. And there are two types, a full mole pregnancy and a partial. Some of them do require treatment after because they can grow back as a cancer. And they only found out that it was caused by two sperm fertilizing the egg quite recently. Charing Cross Hospital is the expert on this.

questions.question: Why is bread exempt from having to be wrapped in supermarkets?

answers.answer: Lots of things are exempt. The only thing I can think of is fruit and vegetables. But you can wash those. You can't wash bread. I think exempt might be a red herring. I'm just not helping at all.

answers.caller: Jack from St Albans (former packaging team at major UK retailer)
answers.answer: The ultimate answer is it's not really driven by any sort of rule. It's based on what the shop selling wants to present the product as. So you'll get some longer life products like your usual sliced white loaf, which will be in a plastic bag designed for take home, sit on the counter for a week. Then you get your more premium in-store bakery style product, which is supposed to look more artisanal. Therefore, you'll get them either loose or in nice paper bags to give the idea of going back to traditional baking. So it's psychology more than anything else. If it's not wrapped up, it's a more premium product. You see the same with pastries. People expect to pick those up in store, walk out and start eating them. Whereas if it's something they're expected to take home and keep for a while, you've got that bag there to either prolong shelf life or provide ease of use.

questions.question: My daughter Grace, age 8, would like to know if there's a proven cure for hiccups. She suffers from them at least three times a day.

answers.answer: I don't think there is, is there? Because we'd know, wouldn't we? I mean, hiccups are your diaphragm kind of spasming, isn't it? So I have no idea how any of these things would help.
Finger in each ear. Have someone that you trust raise a glass to your lips and you have to drink at least half the glass full, your hiccups are gone.

questions.question: How do we know with such certainty what the layers of the earth are? We haven't dug all the way down to the middle.

answers.answer: Maybe your boy's the first one to actually pick up on this and it's all been a huge con visited upon the human species for about 150 years.

answers.caller: Sam from Hampstead (exploration geologist with Masters in geophysics and geology)
answers.answer: The reason we know the Earth's different layers is because of geophysics. When there's an earthquake on one side of the planet, we can measure the different types of waves - body waves, pressure waves and surface shear waves. Shear waves don't travel through liquid. They can only travel through solid materials. So when they hit the liquid mantle, they stop and we can measure that. P waves travel through both liquid and solid. As they travel through the different Earth layers, they change propagation and stretch and squeeze. So we can measure that it's going from liquid into solid, into the core. It's quite recent science - probably early 20th century.

questions.question: Why is it that when aircraft are coming for landing, they turn all the lights off?

answers.answer: To get your eyes ready for the darkness in case there's an accident. Because if it's pitch black, it makes it more awkward to get out of the plane. But the lights are going to go off as a consequence of the emergency anyway. So they're trying to get your eyes accustomed to the darkness in case there's an accident on landing. Think about it - every second is going to be precious in that context.

questions.question: Is there some kind of criteria for the decision making about the colours of football shirts? Why do clubs choose the colours they do?

answers.answer: The fundamental answer will be because at some point in history, they chose those colours. That's it. But then you start saying, well, why did they choose those colours? And then you'd be here forever.

answers.caller: Jim from Whitley Beer (grandfather played left back for Sunderland)
answers.answer: A long time ago, when the clubs were first starting, they tended to have the Catholics and the Protestants separated within one town. The Catholics went for a red shirt. The Protestants went for a blue shirt. If it was two different teams in the same town - look at Everton and Liverpool. Manchester City in blue, Manchester United in red. The story about Juventus and the black and white stripes - it was actually a private World Cup. Tommy Lipton invited a small mining team from West Auckland who played in black and white stripes because they followed Newcastle United. And of course they won the World Cup.

questions.question: Why are some people in Belgium called Flemish?

answers.answer: Flemish refers to a dialect/language. Most people in Belgium are Flemish. I'm not sure where the country of Fleming is or what the origin is.

Belgium is divided into two sections. One is French-speaking (Walloons) and the Dutch-speaking section is Flemish (Flanders). In Dutch, it's Flandern, which we've anglicised to Flanders. The people speak Flemish. It's like Dutch but bastardised. Most Belgians can speak both Flemish and French.

questions.question: What is it about glass that allows light to travel through it, but for other solid objects light can't?

answers.answer: It's transparent. Transparent means light can pass through it.

answers.caller: John (Leamington Spa) - Master's in Chemical Engineering
answers.answer: Light waves from any light source don't interact with the solid structure of glass. Infrared and UV waves can be blocked, but normal white light waves aren't blocked at all.

questions.question: Where does the suspense music 'dum, dum, dum' originate from?

answers.answer: Silent films had musical accompaniment. I'm pretty sure that's right.

questions.question: If a man is 70-80% unwell (has a cold or flu) and his partner is ovulating, would the sperm be less than 70-80% quality? Would a child conceived be only 70-80% healthy?

answers.answer: Your fertility and quality of sperm can be affected by things like flu. It lowers the likelihood of fertilising the egg. But to get through, a sperm has to be in pretty good nick, so it wouldn't mean subpar children. It doesn't work like that.

answers.caller: Ollie (Lingfield) - Farm animal veterinary surgeon, bull breeding soundness specialist
answers.answer: Anything that raises body temperature (gives you a fever) can kill off sperm because spermatogenesis is very temperature-sensitive. That's why testicles hang outside the body. A temperature will drop sperm count (viability) but won't affect genetic makeup, which was set weeks in advance. The sperm that have been produced during illness can be affected in terms of viability (ability to swim, penetrate the egg) but genetically they are set. Even in fertility treatment/ICSI, they look for the most wriggly sperm anyway.

questions.question: Why are taxis legally exempt from child seat/safety belt laws for young children? Why can you take a week-old baby in a taxi without a car seat?

answers.answer: It could be about time saved between passengers. It might be a cost-benefit ratio calculation about harming taxi drivers.

answers.caller: Steve (Oxford) - GMB union officer for private hire and taxi drivers, drove for 26 years
answers.answer: Private hire taxi drivers cannot be sure of what passengers they may collect or whether they'd have appropriate seats. Certain public hire vehicles cannot guarantee they'd have appropriate child seats available. There are questions over liability - there was a recent case where a passenger had a child on their lap, took off their seatbelt and were stopped by police, raising questions about safety and fit and properness. Drivers also don't have to wear seatbelts when driving passengers. Under three-year-olds being unrestrained is also covered by government law. The primary reason is drivers can't have a selection of seats available. If someone pre-books with a car service, it can normally be arranged.

questions.question: When you write a word multiple times, why does it start to look wrong?

answers.answer: That's a great question. I'll be amazed if we get an answer.

It's called semantic satiation. It's when we repeatedly say or write a word and there's a breakdown of long-term auditory and verbal memory. We look at it several times and that function weakens and gives up because it's assumed that you already know it - it's in your long-term memory. It's a phenomenon known with language and auditory information.

questions.question: Is birds singing at night a new thing? Our cats have started watching TV on a new Samsung OLED.

answers.answer: Could be the new development and street lighting confusing the birds, making them think it's daylight. Motion sensor lights might be affecting it.

questions.question: Why have my two 12-year-old cats started watching TV suddenly? We got a new Samsung OLED TV. They never watched TV before. They watch YouTube cat channels with squirrels.

answers.caller: Chris (Coventry) - Has four cats, avid fan
answers.answer: Modern TVs, especially OLEDs, have a higher frame rate. The human eye needs 15-20 frames per second for fluid motion, but cats need around 100 frames per second to see it as fluid. On older TVs, cats essentially see a slideshow - black, coloured, black, coloured. Now they're seeing it more clearly and more fluidly. The higher frame rate makes it interesting to them.

questions.question: What's the German word for rucksack?

answers.answer: Ruck means back in German. So rucksack literally means back sack.

questions.question: Why do my fingernails split when I use scissors with my left hand to cut the nails on my right hand, but cut fine when I use scissors with my right hand on my left hand nails?

answers.answer: It's because you're right-handed. You would have the same problem with clippers.

Scissors for left-handed people have the blade cut in a different direction. You need to buy specially engineered left-handed scissors - it's not just a matter of flipping them upside down. Dave has right-handed scissors which is why his nails split when cutting with his left hand.

questions.question: What's the difference between 'falling over' and 'having a fall'? What are the criteria?

answers.answer: It's when you can't get up without help. Someone who struggles to get back up again has had a fall.

questions.question: What happens to your stomach when you go over a hump in the road and why doesn't it affect everyone every time?

answers.answer: It's about G-force. When you go over a humpback bridge, you briefly experience 0G (weightlessness) for about half a second, then increased G-force (around 2G) as you come out of it. Your organs move up because gravity isn't holding them down anymore, then they fall back down. It happens on humpback bridges but not on steeper hills or longer gradients because it requires that sudden parabolic movement. The diaphragm moving up and down contributes to the strange feeling.
The diaphragm shooting up and down is definitely part of it.

questions.question: Why do trees on the roadside of A roads seem to create an arch or space for vehicles without any evidence of pruning? Does a tree feel the movement of air and realize it's a hostile environment to grow into?

answers.answer: Trees are reactive. They will put more leaves on the side that has more benefit for photosynthesis. When vehicles brush underneath them, they're knocking the leaves off, so the tree doesn't have the ability to photosynthesize there and puts its growth elsewhere. If vehicles are frequent enough, minimal growth occurs in those areas. It's a form of intelligence - the tree registers not to put more effort into that zone. If the bus route changed, after a couple of years it would start growing back.

questions.question: Where did my African grey parrot learn to do the wolf whistle and the 'come here' whistle when it was raised as a chick with no humans whistling around it?

answers.answer: Parrots, parakeets, and cockatiels naturally make these sounds - it's the timber they use that resonates with us. It's a natural song they sing, not learned from humans. African greys pick up a lot of things from us but not this particular whistle. Chicks respond to it, particularly when they need feeding - it's to bring the chicks towards them.

questions.question: Why is it that after 10pm (post-watershed), if a footballer accidentally swore in a post-match interview the interviewer still apologized, but if the same word was used in a drama or comedy show at the same time, it would be acceptable? What's the difference between broadcasting rules in sport versus entertainment?

answers.answer: The presenter was just being cautious. There's no real problem post-watershed, especially for mild language. It becomes more problematic when using profanity to refer to body parts rather than just as an expression (like 'it was all a load of B'). Broadcasters have a reflex action to apologize for any profane language, and there's no downside to being over-cautious.

questions.question: Before the invention of communication technologies like telephone or telegraph, how did people book holidays abroad? How would they book hotels or transportation?

answers.answer: By letter. Hotels would advertise in newspapers (which have existed since the 16th-17th century), and people would write to P.O. boxes to make bookings. It would take weeks for correspondence and required planning well in advance. Even into the 20th century, as seen in Agatha Christie novels, much business was conducted by letter.

questions.question: When do rainy days or windy days become a storm? What is the threshold?

answers.answer: It's going to be a measure of how strong the wind is, or pressure, or wind speed. There must be a way of doing it since you see it on the weather map.

The UK's Met Office doesn't actually use simple thresholds. It's a scale, a risk matrix based on likelihood and impact. A deep area of low pressure over Cornwall or the Welsh Mountains over winter wouldn't necessarily warrant a warning, but the same system over a populated area like London could constitute a warning. It's called the National Severe Weather Warning Service with amber, yellow, or red weather warnings. Yellow is to be aware, amber is to be prepared. The chief forecaster meets with civil contingency advisors to discuss local impacts.

questions.question: Why was Napoleon known by his first name, whereas most other dictators in history like Hitler and Stalin are known by their second name?

answers.answer: If you're an emperor, they go with your Christian name - Emperor Nero, Emperor Napoleon, Queen Victoria. The first name goes with the honorific. Neither Stalin was emperor. He achieved royal status by becoming emperor.

questions.question: Why do racehorses have such strange names?

answers.answer: Horses in general don't have strange names - you could call a horse Dobbin. But when there's gambling involved and it's such a big organised thing, you've got to prove the lineage. So you can't have a dog called Spot. The dog has to have a name recognised by the Kennel Club that is specific to that dog so you can pay a premium for a puppy sired by that dog, in the same way you pay a premium for a foal sired by that stallion. The reason for complicated names is for the descriptive exclusivity.

When horses are foaled, they're unnamed. The owner of the foal gets to choose a name. They're allowed 18 characters. They quite often do fancy wordplay related to the sire and mare (mum and dad). They create the name and check it with the British Horse Racing Authority to make sure it doesn't exist because it can't be the name of a live racehorse. There are certain things you can't put in - rude things, words like 'Colt' and 'Filly'. You're not allowed a number but you can spell out a number. So if you're a golfer you can have 'Three Under Par Five'.

questions.question: How does a dog know which person to go to when two people with identical whistles from the same shop blow them at different ends of a field?

answers.answer: If you blow two different whistles or if somebody with you blows two different whistles, the dogs both make their way to their own owner. The only explanation is that the whistles are, from the dog's point of view, making different noises. The whistles might be ever so slightly differently calibrated, or you might puff differently and the dog's hearing is so finely tuned that if we both blew into a tube we would have different strength of blowing. The answer is probably the different puff - the personal puff.

answers.caller: John from Birmingham (archivist at Acme Whistle Company)
answers.answer: All dog whistles are manufactured to a very tight tolerance so they produce a consistent sound. When training your dog, you would typically train it to respond to specific commands - two pips for one command, three pips for recall. But inevitably, most dog trainers will tell you that your own personality comes into how you blow the whistle. Your dog will start to instinctively know it is YOUR whistle they are responding to. It's the relationship between the whistle and the blower. The only exception is the silent dog whistle with a screw piston - you can tune the frequency to your dog's ear if you wish.

questions.question: Why does the pitch of tinnitus change when I press different parts of my head with different pressure?

answers.answer: Would it just not be the same as your head as a bell? If you put some pressure on a bell, the tone of the chime will change. It must be linked to your ear.

The reason you get tinnitus is because your auditory nerve in the inner ear is irritated for whatever reason and it produces sounds. If you press different areas of the head around the ears - soft tissue - you might change or irritate the conduction going through to the auditory nerve, so you might change the tone. If you put your hand on your forehead, it's mostly bone, that probably wouldn't change the tone. Once you go past the tympanic membrane, it's all liquid and you've got little bones and semicircular canals and then the auditory nerve. It gets conducted more easily behind the tympanic membrane than in front of it because it's air versus fluid. So it depends how hard you press and how much the conduction goes to the auditory nerve and annoys it.

questions.question: Do the people who do voiceovers in commercials actually speak like that in real life, or do they put on voices for the ads?

answers.answer: Gav, who does the Coco Pops monkey voice, categorically doesn't speak like that in real life. It's a really exaggerated voice.

We'd like to think not. But we are kind of vocal chameleons in many situations. If we're just talking to family and friends, probably not really. But over 20 years, your voice naturally becomes this way, like an actor's. Natural talent always wins out over performed accents. In terms of range and tone, it's a skill. I'm proudest of recently doing the new advertisements for Adele's tour in Munich, which required a slower, more deliberate timbre.

We know of each other. There's so many voiceovers it's not competitive between us. The biggest competition at the moment is AI, which is replacing a lot of voiceovers. Career highlights include BBC Three, the Olympics, and the voices in the plants (LBC).

questions.question: Is it ever too cold to snow?

answers.answer: Technically no, it is never too cold to snow, but once you get very cold (like minus 9 or 10 degrees), there wouldn't be enough moisture in the air to create snow.

questions.question: Why can I see clearly underwater when wearing my daughter's non-prescription perspex goggles from the pool foyer, despite having terrible eyesight?

answers.answer: It's because the rain has gone (clearly meant as a joke). It's all about the moment - spotting the opportunity. The rain has gone. He could see clearly now.

answers.caller: Simba from Brighton (domiciliary optometrist for 10 years)
answers.answer: Twofold reason. One is the goggle - water interacts with the cornea and blurs your vision, so having the airspace in the goggle gives your cornea the ability to focus clearly. And secondly, water itself has a different refractive index to plastic. He's probably got a slight refractive error which coincides with the index of the water, which allows him to see much clearer.

questions.question: How would our tides change if we had two or three moons like some other planets?
Has there ever been a conspiracy theory that at the time was deemed crazy and derided that actually turned out to be true?

answers.answer: In prohibition era America, there was a conspiracy theory that the government was poisoning alcohol to stop people drinking, and that actually turned out to be true.

MK Ultra - a CIA mind control program from the Cold War era where the CIA experimented with drugs, particularly LSD, on Americans to see if they could brainwash or mind control people. It was kept hidden underground until it was disclosed post-Watergate in the 1970s.

questions.question: TV continuity announcers - what do they do the rest of the time when they're not announcing between programs?

answers.answer: They have to be there in case things go wrong. If the TV falls off air, they have to alert the news. It's not as easy as it sounds - they have to be on constant alert.

Shifts start at 4pm and the last announcement goes into the news at 10pm - that's a six-hour shift. They sit and watch TV waiting for something to go wrong. If the TV falls off air, an alarm goes off and they get instructions on what to say. They write all their own scripts which get approved daily. They get about 10-15 seconds for idents (going into programmes) and about 15 seconds on end credits.

questions.question: Why is 'sheep' the same word for singular and plural? Can you think of another animal that's the same?

answers.answer: Suggestions included: fish, deer, moose, buffalo, antelopes, wildebeest, zebras.
