The original word for sheep in Anglo-Saxon is 'shea-up' (pronounced 'sheap'). In Old English, it wasn't plural then either. Fish is similar - in Old English, there is no plural; it's just 'fish'. Both are Anglo-Saxon words where Old English didn't have plurals. In modern English, we pre-pluralise the word - 'look at those sheep' or 'look at that sheep'.

questions.question: Is it true that some animals mate for life (penguins, swans, etc.)? Has a species that mates for life ever broken up? Like a penguin leaving a penguin?

answers.answer: His wife is a zookeeper at Blair Drummond Safari Park in Stirling. Two penguins called Damo and Pete were partners for their adult lives. A new penguin called Cliff arrived, caught Damo's eye, and she left Pete for Cliff. Pete was definitely down in the dumps afterward.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to put a cold flannel on a child's head when they have a temperature? Her daughter keeps being told by doctors not to do this, and her grandson has had four febrile seizures.

answers.answer: The caller was right that there's a risk of febrile convulsion. Trials have compared using cold flannels or sponges versus giving paracetamol or ibuprofen. The cold flannel works for about an hour to an hour and a half, and then the temperature comes back. Paracetamol or ibuprofen lasts much longer. They don't want parents to be falsely reassured by using a cold flannel - the temperature appears to calm down but returns later.

questions.question: When filling up helium balloons, is the helium canister getting lighter or heavier as it empties?

answers.answer: The helium is lighter than air and pushes the canister up. As it empties, air would fill the space. The empty canister could be full of air or a vacuum. The canister is very thick, possibly because it is a vacuum - if it wasn't, the pressure would crush it.

Boyle's Law - the volume of gas increases as the pressure decreases. The canister is a fixed volume. When you charge it, you're putting more in, so it gets heavier. Conversely, as you empty it, it gets lighter. There's no vacuum involved because it's never completely empty - the helium expands as pressure decreases and can't all be forced out.

questions.question: Why are TV competition PO box numbers always in Derby? Why not London? Has anyone ever won by posting entry?

answers.answer: There must be one company that runs the free postal entry option for all TV competitions, and it must be in Derby. This is based on legal requirements to offer free entry alongside premium rate text and phone lines.
There are two main companies who do competition verifications: Nunkey in Derby and Royal Mail. Most broadcasters use Nunkey, which is based in Derby, so that PO box is in Derby.

questions.question: Why do children start getting afraid of the dark not when they're babies or toddlers but suddenly around school age?

answers.answer: It's because of imagination - at school age, imagination is developing. When lights are on, you know there's no wolf in the room. When lights are off, there could be a wolf there. Our imagination fills in the gaps. It never stops - you're always frightened of the thing that might be round the corner.

Three headings: 1) Evolution - we are frightened of threat, and when we can't see threat, being frightened is good because it means you're less likely to be eaten. 2) Carl Jung's shadow self theory - children become aware of the darker side of themselves, which manifests as fear of monsters under the bed. 3) Separation anxiety - it's not so much fear of the dark but fear of separation from parents. The transition from being together all day to suddenly being on your own at night is a big challenge. James ranked them: evolution first, separation anxiety second, Jung's shadow self third.

questions.question: Why do some ancient manuscripts have to be handled with gloves and some don't?

answers.answer: The glove is designed to stop moisture and oils from sweat on fingers from getting into the paper. It depends on how the papers have been stored - if they're not desiccated or dry.

Clean washed hands are fine for most manuscripts. You only need to wear gloves when objects have metal on them like gold or silver. However, you should NOT wear white gloves or cotton gloves because they have no dexterity. You should wear nitrile surgical gloves instead. The skin's oils could affect metal but are fine with actual paper.

questions.question: Are the oldest child's genes stronger and do they tend to live longer because parents are younger when they first had children?

answers.answer: I don't know if there's research on this. I wouldn't worry too much if I were you.

answers.caller: Ali (Barnet) - Biology Teacher with First Class Degree in Pharmacology
answers.answer: The evidence is inconclusive but there are interesting studies. First-borns DO tend to live longer, but it's dependent on the mother's age when she had the child. Before age 30, egg quality is higher, giving children better chances and less predisposition to genetic conditions. Younger-born siblings are also more likely to engage in risk-taking behaviours. It's complex - involves epigenetics, chromosomes, telomere lengths. Research is mainly on animal studies with small sample sizes.

questions.caller: Trevor (Frimley) - on behalf of daughter Eloise
questions.question: Why when we eat pickles does one eye go all squiffy (twitch)?

answers.answer: It's probably the sourness triggering a twitch. This is actually a superb question and I really want to know the answer too.

questions.question: Why are children of school age afraid of the dark? (Additional input to Clare's question)

answers.answer: Three theories: 1) Evolution - being frightened of what you can't see is protective. 2) Jung's shadow self - children become aware of their darker side which manifests as monsters under the bed. 3) Separation anxiety - at night it's a big separation from parents, the transition from being together all day to being alone. Children don't have insight into what they're really afraid of. Around age 5 there's also a 'theory of mind' development where children become aware others think differently - this is brain development.

questions.question: Why does the sound of water from the tap change as it gets warmer? Hot water sounds softer than cold water.

answers.answer: Hot water atoms and molecules are bouncing around more, so physical properties are different from cold water. The interaction with the hard surface of the basin would be different, and the transfer of heat and kinetic energy into sound energy would have different ratios.

answers.caller: Ed (Mere) - Retired Mechanics of Fluids Engineer (60 years)
answers.answer: All fluids, liquids and gases are affected by change in temperature. Change of temperature changes the density which alters the speed of sound. Cold water will sound louder than warm water. Bubbles in the liquid also affect density.

questions.question: When you look at a shooting star going across the sky, can you see them if they're coming directly at you?

answers.answer: No one would ever have seen it if it was coming directly at you because you wouldn't see anything. What would you see - either a shooting star or nothing?

answers.caller: Adrian (Elverchurch) - Amateur Astronomer, UK Meteor Network member
answers.answer: If it wasn't going across your path, it would still burn up. You would see it as a point of light that would quickly get brighter and then fade. The UK Meteor Network has cameras across the country that can work out trajectories. When meteors are large enough to land, the cameras are so accurate they can work out within a few hundred meters where the meteorite will land - they found one before weather degraded it.

questions.question: Is it true that during the French Revolution after they guillotined Louis XVI, they changed the order of playing cards so that aces became bigger than kings?

answers.answer: It seems very unlikely to me. I don't know if we can go definitive on it.

questions.question: How do they make synthetic hair extensions? How are they made in the factory without getting tangled up?

answers.answer: The question is on the list. (No answer provided)

questions.question: When in American history did the American accent that we know today become recognizably American?

answers.answer: There's no such thing as THE American accent any more than there's one Irish accent. (Acknowledged that 17th century British English sounded closer to American accents than British accents do today)

The American accent that Americans have is actually old English from the 17th or 18th century. With no telecommunications or rapid transport, varieties diversified and stayed diversified. In the 18th century, most British English lost the R in words like 'car' while American English retained it. American vowels changed - the distinction between long and short vowels disappeared, rounded vowels became unrounded (e.g., 'job' instead of 'job'). It's an oversimplification to call it one American accent - there are also Latino and Eastern European influences.

questions.question: What is the significance of Alverchurch in the history of British radio?

answers.answer: Godfrey Baisley, the creator of The Archers, was from Alverchurch in Worcestershire.

questions.question: What is the answer to the mystery about something that may help stave off Alzheimer's?

answers.answer: The answer is Viagra, reportedly may help stave off Alzheimer's by a factor of about 18%
I don't know what the answer is
Good luck running a double blind test on that one

questions.question: What were electric eels called before electricity was discovered?

answers.answer: It probably didn't have a name before the taxonomy and Darwin era in the 18th-19th century. The technical term is Electrophorus. It's a South American freshwater fish, not actually an eel.
They were all called 'nice' back in the day

questions.question: When cremated people with metal hips, gold teeth, etc., what happens to those metal bits that don't burn?

answers.answer: Vague recollection that someone told him they'd kept a knee or hip, but not sure

The body goes into a cremulator which breaks it down into ashes. They run a magnet across the ashes and remove all metal bits, which go to metal reclaimers and are melted down and reused. Unless you tick a box when arranging the funeral to have them returned.

questions.question: Why are the numbers on a dartboard in the order that they're in?

answers.answer: It's a careful calculation so that if you miss a high number by a bit, you hit a low number, and if you miss a low number by a bit, you hit a high number. The highest numbers are placed next to the lowest numbers.

Brian Gamlin in the 1890s came up with the configuration. It was designed to increase accuracy and prevent lucky shots. There are over two million other possible configurations but his just worked the best.

questions.question: If the source of a river is a trickle like a spring, and the mouth is massive, where does all the water come from?

answers.answer: The sky - all the rain. Water finds its way to the lowest point. Rainwater that once absorbed blanket-like into the earth is now concentrated into a channel.

Two elements: groundwater contribution (from permeable rocks like chalk that hold water and emit it through springs) and the broader catchment itself. The Thames isn't just one river - there are hundreds of tributaries (Brent, Fleet, Tyburn, Kennet, Colne) that all contribute. Heavy rain falls on higher ground and all small rivers coalesce into bigger ones. It's the water cycle.

questions.question: Why does smoke from a bonfire always seem to follow you around, even on a still day?

answers.answer: The parameters of the question may not be true - you're only standing where you're standing, so if you stood elsewhere you'd be equally smoky

As the bonfire burns, it draws in cold air at the bottom and heated products of combustion go up vertically. When you stand near it, you're interfering with a portion of that airflow and creating a vortex - you become an air dam. The smoke will follow you wherever you move.

questions.question: In America where all denominations are the same size, how do blind people know what they're paying with?

answers.answer: It may be a question of ordering them with help from a sighted person, knowing what's at the front and back of the money clip. Some countries may have indentations on their currency.

Blind person speaking - US money is all same size AND same colour, so colour blindness doesn't help either. In Canada, money is different colours and has Braille. Americans sometimes fold money in certain ways to distinguish denominations. There are small machines that can identify bills, made by the Canadian government for US money. Apps like 'Be My Eyes' also help.

questions.question: Why does air from pursed lips (like blowing out birthday candles) feel cool, but saying 'ha' with an open mouth feels warm?

answers.answer: Windchill factor - it's not necessarily cold air, it's about what happens when it hits your skin, withdrawing warmth from the skin

When blowing through pursed lips, you're increasing air speed/velocity which decreases its temperature. When blowing through an open mouth, air comes out at much lower speed at body temperature (heated by circulating blood). Your hands are colder than your body interior, so you perceive the open-mouth blow as warmer.

questions.question: When did dogs become known as 'man's best friend'?
Can DNA be transferred from one place to another - like if someone touches something you've touched, can they then carry your DNA to a crime scene?

answers.answer: Yes, DNA is mobile and portable. Anything containing your DNA can be transferred.

DNA is absolutely mobile. When we leave DNA at a scene, we shed it through hair follicles, skin cells, blood, or other fluids. This is a real problem for investigators - secondary transfer means DNA can be moved around within a scene or unknowingly carried to other locations. Defense lawyers love this because someone's DNA could be walked into a crime scene after they stepped in saliva on the pavement outside.

questions.question: Why do police always say a dog was 'destroyed' rather than 'killed' when shooting a dog?

answers.answer: Dogs are legally classed as 'chattel' - intangible personal property. This dates back to when dogs had value for services provided rather than companionship. You can't legally say a dog was 'killed' because legally it's property that was 'destroyed'. However personally I would say dogs were killed because I love dogs.

questions.question: When you look on your phone and it gives you the temperature for the day, and next to it it says 'feels like' something else - how do they figure that out? Does somebody go out and stand in the cold?

answers.answer: It's the function of your human body's ability to get rid of our body heat. The actual temperature and the feels of temperature would be very similar in light winds and average humidity around 80%. But if wind increases, it makes your body's ability to lose heat faster, so it feels like a lower temperature. However, if humidity increases past 80 up to 90, 95%, your body ability to sweat decreases massively, so it feels like a higher temperature. They use calculations, an algorithm into which you punch humidity, temperature, windiness, and UV index.

questions.question: On a plane, sometimes the flag is printed back to front. Why are the flags printed back to front on a plane sometimes? The Maltese flag was printed back to front with the cross to the other side.

answers.answer: If it was an Italian flag and you were flying towards Italy, it would be the correct way round. But if it was an Italian plane and you were flying away from Italy, it would be reversed.

You mentioned you're looking at a flagpole, and the flagpole is to the left of the flag flying. That's called the hoist, nearest to the flagpole. The flag at the far end is called the fly. If you are looking at the flag such that the flagpole is on the left, it will look to be the right way round. If you go round the other side and look at it so that the flagpole is on the right of the flag, the flag will effectively be backwards. On aircraft bodies, they're effectively like a flagpole. From the port side, it will be the right way round. From the starboard side, it will be backwards. You just need to imagine that the tail fin was made of glass, and you only had a flag on one side.

questions.question: Why aren't there more left-handed people? Why is the population not more 50-50 split between left and right handed?

answers.answer: Handedness is linked to bipedalness in mammals. Only left-handed kangaroos exist. Due to a part of the brain in the left hemisphere linked to tool use. From archaeological data like cave paintings, it was always right-handed tool makers. All Neanderthals were right-handed. They think back in history all humans were right-handed. Left-handedness came from a random mutation of genetics. Certain sports like boxing and MMA - left-handed boxers and fighters have a better win rate because most people who are right-handed expect a blow from the corresponding hand. So although there is a lower level of left-handedness, it's a gradually increasing one. It is evolution in action.

questions.question: Old recipes use 'cup' measurements - if it's proportional, why call it a cup? And if cup relates to proportion, what was a 'stick' of butter? Because if a stick is denoting weight, it can't work the same way a cup does.

answers.answer: I think there is consensus on what a cup is. An American cup is different from a UK cup. Regarding the stick of butter - it probably would have been a way for them to sell it back in the day. A stick because a block would go off quicker in the days before refrigeration.

questions.question: Humans have an umbilical cord connected to the afterbirth that is cut manually and clamped. What happens to other mammals in the animal kingdom? How do they manage their umbilical cords? They can't clamp them, so what do they do?

answers.answer: The umbilical cord doesn't contain a huge amount of blood and it will only deliver blood for as long as the placenta is still attached to the wall of the uterus. As soon as the placenta detaches there's no longer an active blood flow. So you can just chew your way through it and then it'll just wither off. We clamp and cut the cord and try to do delayed cord clamping now because when the baby is born a third of its blood volume is still in the placenta so we give it time to come back. It's called placental transfusion and that protects them against childhood anemia. There's a valve inside the abdomen at the umbilical cord base that then closes. The majority of animals will when the cord has stopped pulsating just chew through it. In mammals that are really tall like elephants and giraffes, their infants fall to the ground and the cord snaps. But because they're larger animals they have a greater circulating volume so they can afford to lose a little bit.

questions.question: Has the gestation period for our species always been the same, or has it changed through evolution? Baby monkeys can grip their mum on day one, but human babies are completely helpless. Were we able to do that when we were monkeys millennia ago?
MRIs are so loud. They go clonk, clonk. Why are MRI scanners so loud? Why hasn't someone come up with a quiet one by now?

answers.answer: It's a large magnet spinning around and changing direction to do the imagery. The machinery used to move it makes a lot of noise. The mechanicals of moving the magnet, essentially.

Nothing actually moves in an MRI scanner. It doesn't actually spin. There are three real things that make the noises. First, there's a background noise that makes a dunk, dunk every couple of seconds - that's called the cold head, a compressor compressing the helium back into liquid helium because the main coil is bathed in liquid helium. Then there is the RF coil (radio frequency coil) which sits closest to your head and makes those chirpy, high-pitched noises - like being in a fax machine. Then outside the RF coil there's a gradient coil which makes the bigger, more substantial noises. We rotate the magnetic field in the coil. Nothing actually physically moves. And there's the three things that generate three different types of noise.

questions.question: Why are albums called albums? The word album means white or albus means white. But an album as a collection of things has nothing to do with the color white. Also, why do stamp collectors collect stamps in a stamp album?

answers.answer: Multiple answers: Greg suggested albumen (egg white) encloses the yolk, so a stamp album contains stamps the same way. Dan Zinkroyd (touring musician for 20 years, studied music theory) explained: The word can also be translated as blank - Spanish blank, blanco. You'd have a photo album as a blank album and put photos in it. Musically it goes right back to the early 19th century - no, further. They used to have it in the marketplace in ancient Rome - a chalked up space you could write stuff on. Then blank music sheets where they would write notation that became a piece of music, which then became an album. It's a space into which you put stuff.

questions.question: When somebody passes away and they have tattoos, do those tattoos retain their colour? Do they go instantly? Do they not go?

answers.answer: When a person passes, almost instantly you can see the skin colour and texture change. His father had lots of sailor type tattoos. When he passed, his skin became translucent - you could almost see through it. Some of the reds became slightly more vivid. The blacks became a little bit duller. But the tattoos were still there. He visited several times before they closed the casket and they were still there. Even over time the skin changes. His father was embalmed but his mother wasn't, and her skin texture was very different. She'll still have her tattoos and they'll still be there for her family to see.

questions.question: How does glow in the dark work? The emergency exit signs and stars on ceilings - how does that work without batteries?

answers.answer: It's all to do with electrons. Light shines on electrons and they absorb that energy and get excited. Some materials let out light immediately, which is fluorescence (like high-vis jackets). The plastic items that glow in the dark work differently - the electrons get excited but retain that energy and don't come back to ground level so fast. They come back slowly over time, emitting light. It's called phosphorescence.

The previous answer was partially correct but went off at a tangent about high-vis jackets. High-vis jackets are actually pure physics - you coat a surface with small glass beads such that light comes in, is totally internally reflected, and comes back in the direction it was illuminated from. That's different from glow in the dark materials.

questions.question: Why do we in English write I with a capital letter?

answers.answer: It's to do with printing. On printing presses, a single lowercase letter 'i' wouldn't stand out enough on a line of text. If it had been a three-letter word it would all be lowercase, but a single letter needed to be capitalised for visibility.

questions.question: Why are there no great white sharks in UK waters? We get dogfish but no great whites, even though there's plenty of food (Selsey is known as Seal Seal Island).

answers.answer: Great white sharks are endothermic - they can regulate their body temperature - so it's not because of cold water. British waters display near-praxic habitat and feasibility. The answer could come down to migration - some say the migration isn't worth the energy to come to our shores. Others believe they are actually here but remain apart from occasional speculative sightings. The problem is that people confuse basking sharks for great whites. If a great white did visit British waters, most likely it would be one from the Mediterranean swimming at such depths that it wouldn't be confirmed. The truth is nobody really knows.

questions.question: What determines whether a belly button is an innie or an outie?

answers.answer: It's to do with how the umbilical cord is clamped at the point of cutting. If it's further away from the body, it tends to be an outie. If it's closer, it tends to be an innie. It also has an element to do with how the skin heals. There's no exact science to it.

questions.question: Why can you see stars when walking in the peaks on a clear night, but when you see photographs of people in space, there are no stars in the background?

answers.answer: It's a photography question, not an astronomy question. When you're in space and there's a lot of light (like on the moon), the camera is exposing for that light. If you go outside in the dark here and try to take photos of stars, you won't get them on your camera unless you let it expose for a long time. The camera lets in a lot of light and you have to be very steady. When you're in space with lights on the spacecraft, you wouldn't get stars on the film either.

questions.question: What happens when we extract billions of barrels of oil from deep underneath the oceans? Doesn't nature abhor a vacuum? Does this affect sea levels?

answers.answer: The idea that oil exists in lakes under the ground isn't correct. It exists in matrices or formations in rock - like a waffle, not a cavern. The formations vary: some are hard like granite, some are like wet sand. When you remove oil, in hard formations the pressure decreases but it doesn't make a difference because the formation is so hard. In places like Northern Holland where there are gas wells, the removal of gas reduces pressure and can cause formations to crush and compress, which is why there have been earthquakes. There are no enormous empty caverns full of oil. When oil is extracted, the rocks stay exactly where they were. Water can't get in because formations are often a mile below the seabed, and they go out of their way to avoid water flooding because it's difficult to extract oil after that.

questions.question: When and why did humans first start to shave their facial hair? Early sapiens didn't have big beards, then Jesus had a beard - when did it start?
When you pick up a freshly laid egg from a farm hotel, how do you know whether it's an egg for eating or whether there's a baby chick growing inside?

answers.answer: The hen will always lay eggs, but it takes a cockerel to fertilize them. In commercial settings, they hold eggs up in front of bright lights when packing them to see what's inside - because the shell is slightly opaque, light passes through and you can see the silhouette. That's also how they spot double yokers. Hotels probably don't have cockerels near the hens, so the eggs are likely unfertilized.

questions.question: What is the difference between white noise, brown noise, pink noise, green noise? And is there a black noise?

answers.answer: White noise is a combination of all audible frequencies from 20 hertz to 20,000 cycles per second. Pink noise is a weighted range of frequencies - it turns up the ones our ears are less sensitive to and turns down the ones we're more sensitive to. Brown noise is shifted more towards the bass end. There is no such thing as black noise.

questions.question: What is the chemical process that happens when cooking Brussels sprouts, and why does putting a bay leaf in neutralize the pungent smell?

answers.answer: Brussels sprouts release hydrogen sulphide when they cook. Bay leaves both contribute acid, which helps neutralise the smell, and also release essential oils which compete with the smell. It's a chemical reaction and simple perfumery.

questions.question: What's the difference between a porter and a stout? Is it how they're brewed or where they're from?

answers.answer: I think one of them is roasting and malting the barley differently. They have different relationships with roasting and malting the barley. But I can't remember which way round it is.

answers.caller: Michael from Brentwood (nano brewery owner, home brewer)
answers.answer: Beer is made of four ingredients: grain, water, yeast, and hops. Porter is a London beer from Victorian England, brewed specifically because there was bad water - it was cleaner and healthier to drink beer than water. The difference between stout and porter comes down to water minerals and how deeply the grains are roasted. You're never going to get a scenario where someone says, oh, have a porter, and someone else says, no, I think you'll find that's a stout. It's too blurred a distinction.

questions.question: Why are there four blood groups? Why is there not just one blood group? Is it like planets where they're numbered? And when's the fifth one coming?

answers.caller: Susan from Inverness (34 years as transfusion medicine specialist)
answers.answer: Blood groups are determined by chemical structures on the surface of red blood cells called antigens. There are hundreds of different red cell antigens. The ABO groups are most important because there are naturally occurring antibodies. If someone with type A gets type B blood, the antibodies will react chemically and cause breakdown of red blood cells. This wasn't discovered until blood transfusions began. Why aren't there just one? It's genetic variation - like asking why isn't there just one eye colour or one hair colour. The ABO group is important because you can have a fatal transfusion reaction without ever having been exposed to blood in the past. The other antigens have to be stimulated by previous exposure either during pregnancy or transfusion.

questions.question: Why do marine mammals have a horizontal tail fin and fish have a perpendicular tail fin? If evolution was in place, wouldn't they have the same?

answers.answer: Because evolution would favour whatever is most effective in the water.

answers.caller: Dane from Stoke-on-Trent (science educator at City Museum)
answers.answer: It's because the up and down spine movement is the ancestral condition for mammals. Way back in early dinosaur era, 200 plus million years ago, mammals had limbs oriented under the body and it was more efficient to move with spines moving up and down rather than side to side the way lizards do. That set the template for the mammal body plan. When they started moving into water after the dinosaurs were gone, that up and down movement stayed and it's been taken to the extreme. It's a holdover from when they had feet. You see it in otters too.

questions.question: Why are so many places in Cornwall named after saints? In Devon there's next to zero.

answers.answer: Celtic Christianity spread from middle of Europe, from somewhere probably in Switzerland. These were very holy men who wanted to get far away from civilisation, as far to the west as they could. So there were more ecclesiastical establishments in Cornwall than elsewhere - more churches, monasteries, individual hermits setting up in places. The pattern is spread up the whole west coast of Great Britain and to Brittany in France. The furthest away from the point of arrival for clerics seeking an ascetic lifestyle.

Christians sailed down the Irish Sea from Scotland, Ireland and Wales. They'd arrive at Cornwall on the north coast, get out the boat, walk across Cornwall, get on another boat, and sail down to France to Lourdes and Santiago de Compostela. They basically walked across Cornwall and went, this is a nice place, and that's the name of the place. It was to do with sea routes.

questions.question: How do they manage replacing a lost or broken cricket ball? They can't replace it with a new ball - they have to use one that's faced just about the same amount of overs. How do they age cricket balls?

answers.caller: John from WhatsApp (watches a lot of cricket)
answers.answer: Every cricket match finishes, but they don't always finish at the end of a cricket ball's life. In a 50-over match, if a team is bowled out after 30 overs, the ball goes into a box marked 30 overs. If the ball goes missing later (hit out of the ground), they pull out the box marked 30 overs. The umpires look at the balls in the box and pick the one closest to the condition of the ball being replaced. In test cricket, when a bowling team complains the ball has gone out of shape, the umpire brings out a gauge to measure if it's still circular. If not, they get a new box of balls to compare.

questions.question: What is the source of the name John Smith being used as an alias? Why is it the default name for an alias?

answers.answer: It's because Smith is the most common surname in the country, and John is the most common Christian name. So if you needed a random name, John Smith would be the one.

questions.question: When we vote, why do we vote in pencil?

answers.answer: You DON'T have to vote in pencil. Pencils are provided but you can take your own pen. There is no legal requirement for ballot papers to be marked with a pencil. James cited Newham Council's FAQ as evidence.
Confirmed: You are allowed to use your own pen. During the Brexit referendum some people really believed someone was going to erase their vote.

questions.question: Why does tea taste wonderful one moment and then taste like bin juice 10 minutes later when made in the same cup, same kettle, under the same conditions?

answers.answer: Bone china isn't porous, so you're just tasting the tea itself and not the cup or whatever else was in it before. It doesn't matter if it's been through the dishwasher. If you drink from an old mug, it's far more porous, so any other liquids that have been in that cup leave a slight taint to your tea.

You can only taste six different flavours; everything else comes from aroma. We can smell over 90,000 different aromas. The vessel you drink from massively affects how the flavour reaches you - the thickness of the lips, the width of the opening, how well it insulates the heat. Slurping tea atomises it and increases oxygen, spreading the volatile aromas through your mouth and enhancing flavour perception.

questions.question: Why don't flocks of parakeets bump into each other when they fly over my house close together, very fast and changing direction? Same question applies to murmurations of starlings.

answers.answer: In those big murmurations, starlings are touching wing tips, so they're able to manoeuvre their bodies without colliding. It's not radar or sonar. Birds like peregrine falcons and sparrowhawks that fly through trees have much faster reactions than humans, like F1 drivers versus regular people, so they can quickly move out of the way of each other.

questions.question: Why do some areas like Bristol use such affectionate terms of address (like 'my love', 'darling')? Is this a geographical or class thing?

answers.answer: The question is whether there's a difference geographically in the affectionate nature of language used. A cockney will call everyone darling or sweetheart. This seems more of a class thing than a geography thing.

People from Bristol tend to say positive things like 'cheers drive' or 'my lover'. It engenders a positive reaction in the listener. I think it's just the regional accent - it sounds better in a Bristol accent.

questions.question: As we age, why does our hair go grey, whereas cats' hair (fur) doesn't?

answers.answer: It's fur, not hair. That's the answer. You're comparing apples and pears.

Dogs do go grey - around the muzzle and chin. Humans a couple of hundred years ago had much shorter lifespans (30-40 years), which is when most people start going grey. So back then most people would have died before showing grey hair. Now with better healthcare and food, we live longer and have more chance for the pigmentation to fade.

questions.question: What would happen if your dog was suffering from a really bad headache or migraine? How would the vet test for that since the dog can't discuss its symptoms?

answers.answer: They can't diagnose it. They can look for a tumour or something like that, but if there's no physical symptom, they can't leave him with a cone for his head if he had a headache. It's a much better question than I'm giving credit for.

questions.question: When I watch the sun in the sky, is the sun really there at that moment? Light from the sun takes eight minutes to reach us, so am I seeing the sun's position eight minutes ago?

answers.answer: You were right. The sun is only 79 million miles away, and if light takes 8 minutes to get to Earth, you're not actually seeing the sun where it is now when you look at it. If you look at a star many light years away, it may have exploded or gone out many years ago but you're still seeing the light reaching you.

questions.question: How much time has to elapse before it becomes acceptable to start digging up dead people from burial grounds or battlefields?

answers.answer: The MOD has a team called the Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre Commemorations Team. Whenever a body is discovered on a battlefield from World War One or anything since 1914, they go in and endeavour to find out who that person is so they can be given a proper burial in a Commonwealth war cemetery.

In the UK we have the Scheduled Monument Act. If anything is discovered on your land that has historical or archaeological significance, you can't touch it. Graveyards generally go into the archaeological record within 100 years in the UK, which is why graveyards can get moved or housing estates get built on old burial grounds. Once anything has historical significance, it gets protected.

questions.question: Where does the air inside a bell pepper come from? If it was grown in Morocco, is that Moroccan air inside the pepper, or is it British air from the supermarket?

answers.answer: Peppers are porous to a degree because they're living organisms that need to respire to allow air through. So it's probably going to be the local air - the air from wherever the pepper currently is, like the supermarket, rather than where it was grown.

questions.question: How were measurements of time and weights measured? When did a second become a second? When was a second invented or worked out? How did they agree upon that measurement and was it the same 500 years ago?

answers.answer: The modern second didn't become important until the invention of mechanical clocks in the 16th century. The division by 60 comes from the ancient Babylonian counting system, which is base 12. The first clocks with seconds were in the early 16th century. It was Huygens who invented it. The second was defined differently in pre-modern times. Pre-modern people didn't need them so they didn't have them. Now they are defined according to atomic clock but back then different clocks would disagree on the length of time.

questions.question: Why does the head at the top of the neck of a violin, cello, or double bass always have the shape of a spiral? Does the shape have a function? Strings wrap around the peg, not the scroll.

answers.answer: The scrolls on a stringed instrument serve no function. They're purely decorative. It was often used as a marker of the maker's skill set to display how fancy they were or how good they were at making the instrument. My mum was in the London Symphony Orchestra playing viola for 30+ years. It's all in the inside of the instrument - that's why it has cut out sections on either side.

questions.question: Where does the king go to the toilet when he's on a long car journey? If he's driving back from Brighton to London and suddenly needs to go, does he stop at services? Do they have private facilities planned? Is it like bus drivers with a special key?

answers.answer: The route is always pre-planned several months in advance. The venue will be scoped by a forward intelligence team. They'll know every area they could go to - police stations, hospitals. There will be designated P posts on the way to and from. For long distance, they'll travel by aircraft. If needs must, they will send the forward intelligence team ahead. They'll go in with escort motorbikes - it's all fast lane stuff. They don't travel at the same speed as us.

questions.question: What dictates how many blades go on a helicopter propeller? I've seen some with two and some with seven or eight.

answers.answer: The reason helicopters have different numbers of blades is really to do with the amount of lift that's required. Helicopters are rotary wing aircraft - the rotor is essentially a wing. The lift is generated by the area and the power. If you had a big old helicopter like a Chinook or Sea King with only two blades, they'd need to be ridiculously long. So they add other rotors so you can have a smaller disc area while still having the amount of power. The more rotors you have, the more lift you create. Whenever you create lift, you also create drag and weight, so it's a trade-off. Heavy helicopters need more blades.

questions.question: Is man flu a real thing? Do men suffer from flu more severely than women? Is there a scientific basis behind it?

answers.answer: Man flu is probably real because it's a hormonal thing. Men have more testosterone than women. Testosterone tends to impede the functioning of the immune system, so men suffer more.

questions.question: Can animals see their noses? Humans can see their nose but the brain cancels it out. Does the same apply to all animals - dogs with different nose sizes, penguins with beaks, horses with long faces?
Why do birds stand on one leg? I saw a seagull on a lamppost on a windy day with only one leg visible, felt sorry for it, then it flew off and landed with two legs.

answers.answer: To conserve energy. Half the bird sleeps - the left half - while the other stays awake to be vigilant. Standing on one leg also conserves heat that would go out through the foot.

questions.question: If you mix two different factors of sunscreen - say SPF 20 and SPF 50 - are they diluting each other or adding to each other? Do you end up with SPF 70 or SPF 35?

answers.answer: There are different types of sunscreen. Milky sunscreen has zinc as the sunblocker. If you mix factor 20 and factor 10, you'd end up with the median, factor 15. However, there are also sun oils and tanning oils with different viscosities that don't mix. If you mix incompatible types, you'd get an emulsion where you have bits of SPF 20 and bits of SPF 10 next to each other - you'd end up speckled like a Dalmatian or with tiny spots depending on how hard you shake it. But it cannot dilute the factor down - the SPF protection would be inconsistent rather than reduced.

questions.question: Why do the numbers on a microwave or LCD clock jiggle and bounce around outside their frame when brushing teeth with an electric toothbrush, but nothing else appears to jiggle?

answers.answer: LCDs and LEDs don't stay on like incandescent bulbs. They flicker - they pulse 50 times a second (50 Hertz, our electricity frequency in this country). When you use an electric toothbrush, your head is vibrating, as is your skull, brain and eyes. So you're only catching very brief glimpses of that pulse of light, making it look like it's bouncing all over the place. Your brain is trying to process that pulse of light at any one moment. If you use a manual brush, you won't notice it. You can see the same effect with LED TVs or car headlights when viewed through a camera.

questions.question: Why do they still do the scores on paper with two people writing scores on either side of the dartboard when there's electronic digital readouts? What is the history of this and why does it persist?

If a UK passport holder goes to Europe and overstays their 90 days, what is the penalty? If they get stopped by police or on their passport, or if they come back after overstaying 90 days to the UK, what's the penalty?

answers.answer: Here in Spain, it's a 2,000 euro fine immediately. And you're banned from entering the country for as long as they think appropriate. But a lot of people don't realize that those days start as soon as you put your foot on French soil. So there's no way that someone can drive to France, think oh I'll pop over to Portugal for a couple of weeks, then pop over to Spain for a couple of weeks, then pop over somewhere else in the EU because that all adds up to your time in the EU. It's 90 days in the EU from the moment you put your foot on French soil or your tires. The punishment may change from country to country but the clock is ticking. But also, here in Spain, even though people keep asking, there's no proof that it's happened to anyone yet.

questions.question: Why are the majority of fruits round or at least globular?

answers.answer: The reason any plant makes fruit is to disperse seeds. So they want the seeds as far as possible. If that fruit is round, as it falls, it's going to travel as far as it possibly can. As it's going to roll, so it's going to cast those seeds nice and wide as possible.

questions.question: Why do blind people's eyes move when they're reading Braille?

answers.answer: If they lose their sight either if they've been blind from birth or at a very early age, then you develop a condition called nystagmus which is an involuntary movement of your eyes and usually from left to right. It can be up and down as well. So it would actually be happening all the time and we just notice it more perhaps because it seems a bit anomalous when people are reading Braille. It's more common amongst blind people and people who are visually impaired. That's why a lot of blind people wear sunglasses, why Stevie Wonder wears sunglasses, because he has involuntary eye movements.

questions.question: Who named people black or white? Why are the majority of Africans or Caribbean called black? When did we start referring to ourselves as black and white people?

answers.answer: The current idea of black versus white, rather polarised like that, goes back to European colonial times mainly. Until then, a lot of people seldom met someone that different from themselves in skin colour. Once European colonisation happened, especially with the institution of slavery, there was clear polarisation between Europeans and Africans and Afro-Caribbean people. White people aren't really white, they're more pink - Steve Biko said that once. When I lived in Southeast Asia, we met some people who were even blacker in skin colour than most Africans, South Indian people, Tamil speakers, some of them were very black, but they weren't described as black because they weren't Africans or Afro-Caribbeans. In the ancient world, for example in ancient Greece, there isn't much discussion of skin colour, it's more a question of what culture people were from. So you have to introduce the hierarchy almost to justify the colonialism. Even if they did use a skin colour, sometimes the Greeks described Egyptian people as red in colour. The Greeks were different from Egyptians who were darker in hues. The word would have kicked in particularly when European-driven slave trade happened and people were coming into contact with African people and it became important to be very decisive about the difference. There's not going to be a hard date.

questions.question: If in the past I dated Kate Middleton or Diana Spencer before they met their royal husbands, what's stopping me writing a tell-all book about my time with them?

answers.answer: Nothing. But I've never seen one. James Hewitt did, albeit he had his relationship with Diana after she'd married Prince Charles. If there were any rules in place to stop people from doing that, you'd think they'd kick in more post-royal marriage than pre. I just think they have the discretion, keep it in the social circles, in the elevated social circles. It's like a gentleman never tells. Same for a lady. So it is just convention and tradition. There's no royal decree saying if you have been in a relationship with the queen-to-be you are not allowed to write about it. Categorically not.

questions.question: If you have a choir of 10 people and they're all singing, if one sings out of tune it's immediately obvious. If you have 1,000 or 10,000 people in a crowd singing, at least 10% are probably singing out of key but you cannot hear them. What's the cut-off point? Is there a magic number whereby if you have more than this number, you can no longer hear the out-of-tune singers?

answers.answer: The reason why you're not going to hear the 10% singing out of tune is because they're not all going to be singing the same notes. The 90% are singing the correct notes, let's say they're singing C major. But the 10% singing out of tune are not all singing a semi-tone above or a tone above or slightly sharp or slightly flat. They're all singing all over the place. So that's why you're not going to hear them. Your brain also kind of self-corrects a wee bit as well. And if there's 10 people and one person out of tune, you're going to be all over it, you're going to notice it. If one person is singing a semi-tone sharp, you'd probably hear that. But for the fact that the out-of-tune singers aren't all singing exactly the same notes out of tune, if one is singing sharp and one is singing flat, they're actually together and that would sound in tune - it evens out.

questions.question: Why are certain viruses like chickenpox causing significantly milder symptoms in children than they do in adults if you contract them as an adult? There are others like hand, foot and mouth. Mumps was much more dangerous to contract as a boy because it could affect fertility. So maybe it's got something to do with puberty but why are some viruses much more unpleasant for adults?
When we think of the first rainbow, why does it arc? Why is it a bow?

answers.answer: The rainbow that we see on Earth is only actually half the picture. A full rainbow is actually a circle. You can view the sun as a point source. The light rays come from it, they hit the atmosphere at the correct angle, hit the droplets, and there's a process called total internal reflection where they get bounced off the back of the raindrop at an angle, hit the back again, and then come out through us and it disperses into a spectrum. Sometimes you'll be able to see it in an airplane. If you're very lucky, you'll see the rainbow full circle.

questions.question: Why isn't there an abundance of Welsh specific surnames? Scots have Mac names, Irish have O names, but I'm not aware of Welsh Christian names. Jones is just son of John, Williams, Evans, but nothing distinctively Welsh in the way the others are?

answers.answer: I think there are absolutely loads. There's Llewellyn, Cadwalader, Davies, Owen, Owens, Parry, Powell - there's a lot of Welsh names. The problem is there's been much more crossover from Welsh into English names so you don't realize that names we think of as English are actually Welsh. Even the Earl of Cadogan who owns half of Chelsea is a Welsh name. I think the Welsh are very well represented.

When Welsh surnames traditionally used to be the person's name, then app, then the father's name. So for example, you would have Pwish App Sean which would be Pwish son of Sean. When the English made it up, that was too difficult for them to remember and keep track of, so they started anglicising some of the names. Someone like Pwish App Sean would then become Paul Jones because it sounded more like Jones so it was easier for them to keep track of. There's a lot of Welsh names that you could probably translate into English but the real sort of hardcore Welsh names got ridden out by the colonisers, by the conquerors. So somebody who's called Davis, their original Welsh name probably would have been Ap Davies or something like that.

questions.question: Are we witnessing a miracle every single day with the moon? The moon never changes, it only presents one side of itself. It's exactly the right size to cause the solar eclipse effect. The fact that we only see one side of the moon doesn't that strike you as being a bit weird? Is it a miracle?

answers.answer: The Earth-Moon orbit doesn't follow strictly over the equator and it is elliptical, not perfectly circular. Together with the Moon, our orbit around the Sun isn't perfectly circular either. In order to get a total solar eclipse, the three have to line up quite precisely, and that happens somewhere in the world about once every year or 18 months. The last one was in Western Australia in April, the next will be in the United States and Mexico in April. Because the orbits are elliptical, sometimes the Moon when it's lined up between the Earth and the Sun is slightly further away and sometimes it's closer. So you don't always get a total eclipse, sometimes you get annular eclipses where the Moon doesn't cover the entire disc. It's not some miraculous geometrical miracle, it's just laws of physics. Also, the Moon is actually spiralling away from us about an inch or so a year. Buzz and Neil left mirrors on the surface of the Moon when they went up on Apollo 11, and there's been a bloke in Texas ever since pinging a laser off the mirrors, and that's how we've measured over the last 50 or 60 years that it's spiralling away.

questions.question: Why is it whenever I, no matter how neatly I fold away and put away my cables in a drawer, whenever I open the drawer, they come out all tangled up?
How did the graffiti artist get that graffiti onto the motorway bridge?

answers.answer: There's multiple ways you can do it. All of it involves abiding by the dark arts of the three o'clock in the morning rule. You can either use a whopping great ladder, park near and walk in. There's often people with climbing harnesses on, like abseiling equipment. Wearing a high-vis vest would oddly be quite a good idea in this context. And a hard hat. Some of them you can just... There's a ledge, and you can just take your life into your hands and walk across the ledge.

questions.question: Why do some people stick their little fingers out when they're drinking?

answers.answer: It goes back to a medieval custom known as a spice finger. At medieval banquets eating with your hands, you wanted to keep your little finger up and away from your mouth and food so you didn't get covered in sauce or gravy. In the center of your table were communal pots with salt, pepper, nutmeg, and spices. If you wanted to add spice to your food, you dipped your little finger into one of these pots. It's nice and clean. You put as much as you can on the back of your little finger and then sprinkle it across your food. It's a learned behavior that we've inherited.

questions.question: Why does water spontaneously turn into water vapor? Why does water, all on its own, turn into water vapor, which is still a liquid but floats away?

answers.answer: Water vapor is a gas. Water has a property called specific latent heat of vaporisation - the amount of energy it takes to turn water from a liquid to a gas. The water isn't turning into gas spontaneously - there's some energy coming in from sunlight or a flame. Water will vaporise at a lower temperature if it already has some energy. Vapor can be for any liquid, whereas steam is specifically water. Water vapor is just saying it's the vapor of water, but it has another name as steam.

Water vapor is the gaseous state of water. Above the kettle where it's clear, that's the gaseous state. Where it turns white like a cloud, that's an aerosol - liquid suspended in air. So steam is liquid in air. Water vapor is the gas form, which confirms Steve's question - water does turn into gas.

questions.question: Why is my chewing gum dissolving after eating chocolate?

answers.answer: It's the fat in the chocolate. The fat's acting as a solvent, dissolving some of the solids in the chewing gum, making it all gloopy and horrible. He has personal experience with this - he tried it with almond butter and chocolate then chewing gum.

questions.question: Why don't bottles of scotch or brandy have flammable warning diamonds on them like other hazardous products under the sink?

answers.answer: The red and white hazard pictograms are under a regulation called CLP (Classification, Labelling and Packaging regulation) in the EU/UK. But that regulation doesn't cover alcoholic drinks - it doesn't cover food. Alcoholic drinks have their own specific, more stringent legislation. Cosmetics also don't need to be labelled with hazard pictograms under CLP because they're already covered by their own specific regulations. The hazards have already been mitigated through consumer protection in those specific laws, so there's no need to communicate a general hazard.

questions.question: Why are tins cylinders rather than squares? Wouldn't you get more in a box if they were square?

answers.answer: It comes down to manufacturing cost. You get a lot more bang for your buck when they're circular. Even though you'd be able to store more in the same space if they were square, you're using a lot more material if you're making them square, so it comes down to manufacturing cost of the cans themselves. A round can is also stronger for transport purposes.

questions.question: Could there become a point where we add too much weight to a country like the UK, or a continent, or the globe, where the ground breaks or sinks?
Is empathy inherited or developed through experiences?

answers.answer: I think, as with almost all nature and nurture debates, it'll turn out to be a little bit of both. I think it has to be inherited because I think the opposite has to be inherited as well. Because otherwise, humanity would have rendered everybody empathetic by now. Because it would be in the general interest of the greater good. We reward lack of empathy. So it must be inherited. And if that's inherited, then the opposite must be inherited too.

There are two forms of empathy - cognitive empathy and emotional empathy. Cognitive empathy is when you can understand someone's perspective and rationalize what it's like to be in their shoes. Emotional empathy is when you actually have a shared emotional experience and feel distress alongside someone else. There was a study done by genetic companies that found there is a gene for empathy, but it only accounts for about 10% of your emotional response. The other 90% is learned behavior. This is backed up by the fact that women are normally identified as being more able to empathize than men.

I'd challenge that - I'd go with the nurture side. As children, when we fall over, our parents pick us up and help us understand what we're feeling and what we need. We learn about ourselves first, then we're able to do it with somebody else. This is the work of Peter Fonagy and Anna Freud Center, and Gabor Mate. If parents haven't been taught empathy, they can't teach it to their kids. Boys particularly get told 'you're fine, get on with it, big boys don't cry' which affects their emotional literacy.

questions.question: Why have dogs got jagged lips? Like when you pull down the outside of their mouth, inside they've got a jagged lip that goes round, like really teeny shark teeth.

answers.answer: I'm a dog walker and I'm looking at my dog's lips right now. They're called Ruger and they assist basically in gripping things. When a dog's carrying something, it just adds a little bit extra grip. It's similar to how when your hands are in water for a while, you go wrinkly. So it assists in grip. It's an evolutionary development - the dogs that were better at gripping things because of their lip structure managed to have more puppies and passed on the trait. The smaller the teeth towards the back, the ridges tend to start there, so as teeth got smaller, the lips kind of fill in a little bit.

questions.question: Why is it that some foods when you eat them affect your mouth, like spicy food and curries, yet other foods like wasabi affect your nose?
If someone has a higher pain threshold than me, are they feeling the same amount of pain but better at processing it, or are they actually feeling less pain than me?

answers.answer: Pain is subjective. In clinical practice, pain is measured on a scale from 0 to 10 based on patient self-report. There's no way of physically measuring pain in patients - otherwise we could identify drug-seeking patients at A&E. Pain is affected by many things: how much sleep you've had, if you've had a good meal, your mindset, whether you're prepared for the pain. If one person has meditated and gotten good sleep and knows what's coming, their experience of pain would be less. Neurodivergent people have lower tolerance for sensory stimuli including pain. Women generally have showers hotter than men. It's truly subjective and affected by environment.

questions.question: Why is it that when someone says something that can produce a smell, when I breathe in through my nose, I can smell that thing just for one breath? Like if someone says 'do we want onion in the pasta' I can smell onion in that next breath. Or if someone says 'those hot dogs were delicious' I get a whiff of hot dog.

answers.answer: It's just a sense memory, isn't it? I would be interested if anyone has any other thoughts on it. Everyone's got a sound memory, haven't they? Some people can't imagine a piece of music in their head. But a smell memory... I don't think I've got the ability to remember smells. But you do. So are you a one-off? Are you the only one?

questions.question: Black hair dye sticks to my ears, forehead, and back of neck for about 24 hours, but on my scalp it doesn't stick at all. I have patches of alopecia so I can see my scalp easily. Why does dye affect some parts of our skin and not others?

answers.answer: Generally, when you wash hair dye off, you emulsify the hair dye into itself on the scalp. If you went into a hair salon, they would apply a small amount of water and emulsify into your skin, which is why when you go to a salon you get less stain. The reason it's stuck to his neck and ears is because he hasn't washed them - he hasn't emulsified it. When you apply dye to your head, before washing it off, you apply a small amount of water and emulsify it with your hands. The bits that have reached your tips of ears and forehead, he hasn't done the rubbed it into itself step.

questions.question: How did cartographers map out the world before the invention of satellites, hot air balloons or airplanes?

answers.answer: You need basic equipment: a theodolite, which measures angles; a level, which measures the height between two fixed points; and some sort of measuring device like a chain, rope, or even paces. Using calculus and geometry between those three sets of information, you can work out the distance, height, and angle of any fixed point in the landscape. That's triangulation - trigonometry. You can do coastlines the same way, just in two dimensions rather than three.

questions.question: Why are some places translated? Napoli is Napoli but we call it Naples. London is called Londres in French. Why isn't it just stayed the same?

answers.answer: Italian place names mostly end in vowels - Roma, Torino, Napoli. English, from Indo-Germanic origins, is heavily consonant-ending - London, Bristol, Nottingham. We don't have mostly names ending in A or E in general. Russian, which I'm studying, is also heavily consonant. So if you said 'I live in London' to a Russian speaker, they'd say the same because it fits their language pattern. It depends on the rule of the language. But we mustn't forget that the name of the town is the original one - that's the locals' name. We translate it into English.

questions.question: How many combinations are there for a Yale lock key? Is there a finite number, and could there be duplicate keys? What are the odds that two randomly selected Yale keys would open the same lock?

answers.answer: About 1100 differs on a standard Yale lock. If you've got 1100 keys, you could eventually open any Yale lock. I've been a locksmith for over 40 years and it's only happened once - a customer came in after a burglary, I changed the lock, and their old key still worked. One in 1100 chance that actually happened.

questions.question: Why do I need to readjust my rearview mirror every morning even though I'm the only person who drives my car and nobody else gets into it?

answers.answer: You're taller in the morning than you are in the evening. When you stretch out in bed, your spine elongates by a couple of centimetres. When you sit in the car, you're at optimum height and the seat is at optimum foam expansion, so the mirror position is different. During the day you both shrink and sink into the seat gradually, and you don't notice the tiny incremental changes. So in the morning when you wake up, you've got the biggest differential between your optimal morning position and where you left the mirror.

questions.question: Are seagulls in Brighton more aggressive than in other seaside resorts like Bournemouth, and if so, why?

answers.answer: There are different species of seagull. The Bournemouth ones are common gulls. Brighton and Hastings have herring gulls, which are about twice the size and very aggressive. The difference is likely related to the fishing industry - herring gulls will chase fishing boats and trawlers, and they steal food. Bournemouth doesn't have a significant fishing industry.

questions.question: How did the non-darts player on Bullseye prove that their skills were inadequate enough to qualify as a non-darts player?

answers.answer: There wasn't really any checking system as to how good the non-playing dart player was. It was more to do with how they answered questions. There have been instances of top-level county players appearing as the darts player, and sometimes the non-darts player was also good at darts - that was an absolute bonus. You would pick someone who was brilliant at answering questions, and if they happened to be good at darts, you were over the line. There was no limit on how good they could be at darts - it just had to be that they weren't too good to be on the show.

questions.question: Why would my wheelie bin have a noise rating of 95dB stamped on it?

answers.answer: It's a European Union regulation introduced for manufacturers of wheelie bins to put a limit on the amount of noise a bin could make while being wheeled along or having its lid shut. 95 decibels is the maximum limit - bins can't go any higher than that. They have to use a different composite of plastic or higher quality wheels. It's a limit, not the actual expected noise level. If you slam a bin lid as loud as you possibly can, you might get close to 95dB in that tiny moment.

questions.question: Why do your joints and muscles hurt when you have the flu, including the soles of your feet?

answers.answer: The muscle pain from flu is called myalgia - inflammation of the muscles. When you get infected by a virus, your body fights it off, which involves white blood cells joining onto the virus. But part of this process creates a cascade of inflammatory chemicals called cytokines, which are irritants elsewhere in the body. These cause inflammation within the muscle cells and the lining of joint cells, resulting in the aches and pains in joints and muscles.

questions.question: Is there any sort of limit to how much memory you can have, like an SD card - is there a limit to how much knowledge you can cram in?

answers.answer: Memory is hugely complex but essentially there are two types: short-term memory (where you have to repeat items over and over to keep them) and long-term memory (created by neural connections). There is probably a finite limit to the number of neural connections, but to all intents and purposes, we never reach it. The more you use a particular memory, the stronger that neural network becomes. As you get older and amasses more information, if you don't use certain information, the neural network breaks down and you forget. So theoretically there's a limit, but practically there isn't.

questions.question: Why is dark beer called IPA (India Pale Ale)? What's the connection with India?

answers.answer: IPA was originally brewed around the 1820s-1830s for export to India. They over-hopped it and made it slightly more alcoholic because both hops and alcohol have preservative effects. Normal beer would spoil during the four to six month journey in wooden casks on galleon ships. The extra hops and alcohol preserved it. When diplomats from the East India Company came back to the UK, they liked the beer and wanted it here, so it became available in Britain and caught on.

questions.question: Why do we break wind more as we get older?

answers.answer: I don't think there's a reason linked to age. The only real answer would be that you're eating more food as you get bigger, and the chemical processes of digestion cause an increase in gas. Your diet might get worse as you get older, you're drinking alcohol - though Alex says he drinks less now than when he was younger.

questions.question: Why does Liechtenstein's national anthem sound exactly like God Save the King?

answers.answer: Many German-speaking nations used the same tune. Liechtenstein is the only one that still uses it. There were German-speaking nations that had it as their national anthem, possibly Prussian National Anthem in Bismarck's time was the same tune. There's no particular reason why it shouldn't be - German-speaking nations shared it, and Liechtenstein just kept it. It might be because the Kaiser and the King were cousins, or they just liked it and put their own words to it - 'Oben am Jungenrein' means 'High on the Young Rhine'.

questions.question: When does a war become a world war?
When professional tennis players are about to serve, they look at their tennis balls and discard one. What are they looking for?

answers.answer: They're looking for the ball which is the freshest, the one which is the least fluffed up. The less fluffy ball will have less wind resistance and fly faster through the air. For the second serve, they'd look for a more fluffy ball because they're going to put spin on it. There can also be an element of superstition if they won a point with a particular ball.

questions.question: Do dogs catch human viruses?

answers.answer: The term is zoonosis - infectious diseases that can be transmitted from animals to humans (and vice versa) under certain conditions. Rabies is an example. So it does cut both ways.

questions.question: Is there a limit to how fast wind can blow? What is the fastest wind speed possible?

answers.answer: The Earth's rotation effectively limits wind speed on Earth. At the equator, it rotates at about 900 nautical miles per hour (roughly 1,000 miles per hour). However, the fastest recorded wind speed on Earth is about 500 miles per hour in major hurricanes. Solar winds - which are not on Earth but in space - can travel much faster, potentially up to a million miles per hour, which scientists are researching for interplanetary travel using solar sails.

questions.question: What is the universe expanding into?

answers.answer: The universe creates space as it goes. It was infinitesimally small at the Big Bang 14 billion years ago, and all matter created then is still around now. The universe is expanding into itself - like putting spots on a balloon and blowing it up. There's nothing outside it. The distances between galaxies simply expand. There may be a multiverse with other universes expanding away from each other faster than the speed of light (because space itself can travel faster than light).

questions.question: Why doesn't my own snoring wake me up but my wife's snoring does?
Why are there no sounds on GIFs?

answers.answer: A GIF is actually just images broken down into individual frames - not video. Since it's an image format, images don't have sound. It goes back to the origins of the technology when file sizes needed to be kept small. While that's less of a concern now, the format has survived from that era.

questions.question: Why do I remember my dreams when I sleep on my right side but not when I sleep on my left side?
What happens to the DNA of a donated organ once it's in your body? If I donated my kidney to you and you were then murdered, whose DNA would be detected from that kidney - mine or yours?

answers.answer: DNA doesn't change with a transplant. The DNA in the kidney would still be the donor's DNA. Your body accepts the organ but doesn't change its DNA. As a kidney transplant patient, I've read up on this.

questions.question: Why are there two tides a day when the Earth only rotates once a day?

answers.answer: The moon's gravity pulls on the water on the side of Earth closest to it, creating a high tide there. It also pulls less strongly on the water on the opposite side of Earth, causing water to bulge out there too. As Earth rotates once per day, you pass through both of these high tide bulges, giving you two tides per day.

questions.question: Why doesn't granulated sugar have a best before date when other things do?

answers.answer: Sugar doesn't go off due to osmotic pressure and lack of water content - life needs water to grow. As a chocolatier who works with sugar constantly, I can confirm granulated sugar is just sugar. However, I can't explain why icing sugar would have a best before date when granulated doesn't - perhaps something is added to it, or it's a labelling quirk.

questions.question: Why are children noisier and wilder on windy days at school?

answers.answer: As a child psychotherapist who observed toddlers for a year, Zara explained it's likely a dysregulation thing. Children are more susceptible to environmental changes. When the atmosphere is chaotic and unstable, some children seek comfort while others reflect that chaos in their behaviour. It's a primitive response - the disruption in the atmosphere contributes to a dysregulation in the child's behaviour.

questions.question: Where does the etiquette of touching/tipping your hat come from?

answers.answer: It goes back to knights lifting their visors on armour to show they were friendly and not about to fight. When we stopped wearing armour, we carried on lifting the visor even though there was no visor there - so we tip our hat instead.

questions.question: Why don't laundry detergent pods dissolve from the inside out given they're filled with liquid?

answers.answer: Chris, who wrote software for the detergent manufacturing process for a major brand, explained that the pods are made of a polymer (polyvinyl alcohol) that dissolves in a certain saturation of water. Because the liquid detergent inside is super concentrated, it can't physically dissolve the membrane. There's not enough water in the concentrated liquid to dissolve it. That's also why they can start dissolving if you have steam in your kitchen.

questions.question: Why is the extra day in a leap year added to February (the shortest month) rather than another month?

answers.answer: The calendar is based on the Roman Julian calendar. In Roman times, they initially had 10 months - September was the 7th month (septem=7), October was 8th, November was 9th, December was 10th. They later added January and February. February was the last month to be added, and when making adjustments, they added days to the last month. The year used to end in February - it was a festival of purification and transition. So actually, February WAS the last month.

questions.question: Do other languages have collective nouns like English does - such as 'a murder of crows' rather than just 'a flock'?

answers.answer: In German, it's also common to have different collective nouns for troops of animals. For example: 'a Sprung of deer', 'a Rotte of wild boars', 'a Herde of sheep'. Some have double meanings like in English - 'Schule' for a school of fish (Schule also means school/learned institution), but Rotte always just means a troop of wild boars with no other meaning.

questions.question: If a King's Guard horse trod on someone, could they sue for damages?

answers.answer: Phil, who is majoring in the army and writes health and safety risk assessments, explained that troops before the King's Guard are given specific orders. As long as they follow those orders, they're following a lawful order. Until the late 80s, defence had crown immunity and was exempt from civil action - but that's no longer the case. Now individuals could raise a case, but they'd have to prove the soldier didn't follow proper procedure, warning signs, etc. If they followed all training and rules, it would be very hard to prove unlawful action.

questions.question: Where does all the blood go in chicken? You see blood in raw beef but never in chicken - do chickens have blood?

answers.answer: Kay, whose son is a newly qualified biology teacher, explained that the red liquid in meat isn't blood - it's myoglobin, a protein found in muscle pigment. Mammals have a much higher concentration of myoglobin than birds or fish. Pigs have different muscle structure that's less dense than cows, which is why pork is more of a white meat. The blood itself is drained out during slaughtering.

Tony, who used to service the trailers that collect chicken blood, explained the process: chickens are hung up and the blood drains into a stainless steel gutter that runs to the end of the plant into a tanker (like a petrol tanker). It runs 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. The blood is taken away and mostly made into dried blood fertilizer for plants.

questions.question: Why are competitive/gala swimming pools colder than leisure pools?

answers.answer: Ian, a British Swimming referee with four daughters who swim competitively to national and international level, explained: athletes sweat when swimming. The hotter the temperature, the more they sweat, which affects biomechanics and slows them down. Also, larger competitive pools are easier to keep cooler than smaller heated pools. Ian's own club once had a heater malfunction - when the water got too hot, after 10 minutes the kids were like lobsters, bright red, and couldn't work properly.

questions.question: Is there a proportional relationship between finger girth and nostril width? He couldn't fit his finger up his girlfriend's nostril while messing around.

answers.answer: Ben revealed he hasn't been able to pick his own nose since childhood - his fingers don't fit up his nose. He realized around age 18 that this was the case. He's not sure if he has particularly narrow nostrils or particularly fat fingers, but either way, his fingers won't fit his own nose.

questions.question: Why do orchestras always have to read from the sheet music? Why don't members of the orchestra know the bloody music instead of having sheet music in front of them?

answers.answer: In an orchestra, you're one of many. In a two-hour performance, you're not playing for two hours unless you are the virtuoso violinist. You need to know where everybody else is. It's almost like in English class when everybody has to read out a certain paragraph - you might know your exact paragraph off by heart, but you need to know when to come in. Everybody is basically just keeping up the pace as to where the piece of music is.

questions.question: What happens in our brain when we get over a certain fear? How do we overcome what feels like a genuine foe? Is it just exposure? Does it happen because you've had to, or because you just sort of... it wears out?
