Why is it so hard to remember dreams after you've just had them? Even as I was waking up, I was trying to hold on to it, and it's like even as you're trying to remember it, it's already going.

answers.answer: The dream phase of your sleep is only about a quarter of the whole time that you spend asleep. Whether or not you remember your dreams depends very much on whether or not you wake up while you're dreaming. If you wake up while you're dreaming, chances are you'll remember it, or just after you've come out of dream sleep. If you're in deep sleep, you won't remember it because your brain rinses all that off. Dreaming is the way that you deal with what you've done during the day or things that are going on in your brain, and it has to process and dump a lot of that.

questions.question: When you put a bottle of water in a freezer and freeze it, why does the water expand rather than contract? Why would it contract? When you cool things down, they get smaller, don't they? Why does water act different to everything else?

answers.answer: Think of the space that is available for molecules and water fills that space in liquid form. When it freezes, it forms into a crystal structure. The crystal structure of ice means that the molecules take up more space than they do when they are floating around randomly. And that is why water expands when it freezes. It's turning into crystal structure. This also means ice is less dense than water, which is why ice floats.

Water molecules have a rigid shape because hydrogen has a magnetic charge. When they're in liquid form as a fluid, they kind of flow around against each other, like a ball pit. Once it starts to freeze, they start to form a rigid structure almost like the carbon atoms in a diamond - crystals. And that actually creates more space between them than when they're in their fluid form because they have to fit together. That's why if water is freezing in a little crack in the road, the road will crack. The force of the freezing is immense. It's also why water at the bottom of the ocean doesn't freeze, even though it's extremely cold - there is so much water pressure on top of it that they physically can't move into that crystal form. Water is most dense at four degrees Celsius.

questions.question: Where should you keep your toothbrush? Is it dangerous to keep it in the bathroom because of poo particles flying around when you flush the toilet? Some adverts say poo particles are flying around the bathroom.
The letter H is spelt A-I-T-C-H. Why do so many people say H? Why do we say 'H' instead of 'aitch'? Why do people pronounce it that way when we don't say 'Zez' for Z, or 'Cess' for C, or 'Nem' for N?

answers.answer: It's basically snobbery. A lot of our words from Old English and words that have come over from places like France originally wouldn't have had the H sound. Things like 'erb' (herb) originally was pronounced without the H, which is how they still say it in America and Australia. They were less bothered about the class system than we were. In the 18th century, people suddenly got very uppity about how we sounded - people thought dropping H's made you sound common, so they started adding H sounds to words to try to sound posher. But actually, over 200 years later, that has made them sound the opposite of posh - it's made them sound like an insufferable peasant.

questions.question: Why don't we eat turkey eggs and especially leading up to Christmas? Is it because there are lots of turkeys around so there should be lots of eggs? Or are they not nice to eat? Does anyone know what they taste like?

answers.caller: Adam from the Forest of Dean
answers.answer: Turkeys lay only about 100 eggs a year whereas a chicken will lay 300 plus eggs a year, and they're bigger birds so it's just not viable. If you're trying to feed an egg market then you might as well use chickens. It's nothing to do with Christmas - a turkey will lay an egg every three days whereas a chicken will lay an egg per day. Turkey eggs are actually very creamy and make the best scrambled eggs.

questions.question: I'm over 50 and my hair is growing in my ears, noses, and eyebrows. Why is it that we lose hair from places where we want it while growing it in places where we don't?
What is the melody of the big ben chime? It's so iconic but it's repeated all over different towns with town clocks. What's the melody called?

answers.answer: It's called Westminster Quarters. It's a piece of music written for church bells, not specifically for Big Ben or big bells. It's one of the most popular little tunes because we can both remember it - that's why it's really effective for telling the time.

questions.question: Why is it that when you're driving along on dual carriageways or motorways, birds swoop down across the road instead of flying straight across? Why do they choose to swoop down and then go up the other side?

answers.answer: Birds evolved before cars, so this is an evasion strategy against predators. Not all birds do it - some birds like starlings fly very direct. But pigeons, wood pigeons particularly, do the same flight pattern whether they're crossing a road or not. If you're walking down a field, you'll see them do that same up-and-dip pattern. It's to evade mainly things like peregrines - being a more moving target is harder to hit. Moving erratically is harder for predators.

questions.question: When you make a cup of tea or coffee, why can you taste a difference when you've boiled the kettle for a second time?

answers.answer: When water is boiled, oxygen bubbles are released making it taste flatter. Also, when water evaporates during boiling, chemicals become more concentrated in the remaining water, giving metallic and other chemical tastes the more you boil it. Different areas of the UK have different fluoride levels which also affect concentration.

questions.question: Where have all the kippers gone?
Why does water go up into a sponge when you just put the tip in? It seems to defy gravity.

answers.answer: The action is called capillary action. It's the intermolecular forces between the surface of the sponge and the liquid, and they overcome gravity, causing the water to move upwards. Qualifications: PhD in physics.

The caller (regarding Luke's chlorophyll question) also mentioned capillary action and explained it involves adhesive properties of water molecules sticking to the sponge, plus cohesion between water molecules - 'water is sticky and pulls other molecules with it, like a chain'. This is the transpiration stream that allows trees to take water from ground to the top - a massive feat.

questions.question: Have we discovered any chemical elements in space that don't naturally occur on Earth?

answers.answer: No elements have been discovered in space that don't appear on Earth. However, helium - the second most common element in the universe - was discovered on the sun before it was discovered on Earth. It was discovered from a back garden in Wimbledon around 1860 during a total eclipse. Every element generates light at particular wavelengths (like a fingerprint). He also mentioned Cecilia Payne, an English woman in the 1920s who discovered hydrogen and helium make up 98% of the universe, but was written out of history. Qualifications: Marcus Chown, author of science books including 'The Ascent of Gravity'.

questions.question: Why do some plants have reddish or purple leaves instead of green? If it's because of chlorophyll for photosynthesis, do they not have chlorophyll?

answers.answer: All leaves have a range of different pigments but chlorophyll is usually the most dominant, which is why leaves appear green. There are actually two different chlorophylls - chlorophyll a and b - which absorb slightly different wavelengths of light to maximize light intake. Other pigments like carotenoids and xanthophyll are normally masked by chlorophyll. In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down revealing these other colors. Bright light actually damages chlorophyll so it breaks down over summer/winter and is re-synthesized. Some plants always have red/purple leaves due to their evolution in shade-tolerant environments. All leaves do photosynthesize. Qualifications: Biology teacher.

questions.question: How would we know that dinosaur stress hormones are exactly the same chemical compound as human cortisol? We have fossil records, but how do we know what chemicals were produced in their systems?

answers.answer: Cortisol is part of a group of hormones called glucocorticoids, which are common across all animals - fish, reptiles, birds, humans, mammals. Fish and sharks predated dinosaurs and have this stress hormone, so it's a simple deduction that dinosaurs must have had these stress hormones too. The odds of them not having it would be astronomically small. Qualifications: Degree in medical genetics.

questions.question: How do people know that dogs age seven years to one human year? And is it the same for every breed of dog?

answers.answer: A puppy is equivalent to a newborn human baby. The first couple of years of a dog's life (roughly two to two and a half years) is when they grow to full size and become fully mature - going from puppy to adolescent. At that point, a dog's maturity rate slows down compared to humans. Different sized dogs live to different lengths, so seven years is an average. Qualifications: Runs a pet care and dog walking business with various dog-related qualifications.

questions.question: What are the odds of being dealt 7 red cards and having his granddaughter dealt 7 black cards (14 cards total dealt from a 52-card pack)?

answers.answer: The probability is 1 in 14,030 (actually 14,030.558). The calculation involves: 26/52 × 25/51 × 24/50 × 23/49 × 22/48 × 21/47 × 20/46 for the first 7 cards being black, then 26/45 × 25/44 × 24/43 × 23/42 × 22/41 × 21/40 × 20/39 for the remaining 7 being red. That's approximately 0.000071 (0.0071%). Qualifications: A-level statistics.

questions.question: Why are bin bags, and indeed bins, measured in litres?

answers.answer: Litres are an SI unit - one litre at atmospheric sea level will occupy the same volume no matter where it is. You can't compress water. The shape doesn't matter - whether you've got an octagonal bin or a long and narrow bin, what you need to know is the amount it will hold, not how tall or fat it is. If you've got one metre by one metre by one metre of water, you've got one ton of water.

A bin is measured in many ways, but what we're measuring with litres is its capacity - how much it holds. With a bin liner, because it's so malleable, you can scrunch it up to the size of your hand and that size doesn't help anyone. The only thing you can measure is its capacity. Volume is how we measure it, capacity is how much it holds.

questions.question: You have airports and seaports, but why don't you have a train port or a plane station? What's the difference between a station and a port?

answers.answer: Airports basically have full-time customs facilities. These were migrated from sea ports where customs officers were stationed traditionally. When airports came to have customs facilities, the customs officers would have migrated from the sea ports to airports. So 'ports' have customs facilities traditionally, and that is why they're called ports. Stations generally don't, even though they might now.

questions.question: I have a tabby cat with multicoloured fur, but when I brush her, all the fluff comes out grey as one colour. Why is that?

answers.answer: When brushing the cat, you're brushing out the undercoat, which is grey. Underneath the coloured hair, there's a really short coat that keeps them warmer and sheds seasonally. The coloured fur, the tabby part, just stays. That's what comes out according to the seasons - the undercoat.

questions.question: What is the purpose of vibrato in music? Why do we add it to instruments and voices when a straight note is natural?

answers.answer: The wave in the voice is something that seduces people and they like it more. It's nicer to listen to, it's easy on the ear. It creates vibration and evokes something primeval in you. It goes through your body. Vibrato is oscillating your vocal folds, making them bigger and smaller in a wave. It's cultural and learned - certain nationalities like French singers have a much faster vibrato because they grow up hearing it and develop it as a style. You can grow it if you don't naturally have it.

To have a true vibrato, particularly the rich vibrato an opera singer has, it's all to do with skill from diaphragm support. When you're singing properly with your support and breath work fully engaged and trained, it allows the vocal box and vocal folds to relax so you can create that beautiful sound. It allows you to sing stronger without tiring your voice. It's actually a sign of skill and talent more than for the pleasing of the ear - though both are true.

questions.question: Why are the whites of human eyes always visible? Why don't other animals have visible eye whites?
Can identical twins be different handed?

answers.answer: Yes, identical twins can be different handed. They can also have different fingerprints and different palm or foot prints. There are also mirror twins who tend to have opposite characteristics.
I'm a mirror image twin. I'm left-handed, my brother's right-handed. I'm left-footed, my brother's right-footed. And we've got asymmetries in our faces which are reproduced on both sides.

questions.question: Why does water pressure from a jet washer seem so much more powerful than from a tap? When the tap is rubbish, plugging in the hose makes it powerful.

answers.answer: The hose that supplies the water will supply at a very low rate, usually about 1 bar which is 30 PSI. Then there's a little brass pump in the pressure washer that pressurises the water, and it's trying to push it out through a really tiny hole at the other end. The key is the constriction at the other end of the pipe. If the aperture on the hose was the same width as the aperture on the tap, you wouldn't have much pressure at all.

questions.question: Is the UK the only country in the world which has a national anthem dedicated to a living individual?
Why don't you ever see a seagull in a tree?

answers.answer: Because they have webbed feet and can't grip branches - they can only settle on flat surfaces
Webbed feet - their feet are adapted for paddling and don't bend properly to grip branches. Same reason you never see ducks, swans, or geese in trees. It's a physical limitation of water birds.

questions.question: Why is one side of a bar of soap soft and the other side hard?

answers.answer: Suggested it might be because one side gets wet and the other doesn't

It's about the mould the soap is made in. The side that contacts the mould stays softer, while the side exposed to air cures faster and becomes harder. Not every soap does this - it depends on the mould type used.

questions.question: Why is a scientific calculator called a scientific calculator when it's used for maths?

answers.answer: Probably just a synonym for 'fancy' - they invented a calculator that could do logarithms and needed a name, so they called it a scientific calculator rather than a fancy one
There's nothing inherently scientific about them - it's just that they can handle more complex calculations. It's just a way of saying 'fancy calculator'.

questions.question: What do they add to gas to make it smell?

answers.answer: Mercaptan - a sulphur compound that smells like rotten eggs at low concentrations. It's added to gas so you can detect leaks. Same additive is used in the Merchant Navy for LPG. It comes from coal.

questions.question: Why do you do that little shiver or judder, particularly after having a wee?
Is there really such a thing as a seafood allergy, since prawns, fish, and mussels are all completely different species?

answers.answer: Yes, seafood allergy is a real thing - it's a specific protein found in three categories: mollusks (oysters, mussels, clams), cephalopods (octopus, squid), and crustaceans (prawns, crab, lobster). Fish is separate. So technically if someone's allergic to seafood they should also be allergic to fish. The protein can be denatured through drying, pickling or fermenting.

questions.question: Why are our teeth so weak and crumbly from an evolutionary perspective?

answers.answer: Humans used to have tribes that would look after them. Evidence shows an elderly woman who lost all her teeth at 40 lived another 20 years because her tribe chewed food for her. Also, people had children before losing teeth, so it didn't affect reproduction. The tribe would look after you.

questions.question: Does any other animal apart from humans go through menopause?

answers.answer: Yes - whales. We've covered this before. Killer whales and narwhals specifically. Not all whales, but many.

questions.question: Why don't you get red champagne?

answers.answer: You kind of do - there's something called Coteaux Champenois, which is a red wine from the Champagne region. The reason red champagne isn't common is that the attributes that make champagne valuable (lightness, crispness) don't align with what red wine offers.

questions.question: Answer about national anthem

answers.answer: Jordan's national anthem is dedicated to the king.

questions.question: Answer about national anthem

answers.answer: Saudi Arabia's anthem is dedicated to a living person - 'God save the king for our flag and the land.' It has many similarities to the UK anthem.

questions.question: Why do seagulls fly over the sea?

answers.answer: Because if they flew over the bay they'd be bagels.

questions.question: I get sleep paralysis sometimes - when I wake up I can't move or talk, my whole body's still and it scares me. How long does it last for?

answers.answer: Sleep paralysis is caused by two chemicals in the brain: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) and glycine. These chemicals are excreted during sleep to keep you paralyzed during dreams, otherwise you'd act out your dreams. When you wake up, these chemicals normally drain very quickly and adrenaline keeps your body from moving. Some people have these chemicals blocked by drugs or alcohol. It usually lasts seconds but feels like hours because you're paralyzed and can't scream. It's terrifying but intermittent for most people.

questions.question: Why don't London-based football clubs have London in their name, like other cities and capitals do - Sporting Lisbon, Paris Saint-Germain, Real Madrid? Is it just because there are so many London clubs?

answers.answer: It's about the evolution of the clubs - they all played against each other from the earliest days, so you can't claim to be THE London club. Arsenal was Woolwich Arsenal, Tottenham, Brentford, Chelsea, etc. - they were all named after their specific districts.

Clubs were named after the district or area of London they were from - Crystal Palace, Fulham, etc. West Ham was originally Thames Ironworks. Arsenal was originally Woolwich Arsenal, based at a munitions factory. The closest was Chelsea, where one proposed name was London Blues, but they rejected it because they didn't have the audacity to claim the whole city for themselves. No club ever claimed to be THE London club. Manchester United and City both think they are Manchester.

questions.question: When was 999 first used on the phone as a way of getting through to the emergency services?

answers.answer: The 999 service was invented in the 1930s with the rotary phone. If you get to the end of the circle on the dial, you always hit 9, so if you do that three times you get 999. On a touchpad phone, if you follow your finger from the 5 (which has a dot on it) downwards, you'd always hit 9. So you can find it in the dark, with eyes shut, or in a smoke-filled room. The date James provided: June 30th, 1937.

questions.question: Is there rhyming slang in any other world languages or equivalents to Cockney rhyming slang?

answers.answer: I can't think of anything. It seems feasible but unlikely because you'd need to know a foreign language well enough to know two words that rhyme.

The Burmese have rhyming slang and the New Zealand Kiwis (Maori) have it - in their own languages, not just English. The speaker's father was in the army (PWRR - Prince William's Royal Regiment) and played rugby against army and navy. After matches in the bar, Gurkha lads from Nepal and Kiwis would argue about the way commands were shouted and insults used. The father explained that as he was born and bred in London, it was their version of Cockney rhyming slang.

questions.question: When I was a little girl we used to stand in a door frame, press our arms against the frame pushing outwards for about a minute, then turn sideways and our arms would float up in the air as if we had no control. What causes this? Is it muscular, neurological, or autosuggestion?
On a standard bath towel, at each end there's always a stripe of coarser, shinier, less fluffy material. What is that for? Is it on all of them?

answers.answer: I think it's so when you fold it and put it on the bath rail or radiator, it just looks nicer. But I'm not sure.

questions.question: Do companies buy a batch of barcodes, or is there some mega-computer that produces them? There must be thousands of products being barcoded every split second - do barcodes ever get duplicated?

answers.answer: Barcodes are just a different character set, like choosing Chinese or English in Word. When you select a letter, instead of appearing normally, there's a certain length and width of black line that depicts it. Different countries and industries have their own barcode languages starting with EAN (European Article Numbers). The relationship is only between supplier and seller - there's no central database. You get given a range of codes like car registration numbers.

Paul's answer was wrong - there IS a central database. The biggest one in the world is GS1. They set the standards. You cannot just encode a barcode willy-nilly. If you're Tesco, you pay a subscription to GS1 who allot you a range of codes. The first digits of the barcode say who the brand owner is (e.g. Tesco). The next part tells you what the SKU is - a bacon sandwich, Coke, etc. The last part is a check digit to avoid duplication. If you buy a Coke in Asda or anywhere else, it always scans as the same 500ml bottle because of the central database. EAN28 doesn't exist.

questions.question: I understand this country has 'policing by consent' but I don't know what it means. I've never signed a document consenting to being policed. Is it something to do with armed police being more of a police force than a service? Is it just us?

answers.answer: Policing by consent dates back to 1829 when Robert Peel founded modern policing. Before that, there were watchmen, local constables, Bow Street Runners - it was all haphazard and some were like protection rackets, open to corruption. Peel's nine principles established that you need public support and consent to police effectively, only using force when absolutely necessary. It's consent on a societal scale - we imbue the institution with authority based on transparency and integrity. The impetus came from the Peterloo Massacre in Manchester when magistrates had to call in the military to enforce orders, leading to cavalry charges and deaths. Other countries that model themselves on us - Australia, New Zealand, Canada - have it too.

questions.question: If I buy a company today for £10,000 and tomorrow it's worth only £5,000, where does my money go? Why is a share different from an apple or a car? The money doesn't just disappear into thin air.

answers.answer: The money goes to the person you bought it from, just like with a car. The thing you swapped your £10,000 for isn't worth £10,000 anymore - it's worth £5,000. It's not like a finite amount of money in the world is being redistributed. There isn't a finite amount of money in the world. The share was worth £10,000 when you bought it, now it's worth £5,000 - like a car being worth less the minute you drive it off the forecourt. The money doesn't go anywhere, the value just changes. You only establish the value when you sell.

questions.question: Why does food and drink taste better when somebody else has prepared it?

answers.answer: Discussed the premise with Gethin, noting he experiences the same thing with Christmas dinner - not enjoying his own cooking as much. Suggested it might be the juices or marinade.

Taste is linked to smell. When sensory cells in your nose detect chemicals, signals travel to your brain via neurons. Between synapses are neurotransmitters. If you're surrounded by a smell constantly, the neurotransmitters run out and you become habituated to it. This is why your own cooking doesn't taste as good - you're habituated to the smell.

questions.question: Is there a reason why Thursday is the day books are published?

answers.answer: It's because of the charts. Wednesday night is when you find out if you've made the Sunday Times top 10 bestsellers. That would be seven days - Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday - giving the full week to maximize sales and get into the chart.

questions.question: Do snails get dizzy?

answers.answer: Said he'd find out. Mentioned it depends on their nervous system and what causes dizziness.

No, snails can't get dizzy. Humans get dizzy because we have little canals in our inner ear with fluid in. When we tilt our head, this triggers synapses and that's how we feel dizzy. Snails don't have these inner ear canals, so they can't get dizzy. You can prove this because you've never seen a snail fall over.

questions.question: What happens at the borders of countries that drive on different sides of the road?

answers.answer: Mentioned he saw a bridge once that was the most astonishing piece of engineering - you drove onto one end and when you drove off you were on the other side of the road. It was almost like a figure of eight with one lane going under and one going over.

Until 1972, Sweden drove on the left and Norway on the right. At the border, they had a permanent barrier across half the road. If approaching from Sweden, you're driving on the left and there's this barrier in front of you saying 'Welcome to Norway.' You go around the barrier and you're now driving on the right. Same barrier works for both directions.

Confirmed the Lotus Bridge between China and Macau works the same way. Ross has been over it multiple times for work - described it like a figure of eight Scalextric where cars change lanes for the second half of the track.

questions.question: When a storm whips up seawater and dumps it inland as rain, where does the salt go?

answers.answer: Explained that when you boil salt water, the salt stays behind. The steam coming off doesn't contain any salt. This is basic chemistry - the first experiment ever done.

answers.caller: Hal (Brighton) - Professor of Public Understanding at University of Brighton
answers.answer: When the sun or wind picks up water, it evaporates, rises, and recondenses at a certain temperature. That's the water cycle. The boiling point of sodium chloride is about 2,000 degrees, so it never evaporates. Even if salt gets whipped up, it just falls back down. Evidence includes salt streaks on black T-shirts from sweat evaporating, and salt flats in places like Maldon.

answers.caller: Alistair (Orpington) - PhD in rainfall and radar 50 years ago
answers.answer: Most spray over the sea falls back down, but some goes higher as very small particles. Each tiny water particle can have a small piece of salt in it. When it evaporates, the salt particles remain high up. Later, these form the nucleus for raindrops to form. Every raindrop needs a solid nucleus to form around - salt, sand, or vegetation particles. Raindrops are a millimetre or more, so they're not very salty by the time they fall.

questions.question: Why are sleeping cartoon characters shown with Zs? What is the origin of that?

answers.answer: Didn't know. Speculated it might be the exhale rather than inhale. Suggested it might have been DC Thompson or one of the early comic artists where it first appeared. Acknowledged he didn't know whether it came from literature or song.

questions.question: Why does my mouth feel drier when I drink more water than on days when I don't drink as much?

answers.answer: Mentioned 'osmosis' as a possible answer, but acknowledged he didn't know and said he'd find out.

questions.question: How does WhatsApp make money if it's a free app?

answers.answer: Said he'd find out. Noted WhatsApp is part of Facebook (Meta).

WhatsApp follows the WeChat model from China. WeChat has a business directory where plumbers, shops, tradesmen, doctors advertise and consumers subscribe. WhatsApp does something similar in India with bank business accounts. They're trying to increase consumer base and data collection. WeChat has one of the highest ARPU (average return per user) in the industry. It's about getting more customers and data.

answers.caller: Patrick (Reading) - worked in data for 10 years
answers.answer: Facebook bought WhatsApp primarily for phone numbers. They're making money through data, not directly from users. They can merge fluid data on Facebook (likes, purchases, political leanings) with static phone number data, making it more valuable to companies and political parties. In the US you can use this data for targeted advertising. There was a huge multi-hundred million dollar fine for data mining.

questions.question: Why can you drink a pint of beer after a huge meal when you can't eat another morsel of solid food?

answers.answer: Speculated that liquid might run between the cracks like cement between bricks - your gut is full of 'bricks' (food) but liquid can fit in the gaps. Said he'd find out.

questions.question: Why is a Mr Whippy 99 called a 99?

answers.answer: Best available theory is the flake - in the 1920s, a half-flake was called a 99.

Said it's an urban myth - one theory involves Regiment 99 and Italian migrants naming their ice cream after something good. Another theory is that the first person to stick a flake in an ice cream had a shop at number 99 on a road in Scotland. No one knows for certain.

questions.question: How does a self-sourcing pudding work?

answers.answer: You pour a mixture of boiling water and sugar over the top of the batter before it goes in the oven. Miraculously, whilst it's cooking, the liquid goes to the bottom and the pudding rises to the top. The crust forms on the top and the liquid underneath is actually uncooked sauce.

When you heat the batter up, it becomes less viscous and the sauce elements drop to the bottom. As you continue to cook it, the sponge sits on top of the sauce elements. When you turn the bowl out, the sauce is at the bottom. The heavier elements drop to the bottom, and there wouldn't be any baking powder or flour in the sauce because that's what cooks and rises. The baking powder makes it rise.

questions.question: Does the body prioritise where that liquid is needed most?

answers.answer: Most of your water is held inside your cells. As they use up water, they draw water from outside the cells which is just in tissues. Your body senses a drop in blood pressure. When you drink, water is absorbed through your large intestine and smaller intestine, fills up your blood and is distributed around your body evenly. Your body doesn't prioritize water anywhere but in your blood and tissues. You hold about 70% of your water in your cells. It's about where water burns is more important - it might be used up in muscles sooner if you've run a marathon, but gradually your body will distribute water evenly throughout.

questions.question: Why do we find beauty in inanimate objects? What is the evolutionary benefit?

answers.answer: As a photographer, it's about composition. In nature you get rules of thirds, golden ratio. A photo that went viral used golden ratio. But this doesn't explain why a waterfall is beautiful but a microphone isn't - both use symmetry.

We are genetically programmed to find environments most suitable for our species. It's called prospect and refuge. There's always an open space where we could find prey or plant food. We universally find flowers attractive because there's a location of future fruit. And there's always a little protected bit - refuge - hiding away from predators. There's always fresh water because our species needs that. This is hardwired into our DNA and the basis of every picturesque painting and garden design.

questions.question: Why do wheel hubs on the front wheels of big vehicles poke out while on the back wheels they don't?

answers.answer: On the front you have a steer axle with a single wheel. All the other wheels are doubled up on the same axle. To get two wheels on one axle, one wheel goes on the right way, and the second wheel is turned 180 degrees, almost face-to-face, and goes on backwards. Hence why the wheel nuts appear deeper inside on the back wheels. So they appear different. The front wheel is offset to allow all the gubbins underneath like brake calipers to fit inside the wheel. The inner wheel at the back goes on the same way as the front wheel. The outer wheel goes on backwards, bump-to-bump.

questions.question: How are words peculiar to foreign languages signed in British Sign Language?

answers.answer: It doesn't make any difference if the signer is signing a word in a foreign language or in English because BSL is its own language. BSL doesn't work on translating word for word - it's all about the meaning. There will either be a way of conveying what is conveyed by words like saudade and phylloxenia in British Sign Language, or there won't. As long as the signer knows what that word means, they can get the meaning across. For example, Schadenfreude in BSL: you point to a weight from yourself to an imaginary person and show them with a miserable face, then point to yourself and give yourself a smiley face.

questions.question: Why can't I ever get a hangover?

answers.answer: You could be born with a bigger liver. Some people are born with bigger stores of certain enzymes that break down alcohol. They're able to get rid of it quicker. Booze builds up more enzymes over time, but Kevin seems to have been born with that capacity.

questions.question: When it rains, why do wood pigeons sit out on rooftops and get wet while all other birds take shelter?
Question about the water question (osmo regulation)

answers.answer: [Answer about/osmo regulation attempted but line was too poor to hear clearly]

questions.question: Why is the number 8 in rugby just a number when all other players have proper position names like fullback and winger?

answers.answer: Rugby numbering started with the All Blacks using numbers to make players more recognizable to the public. The number 8 was originally called 'lock' because he locked the scrum. When second row players started being called locks, the number 8 became '8th man of the scrum' in Wales, which evolved to just 'number 8'. In France they still use the old term.

questions.question: Why do we have a sense of humor? Does it have an evolutionary purpose?

answers.answer: Humor is sexually attractive because it's an unfakeable demonstration of intelligence. When you listen to someone freestyling comedy, you're in the presence of genius. Panel shows are popular because the speed and quick-wittedness shows pure intelligence. People aren't aware how much they value intelligence in mates. This gets passed down genetically because it helps spread genes - it's like a peacock's tail showing genetic fitness.

questions.question: Why do we stroke our chins when being skeptical? Where did phrases like 'chinny reckon', 'Jimmy Hill', and 'toot and car moon' come from?

answers.answer: Female pharaohs used to don fake beards to appear more masculine and therefore more godlike. That became synonymous with a fib or a fake. People in Egyptian society used to stroke their chins when skeptical of what others said, and this gesture has now gone worldwide.

questions.question: Why do menopausal women get hot flushes? Why specifically heat when other symptoms are about mood?

answers.answer: Oestrogen closes capillaries, progesterone opens them. When oestrogen drops during menopause, the capillaries close, then when they open again suddenly, blood pumps through at greater rate - this is thermoregulation gone wrong, causing the flush.

questions.question: What makes an assassination different from a murder? How important do you have to be to be 'assassinated'?

answers.answer: Assassination is about public reasons, not private ones. It's when a public figure is killed precisely because of their public status. If Mrs Lincoln had killed Abraham, it would be murder. But when a politician is murdered by a terrorist for political reasons, it's an assassination. JFK, Martin Luther King, Jo Cox were all assassinations.

questions.question: Do handheld fans actually cool your body temperature or does the energy used in fanning make you hotter?

answers.answer: Fans work through evaporative cooling. When sweat evaporates from your skin, it cools you down. The cooling effect from evaporation is so powerful it overtakes any heat generated by the physical motion of waving. This principle is the same as air conditioning units - instead of using your hand as a fan, it uses refrigerant gas through a condenser.

questions.question: Where do released wedding doves go? Are they wild doves, homing doves, or do they return to the wedding planner?

answers.answer: Wedding doves are homing doves trained to return to their loft. When released, they do a circuit of the venue and then head back to where they came from - in my case, Essex. The dove man told me they're homing doves, which explains why they come back.

questions.question: Why are hills like the South Downs and Epsom Downs called 'Downs' when they're clearly up - high ground?

answers.answer: Downs is a corruption of the Anglo-Saxon word 'dune' meaning hill. This is still with us in 'sand dune'. Britain had wave after wave of migration (Romans, Angles, Saxons) and each new group described landscape topographically. Since there were no maps, travelers knew where they were by landscape features - so 'Birch Hanger' meant a gentle slope with birch trees. Place names like Cheeswick (cheese farm), Brentford (ford over River Brent) all came from this system of geographical description.

questions.question: Why do we swing our arms when we walk? Jeffrey Dahmer taught himself to walk without swinging his arms.
How much energy does it take for a spider to spin a web? And what would the human equivalent be? Would it be like running around the block? Or like a full day's work?

answers.answer: Clarification - not all spiders make webs. For spiders that do make webs, picking a funnel web spider, it takes about 30% of their body energy. A garden spider will eat its web and remake it, using the amino acids and proteins. So a third of the available calories from their last meal.

questions.question: Why aren't smaller rivers and lakes affected by the tides? Why aren't they tidal? Even puddles are tidal, but the movements are so incremental we can't see them.

answers.answer: The question is bound around gravity - there are three main components where gravitational force comes from: the Earth, the Moon, and the Sun. The primary gravitational force on any body of water comes from the Earth, and when it comes to the oceans, because it's already found a level, the secondary effect of the Moon and Sun then dominates the additional movement. With lakes, the same effect is going on but almost imperceptible. With rivers, because they haven't met their settled state as a result of reaching a point where the water becomes level, they're still acting under the primary gravitational force of the Earth - the rainfall on higher ground works its way down to find its own level. Teddington is the point where the force of water coming downstream meets water potentially coming upstream, and that's where tides stop affecting the river. The bed level of the Thames is essentially lower than sea level up to the point where it meets a point on the land where the water level is higher than sea level. Everything has got a tide, even a puddle, but it would just be too tiny to see because gravity is a fairly weak force.

questions.question: Why don't the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire (home in Derbyshire/Chatsworth), Lord Carnarvon (home in Hampshire), and the Earl of Leicester (lives in Norfolk) live where their titles are named after? Why do some of them live miles away from where their title is named?

answers.answer: These Entitled nobles have about half a dozen different titles each. So he might be the Duke of Norfolk living in Leicester, but he's also going to be half a dozen other titles. That's why they don't know where they live - because they've been collecting them like Top Trumps or Pokemons. They go by the name of the biggest title, which would be the Earl of Warrington or something, but they might also be the Duke of so-and-so depending on what gets passed on to which progeny.

questions.question: When paying using coins at the self-checkout, will the machine realize if we're using coins from a different currency? As long as it's the same dimension?

answers.answer: I work for an EPOS company that supplies point of sale systems to retail shops including self-checkouts. These machines are configured to follow Bank of England authorized standards. The machines are very clever in their design - even if a coin is the same weight but is fake, the machine can recognize it. They use technology inside to recognize if it's a real coin by the material. The machines are configured for specific currencies - UK machines use pound configuration, European machines use Euro configuration. There's no crossover because it has to go through the standard. They will reject every single foreign coin or fake note.

questions.question: Is there an accent that's in between English and Scottish? Once you get over the border, is there people that live on the border that have got a mixture of accents? How does it change gradually? Where does Scotland actually kick in?

answers.answer: I lived in Berwick-upon-Tweed for 18 months. The accent there is genuinely a hybrid between a Geordie accent and the accent in Edinburgh - the refined Scottish accent. If you then said to someone from Berwick that their accent was Scottish or Geordie, they would not like that very much because they're conscious of it. Carlisle may be an even better example. The further north you go, the stronger the accent gets. So they have their own unique accent around Berwick-upon-Tweed and Carlisle.

questions.question: I put fizzy water in a regular plastic bottle and it exploded at the airport. Why doesn't that happen when you buy shop-bought water?

answers.answer: You over-fizzed it with the SodaStream. When you have a SodaStream, there's different levels of amounts of gas you can put in depending on how many times you press down.

questions.question: How does a silencer work on a gun? When the hammer hits the back of the bullet at the back of the gun, shouldn't the explosion be heard there?

answers.answer: What makes the noise when a champagne cork opens is the gas being released. What makes a gun noise is different gas - the gas propelling the bullet up the barrel. A silencer is thick and screws on the end, wider than the barrel. It contains baffle - the barrel of the silencer is perforated with holes in it. The gas moves into the second barrel (the silencer) and dissipates into the wadding and baffle behind the holes. By the time the bullet gets to the end of the silencer, the amount of gas that pops out is significantly reduced - so you get a little fut instead of a big bang.

questions.question: What's in Dulwich Picture Gallery and why is it so famous?

answers.caller: John (Daljit) / Rosemary (volunteer at Dulwich Picture Gallery)
answers.answer: It was founded by Noel de Saint-Fan and Francis Bourgeois, who put together the old master collection for the deposed King of Poland living in Dulwich. They were left with the collection on their hands, subsequently housed in the Soane Building, the first purpose-built public art gallery. Sir John Soane designed the gallery.

questions.question: Is it true that if you don't get a good night's sleep, you'll get bags or shadows under your eyes? And if so, why?
Why do pigeons congregate on some roofs and not others? They congregate on one side of a semi-detached property. And it's quite often older people's properties. Is it heat rising?

answers.answer: Pigeons actually like listening to human voices. Older people have their radios turned up quite high, and so pigeons settle on the home where the radio is on higher. That could be it. Or televisions.

questions.question: What does the H-A-M at the end of place names like Durham, Hexham, and Walkingham mean?

answers.answer: Ham with one M is Anglo-Saxon for a settlement (like hamlet). A double M might relate to a fen or water meadow.

Ham means a farm from Saxon. Hampton comes from hemp (flax used for clothing/ropes) with 'ton' meaning a plot of land. They may not be etymologically related - some names got corrupted over 500 years. In the case of Southampton, it's a ham (just for pronunciation ease), not hemp.

questions.question: Why do we never have female juniors? Why don't we see daughters called junior like sons are?
Why do I lose weight (about 2-3 pounds) overnight when I sleep?

answers.answer: We break down fat while we sleep. Fats are triglycerides (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen) which break down into water and carbon dioxide, and about four-fifths of fat is breathed out. Since we metabolize most fat when sleeping, that's when we burn the most. There's a vicious circle - being overweight affects sleep patterns, making it harder to burn fat.

It's a chemical reaction. Every cell in the body uses glucose to make ATP (energy storage molecule). The body can divert energy to making heat instead. When body temperature is low, it diverts more to heating.

questions.question: How is heat generated in the human body? How do we maintain 37 degrees and where does that heat come from?

answers.answer: It's a chemical reaction. Every cell uses glucose to make ATP and can divert energy to heat energy. The body has a built-in thermostat that knows where it should be.

questions.question: Why do some natural features have the descriptor before the name (river Thames, ocean Atlantic) while others have it after (Black Mountains, Forest of Dean)?

answers.answer: In languages like Latin, the head comes first (Mons Vesuvius = Mount Vesuvius). In languages like German, the head comes at the end (Neandertal = valley of the Neander). England has a mix due to its mongrel heritage with influences from Anglo-Saxon, French, Latin, and others. Newer countries like America have more homogenous naming patterns.

questions.question: When you transplant an organ, all the blood vessels and nerves are cut. How do they reconnect the nerves to the brain?

answers.answer: For heart transplants, we don't reconnect the nervous system. The heart has intrinsic cells that beat on their own. In a normal body, faster and slower fibers control the rate (running about 50-60 beats per minute). After transplant, the heart beats at its intrinsic faster rate. Organs like kidneys and lungs work more independently and don't need nervous system reconnection. There is some evidence nerves find their way back over time, but it's never the same.

questions.question: Why do we dance? What's the origin of dancing?

answers.answer: There's no real definitive answer but dancing is a human universal - all cultures do it. The best thinking is that our sociality was so important early in human development that dancing probably predates language. There are links to the womb and heartbeat in utero. There is evidence of brain structures that suggest it's completely innate - three-month-old babies will move to music.

questions.question: As a child into her 20s and 30s, as she was drifting off to sleep, she felt body parts (head, foot, arm) were either huge or tiny - like a pinhead. Is this a known phenomenon with a name?

answers.answer: It's called Alice in Wonderland syndrome - a neurological syndrome. Jamie suffered from it horrifically as a child, particularly when feeling anxious, and still gets it at night. It affects perception of your own body and other people. When suffering from it, fingers felt like huge sausages.

questions.question: Why do we only spray antiperspirant on our armpits? Why not other body parts?

answers.answer: Body odor is not sweat itself but stale sweat. Armpits produce more sweat and because arms are usually by your side, the sweat stays there. The fold of skin creates an environment that engenders more staleness. Other body parts don't sweat as heavily so the sweat doesn't go stale in the same way.

questions.question: Why are vinyl records specifically 45 RPM, 33 and a third RPM, and 78 RPM? Why those exact numbers?

answers.answer: Columbia invented 33 RPM (from radio transcription disc standards). RCA invented 45 RPM to compete. 78 was the original but varied between 70-90 RPM. The numbers don't relate to each other mathematically - they're purely about how much could fit on a disc, market dominance, patents, and competition between record companies (like VHS vs Betamax).

questions.question: Why do people develop allergies at any age? They aren't innate, are they?
Why are mammals the only animals that aren't brightly coloured - no blue or pink, unlike fish, insects and reptiles?

answers.answer: It's to do with camouflage and evolutionary adaptation. Tropical fish with bright colours live where there's coral to blend in with. If a mutation makes an animal a colour that helps it survive longer and breed more, that gets passed on. The colours could be impurities too. It's the same answer to all these questions - evolution.

questions.question: Why do your legs give way when you look down from a great height?

answers.answer: It's all to do with fight or flight and adrenaline. The adrenal system runs adrenaline and lactic acid which makes muscles move smoother and faster. When you experience fear, the adrenaline kicks off your lactic acid system which coats the muscles so they can contract quicker - your body is preparing for that flight action. Your legs go wobbly because you're not actually using the muscles immediately. You get exactly the same response if you bump into a lion in the woods.

questions.question: What happens to all the glass bottles we put out for recycling every week? Is it any good?

answers.answer: They get it up to such a high temperature that all the impurities just get burnt off.

Glass is infinitely recyclable - it can be recycled over and over without loss of quality. They want bottles intact and clean. If not perfect material, it's crushed up and goes into tarmac (you can see it glittering in car parks) and road markings for reflectivity. It goes through an automatic process with eddy currents on conveyor belts to sort metals and contaminants, then manual picking. They try to rescue bottles for reuse. councils collect and segregate waste specifically for this.

questions.question: Why can't you put metal into a microwave?

answers.answer: It's a different sort of metal, perhaps with some sort of plastic coating inside.

A microwave has a magnetron that creates RF energy at about 2.4 gigahertz. The metal box including the mesh on the door is a grounded Faraday cage that absorbs all RF frequency not absorbed by anything else. Putting metal in is about the shape of the object - a round steel ball bearing won't do anything as absorbed energy just gets grounded away. But if metal has points where it can arc or create plasma, it releases that energy. The gold foil on cup rims is particularly problematic because it's basically small pieces of metal in emulsion.

questions.question: Why do redheads have a very high pain threshold but need more anaesthetic in operations?

answers.answer: Redheads have a gene called MC1R which alters how they process hormones and vitamins. They process Vitamin K really well (needed in northern latitudes without much sunlight) and process endorphins differently. Almost all redheads have this gene which gives them higher pain tolerance. They also don't sense smell as much and are more tolerant of obnoxious smells. Regarding anaesthetics, they don't tolerate lidocaine well and need more. Because more is used, they tend to be feisty when coming round. He had an argument with the anesthetist while still under because so much was needed to keep him under.

questions.question: Why do we call some sentences 'life sentences' when the offender won't serve the entirety of their life?

answers.answer: You're mistaking a life sentence for a prison sentence. Unless a judge stipulates a whole life term, you become eligible for parole. If agreed you no longer pose a threat, you're released but always under licence - if authorities decide you do pose a threat, even without committing any offence, you go straight back to prison. This stays until your dying day. So it's a life sentence but not a life prison sentence. The sentence never expires.

questions.question: Where do we 'see' things when we imagine them? If you're looking at your wall, how can you imagine your dog or a picture of the studio?

answers.answer: It's probably the same part of the brain - all we're seeing is lights and our brain processes them. The brain can probably work without inputs and stimuli and still create images in your mind's eye. When you imagine something you've never seen, you're using general concepts your brain has of that thing.

It's to do with visual imagery and memory - you can't conjure up an image you haven't seen before. Even if you've never seen a specific house, you're conjuring up images associated with the word 'house' in your brain.

questions.question: What makes one conductor better than another?

answers.answer: The job is twofold. First: ensuring all players play at the same time to the same tempo - you need to be crystal clear as a conductor, that's where you can be better than another conductor. Second, bigger job: interpreting music. Interpretation is subjective like art - no right or wrong, it's about what you feel is right. How do you communicate that? Through rehearsal. 90 percent of conducting is preparation - you tell them exactly what you want. The actual conducting is reminding them of what you've already told them, plus throwing your passion and emotion physically so they react and play better. You can't just turn up and knock it out of the park - even the best conductor in the world needs the preparation.

questions.question: Why is a celebrity rider called a rider?
Why can you get a sandy beach and a pebbly beach almost right next to each other?
Why do certain parts of your body take longer to tan than other parts of your body?

answers.answer: Melanin distribution - parts of your body that are exposed to sunlight least are the bits that tan hardest. Legs see less sunlight than other body parts.

Tanning relies on three things: levels of melanin, skin tone, and thickness of skin. Some areas tan quicker. Karen's tummy goes brown quickly partly because it's out more when wearing a bikini, and the skin there is thicker.

questions.question: What possible nutrition can moths get out of eating wool and keep living?

answers.answer: Wool is organic material, so anything organic is nourishing. If energy was taken to create it, you can break it down to release energy.

Moths eat keratin. Keratin is a protein found in hair, fingernails, and rhino horn. They also need humidity from the air - moths get nutrition from both the wool and moisture. If you freeze clothes in a bag for a couple of days first, you kill any eggs or larvae.

questions.question: Why do we lick our thumbs to make them sticky to turn pages on newspapers and books?

answers.answer: Speculated that it might create some kind of bond, like glue. He noted that the tambourine example shows the skin isn't absorbent, so it's not just absorption.

Three factors at play: 1) If you've got dry skin, moistening it makes it more flexible and better at gripping. 2) Water is cohesive - water on your thumb sticks to water on the page, creating a glue-like bond. 3) Liquid also lubricates between surfaces, which sounds counterintuitive but the water molecules move over each other while still bonding enough to pick up a page.

questions.question: Why do train drivers sound their horns? What are the rules?

answers.answer: Couldn't give a definitive answer but noted it's probably for safety when going through stations at high speed.

There's a massive rule book that's been developing for 100-150 years. Horns are blown at foot crossings to warn pedestrians, and when engineers/workers (the orange army) are on the tracks - they then acknowledge and stand aside. You can toot between 6am and midnight; outside those hours you need a reason but can still blow if necessary. There are different horns: low tone, high tone, and some trains even have a depot whistle, each conveying different messages - warning people on platforms to stand back, alerting at foot crossings, or emergencies like brakes failing.

questions.question: Why do golfers only wear one glove?

answers.answer: Didn't know - speculated about friction and which hand wears it.

The glove is worn on the lower hand (underneath the shaft) - for right-handed players, it's the left hand. It's there to help with grip because without it, hands don't grip properly - there are gaps between fingers and the club shaft which cause wobble. The lower hand does the bulk of the gripping, so you only need one.

At the change of direction in the golf swing, the club goes from its lightest point (upside down) to its heaviest point, and this forces the hands open - especially for beginners, who get calluses and blisters. The glove offers protection. For good players, it offers adhesion between grip and palm. Some experienced players don't wear gloves because they've built up calluses over time.

questions.question: Can we influence our dreams? Why do I never dream about my cancer even though I think about it constantly?

answers.answer: His subconscious goes way beyond the diagnosis when he's dreaming. He suggested you can influence dreams deliberately - he used to be able to dream about playing football when he wanted to.

questions.question: Why do we get different types of rain - drizzle, normal rain, heavy downpours? Why doesn't the cloud just release a set amount of water at a set speed?

answers.answer: Didn't know - speculated about drop size or wind pushing rain down faster.

It's about thermodynamic properties - temperature, humidity, and pressure. In summer, direct heating makes air parcels rise quickly as warm air becomes less dense. This instability causes quick downpours (convective thunderstorms). For every 1 degree temperature increase, the atmosphere holds 7% more water vapour - that's why we'll see more intense rainfall with climate change. In winter, cooler atmospheres bring more frontal rain - longer duration (12-24 hours) but less intensity. Antarctica is technically a desert because it's frozen and dry, so even though it has lots of accumulated snowfall, there's no humidity.

questions.question: What do we see when our eyes are closed? Do you see shapes drifting across what would be your field of vision?

answers.answer: He confirmed he sees the same thing - shapes and colors drifting across vision. It could be ghost images from looking at light.

These are called phosphenes - little electrical charges generated in the retina. The condition is known as photopsia. They can also be random electrical signals from neurons in the occipital lobe (the vision center at the back of the brain). You can induce them mechanically by rubbing your eyes - it creates a vivid flower display.

questions.question: When a car accelerates and you're looking at the alloy wheels, they go forward as you'd expect, but at one point at a certain speed they appear to go backwards. Why does that happen?

answers.answer: It's because of the speed with which your brain can process what's coming through your eyes. Think of snapshots - if your brain was processing the snaps as quickly as the wheel was turning then it would constantly be moving forward but when you're only getting one snap in five, you're not seeing all the snapshots so it will appear to be going backwards.

The TV thing is called the cartwheel effect, and it's most noticeable in 1940s westerns - cartwheels were going round but not going round as quickly as the frame rate of the film. Each time the next frame comes up, the cartwheel hasn't quite caught up so it appears to be going backwards. It's the flipping camera, not your eyes. Your eyes have something called nystagmus that stitches together pictures into one continuous vista.

questions.question: Why is champagne the drink of celebration?

answers.answer: The most expensive drinks are the fizzy ones because they were much harder to produce and therefore more expensive, so when it's a special occasion we'll get the champagne in.
It's the pop of the cork, the celebratory nature of the popping cork like a firework.

Champagne is linked to celebration because the French kings were coronated in Reims back in the 12th century, and they invited the British aristocrats and kings. They thought 'this is quite nice' so they imported it back to the UK, and then that's why it was linked to celebration.

questions.question: Why do moles accumulate more hair - why is the hair on a mole denser and thicker than the hair elsewhere on the body?

answers.answer: There's something happening in your skin that creates a mole and something happening in your skin that creates hairs in the same place. The thing that creates the mole is the melanin which leads to the conclusion that the melanin is also having an impact upon the hair follicle production.

questions.question: Why does my left armpit smell worse than my right armpit after a sweaty night's sleep? My girlfriend tested this on herself and the same thing happened to her.

answers.answer: It's probably a ventilation issue or sleeping position. The side you sleep on is going to have a different armpit result than the side you're not sleeping on.
I suspect it's the arm that does more physical work during the day, which creates more perspiration and hence more sweat. The right arm is supposedly the dominant one for most people.

questions.question: When we used to camp in France, mice would come up through the floor of the tent. The campsite owners always said the same thing: where you get mice, you don't get rats. Is that true, or only true in France?

answers.answer: You may have a category error here - I think that would be referring to domiciles, to buildings, not a field. I don't think they'd say that in a field. A pest control person might say if you've got mice, you haven't got rats.

Generally they won't be in the same area because the rats will eat the mice. It's that simple. So it's not like the mice keep the rats away - it's that the rats eat the mice. On Louise's French campsite where there were lots of mice, the rats just hadn't turned up because there's no permanent residences there. A rat will need a higher amount of water - they need more water than they do food. Mice can survive without water as long as the food content is above 16% moisture.

questions.question: In winter, being told to turn the thermostat down to 19 degrees feels cold inside. But when it's 18 degrees outside in Scotland, people are walking around in shorts with their tops off. Why does the same temperature feel so different?

answers.answer: It's probably not the same, is it? Even at 19 or 20 degrees in the winter you'd have a jumper on, maybe your house gilet.

If it's a bright day outside, you've got the sun's radiant heat. The radiant temperature can be significantly higher than the air temperature. When you come into your house and set your thermostat to 18, you've lost that radiant heat from the sun and it's just the air temperature you're feeling. It could be t-shirt weather on a cold day if the sun is shining brightly, or it could feel very cold if there's wind chill even with the same air temperature.

questions.question: Why does a single loose hair that lands on my shoulder irritate me like a mosquito, but hair that's still attached to my head and touching my shoulder doesn't irritate me at all?

answers.answer: A lone unattached hair is tickling you like a feather - it's the lightness of the individual unattached hair that is causing the irritation. A ponytail wouldn't tickle because it's too heavy. If you could separate a single hair still attached to your head and tickle your shoulder with it, you'd get the same effect.

questions.question: My Irish neighbour tells me that 'O' as in O'Brien is to express surprise. Is that true?

answers.answer: Both O and Mac denote descendant of. For O'Brien, it's usually believed to be Brian Boru, a sort of king of Ireland. Originally there wouldn't have been an apostrophe - it was a fada above the O. When the English started killing us all for fun, they wanted to anglicise our names, so they got rid of the fada and often the Mac. Some of us kept an apostrophe instead, so the apostrophe is best understood as an anglicised fada. The O means of the clan of.

Mac is actually the son of - it specifies a male descendant. Nic, N-I-C, would be the daughter of. So Mac Sweeney means the son of Sweeney, Nic Sweeney means the daughter of Sweeney. The O means of the clan, not the child of, just of the clan of Brian.

questions.question: What is the origin of horsepower? How was it decided? Did they actually use horses? Did they take a hundred horses and measure the output? Did they take one horse? Which type of horse?

answers.answer: In the old days when everything was done by horses pulling, pushing, lifting, dragging, horses provided a stable way of doing tasks. Then along came Mr. Watt and Mr. Stevenson and created steam engines. To persuade people to move from horses to steam, they would calculate particular things - down the mines it was known there was a big issue with flooding that had to be extracted using horses operating pumps or pulling large vessels. Mr. Watt created an engine that could replicate two or four horses, and that was used as a measure of the engines - two and four horsepower. It started on the pumps rather than trains or steam engines.

questions.question: Does a tree know when it's planted where those branches are going to come out? Or does the branches come out in time because of the place it's been planted? Would a tree turn to the sun like a sunflower? Is branch dispersal determined by nature or nurture?

answers.answer: It's both predetermined and circumstantial. Any branch that you cut back will produce three new branches for every tree. But there's also circumstantial elements. There's no first branch - it goes straight up as a straight shoot, then comes a leaf. If you cut back the first shoot, it turns into three branches. Every year puts on a new layer. If a tree grows in a forest where it's tightly packed with other trees, it will grow straight up to reach the sun. A meadow tree behaves very differently from one in a dense forest. The straighter the tree, the more valuable it is for making boards and planks of wood.

questions.question: Why does your tongue get stuck to a frozen lollypop? Just like in Dumb and Dumber when his tongue got stuck to the pole on the ski slope.

Where does the money go when interest rates rise? I've got a mortgage with Nationwide, they put the interest rate up because they need to get more money to pay the Bank of England. When it filters up to the top at the Bank of England, where does that money go? Does it go to the government? Does it go to the Bank of England? Somewhere there's a huge pile of money. Where does it go?

answers.answer: The guy who phoned in has it a little bit wrong. The system was designed so that banks use interest to regulate loans and to regulate savings. When the Bank of England wants people to stop spending so much, they put the interest rate up to encourage people to save money. But the bank still keeps the interest because the bank is using the interest to fund the other side of the business. Your money in savings pays for the loans they give to other people. They do pay some kind of fee to the Bank of England to keep a certain amount of money there to keep them stable, but the Bank of England doesn't see that money when they put the interest rate up. That's not what they do it for. It stops with the individual institution. That's why HSBC posted profits of $8.8 billion. Bigger banks with bigger cash deposits can afford to offer lower rates, smaller banks have to offer higher rates.

questions.question: Why are police officers known as coppers?

answers.answer: If you think of the phrase 'cop it', you're going to cop it. It's a bit chicken and egg. The phrase 'you're going to cop it' comes from copper being slang for cop, but actually it doesn't - cop is a synonym for capture. The Latin was capere. Going back to medieval times, 16th, 17th century, cop would be just another word for capture. So the copper is a capturer, and ergo police officers became known as coppers because they were the ones that were going to capture you.

questions.question: Why does the temperature in the atmosphere go colder as you go up, then hotter in the stratosphere, then colder again, then hotter again in the thermosphere? Why does it get colder the further you go up, then hotter as you head towards the sun, then colder again, then all the way up to 200 degrees in the thermosphere?

answers.answer: It's atmospheric stratification. In the troposphere, as you go up vertically, there is a reduction in the quantity of gases within the atmosphere, so there is less absorption of the radiation at the higher levels than at the lower levels. When you get to the top of the troposphere, there's a temperature inversion called the tropopause, then it goes into the stratosphere. In the stratosphere, the principal gases are ozone, which is a powerful greenhouse gas with a high absorption rate of solar radiation, therefore there is an increase in temperature as you go up through the stratosphere. Then there is a layering of those gases, it moves into the next layer which has a different composition again with less properties for absorbing radiation, so it gets colder again. They are just different atmospheres with different gas ratios.

questions.question: Why do you suddenly get an itch in a hard to reach place like between your shoulder blades, especially when you're driving?

Why is it so difficult to predict the exact date that a baby is going to be born? Even if a doctor examines the woman, they still can't say when she's going to go into labor. Apparently 90% of babies are born two weeks either side of their predicted due date. Why with all the science we have cannot we get that exact?

When you play back a recording at a faster speed, voices go up in pitch and you sound like Pinky and Perky or the Smurfs. But if you just speak quickly in real life, it doesn't happen. Why does the pitch change when you press fast forward on a recording?

answers.answer: When you speak or record some sound, you produce a sound wave. If you play that sound wave back over a shorter period of time, you're squeezing it, making the wavelength shorter, and therefore the pitch goes higher. It works in reverse too - if you make the sound wave longer, the pitch goes lower. Think of it like a spring - if you stretch the coils further apart, the pitch is lower, if you push them nearer together, the pitch is higher.

questions.question: If I kick a normal leather football with the inside of my right foot, the ball curves to the left. But if I kick a plastic football exactly the same way, the ball curves to the right. Why?

answers.answer: It must be down to the material - either the lightness of the plastic ball or how it interacts with the boot

The seams on a football play a very important role - they mix the air up and make it turbulent. If you add roughness to a ball (like dimples on a golf ball), it makes the air turbulent and actually sticks to the ball longer, making it fly better. With a smooth plastic ball, the air on the right side of the ball (travelling faster) becomes turbulent while the left side stays laminar. The laminar air pushes the ball towards the turbulent air, creating the opposite curve direction. This is similar to how cricket bowlers smooth one side of the ball to create swing.
answers.qualifications: Worked in sports engineering for 19 years, has a PhD in the area

questions.question: What causes us to slow down as we get older? Christine Harigu went from Olympic champion in 400m in 2008 to not qualifying for the final in 2016. What happened to her body in those eight years?

answers.answer: It's wear and tear - we need new knees, new hips, less fluid in joints so we walk and run more slowly, muscles get stiffer, things just wear out

At the sharp end of sport, the difference between success and failure is pretty small. It could be she ate something bad the night before, or was injured six months earlier and only trained for the last four weeks. Or having won the Olympics once, the fire in the belly isn't burning as bright. The comparison between two moments in time isn't necessarily showing she got slower - if she'd run the Olympic winning race the next day, she might have come last.
answers.qualifications: Former Olympic 400m hurdler, 1984 Los Angeles

questions.question: Why do I get really red face and sweat so much in my face during a run, while my friend Laura doesn't sweat on her face but sweats on her back?
Where is the deepest part of the ocean, and how do they know that? Surely not every nautical mile of the sea has been scoured through.

answers.answer: It's the Mariana Trench, and they know through sonar

It's the Mariana Trench, specifically a part called Challenger Deep, which is 11,000 metres deep. Two American naval officers went there in the 1950s in a bathysphere. To measure the depth, they use explosive ranging - they set up hydrophones (underwater microphones) and set off dynamite to create a pressure wave strong enough to reach the bottom and bounce back, measuring the echo.
answers.qualifications: Chief officer in the Merchant Navy and lecturer in navigation, stability and cargo

questions.question: When did surnames become locked and permanent? In medieval times, John the Miller's son who became a barrel maker might be John the Cooper. At what point did this stop and surnames become inherited rather than based on occupation?

answers.answer: Around the 15th-16th century. The Black Death in 1398 halved the working population, so people left the land and moved to cities. With the growth of mercantilism and shops, people lost that identification with their surname as a profession. When you were living in the town, it became your name rather than your job description. Surnames cross-fertilised back from towns to the countryside. The Doomsday Book only included landowners, not peasants.
answers.qualifications: Professor of English

questions.question: Who would have been the last English monarch whose language we would not understand today? If you lined up all English monarchs and King Charles tried to have a conversation with each one, how far back would he get before he couldn't understand them?
Why do we get liver spots/age spots as we get older?

answers.answer: It's the melanin - pigment cells going into overdrive and just starting to work incorrectly. It happens on hands because they get the most sunlight. UV light triggers it. The more exposure you get, the more likely you are to get them. It's the same thing that creates freckles or gives you a tan, but the pigments producing melanin are just working a bit skew-wiff.

questions.question: When one of my chickens dies, within half an hour it goes into complete rigor mortis like a board. But when I buy a chicken from the supermarket, there's no rigor mortis at all. Why the difference?

answers.answer: Rigor mortis isn't permanent - it sets in and then goes away again. Chickens do go into rigor mortis very quickly. If you came back after a day, it would be soft again. The supermarket chicken has already gone through rigor mortis and come out the other side.

questions.question: Why do we slow down as we get older?

answers.answer: It's because of accumulated DNA damage that your body accumulates over time. Like monks copying the Bible - each monk would make a little mistake and the next monk would copy the mistake. That's happening in every cell in your body all the time as cells divide. Gradually over time, lots of little changes slow down different cells - it reduces hormonal activity. UV light also causes DNA damage which turns pigment cells into rogue cells producing liver spots. Your body is trying to compensate for damage.
answers.qualifications: Degree in medical genetics, dissertation in premature aging (progeria syndrome)

questions.question: Why do we slow down as we get older?

answers.answer: Underlying it all is the genetic mistakes that build up over time, resulting in cumulative loss of motor units - the link between nerves and muscles. As we get older, we have a gradual loss of motor units so muscles become weaker and less powerful. The cardiovascular system weakens over time, reducing delivery of energy and oxygen to those motor units. It's also multifactorial - loss of collagen, loss of elasticity in tendons and muscles, loss of higher brain function in terms of how we control muscles and react to things like the starting pistol. All of that accumulates and results in gradual loss of performance.
answers.qualifications: Undergraduate degree in human biology, anaesthetic consultant

questions.question: Why do pub signs have pictures of things like foxes or dogs?

answers.answer: Back in the day, literacy levels were very low. A pub sign would be a pictogram - if you and I were going to meet at the Black Bull and neither of us could read, you'd need a picture to identify the right pub. When you come across odd pub names, it may be because landlords added things to distinguish themselves from nearby pubs with similar names - for example, the Bell and Crown probably had two bells nearby and the landlord added a crown to distinguish his pub.

questions.question: Why are [toast soldiers] called soldiers?

answers.answer: Toy soldier - rigid sides, stand straight as a soldier, line them all up on the plate
Humpty Dumpty and the Great Fall - depicted by an egg, connected to children eating eggs and soldiers

questions.question: How far does pollution travel?

answers.answer: Pollution can travel miles, clouds travel, if we stopped pollution it would still come here from India. CFC travels from around the world to create holes in the ozone layer over Australia

questions.question: Why do dogs love balls and does it have anything to do with Wimbledon and the Ashes and why humans love balls?
