answers.answer: Prey - nothing in the wild that resembles a stick but ball is like a little bird or rodent, movement activates evolutionary predator instinct

Individual thing. Some is prey driven, some is breed tendencies, some are trained. Texture preference - soft vs hard things. Human factor matters - if you approach a dog assuming they love balls, your excitement affects them. It's about interaction not the ball itself.

questions.question: Are there any animals that purely ate for pleasure, rather than just survival?

answers.answer: Most animals eat more than they need. Truffle pig - must find them delicious. Put fresh salmon next to dry cat food and cat prefers fresh salmon, that's eating for pleasure
Dopamine feedback from eating - you get pleasure from eating so all animals eat for pleasure

questions.question: What causes some people to almost shriek when they sneeze and it makes other people jump? Is it physiological or psychological?

answers.answer: I think it's a little bit performative. I sneeze like an idiot but if I remember in time I can do a muted sneeze. On public transport I don't sneeze like an idiot. Anyone who sneezes very ostentatiously doesn't have to unless they have a need for attention

When you sneeze you're releasing energy from both mouth and nose. Sneezing through both is a more relaxing release, more pleasurable, that's why people do it. And that's why if you're in a situation where you don't want tension you can do it more quietly

questions.question: Why do some foods make you feel sick? Not in the repulsive way but halfway through a slice of cheesecake at a coffee shop I felt absolutely nauseous

answers.answer: Too rich. With cappuccino and cheesecake together there's a lot of dairy. Might also relate to chocolate brands - Galaxy makes you feel nauseous but Dairy Milk doesn't. How much is objective vs subjective, from context to context. If you've just eaten a big meal you can't eat as much cheesecake but could eat your body weight in watermelon

questions.question: How do they measure tennis serve speed? 132 miles per hour. Like a police speed gun bouncing off a car?

answers.answer: I think it's quite straightforward - video it and measure the speed of the ball quickly. Not a complex answer
Same as a police radar gun - gun sends out pulses, pulses hit the ball, come back, measures the time difference, converting the changing frequency of pulses into speed via the Doppler effect

questions.question: Is every piece of popcorn unique, like snowflakes?

answers.answer: It probably is, isn't it? Is every piece of popcorn unique?

questions.question: Do people who create or discover things like DNA and the internet get any recompense from other countries who use those ideas?

answers.answer: The question is can you own a discovery? Tim Berners-Lee could have commoditized the internet if he'd wanted to. DNA once discovered, I don't know how you'd own it. Scientists have the thrill of discovery. You could patent the applications like vaccines. You can't patent work, but you can get recompense

Scientists are very mission driven. They don't want to patent something to necessarily make money. If you go into industry you're more likely to patent and make money. Those who discover and share DNA are mission driven. They get funding from universities and institutes to grow their group and discover more. The rewards are different - it's a category error to apply commercial parameters to scientific discovery

questions.question: Why do the Irish say 'top of the morning'?

answers.answer: Translation - 'top' as synonym for 'best'. In Irish, 'I wish you the best of the morning' translates to 'top of the morning' in English. They don't say top of the afternoon or evening, it's like saying have a great day - a morning greeting

questions.question: What does SPF mean on a bottle of sunscreen? Is it based on something or just a scale?

answers.answer: The factor printed on every sunscreen is a reference to time. Factor 20 means you can stay in the sun 20 times longer before being burnt than with no cream on. They test this on pigs (male pigs called hogs) because pig skin is very similar to human skin. The flaw is that different skin types react differently.

questions.question: Why don't we have solar panels on our electric cars?

answers.answer: Suggested it wouldn't be efficient - you wouldn't get enough energy from a solar panel on a roof to justify the engineering and expense

They have put solar panels on a few electric cars. The problem is you'll only get about seven miles of range per day. They're usually used to power climate control and infotainment. Problems: most people keep cars in garages (no benefit), and if you crash, they're expensive to replace. It's more of a gimmick. Hyundai released one in August 2019 with solar roof to help charge battery.

questions.question: Why do long kitchen knives have sharp points? Is it necessary for safety reasons?

answers.answer: There are two types of knives - Japanese chopping knives/hatchets (sharp edge on one side) and slicing knives (need a fine point to slice). With any knife with a sharp edge, you'll always have a point because you can't have one side with a sharp edge without it meeting at a point. For stabbing, you could use a chopping knife but it would be harder. For slicing, it's a rolling process which naturally brings you to a point. Even a hatchet has a point because otherwise it wouldn't have a sharp edge. If you thrust it horizontally into wood, it wouldn't stick as easily, but with a chopping action it would.

questions.question: How do super injunctions work? If the court that grants the injunction has to keep it secret and contact every media organisation in Britain to say 'do not talk about this', doesn't that defeat the purpose of keeping it secret?
Why does the handrail on escalators sometimes move at a different speed than the steps, particularly at King's Cross?

answers.answer: Explained using analogy of big wheel and little wheel with belts around them - the belt at the bottom attached directly to wheels moves at different speed than the other belt because it's bigger. Suggested escalators with negligible wheel size difference won't show this effect, and it's most noticeable on very long escalators.

answers.caller: Terry from Bournemouth (former apprentice electrician on British Rail)
answers.answer: The belt does travel further because there's a whole gearbox mechanism underneath the ground surface with motors and drives, including cleaning and maintenance access. The belt has to go further round. It's also to do with the measurement from where your feet are (a radius). Could be to do with tension or a slipping clutch mechanism.

Both escalator handrails have a wheel underneath which drives the handrail. Theoretically the handrail should run exactly the same speed as the steps to stop people from slipping forward. When it slips backwards, it's because there's not enough pressure applied - a bank of rollers push the handrail against the wheel, and if it's not tight enough against the wheel, there's not enough pressure, so it slips. The steps run off a sprocket connected to the motor, and there's a chime between the sprocket of the steps and the handrail drive.

questions.question: Why do children see mirages on roads but adults don't? When driving as a child, he saw wet patches on roads that weren't there when he arrived. Now he doesn't see them - is it because he's driving or because he's taller?

answers.answer: Described it as an optical illusion caused by heat from the road affecting light through molecules

answers.caller: Dave from Stamford-le-Hope (mental health support worker, former teacher)
answers.answer: Mirages occur when heat on road surface heats the air around it, causing light to bend - creating a mirror effect. In terms of children seeing them but not adults, it's to do with the brain's capacity and survival instinct to look for danger and threats. A child in a car isn't scanning for threats, whereas a driver or passenger is distracted, especially a driver whose concentration levels are much higher. It's about cognitive distortion.

questions.question: Why do we eat popcorn at the cinema? It makes terrible noises and goes everywhere. Why is it the thing we crave when we go into a cinema?

answers.answer: Suggested historically it was cheap and easy to do, then just caught on as a tradition. Profit margin is absolutely off the charts - costs about 2p to make a giant tub, you pay around £5.95

Popcorn predates cinema - it goes back to travelling circuses and carnivals in America, long before cinema existed. It's very profitable, very transportable when tiny, and doesn't go off. During the Great Depression, cinemas picked it up because it was cheap, portable and imperishable. Compared to potato chips which go off, are heavy to transport, and need oil to make. All you need for popcorn is heat sauce. Mentioned that cinemas don't pop it on site anymore - giant tubes of popcorn are delivered by lorry and then heated up.

questions.question: If you give a dog everything it needs (food, fresh water, big garden with walls), why would it ever run away? It goes against survival instinct

answers.answer: Suggested dogs are fascinated by smells and led by their nose. Smells are like drugs to them - they love it. When a dog gets its nose into something, they're quivering with joy. They don't think 'got my food, got my water, taking it easy'. Their instinct is curiosity, smell, and excitement, not security.

answers.caller: Alan from Faversham (runs doggy daycare service)
answers.answer: The wording of the question was slightly wrong because dogs don't run away - they're not running away from something, they're running FOR something. The owner actually answered his own question because he said 'you give them everything but you don't leave the door open.' So the one thing they haven't been given is the freedom to wander off whenever they want to. Their intention would be to wander back provided they don't get lost.

questions.question: Do any other primates bite their nails as a consequence of stress or anxiety, or is it just humans?

answers.answer: Yes, other primates do bite their nails. It's the same theme as the nail-biting question from earlier.

questions.question: Why do humans bite their nails through stress when other animals don't?

answers.answer: Animals feel stress in the moment (like a gazelle being chased by a lion), but they don't fear the future. Humans are the only ones with perception of death, so we feel anxiety about the future, leading to nail-biting and other stress behaviors like parrots pecking their feathers.

questions.question: Do sheep get sunburned?

answers.answer: Seems highly unlikely since sheep exist in hot countries too, but the wool has been shaved off.

Yes, absolutely. My brother's pet sheep Dolly got sunburned on her forehead and turned purple and scabby. The vet confirmed it was sunburn and they had to apply sun cream daily. Only the muzzle area was protected.

questions.question: Why don't women find baldness attractive, given that it indicates high testosterone levels?
Why do we cry when we're sad or happy?

answers.answer: When you're happy or sad, your brain releases chemicals. These chemicals have to come out through your system, and they exit through your tears. There was a study that analyzed the chemical components of tears and found they differ based on emotional state. It's your body washing out the chemicals - a normal bodily function.

questions.question: What is the significance of throwing a pinch of spilled table salt over your left shoulder?

answers.answer: In cartoons like Tom and Jerry, there's a devil on the left shoulder and an angel on the right. The devil whispers bad ideas. Historically, the devil is perceived as sitting on your left shoulder, so when you spill salt (bad luck), you throw it over your left shoulder to cancel out the bad luck by hitting the devil.

questions.question: Can butterflies and moths crossbreed?

answers.answer: I don't think they can, but you might be right that it's a moth.

No, they cannot crossbreed. They're genetically quite different, though both belong to Lepidoptera (Latin for 'scales on wings'). Moths have about 2,500 species in the UK versus about 60 butterfly species. The genetics would never line up - it's never going to happen. Moths and butterflies use similar mating rituals with pheromones but they're very species specific.

questions.question: What is a monger and why is it only used for fish, iron, war, and scandal? Why don't we have shoe mongers or hair mongers?

answers.answer: Monger comes from Latin and means a trader or dealer in a specific product. Over the years it has narrowed down to specific trades: fishmonger, cheesemonger, ironmonger, costermonger. We probably once had beer mongers and salt mongers, but those terms just didn't survive. When used in war monger or scandal monger, it has a negative connotation, but it's just that some terms survived and others didn't.

questions.question: Are humans the only species that, when sober, suffer from dizziness and balance issues?

answers.answer: This might be a category error - you've only seen animals that can balance. You wouldn't see an elephant on a fence. If you made a dog walk along a fence, the dog would wobble.

Anything over the size of a medium-sized cat would have to have a stabilizing mechanism due to physics. Dogs have a lower center of gravity than humans. Cats smaller than medium-sized are less affected by gravity due to their mass. Larger cats actually struggle more with climbing and fall more frequently. It all comes down to center of mass relative to overall size.

questions.question: Why do cricket players still wear trousers instead of shorts, given cricket is a summer sport?

answers.answer: Three reasons: 1) It gets cold when you're standing around doing nothing (80% of cricket). 2) When you strap pads on, you don't want to catch flesh in the buckles. 3) You need to shine the ball on your trousers.
I'm not convinced - it's ridiculous now.
Back in the day women wore skirts, not trousers. Trousers weren't allowed historically, and that's become tradition.

questions.question: My 94-year-old mother has dementia and every time I take her out and bring her back to the care home she says 'home again home again washington/whittington thou lonely citizen'. What is this from?

answers.answer: I think it's Dick Whittington. It's the bells - after he'd gone to London to make his fortune and was going back to Worcestershire having failed, the bells called to him to come back. 'Home again home again thou lonely citizen' - if anyone can slot those words into the story they go straight to the top of the class.

It's not exactly 'home again home again' but there was a folk song called 'Turn Again Whittington' and in there it says 'turn again though wise is those the wisest men or something dick whittington little mayor of london' - 'thou worthy worthy worthy citizen'. It was around about the 30s, written as a folk song. This would fit with Sally's mum being 94.
[Singing] 'Turn again Whittington, now we're here we're... worthy citizen Lord mayor' - that's it.
[Singing with Greg in round] 'Turn again Whittington' - the same as Greg's.

The song is a 17th/18th century broadside ballad. The full lyrics include 'turn again Whittington thrice mayor of London town and thou worthy citizen' and 'turn again to market, turn again thou worthy citizen'. Sally's 'home again' is mixed up with something else but it's the same song.

questions.question: At what point does a war become a world war?

answers.answer: It may not be a technical threshold. I don't know. Maybe it's the number of countries on each side - the alliances drawn rather than the amount of geography covered. The Roman Empire or Genghis Khan might have conquered more territory than the Nazis but the Nazis were in cahoots with the Japanese and the Italians.

questions.question: Watching a program about the serengeti - carcasses rotting away and lions/tigers eat the meat but don't fall ill, whereas a human would. How does that work?

answers.answer: The obvious answer is they're not humans so they've got completely different digestive systems. They don't eat cooked food, their immune system is already stronger to process the bacteria in raw meat. I suspect it's the same answer - how can animals eat raw meat. They probably don't eat the really rancid stuff, they look for relatively fresh meat.

It's the strength of the acid in the stomach - it's a lot stronger than humans, so strong it'll dissolve bone because it eats raw and rotten meat. I used to sell raw dog food and the manufacturers explained that the acid will dissolve bone so it'll dissolve most things. Dogs have remarkable constitutions.

Dogs don't get hurt because they have stronger stomach acid than humans - they actually produce more. Animals like dogs and primates have the genes to process raw meat. Humans, because for hundreds of thousands of years we've been eating cooked food, have lost those genes. We don't produce as much stomach acid or have the things to break down proteins. We use that energy for our brains because we process food through fire. So we can handle less than animals can.

questions.question: When someone has passed away, why are they referred to as being 'the late'? What exactly are you late for when you're no longer here?

answers.answer: Think of it as 'lately' - 'lately of this parish' meaning they were here not long ago but they're not here now.

questions.question: How can you tell the accuracy of a mirror when you buy one? My daughter's has a mirror we call the 'thin mirror' where everyone looks supermodel-ish, and mine is the 'fat mirror'. In a changing room mirrors were really unflattering. How do you know if a mirror gives an accurate reflection?

answers.answer: I would have asked why do some mirrors make you look thin and other mirrors make you look fat. But I don't know what you're talking about because it's not PC. You'd think if it was possible to create more flattering mirrors you'd fill fitting rooms with them.

It's to do with what's called perspective distortion. To check that the mirror is accurate you need to measure the glass with a very flat edge to make sure there's no deviation from that flatness. When you go to fairgrounds and look in house of horrors with wonky mirrors - if it buckles in the middle (concave) it will give a thinner perspective. Convex makes you look a bit bigger than you really are. If it's cheaper it's more likely to do this. It's not necessarily done deliberately. I'm a photographer and this is similar to what we look out for in perspective distortion on the edges of camera lenses.

questions.question: In Bulgaria people nod for saying no and shake their head to say yes. There's a legend it comes from the Ottoman period 500 years ago - when you had a sword under your chin you don't move your head much. But I'm not completely convinced because Ottomans were everywhere. Why do we nod for yes and shake for no, and why do Bulgarians do it differently?

answers.answer: It can't be because of the Ottomans because then they'd be doing it differently in Turkey and loads of other places. I can't believe it's the second question today that I'm trying to edit and change because I'm more interested in why Bulgarians do it differently.

It's the most stark obvious version of semiotic temporal drift. It started from pre-linguistic society when showing the top of your head became acquiescence - animals still do this. It became transgression from acquiescence/submission to meaning yes. Bulgarians just have a different societal implemented change which is regional. The rest of the world does it because it's a transition from pre-spoken pre-linguistic animalistic behavior.

questions.question: When driving across county borders, the 'Welcome to Dorset/Wiltshire' sign and the 'You are now leaving' sign are never directly opposite each other - there's always a 100-200 meter gap. Why doesn't it make sense?

answers.answer: The answer is probably boring - the sign can't be put anywhere, it has to be put in the best place for the sign, like corners. Or the border might be on an angle that cuts across the road like a hypotenuse of a triangle. You're presuming it gives them those ones. But usually the road is straight. I might have accidentally stumbled into the answer - there's absolutely no reason why a road would be perpendicular to a boundary.

questions.question: In Scotland the little grocery stores that sell alcohol have 'Off Sales' written in the window. Where did that come from? Why 'off sales'?

answers.answer: It's for drinking off the premises. It's as simple as that. There's a pub on the corner of Holland Park and Ladbroke Grove that still has the carving - it may even say 'off sales' rather than 'off licence'. It was a separate part of the pub where you could buy a takeaway. The difference between off sales in Scotland and off licence in England - I do not know.

questions.question: If I walk a mile down a steep hill and then a mile back up, compared to walking two miles on the flat, how much energy would I use? Is it more or less?

answers.answer: 99 percent certain that going up and down a hill uses more energy than staying on the flat.

The physics says one plus one miles equals two miles. The energy is always conserved - you've transferred kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy and then brought it back down again when you walked down the hill. However, our bodies store energy in ATP and consume it no matter what. If you lift a one kilogram barbell and hold it there for a meter, physics says you've expended one joule and that's all you're ever going to expect. But your body says 'I'm having to support this, I need to clinch my muscles, ATP, ATP, ATP' which is why it feels like it takes more energy. In terms of calories/glucose/ATP you probably are converting more energy than on the flat.

questions.question: How do they predict pollen counts? For weather we have satellites, but how do they know about pollen? Does it vary by region or is it the same for the whole country?

answers.answer: It varies according to region. I don't know how they count or predict pollen. I'll try to find out.

You take it for a burqa (sic - likely 'aerosol' or sampling device), trap it on a sticky piece of paper, give it to a palynologist under a polarized microscope and they count the pollen. The more pollen there is, the higher the number. There are loads of these around the country.

questions.question: Why are steps outside and stairs inside? Trafalgar Square has steps, you'd never call them stairs. Also, banisters are inside but handrails are outside.

answers.answer: Staircase is the key. A staircase is fitted into a space between floors - it links vertically stacked levels. Steps are not between two floors, they might go from one level to another in the same building like an atrium. Steps are external/physical entities. You take a step to climb a stair, but steps don't connect stacked floors. If you had a big house with an atrium at a different height than the rest of the room, they'd be steps not stairs. Stairs go above each other, they're stacked.

questions.question: Why does a biscuit soak up hot tea more effectively than tepid or lukewarm tea?

answers.answer: Because there is an exothermic reaction where the heat in the water works on the molecules and atoms within the biscuit. When molecules get hotter, they move faster and absorb more water. The heat causes the molecules in the biscuit to start moving and activating so they soak up liquid more.

Biscuits have a thin patina of sugar. In hot tea, the sugar dissolves very quickly, allowing the tea to reach all the nooks and crannies of the biscuit so it swells up. In cold tea, the sugar takes longer to dissolve, so the reaction is much slower. Also, biscuits have higher fat content (lipophilic) and you need higher temperature for water to make contact with the biscuit. Hotter things cause more molecular vibration, encouraging dissolution.

questions.question: Why do Scots people walk on the right when English people walk on the left?

answers.answer: We walk on the left to keep our sword hand (right hand) free. Napoleon was left-handed so he made his French armies walk on the right. Scotland is visited by many tourists who don't know UK rules and walk on the right. Also, single-track roads and right to roam culture might play a part.

questions.question: How do high-visibility strips work? When you shine light on them, they light up like a Christmas tree - what causes this?

answers.answer: The material has a textured surface with millions of tiny three-sided corner shapes (like cube corners scaled down). When light hits these angles, the ball bounces straight back out the same way it came in - like a reflector on a car or bicycle but in miniature.

questions.question: Why do you need a blanket to fall asleep even when it's really hot and you don't need the warmth?

answers.answer: Multiple reasons: 1) Body temperature drops when we're asleep and the blanket helps regulate it. 2) It regulates moisture and stops skin drying out. 3) It's a sensory thing - feels like being cocooned/hugged. 4) Related to serotonin and melatonin (the sleep hormone our brain releases). 5) It's a routine/habit thing - the brain thinks something is missing without it.

questions.question: How does a tiny spider spin a web across a distance of a metre or more when they can't fly or jump?

answers.answer: The spider climbs high, releases and lowers itself like an abseiler, then waits for wind or generates motion and swings across like a pendulum.

The spider actually spins out a thread and waits for the breeze to blow it. The longer the thread, the better. It's very sticky, gets blown by the breeze, tangles on the other side, and then the spider starts spinning the web from there.

questions.question: Do other mammals go through menopause?

answers.answer: Orcas (killer whales) experience the menopause. The reason it's so rare is because it's about the richness of the culture of their society - they have a lot of knowledge to pass on to their children (like humans spending 18 years raising children). Grandmothers are useful after their breeding time has finished. Natural selection means there's no point having females around once they've lost the ability to breed. Other great apes might also have menopause due to their rich cultures.

questions.question: Why do running/athletic clubs always have 'harriers' at the end - e.g. Queen's Park Harriers, Sheffield Harriers, Kidderminster Harriers?

answers.answer: Hare and Hounds was a game played at school - someone was the hare and everyone else was the hound, like cross-country running with the thrill of the chase. A hound used for chasing hares in real life was called a harrier. Most athletics clubs have origins in long races or cross-country running, ergo the runners were harriers.

questions.question: Why do mosquito bites sometimes start itching again about two weeks after you've had them?

answers.answer: Type 1 hypersensitivity reactions happen immediately with lots of histamine released. But there's also Type 4 hypersensitivity (delayed type hypersensitivity) using the immune system, antibody-mediated by T lymphocytes. This takes much longer to develop and settle. Deborah is getting both reactions - immediate hypersensitivity followed by the delayed one, so two reactions are going on. Antihistamines don't work as well for the Type 4 reaction.

questions.question: Do all flies buzz at A flat, or do different flies buzz at different notes?

answers.answer: They probably don't all buzz at A flat - the size of the insect affects the pitch. A tiny little fly goes high, mosquitoes go really high, and bigger flies have deeper buzzes. Like instruments in an orchestra - small instruments like violins play high and double bass plays low. No reason they should all be the same note.

questions.question: How did prehistoric people cut their toenails before nail clippers were invented?

answers.answer: There were implements that make cutting nails easy. There's quite a strong chance we didn't. They grow to a certain length or you just snap them off when they get really long.

If you're living outdoors, especially without shoes, running around barefoot, there's natural abrasion. The skin on your feet hardens and the nails wear down. You wouldn't need nail clippers. And if they got too long, you could just fold and snap them off or file with a stone.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'salt of the earth' and why do we use it as a compliment?

answers.answer: It's from the Bible, Matthew 5 verse 13. Jesus says to his disciples they need to be the light of the world and the salt of the earth. Salt was indispensable for preserving food. Salt and light - those are the two absolute essentials for humanity. You need to be out there doing the business.

questions.question: Why does memory become so much worse after giving birth? Where does the memory go?
Why do pigeons always finish their cooing with that little short note? Why don't they just carry on?

answers.answer: Pigeons are non-oscines - they're born with their sounds innate and can't learn to vary them. Unlike songbirds (oscines) who can add flourishes and learn new sounds, pigeons and doves are genetically programmed to make only one sound. The five-syllable call is their genetic programming. A dove does a three-note version. They're just announcing to the rest of the bird world 'I am a pigeon, I'm here'. That's it. They can't learn to do anything else.

questions.question: Why doesn't every dog in town come running when I blow my dog whistle?

answers.answer: Not all dogs are whistle trained. When you first blew the whistle, your dogs came over to investigate the noise. If you gave them attention, treats, or praise, they learned to associate that sound with coming to you - classical conditioning. If you made a fuss of random dogs in the park, you'd become the Pied Piper of dogs.

questions.question: Is swimming easier and faster in deep water or shallow water? Craig thinks shallower is faster, his wife thinks deeper is faster.

answers.answer: Deeper water is faster. In shallow water there's more wave feedback and resistance coming back at you. Olympic pools are uniformly three metres deep with no shallow or deep end. If there are walls close to the pool edges, you get feedback off them too. Pools that have water lapping over the edges are easier to swim in because the waves escape.

questions.question: When you're trying to recall a memory, your brain replays the same pattern of neurons that fired at the time. How does the brain know which memory file to pull out? You can't see the file to know which one to pick without pulling it out first.
What is the easiest Guinness World Record to break?

answers.answer: Fancy dress running records. A few years ago Guinness introduced new categories for running half marathons or marathons in different fancy dress. The bar was set very low - about two hours for a half marathon. I ran a half marathon dressed as a charity awareness ribbon in 1 hour 49 minutes and got a world record certificate. I held it for 9 months before someone beat it. There are crazy categories like running a half marathon in handcuffs in 1 hour 20. Guinness keeps inventing new categories because so many records are unbeatable now. You just need to find a category nobody's done before and do it in under the target time.

questions.question: What is the national anthem of England? Why do they sing Jerusalem at the Commonwealth Games instead of God Save the King like at football matches?

answers.answer: Jerusalem is the English national anthem - a poem by William Blake set to music by Hubert Parry. There was apparently a referendum and 52% voted for Jerusalem, with God Save the Queen/King coming second.

questions.question: Why do flights from the west always have to come in over central London to land at Heathrow from the east?

answers.answer: Runways are one-way at Heathrow - unlike airports like Chicago, Heathrow can only accommodate flights from one direction.

It's about wind, not one-way runways. Heathrow has two parallel runways that alternate. Planes take off and land into the wind to increase apparent speed over the wing, giving more lift and more control while reducing thrust needed.

questions.question: Do birds get any better at building their nests over time? Like generationally?
Is there any animal that can see microscopic things?

answers.answer: No, they can't. We see by light reflecting. The lowest wavelength of light we can see, called the diffraction limit, is around 200 nanometers. Anything that size or smaller is too small to reflect light back to our eyes. Even in the best optical microscopes with glass lenses, you can see something a thousand times bigger, but that's still big cells, not bacteria and viruses.

questions.question: Why do Chinatowns and gay villages so often exist next door to each other in big cities?

answers.answer: Two factors: First, immigrants usually pick the cheapest and most run-down areas of the city. So Chinatown usually comes first. Then historically, in the nineties and noughties, using Canal Street in Manchester as an example, the gay community was seen as having lots of money - called the Pink Pound. They regenerate the area because people feel safer there. Then through time it becomes gentrified and everyone uses it. Discrimination was so bad that gay people needed exclusive bars and nightclubs where they wouldn't get victimised, so they went to the same run-down areas that immigrants had colonized for the same reasons.

questions.question: Why do we call it a birthday when it's actually the anniversary of your birthday? You only have one birthday.

answers.answer: There are two Old English words that combined in the Middle English period to create the word 'birth'. So saying 'happy birthday' in Old English was something like 'yestally a birthday to thee'. Culturally, why we wait and celebrate is probably down to high mortality rates among children during the Middle Ages - so you're celebrating almost survival.

questions.question: Why don't I wake myself up with my own snoring, when if someone else made the same noise they'd wake me up?
Is there currently a system that sees data transmission visually? Like seeing the constant data from phones to satellites, GPS signals?

answers.answer: No, you can't see it. Wireless communication is done through infrared, radio waves - forms of light. If I were to shine a torch across your field of vision, not into your eyes but perpendicular, if there was no dust in the way, nothing reflecting that light, you would not perceive that light at all. Same with radio waves - if you had an eye that could detect them and did the same thing, you couldn't see it. You could model it, draw the lines, but you couldn't actually see the data.

questions.question: What do newborn babies dream of?

answers.caller: Gavin in concert in County Durham
answers.answer: Newborns spend about 18 hours a day asleep and half of that time in REM, which correlates closely with dreaming. There are theories that they have zero content because they have no identity yet, but actually there's insight from the conflict right from the beginning: whether to eat or breathe. When first given milk, it's a massive conflict and they have to work out how to do both at once. That's quite stressful. When they wake up stressed and crying between sleep stages, it's probably to do with that stress they've already experienced from the first attempt.

questions.question: How can you have dry eyes but also watery eyes at the same time?

answers.answer: Tears are complicated - they've got different layers: an oily layer, a watery layer, a greasy layer. The reason her eyes water all the time is because she's lacking the oily layer. So the actual surface of the eye, the cornea and conjunctiva, is not being sufficiently protected. It feels dry, which is why she's producing too many thin watery tears when what she needs is the more viscous, greasy layer to protect it.

questions.question: When a sign says you're 150 miles from London, whereabouts in London is that measured from?

answers.answer: Charing Cross - the cross outside Charing Cross station. That's where they measure all distances from.

Actually it's the statue of Charles I right in front of Trafalgar Square, which looks down towards Parliament. That's where all the road markings count to. The original Charing Cross was there, with a small plaque marking the official centre of London. You're about 200 metres out with Charing Cross.

questions.question: Why do people with Tourette's often deploy naughty words during their tics as opposed to non-naughty words?

answers.answer: Most tics are physical, not vocal. Of vocal tics, a very small percentage come out as swearing. TV shows highlight the swearing because it makes better TV - blinking or pushing fingers together doesn't make compelling viewing. There may be some truth that the brain seeks out shocking words, but it's actually quite rare. Even if verbal tics are present, they're usually not swear words.

questions.question: Can a dog (Bertie) smell a specific breed of dog? Bertie is blind but goes crazy around French Bulldogs and nothing else.
Why can we not resist the temptation to keep going back to a place we've already checked when we've lost something?

Why do Europeans, i.e. Italians, Spanish, Portuguese, have such an affinity with coffee? As in like espresso? As in their love of it, as in almost their ownership of it. And why did the UK bypass European cafe culture?

answers.answer: The cafe culture is an offshoot of the product itself. Coffee is a tropical crop brought back as a backhaul cargo by the trading states - Spanish, Portuguese, Italian - to fill up their holds. It was popular in the UK too. But when the British Empire expanded east and got the India trade and China trade, we used to bring a huge amount of tea back with us. So we didn't have as big a presence in the New World. We were Eastern traders and brought tea instead of coffee. The coffee houses got squeezed out and that supply, access, and provenance made a difference. It meant all the effort went into flogging tea instead of coffee. What brought it back is tropical tree plantation crops moving around by colonial trading - like coffee started in one place and is now grown extensively elsewhere. The climate in Europe gives them the cafe trade that we don't really have here, where everyone gets up very early, go to bed in the middle of the day, and stay up very late. In Italy now, it's illegal to charge more than a certain amount for an espresso.

questions.question: Was there a designated survivor for the coronation? If the worst had happened and the whole royal family was in the abbey, would there have been someone hidden away back at the palace to take over?

answers.answer: There is no designated survivor at all. But there is a line of succession, and the next in line would be Archie. Since he is only four, Meghan would probably be the mother regent who would reign in for her son until he was of age.

questions.question: When you have a glass of still water and it's left out for a while, it starts to form bubbles. What causes that?

answers.answer: Water has gases dissolved in it - oxygen, carbon dioxide - much the same way as you could dissolve salt or sugar. The weird thing about gases is that they do the opposite to salt and sugar in that they're more soluble when the water's cold. So as the water heats up, because it's come out the tap or out the fridge, the gases start coming out of the water and you can see them as bubbles.

questions.question: Why do they have ashtrays in the toilets of modern airplanes when smoking's been banned on planes for at least 25 years?

answers.answer: People will still smoke even though they're not supposed to, and it's much safer to put it in an ashtray than it is to put it down the toilet because the toilet will melt.

It's only illegal to smoke on an aeroplane if you're on a public transport flight - a commercial flight. To sell tickets, an airline has to be operating under an AOC (Air Operator Certificate), and one of those regulations is you can't smoke on a public transport flight. However, if you're rich enough to buy your own aeroplane, you can smoke on it. The toilets are effectively fitted to the aircraft - they're a standard fit - so you have to have ashtrays because if you were rich enough to buy your own 737, you could smoke on it.

questions.question: Why is it that when you get into a bath that's just a little bit too hot, you want to have a wee? Even if you don't want to have a wee before your bath, you want to have a wee.

Why do surnames not reflect sea-based professions? We have lots of surnames that reflect historical land-based professions - cartwright, cooper, etc. But we don't have names for people who catch fish, make nets, repair lines, gut fish, sell fish. We have butcher but not fishmonger. Why do they reflect land-based professions and not maritime ones?

answers.answer: List of maritime surnames: Fisher, Mariner, Seaman, Shipman, Boatman, Sturgeon, Salmon, Haddock, Purser, Chandler, Waterman. Also: Carrie Fisher, Dennis Waterman, Peter Hook, Michael Fish.
Fisher is a huge name. There are also: netmakers, cooper (make barrels that go on ships).

questions.question: What makes us, with some things, go back to things that we know are terrible? I ran the London Marathon and it's awful, I hate marathons, I always say never again. Yet two days later I'm signing up to another one. I even hold the world record for the fastest marathon dressed as Mr. Potato Head.

answers.answer: The answer is how good you feel when you finish - that sense of satisfaction is like nothing else. It could be endorphins.

questions.question: During the King's coronation, I noticed there's a distinctly different drum sound between the English military retinues and the Scottish military retinues. The Scots sound as though they've got a much deader, less percussive drum sound. The English seem to have a much more percussive drum sound. I wonder why this is. Is it a tradition?

answers.answer: In the latter half of the 20th century, it became a trend for the pipers to tune the bagpipe to a higher and higher pitch. In order to complement that, the drummers would crank their drums down even tighter. It came to a point when the drums could no longer cope with that tension. In the late 70s and 80s, they started to use drum heads made of Kevlar, and they had differently designed drums with extra bolts to take that higher tension. The pipe band snare drum is usually tuned to a much tighter pitch, and the drum is designed to take that higher tension. It also enables the drummer to get more clarity and play far more intricate drum scores. Scottish regiments traditionally all have their own pipe bands while English regiments are more likely to have brass bands. So the Scottish drums are tighter.

questions.question: You can look inward with your eyes toward your nose (cross-eyed). Why can't you do the same outwardly? Why can't you push your eyes out wide?

answers.answer: We don't have the muscles in our eyes to do it. Some people can move one eye to the left while keeping one straight, but we can't go wide. There's no real evolutionary need for it because we have pretty decent peripheral vision. You can focus on the end of your nose because there's a point for focus to pull your eyes to - there's a design purpose for that. But there's no purpose to going outward - it would just create a weird blur with no focal point. It's like being double-jointed - there's no purpose to it.

questions.question: Why does nobody make mouse-flavoured cat food?

answers.answer: Whiskers tried to introduce a mouse-flavoured cat food, but unfortunately the cat responsible for catching the mice kept eating them and was sacked for gross misconduct.

There's actually mouse-flavoured cat food made in Germany that says '100% mouse' on the tin. However, cats don't really like it. When cats eat mice in the wild, they eat all the internal organs, heart, liver and little bones. But cats turned their noses up at the German mouse-flavoured food - it's expensive at £4 a tin and cats just walk away from it.

questions.question: How is it possible to identify whether someone is black or Asian just from hearing them talk on the radio, even when everyone was born and raised in the same environment?

answers.answer: It's about linguistic rhythms learned from parents. If parents have strong accents, it gets diluted by exposure to other accents from friends, school and family. Someone listening can make a broader guess about where someone's from based on these diluted patterns.

It's code switching. People from South Asian backgrounds often grow up in extended families with grandparents who learned English with an Indian accent. This creates different tones and nuances - heavier sounds in Ds and Gs. People who share similar backgrounds can hear these differences immediately because it sounds so familiar. It's a form of sonic osmosis - absorbing and repeating without conscious awareness.

Voice is also dependent on how your mouth is sized and shaped. A black person or Asian person has different physiology - different mouth cavity size, teeth size and arrangement, and possibly skull resonances. This contributes to being able to distinguish voices.

questions.question: How do the French take the rise out of the English? Do they do it in French with a weird pseudo-English accent, or do they do it in English with a French accent?

answers.answer: The French might be more mature than us and not feel the need to poke fun at the fact we speak differently. It could be another example of English exceptionalism.

The French do absolutely take the mickey out of the English, but probably less often than the English do with the French. When they do it, it's not particularly Cockney - it's just a standard British person trying to speak French but exaggerated. It's pretty much the same as what we do, just slightly the other way around, but not as often because the French are probably not as culturally fragile as we are.

questions.question: If puppies are separated from their mother and siblings at eight weeks, would they recognize them if they bumped into each other later?

answers.answer: There have been scientific studies on this. Dogs routinely sniff the bottoms of complete strangers, so the question is how would they demonstrate recognition of a parent?

Yes, dogs can recognize their mothers. I know from experience - my poodle Poppy lived 100 miles from her mum and after six months, when we did a reunion, she recognized her mum absolutely instantly. She ran up to her, licked her, cried and whimpered and jumped up and down. We've met the breeders and her mum twice again on beaches and she made a beeline for them each time. There have been studies showing dogs retain their smell and understand their mum's bark for years. Siblings - she recognized them in a playful way at six months, but that could just have been playing with any poodle. The smell may be different by the time they're older. But her mum - she was over the moon every time.

questions.question: Which of our internal organs are able to feel pain?

answers.answer: A kidney stone is in the middle of the kidney and causes tremendous pain, so that can't just be surrounding muscles. Different organs likely have different answers.

As a palliative care nurse, some organs don't have many nociceptors (pain receptors). However, any area can have pain if it has inflammation because the body creates chemicals like prostaglandins that create pain. Even the brain, though it has fewer pain receptors, if it became inflamed, it would still hurt because of inflammatory chemicals being released regardless of the receptors. Also, brain surgery patients are under conscious sedation with sedatives and pain relief, so they're not completely in pain even though they're awake. The skin is an organ and it has a lot of nociceptors, which is why it hurts so much.

questions.question: What gives England the right to sing God Save the Queen as the national anthem when playing sport, while Scotland has Flower of Scotland and other nations have their own anthems?

answers.answer: It's Big Brother syndrome - England is the biggest part of the union so they just have the national anthem. The anthem has an anti-Scottish verse that has been dropped but was still there when singing started. The other home nations have adopted the English national anthem.

England doesn't have dibs on God Save the Queen - Northern Ireland also sings it. When England played Northern Ireland in qualifiers last year (women's football), only God Save the Queen was played. At the Commonwealth Games, England sings Jerusalem, not God Save the Queen - probably because all home nations compete there. At rugby, Ireland plays as one united team so there's no division. For Scotland and Wales at football, they have their own anthems. If Scotland or Wales wanted to sing God Save the Queen at rugby, they'd have as much right as England, so you'd either get both singing it or neither.

questions.question: What is the smallest type of animal that an average high street vet will work on?

answers.answer: Vets can probably have a crack at anything if you're paying. There will be arachnid specialist vets. You could turn up with a ladybird and ask them to splint its leg. It might not be definitive but we'll find out.

questions.question: What is the legal requirement for knowing where things are made? Why do products have 'Made in Italy', 'Made in China' labels?

answers.answer: It's for trade agreements, customs duties, tariffs and friction. If there's a free trade agreement, goods move cleanly. If not, there are costs. It's not for the consumer.

Products are labelled with origin for trade preference - where you have a trade agreement with other nations under WTO rules. If you have an agreement in place, the label identifies origin and allows goods in free of duty (you still pay VAT). If you don't have an agreement, you pay the full duty rate, making products more expensive. Even if goods pass through Germany or France from China, they still have to provide origin because current agreements only allow European origin goods in duty-free.

questions.question: Can drum patterns be copyrighted?

answers.answer: No, you can't copyright a drum beat in the same way that you can a melody or a song progression or lyrics. James Brown's 'Funky Drummer' beat by Clyde Stubblefield has been sampled millions of times with no royalties involved. Drumming is a combination of single strokes and double strokes with human variations, making it very difficult to play identically.

questions.question: What is stamina? And how does it make me run around like a headless chicken when I'm older?

answers.answer: As you get older, your heart and lungs get worse at delivering blood and oxygen around your body. When you do exercise, lactic acid builds up in your cells. Lactic acid causes pain and also causes your muscles to stiffen up and seize up. Oxygen is what your body uses to remove lactic acid. The more exercise you do, the slower that process of decline will be.

questions.question: Where did the word 'nickname' come from? What does it mean?

answers.answer: It comes from Old English. The Old English word 'eek', which was spelt e-k-e, means 'also' or 'other'. So it's your other name. As it's been corrupted over the years, it's turned from an 'eek name' to a 'nick name'. This is why people like Charles the Bold or William the Conqueror had 'eek names' - they were their other names.

questions.question: When is a bridge a tunnel?

answers.answer: Never. A tunnel and a bridge are both verbs as well as nouns. If you punch a hole through a hill, it's a tunnel. If you span something, it's a bridge. Nothing has been bridged if something has been tunnelled. You have to have been tunnelled to be a tunnel and bridged to be a bridge.

questions.question: Why do we spell it M-O-M (Mum) in the Midlands?
Why does lemonade seem fizzier than any other carbonated drink?
Why do we have different spice tolerances?

answers.answer: You've got TRPV receptors in your mouth. The more receptors you have, the more sensitive you are to spicy food. If you really like spicy food, it's not a question of liking it or not liking it - it's a question of how much pain you're in when you eat it. If you've not got many receptors, you will have a very different physical experience from someone with lots of receptors.

They're called TRPV1 receptors - thermoreceptors. Chilies make you more sensitive to your body's own heat, and things like menthol and mint have the opposite effect - they de-sensitise them. It's probably about greater or lesser number of receptors per square millimetre. Birds don't have thermoreceptors in their beaks, which is why birds will eat chilies but mammals won't - the plants want their seeds dispersed by birds whose digestive systems allow germination far away from the parent plant.

questions.question: Why does the saying 'the chickens are coming home to roost' have such a bad connotation? If you have chickens, you'd want them home safely.
Why do some people dream in black and white and some in colour?
How did ancient people measure time? If you remove the birth of Christ from the equation, what year was it when people like Pythagoras were doing their stuff?

answers.answer: The Romans officially counted from the date when they thought Rome was founded - 753 BCE. They called it Ab Urbe Condita (from the founding of the city), but they didn't use that system much. Instead they named each year by the two people who were consuls in that year. In Greece, each state had its own system - if you went from Athens to Crete you could be changing years completely. Some people counted by the Olympiads, the four-year period to the Olympic Games. In Assyria there was the Limu list, a list of leading magistrates.

questions.question: Why does my gold necklace only burn me when it comes away from my skin and then returns to it in the sauna?

answers.answer: When the pendant is touching your skin, it's heating up gently and dissipating into your skin so you don't notice. When it comes away from your skin, your skin cools down a bit. When it swings back onto your skin, you notice it a lot more because it's at sauna temperature and your skin has cooled. If you leave it there, it stops burning because the heat starts dissipating again - like the frog boiling analogy where gradual change isn't noticed.

Gold has very high electrical and thermal conductivity. When it's in contact with your skin, the outside of the jewellery will be at sauna temperature and the inside will be at skin temperature, driving heat through it into your skin but remaining at skin temperature or some equilibrium between sauna and skin temperature. If it moves away from the skin, it then heats up to sauna temperature. When it swings back onto the skin, it's hotter than the skin is, so it will burn.

questions.question: I have two passports, a British passport and an Irish passport. If I leave the UK on a package tour, they ask me to give details of one passport and use it. Can I leave the UK on one and return on the other?

answers.answer: It's going to depend where you're going because if you're going into continental Europe (apart from Ireland) they need to keep count of your 90 days. If you go in on the Irish passport they won't bother counting because by dint of having an Irish passport you can spend as long as you want in the European Union. There's no reason to return on a British passport and no great benefit to doing it.

You can definitely use one passport to go out and come back on another. I work in corporate business travel for 30 years. There are circumstances where you might get pulled over for doing it - if they keep count of your days in a certain territory. It's very popular in corporate travel. For instance, if you had Australian and UK dual nationalities and were flying to Australia, you'd use your Australian passport going out because you don't need a visa, and then come back on your UK one because customs would be quicker. With the Anglo-Irish agreement, it doesn't matter which you use.

questions.question: Why are there so many pubs in little villages with tiny populations?

answers.answer: You need to stop thinking of a pub in the modern sense and think of it as a house where one room was given over to selling ale. It was commonplace, it was homes, houses where there would be one room given over to selling ale that was usually brewed on the premises. If you think of it in those terms, you'd only need seven or eight customers.

The farm I work at is 500 acres. In years gone by, there would have been hundreds of people working on this farm instead of just me. They would all have wanted a drink, there would have been no TV at home, no entertainment at home. You only got straight down the pub. Added to the fact that pubs would have been houses with one room where you could drink beer, that's why there would be so many of them.

questions.question: Why when you take off and land do you have to put your seat arms down?

answers.answer: If you jar on landing and have a really bad landing, you're going to be thrust into your upturned arm. The upturned arm goes behind you but you've been shoved sideways. If your arm is up and it's an unlikely angle, you're massively increasing the chance of you being impaled upon your own seat arm.

questions.question: Why do snooker players twitch their middle finger before playing a shot?

answers.answer: I think it's like sticking your tongue out when you're threading a needle - drawing your attention, focusing your attention down to the tip of the cue area. It's not that anyone's copied, it's reflexive and some do it and some don't in the same way some people stick their tongue out when threading a needle because it helps them concentrate.

It's for tempo. Some players will count to six, five, four, whatever the number is, and it's done so they don't snatch at the shot. They pull the cue back and forward when they're doing it - it's a warm up, concentration, it calms them down. It's very deliberate.

questions.question: Why is it that most of the time the wind comes in gusts rather than a continuous flow of air?

answers.answer: When you're flying and doing navigation, anything above 2,000 feet the wind is constant. You take the wind as constant above that altitude. Anything below 2,000 feet is being affected by the friction of stuff on the earth - buildings, houses, mountains, trees, hills. The lower you come, the more obstacles it has to steer around and therefore it hits you in a gusty fashion. That's why when you come into land, especially in a slower airplane like a light aircraft, the approach is bumpier than the flight.

questions.question: At what age or what point in a lamb or sheep's life do they lose their bounce?
If camera lenses are round, why are photographs square?

answers.answer: It has everything to do with the light distribution to the sensor. For the light to hit the sensor evenly, the distance from the edge of the lens to the sensor must be equal distance. A round lens achieves this - the edge to the centre of the circle is equal distance. With a rectangular lens, the distance from the edge to the sensor is not equal distance, which would cause vignetting. You need very high quality glass lenses to eliminate the vignetting, which is why some lenses cost thousands of pounds.

questions.question: Why is it the year 2080 in Nepal?

answers.answer: It's the Nepalese New Year or the Nepalese year. Their calendar is based from the reign of a king called Vikram Samrat. He's a sort of King Arthur-ish, Buddhist-type figure. They measure from him - it's religious stroke royal.

questions.question: Why do we grab people by the ankles and wrists and throw them up in the air for their birthday bumps?

answers.answer: It's just a mode of counting - doing one bump for each year. I think it started in Scotland, oddly, and it may have been called 'the dumps' at one point rather than the bumps. It's more fun than just counting candles.

questions.question: Why do Americans call petty theft 'petit' with a T, P-E-T-I-T, spelling it the French way?

answers.answer: It comes from the French - we have anglicised the spelling and they haven't. There was French influence on American jurisprudence. 'Petty' is an anglicisation of the French word for 'little' because it means the theft of something of low value, whether you're in America or the UK.

questions.question: Why do you wake up when someone says your name while you're asleep?

answers.answer: It's Trousman's theory of attenuated attention. The idea is that our ears are listening all the time but a bit of our brain switches it off for obvious reasons. But if something triggers that - like your name or perhaps your occupation - it's a bit of a shock, it switches it back on and you become attentive. It's also known as the cocktail party phenomenon, where you're in a crowd and suddenly something gets your attention.

questions.question: How do Five Guys peanuts get salty inside their shells?

answers.answer: They're soaked in brine before they're roasted. So therefore the salt penetrates through the shell during that process.

questions.question: Does the first crane on the site get assembled without something to support it, and equally at the other end when it's dropped and finished?

answers.answer: I think that the first crane is on wheels. And that starts building the bigger crane. But I can't remember fully.

The initial crane installation will be carried out by a telescopic mobile crane which will turn up on site with a gang and they will put the tower crane up in sections. You do get some self-erecting tower cranes, the smaller ones. They come on the back of a lorry, and they erect themselves. The tower cranes are long-term hires. They're much cheaper than hiring a mobile crane. Often you'll find, especially in things like skyscrapers, the tower will be inside the building, so they'll use the first tower crane to then erect a taller one.

questions.question: Why are there two different types of heads on a screw? A flathead and a Phillips or a posi screw head? Why don't we unify it to one?

answers.answer: The Phillips is better. You get more purchase on a Phillips than you do on a flathead one. Aesthetics? The line looks nice on some woodwork.

Years ago, they used to make screws with a straight slot known as a slotted screw. Different types of screw have different heads. The manufacturing is different - when they make screws by the billion, it's done on a very fast machine. If you're working in an old Victorian house and putting brass hinges on a lovely oak door, you wouldn't dream of using a posi screw on it - it would look wrong. A slotted screw doesn't work in a drill driver. Whereas all the other screws - Phillips, posi, or Torx - work with a drill driver. The Torx ones are much tighter than Phillips, that's why some appliances use them to stop people mucking about with their tumble dryer. It's tradition and aesthetics really.

questions.question: Are homophones and homographs exclusive to the English language?

answers.answer: It's not exclusive to English. English has a lot more of this than many languages because it has a big vocabulary taken from lots of different other languages and it's lost most of its grammatical endings. For example, in French there are words spelled differently but pronounced the same because of silent letters - 'sept' meaning seven and 'cette' meaning this. In German, words like 'schienen' (to shine) and 'schauen' (to see). In Chinese, where characters represent words not sounds, there are many homophones. You also get homonyms - words spelled and pronounced the same but with no connection, like 'bank' (financial institution) and 'bank' (edge of river). Words can have opposite meanings in the same form - 'let' meaning to allow but also meaning to hinder (as in 'without let or hindrance').

questions.question: When you start a series of anything, movie-wise, why is the first episode always called Pilot?

answers.answer: It's the one they made in the hope of getting a commission. It's like a prototype. Pilot, like in a river, the pilot would go in front of the barge and steer the boat into a dock.

When you make a television program, you have to work out technically how to make it because everyone is different. You have to get the artists to understand where they are and how to move and speak. You're also looking to see how the script works so you can make changes before going into making the series. You want to test it on the audience to make sure it's doing the job it's supposed to do. The reason it's called a pilot is exactly as it is with a pilot going down the Mersey - they negotiate the way, going up and down the river.

questions.caller: Craig from Lawrence Cook in Aberdeenshire
questions.question: Why are shampoo bottles generally larger than conditioner bottles when you use more conditioner compared to shampoo?

answers.answer: You're supposed to shampoo your hair twice before you condition. That would mean you go through shampoo twice as quickly.

People misuse conditioner and use too much of it. Conditioner doesn't have foaming agents or sulfates, so it doesn't bubble up and you don't feel you've got enough on. But it is actually doing its job. You're technically correct that you should shampoo the roots and condition the mid-lengths and ends. In theory, if you're using shampoo twice on roots and a 10p piece size of conditioner on mid-lengths and ends, you should get roughly the same time. The bigger bottle is more of a retailing angle - if you make everything exactly the same times, people often complain they can't see the conditioner word on a bottle so they don't reach for the wrong one in the shower. Conditioner masks also go off quicker so they have more preservatives.

questions.question: Who decides what clothes are in fashion?

answers.answer: No one decides. It's cyclical. You've got haute couture at the top of the pyramid influencing diffusion lines, which influences what's in shops. You've got subcultures starting off with trends that then get taken up by the mainstream. It's a combination of commercial and organic. It's a form of osmosis in that you see someone else wearing something and absorb the desire.

The cycle is majorly based on rebellion - children tend to dress opposite to how their parents dressed. Celebrities and influencers set trends leveraging the idea that if you wear what they're wearing, you're cool - it's identity building. Subcultures are about group affiliation - proving you're a member of a group rather than being cool. The biggest influence now that wasn't covered is trend forecasting agencies. Because production of a collection takes around a year or two, brands rely on consultancies to tell them what's going to be in fashion in two years. The trend forecasting agencies run a self-fulfilling prophecy - they all say the same thing, then brands produce it. When it goes wrong it's a very costly error, which is why fast fashion exists to turn things around quickly.

questions.question: Why does my appendix scar hurt when the weather's about to change?

answers.answer: There might be a bit of a chicken and egg problem - it might be hurting for completely different reasons but then the weather changes and you've just linked it in your mind. It might just come and go and you only remember the times when weather follows. Kyle insists he's right though.

questions.question: Why do TV programs and films put copyright dates in Roman numerals at the end of credits?

answers.answer: The general consensus is so that, apart from clever clogs like you, most people can't work out how old the program is. It camouflages the fact that they're putting on old stuff. Everyone likes to think they're watching something new. The same tape will be used in 20 years time so no one can tell it's 20 years old.

questions.question: Why is it called chicken pox?

answers.answer: There's no definitive answer. One theory is that the scars look like little chickpeas. Another theory is that it looks like a chicken has pecked you. The kids prefer that one.

questions.question: Is there a medical reason why I get really ill for about five days when I go on holiday from my desk-based job? When I relax, it seems to let the bad in. Is there any medical reason for that?
When people were digging for coal or iron ore, how on earth did they know that what they were looking for was there?

answers.answer: Some of it makes its way to the surface and that's when you start digging. Especially with diamonds, you find a diamond somewhere and then you dig. If there's gold coming down a river, you'd probably go back to the hill that the river started and dig into that hill. They weren't deep to start with - they'd have found coal and then carried on digging looking for the seam.

There's something called the Order of the Strata put together by William Smith. He recognised that there was some sort of sequence - for example, if you find sandstone, then you might find limestone, and above that you might get mudstone, and then above that you might get coal. He recognised that too. The sequence of rocks repeats itself over time and you can fix these in time using the included fossils. So you know where you are in time and then you can figure out where you are in space. It's a great predictive tool. If you know the geology of a particular area, you can pretty much guarantee where you're going to find the coal. You go out and do some mapping and see where the rocks might be folded or where they're flat, follow these layers as they go up and down and cite your test drilling rigs accordingly.

questions.question: Why is handwriting going worse? In the Victorian times, everyone had good handwriting and everyone was taught the same. But nowadays, it seems those in the past have better handwriting than us right now.

answers.answer: In Victorian times, there was the practice of uniformity where all children who were lucky enough to go to school would have been encouraged to write copy. It was very much a mark of moral rectitude - tidy hand, tidy minded - with strict uniform and rigorous discipline. That would have been the bedrock of tidy handwriting that stayed even as it became less formal over the decades. By the 60s and 70s, everyone was relaxing a bit. Then along came keyboards, not so much typewriters as computers and smartphones, and you just don't do it anymore. That's the final nail in the coffin of general tidy handwriting.

questions.question: Why do I take my reading glasses off to hear better on the phone? Also, I close my eyes when somebody passes me a spoon - to check if a dish has the right amount of seasoning. Is it that our senses work better individually rather than in collaboration, or am I just odd?

answers.answer: I'm gradually going blind over the past 18 months. My hearing has heightened somewhere between 25 and 50 percent since I started losing my vision. I've got something called optic neuropathy which means my eyes aren't sending the right messages to the brain properly. I think it's something to do with the brain remapping - parts of the brain possibly recalibrating. I could give examples but I'd be here forever. It's a clinical study of one.

questions.question: Who decides at what age a person should be flagged as vulnerable on their bank account? I am 90 but my marbles are still here. For the last three months I've had difficulty accessing various things and things were terminated. I wasn't told. Why is there some rule that they have to put that on your account?

answers.answer: It's just one of the protected characteristics that the FCA deems as potentially vulnerable. Protected characteristics cover a multitude of sins. Someone who is maybe 18 beginning their financial life could be vulnerable. Anyone over the age of 75 may be deemed vulnerable, and after 85 additional measures kick in. Vulnerable to what? People at certain ages or generations may have been used to people knocking on their door offering to do windows or fix gutters, and they'd go ahead. They might then go to the bank to withdraw a large amount of cash for paying. It's putting in place a safeguard to ensure people... without telling them. The suddenness of the designation may have been triggered by a particular transaction - for example, a larger amount being transferred to a new payee or drawing money out in cash. It falls somewhat into the generational element. The bank should probably have told her but it's nothing for her to worry about - quite the opposite in fact.

questions.question: Why have the stone walls surrounding sheep flocks in Yorkshire got higher? They put wire deer fencing on top of the walls by maybe another foot or two, with stakes at a diagonal. So have the sheep got higher or have the walls got smaller?

answers.answer: Probably the walls have collapsed and the stones were taken away to make other walls. The ground builds up over time. The sheep's breed has probably changed too.

The ground over time builds up with muck and grasses and things like that - that's what I meant by the walls getting smaller. Also these days the sheep are actually bred bigger and more muscular so they can hop over the walls. An upland hill sheep is far more likely to get over a wall. The walls get smaller as the ground rises and the sheep get friskier as a consequence of being selectively bred. It's a lot cheaper to put a metal fence on top of a dry stone wall than to get a dry stone wall builder to come around and do it.

In the Howarth area they put long poles up with barbed wire on the top of walls for cattle, not for sheep. Cattle are nosy and they like to rub their necks on walls. They put their head over the walls and pull the top stones off, so you put a long pole with some barbed wire on the top to prevent this.

questions.question: When you go to a petrol station and fill up, if you add in say 5p extra, is there any point? Are you actually getting that much? How accurate is it? If you turn the nozzle upside down a little bit, will it drip out?

answers.answer: Petrol pumps are mechanical, so the meters are mechanical meters. They don't run perfectly. You'll see a sign on the petrol pump - Minimum delivery two liters. That's because up to the first two liters, the meter is sort of getting into its stride. But after that, it's evened up and running smoothly and you should be okay. Once they get past the first couple of liters, they run pretty smoothly after that.

questions.question: How do pine cones know when it's going to rain?

answers.answer: They respond to humidity. The fibres in the wood expand when it's humid and as it expands the pine cone opens. When it dries the pine cone closes again. So they start opening when there's moisture in the air, before it actually rains. That's better than the weatherman.

questions.question: What happens to a person's assets if they're sentenced to long-term imprisonment? If you have a five-million-pound house and all the bits and pieces, and there's no one else to look after it, does it go to rack and ruin or do you have to make arrangements?
Why do people get ill when they go abroad?

answers.answer: It's quite simple. It's not the water so much. It's the ice they drink. You have a drink with ice in it and what you're not used to in your own country is how it's treated. It's about susceptibility - one member of the family gets poorly and other members don't. It's about how the water's treated. I have a PhD in biochemistry and biochemical analysis and used to work for Pfizer's.

questions.question: What was the first ever film to have a recognisable soundtrack where you could buy songs, not incidental music?

answers.answer: The Graduate is the first film to contain songs that were not sung by characters in the film. The first commercially released soundtrack was Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, but that had characters singing.
The Graduate is the answer to Alan's question about the first film soundtrack with songs not performed by characters in the film.

questions.question: Why are there more potholes on country roads than A roads and motorways?

answers.answer: The classification is the volume of traffic the road takes. The busier the road, the more effort and money invested in maintaining it to a better condition. They fix potholes overnight when it's quieter.

questions.question: Why and who decided white sticks should be white? Does white register more effectively?

answers.answer: White is most reflective to light so it can be seen from a greater distance. Other colours like blue, green, or red could be confused with each other.

James Biggs allegedly invented the white cane in about 1921. He was an artist who lost his sight and could no longer work. He was concerned about traffic and painted his walking stick white so traffic could see him better.

questions.question: Why do pirates say 'shiver me timbers'?

answers.answer: Timbers are the wooden planks of the ship. When there's a storm and the ship is getting battered, the timbers start shaking. Pirates would be scared, so 'shiver me timbers' means literally my timbers are shivering and I'm scared because of it.

It's about shock rather than fear - 'knock me down with a feather' means surprise/shock. The word 'shiver' in the context of splitting wood means to strike it hard and watch it move before it splits. It later became associated with the involuntary skin movement meaning cold or fear.

questions.question: What is the oldest recorded joke?
Is brain freeze medically bad for you?

answers.answer: It's really just your blood vessels constricting, which sends a message to your brain - it's a neurological response to pain. They constrict and then open again. There's no lasting damage or change, no damage whatsoever.

questions.question: Why do babies blink so much less than adults, and why do we blink more as we grow older?

answers.answer: The front of the eyeball (cornea) is very sensitive and needs to be covered by a layer of tears all the time. Every blink squeegees tears over the eye which then evaporate, causing you to blink again. As you get older, the chemistry changes and adults have thinner tear films than children, so adults need to blink more frequently to keep eyes lubricated.

questions.question: Why do scabs itch from an evolutionary perspective?

answers.answer: Itching has evolutionary benefit - you spot an insect crawling on you and remove it before it can bite and infect you with malaria. The sensitivity of your skin is worth the price of an itchy scab.

When healing, there's higher blood flow and more inflammatory markers including histamine, which makes the area itchy. Histamine is more of a warning shot that something's wrong, isolated to that area. The production of histamine in other contexts (like allergic reactions) is an evolutionary positive, but in scabs it's actually bad because it makes you more likely to scratch.

questions.question: Why do we say an alarm 'goes off' when it turns on?
