answers.answer: It's linked to an explosive - a bomb goes off. It releases. But that answer wasn't very satisfactory.

For alarms, we set them as an output. They are on all the time - even when you're not hearing noise, the alarm is on (primed). So when something happens, it goes off - it releases. You turn the alarm on when you leave the house, but it's not making noise because it's primed. Then it goes off when triggered.

questions.question: Where does the term 'a barrel of laughs' originate?
Do farm animals have friends?

answers.answer: Has three pet chickens. Two raised from chicks go everywhere together. If one is picked up, the other follows. If one doesn't know where the other is, they will start calling for each other, and when they find each other, they run to each other. They're mates.

Farm animals do have friends. In a flock of over 100 sheep, you have all sorts of personalities. Orphan lambs raised together will stay together, play together, and grow up together. You have matriarchs, bullies, and ones that are jokers. Pigs also form friendships - when four were taken for slaughter, the other four mourned and called for days. Even cows' heart rates slow when they're with their friends. They relax more. They have amazing memories and recognize people.

questions.question: Why is planet Earth called planet Earth? We know that Jupiter and Venus and Mercury are named after Roman and Greek gods. Why is Earth different?

answers.answer: The Romans called the Earth Mother Earth, which was Terra Mater, and in Italian the word terra is still the word for earth. The word Earth is Germanic - German is Erda, and in English it's from Old English Anglo-Saxon.

The word Earth is old Germanic Saxon from the 8th century. German is Erda. Lutherans used this word in the German Bible and when Henry VIII did the first English Bible, the Germanic word was used. It means the ground literally - it's the same word for the stuff we're standing on and for the planet.

questions.question: Why do we use the word 'ship' after certain words like lordship, sportsmanship, hardship? Why does the same word we use to describe a big boat get stuck on other words?
Why do we only get growing pains for a relatively short amount of time compared to how long we grow for? Why do they stop before we stop growing?

answers.answer: When you get a growth spurt, the bones grow quicker than the tendons, and that's what causes the pain. It can also make you very clumsy. Kurt learned this from his wife whose brother had gone through groin pains.

Growing pains is a bit of a misnomer - it's not actually to do with growth. It affects children who happen to be growing, but we don't actually know the cause. Bone growth happens at the edges, at the joints, but growing pains affects the whole length of the lower limb. There are theories: juvenile bone not being structured well enough to tolerate growth, or kids not having enough stamina when exercising. It's a diagnosis of exclusion - you rule out serious conditions and what's left is growing pains.

questions.question: Can you learn new information in your sleep? If you listen to a French language tape overnight, could you wake up having learnt French?

answers.answer: For A-level Religious Studies, taped himself reading St. Paul's letter to the Corinthians, fell asleep with Walkman on loop all night. For the duration of the exam had almost total recall and smashed it, but by tea time couldn't remember anything. So it got in but not for very long.

People have working memory with the phonological loop (verbal working memory that temporarily holds verbal information like numbers) and the visuospatial scratch pad (holds images, allows you to visualize something while saying it). These work simultaneously, allowing you to remember two things at once. With repetition, this transfers to long-term memory. A suggestion to test Andy's question would be to count cars coming towards you as they don't have regular rhythm.

questions.question: How or why does a boomerang come back? Is it the physics or the way you throw it?

answers.answer: A boomerang is shaped like an airplane wing with a curved top surface and a slightly flatter under surface. When it cuts through air, air travels faster over the top curved surface than under the bottom, creating lower pressure above and higher pressure below - that's what creates lift. When thrown at a slight angle, it creates higher pressure on the outside of the circle and lower pressure on the inside, forcing it round in a circular motion as it continues to spin. It's the same physics as an airplane banking left or right.

questions.question: Can a human being simultaneously count two things in their head which are going at different frequencies/pace? Example: counting your paces to catch up to a runner while also counting paces to pass someone walking toward you.
In most of the world, left-wing parties are red and right-wing are blue. But in America, it's reversed - Democrats are blue and Republicans are red. Why?

answers.answer: It's anomalous to American politics because Republicans used to be the left-wing party. Abraham Lincoln was a Republican and advocated for freeing the slaves. Democrats were the slave-owning class. These were the Dixiecrats in the 60s. The politics flipped in the 60s, possibly related to the civil rights movement. They kept the colors after switching political direction. Learned from watching The Young Turks American news.

Democrats were originally conservative in America and that changed. The red that symbolizes left wing comes from the blood of workers when they first started to fight back and organize. This is why it came back strongly in the 30s with FDR. From Les Misérables - 'It is the song of men who will not be slaves again.' The blood of the workers is red. Qualifications: geek on American politics, watches late night programs.
The blue/red thing happened in 2000 for television purposes. They went with red for Republican because both start with R. Up until Reagan, Republicans were blue.

questions.question: Why does my watch say quartz at the bottom? Is there a rock in there?

answers.answer: There's a tiny bit of quartz crystal in there. The battery does something to the quartz which makes it oscillate. It needs an electrical charge passed through it in order to tick.

questions.question: Why do the hottest and coldest parts of the year seem so separate from the solstices? We're closest to the sun at the summer solstice which should be the hottest point.

answers.answer: The reason is because weather depends on many factors - relief, distance from sea, air masses. Britain is between the ocean and the continent on the battlefield between two weather systems. The length of day doesn't matter as much as these other variables. When we have a cold spell, it's because an air mass is coming from the Arctic bringing those characteristics. Also the Earth being curved means different parts get different amounts of warmth even with the same daylight.

questions.question: When you decorate a room with emulsion, why does cutting an onion in half and leaving it in the room remove the smell of paint?
Why don't we refer to our parents by their names? We say Mum and Dad but we call our siblings by their names.

answers.answer: My theory is it's born out of respect. In my culture coming from Zimbabwe, you'd say Mother of James or Father of James rather than their first names. It's a mark of respect because they're older people. It's like a nickname, a shortening of the word. It probably started as respect.

questions.question: When you're in the supermarket or pharmacy and there are different coloured shower gels and shampoos, why are the bubbles always white even though the liquids are coloured?

answers.answer: It's to do with light hitting them and how thin they are. It doesn't matter what colour they are.

What we see is reflected light. All light comes from the sun and is split into the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Certain things absorb wavelengths and certain ones reflect them. Blue shower gel absorbs red and green wavelengths but reflects blue. With bubbles, it's too thin to actually absorb or reflect - light just passes through, so you see the white light from the sun.

There are two factors. One is the molar extinction coefficient which measures how intensely the compound absorbs colour. The second is to do with how thin the bubble is. The coloured compounds in shampoo are not intensely coloured because they would colour your skin or hair. And because the bubble is so thin, it's still got colour but so pale you don't see it.

questions.question: About two years ago, the Red Hot Chili Peppers song 'By The Way' started making me feel incredibly nauseous - like a bad hangover, bile-wrenching nausea. No other song does this. Why?

answers.answer: It's to do with how it's received and used. It's creating that imbalance like you get with seasickness. That's why he's feeling sick with it. It's an actual thing caused by the beat they've used or something.

He's got a condition called Misophonia. It's a recognised medical condition. The most common example is being irritated by people who eat noisily which creates a physical reaction. As a musician, his ears have been under pressure for years and he's become more sensitive. It's not necessarily songs generally - with him it's one song, so it will be a particular tone in that song that gets him.

questions.question: Why is it 'aid' at the end of lemonade, cherry aid, orange aid?

answers.answer: When they first made a lemon drink, they called it limonata which got anglicised into lemonade. Then whenever they made anything else fizzy, they just stuck 'aid' on the end. The Italians came up with it - limonata. Later 'aid' just stuck to everything fizzy.

questions.question: When did the colour red become synonymous with danger or stopping?

answers.answer: Red has the longest wavelength so it can penetrate through air molecules and be seen from the greatest distance. Also, red is coded into our nature - our brains are hardwired from when mammalian brains developed 100 million years ago to see red as a danger sign because of its visibility. Most animals use red in danger signalling. As a scuba diver, I can say it's the opposite underwater - red is the first colour you lose.

questions.question: Why do we say we're 'looking after' someone? The words 'look' and 'after' don't seem to make sense together.

answers.answer: It's actually a phrasal verb - a verb with a preposition or particle added after it to add meaning of direction or a completely different meaning. Like 'screw' becomes 'screw up' or 'screw around' which has no logical connection to the preposition. It probably originates from Shakespearean times. 'Looking after' means making sure someone is safe, not under attack.

questions.question: Why do drain grates have the direction of traffic flow arrows on them? I'm looking down at them - the traffic flow arrows point the wrong way for water flow.

answers.answer: They're called gully grates. They're all hinged now because people used to steal the old ones and weigh them in at scrap metal merchants. The hinge has to be on the side of oncoming traffic. If the hinge was on the opposite side and you drove into it, it would rip the front wheel off a vehicle. If it's on the right side (oncoming traffic side), cars just knock it back down.

questions.question: Answering the quartz watch question - why does Cameron's watch say quartz?

answers.answer: There's a little tiny quartz crystal inside the watch. It oscillates but only when you pass an electric current through it, hence the battery. A quartz crystal is the only crystal that oscillates at an exact number of times no matter which one you use - every second it oscillates about 3000 times. Inside the watch it counts to that number and then the mechanism advances one second.

questions.question: Why can't people sit facing backwards on trains (with their back to the engine)? Is it physical or psychological?

answers.answer: It's your brain that can't interpret the images it's receiving. Your brain sees you going backwards, sees the horizon going backwards. Your inner ear tells you you're going backwards but the brain gets confused with all the messages. Your inner ear tells your brain something but your eyes tell it something else. The nerves and muscles and joints tell it something else. It gets confused and that's why people feel loss of balance or nausea. Some people are more tolerant to the mixed messages. It can be affected by age.

questions.question: Why do cats' moods change so explosively? What makes a cat bomb go off?

answers.answer: The cat is possibly neurodivergent. I've got an ex-veterinary nurse who's done animal behaviour for years and I've got my first neurodivergent cat. If something changes that they don't understand, they'll lash out, just like neurodivergent children do. For example, when it was snowing, the cat couldn't process why it couldn't go out and attacked.

questions.question: When and why did we start saving our pennies inside pigs? Why are piggy banks pig-shaped?

answers.answer: Pots used to be made from clay called 'pig'. It was spelt P-Y-G or P-Y-double-G. They became known as pig pots. In the same way you'd say a clay pot now. They became money jars known as pig pots, which became piggy banks. It has nothing to do with actual pigs. Eventually they started making them shaped like pigs because we were calling it a pig already despite it not having anything to do with a pig.

questions.question: Why are computer keyboard letters arranged the way they are?

answers.answer: It goes back to typewriters. The problem with typewriters was the arms sticking and jamming. If you pressed keys at once, they would clash into each other on their way to the drum. The arrangement was calculated based on what letter is most likely to follow any given letter, trying to make all frequently recurring pairings as far apart as possible to minimize jamming. It translates to computers even though the problem no longer exists.

questions.question: At 100 degrees Celsius, water evaporates and flashes to steam. Why doesn't it all just disappear immediately when it reaches that temperature?

answers.answer: The water won't disappear in a puff of smoke when it hits 100 degrees because only the bit in contact with the atmosphere evaporates, called the interface. Not until the water level goes down through boiling off will you get more water at the surface. It's just the stuff right at the surface that's evaporating, constantly replenished and replaced.

questions.question: Do men and women generally take their jumpers off differently? Men grab by back of neck and pull over head, women lift from waist/front? And if so, why?

answers.answer: It's to do with the way men's and women's clothes are cut. Men's t-shirts are looser with more space around the armpit and neck. Women's are more form fitting around the armpit and neck. It's a comfort thing. I buy men's cut t-shirts but still take them off the female way - force of habit.

questions.question: Are humans the only animals that suffer with vertigo? Can other animals like birds or tree monkeys get it too?

answers.answer: Animals can get motion sickness. It all comes down to your vestibular system or semi-circular canals. In both sides of your ears, you have three fluid-filled canals lined with hair. As you rotate your head, the fluid moves the hairs telling you which way you're facing. All land animals have an almost identical system. Birds have a similar system but because they fly, it's more adept. Sea creatures like whales and dolphins have similar systems with three canals.

questions.question: How far away in your family tree would you have to go before a genetic test would not recognise that you're related to someone?

answers.answer: Five generations. Either five generations back or five across. By that point, you could tell they were from a similar group like Welsh or Irish, but you couldn't identify the common ancestor genetically. The average person has about 120 distant cousins at that level. Some things like Danny Dyer being related to Richard III are based on marriage records, not genetics.

questions.question: Why does whiskey have to be in a barrel for three years to be classed as whiskey? Why was three years specifically chosen?

answers.answer: It's quality control and branding protection. A Scotch (no E) requires three years and a day, Irish whiskey (with E) requires three years. It's protecting the quality of the product - you know when you buy something that's proper whiskey it's better than bourbon which is only two years. It's like DPO protection for cheese - you can't call it Parmesan unless made in a certain part of Italy. The barrel protects who can make and call it the same thing.

The whiskey question wasn't about why you put it in a barrel (that would apply to bourbon too) - it was about why it has to be three years specifically. The answer should be about giving it colour and flavour.

questions.question: What's at the end of a 60-metre borehole pipe? Is it a river? A lake? Fissures in rock? How does the water source work?

answers.answer: It depends on permeability and porosity - the ability of rock to allow water to flow through it. Imagine a sponge under the earth. Water flows into the rocks above the borehole end and gets pulled up under pressure like a bicycle pump. When rocks were formed they were flat surfaces that got bent and distorted over time. A river could run over porous rock and recharge it. The end of the pipe sits in rock that transfers water through it - like pumice stone or basalt. It's not a lake or lagoon but water-saturated rock constantly replenished as long as the water table remains high. His spring dried up because over-extraction drops the water table.

questions.question: How do Maltesers get their chocolate coating so perfectly round with no visible point of contact or flat spot where they've been sitting?

answers.answer: The Malteser centre is made and unloaded into something called the 'rollercoaster' - two toilet roll centres turning against each other. A big bar at the top drizzles chocolate onto the outside, building up slowly. It then goes into a polishing drum where it's polished against other Maltesers, like polishing stones from a beach to make them shiny. It never stops turning while the chocolate is cooling, which is how it avoids flat bits. At Mars Slough, it takes about 12 minutes for a Malteser to go from start to end of the rollercoaster.

questions.question: Why is Wales the only country in the UK that doesn't have land at the end of it? England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales.

answers.answer: I don't know. The land of the Scots, the land of the Angles... Land of the Irish... What's the ancient name for the Welsh?

The word land is a Germanic word that came to us by the Anglo-Saxons. The Anglo-Saxons didn't necessarily put the word land when they designated a kingdom around them. For example, Mercia borders the Welsh, so they call it Mercia, which means the border in old English. But they didn't call it borderland like we would today. Wales in old English would have been Waelish or Waelia, as in land of the foreigners. They literally just did not apply the word land to that particular kingdom. Sometimes they did, sometimes they didn't. It was random.

questions.question: Why is it possible to eat vegetables from a garden that have been frozen and then defrosted and frozen again multiple times, whereas you can't take vegetables out of a freezer that have been frozen and eat them without getting ill?

answers.answer: The difference between the kale in your freezer and the kale in your garden is that the kale in your garden is still alive. It's still root growth. It's going to grow when it defrosts. When you cut it from the ground, it's no longer attached to its root system. That's the only difference.

When you've got your root system in, the tomato is part of the organism and it's a living thing. As soon as it's picked, it's not. The reason you can't thaw food and then refreeze it is when you thaw it, it starts spoiling. You put it back in the freezer, the bacteria go to stasis. When you bring it out again, it continues to rot. Plants, when it's icy, put lots of sugar into their sap, which drops the freezing point of their sap. So it's a defense against freezing. As long as it's on the tomato plant, it's alive and it's got turnover. The bottom line is it won't rot if it's still connected to the roots.

questions.question: Why do we call our children kids which are baby goats?
When a man goes bald, there's always a strip of hair left from the bottom back of your head. Why don't you go completely bald? Why does that bit survive?

answers.answer: This is for typical male pattern baldness. It's because of a hormone called DHT (dihydrotestosterone). It only affects from your crown to your forehead. It constricts the hair follicles, and that's what makes your hair fall out. That hormone doesn't appear at the back of your head or just above your ears. So you lose your receding hairline, which can recede all the way back, and it comes from the other side from the crown, but the back and the sides often survive.

questions.question: If babies only ingest liquids and gas can pass through liquids, why do they have such trouble burping?

answers.answer: Babies, when they're born, have a basic sucking reflex. Their feeding involves a lot of sucking and they take in a lot of air. As adults, when our stomachs are distended and full of air, we can naturally belch. That process involves relaxing the muscle at the bottom end of the esophagus, called the lower esophageal sphincter. We learn with experience how to do that. But babies don't know how to do that. They don't know how to control that muscle because it's a smooth muscle, not necessarily under voluntary control. When we put them over our shoulders, that puts pressure on the stomach, pressure builds up inside it, and that facilitates the sphincter muscle relaxing and allowing the air to escape.

questions.question: When teaching babies to talk and you say 'say mummy' or 'say daddy', why does the baby never say the word 'say'? Why don't they repeat the 'say' bit?

answers.answer: They're repeating the most emphasised bit of what you're doing. When a baby repeats something back to you, they're repeating a bigger noise. Say, daddy. So that's how you say it. You don't go 'say, da, dee.' You go 'say, daddy.'

It's mostly to do with the kind of sounds that babies are able to articulate at that age. They're not understanding the verb 'say' at that stage of their language development. They're just mimicking what they can hear around them. That's why in most languages, the words for mom and dad or mama, dada, papa all begin with M or D or P because they're easy sounds. If you think about how difficult it is to produce the letter S sound, it's something they don't learn how to pronounce until much later in their language development. So they might even be trying to repeat it, but they're just failing. They're going 'daddy' because the vowel sound is like a schwa sound, just an unstressed vowel.

questions.question: How is a flatfish able to camouflage itself so perfectly - changing colour and even reproducing a checkered pattern on a chessboard - when it has two eyes on the top of its head and can't look underneath itself to see what it's resting on?

Why is it that when we speak, depending on where we come from, we have local dialects and accents, but when we sing, we don't always have an accent? Why don't people with strong accents sing with strong accents?

answers.answer: We all have an accent whatever we're doing, speaking or singing. But when we're singing, it's often the more neutral or less local. When what we now think of as pop music really got going with rock and roll in the 50s, it was an American product. Therefore, the appropriate accent, even if you weren't American, was a pseudo-American accent. Even the Beatles did that at first. This has continued a long time. For example, Elton John is from Pinner in London but sounds pseudo-American when he sings, very different when he speaks. Peter Trudgill did a study of the Beatles and found that at early stages they sounded a mixture of Liverpool and pseudo-American. But by the time they finished in 69/70, both of those had gone down and it was more general British. They pronounced R sounds at the end of words like 'car' 37% of the time on early albums but down to 4% by the end. They'd established their own identity. So it's partly subconscious but we're moving towards a less localised goal of pronunciation. During the punk rock period it became common to try to sound cockney. Folk singers often try to sound Irish or West Country or Scottish.

questions.question: Why is there not a standard size for football pitches for professional teams? Tennis courts are standard size but football pitches vary - Man City and non-league teams have different sized pitches.

answers.answer: Law one of the laws of the game says a pitch must be between 45 and 90 metres wide and 90 to 120 metres in length. That's a huge difference. You can't have an under-10s team playing on a massive pitch that a professional team plays on. So you have to have variation for children. And because there is variation for children, you have variations on adult pitches.

questions.question: When I was born I had a dent in my head. Has it affected my brain growth or cognitive development?
Do other animals have pregnancy cravings? Like does a pregnant cat crave more tuna or weird things like coal?
Does skin absorb water when swimming?

answers.answer: The outer layer of skin, the stratum corneum, is waterproof because it's made of dead flat cells called corneocytes in a mortar of lipids (cholesterol, ceramides). This layer is hydrophobic and prevents evaporation. Nicotine patches work because nicotine is oil soluble. Without this layer, you would dehydrate. The corneocytes can swell and absorb some water (causing wrinkles) but it won't go through the lipid layer.

questions.question: Why does beetroot color make it through the body (pink wee) but doesn't stain hands like black cherries or blackberries?

answers.answer: The answer is betanin, a pigment/enzyme that doesn't get broken down by kidneys. It passes all the way through the digestive system (through stomach acid and saliva) and comes out pink in urine. The pigment in cherries and blackcurrants is broken down by kidneys.

questions.question: Why do men put their arms above their heads when sitting on the sofa to relax?

answers.answer: From a body language training course: placing hands on top of heads signals relaxation, feeling in control, and being unthreatened. When groups of men are together watching TV having a good time, they signal to the group that 'you are safe with me' - it's like yawning which shows you're relaxed and there's nothing behind you. Having arms up is actually a vulnerable position, so it shows trust and safety.

questions.question: Why are the first flush of flowers every season yellow or white?

answers.answer: The majority of pollinators at this time of year are various species of flies which lack colour vision. Yellow and white are the most reflective colours and therefore attract them the most. The evolutionary relationship between pollinator and pollen means insects doing the pollinating at this time will spot white and yellow more easily than other colours, so those flowers come up first and get pollinated. Larger animals with colour vision pollinate later-blooming flowers.

questions.question: If the odds of winning EuroMillions are £16.5 million to one and the jackpot goes over £100 million, could I buy every ticket for £16 million and be in profit?

answers.answer: The odds are wrong - it's not £16.5 million to one but approximately £140 million to one for the EuroMillions jackpot. If it were possible to guarantee a win by buying enough tickets, someone would have already done it.

questions.question: How do they clean the windows on the outside of the Gherkin?

answers.answer: The Gherkin uses a combination of systems: window cleaners work from cradles suspended from a rail that runs around the top of the building, allowing them to go up and down. The cradles follow the curved shape. Additionally, windows at the very top are cleaned by abseilers.

questions.question: Is there a height limit for nudity on a nudist beach, and can you skydive naked onto one?

answers.answer: There is no height restriction on nudity on a nudist beach. Being naked is not in and of itself illegal. You might get arrested if you're likely to cause offence or breach the peace, but landing in a field in the middle of nowhere would be fine.

In April 2018, UK law was clarified: public nudity in pursuit of a lawful activity is not illegal. There are three caveats: no sexual activity, no mental illness concerns (for your own safety), and no intent to cause fear and alarm. The Naked Rambler was arrested for causing fear and alarm or refusing lawful instruction from police, not merely for being naked. So there's nothing to stop you skydiving onto a nudist beach from any height.

questions.question: Why does it take three to four weeks for funerals in England when in Ireland it's two to three days, even including post-mortems?

answers.answer: It's simply a waiting list issue - there's a backlog in the waiting list for post-mortems in England compared to Ireland. Also, there are more priests available in Ireland to perform funeral ceremonies. The undertaker told me my father, who died on Saturday morning, was buried on Monday.

questions.question: Why do owls have such long legs compared to their bodies?

answers.answer: Owls can catch surprisingly large prey, and you need quite long legs - possibly the musculature of the leg that propels the talons at sufficient speed to catch prey. It's linked to their hunting skills.

The fidgeting and foot shaking is a sign of nervous energy. When people have worries or are preoccupied, they don't know how to manage it, so finger tapping gives a release of nervous energy. The best way to manage it is to find a displacement activity - rhythmical or mathematical - to move the mind away from the preoccupation. Like fishermen making nets in Cornwall who still do this activity.

questions.question: When you go to buy hens' eggs in Denmark, they are white, completely white. In the UK, they're normally brown. Why is that?
If I eat an apple and plant the pip, I get a tree and more apples. Same with an orange. But how do I get seedless grapes if I have no pip to plant?

answers.answer: You have got a pip to plant. It's just a very soft pip that you eat when you eat a seedless grape.

questions.question: Why is it that certain daily newspapers change their name once a week? For example, the Sunday Telegraph versus the Daily Telegraph.
Whenever I buy a tailored item or clothing, the pockets are always stitched together. Why?

answers.answer: After manufacture, but before being put on for sale, the garment will almost certainly be pressed so that it looks as good as possible on the rail. If the pocket was open, then it would crumple and crease under the pressure of the ironing. The lining of the pocket could get crumpled and creased, and then if you ironed over a crumpled internal, it would get reflected on the surface of the outer cloth.

The pockets are sewn quite early in construction, so it's not just the ironing that might cause distortion, but they could become distorted during construction of other parts of the jacket, like adding the sleeves.

questions.question: N/A - Answer about egg colors

answers.answer: If a chicken has got white ears, they will lay white eggs. If they've got brown ears, they will lay brown eggs. It's the colour of the ears. She showed me and they matched. I looked into it online and it confirmed what she told me.

questions.question: N/A - Answer expanding on egg color question

answers.answer: The colour of the egg is entirely down to the breed of chicken. The ones that lay white eggs are leg bars or derivatives of hybrids of leg bars. The reason they are the preferred colour of egg in places like Denmark and the States is consumer preference - consumers like buying white eggs there. There's also a commercial advantage: leg bars are a smaller breed but still lay a really good size egg, so commercially they're more viable, they eat less. The lobes (not ears) correlate - leg bars have white lobes generally. But it's not always true - olive eggers produce green eggs and they don't have green lobes. You can also get blue eggs, almost black eggs.

questions.question: When did we first conceive of ghosts as essentially being a sheet with eyes? Can we trace back to the first time that image was used?
N/A - Answer about seedless grapes

answers.answer: With the seedless grapes, the way they propagate them is by cuttings. You can clone plants by cutting bits off, like a stem, and the stem cells can root. The reason for cuttings or graftings for seedless grapes isn't because they don't have seeds, but about the grape you're producing. If you were to propagate by seed, that seed is formed when a flower becomes pollinated, but you don't know what plant it's being pollinated from. So it could be a random grape that you don't have control over mixing with the grape that you're trying to grow. The seed formed is a mix between two varieties of grape, and you want to only grow one variety.

questions.question: Why is a public school essentially a private school?

answers.answer: It starts with the idea that not everybody went to school. If a school grew up and it was really good, then people would start sending their children there - not just local people. So it's not the most literal definition of public, but you have to understand it as being the opposite of local. When they started taking boarders who stayed at the school, they became known as public schools because it was not just for local people.

questions.question: N/A - Answer about grapes

answers.answer: Humans have been growing grapes for over 8,000 years. Once a particular type of grape has a property that people really like, you take a cutting which is grafted onto a rootstock, and the cutting is an identical twin of the mother plant. At some point over the last 8,000 years, a grape plant somewhere produced grapes with no seeds. People liked that, so they take cuttings from that plant, graft them on, and you have a grape vine that produces seedless grapes. When that one gets old, you take another cutting. Most varieties of grapes for table grapes or wine are identical twins, clones of the parent. Additionally, for example, a red grape is original because the grape changes colour to indicate to a bird eating seeds and plant the seed somewhere else. A white grape is a mutation.

questions.question: How do we get vitamin D from the sun, which is essentially a ball of fire in the sky?

answers.answer: There are ultraviolet rays coming out of the sun. In your skin, you have something ending in cholesterol - 7-dehydrocholesterol. The ultraviolet rays are absorbed by this stuff in your skin, and it changes them. It's a chemical reaction - the ultraviolet rays have a chemical reaction with something already present in your skin, and that turns it into vitamin D.

questions.question: Is the world getting bigger? When we use expandable foam on building sites, it comes in a small can but then expands to a larger amount of matter. Is man adding to the size of the world?

answers.answer: No. Everything is in a state of constant - the actual raw materials are the same. We're making it out of materials that already existed. Expandable foam expands because it's filled with something else that already existed. Like blowing up a balloon - is there more or less air in the world than before? No, there's the same amount. New human beings are also made of stuff that already existed - we're converting chemicals into different things. The planet is not getting heavier or bigger. Although meteorites can add slightly to the mass, it's not much.

questions.question: On a trumpet, you have three valves and there's eight different combinations. How can you get more than eight notes out of a trumpet?
N/A - Answer about trumpet

answers.answer: Trumpets and trombones are basically just a tube. Even without putting any valves down, or without moving the trombone slide, you can make a series of notes just by tightening and loosening your lips. You change the aperture, and that changes the note. You can get a whole series of notes just from the lips. With a trombone, moving the slide out one position makes the instrument longer, so the whole series of notes goes lower. A trumpet works the same way but an octave higher. Instead of the slide, valves redirect air through additional tubing. The first valve adds a slightly long bit of tubing, the third valve has the longest bit of tubing, and combinations act like the trombone positions. So you've got seven sets of harmonics to play with.

questions.question: N/A - Answer about public schools

answers.answer: Public schools were originally for poor people - places where clever poor children got educated, largely by clergy. Because they were providing a good education, the sons of the wealthy started wanting to send their kids there as well. The Public Schools Act of 1868 designated specific schools as public schools - there were about seven or eight: Charterhouse, Eton, Harrow, Shrewsbury, Winchester, Westminster, and Rugby. Not all private schools are known as public schools. The act was about government regulation as they moved from being places for clever poor children into places where wealthy parents paid for education.

questions.question: N/A - Answer about vitamin D

answers.answer: Vitamin D is mostly made in the epidermis, the top layer of skin. UVB radiation from the sun penetrates those layers and the energy from that particular wavelength catalyzes a protein called 7-DHC (7-dehydrocholesterol), which converts. The 7-DHC absorbs the UVB and gets converted into cholecalciferol (vitamin D3), a pre-vitamin. It circulates in the body and is processed by the liver, then the kidneys convert it into the bioavailable form our body needs - calcidiol. It is directly linked to melanin in the skin and skin color. People with darker skin have about one-tenth the prevalence of skin cancer of those with lighter skin, but they also need more sunlight to produce the same amount of vitamin D.

questions.question: Why do people rub their hands together in anticipation?

answers.answer: Stimulates blood flow to warm hands before physical tasks. Has become psychological programming for anticipating challenges, girding your loins.

questions.question: What is the mechanism keeping us warm-blooded?

answers.answer: Burning food creates energy which creates heat - metabolism.
Mitochondria in cells take sugars from food and oxygen, burn it, and release heat. Cold-blooded animals may have fewer mitochondria or don't store energy the same way.

The hypothalamus in our brain regulates homeostasis - it tells cells to keep burning sugar at a certain rate to maintain internal temperature. Cold-blooded animals don't have this, so their temperature depends on environment.

questions.question: Why do manufacturers request plastic plates and bowls only go on the top shelf of dishwashers?

answers.answer: They might melt because the heating element is at the bottom.
It's about pressure from water jets at the bottom, not the heating element. Wash temperatures of 40-60 degrees aren't hot enough to melt plastic.

questions.question: What's the point of the dawn chorus?

answers.answer: Birds are either attracting mates, defending territory, or telling their mates where they are.

answers.caller: Jane (the Wirral) - zoology degree, county recorder for Cheshire for birds
answers.answer: Birds sing to proclaim territories or attract mates. At dawn, they have a tight energy budget and can't catch food yet (insects aren't active - they're cold-blooded). So they sing pre-dawn when they can't feed. Sound also travels better and there's less background noise.

questions.question: My twin boys are identical but one is left-handed and one is right-handed - what's going on?

answers.answer: They might be 'mirror twins'.

answers.caller: Adam - PhD in behavioral psychology neuroscience, learning behavior
answers.answer: Referencing Uno Guntergren's research on laterality - the way people lean left or right when kissing matches how they lay in the womb. There's an environmental impact of the womb on brain development. So twins could be lying different ways, making one left-handed and one right-handed.

questions.question: Why do saltwater fish die in freshwater and vice versa?

answers.answer: The salt concentration in the fish's body becomes too low to survive. Might be osmosis.

answers.caller: Professor Hall - Professor of Public Understanding of Science, University of Brighton
answers.answer: Every organism has an optimum level of saltiness called osmotic strength. If you put a salty fish in fresh water, it swells up because water osmose in. If you put a freshwater fish in salt water, it dehydrates because water osmose out. Salt is actually quite toxic.

questions.question: Why do women run 100m hurdles and men run 110m hurdles?

answers.answer: I like that question. I've never clocked it until you mentioned it.

answers.caller: Richardson Barnett - former 400m hurdler, 6th best in country at under-19 level
answers.answer: Men's hurdles are 3 foot 6 inches high versus 2 foot 9 for women. To clear the higher hurdle you need extra distance to generate the power and speed. Women are generally smaller so need shorter hurdles. Men also have longer strides and need more space between hurdles to generate pace.

questions.question: If you put a polar bear in the South Pole and penguins in the North Pole, would their natural navigation instincts be messed up because they're in different hemispheres?

answers.answer: I don't think so, no. Animals would probably be fine as long as conditions are similar.

questions.question: Is it true fish have a two-second memory? And if so, how is that known?

answers.answer: Imagine giving a fish a small electric shock that hurts but doesn't kill - enough to make it swim away. Then you time how long before it goes back. That's how long a fish's memory lasts.

answers.caller: Howard (Sydenham) - psychology degree from Northumberland University
answers.answer: They did actually do this experiment with goldfish and electric shocks. The fish could remember for several days. The head of department shut it down for cruelty to fish.

questions.question: Why does burning paper create so much more ash compared to burning wood?

answers.answer: Paper and wood are both primarily made of carbon. The difference is that paper has a much greater surface area - carbon molecules are all around the top, bottom, and sides, so it can be attacked and combusted by fire everywhere at once. Wood has carbon molecules stuck within the inside of the plank, so it has to be attacked from top and bottom. However, if you burn the same weight of wood and paper, they should create roughly the same amount of ash.

questions.question: How do scientists rate animals' intelligence? How do they determine that one animal is more intelligent than another?

answers.answer: By giving them problems to solve. Tools usage is also considered.

They use various tests including grid tests with multiple images where there are duplications. The animal has to identify where the matches were based on memory. They assess the number of associations they can make and the speed to which they can memorise the grid. This is used on pigs, chimpanzees, apes, and crows. Some animals greatly outperform humans on these tests.

questions.question: Is there less oxygen in the wintertime when there's no leaves on the trees and no plants growing?
Where do moles go in the summer? You only see mole hills in the winter.

answers.answer: In the summer, moles go deeper down because the earth is drier and the worms and slugs (which they feed on) are deeper in the ground. Then in autumn, winter, and late spring when it's often very wet, the slugs and worms come to the surface and that's where the moles follow them.

questions.question: When eating fruit, what classifies something as being a pip or a seed?
Where does 'Tories' come from for the Conservative Party, and why haven't any of the other parties got nicknames?

answers.answer: Tory means outlaw. It comes from the Irish language. English settlers in Ireland were correctly described as thieving outlaws by Irish people. It was picked up in Scotland and later applied to Conservatives by James II.

questions.question: How do they make babies cry for a film on film sets?

answers.answer: Baby wranglers are trained professionals who work with parents to get the performance directors need. Methods include: taking the baby away from the mother (which can set them off, especially if the mother appears distressed), wranglers pretending to cry in front of the baby, making a loud surprising noise like 'boo', or waving something under their nose. If in doubt, they won't film the baby's face and will add a sound effect later.

questions.question: Why does my labradoodle take three pellets of food, go to another room, drop them on the carpet, look at them, eat them slowly one by one, then go back and wolf down the rest?

answers.answer: My vet said it's a social thing. The dog wants to eat with the family at the table, so they bring their food to where the family eats. Even if you're not eating, the dog still brings food there.

questions.question: Why are there so many different types of pasta - rigatoni, shells, spaghetti, flat ones?

answers.answer: Different pasta shapes hold sauce differently. A pasta aficionado would notice the difference.

It's a regional tradition. Italy has 20 regions, each with provinces that have their own traditions, recipes, and pasta shapes. Some shapes do lend themselves better to certain sauces. For example, in Tuscany there's picci - handmade spaghetti that's long and thick, used with ragu.

questions.question: Why is it considered lucky to be pooed on by a bird?

answers.answer: It may be a way of comforting someone who's just been pooed on - there's not much you can do except say it's good luck. Different cultures have different versions: Italians say dog poo is good luck.

questions.question: Why do we put candles on a birthday cake? What are the origins of candles on birthday cakes?
Why is the capital of England called London? Why is it called London rather than Lond?

answers.answer: The Normans didn't rename places. They kept native names to avoid making the natives restless. London (Londinium) was the Roman name and it just stayed, getting trimmed and evolved like other Roman place names. It was never on the agenda to rename it.

questions.question: How do snowdrops know when it's time to flower? They always come up in the second week of February whether the ground is frozen or warm.

answers.answer: All seeds respond to changes of temperature. When snow covers the ground, it creates a magnifying glass effect between the snow and the ground underneath, heating the soil up and making the snowdrops think it's spring. The second week of February timing is due to the gradual warming of the ground as we head towards spring. If there's a particularly cold snap, everything will be late.

questions.question: How do bananas make other fruit ripen quicker?

answers.answer: They release a gas which accelerates the ripening of other fruits. If you put them in a brown paper bag with other fruits it happens even quicker.

It's an ethanol blend gas. She works for a chemical distribution company and her customer sells this gas to ripeners who sell to supermarkets. It's used to ripen bananas and other fruits. Bananas produce less of the gas than other fruits like apples, so actually other fruits can affect bananas more. The gas triggers a ripening hormone.

questions.question: Why does ouzo go white when you put water in it?

answers.answer: It's a precipitate - when you add water it creates a solid or an emulsion. The milkier it gets, apparently the better the ouzo is.

It's called 'looshing' - some of the botanicals used in the creation of the spirit come out of solution and form something that is soluble in alcohol but not in water. It's probably aniseed oil from star anise. It also happens if you chill spirits down - if you put an ice cube in pure gin you'll see a tiny bit of looshing happening too.

questions.question: Why do we get a lump in our throat when we get upset?
Why are films like 'A Fistful of Dollars' and 'The Good, The Bad and The Ugly' called spaghetti westerns? Where did the spaghetti come from?

answers.answer: They were made by Italians. They were usually directed or produced by Italians, most obviously Sergio Leone. That's why they're called spaghetti westerns.

questions.question: Where do winds start? How does wind develop and get stronger? What's the beginning?

answers.answer: Wind is solar-powered. When you heat up a surface, the air above it gets hot, loses density and rises. What's left at ground level is low pressure, which draws air towards it. As air rises it sucks air from elsewhere, causing momentum - wind. It gets deflected by the spinning of the earth (Coriolis force), going clockwise in the north and anticlockwise in the south. Meteorologists can predict where wind will come from by looking at atmospheric and surface pressures using the 500 hectopascal chart.

questions.question: Why do we blush when we get embarrassed?

answers.answer: It's the body's response to stress, anxiety or fear. The sympathetic nervous system (fight or flight) makes your heart rate go up, diverts blood to your muscles, and makes the blood vessels in your cheeks bigger so they go red. Adrenaline hits receptors in the blood vessels and makes them dilate. Even when embarrassed, you have fight or flight response because you want to get out of the embarrassing situation. It also happens when attracted to someone because that's an anxious situation too.

questions.question: Why are the numbers 1, 2, 3 on the top row of a telephone keypad but on the bottom row of a calculator and computer keyboard?

answers.answer: On a rotary telephone, the numbers went 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and then 0 in the middle. The dial mechanism sent clicks to the exchange - one click for 1, two clicks for 2, etc., with 0 sending 10 clicks as it was furthest round the dial. This layout has been passed down to digital phones. On calculators and computer keyboards, 7, 8, 9 are at the top because numbers go in numerical order from top to bottom, with zero at the bottom.

questions.question: What happens to UK number plate systems when they run out of letter combinations?

answers.answer: It's already happened. When I was a kid, the old system had the letter at the end denoting the year (like RBT426T). They've already started again and mixed it up.

questions.question: Why can we sometimes hear people smiling when we talk to them on the phone, even without them laughing?

answers.answer: Your mouth is a vocal filter. When it's relaxed you make a more forward sound in the mouth. When you smile, your cheeks tighten and you get a tighter sound, going further back in the mouth. You have different vocal resonators in your forehead cavity and in your cheeks. As the muscles in your face move with a smile, you use different parts of your head to make the sound.

questions.question: Why is the phrase 'double Dutch' used to mean nonsense? Why Dutch rather than French, Italian or Spanish?

answers.answer: James admitted he didn't know. He offered an unverified theory that many Dutch words sound like English words but with consonants repeated at the beginning (like 'geist' for ghost, 'heilige' for holy). But James later acknowledged this was wrong - the Dutch word for ghost is just 'geist' and holy is 'heilige', and he had been wrong about this for 37 years.

questions.question: Is there a rule about how far apart places with the same road name can be? Can the same road name appear in different areas?

answers.answer: He doesn't think there's a national rule. It's down to individual councils, so there could be an Avenel on both sides of a council border. He suspects there's no requirement in place and no one to enforce it.

questions.question: Why are some colors used as surnames while other colors don't become names? I've met Mr Black and Mrs Brown and Jason Orange from Take That, but I've never met a Mr Yellow or Mr Blue.

answers.answer: Originally names might refer to what you did for a living - that's where Smith comes from or Butcher. Black, white, brown, gray could refer to hair color. Green... might be from green grocer. But nobody has purple hair.
Exactly, nobody has purple hair.

questions.question: Following on from someone asking if lakes have tides - do I have a tide? Does the gravitational pull of the moon affect me? Do I get fatter and thinner according to the gravitational pull of the moon?

answers.answer: The gravitational pull of the moon must apply to all matter in varying degrees. As water moves in and out of oceans and lakes, it expands and contracts according to where the coastline is. But what do you move in and out of? It does affect you because you don't get fatter or thinner... or maybe you do?

questions.question: If I put a cotton T-shirt in a tumble dryer, it shrinks. But if I put it on a red hot radiator to dry, or out on a line which is hot and windy, it doesn't shrink. Why does it shrink in the tumble dryer but not anywhere else?

answers.answer: It's hotter in the tumble dryer. If you put it on cool tumble, it will still shrink.

The tumble dryer is an enclosed atmosphere. You're introducing heat and air to reduce the moisture content. Cotton is a natural fabric with natural moisture content within it. When you exceed the time limit or heat limit, you reduce the moisture from the cotton fibres and therefore you create shrinkage. It's a see-saw - on one end you've got time and on the other end you've got heat. Charles is either doing it too hot or too long, or possibly both.

questions.question: Why do horses get shooed (shoed) but other cattle doesn't? Cows, sheep, goats - they all have hooves too.

answers.answer: Horses in the wild don't have shoes. The shoe is a consequence of being domesticated - they're going on harder surfaces, which means their hooves are affected in ways they wouldn't be in the wild. If you wanted a cow to pull a carriage every day, you would probably have to buy it cow shoes. If you own a horse that never leaves its field, I don't think you need to shoe it. The shoeing is a consequence of domestication and putting the horse to work.

answers.caller: Cheryl (Fraserborough) - Qualifications: 40+ years of keeping horses and being a farmer with cows
answers.answer: Horses don't have shoes on even those that work. These days, it's only those that need shoes because they're doing a lot of work in abrasive sand. Cows can actually be used - they're called oxen. You can get blocks that go onto cow's toes, but cows walk on two toes whereas horses walk on one. If you rode a cow, you'd have to have two shoes on it, not one. Oxen shoes go back hundreds of years because oxen were used as beasts of burden for ploughing. Most horses are not shod these days unless they're going on the road or doing work - even ridden horses might need shoes depending on breed, quality of feet, and nutrition.

questions.question: Why when something hurts do we say that it's smart? Is this just American or do we say it here too?

answers.answer: Smart meaning hurt - that is a familiar figure of speech. I'll give you £50 if it's not German originally. It sounds German - smarte? It might be Saxon, Viking invasion, Northern European or possibly German. We'll find out.

The word for pain in Norwegian is 'smerte' (S-M-E-R-T-E). It's from the Proto-Germanic 'smerte' and also Middle Dutch 'smerten' - it just means hurt. The Vikings brought it over. There are so many English words from Scandinavian countries - like 'window' which is 'vindu' over there.

questions.question: Why do we have the 'aid' at the end of lemonade, cherry aid, lime aid etc.? Where does the 'aid' come from?

answers.answer: Where does the 'aid' come from? Does it denote fizziness? It's not always fizzy - if you buy fancy lemonade it won't be fizzy. We could go on all day about lemonade - not all are fizzy. I used to sit in Covent Garden, turn to my little dog and say 'you're not in Kidderminster now Toto.' I don't know why it's called lemonade, I'll try and find out.

answers.caller: Peter (Wallingford) - Qualifications: Expert Etymologist who wrote 'Well I Never Knew That' series of books on origins of words and phrases
answers.answer: The 'aid' comes from the Spanish ending 'ada' which comes from Latin 'ata'. It converts a verb into a noun. If you were a soldier fighting for the cross, you were a crusader. If you have a building with an arch, it is an arcade. If you're part of a community, you're a comrade. Therefore if you have a drink that is made from a fruit, it is lemonade, orangeade. When it's spelled A-I-D in a drink, it's normally when a copyright has already used the ending A-D-E and to be allowed to sell the new name, they cheat and use A-I-D, like Kool-Aid. In Italian it's still limonata - the ATA ending. In Spain it's ADE. Blockade is a good example because 'block' is a verb.

questions.question: How do opticians know when a baby's eyesight is right when the baby can't talk?

answers.answer: The eyes will follow something. If you hold a little toy in front of a baby, the baby's eyes and possibly its head will follow the toy around.
No, James. They will follow. You try it - get a baby and call me back.

questions.question: Why aren't there clocks on London Underground tubes? You have clocks on the overground, National Rail, buses. But on the carriages themselves, there's no time display. Even on the new trains, there isn't any.

answers.answer: Where would they put them? If it ain't broke, don't fix it - they've never had it. If you're stuck underground and need to know the time, ask someone. If there's no one else in the carriage, buy a bloody watch. It's possible you might need to change your fashion based on... I don't know if there's a genuine reason. I do too now. I've never really clocked that before.

questions.question: Why can you go into a supermarket and buy chicken eggs or duck eggs but you can't buy turkey eggs when there are millions of turkeys in the country?

answers.answer: No one wants them. All turkey eggs are hatched because the market wants loads of turkeys in the right place at the right time - i.e. Christmas. If they are farmed, they're farmed for the meat. They're just not farmed for the eggs. You can't really buy goose eggs either.

answers.caller: George (Wembley) - Qualifications: Used to work on a turkey farm
answers.answer: There are two factors. One is that the taste of turkey eggs is so awful that nobody would want to buy them. There's too much fat in them. Economically, turkeys don't produce as many eggs as chickens do, so there's a commercial reason but also a culinary reason. It tastes like eating fat on its own - gross.

questions.question: Being as the planet Earth is billions of years old, why hasn't it cooled down? Why are we still getting volcanoes going off and geysers? You can understand why the sun is hot because of nuclear energy, but the Earth is just a rock.

answers.answer: You're thinking of it like a pie you've just taken out of the oven. First of all, there's no oven. The planet is so enormous and so hot to start with that there's still loads of lava and magma. It's like a thermal flask. Eventually they do cool, but over a very long period of time - billions of years.

answers.caller: Professor Hal (University of Brighton) - Qualifications: Professor of Public Understanding of Science
answers.answer: Yes, the Earth absolutely should have cooled down by now, and the reason it hasn't is that in the mantle there's an awful lot of radioactive isotopes which are decaying and thereby producing heat - lots of uranium uranium-238 decaying into thorium and so on. One delightful byproduct is alpha particles which are helium nuclei, so all the helium we get for Valentine's balloons doesn't come from fractional distillation of air but from helium mines, because when helium escapes into the atmosphere it radiates out into space so fast you can't get it from air. Eventually everything will have decayed and we'll have the heat death of the universe - the sun will start using helium and become a red giant. Andrew's heat pump is alright for the foreseeable future - the Earth is creating its own heat for the time being.

questions.question: Is ginger/red hair exclusively a Caucasian thing, or can people from Asia, Africa, or the Middle East also be born ginger?

answers.answer: I've seen ginger hair in cases of albinism, but is it natural? I think someone with darker skin can have ginger hair, but I've got no way of proving it except my Swiss cheese of a memory thinking I'm sure I've seen something somewhere.

answers.caller: Rick (Location not given) - Qualifications: Physics A-Level
answers.answer: Yes, the gravitational pull of the moon does affect humans. Newton's law of gravitation says that every object is attracted to every other object, but it depends on the mass of the object and the distance. Because the Earth is so huge compared to us, we are attracted to it and our internal organs are dominated by Earth's gravity, not the moon's, because the moon is smaller and much farther away. But the principle stands - the moon does affect us, just minuscule compared to Earth.

questions.question: Why is it that only humans have visible whites of their eyes (sclera) that are clearly visible when the eye is in a resting stage, when most animals don't seem to have this?

answers.answer: As a dog behaviourist, I can tell you that you can see the white of dogs' eyes when they're stressed, anxious, or scared - they deliberately show the whites to signal they want nothing to do with another dog or person. But I don't know why human sclera is so much more prominent than for any other species.

In most animals the sclera is pigmented, not white. Humans have white sclera so our irises are more visible - it's linked to communication. Animals are trying to stay away from prey, so they don't want the whites of their eyes seen. It's an evolutionary advantage.

questions.question: Why are potholes called potholes?

answers.answer: Before tarmacking, potters used to dig clay out of the road. The ruts cut through the soil, so to get clay you'd dig in those wheel tracks - known as potholes. Holes dug to get clay to make pots.

questions.question: Does light last forever?

answers.answer: Yes, light does last forever. It's an electromagnetic force, an energy wave that doesn't need any other matter to propagate - it travels on into infinity. However, if there are particles like space dust or rocks, the light gets absorbed. That's why you can't see light forever on Earth, but in space with no particles, it goes on forever.

questions.question: Is seven the record number of former Prime Ministers currently alive - Blair, Brown, Major, Cameron, May, Truss, and Johnson?

answers.answer: No, six is the most since 1951. There have been periods with five, but never seven - until now, it IS a record.

questions.question: Why are some wind turbines switched off when it's windy, given we have an energy crisis?

answers.answer: Because it's either too windy or not windy enough. Or there might be no demand for the electricity. Also, we don't have good storage capacity, so there's nowhere for the electricity to go.

questions.question: How did the first English-speaking person and first French-speaking person translate languages? How did translation begin, especially for abstract concepts like 'feeling'?

answers.answer: You can point at things to establish concrete meanings, then gradually build up a shared vocabulary. But for abstract concepts like 'feeling', you need more sophisticated methods.

The best way is with children. A child under six can naturally pick up a language just by hearing it. In the 18th century in America, children were placed with indigenous tribes to learn their languages so they could later create dictionaries and facilitate translation. With children, you get both languages naturally. Also for Latin-based languages, many technical terms are similar between languages which helps.

questions.question: Why do we say County Durham but not County Yorkshire or County Kent?

answers.answer: It has something to do with the word Palatine - originally it was the County Palatine of Durham. It was a ceremonial title involving the bishop, distinct from other counties which were geographic. Because it was called County Palatine of Durham, it just survived as County Durham.

questions.question: Why do cows lie down when it's raining or when it's about to rain?

answers.answer: Cows want a dry patch to lie on. If it's raining and you decide to lie down, you have nowhere dry. If you lie down before it rains, only half of you gets wet and you stay on a dry patch and warm. They sense atmospheric changes - it's linked to pressure changes and conserving energy.

The answer is yes - it's because they want a dry patch. They send some sort of atmospheric change which tells them it's going to start raining, similar to how seagulls come inland when a storm is coming.

questions.question: Why do things expand when they get hot? If molecules are jiggling more and creating space, where does that space come from if there's nothing there before?

answers.answer: Think of it like snooker balls packed in a box. When you heat it, they jigle more and push the walls out - they're creating the space by moving into it. But Mark challenged: where does that space come from beforehand?
Actually thinking about it, nothing. It's just a slightly weaker interaction between molecules.

You can model metals as spheres (atoms) connected by springs. They jiggle with greater amplitude when hotter, which is why they expand. Within the metal there's just space - the atoms push air out of the way so that space is now occupied by metal vibrating more. Everything has space (atoms are mostly empty space). The air that was there moves away. Also, it's not true that everything expands when hot - water contracts when melted, which is why things crack when frozen.

questions.question: Why does Deep Heat make your shoulders tingle immediately when you rub it on, but you feel nothing on the hands you're rubbing with?

answers.answer: Probably because the skin on your hands is thicker. Your hand has big muscles too. There's a lot of nerves in fingertips but maybe those nerves are different. Not claiming a round of applause for this - I'm leaving it to someone better qualified.

questions.question: Is there scientific basis to my mum's saying that an hour's sleep before midnight is worth two hours after midnight?

answers.answer: Your body goes through 5 sleep stages: stages 1-2 are light sleep, stages 3-4 are deep sleep (very hard to wake someone), stage 5 is REM. Stages 3-4 are when your brain cleanses itself, detoxifies. You cycle through these roughly every 90 minutes. If you get 8 hours, you get roughly 5-6 cycles of these stages. So the quality of sleep matters, not the clock time. Your mum was partly right - deep sleep in early stages is important, but it has nothing to do with midnight specifically.

questions.question: What is the hardest sporting feat an individual can achieve? For example, a 59 in golf, a nine-dart finish in darts, or a perfect game in bowling. Is there a way to statistically measure which is most difficult?

answers.answer: I would say a 59 in golf is the hardest. A hole-in-one is more work, and there have probably only been 10 in the PGA Tour.

My brother is a golf professional. He says golf is the second most difficult sport to play. The most difficult sport is pole vaulting because all the components (speed, pole placement, angle, weather) have to come together at exactly the same time.

An iron distance triathlon is the hardest achievement. The first person to have gone sub-seven hours (2.4 mile swim, 112 mile bike, full marathon) was Christian Blumenfeld in June. Only two men have ever gone under seven hours.

I believe the biggest privately owned house in the country is Wentworth Woodhouse. It's near Yorkshire and looks like Castle Howard. It was the ancestral home of someone connected to a famous Victorian.

An 18 under par 18 hole round would be the ultimate achievement but it's impossible. You can't talk cricket - taking all 10 wickets depends on the batsmen. Hitting six sixes also depends on the bowler.
A 155 break in snooker is theoretically possible with a free ball, which would actually be a greater achievement than a 147. You can't control getting a free ball though.

questions.question: Which private individual in the whole of the United Kingdom, not the National Trust or the Royal Family or the government, can say they've got the biggest house in the whole country?

answers.answer: The biggest privately owned house in the country is Wentworth Woodhouse, which is privately owned. There was a furore a few years ago about them receiving government money for restoration.

questions.question: Can blind people or partially sighted people have hallucinations? When I'm asleep I dream and can see things, but would I see hallucinations when awake like someone might see a dancing gnome in my field of vision?

answers.answer: Yes, visual hallucinations are fairly common, mainly with people who have macular degeneration or possibly Parkinson's. Even someone registered as severely sight-impaired with zero vision could have something appear in their field of vision that simply wasn't there. Most people registered as blind still have 5-10% vision. It depends on what's actually happening with their eyes.

questions.question: Blue cheeses like stilton, gorgonzola, and Danish blue are naturally mouldy and we eat them with impunity. But can you eat a piece of cheese that's not specifically been made to be mouldy, like cheddar that's gone yellow and green? Can you just cut the mouldy bits off and eat the rest, or is some mould good and some mould bad?

answers.answer: The consensus among cheese makers is that the only mould you need to worry about is black mould. Any other colour will not damage you. Your nose is the best guide - if it smells bad, don't eat it. Cutting off mould will stop it from tainting the taste of the cheese but it's not dangerous. Blue mould (Penicillium Roqueforti) is very predatory and will invade other cheeses. The white rind on brie and camembert is also Penicillium mould.

questions.question: How did Jesus find people in his area within his time named Matthew, Luke, John, etc.? These are very Western names.

answers.answer: These are Western varieties of the same root names. Luke would have been Greek-speaking, probably from Antioch. The names in our English Bibles are not the names they would have been known by. John would have been Yanis or Johannes in other forms.

The stories were first recorded in Aramaic, then passed through Greek and Latin, and then anglicised versions of Norman French. That's a five-step translation process. Jesus wasn't called Jesus - he was probably called Yehoshua or Yeshua. Peter was actually called Cephas, which means 'the rock' - a nickname and bodyguard's name. Many of the names were nicknames. Paul changed from Saul - Paul comes from Paulus, a Latin word meaning small, possibly taken from his protector Sergius Paulus. The stories were translated multiple times before reaching us.

questions.question: Why is Snow White?

answers.answer: Snow is made out of lots of tiny ice crystals. When light comes through, it scatters off all the different wavelengths of light because the crystals are randomly oriented. This reflects all the different colours of the rainbow, which adds up to make white.

questions.question: How do football players, in the middle of a football match, hold it when they're really desperate for the toilet?

answers.answer: Players do a wee just before they come on and again at half-time. There's no rule against running off to the toilet and coming back. If you don't drink too much before the game, you won't need to go until half-time.
Gary Lineker's incident wasn't in Japan - it was during Italia 90 when he did the business on the pitch.

questions.question: Why don't you get big variations in size between animals of the same species? Like tall pigeons, or Labradors that are all the same height, or two tall lions?

answers.answer: You're wrong. If you measured a hundred pigeons, there would be a tallest one and a shortest one with 98 in between. The incremental difference between a medium pigeon and a large pigeon would be barely noticeable to us but they exist.
They're different heights, different weights, different sizes. When I used to race pigeons, my mate Mark had a huge blue cock and I've only got a small little red one.

questions.question: Why are four-letter words and swearing offensive? When did they become offensive?

answers.answer: Probably when the Normans came. They tried to change the language to French. Though all Anglo-Saxon words would be offensive, not just the offensive ones.

questions.question: Which is heavier, still water or sparkling water?

answers.answer: We presume water with more air in it is lighter than water without. But it's carbon dioxide, not air. Carbon dioxide might be heavier than air, which would mean it would sink.

Carbonated water is heavier than still water. Density equals mass equals weight. If you take a litre of water and add something (carbon dioxide), you've made it more dense, more massive, therefore more weight. So whether it's a litre or 10,000 litres, sparkling water is heavier than still.

questions.question: Why do Americans on TV shows always bring their groceries home in paper bags without handles and struggle with them, especially going up steps? Why don't they use carrier bags like we do?

answers.answer: My daughter lives in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. When you do go grocery shopping, they always say 'would you like paper or plastic?' Americans prefer paper. And if you're going straight to the boot of the car, plastic bags don't have the same value.

Different policies depending on where you live. I live an hour north of New York City and we have to bring our own bags. No bags at all in stores. The paper bags on TV shows are probably just a nostalgic depiction, like people thinking England is still in fog.

questions.question: Why are some dogs determined to fetch massively, disproportionately big sticks? What is it in their psychology that makes them do this?

answers.answer: A dog sees a stick as a trophy. The bigger the stick, the bigger the trophy. It raises their status and gets them attention. Dogs that do this are using the trophy tactic to raise their status. There are four ways dogs raise their status: trophies (sticks), food (how they eat), hunting (who leads walks), and danger (who protects them).

questions.question: Is there a collective noun for things that go through you - like nails on blackboard, wet tea bags, cutlery on grainy plates?

answers.answer: It's called misophonia. It's the way your brain processes sounds and nerve pain. With conditions like fibromyalgia and ADHD, the brain misreads signals. In certain sounds like nails on a chalkboard or loud chewing, your brain misreads the signal for a pain sound, causing actual physical pain or revulsion. It's a misfiring of signals.

questions.question: Why did my mosquito bites stop itching the moment I landed in London from St. Lucia, even though the red blotches are still there?

answers.answer: Your skin becomes less sensitive in cold weather to protect you from frostbite. A 35-degree temperature differential could cause this. It's an unexpected side effect of evolutionary protections against excess cold.

questions.question: Was it illegal to record the Top 40 off Radio 1 onto cassette tapes as a child? And was anyone ever prosecuted for it?

answers.answer: If you then broadcast it, it would be illegal. But just keeping recordings for personal use - I think people used to say you weren't allowed to do it.

It was definitely illegal. My dad was a composer and my mum was an expert in music copyright. They were part of a campaign to legalise home taping. They even wrote a song about it: 'Legalise home taping, just a few pence on a blank cassette.'

questions.question: When the World Cup's on TV and the fans are singing Sweet Caroline, does Neil Diamond get royalties?

answers.answer: No. You can't get royalties for that. Who would pay them?
No. I've played Sweet Caroline for considerably longer than I would be allowed to play Sweet Caroline for on the radio without paying royalties to Neil Diamond.

questions.question: If you were to go to a therapist and say something that traumatized the therapist, would they be allowed to go to another therapist and breach the confidentiality by talking to them?

answers.answer: They wouldn't be breaching the confidentiality because they wouldn't reveal any details of who it was. All therapists, as part of their training, do two hours of therapy a week themselves. And they do assessment supervision where they talk about their experiences as a therapist with an Uber therapist. So it is a part of the training to talk about what you learn when you are doing your therapy yourself.

If somebody discloses something to us that is disturbing, if it triggers something in us, that's what we take to supervision to our clinical supervisor, not an Uber therapist. And we discuss that. We don't disclose any identifiable details about the person. And it's not necessarily what they went through. It's about how it's triggered something in us, how we're working with it. Supervision is about how we're working - how you are doing your job as a therapist. There are times when we have to disclose information, but they are few and far between. And that's discussed with the client beforehand, so they know what the parameters are before the therapy starts.

questions.question: What are the bristles for on the escalator that are about ankle height coming out the side of the elevator?

answers.answer: I personally use them to polish my shoes when I go down the escalator.
I don't know. I wear trainers mostly these days, but if I'm ever wearing grown-up shoes, I give them a quick buff.

They are purely for safety. They are a barrier between you and the edge of the escalator. They can't have anything fixed on the escalator because you might get snagged in that. So the bristle, you will move through them, but you can feel them. People get their shoelaces caught in the mechanisms or something like that. You see people hanging their jackets down and it's the bristles that stop them getting snagged in the side.

questions.question: Tyson Fury sang the whole of American Pie at Wembley Stadium after annihilating Dillian White. Would Don McLean get a royalty?
