answers.answer: He wouldn't make a royalty for that because it's not an organized public performance or a public broadcast. The key word is organized. Ordinarily venues, stadiums, whatever, they pay a license fee and that covers the performance of music in their venues. But whoever is performing the song, if they're playing a recording or if a band is playing live or whatever, they will send the return to a royalty collection agency to say this is what was performed, this is who wrote it, this is who needs to get the royalties. And that's not going to happen for a crowd. But it would happen for the halftime entertainment - if the stadium was to perform a song live, he will get a royalty because he will have claimed that he did a live performance of his song in front of that many people. For Tyson Fury singing American Pie in its entirety at Wembley, no royalty there because it wasn't organized or scheduled. If it's impromptu, there's no royalties. The royalties come in a pot form via the Performing Rights Society. Every venue pays their money. It all goes into a giant pot. And then you qualify for a slice of the pot if your song has been sung as part of the scheduled event. It depends on size of venue, size of artist, size of song.

questions.question: When you see circus acts throw axes at a target, with a lady standing there with her legs and arms out, it always lands point first. Why does it always land point first and never drop to the floor, considering the axes going 360 degrees and at some point the handle, the blunt part would be facing down?

answers.answer: Because of all the training they do.
I went axe throwing last night. Half the axes didn't stick. Possibly more than half.

There's a right distance from the target relative to the length of the blade and the handle. It rotates a single time, and pretty much every single time it'll stick into the board. It takes a little bit of practice to get to that point. In a circus, you're going to have your mark delineated fairly clearly on the floor. It's one rotation. If you get the distance right, it's one rotation.

questions.question: What's the difference between an evergreen and a deciduous tree? I mean, what causes an evergreen tree to keep its leaves and the deciduous tree? Why do some shed their leaves and others don't?
You see goose fat for sale everywhere in the supermarkets. You never see goose meat. What happens to the rest of the goose?

answers.answer: Geese and ducks are actually the same species, and whether the goose or a duck is completely arbitrary. So maybe the goose meat ends up being sold as duck, and therefore we do get through quite a lot of duck in Chinese food and similar.
You can buy goose to eat. You can buy full birds. You can buy a crown of goose. The fat will just get taken off when it gets sold.

We import it all from France. All the fat. And then we're looking at foie gras and they eat more goose than we do. I've never seen a jar that says sauce at UK on it. It's always from France or other countries where goose is regularly eaten.

questions.question: A fly can fly high, but how high can a fly fly?

answers.answer: It's not so much to do with how high a fly can fly of its own power. It's more to do with the atmosphere and thermals. They get entrained in thermals, which are rising columns of air. The limit is generally towards cloud base, which on a good summer's day could be as much as 11,000 feet. But the rising columns of air continue into the cloud and accelerate when they get in the cloud. And the flies would continue going up. If it were a thunderstorm cloud, that could be several multiples of tens of thousands of feet up to 50,000, 60,000 feet. By which time the fly is pretty much dead and pre-frozen. If it's not flying, it's dead. I would argue that falling upwards is probably akin to flying.

questions.question: When you have a tooth pulled, the nerves and pain receptors know it's gone and that's the end of it. However, when you suffer an amputation, you can still feel phantom sensations and pains in it. Why is that? Why do the nerves not understand one thing's gone but they can understand another has?

answers.answer: None of us feel anything in our fingers ever. What we actually do is feel it in our brain. Your brain hasn't changed, even though your finger has been removed.

Phantom tooth pain is a well-known phenomenon. It's called atypical facial pain. There's a special clinic for that problem at the Eastman Dental Hospital on Gray's Inn Road. It can be post-removal and then they call it phantom tooth pain. The classic scenario is you have a patient with several missing teeth in their mouth and the pain just seems to flip from tooth to tooth. It's a real phenomenon. There's a whole family of things. You can get burning mouth syndrome where a patient's mouth is burning. It's usually a diagnosis of last resort. Once you've excluded everything else, you come to the conclusion that it's not a local problem. It's more to do with the brain pathways of pain that are causing the problem rather than the actual disease itself.

questions.question: Why do we say Charlotte with a sh sound instead of Ch?

answers.answer: It comes from the French. Like charcuterie, which we say as charcuterie not sharcuterie. So it's the way the French pronounce it.

questions.question: Why is it the majority of elderly care homes are named after some sort of tree?

answers.answer: It conjures up nice imagery. Like the Forest Glades Leisure Center in Kidderminster, which was on a ring road and was about as sylvan as a mulberry. It was a multi-story car park, but it was called the Forest Glades. So that's why care homes are called that - it sounds nice.

questions.question: Can chickens have twins? Can one egg produce two chicks?

answers.answer: Yes, chickens can have twins. You can get a double yoker and both yolks can be fertilised, giving you the right initial ingredients for twins. But as they develop, the little air bubble in the egg that's designed as a chick Airbnb for one becomes too small. They can both develop and on an odd occasion both will hatch. Generally either one hatches and one dies, or they both die.

questions.question: Why is dust always grey?

answers.answer: Dust isn't actually grey, but we perceive it as grey. If dust comes from just one thing, like grinding white foam, it'll look white because all the dust is from the same source. But dust in your house comes from many different things, and when you mix lots of different colors together, you generally get an average gray color. It's the same as your television with RGB - you can make gray out of those three colors in equal amounts. The colors all merge into one and that one is grey.

questions.question: Why are some countries on their football scoreboard shown with their own national flag abbreviations like ESP for Spain, but Germany is shown as GER rather than DEU for Deutschland?

answers.answer: It depends on whose feed we're watching. Whoever owns the original broadcast rights decides the abbreviations. Many channels piggyback off others rather than having their own cameramen in the stadium.

If it's a UK broadcast, if the abbreviation is still recognisable like ESP for Spain, they leave it. But if it's completely unrecognizable like Greece which would be ELL in Greek, or Serbia which would be SRB, they change it to something recognisable like GRE and SER. So if it's recognisable, they leave it, if it's unrecognizable, they change it.

questions.question: How do dogs know what time of day it is?

answers.answer: The dog doesn't know it's five o'clock, the dog knows it's dinner time. Its body is telling it at the level of hunger. If you started feeding the dog at four o'clock every day, after a week the dog would come and hit you at four o'clock.

It's based around smell. A study showed that when a person leaves for work, their scent gradually fades throughout the day. The dog notices when the scent reaches a certain level and knows the owner will be home soon. When the clocks go forward or back, the dog gets confused because the gap between feeds changes.

questions.question: Why has denim clothing always been mostly blue whilst clothing made from other fabrics has always been a wide range of different colors?

answers.answer: It's because it stays blue. There's something about indigo that gets into the fabric in a way that keeps the colour more than any other colour. If you dyed it a different colour, it would fade a lot more quickly. Back in the day, it was also about what was available and what wasn't available.

Indigo comes from indicum in Latin, meaning origins from India, about 4000 years ago. It was used in blue ceramic and mosaic until yarn dying came along, which Germany brought to the world in the early 19th century. Indigo latches onto the fibres of white yarn in such a way that it penetrates the molecular structure deeply. Indigo is the best choice because it has the least wash fastness - no matter how many washes you do, it'll fade but it'll never leave the fibre. That's why they favoured it for denim. The fading effect you get from different percentages of dye in the dye baths gives you different shades of blue denim.

questions.question: Where are the flies that invade dead bodies? The coroner said they arrive within 25 minutes. Where do they hang out the rest of the time - in nests, underground, in little holes?

answers.answer: They're not specifically box flies - they're various insects already around in the environment. The body, once it dies, secretes very subtle smells within anywhere between half an hour and three hours depending on temperature conditions. It's the smell of the body that attracts the flies. They're not hiding anywhere, they're just knocking around doing their thing, and when they catch a whiff on the wind, they come in. In hotter countries this happens quicker, in colder countries not so quickly. Within 12 hours the body is more or less consumed.

questions.question: What does 'tog' mean on duvets? Is it a measurement of thickness, heat resistance, or something made up by duvet manufacturers?
Who is Gordon Bennett? Did he ever exist?

answers.answer: He was a New York newspaper proprietor, a bit like Donald Trump before he turned evil - exuberant, rich and known as a bit of a lad. He was a Barnum-type figure coming up with great wheezes. His name became a byword for being surprised because instead of saying 'Gor blimey', you'd say 'Gordon Bennett'.

questions.question: Why are you allowed to have all those small 100ml bottles of liquid at airport security but you can't take a big bottle like a bottle of coke or water?

answers.answer: It's a security measure. If you've got corrosive liquid and you need half a litre to make an impact, having to empty out five little bottles to deploy it makes it much harder. But James acknowledged there are ways around it.

Air Force Security reduces the amount of product you can bring through. If you mix certain products together, particularly things in shampoos and cleaning materials, they can become dangerous and give off gases. By reducing it to 100ml, you don't have enough of the product to bring together to become a hazard. They test the bottles and make you taste them sometimes.

questions.question: Why can you smell things when you breathe in through your nose but then you can't smell them when you breathe out through your nose?

answers.answer: When you breathe in, odorant binding proteins along the mucus in your nose grab what you smell and take it to the receptors. When you breathe out, you're respiring - breathing in oxygen and breathing out carbon dioxide and nitrogen. There's nothing for those proteins to grab and take to your receptors to smell.

questions.question: Why do some of us get goosebumps or tingles when listening to music, but other people don't? My friend doesn't get this with any music.
If you're swimming in the sea and lightning strikes, how far away would you have to be for you not to get electrocuted?
Why do some tins stack with little lips onto each other but others like Heinz soup tins don't stack properly?

answers.answer: It has to do with how they're manufactured. Some tins are rolled up metal that's stuck together, while others like Heinz are pressed through to form a shape with just the lid on top. The pressed ones are higher quality and less likely to have seals break and cause leaks, which is why soup uses the better tin but also why they don't stack. The cheaper rolled tins are used for the beans.

It's to do with the cooking process. When they can beans, they seal them and cook at a different temperature by steam. The ingredients are put in the can, the can is sealed, and then the contents are cooked inside, which creates pressure. Different cans are manufactured to withstand different pressures, and that determines their stackability. The ones cooked under pressure end up with the slightly different shape.

questions.question: Is it possible for a celebrity to copyright or trademark their voice? What stops a company using an impressionist instead of paying for the real celebrity?

answers.answer: Two parts: First, the Advertising Standards Authority has rules about passing off - they wouldn't allow someone to use an impression that leads people to think the celebrity actually sanctioned their product. Commercials go through approval processes. Second, for copyright, it's more complicated. There's a Copyright Act going through Parliament that will change things with AI. Currently, if someone synthesizes your voice, you'd have no rights under the new act. AI companies can scrape information to learn from but not commercialize what they've learned - yet. The government seems to be leaning towards supporting innovation over protecting original artists' rights.

questions.caller: James from Crowthorne (on behalf of 6-year-old son Max)
questions.question: How does your body decide which end to produce gas from - burp or fart?

answers.answer: When we eat, we swallow air with the food. That air builds up in the stomach and the stomach releases it by breathing it out through the sphincter - that's a burp. The gases from the other end are produced during digestion in the intestines and bowels, and it's just too far for that gas to come back up, so it comes out the bottom. When you burp and can taste what you've eaten, it's because it's undigested - the air coming back up brings some of the aromas with it. Very hot food or fizzy drinks make you swallow more air, so you burp more.

questions.question: What was the name of that song on the new A-ha album that James loves?

answers.answer: It's called 'You Have What It Takes'.

questions.question: Why don't you wear a seatbelt on a train? My daughter says it's because it's on a fixed track.

answers.answer: The reason there will be much fewer accidents on a train than on a road is because it's on a fixed track. The much lower incidence of accidents, the fact that you hardly ever have circumstances where the driver's going to slam the brakes on and we're all going to lurch forward like we do in the car means seatbelts are less necessary.

The main reason is the rate of deceleration in a train. Wearing seatbelts protects you from sudden deceleration - you can get injured. On a train, the deceleration even under emergency braking, the train's so heavy and long that the rate of deceleration is still quite gradual. Even if you were stood on your feet and the driver applied the brake in emergency, the likelihood is you could still stay on your feet.

questions.question: How can you find out if you were christened? My daughter is a mother of three and she can't remember if she was christened when she was younger. There must be a central register?

answers.answer: I don't think there would be a central register of christenings. You can find your birth certificate but not christening. You need to know the church. Sometimes you need to prove you're christened - I think the only position is Lord Chancellor or something.

There is no central register for christenings, so if somebody would like to enquire whether they were baptised, they'd have to go back to local churches and ask to go through the registers. Some churches will charge a £10 fee for going through the register. Work out where mum was born and the more likely it is that if they were christened, it would have been in a nearby church. Theologically, you can't be baptised more than once. If somebody was unsure, in the Church of England we would do something called a conditional baptism, just in case.

questions.question: With fizzy drinks, why do they fizz up much more when you have ice in the glass compared to an empty glass?

answers.answer: Surface area is involved. It's not temperature - a frozen glass wouldn't fizz up more than an unfrozen one. The drink meeting a surface area releases the gas.

This is a version of the Coca-Cola Mentos experiment. The ice has got lots of corners and rough edges, and what that does is provide nucleation sites for the dissolved carbon dioxide to come out of solution. It just drops out of solution, whereas in a clean glass there are no rough edges. You can demonstrate this with champagne - the bubbles always seem to come from the same place on the glass because of a little scratch which causes nucleation. When you put soda in your mouth and it gets sparkling, it's because your taste buds are forming rough edges for the nucleation. It's more to do with rough edges than temperature.

questions.question: Why are there 12 people on a jury? It felt a bit biblical but it can't go back that far.

answers.answer: I don't know why 12. It might be biblical or go back to William the Conqueror around 1066 when trial by jury began. You'd think it'd be an odd number so you could always have a result, but the judge determines if it can be a majority or unanimous verdict.

answers.caller: Gina (Exeter, PhD in Arab and Islamic studies)
answers.answer: It comes back from the Crusader era. The Knights Templar picked it up from the Middle East and that derives from Sharia, which means 12-member jury. It's called Islamic Lafif, and Lafif translates to the body of 12. And that in turn comes from the pre-Islamic practice of Bedouin consensus within a tribe - in the desert they would have a consensus before electing a leader or a warrior or a commander, and they had to have at least 12 wise men sit down.

questions.question: The Luck of the Irish - why are the Irish so lucky?

answers.answer: The answer is America and gold mining. The Irish were particularly adept in the gold rush at finding gold, and the Luck of the Irish became an American meme and it then made its way back over the Atlantic to Ireland itself.

questions.question: Why does pain ease when you touch it? When we bang something, the instant reaction is to put our hand on it and it lessens the pain.

answers.answer: I'm trying to think if there's an obvious answer to do with blood flow or something, or warmth? Sometimes it's just reassurance.

answers.caller: Shlomi (Manchester, final year occupational therapy student)
answers.answer: It doesn't actually take the pain away. You're just applying pressure to the area which gives you proprioceptive feedback, which is a very nice feeling. It makes you feel better. And because it's a nice feeling to the same area. But it's only a nice feeling when you're in pain. It's not a nice feeling when you're not in pain. Like babies or people with sensory issues crave lots of input. Pain is not an actual thing - it's something individual. It's not something that's in your head. Both sensations are in your head. It's an evolutionary protection against carrying on doing things that are going to hurt you even more.

questions.question: Why do people across the country in primary schools sing 'good morning' back in a weird melody?

answers.answer: It's the nature of speaking in concert - it's a way to introduce a rhythm so everyone is speaking in unison. Otherwise they'd all be starting at slightly different points. It's just easy to do. Sing-song is the easier option.

questions.question: Why don't we sneeze when we're asleep? As an allergic person I sneeze a lot when I wake up but never once have I startled myself awake sneezing.

answers.answer: We do breathe through the nose when sleeping - you're snoring. Everything relaxes when we're asleep. Lots of things you don't do in your sleep that you do while awake - and I don't think you cough in your sleep either.

questions.question: In multi-cat households, do the cats talk to one another? Do they have conversations?

answers.answer: You're being a bit anthropomorphic. They must have some forms of communication but you're being a bit excessive with the imagination.

Adult cats don't communicate by meowing. They only communicate with each other by body language. They will definitely be communicating with each other - I fostered loads of cats and they always show the new guy where the food is, where the litter tray is, all that sort of stuff. Cats only learned how to meow back in ancient Egyptian times because they realised humans were a bit of a pushover. They tried to mimic the noise that sounded most like a baby because they noticed that's when humans came running. Cats only meow to do impressions of human babies. You will rarely see an adult cat meow to another adult cat - they'll hiss at each other but they won't meow the same way.

questions.question: Why are old keyholes in doors upside down compared to how we imagine modern lock keyholes to be? On old clock tower doors, the round bit is at the bottom and narrow bit at the top, the opposite of modern keys.

answers.answer: I don't know why they're different. It's something we're going to try and find out.

questions.question: With the exception of the 100 metres, every other running event in athletics goes anti-clockwise around the track. Why is it we go anti-clockwise?

answers.answer: I think there was one meeting in the beginning of the 20th century where they ran clockwise and something went wrong.
At the first London Olympics, the monarch had to be on the finish line. They built a stadium, put the Royal Box at the end of the finishing straight, so there was only one way they could run.

questions.question: If the sun's rays are parallel, then eclipses don't cause two shadow types, an umbra and a penumbra. And if rays do come in at all angles, then Eratosthenes' test that we can test the Earth's rotundity is also out. So which fact is true, James?

answers.answer: Both are correct for a given level of correctness. When the rays leave the sun, they fly off in all directions, but by the time they get here, they are more or less parallel and close enough to parallel to make a good guess at the Earth's circumference. If light from the bottom of the sun hits the top of an object and light from the top of the sun hits the bottom, that creates the outer shadow (penumbra). If the top of the sun aligns with the top of the object and bottom of sun aligns with bottom of object, you get the inner shadow (umbra). If they were precisely parallel, you wouldn't get both shadows. But by the time they reach Earth, they're so close together they're as near damn it to parallel.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'you've been fired' come from? I understand someone being sacked because they might get a sack to clear their belongings. But why 'fired'?

answers.answer: Sacked comes from trades - you were given a bag to put your tools in and could go find a job somewhere else. Fired meant your tools were actually burned or destroyed so you couldn't go and get a job anywhere else. So there were different levels of losing your job - laid off was sacked, but if you did something egregious you were fired.

questions.question: What happens when an unstoppable force meets an immovable object? Does this question admit an answer?

answers.answer: The answer is they are mutually contradictory - only one can exist. If something is irresistible, then something else can't be immovable and vice versa. There's also a song lyric: 'When an irresistible force such as you meets an immovable object like me, something's got to give.'

questions.question: We have cheesemongers, fishmongers, ironmongers. Why do we call a butcher a butcher and not a meatmonger?

answers.answer: Monger is an old English Anglo-Saxon expression for trade person - ironmonger was a blacksmith. Butchery, baking, cooking were community services done amongst the community rather than trades in the Anglo-Saxon period. If you wanted meat, you'd buy an ox off a cow herd, take it back to your village and they would butcher it up as needed. Butchery came after the Norman Conquest - it's a French word (boucherie). As we urbanised, we needed specialist people to cut up meat for us.

questions.question: Is there officially a most isolated place in the whole world? I read about a range of mountains in the Antarctic that only about a dozen people have ever seen.

answers.answer: The most isolated place is Point Nemo in the Pacific Ocean. If you're on a boat there, you have to travel over a thousand miles to get to the nearest landmass or any other human beings. It's also called a spacecraft graveyard - when decommissioning rockets or satellites, they plot trajectories to crash there because it's so isolated they won't harm anybody. The closest human beings to you at Point Nemo would actually be astronauts on the International Space Station if they're flying overhead.

questions.question: How are military personnel selected for royal funerals? Why were pallbearers flown back from Iraq specifically for the Queen's funeral?

answers.answer: All personnel on parade are part of Operation London Bridge. Units that traditionally had links to the sovereign were invited to provide people for certain roles - each regiment has plans in place. The pallbearers all came from the Queen's Company, First Battalion Grenadier Guards, of which Her Majesty was traditionally the company commander. There was a minimum height requirement of six foot two (now dropped to five foot ten) so everyone was the same height when carrying the coffin, making it move smoothly and look uniform.

questions.question: At what point does dressing up as a police officer become impersonating a police officer? If you're wearing black trousers, black shoes and a jacket with 'police' on the back, is that impersonation?

answers.answer: Section 90, subsection 2 of the Police Act 1996 covers this. It says if you wear articles of police uniform in circumstances which give you the appearance of resembling a police officer, and it's so close that the conclusion would be you're intending to deceive people, then that's the point. Impersonation requires intent to deceive rather than just appearance.

questions.question: Why do newsreaders always say 'a short time ago in the city' rather than giving a specific time when reporting financial markets?

answers.answer: You can't be too specific because the numbers might have changed by the time the bulletin is read. It's quite hard to change autocue mid-bulletin and it's dangerous to faff about with it. 'A short time ago' gives you a bit of wiggle room.

The bulletin is written a short time before it's read out. By the time the newsreader gets to the studio and reads the FTSE 100 figure, it might be out of date. If you said a specific time like 'at 9:04' and someone checked and it was actually six minutes ago, you'd get into trouble. 'A short time ago' covers you. Former BBC newsreader.

questions.question: When you have cooking aluminium foil on a roll, it has a shiny side and a matte side. Which is the right side, and why are they different?

answers.answer: It's just a manufacturing process involving big hot wheels and melty metal. The shiny side and matte side is a consequence of production and has no bearing on the actual efficacy of the foil. You can wrap your salmon either way and it will make no difference.

During manufacture, aluminium is rolled between rollers to make it thinner. When it gets very close to foil thickness, they put two strips together and roll them together as a sandwich. The shiny side is the side that was in contact with the shiny rollers. The matte side is the middle where the two sheets were in contact with each other. When they separate the two strips, you get one coil with shiny outside and matte inside. No recommendation on which side to use. The rough matte side is more likely to stick to something than the shiny side, so if you don't want your salmon to stick, put the shiny side away from the fish surface. Alan worked in the aluminium industry and with an aluminium foil manufacturer.

questions.question: Why do we say things are old in expressions like 'funny old game' or 'funny old weather'? Why do we use the word 'old' when describing things?

answers.answer: It's a way to convey that this is a long-established trope. 'Funny old game' suggests you've watched so much football over the years that you've concluded it's a funny old game - it's not just a funny game, it's an old game. Same with funny old weather - they've watched the weather for a long time and concluded it's an unpredictable old business.

questions.question: How do toenails or fingernails grow back when they've been removed completely? Is there a root or follicle thing?

answers.answer: Hair and toenails are both made of keratin. That's what I remember from school.

Toenails do grow back as long as the nail bed is still there. The nail bed is part of the bone at the end of your toe - that's where the nail grows from. I've had my toenail surgically removed about four times until they eventually took the nail bed off, and after that it never grew back. So as long as the nail bed is intact, the nail will keep coming back. If you just pull the nail out, it will come back again and again. Geoff's condition was ingrown toenail.

questions.question: Why is a tea towel called a tea towel?

answers.answer: We need to distinguish it from other towels. Maybe it's what you have with your tea. But actually, James confused tea towel with tea cosy. Acknowledged he might be completely wrong. Promised to find out.

questions.question: Where does the wax go once a candle in a jar is all gone? Do we breathe it in?

answers.answer: It's like petrol or wood or coal - it goes up the chimney into the atmosphere. There's a chemical reaction (combustion) that breaks it down into gases which float away. You'll probably get some water which goes away as steam, and some carbon dioxide. The solid is being burnt. The wax is combusted.

questions.question: Where does all the rubber from car tyres go? It's not at the side of the road.

answers.answer: It comes off in tiny amounts, becomes dust, gets blown around in tiny particles. When it rains it gets washed down the drains. That's why roads need to be irrigated.

Around 10% by mass gets airborne (microplastics), and around 90% by mass ends up on the road as a mixture of rubber and minerals because the tyre rubber interacts with the road surface. You get much more of it around junctions and traffic lights where people are braking - the energy of braking or cornering produces the tyre dust. It gets washed to the gulleys to the side of the road, ends up in sewage sludge, in fields, in oceans and rivers. The airborne stuff is a concern because it gets into the sea and some nasty stuff called 6-PPD leaches out of it and becomes highly toxic - it's killing coho salmon in the Pacific northwest of the USA. David runs Tire Industry Research.

questions.question: What shape is a slice of pizza?

answers.answer: It's a triangular prism! It's three straight lines on the sides and a curved base but still has three sides.

On a 2D plate, a pizza slice is called a 'sector' - it has an arc and two radii. On a 3D slice, it's a 'sectorial prism.' 'Triangular prism' is more like Toblerone, not pizza. John in Newcross confirmed: the 2D shape is a sector, the 3D shape is a sectorial prism. Someone suggested 'circular sector' as the answer.

questions.question: Why does cold water taste colder after eating a mint? Why does water seem to have a cooling effect after mint?

answers.answer: It's menthol. Your mouth feels cooler when you eat a mint, everything is cool. In the same way that if you eat a chilli, water helps get the effects of chilli spreading around. Maybe the water activates the menthol receptors more. James thought the receptors were called PH24s but was unsure.

It's not PH13 or PH24, it's TRP. Specifically TRPM8 (transient receptor potential melastatin 8). It's a protein in your mouth that gets activated when menthol is present. When you drink water, it activates more of these receptors, which tricks your mouth into thinking it's cold. Chris is a biomedical sciences graduate.

questions.question: Have you ever seen a baby pigeon?

answers.answer: Yes, I have. I saw one outside KFC in Brentford. A baby pigeon fell from its nest up above on the canopy, and a lovely man had picked it up and was looking after it. They were trying to work out how to get it back up to its nest using KFC furniture.

questions.question: Why does the water seem a lot colder after eating a mint?

answers.answer: It's menthol. Your mouth feels cooler when you eat a mint. When you drink water, it activates the receptors more, spreading the menthol around, tricking your mouth into thinking it's cold. James thought the receptors were called PH24s.

It's the TRPM8 receptors (transient receptor potential melastatin 8). When menthol is in your mouth, it activates these receptors. When you drink water, it activates more of them, so it tricks your mouth into thinking it's cold. There is no known evolutionary purpose for this. Chris is a biomedical sciences graduate.

questions.question: Why do we categorise certain foods for certain meals or times of day? Why wouldn't you have a steak sandwich for breakfast or porridge for dinner?

answers.answer: It's cultural. I worked on ships for about 10 years with many nationalities, particularly Filipinos, and whether you're in the crew mess or officers' mess, there's always a big vat of white rice at every meal. I also think preparation time matters - most people aren't going to cook a steak and eggs on a weekday morning. But mainly it's cultural - stereotypes speak to a culture's breakfast.

The size of the meal might differ - we have smaller meals for breakfast because we've only just woken up. But actually, there's also something about pork marketing - they created the idea that sausages and bacon would be good for breakfast. And Kellogg invented cornflakes as part of some weird health movement.

It's traditional and all to do with going to the paddy fields with a full stomach in the early hours of the morning so that you don't get hungry until lunchtime. The paddy fields could be miles away from your home, so it would be difficult to pop home for a quick snack. For peasant farmers, rice was the most cost-effective and available food item, and the tradition has carried on into modern times.

questions.question: In fantasy and sci-fi, something amazing happens when all the planets line up. In reality, when planets do line up, does anything interesting actually happen?

answers.answer: You'd get an eclipse, wouldn't you? When I was a kid in Australia, we had an eclipse and it was amazing. So amazing things happen when planets align - you get an eclipse.

Contrary to what you'd see in Disney's Hercules, when the planets align, nothing happens. They're basically too far apart. When scientists say the planets align, they don't really align - they're just in the same section of sky. Any gravity interference between planets would be negligible. For a grand conjunction, there's nothing special happening at all. When you look at a picture of the solar system, they're all on a flat plane, but they're actually off kilter. The last planetary alignment was in 2020 - loads of articles popped up and people were worried about cataclysmic events, but nothing happened. It's usually 3 to 5 to 7 planets aligning, not all of them - it takes several thousand years for all of them to align. I used to work at the University of Kent Space School.

questions.question: Why is soapbox racing called soapbox racing?

answers.answer: It's because the original go-karts were made out of boxes that soap came in, weren't they?

questions.question: How is the average global temperature calculated? You need points to measure the temperature - are there satellites? Where do the measuring points come from?

answers.answer: There are weather stations positioned all over the planet on both land and out at sea on ocean buoys. They're positioned away from urban heat islands to avoid the influence of man-made heat. The ones on land are put in Stevenson screens - a box like a beehive - to make sure you don't get direct sunlight on the instrumentation; you just get the air going in and out. The Met Office has several hundred, but data is collected from national weather services around the planet. Prior to modern instrumentation, proxy records were collected from dendroclimatology (tree ring density) and ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica to measure oxygen levels and air bubbles. Climate scientists do hindcast models to understand what impacts would have occurred with and without human influence. My master's was in climate change.

questions.question: Why do you call it bubble and squeak? The leftovers of Sunday dinner?

answers.answer: It makes a bubbling and squeaking sound when you cook it. You've got it all mushed up together so it has air bubbles in it, and that creates a sort of squeaking and bubbling sound when you fry it.

questions.question: There's crossovers between English and French days of the week named after celestial bodies - Monday/Mondi (Moon), Tuesday/Mardi (Mars), Wednesday/Mercury - but in English you have Saturday (Saturn) and Sunday (Sun). But there's nothing for Friday and Thursday. Why isn't there a celestial body for those days?

answers.answer: Thursday is named after Thor, a Norse god. Friday is named after Freya, a Norse goddess. In French, those days are named after the corresponding Roman gods - Jupiter for Thursday (Jeudi), Venus for Friday (Vendredi). So all days are named after gods, not planets - it's the Norse equivalents in English and Roman equivalents in French.

questions.question: Why do we get our age wrong? A baby is born and 12 months later we say they're one. They've experienced their second Christmas, second Easter, second of everything, but we say they're one. How are they one when they've been through everything twice?

answers.answer: How many birthdays does the average human have? One. You're born, and that's it. Everything afterwards is a celebration. When you're one year old, you're having your second Easter. You've already had one birthday (the day you were born), and then you have your first birthday as a celebration of your first anniversary. You're between zero and one. You've gone round again but know it's your second time. It's a bit of a logical fallacy - the chap was confused about the difference between the day you're born and your first birthday celebration.

questions.question: Why are the vast majority of semi-detached houses built living room to living room and not front door to front door? A friend lived in one that was front door to front door and said it meant less noisy neighbours.

answers.answer: I'm wondering if it's anything to do with cost - like electrical wiring, bringing it in and splitting the cost. Or maybe it's the staircases - they might be easier to align. Or possibly chimneys. Semi-detached houses often share a chimney.

Houses are hallway to hallway in the older houses. When they first started running cables into houses, it was paper, wax-insulated cable - very expensive. To save cost of running one into each house, they would run into one and then go back through the wall to the other house to put a meter on each side.
The big one with developers is snobbery. Nobody wants to go into a house next door to the neighbour, so they keep it apart so it doesn't look like a terrace. That's from a developer's mouth.

questions.question: Why does flotsam on the water go in the opposite direction to the tide? When the tide is coming in, the leaves and twigs go back out to sea. And vice versa - when the tide goes out, sometimes the leaves go the other way. It happens every day and it's not the wind.
None - this was an answer to the days of week question that was cut off earlier

answers.answer: We need to think of gods rather than celestial bodies. When looking at French days, we're looking at old Romano gods - Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn. In England, we're looking at Germanic Norse gods and their equivalents: Tiw is the god of war (equivalent of Mars), Woden/Odin is Mercury, Thor is Jupiter/Jerdi, and Freya is Venus (Thor and Freya's mother). So all the days are named after gods.

questions.question: Who's the shortest-serving Chancellor of the Exchequer?

answers.answer: It must be Nadim Zahawi, but it wasn't. It was someone muck someone. I'll find out for you, mate.

Ian McLeod. He was appointed after the 1970 election by Edward Heath. He lasted a month and sadly died in 11 Downing Street at the heart attack, I think on 20th of July. He was replaced by Anthony Barber, who until very recently was regarded as having brought in the worst financial policy in the history of these islands.

questions.question: How do knives work?

answers.answer: How do knives work? Crucial difference. It's GCSE physics - pressure equals force over area. For a given force, the smaller the area, the greater the pressure you're bringing to bear. That's why needles go through skin rather than a piece of dowel, why cheese wire cuts through cheese, and why knives cut through anything. Because they have a very, very small surface area in contact with the mushroom or the piece of meat. The sharper the blade, the greater the pressure. And it's why sharp knives are safer than blunt knives because you don't push down as hard with them.

questions.question: Musical annotation, was that invented by one person or was it just something that evolved?

answers.answer: In about the eighth century, there was a monk in Italy who came up with this idea. In the Middle Ages, they would sing most of the Bible and all of the texts in services, and it was hard to remember. So he came up with a plan and wrote a single line, which was originally read. With one line, you can have three different pitched notes. That was the beginning, and then gradually more lines were added for more notes until eventually there were 11. And that was known as the Great Stave.

The Mesopotamians might have been the ones to have devised what we know now as the notation for music, through archaeology digs in modern-day Syria and Iraq, where tablets have been found with notes etched into clay. It was actually Guido of Arezzo who came up with a relatively similar system. How that started was when they were chanting religious scripts, they put little dashes so that all the monks could sing in unison. It just embellished over the years. It's quite basic - there's only really one way you could do it, a scale with gradations of tone.

questions.question: What's the difference between truth, fact and knowledge? Are they all the same? Are they intertwined?

answers.answer: Knowledge is a collection of facts. Knowledge is the bank and fact is the money. Truth and fact I think are synonyms - an objective truth is a fact. So truth and fact are the same and the place where they reside is called knowledge. If it's objective, it's a fact. A truth is absolutely objective. If it's subjective, it's a belief. And if it's a fact, an objective truth, then it makes up part of your knowledge. The idea is that when I give an answer, at that moment it's a truth, possibly a subjective truth. Then we establish whether or not it becomes an objective truth, at which point it becomes part of our shared knowledge.

questions.question: Why don't novels and books have the same [age ratings/parental guidance] as films?

answers.answer: Because you can judge a book by its cover. There are now attempts in academic institutions to do a form of warning or age rating called trigger warnings. Libraries used to have children's sections, adult fiction is a separate genre. You have a rough idea - if you're in the adult section, it's going to be an adult book. Books have been around longer than the idea that we should be limiting access to them.

You do get age ratings on books, particularly graphic novels. Graphic novels have imagery plus words. Age ratings on books are often marketing ploys. Things like The Boys - you could not give that to a child. And something like Titus Andronicus, the last scenes of it - that would need age rating.

questions.question: I've got a jigsaw, 1,000 pieces from the River Dee in the aqueduct... I've done about 55%, 60% of it. I'm just stuck. I just can't [continue]. What should I do?

answers.answer: You get all the straight bits and you make your edge. There's your frame. You get all the colours - you get your sky bits, your grass bits. You've got to keep putting every bit in. You've got 50 pieces, you get one to fit, then 48, 47, 46, 45. In the end, the last one goes in. You've just got to be bloody-minded. Just keep at it.

questions.question: Why is the first meal after you're married called a wedding breakfast considering they don't serve cereal, and it's an evening?

answers.answer: Married couples used to have to fast before they got married for religious reasons. So technically, you'd be breaking your fast when you have that first meal together. In the olden days, you'd be in the church, you'd be coming out of the church, and you'd be having a bit of cake or a biscuit or something. You'd be breaking the fast with a lovely treat. That's why it's called the wedding breakfast - it's literally breaking your fast.

questions.question: Is [a Shire horse] pulling the plough or pushing the plough?

answers.answer: The horse is pushing the yoke. The yoke is attached to the cart or plough. The horse pushes into the yoke, which in turn pulls the cart. So the horse is pushing the yoke, but that is why the horse is pulling the plough. You're both right. The yoke is the weapon, a means to an end. The horse is pushing the yoke but pulling the cart.

questions.question: Electronic readers like Kindles, how do books get on there? If it's a classic, would it have to be rewritten? Is there a way of photographing it with text recognition?

answers.answer: Someone's typed it in. They're going to have to retype all the classics. There are millions of books on these things. Everything that's available on paper now will have been electronically typeset. That's what they would use to put it onto a Kindle.

It's called OCR, Optical Character Recognition. You scan or photograph the page, the computer recognises the shapes of the letter. That is then translated into text and then it just needs to be proofread. So somebody somewhere has scanned every book ever written into a computer so that it could then appear on a Kindle. I spent 30 years in the railway signalling industry and we used OCR to translate standards originally typed on a typewriter into the computer.

questions.question: Where does Middle C come from?

answers.answer: I can't answer that one. You'll have to ask that separately... It obviously has something to do with the move from 11 lines to back down to five or six.

questions.question: If a child, like a little boy or little girl, was next in line for the throne and the monarch passed away, would that child be crowned king or queen?

answers.answer: You have a regent, someone who rules in place of until they are of an age. Henry VI was a kid when they came to the throne. Someone would look after it until they're 18 or something.

A child would become king or queen the moment the sovereign dies if he or she is heir apparent. Henry VI became king at six months old. Edward VI became king when he was nine. A regent would be appointed, traditionally the former king's brother if available. Coronation is not essential - Edward VIII was never crowned. If George is nine, he can stand upright and have a crown placed on him.

questions.question: Can deaf people who lip-read identify accents?

answers.answer: Just demonstrating different mouth shapes for different accents.

I am a lip reading teacher and quite deaf. I can't identify specific accents, but I can tell if someone doesn't have the same accent as me. When you're lip reading, your brain works harder than when just listening. For example, someone from the Midlands says 'bath' differently than I do, and it looks different in the mirror. I would know she's speaking in an accent not my normal one, but I couldn't say she was from Manchester or Liverpool specifically.

questions.question: Where did tying cans to newlyweds' cars originate? Just the cans themselves, not the 'just married' writing.

answers.answer: I don't know. Must have been the first person to do it.

questions.question: Is making tea using a kettle the only way to go? My partner says we should all be making tea in the microwave to save energy during the energy crisis. Is it really different?

answers.answer: It's wrong and gross. The water doesn't boil properly - you get little bubbles instead of big bubbles. You'll have a really hot mug. It's not going to work.

The answer is dissolved oxygen. When you heat water in a kettle, it's in contact with a surface at about 150 degrees which drives more oxygen out of the water. In a microwave, it's only ever at something approaching 100 degrees, so you have a greater degree of dissolved oxygen remaining. It just tastes different.

In the interest of science, I made tea using a microwave. Used a jug of water, half a liter. Took seven minutes to boil in a 240-volt microwave. I then poured into a mug with teabag and can report no difference in taste.

questions.question: Why do chameleons change to different colours of objects that come close by?

answers.answer: Chameleons change colour to match their background to avoid predators - it's camouflage. Like a green chameleon on a blue table, an eagle overhead wouldn't be able to see it against the blue background.

That's codswallop. I've been sold a lie all my life. It's not about camouflage at all. Chameleons change colour for two reasons: temperature regulation and communication with other chameleons. There's no evidence that if you put a chameleon on a green thing or a blue table it will turn that colour. It will only turn blue if it needs to change its temperature, or if the chameleon it's trying to attract likes the colour blue.

questions.question: How far along are we physically and mentally in terms of human potential? Usain Bolt ran the 100 metres so fast, but how fast can we really run? And on the mental side, if Einstein was X IQ, how far can we go?

answers.answer: We've been told there are parts of our brain we're not using. When you think of the four-minute mile and how excited everyone got, or the 10-second 100 metres, and now you wouldn't even get near records without modern equipment. If evolution has finished, who knows?

questions.question: Why are waiters called waiters when it's not them waiting for food? It's us that's waiting for the food.

answers.answer: There's the distinction between 'wait for' and 'wait on'. We wait for food, but the waiter waits on us - waiting for us to give orders, waiting for us to finish so they can clear plates. It's a semantic distinction.

questions.question: If I freeze food on its expiry date, when I defrost it a week later, have I bought myself any extra time to use the food, or does the clock start ticking again the moment it comes out of the freezer?

answers.answer: The enzymes would be rewound slightly rather than just picking up where they left off. The enzymes would sort of start again.

You don't get any extension on the shelf life. You don't reverse that degradation by freezing. I've been a chef for 20 years and used to be in charge of food safety for a large pub group. It often says to eat within 24 hours of defrosting. If it's a raw product you can cook, you reset the clock when you cook it. But if it's ready to eat, no, you don't get any extension.

questions.question: Why are goalkeeping tops always bigger/longer than outfield player tops? I had to put them in the same size top and the goalkeeping one is extra three to four inches longer.

answers.answer: The goalie doesn't tuck his shirt in because he's jumping about all the time, diving across. The goalie needs extra length so everyone doesn't see his midriff. Also goalkeepers are generally taller than outfield players.

The reason it's longer is so it stays tucked in when you're stretching for the top corner making saves. It's like a dress shirt - always a bit longer so it stays tucked in. The extra length keeps it tucked in when you're jumping around.

questions.question: Is there an agreed protocol between space agencies for if extraterrestrial life makes contact? Who would lead - would it be NASA, the Chinese, the Russians, the UN?

answers.answer: I haven't got a clue. Everyone would assume NASA, but the Chinese and Russians... I don't know why I said international. I'll find out.

questions.question: Why are green screens green? Why not blue or red or purple?

answers.answer: Green works best because there's very little green pigment in human skin. That's also why they use blue screens - very little blue in human skin. It's called chroma key. You can use any colour but green works best, except for green aliens where you'd use blue.

questions.question: What is the origin of the word 'flea' in flea market? Where does the phrase come from?

answers.answer: The idea is that if you're buying very old furniture, it's likely to have fleas in it. Flea markets began as house clearances.
Marche aux pouces is the French term for flea market

questions.question: Why does holding a car key fob to your temple make it work better from further away?

answers.answer: Your skull works like a bell - it's an amplifier. Your skull has echoing capacity unlike your chest or arm which aren't dome-shaped.
It's what's inside the skull - mainly water. The frequency of water matches the frequency of the signal, extending the range of the RF signal. Your brain is being used as an antenna.

questions.question: What is the longest queue ever in history? Where was it and what was it for?

answers.answer: The Baltic Chain in 1989 - over 2 million people queuing from Vilnius, Riga and Tallinn, holding hands and waiting for freedom/independence from the Soviet Union.
That's not a queue, it's an exodus - they were trying to get out of something, not wait for something.

questions.question: What era are we entering now that the Elizabethan era has ended?

answers.answer: Carolingian/Corollian. Carolingian refers to a whole dynasty (Charlemagne, Byzantine) so Carolian is correct. Also noted King Charles High School in Kidaminum has old Corollians rugby/cricket team founded by old boys.

questions.question: Why don't we have gendered nouns in English anymore? Why do German, French, Spanish still have them?

answers.answer: Indo-European languages historically had masculine-feminine-neuter system going back to animist beliefs where everything had a spirit with gender. English changed faster because it was creolized in the Dark Ages when Norse was widely spoken - similar vocabulary but different grammar, resulting in simplified grammar which is what happens in creoles. Grammatical gender never survives in creoles. Dutch and Scandinavian reduced to common and neuter. Romance languages lost neuter. French deliberately keeps it alive through scholars who decide gender for new words. English also has vestiges like blonde/blonde, he/she pronouns.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'slap-up meal'?

answers.answer: It comes from 'slap-bang meal' - a meal where you slap the money down on the table. Cash on delivery, no faffing around. Has nothing to do with women putting makeup on to go out for a meal.

questions.question: Why can some people raise their ring finger all the way up from a fist while others cannot?
Do military bandsmen recruited as musicians go through regular basic training like other soldiers, or just learn to march? Do they fight in wars?

answers.caller: Terry from Sissinghurst (18 years Royal Army Medical Corps)
answers.answer: All bandsmen are trained as first aiders. Their primary role in war is to move casualties around (traditionally stretcher bearers, now advanced first aid supporting medical stations). However, every soldier's first role is soldier - everyone is taught to fire weapons and basic infantry skills.

answers.caller: Bob from Perth (34 years in Black Watch)
answers.answer: In Scottish Infantry regiments (Black Watch, Scots Guards, Royal Irish), pipes and drums are fighting soldiers first, musicians second. They're allocated to specialist machine gun platoons. English battalion flute and drums are also fighting soldiers first. But the core military music (brass, trumpets) are musicians first. It varies by regiment.

questions.question: When a submarine turns underwater, does it lean into the turn like a plane banks, or does it go flat?

answers.caller: Paul (Ice Cream Man's son, based at Faslane for 20 years on nuclear subs)
answers.answer: Subs have two planes on either side for depth control. When turning quickly in battle station mode, they can roll a bit. But normally, subs don't lean into turns. The rudder alters direction without the sub banking over.

In the 1980s, Steve Wright in the Afternoon had a board game called Steve Wright - a stupid game. His daughter was keen to have it, they played it twice, then stored it in the back of the garden shed.

questions.question: When did we start rating things using stars? Was Shakespeare's plays five stars? When did stars become a symbol of quality?
Why do flowers close up at night? I knew the benefit of them opening during the daytime, but why don't they just stay open?

answers.answer: Flowers close at night to protect the pollen. They open during the day because that's when insects are around to pollinate them. At night, insects are dormant, so they close up to protect the pollen from blowing away and getting wet.

questions.question: As a cyclist, I've noticed women seem to have an intuitive sense even before they can hear or see me behind them, and they move over. Blokes tend not to do this. Why do women have a greater awareness of cyclists approaching from behind?

answers.answer: Could it be your pheromones? Perhaps you're possessed of particularly pungent pheromones blasting down the towpath as you pedal. Or hypervigilance - women spend more time in public worried about threat, so they have a more finely tuned antennae.

Women have better peripheral vision than men, and they also see more colours because they have more cones in their eyes. This is evolutionary. Men are more tunnel-visioned because when they went out hunting, it was useful to see straight ahead at prey, whereas women were left behind looking after children, so it was useful to see predators moving in peripheral vision.

questions.question: Why are some rocky outcrops and headlands named while others aren't, even when they're geologically similar? If I wanted to name one, how would I go about it?

answers.answer: It goes back to sailors, smugglers and fishermen. The navigable bits were given names so people could tell others where they were going. The non-navigable bits were less important.

The Ordnance Survey in the 18th century surveyed the country and made maps. When it came to naming features, they asked local people what they called things. As much as possible, they were faithful to what local people used. If something didn't have a name, it was left blank - they didn't make anything up. There's no way to get something named now because all the maps are already made.

questions.question: Current housing stock in the UK has styles like Gothic, Victorian, Arts and Crafts. What would the houses being built now be called? What era are we in?

answers.answer: Gothic is more architectural style than era, so you could still build a Gothic house now.

The Georgians didn't call their own buildings Georgian and the Victorians didn't call theirs Victorian - they were just modern buildings of the time. So right now we're just building buildings, not post-Elizabethan structures. We might be building modernist or neo-Georgian, neo-Victorian buildings. Also, old ordinary buildings have been knocked down or covered up, so we're only referring to the big grand buildings of those eras.

questions.question: In every single packet of almond fingers, there's always one almond finger without an almond on it. I've checked many, many packs. Friends have spent money testing this. Is this intentional? Is it for people like me who take the almond off? Or is it accidental or cost-saving?
If you accidentally stepped on a tortoise's shell, would your foot go through it like cracking a chocolate Easter egg, or how tough is the actual shell?

answers.answer: I think it's designed to protect from all manner of predation, so I'd be astonished if it isn't incredibly strong - strong enough to survive your foot.

A tortoise escaped from a nearby garden and got under my car. I backed out of the driveway and a passerby stopped me to say there was a tortoise underneath. It was about 30cm long - dinner plate sized. I clearly drove over it but it was absolutely fine. Eventually found the owner three doors away.

questions.question: Why does my hair on my head fall out but my hair doesn't get shorter? If all that hair is falling out and being replaced with new hair, shouldn't I have notable short hair growing at the bottom? The new hair follicles couldn't grow to the length of my existing hair within a day - it would take months.

answers.answer: Hair grows in distinct cycles - anagen (growing), catagen (resting, not growing), and telogen (falling out). Head hair stays in the anagen stage for about 7 years, while eyebrows and eyelashes are only about 8 weeks, which is why they don't grow as long. You do have short hairs growing but you just can't see them - unless you get static and see lots of little short hairs sticking up. Some people's hair grows longer than others before falling out.

questions.question: When money leaves your bank account via Faster Payment or BACS and it takes hours or days to arrive at the other end, where does the money go? Who's benefiting from it? Is someone earning interest on my money in that gap?

answers.answer: I was going to say it goes into a holding account. But someone's got to program the computers and pay the electricity bills for the systems.

With BACS payments, the money sits in the sending bank's account for the 3-day clearing period. At the end of every day, the clearing banks have accounts at the Bank of England and settle up by netting off all their incomings and outgoings with each other. With Faster Payment or CHAPS, it's done the same day. So the money doesn't sit in a huge pot accruing interest - it's unlikely a bank would only receive BACS payments in one day and none going out, so it nets off. The remitting bank has used the money in the meantime, but it's balanced out.

questions.question: Why are only 10% of people left-handed? If you have two hands, shouldn't it be 50-50?
Why do you never forget how to ride a bike?

answers.answer: It's the relationship between momentum and stability - a switch that gets flicked. Once you've crossed that rubicon and understood the relationship between momentum and stability, you'll never go back from that. It's a sense memory, not an intellectual memory.

Procedural memory is a type of memory you never forget. It's to do with procedures like riding a bike, driving a car. Your neurons have already assembled the skill set and can never be disassembled unless you have full memory loss. Clive Wearing is a famous case - he had complete retrograde and anterograde amnesia but could still play piano. He would say he never learned to play piano.

questions.question: What is the red comb on a chicken's head for? Other birds don't have it.

answers.answer: It's going to be sex - to make them more attractive to other chickens. Could also help regulate hydration or temperature.

Chicken combs regulate body temperature. Chickens and hens can't sweat. Both male chickens and hens have combs. In summer combs are big to let off more heat. In winter they shrink to retain heat. Jonathan keeps three chickens including ex-battery hens - when he first got them their combs covered their eyes because they were too hot from being in cages. Now the combs are dramatically smaller. The top bird in the pecking order tends to have the biggest comb.

questions.question: Why don't flies affect my dogs like they affect cows and horses? The flies bother cows and horses particularly around their eyes.

answers.answer: The dogs are moving. If you glued your dog to the floor, it would soon have a fly problem. Horses and cows stand still a lot. The horses in a race don't have a fly problem. Also cows and horses swish their tails.

questions.question: Who does Larry the cat belong to?

answers.answer: The Cabinet Office cat. He's a mouser. That's why he stays when Prime Ministers change.

questions.question: How does the dishwasher know when the dishes are clean? If I put 3 plates on auto it takes less time than when it's full of pots and pans on auto.

answers.answer: I don't know. I only ever put it on when it's full.

There's an infrared transmitter and receiver that shines through the water. It measures the intensity of light the receiver perceives to determine how clear the water is. When water runs clear, the dishwasher knows to turn off.

questions.question: Where do the bullets go when people shoot AK-47s in the air in celebration? Is it unsafe?

answers.answer: They come back down to earth at terminal velocity. At the apex, the bullet stops completely so it starts from zero. It's just dropping a bullet from that height - never going fast enough to be like being shot. It could hurt or kill you if you got desperately unlucky but it's not the same as being shot.

You separate vertical and horizontal components mathematically. For a vertical shot, the vertical component reaches zero at the apex then falls under gravity at terminal velocity (about 140mph for a human, faster for a bullet due to shape). People have been killed by falling bullets. For a horizontal shot, there's no apex - it's immediately falling. The horizontal component is maintained apart from air resistance. Something fired horizontally is beginning to fall immediately.

questions.question: Why is a banana more sinful to eat when it's mashed up than it is to eat it whole? On the Slimming World diet, mashing up fruit and veg makes them more fattening.

answers.answer: You're not chewing as much when you drink a mashed banana in a smoothie. Chewing is exercise - you use calories. Though you also use energy to mash it up, not as much.

There's misinformation around this. People might be referring to the thermic effect of food, but that's more relevant for proteins. For fruit and veg, the effect is negligible. The calorie content stays the same whether you mash it or not. The diet industry has been arguing about this.

questions.question: Can you have a triple or fourth rainbow? Would the colors keep reversing each time? The second rainbow had reversed colors.
Why do priests wear dog collars? And why is it called a dog collar?

answers.answer: Dog collar is just a nickname because dogs wear collars - to distinguish it from a shirt collar. Priests wear cheek collars (little slip-in tabs) with shirts, but with a cassock they wear a tonsure collar (full ring). It's scriptural reference - everything clergy wear has religious meaning. The meaning harkens back to martyrdoms and Diocletian persecutions where Christians were put in collars as slaves. The priest is always reminded he's a slave to his calling.
The white dog collar goes back to the early church, 6th-7th centuries, not for slave reasons but to be identifiable as priests and leaders - to stand out from the flock.

questions.question: Why do swimmers break world records faster than athletics? Is there a 'fast pool'? Could it be water quality or composition?
How is weight monitored in a state of weightlessness for astronauts on the ISS?

answers.answer: It comes down to the difference between weight and mass. Kilogram is a measure of mass, which is constant whether you're on Earth or in space. They use a device called a Newtonian that measures force on you and acceleration using an optical sensor. Force equals mass times acceleration, so mass = force divided by acceleration. They then calculate what you'd weigh on Earth.

questions.question: When you take a frozen loaf of sliced bread out of the freezer, why is the moisture leached to the same side of each slice - one side bone dry, the other with ice crystals - all the way down the loaf?
Why do some people need music or background noise to concentrate while others need silence?

answers.answer: There are perhaps two types of brain - one that concentrates better with background noise and one that concentrates worse.

It's all to do with the dopamine pathway in the brain. For certain brains, like ADHD at the extreme end of the spectrum, the constant need for dopamine means background noise distracts the brain enough and gives that reward of dopamine to allow focus on other tasks. People with greater dopamine regulation find background noise distracting because they're able to concentrate and get their dopamine from the task at hand. This applies to varying degrees across the whole population, not just neurodiversity. Also applies to sleep - some people's minds wander because they're not getting enough dopamine lying still, so background noise helps them sleep.

questions.caller: Philip from Newport on Isle of Wight
questions.question: Do airlines sue guilty air rage passengers through civil courts for losses when planes are held up for hours or diverted mid-flight?

answers.answer: Yes, if an airline has to make an emergency landing somewhere other than intended, the passenger will be expected to pay the full cost. If they don't pay, they will be taken to court, and nine times out of ten, the court finds in favour of the airline. It also depends on landing charges - if an airline has a contract with that airport, the charge is smaller. If not, it's higher. The airline also incurs costs for crew and must refuel. Caller personally witnessed someone being ordered to pay over 20 thousand pounds (around 25-28k), and they received a lifetime ban. The airline loses money while sitting on the ramp not where it's supposed to be.

questions.question: When they set a Sudoku, how do they know if it's going to be easy or difficult to solve? It's not about how many numbers they leave in, because you can have the same number of numbers left in and it can be really easy or really difficult.
Why is a kangaroo court called a kangaroo court?

answers.answer: It comes from the Californian gold rush. Many Australians rushed to California in the 1840s and claimed plots of land to mine. Claim jumping was common - when you got to California and claimed a plot, someone else might come and claim the same plot. When you went to court over a claim jump, it became known as a kangaroo court because kangaroos hop and jump like 'claim jumping'.

questions.question: Does our cat know she's having babies? The cat is still doing everything she did before - jumping off the greenhouse and shed, rolling about - and the caller (Emily) is concerned about protecting the baby.
Why don't we get that glorious petrichor smell when we're watering the garden during a long hot spell, like we do after natural rain?

answers.answer: It's to do with the size of the rain droplets. Small rain droplets create a much stronger smell. The term petrichor was coined by two Australian climatologists in the 1960s. With larger droplets, you can still get the effect but it's not as noticeable. Fine mist from a sprinkler might work.

questions.question: Why is a hot dog called a hot dog?

answers.answer: German immigrants going to the States brought their meat and sausages. The Americans thought they looked like their German dogs - dachshunds.

Hot dogs come from dachshunds. In the 1900s at ball games, vendors used to shout 'come and get your red hots, your dachshund sausages.' Cartoonist T. Dorgan couldn't spell dachshund properly when writing captions, so he abbreviated it to 'hot dogs' and it stuck.

questions.question: Is there a different production line for grab bags vs multi-packs of crisps? The caller is sure the 70g grab bags taste better, crunchier, and have better flavour than the multi-packs, and everyone laughs at him for saying it.

answers.answer: The grab bags are substantially larger. About 60-70% of taste is actually due to the sense of smell (olfactory cortex), not taste buds. The larger bag allows more flavour particles to get into your nose and stimulate your olfactory cortex. The smaller bag has fewer particles. It's the same principle as wine glasses - more nose means better smell. If you did a controlled experiment with identical crisps in identical size bags (like Ziploc bags), there would be no difference. There is a difference in taste perception, but not a difference in the actual crisps.

questions.question: How does the needle (diamond) on a vinyl player create the noise of multi-track recording just by scraping in the vinyl groove?
A theory about sliced bread (interrupting at end of show)
Is the vinyl needle actually a diamond?

answers.answer: Yes, it is a diamond. The diamond fits in the groove of the record. There's only one groove per side. And the deeper the groove, the louder the music.

questions.question: When you put food out for the birds, how come they come so quickly? You can't see any in the sky and then within half a minute there's 20 or 30.

answers.answer: They might have seagulls or pigeons constantly flying around looking for food, and when one finds some they send a message back to the rest.

All birds, but particularly seagulls, can smell from three miles away. Even though you can't see them, they see you and smell you. Bread can be smelled from three miles away. Qualifications: told by a harbour master in Chichester.

questions.question: I've just turned 35 and my hairline's retreated, but suddenly I've got ear hair. How is it more helpful to have hairy ears?

answers.answer: There may not be an evolutionary advantage to it. It might happen when you're older and procreating less, so evolution doesn't care.
Ear hair helps clear ear wax from the ear canal. Testosterone causes hair to appear or become coarser and thicker as men age, which is why older men have hairier ears. The same applies to nasal hair.

questions.question: What's it in the brain that allows some people to do impersonations and accents like Rory Bremner or John Coleshaw?

answers.answer: I think it's something to do with your brain - like a tape recorder that works differently from everybody else's. It's probably the same skill needed to be very good at accents, just even better.

questions.question: How do we know what colour dinosaurs are? My son has a toy carcardontosaurus that's orange with blue spots, but the likelihood it was that colour seems slim.

answers.answer: We don't know for certain. From fossil feathers, they've sometimes been able to work out colours (like black), but most fossils offer no clue. You extrapolate what seems likely - camouflage colours. But some dinosaurs like T. rex would have no need for camouflage. Hollywood has probably influenced what we think. Unless you find fossilised pigment, you won't know.

questions.question: If a married man has another woman, she's a mistress. If a married woman has another man, what is he called?

answers.answer: Mistress comes from the man assuming financial responsibility historically. For a married woman to have a bit on the side wouldn't involve that. I don't think there's a particular term for the male extramarital lover.
It's called a paramour. (Though this can apply to either men or women - it's the technical term for an extramarital lover.)

questions.question: What is Flying Ant Day? Where do all the flying ants come from and why?

answers.answer: It's mating, isn't it? But where are all the ants with wings for the rest of the year? They must live in nests, but that can't be right.

The big ones are virgin queens, the smaller ones are males. They take off, mate, and once mated the queen chews off her own wings and goes underground to start a new colony. She has enough fat reserves to keep going without food, lays eggs, and those become worker ants. Most get eaten by birds. Ants nest all year creating eggs for this day. Males' sole purpose is to mate and then they die. Qualifications: insect geek, member of Entomological Society, keeps ants.

questions.question: Why do photo finishes look blurry and distorted, with runners looking elongated and knees going the wrong way?

answers.answer: It's not really a photo, it's a frozen piece of film. It probably has something to do with shutter speed. But why does it look so different from a normal photo?

It's a still image camera that looks at a very narrow window and captures movement as still images, which are then stitched together. People look wonky because they're captured at different speeds - moving slowly makes you appear wide, moving fast makes you appear narrow. Qualifications: former Formula One timekeeper who rigged and operated these cameras for six years.

questions.question: Why can't horses vomit or be sick? If they eat something bad, how do they get rid of it?

answers.answer: It may be that it's more remarkable to be able to vomit. Horses only eat grass, so the likelihood of poisoning themselves is slim, whereas other mammals eat all sorts of things and need to be able to vomit after eating something hazardous.

They have a valve called a swift tie which is set really low down in their stomach, which prevents them from regurgitating. The valve being low down means when they're at full speed evading predators, it wouldn't allow them to be sick whilst fleeing - they'd have to stop. Qualifications: farrier for 30 years.

questions.question: Before Julius Caesar and Emperor Augustus, there were 10 months in the year, then 11, then 12. How did this affect the seasons? Would seasons have started at different points each year?

answers.answer: The pie stayed the same size - it's just cut into more slices. A season takes 90 days whether it's 10 months or 12. The year was still the same length, they just rearranged the months.

There was an extra month called intercalendis that consuls could insert to sort out seasons. They only accounted for about 330 days originally. They frequently didn't bother inserting it, so seasons would drift. Religious festivals went by the month, not the season, so Saturnalia could end up being celebrated in September instead of December. That's why Julius Caesar reformed the calendar with Cleopatra's help, leading to 365 days. Then Pope Gregory refined it with leap years.
