Qualifications: obsessed with everything Roman since picking up first Asterix book at age 8.

They had a civic year beginning in March running 10 months at only 300 days - not covering the whole solar year. There were 60-61 extra days not assigned to particular months, fitted in when needed for religious festivals between what we now think of as January and February. Because of Greek cultural influence, Romans started wanting 12 months and formally added January and February. Quintilis and sextilis were renamed July and August by Roman leaders after themselves.

questions.question: It hasn't rained for two months and there are no ponds. How do squirrels get water?

answers.answer: I imagine there are puddles or little deposits of water somewhere that they track down. They may not need a huge amount of water.

They drink dew first thing in the morning - little pools of dew that form on broad leaves, even on lawns. What they manage to drink in the morning is enough to sustain them for the rest of the day. Qualifications: lives near woods with famous red squirrel population, knows a local squirrel feeder.

questions.question: How come mirrors only invert left and right (lateral inversion) but not up and down?

answers.answer: I don't know. There'll be an answer - physics or optics. We don't know what it is.

The premise of the question is fundamentally flawed. The mirror isn't inverted left to right at all - it's inverted back to front. Whatever you put in the right side of the mirror is still on the right. When you raise your right arm, the mirror image appears to raise its left arm, but nothing is actually inverted. Qualifications: has a physics A-level and looked it up after it came up on a programme three months ago.

questions.question: How far does electricity travel through water? If lightning strikes the sea, how far away do you need to be to be safe? Does a hair dryer in the bath have less impact than lightning?

answers.answer: It depends on how much electricity there is. There must be an equation - voltage versus volume of water. It's not a simple answer like 40 metres.

It depends on conductivity. Sea water being salty is very conductive, but it's in constant contact with the earth's surface, which is an infinite source of electrons, so current gets dissipated very quickly - it leaks out into the soil and earth's crust. If you had contained water in a bath and made it conductive by adding salt or electrolyte, you could theoretically pass current through an infinite length. If you had water in a trough or drain pipe with sufficiently conductive solution (like battery acid) and sufficient voltage, it would act like cabling. Qualifications: chartered electrical engineer.

questions.question: Is there an international language between air traffic controllers and pilots? If you're flying your German plane into Abu Dhabi, what language will the control tower speak to the cockpit?

answers.answer: English is the international language. Any pilot or air traffic controller needs to be able to speak English to a certain level so they can all speak to each other in a common language.

English is the default universal language for aviation, but if you're flying an aircraft registered in the country you're flying over, you can talk in your native language. So a French pilot flying over France can talk French to air traffic control.

questions.question: Why is cubed pancetta located in the cooked section of a supermarket with the hams and chickens, but you have to cook it before using it?

answers.answer: The staff in High Wycombe think that because it comes in the same crate and from the same suppliers as the hams, because it's cured, it's coming from the ham people rather than the bacon people, so they just put it on the shelves with the hams.
Pancetta is kept with the cold cuts as it's the only uncooked Italian item. It's placed with the Italian hams - Parma ham and prosciutto.

It comes under the category of charcuterie. Supermarket buyers have someone responsible for sausage and bacon as a category, and someone else responsible for cured meats. Pancetta is a cured Italian meat, so it goes with all the other cured Italian meats. The cubed version (pancetta stese) is different from what you'd eat straight from the pack in Italy.

questions.question: Do we think the world gets heavier or lighter or possibly stays the same every day?

answers.answer: The world does change in weight. Planes taking off make the Earth lighter. But you can't create mass or destroy mass. Trees grow and get heavier by taking carbon dioxide from the atmosphere (through photosynthesis, turning gas into glucose), so the Earth gets heavier as trees grow.

questions.question: What is the origin of saving in a piggy bank?

answers.answer: Pig originally wasn't spelled P-I-G, it had a Y in it and possibly more than one G. It's just a type of clay from which a pot would be made. Ancient peasants would put their coins into this pot. Over the years, potters, given that it was called pig, would then make the pot look like a pig as a marketing wheeze.

questions.question: Why do we have eyelids? Why can't we close our ears or nose like we can close our eyes?

answers.answer: The eye is a very sensitive and delicate organ. If you lost the ability to see, you'd be in a huge evolutionary disadvantage, so something that covers your eye and minimizes the likelihood of your eyesight being compromised is an epic evolutionary advantage. Ears and nose are not as highly sensitive - if you poke someone in the ear they can still hear, if you poke them in the nose they can still smell (unless you completely break it, which would be the same whether it had a lid or not). There is absolutely no evolutionary advantage to having ear lids or nose lids.

questions.question: Why do you have to show ID to buy non-alcoholic beer?

answers.answer: It might just be that it makes life easier - anything that's got beer on it, you need to show ID so you don't have to waste five minutes looking for the volume on the till.

It's about not promoting alcoholic drinks to children. Non-alcoholic beer is still promoted in the alcohol aisles in stores, and what they don't want to do is encourage children into that aisle. In licensed premises such as a pub, children can actually drink beer under 0.5% because it's not classed as beer.

questions.question: Why are closes called closes, streets called streets, roads called roads, ways called ways, avenues, lanes, drives, terraces, etc? Why are they called what they are?

answers.answer: Variety, I suppose. You can't have a road and a street in the same place, but you can have an Acacia Road and an Acacia Avenue and an Acacia Close, so it gives you more options. Once you've eliminated the impossible, what else could it be?

The street naming process goes back to the Town Improvement Clause Act of 1847 and the Public Health Act of 1907. Local authorities are legally bound to name properties and streets. In the old days, people would look at a location and name it based on what they see. There are about 14 high-level guidelines including not naming streets after famous living people (to avoid things like Jimmy Savile). Street naming officers try to have themes for new housing developments. 'Avenue' traditionally comes from trees lining the road. 'Close' often refers to dead ends.

questions.question: Why do people feel tranquil when they arrive and look at bodies of water?

answers.answer: During lockdown, he really noticed how much he missed big skies. He looked it up and it makes sense: the more you can see of the horizon, the more relaxed your lizard brain will be because you know there are no threats incoming. If you're beside a huge body of water and it's empty, that's a huge weight off your subconscious. There's also the sound of running water, and probably something linked to the womb, but it's mainly to do with the wide expanse of horizon with no threat on it.

questions.question: Do babies get songs stuck in their head (earworms)?
Why does your voice go up in pitch just before you start crying, before the tears even start?
Why do we cry? Why do we produce tears?

answers.answer: When you get stressed or angry, which is normally why you cry. You produce stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline and other nasties. And when you cry, it's one of the body's ways of excreting the kind of byproducts or the hormones that you don't need. I'm a nurse but I only attended a psychology lecture and that's what the psychologist was telling me.

questions.question: Where does the word 'honeymoon' come from or what does it mean?

answers.answer: If you got married in the olden days, the village would all club together to give you enough mead to last a month. And a month being a lunar month as in one passage of the moon. And that is where honeymoon comes from. Mead is a drink made out of honey, an alcoholic drink.

questions.question: Why is a sweet potato classed as one of your five a day and a normal potato isn't?

answers.answer: It's to do with the structure of the carbohydrate in it. So in potatoes, the structure is starch. And in sweet potatoes, it's basically a sugar. And to be one of your five a day, a fruit or vegetable has to be a non-starchy product. Also in the colored sweet potatoes, you contain chemicals that act as precursors to vitamin A and stuff like that. Sweet potatoes are related to morning glory. So they're part of the convolvulus family where normal potatoes are part of the nightshade family. They're in different categories of food. I think it's called a potato because it looks like a normal potato.

questions.question: Why is a double U called a W and not called a double V when it looks more like a double V on a keyboard?

answers.answer: In the old English or Anglo-Saxon period, we'd use a letter called wynn, which looks a bit like a stylised P. And that's how you make the W sound. It was based on an early sort of Germanic rune. And it's quite, well, we lost most of our Germanic root letters after Norman conquest. 1066. And this is why W is relevant. Because the Normans wanted to make the English spellings more relevant to Norman French. So, rather than using wynn, they would write two U's together to make the W sound. Hence, it became W. And like everything, over time, we've got lazy and shortened it to just look like two Vs. It's an attempt to sound less German and more French.

questions.question: If you dropped a penny off the Empire State Building, would it kill somebody? And if it isn't true, would some clever person know what height you have to drop something off the building for the velocity to kill someone rather unpleasantly?

answers.answer: A penny reaches a terminal velocity after about 50 feet of free fall. The Empire State Building is a hell of a lot taller. So you're not going to kill anyone. It's going to hurt. The terminal velocity is only about 25 mile an hour. Compare this to paintballs going 150 mile an hour when you're playing paintball. They're heavier. You're not going to kill anyone, it's just going to hurt.

questions.question: In what order should I apply my skincare products: coconut body butter, suntan lotion, mosquito repellent, and bite treatment balm? Does it matter? Does the coconut oil attract mosquitoes? Would it cancel out the repellent?
Why do they use the term 'theatre of war' when war isn't in a theatre? It's a big field, not a theatre.

answers.answer: Karl von Clausewitz wrote 'On War' in German. He defined the term Kriegstheater by translating the original Latin term theatrum belli, which means denoting a portion of space over which war prevails with protected boundaries. So it makes it independent. It makes it a specific area. It comes from the Latin, theatrum belli. The whole area, so everything that is contained within that war is in that theatre of war. It also relates to where plays were performed, like an amphitheatre, defining a space in which something specific happens.

questions.question: Does a strand of hair go grey or grow grey? Does a fully grown hair turn grey or does a brand new hair come out grey?

answers.answer: It has to grow grey. The hair's dead as soon as it grows out of the hair follicle. It can't turn grey overnight. It can't just turn grey. We shed quite a lot of hair, don't we? So that's why you go grey, because you're shedding the old hair and growing the new hair, which is grey. And therefore, you cannot immediately go grey. Hair on the body has a shorter life than hair on the head, which is why it may appear to change overnight but it doesn't. You've just grown a new one. I was a colour specialist in London for many years.

questions.question: Why do wisdom teeth come through when they come through? Does stress or hormones have anything to do with it?

answers.answer: Some of us don't have wisdom teeth now because we are phylogenetically superior. We don't need them any longer. It's to do with hormonal changes and growth, just like adolescents. Just as our bone structure isn't fully established till 22-23 years of age, the same applies to wisdom teeth. So if your wisdom teeth haven't come through by the time you're 30, they're never going to come through. It's just the same as your baby teeth falling out. It's a cycle of time. It's an evolutionary adaptation to not have wisdom teeth because we don't need them to chew branches and trees anymore or to chew more uncooked and unprocessed foliage. I'm a medic.

questions.question: Why don't we have symbols above or below English words to indicate pronunciation, like other languages do? For example, we don't have pronunciation guides on words like Loughborough.
If you can have your tonsils removed, what's the point in having them in the first place?

answers.answer: Tonsils help us fight infection. They catch viruses and bacteria. If we have one or two episodes of tonsillitis in a year, that still works in our favour. But if we're having six or seven episodes, the risk of infection turning into something like sepsis means the benefit of removing the tonsils outweighs the purpose they're originally serving. They're useful but not essential and their usefulness can be outweighed by susceptibility to infection.

questions.question: The saying, 'she'll have my guts for garters', where does it come from and what does it mean?
Why do Prime Minister's questions and debates in Parliament have to go through the speaker before the person can answer?
How do birds know how to make nests?
If you fed a cow strawberries, would the milk taste of strawberries?

answers.answer: Cow's milk flavour is affected by the diet. You have to be quite extreme, but from studies and family knowledge, milk from cows that eat too much wild garlic was rejected because it tainted the flavour. Farmers had to make sure pastures didn't have too much wild garlic. If they have a good forage-based, mainly grass diet, they have nice milky milk. It would be possible to affect the flavour with strawberries but nobody's ever done it because you want milky milk, not something else.

questions.question: What do pelican crossings have to do with pelicans?

answers.answer: It's called a PELICAN crossing because it's a PEDestrian LIght CONtrolled crossing. Like a zebra crossing references a zebra, it's named after the control mechanism. The button is controlled by the pedestrian - PE for pedestrian. The term evolved from 'con' to 'can' which is nice and easy to remember. There's also a puffin crossing and a toucan crossing for pedestrians and cyclists.

questions.question: How do people find their tents after concerts at Glastonbury?

answers.answer: The campsites are in colours and divided into north, south, east and west, so you're in Blue East for example. Everyone puts up big flags. People walk along roads and find their own landmarks like a distinctive tent. If you use Google Maps you can mark where you parked. When drunk it gets complicated but generally colours, flags and personal landmarks help you find your tent.

questions.question: Why does concentrating on an alphabetical list of things help you go to sleep?

answers.answer: When we go to bed, what we've avoided during the day rebounds and it's threat-based - future catastrophes, things from the past we haven't processed, our inner critic. This activates our sympathetic nervous system (fight or flight) so we can't sleep. Using the alphabetical technique is neutral-based, bypassing the sympathetic system. You're concentrating hard on something that isn't adrenalizing or threatening to yourself, so you can bypass that and go into parasympathetic relaxation and drift off.

questions.question: Why does clothes dry at room temperature? How does water turn from liquid to gas without boiling?

answers.answer: You need to differentiate between boiling and evaporating. Boiling happens at one temperature - in water's case, 100 degrees. But evaporation happens at all temperatures. In a glass of water, molecules are randomly moving and by chance some move up with enough energy to escape from the body of water - that's evaporation. It's about the movement of molecules. Even ice sublimes - in Siberia they put clothes out, they freeze but still dry. Freeze drying of coffee works on this principle.

questions.question: Did we invent maths or discover maths?

answers.answer: Some of it's invented and some discovered. Things like deciding there are 360 degrees in a circle, a right angle is 90 degrees, how many minutes in an hour - these were human conventions, probably for international trade and contact. Someone had to invent the means for different groups to communicate. But basic laws like three plus four equals four plus three, numbers multiplied by one equals the number, any number times zero equals zero - these had to be proven. When you prove something you hypothesize it and then prove it exists for all situations. Even concepts like bases - we use base 10 but there are other bases. So we invented the concepts and theories but discovered the relationships.

There are basic laws you learn at university like 3+4=4+3 and 3x4=4x3. These aren't intuitively obvious if you're in the dinosaur age. When you prove something, you hypothesize it first and then prove it exists for all situations. The concept of what a number actually is, even things like bases - we use base 10 but there are others. So some of it's invented and some discovered.

questions.question: Do fish feel the water? Do they know they're wet?
Sheila, why did you want to make this podcast?

answers.answer: It was such a big thing that happened to me and nobody was more surprised at the depths of its effect on me than I was. Because to start with, I kind of batted it away as an annoyance, an irritation, something that could easily be managed out of my life, managed away. And I learned the hard way that that's not how stalking works. Stalkers are obsessive. They don't give up easily. They don't stop easily. It takes an awful lot to dissuade a stalker from carrying on. So I was approaching it with too much of a focus on just a simple managing it out, thinking it would be a quick situation. And it wasn't. I was really clear at the end of this experience, if it's not really over, it's never over really. I was really clear that there was a lot to know about this and that I could have managed it differently, better, faster. And there was. There was so much to it that I wanted to dig into, into the issue of stalking. I just wanted to know more about it. And actually, I very actively wanted people to have information about it. And not just potential victims of stalking, but police officers as well.

questions.question: How has this experience of being stalked, how has it impacted on your life? Are there moments, even now, when you look behind you and you start to fear?

answers.answer: It does still affect me now, yeah. To say it had gone away completely would be absolutely wrong because I still check whether he's outside the office. I still check whether he's on a train I'm on. I still check the train platform at my home station. I still sometimes coming out at my front door, mentally see that moment when he was at my gate and I was livid, horrified, shocked, angry. You name it. I still, every now and again, relive that as I walk down those steps towards the gate, you know. So in that sense, it's not over. And I also, I've got a little old cottage that I'm doing up. And if I talk about it on, I don't really talk about it on social media or I don't want anyone to know where it is, there's a newfound protection of my privacy born out of necessity. You know, I really need him not to know where I am. I hope that the sentence and therefore the restrictions he's under applies to him approaching me at all, anywhere, in any way. But I do fear that he could appear somewhere else other than those places named in the sentencing. And even just describing it to you now, I have a sort of dread in the pit of my stomach. So yeah, very much still. In my head. In my mind.

questions.question: Did humans, homo sapiens, ever in any point in history schedule their offspring to be born in the spring like most of the animal kingdom do? Like around spring you see the lambs, in the wild you see the bears, did we ever used to do it?

Why can't the brain recognise an incline when you look at it? We were walking on a road that looked completely flat, but my wife asked if we were walking uphill. Looking behind me I could see the gradient going back down, but looking ahead it looked completely flat.

answers.answer: If it's a straight road, there's nothing that actually indicates the incline. If it was a bendy road, you'd see one bit above another bit. That's why the straightness seems significant.

questions.question: Do chillies actually burn our mouths as in leave lasting damage? The pain from chillies is the same as other things that cause damage, but chillies don't leave lasting damage. So is it actually a burn?

answers.answer: Chillies don't leave lasting damage, so it can't be a burn in the conventional sense. It's about the meaning of the word 'burn' rather than what chillies do to our mouths.

questions.question: Can giraffes swim? Even if they could, the neck is so long that it would almost tip them upside down in water.

answers.answer: I think they probably can, but I wonder if anyone's ever been able to find out.

Giraffes can't swim. I saw it on QI with Alan Davies demonstrating with a puppet. It's the weight of their neck that means they can't get into a swimming position. If they went in deep water, the head would have to come out of the water for them to breathe, which would take them out of viable swimming position.

questions.question: How and why did France develop a system where instead of having a name for 80, they say quatre-vingts (4×20)? Why can't they have a number for 80 like normal languages?

answers.answer: The old counting system dates back to Celtic times. They stopped at 60, which is why we have seconds to 60. It's pre-metric, and France kept the old Gaulic system. Other French-speaking countries like Belgium and Quebec actually do have separate numbers for 70, 80, 90 (septante, octante, nonante). In Paris, when I asked my flatmate why they don't change, he said it sounds ugly. It's an old remnant kept by the Académie Française.

Marc jokes that the French have a base of 20 because they used fingers and toes, whereas we only have a base of 10 because we only used fingers. It was a Celtic base and they stuck to the Gaulic base.

questions.question: Human infants seem to be lulled and even put to sleep by singing and lullabies. Why? How did that come to pass evolutionarily? In a world of predators, having crying babies seems like a bad survival strategy.

answers.answer: The rocking is very much part of it. It simulates the mother walking during pregnancy. It possibly recreates the atmosphere in the womb, or it has the same rhythm as your heartbeat.

questions.question: Can a spider get caught in another spider's web?
How new does news have to be to be considered breaking news? And how old does news have to be before it stops being considered breaking news?

answers.answer: It's not an exact science. It's largely meaningless now - people stick 'breaking' on anything. It just means 'this is happening now' or 'being published for the first time.' The 24-hour rolling news cycle has rendered it utterly meaningless.

questions.question: When a gull swallows a puffin whole, does it stay alive? Does it suffocate? Does it dissolve?

answers.answer: It would be alive to start with, for some of the journey. Probably more likely to suffocate than be killed by stomach acids, or might have a heart attack and die of fear on its way down the gull's gullet.

questions.question: What makes some humans so irresistible to mosquitoes? (Got bitten constantly on honeymoon while wife barely got bitten)

answers.answer: People with thalassemia trait have less hemoglobin (more anemic blood) so mosquitoes particularly hate them. Also mosquitoes prefer warmer body temperatures (they're cold-blooded) and smellier people by their standards (not smelly as humans determine it).

questions.question: Why does a British passport have French text on it alongside English?

answers.answer: French and English are the two most widely spoken languages globally. It dates back to French being the language of international diplomacy - it's called a 'lingua franca' meaning a common language that everyone defaults to. France essentially invented international diplomacy.

questions.question: Why do most landmasses/continents appear wider at the top (north) and taper narrower toward the south?

answers.answer: Admitted he wasn't sure and might need to verify the premise. Suggested it could involve tectonic plates.

During Pangaea, the bottom of South America, bottom of Africa, and bottom of India were all joined together. When they broke apart and moved in different directions, that's why those three continents have that shape. The top of South America butted into the crook of the Gulf of Mexico, which is why Mexico comes down like a finger.

questions.question: From his 8-year-old: How come we are able to have a conversation with ourselves in our head?

answers.answer: Based on 'The Chimp Paradox' - humans developed a human brain alongside a basic 'chimp' brain. The chimp brain handles fight/flight/instinct. The human brain takes longer to kick in and applies logic. Having conversations in your head is the human brain processing and analyzing - it's just thinking. It's a consequence of evolution.

questions.question: Why is it that you can remember the music in some songs but not the lyrics, or vice versa?

answers.answer: Some tunes for musical/technical reasons lend themselves to easier recall, just like rhyming poems are easier to remember than complicated blank verse. Happy Birthday is probably the best example of the easiest tune to remember.

Music is repeated throughout the song and repetition is one of the pillars of being able to remember something. If a song uses a small number of repeated notes, it becomes more memorable. Simple tunes with repetition are easier to recall than complicated sonatas.

questions.question: If we can donate organs after death, why can't we donate bones (assuming they're healthy)?

answers.answer: No one wants somebody else's old bones. A brand new titanium hip is better than a used one from someone who might be closer to needing a replacement themselves.

We do use what's called an allograft - bone from a dead person. Bone is used to create a scaffold for repair. We also do autografts (bone from the patient, e.g., from the pelvis). The donor bone is irradiated to remove damaging cells, then used as a graft. So bones ARE donated, just not whole bones - they're processed into scaffolding for bone repair.

questions.question: Why don't Australians have any regional accents, considering how far they are from each other?

answers.answer: There ARE different Australian accents - three main types: educated, bush (Crocodile Dundee style), and general. But they're more to do with socioeconomic class than geography. Australia is a relatively young country, so regional dialects haven't had time to develop.

Australia hasn't been around long enough for regional dialects to fully develop. There are subtle differences - South Australians sound more English, Queensland has broader speech. Accents can develop from environmental factors - one theory is that squinting in the sunny Australian climate contributed to the accent. You've got white collar, blue collar, and country/bush accents.

questions.question: Why is the Old Bailey called the Old Bailey? Was it ever just 'the Bailey'? Is there a new Bailey?

answers.answer: A Bailey was grounds outside a fortification. The Old Bailey is the street where the Central Criminal Court sits - named after the grounds around the City of London walls. The bailey was the area outside the walls. As the city expanded, that area became 'the old bailey' because it used to be outside the walls.

questions.question: Why don't we have to pick up horse droppings? Lady on a horse said you don't have to, it can go on roses.

answers.answer: Horses are herbivores, dogs are carnivores - different bacteria. Dog fouling is regulated differently in law. There are bylaws requiring horse riders to clean up in certain places, but the Road Traffic Act has no requirement for horse riders to dismount and shovel. It would cause more problems than it solves.

questions.question: How did mapmakers in the middle ages and 1700s know what the UK looked like before planes and drones? Did they have people going around the corners working it out?

answers.answer: Sailors would go around the coast drawing contours. Maps were invaluable for navigators, military campaigns, and privateers. The more valuable a map, the more hand-drawn and rare. This was often done for taxation purposes (like Domesday Book) or military planning.

Prior to the Ordnance Survey, mapping was done by sailors going around the coast by eye. The Ordnance Survey was commissioned in 1741 for military purposes (ordnance = weapons). The first task was the Principal Triangulation of Great Britain using triangles, measured using metal chains across Hounslow Heath as a baseline. Stations near the coastline gave approximations of coastlines; the rest was done by walking and mapping.

questions.question: Why would a magnetic pole flip be dangerous? Could render parts of Earth uninhabitable.

answers.answer: The magnetic field protects us from solar rays. When it flips, the field is interrupted in certain areas, allowing harmful solar rays through temporarily. It can make some areas uninhabitable for a short period. This was discovered through studying iron in ocean floor plates - they show a zebra pattern as the poles flip.

questions.question: Is there a scientific way of measuring pain? The 1-10 scale is subjective.

answers.answer: There are many pain scales. For adults, a zero to ten numeric rating scale is commonly used. Pain is defined subjectively by what someone says it is, so objective measurement is difficult. However, functional MRI can show brain responses to stimuli. For babies, you can measure arm and leg movement combined with crying. In large drug trials with thousands of patients, biases average out and you can show interventions reduce pain scores by 2-3 points. For chronic pain, there are other scales measuring impact on life.

questions.question: Why are stag and hen dos called that? What's the origin?
How can the sun burn in space/vacuum with no oxygen? Six-year-old nephew asked this.

answers.answer: The sun isn't burning - it's nuclear fusion. In the 19th century people thought it was a giant lump of coal, but that would only last 5,000 years. The sun is about 5 billion years old. The sun fuses hydrogen into helium, producing sunlight. No oxygen needed - just hydrogen. It's an unbelievably inefficient nuclear reaction, which is why it takes 10 billion years to burn its fuel, allowing time for complex life to evolve.

questions.question: Why do we still use the year 2022 based on the life and death of Jesus Christ? Why has that become the global standard?

answers.answer: Consensus and regulatory framework. It spread through missionaries and military adventures. Once enough people adopted it, everyone had to agree to have a common regulatory framework. It's madness to remove yourself from such a framework (Brexit analogy). North Korea and some civilizations don't use it.

questions.question: Why were ancient sculptures so beautifully proportioned, but painting didn't achieve similar realism until the Renaissance?

answers.answer: The camera obscura enabled the leap in painting accuracy. Before putting brush to canvas, artists would use a camera obscura to trace figures - a black screen device where they would prick out the outline and then paint it. David Hockney documented this in a documentary and book. This is why earlier paintings often show characters holding objects in their left hands - the camera obscura flipped the image. Once the human brain learned to conceive of such realism, the technology became outmoded.

questions.question: Why is it that if you leave the top off the biscuit tin and return to it a couple of days later, your crisp biscuits have gone soft? But if you play the same trick with a cupcake, for instance, it will have gone hard.

answers.answer: It all comes down to the shortening, how fatty is it? Because oil and water doesn't mix. Fats and water don't mix. So the more fat you have, the more likely you are to repel water and not attract it. Cakes dry out, they lose water, but they don't suck it in from the environmental moisture. Biscuits, on the other hand, have lots more sugar and lots less fat in them and therefore they will absorb water from the air around them and become quite soft. Regarding Jaffa Cakes, there was a big punch-up at the VAT tribunal in 1991, which I teach about to my students because VAT is payable on chocolate-covered biscuits but not chocolate-covered cakes. One of the tests that was done was does a Jaffa cake dry out when it's left out or does it not? And the answer is, of course, it does. Jaffa cakes are indeed cakes. And there was a huge refund of VAT made on that basis.

questions.question: When you move house, how is it that cats know where the new house is? Like, they can find their way home.

answers.answer: Cats have a kind of homing system built in, like a bird. A bird will fly off to the far reaches and come back. They have a homing sense and it works up to about three or four miles. If you drove a cat ten miles away it probably would not be able to come home. I found a scientific report saying that cats do have a homing system but the scientists aren't quite sure how it works. They think it's to do with something similar to birds.

questions.question: About three years ago, we were on holiday in Lyme Regis. My mum was sat there saying, how come you're more moley than your brothers? And I've noticed on my children, they are getting more moley as they get older. Why do some people have more moles than others? And where do they come from?

answers.answer: The reason moles come about is because your DNA in your skin gets mutated and it starts producing melanin. That's why you get them more as you age because when you age, your DNA naturally mutates anyway over time. That's part of the aging process. The reason you can inherit them is because essentially it's a bit like how you can inherit other skin conditions. You inherit some of those mutations that haven't quite become moles yet from your parents. And that's also why you get them more than some and get skin cancer because UV rays damage your DNA.

questions.question: What is the world's contingency plan if we're visited by aliens, like extraterrestrials, or extraterrestrial life? Would the world have a plan or would it be region by region? Country by country or possibly council by council?

answers.answer: There are certain plans and certain things that were put forward by a number of bodies such as SETI, Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence, and I believe the Astronomical Union about first of all, the signal or contact or whatever would have to be verified so they'd have to be extremely certain about this is an individual astronomer finding such a signal or such a signal on the radio and then after that, they are supposed to make the United Nations aware of this. However there hasn't been anything adopted in a concrete sense, so there isn't an international treaty out there as such or any kind of binding international agreement that would have to be followed. So yes and no, there are things in place, but there's nothing extremely concrete. I can say almost quite categorically that I believe there's no domestic legislation at least that I know of.

questions.question: Why do bubbles not pop on mirrors?
How did clapping become the most important way of showing appreciation for a performance?

You've got a frying pan. You put oil in the frying pan. If you left that frying pan, eventually it would spit and it would get hot and it would smoke. But if you put a sausage in there and a piece of bacon, it doesn't set on fire. So how does the oil know that there's food in the pan?

answers.answer: If a frying pan with oil in it is smoking hot, then it's got to be very hot, like 200 degrees plus. As soon as you put a presumably colder room temperature sausage bacon piece of meat in there, that drags the temperature of the pan down and so it stops smoking. Now, the sausage, bacon, what have you is made of mostly water, as most foods are, and so thereafter the heat energy that's being put into the pan by the cooker isn't going towards raising its temperature, it's going towards boiling off the water. And the boiling off water is what makes the spitting sound of frying. So that basically prevents the temperature of the pan getting back up to the smoke point of the oil which is why it doesn't smoke anymore while you're cooking your food. But it will eventually if you were to leave the sausage or bacon in there until it was a completely dried out black mess then there'd be no more water and the temperature would rise and it would start smoking again.

questions.question: If an astronomer looks at outer space and he sees planets and stars, he tells you that we're looking at them thousands and sometimes millions of years in the past because of the amount of time that lights come to reach the stars. If you're able to travel in a spacecraft rocket at twice the speed of light, would you be going backwards or forwards in time?

answers.answer: The faster you go, time slows down. And when you actually hit the speed of light, time ceases to exist as a concept. So if you're going at twice the speed of light, it wouldn't make any difference. In other words, time no longer exists at the point of speed of light. It's a real effect. Things like GPS, so if you're at the top of a mountain and I'm at the bottom of a mountain, your clock will run slightly slower than mine because of course speed over distance, you'd have travelled further. The faster you go, the slower your clock to the point at the point of speed of light the clock stops.

questions.question: Given what's happening in Northern Ireland with the stalemates in the Parliament, where nothing's happening, the DUP and Sinn Féin won't... If that were to happen in Westminster, would it make any significant difference?

answers.answer: I don't think it applies to Westminster because there's no power sharing in Westminster. So if you refuse to sit in the House of Commons, that's just tough, your opponents will win all the votes. I was just wondering whether there was some ancient law. I don't think so, because Sinn Féin don't take up their seats in London. I think the power sharing thing is what means that they can't the installment can't sit if the DUP are refusing to join in. I don't think there would be any equivalent, even if everybody refused to turn up. I suppose you'd have to have another general election or something like that, but I don't think there's a parallel here.

questions.question: Do animals in the animal kingdom, whether wild or domestic, have eyes that change? Are they sometimes short-sighted or long-sighted like humans need glasses later in life?

answers.answer: The truth is we don't know for sure whether animals are affected in quite the same way we are with long-sightedness or short-sightedness because it's not easy to test. However, dogs in particular, as they get older, get a condition called nuclear sclerosis where a cloudiness appears within the lens. It's not quite the same as a cataract. We suspect there's going to be some sort of effect, a bit like slightly clouding and slight lack of clarity in their vision.

questions.question: Where do collective nouns come from? Who dreams them up?
Can people be allergic to butterflies?
Is there anything in the world that is impossible for anyone to be allergic to?

answers.answer: A flamboyance of flamingos, an embarrassment of pandas, a tower of giraffes, a kaleidoscope of butterflies, an obstinacy of buffaloes, a lamentation of swans, a rumba of rattlesnakes.

Yes, your body can produce IgE antibodies to pretty much anything at any time throughout your lifetime. You can be eating strawberries one year and find the following year you're allergic to it. Anything that you can put into your body or anything that your body can come into contact with could, at some point, in someone, prompt an allergic reaction.

questions.question: If water is clear, why then, when there are waterfalls, or even when we have waves, do we see it come up as white?

answers.answer: It's the same reason that clouds are white. The droplets are really, really close together. So light goes into it, gets split into the colours of the rainbow. But it then goes into another droplet and that scatters it out and it goes into another. And eventually, you just have all the light being mixed together, so it mixes back into white light. Clouds and waterfalls are basically crap rainbows.

questions.question: Can babies be scared of the dark?

answers.answer: Babies aren't scared of the dark when they're that little. They only start getting scared when they're toddlers because that's when they get an imagination. Pure darkness is actually the best way of getting them to sleep and sleep training - pitch black is brilliant. The baby is not settling for reasons other than darkness, probably wanting cuddles and closeness like in the womb. I'd suggest swaddling.

questions.question: Will the Sahara run out of sand eventually? If so, how is it replaced? If not, how is it replenished?

answers.answer: No, it wouldn't run out because there's a relationship between the velocity of wind and atmospheric currents with the deposition of sand. The higher the velocity, the heavier the grains are able to be transported. When you see dust on your car window screen, it's always that finer material. The wind only transports the finer stuff and leaves behind the heavier stuff. So it would replenish. In the longer term, millions of years, if climate change made it more humid or maritime climate, you'd stop getting deposition of sand and get deposition of organic material and then the desert would disappear.

questions.question: Do people have different thickness eyelids?
Why is the alphabet in the alphabetical order that it's in?

answers.answer: It goes back before Greek to Phoenician and Hebrew. The names of the letters weren't really letter names originally. You can tell from the word delta which looks like a triangle. Beth means house in Hebrew, became the letter Beth, then Greek beta. They started being used in order relatively late in Greek times for numbers - alpha would be one, beta would be two. Then there was the catalog of the Library of Alexandria when they started to come to the order we know now. Eventually dictionaries in Latin and Greek in the first century. English didn't have dictionaries until the Middle Ages - first biblical dictionaries. It wasn't until about the 12th or 13th century that the order became fixed, and it differs for different languages.

questions.question: Is handwriting inherited?
Why do I never swallow chewing gum by mistake when I swallow everything else eventually after chewing long enough?

answers.answer: It's because it doesn't break down. The message from mouth to brain is that this isn't ready to swallow yet. You carry on chewing but it never breaks down, so the message to your brain never says let's swallow it.

The answer about breaking down was correct but not complete. It's also a learning process - we learn to put chewing gum in our mouth not to swallow but to chew. The first part of chewing and swallowing is under voluntary control, but once it reaches the tonsil area, it's no longer voluntary and you have to swallow it. We keep chewing gum nearer the front of our mouth because that puts it under voluntary control. Children don't have this learned behaviour in place, which is why you shouldn't give chewing gum to little children.

questions.question: If all the ships and boats and vessels around the world were taken out of the water, would there be a noticeable drop in the sea level?

answers.answer: No. Compared to the mass of all the biomass in the ocean, the ships barely register. To make a noticeable difference, if you were to take out all the ships, all the biomass, everything we've put in the oceans, all the garbage, that might make a difference but probably not making a noticeable difference either. The oceans are just so epic and immense. Unlike a canal lock which is a very closed system, the ocean is not a closed system.

questions.question: Why is the number four on a clock face written as IIII in Roman numerals rather than IV?

answers.answer: It was to do with symmetry - to make the four look larger in correspondence to the eight on the other side of the clock face.

questions.question: What is the grinding noise you hear on an aircraft when taxiing along the runway before takeoff? It sounds like a long dog bark.

answers.answer: It's called the 'Barking Dog on an Airplane.' It only happens on Airbus 320 aircraft (A319, A320, A321), like EasyJet. There are three hydraulic systems: green, blue, and yellow. The blue is powered by ground connection, the yellow goes on when the first engine turns on, and when engine one turns on it activates the PTU (power transfer unit) which sends hydraulic fluid to pressurize the green line. That's what makes the noise. If you look at the wings, you may see the aileron droop when you hear that noise.

questions.question: If you have a successful heart transplant from a pig into a person and it doesn't get rejected, would that affect the person's lifespan? Could they live as long as a normal person, or would it be limited to the lifespan of a pig?

answers.answer: I had a pig valve fitted in my heart. Its life expectancy was around 15 years, but I managed to ruin it in seven. It calcified and leaked quite badly, so I had to get it replaced. I think they usually do them now with cow tissues or you get a mechanical valve. I've had two of them in six or seven years.

The gentleman ended up passing away from mass organ failure, which usually occurs with major cardiovascular operations like heart or lung transplants. The heart itself was in very good condition and performing well. The reason he was up for surgery was because he was near end of life and the rest of his body couldn't keep up. The surgeon mentioned a possible virus as well. As of the time, the heart was going strong and performing better than expected. It's really unknown whether a pig heart could be as successful long-term since it's so new.

questions.question: Is there a difference in metals that can go into a microwave? What determines whether metal sparks in a microwave?
Do we still have an air raid siren system in Britain? I haven't seen one for a long time.

answers.answer: Yes, we do still have air raid sirens in places that require them. Here in Plymouth because of Devonport Dockyard, they test their air raid siren every Monday at 11 o'clock. When I first moved here over 20 years ago it was quite alarming. They are also moving towards an emergency text message alert system which was tested this week in Plymouth.

The test siren is actually every Monday at half past 11 on the dot, not 11 o'clock. It is a nuclear accident alarm, not an air raid siren, because of the nuclear submarines being repaired in the dockyard. Testing is part of the safety justification.

questions.question: Did pirates back in the days of empire actually speak the way they are portrayed in popular culture? Like 'ya-har-har' and 'ya-ho-ho' and 'shiver me timbers'?

answers.answer: This started with an actor called Robert Newton who played Long John Silver in a film of Treasure Island in the 1950s. He went on to star in a series called Long John Silver. It was his way of speaking and it caught on so much that it became associated with all pirates. Someone texted in to confirm that modern pirates speak with a 'Newtonian accent.'

questions.question: If I like barbecue sauce and you don't, does it taste the same to us and you just don't like that taste? Or does it taste differently to different people? Since my wife had COVID she used to really like onions but now can't stand the taste of them - they taste totally different to her now.

answers.answer: His wife's condition sounds like parosmia, which is a common after-effect of COVID. It's where the cells in the nasal receptors are picking up distorted signals from their food. This is different from complete loss of taste. The charity Fifth Sense works with people who have smell and taste disorders.

The reason some people taste things differently is genetic. The most obvious example is coriander - about 20% of the population taste it as soapy because they have a different receptor that picks it up more acutely. Bitter taste comes from being able to detect poison, and genetic variability in this helped people survive. If you can detect a poison more acutely and others who can't eat that plant and die, your children live on. So genetic variability propagates if advantageous. With strawberries, if it's not poisonous, it won't negatively select against you - you'll just not like the strawberry. If strawberries became the only food available, those people would die out.

questions.question: Why can you still see images when you close your eyes after staring at something? Like looking at black tiles and then when you blink, you can still see the inverted colours. Or playing Tetris and then seeing it when you close your eyes.

answers.answer: It's called the waterfall illusion for movement. Basically your neurons get tired because you've been staring at that colour for too long. When you look away, those neurons are fatigued and all the other colours are still at normal activation level, so you see the opponent colour instead. The waterfall illusion is the same but with motion - when watching credits go up and then looking at a blank wall, you see downward motion because your up neurons have been firing. It's fatigue of neurons - psychology is all about perception and how your brain and neurons fire.

questions.question: Why do airline pilots sit on sheepskin covers in the flight deck? Is it superstition, tradition, or is there a technical reason?

answers.answer: They do sit on sheepskin and there are several reasons. They maintain temperature - whether it's hot or cold in the flight deck, the seat stays the same temperature. They're also hypoallergenic so won't irritate a pilot's skin. And they don't melt - if there's a fire in the flight deck, the seat cover won't catch fire, and when they do melt, they don't stick to anything. There's probably something modern that could fulfil all those criteria, but it's always been done this way. It's more common on Boeing aircraft because Americans like their traditions more, while Airbus is more modern.

questions.question: Why do we say 'first' and 'second' when they bear no resemblance to 'one' and 'two', but then we use 'third', 'fourth', 'fifth' which do correspond to 'three', 'four', 'five'?

answers.answer: This is called suppletion. In the early stages of a language before it gets fully standardised, you get different parts of the same word from different sources. 'First' is from the same root as Greek 'protos' (as in prototype, protozoic). 'Second' is from a Latin root meaning following or coming after the first. When a language gets more standardised, that kind of thing tends to get evened out and you get the same root for all parts. But with very common and short words, you use them so much that you're very familiar with it and don't feel the need to replace them by more regular forms. This happens with other words too - 'go' and 'went', and verbs in English like 'to be' (I am, you are, he is). Russian uses 40 which has nothing to do with 4 or 10 - that's another example of suppletion.

questions.question: When the Queen passes away and there's a new monarch, what happens to the money with the Queen's head on it? Do the notes get taken out of circulation gradually or all at once?

answers.answer: They've already got Charles on the next note. All the new stuff has Charles's head on it. Then all the old stuff is taken out of circulation at the same rate it would have been anyway. You could still get King George coins around well into the 50s or 60s. They won't be discontinued overnight. They just carry on as normal and gradually get replaced.

questions.question: Why do things stay fresh in a sealed container when the air chemistry is surely the same inside and out?

answers.answer: At the moment of closure, the air inside and outside is similar, but the ingredients will start to oxidise, and if it's in a sealed box, they will run out of oxygen, so they will stop oxidising.

questions.question: How do they calculate food waste? How do they know what everybody's bought, how much they're throwing away?

answers.answer: They probably take a sample and then multiply it to get the bigger population. It's probably going to involve a survey and then a multiplication.

We do it by recruiting a sample of people from across the UK and we literally ask them to measure and weigh everything they throw away, including things like milk that they might tip down the drain or juice that gets thrown away. We collect all of that data and then multiply that and come up with the figure.

questions.question: Why don't tattoos disappear? They just fade. We slough our skin every four or five times a year and apparently our skin changes over seven years.

answers.answer: The tattoo is injected below the skin in a different layer. The ink is deeper than that, which is why it will fade. The ink itself will fade over a really long period of time but it will still be there because it's underneath the skin layers.

questions.question: What does O stand for? And what does K stand for? in OK

answers.answer: My favourite theory is wrong - in Greek you would say ola kala which would mean all good. But I think everybody just says it, nobody really knows what it means.

questions.question: Have penguins got knees? I've never seen a penguin flex their knees.

answers.answer: Probably not, which would make them unique in the bird world. All birds have knees but they flex differently to ours, they flex backwards.

Yes, they do have knees. The femur on a penguin is a very short bone and it's very high up on their body. As a result, they can't really flex them, hence the reason they walk the way they do. We all have hips, knees, femurs - we're all built on the same kind of thing.

questions.question: We're sending all these arms and munitions out to Ukraine. If it wasn't for a crisis like Ukraine, what happens to it all? Does it just go into storage?

answers.answer: Some of the factories can be retooled and repurposed, they might be doing other things the rest of the time like PPE. But munitions and armaments, I wouldn't have thought they'd retool rapidly.

They would have been put into store and weapons and munitions can be stored for an incredible length of time. A large percentage would be taken from store and used in training both in UK as well as NATO. The levels are going to be the same all the time give or take. Weapons can be reprocessed - electronics checked, cordite refreshed and put back into store.

questions.question: Is there a name for forgetting what day it is because of bank holidays? After Easter break I couldn't remember what day it was.
Why is it three square meals a day? Why do we call them square meals?

answers.answer: It's the Navy. Square plates on ships because they're made of wood and you wouldn't make them round out of wood because that would be really hard. And three square meals a day was an inducement for joining the Navy.

questions.question: Sea otters have a pocket in which they keep their favorite stone that they use to open clams. Are there any other animals that have pockets for toys or tools?
When I back all my data up online, how many physical places is it stored? If it's all in one server building and there's a fire or flood, have I lost all my data?

answers.answer: When you store data in the cloud, it gets stored in a data centre with hundreds if not thousands of servers sharing lots of copies of that data. If one server fails, there's another one due to fault tolerance. Data centres are also geographically replicated. They're enormous warehouses. Microsoft even did a proof of concept of one under the sea off the coast of Scotland. The cloud is just someone else's computer.

questions.question: How did the Australian and New Zealand accents come about in such a short space of time after we colonised them?

answers.answer: If you went back far enough, people were more likely to sound Australian in this country than they would be now. Australia and American are probably more similar to each other than they are to London.

The accent in Australia and New Zealand was originally more like what we now think of as a New Zealand accent. The Australian accent reverted back towards the British norm because it's a bigger place with more international exposure. New Zealand was very isolated so it had less of a melting pot effect. The biggest effect is the second vowel shift, which is why New Zealand has very high front vowels - tin for ten. When you look at the distribution of settlers in Australia, there was a preponderance from south-east Anglia, Essex and so on - criminals. The first fleet was in Sydney in the 1780s. If you were in 1780s Essex, the accent would be closer to a New Zealand accent than a today Essex accent. The exceptions were Adelaide which had free settlers with a posher accent, and far south of New Zealand with many Scottish settlers.

questions.question: Why does my dog who has a highly developed olfactory system insist on placing his snout adjacent to other dogs' bottoms and various other unsavory places?

answers.answer: Dogs have what's known as the vomeronasal organ in the nose which opens up when they start really sniffing and takes in all the pheromones, which are chemical communicators. The reason they do that is to take as much of the smell in as possible. They can really tell how the other dog is feeling, what he's had to eat, if he's sick or not, if it's a female, if she's going to be close on heat or not. They might even lick their lips and do that, or lick their noses to make it even more moist.

questions.question: When you have a picture a couple of hundred years old that's black and white, how do people know what colour to add to it?

answers.answer: Black and white photos have many shades of grey, perhaps as many as 50. You can do a calculation to work out what primary colour a particular shade of grey denoted and use that as a rough guide. With a picture now, if you were wearing a blue jumper and red trousers, they'd look different even in black and white. You'd also use some imagination and knowledge - for example, the sky is unlikely to be green.

It is basically guesswork using an educated guess. You know what colour a tree is going to be, what bricks are going to be. The trousers and the jumper aren't the same shade, so if you've got a rough idea. Particularly with trees, you can tell the species as well so you can guess the colour from that.

questions.question: What is the origin of OK?

answers.answer: Back in World War II, when squadrons used to fly back in, people used to say how's the squadron doing? And they'd say OK which was a zero kill.
In two parts of France, north is called Languedoc because they use oui for yes. The south is Languedoc where they use the word oc for yes. The oc is the origin of OK.

questions.question: When does your brain tell your body the nutrition it needs? Why do I get cravings for specific foods like avocados or bananas?

answers.answer: If you have a craving for something, it probably means your levels are depleted. Bananas contain potassium, so if you crave bananas, your potassium levels might be low. Your brain is telling your body that you need certain nutrients.

It's the microbiome. You have roughly 100 trillion cells but only 10 trillion have your DNA. The rest are bacteria living in your gut. These bacteria send chemical signals to your brain telling you what to eat. The good bacteria tell you to eat vitamins and proteins, but bad bacteria tell you to eat sugars and excess fat. The more you feed the bad bacteria, the stronger their signals get.

questions.question: When did the acronym VIP become commonplace? When did 'very important person' become a recognized status?

answers.answer: There's no definitive answer. It might have come around in the 1930s in America where there was a fad for acronyms (FBI, MGM, FDR). It might have come from the huge usage of telegraph where you'd say 'he's on the plane, make sure to look after him, he's a VIP.' It might have come from the Royal Air Force in the 1940s for the same reason - to shorten messages.

questions.question: Where did the black light come from in an LCD telly? You have red, green, and blue pixels to make other colors and white, but how do they make black?

answers.answer: It depends on the technology. First generation LCD screens have three filters of liquid crystals in front of a diode that kicks out white light. You pass current across red, green or blue diodes to get color mixes. Black is the absence of any color - the LED is just off. On newer generation screens, they have 'local dimming' which means they can turn off the backlight per section of LEDs, so that part of a black screen would be darker than the rest.

questions.question: Why does white skin exist? Why did our ancestors' skin get paler as they migrated north?

answers.answer: It's about homeostasis - maintaining a constant internal environment. Dark skin scatters lots of sunlight to avoid cell damage but also allows lots of body heat to escape. White is a good insulator - it keeps body heat in. So in cold environments, white skin allows you to keep more body heat and stop hypothermia. As you head north, you need the reflection more than absorption.

questions.question: What is the oldest gesture in the world? Is the finger-to-lips 'shush' gesture the oldest?
When making icing sugar and buttercream, huge clouds of icing sugar come up. Can I taste it even with my mouth closed. Does that count towards my daily sugar intake?

answers.answer: Yes, some of it gets caught up in your saliva. Your nose and throat are all tubular, so you will end up swallowing stuff that has gone in via your nose. However, it's not going to make a noticeable difference to the amount of calories you're consuming. I don't think you need to go on a diet to counteract inhaling a bit of icing sugar when making a cake.

questions.question: We call the people of Germany 'Germans' and people of Spain 'Spanish'. Why do we call the people of the Netherlands 'Dutch'?

answers.answer: It comes from 'Deutsch' - the German word for German. There used to be High Deutsch and Low Deutsch, and one of them became 'Dutch' for the people of the Netherlands. The people of the Netherlands actually call themselves 'Nederlanders'.

questions.question: Why, when you walk outside and it's cold, do your eyes start to water?

answers.answer: The cold dries your eyes out quicker than body temperature weather, and therefore they need extra lubrication. Your eye sends a message to your brain saying you need lubrication, and then your eyes start watering. It's something to do with how hydrated you are.

questions.question: Why do we have such strange collective nouns for animals? Like 'a flamboyance of flamingos' or 'a murder of crows'. Who decided that?
Are some musical instruments definitively harder to play than others? My mum says trombone is easy compared to cello and guitar.

answers.answer: As a music teacher who has played all three instruments: the guitar is the easiest because you just put your finger in the right fret and pull the string. The cello is in the middle because you have to choose where to put your finger but there's no frets so you'll roughly get the right note. The trombone is the hardest because with all brass instruments you produce sound by buzzing your lips - even a slight difference in lip pressure or air can change a note, so in every position you can hit wrong notes. For the French horn specifically, it's the hardest because the tubing is longer and narrower so the harmonic series is closer together, meaning more chance of splitting notes.

I'd say the French horn is the hardest musical instrument. The harmonic series is so much closer together because the tubing is so much longer and the bore is narrower, so the notes are closer together. That means you have more chance of splitting the notes. That's why professional French horn players play wrong notes in orchestras more than any other instrument.

questions.question: What's the relationship between rubbing your chin and calling someone 'Jimmy Hill' when they're lying? What's the origin of 'chinny chin chin'?

answers.answer: Jimmy Hill had a very big chin, hence 'chinny chin chin' for lying. In some parts of the world they say 'beard' instead.

questions.question: When it rains, is it inevitable that those raindrops fall to Earth, or on occasions, can they get blown back up into the clouds or evaporate before they reach the Earth?

answers.answer: Raindrops can't make their way back up. As raindrops begin to fall from a cloud, if they pass through a layer of colder, drier air, they can evaporate before reaching ground. Cold air tends to be drier. When raindrops fall into that colder, drier air, the raindrop evaporates because the air's moisture level is lower. This is called evaporative cooling. This is more common during winter because air tends to be colder, but it can happen in summer too.

questions.question: Why do we get itchy when we're tired or half asleep?

answers.answer: Getting itchy when tired is a known thing - David and his family don't need to go to the doctor unless they have weird rashes. It's because we don't hydrate during sleep. Every part of our body becomes naturally dehydrated through sweating. That makes the surface of the skin quite itchy. Body temperature and blood flow also increase to keep warm while sleeping, and the rising temperature makes us feel itchy as well. It could all be linked to the dehydration.

questions.question: How do they work out sea level? Because the seabed's not level and the tide goes up and down.

answers.answer: Sea level was originally fixed to Liverpool but the survey moved that location to Newlyn in Cornwall. Newlyn was chosen because it has quite a small tidal range and predictable tidal cycles. Sea level is a fixed man-made concept - the sea can actually be below sea level. The value chosen as zero is the median of the tidal cycle, essentially the midpoint between high tide and low tide. The Ordnance Survey calibrates all contour maps to that value. However, it's not international - different countries and mapping organisations can have their own fixed baselines.

questions.question: What do they do with the voice box? Does it get put in a fridge or what? Or put back in?

answers.answer: A tracheostomy doesn't actually have much to do with the voice box because everything happens below it. Your Adam's apple is just under your chin. A tracheostomy goes in below that - it's a hole from the windpipe or trachea to the outside so they can breathe through that hole or be ventilated. The reason Xander only had air come out when he tried to talk was because no air was making its way past the tracheotomy hole. His voice box went nowhere - it stayed exactly where it always is. The voice box was simply bypassed by the hole in his neck, not removed.

questions.question: Why do we refer to the recently deceased as 'the late'?

answers.answer: 'Late' used to be Old English for 'recently' but not anymore. The phrase 'late of this parish' meant someone who had recently left the parish.

questions.question: Are there any good viruses? I want to know if there are viruses that make you feel better rather than worse.

answers.answer: Viruses don't try to make you feel good or bad - they take over your cells and systems to reproduce, and your immune system attacking them is what makes you feel bad. Regarding bacteriophages - they kill bacteria but they also contribute to lateral gene transfer, which can make bacteria more harmful over time. So bacteriophages are good in the sense they kill bacteria, but they wouldn't affect your mood and can actually make bacteria more dangerous.

questions.question: Why don't we grow another tooth if we lose our permanent teeth?

answers.answer: All your teeth are in your head when you're born - they're stacked up on top of each other in your skull. You can't grow a new tooth because they're all already there, just waiting to emerge. There wouldn't be any reproductive advantage to growing your own teeth, which is the driving engine of evolution.

questions.question: Why are the buttons and the opening on the front of my trousers called flies or fly buttons?

answers.answer: It comes from the flagpole where you fly a flag - the flag flies. The zipper resembles the pole and the tag on the end you use to pull it up and down is the flag, so that's where it gets its name.

After they got rid of cod pieces, there were little flaps of material covering your bits and that was called a fly. It's like a little flag - even if it's a flap on something, it's still flying. The zipper kept the name 'fly' from when it was just a flap of cloth.

questions.question: Is a molehill all dug by one mole, or are there teams of moles that do them? Or are there giant moles?

answers.answer: One molehill is created by one mole. Moles have a territory which they dig tunnels in to get worms which they feed from. They push up the soil from the tunnel to create the molehill.

questions.question: If you're on a flight and have a medical emergency, what happens when you land with regard to customs checks if you're immediately rushed off to hospital?

answers.answer: The pilot would put out a PAN call - PAN PAN - to get priority for landing. On arrival at the airport, you'd be met by Border Force and the police. The Border Force and police would check the documents of the person on the plane before they're removed.

questions.question: When you flip a coin, they say heads or tails. One side is clearly a heads, but why is the other side called tails when it isn't a tail?

answers.answer: It's the opposite of heads. I don't know if it's going to have a meaning. The answer is probably linked to the head versus tail rather than any pictogram or similar on the reverse of the coin. Probably. It was just the opposite of heads. So what do you want? Heads or the opposite, i.e. tails?

It comes from the Romans. Back in the day, when they used to make their coins, they always had on one side the head of whoever was in charge, whatever. Caesar, isn't it, usually? Or whatever, one of them. And on the other side, they used to have a dragon with a great big long tail that used to go all the way round the coin. So when they flipped it to make a decision, it was heads or tails.
When I was about ten, the old 10p used to have a lion on the other side. The heads or tails was around in the 19th century. It could have had a lion on it then.

questions.question: Why do seas have different levels of saltiness?

answers.answer: It's the temperature. The hotter the water is, the more salt it holds. So around the equator, the seas warm up, they hold more salt. And the way to test it is if you've got kids, you get two glasses, put a spoon of salt in each. Pour 100ml of cold water in the one jar and 100ml of warm water in the other jar and watch what happens. The Dead Sea is not a sea. It's a lake. It's salty because the water evaporates off and then you get more salt left in it. Where there are anomalies, it's because cold water falls through warm water and the currents take it along the bottom.

Half right in the sense of evaporation. It will actually increase the salinity of water. But mostly, it's down to the igneous rock of where that ocean is specifically. Certain rocks will emit more salt than others. The seas are huge, by the time it's all mixed it up together, you're going to have all the rocks coming in from all over the place. The experiment with the two glasses of water, one hot, one cold, and which can hold the most salt is the beginning and the end of this. But your point is relevant perhaps to the Dead Sea, because it's a lake. So the igneousness, the salinity of the igneous rocks plus the evaporation is the reason why it's so salty. But it's not a sea, you see.

questions.question: How do we know how dinosaurs sounded?

answers.answer: I don't think we do know how they sounded. There'll be some research that could have been done into their voice boxes and like anatomical specs. And speculation on what they would have sounded like. Someone told me once that we can't know for sure that dinosaurs weren't bright purple, because we've only ever found bones and fossils. So they could have been bright green with massive pink spots. They could have all looked like Mr. Blobby. A dinosaur might sound like a chicken.

It's generally quite difficult to tell what sounds a dinosaur may have made because the soft tissue of the mouth and the throat and so on generally doesn't get preserved. It doesn't get fossilized. However, there is an exception - the Parasaurolophus, which was a herbivorous dinosaur. It had quite a long horn coming out of the back of its head. It looked a bit like the Xenomorph from the Alien film. That has been preserved. Inside that horn there are sort of hollows, which acted as acoustic chambers, almost like sort of little amplifiers. By modeling those acoustic chambers, it's been found that the Parasaurolophus could have made sort of a trumpeting sound, sort of an elephantine kind of sound. Birds are the closest living relative that we have to dinosaurs. So by looking at the bone structure of similar living creatures, like modern reptiles and modern birds, there are inferences can be made, but the Parasaurolophus we're sort of a bit more sure about.

questions.question: Why do we say O in front of telephone numbers rather than 0 or zero?

answers.answer: It's probably because it sounds easier. It's just shorthand. It's verbal efficiency. We all say O, don't we? I couldn't answer it.

Very old-fashioned telephones. Dials. Areas of London. You would use letter codes. The Americans took this to an extreme. They used to say, if you want to phone somebody because you've broken your leg, phone Busted 12758. If you had a string of numbers associated with Busted, you'd never remember. So it's just a shorthand. It's quicker. It's smoother. It's efficiency. It came from the telephone exchanges. It was just far easier to say C-R-O-1-2-3-4. C-R-O, but it was an O. It was an O for Croydon. It wasn't a zero. It was an O.

questions.question: Why do bananas go brown when you keep them in the dark?

answers.answer: I'm not sure that the premise of your question is valid. I don't know that you have sufficiently demonstrated that bananas do go brown in the dark. You need to have two sets of shopping, one in the boot and one not in the boot, in order to conduct an experiment.

It's got nothing to do with the dark. It's basically all about the temperature. If he's left them in the car, bananas don't like the cold, and it sends them browner a lot quicker. If they're in a really cold temperature, you could leave them out in a really cold house, and they would do the same thing. It's got nothing to do with light or dark. It's all to do with temperature.

It's the fact that they're in an enclosed space. Enclosed spaces are normally dark. The thing which makes bananas go off is ethylene or ethene. When you transport bananas over from South America, they'll actually pump in the gas in order to make them ripen at the correct time. So in an enclosed space, you will have the ethene gas ripening the bananas, which they give off as well. It's nothing to do with the darkness. The temperature is going to increase the reaction rate, because obviously rate increases with temperature in chemistry. But not on this one. The colder it is, the darker they go.

questions.question: What makes popping candy pop?

answers.answer: Do you remember Space Dust? You'd pour it into your mouth and your tongue would go nuts. It hits the saliva, it hits some sort of fluid, it makes it pop. But what makes it pop? I don't know.

questions.question: Why were beds in old palaces and Shakespeare's house so short?

answers.answer: People were shorter back then. You've seen suits of armour. They're tiny.

It's to do with the immense paranoia of death. They made the beds shorter so that they could not accidentally slip and lie down. And then they would appear awake so that when death floated past the window, he would just sail on his merry way rather than take them.

questions.question: Would eczema affect your fingerprint in terms of identification?

answers.answer: I think they use acid sometimes to burn off fingerprints. But eczema wouldn't, if that answers your question, eczema wouldn't affect your fingerprint. Someone listening will know. There might be something that does sufficient damage to your thumb so that your fingerprint would no longer be recognisable, but it's not going to be something that's naturally occurring.

I've had eczema my entire life and back in the day when we had fingerprint tech on phones to unlock, I would have to have multiple fingerprints depending on the severity of my eczema on my fingers and I couldn't unlock the phone. Thank goodness for passcodes. It can't be much fun for you. I only get it on my hands now and then nowadays. Luckily, it's face recognition now, so that works.

questions.question: How much of the airspace above your property do you own? Can you zipline over your neighbour's house?

answers.answer: No, he would be trespassing. Going over his neighbour's bits, he would. In the air. So basically it's all to do with trespass and the question of ownership. How high up can you go?
