Because the aeroplanes fly over my garden and they're not trespassing. There's a lower stratum and an upper stratum. The upper stratum is generally where we would hope that the aeroplanes are flying. It will vary because it will be down to the Civil Aviation Authority and what they've applied in those areas. In Hounslow, as planes come into land, that level could be just a few hundred foot. In my part of the world, Concord, County Durham, about 15 miles out of Newcastle Airport, that plane could be up at about 20,000 foot. So it does genuinely vary.

questions.question: How long would it take if you were asleep on your arm for there to be permanent damage?

answers.answer: Different tissues have different tolerance to ischemia. Brain cells die after a few seconds, hence strokes. Heart cells can last about 20-30 minutes. Muscles start early damage at about 4 hours, permanent damage at 6-8 hours. Bone and tendon last longer. In surgery, tourniquets are released after about 2 hours to let the limb re-perfuse.

questions.question: Why are energy drinks sold in short thin cans while soft drinks are sold in short fat ones?
Which culture or civilisation first came up with the idea of the love heart shape?

answers.answer: It's to do with a plant in Roman times used as a contraceptive. The seeds or seed pods were in the shape of what we now call a love heart. It's called silphium or similar.

questions.question: How do different people have different tolerances of spiking?

answers.answer: You can be a non-taster, medium taster, or supertaster, and it all depends on how many taste buds there are on your tongue. The more taste buds, the more you taste. Daniel has fewer taste buds than his 8-year-old daughter.

questions.question: Do colors actually exist or are they a construct of the mind? How would we know?

answers.answer: Colors and light can be measured with scientific equipment. If you take white light and put a filter in front of it that blocks all colors except say red, it can be measured by a photomultiplier tube. The fact that it can be measured means it exists beyond just perception.

questions.question: Why do we clean our teeth with cold water when everything else we clean in everyday life is with hot or warm water?

answers.answer: It's a throwback to the days when hot water was less potable than cold water. Hot water tanks had rats and birds getting in, so people wouldn't drink from hot taps or brush teeth with that water. Now with combi boilers, the water comes from the same source, so theoretically you could use hot water.
Challenged the answer - still advises against hot water because of Legionella in tanks at 55-65 degrees. Caller is a plumber who still deals with hot water tanks, especially in big houses in Chelsea.

questions.question: When did we start using an X to signify a kiss? What's the origin?

answers.answer: The X originally represented the Christian cross and was a way of denoting sincerity or good faith on documents. Over the centuries it evolved into a sign of love. The Christian cross isn't like an X, it changed over time.

questions.question: Is water wet?

answers.answer: Water isn't wet. The term 'wet' describes a liquid's ability to absorb into a surface. Water can't be wet because it can't saturate itself - otherwise 10 gallons would be wetter than 1 gallon which is ridiculous. Using the dictionary definition: something covered or saturated with water - you can't apply that to water itself.

questions.question: What is the origin of the first knock knock joke?

answers.answer: The first knock knock joke is credited to William Shakespeare. It's from MacBeth - the Porter scene where MacBeth is drunk and compares being at the castle to hell. 'Knock knock. Who's there? In the name of Beelzebub.' Sam is an English teacher who has been telling students this for years. The exam board used this extract in a GCSE question and teachers were furious because it's quite rude and difficult to teach.

questions.question: Who first thought gold was precious and why is it a precious metal?

answers.answer: Gold has properties that made it valuable: immutable (can't be destroyed), divisible (unlike a cow), recognizable throughout the world. 'Sound money' came from throwing gold on a table - if it made a sound, you knew it was real. But gold being shiny and rare and moldable into jewelry is the main reason.

Red Bull (energy drink) was invented in Thailand. It did really bad in taste testing in the US. They needed to differentiate it and market it as a medicinal product rather than soda because they didn't think customers would accept it as soda. So they changed the size and shape of the can to look more medical/medicinal.

questions.question: How did they measure the height of mountains before modern technology?

answers.answer: It would be trigonometry. You measure the side, the adjacent... you'd need to be able to see the top. You'd need the top to the ground. You're not going to get a vertical drop.

It's trigonometry but not as accurate as we'd like. You find the height of the mountain - that's an imaginary line of a triangle. You walk a certain distance away - that's another line. From the top of the mountain to where you're standing is the hypotenuse. You need to measure the angle you tilt your head to look up. The sign of that angle is the opposite divided by the distance from the mountain. But you need to be able to see the top. The inaccuracy comes from estimating how much of the base of the mountain you count. This goes back to Pythagoras and Eratosthenes who calculated the circumference of the Earth using a well and a stick.

There is more to that story than Professor Howell indicated regarding the mountain question. The ancients who could have measured mountains include Eratosthenes who calculated the Earth's circumference using a well at Alexandria and a stick down the road.

questions.question: What was the difference between the red and black side of the table tennis bat?

answers.answer: I used to have a Schlesinger bat that was pimply on one side and flat on the other. Both sides seem smooth now and equally sticky. I twizzled the bat for serve rather than technique. It's changed in my lifetime - my Schlesinger was black on both sides but pimply and smooth, and I'm pretty sure that's not allowed anymore.

Your bat must have been an old Schlesinger. Before 1980, John Hilton won the European Championships using the same colour rubbers on each side - pimply and smooth. He won by twiddling his bat so no one could see what rubber he was using. In the 1980s, the International Table Tennis Federation changed the rules so you had to have one black and one red. Although Christian didn't detect any difference between the two sides, there would be a difference if you're using different rubbers on each side. Even if it's the same rubber on both sides, you're not allowed to have the same colour. It has to be red and black - now it must be black on one side and any colour on the other.

The table tennis rules - when Jim Hilton or John Hilton won the title in the 80s, he was playing with a bat that had two different rubbers on it even though they were the same colour. The rules changed so it has to be different colours, even if you've got the same rubber on both sides. It's about fairness for the person receiving your shot. The rules were changed around 1986.

questions.question: Do cartographers change the mapping when coastal erosion happens? Do they keep it for the UK itself or just keep it basic so it doesn't have to get changed?

answers.answer: Not on a scale map it's not noticeable. It happens a lot on the coast in Norfolk - over 20 years the cliff has come up to people's back doors.

It depends on the scale of the mapping. The Ordnance Survey's largest scale maps are at 1 to 2500. When coastal erosion, sea level rise, and sediment accretion happen, at that scale those changes will have to be mapped. The Ordnance Survey continues to do mapping updates and brings those changes onto their systems. But they also publish smaller scale maps - 1 to 1 million, 1 to 2 million - and at that scale these changes are completely undetectable. So yes, it's still being mapped, but it's a question of when it becomes significant enough to be noticed at the relevant scale.

questions.question: At what point does water at room temperature get to the point where it's actually off?

answers.answer: It never goes off. There wouldn't be a point where it's actually off. Only if it got lots of dust in it. Plastic bottled water can go off but that's the plastic, not the water.

Tap water doesn't go off. The reason is that water is made up of hydrogen and oxygen, which are naturally occurring elements, and tap water is treated to remove any microorganisms that might be in the water supply. So there's no potential for microorganism growth to occur in your glass of water if you leave it there for days, weeks, months, or years. Whereas with river water or stagnant water, there'll be something in it that can multiply. Bottled water can go off because the plastic and polymers in the bottle can disintegrate over time and leach into the water. That's why bottled water has an expiry date based on how long the plastic behaves under certain storage conditions.

questions.question: What is the origin of the saying 'tickety-boo'?

answers.answer: A lot of this stuff comes from the Raj and the empire. It might be a anglicised version of native language that we've adopted our own version of. It's probably not used as much now as it was.

Tickety-boo is translated from Hindi as 'Tikka Babu' which means 'I'm fine, sir'. It came about when the British soldiers in India used to say 'how are you doing' to Indian soldiers, and they used to reply 'Tikka Babu, Tikka Babu'. The British took to saying 'Tickety-boo' meaning everything is fine. I heard this from Nick Ferrari's show years ago.

questions.question: Why can we feel when someone's staring at us?

answers.answer: There is a book called 'The Sense of Being Stared At' by Rupert Sheldrake, dedicated to questions like this. He thinks it possibly has some sort of psychic explanation. But the problem is you only remember the times you thought you were being stared at and you looked up and you were. You never remember all the times you thought you were being stared at and you looked up and you weren't. Your brain goes 'oh my God I'm psychic' but you don't remember the millions of times you weren't. This is how a lot of superstitions work - you only remember when the planets align.

I took part in an experiment in the 80s with Dr Wiseman at Hertfordshire University. You had to sit in a room with a little buzzer and there was a separate room with people looking at you via live camera. You had to press the buzzer every time you felt you were being looked at. They wrote to me a few weeks later saying they concluded there is no correlation - people don't know when they're being looked at. It's just coincidence when people feel they have been. You'd remember it when you looked up and they were. You're not going to remember the hundred times when they weren't. Although you could argue that being viewed via camera rather than physically in the same place might be different.

questions.question: Why is a saxophone classified as a woodwind instrument when it is made of brass, like many other brass instruments like cornet and French horn?

answers.answer: It's actually quite boring and simple. What makes the noise that is amplified by the saxophone? Where does the actual noise come from? From the reed. What's the reed made of? Wood. Wood plus wind equals woodwind. That's it - it's that simple.

questions.question: When did dueling stop being a thing? Did it ever actually happen? When was dueling outlawed in the UK?

answers.answer: You can't consent to being killed by someone else. The same legislation that prevents assisted dying would also outlaw dueling. It might have just fallen out of favour. It might not ever have been legislated for specifically, but you couldn't do it now. Alexander Hamilton died in a duel with Aaron Burr. In New York City, there is a rock with a plaque marking where he literally rested as he died after being shot.

I know the site and date of the last duel in England. It was on a hill called Priest Hill in Englefield Green around 1852. There's a plaque up at a pub I used to drink at. So it must have been made illegal soon after 1852. That was the last legal duel. The difference between a duel and a fight is that people get killed in duels - it's a fight to the death.

Whether dueling was ever outlawed - the answer is that it wasn't because it was always illegal. It was never actually allowed, so people just stopped doing it. I wrote a book about it called 'Pistols of Dawn' published about 15 years ago.

questions.question: What are the three lions on the English football team's shirt called? They have a name and it's bugging me because I can't remember.

answers.answer: Huey, Louis and Dewey! I love you James, I love you, don't retire and do not die! Is it like a heraldic term? In heraldic terms, they're called leopards. The three lions of Anjou is also right. But traditionally they're Huey, Louis and Dewey.

The three lions on King Richard III's tabard are called leopards. No they're not - they are lions - but they're called leopards back in the day according to crusader law. I saw this on QI when Steven Fry was explaining to Frank Skinner that the three lions are non-existent and are actually three leopards.

questions.question: When I put my bin out, do the contents still belong to me until it's taken away? And if I saw my neighbour putting their bin out and they've got a picture in it that they got from a charity shop they think is a fake, but I think it's a Rembrandt, can I go and take it out of their bin?

answers.answer: If you put your wheelie bin out, you've already discarded the item, so therefore it becomes waste. The definition of waste is if you discard or require to discard, or if you intend to discard, then something becomes waste. So if you put your wheelie bin out and you have a Picasso in there, you've discarded it, so therefore it becomes fair game.
When you put rubbish in your bin and you put your bin out for collection, it becomes property of the local authority. If you take it out, you're stealing it. The bin becomes council property.

There's case law - Williams and Phillips - whereby two refuse workers were prosecuted for taking stuff out of bins and selling them. It was held by the divisional court that the refuse remained the property of the householder while it was in the bin, at which point it reverted to the property of the local authority when it was collected. But it never became ownerless. It has to have an owner for it to be theft.

questions.question: If you win a really big prize on the National Lottery and you're playing online, do you still just get that email saying you've won a prize, or would you get a telephone call? Am I wasting my time just fantasizing in bed on Sunday morning?

answers.answer: I phoned Camelot up once and asked if anyone had ever won big online. They said yes and told me several people. A work colleague won half a million pounds online and hadn't received an email. He had to go on to his account and then phone them up to confirm. He didn't get a phone call - just hadn't checked his email. So you would only get online notifications.
I won £2,050 on the lottery playing online and they called me. They didn't email me - they just called me. This was five years ago.

questions.question: How come you can safely eat a softshell crab whole, yet with other things such as fish you would have to gut them? How come it's safe to eat the whole thing - guts and everything?

answers.answer: These particular crabs actually shed their shell. The exoskeleton doesn't grow with the crab as it grows, so periodically it has to shed its skin. That's when they're formed. They're selected by producers at the point that they've just shed their skin. In terms of prawns, certain farmed ones are soft but wild ones are extra hard. They're farmed - it's a big business.

questions.question: Why does the front windscreen freeze up but the back windscreen and wing mirrors don't on a cold morning, even when you park in the same place?

answers.answer: The windscreen is a different type of glass to the rest of the car. There are multiple layers - layers of plastic, layers of glass, but also sprayed metal which conducts heat and cold much better than the rest of the car. It's because the windscreen is less conductive.

questions.question: How do painkillers know where to go?

answers.answer: Things like ibuprofen and paracetamol are anti-inflammatory and they prevent the release of chemicals called prostaglandins that cause inflammation. You feel pain in the place where you have pain but it will affect your entire body. There are other types of painkillers called opiates like codeine and morphine which block the nerve transmitters that tell the brain you're in pain and they're also euphoric so they give you a bit of a buzz so you forget you're in pain.

questions.question: How does a whip break the sound barrier? What is the mechanism of action going on at the end that causes the crack?

answers.answer: With the whip, how it creates a sonic boom is the kinetic energy going from the large end where you input it travels down the whip to the focusing point, and that's where the sonic boom is created. Because it's tapered, it gets faster and faster. As you whip it, up and down the loop, the energy multiplies on the way out. You do the movement at the fat end and as it makes its way down towards the thin end, the movement gets bigger and bigger to the point where it breaks the sound barrier.

questions.question: Why is the letter X represented as 'X-ray' or 'xylophone' in alphabet books for children when every other letter has a proper phonetic sound? K is 'k' not 'kay', so why is X not just 'x' like in 'box'?

answers.answer: X is the only way you can pronounce X if you pronounce it as in xylophone it's a Z. Z would be X so it's literally the only way you can say X.

Actually when we go through the phonetic alphabet we say K for both C and K. We now don't teach X-ray and xylophone as the example - we teach fox, fox, fox. It's been a gradual thing. Some places might still do x-ray but the pedagogy at the moment is moving towards fox or box or whatever. They used ox as well.

questions.question: Why do people naturally gravitate to have some sort of cover on them when they go to sleep even in very hot countries? Why don't we just lay in bed without any covers?

answers.answer: We haven't got any fur. Animals nuzzle down into leaves and things to keep warm. If it's warm it's just sort of nice - it makes you feel secure. There's a degree of psychological comfort involved because it reminds you of being in the womb.

We don't take sheets over us in very hot countries when it's hot. Only Westerners in Thailand will have a sheet - Thai people in Thailand won't. I'm Nepalese and I lived in Nepal until I was 23. I never used to take cover at night, nor did my family in summer. But since I came here in 2011, when I go back home now I do take cover even in summer. It's habit - it's what you're used to doing.

questions.question: Why can't I booby trap my house? And why is it called a booby trap?

answers.answer: On long ocean voyages they put a small wire loop on top of the deckhouse on the boat. When a blue-footed booby would land on top of the deck they'd pull the string tight and catch their supper. So it was a particularly dozy bird that hadn't really been predated much, probably with big bright blue feet.

questions.question: Are our sense of taste and smell hereditary?

answers.answer: Some people can't eat coriander - about 20% of the population have a genetic reaction where it tastes rank and horrible. It might be something similar with oranges - a genetic reaction that can skip a generation.

With the coriander analogy, there's a percentage of people who taste it more soapy because they have a variation in their olfactory receptor genes. So with her great-grandmother having it as well, it would have been passed down. It's probably a recessive gene, same principle as the coriander question.

questions.question: What is the oldest language still currently spoken today?
Why is 999 the emergency number? Why is it not 111?

answers.answer: The 9 was the first number next to the little metal stopper at the bottom of the dialer.

When the 999 service was first brought in, the signalling was done via two wires. When the wind blew, these wires would sag and touch, causing a pulse. If you had a signalling for 111, that could easily be affected by the wind. 999 was the hardest amount of pulses that nature could replicate, so the wind would never cause three pulses of 999.

questions.question: Why do you get car sick in the back seat of cars?

answers.answer: It's because your body is telling you that you're moving, but the brain isn't getting the information it needs because you're in the back. You can see your seat but can't see the speed you're traveling. In the front seat, your brain, eyes, and body are in synchronicity.

It's a very ancient response - your ears are telling you something. You've got fluid flapping around in your ears telling you you're moving, but your eyes are seeing static objects. We haven't evolved with cars, so the disassociation between what your ears and eyes tell you makes your body think something's wrong and you need to throw up. When you get to the front, your eyes take in more information that tallies with your ears.

There are three orientation systems in our bodies: 75% is vision, and the rest is the inner ear (two systems - a gyro for circular motion and an organ called the otolith that detects gravity). When you're in the back and can't see much, those three systems aren't agreeing. When you're in the front, you can see the horizon - a steady point in front of you - so your inner ear says you're okay. Pilots get this illusion a lot when flying.

questions.question: If a wife gets a damehood, does the husband get a title? Would we become Sir Stephen or Sir James?

answers.answer: No, the husband of a dame stays as a plain old mister. The female equivalent of a knighthood is a damehood, but there's nothing like a dame for men. It's sexism.

questions.question: Why do countries like Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan all end in 'stan'?

answers.answer: It means land - a family from Pakistan explained that stan means land. It's more of a kind of place rather than just land.
It actually means 'land of' - as in, I am from the land of Turkmens. The tribes were called this when it was all the Persian empire.

questions.question: Why is a corned beef tin shaped like a corned beef tin?

answers.answer: It's partly so you can have the key on top. You can't have that on a round tin because it would snap off. You can't peel back a round tin lid. It's to do with getting the meat out easily.

When they're empty, they can't be nested inside each other. When they have to transport empty cans to very rural or remote locations, they can ship in millions of empty cans, fill them up, and ship them out full. The slicing comes out in one piece - that's the point about the shape. With a round can, it wouldn't come out in one piece. You get corned beef in nice, neat slices rather than like cat food that you'd have to spoon out.

questions.question: Where do birds go to die?

answers.answer: They get eaten by foxes, cats, and predators. It's like leaving biscuits out - they don't last long.

Like a lot of animals, when they feel vulnerable or ill, they don't want to be out in the open. They'll hide away in a bush or undergrowth to die, so other animals don't see them being vulnerable. But then they do get eaten - that's the circle of life.
If they don't get eaten by a scavenger or predator, they'll be eaten by maggots from flies that lay eggs in them, and then worms and everything else - like any dead body.

questions.question: Why does Deep Heat or Tiger Balm make your leg hot but not your hands?

answers.answer: It's the closeness of the bone - the amount of skin between balm and bone that determines the effect. The knee has bone very near the surface so there's less sensation. The thigh is more sensitive. Skin thickness plays a role.

questions.question: (No question, providing answer about oldest language)

answers.answer: The best short answer is Chinese - we have it written from 2000-3000 BCE. There are languages written earlier (like Sumerian and Egyptian) but they're no longer spoken. Chinese has diversified and changed a lot, but the writing system encouraged people to think of it as still the same language. The issue is how much a language changes - Greek has changed but remained one language with the same alphabet, whereas Latin diversified into French, Italian, Spanish. Hebrew was a special case.

questions.question: Why do we sell red wine in coloured bottles (green, brown, black) and not clear bottles?

answers.answer: Light would accelerate oxidisation and oxidisation would make the wine taste rank. But then why wouldn't that apply to white wine?

The question isn't why we store wine in glass, it's why in dark glass. It's to prevent light strike - UV light degrades part of the molecules in the wine, changing them to sulphides, making it unpleasant, slightly eggy, slightly cabbagey. Any wine can be affected by this - the colour of the wine is irrelevant. Wine in clear glass is always a bad idea. Clear glass exists for rosé because when you put rosé in dark glass, sales drop massively. Fancy champagnes like Cristal come in clear glass with yellow cellophane which only lets yellow light through, which doesn't harm the wine.

questions.question: Do all mammals get morning sickness?
Do spiders just live in one web and abandon it and move on, or do they have several webs on the go at once, like trappers setting traps?

answers.answer: Usually it's one spider, one web. They're usually solitary animals so they won't take over another web because one of the key reasons is that they're usually laced with pheromones from a particular spider so they wouldn't take over. But there are some species that are communal and will build giant webs together. You never get an individual spider running several webs.

questions.question: What is the thing called that you put in your mouth and bite down on during surgery before anaesthetic, like when sailors had amputations on ships?

answers.answer: The thing that you bite into, or people historically bit into during surgery, well, it's called a bit. It's used in horse tack and still sort of a specialist bit of equipment. A bit is just something that is bitten that isn't eaten. You bite but don't eat.

In hospital we would just typically refer to it as a mouth gag. Also, Howard might have been confused with a commonly used airway called a Goodell airway, which is a very simple device that you slip into the mouth which prevents patients from biting down on their tongue but it also allows them to breathe. Goodell was an anesthetist in the 1900s who developed this airway in the USA. It holds the tongue forward and allows the airway to remain open.

questions.question: If a baby is born on a cruise ship in national waters, what nationality would the baby be? Would it be anything to do with where the ship is registered? Would it be decided entirely by the nationality of the mother? Or would it have something to do with where the ship was?

answers.answer: There's really three answers. One is the nationality of the airspace or territorial water of where the ship or aircraft was at the time of birth. Or the nationality of the parents, provided the country where the parents are citizens of allows dual nationality. The parents can choose the nationality. There's an international agreement that nobody can be born without a nationality. If you're born under the flag of a country, you'd be entitled to that nationality, but it wouldn't supersede your parents' nationality unless your parents came from a country where you weren't allowed dual nationality.

The nationality question is really about two things - residency and domicile. In the UK, if you're born, you generally take the nationality of your father if he's alive. If you're born on a boat, if your parents are married, you take the domicile of your father. If your father is not alive, you'll take the domicile of your mother. Or if you're not married, you will take the domicile of your mother.

questions.question: What does it mean when weatherman says there's a 22% chance of rain? Does it mean it's going to rain, or does it rain for 22% of the time?

answers.answer: There is no reading of the phrase 20% chance of rain that involves 20% of the time. Because what timescale would you be deploying at this point - 20% of an hour? 20% of a day? 20% of the year? It is a 20% chance of rain, so it's five to one.

Forecasting is done mostly with models these days. Those models are built in what's called an ensemble system. For a particular day's forecast there'll be multiple runs of that forecast using different models. Within your hour window where there's a bit more uncertainty, what that forecast is saying is within that hour window there is essentially a 20% chance of rainfall happening at the location that is being spoken about, based on the number of model runs that are covering for that area.
He set James straight during the break. It was later confirmed by the Met Office. The percentage is the probability of rainfall occurring.

questions.question: When you smell something, if there is a finite amount of aroma or gas in the atmosphere, do you reduce the total amount every time you smell it? Does every sniff remove a little bit of the aroma from the atmosphere?

answers.answer: The molecules in the air which cause smell lock into little olfactory receptors in your nose. While they're locked into your nose, they of course can't be locking into anyone else's, so there will be a marginal decrease in the smell. But they get washed out quite quickly, so they can be recirculated. Your olfactory molecular emissions could end up in someone else's nose. That's how viruses spread.

questions.question: Why do politicians on TV always have their sleeves rolled up when they're in hospitals, as though they're just about to get stuck in? And why is the tie tucked into the shirt?

answers.answer: It's called a policy called 'Bare Below Elbow'. It applies to everyone who's likely to have physical contact with a patient. It means that it's very easy for them to wash their hands and lower arms between patients. It's an infection control measure. A consultant would probably just be talking to you rather than physically examining you - not getting his hands dirty.

questions.question: Why do you temporarily lose most of your hearing when you yawn?

answers.answer: Think of your ear canals as a straw. And then think of when you're having a drink through a straw - when you squeeze the straw you get less fluid through. So when you yawn you tighten your ear canals and they become narrower which means less sound gets through.

There is a tiny muscle in the middle ear behind the eardrum which actually contracts when somebody yawns, temporarily decreasing the hearing sensitivity. This is the same protective mechanism your ear has when exposed to loud sounds - the muscles contract to protect you. The other way to contract one of those muscles is by yawning, therefore your hearing is temporarily reduced.

questions.question: Can foreign nationals who are being spoken to in their language detect which country you're from? So when you're speaking French, would a French person know you were English? Or detect that someone who was German was speaking French?

answers.answer: It's going to be different depending on who you're talking to. Some people are going to sound completely convincing, they're going to sound like a Parisian born French man. And other people who've got just as good French are going to sound like Geordies.

The answer is yes. It depends on what sounds already exist in your language versus the foreign language and how the sounds you're used to making affect the way you would pronounce the sounds in the foreign language. For example, the French R is not the same R that we have in English, so you would obviously have an accent unless you learned it. The more similar the noises are to your native language, the more convincing you will sound when speaking a foreign language. For example, Chinese has four tones and we don't learn tones in English, so the older you are, the harder it is to sound like a native speaker in Chinese because our brains just aren't... The plasticity changes over time. You can take phonetics courses or accent loss courses to help fix your accent.

questions.question: Why do we blow out candles on a birthday cake and not anything else?

answers.answer: It goes back to paganism. Pilgrims worship the moon, so traditionally the cake would be round which symbolises the moon. When you're blowing the candles you make a wish with the belief that the smoke from the candle is going to go up to the moon and your wish will be granted. Pagans also believed that when it was your birthday there were evil spirits out to get you, so in order to show the evil spirits that the person is loved and cherished in the community, they would have a gathering, which is now the party. And that's why presents are given as well, to deter the spirits.

questions.question: When did organic food become a commodified product? I don't remember organic food being a thing growing up. Like you couldn't buy organic food as far as I remember. And then mid-90s maybe.

answers.answer: Chronologically, it's going to coincide roughly with the discovery of how bad pesticides were and the increasing scientific knowledge of what some of the additives and pesticides were doing to our food. Everything was organic before pesticides kicked in, but you wouldn't have made a fuss about it being organic because everything was.

All farming originally was organic. The definition of organic farming is using little or no artificially produced herbicides or fertilizers. If you go back far enough, sort of 5-6 thousand years, all farming was organic. The Soil Association was formed after the war in 1945. I started receiving subsidies for converting my farm to organic in 1983. But the question is when did it become a marketed commodity on shelves in the UK? That would have been probably the last 20-30 years.

questions.question: Why do we consider horseshoes to be lucky?

answers.answer: You're supposed to put them sideways so the devil can't play in them. If you put it upside down, the luck falls out. And if you put it like a U shape, the devil will play in it. So you put it on its side.

Horseshoes are considered lucky because blacksmiths are considered lucky. They used to deal with fire and tend to make the horseshoes and it wards off the devil. Some traditions have demons being unable to bear the touch of cold iron.

questions.question: What makes a British animal native to this country? How long does it have to be in this country before it's classed as native?

answers.answer: I don't know that you ever become native. For example, a peacock. It doesn't matter how long a peacock has been here, they'll never be native. The same with pheasants. There must just be a point where we started listing animals and everything that got on the list back then is native and anything that's come in since then is not.

There's not an exact date, but the range is between 8-10 thousand years ago, which coincides with the last glaciation in North and Western Europe. When the Ice Age began to recede, the waters formed the English Channel which provided the cutoff for any other species migrating naturally over the European land bridge to Britain. The best way to look at it is that non-native species are those predominantly introduced into new regions by human activity. When humans arrived in Britain around 8,000 years ago, all species that colonised our land came during that period. Nothing becomes native after that point.

questions.question: How many people need to know an acronym before it's officially an acronym? When Jacques Cousteau made up scuba, did he just have to know it or did he have to tell half a dozen mates?

answers.answer: There's no official threshold for becoming an acronym. There's no international body of acronym certification. If you tell me your acronym, will that then be an acronym? That is the real purpose of this call, isn't it? Brino (Brexit in name only) was a relatively recently coined acronym. There's no official body that certifies acronyms.

questions.question: Why do we season with salt and pepper? Why is salt and pepper a thing and not salt and paprika or salt and something else?

answers.answer: It harks back to when Venice was at its height of power and the trade routes that came with it. All the Venetian big families brought back lots of stuff across the Silk Road from places like India and as far afield as China. Salt was incredibly valuable - the word salary comes from salt. Having salt on your table showed you were better than the next person.

questions.question: Why can I use my six burner gas hob indoors but not this little pizza oven, when it's burning the same gas effectively?

answers.answer: It may be that you can't, I mean I obviously don't try this at home, but it may be that you can, it's just erring on the side of caution. Or it may be to do with the volume of the way this burns or if there's a different type of gas.

It's to do with the jets on the burner at the back. They're set up so they let less oxygen in, which creates a yellow rolling flame that goes over the pizza on top of the oven. Whereas your burner in your kitchen is blue and really hot, so you're getting a lot more carbon monoxide coming off your pizza oven.

questions.question: Queen's Council is a barrister appointed by the Queen. When the monarch dies, do they automatically become King's Council if the next monarch is a King, or do they have to be reappointed?

answers.answer: The title of QC/KC comes with the sex of the monarch. As soon as the particular monarch dies and it's a new gender, the silk follows the same title. So when Charles ascends to the throne, all QCs will become known as KCs.

questions.question: What is the red in Red Leicester cheese? It's not really red, it's more of a deep orangey colour. Where does the red come from? Do they add something to it?

answers.answer: The Red Leicester comes from the actual cattle that is used. The Red Leicester cattle have very hard milk and the pigment that is added to that milk to make it a dark orange colour is called annatto - from the seeds of the achiote tree. You can be allergic to it.

questions.question: Why is it called a rider? Especially now you've said it could be anything - why would you call it that?

answers.answer: When a musician draws up a contract with a venue, it's the rider who gets tacked on afterwards. It's never part of the contract. So it's something that rides the original agreement, which is where the original word comes from. This would apply to all contracts. It just entered into common parlance because it's most known about backstage requirements. It was Van Halen that did the M&Ms with the brown M&Ms because they figured if a venue couldn't be trusted to do something like that, they possibly wouldn't be good at dealing with all the dangerous electronics and other requirements of a big show.
It's called a rider because something was always sent ahead in medieval times from one castle to another castle to prepare the exact sort of things that the visiting dignitary would want.

questions.question: Why does our voice sound so different when we hear a recording of it?

answers.answer: Your skull is resonant in a way that means what's reaching your ears from almost inside your skull is different to what would reach your ears from outside your skull. If you record it on a tape, you remove the resonance of the skull. When you think about it, it's a bit like asking, if you stuck your head inside a bell and bonged it, why does that sound so different to how it sounds when you're standing over it?

questions.question: What happens if you've got a language which doesn't have the normal Greek alphabet? How does Morse code work in languages like Chinese or Arabic?

answers.answer: I'll find out for you.

For Chinese: They've got a great big book called the Telegraphy Codebook and each of their symbols is on a page of that on a row and a column and they said the four digit Morse thing. So still dots and dashes, they just send the exact same numbers as anyone else would send. So one would be da-da-da and they'd send, say, one, two, three, five and you'd look on page, whatever. For other non-English, non-Latin alphabet languages: Every country's got its own. If they've got a different alphabet, they've got extra Morse symbols for letters that we don't use. For example, there's one that goes da-da-da-da which is H with a bar over it but in Russian it's actually the little Ivan Krakow symbol.

questions.question: Why do the Spanish have upside down question marks and exclamation marks at the beginning of their sentence? Is it that their question marks are upside down or that ours are?

answers.answer: I presume it's because the order of subject, object and verb is different in Spanish and therefore it needs to be established at the beginning of the sentence that it is an interrogatory statement as opposed to a declamatory one... The idea that you need to know in advance because the words won't make it as obvious as they do.

It's not only in Spanish. It's in other languages used in areas where Spain had control at the relevant times. It goes back to the 18th century and a decision of the Spanish Academy, which is like the equivalent of the French Academy. At that time, the Spanish Academy decided it was its duty to rationalize the Spanish language somewhat. In a language like Spanish, there are sentences which in writing could be either questions or statements. And in speech you can tell from the intonation, but not on paper. So they seem to have inverted the symbol to make it more different from existing symbols. It's a form of parenthesis. They've turned it into parentheses surrounding a clause. It's a way of marking the boundary and telling you which type of clause it is.

questions.question: Are humans the only species who can laugh? I mean properly laugh as an experience, something funny and then laugh because something's funny. Not hyenas and stuff like that.

answers.answer: I'll find out for you.
It's a rat. The evidence appears to be yes from all the people sending video clips, including one of a squirrel apparently laughing.

questions.question: Can you have dominant versions of everything when you've got two of something? Do you have a dominant lung? Do you have a dominant kidney like you have a left or right hand?

answers.answer: I'll find out for you. The eye does it feel? Well, you get... you don't have a dominant eye necessarily. Your prescription might be... a dominant eye, you don't have a dominant eye necessarily.

The answer is no, we don't. Although I have to caveat that response that we have to assume that both organs are actually healthy organs. So if you do have two lots of healthy organs, then no. One is not dominant over the other. They actually work on a 50-50 basis. And if you're going to ask me then why do we have two, then, well, the answer is that if you lose one, then the other one can take over the function of the other. Eyes are the best example of that. In terms of one being better than the other, but it being accidental, because your prescription might be different according to each eye. But if it's your kidneys, then one's a bit crook but the other one's going to have to work a bit harder. But it's not de facto dominant.

questions.question: If you were here with me and we swapped heads, what would the green grass look like? Would it look the same to you as it does to me? Does your green look like my green?

answers.answer: If Angus could get a machine that would completely accurately reproduce what the colour he sees when he sees green grass outside his bedroom window, would I see exactly the same thing on the piece of card or the picture that he handed to me?

The answer very simply is no, we don't. My dissertation was on colour blindness. Some people see only black and white. A really small, tiny percentage of people only see black and white. Some people see kind of blues and oranges. And some people see sort of more blues and yellows. We do all see different shades, which is why people have arguments with their spouse about which colours match in the living room.

questions.question: How did the newts get into my pond? I dug a pond a couple of years ago and I've now got newts in it. How do they get there?

answers.answer: Ducks do. A duck would be swimming around. If Socrates the duck has been for a swim in a pond that's got newts in it and he's got some new eggs on his flippers and then he's landed in your pond and the new eggs have washed off. Or newts walk. They're amphibians. They've got legs. They can travel over land. The newts have either been carried there on an unwitting duck undercarriage or they've walked there.

Newts, as you said, they're amphibians, and as long as their skin is damp, because they breathe largely through their skin, they will walk. They will travel over land. No problem. When things turned up in strange places, we always said have a duck's feet because that does happen. They have eggs, almost exactly like frog spawn, strings of eggs turn into little newtlets.

questions.question: Does the amount of water on the planet remain constant at all times? And has it always remained constant?

answers.answer: Some of it will be hydrogen and oxygen, won't it? At some point. So there'll be the same amount of hydrogen and oxygen in existence, but not the same amount of H2O. Because I could make some water now if you just gave me some hydrogen, some oxygen, and a toilet roll holder and a Bunsen burner. You can get a couple of hydrogen molecules and an oxygen molecule, and if you've got the right kit, you can turn them into water, which would increase the sum total of the amount of water on the planet. And I presume you can do the opposite reaction as well. So no, not the same amount of water, but the same amount of hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.question: Plants evolved long before pollinators. How did plants cross-pollinate before pollinators were around?

answers.answer: It's just going to be wind, isn't it? In the absence of insects, how does pollen get from A to B? Wind.

questions.question: How long do letters sent to the 1922 committee remain valid? Do they stay forever unless you withdraw them?

answers.answer: I imagine they stay there until either the vote has been conducted, or the sender has withdrawn it. But we'll get that confirmed, or of course, denied for you.

questions.question: Why do MRI scanners make such an interminable racket? I've been living with MS since the mid-naughties, and had an MRI scan with foam earplugs in my ears and massive headphones, and it was uncomfortably loud. Everything else in life is getting quieter. Why can't we just scan without making such a racket?

answers.answer: I presume in part it's because there's no cost-benefit ratio in making them quieter. It's such a niche market that no one has said you know what we need to do, we need to make the MRI quieter. Waste of energy, though, isn't it? Probably it is.

You're sat in a tube inside another tube, and in between the two tubes is the device that goes round constantly to create multiple layers of a slice of you effectively, and when you put them all back together, it gives you the 3D image. As it goes round, it's making the noise of it being propelled round, plus also the magnetic resonance. If you put something between the tips of it and the body, all you're going to do is diffuse the image that you get. It's technically a bit hard to diffuse the noise. It's the engine then, really. It basically makes a full loop of your body. It's a bit like lying inside a lawnmower and wondering why it's so noisy. Or a spinner on the washing machine.

questions.question: What is the etymology of Kidderminster? There's Yorkminster, there's Westminster. Kidderminster used to be a famous carpet town and there was a famous carpet called Axeminster. What strings it all together?

answers.answer: Minster means a church or a monastery. Kidderminster means Kidders' church. Kidders was a kind of Anglo-Saxon tribal chief. When they first settled on the hill, it was Kidderminster, Kidders' minster, Kidders' church. Yorkminster is the best way of explaining it because it's still called an actual minster. It's a cathedral but it's called a minster because they've never moved on from a minster, which just means church. Minster and monastery are very closely related words.

questions.question: How can you age a tree without cutting it down to count the annual rings?

answers.answer: The answer is to measure the tree's circumference at 1.5 metres from ground level. Every inch of girth is valued at about one year of age. Most trees follow this rule of thumb quite consistently, though some exceptions exist like conifers that grow faster or yew trees that grow slower. A silver birch won't reach the girth of an oak tree because it simply won't live as long.

questions.question: At what point in someone's family history can they lay claim to being indigenous to a particular country or region?
Do onions make any other animals cry?

answers.answer: Yes, depending on the animal. Crying from onions is the body's defence mechanism trying to wash out the sulphur compound which is the irritant. It depends on how the animal's tear duct is designed. Dogs and cats won't like the smell or taste but tear ducts are different. Animals that live underground have much differently designed tear ducts and can actually eat onions raw out of the ground with no irritant effects.

questions.question: Why do oil refinery and timber yard workers have to reverse into their parking spaces?

answers.answer: It's a health and safety measure. When you reverse park in, you drive out front first, which is safer because you've got less chance of knocking someone over. When you come out front first, your front wheels are steering so you can turn on like a sixpence, making it easier to manoeuvre.

questions.question: What would happen if a sitting Prime Minister defected to the opposition party? Would they remain Prime Minister? Who would be the governing party?

answers.answer: The governing party wouldn't change unless it was a majority of one. The defector would cease to be leader of their party, they'd just elect a new leader and that person would automatically become Prime Minister. The defector would effectively become an MP for the opposition - it's up to them whether to make him shadow chancellor or something.

questions.question: When a new word is added to the French dictionary, who decides whether it is masculine or feminine?

answers.answer: There's an institution called l'Académie Française, set up in the 1600s, which actually governs what words are added to the French language. Unlike English where nothing formally governs it and dictionaries just follow trends, French is much more formally organised. They decide whether a new word is allowed and whether it's masculine or feminine, often based on etymology and the root words it's made up of.

questions.question: Why are legal pads yellow?

answers.answer: They're yellow because lawyers work with lots of documents, so when they're writing their notes they need to identify where their notes are in the big pile of documents. The yellow colour helps them slot their notes into the pages, like post-it notes but on full pages.

questions.question: How do we tell how quickly time passes on other planets?
Can dogs recognise themselves in the mirror? One of my dogs goes barmy when he sees himself, the other ignores it.

answers.answer: No, dogs cannot recognise themselves in mirrors. Visual self-awareness tests show they cannot recognise themselves. They can recognise a form but not themselves. However, there are new tests being developed on olfactory recognition - they might be able to recognise their own smell. Some dogs go reactive to the shape or form of another dog, some don't.

questions.question: Does the Queen abide by AML (anti-money laundering) regulations?

answers.answer: No, with a slight caveat. The Queen is subject to sovereign immunity and therefore cannot personally commit a criminal offence. The money laundering regulations only apply to regulated persons - lawyers, bankers etc. However, if the monarchy were to construct the services of any regulated person, they would have to satisfy themselves that the regulations have been complied with. For example, to purchase a new palace they'd have to check the source of funding to ensure it's not the proceeds of crime.

questions.question: What happens when there's a fire in a hospital if a surgeon is mid-operation? What if it's something that can't be stopped?

answers.answer: If you have a patient open on the table and the fire alarm goes off, everyone's informed. You don't proceed any further with any extra surgery. No further incisions are made. No further patients are anesthetized. You prepare patients for evacuation. You finish the stage you're at exactly and wait. If you're given the order to evacuate, you evacuate as safely as you can. If you can't, all non-essential staff are evacuated and the surgical team are asked if they're prepared to stay and carry on, and it's up to them to decide.

In an operating theater, you have separate ventilation systems for each theater. In a normal hotel office building when fire alarm goes off ventilation closes, but in an operating theater they continue to run with fresh air independent ventilation. They remain in positive pressure so any smoke outside can't get into the operating theater. They can continue and decide whether to continue in a safe environment or do an emergency closure and evacuate. They practice that every year with practical exercises. You go through a smoke lobby when approaching theaters, which stops smoke outside getting into the theater areas.

questions.question: Why does the sense of smell get better or more acute during pregnancy?

answers.answer: When you're pregnant, your blood volume increases and your mucous membranes are better supplied with blood so everything works better and you're more sensitive. The theory is also that when you're pregnant you don't want bacteria that could harm you and the baby, so you're more aware of something being off - like an alarm system.

questions.question: Does putting pennies in the bottom of a vase keep tulips standing straight and stop them wilting?
What determines why some people are great singers and some people really sound like a bag of cats?

answers.answer: It's mostly practice but there is an element of physicality - your voice box, the amount of fat on the back of your throat, and the musicality learned as a child. Some people can be taught even if they thought they were tone deaf. If you can hear the difference between two notes, you can learn to produce the difference. It's about training a muscle and the relationship with your ears is learned behavior.

questions.question: Humans can see seven colours in a rainbow. Is there another animal on the planet that sees more than seven colours? And if so, what are they?

answers.answer: In short, they can't... actually some can. We have receptors called cones that detect red, green and blue light and that's how our brains form the rest of the colours the same way a TV does. Some animals have a fourth receptor that can detect ultraviolet light, particularly birds. They use it to find particular flowers they might want to eat. In the context of a rainbow specifically, an animal with a fourth cone would see more colours down towards the bottom of the rainbow past indigo and violet. They light up like a Christmas tree basically.

questions.question: Why can you not stop going to the toilet once you've finally gone after drinking all evening?
How does a rice cooker know to make perfect rice? Why doesn't it undercook or overcook? And why does it stay perfect even if you don't open it for a while?

answers.answer: Rice cookers involve a hot plate, a spring and a thermostat. All rice cookers come with an approximate rice versus water ratio in their book. You throw the ratio in and it depresses the spring which touches the thermostat. When all the water evaporates and disappears, you're left with perfect rice. The bowl pops up off the spring and the thermostat cuts off, leaving it as a hot plate rather than a cooker. Then it just keeps it warm - keeps the steam at the top in the sealed lid to keep the moisture in but not dry out. It's based on weight ratio, not a bimetallic strip.

questions.caller: Tim from Earl Shilton in Leicestershire
questions.question: How do we know when we've chewed enough to swallow? How does a 10-month-old baby know when she's chewed enough?

answers.answer: Babies are born with the ability to swallow - it's a human instinct. When they start biting on plastic toys and different types of objects (usually through teething), experiencing these different textures and feeling the different weight teaches themselves to adjust their motor responses, for example stopping themselves from choking.

questions.question: What is the point of skirting boards?

answers.answer: It's to cover the gap between the bottom of the plaster and the floor because you can't plaster all the way down to the floor. There might be pipe work and electrics behind there as well.
Embellishment: It's to protect the plaster from being knocked off by feet, hoovers, brushes and things like that. The bottom of the plaster would be vulnerable without it.

If you lay any type of wooden flooring - engineered oak, parquet, laminate - you need an expansion joint all the way around between the floor and the wall because timber is dead but still a live material. It expands and contracts with heat. If it didn't have room to expand, the whole floor would buckle and crack over time.

questions.question: Can what you eat before you go to sleep affect the type of dreams that you have? Does eating cheese really give you nightmares?
When is a language considered dead? For example, Latin is called a dead language but we use Latin phrases in everyday conversation and it's used extensively across the Catholic Church.

answers.answer: A language is dead when it's not the lingua franca anywhere anymore, where people don't speak it routinely to each other.

A language is dead when the last native speaker of a language has died out. That's why they send people to Africa and South America to get all the languages transcribed before they stop existing. About 7,000 languages a year die out.

questions.question: Why do Italian sports teams play in blue when there's nothing on their flag connected to blue?

answers.answer: It's the colour representing the former Italian monarchy - the House of Savoy. After World War II, after Mussolini and creation of the Italian Republic with the new flag, the blue colour is a historical harking back to the pre-Republic days.

questions.question: If you used a thermal imaging camera overhead in a graveyard, would you be able to see which bodies had been buried recently? Because obviously when things rot, they give off energy and heat.

answers.answer: Thermal imaging cameras detect infrared energy being emitted from surfaces, not heat. You can't see underground. However, freshly dug graves can be detected because disturbed earth emits different infrared energy - older graves blend in after about a week. Decomposing bodies won't show up unless very close to surface.

questions.question: What is the etiquette for the shared armrest on planes and cinemas? Is there a rule?

answers.answer: There is no official etiquette. Passengers often need cabin crew intervention for disputes. The armrest develops its purpose during the safety briefing discussing brace positions. Safety seats are rated to G-force impacts, and armrests became part of aircraft design as accidents prompted improved passenger protection.

questions.question: How long would it take to get around the world using only scheduled non-air travel (trains, boats, coaches, cars)? Inspired by watching Around the World in 80 Days with his children.

answers.answer: About 31 days. Route: Moscow to Vladivostok via Trans-Siberian Express, boat from Tokyo across Pacific (about 11 days), bus from San Francisco to New York (47 hours), cargo ship across Atlantic (a week), then train from Liverpool to London. Everything has to line up perfectly.

questions.question: What does the word 'Bachelor' mean in Bachelor of Science? Her son saw a podiatrist's BSc certificate and wondered. Neither she nor the podiatrist knew.

answers.answer: From Medieval Latin 'Bacalaureatus'. Bachelor came to mean anyone early in a series of procedures. It then got transferred to mean unmarried man because the idea was that anyone who wasn't a priest would eventually get married - so bachelor means early stage. Some claim it's from laurel but that's disputed folk etymology.

questions.question: Why did evolution result in male seahorses giving birth to babies instead of females?
Who are the people in our dreams? Are they from memory or are they generated? If you're in a crowd scene, who are those people?

answers.answer: Your brain is incapable of creating faces. Every face you see in your dream is a face that you've seen before - you just don't consciously remember where. It may have been someone you passed in a crowd, but it's definitely a face you've stored somewhere.

questions.question: Can you be a soldier if you snore really badly? Would it affect deployment to places like Iraq?

answers.answer: Snoring is acceptable as long as the person is medically fit otherwise. If you're on manoeuvres and the enemy is close enough to hear you snore, you should be awake anyway anyway. Someone will give you a nudge. Historically, loud snorers got boots thrown at them which somehow cured them.

Snoring is not a problem unless you want to be a sniper - snipers are a specialist qualification and work behind enemy lines where there's no one to give them a nudge. Most snipers work in pairs anyway.

questions.question: If a serving Prime Minister loses their constituency seat in a general election whilst the governing party retains a majority, does that person cease to be Prime Minister?

answers.answer: The Prime Minister would retain the position immediately because it's the Queen that bestows and removes the title. However, convention would mean they lose the party leadership, leadership elections would occur, and the new leader would go to the palace and be invited to become PM. In practice, they'd probably resign, but constitutionally they'd remain PM.

questions.question: Would someone with a nut allergy be able to eat the meat of a squirrel?

answers.answer: Yes, because nothing would get into the squirrel that was... It would all be washed out. It would all come out in the butchering process.

When a squirrel digests nuts, the nuts are going to be broken down. And the protein is what you're allergic to in the nuts. So the protein will be broken down into the component of the amino acids. So thus, no longer causing that allergy. The amino acids will then be used by the squirrels to develop muscles, et cetera. So you're not eating the protein that's in the acorn, which is the nut.

questions.question: Why was Queen Victoria known as the Empress of India? Why wasn't she just called Empress Victoria or Queen of India, considering that Britain had an empire at the time?

answers.answer: England's not part of the empire. The relationship between the monarch and the United Kingdom is not imperial. So you can't retrospectively rebrand the monarch as an emperor. I mean, when it comes down to it, I'm not sure I know the difference between a king and an emperor. It's like Kaiser. I mean, it did come... I think because we had kings and queens. We didn't have emperors.

answers.caller: James (King's Cross) - works for what used to be the India Office, now the Asia and Africa Collection at the British Library
answers.answer: There was a period in time during roughly the 1870s where she was seen as being too far detached from certain parts of the empire, namely India, and Benjamin Disraeli pushed it through the House of Commons in order to make her the Empress of India. It was a political decision.

questions.question: Why do we say 'touch wood' to avoid bad luck? It is not going to stop me getting a cold, is it?

answers.answer: The wood of the cross is one of the theories. You touch the wood of the cross. So it was a kind of Christian thing. But before that, as with lots of things, there's a pagan one as well. Is it spirits lived in the woods? So that there'd be a spirit in the wood that you were asking for help or asking for support with your luck.

It's back when humans were tree dwelling, they used to touch the bark of trees to invoke the fairies and spirits that they believed lived there for protection. I read it in Otto English's book, Fake History.
Another theory is you touch wood so that the malevolent spirits in the wood can't hear what you're saying. So you say, oh, I hope we're all right, oh don't let the bad spirits hear it.

questions.question: Are spiders scared of conkers? Are they repelled? Do conkers keep spiders away?

answers.answer: They are repelled. There is a gas released by horse chestnuts which spiders have a problem with. I remember someone ringing in and saying, oh yes, conkers release noxious substances which repel spiders. And that is why you are advised, if you have a problem with spiders, to put conkers around your doorways.
Spiders are not repelled by whatever chemical conkers may give off. It's a myth. I got this from a quiz game that I got for Christmas.

questions.question: How do parrots pronounce certain letters, for example P, without lips? When we pronounce, we use our lips to form the sound. We do. But a parrot doesn't have lips.

How in nature is it possible, or how has it become possible, for animals and insects to camouflage themselves? For example, insects which suddenly turn from their normal colour into to hide themselves on trees, or animals, insects or reptiles which can change the colour to disguise themselves. At one point, did the newborn insect become camouflaged?

answers.answer: It was a genetic glitch that occurred at some long-distant point in the species' past, and it equipped them with something beneficial, which meant they could breed more, and the glitch got passed down to generations until all that survived were descendants of the glitched origins. They were born with the ability to camouflage themselves, and it would have been a freakish genetic glitch, but it turned out to be really useful. This gets passed down through reproduction.

answers.caller: Professor Hal (University of Brighton - Professor of Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: Evolution is not driven by purpose. Evolution is a series of chances causing mutations. So the chance that an insect looks a bit more camouflaged means it's likelier to reproduce and not get eaten. Some mutations which cause harm also cause benefit. And it's the same with the giraffes with the longer necks. The peppered moths went black and then they went white because of the industrial revolution. So they'd get eaten when they were white because they'd stand out against the black background and then they went black again when there was pollution on the black background and then they went white again when things cleaned up a bit.

questions.question: Why do we have the urge to squeeze cute things like kittens or the chubby bits of baby's legs? Sometimes even like a bit of a bite.

answers.answer: Is it things that we would normally cuddle, but they're too small to cuddle, so we kind of subconsciously translate?

answers.caller: James (Dunoon) - took child and adolescent development at university
answers.answer: The urge to bite, squeeze or pinch cute things is known as 'cute aggression' or 'playful aggression'. In humans, it's so we can perpetuate the species and we have to give care to young. And so we have this mechanism in our brain that says, oh, we have to take care of this. But if it's so cute that we're debilitated and can't function in life, that's detrimental. So we have this aggression to break that urge of cuteness. To overcome the paralysis of cuteness.

questions.question: Does the Prime Minister know the questions he's going to be asked at PMQs in advance? I just wanted to know whether the Prime Minister knows the questions he's going to be asked.

answers.answer: He doesn't know the questions in advance, but they spend quite a lot of time preparing, trying to work out what the questions will be. They do quite a lot of modelling. Michael Gove would play the role of the opposition leader and they'd rehearse it.

answers.caller: Ed (Edgware) - worked for the PM and the Whip's office
answers.answer: The PM knows about half of the questions in advance - the leader of the opposition's questions, not the MPs' questions. The leader of the opposition's office would be in advance telling us what questions to ask. That's why MPs will ask a version of the question they're asked and at the end shoe in something about their own constituency.

questions.question: Why in all countries in the world is the Conservatives called the right and Labour or the Democrats called the left? Why is one of them right and one of them left?

answers.answer: It's post-revolutionary France. It's where they sat in the first French Parliament after they'd got rid of the royal family. The first estate is the monarchy. The second estate is the aristocracy. The third estate is the people, the tribunes of the people. The Speaker would have the nobility, the aristocrats on his right and the Robespierre lot on the left. And that's where it comes from.

questions.question: Why is it that the English Channel is called the English Channel and not the French?

answers.answer: The French call it La Manche. All the maps you've looked at are English maps, and if you looked at a French map, it would say La Manche.
La Manche means a sleeve because of the shape of the channel.
La Manche translates as 'the sleeve' because of the shape of the body of water.

questions.question: Why do some parts of the body grow back, but others won't? Like bones vs skin vs nails - why can't we regrow fingers but can heal cuts?

answers.answer: The less sophisticated the function of a body cell, the more likely it will regenerate. Skin and bones heal because they're simpler cells. Heart tissue and brain/spinal cord tissue don't regenerate because they're complex. If you amputate a finger and get to hospital quickly with it packed in ice, it can be reattached. You're not really growing back - you're repairing.

Bones, nails and skin grow all the time. Bone is covered by periosteum which stops growth - when breached, osteoblasts produce bone and periosteum races to cover up. Nails grow from nail beds similar to hair follicles. You're not regenerating, just repairing. For limbs to regrow, cells would need to be stem cells (totipotent) - once they become muscle or nerve, they can't go back and change.

questions.question: Why does it feel colder when you step inside your car than it does outside, even though it's not actually colder?

answers.answer: Car interiors are mostly black which absorbs heat well but also releases it quickly. So any heat in the car escapes, making it feel colder than outside.

The difference between being in a car and outside is due to conduction versus convection. When you're touching something and conducting, you transfer heat to it quickly, so the coldness is coming from the car.

questions.question: In boxing, why does the referee wipe the fallen boxer's gloves on his shirt before letting him continue?

answers.answer: When boxers go down and use their fists to get up, little bits of resin, dust and grit gather on the canvas. These need to be wiped off so they don't cut the opponent when punching - it's a safety measure.

questions.question: When did people first start referring to their girlfriend/boyfriend as 'baby' specifically in songs?

answers.answer: Mentions Louis Jordan's 'Is You Is or Is You Ain't My Baby' from late 40s/early 50s as an early example.

questions.question: Why does time fly when you're having fun? And conversely, why does it slow down during dangerous situations like a car crash?

answers.answer: When you're in danger, your brain focuses intensely on one thing - adrenaline gives you more reaction time. Time flies when having fun because you're so engrossed you don't notice the time passing.

It's all about subjective perception. When you're really enjoying yourself, you don't look at your watch. When you're in danger, you're really focused on that one thing and your brain processes more information, so time seems to slow down. It's about the degree of focus on a particular event.

questions.question: Why are drag queens called drag queens? Where does the word 'drag' come from?

answers.answer: From Shakespeare times - all female parts were played by men, and in script footnotes they'd write D-R-A-G meaning 'dressed as girl'. Rupaul told Helen Mirren this on Graham Norton. 'Queen' comes from it being a gay term of endearment.

Can't give a precise answer - etymology is often obscure. The word 'drag' isn't recorded until about the 1870s to describe a man dressed as a woman. The claim about Shakespeare footnotes is almost certainly wrong - we don't have original stage directions like that. The most plausible answer is it might be related to 'drag' at muscadine balls. Acronym theories are usually nonsense.

questions.question: Does red really make a bull angry, and if so, why?

answers.answer: It's the movement, not the redness - bulls are colorblind.
Bulls are colorblind so they're not affected by red. The waving of the cape around is what annoys them.

questions.question: Is there a physical pole/marker at the North Pole like there's a marker for the equator in Kenya and the meridian at Greenwich?

answers.answer: There's no physical marker at the North Pole because it's sea ice with no landmass - too unstable to put anything permanent. At the South Pole there ARE markers, but even there they have to keep adding new ones because the ice sheet is still moving.

questions.question: When birds fly in V formation, how does the bird at the front know it needs to be at the front?

answers.answer: Stronger geese take turns at the front. The lead goose breaks the wind and when it gets tired, it drops back. The next strongest goose moves to the front. They do it on a shift basis - like drafting in Formula 1 with the slipstream.

questions.question: Why is my 9-year-old English bulldog eating so much grass every time I take her in the garden? She's not sick with it and she's fed good quality food.

answers.answer: Grass settles an animal's stomach - cats and dogs eat it when feeling unwell. It's the first sign they're not feeling well. Could indicate dietary issues or a bit of an upset tummy, maybe the food isn't agreeing with her. Some dogs don't like chicken or turkey in food. It's a natural soother - like us taking an antacid.

questions.question: Can doctors treat animals and can vets treat humans? Is it true that vets can legally treat humans but doctors can't legally treat animals?

answers.answer: The reason vets can treat humans and doctors can't treat animals is that animals can't speak back to tell you what's wrong with them. Vets can ask humans what's wrong and get an answer, but doctors can't understand animals. Both verified this in their medical schools.

questions.question: Why do MPs and the Speaker refer to each other as 'honourable' and 'right honourable'? Where does it come from and when did it start?

answers.answer: Right honourables are members of the Privy Council, past and present, and honourables are everybody else. All members of the House of Commons are considered to be 'honourable' which is why unparliamentary language like calling someone a liar is not allowed - it's supposed to be an 'honourable' institution

questions.question: When boiling pasta in a saucepan without the lid on, it boils over. If you place a wooden spoon across the top of the saucepan, it stops it from boiling over. Why?

answers.answer: Bubbles build on bubbles. If you pop the top bubbles, nothing can build on them, so it bubbles no higher than the level of the spoon

If you put something hydrophobic (it doesn't absorb water) across the top of the pan, it compromises the structural integrity of the surface area of the bubbles. Anything that doesn't absorb water will work - a metal spoon, a coat hanger - not just wood

questions.question: Do sign languages have an equivalent of 'um' and 'er'? Is there a sort of pause or filler sign?

answers.answer: Yes, we do have fillers in sign language, but it's mostly gestural and through facial expression. It's like twiddling your fingers before you can think of the sign you want to use - it's more of a fill in the space. It's like a 'thinking face'

questions.question: How does your brain remember something that it's forgotten? When you rack your brain trying to remember someone's name, then later without any prompt it just suddenly pops into your head - where does that come from? How does it work?

answers.answer: Long-term memory - anything longer than about 20 seconds - is coded along with all the environment and things in our environment (the room we're in, the place we're in) as well as our internal state (if we've had coffee, wine, if we're feeling sleepy). We need those cues to pull the memory back into our working memory. When you're wandering around and something triggers that part of your brain where the information was stored but temporarily inaccessible, the memory becomes accessible again

questions.question: What's better for the environment - keeping an artificial Christmas tree you've had for several years, or cutting down a fresh one every year?

answers.answer: Real trees are better for the environment once you factor in all the production costs and travel costs. An artificial tree only becomes better for the environment if you keep it for about 20 plus years. The best answer is to grow one in your garden, cut it for Christmas, then replant it

questions.question: How can the Pacific side of the Panama Canal be higher than the Atlantic side, requiring locks and weirs to manage the water level difference? If they're both sea level, how can they be different heights?

answers.answer: Think about filling a plastic tub with water and pulling it towards you - the water moves away and piles up on one side. The Earth is always spinning to the east, so if you're pulling the water towards you (which the Earth is doing), it piles up against the Americas.
