The Atlantic/Caribbean water piles up against the land, while the Pacific is a much larger body so the effect is much more limited. The difference is about 2-4 meters. Without the locks, water would pour through one direction until the middle of the canal was level

Adding to the Panama Canal answer - there's also the Earth's geoid, which is the shape the Earth makes because it has variable density through it. The sea follows that perfectly, so some areas of sea level are literally higher than others. Even if the sea level was different at either end, it would still be flat - the water wouldn't flow because it's an equipotential surface. The water level in the locks is controlled by water coming from big lakes within Panama

questions.question: Birds of a feather flock together - but do birds of different species communicate with each other beyond the basic alarm call? Is there something else going on?

answers.answer: All different species of birds have very simple communication systems with a finite number of calls. Each call isn't divided into call parts - it's not like human language with grammar. If two species are physiologically similar (closely related), there's a fair chance they'll share some calls with similar meanings. The most obvious example is alarm calls. It happens more by chance because the system is so small there's not much room for variation. There's no research showing that birds of different species communicate beyond this basic level

questions.question: Why do people sound different? Not accents or dialects - but physical reasons. For example, why does someone look nothing like their brother but on the phone people can't tell them apart? Why does Brian Blessed have a booming voice and Joe Pasquale have a squeaky one? What determines the depth, tone and register of our voices?

answers.answer: It's about the vocal cords, the shape and size of the tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavities. Two brothers who look different externally are still more physically similar internally than they realize, and that's what determines their identical sound

questions.question: Why do we need to know when commercials are about to come on TV? There's the white dot in the corner to signal adverts - why do we need that warning?

answers.answer: It's to sync up with the networks, not for the audience. Different regions (ITV in London, STV in Scotland, UTV in Ulster) show different commercials. The symbol tells the networks' computers when the main show is about to resume so they can cut back from regional ads. It lets them know 'OK, we're about to go back' so everything can be ready and they can cut out a few seconds here and there to sync up if needed

questions.question: Why does a remote control start working again when you take the back off and spin the batteries?

answers.answer: The electricity in a battery is like leftover aftershave at the bottom of the bottle - schwooshing around but not making contact with the tube (the connection). Moving the batteries around is like schwooshing the aftershave to the bottom of the tube so when you press the button, it sucks up the electricity and your remote works

A battery is a store of chemicals and chemical energy. When you complete the circuit, you're converting chemical energy to electrical energy. Twiddling or rubbing the batteries adds a tiny bit of heat to the conversion, and that heat gives just enough electricity to get one more channel change

questions.question: Why do we cross our legs?

answers.answer: James provides some speculation - sometimes because we need a wee, sometimes to rest a book or phone on folded knees, sometimes it feels nice.

Two-part answer: For ladies, they were told as children to cross their legs as it's polite - 'because people might see your knickers otherwise.' For children who wrap their legs around each other, research suggests it's a sign of the two halves of the brain not quite working together. James notes this covers female and psychologically interesting male leg crossers but not the basic male leg crosser, so he adds his own view that it just feels comfortable.

questions.question: Why is it called 'shipping' when it arrives by car or van, but 'cargo' when it arrives by ship?

answers.answer: Cargo comes from 'cargar', Spanish for 'to load.' Shipping relates to any contract of carriage, first properly established in the Hague-Visby laws which covered carriage specifically by sea, then extended to land. So when loaded onto a ship it's cargo, and to ship something is a verb that's become a noun based on those contracts of carriage. Ash is a Merchant Navy Chief Officer and lecturer at Fleetwood Nautical College.

questions.question: Why do bingo numbers only go up to 90? Why not an even 100?

answers.answer: James admits he doesn't know and puts it on the board.

It's about permutation. You buy six books and when he calls, you've got that number on your six. If you went over 90, it would run out of permutation and you'd get double numbers. With 15 numbers per ticket, going to 91 would take it to 16 numbers. Ricky works as a bingo caller for Mecca and has been in the business 42 years.

questions.question: How many children does Boris Johnson have, and is it a record for a sitting Prime Minister?

answers.answer: James acknowledges legal matters prevent him from giving a definitive answer. He notes Johnson went to court to try to keep the existence of one child secret, so he could have gone to court to keep others secret. James says 'He might still be in the lead with the ones that we know about' and seems unsurprised.

Knowles heard 'somebody on LBC' say Boris had seven children but refrains from taking that at face value, stating 'those are the ones we know about' - essentially echoing James's earlier caution. For the record question: the second Earl Grey had 17 children from his wife and sisters, making that the Prime Ministerial record. Knowles has a BSc in policy studies and a keen interest in history.

questions.question: The tyres on my bike kept inside deflate within about three weeks, but the tyres on my bike kept outside stay inflated for months. Why?

answers.answer: James guesses it's about temperature.

As temperature cools, molecules in the air get less energetic and can't penetrate through the walls of the tyre as easily. tyres and inner tubes are slightly porous to air/gas molecules. Higher temperature means more energetic molecules that can penetrate the walls faster. This is why cars with tyre pressure monitoring systems alert you when temperature drops. David runs a company called Tire Industry Research.

questions.question: What is the next human evolutionary trait that we will see?

answers.answer: James says he can't know but puts it on the board, noting that medicine means things that might have evolved to improve haven't needed to.

As a former dentist for about 12 years, Daniel was taught that jaw sizes have got progressively smaller over centuries because we're no longer eating the foods cavemen ate. We're eating much softer food now, so we don't need strong jaws or big teeth, which is why orthodontists constantly work to create space for teeth. Daniel suggests the mouth is the area most susceptible to evolutionary change. He's now a comedian and former airline pilot aspirant.

questions.question: Where did the design for the treble and bass clef come from in music? Why are they designed the way they are?

answers.answer: James doesn't know and puts it on the board.

It goes back to medieval periods when music was controlled by the church and was mostly vocal. There are four clefs: treble, alto, tenor, and bass, corresponding to the different voice types used in church singing. The position of the clef indicates which notes they represent. A treble clef (also called a G clef) wraps around the line indicating the note G - and it designed to look like a G from medieval times. Alto and tenor clefs are C clefs, which look like a C. Bass clef is an F, wrapping around the line for F and designed to look like an F. Kayleigh has a music degree including a module in medieval notation and is a qualified music teacher. James notes she was named after the Marillion song 'Kayleigh'.

questions.question: Why are cowboys called cowboys when they ride horses? Shouldn't they be called horse boys?

answers.answer: Cowboys were responsible for driving huge herds of cattle across the Wild West, from one ranch to another for pasture. So they were literally cow herders on horses - they worked with cows, that's where the name comes from.

questions.question: What state of matter is fire? Solid, liquid, or gas?

answers.answer: Fire is solid and gas - the flames themselves are gas, and it's the solid that's burning. Possibly a bit of liquid too if exothermic reactions involve liquid emissions.

James was kind of right. Fire isn't just solid and gas - it's actually plasma, which is a fourth state of matter. Plasma occurs when material gets superheated and electrons get stripped from atoms, becoming ionised. Fire is superheated ionised gas - plasma. Peter has an MSc in chemistry where his project was plasma catalysis.

questions.question: Why do we blush when we're embarrassed?

answers.answer: The reason you blush is because your brain detects awkward situations and fires chemicals around your body to increase blood flow and increase the size of veins in your face. It's a social cue thing - you're communicating to your social group that you're embarrassed.

questions.question: Why do we use capital letters at the start of sentences?

answers.answer: It's mainly a matter of the Roman alphabet which didn't distinguish between small and capital letters until relatively late. Roman inscriptions are all capital letters. The insistence on capital letters at sentence beginnings didn't really start until the origins of printing. Even now, printed Latin is normally without sentence initial capitals. There's a similar pattern in Afrikaans where the indefinite article never takes a capital letter even at the start of a sentence.

questions.question: When did we start wearing black armbands as a symbol of mourning?
Is it detrimental to your health to stifle or hold in a sneeze?

answers.answer: When we sneeze, our body builds up pressure to help get rid of something in our nasal passage that shouldn't be there. If that pressure isn't released through the mouth or nose, it can cause blood vessels or even eardrums to burst because the pressure has to go somewhere. Better out than in.

questions.question: When did sports people first start spraying champagne to celebrate a victory?

answers.answer: It was done by accident in 1966 at the Le Mans 24 Hour race. It happened because of the hot weather and the champagne sprayed out due to pressure. The tradition of awarding champagne bottles goes back to the first Grand Prix in 1950 in the champagne region of France. An American driver then copied the spraying tradition at the Indy 500.

questions.question: Do dogs recognise their own breed?
Is sign language a universal language or do people sign in different languages?

answers.caller: Dr. Kate Rowley (via Kate Ferby interpreter)
answers.answer: Sign language is not universal. It evolved in different countries all over the world. While many signs are iconic (like tree - you make the shape of a tree with your hand), other signs are arbitrary (like who, what, why, where) and these differ in different sign languages. British Sign Language and American Sign Language have different representations for the same objects. Even Japanese sign language is iconic but chose different representations.

questions.question: Where does Whamageddon come from?
When you take items out of the dishwasher, why do plastic items always seem to be full of water droplets while other items don't?
Is PL (Plymouth/Cornwall) the biggest postcode area in the UK by geographical area? If not, what is?

answers.answer: Inverness (IV) is the largest postcode area in the country with 52 postcodes. This refers to the number of deliverable addresses.
Belfast is actually the largest single postcode area because it covers the entirety of Northern Ireland in terms of surface area. Inverness is possibly third behind Perth.

questions.question: Who has the longest official documented family tree in the world?

answers.answer: The Japanese Emperor. It goes back about 1500 years. They have the oldest continuous hereditary monarchy.
Confucius (Master Kong) from China. The Chinese have been keeping his lineage going for over 2,000 years in really detailed scrolls. Many living descendants exist in China today.

questions.question: Is there any basis in food really tasting better the day after it's been cooked?

answers.answer: Sauces and stocks with spices break down over time, creating stronger flavors. Meat acts like a sponge, absorbing flavor the longer it's left. As a former chef who went to the International College of Food, he explained that Indian restaurants make their base sauces weeks in advance and freeze them, making them more potent.

questions.question: Can you get two colds at the same time?

answers.answer: I presume you can, because it's just a virus, isn't it? I shall find out for you.

Yes, you can have two colds at the same time. It's called co-infection. His son was sick for three weeks with a cold, got better, then got worse again. The doctor explained you can have two colds one after the other or at the same time.

As a GP, he explained that a cold isn't a disease, it's a symptom. You can have a viral infection that gives cold symptoms, and then get what's called a superimposed bacterial infection which gives you the same symptoms but caused by a different organism. That's co-infection.

questions.question: Where did borders, country's borders actually begin? Where was the first ever border?
Why is belly button fluff always blue?
Why do airplane propellers appear to slow down and then run backwards when the plane is speeding up on the runway?

answers.answer: Your eye is like a camera that can only take a finite number of frames per second. When the propeller moves faster than your eyes can process the information, your brain tells you it's going backwards. James called it 'ocular acceleration syndrome'.

The wagon wheel effect only happens on film when the frame rate matches propeller rotation. What John saw in real life is called nystagmus - you see jerky eye movements on trains because you remember each still for a fraction of a second after seeing it. These are two completely different effects.
Contesting Professor Howell: Propellers DO go forward and backwards and you can see it without being on film. He was a propeller watcher.

questions.question: What is the fundamental reason for the BODMAS rule in mathematics? Why does multiplication come before addition?

answers.answer: The reason for the rule is that there needs to be a rule, otherwise there wouldn't be consensus on what 2+2x4 equals. You can't have a right answer without a rule. The rule came after the confusion.

Multiplication is repeated addition, so it takes precedence over simple addition. Division is repeated subtraction, which takes precedence over simple subtraction. This is the fundamental reason for the order. She was a business, economics and IT teacher who also taught some math.

questions.question: Why does your hair get darker or change color as you get older from childhood?
Why are cats so temperamental? They can be worst of enemies one minute and best of friends two minutes later.

answers.answer: Humans are like that too, just not as quickly. It might be odder if mood changes took a long time. With seven cats, they've got six other cats getting on their nerves constantly.

questions.question: If we're receiving a radio signal, how do you know how many people are receiving or listening to that signal?

answers.answer: It's done through surveys and diaries (RAJAR). People get visited door to door or sent diaries and asked what they've listened to during the week. They take a sample and extrapolate to the broader population. With digital listening, it's becoming more reliable.

questions.question: Why is the rugby ball shaped like that? At what point did it go from being a football to this ovoid shape?

answers.answer: They were shaped after pig's bladders. Originally rugby and football used the same shape ball. In 1892 they standardised the ovoid shape. It changed again in 2004 when they made it longer and used synthetic materials. The ovoid shape is for grip and aerodynamics - it spins better through the air.

questions.question: Do dogs on heat get warmer? And if they don't, why is it called 'dogs on heat'?

answers.answer: No, they don't get hot like humans do. Female humans have a temperature raise during their heat cycle that can be measured, but not with dogs. You can't time it - there isn't a pill for female dogs because you just don't know when it's going to happen. There is a slight temperature change but that's probably just due to excitement and meeting other dogs. The phrase probably comes from humans presuming dogs would be the same.

questions.question: Do lakes and large bodies of water have tides? If so, how large does the body of water have to be before the moon affects the tide?

answers.answer: In theory, all bodies of water will have a tide no matter how tiny. The smaller the body of water, the smaller the tide. The moon's gravitational attraction pulls water upwards. In a lake, water heapes up in the middle and pulls away from the sides. Even a puddle would have a tide, though it would be so tiny you couldn't measure it. The Baltic Sea has tides of about 25 centimetres because the narrowness of the channel connecting it to the ocean restricts the tidal flow.

questions.question: At what age does a bone become a fossil? We find human bones and mammoth bones that aren't fossilised, but dinosaur bones are always fossils.

answers.answer: You can get human fossils. It's all about the process, not time. Water is needed - if an animal dies in a desert, the body rots away leaving just bone. If it dies in a riverbed and gets flooded quickly, it gets buried in sediment. Layers build up and push down, turning the surrounding area into sedimentary rock. Water from the river seeps into the bones, there's a chemical reaction, and the minerals turn into stone. Anything can be fossilised.

questions.question: Does a fish really rot from the head down?

answers.answer: Yes, it does rot from the head down. The first part of a fish that rots is the gills, which are within the head. The gills have a very large surface area, they're surrounded by air causing oxidation, and they're full of blood which is high protein that bacteria loves. The bacteria then spreads down the fish along the main vein that runs down the back line. A very fresh fish has runny blood, and as it ages, the blood at the head congeals first while the blood in the tail is still runny.

questions.question: Why does the moon not rotate? Why is there always a dark side of the moon?

answers.answer: The moon does spin on its axis. The reason we see only one side is tidal locking - Earth's gravity pulls on the moon causing it to bulge. Over 10 billion years, like a spinning ice skater who opens their arms and slows down, the moon's rotation became locked to Earth's. The pointy bit (bulge) is always nearest Earth and they rotate almost in tandem, so the dark side is always on the other side. We actually see about 59% of the moon total due to slight wobbles.

questions.question: What is the earliest record of a human name?
If both parents are left-handed and their first child is left-handed, will every child after that be left-handed?

answers.answer: That is not true. Colourblindness sits on the sex gene, whereas left-handedness doesn't sit on the sex gene. Other callers have said they've had two children - one left-handed and one right-handed - so left-handedness doesn't guarantee all children will be left-handed.

questions.question: Why do we call astronauts from English-speaking countries but cosmonauts from Russia? They're both English words for the same job.
Why is the east of England so flat compared to the west?

answers.answer: When tectonic plates push together, hills pop up. The west of England must be directly over a point where plates have pushed together.

The west of England is much closer to the edge of the European tectonic plate, so there's activity there. On the east, the Dogger Bank was a land bridge from Britain to Europe, and that being flat, there's not much underneath. When it sank, it stretched the land. The east is closer to the middle of the tectonic plate, which is why it's flatter, while the west pops up with hills due to the activity at the plate edge.

questions.question: Does everybody who looks at an object with colour perceive the colour in their minds the same way as you do? How would we know?

answers.answer: No, we all interpret colours differently. The best example is the viral dress picture - black and blue or white and gold. As a retoucher for a fashion company, colleagues often disagree on whether something looks too blue or too green.

From his brain injury and visits to Moorfield Eye Hospital over 10 years, he learned that colours are processed in the left side of the brain rather than the right. He's partially sighted and can't see colour properly - sees black and white, and with red can see something slightly different.

The way we see light is down to colours. Working in print for 26 years, ink manufacturers have shown that colours look different depending on light conditions - both the light source and individual eyes affect perception. Even in the same room with the same light, people see different things.

questions.question: When a by-election is triggered, people tweet that the Chief Whip has moved the writ. What is the writ? Where is it moved to and why?
What was the earliest known form of currency to be used? Money as we understand it, not barter - a token worth X.

answers.answer: Probably Babylon or ancient Egypt.
The Mesopotamian shekel. Units of shekels were being used about 5,000 years ago, but the first mints were around 650 BC. Prior to that you'd swap a chicken for a pumpkin.

questions.question: When we no longer have a queen, what happens to our currency? How long after does it change? How long is it legal for?

answers.answer: He doesn't think it's any different from normal - coins just get taken out of circulation. If you were around years ago, you'd still have had coins in your pocket after the queen's head appeared that had her dad's head. She was on the throne when we decimalised, so a coin with her father's head might still have been legal tender.

When Charles is crowned king, his head will face the opposite way to the queen's on coins. The queen's money will still be legal tender until the Royal Mint decides to either redesign the coin or just decide it's not. When he was at the Royal Mint four weeks ago, they minted their own 50 pence piece for an anniversary of decimalisation which didn't go into circulation due to Covid.

questions.question: Can birds fly upside down?

answers.answer: Aeroplanes can fly upside down but they don't flap their wings.

Yes, but they don't do it often. Hummingbirds are well known for it - they have rotator cuff muscles enabling them to put their wing in any position, moving it in a figure of eight, so they can fly upside down to take nectar from awkward flowers. Ravens also fly upside down as a mating display to show dominance. Geese do it to stall in the air before landing on lakes. Small wading birds do it to evade predators.

questions.question: When squirrels go back to get their nuts, are they always going to be there or is another squirrel grabbed hold of their nuts?

answers.answer: If a squirrel could find your nuts by looking for them, it would remove the reason for burying them - so no, probably not.

Squirrels have a very advanced sense of smell. They bury nuts at times of plenty, and the nuts start to decompose in the soil. When they want to go back, they rely on their sense of smell - they put their nose on the ground moving side to side, attracted by the odour of decomposing nuts. The partially broken down nuts are more digestible. They're not remembering where they buried them; they're attracted by the smell. Squirrels are not particularly territorial - you'll see six or seven in a garden, all relatives. They'll eat whatever nuts they come across, regardless of who buried them. They sometimes forget, which is why you get oak trees growing in gardens.

questions.question: Why is the acting so wooden in children's TV when these people go on and become good actors?

answers.answer: It's not wooden - it's the opposite. It's more pantomime-y, exaggerated. They're doing everything in a more exaggerated fashion because children process entertainment differently. The shows are almost like human cartoons with cartoonish sensibilities - exaggerated accents, physical expressions, and reactions.

Children don't develop the ability to recognise nuanced emotions until later in their development. It's very purposely exaggerated in child acting so that they can recognise happiness, sadness, and other emotions - almost like signposting their emotions.

questions.question: Elizabeth I died, people were called Elizabethans. George died, they're Georgians. When Charles dies, we'll be Carolines. What happens when William dies? What would the age be called?
Why do we say 'whoops-a-daisy' when we've had an accident or been clumsy?

answers.answer: He remembers from school that when somebody died or fell over, people would say 'whoops' and to cover the smell they put a posy of daisies on their body.

questions.question: If I was to plant one thing in my garden, what would absorb the most carbon dioxide?

answers.answer: For pure CO2 absorption: pine trees like Picea abies (Norway spruce) because they have very fine needles with high density of absorption, and they're evergreen so they work all year round. However, they're not native and have little value to nature. The better answer for both carbon and biodiversity is an oak tree if the garden's big enough. Oak trees are the most biodiverse tree in the UK, support hundreds of species, absorb carbon for much longer (centuries), and you can get native UK-grown saplings from the Woodland Trust.

questions.question: How do deaf people learn to read? My three young boys have used phonics and sounds to learn to read, but deaf people can't hear the sounds being made out loud.

answers.answer: Deaf children learn to read through visual association, connecting signs or objects to printed words. If they have access to spoken language, they can make the connection between what they see and hear and the printed word. Many deaf children learn sign language - they learn the sign for an object (like 'ball'), understand the concept, then see the printed word and make the connection. For abstract concepts without physical representation, it works the same as hearing children - through conversation and language exposure. The more signs and language they have, the better their reading will be. Dr. Rowley is a deaf psycholinguist at the Deafness, Cognition, Language and Research Center.

questions.question: On the International Space Station, which country's laws apply? If you committed a crime, which country would have jurisdiction?

answers.answer: According to the Outer Space Treaty, space has the same laws as international waters - no country can claim space just as no country can claim the high seas. The criminal will be prosecuted by the country they're from, under that country's laws. So it's essentially based on the country of nationality of the person involved.

questions.question: What is the biological difference between cold-blooded and warm-blooded animals? How is the blood heated in a warm-blooded animal?

answers.answer: Warm-blooded (endothermic) animals can regulate their own body temperature internally - mammals keep around 37 degrees by burning food energy. Cold-blooded (poikilothermic) animals don't have that ability and must move around to regulate temperature from external sources. Lizards shuttle between sun and shade to warm up or cool down, and in cold weather may go into torpor to conserve energy.

questions.question: When was the heart symbol or heart emoji first used in popular culture to mean love?

answers.answer: Mentioned in ancient Egyptian civilization - in hieroglyphics as a symbol representing the center of emotion and love. Also referenced in Greek texts and the Quran. But this was not a definitive answer - James said Abu Omar wasn't getting a Ray Liotta because the answer wasn't conclusive enough.

questions.question: Why do you put chalk on a pool cue? You just use chalk for grip in climbing and weightlifting, but in pool you're not gripping anything - you're just impacting the ball.

answers.answer: You put chalk on to stop a sheen appearing on the tip so you can impart spin on the ball. Without grip (purchase) on the cue tip, it slides off the ball and you miss. The chalk creates purchase at the point of contact, allowing you to put spin and screw on the ball - for example, making the ball roll back on itself when you hit it hard underneath. Professional players need this for the more nuanced shots, not just basic impact.

questions.question: Why is there an abundance of helium-3 on the Moon but not on Earth?

answers.answer: Professor of geophysics specializing in geomagnetism. The helium on the Moon comes from the solar wind from the sun. Earth's magnetic field blocks it from reaching Earth, but doesn't extend far enough to block it for the Moon. Earth's helium-3 is mostly primordial from when the planet formed, plus some from nuclear testing. In principle, we could mine it from the Moon, but whether it's practical is another matter.

questions.question: How do nasal sprays like Vicks work to clear a blocked nose? You just breathe something in and your nose clears up - what's actually happening chemically/biologically?

answers.answer: GP. Nasal sprays contain drugs like xylometazoline or oxymetazoline. They don't get rid of snot immediately - they shrink the blood vessels causing vasoconstriction. What's blocking your nose is the swollen mucosa (blocked walls of your nose), and the spray makes those blood vessels get smaller, rapidly opening up your nose. Warning: these can cause rhinitis medicamentosa - if you use them for more than a couple of days, your nose becomes dependent on them just to open up normally. In some countries they're not freely available because of this addiction risk.

questions.question: When a song or a composition is described as being in an uncertain key, what does it mean? What is a musical key?

answers.answer: Explained that a key is essentially the scale in which music is played. The key determines which notes you can play and which notes you can't play. If you play notes outside the key, it sounds wrong.
A key is a series of semitones and tones put together. The series of jumps between notes has to be the same for each key. A major scale forms a key with specific tone/tone/semitone patterns.

questions.question: Can you be allergic to water?

answers.answer: It's called aquagenic pruritus. Some people suffer really badly - if they sweat or cry, their skin feels like it's on fire. Ed has a mild form himself.

questions.question: If the human race became extinct tomorrow, what would be the last surviving piece of evidence that we ever existed? Something that aliens visiting in 50 or 100 million years time could find.

answers.answer: Highly enriched uranium-235, like what's used in nuclear bombs, would be the last remaining evidence because it's artificially enriched to 80% concentration which is impossible to find in nature. Materials with half-lives of tens to hundreds of thousands of years will last a long time in one location.

Jack's answer was in the millions of years. The actual answer is in the billions of years - the Voyager space probe. When the sun expands to consume the Earth as a red giant, only Voyager will remain as the last trace of humankind.

questions.question: Why does ice make Coke go flat? We add ice to our cola at the restaurant and it goes flat within minutes. We've tried rinsing the ice and it doesn't help.

answers.answer: The real problem is not the ice but that they're serving from two-litre bottles (which lose gas once opened) and not refrigerating the bottles. Adding ice to warm, already partially flat Coke makes it worse.

It's about surface area and nucleation points. When you put something like ice into a liquid, you're increasing the surface area inside the glass, giving bubbles more places to grow and float to the surface. The melting isn't the major issue - it's the nucleation points.

questions.question: Why do we call them a 'pair of pants' when pants are just one item of clothing? Why hasn't the word changed?

answers.answer: In medieval times, pants were originally like a pair of tights - two separate pieces joined at the top. Men had a separate codpiece to cover the middle bit. So it was literally a pair, and the name stuck even after the garment became a single piece.

questions.question: When humans walk, the bottom part of our legs bends backwards. But wetland birds' legs bend forwards. Why do wetland birds have legs that bend differently?

answers.answer: We evolved to walk on dry land; wetland birds evolved to walk on soggy ground. The hydraulics of walking change according to the sogginess of the terrain.

The part of the bird's leg that bends outward is actually their heel - they've got an extended foot. Their knee is equivalent to the end of their drumstick, which is usually inside their body. This has evolved to be a better way of walking for them.

questions.question: What makes cats chatter - like a shudder or jaw movement - when they see potential prey like a bird on a fence? Even when they're alone?

answers.answer: He speculated it might be stretching their jaw, like a tennis player warming up.
It's to do with exercising their jaws, so when they do eventually catch the bird, their jaw is ready.

questions.question: Why do the Canada geese in our local reservoir stand on one leg when they come out of the water?

answers.answer: It's not actually purely just geese. It's the majority of birds do that. And they do it to retain body heat because obviously the birds' feet are just literally exposed skin. So they literally took a foot up so they can retain body heat. It's not that they're warming their foot up, so to speak. It's just that they're turning off the tap of exothermic, of heat emissions and air.

questions.question: Clouds are made of water, why is it that you can see through water but you can't see through clouds?

answers.answer: The gas has a different state from the liquid... I should have listened to science. I think it's a gas... when water turns to steam or water turns to a vapour, it changes its state and it also, its properties therefore change.

When water evaporates from all the sources, like the ocean and stuff, and goes up into the air, it returns back into water droplets. Tiny. And they're like micro droplets. Tiny, tiny droplets. Yeah. And there's billions of them, so they're not a gas. They're actually water droplets. And it's only when they mix with particles and dust, they become heavy enough to fall again into rain. Right. And that's why you can't see through them, because they're water droplets. And they'll be all the reflection on each drop. This is the same as fog. That's it. If you put your main beam on in fog, you're blinded. Yeah, because the light's coming back at you.

questions.question: If I were to dig a hole straight down through the middle of the earth, out the other side, I put down my spade and I jump in, what would happen when I reached the centre of the earth?

answers.answer: First of all, if you jumped through, you'd obviously get burned up. We're ignoring the molten core. The second thing is air resistance. So, assuming you're in a perfect vacuum and that you can survive that, you've got potential gravitational energy. So that would pull you through right to the centre of the earth. And until you got to that point, the earth would be pulling you through. Once you get to that point, you've got enough momentum that you'd get through to the other side and you'd essentially just hop out at the other end. But with air resistance, your momentum wouldn't carry you far enough because of your loss of energy. So, you'd get through and then you'd end up just kind of ping-ponging until you ended up losing all your momentum and just stayed in the centre of the earth. You'd be going ba-doing, ba-doing, ba-doing for quite a while. For a millennium or something like that.

questions.question: Sunflowers open up in sunlight... how do they do that if they've not got a brain?

answers.answer: I mean, brain is a really misleading thing to bring into the conversation. It's not... in the same way that... you know, how does it draw water in through its roots if it hasn't got a brain? How does it end up yellow if it hasn't got a brain? And it doesn't... it's not the absence of a brain that is... But it can actually move. It's the same reason that if you go into a forest, the trees will be long and thin because they've got to try and get the light.

It's not about moving. It's about growth. And I think it's called heliotropism. And it just means that it's growing towards light in order to get the energy from the sun, in order to photosynthesize. So all plants do that.

questions.question: Why don't you forget how to ride a bicycle?

answers.answer: I think you've just answered your own question, haven't you? It's a lot harder to play a musical instrument than it is to ride a bicycle. So it's just a number. If you think of learning to ride a bicycle, in order to learn to ride a bicycle, you have to tick X number of boxes. It's only probably four boxes, isn't it? Keep your balance. Two boxes. Keep your balance. Pedal fast enough. Once you're ready, physically ready for it, your dad takes your stabilizers off, you go down the park, bish bosh, you're off. First time. First day. You don't have to redo that again 20 years later.

questions.question: Why is it perceived as rude to eat with your elbows at the table?

answers.answer: During our era as a major maritime nation in this sceptered isle, the practice aboard ships... Space used to be a premium. So they would bring out a trestle table. You'd have a sort of triangular shaped framework upon which you would lay a large flat surface. Now imagine you were to put your elbows on large flat surface and lean down with a degree of pressure. The entire table would go belly up. And that is why putting your elbows on the table was considered to be, well, was sort of a very bad thing to do. And as with many issues of etiquette, it segued effortlessly into a good manners scenario as opposed to a practical scenario.

The caller offered his own theory: I thought it was pirates eating at the table on a ship. The ship would rock and make the table rock also. So pirates would have their elbows on the table. But because pirates are rude, it then became rude.

questions.question: When you apply antiperspirant or deodorant, where does the sweat go that's supposed to leave your body?

answers.answer: It comes out in your wheel. Something like that. No idea. That's why I'm phoning in. I think that's the answer. You just wee it out. Well, I'm sure someone will phone in and give us the scientific explanation. Someone can ask next week.

questions.question: What is the longest amount of time a baby can have a blank birth certificate for?
Why are we born with different blood types?
When you shake an egg before frying it, why does the yolk stay centered?

answers.answer: It's like stirring a cup of tea - the liquid on the outside goes faster than the liquid in the center, which forces the heavy object to the middle

questions.question: If you jump on top of a moving train, you land in a different spot, but if you jump inside a train you land in the same spot - why?

answers.answer: Wind resistance would cause you to land in a different spot on top of the train. When you're inside the train, you're within its envelope, so you maintain the same speed. The chicken-in-a-lorry paradox - if all chickens jump, the lorry doesn't weigh less because they're still part of the system's mass

questions.question: Why do cats pad/knead on soft surfaces like dressing gowns?

answers.answer: As kittens, they knead to stimulate milk from their mother. As adults, it's a pleasurable reflex - a memory of that comfort. The texture of toweling mimics the softness of their mother's fur. His girlfriend is a veterinary nurse specializing in feline behaviour

questions.question: Are there seasons in space? When would be the best time to visit the moon?

answers.answer: Any body tilted on its axis will have seasons. The moon is tilted 5 degrees on its axis, so there are seasons, but they're more about length of days than temperature changes. He has a degree in geology and physical geography

questions.question: What did people use before microphones to be heard in large crowds?

answers.answer: Before electronic amplification, people relied on specially designed acoustic spaces like Epidaurus theater in Greece, town criers who practiced voice projection, and the human microphone relay system where speakers repeated to people who repeated to others further away

The human microphone system - the speaker says a few lines, people closest repeat them in unison, then a second group repeats, passing it on like a relay. Used for thousands of years. David Graeber wrote about this. Now activists call it 'mic check'. He's an activist and fan of David Graeber's work

questions.question: Is sound magnified in the womb when you tap the belly, like it is when your head is underwater?

answers.answer: The sound changes medium from air to liquid, but energy can't be created or magnified - it can't be louder inside than the energy input at the point of entry. The baby only knows what it sounds like in the womb, with no comparison to outside. He works in acoustics with a physics degree

questions.question: Why is a honeymoon called a honeymoon?

answers.answer: It's mead (booze made from honey) plus the moon. Newlyweds would drink mead during the first moon cycle of marriage, when there was more time and likely increased conception. One moon cycle plus lots of mead equals honeymoon

questions.question: How far can you actually see when looking at stars? Are you seeing millions of miles away or is it an illusion?

answers.answer: The theoretical limit is the observable universe - 13.8 billion light years away. Since the universe is 13.8 billion years old, light from anything further away hasn't reached us yet. You can see theoretically if something is bright enough. He's a space enthusiast who watches lots of YouTube videos

questions.question: Is there a place in the world where East meets West? What determines those points?

answers.answer: The Bosphorus in Turkey - the bridge over the Bosphorus is widely regarded as the meeting point of East and West, Europe and Asia. Constantinople was the gateway from East to West

questions.question: Water is transparent, right? So you can see through it. So my question is why, when you put clothes into water, they go darker or into the washing machine or into a bowl or whatever. Why do they go dark and then when they dry out, they go back to their original colour?

answers.answer: It's called internal reflection. Liquids have a reflective surface. When you intertwine that reflective surface into the fabrics of a fabric or a jumper, what happens is where that reflective surface is introduced in between, it reflects some of the light back in on itself, making it appear darker, but it's not actually darker. Some of the light that we would normally see is reflected back so you don't see it, giving the illusion of it being darker.

questions.question: Why don't other animals cry?

answers.answer: Yes, from my experience it's a bit of a yes and no answer. They can cry but it's not because they're upset or with any empathy. It's generally due to a physical cause, usually like an illness or some kind of wound. That's why I said weeping.

questions.question: Why does this spider keep coming back to my house after I remove it? How do spiders find their way home?

answers.answer: There are some spiders that can navigate, but those are very advanced spiders, mainly jumping spiders. There's a particular type with the Latin name Portia that is debatably the most intelligent spider that hunts other spiders. But from the description, it sounds like a house spider, and those are not advanced spiders. They have very poor eyesight and generally only respond to external stimuli. So logically, the only thing that could be attracting him so much to that house is lots of female spiders. The only logical answer is that there must be more female spiders in that room or near that lavatory than there are in any of the other surrounding areas. And they're probably ambush predators who stay in a little hole the whole time anyway.

questions.question: You can pay a company to put you in cryogenic suspension when you die with the hope of being revived in the future. My question is, what's the time limit on that?

answers.answer: It's actually a non-question because as far as our current scientific understanding goes, you can't be unfrozen. They invented the microwave to defrost cryogenically frozen people. To defrost mice, because they were looking into cryogenic freezing, they found that you can actually freeze and refreeze mice multiple times and they were fine. But you can't do it any bigger than a mouse. It's to do with the surface area.

questions.question: Does mixing your drinks make you more drunk than not mixing your drinks?

answers.answer: Generally, the darker the drink, the more congeners you have. These are chemical clutter that irritate the brain. Vodka is mainly water with alcohol and has very few congeners, so you get drunk but don't have that chemical clutter. Whiskey has lots of organic chemicals that leach out from the barrel and irritate the brain. Red wine has phenylethylamine in it, which is a vasoconstrictor. Mixing drinks does make a difference because strong drinks can inhibit their own absorption. If you drink whiskey and then lager on top, it dilutes the whiskey enough so it starts getting absorbed. So if it's a strong drink mixed with a weak drink, it becomes a semi-strong drink which doesn't inhibit its own uptake. The never-mix grain and grape rule follows but for a different reason.

questions.question: Why is the President's emergency briefcase called the nuclear football?

answers.answer: It's called the football because originally the bag was a small brown leather case that looked a bit like a football. They also named an operation, a war plan, called Operation Dropkick because you need the football to do a dropkick. The briefcase just looked like a football. Kemsley met one of the military aides that carries the football a few months ago when he met Jill Biden through Walking With The Wounded. He saw the football when it was last in the country.

questions.question: Why is milk stout called milk stout?
Are crows intelligent?

answers.answer: Crows are highly intelligent. They're part of the corvid family and all corvids are really intelligent. They're one of the most intelligent birds. They can use tools, they can mimic human speech, they can work out puzzles. This was from research into ravens at the Tower of London for a children's book.

questions.question: What is the difference between a ballad and a song? When does a song become a ballad?

answers.answer: A ballad is a story. Going back to the medieval Middle Ages, balladeers with lutes would travel from court to court telling stories put into song so people could remember them. That's where the name comes from - commercial and touring. 'Living on a Prayer' by Bon Jovi is a ballad because it's about Tommy who used to work on the docks. Fresh Prince of Bel-Air would be a ballad because it tells a story all about how his life got switched upside down. There's very little between Will Smith and someone who played the lute 500 years ago.

questions.question: Will Brighton Beach ever become like Copacabana Beach? Will it eventually be sand?

answers.answer: Unfortunately, unless there are significant changes in tidal flows along the south coast of England, Brighton will always be Pebble Beach. The larger rocks get ground down into gravel and eventually sand and then silt, but the speed of the water carries smaller particles along. At Brighton, the gravel comes in and will always be the same size - it heads down the coast towards Worthing and Hastings where sand is deposited as the tide slows. You would need to put in breakwaters or groins to slow the tidal flow and encourage sand to accrete, but that would steal sand from neighbouring towns.

questions.question: Why does sweat smell differently in different parts of your body?

answers.answer: You have different bacteria in different bits of your body and they excrete different smells. Sweat itself doesn't smell - it's the bacteria.

Different types of bacteria inhabit different parts of your body and these produce metabolical by-products. The smell of these by-products will differ based on different environmental factors such as temperature and moisture availability. It's hotter and wetter under your armpit than on top of your head, therefore the sweat behaves differently and the bacteria behaves differently.

questions.question: Do animals, and dogs in particular, suffer from mental illnesses in the same way as humans? Specifically things like paranoia, schizophrenia, bipolar?

answers.answer: Yes, they can get mental illnesses. The most widespread are dementia and depression. Canine cognitive dysfunction is very similar to Alzheimer's - a deterioration of the brain. They can also get PTSD, for example if a young dog is bitten by a much bigger dog and hurt. The U.S. Army has a center in the States for PTSD service dogs. They used to find out that dogs get PTSD six months after the handler gets it, and then the dog would go into depression when the handler was getting better.

questions.question: Why does her face go very bright beetroot red after a run while the rest of her body stays her normal skin colour?

answers.answer: When you exercise, body temperature goes up and your blood vessels vasodilate (get bigger) to lose heat through your skin, which is why you go redder. This happens more in your face because you have a high percentage of capillaries in your face - they're closer to the surface. Heather doesn't have capillaries as near the surface of her skin in any other parts of her body.

questions.question: If central banks print money for governments to borrow, where do the interest payments go? Do governments borrow from central banks?

answers.answer: Treasuries issue bonds and central banks buy them. The interest gets paid by the bondholder. The central bank keeps the bond on its balance sheet and pays the interest to itself. It either keeps the interest proceeds and reinvests them to buy more bonds, or sits on them until the bonds expire. In effect, it's a firebreak - the bonds keep the bond market going while the treasury is on the hook for its own debt. The central bank buys that debt and creates money into the system. It's not direct printing like helicopter money which leads to Zimbabwean-style inflation.

questions.question: How long does an average brick-built house last before it becomes uninhabitable or falls down?

answers.answer: Houses depend very much on how they're built. At college I was taught that a modern house was designed to last 100 years. It will last a lot longer than that, obviously, but it depends on materials, weather, whether walls are north-facing, salty air - there are 101 things. I've been in the building trade nearly 50 years. Roughly 100 years per house.

questions.question: Why does gooseberry jam come out reddish pink when other jams come out the colour of the fruit (strawberry red, blackberry dark)? Why isn't it green?

answers.answer: It depends on the variety of the gooseberry. It's quite natural for it to be pink. The gooseberries start off with a pink pigmentation in the skin. It's not the skin making it pink - it's taking the pigmentation from inside the natural variety. The longer you boil the jam, the darker the colour will be.

questions.question: Where does weight go when you lose it? I've been thinking about this and I can't find an answer. When people say 'I've lost weight', where did it go?

answers.answer: Discussion: You're burning fat, turning chemical energy into heat and kinetic energy. The log on fire example - the log is fat, it turns into heat, there's ash left. Carbon dioxide breathed out is our ash. Water vapor as well.

Fat molecules shrink when you expel energy. By-products are carbon and water. When you breathe out, you're getting rid of carbon. When you go to the toilet and sweat, you're expelling water. Movement uses energy.

answers.caller: Alex (Wirral) - Professor of Small Animal Medicine at University of Liverpool
answers.answer: When you lose weight, the bulk of what you lose is carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. This comes out as water and carbon dioxide. About 16% of weight loss is water, and about 84% is breathed out as carbon dioxide. So the weight is mainly breathed out.

questions.question: Is there anything remaining in British law that still requires a minimum age of 21?

answers.answer: Discussion: Could be becoming an MP, joining the army, age of consent, getting married. James suggested maybe MP, but Mari Black (SNP MP) was elected at 20, so that fell apart.
To adopt a child in the UK, you have to be 21 years old or older.

questions.question: When you look at a flat map of the world, why is it split by the Pacific Ocean and not the Atlantic Ocean?

answers.answer: The map is arranged with the UK in the middle. The Pacific is where it is because the UK has been prioritized in the plotting of the map. If you went to America or Mongolia, maps in schools wouldn't have Britain in the middle.

It's because the Greenwich Meridian is in the UK, and that will also be in the middle of the map. If Greenwich is the longitude and latitude middle for all navigations, ergo the map is arranged around it.

When there was more trade and the Empire existed, people needed to standardize maps so they could collaborate with other ships and sailors. Because it was such a big Empire, many countries used the UK version of the map. It's about standardization due to political power.

questions.question: Does everybody say 'achoo' all around the world when they sneeze?

answers.answer: Discussion: Could be learned behaviour. Different languages have different sounds for animals (France says cockerico for rooster). The blessing 'bless you' after a sneeze came from the 17th century plague fears.
In Poland, they say 'apsik' when sneezing, not 'achoo'. It's like a psh sound when air comes out through the mouth.

questions.question: Can you tell me why the home counties are called the home counties?
Why does the Royal Coat of Arms have a unicorn on it? I noticed it for the first time watching the news last night.

answers.answer: The unicorn is the national animal of Scotland. Since James VI (of Scotland) ascended to the throne, the unicorn has been alongside the lion. It's the Lion of England and the Unicorn of Scotland. The Scottish coat of arms had two unicorns before the crowns merged.

questions.question: If I'm cycling at 20mph with a 20mph tailwind and then the same wind becomes a headwind, is the extra effort required into the wind exactly equal to the effort saved coming with the wind? Does that make sense? Are they equal and opposite forces?

answers.answer: Intuitive feeling that you need more effort into the wind than you gain from a tailwind. Probably friction related. Needs scientific answer.

Aerodynamically, resistance goes up quadratically with wind speed. If you're cycling at 20mph with no wind, your aerodynamic term is 400 (20 squared). With a 1mph tailwind, you're effectively at 19mph, so 361. With a 1mph headwind, you're effectively at 21mph, so 441. The tailwind saves you 39 units but the headwind costs you 41 units. On average over the two journeys, you use more energy than a still day because aerodynamic resistance increases more with headwind than it decreases with tailwind. This is because there's no resistance involved when the wind is behind you helping you - the resistance is what makes you go faster if the wind is behind you, but the same resistance slows you down more when it's in front.

questions.question: Why do grey hairs on men predominantly always start in beards or sideburns rather than on the top of the head?

Why are the beaches on some volcanic islands white and on other volcanic islands they're grey or black? St Lucia is volcanic but has white beaches, while just over the way there's an island with black beaches.
If I was on the moon, what would the time difference be? Would I have to put my watch forward? Or would I have to take it back?

answers.answer: You would just calibrate your watch with mission control. When they want to talk to him, they have to call and give him a time to wake up so they can talk to him. So it'll be the same as mission control.

The time on the moon conforms to UTC (Universal Time Coordinates), which is exactly the same as GMT. Every operation or mission outside of Earth is coordinated to UTC. The military use UTC quite a lot - even the Russian military.

questions.question: In football, has a referee ever been sent off?

answers.answer: The referee is the only person with authority to send people off, and there's no provision for sending himself off. The only way it could be done is the referee can abandon a match at his discretion. It would be abandoning the match to be probably replayed at a different time.

There is no FA ruling on whether a referee can or can't send himself off. Joe mentioned from his inbox there's been one incident - a Sunday League match in Peterborough in 2005 where the referee had a tough day, lost his rag with a goalie, sent himself off and abandoned the match.

questions.question: What's the difference between Diet Coke and Coke Zero? Is it just a marketing plot?

answers.answer: There's very little difference in actual ingredients. Coke Zero is specifically marketed at people who don't want to drink a drink with the word 'diet' in it - very often men, who might see it as perhaps soft or effeminate if it has the word diet in it. They do the same job but are aimed at different markets.

The caramel content in both products is varied and different - more in Coke Zero than Diet Coke. The acidity and carbonation levels are different too. Coke Zero tastes more like regular Coke, which is why people who want the taste but no sugar would drink it. Diet Coke was for people who prioritized diet over taste and ended up preferring it. Coke Zero used newer techniques and technologies to sound more like real Coke.

questions.question: What are those poles with bunting across the top on motorway roadworks for?

answers.answer: It might be health and safety or where different legislation begins and ends.

They're used to indicate to drivers and workers on the motorway that there are overhead powerlines and to avoid hitting them. This is for trucks, diggers, or plant equipment. A driver didn't see the poles and ended up lifting his tipper body into a 33 kilovolt powerline. The poles are for vehicles that become higher when tipping or have big arms on them.

questions.question: Do dogs prefer to sleep in the dark?
Why do children have growth spurts as opposed to just growing constantly, but slowly?

answers.answer: The determinants of longitudinal bone growth (growth of arms and legs, which is the main determinant of height) is controlled by the release of hormones by a little gland at the base of the brain. The release of hormones that control this - things like growth hormone and sex steroids - is not continuously released. It's released in a pulsatile way, which increases to its maximum at the point of growth during puberty, and therefore you grow in these spurts as opposed to continuous growth.

questions.question: Ice cream vans - when purchased, does the ice cream man get to pick the tune or does he get what comes with it?

answers.answer: It's a tape and you can put whatever you want on it. It's unlikely you can't change the tune.

answers.caller: Oosie (Tower Hamlets) - Ice cream van driver
answers.answer: If you make your own van through Whitman Morrison (main manufacturers), you can request your own tune. But if you just buy a van as an independent seller, you get the tune that's given. It's also quite easy to replace - you can go online for the tunes box made by Harvey's with an amplifier, buy on eBay. New vans are more technical, run on electricity, are more polyphonic with a richer, deeper sound. Oosie's tune is Oh Sole Mio but he doesn't play it because he's static pitch working at Victoria Park, only for children when they ask.

questions.question: When we look in the mirror, we're told we see everything in reverse because light bounces off the mirror into our eyes. Why don't we see things upside down then?

answers.answer: Eyes are horizontally aligned rather than vertical, so we see things reversed (horizontal crossover) rather than upside down (which would be vertical). If eyes were vertical, you would probably see your face upside down.

It depends on the shape of the reflective surface. With a flat mirror, you get an exact mirror image. But in your eye, the crystalline lens behind the pupil is convex-shaped, which inverts the image onto the back of your retina. Your brain then decides you're seeing the image upside down and inverts it in your head. Your brain is rejecting what your eyes are telling it. If you wear glasses that invert your view, after about 3-4 days your brain will work it out and invert the view again.

questions.question: How many words are there in the English language?

answers.answer: Approximately 250,000 words in general use, 750,000 in total. Mike developed a board game called Word Blind based on etymology.

questions.question: When did they decide that horses needed to wear shoes?

answers.answer: The Romans first started putting steel iron shoes on horses to extend the range of the animals. Steel ones came around 900 AD. The Romans were around 300-400 BC. Across Asia at the same time, they were doing it with plant materials but strapping them to feet.

questions.question: What actually happens when someone objects at a wedding? Is there an official procedure? Does the priest check? What is the legal procedure?

answers.answer: If somebody objects to the wedding with a legitimate reason that could make the marriage invalid, you have to stop and investigate. Legitimate reasons include: coercion, if one party didn't really want to do it, if they're too young, or if already married. You do your due diligence before the ceremony by checking paperwork and speaking to bride and groom separately. The only one you might not be able to nail down on the day is the coercion question, but you get a feel for it beforehand. People sometimes joke around and object thinking they're funny, and you just say 'moving on'. There's a pause where you wait to see if anyone has anything to say and everyone coughs.

questions.question: Can a former president run as vice president after he's fulfilled his two terms?

answers.answer: There is an amendment in the Constitution (22nd or 23rd amendment) which states a president can only be elected to the position of president for two terms. However, you could technically run as vice president and succeed an elected president if that president dies or resigns. You wouldn't be able to run again as president, but you could see out that term. This amendment came in after FDR, who served four terms.

questions.question: What are the origins of head lice or nits? How do schools get them? If there's a first case, where did that come from? Why can't you make them extinct?
Has there been a reduction in emergency gas call-outs since COVID, given that people lost their sense of smell (anosmia)?
Why are reheated chicken nuggets from the microwave soggy, but much better when reheated in the oven?

answers.answer: It's the difference between how the two ovens work. A conventional oven works by heating up the air, which then heats up the food. That hot air is hygroscopic and draws moisture out of the surface of the food. In a microwave, the air stays cool, making it more humid, so the hot food draws moisture in the opposite direction - into the crispy coating. If you put stale bread in a microwave, it becomes moist, not from steam coming out, but from moisture already in the microwave's atmosphere.

questions.question: Is there any scientific evidence that sea air is beneficial for us?

If a 70-year-old had all their organs (heart, liver, lungs) transplanted with healthy organs from a 20-year-old, what would their life expectancy be? Would they live longer than they otherwise would have?

answers.answer: They wouldn't live anywhere near as long as they would in natural life. The main issue is immunity suppressants you have to take after any transplant. With a PAC transplant (pancreas, liver, small bowel, large bowel, bladder and kidneys), there's also the danger that the PAC can reject the body, not just the body rejecting the organs. Immunity suppressants compromise your natural health and immunity, making you subject to COVID, flu and other dangers. This profoundly affects longevity.

questions.question: How do they measure UFC statistics for significant strikes landed, significant strike attempts, and breakdowns by head, body, legs? The fights go too fast for anyone to count in real time.

answers.answer: It's literally done by eye. There are three judges on ringside with monitors. They watch closely and presumably press buttons or write things down as they see contact being made. They'll look at the percentages in the event of a tie. It's not scientific but it's reliable.

The three judges' job is strictly to judge the fight. They actually have separate employees from a company called Fight Metric to count the strikes. There are three judges and another two or three employees whose job is to count the strikes specifically.

questions.question: Does the depth of the punt (indentation at the base of a wine bottle) indicate the quality of the wine?

answers.answer: There isn't a direct correlation between the depth of the punt and the quality of the wine. It's one of those urban legends, like the teaspoon in champagne bottles. There is a valid reason a more expensive bottle might have a deeper punt - it gives a greater surface area of glass at the bottom, helping structural integrity. Producers can either use a thick base (like Louis Roederer Cristal Champagne which has a flat but very thick base) or go with a deeper punt but a lighter bottle. The deeper punt is also being adopted more for environmental reasons as heavy bottles cost more to transport.

questions.question: Is there a rule about how big goalkeeper's gloves can be? What if goalkeepers have small hands but wear massive gloves? Like Kenny Everett with big hands.

How can you make an emergency call on your mobile when you have no signal? In places like cinemas where coverage is blocked, you can still only call emergency numbers. How do those calls get through when others can't?

answers.answer: All carriers have a universal agreement that your mobile phone can jump from network to network to make an emergency call. It will use the strongest network at the time. There will still be places with no coverage at all where you can't make any calls.

questions.question: Why does the tax year begin and end on April 6th? Is it connected to Christendom?

answers.answer: In the Middle Ages, rent was paid on quarter days tied to religious festivals. Lady Day was March 25th. When they moved from the Julian calendar, people would have had to pay rent 12 days earlier to compensate. They moved the financial requirements away from quarter days to avoid this. That's why April 6th became the tax year date - an anachronism from centuries ago.

The Julian calendar was inaccurate by about 10 seconds a day. By the 1700s it was 10 solar days off. The Treasury worried about missing tax revenue when switching to the Gregorian calendar. They added those 10 days to March 25th, moving it to April 4th. Then in 1800, which was a leap year in Julian but not Gregorian, another adjustment was made.

questions.question: Why are so many guide dogs Labradors? I've got a 13-year-old Staffie - why can't she be a gay dog?

answers.answer: Labradors are genetically and temperamentally predisposed to the training and最适合 it. It's about breed traits. But not all guide dogs are Labradors - there have been German Shepherds, Golden Retrievers, and other breeds.

I've had four guide dogs - only one was a Labrador. The others were a bearded collie, German Shepherd cross retriever, and a balder collie cross retriever. Dogs are matched based on the handler's height, walking speed, and ability to handle the dog. A 4'10 person wouldn't get a 100-pound Labrador. They also do Labradoodles for hypoallergenic and non-shedding. Labradors are still the main breed people think of, but there are lots of cross breeds being tried.

questions.question: What language does a referee use in international football matches? How can the referee communicate with players who have different mother tongues? Airline pilots use English, but isn't that asking a lot for every international player?

answers.answer: International referees must speak four languages: French, Spanish, German, and English. Players know the rules of the game. In internationals, there's less conversation with referees because his word is final and that speeds up the game.
Red card, yellow card, free kick, goal kick - the players would understand these basic signals.

questions.question: How can a civil case brought abroad be taken over as a public case in another country? Why are they going after Prince Andrew in America? Why is the commissioner investigating Jeffrey Epstein for crimes in this country if they weren't committed here?

answers.answer: Civil case cannot become a public case - that's what civil means. They report on foreign civil cases the same way they report on wars in other countries (foreign news). Prince Andrew cannot be prosecuted in the UK for crimes allegedly committed in America. Julian Assange is a public case, not a civil case.

questions.question: When a group of people are under stress (like waiting for exam results), do they emit enough chemicals for others to detect? Or do we just feel the tense atmosphere because we've noticed behavioral changes like quietness?

answers.answer: Humans are social creatures with lots of social signaling. When people are stressed, they have a threat response - they become more rigid, shut down, less facially expressive, move less, and their voice becomes less variable. You're picking up on behavioral changes rather than chemical releases. This is almost genetic - your mind constantly reads the room. There are cultural and social variations, but broadly this is what you're detecting when you walk into a room and feel the atmosphere.

questions.question: Why is a skip called a skip?

answers.answer: My grandfather was a sailor in the war. Before a ship would put to sea, sailors had to give it a good clean and get rid of all the rubbish. They'd have a container into which all the rubbish would be thrown, and that container became known as a 'skip' - done on the orders of the skipper.

questions.question: How do beekeepers know which flower honey comes from? Local honey is labeled as lavender, clover, dandelion, eucalyptus - how do they know the nectar came from that specific flower?

answers.answer: Look at the bees' backs when they return - the color of pollen indicates which plant they visited. Some are bright yellow, orange, white depending on the plant. All bees in the area will visit one particular plant at a time, all returning together in a flood. To collect specific flavored honey, you'd wait until they've capped off that frame and bottle just that one. Wind-borne pollen doesn't get collected by bees, which is why honey won't cure hay fever - hay fever pollen is wind-borne.

questions.question: If I knew sign language and met someone from Scotland, would I understand them? Do different regions have different sign language accents?

answers.answer: Sign language doesn't have accents - it's like written words, the same across accents.

There are regional variations in sign language - like dialects and colloquialisms rather than accents. For example, Glasgow uses different signs than elsewhere, sometimes punching your fist into your palm. It's more like regional slang than an accent.

questions.question: Why don't they use Dubai's cloud seeding technology (sending drones up into clouds to make it rain) to fight forest fires?
If the UK devolved into its four nations, would the previous sovereign's relations come back to rule those nations? Would Scotland go back to Bonnie Prince Charlie's line? Who would get Wales?

answers.answer: There are two main kit men who travel with the Welsh national football team to tournaments like the Euros, plus two others in the background. Presuming England, Scotland, and Northern Ireland have similar setups, there are currently eight international kit men in the country.

questions.question: How is it that horses are able to sleep standing up?

answers.answer: It's because they've got four legs. Why don't they fall over when they're asleep? Same reason tables don't.

Horses don't actually sleep unless they're lying completely flat out. They only need to do that two hours in every 24. When you see them in the field looking like they're sleeping with one leg bandy at the back, they have a mechanism in their hind legs that allows them to lock one leg - like a table. They'll only get proper REM sleep when laid completely flat out. When they're in a horse box, they don't go to sleep at all, they're continually managing their balance with their legs, which is why there are limits on how long you can have a horse in a trailer.

questions.question: How did they discover that beer was safer to drink than water when they hadn't made beer before? Would they accidentally kill themselves with water first?

answers.answer: Someone probably just noticed that the fella drinking beer all the time didn't get sick when everybody else drinking water did. They put two and two together and realised it was the fermentation process being a form of purification. It would have been observing the available evidence - if you drink beer you won't get sick, if you drink water you will.

John Snow observed that brewery workers across the road from the Broadwick Street pump did not get cholera. The water used in brewing came from the same pump but was boiled with hops to flavour the beer. Boiling kills all the bacteria - it's not the fermentation but the boiling process. Before John Snow, people believed cholera was caused by bad air. He realised it was waterborne.

questions.question: Is it illegal to destroy money? How come machines at tourist attractions that let you stamp pennies with logos are legal?
Why do some sports have umpires (cricket, hockey, tennis) and others have referees (football, rugby) when they're basically doing the same job?

answers.answer: The difference is very simple - referees work alone (there's only one on the pitch in football, rugby etc), while umpires always work in pairs or more. Even in hockey there are two umpires.

questions.question: Do cats need to have sunshine to get their daily dose of vitamin D? My cat never goes outside.

answers.answer: Your cat seems healthy so probably not deficient. If she was a plant she'd need sunlight for photosynthesis, but she's a cat.

Cats don't absorb any vitamin D from the sun whatsoever. They get it all from their diet - cat food is loaded up with vitamin D. Although they don't need sun for vitamin D, there is some thought that lack of sunlight can cause depression in cats, like seasonal affective disorder.

questions.question: Why does bi-weekly mean twice a month rather than twice a week?

answers.answer: It's because 'bi' refers to two. It can mean two times in a week OR every two weeks. You need to focus on the 'bi' part and think about how the 'two' plays into the word 'weekly' - it can mean either two times in a week or once every two weeks. It doesn't work the same way with bi-monthly because the linguistic glitch is specific to weekly.

questions.question: What happens inside your body that decides whether gas comes out of your mouth or the other end? What's the difference between a burp and a fart?

answers.answer: Your gut from mouth to tail is one long pipe. There are valves throughout - the pylorus between stomach and small intestine, and the ileocecal valve between small and large intestine. Air you ingest while eating stays in your stomach and can only go backwards as a burp. Gas produced by bacteria digesting food in your colon can't move backwards past these valves and comes out as flatulence. This also explains why burps don't smell as bad as the other emissions - burps are predominantly air you swallowed, not gas from food breakdown.

questions.question: When you're diffusing a bomb, does it matter which wire you cut first?

answers.answer: The first thing you need to do is disconnect the power supply. IEDs work through an explosive chain - a small power supply creates a spark (like a short circuit or lighter flint), that initiates a slightly bigger explosion going into the detonation core, then finally the main charge. You establish where the power source is, then set up a remote device with a scalpel on the end using highly pressurised water, walk backwards, and fire it from a safe distance to cut through all the connections. The red, blue, green wires you see in films are mostly just for drama. The Oklahoma bomber was actually a former bomb disposal expert himself, which made his device very sophisticated.

questions.question: How come it's legal to use those penny press machines at tourist attractions when surely it should be illegal to mutilate currency?

answers.answer: The sign explained it's no longer illegal because of the Coinage Act, which now has an exception for these tourist attractions. The exception came in around the 1970s.

questions.question: Would facial recognition software work on animals?

answers.answer: Yes, Bellingcat (journalism organization led by Elliot Higgins) used pattern recognition technology on animals to track endangered species being used as tourist attractions. They applied the same technology used in facial recognition by analyzing gaps between stripes on snakes, ocelots and other animals to establish that the same animals were being used in different scenarios.

questions.question: Why is Liverpool's accent more heavily influenced by Irish immigration than Manchester's?
