answers.answer: Various factors influence accents: Irish immigration spreading like ink on blotting paper, environmental factors (pollution causing people to breathe through mouths more), historical influences from Viking invasion and Norman conquest, and less mixing in olden days when people rarely traveled far from where they were born. Liverpool and Manchester are more similar to each other than to Bristol or the Southwest, and accents have evolved over time - even the Beatles' lugubrious Liverpool accent has virtually disappeared.

questions.question: Why is Team GB called Team GB when Northern Ireland is included? Shouldn't it be Team UK?

answers.answer: James admitted he didn't know the answer but found it a great question.

The official team name is Team GB and Northern Ireland, but 'and Northern Ireland' was dropped for marketing purposes to make it roll off the tongue easier. The United Kingdom includes Channel Islands, Falkland Islands, Gibraltar and other territories. The abbreviation was originally GBNI and is still used officially by the British Olympics Association.

Most sporting bodies in Ireland are all-Ireland (Northern Ireland and Republic together), apart from soccer. So most sportspeople from Northern Ireland would be represented by an all-Ireland union. Also, Ukraine already has UKR as its abbreviation, so UK couldn't be used as it would be confusing on TV.

questions.question: Why are police car lights blue? His son Alfie wanted to know.

answers.answer: James speculated it might be Occam's razor - blue cuts through the spectrum most effectively in all lighting conditions, whereas red would get lost in sunlight. Modern police cars often have combinations of blue with white or red for different purposes.

In America they introduced flashing red lights on top of vehicles but they caused problems in fog, rain and bad visibility conditions. The UK decided to come up with a color that would be effective in all weather conditions. White headlights, red tail lights and amber indicators already existed, so they chose blue because it gets through fog, rain and bad weather conditions most effectively. Spain has always used amber on ambulances but is standardizing to blue to match the rest of Europe.

questions.question: Why are swimming lanes numbered 1 to 8 from right to left (with lane 1 on the far right and lane 8 on the far left)?

answers.answer: James argued that swimming pools have four sides, and on three of those sides (75% of viewing positions), lanes would appear numbered left to right. Only the side where swimmers enter (behind them) would it be reversed. He insisted this was logical but acknowledged he was getting 'incredibly strident about a subject I know nothing about' and was 'moments away from thumping the table.'

Health and safety dictates you generally enter a pool from the shallow end. You walk in from the shallow end, so lanes are numbered 1-8 left to right. When diving in from the other end (deep end), it would be 8-1.

questions.question: If our internal body temperature is 36.5 degrees Celsius, why does that temperature or even 30 or 27 degrees feel hot to us? Even in water at those temperatures, why does it feel hot?

answers.answer: James admitted he didn't know and couldn't remember the answer.

Our bodies are like car engines - they produce heat and need apparatus to remove it. We need to keep our body temperature relatively constant by radiating heat. All our cells are breaking down glucose to produce heat constantly, and we need to radiate it more or less at the same rate. This requires a temperature gradient - heat always goes from hot things to cold things. If you insulate your body, you have no way of getting rid of that heat and you get sick. When we have a fever, it's the body's attempt to kill bacteria by raising temperature so their enzymes get denatured. It's exactly like a car engine trying to radiate heat as fast as it's being produced - if you lose coolant and the car produces heat faster than it loses it, the engine overheats.

questions.question: [No question - Damien answered a question from the previous episode]

answers.answer: Gibraltar has many Spanish workers who commute daily. When calculating the vaccination percentage, they included these workers in the population count. So they've vaccinated more people than the actual resident population of Gibraltar, hence over 100% vaccination rate. Damien heard this on the More or Less podcast by Tim Harford and is a government statistician.

questions.question: Why are movie credits always dated in Roman numerals?

answers.answer: James didn't know the answer and put it on the board.

Roman numerals obscure what year the film was made. In the early days of cinema when films were distributed across states, distributors didn't want audiences to know they were watching an old film (even one year old) as it would affect sales. By using Roman numerals instead of Arabic numbers, the production date becomes less immediately obvious.

questions.question: Why are about 90% of humans right-handed? What is the evolutionary advantage when our nearest relatives (apes and gorillas) don't show a hand preference?

answers.answer: James didn't know the answer but acknowledged there must be an evolutionary reason. He noted that left-handed people have problems with things designed for right-handed people, but that's a chicken and egg question.

There are two main theories: 1) Most humans use language in the left hemisphere of the brain, and the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body. Humans are very expressive animals and gesture while speaking, which is why right-hand dominance developed. 2) The Neanderthal theory - a Neanderthal's front teeth showed scuff marks where he'd been holding leather with his left hand and scraping with his right, showing most Neanderthals were right-handed. Since we interbred with Neanderthals, we may have inherited right-handedness from them. Also, kangaroos are mainly left-handed. Lewis has a medical genetics degree and is left-handed himself.

questions.question: Why do they say 'Roger' in aeroplanes? Roger, over and out, especially during wars and now.

answers.answer: Roger means received and understood. In radio communication, 'over' means you're expecting another message, 'out' means end of message, and 'Roger out' means I've received and understood, no further communications required. It shortens messages because air time is precious. The word Roger came from the old American phonetic alphabet where R was 'Roger'.
In the olden days, more than 50 years ago, the phonetic alphabet used 'Roger' for the letter R, particularly in the US and probably the US Air Force. We've since replaced it with 'Romeo'.

questions.question: What happened to Skyphones? In the 1980s you could fly on a plane, put your credit card in, and make a call from your seat. I took a flight this weekend and it's not possible anymore.

answers.answer: Skyphones were removed around the mid-2000s. They were too expensive to maintain for the airline. Aircraft have limited channels on the satcom system with about 300 people on board, and only six or seven people could be online at once. It was also disruptive to other passengers listening to everyone's phone conversations - the 'Dom Jolly effect' of some yuppie saying 'I'm on a plane' was irritating.

questions.question: The Queen doesn't vote in elections by convention, and that extends to her immediate family. But who's the closest relative of the Queen that usually votes? How far down the line of succession do you have to go to find someone we know has voted?

answers.answer: Anybody who sits in the House of Lords or is entitled to sit in the House of Lords is not entitled to vote at a parliamentary election. The Queen's siblings have dukedoms or earldoms and are entitled to sit in the House of Lords. On the electoral register there will be an 'L' against their name if they've registered to vote. They can vote in local elections or referenda but not for parliamentary elections.

questions.question: Why do dogs love sticking their heads out of car windows? They absolutely love it and I don't know why.

answers.answer: The main sense of a dog is their smell. They've got olfactory glands in their nose. When they stick their head out the window, it gives them a complete and utter overload of smells and they love this. It's like fireworks going off in their doggy heads - a unique sensation that's very hard to explain.

questions.question: In England, banknotes are different sizes and have braille on them for blind people. But in America, dollar bills are all the same size with no braille and no raised bits. How does a blind person know what they've got?

answers.answer: Unfortunately blind people have to just trust people. There is no way to distinguish denominations and it's a known problem. People have been advocating for change but it's very hard to implement. I work in the assistive technology industry and have a blind friend who has to rely on other people for independence.

There's an app you can download on any bog standard phone. It has built-in text-to-speech and I use it for identifying euro bills when on holiday. You can sort money in your wallet into different sections once you've identified denominations. This would help Gemma's friend if he doesn't already know about it.

questions.question: Why is BC in English (Before Christ) while AD is still Latin (Anno Domini)? BC means before Christ and that's an English term. Why is one English and one Latin?

answers.answer: AD (Anno Domini - in the year of our Lord) started in the 6th century after the Western Roman Empire ended, when the main centre was in Constantinople. They wanted a dating system reflecting current Christian beliefs. The earlier Diocletian system was rejected because he persecuted Christians. Most countries didn't keep the Latin AD - for example, the French use 'apres Jesus Christ'. English is unusual in sticking with the Latin for AD. BC (Before Christ) came from Latin 'ante Christum' around the same time. As English became the main written language in the Middle Ages, people started using the Anglicized BC. AD stuck because 'Anno Domini' is shorter and easier than 'Year of Our Lord', while BC is an abbreviation of the Latin. The odd one out is English hanging onto the Latin for AD.

questions.question: When they do line-ups in police stations, where do they get the other people from? Do they use actors? Do they pick people from a prison? Do they grab people who have been arrested that day?

answers.answer: You have to go out on the street and find somebody of similar age, height, and color and bring them in to the police station. They used to get paid a tenner for their service, now it's gone up to £15. The lawyer has the right of refusal - if they say 'I'm not having number two or number six because they don't look anything like him,' you have to go get somebody else.
Years ago I was homeless and hanging around Liverpool Street Station. Two City of London police officers came up and asked if I'd stand in a lineup for £15, and I did.

questions.question: As a gardener, I can work with horse manure in borders but I would walk away from human poo or dog poo. Is it the plant-based diet that makes the difference? If a mammal consumed only a plant-based diet, would their excrement be as beneficial as a horse's for fertilizer?

answers.answer: We need fertilizer to put nitrogen back into the soil because it's the one thing we can't store. Humans are programmed to avoid their own manure, vomit, and urine because it's septic. We prefer to use manure from two or three species away from us. Vegetarian manure is more acceptable than an omnivore's manure - pig manure isn't very nice either. Both human and horse manure can technically be used, and in North Korea and China they do use human manure (there's actually a market for it there). The downside is contamination from things like tapeworms, which you often get.

questions.question: When you bite too much off a lolly ice and swallow it, why do we get brain freeze? Why does your head really hurt for a few seconds?

answers.answer: The blood flow to your brain runs through the roof of your mouth. When something really cold hits the roof of your mouth and you keep it there long enough, the blood gets cooled and that chilled blood flows to your brain, giving you brain freeze. It's like the pipes in a house. To get rid of it, Bill Bryson's book 'The Body' suggests you hold your tongue to the soft palate behind the roof of your mouth to warm the pipes back up.

When you have something really cold against the roof of your mouth, the blood capillaries constrict. As a response, the body tries to save the brain from freezing so it opens up the capillaries, letting a lot of blood flow through up to the brain, and that's what causes brain freeze.

questions.question: When watching football and the camera zooms into the crowd after a missed goal, every single fan puts one hand to each side of their head. Why do we do that? It's the same reaction when you realize you've left the gas on. Is it instinctive or learned behaviour?
Why aren't dogs ticklish? Or indeed cats, I suppose. I have one of each and I've tried on both of them and I know they can't laugh but why aren't they ticklish?

answers.answer: The question might be why ARE humans ticklish? Because I can't think of any other animals that are. The tickle might not be on the skin, it's under the skin. There are two types - the feather on balls of feet type and rib tickling. Dogs like being tickled, they enjoy it but it's different pleasure than we get from tickling.

Humans are ticklish and laugh when stimulated but rats do as well - you need a bat detector to hear their high frequency chuckling. Monkeys can be tickled and enjoy it in the same way a dog will - they get a shivery pleasant feeling but won't laugh. Monkeys will laugh in mimicry of other animals around them, which is a language function rather than a reflex stimulus.

There are actually two types of ticklishness. Some ticklish behavior makes you cringe - like a feather running along the sole of your foot. Many animals are ticklish - if you touch the side of a dog where a bug might bite, the dog will scratch and you can reproduce that reflex. Some dogs will widen their paws when tickled between them. Cats do that too.
Gary tried to tickle his client's dog and it nipped him - living proof of what Vieri was describing.

questions.question: Who or what is Larry and what did he have to be so happy about?

answers.answer: The answer is a boxer called Larry who won and it appeared in a headline. It's from Australia or New Zealand, got picked up in papers and became a figure of speech through verbal osmosis. Another suggestion is 'larrikin' - a word for a geezer, also Australian or New Zealand.

questions.question: Why when you buy trousers and jackets are the pockets sewn up? Sometimes you don't realise and get a nice surprise after two years that there's a pocket in the jacket but it's sewn up.

answers.answer: If the pocket wasn't sewn up then the pocket lining could get creased. When you iron the suit jacket it would look creased on the outside. So it's just so that when it's hanging on the hanger in the shop it looks absolutely smooth.

questions.question: You get a power surge at half time with a football because everyone turns the kettle on. Do the reservoirs drop as well because people go to the toilet?

answers.answer: Yes, the reservoirs do drop during halftime. They planned a shutdown on a reservoir for Severn Trent and had to cancel it because of the demand during the England game. You couldn't see it visually but you could see it on computer readouts and level sensors.
Reservoirs don't reduce their level when we all flush our toilets at the same time. What happens is the pressure in the cold water mains drops.
So they're both right - the water level does drop but it's the pressure that changes.

questions.question: I'm wondering about grammatical gender. In French you get masculine and feminine nouns, in German neuter as well. What is that for? It seems to just make everything more complicated and harder for foreign people to learn. It doesn't impart any extra information. Why do some languages have gender?

answers.answer: Grammatical gender is one of the features of human language which some families of languages don't have at all - Finnish doesn't have it. Where it does exist, it seems to go back very far and relates to cosmological and mythological beliefs about the world. Many peoples have believed that all creatures, things, trees, rocks have spirits which have gender - some male, some female. This goes through even to ancient Greek times. Things are assigned to a gender, often with a neuter gender for things not assigned to male or female. Young living things which haven't reached sexual maturity are often assigned neuter gender - this is why in German, das Mädchen (word for young woman) is grammatically neuter, not feminine. In French, son is male and la lune (moon) is feminine. But in German, the moon is male and the sun is female - because of their different mythological heritages. As these beliefs faded, the gender systems got reduced.

questions.question: What is the line between a murder and an assassination? How important somebody has to be for it to be an assassination? What kind of height of celebrityism?

answers.answer: An assassination is when somebody is killed because of their status or their role, as opposed to who they are personally. A politician would be assassinated by a terrorist but murdered by their husband or wife. If someone is killed because of what they do, their status or role, then it's an assassination. But if the same person were killed by their partner in a domestic incident, that would be murder. Even a relatively unknown celebrity, if they were killed by someone who had no previous connection to them and was motivated by the status or role of the victim, that would still technically be an assassination. Everybody who was assassinated was also murdered, but not everybody who was murdered was also assassinated.

questions.question: Going back to when we evolved into speaking different languages, how did the various continents derive to whatever language they spoke? Why didn't all the continents speak Japanese or French or English? What made different continents people speak the different languages?

answers.answer: When the Great Exodus or diaspora began from Africa, from which all human life is descended, that would be pre-language. Then human communities grew up in all different parts of the world. Humans started living together before anything had evolved into what we'd recognise as language. Languages developed in all different parts of the planet simultaneously, with no absolute reason to expect them to evolve the same way. If you're in Ulaanbaatar and I'm in Kidderminster and we're the first people in our tribes to develop the rudiments of language, and you point at a stone and say 'Freck' and I point at a stone and say 'stone', that's how it happens. Language evolved in human communities that were so spread out that it evolved in completely different ways.

The theory is the first word ever spoken was 'agua' (Spanish for water). People telling each other where water was because otherwise they'd die. Whether it's 'agua' or something else would depend on where you are in the world - it's contextual.

questions.question: They say 27 million people watched the football last night. How accurate are those figures when we saw footage of thousands of people watching in clubs and pubs? How sure are they that there was 27 million people watching?

answers.answer: These ratings are done the same way that opinion polls are done. They ask a relatively small number of people - those with BARB boxes in their homes. They multiply that by the population, finding what percentage of the population is watching and turning that percentage into a number. They know how many people were watching the box, how many people are in the household. But specifically about large audiences watching the same screen in pubs - I don't know. Would it be significant enough in the context of 27 million? Probably yes.

My husband works in TV as a brand and marketing manager and tracks the success of shows. Some people have what they call radar boxes on their TVs which track their habits - it's not an accurate figure. Pubs don't have these radar boxes because their viewing figures would be all out of whack because sometimes they'd be closed. So the overall numbers are independent of people watching together in the pub - they make an average based on people with radar boxes.

questions.question: Why don't birds cross-breed like dogs do? You see cross-breed dogs, cats, and mongrels, but never see cross-breed robin and sparrow or blackbird and starling. Why can't birds do this?

answers.answer: Bob is confusing species with breeds. All dogs are the same species, so they can interbreed and produce fertile offspring with different physical characteristics. Birds are classified as different species - a robin and a magpie cannot interbreed. Even ligers (lion and tiger cross) are not fertile, proving they're different species. Cross-breeding in dogs is the result of 10,000 years of human breeding for physical traits.

questions.question: In cricket, why can't you be given out LBW if the ball pitches outside the leg stump, even if it's clearly going to hit the wicket? If it's going to smash the middle stump out of the ground but hits the pad just outside leg stump, the umpire gives it not out. Why?

answers.answer: The reason is to stop negative bowling. It's very difficult for a batsman to hit the ball when it's going down the leg side - they have to chase it around the corner. To stop bowlers from bowling negatively on the leg side and preventing scoring, they said you can bowl there if you like, but the batsman can just pad it away and cannot be out LBW. The historical reason is Bodyline in the 1930s when Harold Larwood bowled short-pitched stuff outside the leg stump and the Aussies could only play around the corner with fielders everywhere. It was considered ungentlemanly.

questions.question: How come they found a vaccine for COVID within months, but we've never found a cure for the common cold? Why can we solve one but not the other?

answers.answer: The common cold isn't one illness - it's a description of symptoms (scratchy throat, cough, fever) caused by hundreds of different viruses, mainly rhinovirus but also some coronavirus. There's no cure because: 1) It doesn't kill you, so there's no market to recoup the billions spent on vaccine development. 2) The viruses mutate constantly, like COVID variants. There would never be one 'cure for the common cold' - it would have to be specific to each virus type, like cancer cures being specific to cancer types. We got the COVID vaccine quickly because: we'd been trying to build vaccines to this type of virus for years, AND every pharmaceutical company on the planet focused on one specific virus with one RNA strain. The flu shows it can be done, but it changes every season so the goalposts move.

questions.question: Who owns the riverbank? Specifically the bits of the Thames riverbank that aren't attached to private houses. Some of it is mowed and neat, some is overgrown. Why isn't it all done? Who is responsible for the public towpath bits?

answers.caller: Catherine (flood risk officer for Cambridgeshire County Council)
answers.answer: The Riparian Landowner under the Land Drainage Act 1991 owns the riverbank. The landowner on either side up to the centre line of the river owns the riverbed and bank. The reason some bits are kempt and some aren't is simply that different landowners maintain their sections differently. Public rights of way are a separate matter - people can walk on it but the soil belongs to the riparian landowner. So if a pub has outdoor seating by the river, the pub actually owns that bit of riverbank. Many people don't realise they're responsible for the ditch or river running through their land, which is why flooding sometimes happens.

questions.question: Why does aerosol deodorant always come out cold, even when it's been sitting in a hot car? The steering wheel is red hot, the seat is hot, but the deodorant is freezing cold. What is the physics behind this?

answers.answer: It's the law of conservation of energy. When you press the button, the gas escapes and gets kinetic energy - energy through movement. To equalise its energy, it goes cold. This is Bernoulli's theorem from fluid mechanics. The speed with which the gas emerges from the nozzle means the volume of gas has gained energy through movement, and the only way for conservation of energy to work is by reducing temperature. The reverse is also true - when you inflate a tyre with a pump, it gets hot at the end.

Ron was wrong about Bernoulli's theorem. The correct explanation involves auto-refrigeration. The aerosol contains chemicals like isobutane that cannot exist as liquid above minus 9 degrees at atmospheric pressure. When the droplet leaves the pressurised can and hits atmospheric pressure, it can't stay liquid anymore - it has to boil. But the heat it needs to boil comes from itself, so it instantly cools down to around minus 9 degrees. This is why if you spray onto a surface, the liquid sitting there is freezing cold - you can burn yourself on it.

questions.question: When you plough a field, however far inland you are, it attracts hundreds of seagulls. They come from nowhere - you never see them in that area normally. But as soon as you start ploughing, hundreds appear. Where do they come from and how do they know?
Can you smell in your sleep? If you're asleep and someone breaks wind nearby, can you actually smell it, or are your senses too dulled?
When you pour a pint of beer, it gets a nice thick foamy head. But when you pour a pint of cola or lemonade, it doesn't. Why is that?

answers.answer: It's all about the gas used to push the drink from the barrel to the pump. Coke and soft drinks use 100% CO2. Guinness, Worthington, and cream flows use 70-30 gas (a mixture of nitrogen and CO2). Some lagers use 60-40. Nitrogen creates smaller, tighter bubbles that take longer to pop, giving a smoother, creamier mouthfeel and better head. CO2 gives a crisper, bubblier result. From a cask with an air compressor, there's not much head because no nitrogen is introduced.

answers.caller: Mike in Maida Vale (chemical engineer, lectured in foaming situations)
answers.answer: Sam is right about the gas, but there's more to it. It's also about the nature of the liquid itself. Complex liquids like beer contain many molecular species that like to sit on the interface between gas and liquid - these are hydrophobic or hydrophilic molecules. They stabilise the bubbles. The size of the bubbles matters too. It's a combination of the history of the fluid, the bubble size, and most importantly the nature of the liquid.

questions.question: Why does it say 'pound sterling' on Scottish banknotes but not on Bank of England notes? I have a Bank of Scotland £10 note and a Royal Bank of Scotland £20 note that both say sterling, but a Bank of England £20 note just says £20.

When my mates watch football, the host cooks the food of the country we're playing. Easy for Italy (pasta, pizza), but this week it's Ukraine and nobody knows what to cook. What is the national dish of Ukraine?

answers.caller: Niall (Irish-born, lives in Ukraine with Ukrainian family)
answers.answer: The most internationally known dish is Borscht - a beetroot and cabbage-based soup. Other dishes include Varenyky (dumplings) and Holuptsi (stuffed cabbage rolls). Chicken Kiev is more popular internationally than domestically, but it's known everywhere. The first thing a Ukrainian person will say is Borsh. For a watching party though, Chicken Kiev with chips is probably the better option - it's easier to serve and less likely to stain the sofa.

questions.question: How do they design Sudoku puzzles? They normally prime the grid with numbers. But how do they know they've left enough logic in there to be solved?

answers.answer: You use software that's got two parts. One part randomly fills in the grid and then takes away one digit at a time. The other part is programmed with all of the logical steps that a person might use to solve a Sudoku puzzle. Every time you remove a number, that solver tries to solve it. If it can't, you've broken it, so you re-add the last number. This makes it highly unlikely that an unsolvable Sudoku would escape into the wild.

questions.question: Is subtitling done by someone typing it quickly or by voice recognition? How does it get in, particularly to live broadcast where it is immediate?

answers.answer: There are several ways subtitling is done. For live subtitling, it's done partly by stenography (like in a courtroom) where someone with particular skills types out verbatim words. There's also a re-speaker who has headphones, listens to the programme live, and speaks into a microphone enunciating properly with punctuation, which goes straight onto the screen. They use voice recognition software that creates a voice model recognizing their voice. You couldn't use voice recognition straight onto an interviewee's voice.

You can actually use live speech-to-text for multiple people now. There's software like Otter that records meetings and transcribes in real-time, showing who said what. The software uses signal processing algorithms and machine learning - frequency analysis looks at voice patterns like fingerprints. It takes several months for a computer to learn someone's voice perfectly, requiring about a million samples for machine learning to improve accuracy.

questions.question: If you throw a spider out of your daughter's bedroom window, do they die if they hit a roof or the pavement, or are they going to be okay? I don't want to kill them.

answers.answer: The ratio of body weight to volume is critical for spiders falling. Spiders are not very aerodynamic - they're covered in little hairs which creates lots of air resistance as they fall. Usually that saves them. If it's a very heavy spider like a tarantula, that excess body weight can cause them to be injured, but their exoskeleton is very resilient. So generally spiders will survive being thrown out of a bedroom window.

questions.question: Can you tell where someone's from in the UK by the characteristics of their face? There are a wide variety of accents in the UK, each requiring different facial muscles and movements to pronounce them.

Balls - specifically about snooker balls. Back in the day, how did they make them so perfectly round when there wasn't any laser technology or anything like we'd have today? Also ball bearings used in tanks.
Is hot food better than cold food in terms of digestion and nutrition? His girlfriend is horrified that he eats leftovers straight out of the fridge (chili, jambalaya) without warming them up.

answers.answer: The more processes you put food through, the less nutrition you get out of it. Raw food (not chicken) is better - you get more out of it. The more processing, the more nutrients disappear.

questions.question: How many nuclear weapons or fissionable material has been unaccounted for in the last 60 years? Looking at ballistic missile treaties between US and Russia, post-Soviet era destruction, and recent treaties that have attempted to count weapons.
When you go to a supermarket, you can buy eggs with double yolks. How do they know that they have double yolks inside?

answers.answer: They use a really bright light - called candling - so you can see through the shell. They also likely breed chickens with a propensity for laying double yolks.

questions.question: How do cats cool down when it's hot? They don't sweat because they're covered in fur. They can't take the fur off. They don't pant like dogs do.

answers.answer: Unlike dogs, cats don't pant obviously. They groom their fur using saliva and go in the shade. But they also expel heat through their ears - the blood vessels are close to the surface. The pads of their paws (called beans) also help.

Cats cool through their ears because the blood vessels are so close to the surface. They also sweat through their paws - you can see paw prints on cold tiles on hot days. They do pant but only if they've got heat stroke.

questions.question: In elite sports, I'm thinking mostly along the line of athletics and things, are people who are pacemakers allowed to win the race?

answers.answer: The pacemakers have to register for the event in the same way that any other entrant would. And so, yes, they can go on and win the race. I'm sure this came up when we were on an athletics club trip away.

It has happened, and it happened to an American pacemaker called Tom Byers. I think it was at the Bislett Games in 1981. And sometimes what happens is sometimes the top guys think, well, you know what, I don't fancy sticking behind the pace. We're just going to hang back a bit. And Byers thought, well, I'm feeling good. He was on the last lap. He said, yeah, we're going to do it. And he just went for it. And by the time the top guys thought, he's not actually going to stop, is he? They went for it. They couldn't catch him.

questions.question: A week ago I had a weird dream where I was on the moon in a swimming pool... inside a dome, obviously. Would you be higher up in the water than you would have been on Earth?

answers.answer: You would swim at the same level that you would on Earth because the gravity is having the same effect on the water and your body. The moon only has a sixth of the gravity of the Earth, so the water is going to weigh a sixth, but also you are going to weigh a sixth. So you will displace the same amount of water. You'll be swimming at the same level as you would be on Earth.

questions.question: If the last time we walked on the moon was in 1972... why is it that we've never been able to land and put a man on the moon since then with far superior technology?

answers.answer: I don't think the question is that we haven't been able to. It's just that we haven't. We've chosen not to. Obviously there's all this talk about landing on Mars and looking for alien life forms, and yet there is a... The boring answer is that we've been there and we've done that.

questions.question: When a baby is inside the womb, it's surrounded by amniotic fluid. Is there also another function for that? Like, does it provide nutrients? Or does it form a part of the development other than just to protect the baby?

answers.answer: Amniotic fluid provides quite an important function in the development of a baby's internal organs. A baby swallows the amniotic fluid, it passes through the stomach and the kidneys and is urinated out. So amniotic fluid is actually baby urine and it is a homeostatic process. It's a constant swallowing going through the system and urinating out and that continues throughout the pregnancy. And if there's too little amniotic fluid or too much it's a potential indication of a problem.

questions.question: Evolutionarily speaking, why do we blush? I understand what causes us to blush, but why do we blush?

answers.answer: I'm just trying to think what possible purpose does this serve? Unless it's a side effect of something else. So unless it's a side effect of the adrenaline that is part of the fight or flight response that is advantageous to you.

questions.question: I have a laurel bush outside my kitchen window. I noticed insects were going underneath new leaf shoots where the leaf meets the branch. There's some kind of gland where nectar comes out. I wondered what's in it for the plant?

answers.answer: The plant needs to attract insects. And if the price it pays for attracting insects when it needs the insects is attracting insects when it doesn't need the insects, then evolutionarily speaking, that is a price worth paying.

questions.question: As in the bubbles that kids play with. Obviously when you blow bubbles, sometimes you get a really nice good-sized one. I just wondered, in the right circumstances, could you freeze a bubble?

answers.answer: I haven't been able to test that out because it's never been cold enough but I saw on a video that I think it was in like Russia or Alaska when it's really cold. If you blow a bubble when it's cold enough it will very slowly freeze into like really thin ice.

questions.question: Why is it easier to remember lyrics to a song than it is just to remember the words of a poem, for example?

answers.answer: When you're having to remember the structure or the layout of words as well as the words at the same time, our brains can't process it as fast. So if you've got the construct, if you've got the structure laid out, you know the rhyming pattern or you know which lines are lined two and four, it's much easier for your brain to process the remaining information in time for you to recall it at the moment you need to actually say it. The alphabet is a brilliant example of this. So in fact if you were struggling to learn a poem then setting it to some sort of music would be a good way of doing it.

questions.question: If the earth blew up, what would happen to things on Earth that don't burn? Like my birdbath or the statue of Queen Victoria in EastEnders. Would they just float in space forever?

answers.answer: Just because you can't set fire to it with a big lighter, doesn't mean it's not going to burn in an interplanetary conflagration. Everything burns if you get a temperature high enough. And if the temperature is high enough to explode the entire earth, it's high enough to burn your birdbath. The answer is no, nothing would survive.

questions.question: Why don't birds get electrocuted when they land on electric wires?

answers.answer: If a bird is sitting on a high-voltage wire, as long as it doesn't connect to the ground or the wire next to it, there is no circuit. So even though it might have two legs on the wire, there is no electrical circuit between those feet. If you were able to glide down on a parachute very slowly and land on a high-voltage wire, as long as the parachute was ejected and didn't touch any of those other wires or earth, you also could stand on that wire without any fear of electrocution.

questions.question: Will I have the same exercise effect training for a marathon on a gym treadmill as I do pounding the streets? I want to run a sub-four-hour marathon in October.

answers.answer: On a treadmill it's softer impact but easier because there's no wind resistance even on a calm day. You also don't have to deal with weather or corners. However, setting the treadmill to a small constant incline would be cheating but would help. Marathons vary in difficulty - Edinburgh Marathon is more downhill than others.
answers.qualifications: Two-time marathon runner, best time 4:12

questions.question: Why haven't all little garden birds learned to be as trusting as robins, who clearly know when there's an easy meal to be had when they see somebody digging?

answers.answer: Different diets - robins eat insects, grubs and worms that humans digging expose, while other birds eat seeds.

questions.question: How old are electricity pylons? I've never seen anyone putting them up or taking them down. What's their lifespan?

answers.answer: Pylons don't have a fixed lifespan - it depends on variables like weather and corrosive conditions. In coastal areas they wear faster. The big metal towers have installation dates stamped on them. Wooden poles also have dates chipped into the wood. You can see the year and type when you look at poles. Some UK towers are 60-70 years old and still standing strong. Electrical runs also use wooden poles in rural areas.
answers.qualifications: Asset inspector for energy supplier, inspects assets to make sure they're not falling over

answers.answer: In former life worked as concrete structures designer in Middle East with pylons. They protect pylons with sacrificial anodes buried in ground - these corrode first instead of the pylon. Anodes are replaced every 5-10 years depending on environment. The pylon itself is very expensive so you don't replace it often. This is cathodic corrosion protection, same system used on ships and boats.
answers.qualifications: Former concrete structures designer, now makes specialist breathing equipment

answers.answer: First steel lattice transmission towers in the UK were erected in 1929 as part of the first national grid build, brought into service 1933 by Act of Parliament, developed by engineer Charles Mertz. That power system has never been de-energised - we've never switched the country off. They typically last 50-80 years. The thing buried in the ground is actually an earth connection to help protection systems work if struck by lightning. We paint them periodically to maintain them.
answers.qualifications: Chartered engineer, works for National Grid, keeps the lights on

questions.question: Is it illegal to project something, specifically an ad, onto a building? What laws govern that? Does it depend on the building? You're not physically altering the surface like graffiti.

answers.answer: They used to project onto the MI5 building every Saturday as part of Strawberry Sunday club night in the 90s. Police would come over but there was no law against it. As long as it's not nude pictures or rude words, just images, no problem at all.
answers.qualifications: Was involved in Strawberry Sunday, used hard house moon flower projector

questions.question: Why don't we sneeze in our sleep? I have chronic hay fever and can sneeze all day, but when I fall asleep I won't sneeze for eight hours, then wake up and sneeze uncontrollably within two minutes.

Why does a steam sterilizer stay sterile for six hours if unopened, but only half an hour if you open it, take one bottle out, and put the lid back on? Everything inside is still hot and running with steamy boiling water either way.

answers.answer: The obvious answer is bacteria gets in when you open it. Still hot but not boiling hot. Bacteria needs time to become a problem - about half an hour. With lid on, it takes even longer but it's not airtight so bacteria still gets in as it cools down.

questions.question: Is there a maximum speed that a passenger aircraft can travel? I've seen the speed displayed on monitors during flights.

answers.answer: Aircraft have ground speed and air speed - they're different concepts. Aircraft are designed and certified to withstand certain air speed limitations. There's a structural limit that pilots must not exceed. It varies from plane to plane - a 737 has certain structural limitations different from other aircraft. You could be flying at 700mph through the air but ground speed might be 500mph if you have a headwind.
answers.qualifications: Private pilot

questions.question: Is the reason robins are so friendly and different to other birds that they've never been on the menu since time immemorial? Even Henry VIII had swans and geese but never robins.

answers.answer: Robins have never been hunted or eaten - they've not built up that fear of humans that other birds have. Songbirds were eaten in other cultures (France) but never robins.

questions.question: What does ER2 mean on lampposts and bins, and will they be changed when Charles ascends the throne?

answers.answer: They won't replace all existing lampposts with ER2. New ones will have Charles's reference (CR3). Postboxes show this - you can still find Victorian postboxes with VR (Victoria). They won't take down all lampposts and replace them just because of a new monarch.

questions.question: If four cars arrive at a mini roundabout simultaneously, who has right of way?

answers.caller: Mustafa from Pinner (Driving Instructor, 10 years experience)
answers.answer: Whoever turns up first would normally have right of way. If everyone turns up at the same time wanting to go straight ahead, one of them would have to give way. You teach students to give way to the car on their right, and once one goes, the situation clears.

answers.caller: Gerry from Tunbridge Wells (Student, 17 years driving experience)
answers.answer: The previous instructor was wrong. There's no such thing as 'right of way' in driving - it's 'priority.' Everyone having right of way is the complete opposite. The car on your RIGHT has priority. Nobody has priority and everyone has priority - it's philosophy.

Whoever has double white lines (two single lines instead of double dash) on their entrance to the roundabout has priority - it normally corresponds to the main road. But James disputed this applies to mini roundabouts.

questions.question: Why are houses numbered 1,3,5,7,9 on one side of the road and 2,4,6,8 on the other?

answers.answer: Something to do with the post office - that's all James could initially offer.

answers.caller: Michael from Tunbridge Wells (Former cartographer, now vicar)
answers.answer: It's all about future-proofing. If a road is extended, you can just add the next numbers sequentially. If you numbered sequentially up one side then down the other, you'd have to renumber all houses when extending. With odds and evens, you just continue adding.

questions.question: Do we actually swallow while we're asleep?

answers.answer: We must do because of mucus and other stuff going on. But James couldn't provide a definitive answer.

answers.caller: Sue from Twickenham (Speech and language therapist, feeding specialist)
answers.answer: Yes, we do swallow at night. Adults swallow 2,000 times per 24 hours, mostly during the day around eating and drinking, but we still swallow 3-6 times per hour at night. We have to keep mouth tissues moist and deal with secretions. Otherwise we'd wake up coughing, choking, or with our tongue stuck to the roof of our mouth.

questions.question: A farmer has 322 cows. He takes one shot and gets all the cows. How did he do it?

answers.answer: He took a PHOTO. One shot = one photo. The riddle uses the ambiguity of 'shot' (gun shot vs photographic shot).

questions.question: What do the colours of the Olympic flag represent?

answers.answer: Continents.

The five rings represent the five continents: Africa, Americas, Oceania, Asia, and Europe. The colours (red, yellow, black, green, blue) - one of those colours appears in every single country's flag. They're all interlocked symbolizing that the Olympics unites the world.

questions.question: Why is there 360 degrees in a circle and 90 degrees in a right angle? Could geometry be metricated like the metric system?

answers.caller: Gary from Lincoln (Physics and astrophysics graduate, radiotherapy physicist)
answers.answer: It's because ancient civilizations (Babylonians, Aztecs) believed there were approximately 360 days in a year from their astronomical observations. 360 also divides by so many numbers which makes it practical. Yes, geometry could theoretically be metricated into 100 units per circle, but it would involve too much paperwork to change.

There ARE other systems for measuring angles - radians (2π radians in a circle, useful for complex numbers in mathematics) and gradients (100 gradients in a right angle, used by surveyors). Gradients would be the metric equivalent James was looking for. But the Babylonian/Aztec system got there first.

questions.question: Where did the 'ba-dum-tish' drum roll that follows jokes come from?

answers.answer: It comes from music halls, working men's clubs, and comedy clubs where the turn would do comedy and songs with a drummer on stage. The drummer would provide the ba-dum-tish after jokes.

It started in pantomime around 1670. They used drummers to accompany actors with sound effects including pratfalls. This was stolen from Commedia dell'arte, which turned into the Harlequinade. The minstrels on stage would do the drum to deliver punchlines and other sound effects.

questions.question: Why does hot water dissipate bubbles in a bath more effectively than cold water?

answers.caller: John from Golders Green (Masters in Material Science)
answers.answer: Hot water is at a higher temperature with less pressure. Therefore the bubbles can survive and increase in size longer. Cold water has higher pressure which collapses bubbles more quickly.

questions.question: How are bitcoins made?
During the Second World War, at the start of the bombing blitz, did London Zoo have any plans in place for where the animals would go, especially the dangerous ones?

answers.answer: Most of the animals got transferred to other zoos, most went to Whipsnade Zoo. Some of the more endangered ones like the Komodo dragon went to Blackpool. All the venomous animals that they thought might cause a danger to the public were killed.

questions.question: What color is a bee's skin? Her 8-year-old daughter Amelia wants to know - the fur is black and yellow but what color is the actual skin underneath?

answers.answer: The fur is actually very light in colour and almost appears to be see-through, so what you're seeing is the colour of the bee's skin underneath rather than the fur colour itself.

questions.question: Why do crows hang around graveyards? What's the association? Is it just graveyards or do they hang around all parks and open spaces?

answers.answer: Three reasons: First, crows like ledges and graves provide high perches in quiet areas away from humans and larger predators. Second, crows are genetically related to ravens and vultures and are drawn to the smell of meat. Third, small animals like hamsters and rabbits burrow in graveyards making easy food for crows.

questions.question: Is there a rule anywhere that says football referees have to have short hair?

answers.answer: There's nothing in the rules to say you can't have long hair while refereeing. You just have to look presentable for respectability reasons. Roger Milford from Bristol was a famous referee who had a perm at one point.

questions.question: Why do we hang meat? I keep seeing adverts for meat that's been hung for 21 days. Why does it need to be hung and does it improve the flavour?

answers.answer: When an animal first gets put down, its pH is slightly above 7. As you hang it, lactic acid kicks in making it acidic. The longer you hang it, the more acidic it goes, breaking down the material and the joins between the meat, giving ease of eating and juicy flavour. You don't have to do it but it improves the meat. With pork you wouldn't do it because pigs eat anything and everything.

questions.question: Can particles leave our stratosphere? Like microbes in the air - on the space station there are microbes growing outside it. Could particles just float off into space?

answers.answer: Yes. If you imagine sand, oil and water in a container that separates out with the heaviest at the bottom and lightest rising to the top - similar happens in the atmosphere. The very lightest atoms like helium and atomic oxygen travel upwards through the mesosphere and thermosphere, and if they have enough energy they can leave the atmosphere completely and travel off into deep space.

questions.question: Can you get a complete tiebreak in a frame of snooker? If you're both on 8-8 and it's first to 18, can you end up tying?

answers.answer: No, because it's first to 18. If it goes to 17-17 and ends equal after the final black, they just re-spot the black and put the white back. So there's no complete tiebreak within a frame itself.

questions.question: What medical criteria needs to be met for an injury to classify as being serious? What is the threshold for an injury to be described as serious in media reports?

answers.answer: It's basically a life threatening injury or life changing injury. So it could be life changing as in someone broke their leg but it won't heal very well, so they'll have life changing injuries. That's the difference between serious and non-serious.

questions.question: (Answering the Bitcoin question)

answers.answer: Bitcoin is a decentralized computer system stored on everyone's computer rather than one central location. You don't make bitcoins - you mine them. There are only 21 million bitcoins ever. Mining involves using hash functions and computer algorithms - essentially a one-way function to find the next Bitcoin. Bitcoin miners worldwide with fast computers race to solve mathematical puzzles to find the next block in the blockchain. It's similar technology to encrypting passwords. It's called SHA256 encryption.

questions.question: (Answering the Bitcoin question)

answers.answer: Mining is like giving everyone in a room a thousand piece puzzle scrambled on their desk. Whoever completes it first gets a reward in bitcoin. When you send a bitcoin transaction, you need someone to verify it goes through the network without being stolen or double-spent. You solve the puzzle to push the transaction through, then all computers on the network confirm the transaction is valid. Once solved, the transaction gets rubber-stamped and recorded on the blockchain.

questions.question: (Phone line issues - couldn't deliver question)
Why are babies born without kneecaps?

answers.answer: Babies are born with cartilage instead of bony kneecaps. The cartilage hardens into bone between ages 2 and 6. The purpose is to allow flexibility for crawling and movement - they're more flexible and bendy, which helps them crawl. If you drop them, they bounce.

questions.question: Why do kettles boil for 20 seconds too long?

answers.answer: If the kettle isn't full, it has to boil longer to heat up the bimetallic strip because there's more water to heat.

Most kettles work via a steam tube - when water boils, steam builds up and travels down the tube to a bimetallic strip at the bottom, which switches the kettle off. If the kettle is half full, there's more water to heat before enough steam builds up to trigger the switch. This causes the delay. Electronic kettles without steam tubes don't have this problem.

questions.question: How do manufacturers industrially shell peas?

answers.answer: Similar question was asked about prawns - the answer involved high-pressure hoses. The prawn is on a spiky conveyor belt and water blasts the shell off.

Peas are gravity fed into a hopper. They land on a sieve-like mechanism. Blades or belts run in opposing directions - the friction pops the pods open, peas fall through the holes, and the shells don't because they're bigger. Peas are then blown into silos for batch processing.

questions.question: In what century did Italians start eating spaghetti?

answers.answer: Marco Polo - probably 14th century. Somewhere in my memory banks I've got the noodle-spaghetti relationship filed away.
It actually started with the early Romans - way before Marco Polo. Marco Polo may have resurrected or reinvigorated the pasta industry, but Romans had it before.

questions.question: Can police legally commandeer a vehicle when pursuing a criminal?

answers.answer: I think we've done this before and the answer is yes, but I could have imagined the whole thing. A lot of these conventions weren't actually ever legal - they were just accepted. Like it's still illegal to go through red lights but it's accepted.
Yes, police can commandeer vehicles but it rarely happens because of the insurance aspect. If they have an accident, who would be liable?

I did it two weeks ago to a bin lorry. It was the only vehicle available and I needed to get to the other side of a large block of buildings to arrest someone who was jumping fences. The bin lorry driver agreed and even put his orange lights on. I didn't catch him - I should have run.
The only way police can commandeer a vehicle is if there is life in danger.

questions.question: Why does the police recording beep at the start last so long?

answers.answer: This is old-fashioned from when police used tapes rather than CDs. The high-pitched beep indicates the start of the recordable part of the tape. It's there so officers know they can start speaking and won't miss the beginning of the interview on the recording.

questions.question: If the Queen, Prince Charles, and Prince William all died, would Prince George become crowned king?

answers.answer: I presume he would, but there'd be a regent involved, a counsellor.
It would be Prince Andrew. If Prince Charles died before the Queen, the next in line is Prince Andrew. You can't skip a generation. Andrew would have to abdicate.

It would be George. The line of succession is set - it never goes to a sibling if there's an heir below. For Andrew to inherit, both William and Harry and all of their children would have to die. Eugenie and Beatrice are surprisingly high up the line but not high enough to change anything.

questions.question: How are antibodies from COVID vaccine different from antibodies produced by having the virus?

answers.answer: Virus particles in vaccines are not complete viruses. The antibodies stimulated will be specific to certain parts of the virus. If you've been exposed to a live virus, you'll make the same antibodies as the vaccine plus antibodies to other parts of the virus. For example, with Hepatitis B, the vaccine stimulates antibodies against the surface antigen only, whereas natural infection makes antibodies against the surface antigen, core antigen, and envelope antigens. Your own immune system makes a broader range of antibodies from natural infection, but the vaccine selects the most relevant antigen to help you clear the virus as soon as possible.

questions.question: Where was the first known use of wallpaper?

answers.answer: The Chinese used wallpapers for decoration 200 years B.C. The knowledge came through the National Trust where there are 16 properties with Chinese wallpaper dating from the 1700s.

questions.question: How far can you see with the naked eye before the curvature of the earth stops you seeing any further?

answers.answer: The formula is 1.23 times the square root of the height in feet equals distance to horizon in miles. If eyes are 6 feet above the ground, the square root of 6 is roughly 2.4, and 1.23 times that is roughly 3 miles. If something is 100 feet above sea level, that's 12.3 miles.

questions.question: Can you eat any egg from any animal (snake, lizard, bird) without getting poisoned? If you found eggs in the jungle and steamed them in bamboo, could venomous snake eggs poison you?

answers.answer: The venom sacs in snakes develop quite late in the embryological process. There's a clue in the fact that venomous snakes and their eggs have been eaten for eons by humans with no ill effects. As long as you remove the venom sac, it tastes like chicken. Nobody eats an egg without cracking it first, so by the time the venom sac has developed, you've got a fully-formed snake in the egg.

questions.question: Why do electric cars have to have this specialized plug to plug in your house? Why can't it just be a three-pin plug like we plug everything else in with?

answers.answer: It's all to do with the rate of charge. If you plug an ordinary mains plug type charger that's normally supplied with the vehicle, it takes a long, long time to charge. Think of electricity like water - if you had a tank of water with a tiny little pipe, it would take ages to drain down. Whereas with a large bore pipe, it would drain down really quickly. Those big powerful chargers are charging at hundreds of volts (480 volts for a Nissan Leaf). With a 13-amp plug it would take flipping ages, whereas with a specialist charger the current flow is much faster.

questions.question: When does a roundabout cease to be a roundabout and start being a gyratory system? How large does it need to be?

answers.answer: In a roundabout, even with two lanes, if you get into one of the lanes, you could continue going round and it wouldn't lead anywhere - you just continue going round the roundabout. With a gyratory, the lanes are designed in such a way that you can't - they spit you out at the right exit, so they sort of course you outwards as it goes around. Providing you've selected the right lane to start with, you will leave at the right exit. In theory you could continue going around a gyratory but you'd probably annoy a few people.

questions.question: Is light pollution naturally luminous? If you turned off every light source in London, would the night sky still glow orange as it currently does? Or would the glow go away?

answers.answer: If you shine a torch at a football, the ball gets lit up and so does the rest of the room. All the street lights, car lights, and light sources in a built-up area give off light pollution. It goes up into the sky. If you turn off the torch, the ball is still there but the rest of the room is dark. So the sky would be dark. The glow is all the spare light going up into the sky. Amateur astronomers have to travel out of London to get a better view of the night sky.

questions.question: Do Boris Johnson and Simon have to move out of Downing Street flat and keep the furniture? Do they have to declare it as imputed income?
Why do they cover speed cameras with a sack or sign saying 'not in use' when surely it would be beneficial to safety to have people believe it is still operative?

answers.answer: Under legislation, you've got to notify motorists that there are speed cameras or radar cameras. The 'not in use' sign is to notify motorists that the camera is not in use. They usually set up ready for roadworks or average speed cameras. The presumption is there aren't any speed cameras in a built-up area, so they notify people that there are speed cameras. When the camera is broken, they notify you it's not in use so you know there's no average speed camera operation happening.

questions.question: When dogs are looking to go for a toilet, what is it that they are sniffing for before they go? Why don't they go until they've had a good sniff?

answers.answer: Dogs are just trying to find the sweet spot. They need to have a good sniff before they go. As for why they turn around in circles before they poop (not before they pee), 80 dogs were watched for two years by German and Danish students. The reason dogs turn around is because they're trying to align themselves to about 90% of the time on the north-south axis of the Earth's magnetic field. This proves mammals are magnetosensitive, similar to migratory birds and insects.

questions.question: St. Paul's Cathedral is in the City of London, Westminster Cathedral is in the City of Westminster. Why isn't Southwark Cathedral in the City of Southwark?

answers.answer: Southwark wasn't built as a cathedral originally. It was a big church and Southwark is a pretty new diocese, only about 100 years old. It used to be part of Rochester or Winchester.

A cathedral doesn't necessarily confirm city status. Chelmsford only became a city in 2012 but has had a cathedral for about 200 years. Brentwood also has a cathedral but isn't a city. That's the long and short of it.

Cathedral is derived from the word for a big seat or throne, which is the bishop's throne. Unless you were a big bishop, you didn't get one. The moment you got one, where your throne was, your official seating place is, that church becomes a cathedral.

questions.question: How far away is the horizon? Is it always the same distance?

answers.answer: It's dependent on your height of eye. If you're at 2.5 meters, the distance to the sea horizon is 3.3 miles. Double that to 5 meters height of eye, and the distance is 4.7 nautical miles.

questions.question: Why does bright sunlight make me sneeze?

answers.answer: It's probably an evolutionary defence against pollen. The brighter the sunlight, the more likely the pollen count is to be high and therefore you're cleaning out your nasal passages.
It's called a photic sneeze reflex. It only affects about a third of the human population. A 2010 study linked it to a specific chromosome but we're still not entirely sure of the reasons behind it.

questions.question: When the clocks go back at the end of October, that's approximately seven weeks before the winter solstice. But when they go forward again, it's approximately 13-14 weeks after the winter solstice. I wonder why there's a disparity because the light should be the same either side of the winter solstice.

answers.answer: Daylight saving was originally brought in for the First World War, mostly to do with farming, giving longer daylight during the war. And then over the winter. And then as spring starts to come in and farming picks up again, that's why you've got that offset. The harvest time would be September into October, so it is done to save daylight.

questions.question: Does the Queen have a will or does she have to write a will?

answers.answer: She probably does have a will. Some stuff is hers and some stuff is the Crown's. Stuff passes on to the next monarch. But she's going to have private gear like a tiara that she wants to leave to someone specific.
The Queen has a huge private estate which belongs to her personally. If she didn't make a will, it would go under the laws of intestacy, which she wouldn't want. So of course she has a will.

questions.question: How can you get a Ray Liotta on a board game?

answers.answer: The Ray Liotta is being kept exclusively for radio entertainment and not on the board game. You won't be able to get a Ray Liotta on the Mystery Hour board game.

questions.question: Thunderbird 4, the yellow submarine, is delivered inside a pod inside Thunderbird 2. The pod is floating on the water and Thunderbird 4 goes down a ramp into the sea. How does Thunderbird 4 get back inside the pod when it's done its mission?

answers.answer: Thunderbird 4 has wheels underneath it which allows it to get back up the ramp into the pod. You don't see this on the TV show but you do see it in the comics. In an episode called Terror in New York City, you see the wheels working.

According to a technical manual issued on the 50th anniversary edition of Thunderbirds, approved by Anderson & Co, the launch and recovery rail is the main way of deploying and recovering. There's also a magnetic retractable ramp but it would need wheels to get there.

questions.question: Why is it that in this country we get a few days of hot and humid weather but then it tends to turn into thundering showers, whereas if you go somewhere like Cyprus or the Med, the hot and humid weather just carries on through the summer without thunderstorms?

answers.answer: It's standard GCSE geography stuff - it's just conventional rainfall. If you've got a wet climate, the sunshine evaporates a lot of water out of the ground and lakes, the air gets saturated, so it starts to rain. So because it's wet, it's wet.

questions.question: Has anyone ever smoked a cigarette in space?

answers.answer: Yes, Jerry Linegar, who was a US astronaut on the space station Mir, said in his autobiography that the cosmonauts used to get cartons of cigarettes delivered.

questions.question: Is there any muscle in the human body that we haven't got conscious control of? If so, what is it, where is it, and could we practice to use it?

answers.answer: Your heart - you can't just flex it consciously.

Graham has Tourette's with motor tics in his neck, shoulders, eyes, and breathing - he has no control over when he does them or how often. It's caused by chemicals in the brain that communicate incorrectly, sending muscular impulses in wrong directions.

questions.question: In darts, why is it called a Shanghai when you hit single, double, and treble all in the same segment?
Why does wind gust? Why isn't wind constant during a storm, especially on the coast with nothing in the way?

answers.answer: Wind gusts because of fluid dynamics - there's laminar flow where everything flows smoothly, and turbulent flow where things tumble. Turbulence is caused by roughness of the ground the air travels over - houses, trees, hills. The irregularities propagate themselves (like the butterfly effect). Also, hot air rising and pressure changes create turbulence, punching holes in otherwise uniform flow.

questions.question: Why do cartoon characters typically have four fingers instead of five?

answers.answer: Economy of line - hands are the hardest thing to animate/draw, with so much movement and angle. It makes life easier to draw three fingers and a thumb.
In The Simpsons, the only character animated with five digits was God.

Economy of draftsmanship applies, but there's also a neurological reason - the thumb is overrepresented in the primary motor cortex and primary sensory cortex, so readers don't need five fingers for their inner eye to understand comics. You'd miss a thumb though, not the other fingers.

questions.question: When they first built and tested the atomic bomb, who decided how far away people should stand? How did they arrive at that figure?

answers.answer: His grandfather was at nuclear tests on Christmas Island in the 1950s. They were 20 miles away, decided by the Ministry of Defence. Some people weren't far enough - one pilot flew through the mushroom cloud to collect samples and many died young of rare cancers. His grandfather died in 1969 of blood cancer, 10 years after washing down an aircraft that flew through the cloud. There wasn't really a hard and fast rule; they were making it up on the spot. Some sat on the beach with their hands over their eyes, backs to the sea, then were told to turn and look, seeing bones in their hands during the flash.

questions.question: Why is someone born with allergies when the mother and two previous grandchildren weren't allergic to anything? Why is the baby allergic to eggs but the mum isn't?

answers.answer: Allergies are partly genetic and partly environmental. You're more likely to be allergic to things if your parents are, but it's not guaranteed.

It's both nature and nurture - genetics and environment. You get antibody packs from both parents, shuffle them up, and make a certain sequence where a snippet corresponds to an allergen shape. Environmentally, IgE (allergy antibodies) was originally for parasites and worms. Since we don't have parasites in modern clean societies, the genetic pressure to make good antibodies against parasites is gone, so now all the pesky allergy antibodies get through unchecked.

questions.question: Why do lab technicians and doctors always wear white coats when that's most likely to get stained?

answers.answer: White shows the stains - you want to know that the doctor is clean. If someone is going to cut you open, you'd want to see they're wearing something you can see stains on, not a manky old apron where you couldn't see if they're filthy.

questions.question: Why do refs in football wear long socks?

answers.answer: The only kit referees have is football socks, which are long. James suggested it could be to keep calves warm or just part of the uniform making them look smart.

questions.question: NA - called in with ANSWER about Shanghai darts

answers.answer: Shanghai is a popular darts game in pubs where everyone can play. One person goes for one number, you total up scores, then move to three, and go around the clock to 20, ending with bullseye. Everyone puts a pound in and plays. Marcus mentioned the Earl of Dartmouth invented the game and went to China where he discovered it.

questions.question: Why does Australia start the day before we do? Who decided or how did it come about that the 4th of March would begin in Australia before it begins in England rather than beginning in England and then working its way around to Australia?

answers.answer: It's all to do with universal coordinated time and Greenwich Mean Time. There's the Prime Meridian and Greenwich Mean Time and the 180th Meridian Line. An Italian first suggested it, and because we were such a powerful maritime nation, we kind of wrote the rulebook for maritime rules and regulations. We also invented standardised time because before standardised time, we set our clocks to the sun. When it was midday, it was high point in the sun. And then because of railways, the explosion in railways, we standardised our time within the UK and then exported it around the world.

We were the foremost naval nation. It was decided officially that we would recognise Greenwich as the prime meridian. That's the line of zero longitude. The international dateline is 180 degrees opposite Greenwich which happens to be in the Pacific. It has to have a common calibration in order to have internationally meaningful measurements for navigating. The source is Greenwich and the international dateline is exactly opposite Greenwich on the other side of the globe so that Greenwich appears halfway through the 24 hour cycle.

questions.question: Why do all the lemons I buy have pips, but all of the limes I buy do not? How do the limes grow if there's no pips to replant?

answers.answer: Limes have been bred so that they'll produce a fruit which doesn't have a seed. People breed limes until they find one that doesn't have a seed, and then they'll graft it from then on. They'll take a graft of that and put it onto a root, and that root will grow into a plant which will produce fruits that don't have seeds. It's a process of grafting.
All of her limes actually have seeds in, which doesn't completely tally with James's information from one of the country's leading botanists, James Wong.

questions.question: Why do vitamins go A, B, C, D, E and then jump to K? What happened to F, G, H, and I?

answers.answer: Vitamin F is actually not a vitamin as we know it - it's a combination of two fats, linoleic acid, for brain health. Vitamin G is actually one of the B vitamins, reclassified as B2. Vitamin H is B7. Vitamin I doesn't exist because it would look like vitamin 1, just confusing. Vitamin J was looked at as being very similar in property to vitamin G (B2), so they dropped it. That takes us to K. There are no vitamins after K.

questions.question: Is a coconut a fruit or a nut? Why can't it have a classification all of its own?

answers.answer: A coconut is a drupe, not a nut. A drupe is a type of fruit with a fleshy outer coating and the seed in the middle. Examples include walnuts and mangoes. A coconut we buy in the supermarket is the seed, and the drupe is determined by the fact that the seed is inside the fleshy casing like a mango. Because it's hollow we get all confused.

questions.question: What determines the total amount of money that's in the world? How do we calculate how much money there is in the whole wide world?

answers.answer: All the central banks in the world follow the M1, M2, M3 money supply calculations which categorise money per cash, per deposit, per investments etc. They keep a running tally of all the banks' money supplies worldwide. Cash in circulation is only a small portion of the total amount of money on the planet.

questions.question: What is the genetic determination for how tall someone can grow? What determines how tall someone is?

answers.answer: We all have growth hormones - a certain amount of growth hormone when we're born that determines how tall we would be. Also the height of your father and your mother - the height you'll grow to is usually between their heights. You get it in the baby book, you can make a rough estimate if you know how tall mum and dad are.

questions.question: Before the advent of emails and Twitter, what was the @ button used for on the keyboard?

answers.answer: It was used for accounts - like '45 barrels of apples at £10 a barrel' when typing up accounts.

questions.question: Do astronauts when they go to space take any sort of weaponry with them? Like guns or a revolver or a sidearm? In case they land in hostile territories when they come back to Earth.

answers.answer: Yes, they can carry guns in spaceships. At the Science Museum, there was an exhibition on the Soviet space race, and she was told that astronauts would have a gun so that if they landed in the forest and were attacked by a bear, they could defend themselves.

questions.question: Why does your last finger always bring in the ring finger when you try to move each finger independently towards the centre of your hand? Why can't each digit move independent of the other?

answers.answer: Each finger has two tendons that bend them - one that bends the middle knuckle, one that bends the end knuckle. The extensors that straighten them are more simplistic - each has generally one tendon. The crucial thing is between some of those tendons on the back of the hand, there are structures called juncturae that tether the extensor tendons together of some fingers. So when you're bending them down, the tethered extensor tendons pull the one next to it down. Martin probably has more tethering than James, putting him in the majority. There's also something called palmaris longus - a tendon at the front of the wrist - which tethers when you start bending your fingers, and those are residual from monkeys swinging through trees.

questions.question: How accurate is the world's population at any given point, and does it take into account the world's tribal and indigenous population?
Why do lemons have pips and limes don't?
What all these conspiracies regarding 5G and that they're bad for our health? Is there any truth behind that?

answers.answer: No.

questions.question: Why specifically is anything to do with the DVLA situated in Wales? Why is the passport office in Liverpool? Why is the Museum of Film and Television in Bradford?

answers.answer: The DVLA going to Swansea is like lots of other agencies at the time. They were pushed out into places where heavy industry, late 60s, early 70s, heavy industry was shrinking. There was a lot of joblessness. It was a means by which government could post high-paying, high-quality jobs into areas that were changing rapidly because heavy industry was going.

questions.question: Why do most almost all wetsuits do up at the back? Surely doing up from the front would make much more sense.

answers.answer: Wetsuits used to all zip up the front and were horrendously uncomfortable when surfing. The zip is the easiest way for water to get in and out. As material became more stretchy, you were able to get in and out of a wetsuit with a really short zip up the back. That makes the wetsuit warmer and more comfortable when you're lying on the board and paddling. The shorter the zip, the better the wetsuit.

Body mechanics means that whenever we move, the back will expand and the front will contract as you bring your arms in. The only part of a wetsuit that doesn't expand or contract is the zip. So by putting it on the back where the material expands further, it'll only get closer in. If we put it on the front, that material contracts, the zip doesn't, meaning the seal's a little bit less efficient.

questions.question: How comes that when you make Yorkshire puddings, as I do every Sunday for roast, plain flour makes the Yorkshire puddings rise, but if you use self-raising flour, they come out like little dumplings?

answers.answer: The main way that you rise a Yorkshire pudding is you need very large bubbles, and the eggs help with that and the gluten stretches around it. But in self-raising flour, you have bicarbonate of soda which produces lots of very little bubbles, far too many of them. You end up with a very spongy texture and it cooks far too quickly and ends up as a lump. Self-raising flour works very well on cake, but not on Yorkshire puddings.
