questions.question: I'm wondering who decides when that man comes up or woman comes up on the TV. How do they decide which programmes get signed and which programmes don't? They might only pop up for two minutes or three minutes and disappear again.

answers.answer: Ofcom sets targets to broadcasters for all different accessibility including subtitles and audio description. These targets are over 10 years. It's up to broadcasters - BBC, Channel 4, ITV - to meet a quota. A percentage of programmes have to be accompanied by sign language each year. They'll lean largely towards the most popular programmes. Deaf people don't have access to information, so they also try and choose programmes that will convey information like press briefings. There was a campaign and court case about the Downing Street interpreter not being in the room with the Prime Minister due to social distancing.

questions.question: Why is it that my washing machine has a little window so I can see what's going on inside it, but my dishwasher and my tumble dryer don't?

answers.answer: If you opened your dishwasher mid-cycle it just stops. If you opened your washing machine mid-cycle it would get your floor wet. Ergo, you need a window on your washing machine but you don't need one on your dishwasher.

The simple answer is so you can see what's going on inside. If you can see inside, you can see if there are any faults with the door lock opening. A pressure switch will keep the door locked if there's water pressed in the drum. Also by seeing in the drum, you can see if there's water in the drum. If there's anything causing an issue or anything that might need a repair.

questions.question: Why is it you fill your car up at the pump in litres, but your fuel consumption is miles per gallon? Why do we sell petrol in litres but measure its efficiency in gallons, miles per gallon?

answers.answer: It's historic. We used to measure everything imperial in gallons and the figures have stayed stuck. It's purely tradition. We went metric on the measurements for selling stuff but we haven't gone metric on the measurements for measuring stuff.

questions.question: Which is the more efficient - if you're boiling a litre of water or a pint of water or even a gallon of water, a kettle or a pan?

answers.answer: The kettle is more efficient because the water's in immediate contact with the element and it's got a lid on it.

It depends on three factors: the materials the kettle is made of (many modern kettles are made of non-conducting plastic which gives them more efficiency), the surface area of both items (a large metal pot has a large surface area which wastes heat even as you're heating it up), and the rate at which you're heating. A kettle is usually more efficient because you're heating very fast and that gives less time for heat to be radiated out from it. A pot is usually not receiving heat so fast in relation to the rate at which it's losing heat.

questions.question: Why does the letter Q almost always follow with the letter U? QI is a word in Scrabble.
How important do you have to be to be assassinated rather than murdered? Is it political?

answers.answer: Assassination is basically the murder of an important person for either political or religious motivations or if you're getting paid to murder (hitman).

questions.question: Are viruses really alive? Because people talk about them as if they are, but I'm not convinced. Are they actually alive or bacteria are alive?

answers.answer: No, they're not alive. They are inert particles that are not dead but not alive either. The definition of life includes the ability to reproduce by yourself, and a virus needs to colonize a cell to reproduce and use their machinery. So they don't have the ability to reproduce on their own. That's why they're not alive.

questions.question: Is there mutual responsibility between UK twin towns and their European counterparts? Does it work the other way? Could it have anything to do with translators?
How come last week when it was so bitterly cold, there was no frost on my car?

answers.answer: Presumably because there wasn't enough moisture. If it's cold enough to freeze water and you can't see any frozen water, there must be a shortage of water.

When you look at a weather map of the UK, you get areas of high and low pressure. Different parts of the country have slightly different local pressures. The atmosphere is made up of gases including water vapour as a gas. As temperature and pressure changes, it changes the behaviour of the water vapour. You can get ice formation one day, and the next day it's still cold but the pressure has changed and you don't get ice formation. Relative humidity is altered by both pressure and local temperatures. Also, cars and metal work chill down below what's called the dew point, and the metal radiates away heat, dropping below the dew point where you'll start to get ice formation.

questions.question: I wondered why they vaccinate in your left arm. Also, if you're left-handed, can you have it in your left arm? Is it optional? Can you have it wherever you want, for example, your buttocks?

answers.answer: You're probably right - you're more likely to put it in the arm that is used less because it makes the arm go sore.

It is quite simple. You can have it in either arm. She asked me whether left or right. I said write my left arm. And she said in that case, you'll have it in your right. You could have said no, thank you. And you can have it in your leg. I asked because I'm really scared of needles and said jokingly what if you haven't got no arms? She said we're doing your leg. She wasn't very happy that I asked.

questions.question: Who determines the feels like factor when they talk about the weather? Is that the same as wind chill? Do they do it the other way around? Do they do it's 20 degrees but it feels like 25?

answers.answer: It's based on the wind mile per hour. It's that simple - you multiply the temperature by a factor of wind speed. The current temperature minus a factor of wind.

questions.question: Why do certain birds change colour between summer and winter with no apparent reason? Particularly the black headed gulls mix in Melbourne.

answers.answer: Black-headed gulls, along with a lot of animals, change colour during the mating season to darken their feathers. The reason they turn back white is partially due to breeding - it's a variation of the environment that dulls their feathers over time. But also it's hypothesised that because our weather way, way back when was more snow, more cold, more dark, they changed back to white to avoid predators then. Though it looks out of place now, it was effective at the time so they survived past others. It's like the peppered moths in Manchester at the turn of the century that changed colour due to soot. Sometimes animals just change because it's sexy - there's a hypothesis in zoology called the sexy son theory where mothers select mates that look more attractive because they're expending energy and it shows they're healthy.

questions.question: Do animals in the ocean ever get thirsty? Specifically mammals like whales or dolphins - is a dolphin swimming up the Thames seeking fresh water to slake its thirst?

answers.answer: They don't in the sense that they want to drink fresh water, but if you use dolphins or cetaceans as an example, they do need to eat fish in order to remain hydrated. If they become malnourished, they do dehydrate, and that's often why they wash up on the shores here in the UK.

questions.question: Why do we roll our eyes?

answers.answer: In the 15th and 16th century, playwrights like Marlowe with Dr. Faustus and Shakespeare would use characters rolling their eyes in court to show lust or love for a character. Over time, down the emotional spectrum of conveyance, it went from showing lust or desire and evolved into showing contempt or annoyance. It was born out of a time when people couldn't really show how they wanted to feel and evolved into a way of letting people know exactly how they feel when they're upset. Also, it allowed actors to convey something that wasn't necessarily in the script.

questions.question: Does honey go off? I had some honey dated 21st April 2020 and it had hardened - how come it's not gone off?

answers.answer: They discovered honey in the pyramids when they were opened that was still edible. It can last hundreds or thousands of years. It's basically sugar so it doesn't rot in the sense that other foods go off - nothing gets in to start the process.
Bacteria that would otherwise make things go off are killed in a high concentration of sugars because they have all their water sucked out of their little cells by osmosis.

questions.question: Where does the tradition of ringing a bell at the beginning of the last lap in sporting events come from?
What's the difference between first and second class post? Not in cost, but in process/service/action.

answers.answer: First class goes first. Second class gets pushed aside and dealt with the next day. Letters go to the mail centre where a machine reads the addresses. They're sorted by hand into different areas. First class stamps go first, second class goes after or next day.

questions.question: Why are newborn babies who are born before midday classed as a day old at midday?

answers.answer: They have to put the line somewhere - it's about registry and writing stuff down. 12 noon has more going on than midnight.

answers.caller: Kay (Ayrshire, Registrar of births and deaths)
answers.answer: Birth certificates only record the date and time of birth. Your age changes as you get older. Age is only mentioned when someone passes away. The rules are: up to 60 minutes old = in minutes, up to 48 hours = in hours lived, up to 14 days = in days lived, then weeks up to 6 months. The question was based on a misunderstanding - a baby born at 10 to 12 who died at 10 past 12 would be recorded in minutes, not as one day old.

questions.question: Can scorpions sting themselves to death? Are scorpions immune to their own venom? Can two scorpions of the same species sting each other to death?
Are big spiders older than little spiders, or do they just eat more?

answers.answer: Most species of spider are sexually dimorphic. Females grow much bigger than males, which is why males often get eaten when trying to reproduce. If you're seeing massive spiders, it's likely a female. Males have narrower abdomens and boxing gloves on their front legs for mating. Older spiders shed their exoskeleton and can expand further if they eat more. If you had to pick one answer, it would be sex.

questions.question: Why do we capitalise the letter I in English when no other languages do the same?

answers.answer: 10 pounds says it's to do with printing presses - when printing was clumsy and primitive, a little 'i' could be confused with part of another word, so it got capitalised to stand out.

I is a personal pronoun, not a proper noun. We capitalise it because it replaces a name - just as 'James' has a capital letter, 'I' is your name replacement. English developed by roughing up other languages and stealing grammar - it's a mixture of Saxon, Latin, Romance languages, and Greek. Because it replaces a name, it follows the same rule. That's why other languages don't do it - they're not English.

questions.question: Why can't multivitamins just be 100% of everything you need?

answers.answer: Because you also eat and drink. If you took 100% in a tablet plus a balanced diet, you'd be overdosing. Vitamin B12 you just wee out, but too much vitamin D could do you some damage.
Supplementary: They're called vitamin supplements, not vitamin replacements. That proves James was right.

answers.caller: Damien (Camden, runs Form Nutrition - vitamin manufacturing company)
answers.answer: Every ingredient takes up different amounts of space. To get the daily recommended allowance of zinc takes much more weight in the capsule than vitamin B12. It's a formulation decision based on the limited space in capsules. The 100% recommended daily amount is actually a minimum, not a maximum. Manufacturers stay well below maximum tolerable levels defined by the EU. James's overdose theory was completely wrong - while vitamin overdoses are possible, the formulation is about fitting ingredients in limited space, not avoiding overdoses.

questions.question: Why does her battery wall clock cause her radio to go off every time it chimes?

answers.answer: Maybe the clock is setting itself remotely and picking something up.

It's an EMC (electromagnetic compatibility) problem. Exactly like when you put a vacuum cleaner next to an old cathode ray tube TV. The electromagnetic current coming out of the clock when it chimes is interfering with the radio. The easiest fix is to move the radio or clock further away. Or coat it in something like a tinfoil Faraday box.

questions.question: Why does a black-headed gull change the colour of its head between seasons? (Black cap in summer, white with black blusher in winter)

Why is it that when one peels potatoes ready for boiling, that by the time you've finished your pile of potatoes, the cold water, that you put in the saucepan to put the first potato in, is lukewarm by the last potato?

answers.answer: Something to do with starch is my early guess, but I wouldn't even dream of suggesting that's going to come close to definitive.

The water doesn't actually get warmer. Your hands just get used to the cold. It's like when you go swimming in a cold lake. You feel as if the water's heated up, actually. Your blood's just rushed to your skin.

questions.question: Once a suppository goes in there, how does it actually get around the system?

answers.answer: Think of it as being the same as putting it under your tongue. But under your tongue, it goes into your mouth and then it gets taken to the right place. It's a blood stream. It needs to get into the blood stream, doesn't it? So anywhere that's absorbent.

It's absorption rates. It goes in faster than it would elsewhere. It has to be absorbed through the stomach, through the gases and food that's in your stomach. So it takes time to be broken down. So if you take something sublingually, they're made to dissolve for slow release. So if you put something under your tongue or into your anus, they're made to dissolve. That's why babies are given paralytic suppositories - it's a really fast acting way to get the job done quicker.

questions.question: Why is it that a courtroom artist can only draw what they see in the courtroom after they have left?

answers.answer: It's all down to the Dr. Crippen case. When the huge publicity was, photographers were actually in court because they were allowed in those days. There was so much disruption that they brought in a new law. They said you couldn't take photographs, and the courtroom artists also had to effectively do all their scribbling outside the court. They were effectively collateral damage.

questions.question: Can a dog tell when a strange dog is of the same breed? And is it a bit like greeting a long-lost relative? Does it make any difference to their behaviour around them?

answers.answer: I wouldn't have thought so... They've got such an acute sense of smell. They can find out a lot of things just by having a sniff. But they are not averse to a little bit of the other with dogs of pretty much any other species. So that would suggest that to a dog, you are either a dog or you are not a dog. There are not distinctions of dog.

Dogs actually recognize each other through not just their looks, but breed typical behavior. If you think about the difference between a golden retriever and a French bulldog - French bulldog doesn't have a tail, has huge little ears and is very frontal. Whereas a golden retriever has a huge tail and wags a lot and the whole body wags and is very smiley. Each breed has a specific way of communicating, of behaving. Dogs really recognize that. Same size dogs will tend to match and same breed as well. When a golden retriever sees another golden retriever, he'll go there. It's about reducing the uncertainty of conflict. Dogs want to try and prevent conflict. They get together with somebody who looks pretty much like me, so I guess he'll be pretty cool too. It's a breed attraction magnet.

questions.question: Why all the recipes I've come across say use unsalted butter with salt? All I have in my fridge is salted butter. I put that in. It tastes fine. But why can't I just throw in salted butter?

answers.answer: I wonder if it might have something to do with temperatures. Because when you're making a dough or a pastry, you want your butter to be... Maybe salted butter has a lower melting point, I don't know.

Whoever's writing the recipe can't tell how much salt is in the manufacturer's butter, because they may vary. Therefore, you put in non-salted, and then you add the salt to make it accurate. It also makes the amount of salt you use unreliable, and the amount of butter you use unreliable as well because the weighed butter contains salt. The bigger the quantities you're making, the more hazardous using salted butter would be. When you start faffing about with phyllo or choux or tougher pastries, these proportions will become pertinent.

questions.question: If Tony and I were to go to Button Moon with a magic spaceship that could pass through the gaseous planet, would it pass through or would it get stuck?

answers.answer: Intuitively, you're thinking yes, right? It's gas. Gas, when a kettle boils, that's gas, isn't it, the steam? You can put your hand through that.

As far as I know, I can answer it for Jupiter, but I assume it's the same for the others. So theoretically, you could if you had an indestructible spacecraft. But with any kind of spacecraft that we have at the moment, it would collapse through the atmosphere by the time it got to the core, because they do actually have solid cores. The gaseous bit before you get to there is about 10,000 miles. So the core is probably about 1,000 miles. It's big enough to stop a fictional spaceship possessed of superpowers. It would get consumed or subsumed. It would become part of the planet. If it was infinitely dense, it would just halt - it can't crash through.

questions.question: Does the International Space Station get rusty?

answers.answer: I don't think it could, because there's no atmosphere in space. There'd be no oxidisation, because there's no oxygen.

questions.question: Why is it illegal to die in the Houses of Parliament?

answers.answer: Are you sure it's true? It's not one I've heard before. You may have misheard or misremembered, but it does have that sort of ring of plausibility. It's one of those weird laws like being able to drive a flock of sheep over Battersea Bridge.

Unfortunately, it is not illegal to die in Parliament. The story is that if you died in a Royal Palace, you'd get a state funeral. But we know this isn't actually the case because the only British Prime Minister ever to have been assassinated was Spencer Percival in 1812, and he did not get a state funeral because his family requested that he didn't. So the urban myth is that if you die in the House of Commons, you're entitled to a state funeral, so they transport your corpse outside before declaring you dead so that you don't qualify. But that's not true because that would break all kinds of doors these days. Forensics would not be happy with you either.

questions.question: When did celebrating birthdays become a thing?

answers.answer: I imagine it started with posh people and then worked its way down to the plebs. So you'd know the birthday of the king, but you wouldn't know your own birthday back in the day. No one could write anything down. Literacy might be a factor.
The first time that we hear about someone celebrating his birthday is actually in the Bible with Pharaoh.

questions.question: When someone is deemed to have died of old age, how old do they need to be? Is there a definitive age that you need to have died of old age?

How can the same device be broadcasting the same thing and it coming out two different ways? If someone is on FaceTime or Skype, it comes through perfectly. But when someone phones up on the same device via the phone line, it's rubbish. Why is the phone line not better than the internet?

answers.answer: You're coming down the phone line. You're not coming over the internet, mate. It's the same device using different networks. An internet call comes over Skype and FaceTime, whereas a phone line call comes over a phone line. They're two different things.

questions.question: Why does the City of London have its own Lord Mayor, tax office, and police force? Do these have any legitimate power, or is it purely ceremonial?

answers.answer: The City of London was the original London, enclosed by walls. They had their own police to protect citizens from outside threats, locking gates at night. As London expanded and walls became redundant, new institutions were introduced but the old ones just stayed.

questions.question: When someone commits a crime like weapons charges or murder and they get pardoned, what happens? Are they free to go or are they kept track of?

answers.answer: I don't know the answer. Someone listening will know.

There's a difference between a full pardon and commuting a sentence. A full pardon wipes it away completely - no history of being a convicted felon. Commuting means you're let free but it's still on your record. In most states, being a convicted felon prevents you from getting firearms and certain jobs for the rest of your life.

questions.question: What happens inside a wine bottle that makes certain wines become vintage and high quality after years, while others only peak after 4-5 years and never get better?

answers.answer: It's mainly due to how it's stored and the cork seal - oxidation can happen if the cork isn't tight. Also atmospheric conditions when grapes are growing.

Main factor is the grape variety - some have greater affinity to age. Most red grape varieties age well, but Cabernet Sauvignon has greater aging potential than Pinot Noir. For whites, Chardonnay ages better than Sauvignon Blanc. Also vintage variation - particularly good years with ripe tannins help preserve wine. Yield matters too - high yielding industrial vineyards make wine meant to be drunk immediately, while controlled-yield vineyards in places like Bordeaux aim for premium wines that can be laid down.

questions.question: What happens if more than one player scores a hat-trick in a football game? Who gets the match ball?

answers.answer: Anyone who scores a hat-trick gets to take a match ball. These days so many balls are used in the game that both get to take one home. Back in the day when only one ball was used, it would go to whoever scored the most recent hat-trick to the final whistle.

When two players from the same team score hat-tricks, they actually decide between themselves. I saw this happen in an Arsenal vs Southampton 6-1 game where Jermaine Pennant and Robert Pires both scored hat-tricks. Pennant, being younger, went up to Pires and said he scored the hat-trick first and wanted the ball - and Pires agreed. So it's a negotiation.

questions.question: What is a Wellerman and what do they do in sea shanty songs?

answers.answer: It has nothing to do with Cornwall and everything to do with New Zealand. The Weller Brothers ran a company that delivered supplies to people working on shore, chopping up whales with an H in New Zealand. The Wellerman was a man who worked for that company on a ship - bringing rum, tobacco, and vittles. They're waiting for his arrival with supplies.

questions.question: If Joe Biden couldn't finish his term and Kamala Harris took over for the remaining 2 years, could she then run for president twice more, serving 10 years total? Or does that 2-year sub-term count as a first term, limiting her to 6 years?

answers.answer: I don't know the answer. Lyndon Johnson took over after JFK was assassinated and won re-election in 1964, and very nearly ran again in 1968. That suggests it might be possible, but I'm not sure about the distinction based on how long you've served.

LBJ became president in 1963 after Kennedy was assassinated, won in 1964, and very nearly ran again in 1968 but chose not to. The fact he could have done it means it's possible. But there's a distinction about whether it counts as a term if you've taken over before half-time.

It's to do with the wording of the 22nd Amendment. If someone serves as president for less than two years after taking over, they can then be elected twice. If they serve more than two years, they're limited to one additional term. The rules were changed after FDR died and Truman came in.

questions.question: Due to tectonic plate movement, would the Greenwich Time Meridian shift over 200 years, moving the actual line on the ground 10 meters either way?

answers.answer: Yes, everything moves. The UK moves about 3-4cm per year eastward due to being pulled apart from America along the middle of the Atlantic. In 200 years that's about 60cm. It's not going to bother most people, but GPS systems already account for this with receivers all over the world. Time zones are defined by country borders anyway, so 60cm isn't a problem there. Only very precise navigation is affected, and that's already handled.

questions.question: Is it possible to reenter a dream once you've already woken up from it?

answers.answer: Yes, I've done this. You drift back off to sleep and start conjuring up the dream in your imagination, and you can re-enter it. It doesn't mean everyone can - some people don't even have visual imagination or an inner monologue.

questions.question: How do starling murmurations work? When they all turn in multiple different directions simultaneously, which bird do they follow? How do they know when to turn?

answers.answer: I watched a documentary about this but got too hypnotized by the murmurations to pay attention to the explanation. The documentary suggested the swooping is to check for predators before roosting, and they stop doing it once they've been somewhere a while.

Each starling uses either five or seven other starlings around it to determine where to move. They move in little clumps that form the whole. Each starling only gets information from its nearest neighbors - it's a local information system. An external stimulus starts it - one bird moves, then it goes like a domino effect and they all move in sync. They return to the same roosting places, so there's a mass intelligence of where they're going.

questions.question: Can I bury my nan in my back garden?

answers.answer: The important thing is that the land that you do the burial is your land. So you can't be a tenant or anything like that. So it's your property. Nothing to stop you from burying a relative in your garden. And to be honest with you, it's becoming more and more popular these days. All you need to do, you don't need permissions. You need to make sure it's recorded on your D. I.e. the location of the burial plot. And when you go to register the death, you need to get a cremation form. And on that burial form, you need to put, again, the location of the plot. Now, here comes the problem. So you've got someone buried in your garden. You've got to imagine that after so many years, you might want to move away and go to a different home or whatever. You obviously have to declare that. And you can imagine, I would expect the value of the property would decrease. The main, in the main, the people that do these have got a lot of money and a long history with the land or the property. They've lived there for generations. If they put up a memorial to that person on the grave, that needs planning permission. And if they then decide eventually to move and take the remains with them, that would require certain consents as well from the local authority.

questions.question: How does a digital camera know when it's in focus?

answers.answer: Most cameras use what's called the contrast-based autofocus detection system. So essentially what's happening, and this can happen tens or a hundred times a second. It really depends on your camera or your phone. Your camera is analysing what your centre sees and ever so slightly shifting the focus of the lens back and forth. And what it's looking for is a really high contrast area. So if you, for example, looking at your face. So clean lines. When does the clean line appear? When the clean line appears, that's when it assumes it's in focus. So sometimes on older DSLR cameras, for example, you may see it goes back and forth and that's called hunting. It's just because the system or the processor in that camera is not as quick as what we have in some of the smartphones now. So it takes a little bit longer.

questions.question: Why can't babies use pillows?

answers.answer: When babies are born, the bone on the back of their head is called the occiput. And that's really, really rounded. And babies, airways, they need to have their head in a neutral position to be able to breathe properly. So whereas if you were doing CPR on an adult, you have to tilt their head backwards to open their airway. But babies need their head in a neutral position. So if you put their head on a pillow, it's going to force their chin down and it will occlude their airway.

questions.question: What would happen if you reached the edge of the universe and kept going?

answers.answer: You kind of have to rethink how you think the universe because basically it's constantly expanding, but it's the dimension start expanding as well. So you could never actually reach the edge of the universe because it would all be moving away faster than you could get to it. The universe is constantly expanding, but there's nothing at the edge of the universe for it to exist in. It's basically the universe is all of our dimension. So it's all of space and time. So there's nothing beyond there for it to exist in. It's kind of like if you think of the universe as a bit of paper and you just exist on that bit of paper, you won't be able to experience anything else on another bit of paper. You really have to change how you think about the universe because it's what we exist in.

questions.question: Can migratory birds stop migrating if they are happy somewhere?

answers.answer: Starlings that are in London in spring move further north as the weather gets better, and starlings from further south move up into London, and then in the autumn it's repeated in the opposite direction. So the ones going north have another bunch behind them who were going north, but only to the place where the other lot set off from.

There's two populations in the UK over winter. There's the resident British population, which are here all year round. And then the migratory ones, migrating from Europe, continent for winter, because they eat for food. They come in, they stay here, and then in the spring they migrate back. And they do that because it's instinctive in them. So Cordelia's starlings are staying all year round, but not necessarily, well, not because she feeds them, but because they just live there. She might even have a mixture of migratory and residential starlings at the same time.

questions.question: When you see a road sign and it says London 20 miles or Manchester 50 miles, where are they actually measuring it from?

answers.answer: Every major town in Great Britain had a main post office at one time, and the mileages were taken from the main post office. And subsequently, the small post offices in the villages.

questions.question: Why does Hawaii have a union flag in the top left corner?

answers.answer: The Hawaii was gifted to America by, I believe, Queen Victoria.

It was never part of the British Empire. It was an independent kingdom up until about 1880s or something. And it was taken over by coup by America, by settlers. And it had a rich flag on it as a sort of like flag of convenience to get itself approval ratings from the British Empire at the time. As almost like a kind of car sticker in your window. Saying we support, we love you. Come and do some business with us.

questions.question: When police announce an amount of people at an event or a march, how do they come up with the figure?

answers.answer: You select an area, count the number of people, look at the overall area, and that's the calculation. And then the organisers say it was a lot more. They never say, oh, no, you're wrong. It was much less than that. They never say that. In the days before drones and those clever things, the technology was somebody standing on the top of a police carrier. So you just need to be able to multiply the number of squares by the number of people in a square.

questions.question: Why is it after someone has died, they're referred to as late?
Is it true that we only use 10% of our brain? And if the person answering could elaborate on why there was so much space left unused

answers.answer: We actually do use all of our brain. If we didn't, it would be smaller because it takes a lot of energy. The grey matter has a certain type of neuron which is different to the white matter and they all are used. The 10% myth might come from the fact that we don't use all of our brain at once - we use specific neurons that trigger other specific neurons in certain pathways. But actually, we do use all of our brain at one point, even just doing one day.

questions.question: Why the expression 'Philadelphia lawyer'? Why not Edinburgh, London, Chicago? Why specifically Philadelphia?

answers.answer: Philadelphia had a much more complicated constitution than other states, so to be a lawyer there you had to be much more knowledgeable and informed than elsewhere.

The Philadelphia lawyer refers to Andrew Hamilton, a lawyer from Philadelphia who defended John Peter Zenger in about 1740 in a landmark case. Zenger was a German immigrant publisher of the New York Journal who aired grievances against Governor William Cosby and was imprisoned. Hamilton's argument was that the jury could decide whether what was published was true, and if true, it could not be malicious. Zenger was acquitted, establishing truth as a defence of libel. The phrase's meaning changed over time - from about 1800 it meant competent and diligent, but in the second half of the 20th century it came to mean sleazy lawyer.

questions.question: What is the height when you lose mobile signal when descending or landing on a plane?

answers.answer: 32 kilometres is the theoretical maximum distance, but practically it's far less. The problem is you have so many towers talking vertically and the phone just can't decipher which tower it wants to speak to.

32 kilometres is specifically the limit on the digital mobile network because of the time slots given for mobile phone signals. You have 32 mobile phones on one channel, multiplexed, listening for each one in turn rapidly. If you're further than 32 kilometres away, your radio signal travelling at the speed of light (186,000 miles a second) will miss the slots. The base station physically won't hear you because your signal won't have reached it in time.

questions.question: Do dogs have dominant front paws? One or the other?

answers.answer: Yes, dogs do have dominant paws. Food eating and hunting would be the ways to determine this. Bina confirmed her dog shows this - one paw like Muhammad Ali and the other like Larry Grayson. When a dog gets a scent, they often get up on one paw - always the same paw.

questions.question: Are there any viruses that are actually beneficial to us? Whether they attack other cells, dying cells in our body or attack bacterial cells that are no good for us?

answers.answer: There are things called Bacteriophages (or just phages) - viruses that kill bacteria in the human body. They were used as alternatives to antibiotics in Russia and Eastern Europe over the past 50-60 years. They go into the body and use the bacteria causing a problem as a host, then destroy them from within.

The vaccinia virus is a really good example of a helpful virus - it's the virus used in the smallpox vaccine that eradicated smallpox. There's also a theory about human placenta genes possibly coming from viruses, though that's not proven. We definitely know there are some retroviruses which can regulate the expression of human genes and might be playing a role in evolution.

questions.question: Why does oil become iridescent when it hits the ground when wet? Why do you see multicoloured shiny rainbows?

answers.answer: The shininess is the viscosity. The oil and water are different thicknesses of lenses and the light passes through in a way that diffuses or diffracts, breaking down into all the colours of the spectrum.

answers.caller: Andrew from Brentwood (A-level physics teacher and engineer)
answers.answer: It's interference. When the same wave gets split or reflected, you end up with two versions that either add together or cancel. Depending on the angle you're looking at the surface, you get a different path length through the film. You will either get enhancement or cancellation of that particular wavelength. They're not actually rainbow colours - they are different wavelengths being enhanced or cancelled at different angles. The amount of light reflected at the interface is similar so you can get real good cancellation.

questions.question: If you're watching a film in English and there's a character speaking a foreign language who swears, does that affect the film's rating in the UK? And what happens when that film gets translated to a French audience - do they still swear in French?
Why don't we greet people with 'good night'? We say good morning, good afternoon, good evening, but we don't say good night as a greeting. We only say it when leaving.

answers.answer: In Charles Dickens' 'The Signalman', characters greeted each other with 'good night'. It was used historically. The answer is probably that it simply fell out of fashion, like not saying 'gadzooks' anymore.

questions.question: What is the most photographed thing or object in the world?

answers.answer: If defining photographed as printed, it would be Nottingham Castle
France is the most visited country on the planet, Paris is the most visited city in France, so likely the Eiffel Tower

questions.question: Why do kettles go quiet just before they boil?

answers.answer: The noise is from bubbles created on the element collapsing in water not at boiling point. When water reaches boiling point, bubbles no longer collapse and instead rise to the surface as steam, so it goes quiet

questions.question: In athletics, why are track events anti-clockwise?

answers.answer: Standardisation for record-keeping purposes. Most people are right-handed and right-footed, so forces go onto the right leg and right arm comes across the body. It's more comfortable to run anti-clockwise
Something about a vein that takes blood to the heart - running anti-clockwise works better for blood flow
When Greeks first ran tracks, they believed natural eyesight moved left to right (like reading), so they ran left to right (anti-clockwise)

questions.question: What animal grows the most relative to its birth weight? (Biggest differential between birth weight and fully grown size)

answers.answer: It's a marlin - they hatch from grams and can grow to 2,000 pounds (multiple of thousands)
Take a fish - go for the biggest fish in the ocean: whale shark
Red kangaroo - they have a month gestation, give birth to young the size of a grain of rice, and adults are 7-8 feet tall (tens of thousands of times heavier)
Coral reef - it's a single animal made up of billions of tiny polyps and can be miles wide
Whale shark - they give birth to 30cm babies but grow to 30 metres (Baby shark, doo doo doo doo)

questions.question: How do you steer in space?

answers.answer: Rockets

Newton's third law - every force has an equal and opposite reaction. The rocket exhaust pushes against the rocket itself, not the air. If you're in a spacesuit pushing away from a rocket, both would move but the heavier rocket moves less

Half right about Newton's law but should have said mass not right. You could squirt orange juice out of a spaceship and it would work. They select rocket fuel because it's the 'rightest' - costs so much per gram to get anything into space

questions.question: What is the difference between a philharmonic and a symphony orchestra?

answers.answer: Orchestras: chamber orchestras play chamber music (smaller), symphony orchestras are bigger. Symphony and philharmonic are essentially the same - both play symphonies. Philharmonic is just a name applied to orchestras in particular places, like Glasgow Rangers/Celtic rivalry. You can't be a philharmonic if you're James O'Brien's orchestra - just the rules

questions.question: If I'm given a vaccine for any virus and then I give blood and that blood's used to treat somebody, do they then take on the vaccine that I've been given?

answers.answer: I wouldn't have thought so, but I have not got a clue.

If you are vaccinated and have an antibody response to it and then went to give blood, there would be some of the antibody in your blood, but highly unlikely that there would be sufficient in order to protect the recipient of your blood. For years there was a practice of taking plasma, specifically not blood, from hyperimmune donors who've either been exposed to a virus or a specific antigen. They have developed a very high antibody level to it. The plasma was pooled together and subjected to a process called fractionation, which split off the bits you didn't want and left the antibodies or the immunoglobulin. That immunoglobulin was then put into vials and used to provide passive immunity for people exposed to that particular virus. But it only is passive and doesn't give long-lasting immunity, and would have to be pooled from thousands of donors.
answers.qualifications: 33+ years working in the blood transfusion service, recruited donors to donate hyperimmune plasma.

answers.answer: If you've had a vaccination, you've got to wait four weeks before you can donate blood. I was looking to donate my antibodies but unfortunately my antibodies weren't high enough. It's just a normal blood donation centre within a couple of days you can get an appointment.

questions.question: Corned beef comes in a can that's pyramidal shaped and has a key. Nothing else comes in a tin like that with either a pull tab or use for a tin opener. I wondered why.

answers.answer: Isn't it so that you can serve it whole? I think you could have opened a tin and poured it out. I'm trying to remember.

If you pierce the small end of the tin, that releases the vacuum even easier and lets air in at the back, so it just pops out onto a plate like a rat up a drainpipe. It just slides out smooth as you like, so you can slice it.
answers.qualifications: Used to eat a lot of corned beef.

answers.answer: Corned beef tins are actually square because they take up less room on a pallet and they were initially tinned for the military so their protein went out on operations. They can tear the top off the tin with the key provided and use the tin as a container to eat the meal. They're stronger and more reliable and you pack more in a smaller space.
answers.qualifications: Learned it in a general knowledge quiz years ago.

questions.question: Assuming the sun isn't a ball of gas... it's not constantly fed by gas... it must be solid. My question is, whatever it's made of, when is it likely to burn out? When will the sun burn out?

answers.answer: When will the sun go out? And have I got time to get home before it does? We'd be dead in a nanosecond, wouldn't we? I'm 99.99999 recurring confident that the sun is a ball of gas.

The sun is actually made from gas. It's hydrogen. Because it's so hot, the electrons get knocked out and just protons remain. They get fused in what's called nuclear fusion and make helium. That difference of some of the mass is lost and transformed to energy. This gas will run out and it's estimated to be five billion years with a B. In about two billion years, the Andromeda galaxy is approaching our Milky Way galaxy so within two billion years that would... Actually within five billion years the sun will run out of fuel.
answers.qualifications: BSc in biomedical and PhD in genetics. Loves physics. Recommended book: Just Six Numbers by Martin Rees.

questions.question: How did curry sauce become so ubiquitous with the chip shop?

answers.answer: I bet it has something to do with Chinese chip shops as opposed to British-owned ones. It's very mild, closer to the curry we introduced to Japan rather than the curry we bought over from India. Maybe katsu curry type was a British thing.

Curry went to Hong Kong with Indian troops and soldiers. The Chinese in Hong Kong adopted it as a staple in their diet and it was also prominent in Singapore. A curry sauce that's very popular in Asia is a Malaysian curry sauce which is much milder than an Indian curry sauce. When the Hong Kong restauranteurs opened up and boomed in England, then it came back with them.
answers.qualifications: Lived in Hong Kong.

questions.question: On the odd occasions when we have moths or I spot moth holes in clothes, they always tend to be in the same sort of region, which is at the front, around the belly button area. I've always wondered why.

answers.answer: How do you store your clothes? When you put them away, do you fold them and put them in drawers? If they're piled on top of each other, they'd be the point of access. But they're hanging up in a wardrobe... Are you sure? Because once you've got an idea like this in your head, you could see a hundred moth holes and only four of them would be in the belly button area but you'd only notice those four because they fix your theory. It's like being a Brexiter, claiming that the vaccine had something to do with Brexit. You see what you want to see.

The holes around the belly button area are caused by friction - your button on your jeans, for example, rubbing from the other side, or where you put your safety belt on in the car crosses over the point and causes friction between the button or the buckle and the jumper. They're not caused by moths. Tracy's hygiene concerns were completely unfounded.
answers.qualifications: Texts coming in from listeners confirming the belly button area pattern and friction explanation.

questions.question: I'm currently looking at a bank £20 note. It states on the note: 'The Bank of Scotland, PLC, promises to pay the bearer on demand £20 sterling.' What would happen if I walk into the bank and demand £20 sterling?

answers.answer: If you go in and say 'I am the bearer, can I have my sterling please?' - because the note is not worth anything unless we decide collectively as a society that it is.

If you went into the bank with a £20 note and asked them to exchange it, you would get nothing in return. Had that been before 1931, the bank would have been obliged to swap it for sterling silver. At that time we ran on the gold standard, so every bill was an actual claim check on some gold or valuable metal in a vault. We abandoned that in 1931, moved to the Bretton Woods system which pinned it to the American dollar, abandoned that in 1973, and now we have fiat currency - the only reason it has any value is because we all agree it does, and nothing more.
answers.qualifications: Had to research it for a speech for a speaker's club competition and made the speech three or four times.

answers.answer: Correction - the promise is actually to exchange it for another £20 note, so you could swap a manky old one for a new one just for purposes of cleanliness. But you're not going to get sterling silver or gold - just another note.
answers.qualifications: Read it in one of Tim Harford's economic books. Really hates being wrong.

questions.question: When you're nervous or under moments of quite high suspense, why do people shake their leg? Their leg wobbles up and down when they're nervous or under high suspense. Why the leg and not another limb?

answers.answer: I think it is just a release of anxiety, a release of tension. The leg and not another limb will probably be to do with the amount of blood and muscle. So it's the biggest thing you can sort of jiggle. It's a bit chicken and egg - we shake our legs because we're tense and you're tense because we shake our legs.

It's part of the fight, flight or freeze response. When you are feeling nervous, various things happen in your body. Adrenaline gets pumped around your system, cortisol, stress hormones, and all of those are preparing you to respond to the threat. So if you're being chased by a tiger, you need to run, you need all that pumping through your system to be able to run away. Those people are sat there watching whatever it was, the Formula One, and the legs are wiggling - it's like keeping the engine running because they're not actually flying away. They're not actually fighting or running. So the body's preparing for that action but they can't actually do it in that context, so the energy goes into shaking their legs.
answers.qualifications: Counselor therapist who works with young people and adults with anxiety and depression, learned this as part of training.

questions.question: What happens when an astronaut dies in space? The body is up there and they can't just call a funeral director. What's the procedure?

answers.answer: I presume they just have to keep it somewhere until it's time to come home. A bit like on an aeroplane, maybe. Unless the death meant that they couldn't do the mission or the astronaut was essential. I wouldn't just sling them out the window, would you? That's what my partner kept telling me - launch them into space.

questions.question: I'm trying to buy your book unsuccessfully. I've used your link on Twitter and the site keeps saying my postcode is incomplete. I've typed it in with and without a gap. Is there an error on the site? I need to give it to my boyfriend for our anniversary on the 17th.

answers.answer: There are other websites you can order from, although you may have issues with some of their business practices. But the bookshops are open again - get yourself down to any bookshop. It's in all good bookshops and the rubbish ones as well. 'How Not to Be Wrong: The Art of Changing Your Mind' by James O'Brien in all good bookshops now.

questions.question: Why is it called a whip in Parliament? Why is it called the Whip's Office?

answers.answer: It's a hunting term. The whippers-in were the chaps who would keep the dogs in order so they wouldn't go straying and lose the track. The whip's job is to get the MPs through the correct lobby, controlling them like the whippers-in controlled the dogs.

questions.question: Why are logos on polo shirts or sweatshirts always on the left? Why is it never on the right?

answers.answer: It's so that if you shake hands with your right hand, it wouldn't cover up your logo and people wouldn't be able to see your logo.

Pockets were traditionally on the left-hand side because soldiers were mainly right-handed and would keep all their cartridges in their left-hand pocket for easy access. Logos evolved from military insignias which were always on the left side. This tradition transferred onto shirts.

It goes back to the knights of old having to show their colours. Most knights were right-handed, so on the left they carried their shield, and on the shield was their logo. As they went into battle, you wanted to see who you were fighting. This got transferred onto the tabard - the loose-fitting tunic worn over chainmail - and by inference onto clothing.

questions.question: Can you get two or more viruses at the same time?

answers.answer: Yes. The doctor's advice was that if you contract influenza and coronavirus at the same time, your likelihood of death is far higher. That's why people with asthma are encouraged to get the flu jab.

questions.question: Why, when we see somebody hurt themselves, do we take a sharp intake of breath?

answers.caller: Robert (Portsmouth) - Thatcher, studied geology, watched documentary on spirituality
answers.answer: We have something called a mirrored neuron, which we share with a handful of other animals. When something happens - somebody gets hurt - we feel that visceral feeling of an intake of breath or pain in our stomach, we wince. The evolutionary reason is probably that if you're going to get smacked next, you're bracing for it, which means it would hurt less. It's like sympathetic resonance where playing a C chord on one piano makes another piano vibrate. It's also like yawning - when you yawn, I yawn because it means there's nothing dangerous behind me.

questions.question: In 1965, the Queen gifted the US an acre of land next to the Magna Carta in Surrey at Runnymede for the JFK Memorial. If a crime was committed on that acre, which is technically US soil, who would have jurisdiction to investigate?

answers.caller: Alistair (Egham) - Professor of Geopolitics at Royal Holloway
answers.answer: Even though that acre of ground is owned by the American government, it is not an extraterritorial space. British law still applies there. An act of Parliament - the JFK Memorial Act in 1964 - was passed to gift the land to America, but without giving away British sovereign rights over that space.

questions.question: Which is the first country in the world to turn to the next day? Who celebrates New Year's Eve first?

answers.caller: Joe (Croydon) - read Maya by Jostein Garda as a teenager
answers.answer: Fiji celebrates it first and last. The international date line crosses some of the Fijian islands.

The first place that celebrates New Year is the Pacific island of Tonga. Tonga, Samoa, Kiribati and Christmas Island are all in the same time zone. The funny thing is American Samoa is the last inhabited island to celebrate New Year. There's actually a 25-hour gap between Tonga and American Samoa, but they're only about 500-600 miles apart.

questions.question: Where did the idea of throwing spaghetti against a wall to test if it's done originate?

answers.answer: The claim that sticking to the wall proves it's al dente may actually prove the opposite - that it proves it's overcooked because there's too much starch in it.

questions.question: The space station is 250 miles above Earth and SpaceX travels at 17,500 miles an hour. Why does it take 27 hours to get there?

answers.answer: SpaceX doesn't go in a straight line. It goes in a spiral orbit, rounds the Earth a few times, moving out all the time, and eventually catches up with the space station. The space station itself is travelling at pace, and you have to meet it at exactly the right speed. You have to catch it and slow down, so when you dock, you're going the same speed. It's like Wile E. Coyote chasing the Roadrunner - if he's only running marginally faster, it's going to take a long time to catch up.
They wanted the astronauts to have a good sleep. They got out of their space suits, into their comfortable clothes, and that's the reason why it took so long. They could have got there quicker.

questions.question: Why do we say 'rabbits' at the beginning of the month?
What is the meaning of James's regular references to 'Ray Liotta'?

answers.answer: Ray Liotta is the American actor from Goodfellas who also did the voiceover on Field of Dreams saying 'if you build it they will come.' When he came over to be interviewed, he recorded the voiceover for the show. It's an award reserved for people whose qualifications for answering are almost too good to be true.

questions.question: What's at the bottom of a black hole?

answers.answer: Black holes are not holes but spheres. At the centre there's a singularity of mass - all mass crushed down to a single infinitesimally small point. If you took the mass of Earth, it would be a black hole the size of a ping pong ball, but that's just the event horizon. The actual singularity is inside. As you approach the event horizon, time slows down. So it's more a vortex in space and time, not a hole with one side and another.

questions.question: How do you lock an airline jet? Is there a set of keys for each plane?

answers.answer: You can't lock them in a conventional sense. On an Airbus, it has two large batteries. You need electrical power and air capability. You can fire up the auxiliary power unit in the tail (a small mini engine). Once you have good electrics and air, you need to put two more switches in the correct position and the engines will be up and running.

questions.question: Can dogs see in the dark?

answers.answer: Yes, dogs can see in the dark. They can see approximately six times better than humans. Their eyes are built differently - they have more rods which concentrate light. Their tapetum is bigger, which is why a dog's eyes reflect when you shine a light at them and ours don't.

questions.question: Why are there two different forms of the lowercase letter G?

answers.answer: The loopy G is called a double-story G (same as double-story T). It comes from Roman type style. To make lowercase G more obviously different from lowercase C, they added the tail and loop. It was the most common European manuscript style in the 15th century when printing was invented (William Caxton). In serif styles like newspapers, you get the double-story G. In sans-serif styles (more like handwriting), you get the single-story G. Now it's a stylistic choice.

questions.question: Why don't continental shoe sizes consistently match UK sizes? Why doesn't a size 10 always equal EU 44?

answers.answer: Your comment about English exceptionalism wasn't entirely wrong, though turned on its head. There isn't one continental sizing system - there's the French sizing system which is more common and uses different increments (about 6 and two thirds millimeters). So there's no such thing as 'the continental sizing system' - there are various different ones.

questions.question: Why do men's bikes have the crossbar at the top and women's have the step through design?

answers.answer: Historically it's about decorum - women rode side saddle on horses to avoid straddling. That same thinking transferred to bicycles (the 'ankle theory' - if a man got aroused by a woman, it was always the woman's fault). However, structural integrity is also a factor - a bike with a crossbar is stronger. With modern tempered steel and carbon fibre, that probably doesn't matter anymore, which is why step-through bikes are becoming more popular for everyone.

questions.question: What's the relevance of the term 'blue' when associated with movies? And 'turn the air blue' when using bad language?

answers.answer: The censor used a blue pencil. So 'blue' became the phrase used to describe stuff that should be censored - the censorship would be done with a blue pencil, on film and on paper.

questions.question: Can lip-readers see accents? Do mouth shapes differ for different regional accents?

answers.answer: Saw a documentary (possibly World War II in colour) about a lady who could identify regional accents by the shape of the mouth from a soundless film. She could still lip-read and identify accents from mouth movements.

questions.question: Why does the leader of the opposition always ask six questions? Is it a legal requirement or just that they get six questions? And if it's just because they get six questions, why do they always ask them because the sixth question just opens the door for an unrelated diatribe from the Prime Minister?

answers.answer: The leader of the opposition does not have to ask six questions. Ed Miliband was notorious for only asking five, because it meant that the Prime Minister had to ask five questions, and the Prime Minister couldn't deliver the final prepared flourish on the sixth question.

questions.question: Can plants feel pain? They've recently done studies where they can put plants to sleep, suggesting plants have a nervous system. Plants can communicate with each other through their roots, trees, et cetera.

answers.answer: Plants have a diffuse nervous system. They communicate when being eaten via pheromones, root systems, and leaves releasing chemicals. They are aware when being eaten but couldn't possibly feel pain because they would never have evolved in the way they evolved if it hurt them when we bite them.

questions.question: Who first theorized the water cycle? Did ancient Greeks know about it? Was it a person or did the ancient Greeks just work it out?
Why do we have a Royal Air Force and a Royal Navy, but it's not called the Royal Army? Why is the British Army the only one of the armed forces that is not royal?

answers.answer: The Army is much older and was not always raised by the Crown, whereas the Navy and subsequently the Air Force have always been one cohesive unit in their own right, raised by the Crown, and have been given the Royal title. Various units and regiments like the Royal Engineers are given the Royal title as an award.

questions.question: How do babies know how to dance? It seems to be inbuilt in them that they have rhythm, whether you turn music on or not in their infancy. Is rhythm innate in humans? It seems to be inbuilt as babies from them being born that they can dance.

answers.answer: Babies' auditory and motor systems are inextricably intertwined. They will start to sway with rhythm as electrons are emitted from their brain in preparation for crawling and expressing rhythm. Expressing rhythm is just part of their development. This is based on a study called Action Simulation.

questions.question: When you dream and your eyes are closed, where do the images come from? How can you see in your dreams when you can't see with your eyes closed when you're awake? Because your eyes aren't working in a dream.
All other months have 30 or 31 days. Why does February have 28 days? Where does 28 come from? They nicked a day from February to put on other months. Why was February the one that got picked on?

answers.answer: They nicked a day from February when Julius Caesar wanted July to have an extra day, and when Augustus Caesar wanted August to have an extra day, he got it from February as well. It's to do with the redistribution of days under the Julian calendar, but I don't fully understand why February specifically was chosen.
The extra day in February (29th in leap years) exists to balance out because the circuits that the Earth makes around the Sun are not as perfect as our clock would have us believe - it's 365.25 days.

questions.question: At what point in human history did we start using surnames? Who was the first person to have a surname? Adam and Eve didn't have surnames, so when did we start?
Do animals get headaches? How would we know if they get headaches?

answers.answer: Mammals very likely get headaches because they're very similar to humans neurologically and in blood system. They show pain, bang their heads around the corner. Insects and fish - probably yes too. Unfortunately, animals can't tell us whether they have headaches because they can't speak.

questions.question: How does conditioner work? Soap and shampoo break down fat and oil, but how does conditioner work?

answers.answer: Conditioners contain a surface active agent (surfactant) which leaves a very mild positive charge on the hair fibre. As positive charges repel one another (like magnets), each hair then repels one another, making the hair feel smooth and silky. It does not leave a waxy film. This is the same principle as fabric softener.

questions.question: What is the longest duration an extra time has lasted for after a football match?

answers.answer: The longest added time was in the last couple of years at Burton Albion in the League Cup. It was about half an hour because the floodlights kept coming on and going off. The referee is the sole timekeeper in a game and there's no actual time limit. Ian mentioned a game where they waited 40 minutes for an ambulance to take a player away and still carried on.

questions.question: If you're living in a camper van parked legally on the side of the road with the engine off, do police need a search warrant to come in?

answers.answer: Police need a power of entry granted by some section of the law. It is considered a residency and they would need some kind of power, not necessarily a warrant. It could be under Section 18 of PACE or Section 32 of PACE. If he was at his premises at the time of arrest, it could be searched under Section 32. If he was arrested away from his premises, Section 18 would require signing off by a police inspector, not a court, but it is still a legal power to go in and search. It is also considered a residency under the Theft Act, so it can be burgled because it is being used as a residency with a degree of permanence.

questions.question: During space travel with zero gravity, has anyone decided which way up is in space?

answers.answer: He suggested that if we encounter an alien species, we would have to take their views on board before putting down a rule that would apply to both of us. He noted it's a bit like sovereignty - a bogus argument that requires agreement from all parties.

The Millennium Falcon above or below the Star Destroyer - if it's above your head, then it's above the Star Destroyer, but why would you think that? You could be upside down. In fact, the Millennium Falcon often flies upside down.

questions.question: Is it true that you can get a cold from actually being cold, or is that an old wives' tale?

answers.answer: You can't catch a cold from just being cold and wet because colds are caused by viruses. But if you get soaking wet and freezing cold, it does impact your body - your immune system is less able to produce the cells needed to fight off infection. So not directly, but indirectly: if there is a virus around and you're shivering and cold, you are more likely to fall victim to it than if you're feeling chipper. Your body has a certain amount of energy to expend, and if you're freezing cold, it's having to keep you warm, leaving less energy to produce your immune response.

questions.question: The Black Death was spread by the fleas of rats. Were the fleas actually affected themselves by the Black Death?

answers.answer: Neither the rats nor the fleas have any symptoms - it's only harmful to humans or potentially other mammals, but not to rats or fleas. There was research not long ago that tried to remove fleas from the equation altogether and claimed it was human body lice responsible for passing on the plague.

Fleas DO suffer symptoms. Their stomachs become filled with the bacteria, which blocks their feeding tubes, causing them to essentially starve to death. This is important in the spread because rat fleas by their nature only feed on rats, but because of the starving, they become less choosy on who they bite. When they turn their attention to human hosts, that's how humans get it. You can only get bubonic plague by a bite - you can't get it through droplets in the air.

questions.question: Why is it, if you're in a dark room with the door open, you can see a lit-up room, but if you're in the lit-up room, you can't see into the dark room?

answers.answer: It's to do with the pupil in your eye. In daylight, the pupil dilates and gets bigger to let more light in. When you go into a dark room, it contracts and goes very small, allowing less light in. The transition period between light and dark places takes about 15-30 seconds for the pupil to fully dilate, which is why you can't see into the dark room from a light room at first, but you can later when it's pitch dark. In the dark room, your pupils are wide open so you can see the light coming in.

questions.question: Do dogs get hay fever like humans do?

answers.answer: Yes, dogs do get hay fever and you can treat it. They get the full human deal - runny eyes, sneezing, itchiness. It's an allergy to pollen just like humans. The skin can also get irritated with some dogs.

questions.question: Why is non-fiction called non-fiction as opposed to a word of its own like 'factual'?
In America, Democrats are red and Republicans are blue - opposite to the rest of the world where left-wing/communist parties are red. Why are the Democrats red?

answers.answer: The colour coding emerged from television media needing colours to identify states as they turned on electoral maps. The notion of calling them red and blue only became solidified in the 2000 George Bush election. Prior to that, there were examples of colours being reversed in the early 70s. It was actually more the TV media and the fact that they weren't coloured that necessitated the need for colours to be associated with parties in America being such a media-oriented country. There's a belief that red is the communist colour, but it's actually a televisual convention with nothing to do with ideology or politics.

questions.question: When you're flying close to the clouds, why does it feel slower than flying the same distance from the ground at the same speed?
Do magnets get weaker when applied to bigger objects?

answers.answer: Magnets don't get weaker based on the size of object they're stuck to. If they did, they'd eventually fall off the object as the magnetic pull diminished.

Magnets do lose their magnetic pull over time, but it's not a consequence of how big the thing that the magnet is attached to is. It's because the atoms within the magnet aligning towards magnetic north is not diminished by the size of the object. Also mentioned that vintage guitars from the 50s and 60s sound mellower because the magnets have lost some of their pull.

questions.question: Why don't birds on electricity wires fry?

answers.answer: Because they're not earthed. If you had a string attached to the bird's foot and you were holding the string on the ground, then you'd both fry.

questions.question: Where does the modern game of chess come from?

answers.answer: Mentioned the Lewis chessmen found on the Isle of Lewis that predate medieval times, likely brought by Vikings.
Chess stems from an ancient Egyptian game called Kness, which has been modified over the years.

answers.question: Where does the modern game of chess originate?
answers.answer: Chess goes back about 1,500 years, possibly longer. But the modern game changed when the queen and bishop became much more powerful pieces. In the modern game, the queen can move anywhere and bishops can move diagonally from one end to the other. This change happened through Spanish development in the Middle Ages. The Lewis chess pieces date to the 12th or 13th century but the queen didn't have as much power then as she does now.

questions.question: Why do all, or at least 99%, garden centre trolleys only have two wheels?

answers.answer: The trolleys have hinges at the front so they can slot into each other and be stacked in a smaller space. Otherwise, you'd need a trolley-sized space for every trolley.

questions.question: Why is it unlucky to open an umbrella indoors?

answers.answer: It's probably an old wives' tale invented to stop people opening umbrellas indoors so they wouldn't knock ornaments off the mantelpiece.
Back in ancient Egypt, umbrellas were used as sunscreens to protect the nobility. It was seen as an insult by the sun god Ra to stand underneath an umbrella, either in the shade or indoors anywhere.

questions.question: Where does the word 'mufti' come from to describe non-uniform?

answers.answer: A mufti is a Muslim word for a scholar or Islamic religious figure. When the British army was off duty in the 19th century, they would sometimes dress like the natives as a form of integration, wearing robes and tasseled hats. Therefore, dressing not in uniform but wearing local clothing became known as going mufti.

questions.question: Why does hair lose its colour when you age?

answers.answer: As you get older, you lose melanin in your hair follicles, which causes the colour loss in your hair. When dark hair starts losing colour, it appears grey from a distance but it's actually white hair.

questions.question: Why are essential oils called essential when we don't realistically need them?

answers.answer: The word 'essential' derives from 'essence'. When you have a pot of stuff and you split it into all the different constituents, when you've got the constituent that can't be split any further, it's an essence. And if it's an oil, it is therefore an essential oil.

questions.question: Why do we say we went 'in' the car but 'on' the bus or train?

answers.answer: With a bus or a train, you could think of it as a constantly circulating route onto which you hop, whereas in a car you've got autonomy and independence.
When planes and trains and buses were first designed, they didn't have roofs, so you were open to the elements and you were on them rather than in them. Cars all had roofs, so you were in a car.
When you had horses, you would go on a horse or on a cart. When cars were made, they were all open, so you would have been going on a car. When they had roofs, you were going in a car.

questions.question: Why is it a tradition to bring grapes to visit someone who is poorly?

answers.answer: Grapes allow you to have a little bit of fruit without the rest going off. If you had an apple, you'd take a bite and not finish it. If you had a melon, you'd only want a little bit. But with grapes, whether you've eaten 10 or one, the fundamental integrity of the bunch remains and the freshness of each grape remains intact for the longest time.

questions.question: Why is the crane fly known as the daddy long legs?
Where does the tradition of smashing a bottle of champagne against the hull of a boat before it makes its maiden voyage come from?

answers.answer: The tradition goes back thousands of years to good luck ceremonies invoking Norse gods before launching ships. Prior to Queen Victoria, they used goblets filled with wine and smashed them against the ship, but launching so many ships got too expensive so they switched to champagne. Queen Victoria was the first to use champagne for ships with royal names. During American Prohibition, they filled empty water bottles with water and smashed those instead.

questions.question: How does breathable paint work? Unlike fabric which has an inside and outside, paint just gets painted on one side - so how does it know to let moisture out from the timber but not let rainwater in?

answers.answer: Breathable paint has less vinyl or acrylic in it. Standard paint is generally porous - water will pass through it. The more vinyl or acrylic you add, the more potentially waterproof it becomes. The shinier the paint, the more vinyl it has (gloss = high vinyl, matte emulsion = lower vinyl). If you put vinyl silk directly on bare plaster, the moisture trying to escape from the plaster will push it all off. Mineral paints are for lime plaster on older buildings and have no vinyl or acrylics.

questions.question: Do commercial airliners have horns?

answers.answer: Yes, they do have a horn - a small one on the nose of the aircraft. It's not for getting attention of other aircraft but for the flight crew to get the attention of ground crew, engineers and handlers. It sounds like a squeaking duck with some distortion to it, not very loud. When the aircraft arrives on stand and is met by ground crew who usually plug their headset in, if they're not there or the crew needs their attention quickly, they'll hit the horn so people can hear and go plug in their headset.

questions.question: When you freeze beer bottles and then thaw them out, why are they much less fizzy than before? The gas should still be inside the sealed bottle.

answers.answer: The seal gets broken during freezing. When the beer expands as it freezes, it breaches the seal - not enough to blow the lid off completely, but enough for gas to seep out. This is why frozen beer goes flat even though the bottle appears sealed when thawed.

questions.question: What constitutes classical music? Is it a time period? Can there be modern classical music? Can classical music not performed by an orchestra still be classical? What are the actual parameters?

answers.caller: Steve (St Albans) - Senior Lecturer/Associate Professor in Music at University of Leeds
answers.answer: There are two types: Classical with a capital C refers to the period roughly 1730 to 1820 (Baroque was before with Bach, Romantic came after with Tchaikovsky and Liszt). But Classical with a small c is a generic term - some use it to contrast with popular music, others call it 'art music.' It's a complicated term tied to ideas of proportion, structure and correctness from Greek and Roman classics. Examples that challenge the distinction include West Side Story (opera or musical?) and Schoenberg or John Cage would be called 'art music.' Even the term has classist connotations - why isn't Elton John art music?

questions.question: Why are car number plates white at the front when they're yellow at the back?

answers.answer: It's a legal requirement - you're not allowed to show a white reflection at the rear of your car. Yellow was chosen for the back because black numbers stand out more proudly against it. White must be at the front. The reasoning is so drivers can tell which direction a vehicle is traveling, particularly in the dark when you can't see other visual cues like headlights or taillights.

questions.question: What is the origin of the British military salute?

answers.answer: The generic origin is the lifting of visors by knights to identify themselves and show their faces. The specific British military salute involves an open palm to demonstrate the hand is empty - back in the day when messengers were sent to parley, they had to show their hand was empty with no knife or blade. The arm is held at a 45-degree angle with heels together in formal salute position.

questions.question: Why do we celebrate birthdays with cake? When did that start?

answers.caller: Basil (St Albans) - references book by Peter Haining on Laws and Superstitions
answers.answer: To understand birthday cakes, you need to understand the origin of birthday candles. In ancient Greece, when people wanted their prayers heard by the gods, they would bake little cakes or bread, put a candle on top, light it, and leave it on the windowsill at night. When the wind blew out the candle, the smoke (symbolic) would carry their prayers up to the gods to be heard. This is why we make wishes when blowing out birthday candles today - it evolved from this ancient superstition.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'by the way'?

answers.answer: If you're walking up a road, the main bit of business is the road itself. Something additional or alongside the main business is 'by the way' - like blackberries growing by the side of the road. So when you're telling a story about X but want to add Y which is vaguely relevant, you say 'by the way.' It introduces a new topic not directly relevant to what was previously under discussion.

questions.question: Why is the Deputy Speaker always in the chair for the Budget speech rather than the Speaker? For something so important, I'd have thought it would be the Speaker.

answers.caller: Theo (Leicester Square) - Political Journalist at LBC
