answers.answer: The Deputy Speaker is also the chairman of the Ways and Means Committee, which initiates proposals for raising taxation and the budget. Since the Budget is fundamentally about taxation, it's customary that the Deputy Speaker chairs that debate rather than the Speaker himself.

questions.question: Why do we call people left-wingers and right-wingers?

answers.caller: Theo (Leicester Square) - Political Journalist at LBC
answers.answer: The terms come from the post-revolution French Parliament in 1789. Those who sat on the left side of the chamber were the revolutionaries or radicals, and those on the right were the loyalists or royalists. 'À gauche' (left) and 'à droite' (right).

questions.question: When were birth certificates first introduced?

answers.answer: 1837 in the UK. Before that, churches kept records. It became mandatory to record births then, with registration within six weeks of birth.

questions.question: What is the longest bridge in the world?

answers.answer: The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge in China. It's about 100 miles long and is part of a high-speed railway.

questions.question: Why do motorways have numbers and why are they not numbered in the order they were created?

answers.answer: Motorways are numbered because they follow the A-class road that goes to the same place. The M4 follows the A4, the M2 runs down through Kent, the M3... They were named because they were relieving the A road.

The A-roads are actually numbered radially around London like a clock. The 1s go north, 2s go east/southeast, 3s go south/southwest, up to the 60s for the Midlands, and the 7s, 8s and 9s are in Scotland.

questions.question: Why do champagne bottles have exactly 6 twists on the wire cage?

answers.answer: There are only two manufacturers that make them (one in Italy, one in France), so they both use the same number. It's so you can count six twists without looking, rather than looking down at the bottle.
Backing up the previous answer - it's for the service standpoint so staff can count six turns in their head when engaging with customers.

The pressure in the bottle is six times more than atmospheric pressure. Each twist prevents the cork from popping unexpectedly. When you start releasing it, you put your hand over the top to stop the cork.

questions.question: Why do shampoo bottles have the lid on top while conditioner bottles have the lid on the bottom?

answers.answer: Two reasons: First, so you can identify which bottle by touch when your eyes are closed (don't grab the shampoo again). Second, and primarily - viscosity. Conditioner is thick, so the lid at the bottom means it's backed up and ready at the nozzle when you flip it, like ketchup bottles with flat tops.

questions.question: Is an 18th century law still valid that allows a man to urinate in the street if he shouts 'relief' three times?

answers.answer: Clearly not valid, as you can get arrested for urinating in public. James suggested Edward test it by doing it in front of a police officer.

Historically true - in bus driver training around 1987, they were taught you could relieve yourself against the offside rear wheel as long as you shouted 'relief' three times. Same was taught to taxi drivers and police. But you'd get arrested now for indecent exposure.

questions.question: If a crime is committed on an airplane, who has jurisdiction?

answers.answer: Jurisdiction belongs to the destination country. Wherever you land, that's where you'd be arrested and dealt with. While at altitude, the law is upheld by the crew in the name of the commander (captain). They can restrain disruptive passengers. If it's a serious crime, they might divert, but often that's not possible. Better to be heading to London than somewhere like Bangkok.

questions.question: Is there anywhere in London where young people still speak with a traditional Cockney accent?

answers.answer: Bermondsey was suggested as one place.
Plenty of Cockneys still in Bow, Bethnal Green, East London. The test for a true Cockney is that they never use the letter H at the beginning of words. Born in Bow, within earshot of the Bow Bells.

questions.question: Why is it called 'heads and tails' in a coin toss?

answers.answer: The coin used for tossing traditionally wasn't currency coins but had animal imagery on the back - donkey tails, etc. Tails refers to the animal tail side of the coin. Jason collects toss coins featuring African wildlife (lion, rhino, elephant, hippo).

questions.question: Why is clockwise clockwise?

answers.answer: It comes from sundials. The clock face was modeled after how sundials work, with shadows moving in that direction. It wouldn't have had a name before clocks existed.

questions.question: Is there any truth in the way two place names came about to be named during the Black Death, which is Tilbury and Gravesend? So if someone was to die during the Black Death, apparently they would be taken to Tilbury, and that's Tilbury. Til they're buried. Til they get buried, and then they get carted across to Gravesend. Gravesend, correct. Is there any truth in that?

answers.answer: Lots of place names have names that don't mean anything about from their existing spelling. They go back to the Doomsday Book of 1066 and beyond. And Gravesend is the name of the town. The council name of Gravesham was selected in 1974 for the new area. And they went back to the Doomsday Book to find what Gravesend was called then. And it was Greve's Sham or Greve's Ham, the home of the Reve. And the Reve is a ruler like Sheriff. So Gravesend has nothing to do with the plague because it's a derivation from a name that's been around since the 11th century at least. Similarly with Tilbury, the burying part is nothing to do with death. Lots of place names end B-U-R-Y because bury is a wood. And often there is a name of a village and then a location further away is the same name but with bury on the end.

questions.question: My friend was sitting in the garden and I mentioned it must be well over 30 degrees today. He got on his phone and said no, it's 29 degrees from the Met Office. I didn't believe him, so I got a glass thermometer out, put it on the table, and it measured 35 degrees. I then put it in the shade, it still measured 35 degrees. He said you can't measure temperature accurately with a glass thermometer. Is my medical thermometer more reliable than the Met Office's?

answers.answer: Your mate was right. If you put it in the shade and it didn't change, that means it's not taking a reliable measurement. I wouldn't have thought that your medical thermometer was of any use at all in this situation.

He wanted to know whether or not his medical thermometer could be used to measure the temperature in his garden. Well, it could be, but he'd have to be very careful. They're made so that when they record the temperature, the mercury doesn't go back into the bulb. It actually stays at the temperature it records. So it'll go higher, but it won't go lower. There's a tube with mercury in with a tiny little kink, a sort of restriction. That's why you see doctors and nurses flicking them. If he took it outside, got into a shaded place, shook it down and then let it rise, he'd get a rough approximation of what the temperature is like in that place. If he let the sun on it for just a very short space of time, the mercury would shoot up. They're made so that they'll take the temperature fairly rapidly, but they won't go back down again.

questions.question: Why don't publishers release a book in hardback and paperback at the same time? I hate reading hardback books. Usually I've got books from Christmas sat on my bookshelf that don't get read because I don't like reading hardbacks.

answers.answer: Anyone who rises to that epic challenge of writing a book deserves to be amply rewarded. And a hardback book costs more than a paperback book and it just provides two tiers. You get first dibs on it if you pay a bit more and that will be the hardback. That's the answer, but I'll leave it on in case there's sort of publishing type listening. And there might be a historical origin story for this. You know, the reason why it was published in hardback first, maybe more than just commercial consideration.

The short answer is profit, but actually it's more nuanced than that. Hardbacks rarely make money. A small percentage of them do. If it's a massive bestseller, a brand new Jamie Oliver cookbook, Delia Smith cookbook, David Attenborough book tie-in with a BBC series, Harry Potter, hardback. When a publishing company decides to publish a book, all of the costings and sales projections are done on the hardback and the paperback together. The sales of the paperback, which are always much, much greater, offset the cost of the hardback. Hardbacks nearly always lose money, paperbacks bring the money in. It's also traditional, and it's partly snobbery, because most reviewers won't review paperbacks. There have been publishers over the years, particularly Transworld, who've tried to go straight to paperback, but it hasn't worked because the reviewers want the hardback.

questions.question: Why is a red onion called red when it's obviously purple?

answers.answer: It's to distinguish it from white onions. And it's arguably red. It's more purple than red. It's burgundy. Burgundy is red. It's red wine. It's red on the inside, isn't it?

It goes back to many hundreds of years when there weren't so many terminologies with different colours. Yes. As in red hair, robin red breast, the whole lot was classed as red. So anything remotely red was red. Absolutely, because they didn't have a word for purple or mauve or anything like that. So it's that simple. It's linguistic evolution, really.

questions.question: Why does your nose run when you cry? We understand the functions of crying - it demonstrates that you're unhappy socially and it cleans your eyes in case there's a predator. But why does your nose run when you cry?

answers.answer: Is it not because the tear ducts, although mostly servicing the eyes, I think the short answer might be gravity, mightn't it? Your tear ducts are pushing tears into your eyes, but gravity's causing some of them to... I think it's a side effect of an evolutionary advantage than a design flaw. If you're crying because you want someone to cuddle you and you've got snot all over your face, I don't think that's ideal.

The eyelids where they meet above the nose are called inner canthus. Tears are produced above the eyes, sort of under the eyelids. And when we start crying, of course, the tears flow into the inner canthus where there are little canals and they end up into the nose. Hence, the nose starts watering. When somebody cries immensely, then, of course, these little ducts can't cope. Hence, you get tears on the cheek.

questions.question: Is an ambulance that's already en route to hospital in any circumstance allowed to stop and render assistance to another one? Like, if you've just been transported to hospital and they come across a horrible car accident, are they allowed to stop and render assistance in any situation?

answers.answer: We have to stop if we do come across, if we're travelling someone with somebody to hospital and we come across something quite serious, then we do have to stop, assess the situation. It's called a running call. Assess the situation, decide if there's another ambulance that's needed, maybe stay with them until that ambulance is there. But it all depends on the situation, really. If you've got someone in the back who needs to be, I don't want to be irresponsible, but you mean somebody in the ambulance for whom speed is of the very essence, lost seconds could be the difference between survival and non-survival. You wouldn't stop then. It would be a difficult situation. You would have to possibly just call up our control to let them know that something terrible has happened on the road. It might not have been rung in yet. But it all depends on the situation. I've stopped a couple of times, yes, with a patient on board for calls. I had to assess the situation. Usually I've got two people on the ambulance, so the other person will sit with the patient and watch them.

questions.question: Do we travel among the dead? So, you know, if you go on holiday and then if someone passes away and then you travel home, are they underneath us in the plane with the baggage? And should we know about it as well?

answers.answer: I know from unpleasant personal experience, a friend of mine whose father passed away in Dubai, they had a right home there. It was horrible. But they came back on the same plane. The answer to your question is yes, based on personal experience, but also on just reasoning in that it's impossible to think of how else you would do it. We know that people are brought back if they pass away on holiday, they're brought back home to be buried or to have their funeral. It costs a lot to repatriate dead relatives. But that's on scheduled airlines. The idea of chartering your own jet, you'd never get anybody home from abroad unless you were super rich.

The human coffins are flown around the world with regularity. They have to follow IATA regulations whereby they have to be declared on the load sheet to the captain. And they're actually designated as a three-letter code of HUM for human remains. But interestingly, if there are dogs that are being carried around in the same hold, there has to be a minimum distance between the human remains and the animals, say, dogs or cats, because of their acute sense of smell. They can actually smell the remains and they get quite disturbed and distressed. Of course, if someone passes away on the flight, you have to leave them in their seat as well. There are also other human remains that are carried as cargo, which are ashes in an urn.

questions.question: What ecological disadvantages would we suffer on the planet if flies didn't exist?

answers.answer: They eat each other. If you've got aphids, for example, there's big news at the moment about nicotinoids and sugar beet crops in Europe. The aphids have taken over the sugar beet fields but they have predators that are also flies. Recycling. There's your first answer. There'd be a lot more poo around. They'd turn mammalian waste into kinetic energy, chemical energy.

Biodegradation is absolutely correct. The waste is obviously only one half of the biodegradation. Also, in their larval stages, so maggots will get rid of a lot of dead bodies as well. There'd be a lot of unpleasantness around if there weren't any flies. Also, from an ecological point of view, they provide a food source for a great number of animals, amphibians, other insects, birds, even some small mammals. And from a human point of view, there are some parasitic versions, but they also provide a bit of a defence against plant pest species like caterpillars and grasshoppers. So there's a lot going on. It's not that bad after all. Be nice to flies is the lesson.

questions.question: Why do you close your eyes when you sneeze?

answers.answer: If you don't close your eyes when you sneeze, they'll pop out.

We sneeze to clear our lungs. The pressure that builds up, if we didn't close our eyes when we sneeze, you'd blow your eyeballs out. There is a risk of the pressure building up in such a way that you might actually blow your own eyeball out of your face.

questions.question: Why are there so many satellites in the sky?

answers.answer: There are so many because of all the technology on Earth - mobile phones, GPS technology, and communication satellites. Because there are so many computers and smartphones and tablets, the satellites are needed to keep us all in touch with each other.

questions.question: What are the chemicals that water is made up of?

answers.answer: Hydrogen and oxygen. H2O - that's the chemical formula for water. It means you've got two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.question: How do they measure a wave?

answers.answer: Modern satellites can radar wave heights. Ships at sea report on a daily basis weather reports to the Met Office - they just look out the window and estimate. In surfing competitions, they're just doing it with their eyes based on previous experience. Oil rigs have wave measuring radar that points out and measures exactly how high the waves are.

questions.question: We know that Earth was created by a big bang and rocks colliding. Well how was space created and what was before space?
What is the difference between a trap and a booby trap?

answers.answer: Booby is an adjective. So you booby trap something. All booby traps are traps, but not all traps are booby traps. The difference between a booby trap and a trap is that for a booby trap you need to have an object that has been 'boobied' - disguised as something else. Something disguised as something else is a booby trap. You booby trap an object like a fridge - you'd wire it up so it squirts water or gives you an electric shock. A mouse trap is just a trap - no one's boobified it.

questions.question: Are black holes dangerous to the universe?

answers.answer: If a person was to enter a black hole, there wouldn't be any oxygen, so you wouldn't be able to breathe. It contains extreme levels of dangerous radiation, which could give you really bad radiation sickness or you could die. If you'd fallen out of your spaceship, you'd probably be dead already. Nothing can escape from a black hole - once it's in there, it's there forever.

questions.question: Why is County Durham the only county in the world that has a black hole? (meaning: Why does Durham have 'County' prefix unlike other English counties?)

answers.answer: The county is prefixed by County Durham to distinguish between the county and the county town, which is Durham City.

County Durham came around later on, after Durham existed. There's constantly changing county lines. 'County' is a very old English term. It was Durham, and then it became the County of Durham. So they just called it County Durham. It's more to do with history than geography - a linguistical preference at the time it was founded. Places like Avon were originally kingdoms.

questions.question: Where do robins originate from? And do robins migrate?

answers.answer: I think it's because of their red breasts that just gives them a bit more confidence or it makes us like them more. They sing beautifully.

Robins are spread widely across Europe. They're quite local birds, tend to live within a sort of five-mile radius. They don't tend to migrate - they change their eating habits instead: insects and larvae in spring/summer, nuts and berries in winter. The wide-held belief about why they're so friendly is that because they're ground-feeding birds, they've developed a symbiotic relationship with gardeners. Because we till the soil, robins believe humans aren't a threat because we're also ground-feeders. Their lifespan is about 30 months. When near country boundaries, they might cross the Channel for warmer climates or food availability in winter, but generally they're sedentary birds, not migratory. Its full name is the European Robin.

questions.question: Can spiders get trapped in other spiders' webs?

answers.answer: Yes, it can happen but very rarely. Spiders tend to stay away from each other. When spiders get near each other, they tend to fight. Spiders have knowledge of silk - they make several different types of silk. There's piriform silk which they make specifically to navigate around the web with, and that isn't sticky. They cover that with another layer of sticky silk. Their legs are specifically designed to walk on webs with their hair. Spiders can detect silk instantly and usually go away because they think there's another spider there. Most spiders stay on their silk. In normal circumstances, no. But in freak circumstances where a spider gets blown out of a tree and lands upside down on another spider's web making contact with parts of its body that aren't legs, it could get stuck.

questions.question: What was the first thing to ever be alive on planet Earth?

answers.answer: It would be something tiny like a bacteria. Everything evolved from a creature that lived in the sea, but that creature was already quite evolved compared to the very first instance of life.

questions.question: Why do we have to mark our election ballot papers in pencil? Why are we not allowed to mark them in ink?

answers.answer: You're allowed to use whatever you like. The reason we prefer pencils is that when you fold your voting paper, pencils don't blotch onto another option and contaminate your vote. There's no danger of accidentally spoiling your ballot by dint of a leaky biro.

questions.question: Where did algebra come from?

answers.answer: Algebra is Arabic. The Babylonians would have been the first people to have algebra as mathematical formulae, around 500 BC.
It wasn't the Babylonians - Islam didn't exist until about a thousand years ago, and algebra has been around since about 500 BC. (This corrected James's claim about Babylonians.)

Algebra means 'reunion of broken parts' or 'small parts' in Arabic. There is an Islamic scholar known as the father of algebra, but that relates to the title of the book he wrote rather than the actual discovery of mathematical formulae, which was first recorded by the Babylonians around 539 BC.

questions.question: How many stars are there in the galaxy and how do we know that? In all the galaxy... I mean in the universe?

answers.answer: The answer is 11. And I know because I counted them. You're a star.

We can't tell how many stars there are in the whole Universe because the Universe is expanding and we can only see stars whose light can actually reach us. In our own galaxy, we do know but I can't remember the number. They count by taking photographs of sections of the galaxy and working them out - they can take sections and multiply, though they have to account for variations because the galaxy is different in different places with a thick middle with lots of dust, spiral arms, etc.

questions.question: Why do some animals have the name dragon in it, like dragonfly or Komodo dragon?

answers.answer: They look like dragons. Komodo dragons look like giant lizards, like dinosaurs. Dragonflies look like dragons with wings. The dragon snake has a ridged back, bumpy scales, which is what we thought dragons looked like.

questions.question: How deep can you dig a hole before it gets too hot?

answers.answer: As you dig down, temperature increases due to the geothermal gradient. The global average is about 25 degrees centigrade increase for every kilometre you go down. At 40 degrees centigrade, enzymes start to denature, which is when you start getting biological problems. So you can get to nearly two kilometres before it becomes dangerous for humans without cooling. The deepest hole we've managed to dig with a drill is about four kilometres. For a practical answer, about 125 metres would give you about 3 degrees change.

questions.question: Why aren't animals still evolving today?

answers.answer: Animals are still evolving - you just can't see it because it happens over such a long period. Evolution happens when an organism is born with a mutation in its genes. If that mutation helps survival, that organism has more children, and over thousands or millions of years, the species evolves. Example: in Manchester during the Industrial Revolution, white moths on grey buildings got eaten, but grey moths could camouflage themselves on soot-covered buildings, so the species changed colour very quickly.

questions.question: When an adult is kidnapped, why is it still said to be kidnapped when there's no kids involved?

answers.answer: The word was coined to describe children being taken away, then it got applied to adults being snatched as well. Like 'taking candy from a baby' - your dad wouldn't actually be a baby when you beat him at Mario Kart, but the phrase still applies. Kidnap applied to children when first coined, but as the word developed, it also applied to stealing or taking adults away against their will.

questions.question: Why is a hen and a stag do called a hen and a stag do, because they're different species? Why isn't it a hen and a rooster or a stag and a doe?

answers.answer: There are two origins for these words. In Middle English going back to Tudor times, 'hen' was actually the female name for any bird - not just chicken. Pea hens, etc. That's how it became associated with women. The stag party actually goes back to the 5th century in Sparta when they would have a pre-wedding feast for the men and go out hunting stags. There are also origins of the hen party in the Middle East and Asia hence the henna party where they tattoo females, which may be part of the etymology from henna to hen.

questions.question: Why don't cats like water?

answers.answer: It's because their fur gets heavy when wet and it confuses them because their balance is different. Dogs don't mind as much because they don't jump that high or spend their life up trees and climbing places, so balance isn't as important for dogs. The longer the hair, the bigger the problem with getting wet for a cat.

questions.question: Who or and when had the idea of democracy?

answers.answer: The Greeks claimed they invented it and generally they invented the word. Demos is the people and kratia is rule. So the rule of the people would be a Greek invention, going back thousands of years. Though not every person got a vote in ancient Greece - you had to be a man and a property owner. Greece is called the cradle of democracy.

questions.question: Why is it called Greenland if it's white and covered with ice?

answers.answer: Eric the Red fell out with other Vikings and wanted to settle somewhere else. He wanted to get a message back to Norway and didn't want his enemies to chase him. So he described Icy Place as Greenland in the hope that other Vikings would head in that direction and leave him alone. It was like a medieval marketing campaign to persuade other Vikings to go where everything was green instead of going where he was. He might have actually been in Iceland which is greener than Greenland.

questions.question: Why do only humans and apes have opposable thumbs? Why can't cats and dogs?

answers.answer: It's not just humans and apes that have opposable thumbs. Some bears have them, some frogs do. Koala bears have opposable thumbs, and pandas do too. Some birds have something like an opposable claw. The answer is evolution - to be simplistic about it.

The reason thumbs have evolved is because there's a basic body plan that many animals share with five digits, which have been adapted in many ways - like the fins of whales and dolphins. When animals start using their forward limbs less for locomotion and more for other uses, that's when the evolutionary adaptation to having something to grip with develops. The panda's thumb is particularly interesting - it isn't actually a thumb, it's a bone in the wrist that has evolved to take the place of a thumb and serves the same purpose.

questions.question: Why are jumpers, as in clothes, called jumpers? Because there ain't no jumping involved.

answers.answer: If you go back to the really olden days, certainly in Scotland and I think in England, you would wear something called a jupe. J-U-P-E. And over the years, for reasons I don't know the answer to, that word has evolved into the word jumper.

questions.question: How much does it cost to make a £20 note?

answers.answer: No answer given during the episode.

questions.question: Why did people tip their hats as a sign of acknowledgement, and when and why did the practice phase out?

answers.answer: This dates back to medieval times with knights in armour on horseback. When they approached each other on a battlefield, they would raise their hand and lift their visor - effectively tipping their hat. It was a sign of respect, making eye contact with your adversary, and saying 'let's not stab each other for the next 10 minutes.' It originated as lifting the visor, became a helmet, then a hat, and the doffing of a cap.

questions.question: What is a parallel universe?

answers.answer: Parallel universes are part of a theory based on weak gravitational fields. Some people think there could be 12 parallel universes and the combined actuality creates a reality that shares an overall gravity, but that's probably fanciful nonsense. They're also believed to be like sliding doors moments - a slice in time where if you made a certain decision, it would go off that way. But that doesn't actually exist - it was only ever a potential until what would be considered a collapse of the waveform. Nature is a lot simpler than that.

questions.question: Where did the 5-day working week come from?

answers.answer: Sundays were already not used for working in mills because it was considered a religious day. During the Victorian period, the average working time was around 60 to 80 hours a week. The Factory Acts gradually reduced this by protecting particular groups like children and women. There were various strikes in the 1880s by gas workers who said 'shorten our day to lengthen our life.' It wasn't until just after World War II that a lot of firms stopped working five and a half days and got rid of Saturday morning, giving us Monday to Friday. Trade unions played a massive part in this.

questions.question: Why do mobile phones require you to dial the number and then press send, whereas landlines you press send and then dial?

answers.answer: It's to conserve battery. How mobile works is every so often it connects to the network to tell the network where it is. If it was continuously connected to the network, it would drain your battery. That's why if you're out in the country with no mobile signal, your battery goes down really quickly because the phone is constantly trying to connect to the network. The base station is connected to the electricity supply, so landlines are always on.

There are two answers - one is analogue and one is digital. On analogue systems (landlines), when you pick up the phone, that engages a strawager unit. You dial by running your finger along a comb-like device, with each tooth representing a digit. On digital systems (including cordless phones), you put the number in first and the phone stores it, then gets the line and pumps the number down.

questions.question: Why does an 18-month-old blink when someone else bangs a toy, but not when he bangs it himself?

answers.answer: It's the same reason you can't tickle yourself - subconsciously your brain tells your nerve endings what is happening, and it can only be done subconsciously by the person doing it. Even if the baby can see the drumstick heading towards the drum, there's still an element of surprise involved. When someone else does it, their brain can't send the message to your nerve endings saying 'it's coming, don't react.'

You don't actually blink when someone else claps - it's all about being ready for it. Being expected is what matters. A baby can still tickle himself because he doesn't yet understand what's going on and his brain doesn't send a message to his skin saying 'don't get ticklish.' The older you are, the easier it would be to train yourself not to blink when someone claps.

questions.question: Who was the first teacher?

answers.answer: James suggested it might be Socrates or Aristotle, but the episode was cut off before finding a definitive answer.

questions.question: Who decided that the fork would be in the left hand and the knife in the right?

answers.answer: Back in the day there were no forks, only a knife. You'd cut a bit off with the knife and then spear it and put it in your mouth. Since almost everybody is right-handed, the knife would naturally be in the right hand. When the fork was invented to make life easier, people kept the knife in the right hand and put the fork in the left.

Livvy confirmed James was right - knives came first. They were used in the right hand because most people are right-handed. The reason a lot of children eat left-handed is because they sit opposite their parents, so they mirror what their parents do.

questions.question: How accurate are GPS coordinates? If you buried treasure and gave someone coordinates, could they be a metre out or a centimetre out?

answers.answer: It depends on the number of decimal places. A latitude and longitude of 0.01 degrees will get you to a general area, but the further down you get into decimal places, the more accurate you get. It can be infinitely accurate - you could get a coordinate down to a grain of sand if you used enough decimal places. To get to someone's front door, you need eight decimal places. To get to a doorknob, you'd need 18 or 80 decimal places.

questions.question: How and when did plants evolve to have poison as a defence instead of physical defences like spikes and thorns?

answers.answer: Evolution depends on random mutations. A plant might grow from a seed that was slightly different from others - a random mutation. If that mutation involved something that made the plant taste horrible, a cow might sniff it and go on to the next plant (which doesn't have the mutation). The plant without the mutation gets eaten, while the one with the mutation reproduces more. That plant's seeds will carry the same mutation. Eventually, the mutation-carrying plants take over because the others keep getting eaten. You can't estimate when it happened, but that's how poison defence sustains itself.

questions.question: Do bees fart?

answers.answer: Yes, bees do break wind. It's because of air getting caught in the fecal matter, apparently. It's essentially an exhaust after the chemical reactions of digestion have occurred.

questions.question: Why do we call it a 'lap' when we're sitting, but not when we're standing? It's still our thighs when sitting, but we call it a lap.

answers.answer: No answer given during the episode.

questions.question: What happens to clouds when it's sunny, and where do they go?

answers.answer: No answer given. James attempted to explain that clouds turn into rain when they get colder and fall out of the sky, but didn't finish the explanation about where they go when it's sunny.

questions.question: When you go into the sky on a plane, the sky is blue. But when you go into space, the sky is black. Why is this?

answers.caller: Lydia from Southend (research scientist, physics degree)
answers.answer: The light is coming from the sun. When you look at the sun in space, it looks white because it's really bright. There's no atmosphere in space so the light isn't scattered. But when light reaches Earth, it hits the atmosphere and scatters. Light isn't actually white - it's made up of loads of different colours. When light hits oxygen and nitrogen in the atmosphere, it turns blue, and that's what you see.

questions.question: When you drink water straight out of the fridge, is it much colder than when you drink orange juice from the same fridge?

answers.answer: Every material has what's called specific heat capacity - it takes a certain amount of energy to add a certain temperature. Water and orange juice have different specific heat capacities. They absorb the same amount of heat energy from the fridge but because of different heat capacities, the temperatures will be different. Orange juice, though largely water, has other components that change its heat capacity.

I did an experiment - water and orange juice are the same temperature in the fridge. But a thermometer cools down quicker in water than in orange juice. The difference is in how your mouth takes the heat out of the substance - it's the specific heat capacity that makes them feel differently on your tongue.

questions.question: When you get on a horse and get off, why do you get on and off with the left side?

answers.answer: Back in the old days when we used to wear swords, we wore them on the left-hand side. You would pull it out with your right hand. If you tried to mount from the right-hand side, you'd get tangled up with the sword. So traditionally you got on from the left. Also, because the massive majority of us are right-handed, it's easier to swing your right leg up to get on.

questions.question: Why do we get beauty spots?

answers.answer: A beauty spot is essentially a massive freckle. Freckles are a product of melanin concentrations. When you go out in the sun, melanin comes to the surface because darker skin protects you. The melanin isn't spread evenly - it's like spreading butter on toast. Some bits have a globule of butter (melanin) and your beauty spot is where you've got a big lump of it.

questions.question: Can rabbits from different warrens visit each other's warrens?

answers.answer: Yes, rabbits can share warrens. Particularly when startled by predators, they all jump into the nearest burrow they see.

questions.question: Why do colourful fish turn white when they die?

answers.answer: Two reasons: First, stress - if fish are kept in captivity and moved to a new aquarium, stress weakens their immune system making them vulnerable to diseases and parasites which make them lose colour. Second, when fish die they sink to the bottom where there's less light, and less light exposure causes them to lose colour. Something chemical happens to the fish with regard to colour that is caused by sunlight, so when that stops, the colour goes.
[Attempted to add to the fish answer but phone line was unstable]

questions.question: If a baby animal got separated from its parents - for example a lion cub - how would it know if it was a carnivore or a herbivore?

answers.answer: There's a close connection between the sense of taste and smell in all animals. If it smells good, it tastes good. Animals have this evolutionary inheritance - they would know from the smell whether they're going to enjoy eating something. Herbivores can smell their food automatically. But predators like lions have to be taught how to hunt because they can't just smell their food in the same way - they'd follow their parents and the parent would show them how to catch prey.

questions.question: How do we get déjà vu?

answers.answer: It's basically a mini seizure - a very quick rewiring of your brain. It goes to a place in your brain where memories are made to exist. That's why it feels like you've already done it before, even though it isn't - it's triggered in the same part of the brain as memories.

questions.question: Is there a difference between the number of atoms in water and in a solid like a rock?

answers.answer: Two parts to the answer: First, it's to do with state - in a solid, atoms are closer together than in a liquid, so in a given volume of rock there would be more atoms than in the same volume of water. Second, it's also about what the atoms actually are - different atoms weigh different amounts. If you take one kilogram of iron (atomic number 26) versus one kilogram of lead (atomic number 82), there will be fewer atoms of lead because the atoms themselves are heavier. It's not purely a solid-liquid split.

questions.question: Why are badgers called brock?

answers.answer: The words 'badger' and 'brock' come from French and Old English. 'Badger' means to dig down because badgers can dig down really quickly. 'Brock' means badger in Old English. Originally, brock was a nickname for people who look like badgers. In the cartoon Peter Rabbit, the badger character is named something like Brock because they name characters after linked words.
It's one of those words that comes from Vikings or Celtic origin. I think brock was a Viking word that applied to badgers, possibly linked to colouring.

questions.question: Why do people use the word boo to scare someone, and what makes the word boo scary?

answers.answer: I don't know. I like it a lot. I shall try and find out for you.

The word boo starts with B which is a plosive or stop consonant, created with a buildup of air that's suddenly released. It's a bilabial plosive. The sudden release of air is the key - it probably has an evolutionary explanation as it's similar to dangerous sounds in the wild like a crack of a tree or a rock hitting a rock. It's the nearest articulable sound to something dangerous.

questions.question: If you put your elbows on the table, close your eyes and rest your eyes in the palm of your hands, why do you see colours and shapes?

answers.answer: You see weird kind of images and lights almost. I need to find out.

There are lots of really delicate nerves in your eyes. When your eyes are open, they react to light. But when you press on your eyes, you mechanically press on them, and that stimulates them to go off even though they're not getting any light coming in. They start sending information to your brain to say you're seeing something, but there isn't really anything there. So you see weird stuff that your brain just makes up and puts there.

questions.question: Why is there a child safety cap on children's vitamin sweets and not alcoholic drinks?

answers.answer: Because children's vitamins might be kept in the bathroom cupboard, somewhere children could realistically get hold of them. But parents don't leave alcohol where children might get hold of it. It would be too expensive to put children's safety caps on bottles. I don't know is the short answer. I shall try and find out for you.

questions.question: Why is blowing a raspberry called blowing a raspberry?

answers.answer: I don't know. I don't know.
It's Cockney rhyming slang. Raspberry tart rhymes with another term for breaking wind - fart.

questions.question: Why do you get freckles?

answers.answer: If you're in the sunshine and you sometimes go brown, the chemical in your skin called melanin makes all of your skin go brown. A freckle is like a deposit of melanin that is there anyway. Usually you get more freckles in the sun. So it's like a suntan when all the skin is equally bringing the melanin to the surface, but a freckle is a little concentration of the chemical called melanin.

questions.question: Why does light not travel through walls, but radio waves do?

answers.answer: I haven't got a clue. That's the sort of question I'd expect from a university student.

Light waves are in the middle of the electromagnetic spectrum. Radio waves are at the opposite end with long wavelength, low frequency, and low energy. Gamma rays are high wavelength, high frequency, high energy. Because of those properties, gamma rays have sufficient energy to penetrate the molecular structure of a wall, whereas visible light doesn't. But if your wall was glass, the wavelength and frequency of visible light does pass through. It's all to do with energy, wavelength, and frequency interacting with the molecular structure of the wall.

questions.question: Where does helium come from?

answers.answer: Last time I had some helium, it came out of a canister.

Helium is made in stars. When two hydrogen nuclei combine, that creates a helium atom because it has the right number of protons and neutrons. Then some star a long time ago exploded in a supernova, and that caused the helium within it to be spread far throughout our galaxy. When Earth formed around the sun, it took on this helium from the supernova, which became part of Earth's crust. That's how we dig it up and get it today.

questions.question: When lightning strikes the sea, why doesn't everything in the sea die?

answers.answer: There is still quite a lot of stuff in the sea, and lightning must have struck it quite a lot of times, so it's highly unlikely that everything in the sea dies whenever it gets struck.

As the lightning strikes the water, the energy slowly diffuses, so it becomes less and less powerful the more it spreads out. That's why only the sea creatures right where the lightning struck get injured. It's like having a huge piece of toast but only a small amount of butter - by the time you've spread that little bit of butter all over, you can't taste it anywhere. There's barely any once it's spread out.

questions.question: If two people taste something, do they taste it in the same way? How could we ever know?

answers.answer: That's a brilliant question. We could be here all day. I shall find out for you. It's all about how your neurons fire up. Everybody's brain is wired up differently. You can't claim that everybody sees green the same or blue the same in the same way that you can't claim everybody tastes things the same, because it all depends on how your neurons fire up.

questions.question: Has the lockdown helped improve climate change?

answers.answer: Pollution has gone down a lot because there have been fewer cars and a lot less planes. But I don't think anybody knows whether anything permanent would have happened via this temporary change. And we don't know for a couple of years whether it's going to change our behaviours.

questions.question: Why do judges wear wigs?

answers.answer: It's to do with a uniform so that you know the judge is not just a person but the embodiment of the law. I kind of know this but it's quite hard to explain.

It was derived from anonymity. It was part of a larger uniform and the wig has just become a mainstay. So that you couldn't identify a judge outside of the courtroom and maybe wreak revenge for the heavy sentences they'd handed down to you or your favourite uncle.

questions.question: Why do snakes have forked tongues?

answers.answer: I haven't got a clue, mate. I shall try and find out for you.

They flick their tongues out to sense the world around them - up and down, left and right. They need forked tongues to sense left and right as well as top and bottom. If there was a delicious snack around the corner, they wouldn't know whether it was around the left corner or the right corner unless they had two separate bits of tongue to tell them.

questions.question: Why is cotton wool called cotton wool if it's 100% cotton and 0% wool?

answers.answer: It looks like a tiny sheep. If you imagined an enormous load of cotton wool with four little legs poking out the bottom, it would look like a sheep.

Cotton isn't native to Europe. For hundreds of years, Europeans had no idea what it was but knew it looked like wool, so people thought it was just wool that grows on a plant. The Germans called it 'tree wool' and many people genuinely thought little sheep and lambs grew on trees in India. There are old 12th century pictures of cotton plants with sheep growing out of them.

questions.question: Why does alcohol make you drunk?

answers.answer: You have to understand the blood-brain barrier first. Alcohol (ethanol) passes through the blood-brain barrier into the bloodstream where it interferes with neurotransmitters, slowing down your system reactions and making you drunk. Ethanol shakes up your neurotransmitters - your aerial - so your inhibitions are reduced, motor skills compromised, speech slurred, vision cloudy, and you might laugh uproariously at things that aren't very funny.

questions.question: Why do wind turbines have three blades?

answers.answer: They made turbines with one blade, then two, then three, then four, then five blades and just watched which one went faster.

If you have too many blades, the disturbances from the tips cause the other blades to be less efficient. With four blades, the wake hasn't had enough time to dissipate before you get to the next blade. Three blades is the optimum for efficiency.

questions.question: The Conservative Party nickname is the Tories. Why is that?

answers.answer: It was originally used as a derogatory term. They were strong supporters of James II's claim to the throne and were called 'abhorers' through legislation in Parliament. They were extreme monarchists and parliamentary opponents to the Whigs. The term had connotations of Papists and outlaws, and it became shortened to Tory.
The origin of the word Tory is from Ireland and it means bandit, outlaw or brigand. It's from the Scots Gaelic word 'Toraid' (T-O-R-A-I-D).

questions.question: If you leave paddling pool water in the pool for too long, it grows algae. Can this happen to a bath?

answers.answer: I think it's the sunlight that causes the algae. It would only happen in your bath if you carried your bath into the back garden, which would be very difficult to do.

It's the same reason you don't get algae in swimming pools - they have chlorine filtration systems. You can get a little flotation device with chlorine tablets that kills all the bacteria. For a chemical-free lifestyle, use silver hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), which is water-based and environmentally friendly while killing bacteria.

questions.question: If Cinderella's shoe fitted perfectly, how come it fell off?

answers.answer: Glass is really slippery. When Cinderella danced enthusiastically with Prince Charming for hours, her feet got sweaty. Sweat is a liquid, making her feet slippy. Glass is slippy. If you licked your finger and ran it down a window, it would be more slippy than when dry. Slippy feet, glass slipper, slips off.

questions.question: Why do we sleep with our eyes shut? And why do we dream?

answers.answer: Dreams are to do with emotional processing. Studies showed people who slept after seeing distressing images found them less distressing when re-shown, while the awake group didn't. The brain processes emotions through dreams, and brain scans show people who dream process images better and feel them less emotional the second time.

When we blink, there's a liquid that goes over our eyes and renews them, keeping them from drying out. If you had your eyes open all night, you'd have a problem with them drying out. When you sleep, your whole body goes through a repair process, and having that protective covering also helps with the repairing process.

questions.question: Why are oranges in segments?

answers.answer: It probably has something to do with spreading the pips, spreading the seeds around.

Every fruit has evolved to optimise reproduction for the plant producing it. The outer skin of an orange is bitter so animals won't bite into it - they'll take the skin off. The segments optimise the chance of reproduction by spreading seeds across the widest area. One cherry equals one potential cherry tree. One orange equals ten potential orange trees because each segment contains a seed. The bitter outer layer ensures primates with opposed thumbs remove it, and humans then spread the seeds through soil when the fruit passes through.

questions.question: Why would you get sucked into a black hole?

answers.answer: It might be like a giant plug hole in the bath - when the water starts going round, it goes down.

A black hole has an incredible mass and therefore a huge gravitational field. Once you pass the event horizon - the outer limit - nothing can get out. Heavy stuff does attract things, due to Newton's gravitational constant. If the mass is absolutely huge (roughly 18-20 orders of magnitude greater than our sun), you will be attracted to it. They're very large objects and because they are so large, they will draw other objects to themselves.

questions.question: Do nettle stings hurt animals?

answers.answer: I'd be surprised if they didn't, because they probably evolved the sting to stop themselves being eaten by animals.

Yes - my dog was stung by nettles at the back of my mum's garden. Her whole body was squirming, she was terrified. I took her to the vets and she was on steroids for a week. When we get stung by nettles we feel it in a certain area, but for the dog it was like that through her whole body. The stings must exist to stop animals getting among them or eating them.

questions.question: Why are queen ants usually darker than worker ants?
If the coronavirus is taking over all the news in the UK then what's happening with Brexit?

answers.answer: On a scale of one to ten, where one is good and ten is bad, Brexit is going worse than ten.

questions.question: Why do we eat popcorn when we watch films?

answers.answer: It stems back to the introduction of television in America. Once television came in, people were no longer going to the cinema for news reels. So cinemas had to find a way of making cinema more of an experience to attract people in, so they'd start selling snacks. Popcorn was cheap. It also coincided with the Paramount decision in America that meant they could show fewer films, so they needed to offer something that added to the experience.

questions.question: When my dog comes to cuddle me, he buries his head and hides his face. Why?

answers.answer: It's a submissive gesture that shows a lot of trust. When a dog puts its head down and nuzzles right into you, it's not challenging at all. Its teeth are away, it's not looking at you, it's saying 'I trust you, you're not going to hurt me, you're the boss.' It also exposes the neck, which is a dangerous position, so the fact the dog will do it shows how much it trusts you. The circling before settling down is because they're establishing there are no threats nearby. When they tuck their head in and curl up to sleep, it's a central heating system - hot air from their nose gets trapped underneath their body and keeps them warm.

questions.question: Why do some viruses last longer than others?

answers.answer: Everybody has an immune system which consists of different antibodies and white blood cells. Each person's immune system is different, so some may be stronger than others and fight off a virus quicker. The speed with which you fight off a virus will have a lot to do with what's going on inside your body rather than just what's going on inside the virus. But the virus also matters because the stronger the virus, the harder for your body to fight it.

questions.question: If cars and ships are female, do buildings have genders?

answers.answer: No, buildings don't have genders. Ships are called 'she' because in the 18th century when ships came into power, it was a very superstitious environment, so they thought if you take care of the ship, she will take care of you, like a woman at that time. And it takes an experienced man to handle a ship.

questions.question: How were magnets discovered?

answers.answer: The first magnets weren't invented but discovered. The first magnet recorded was accredited to the Greeks. It's from a mineral called magnetis which is iron hydroxide, and it's formed naturally around volcanic areas. There was a story about a philosopher, scientist, and shepherd herding his sheep who had nails in his shoes that magically stuck to a rock. He named the mineral magnetis, and from then on they made compasses, with Vikings being among the first to use them. This would have been somewhere between 500 and 1500 years BC.

questions.question: Who decides what to call new roads?

answers.answer: Each council, district council, will have a street name and numbering department, and they will work with the developer of a new estate on what that should be called. It's then sent down to the parish council for their comment, and if everyone is in agreement, that's what they're called. You can lobby or petition to have someone commemorated with a street name. Unfortunately, you're not allowed to name someone who is still alive.

questions.question: Why do record players have two speeds - 45 and 33 and a third revolutions per minute?

answers.answer: It was an improvement in technology and was all about the number of slots in the grooves and the improvement in needles and so on. The fastest speed with smaller discs may have been about the advent of seven-inch records as opposed to albums which existed before. It was about the number of slots in each groove and the ability of needles to reproduce that sound through the amplifier or speaker. Almost by trial and error they came up with the optimum speeds. The size of the groove would determine the speed of the RPM - you could pack more into a faster moving speed than into a slower moving one because of the technology of molding.

questions.question: If I hit myself hard and it hurts, would I be weak or strong?

answers.answer: This is a philosophical paradox. It's similar to the question 'could God create a mountain that was so heavy he couldn't lift it?' These are questions that have plagued philosophers and theologians for centuries. Essentially there isn't an answer because if she hit herself hard and it hurt, she could say she was weak, but if she hit herself hard and it didn't hurt, she could say she was strong - but she can't do both at the same time. It's a way of thinking about logic and questions that don't have answers. Also, 'strong' and 'weak' are subjective judgments, not objective measurements, so there are too many variables.

questions.question: What triggers a phobia?

answers.answer: Sometimes it's as simple as something very traumatic happening to somebody - it's so scary they become scared of that thing forever. But other phobias, like fears of spiders, snakes, rats - these are explained by evolutionary psychology. Before we were fully human, back in our evolutionary history, we had to be frightened of certain things to protect ourselves and stay alive. We would instinctively fear a snake because we don't know if it's venomous, a rat might have bubonic plague, a spider could be venomous. Our instincts would tell us to run the other way and not touch it. Some phobias are learned behavior (like balloons and clowns), but others hark back to our ancestral survival instincts.

questions.question: Why do moulds appear?

answers.answer: There are cells in our skin called melanocytes and they're the ones that give us a suntan. When we get exposed to UV light or sunlight, wherever those cells are really clumped together in a very small space, that turns into a freckle or a mole. It gets a lot darker and grows a lot faster than it would in the rest of our skin. A mole is raised while a freckle is flat. It's the same thing that makes you get a suntan, but the relevant chemical concentrates in tiny little spots rather than spreading equally all over your skin.

questions.question: Do animals that have fur get split ends?

answers.answer: No, I don't think they do because I don't think fur is made out of the same stuff as hair, but you're probably thinking this blokes not really clever enough to answer this question.
Some animals shed and they have shorter hair than us. So, they don't have split ends. But if they do shed, then they can have split ends. Dogs can have split ends if they don't shed.

questions.question: How come when you tickle yourself, you don't laugh when other people tickle you, you do laugh?

answers.answer: It is not possible to tickle yourself. Yes, a part of your brain warns the rest of the brain that you're about to tickle yourself, so your brain ignores the resulting sensation.

questions.question: My mom and her sister and her friends speak a secret language called other guys where they add other gov to vowels. Where did this originate from?

answers.answer: It's called back slang. It apparently came from the Victorian times and market traders used to make up this language so they could talk behind their customers' backs and pass on lower grade items to their customers.

questions.question: How do we know that cavemen couldn't speak? How do we know that?

answers.answer: George, who was eight, was asking how we know cavemen couldn't talk. As we understand it, it seems fairly uncontroversial that they could speak. There used to be a theory that Neanderthals couldn't, just because of the shape of their voice box, but as far as I understand it, that has also been disproved as well. There's no reasonable doubt that they could definitely make a range of sounds.

questions.question: Why is it when bees sting they die but when wasps sting they stay alive?

answers.answer: A bee leaves its sting inside you. A bee's sting is used very rarely and once the sting has been stung it stays in you and they can't survive without it. With a wasp it's more like a poisonous bite.

The answer is that a bee sting has a barb, and a wasp sting doesn't. Both are like a hypodermic needle coming out their rear end. Both squirt poison into you through the hypodermic. But the barb means the bee can't get it out again, so it flies off leaving its sting and quite a bit of its inside behind. There's a little muscle in the bee sting that keeps pumping while it's in your skin, so the venom keeps pumping into your bloodstream unless you scrape it off with a fingernail or hive tool rather than pulling it out which squeezes more venom in. The bee sting probably evolved before mammals evolved - they evolved to sting other insects. A worker bee is sterile so it doesn't care about its own life, the hive is the organism. The queen bee has a sting just like the worker but it doesn't have a barb because the only thing a queen bee will sting is another queen bee.

questions.question: Why do we brush your teeth with cold water and not hot?

answers.answer: In the olden days, the water that was hot was kept in a tank and the water that was cold came in normally through the pipes. The water in the hot tank wasn't necessarily drinkable because it would hang around for quite a long time and stuff might get into the hot water tank that meant it was all right to wash your face with but you wouldn't want to drink it. These days the water comes in through the same pipes and gets heated up on its way into the house, so you probably could brush your teeth with hot water, but we all got into the habit of brushing with cold water because there was a possibility that the hot water wasn't very healthy.

questions.question: Do animals cry when they're sad?

answers.answer: Darwin thought that emotion could be shown in either the face or the voice. There's an evolutionary aspect to showing emotion in the voice. Yes, definitely animals do cry - any of them that have an emotional connection to something. I'm thinking of puppy whining - that's sort of a vocal connection to emotion going back to that evolutionary aspect.

questions.question: How did the idea for people putting rainbows in their windows for NHS workers come about?

answers.answer: It was a way of making sure we all look forward. The campaign was announced on TV and the slogan behind it was 'After a storm comes a rainbow.' The One Show was asking kids to draw rainbows to put in their windows.

questions.question: In India every morning in school they sing the national anthem. Why in UK schools do we not get taught the national anthem?

answers.answer: Most people don't believe in God or the monarchy, so they feel they don't want to sing praising either one of those. There was previously a line in the anthem saying 'we will crush the rebellious Scots' and many people feel, especially Scots, they feel offended by it.

questions.question: The hair on your arms, your legs, and your head continues to grow, but why do your eyelashes not grow at the same rate?

answers.answer: I don't think there's a difference. Usually the answer to questions like this is that the hairs fall out, and then new ones grow. So it's not a question of them not growing, it's a question of them being replaced.

All follicles are genetically programmed to only ever grow to a certain length. So even though it's all the same material on your head, on your arm, on your eyelashes and so on, eyelashes will only ever grow to a certain length. Then they go into a dormant bit and then they fall out. The biological principle is actually the same apart from head hair - head hair doesn't have a follicular shelf life but it would eventually stop growing at a given length when it reached its genetically predisposed length.

questions.question: How deep can a meerkat dig?

answers.answer: A meerkat can dig 6.5 feet deep. This was explained in a National Geographic documentary.

questions.question: If you are in international waters, in a boat, and you come across an unclaimed island, would you then be able to claim it as yours?

answers.caller: Oliver on an island in Stafford
answers.answer: Yes, if they're in international waters, they could claim it. There's an example of Surtsey off Iceland, a volcanic island discovered by fishermen where the French press tried to claim it for France, but it was within Icelandic boundaries so went to Iceland. If it was genuinely in international waters, Charlie could keep it.

questions.question: If you've been blind since you were born and you've never seen anything, could you see in your dreams?

answers.answer: Her brother has been blind since birth. He dreams about music, not pictures. He doesn't have an understanding of what pictures are. When he was younger, he had nightmares about music being out of tune or performing in a band with things going wrong. They dream with the senses they have, not the sense they don't have.

questions.question: Why don't animals wear glasses? Do they not have eyesight problems? Or do wildlife zookeepers not care to help them?

answers.answer: Animals can't tell you what's wrong with their eyes. They can't look at a chart and read letters. You could measure their eyes with something like an electroretinogram, but why would you do that for every animal?

Different species see differently. Hamsters are notoriously short-sighted. Dogs rely more on smell than vision. Many animals don't see in color because they don't have the right cells in the retina. Cataract surgery is done on animals—racehorses, tigers, dogs. They can remove lenses and replace them or use temporary contact lenses for eye injuries.

questions.question: Why does your skin get wrinkly in the water after your bath?

answers.answer: The answer is osmosis. Water molecules are smaller than solute molecules and move through semi-permeable membranes more easily. Water moves into skin cells because the concentration inside is greater than outside. The dead skin cells on the surface swell and they don't swell uniformly, causing wrinkles rather than uniform inflation.

The previous answer was the old received wisdom. Actually, it's your nerves reacting to the water that makes your skin go wrinkly. One reason we think this happens is so you can swim better or have better grip underwater. Evidence: people with nerve damage in one hand only get wrinkles in the other hand when placed in water. It's an evolutionary adaptation that improved our ability to get hold of things underwater or improved swimming abilities.

questions.question: What's the difference between a disease and a virus?

answers.answer: Disease describes what's happening in the body. A virus is the infective agent that causes the disease. With coronavirus, the virus is called SARS-CoV-2 and the disease is COVID-19 (Coronavirus Disease discovered in 2019). A virus is usually genetic material wrapped in protein and fat. Diseases can also be caused by bacteria, yeasts, and fungi. The virus is the cause, the disease is the effect on the body.

questions.question: Why do people have different eye colours? Why don't we just all have the same coloured eyes?

answers.answer: It's about melanin. When we're born, we have a certain amount of melanin in our body. If you're born with very little melanin, you'll have blonde hair and blue eyes. If you're born with lots of melanin, you'll have dark brown hair and dark eyes. The more melanin you've got, the darker your skin will be too.

questions.question: I was banking a cheque online and had to photograph the front of the cheque. Why do I need to photograph the back of the cheque, which is blank?

answers.answer: Some cheques have got stuff on the back of them. Not all cheques are blank on the back.

Cheques can be open or closed. A closed cheque has two vertical lines in the payee and amount section. An open cheque can be endorsed from the payee to the person cashing it, and that endorsement takes place on the back. Banks require pictures of all backs of cheques to avoid the risk of missing information even when blank.

questions.question: Who taught the first teacher?

answers.answer: It might have been Thales of Miletus, a Greek pre-Socratic philosopher, who may have taught Pythagoras. Pythagoras would have called him his teacher, and then Pythagoras came up with most of his stuff himself and decided to pass it on.

questions.question: Why don't small flying insects get knocked out when it's raining?

answers.answer: Small flying insects like gnats have adapted to moist environments. Particularly mosquitoes—if they've adapted to moist environments they can normally fly in the rain. Their bodies are adapted to work well in these conditions, including hairs on their body.

questions.question: How can a baby survive in its amniotic fluid for nine months? Why is it that a baby can breathe underwater after being born?

answers.answer: The most amazing organ humans produce is the placenta. It's attached to the inside of the mother's womb and connected to the baby through the umbilical cord at the tummy button. Through this, the baby gets oxygen from the mother's blood system and gets rid of carbon dioxide. The amniotic fluid doesn't carry oxygen—it mainly protects the baby.

questions.question: How does stripy toothpaste get in its tube and stay stripy when it comes out?

answers.answer: The bulk of the toothpaste is white, and in the nozzle there are some little ridges with colored dye. As you squeeze it, the red dye goes into the toothpaste or sits on the surface. If you chopped the tube in half, it would be white inside at the bottom.

When the toothpaste is made, it's made out of white and the other colours in different tubes/nozzles. When it's pumped into the tube, because of the viscosity, it all sticks together. The stripes run from top to bottom - you can see this with pump toothpaste.

questions.question: If two bees from different hives land on the same flower, do they fight over pollen?

answers.answer: No, they don't fight. All bees are docile away from their hives or nests. If a bee sees another bee on a flower, it moves on to find another flower. They won't fight over such a tiny space when there's always another flower nearby.

questions.question: Can you see cold-blooded animals through infrared cameras?

answers.answer: Yes, cold-blooded animals can be picked up on infrared cameras assuming the ambient air temperature is a certain height. Cold-blooded doesn't mean cold creature. Their body temperature is controlled by their surroundings, so their bodies would still show up on infrared.

questions.question: What is the first board game ever made?

answers.answer: The oldest board game is a Viking/Norwegian game called Tafel. It's very similar to chess. (This was later found to be incorrect)
Senet is the oldest known board game - an ancient Egyptian board game from about 3000 BC. It's a three by six tiled game. It looks like a combination of chess and checkers with counters on a board.

questions.question: Why do tins of food have ridges in them?

answers.answer: The ridges are there to keep the cans stronger and give them rigidity. If you had smooth, plain cans they would be very flimsy.

questions.question: Who decided to think of a 24-hour clock? Why 24 hours divided into 60 minutes, and who came up with saying 1300 hours for 1pm?
Do stars grow as you get older?

answers.answer: Stars don't grow in terms of mass, but they do grow hugely in size as they get older. Powered by fusion in the core, our sun has been stably fusing hydrogen for 4.5 billion years. In about 4.5 billion years, when hydrogen runs low, the core contracts and heats up, pushing outer layers massively out into space. The sun will swell to engulf Venus, Mercury and possibly Earth. Eventually the outer layers drift away as a nebula, leaving a white dwarf.

questions.question: Is the coronavirus in space?

answers.caller: Patrick (biology teacher, studied viruses at university)
answers.answer: No, there wouldn't be any viable virus in space. As virus particles drift up through the atmosphere, they're exposed to increasing ultraviolet radiation, which destroys nucleic acids (that's why we get skin cancer from UV). The virus has a fatty coat rather than a protein coat, making it quite unstable. Even if you could get it into space avoiding UV, it wouldn't survive anyway.

questions.question: How does your body know to stop your bones from growing? Why do bones stop growing?

answers.answer: There are two bones in each hand. As you grow, they slowly join together. Once those two bones touch/fuse, your body stops growing. (James notes this raises a chicken-and-egg question about whether bones meet because growth stops, or growth stops because bones meet.)

questions.question: Do fish drink water? I know they're surrounded by water but they don't have a system like us to drink water.

answers.answer: Fish absorb water via a semi-permeable membrane using osmosis. (James seemed uncertain about this answer and there was some confusion during the call.)

questions.question: We all speak different languages around the world, but yet we all laugh the same. Like, is it just bred into us or... I just don't understand how we all, no matter what, everyone seems to laugh the same around the world.

answers.answer: Babies laugh before they've even got language. So it's just something that we naturally do. Because laughter is in place before language, there is clearly no case for arguing that laughter is linked to language.

Laughter is not learned behavior. Babies laugh naturally. On epigenetics - if you stress a mouse and make it smell lavender, then breed it, two generations later the mouse born will have a negative reaction to lavender. That's genetic inheritance passed on because genes get turned on and off.

questions.question: She swims under the water really easily, but struggles to swim normally. But how do we learn to float? Like, what's the how? Who? How?

answers.answer: Short answer is you don't learn to float. It's determined by the way your weight and your composition, whether your bone or fat, or muscle, etc. The size of your lungs in terms of your body composition. So as you float, your body's pressing down on the water and the water presses back, pushing you up. So you're not learning to do anything. It's your body composition that determines how high you float in the water. Practice is in terms of compensating for your natural buoyancy. If you just relax, you will float to the surface. When you're swimming underwater, you don't need to worry about buoyancy. Whereas when you're swimming on the water, you've got to maintain that buoyancy, which involves a redistribution of various variables. Everybody floats because when you're unconscious, you float as well. Even kids have different composition and two different humans are going to be different levels of floatiness.

questions.question: Why is garlic in every single cuisine you can possibly think of?

answers.answer: Because it's so delicious and it's so easy to grow.

The garlic was originally sent out around the world from wherever they started from, as medicinal and as a preservative. They were sent out in different types of food, and people who then got it in a particular country said 'oh, this tastes nice' and decided to grow it and put it in part of their cuisine. For example, vindaloo is an Indian dish but it's actually Portuguese. The Portuguese sailors who went to India used wine turned to vinegar, and they put chicken meat in there with garlic as a preservative. And 'aloo' is garlic in Portuguese. That formed the dish vindaloo. The bottom line is it's so flavoursome and so easy to grow. As soon as people started travelling, garlic would have been a really obvious thing to travel with because it is such a useful preservative. When they got it in whatever country they exported this food with the preservative, they liked the taste of it and thought it was so easy to grow, so they decided to grow it and put it in part of their cuisine.

questions.question: Why do bagels have to have holes in them? Do they have to have a hole in to be a proper bagel?

answers.answer: So they cook evenly. (From Jamie Oliver's recipe book)

Back in the old country, back in Poland or East Germany or wherever it was, they used to be sold in markets individually and the people that carried them around carried them around either on sticks or on strings. It was the best way of dispensing them. Same with pretzels - they've got holes in so you can string them on something for ease of carriage. Bagels is basically pop-up food, street food.

questions.question: Why can't I throw a successful punch in my dreams?

answers.answer: When we dream we go through different stages of sleep - we start off light sleep, go down two stages to deep sleep, then when we come up again to light sleep it's called REM sleep and that's when we've been shown through various studies that we dream. When we dream we do all sorts of things connected to the day we've had and plans ahead of us, which often involves actions. If we lived out all those actions we'd get ourselves into a bunch of rubbish. So people can drive a car in their dreams and feel like they are, but when you try to do something in a dream like a punch, your arms and legs don't move. You are effectively paralyzed. The part of the brain that is controlling physical movement, feelings and balance is effectively paralyzing us so we don't all go out and physically live out our dreams and punch people.

When you're asleep and dreaming, your mind does all sorts of wonderful things, your imagination runs wild. But it's still connected to your nervous system, so it responds to sensations you're feeling in real life. If you're really thirsty in real life, you're thirsty in your dream and you try to quench that thirst. The reason you can drive in your dream and it feels like you're actually driving is the sensations of driving - pressure on your bum and back and maybe a bit on your hands, movement. It's not hard to replicate when you're sleeping. But if you're running in your dream, the sensation is your feet impacting the floor, feeling that resistance. If you're running in a dream, you're not getting that resistance against your feet. These are quite big sensations. The bigger and more powerful the physical sensation is in real life, the harder it is to replicate in a dream. If you were to punch in real life and not feel anything on your fist, it would feel weird, like you're not really punching. And it's the same in your dream.

questions.question: Why is it when you put halloumi in a frying pan or on a barbecue it doesn't melt? What is in it different from other cheeses?

answers.answer: It's going to have something to do with the relationships between proteins and carbohydrates and molecules.

answers.caller: Adam from Forest of Dean (cheese maker)
answers.answer: Halloumi is already cooked. That's why it doesn't melt. Same as Indian cheese paneer - when it's already in the cooking process, it doesn't melt. So you get your milk, you warm it up, you add your rennet, and then it splits the curds and whey. You get your curds, then you press them, then you cut them, then you bring your whey back up to temperature, just below boiling point. You put your curds back in, and after about 20 minutes it floats to the top and it's cooked. Then you cool it, slice it, and away you go. So the point is it's already a cooked cheese. When you cook it, you just warm it through. If you put it on a really low heat for a really long time, it will actually melt. But just a really hot pan seals the outside.
