questions.question: Why do we have a pair of shorts, a pair of trousers, a pair of pants, but we don't have a pair of jumpers? We don't have a pair of cardigans?

answers.answer: Originally you would have had two. This is what a codpiece was for. So you'd have worn two stockings or two leg coverings, and then you'd have had another middle bit that was the third item of clothing, and from that all else has evolved. Think of stockings - you have a pair of stockings, and then the language evolved with the evolution of the clothing. So a pair of stockings becomes a pair of tights, despite the fact that you've only got one item in your hands. Upper body wear has never involved separate sleeves with a linking middle piece.

questions.question: How do police operations get their name? For example, every operation has a name like Operation Swordfish. Who decided?

answers.answer: There are two different ways. If it's a small local operation, the local police officers will come up with the name. I once got told I couldn't call a series of thefts from McDonald's Operation Hamburglar. But nationally, like Operation Bumblebee to prevent causing any kind of offence, they're completely random names that are picked out of a book. There's like a list of operational names centrally. They've all been centrally approved and then you just go through it and pick the next one along. It's like hurricanes - you just pick the next name. So it doesn't cause any offence to anybody. If it's local, you pick it yourselves, although with a few caveats on suitability. If it's national, it comes out of a central register.

questions.question: Who first decided that gold was valuable? When those people went up to Alaska and pulled that yellow metal out of the ground, who decided it was valuable?
Commercial aircraft, why does the pilot always sit on the left?

answers.answer: 85% to 90% of people are right-handed. Engine management controls and any instruments that need adjusting would be on the right-hand side, purely for ease. You've got all your gubbins in the middle, so your right hand is going to be favoured, so you'd sit on the left.

When you apply power to the aircraft on the runway, because of the down-going blade being from past the centre axis, aircraft blades spin clockwise so the nose tends to yaw to the left so you apply right rudder. In the old days, you would turn left in traffic patterns because it's easier to turn left. With multi-engine piston aircraft, the critical engine is the left-hand engine because the right-hand engine produces more torque, so it turns the aircraft to the left. Historically, from navigation, if you were to follow a road or river, before GPS, you are supposed to fly on the right-hand side keeping the feature to the left.

questions.question: How do weather forecasters predict the gustiness? They can predict wind levels accurately but how do they predict gust levels?

answers.answer: As a basic rule of thumb, you'd take the mean wind speeds and double it for the gusts. So if it's going to be 20 mile an hour sustained winds, you'd expect about 40 mile an hour gusts. It's a bit more complicated than that though. It depends how buoyant the air is as well. The more unstable the air, the faster the air rises under low pressure and you get stronger gusts. Exposed areas and higher ground tend to see higher gusts than central London would just because it's a lot more open and the air can move more freely.

questions.question: Why does the white ball go down a different hole on a pool table and get returned to the players, while coloured balls are retained?

answers.answer: All the object balls are two inches in diameter. The white ball is one and seven-eighths inch. The balls go past a little gap and all the object balls go across the gap while the white ball falls down there. It's like a little pit and it comes out the different end.

questions.question: Why is dog wee always really yellow regardless of how hydrated the dog is? My dog drinks loads but whenever it goes out for a wee, the wee is really yellow.

answers.answer: It's actually to do with dehydration. We might think our dogs are drinking enough water, but they're not. I would encourage people to take water out on walks. If their wee is still quite dark, it'd be down to their nutrition and the moisture content in that. If it is very, very dark, I would recommend vets because there could be an issue, albeit minor, with kidneys and red blood cell issues can affect the dog's urine, making it dark.

questions.question: Why do sportspeople after they miss put their hands on their head? They cover their faces, they cover their heads. Why that reaction?

answers.answer: There are two different reasons for both actions. The one behind the head is due to the fact that when you're a baby your mum cradles your head. So it's a natural reaction of support and comfort. The reason for the hands on the face is to hide your face due to embarrassment. Behind the head is a reflex comfort gesture that emulates being cuddled as a baby. The other one is shame-prompted hiding of face.

questions.question: On a motorbike with a sidecar, if I want to go to France, does the sidecar have to go on the left-hand side of the bike?
Why do boxers and wrestlers use belts and not trophies or another form of award? Most sports use trophies and cups but boxing and wrestling use belts.

answers.answer: The reason they don't have trophies when they wear belts is because they have gloves on, which are very difficult to remove at the end of a match. Therefore it's far easier to present them with a belt rather than a trophy. The belt just gets draped over their shoulder or they can bolt it around their waist. That just leached into wrestling, where they don't wear gloves.

questions.question: Most pubs now have modern high-speed hand dryers with a blue light. What is the blue light for?

answers.answer: They're UV lights and they sterilise and kill the germs.
It's not UV. It's to direct your hands into the area of maximum drying capability. It just shows you where your hand should be to get the best blow.
It's a guide light, it just shows you the maximum where your hand should be to get the best blow.

questions.question: Why are they called midwives? Is 'mid' like a German word for 'with'?

answers.answer: Mid is like the German word for with.

It's from Old English or Middle English. 'Mid' means 'with' and 'wife' means 'woman'. So it just means 'with the woman'. The German word for 'with' is 'mit'. This makes a mockery of the idea that men can't be midwives because it doesn't refer to the gender of the person - it refers to the gender of the person that they're 'mit' or 'with'.

questions.question: Where did we get the idea from that the moon is made of cheese?
What is the difference between a concerto, a symphony, and a sonata?

answers.answer: A sonata is a piece that is typically played for one instrument, usually piano but doesn't have to be. A symphony is a work composed for the whole orchestra - violins, timpani, strings, brass, everything. A concerto is a piece for one instrument plus orchestra - a soloist plus orchestra. So symphony is orchestra only, sonata is soloist or soloist plus accompanist, and concerto is soloist plus full orchestra.

questions.question: Do we feel the pain more when it's cold?

answers.answer: I recognize what you described. It might be physiognomy or it might be a trick of the mind.

Anecdotally we know it is - people with chronic pain conditions say cold weather causes flare-ups. However, the evidence base or literature would suggest there's no link. My favourite theory is that cold weather makes people sad and that increases pain sensitivity. But there's no scientific evidence for it, just lots of people who believe it.

questions.question: What does best boy do on a film set?

answers.answer: I think it's a camera assistant or someone in charge of winding up the cables and stuff like that. Gaffer as well - you used to get gaffer on.
The best boy is the gaffer's assistant. The gaffer is the electrician, the chief electrician. Andy was a dolly grip, which means he pushed the camera along the track for tracking shots.

questions.question: Why in the United Kingdom do we no longer have national days of mourning? When was the last one?

answers.answer: I presume that we actually haven't lost anybody of sufficient significance. I'm sure that if we were to lose the Queen, we would have some sort of day of mourning.

questions.question: Why did my car windscreen freeze when all the house windows in the street didn't freeze?

answers.answer: The car was colder than the house. The house is insulated, the heating would have been on during the day, the bricks would have retained some heat. Do you have double glazing? Well, have you got double glazing in your car?

questions.question: Why are televisions not round?

answers.answer: I think it might be because film is rectangular. You record it on film, shine a light through a square bit of film to project it onto a square screen.

The simple answer is that because films are rectangular. The TV's always been catching up with the cinema technology. The further you go back, Charlie Chaplin movies were square formats, and the first TV sets were square. It's to do with the shape of film going through a projector or lens. Also, a rectangular picture is able to show you more things. Now it's become so normal that no one would want a round television. Victorian magic lanterns had round pictures.

questions.question: Why do police cars have giant numbers on the roof?

answers.answer: They're for identification if you're doing it from a camera or a copter. It's the same as the registration number.

Each number represents the force - 41 would be Hertfordshire. Then there's another number to identify the car. There are also letters which I think reflect the registration plate. If police cars go cross-border, they can be tracked on the helicopter.

questions.question: Why are people from Holland known as Dutch when people from other countries get their nationality names?

answers.answer: I think it's Deutsch. So we thought they were German. They said Deutsch, Dutch.

Holland was a term used from the 10th to the 17th century for a former region which consisted of South and North Holland. After the 17th century, Holland became a bigger trading nation and formed the Republic of the Netherlands.
Dutch and Deutsche as in Deutschland means nation. Old English.

questions.question: Do pre-talking babies in the babbling phase know what they're saying, or is it completely random?

answers.answer: The answer is yes and no. Sometimes she will be trying to articulate externally something that she understands internally, and sometimes she will just be babbling.

Babbling in itself doesn't represent any sort of words or meaning to the child because they're practising their movements in their mouth and lungs, moving their tongue to make sound and get that coordination going. But at ten months, they will start to make associations with their babble sound with things they mean. A tip is to show the child objects at eye level and say the word - like showing a dog and saying 'dog'. The child connects that babble into words as it develops.

questions.question: Where do birds go in a storm?

answers.answer: If you were a bird, you'd want to stay low and stay hidden. They're probably all in your hedge.

When storms come, the birds know beforehand. The farmer told me they go out the day before and collect extra food because they can tell it's coming. They hunker down in an evergreen hedge. You can see them - just all curled up in little balls in the hedges.

questions.question: How do satellites stay in orbit? What keeps them from floating off?

answers.answer: Once you're in orbit, you don't need any propulsion. That's how planets work. You might as well ask why the Earth stays in orbit around the Sun and doesn't just float off.

They actually do require some movement when they're in orbit to prevent them from falling out of the sky. They have their own fuel supply and use some sort of jet propulsion system. They do have to be decommissioned after a certain amount of time. Like Skylab.

questions.question: Why is the cabinet called the cabinet?

answers.answer: It's not as disappointing as Cobra, is it? Everyone thinks Cobra stands for something cool but it stands for Cabinet Office Briefing Room A. I don't know why it's called the cabinet.

It comes from the 16th century when they used to describe the cabinet council, which was used as a term of abuse saying it was a foreign habit. The idea was the previous council would be in a cabinet, which in those times was a small room rather than like a cabinet. It's a French word from the Italian cabineto.

questions.question: Why don't the palms of our hands get sunburned? At what point in human evolution did that occur?

answers.answer: Palms can get sunburned if exposed. The answer involves two parts: 1) Palms don't have melanocytes in the skin, which produce melanin that protects against sun. 2) Because of human posture - hands hang down facing our legs, so they're not usually exposed to the sun. If you lay on a sunbed with palms facing up, they would burn.

questions.question: Where does the universal recognition of little green men or aliens come from? Where did the inverted teardrop head with big eyes instantly recognised as an alien start?

answers.answer: The big head with big eyes stereotype came from Betty and Barney Hill, who were abducted in the late 1960s on their way home from Canada. They reported being taken up in a ship and described their captors as small with big heads and big eyes. The cultural meme adapted from there. The green element may come from Dan Dare comics featuring the Mekon - a green-skinned enemy with an enormous head - which predates the 1960s.

questions.question: Why do birds not crossbreed?

answers.answer: It's a myth that birds don't crossbreed at all - it happens when birds have very similar needs. Examples: white-headed duck has mated with ruddy duck (invasive species threatening the native one); Spanish sparrow has mated with common house sparrow. In falconry, merlins are mated with peregrine falcons to produce purlins. A house finch was bred with a canary. However, unlike dogs which are all the same species, birds are many different species, so you can't crossbreed across species boundaries like you can with dogs. A fox doesn't breed with a dog because they're different species.

questions.question: Can a farmer legally shoot me for stepping on his land?

answers.answer: No, this is not true. The only circumstances in which you can kill or shoot someone is in self-defense with a legally held firearm. Even then, it would be questionable. A farmer cannot shoot you for trespassing on his field. However, there is a separate legal proposition: if caught in bed with his wife, that could be considered a crime of passion (crime passionnelle) and might provide a defence.

questions.question: When will my body replace the blood I donated?

answers.answer: It depends what you want to know. Blood volume returns in 12 to 48 hours. However, blood is not just fluid - it's blood cells suspended in plasma. The plasma (fluid) comes back quickly, but the red blood cells take longer because your bone marrow has to produce new ones. This is why NHS Blood and Transfusion sets a time limit on how often you can donate - to allow red blood cells to replenish.

questions.caller: Mark (Radlet, on behalf of 9-year-old daughter Summer)
questions.question: What happens if the Queen is travelling somewhere and she needs the toilet?

answers.answer: For travel from north to south and east to west, there are designated stopping points at police stations where the Queen can rest and use facilities as needed. There's a massive police station near Wakefield with a big suite where they can stop - sometimes they land there in a helicopter, then get into a car. Your friend in the police told you this.

questions.question: Where does the saying 'dumb blonde' come from?
Why do I get a metallic taste in my mouth when a metal spoon scrapes against a metal bowl near my mouth?

answers.answer: The metallic taste is caused by an electrolytic action, similar to when a spoon is put in the mouth. However, the caller had clarified this happens when metal is near her mouth, not in contact - so this answer may not fully apply.

questions.question: Why were children in schools historically restricted and reprimanded for writing with their left hands?

answers.answer: In Roman culture, left-handedness was considered highly odd and unusual. The Latin word for left is 'sinister'. Through the spread of the Roman Empire and subsequently Catholicism, this association spread throughout Europe. It started as just being considered odd, then became associated with evil/wrongness over generations.

In historical times, people wrote with quills and fountain pens, dipping quills in inkwells. If you're left-handed, you drag your hand over what you've just written, smudging it. There were historical ways around this - left-handed people wrote from above.

questions.question: If all trees are that important to the world, why are they not all protected? Why every single tree?

answers.answer: It would be too hard to implement and the costs would outweigh the benefits. Using the Tube platform edge doors example - not all stations have them despite them saving lives because someone decided it wasn't worth the money. If we put protection orders on every tree, we'd need two million tree officers and prisons would be full from prosecuting everyone who chops them down.

questions.question: If no one turns up to the cinema, do they turn the film off?
Have any of the other 27 letters got a spelling?

answers.answer: Yes - W is spelled with a D (double-you starts with D), so W should be called 'double-u' but spelled with a D sound. Scott Balcony pointed this out on Twitter.

questions.question: Why do we cross our legs? Why is it more comfortable to contort our body rather than sit straight?

answers.answer: It's to cover delicate parts in socially difficult or challenging situations, similar to how men put hands in pockets and women cross arms. Manspreading is a subconscious way of saying 'come and have a go if you think you're hard enough'. Hands behind head and elbow waving is aggressive.

questions.question: Where does all the goose go? When you're in the supermarket, they sell goose fat in jars but I don't see any other product that contains goose meat. Where does the rest of the goose go?

answers.answer: Some geese are bred for foie gras - in fact, a lot of them. When they've gone past their use-by date, the geese are quite old. The roasted fat is saved because the fat is worth more than the goose meat. The meat is thrown away. Also, geese are used for feathers.

questions.question: Is there a reason why we nod our heads for yes and shake them for no? Is it universal, or are there cultures where the opposite applies?

answers.answer: There is definitely somewhere in the world where they nod their head for no and shake their head for yes.
It's Bulgaria that nod for no and shake the head for yes, which is confusing when you ask for a drink in a restaurant.

questions.question: Who was the first person to make up the word Brexit?

answers.answer: A bloke called Peter Wilding, who was chairman of British Influence and a specialist in EU law, coined the word Brexit. He was pro-Remaining. James mentioned wanting to speak to him about it.

questions.question: Why do we talk in our sleep? The other night I was apparently peeling potatoes on a bus, and my uncle Alan apparently builds bungalows in his sleep.

answers.answer: It's an extension of dreaming. The reason you were peeling potatoes on a bus is probably because you're worried about having enough money to buy food to feed the new baby. Your uncle Alan building bungalows is probably because he's terrified of stairs.

questions.question: Why did they change tennis balls from white to yellow at Wimbledon in 1986?

answers.answer: I think it's because colour television became more common, making it harder to track the white ball on a colour screen. I can't prove it, so I'll leave it on the board until someone comes with a better answer.

questions.answer_to_question: If no one turns up to the cinema, do they turn the film off?

answers.answer: Yes, we do turn off the projections when screens are empty. The lenses are very expensive, so to save them from breaking we just turn them off. It's all computerised now - there's no human projectionist. I once accidentally turned off the sound in a wrong screen while the film was still playing.

I worked in a cinema about 15 years ago and had the same conversation with my manager. He said we are contracted to show the film a certain amount of times, so it has to be shown even if no one's there. Something may have changed in the last 15 years.

questions.question: What would happen if the Queen committed a serious crime like murder? Is she above the law?

answers.answer: Historical precedent is unhelpful because monarchs used to kill people with impunity. James wonders if a medieval historian could prosecute Henry VIII retrospectively for killing Anne Boleyn.

answers.caller: Tom (City of London) - solicitor and constitutional buff
answers.answer: There's a doctrine called Sovereign Immunity which suggests the sovereign cannot be subject to criminal law. The waters have been muddied since we moved to constitutional monarchy - there's the Crown as government (which can be taken to court) versus the person of the Queen herself. Like the Trump/Mueller situation where the DOJ concluded a president can't be criminally charged while in office. The only historical example of a monarch being tried was Charles I in January 1649, but only after beating him in a civil war. It would be more of a political and constitutional question than a pure criminal legal question. Interestingly, murder is a common law offence defined as a killing 'under the king or queen's peace'.

questions.question: Why can some fish live in fresh water, some in salt water, but some can live in both?

answers.answer: Fish that live in both are called brackish water fish - they live in the part of a river closer to the sea where saltwater dilutes into fresh water.

There are two types of fish: stenohaline (can only live in one type of water) and euryhaline (can live in both). Stenohaline fish placed in different water have bodies with such a concentrated salt level from evolution that fresh water dilutes their bodies through osmosis, causing them to die within hours or days - similar to water poisoning in humans.

questions.question: What's the difference between grave robbery and archaeology? Is it archaeology if you didn't realise it was a grave?

answers.answer: If you're digging up a field and find remains you didn't know were there, that's not grave robbery. If there's a marked grave with a stone, that's grave robbery. If it's consecrated ground, it's grave robbery. If not consecrated, it's archaeology.

Grave robbing is done for profit while archaeology is done for research purposes or when remains are under threat from grave robbers. Archaeologists are looking for knowledge; grave robbers are looking for jewellery. Most archaeology doesn't involve digging people out of the ground anyway - it's more like using a nail brush to clean up a mosaic. Historical figures like Howard Carter were essentially tomb raiders before modern scientific archaeology developed.

questions.question: Why is Japanese knotweed so destructive to property?

answers.answer: The roots burrow through bricks and foundations, causing structural damage to buildings. If you've got Japanese knotweed in the vicinity and you're trying to get a mortgage, insurers won't cover you if they can see knotweed, which means you can't get a mortgage.

Japanese knotweed was bought by the Japanese who thought it was fast-growing bamboo. When it turned out to be just a weed they couldn't sell, they dumped it around railways - which is why houses near railways often have it. It grows incredibly quickly, gets everywhere including foundations, and is very hard to kill. No easy solution exists; specialist companies handle it but it's very expensive.

questions.question: How old is the water that comes out of the tap?

answers.answer: It's probably been drunk already seven or eight times by the time you're pouring it - it's gone through the sewage treatment places and come back round the water cycle. There's no such thing as new or old water.

There's no definite answer because water's recycled time and time again. Each molecule could be at a different stage in its process. Once cleaned and pushed out, it sits in tanks for weeks to months - always being turned over. Drinking water actually goes through more testing (about 7 tests) than bottled water (about 4 tests). You can't know the age of a glass of water with a number or even a calculation.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'cheesed off'?
Why do we always get on planes on the left-hand side?

answers.answer: Port out, starboard home - it's a throwback to how boats dock. Planes still use port and starboard terminology.

It's to do with how planes are designed. Airbus and Boeing generally design planes so cargo holds are on the right side. You board on the left, load cargo on the right, and refuel on the same side you board. So it's not about efficiency with multiple gangways - each side has a specific purpose. Air bridges are generally put on the left side for safety.

questions.question: Clarification on the plane boarding question

answers.answer: The port out/starboard home thing is partly true. Port is actually the left side and starboard is the right side (correcting James). The origin is from sailing to India - people with money would stay on the port (shady/cooler) side going out, and starboard side coming home. Also, you couldn't load planes on both sides because wings would clash - they need to be further apart, hence loading from one side.

questions.question: What happens to all the turkey legs from supermarket turkey crowns? Why can't you buy them anywhere except a butcher?

answers.answer: The leftover bits get cut up and go into processed products - tinned food, pies, and probably pet food. It's not special. Any turkey snack-based product uses the less desirable parts of the bird. Prime breast would be too expensive to waste on pies.

questions.question: Possible answer to 'cheesed off' origin

answers.answer: It might be to do with grating cheese - you're getting 'grated off' when something grates on you, like being cheesed off.

questions.question: Possible answer to 'cheesed off' origin

answers.answer: It's the opposite of saying 'cheese' when you smile for a photo. Cheesed off means you look sad rather than happy.

questions.question: If my trampoline, which I haven't pinned down, takes off in the wind and smashes through my neighbour's greenhouse or hurts somebody, would I be liable or prosecutable?

answers.caller: Jonathan (barrister in criminal and civil law)
answers.answer: Yes, he'd be civilly liable and would have to pay for any damage. The neighbours could pursue him for negligence for not securing it, or for nuisance, which is a tort where you can sue someone if something dangerous escapes from your land. Criminal liability is unlikely unless he specifically planned it on a windy day with intent to damage his neighbour's property.

questions.question: On the back of your debit card, you've got your last three digits. What about those other digits? What are those for? Are they not the last four digits of the card on the front?

answers.answer: They're the last four digits of the long number on the front. James checked his own card and confirmed they match.

questions.question: A bee landed on my windscreen while driving from Sheffield to Manchester over Woodhead and I took it all the way there. When I arrived, it flew off. What's going to happen to that bee? Will it try to find a hive in Manchester? Will it be homeless? Will it try to find its way back to Sheffield?

answers.answer: If the bee manages to find another colony of its own species - whether that's a beehive in someone's back garden or a naturally occurring colony - and if he's got something useful with him like nectar or pollen, they'll welcome him into their colony. It's not hard for a bee to find a colony. If he can't find one, he's in trouble. The worker bees are all female, so it could be a she-bee.
Worker bees are all female. The drones are essentially just love machines serving the queen.

questions.question: Modern TVs just go into standby mode when you turn them off. When I was a kid, you had to actually press a button on the TV to turn it completely off and my mum used to unplug it from the wall. Are modern TVs using a load more electricity because we can't actually turn them off?

answers.answer: All TVs have an on and off button on the back, but most are mounted on walls making it difficult to reach. Electricity usage on standby is minimal - about a quid a year. Keith had looked into this and confirmed it.

questions.question: Why does the Queen always look to the right on all of her coins?

answers.answer: Monarchs alternate left to right on coins so you can easily recognise whether it's a new coin or an old coin. Edward VIII was the exception because he was vain and thought he had a good side and a bad side, so he didn't want to be part of the alternation. So George VI faced left, the Queen faces right (alternating), and Charles would face left when he appears on coins. The questioner had it backwards - the Queen faces left, not right.

questions.question: Do dogs bruise? I've seen dogs bump into things all the time and I've never seen one bruise. Even on vet programmes with hairless dogs, I've never seen a bruised one.

answers.answer: Yes, dogs do bruise, but not like humans. The process is the same - blood coming out underneath the skin. The big difference is that dog skin (the epidermis) is much thicker than ours. Before you can see a bruise, you need a really major thump. When you do see bruising in dogs, it's usually pretty serious. There are certain parts of the body where the skin is thinner. Plus they're covered in fur so you can't see it immediately unless you shave the dog, which is not recommended. Dogs are hardier than us - we bruise more easily than dogs do.

questions.question: How do directors and film crews make babies cry on TV and in films? Is it not cruel for the child to be lying there screaming and crying while people are acting with lights overhead?

answers.answer: If you don't see the face of the baby, it's not a real baby - it's smoke and mirrors. It doesn't take long for a baby to cry in general. Usually when you see a baby crying, they're not necessarily filming when the baby is crying - the crying could be completely out of sequence. Babies spend most of their time crying anyway, so they just bring the baby in and hope for the best. For more sophisticated shots where you can see the baby's face and tears, they have loads of recordings of baby crying that they can put in as a soundtrack afterwards. It's mostly fake.

questions.question: What makes kissing so pleasurable?

answers.answer: It must be to do with nerve endings. There's a high concentration of nerve endings in the lips. When we eat we use the same area but it's not as pleasurable as kissing - unless it's a truffle. There's something special about kissing that eating can't match.

questions.question: If you were ordered in court to reveal how you voted at the last election, would you, on your oath, have to reveal it? Could a judge order you to answer the question?

answers.answer: You can't be compelled to reveal how you voted because there's no way of establishing whether you're telling the truth or not. Your conscience is the only measure. A judge could order you to answer the question, but they can't make you tell the truth - that's up to you. The secrecy of the ballot is protected.
A judge could find out how you voted because each ballot paper has a unique identification number on it, which is reported against your name when you collect your ballot.
I don't think that's legally allowed. I don't think you are legally permitted to establish how somebody voted, even if you could technically achieve it.

When a situation like this arises in court, the witness is treated as a hostile witness. The judge has discretion as to whether or not to compel the witness to give the evidence, but must also consider the impact on the trial and relevance of the evidence. The secrecy of the ballot is likely protected under human rights legislation.

questions.question: Why are pubs and drinking establishments always named after royal figures and limbs of royal figures?

answers.answer: It's about pictograms. In an era where literacy was rare and pubs were popular, they used recognizable pictures so people knew which pub they were entering. The Duke's head or Queen's arms would be instantly recognizable. Also, the population wasn't very mobile, so you'd know the local coat of arms because the family probably owned your house.

It goes back to the English Civil War. A pub would show its allegiance to either the parliamentarians or royalists. If they put the king's head up, it meant they wanted the king's head lopped off (parliamentarian). King's arms meant they supported the monarchy. Pubs often changed signs depending on who was in power.

questions.question: Will a spider ever give up on a web as a bad thing and move somewhere else to build another one? Not because it's blown away or damaged, but because it's not fit for purpose and not catching any flies.

answers.answer: Liked the question but didn't have a definitive answer. Shared an anecdote about a spider that kept spinning in a sealed metal bin with no chance of catching flies.

Spiders do give up on their webs, but it's not because they haven't caught flies. It's because the web has captured dew in the morning - that's how they drink. Indoors where there's no dew, they would never abandon a web just because it hasn't caught flies. They might move elsewhere and build a new web somewhere else, but they wouldn't abandon a web indoors.

But my logic is also sound - if a spider never catches any flies indoors, wouldn't it starve? It would just leave the web up but move somewhere else to build a new one. So they are abandoning a web because they can't catch enough flies.

questions.question: When you go to a loud music venue or a gig, why do your ears ring the next day? What is actually going on?

answers.answer: The ear does something to cope with the loud noise that then has a side effect or knock-on effect later, but admitted he didn't know the specifics.
Your ears ring after a concert because your ears are trying to repair the damage caused by the loud music. The ringing is your ear trying to repair itself by pumping blood to the damaged area.

questions.question: Do birds feel that weird sensation in their tummy when they plummet down through space very quickly, like we do?

answers.answer: Probably not, because they can fly. Humans need an evolutionary warning that they're falling at potentially dangerous speed because we can't fly. Birds don't need that warning.

Birds don't actually get that sensation if they can predict what's about to happen. They've evolved different methods of coping with their physical environment - they have acceleration sensors in the inner ear. If they have a surprise on the way, they get a little tickle, but if everything is as they predicted, they don't get any sensation. It's not necessary for them because they know what they've signed up for by dint of being birds.

questions.question: When was the first currency exchange rate set? When did someone calculate how much your money was worth in one currency when you held it in another?

answers.answer: Liked the question but admitted he didn't know. Noted the Bible mentions money lenders but that's money changing, not currency exchange.

The Knights Templar during the Crusades were the first international bank. If you had money held with the Knights Templar in London, you could travel somewhere else and cash it in with a letter of introduction. Not every country valued gold the same way - some dealt in seashells or pearls - so there must have been some kind of exchange rate process.

The first time people started publishing lists of equivalent values of coins from different places was in Antwerp in the 1530s, a major international commercial centre. Before that, medieval money changers used weighing scales based on the weight and purity of the metal in the coin, not the nominal value or where it was from. Most merchants didn't use cash - they used letters of exchange and notional value.

questions.question: Why does putting a spoon upside down in an open bottle of Prosecco keep it fizzy for a couple of days?

answers.answer: The heat conduction qualities of the spoon mean the neck of the bottle becomes even colder with the spoon in than without, even in the fridge. This makes the area full of air colder, which changes the pressure and keeps the bubbles present. The bubbles can't rise and disappear as much.

answers.caller: Professor Hall (Professor of Public Understanding of Science, University of Brighton)
answers.answer: It's a red herring - correlation and causation. Prosecco is a super-saturated solution of carbon dioxide. The solubility of CO2 is affected by temperature and agitation. A spoon, fork, or pencil makes no difference whatsoever. The fridge does the work. The spoon is the same temperature as everything else in the fridge. Whether you put a spoon in or not, the result would be the same because it's the temperature that matters, not the spoon.

questions.question: What is a vitamin? What defines something as a vitamin A, B, E, or K?

answers.answer: A vitamin is basically a group of carbon-based compounds that are essential for normal metabolism and body function. The body can't build them itself so you acquire them from dietary sources. For example, with the sun you get vitamin D metabolized by the body from sunlight, or from fish oils and fats. It's a nutrient or micronutrient needed for chemical reactions that sustain life. You differentiate it from minerals which aren't necessarily carbon-based.

questions.question: If both the pilot and co-pilot become unresponsive on a plane, what's the protocol to land it?

answers.answer: A member of crew would step into the seats and get instructions over the radio.

There is no actual protocol written down to cover that eventuality. If both pilots became incapacitated, you'd effectively have an aeroplane flying on its own, left with the last instructions given to it. Bright-minded cabin crew would hopefully recognise the situation, extract one of the pilots from the seats (they might be locked over the controls), and attempt to contact air traffic control who may get someone. The protection the public have is that pilots try to avoid that situation - both pilots eat different food, come to work well rested, and don't come to work if ill.

questions.question: What's the origin of the phrase 'top drawer'? Why does the top drawer mean something is good quality?

answers.answer: In olden days in England, in a woman's dresser room, they'd have a dresser with a few drawers. The small drawers at the top were where they sat in front of with the mirror to do their makeup. The top drawer is where they kept their jewellery and valuables. That's why top drawer means high class.

questions.question: Why are the loose bits of skin under older women's arms called 'bingo wings'?

answers.answer: Because the demographic that gets bingo wings is associated with bingo halls. Women who go to the bingo rather than the gym tend to be of a certain age and have this phenomenon. It's as simple as that - bingo women with wings. The women who are drawn to the bingo raise their hands a lot pressing dobbers so they are exercising a bit.

questions.question: When do we stop saying Happy New Year to people? What's the cutoff point?

answers.answer: You'd probably say it for the first half of January to anybody you haven't seen since last year. It would sound odd in February.
This weekend. First week. You're allowed to do it more than just on January 1st. No one has a strict rule about this.

questions.question: We have two dogs, Harry and Hugo, who are father and son. Do they know they're related?

answers.caller: Vieri (Rome, Italy) - dog behaviourist / Dr. Dog
answers.answer: No, they don't know they're related. They just know they grew up together very closely and formed a bond. They could just be friends. Puppies tend to recognise their mum after two years due to pheromones and oxytocin, but after a certain period it's just a question of familiarity. Dogs tend to recognise the same kind of dog as themselves rather than actual relatives. The two dogs who live together are just very close friends.

questions.question: Why do we never see female police officers wearing the tall domed police hats (custodian helmets)?

answers.answer: Female police officers are still issued certain types of uniform different to males. The custodian helmet was part of the uniform when police wore tunics with capes and women weren't in the service then. Female PCs are issued the same number one dress uniform but have one hat whereas male officers have two hats - the flat cap and the custodian. The custodian doesn't fit inside a police vehicle and is impractical for getting in and out of a van. If you're in central London, policing around the Mall, Buckingham Palace, any public engagement, any foot patrol in high-profile tourist areas, you'd be expected to wear it because it makes you visible in a crowd. It's purely traditional now and tourists love seeing it.

questions.caller: Elsie (8 years old, via Tracey from Torquay)
questions.question: Why do we say someone is on 'cloud nine' when they're happy? Why nine and not another number?

answers.answer: There was an international cloud atlas that registered ten different types of clouds. The ninth one was the highest cloud. Therefore if you're at the highest level, you're as happy as you can be - Cloud 9.

questions.question: Does chewing gum help you concentrate? Why or why not?

answers.answer: Yes it does help with concentration. When you chew, your body receives pressure around your mouth and jaw, and that pressure is calming for the body. If you have a massage and people press your body hard, that is calming all over your body. If somebody runs their hand lightly over you, it's alerting and sets you going. Chewing bread, anything chewy or crunchy, gives mouth stimulation which calms you down. If you're calmer, you can concentrate better.

questions.question: Why do we say someone has 'kicked the bucket' when they die?

answers.answer: It's to do with hanging. To get the noose over someone's head, they need to be higher than where they would hang. Traditionally you stand on a bucket, kick the bucket, and it's curtains.

When a pig was slaughtered, it was hung by its trotters over a bucket to catch the blood to make black pudding. When the throat was cut, the spasm of the back legs kicked the bucket. So when you say you've kicked the bucket, it means you're dead. The best black pudding comes from Scotland - Stornoway.

questions.question: Who gets the royalties on Live Aid and Band Aid? Specifically, who gets the royalties on 'Do They Know It's Christmas Now'?

answers.answer: According to the PRS (Performing Rights Society), the songwriting royalties go: 25% Midge Ure, 25% Bob Geldof, 50% to a publishing company. Jim noted he looked it up on the PRS portal and even received a distribution that very morning.

questions.question: Why do we put a penny or coin in a Christmas pudding?
At what point in time would we first have ever seen a man-made land border? Like an arbitrary line on a map dividing countries, not a river or mountain range.

answers.answer: The first land border was the Andorra border between France and Spain, dating from around the mid-1200s. It's a feudal arrangement where the co-rulers are the French President and Spanish Prime Minister. This was the first time there was a legal line you could walk over between countries.

questions.question: Why are supermarket ceilings so high when nobody can reach them?

answers.answer: Supermarkets are built high so they can add a mezzanine floor in the future if they need to expand. It's cheaper to build up than to buy additional land to build outwards.

answers.caller: Ian (Guildford - 40 years in construction, Chartered Institute of Building)
answers.answer: The high ceilings are due to structural requirements. To achieve wide open spaces without pillars, you need deeper structural beams, which requires more height. The beam depth determines the possible span of the building.
Larger air volume inside a building makes it easier and cheaper to regulate temperature. The bigger the building, the more constant the temperature due to air movement.

questions.question: Why do we associate penguins with Christmas when they're from the South Pole and Father Christmas lives at the North Pole?

answers.answer: The association is because people think penguins come from the North Pole where Father Christmas lives. James suggested it's 'lazy geography.'

questions.question: How much does the world weigh?

answers.answer: The question should be 'what is the mass of planet Earth' since weight varies with gravity but mass is constant. To measure mass, the Earth would need to float in water - the displaced water weight equals the object's mass.

The mass of the Earth is 5.19 x 10^24 kilograms. In the 1770s, Neville Maskellane (Astronomer Royal) calculated this by building a pendulum on top of Schiehallion mountain in Scotland and measuring how much the mountain's gravity deflected the pendulum.

questions.question: Why don't certain body parts like eyeballs or the tongue get fat?

answers.answer: You don't gain new fat cells in your body - you only have a fixed number. The fatter you get, the more fat deposits inside those existing cells. Since eyeballs and tongues don't have fat cells, they can't get fatter. Genetics determines where your body stores fat first.

questions.question: In theatres and TV studios, why is the green room called the green room?

answers.answer: Some suggestion it was to do with lime lighting in theatres, giving a greenish tinge

answers.caller: Martin (Maastricht - TV judge on Robot Wars, Tomorrow's World etc)
answers.answer: Green rooms are painted green because green is a calming, relaxing colour. From evolutionary psychology, people feel more comfortable seeing green - it reminds them of plentiful food and pastures. Actors tend to be nervous, so the green room helps relax them.
The London Palladium ushers used to wear green jackets, which they hung up on pegs in the room, making it look green. Also mentioned it might be rhyming slang - green gauge stage.

questions.question: How far down the royal family would the restriction on voting go? Would Prince Andrew be allowed to vote? What about Princess Eugenie?
If you played sad music (like Chopin's Funeral March) to an animal, would it feel sad?

answers.answer: Yes, mammals do have emotional reactions to music. Her friend completed a master's thesis on horses' reactions to music - they measured heart rate as an indicator of comfort/discomfort. Rock and heavy metal music made horses uncomfortable (increased heart rate, respiration), while classical music calmed them down.

questions.question: Why did Germans have Christmas trees in the first place?
How many taps would you have to run in one city before the water just stops running?
Why do we put pennies in Christmas puddings? (Answering John's earlier question)

answers.answer: The tradition dates back to Edward II (1300s) when puddings were eaten on Twelfth Night. A pea or bean was baked in, and whoever found it became king or queen for the day. This evolved to include charms, pennies, and symbols - finding a ring meant you'd get married, etc. It eventually simplified to just pennies for luck.

questions.question: When did the Americans make a conscious decision to speak American and spell American as opposed to English?

answers.answer: Before about 1828, there were lots of different spellings for lots of different words. In 1828, a guy called Noah Webster, who was American, wrote a dictionary and he basically picked out his favorite spellings, preferred forms. So there wasn't even a right and wrong before that. You could have spelt it in a variety of different ways and everyone would have known what you were talking about. James noted some people said 1806 for 'A Compendious Dictionary of the English Language.' He learned 26 languages, including Anglo-Saxon and Sanskrit, in order to research the origins of his own country's tongue.

questions.question: When did the convention of taking your husband's surname originate?
Why is medication in tablet form a variety of different shapes?

answers.answer: The answer is recognition/marketing/branding. Everyone knows the blue pill and knows what it does. It's like branding so you know what it is from looking at it so you don't take the wrong one by accident. He worked for pharmaceutical companies for 20 years selling drugs.

questions.caller: Cara (Edinburgh) - question from her son Idrissa, age 7
questions.question: How are street lights actually operated?

answers.answer: It is a photovoltaic cell. When the light of the sun comes up, there's enough electricity generated within the component. It then opens the circuit and the lights switch off. And vice versa. At substations, the photovoltaic cell would be at the substation to avoid the aesthetic of the lamp being removed. He is an electrical engineer.

Photo cells that turn the lights on at dusk and off at dawn are quite an old system now. Many local authorities are now employing central management systems. The sensor on top of the light is a complicated device that can transmit and receive radio signals. The central management systems send a signal to turn the lights on and another signal to turn them off. You can turn an individual light on or off or a group of them and you can also dim the lights. These devices record the amount of electricity the lamps are burning so they can be interrogated. He is an electrical contractor who maintains and repairs street lighting.

questions.question: Is there an evolutionary benefit in chillies being hot?

answers.answer: It's about evolution but not in the way you think. Chillies evolved so that mammals won't eat them because the seeds get destroyed in mammalian stomachs which are pH 1. Birds on the other hand don't have such low pH. Birds will eat chillies and disperse the seeds beautifully so they're evolutionally programmed to be attracted to birds but not to mammals. His top tip: if you've got something that's too hot in your mouth, drink milk because the fat in the milk dissolves it much more effectively than water or beer. He is Professor of Public Understanding of Science at the University of Brighton.

questions.question: If you were really super dehydrated, could you rehydrate yourself simply by submerging yourself in water rather than drinking any water?

answers.answer: You can't do it because your skin is made of stratified squamous epithelium that's impermeable. Water can't permeate through your skin to rehydrate. It will get into the layers of the cells so they'll swell up if you get in a bath but it won't go any further. It won't go intravascular. She is a doctor.

questions.question: Why do cats and dogs and lots of other animals like their ears rubbed so much more than humans do?

answers.answer: There are three reasons. First, dogs hear much higher pitches than we can so their spectrum of hearing is much broader. Second, dogs have 80 muscles per ear whereas humans have 2, so they can turn their ears in different directions. Third, when you stick your finger in a dog's ear, it will feel the tickle because there are so many hairs growing there. He's also known as Dr. Dog - website www.dr-dog.eu.

questions.question: If the Earth stopped spinning, would we be able to feel the difference?

answers.answer: Yes, we would notice. If it stopped spinning all of a sudden, the atmosphere all around us would still be spinning at whatever the speed it is - 1100 miles an hour, 1200 miles an hour. So everything that wasn't attached to the bedrock would be swept up into the atmosphere. He learned this at school in physics many years ago.

questions.question: What impact would continental drift have on the Channel Tunnel?

answers.answer: We are not drifting away from mainland Europe. The UK and the whole of Great Britain and mainland Europe are all on the same Eurasian continental plate, so we're not drifting apart. There might be erosion from the Chalk Cliffs but we're on the same plate.
France is on the same plate as the UK. We're on the Eurasian plate together.

questions.question: How is it that air fresheners in cars don't taste the way they smell? They smell nice but would taste gross if you sprayed them in your mouth.

answers.answer: If you diluted it enough, it would taste like it smells. This is a question of concentration. To get a smell that will fill a room, it's got to be really concentrated to a degree that if you stick it in your gob, it'll be gross.

The perfume contains chemicals that are recognized as a smell and chemicals that are registered as a taste - two different chemicals within it. Your taste receptors work differently to your smell receptors. When you sense a smell, it signals directly into your limbic system where emotions are felt, whereas taste, sight, hearing, and touch are cross-referenced in your brain first. Perfumes don't taste like they smell because they're made up of different chemicals. When you distill rose, you get different chemicals coming off at different temperatures - the oil part versus the floral water. It's a question of concentration.

questions.question: Why does grapefruit specifically cause it to interact with medication? My auntie was on HRT and had terrible headaches until she stopped drinking grapefruit juice.

answers.answer: Grapefruit contains certain compounds or chemicals that interfere with the metabolism of drugs. When humans ingest drugs or medicines, they get metabolised by the liver. Those chemicals in grapefruit interfere with enzymes in the liver that break down drugs. So drugs are not broken down quickly or strongly enough, and you get high levels of drugs in the blood that give nasty side effects. The grapefruit juice has something in it that can block the enzyme from working. However, the enzymes in grapefruit juice only affect certain enzymes in the liver that metabolise certain drugs.

questions.question: When they build skyscrapers like the Shard in Dubai and other buildings, they've got a tower crane right on top. How do they get that crane back down when the job is finished? If they have a crane big enough to get it down, why didn't they use that crane in the first place?

answers.answer: There was an urban myth that for some of the massive basement excavations in Mayfair and Chelsea, it was so expensive to get the JCB out that they buried it and dug another hole. It might be that every massive skyscraper has a secret crane inside.

The crane will take itself down. They'll put a jack on the mast and unbolt it. They'll clamp two sections of the actual mast, then the section in the middle they'll unbolt and hook onto the crane. Then they'll lower it down. You come down bit by bit until you're low enough that mobile cranes can get to you. Then you'll come out of the crane and they'll take all the other sections away. The mobile cranes can't reach as high as the tower crane, which is why you don't use them in the first place.

Steve's answer described what happens but didn't use the technical term - it's a derrick crane that stays up on top of buildings like the Shard. It also takes the crane down to the level. Steve's description was accurate but there is a derrick crane involved.

questions.question: Who decides how to number roads? Is there a logic to it?

When you don't know someone's name, you know what it's not. For example, if someone said it's Bob, I'd know it wasn't Bob, even though I don't know what it is. What's happening in your brain when that happens?

answers.answer: It's associated with the long-term memory, not the short-term memory. When new information gets processed by the brain, we associate it with either an association clue or a clue like how you wear, color, or smell. It gets imprinted that information. When you can't remember what it is but know what it isn't, we call it freezing - brain freezing. Nobody knows exactly why this happens. We are still working on this.

questions.question: How do smartphone gloves work? Why can some gloves work a smartphone but an ordinary pair of gloves won't? I've got woollen ones with three different coloured finger ends that allow you to use a smartphone.

answers.caller: Steve (Milton Keynes) - Former smartphone manufacturer employee
answers.answer: It's about conductivity. There's such a thing as conductive thread. They'll loop through conductive thread, connecting it to the inside where your hand is. The conductivity from your hand makes connection with that thread, and then they loop it through to the outside of the glove so it makes contact with the screen. Wool and cotton are not normally conductive. The different coloured finger ends are just to make it identifiable quickly so you know which one has the thread.

questions.question: How did they work out that Beaconsfield is 60 metres higher than Uxbridge? How do they measure the height of places above sea level, and where do they measure sea level from?
When there's a big storm and the news says there were 18,000 lightning strikes that night, how do they actually record how many lightning strikes there have been?

answers.answer: There are storm trackers online where you can track exactly where lightning strikes are. They triangulate via weather stations. Weather stations on the ground have sensors that pick up a flash. When lightning strikes, different weather stations pick up the flash and they triangulate the location. They just count them up.

questions.question: My eight-year-old son wants to know: who decided who the first king or queen would be?

answers.answer: The answer is Athelstan. He was one of the children of Alfred. Athelstan was the first person who could reasonably be described as a king of England. There were other kings, but he was the one that united all the different warring factions - the Angles, Saxons, Celts, and all the pre-Norman, post-Roman factions. He would have been the first united king of England (though not Scotland, the Picts were separate).

questions.question: Why do the most venomous creatures live in hot countries? You don't get black widows in England, rattlesnakes in New York but you would in Texas, and in Australia everything's trying to kill you. Why are venomous creatures confined to hot countries?

answers.answer: The very simple answer is that they are cold-blooded. Venomous creatures are cold-blooded, so they wouldn't be able to survive in cold areas. They survive in warmer climates because they use the heat to regulate their body temperature.

questions.question: Why is number 10 Downing Street still called number 10 when there aren't 10 houses on Downing Street? There are only four, nine to 12.

answers.answer: They knocked down the other side of Downing Street to make room for the Foreign Office. They left 9, 10, 11 and 12 there. And also because number 10 Downing Street had become synonymous with the seat of government, they couldn't have renamed it.
Number nine is an office for the Chief Whip, not where the Chief Whip actually lives. He used to live at number 12, but that's now all offices too.

The Royal Mail has no ownership of address data. Every single property in the UK has a unique ID called a UPRN (unique property reference number). You wouldn't rename the houses because you have historical records. 1 to 8 was knocked down when Victoria was on the throne in the 19th century, so they just wouldn't change it.

questions.question: What is England's national dress? If you look at the Middle East, the thobe is worn across the Middle East. Look at India or the Asian subcontinent, they wear a sari or shawakamese. Scotland has national dress. What dress or garment would say that person is from England?

answers.answer: I think you know that there isn't one. Otherwise you wouldn't have asked the question. I suppose at various points in history, we could have claimed that the sort of bowler hat and the chalk striped suit represented some sort of national dress, but not if you worked in a factory.

We do not have a national dress in England. National dresses tend to be very, very old - hundreds and hundreds of years old, like a toga. Back at the point where national dresses were formed, we weren't actually a nation. Which is why we have Pearly Kings and Morris Dancers and all the different regional dresses, rather than one national dress.

questions.question: What was the origin of the phrase 'shouldering responsibility'? Is it to do with the military, in the sense where rank moves from the sleeve onto the shoulder?

answers.answer: Shouldering is simply a synonym for carrying. You'd shoulder the weight, and then it just gets semantically evolved into a metaphorical shouldering. The military angle is a complete red herring. You shoulder a physical burden, and then that evolves into a metaphorical burden. So you shoulder responsibility.

questions.question: What was the origin of shouldering responsibility?

answers.answer: Shouldering is simply a synonym for carrying. You'd shoulder the weight, and then it just gets semantically evolved into a metaphorical shouldering. It's a complete red herring.

questions.question: Why is it whenever you see athletics on the television or go to a track, they always run anti-clockwise, never clockwise?

answers.answer: They don't always. It's convention rather than rule and regulation.

We do still run the other way for different events. It's to do with the heart being on the left-hand side of the body. When you run round the track one way, it creates more force and it tires people out more because of the centrifugal force. Most people are also right-footed.

questions.question: When a bag of satsumas goes mouldy, why does one go blue and the ones surrounding it not get affected at all? With apples or pears, they all go squishy at about the same rate. But with satsumas, a rogue outlier goes blue while the rest are fine.

answers.answer: I'm an ex-greengrocer and they're coated with a chemical called diphenylthiobendazole. It's a chemical wax put on fruits to stop one rotting the next one. So it wouldn't just be satsumas, but it would most obviously be satsumas. Normally citrus fruit - oranges, lemons, that sort of thing.

questions.question: Can a cemetery be sold off for property development? And if so, what would happen to the bodies?

answers.answer: Yes. The Westminster Cemetery scandal was a British political scandal which began in January 1987 when Westminster City Council sold three cemeteries, three lodges, one flat, a crematorium, and over 12 acres of prime development land in London for a total of 85 pence.

In practice, not really. Apart from when they were in Westminster in 1989. Spitalfield, All Saints Spitalfield in the 80s is a good example. Crosswell recently dealt with a very large known historic cemetery. But Crosswell was a huge national infrastructure project so it took priority. Normally they wouldn't do it. But theoretically, and occasionally, it happens. As an archaeologist, I can tell you that bodies get excavated in a controlled fashion by specialists. They're probably sat in a store somewhere awaiting analysis. The skeletons will be sexed and aged, looking at pathologies, teeth, diet. Scientific analysis can show what kind of diet they were eating. And then eventually they will be reburied on consecrated ground. This is why cemeteries tend not to get developed on - because there's going to be too much there and it's going to cost a huge whack to relocate.

questions.question: Why, when you go to an ice cream van and you buy a vanilla ice cream cone, and he sticks a chocolate flake in it, why does it then become a 99?

answers.answer: Nobody knows. There's no definitive answer to the question. There are all sorts of rumours about the cost of it or the brand name, but no one knows. Even Cadbury's couldn't answer your question. Even they wouldn't claim to have answered the question. There's three or four different theories on where it might have come from, one from Scotland, one from Manchester, but no one knows.

questions.question: When a banana goes brown, does the calorific content change? When a banana goes brown, it becomes sweeter. Is it then more calorifically contained?

answers.answer: A banana when it's been picked is a closed system - where would the calories come from? It's a beautiful question. Unripe fruit contains the same amount of energy, but in the form of starch, which doesn't taste sweet. It then breaks down to sugars. There won't be any calorific changes in total. It's just the way you extract the calories. The starch gets broken down in your gut to the same sugars and the calories go the same way. So she could eat a banana in any state and it wouldn't have a different effect upon her diet.

questions.question: When you're looking at a baby six to eight months old, they're staring at you, thinking etc. What language do they think in?

answers.answer: They don't think in any language until they can speak. They'll just be registering sensations and feelings. They haven't given the name to them yet. It's wind. Seriously, I spent months thinking my oldest had started smiling. Turned out she was breaking wind. They might start thinking in the language spoken to them by their parents, but it won't be there at six months. It's like why their first word is almost always descriptive - mama, dada, dog. It's very rarely going to be discombobulated or anti-disestablishmentarianism.

When they're looking at their dad, they wouldn't be thinking in that sense. They're looking at their dad because their pull of a social interaction is much greater than anything else at that stage. They have to go through the understanding that a word represents an object, and that comes long before they can produce a word and before they can link it together.

questions.question: Where did the British accent develop over time? How did we get to having Scouse, Geordie, Scottish, how did that actually originate?

answers.answer: We were a hell of a lot less mobile until surprisingly recently. Until the invention of the motor car, unless you had a horse, and most people didn't, you'd very rarely leave your own village. That will be part of the answer - it explains why you can have two such different accents between two stops on the train.

Language and accent in particular comes from mimicry, because we are social creatures and we mimic one another to fit in, up to and including how we speak. So you sound like the people you most spend time with.

questions.question: How was money introduced into the world? Because at one point, people would have had no money. And money would have been subsequently invented. How was it distributed and integrated into society? And was it integrated evenly? Did everyone get it?

answers.answer: Historically, gold was deposited with goldsmiths who gave receipts. Those receipts became standardized and exchangeable as 'I promise to pay the bearer.' This made receipts as good as gold. Goldsmiths then realized no one was coming back for their gold and started lending gold, creating the basis of modern fractional reserve banking. The first recorded money would be the point at which someone turned precious metal into a disk with a number on it - like Roman denarii. Paper money is called fiat money - money with no intrinsic value. Coins were commodity money, worth what the metal was worth.

When you first fill the kettle, the water is filled with oxygen. As the kettle heats up, the oxygen boils off, which is what makes the noise. If you let the kettle get completely cold and boil it again, it's even quieter - makes no noise at all. The oxygen has boiled off.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'there's no skin off my nose' come from?

answers.answer: It originated as a medieval judicial punishment where the nose was taken off from adulterers. The idea was to make the adulterer too ugly to have another affair. It mainly applied to female adulterers. The phrase means something doesn't affect you or bother you.

questions.question: Moths always come out at night and fly to light bulbs. Why don't they just get up in the morning and come out in the light and save all the hassle?

answers.answer: They've evolved to be nocturnal because their predators - birds - are generally operating under the benefits of daylight.

questions.question: Why do kettles go quiet before they boil?

answers.answer: When you first fill the kettle, the water is filled with oxygen. As the kettle heats up, the oxygen starts to boil off and this is what makes the noise. If you let the kettle get completely cold and boil it again, it's even quieter - it makes no noise at all when it boils. Most of the oxygen is burned off.

questions.question: When Parliament votes, the speaker takes the result, reads it out, then bellows 'unlock'. But he never said 'lock' first. Why does he shout unlock?

answers.answer: MPs have 12 minutes to vote after bells ring. At the end of those 12 minutes, to make sure only people that got there in time can vote, they lock the doors. The speaker does shout 'lock the doors' before, but this happens during a muted bit so people don't hear it. After the votes are counted, the speaker shouts unlock to release the doors. MPs go in through different doors depending on how they're voting - yes on the right, no on the left. They genuinely lock you in.

questions.question: Why do some butchers wear blue striped aprons and others wear white plain aprons in the same shop? Is there some ranking system?

answers.answer: It's probably nothing meaningful - just random. Whichever apron came out of the laundry first. Butchers wear white so you can see the stains and know you've got a clean butcher. Blue is used in catering because you don't often get blue food so you can see if it ends up in the food.
Plain aprons are for apprentices. The stripey ones or pinstripe are for elder butchers. The higher up the butchery chain you are, the wider your stripes are.

questions.caller: Sally (Farnborough) - on behalf of Sam (10 years old)
questions.question: When you breathe out through your mouth, you get warm air. But when you blow out, you get cold air. Why?

answers.answer: It's to do with wind chill factor - the speed with which the air is hitting your skin and the heat being transferred.

It's due to the expansion of gas. Expanding gas cools. When your mouth is open, the gas is already expanded and when you purse your lips and blow onto your hand, the gas in the air expands and cools your hand.

questions.question: Her 14-week-old daughter yawns when Stephanie yawns, but when the daughter yawns, it doesn't make Stephanie yawn. At what age do you start catching yawns?

answers.answer: About two years old. Yawning is one of the earliest forms of human communication and signals that you're safe.
When you develop empathy - you understand concepts like safety and security. There wouldn't be a fixed date like two years, three months and two days.

questions.question: Brazil was named after the nut. Is that true? Or is the nut named after the country?

answers.answer: Instincts say country first, nut second

It's got nothing to do with a Brazil nut. The country was named after a tree the Portuguese found called Pau-Brasil which gave them red dye. The nut was named after the country afterwards because they only had the nut over here and decided to call it Brazil nut.

questions.question: What officially makes a castle a castle and not just a big building or house?

answers.answer: It's a luxurious living residence that belongs to someone, fortified for military purposes. A fort belongs to someone but the people living there might not own it, whereas a castle belongs to the gentleman or his family living there. When properly reconstructed, castles were actually bright and beautiful buildings inside with plastered walls and painted scenes.

questions.caller: Dave (Isle and Royal Manor of Portland)
questions.question: Does James consider himself a journalist, a presenter, or a philosopher?

answers.answer: First and foremost a friend, followed by an entertainer, and last of all a confidante.

questions.question: Where did the heart shape on Valentine's cards come from? Why was the actual biological human heart shape substituted for the heart shape we see today?

answers.answer: The heart-shaped symbol comes from the seed pod of a seed called the silphium. It was distributed in the Roman Empire on coins and was associated with fertility. It's extinct now. During the age of chivalry, it became a romantic symbol again. Qualifications: studied ancient history at university.

questions.question: Is handwriting genetic? Do you inherit it? My mum posts to me and my husband recognises her handwriting instantly. My brother has handwriting similar to my dad, but I'm a twin and my handwriting isn't similar to my twin's.

answers.answer: When you're learning to write, generally your parents teach you how to write, so you copy the way they write. It's learnt behaviour, not genetic. Qualifications: did a bit of evolution, behaviour and genetics at uni.

questions.question: If I'm on a train and I have a ball and I chuck it up or forward, why does it not move differently? The train is moving, so shouldn't the ball move?

answers.answer: The ball is moving at the same speed as the train. So as far as the observer on the train is concerned, the ball is moving up and down in one plane. It's still moving at 80 miles an hour.

This is what Einstein talked about - relativity. If you're on the train bouncing a ball up and down, from your perspective the ball goes up and down in a straight line. But if someone at the side of the track could look through the glass, they'd see the ball traveling in a wave form - different distances in the same time. From this Einstein worked out that time travels differently at speed. We're never standing still - the Earth is moving, the solar system is moving.

questions.question: Why are goldfish called goldfish when they're orange, not actually gold?

answers.answer: The word orange is a relatively new addition to the English language (16th century, comes from Naranja - the orange tree). So before then, Anglo-Saxons used a word called geoluread which meant yellow-red. Robins don't have red breasts - they have orange breasts. Red kites are orange. Red foxes aren't red - they're orange. Many animals we call red or gold are actually orange because there was no word for orange. In France, a goldfish is called 'le poisson rouge' (the red fish). Qualifications: I'm a zoologist who writes about the naming of animals as a hobby.

questions.question: My 10-year-old son Archie is a budding paleontologist. At what temperature will a polar bear freeze to death?

answers.answer: Polar bears can survive in temperatures down to around minus 70 (which is what the Arctic can reach). But it's not just about temperature - it's about how much food and fat reserves they have. A healthy polar bear would last longer than an unhealthy one. Roughly, even the scrawniest polar bear wouldn't freeze to death at minus 20 - that would be dying from lack of food. For a very thin polar bear, around minus 63 could be fatal. Qualifications: I've been doing a project for around five years to raise awareness of endangered species. I make limited edition screen prints with my brother that reveal the skeleton under UV light, with proceeds going to charities like Polar Bears International for polar bears. Website: undertheskin.co.uk

questions.question: Where did the term Black Friday come from?

answers.answer: Thanksgiving in the US is on a Thursday. Americans get Thursday off work and make it into a long weekend by also taking Friday off. Nobody goes to work on the Friday, everyone goes shopping. That's why it's the biggest shopping day of the year. Qualifications: I heard it on the news.

The reason it's called Black Friday is because all the stores are supposed to go from red to black - meaning they go from making a loss to making profit for the rest of the year. It's the biggest shopping day so that's when most stores hit that threshold. Qualifications: I was an accountant originally in New York, now work for Network Rail.

questions.question: I'm getting married next year. Where did wedding dresses come from? When and where were they first worn?

answers.answer: It's all about Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. They were the biggest celebrities of the 19th century, like Christmas trees and Christmas cards - he was the first to send Christmas cards and everybody copied. Queen Victoria wore a white fancy dress on her wedding day and after that point, all women who sought to emulate the royals bought similar dresses. It had a veil and a train.

questions.question: Why do windows in continental Europe generally open inwards and windows in Britain and Ireland generally open outwards?

answers.answer: Continental Europe has very common shutters. If you've got shutters, you don't want a window that opens outwards. So shutters are likely the reason.

questions.caller: Eleanor in Canary Wharf (for her dad, retired firefighter)
questions.question: In tennis, why is zero referred to as love?

answers.answer: When we first started playing tennis, the lingua franca of the sport was French. The French word for egg is l'œuf, which sounds like 'love'. The shape of a zero looks like an egg. And 15, 30, 45 comes from using clock faces to display the score.

questions.question: When you get hair on your head it's called a head of hair, armpit hair, leg hair. But when you get hair on your face it's called a beard. Why is a beard the only collection of body hair that has its own specific name?

answers.answer: Beard is just a general term for facial hair. It's not the answer to the question.

Beard is a style, same as you could have long hair, dreadlocks, buzz cut. So you could have a beard, moustache, mutton chops on your face - they're all types of facial hair. Crew cut, buzz cut, Mohawk are all haircuts. Beard has become a generic term like hairstyle. Qualifications: Just something I know.

questions.question: Do pigs go back to the same shelter every night when they sleep in fields?

answers.answer: They will have their own dedicated sties.
I moved pigs four or five fields away and overnight they trotted back to where they started. Very clever animals.
