Generally if they're with their mothers, they'll always go back to the same pig arc. If you put five pig arcs in, they'll always go back to the same pig arc. But mothers might suddenly decide to move pig arcs.

questions.question: When did Halloween become a thing?

answers.answer: All Hallows' Eve is the origin. It comes from America, but you could trace it back to All Saints Day.

Halloween goes back to the Celtic festival of Samhain, thousands of years old. In Scotland and Ireland they've celebrated All Hallows' Eve continuously with guising. It spread from Celtic regions to America via Scottish and Irish migrants and then came back to England.

questions.question: Why are chickens seen as weak animals? Why do we say 'chickening out'?

answers.answer: If you try to catch a chicken, the chicken will run away. Ergo, running away and chickening out became interchangeable.

questions.question: Are a dog's front legs classified as legs or arms? My wife says arms, I say legs.

answers.answer: I would class them as legs. You talk about shoulder of pork, shoulder of lamb.

Front legs are classified as fore limbs and hind limbs, not arms or legs. But physiologically, the front limb is shaped and built like our arms. The person who asked hoping his wife would look stupid has ended up looking stupid himself.

questions.question: Are we any more intelligent now physiologically than we were thousands of years ago? Are our brains any better?

answers.answer: Darwinian evolution suggests there may be diminishment in average intelligence when a population gets very comfortable. But whether there's been physiological improvement is a beautiful question.

There's a report stating that if a child from pre-Caveman times was brought up in school today, they would be just like any other child. There's a conflation between intelligence and consciousness. We've become more aware and conscious, but intelligence specifically? I'm not so sure.

questions.question: My 8-year-old daughter Sarah asks: Why do we have drinking straws? When did drinking straws come about?

answers.answer: Straws go back thousands of years. First straws would be grasses so you could drink liquid off the top of beer without getting gunk at the bottom. The modern paper drinking straw was invented by a bloke involved in the tobacco industry, but I can't remember his name.

questions.question: How does honey get labelled as from a particular flower (e.g., lavender honey)? Do bees prefer certain flowers?

answers.answer: Bees forage within about a three-mile radius. The beekeeper knows where they've been foraging and deliberately places hives near specific crops to get particular honey.

The bees will forage for whatever's around them. If you put a hive in a field of lavender, you get lavender honey. They'll forage within about a three-mile radius. The beekeeper deliberately places the hive to increase the chance of getting acacia or lavender honey.

questions.question: Who is responsible for the convention of eating with fork in left hand and knife in right hand?

answers.answer: Originally you only had one tool, a knife. Forks probably came after knives. It's a convention - knife on the right, fork on the left.

Forks didn't arrive in the UK until about the 1600s. People cut with their right hand and held food steady with a knife. When forks arrived from the continent (probably Italy), they were just used to hold meat steady while cutting - you didn't actually eat with it. So it slipped into the left hand because the right hand was doing the heavy work with the knife.

questions.question: Why don't trains have seatbelts?

answers.answer: The Rail Safety Standards Board researched this. They found 8 times more injuries would occur with seatbelts because trains deform in accidents and people strapped in can't move. Also, seats would need to be strengthened, and standing passengers would hit stronger seats and get more injured.

questions.question: When was the TV watershed invented and why is it called a watershed?

answers.answer: A watershed is an area of high ground above a river system that drains into the river - it 'sheds' water. It's a tipping point. In TV terms, it's the point at which you can have a bloody good swear.

questions.question: Is ketchup a food or a drink?

answers.answer: It's about viscosity - the flow characteristics determine classification. Food measured by weight, drink measured by volume, but ketchup's viscosity makes it a food.
The question was flawed. Ketchup is a food because you get satisfaction from it and you don't quench your thirst with it. You can put ketchup in a sandwich (unlike a drink).

questions.question: Why do you never see any aeroplanes in satellite photographs of Earth?

answers.answer: You do see planes in satellite images if you look closely. Books like 'Pictures of Earth from the Sky' wouldn't publish images with planes. Also, as you zoom in on Google Maps, images switch from satellite to aerial photos taken from planes flying below regular airline altitude. There are ISS photos showing planes if you know where to look.

questions.question: Can a Boeing 747 physically do a loop-the-loop?

answers.answer: Commercial jets have asymmetrical wings designed to work efficiently flying right way up. To fly inverted you'd need such angle of attack it wouldn't work. Also, the 747 doesn't have enough power to overcome stall speed at 90 degrees. If it somehow got over the top, the structure would give up because wings experience loads they weren't designed for. Both stalling and wings falling off are risks.

answers.caller: Martin from Cornwall (PPL pilot with aerobatics rating)
answers.answer: The previous answer was completely wrong about asymmetrical wings being the issue. You gain airspeed by diving, then pull into the loop. As long as you have enough speed to get over the top, you'll complete it because airflow is relative to wing angle, not orientation. However, when coming out the bottom, pulling through the last quarter puts enormous stress on the airframe and wings would break off. It would be possible with the right pilot, but dangerous.

questions.question: What is a 'donkey's years' and where does it come from?

answers.answer: Donkeys live for ages - about 60 years. That's why it means a very long time.

It's actually rhyming slang. 'Donkey's years' is short for 'donkey's ears' which rhymes with 'years'. When you say 'donkey's years', you're giving away the rhyme - proper rhyming slang only works if you don't say the rhyming word (like 'apples and pears' becomes just 'apples').

questions.question: What is the oldest musical score that we know of? Like music that's been written down.

answers.answer: The earliest I can't give you an exact date, but it's around about the Gregorian chant, sort of monks from the 14th, 15th century. If you have written down music, that would be it.

The answer is not Gregorian chant, which is obviously in the Christian era. It's actually 1800 BC and it comes from what is now Syria, which was part of the Hurrian Empire, and it's a love song to the moon goddess Nikal. It's written in what's called tablature, which tells you where to press your fingers on the strings of a harp.

questions.question: At what stage in human development did we become carnivores?
Why does the moon look massive when it first rises on the horizon but much smaller a few hours later?

answers.answer: It's got nothing to do with the orbit of the moon. It's an optical illusion that's caused by the curvature of the Earth. When the moon is closer to the horizon, it appears a little bit wider based upon the fact that the image is being distorted by the curvature of the Earth. The same thing happens with the sun as well.

It's an optical illusion but the slight distortion through the sky isn't the reason. It's because you've got a reference point of the ground. When the moon's in the middle of the sky, right above us, it's exactly the same size as it was on the horizon. It might be a bit clearer because it's going through less atmosphere, but it's the same size. No one really knows why our eyes fool us into thinking it's bigger when they're on the horizon.

questions.question: When were swimming strokes formally delineated? Who decided what was what with front crawl and backstroke?
Who was Gordon Bennett?

answers.answer: There were two Gordon Bennetts. His father founded the New York Herald. The son was a bit of a playboy who got stocious at his engagement party and behaved abominably, allegedly urinated in his future mother-in-law's fireplace. He was horsewhipped by the brother of the woman he was engaged to, fled America in disgrace, and ended up living on a massive yacht. His name became a byword for flipping heck.

The phrase Gordon Bennett came from because he was an amateur magician. His favourite party piece was whipping tablecloths away from people when they were eating. The trick was to leave everything sitting on the table. However, most of the time he was nine-tenths cut and everything ended up on the floor. So whenever he entered a room or restaurant, the cry went out 'Gordon Bennett!' and everybody hung onto their tablecloths and cutlery. He also ended up in France and set up the International Herald Tribune.

questions.question: If I could travel at the speed of light in a spaceship, what would I see out of the window?

answers.answer: We can't travel at the speed of light because as you get faster, you get heavier and at light speed your mass is infinite. But if you could travel at the speed of light, using the speed of sound as an analogy - when a plane travels past at the speed of sound, you don't hear it at all until it's right on top of you. It's the same with light. As you travel forward, everything gets foreshortened. Those little columns at the beginning of Star Wars aren't a whole lot away from the truth. Everything in front appears blue, everything behind appears red because it's like the Doppler effect. It's red shift and blue shift. When you're going towards the light, things are elongated towards you but sideways there's not really much difference. You end up going through like a tunnel effect.

questions.question: How do sharks at the bottom of the ocean that are 400 years old survive the pressure? Why don't they get crushed?

answers.answer: The part of the thing that causes crushing is having an air space or a space for gas in your body. These animals, the water forms an integral part of their body. They don't have any gas spaces and therefore there isn't for the pressure to be exerted upon the gas. They're made of water, essentially.

questions.question: How long have humans been eating meat?

answers.answer: I think we've always been meat eaters. We know for a fact that chimps are carnivores. They hunt in big groups.

questions.question: Why doesn't your tongue keep growing? It's a muscle, so it should keep growing when your body stops growing.
Why do you get a drippy nose when you go for a walk, particularly on a cold winter's day? What's your body doing to protect you?

answers.answer: When you are cold, your body temperature rises to compensate and that liquefies your snot. Your whole body is trying to compensate for the outside temperature being cooler. It goes up and that makes everything more liquid. That's also why you get a red nose in the cold.

questions.question: Who cleans up after guide dogs? And if it is the person with the dog themselves, how do they do it?

answers.answer: It's their owners or users that clean up after them. During puppy walking training for Guide Dogs Association, they teach the dog to go to command using phrases like 'get busy' for number one and 'big busy' for number two. After enough training, the dog will try to go even if they don't need to, which means visually impaired owners can prepare and clean up.

questions.question: Why can some people mimic accents and others can't? Is there some sort of thing with your vocal cords?

answers.answer: The reason she can do accents is because she's a musician. She can hear the music in the words and in the accent. Each accent has its own very particular movement and sound. If you've got a good ear for music, you'll probably also have a very good ear for doing accents. She noted her kids who are musicians can also mimic accents. However, she cannot do impersonations - she can do accents but not impersonations of specific people.

questions.question: What was the first TV advert on ITV?

answers.answer: The first TV advert was Gibbs SR (toothpaste).

questions.question: Why is it that any clothes you wear on the lower part of your body are referred to as a pair - a pair of trousers, pair of knickers, pair of underpants, pair of shorts? Nothing you wear on the top part of your body is referred to as a pair.

Is there an international board that can veto what goes onto a national flag? If someone started a new country and put the poo emoji on their flag, is there someone who could say no, you can't have that flag in the UN?
Why do men have nipples?

answers.answer: When an embryo is in the womb developing, before it becomes male or female, the nipples develop. By the time the Y chromosome emerges to make the embryo male, the nipples are already in place. Every embryo starts sexless and has nipples before sex differentiation.

questions.question: Why do we have the reaction to wince or brace ourselves when we're about to hear a loud noise? You can't protect your ears from a noise, but you still brace your body.

answers.answer: With the eardrum, sound waves hit the eardrum. When you brace yourself, the pressure inside through the eustachian tube and the auditory tube that goes between the inner ear and the back of the throat compresses to match the pressure that might arise from the outside. It's like muffling a drum - putting your hand on a drum before you hit it gives you a less resonant sound.

questions.question: When leaves fall off trees during autumn, is there a noticeable decrease in oxygen in the air? Is air quality worse?

answers.answer: When it is autumn in the Northern Hemisphere, it is spring in the Southern Hemisphere, so leaves are growing there. Oxygen is a planetary issue, not a geographically specific one.

questions.question: What do you do with your napkin at the end of a formal dining experience? Do you refold it or leave it crunched?

answers.answer: Scrunch it up and chuck it on your plate or next to your plate. Members of the aristocracy don't tend to care about these things - they're middle-class concerns.

questions.question: If you trace your family history back, you've got two parents, four grandparents, eight great-grandparents, etc. How many generations back do you have to go before you're related to everyone who was on Earth at the time?

answers.answer: I don't know. It's probably answerable - it's only maths. There must be a time when the number going backwards makes the same number as going forwards.
Tudor times. My genealogy tutor said if you can trace your lineage back to England in Tudor times, you're related to everybody in England.
According to geneticist Brian Sykes, there are 30 known women that can all trace their lineage back to a single woman in Africa, around 140,000 years ago. That's through mitochondrial DNA analysis.

questions.question: When you buy gold on the stock market, do you actually own that gold? If you wanted it delivered, could you have it delivered? Or is it just virtual?

answers.answer: Usually when you buy it, it's kept in some sort of facility for you. But if you absolutely insisted on having it delivered in bullion form or coin form, then you could.

If you just want to benefit from the ups and downs, you can buy the spot price or forwards price. If the young fellow wants physical delivery, he can do that through a futures contract. The small problem is the minimum contract size is $1 million for gold.

You can buy futures contracts for gold (million pounds worth), or exchange-traded funds backed by gold in much smaller amounts. The gold is kept in vaults with big global banks. The fund is backed by gold derivatives. You can also buy physical gold - a gram at a gold dealer for about 40 quid.

questions.question: What's the science behind the 'dessert stomach' phenomenon? How is it possible to be really full after a main course but then suddenly recover hunger for dessert?
Do Parliament have the power to remove power from the Queen? Could they pass a bill abolishing the monarchy? Would that have to go via referendum?

answers.answer: Yes, Parliament could abolish the monarchy. You don't need a referendum to do anything like this. The Queen would have to sign it - she'd have to sign her own P45.

Parliament is sovereign. They can sack the Queen. Case law (12 Co Rep 74) established that the King has no prerogative but that which the law of the land allows. She would have to sign the bill for royal assent.

questions.question: How does rocket fuel going into space propel itself without the element of oxygen?

answers.answer: They take their own oxygen with them. The fuel plus oxygen - you need both. Once you get out of the atmosphere, you carry on moving at whatever speed you were travelling.

Rockets carry their own fuel plus their own oxidant. In your car you have petrol and air. The Saturn V rockets used kerosene and oxygen. Even fireworks have fuel and oxidant (potassium chlorate). The Space Shuttle had liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen plus solid fuel boosters. That's why multi-stage rockets are more efficient - you don't want to be carrying an empty fuel tank.

questions.question: Why is Friday the 13th considered an unlucky day?

answers.answer: Is it the day Jesus got crucified? He definitely died on a Friday. Was it the 13th? I think so.
It dates back to when the King of France rounded up the Knights Templars all at once because he wanted their money. He was broke and wanted to win money on war.
Jesus was crucified on a Friday. He and the 12 disciples were at the Last Supper, so there were 13. Friday the 13th became unlucky because 13 at the Last Supper echoes the biblical story.

questions.question: When and why did baked beans become part of a full English breakfast?
At what point does a courgette become a marrow? I've grown courgettes and left one over a foot long - when did it become a marrow?

answers.answer: It's a bit like when does a puddle become a pond. It's probably more measurable. You need a local show - they'll know. Someone who does food competitions would know.
A courgette is just an infant marrow. All marrows start as courgettes. Marrows tend to have much thicker skins than courgettes.

Courgettes, when they start to grow, are a dark greeny colour. The bigger they get, they get lighter. There's no specific time when they become a marrow - it's all to do with weather and temperature and sun.

questions.question: Why after it rains are there so many snails about?

answers.answer: The ground gets slitherier when it rains, and snails find it easier to slither around. You don't see as many when it hasn't been raining because they're not slithering around as much.
Snails come out when it's raining to stop them from drowning. When they're in the ground and the ground gets saturated with water, they drown. So they always come up when it's raining.

questions.question: Walls ice cream and Walls sausages - is Mr or Mrs Wool one and the same person or are they related?

answers.answer: Yes, it's the same company. I believe it started early 19th or late 18th century with a market stall. They started selling sausages first because ice cream didn't exist in 1786 without industrial refrigeration.

Walls started as a butcher's stall in St James's market in the late 18th century. At the beginning of the 20th century, the boss got uncomfortable about laying off staff during summer when people didn't want as much meat. So he came up with the idea of selling ice cream during summer to make up the shortfall.

questions.question: Why does yeast always come in seven gram packets? When me and my dad make bread, the flour comes in different amounts but yeast always seems to be seven grams.

answers.answer: They've worked out an average loaf. You need a lot more flour than yeast to make bread. Once you open a packet of yeast, it can't hang around like flour does - you need it fresh, sealed up, otherwise it starts yeasting all over the place.

Seven grams of dry yeast is the equivalent of one ounce of wet yeast. Recipes used to be in wet yeast amounts with ounces. For a kilo of flour you need 7g (one ounce for a two-pound loaf). The sealed packet is specific to the kilo of flour for a standard bake.

questions.caller: Steve (Camberwell) - on behalf of daughter Cassie
questions.question: Why is bird poo predominantly white while other animal poo or insect poo is of a darker colour like brown or black?

answers.answer: Probably diet. What do birds live on? Insects and things.

If you get pooed on by a bird, there's a white bit and a dark bit. The white bit is what the bird produces instead of urine. They don't actually pee. The white soupy substance is their urine equivalent and the dark stuff is the actual poo.

questions.question: If somebody owns a Grade 2 listed building and does something they're not supposed to, what are the consequences?

answers.answer: You're often ordered to build it back up again. Near my old place, there was a Victorian pub frontage and the developers had to leave it up. When it fell down, they had to put it back up again.

The punishment can be as serious as imprisonment. You can get fines with no limit. You can be asked to reinstate things, and if that's not possible to do, you're more likely to get a bigger fine or even a prison sentence. You can get retrospective planning consent but there's no guarantee you'll succeed. It's a criminal offence.

questions.question: We eat chicken eggs, duck eggs, quail eggs, turkey eggs (at Christmas), but why do we never see turkey eggs for sale in shops?

answers.answer: The answer is Christmas. Turkeys are very seasonal. All the eggs get hatched - they need them to grow into turkeys. Most turkeys get eaten at Christmas, they save a few to produce next year's Christmas turkeys. The market for the bird rather than the egg.

It's a matter of cost. Turkeys lay about two eggs a week. Chickens can lay one to two a day. Turkeys take considerably more space and more food than chickens. They haven't been bred for egg production. If you wanted turkey eggs, you can get them, but it costs an arm and a leg. The farms either hatch them or throw them away.

questions.question: Why are there jokers in a deck of cards? They're just pointless.

answers.answer: It goes back to when cards were used for more than mere games - for fortune telling, tarot, rune reading. Jokers were there for that purpose as a hanger in the deck. When someone draws the Joker, they ask where's death? And it's the Ace of spades - can't dig a grave without a spade.

answers.caller: Israel (Peckham) - tarot card reader and teacher
answers.answer: The Joker does originate from the Tarot - it's the Fool card. The premise is that when people go for Tarot readings, the person consulting the Oracle is somewhat of a fool, in a world of unknown. The Joker is a wild card that doesn't even have a number - given the number zero. It's the first card in the Tarot deck. That's the wildness and unknown about the Joker.

questions.question: Why is there only one King Stephen and only one King John? Does it mean these were bad kings?

answers.answer: I questioned the premise. Stephen and Matilda, both grandchildren of William the Conqueror, had a civil war. Stephen lost, Matilda's son became Henry II. Names fall out of fashion for various reasons - Henry fell out after Henry VIII, Richard after Richard III.

The short answer is bad luck rather than bad kings. Stephen was in a power struggle with Matilda (daughter of Henry I) and he lost. She founded the dynasty - her son became Henry II. Both were grandchildren of William the Conqueror. Stephen's name fell out of fashion the longer it went. If he'd won the war between himself and Matilda, we would have had more Stephens. It damaged the brand of the name.

questions.question: Where is the Second World country? If there's a First World and a Third World, where's the Second World?

answers.answer: It has something to do with NATO and the Warsaw Pact. First World countries are NATO countries, Second World countries are the communist bloc/Warsaw Pact countries, and Third World countries are those in neither - non-aligned countries.

questions.question: Where does the famous Big Ben chime come from? The dong dong dong dong that has made its way into doorbells everywhere. I've heard it in Europe as well.

answers.answer: I was on a bus tour in Vienna on Monday. The second largest bell in the world is in Vienna - it probably has something to do with bells. There's only a certain amount of notes you can get from bells.

answers.caller: Ben (Hitchin) - on behalf of granddad Tom
answers.answer: It's something to do with military history - Portsmouth football club, Navy town. They used to play a tune to signal when to finish the match. The crowd would sing it so the bells would ring because the bells were how the referee knew when the game was supposed to end. This is part of the history but probably not the original origin.
It's a piece called Westminster Quarters, originally called Cambridge Quarters. It was played in Great St Mary's Church in the centre of Cambridge.

When I was about 12, my dad bought a grandfather clock which had Westminster Chimes. We took it to pieces to fix it - the chimes weren't working. We went to the library and did a lot of research. It was for a church in Cambridge, written in the 18th century, possibly by Handel.

questions.question: Where did the term 'ruck' come from? (from rucksack)

answers.answer: Ruck is the German for back. So it's a back sack. A rucksack. We've just adopted the German word.

questions.question: Why does the number pad on a keyboard go 789-456-123-0 while phones go 123-456-789-0?

answers.answer: The computer keyboard copies the layout of the calculator. Originally you'd be using that little keyboard with numbers across the top above the letters, then you've got the number pad which doubles up as a calculator.

questions.question: Why do men's shirts have buttons on the right-hand side and women's shirts have buttons on the left?

answers.answer: Ladies' shirts were done up by their maids. And so we are mostly right-handed. So a bloke who does up his own shirt, right-handed, button in right hand, through hole, job done. Now turn around and you're putting on someone else's shirt, whether it's male or female, and having the buttons on the right-hand side means that you're going to be using your left hand to do the tricky fiddly bit. Ladies' maids, right-handed, ladies wearing blouses, buttons down, left-hand side.

questions.question: Does a bee know that when it stings you, it will die?

answers.answer: No. He would never do it. Would it be altruistic of him to do it anyway? No, because there's no altruism involved, really, in stinging someone. He doesn't help anybody else. It's an evolutionary mistake. He doesn't know he's going to die if he stings you.

Bees are not aware they're going to die when they sting a mammal. It only happens when they sting a mammal - if they sting any other type of insect or animal then it doesn't happen. It's only the guards mainly that do the attacking and they set off a pheromone that entices the others to come along. They're only interested in protecting the collective. Their individual lives as far as we know, they've been keeping bees for 10 years, they're only interested in the actual collective. The honeybee has a small hook at the end of its stinger. The problem with mammals is we've got the elasticity in our skin and as soon as they sting and stick it in it gets caught. The bee wouldn't have a clue - it's an evolutionary mistake.

Bees ARE aware they're going to die when they sting someone. When you see a bee injure itself and land, you see it pumping its abdomen where the sting comes from - that's them pumping all the adrenaline into themselves to get ready for the final act, the kamikaze act. They release an electrical spike during that few seconds. They are aware because of all the actions they do in their life.

questions.question: Why are UK elections always held on Thursday and not Sunday like in Europe?

answers.answer: Mystery Hour is on a Thursday because elections are on Thursday. And when there's an election, we're not allowed to talk about the politics. So we came up with some games. And this one proved really popular. So we stayed with it. But why on a Thursday? I do not know.
I've heard that a vicar could give a sermon on a Sunday and be politically biased towards a certain party. So by the time Thursday comes along, hopefully that opinion may be forgotten.

Elections are not always held on a Thursday. They have been since the Representation of the People Act with exceptions. There is no definitive answer. Theories include payday on a Friday and church influence (Christians on Sunday, Muslims on Friday, Jews on Saturday), but ultimately there's no statute and it's not always the case.

questions.question: Why does double A represent a smaller bra size rather than a larger one? Since it came after A chronologically, shouldn't it be bigger?

answers.answer: The original scale was overtaken by the dizzying array of boob sizes and the bra measurement scale had to catch up. They needed something smaller than an A but had already used A, so they called it double A. Same at the other end - needed something bigger than F but had G, so they made double F.

questions.question: When or why did we associate the color blue with obscene or rude things? (blue comedian, blue movie)

answers.answer: When they started making pornographic movies, the production values were incredibly low and it had to be done in secret so they'd use cheap black and white film. Cheap black and white film often assumes a bluish hue because there's not enough lighting. A bluish tint would appear on the film which you could have got rid of if you'd had more money or better quality film or better lighting. Blue became a synonym for rude and it started with the film.

questions.caller: Graham from Basingstoke (daughter Eva, 6 years old)
questions.question: Why do itches move around? When you scratch one spot, it moves to another spot.

answers.answer: There are two different types of scratches: the pleasure scratch (Baloo the Bear style) and the itch scratch. The pleasure from being scratched on your back moves all over your back, so you keep asking for more scratches in different spots. But when you've got an actual itch somewhere else, once you've scratched it, the itch has disappeared. It's two different pleasure principles - a back scratch is a joy regardless of whether you're itchy or not, whereas an itch on your calves is just annoying and once scratched, it's gone.

questions.question: Why can't you digest sweetcorn? Why does it come out whole?

answers.answer: It's the membrane. Sweetcorn has a quite thick membrane, so you need to chew it properly. If you chew it, you'll absorb and digest it. It's not that you can't digest it - you haven't chewed it properly.

questions.question: Is there anywhere in London that's just called 'London' with no other name?

answers.answer: London is the City of London. The places within the City of London are building-based or smaller than a borough, linked to a river or geographical feature, or named after gates.
Apsley House in Hyde Park Corner is known as 'Number One London' - there's no other address for it at all. The Duke of Wellington lived there.

questions.question: Why do golfers shout 'four' when doing a wayward shot?

answers.answer: It's short for 'before' - 'before you get hit on the head.' It comes from shooting galleries or firing squads - you wouldn't wander around in front of a gun without warning, so 'before' became 'four' and got adopted into golf.
It's 'four warns' - B4. You say it because by the time you got to 'warn' the ball would have hit the person already.

questions.question: Do you get more wet by running or walking when it's raining?

answers.answer: It depends on wind, how heavy the rain is, how fast you run. Mythbusters arrived at both conclusions - whichever one they arrived at second they went with. I'll leave it on the board.

answers.caller: Professor Hallett (Professor of Public Understanding of Science, University of Brighton)
answers.answer: Think of it like a shower - if you saunter through slowly vs run through as fast as you can, you get WETTER when you walk and DRIER when you run. The faster you go, the less you're exposed to the flux of water hitting you.

questions.question: When we talk about massive international trade figures in the billions, is it a thousand million or a million million? When they're talking about government spending plans and international trade, which billion is being used?

answers.answer: The market convention is it's a thousand million and it's always been that way. So if you're talking about a billion dollars or a billion sterling in the city of London or in New York, it's always a thousand million.

questions.question: How did regional accents develop in the first place? My son was asking last night and I changed his simple question into this bigger one.

answers.answer: The accent in parts of the country like the Black Country and the Potteries was in part informed by the scale of industry. If you go for a full-on Black Country accent, it has a blocked nose flavour because people weren't breathing through their noses due to smog and pollution.

Accents are vestiges of regional dialects, which are themselves vestiges of regional or tribal languages. Geordie is distinct from the rest because it was a Danish stronghold - one of the last strongholds of the Vikings. Before the industrial revolution, people didn't move around much, so regional dialects were really regional languages - they couldn't understand each other from one end of the country to the other. There's also loan words from other languages, notably French. From Shakespeare onwards, when people started reading and language was standardized, these regional dialects or languages became accents.

questions.question: When you're on a plane and it's about to take off, why do they put the shutters up for safety? In case the engine catches fire?

answers.answer: They need to be able to see the wings.

It's to do with pupil dilation and the taxi, take-off and landing. You're trying to keep the ambient temperature and ambient light the same during those emergency situations. You don't want to go from extreme light to extreme darkness in case of emergency because obviously you'll lose all aircraft power. That's what it's trying to compensate for.

questions.question: I've often noticed that when music is played softly, it sounds out of tune. When it's played out of my phone and the volume isn't high enough, it sounds out of tune. Is this just me or is there a scientific reason?

answers.caller: Paul (caller who gave his name as Tom initially)
answers.answer: I'm a musician and producer. If you don't get the full range of harmonic or EQ frequencies, you don't get the full balance of a mix. When you listen to something through a phone, which is why music always sounds awful through a phone, you don't get the full harmonic balance. As musicians, when we put this stuff together, we're considering the full harmonic balance. Bass frequencies don't travel at the same pace as high end frequencies. What's reaching your ear is less complete and therefore it sounds less tuneful.

questions.question: Oranges arrived in England in the 15th century and we named the colour orange after them. What did we call orange things like carrots before the fruit arrived?

answers.answer: It was red. It was literally everything was just a different shade of red. The best illustration is the fact that we call people redheads and that goes back to way before the 15th century.

questions.question: Are there any other insects or animals, like the butterfly, that when you spoonerise the name describes what it does? Butterfly becomes flutterby which is more poetic and accurate.
We have the Royal Navy and the Royal Air Force, but why is it just the British Army and not the Royal Army?

answers.answer: Royal patronage is established at regimental level rather than whole force level. You have Royal regiments within the British Army like the Royal Fusiliers and Royal Grenadiers. The Royal Navy is like the Royal Fusiliers - it's just one regiment of the broader force.

Go back to the English Civil War. There were no standing armies in those days. The parliament decided to raise the first proper English standing army, and that army fought against the King. Therefore it wasn't royal - it was republican. And that's the reason why it's called the Army and not the Royal Army. The Royal Navy didn't fight against the king, so it kept its title. The Royal Air Force was formed way after that, so it got the title Royal. The army was never a homogenous force - it's always been a conglomeration of regiments, some royal and some not.

questions.question: Why do we say cats have nine lives? Where did that myth come from?
The word hello on the phone - what's the etymology? Why is it the first word we say when answering the phone? In Greece they say 'Ella' which means come on.

answers.answer: Hello was only really popularised as a way of greeting and introducing yourself on a telephone call after Thomas Edison accidentally did it. With Edison, because there was competition between Edison and Graham Bell, they were like 'if you use my phone, you've got to say this.' But the word hello was recorded before the telephone was invented.

questions.question: Why does putting your car key fob next to your head when you press the button increase the efficiency and range of the key fob?

answers.answer: Your body amplifies the aerial or amplifies the signal that the remote sends out. If you're listening to the radio and the reception is bad, if you hold the aerial it gets better. It's the same thing - your whole body has become the transmitter.

questions.question: A sommelier in France has a budget of half a million to a million pounds to buy wines. Some of these wines are 100 years old. How much better would those fine wines actually be? Would I be able to taste the difference between my Chateauneuf-du-Pape and a wine worth thousands?
How many helium balloons would it take to lift a 12-stone man off the ground?

answers.answer: Roughly 3,900 balloons (5-litre size, 5 grams per balloon). Alternatively about 4,000 for safety margin.
One litre of helium lifts one gram. To lift an 80kg man, you need 80 cubic meters of balloon volume. With 10-litre balloons, that's about 8,000 balloons just to hover a few inches off the ground.

questions.question: What is the origin of the 'wooden spoon' given to people who come last in a contest?

answers.answer: The wooden spoon was traditionally given to the Cambridge maths graduate with the overall lowest score. It then passed into sport.

questions.question: Why don't migrating birds fall out of the sky when they sleep?

answers.answer: Birds can fly with either one or both halves of their brain asleep. They go into a semi-sleep state while maintaining muscle tension. They actively navigate in this state. Migratory birds glide on air currents rather than constantly flapping, which is why they don't fall out of the sky.

questions.question: When was the first canned laughter used?
Why do we suddenly need to go to the toilet when we get close to home?

answers.answer: This is Pavlovian conditioning. Every time you've gone home in your life, the first thing you've done is go to the loo. Your mind makes that association. As you approach home, psychology takes control of biology - your brain signals that you're almost there and can now 'evacuate'.

questions.question: At what point does somebody consider themselves fluent in a foreign language?

answers.answer: When you think in the language rather than translating in your head.

When you start dreaming in the language. She started dreaming in English after about 4 years of living in England. You get a 'switch' going on where your shopping list is in English and you think in English.

Fluency isn't just about thinking in a language individually. It's fundamentally about social interaction - being able to negotiate meaning with members of the community where that language is spoken. Thinking in a language doesn't mean you can make yourself understood.

questions.caller: Stefan (Luxembourg) - asked as answer but is essentially a question
questions.question: Is 'Herr' the correct term of address for Jean-Claude Juncker?

answers.answer: In Luxembourg, there are three official languages (German, French, Luxembourgish). You can call him 'Herr' or 'Monsieur' depending on which language you're using.

questions.question: Why do European languages like French, Spanish, Italian attribute masculine and feminine genders to inanimate objects?
Why do we paint our ceilings white? Why do we associate white with spaciousness?

answers.answer: Colour absorbs light. You paint a ceiling white to reflect light rather than absorb it, which keeps all the light in the room and makes it feel more spacious.

questions.question: Is it true that a two word Google search requires to use the same amount of electricity as a kettle being boiled?

answers.answer: I shall find out for you. I like this one.

It is a misconception and a misunderstanding on how things work. If you were the only person doing a search at that moment, no one else was online at all, then yeah, boil a kettle all you like because all the equipment along the way will use the amount of energy to take to boil a kettle, not a problem at all. But a few more than you doing a search at any one point in time then you dilute it by millions and millions and millions.

questions.question: What is the fastest something could travel on Earth? Bearing in mind, when meteors and asteroids come into the atmosphere, they burn up. If something went quick enough on Earth, would that burn up? Does it, do they burn up? Because, no, I see what you mean. They don't burn up because of the speed they're going. They burn up because of what happens when they come into our atmosphere. So what's the maximum achievable speed on Earth? Of anything, yeah.

answers.answer: The fastest something can travel towards the Earth powered by gravity is about terminal velocity. An anvil weighing 500 kilos with a cross-sectional radius of half a meter would reach 280 miles an hour, 446 kilometers per hour. Human beings in free fall reach about 120 miles an hour. When powered by an engine, as you travel towards the speed of light, your mass starts increasing, so you can never travel faster than the speed of light because at the speed of light you have infinite mass and need infinite power. You can technically travel up to 99% the speed of light if you have enough energy.

questions.question: You can't burp in space. And I wondered why?

answers.answer: It'll be gravity.

You can't burp in space because there's no gravity. If there's no gravity, then loads of food might come with it as well, so you can't burp without running the risk of being a bit sick in your spacesuit.

questions.question: Why don't I get hundreds of apples growing in the shadow of my apple tree? Every year that apple tree drops hundreds of apples.

answers.answer: I think you need... I think the pips actually spread through... someone eats the apple and then the seed gets pooed out the other.

When the apples drop on the ground, apple seeds from the apples are not self-pollinating. You need a seed from another apple tree to pollinate the seed. So if you wanted to personally grow an apple tree and you took a seed from one apple tree in your garden and planted it, it wouldn't grow. If you took one from a Granny Smith and the Royal Gala apple tree in your garden and you planted them together, they would pollinate and then you would get an apple tree. Most apple trees are going to come from grafting rather than from a seed.

questions.question: Why when you see someone hurting on TV or in a movie, why does the shooting pain go up your foot or up your leg? And why the people... My mum gets it in her behind. I get it in my feet. It's like a sharp... like an electric shock. Like a contraction of the muscles.

answers.answer: It's a condition called mirror touch synesthesia. If you're watching something on the TV you have someone sort of like puts the hand on someone's shoulder and you feel the same sort of... it's just how it affects you as an individual. I have it and that was about four or five years ago watching things like 'You've Been Framed'... why do I always feel uneasy when I watch these things on the TV? It's because you're the one getting swiped around the back of the head by a penguin or whatever like in the thighs I get it like a knotting feeling.

questions.question: Why do humans have different body shapes? So, for example, you have pear-shaped, you have apple, you have square... But in nature, all animals, but in certain species, are the same shape. So if you take a bottlenose dolphin, all bottlenose dolphins are the same shape. You don't get one that's got a bigger bum than another one, or a smaller fin, waist, etc. I just didn't know if it was because of certain environments that we...

Why does the Queen have to bow to come into the City of London? I was going through an interview done by a very known English political commentator. He was saying that because the City of London is not within the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom, it's international. I've seen a video online on YouTube of her doing that to the Mayor of the City of London.

answers.answer: She doesn't. The city of London has a lot of special status and special traditions and heritage and it may be a garbling of the fact that within the city of London, it's a city of London, so if you're in the square mile nobody takes precedence over the Lord Mayor except the Sovereign. Within the city of London, if the Queen is in her coach and she was coming to the city of London she would stop at the boundary of the city which is Temple Bar, the Lord Mayor would meet her there, she would touch the handle of the Lord Mayor's sword which he is presenting to her and then that shows that she trusts him there's not going to be any trouble and then he will escort her into the city. But any bowing is going to be from the Lord Mayor to the Queen, not the other way around. The Queen bows to nobody.

questions.question: Why is there no pork-flavoured cat food? They seem to have like beef and chicken and fish. But they don't do a pork one. Is it halal or something like that?

answers.answer: I would imagine that just commercially, there hasn't been a need. Pork more than anything else gets turned into offal. Pork scratchings, sausages, bacon. I can't imagine there's enough left over for cat food. It's probably that simple. I don't think there's any medical reasoning.

The reason that they don't have pork-flavoured cat food is cats only have 500 taste buds. It's not really about taste of cats. Same for dogs they have 1,700 taste buds. It's much more about aromas particularly with cats it's about the temperature of the food, they prefer it at prey temperature, also how it feels inside their mouth, they're quite sensitive to those things as well and how good it was for them after they've eaten it so post-ingestion they can analyse how good that food was for them and whether they would go back to it. It's really, really not about taste at all. Also, I suspect there's not any left over with pork production because you can feed they even feed it back to the pigs at some point. They can use pork protein in some dog food and in some cat food but when it comes to flavouring actually there doesn't have to be any of that ingredient in order for it to be a flavour for you to claim it on the packaging.

questions.question: In a supermarket, when you're going down the vegetable aisle, why is it only mushrooms that have brown paper bags and the rest of the vegetables are all plastic bags?

answers.answer: Moisture. If you leave your mushrooms in a plastic bag they go manky much quicker than they do in a paper bag. That's the reason.

Mushrooms actually breathe. They breathe oxygen and release carbon dioxide. So if they're in plastic packaging there's no way for that carbon dioxide to go, the moisture is not present when they're bought they actually produce moisture themselves that needs to be absorbed. If they're in plastic packaging the carbon dioxide really stays in the bag and then it just ends up rotting and killing the mushrooms off.

questions.question: Where do urban foxes get their water from, especially in hot weather like this?

answers.answer: They go to ponds, puddles, canals, and rivers. They can find bits where they won't fall in. They lick water off stuff. It's like asking where a dog gets water from - they go down to the water's edge and have a lick.

Urban foxes are highly opportunistic and modify their behaviour to adapt to urban stresses. They choose home ranges that ensure basic needs including water are met. They find water in food, through rubbish bins, bite through plastic bottles, and do what dogs do. Some societies recommend placing bowls of water out during drought periods when natural sources dry up.

questions.question: How are magnets made? I took my washing machine apart and found lots of magnets.

answers.answer: You can make a magnet if you've got another magnet - rub it and draw the north pole away to polarise another piece of magnetisable metal. But that requires an existing magnet. Presumably you dig metal out of the ground and it's already magnetic. There are naturally occurring magnetic bodies called lodestone.

You get iron out of the ground, add impurities like rare earths such as cobalt in small percentages, which make it much easier to magnetise strongly. Then you put it in an electromagnetic field and turn the electricity on. There is naturally occurring magnetic material (lodestone) but it's very weak and impractical for modern uses like speakers. The materials technology has advanced because now they can look at materials at molecular and atomic levels to figure out the best combinations.

questions.question: How is caffeine extracted from coffee and tea when it's naturally contained in them? How do you make decaf coffee?

answers.answer: Put the question on the board - I knew this once and have forgotten.

answers.caller: Jonathan (Congleton, Cheshire - works in coffee industry)
answers.answer: The decaffeination process happens when the coffee beans are picked and the caffeine is soaked from the beans before they are roasted. It's done at a certain temperature so the coffee flavour stays. The beans are then dried out and imported as green coffee beans before being roasted.

answers.caller: Professor Howell (University of Brighton - Professor of Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: The problem is you want to remove one organic compound (caffeine) while leaving all the others in. There are several methods: 1) Soaking beans in a solvent like ethyl acetate (the smell of pear drops) or ethylene chloride. 2) The Swiss Water Process - you make a huge vat of incredibly strong coffee completely saturated with everything except caffeine, then soak new beans in it. The caffeine migrates into the water because the saturated coffee cannot dissolve anything else - only the caffeine moves, leaving all flavour compounds in the beans. Then you drain away the very hot coffee, remove the caffeine, and reuse it.

questions.question: If a member of the royal family (e.g., Prince William's children) were to ascend the throne and were gay, would they constitutionally be allowed to marry a same-sex partner? Would that partner be given a title?

answers.answer: There's no constitutional reason they wouldn't be allowed to marry a same-sex partner. I would hope they would be allowed. Of course they'd be given a title - like the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall. It's never happened before so there's no precedent.

Prince George would be the first male royal born into the family after equal marriage legislation was introduced. If he had a same-sex marriage as his father Prince William has said he'd be perfectly comfortable with, what would his partner be called? What title would his partner get?

questions.question: Why do people walk down the red carpet at posh events as opposed to any other colour?

answers.answer: It goes back to the ancient Greeks - important events like at Gladiators. The crimson path was for important occasions. Red was the most expensive dye, like purple was for Romans. The red carpet was the poshest, most expensive carpet.

Rolling out the red carpet for important visitors comes from ancient Persia - trading stations on the Silk Road were lined with camel hair carpets which were dyed red. Red is the most common plant dye in that region, and camel hair carpets are extremely hard wearing so the roads didn't wear out. My other half is Persian so I know about this.

questions.question: Why aren't there motorways numbered M10, M11, etc? And why don't we see dead birds?

answers.answer: There is literally only one rule in Mystery Hour - we never take motoring questions. They are boring.

questions.question: When did we tarmac all our roads?

answers.answer: Tarmacadam was invented by someone called Macadam. It would have happened shortly after tarmac was invented, though WWI, the Depression, WWII, and 1970s recession would have interrupted progress. I don't know off the top of my head but I'll find out.

questions.question: Why do we say 'for Pete's sake' instead of using the other word?

answers.answer: Instead of saying 'for God's sake' (which would be blasphemy), you substitute Jesus's best mate Peter (Saint Peter). So 'for Pete's sake' is a euphemistic version of blasphemy that everyone would understand as swearing. 'For crikey's sake' probably came from this tradition too.

questions.question: Why is it 'Dutch Courage'? Why not English Courage or French Courage?

answers.answer: Gin was almost always Dutch and was the strongest alcohol you could buy. Having a tot gave you a bit of confidence / 'lead in your pencil'. Because gin was Dutch, it became known as Dutch Courage. This connects to Hogarth's Gin Lane - most gin came from Holland through trade.

questions.question: Dutch Courage - was it actually about Dutch sailors bringing provisions into London during the plague, drinking themselves into a stupor to get courage to sail into plague-ridden London?

answers.answer: My understanding is that Dutch sailors bringing provisions into London during the plague drank themselves into a state of stupor to give themselves courage to sail into plague-ridden London.

questions.question: Does Stonehenge have a roof, or do we have any evidence to suggest that?

answers.answer: It's a henge and no one has ever suggested they might have roofs with a straight face. The sun's shadow operating on them would be hard with a roof. There are doorways between the arches.

questions.question: When or why did people first start putting milk in tea?

answers.answer: Probably British, probably 19th century. Tea wasn't big before that - people mostly drank beer and gin.

questions.question: Back in the old days when everything was filmed in black and white, how do they colourise it in modern day?

answers.answer: I have a vague memory it's done by hand, which is why there's so little of it. If it was easily done technologically, every black and white film would be available in colour.

questions.question: How long do you have to be dead for a doctor to declare you officially dead?

answers.answer: A doctor has to declare them dead at that moment in time. It depends on how long the doctor holds the wrist for looking for a pulse.

Within the NHS: First check for visible signs of life (skin colour), check if they respond to verbal stimulus (go close and say 'can you hear me?'), check for response to pain (squeezing a finger or trapezius muscle), put stethoscope on chest listening for heartbeat and breath sounds, feel for central pulse (carotid). Different hospitals have different guidelines - Cambridge requires 30-60 seconds for each check, some universities say 2 minutes for each. There's no hard and fast rule, it's at a doctor's discretion. Two doctors usually check at different times.

questions.question: What do fighter jets actually do when they escort planes into airports during bomb threats?

answers.answer: In the case of a bomb threat, they would shoot the plane down if it poses a threat to life on the ground. It's about minimising damage and casualties.

questions.caller: Ian (Marbella) - Former hostage negotiator at Scotland Yard
questions.answer: An airport has to be designated so there's a plan in place when something like this happens. All services know where to go. It has to be in a place where there's less likelihood of collateral damage. There's a designated 'warm area' where the aircraft would be taken. If everything's intact (e.g., a hijack), they can conduct hostage negotiation. The escort jets are there to get the plane into the airport. If it doesn't go where they want, they threaten to shoot it down.

questions.question: Can astronauts and people that go into space take fresh fruit on their missions or is fresh fruit banned?

answers.answer: They might be able to have a banana on the first couple of days, but what would they do with the peel? It would rot in the absence of microbes.

questions.answer: They did used to get deliveries of fresh fruit in space. One of the things the crew always looks forward to is a visiting cargo spacecraft. Usually the ground crew pack a small supply of fresh fruit at the top, near the hatch. Fresh oranges were incredibly powerful in the stale atmosphere. Fresh fruit was a huge treat for all the crew.

questions.question: Why don't most animals sweat?

answers.answer: Most mammals sweat a bit. Horses and monkeys have proportionally the same sized sweat glands as humans, but other mammals have much smaller ones. It's about regulating body temperature, and if you've got fur you do it in different ways. Pigs do sweat but not on the same scale as humans.

questions.question: When you run a really, really hot bath, and you get in, you put your toe in, why does it feel like freezing cold for a couple of seconds?

answers.answer: I don't know. I wonder whether it's like nerve endings with something really hot and really cold.

questions.answer: It's about the temperature difference between the water and the air. The body has to adjust. When there was a big change between air temperature and water temperature, people would complain it felt really cold when it wasn't. When the bath is boiling hot, you feel it more.

You've got two kinds of receptors for hot and cold in your skin, and they work at different temperatures. But as you approach 40 degrees, the cold receptor fires off very strongly all of a sudden. It's not known why this happens, but this is why you feel cold when you put your toe in a hot bath.

questions.caller: Karen (Oxford) - has MA in Early Modern English History, qualified City of London guide
questions.answer: The practice of putting milk in tea coincides with the development of bone china. Tea was a more genteel drink than coffee, favoured by the queen. Ladies would drink it from very fragile bone china cups, so they put milk in to cool the tea down. The custom in England was to put milk in first, then tea, so you wouldn't shatter the cup. Tea in England started around 1660 (Pepys diary reference, Catherine of Braganza). The addition of milk when bone china became commonplace was much later - early 18th century.

questions.caller: Helen (Edinburgh) - worked in visual effects for almost 20 years
questions.answer: They use a process called rotoscoping. You isolate a particular part of an image on each frame of the shot you're working on. In layman's terms, you draw a line around it and fill it in. For the hat, they will have rotoscoped each hat for each shot. Then they can make that a certain colour and the background a different colour. It's phenomenally time-consuming because you have to do it for every single frame. That's why there isn't more of it.
The phrase 'sweat like a pig' actually comes from pig iron, not the actual animal.

questions.question: Do trees have memories? Specifically, why do trees grow in a way that means buses don't hit them? Even when trees aren't there, buses hit the branches.

answers.answer: It's air pruning. The leaves get pruned where they're constantly being pruned by the air flow from buses. It's the same way trees are grown in pots with holes around the outside - if the fibrous roots reach air, they stop growing because there are no nutrients there.

questions.question: Why don't pigeons swim? I saw ducks in a park diving and splashing in the water, and all the pigeons were just standing around watching.

What defines an island? My daughter's gone to the Isle of Purbeck this weekend. Surely most coastal regions you can't reach without crossing over water. So what makes the Isle of Purbeck an isle as opposed to just an outlying bit of land?

answers.answer: The dictionary definition of an island is any land that is completely surrounded by water. However, the Isle of Purbeck is actually a peninsula, not an island - it's only misnamed.

questions.question: Why is there only one Monopoly Commission?

Do dogs have a concept of time the same way that human beings do? When I go on holiday and put my dog in a kennel for a week, does he miss me? Does he miss me more after a week than he would after a month or a day?

answers.answer: It's called mental time travel. Some animals have it, some don't. Animals have a sense of time, but it's different from humans. Dogs have a concept of time but it's different from ours - related to what's called mental time travel.

There are two types of memory - conscious and subconscious. Conscious memory is when you're aware of wanting to learn something. Subconscious memory is when you learn to ride a bike and can still do it years later. Dogs have both. Pavlov's famous experiments showed dogs have memory and subconscious association to events. The memory stays with them for the rest of their life. When a dog goes mad when you come home after just going to empty the bin, it's not because she's forgotten - she's just very happy you're back. Dogs also respond to sounds and smells that predict events - like a dog running to the back door when you open the kitchen drawer where you keep the key.

questions.question: Why do humans dance to music like we're pre-programmed to dance to music? From babies, if they hear a certain beat, they'll just dance. They've never been taught to do that. It's already in them.

answers.caller: Lewis (Cardiff - PhD in Physiology with interest in anthropology)
answers.answer: We dance as a happy accident of evolution. It's emerged as a by-product of our ability to imitate sound. Any animal that is a vocal learner, like birds and humans, can dance. Those who aren't vocal learners, can't. A study looked at about 5,000 videos and found birds and one elephant could move in sync to a beat. Animals have a very close connection between the auditory and motor circuits in their brains.

questions.caller: Chris (London - black cab driver, John in the Counterfeit Beatles tribute band)
questions.question: Back in the old days when cabs were horse-drawn, how long did a horse last? How long would you get out of a horse?

Where does the tune for Happy Birthday come from? Anywhere you go in the world, it's the same tune but in different languages. I know in the UK, France, Germany, Israel, Spain they all sing it to the same tune. Why is the tune universal?

answers.answer: It was penned by two American sisters in the late 1800s. They were schoolteachers and the original tune was 'Good Morning to All' - a song they used to welcome children into class in the morning. It was used in a 1930s film and someone spotted it and it became Happy Birthday. It went on to become the number one royalty-earning song of all time until it fell out of copyright a couple of years ago, which is why there was a lawsuit.

questions.question: Why is it that there's so many more right-handed people in the world than left-handed? You would think it would be 50-50.

answers.caller: Paul (Staplehurst - psychologist with specialism in behavioural preferences)
answers.answer: Two main reasons: First, conflict avoidance - protection of critical parts of the body, particularly the heart, meant a shield was used by the left hand leaving the fighting arm (right hand) free. Over time, those who were stronger at that became dominant. Second, the left side of our brain controls the right side of our body and also controls functions like logic and critical thinking. In the Western world, these functions are valued, so the left side of the brain becomes more developed and dominant, which exacerbates use of the right side of the body. This is why in different cultures with different values, you could end up with more ambidextrous or left-handed people.

questions.question: Why do auctioneers do that rhythmic jibber-jabber thing in between bids? It can be confusing and seems exhausting.

answers.answer: From personal experience doing an auction for Combat Stress charity: it's about creating excitement and momentum. The noise and rhythm, the teasing, the interaction with the crowd, getting people riled up - you can get more money out of people by getting a sense of the value of the money. It's about not letting the other bidder get away with it.

It goes back to old yard livestock auctions. There are two reasons: First, it hypnotises the audience so they're much more relaxed. Second, dead air is an absolute nightmare when you're trying to focus. You do it partly for yourself because it helps you continue to speak. You go 'who's going to give me 100? 100 on the left, 200 on the right. That's good. 200 on the right. Put a hand up. At the back. That's 300.' It just allows you to keep talking.

questions.question: Is there a minimum amount of time that someone would have to live in a property before they can get a blue plaque outside?

answers.answer: It's not time-limited based on the amount of time that you've lived in a house, but it has to be your principal place of residence during your lifetime. Originally it was a London run scheme. Mozart was only in London for a matter of months as a child prodigy on grand tour of Europe, but because that was the place he spent most of his time when he was in London, it qualified. He stayed with a barber named Cousins.

questions.question: Why did we pick Cancer and Capricorn out of the 12 zodiac signs for the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn?

answers.answer: The earth is tilted 23.5 degrees and when the sun is at its highest point north at 23.5 degrees, that point is called the Tropic of Cancer because at that latitude the sun was in Cancer. The same applies for Capricorn. The constellations got their names from Greeks - Cancer because the stars look like a crab. Humans have the ability to make patterns out of stars.

questions.question: Why do they have to sing Abide With Me at the FA Cup final?

answers.answer: Arthur Elvin was the owner and instigator of Wembley Stadium and it was his favourite hymn. He requested that of every game of importance, they would sing Abide With Me. He also requested that the third line of the hymn was removed (reason unknown). Sam's great-grandfather was Arthur Cager, known as the man in the white suit, who conducted the community singing before every match in the 1920s and 30s. Arthur Elvin himself asked Arthur Cager to do Abide With Me at every single game of importance. They have a note to prove it.

questions.question: If you've got a stutter and you're an English speaker, does that mean if you learn a foreign language you'll have a stutter in that as well because of tonal inflections and things like that?

answers.answer: I speak English and also speak Punjabi and I stutter in both languages. If I had to do it in French, I'd even stutter in French as well. It's very difficult. Whatever language you speak, you will stutter.

questions.question: Where do the doves go when they're released at ceremonies like the D-Day celebration?

answers.answer: They're trained to go home to where they came from, like homing pigeons. I know this because my daughter got married a couple of years back and they released a dove. I asked the fellow who owned the doves where they go and he said no, they're trained to come back to where I keep them. It's a business - you basically rent the doves. People started getting owls after Harry Potter to fly up the middle of the church and deliver the rings to the altar.

questions.question: When did the Hollywood sign become just 'Hollywood' instead of 'Hollywoodland' and why?

answers.answer: In 1949, they had to refurbish and rebuild the sign. The area was becoming less land and more urban housing districts. They got rid of the 'land' because there was just less land. It used to be like a massive park land and then it became a residential area, so calling it land seemed silly. You still have all the Griffith Park which is huge.

questions.question: How memory works when it comes to memorising numbers and memorising text. I grew up speaking Pashto and Dari and find it easier to memorise English text than numbers - I have to memorise telephone numbers in Dari.

answers.answer: There are different types of memory: episodic, semantic, linguistic and numbers. Linguistic memory and semantic memory are closely linked so it's easier to remember a language than numbers. Famous mnemonicists turn numbers into stories - making them linguistic - which is why someone who remembers pi to 500 decimal places turns numbers into a story. The caller is unconsciously turning numbers into Pashtun to make them linguistic memory.

I see numbers in colour - I have synesthesia. If both letters and numbers trigger colour associations in the same way, they're processed the same way. But since I don't have it with words, that suggests maybe the brain processes words and numbers differently.

questions.question: Do chickens and other egg laying animals have the emotional intelligence to be sad when we take their eggs away?

answers.answer: Chickens have been bred to lay an egg a day - they don't lay an egg a day in the wild, they lay and sit on it until it hatches. When I had chickens they laid an egg a day and I didn't detect any signs of sadness.

I kept Peking Bantams which are very maternal. They never want you to take their eggs away. If you take the egg away, they just keep on laying. China imitation eggs exist to put underneath them. One hen used to steal eggs from another and roll them across the lawn to her nest. Peking Bantams are famous for being incredibly maternal. The very fact that China eggs exist for comforting chickens suggests they do have an emotional response.

questions.question: Why are cups given in sports finals and in tournaments when you win across the world? You get a celebratory drink but generally they don't do that anymore - maybe back in the day it'd be full of wine.
When they put in a new roundabout or change road layouts, how long does the sign saying 'new roundabout, new layout, priorities changed' stay up? There's been a sign up in my area for ten years.
What makes us warm-blooded and more specifically, what part acts as the radiator which generates the heat?

answers.answer: All cells in the body generate small amounts of heat through exothermic chemical reactions as they use sugars, proteins and fats to generate energy. Different organs generate different amounts of heat. Blood isn't particularly active in generating heat itself. Cold-blooded creatures still eat and obtain energy but aren't as metabolically active, so they don't use the same amount of energy. It's advantageous for them to live in hot environments where they can lie in the sun until their muscles are warm enough to move. Hot-bloodedness is evolutionary - it allowed mammals to survive in northerly and southerly climes.

questions.question: How fast does electricity travel in miles an hour? From a power station to a plug in your house - how long does it take at what speed?

answers.answer: Electric current flows at a maximum speed in metallic conductors of about two-thirds the speed of light - roughly 450 million miles per hour. However, there are discontinuities in the system: switches, transformers, fuses, electricity meters - all present different characteristics that cause the current to speed up or slow down. The typical speed would be about 350 million miles per hour. But to all intents and purposes, it's the blink of an eye - you cannot detect these speeds with the human eye. When I throw a circuit breaker, you see instantaneous light.

questions.question: Why when you walk from sunlight to shade, you don't cast a darker shadow in the shade given that there is less sunlight going through?

answers.answer: A shadow is caused by sunlight hitting something solid. It's an absence of light. The light has to be passing over the body for it to be removed from what you see. When you're in shade, it's not pitch black because there's not enough light to cast a shadow - the more light you have, the more shadow you have, the darker the absence of light becomes.

questions.question: Is there a mechanism by which the producers measure the number of people who might suddenly switch off their radio or change stations - for example, for an irritating ad?

answers.answer: No. They measure audience by using diaries - some electronic, some paper. People fill in their listening habits, and they extrapolate a broader national picture. There's no way to identify a specific radio being switched off. There's nothing in place that would measure or count how many people were switching off as the result of a specific advert.

questions.question: What's the largest score you can get with a single rack in Scrabble?

When will the earth's surface reach the ozone layer? Plant growth divides and grows, we pull oil out of the ground, and when archaeologists dig up relics they're often 20-30 feet down. How many millions of years before it reaches the edge of space?

answers.answer: No. The Earth hasn't put any real mass on since the late heavy bombardment about 3.8 billion years ago. You can neither create nor destroy matter. Matter is energy and energy is matter.

questions.question: Why in aeroplanes does the pilot sit on the left-hand side and in the helicopter the pilot sits on the right-hand side?

answers.answer: Helicopter pilot sits on the right because the cyclic (stick between legs) and collective pitch lever are positioned for right-handed people. In military helicopters, weapon systems are on the left attached to the cyclic.

A helicopter needs to always be flown with hands on controls - if you don't, the helicopter will crash. An aeroplane can fly on its own so pilot can move around. It may be to do with ergonomics or tradition from port and starboard. One of the first helicopter designers was Sikorsky.

questions.question: What's the link between the word blighty and Britain?

answers.answer: Blighty was derived from an Urdu/Hindi word meaning foreign. It's been taken over and hijacked by people who don't know its meaning.

questions.question: What is the smallest animal that could kill a human in its own right?

answers.answer: The banana spider is about two to two and a half inches. They sit between fruits when picking bananas and can kill the pickers.
The harvester ant, about the size of a Tic Tac, has the most toxic bacteria of any insect in the world and uses it to kill prey. They hunt in packs in the southern United States.

questions.question: Why is a hen's called a hen and a stag's called a stag? Why isn't it a hen and a cockerel or a stag and a doe?
Why do road signs for eateries and pubs show a spoon and a fork instead of a knife and a fork?
Why do we call a rabbit a bunny?
Why have we not put another man physically on the moon since 1972?

answers.answer: Because it costs so much money and they've done a cost-benefit analysis deciding it's not worth it. No other country has prioritized it enough.

questions.question: At what speed does it become more efficient to run than to walk? What's the biomechanical reason?

answers.answer: When walking, you always have one foot planted on the ground. When running, there's a part of the motion where you have no feet on the ground. The speed at which it becomes more efficient varies by individual depending on leg length etc.

questions.question: Where does 'Luke' come from in the phrase 'lukewarm'?

answers.answer: It comes from a 15th or 16th century old English word 'lewk' pronounced Luke, which meant sunny or warm.

questions.question: How are crabs able to breathe both underwater and out of the water?

answers.answer: Crabs have 'dead man's fingers' which are their gills. They have two separate respiratory systems like a lobster.

questions.question: ANSWER - Hen night and stag night parties origin
When does a murder become an assassination? How far up the pecking order do you have to be before you get assassinated, rather than a murder?

answers.answer: I don't think it's a pecking order. I think if it's done for political reasons, it's an assassination. Donald Trump tweets that he has received more attacks than any American president in history. And somebody points out that four of them have actually been assassinated. And that word fits there, because you're thinking of an American president. But if anybody... And then you think of British politicians who were murdered by the IRA, like Airy Neve, Lord Mountbatten, they were assassinations. For my money, and I think under the technical terms of the definition, we'd have to say that Joe Cox was assassinated by a terrorist, a white supremacist in that case, because it was done for political reasons. So, I think it's the day of the jackal they were trying to kill de Gaulle. I think it's an assassination when it's been done for political reasons.

questions.question: When I'm sat in my car and I look in my rearview mirror, the object seems further away. When I look in my wing mirrors, they seem closer. So which mirror is accurate?

answers.answer: Interior mirror is flat and gives a true reflection of distance. Exterior mirrors are convex and give a distorted distance to make things look nearer so that you act more safely. If you've ever been to the states and you look in a wing mirror in the states it's etched onto the glass objects in this mirror are closer than they appear.

questions.question: Why does crossing of fingers symbolise hopefulness?

answers.answer: It's a little prayer. In the Christian church, what is an item of worship? The cross. Ergo?

questions.question: Why do babies and why you grow into adults as well, why the bottom lip comes out and quivers when they cry?

answers.answer: When I was having my son's vaccinations done, a midwife told me this.
