The reason they curl their bottom lip when they're crying is because due to all the emotions going through them at that moment, it helps the mother soothe them when she latches them on. It helps them latch on to their mother. Otherwise if they didn't roll their bottom lip they couldn't get soothed by a bottle or by mum and they wouldn't be able to feed and relax them.

questions.question: Me and my wife are big gin fans but we're really annoyed that you can only get tonic bottles in one like dinky little one liter size. Why is that?

answers.answer: The answer to this might be that you and your wife aren't quite as big a gin fans as you think you are because the idea is with a decent measure of gin that's the amount of tonic you need for a single drink. If you still want to be able to taste the gin, if you poured a whole can of coke into a... you don't really have gin and coke but you might have rum and coke. If you put a whole can of coke into your jack daniels or your rum you wouldn't be able to taste the jack daniels or the rum. And if you poured a 330 mil measure of tonic water into your third of a gill of gin you wouldn't be able to taste the gin mate. It's a measure for one drink and if you opened a tinny of tonic... the bottles... you can put the lid back on. It's a measure for one drink and it stays fizzy.

questions.question: Some churches have spires and some have kind of square turrets. I was driving back from Shropshire then I noticed it was more up north. The closer I got to London the more the church has had spires. Why do some church spires/towers have round steeples and some have square towers?

answers.answer: Norman churches have square towers. Anything built after the Norman period before that generally round towers were made of flint. In places where there is suitable building materials and money then you get square towers because obviously it's very difficult to make corners out of flint if you mix it with mortar but if you actually build something out of stone it's much easier to build a rectangular shape.

Where I wanted to see if the actual answer was was where you have a square tower and on the top of the square tower many of these churches used to have a round spire made of wood. And in the rural areas this would frequently become damaged and then it would fall over. And it was never repaired. A lot of these square towers are actually made of wood. The square towers probably used to have spires but because they were damaged and fell over and because they're in rural areas where there isn't obviously the wealth to rebuild them they stay where they are.

questions.question: Why does it smell when we cut the grass?

answers.answer: It's the plant release, grass releases the chemical when it's cut that actually helps deter herbivores. It's the chemical that comes off is like a warning to other grass plants that it's being eaten. And it allows them to see and start building toxins up in the leaves. That's why you might see a herd of sheep grazing in a spot and all of a sudden they'll just walk across to another pack. They won't keep moving in the same bit they're grazing. It's just the plants have released enough toxins to actually start warning them away.

questions.question: Why do towns in different parts of the world twinning? Who does it and are there any perks?

answers.answer: The councillors get to go on lovely jollies with the towns and cities with which they are twinned and they are reciprocated, so they get a free holiday out of it. You also get a little bit of cultural cooperation and what have you and it is arranged by your local authorities, whether municipal or county councils back in the day or whatever it may be.

questions.question: Why is a carpenter's pencil flat when a normal pencil is round?

answers.answer: To stop it rolling away. There are a number of different things you can do with carpenter's pencils. They can be used as a measuring implement in as much as their dimensions are the same, no matter where you get them. They're half inch wide and a quarter of an inch thick. So even though you've used it a lot, it's the width and the thickness, it doesn't matter about the length. The lead, if you look at the end of the carpenter's pencil, the lead is the same shape as the whole profile, but smaller. You can sharpen it blunt. So you can use it on rough surfaces, such as brick or concrete. Because you've got a really thick nib, so to speak.

questions.question: When I was doing my Duke of Edinburgh expedition I learned to do bell ringing in church. At the end of a bell rope, which is where you do the hand stroke, there's a piece of what was carpet then that was called the sally. I just want to know why it's called a sally.

answers.answer: The word originates from a French word which means the action of a jumping rope. So that's why they called it the Sally. But one of our older bell ringers used to call it a fillet as well, which I believe he explained is another rope term for meaning something to do with a corded rope. The French word is salure. Saliure. And then it becomes a sally.

questions.question: What is the kind of origin, or when did we start sleeping in bed? When did we start sleeping with a duvet and a fluffy pillow?
Why is an MP's regular opportunity to meet with constituents called a surgery?

answers.answer: Surgery actually just means any work done by hand. So any work done personally by hand. It's from the Greek. Kirogia. It's just work done by hand. Handy work. Hand work. Greek word for hand. So it's any work done personally. And therefore a personal meeting with your MP rather than having to go through the office and deal with somebody else. And because originally surgeons here, it was all done by barbers. So all the original surgeons were done by barbers because they did all the stuff by hand.

questions.question: Why do earphone wires seem to go into knots more than other wires? Is there some sort of scientific explanation?

answers.answer: It's just the nature of our relationship with our earphones, perhaps. When you carry around a gubbins drawer, all the wires end up tangled together. But if you put earphones by themselves on a table, they still tangle. I don't know.

When people get their headphones, they just shove them in their pocket or fold them up and put them down. When they pick them up again, they pick them up from the wrong end, causing entanglement. Audio engineers have a set method - they always coil it in a specific way so when they untie it, it won't knot and will just come out flat.

questions.question: Which country has the most official languages?

answers.answer: Off the top of my head, you'd be looking at something like Switzerland or possibly the former Yugoslavia. But I don't know about India, Southeast Asia, China - China has Cantonese in the south, Tibet, Xinjiang province have their own languages.
South Africa has 11 official languages and soon to be 12 with sign language being officially recognised legally. I studied African politics and African international relations.

India has 22 official languages nationwide, depending on the state. Zimbabwe has 16 official national languages approved by Parliament. South Africa's languages are just not legally recognised nationwide. I'm a linguist doing my MA at Poznan University.

questions.question: Why are bags of fertiliser or topsoil measured in litres rather than kilograms when litres is usually for liquids?

answers.answer: I think it's to do with moisture content. A wet bag of log chippings weighs more than a dry bag. If you're charged for the quantity put in the bag at source, they do it by volume rather than weight. I'm not being definitive here.

When purchasing pots, they're measured in volume - you'd get a 5 litre pot, 150 litres, 70 litres. And to know how much soil you need to fill those pots, they also measure soil in the same amount (volume/litres). So it's consistent. I used to run a garden centre in Streatham.

questions.question: Why is the cardboard tube in toilet rolls and kitchen rolls cut spirally/diagonally rather than horizontally like the actual roll itself?

answers.answer: I imagine it's because it's the easiest way to roll up the cardboard in the massive things that then get chopped up into little bits. But I don't know why on a toilet roll specifically it's sliced diagonally when the actual bog roll is sliced horizontally.

Tubes can be made two ways - spirally wound or lap wound. Lap wound is like taking a sheet of A4 paper and rolling it up. The more common way for toilet rolls and postal tubes is spiral winding - you take big reels of paper, put them around a spinning metal mandrel, add glue, and as it makes its way along you get that spiral effect. It comes off and gets chopped up. Spiral winding is easier and has better structural strength. I work in packaging and spent three years selling cardboard tubes. The biggest one I sold was 40 feet long.

questions.question: If referring to directions, what is meant when someone says 'as the crow flies, it's about 25 miles'?

answers.answer: It's point to point - the straight line from A to B without taking into account the actual roads and paths and trains you'd have to go down.

questions.question: What word in the English dictionary has the most meanings? Words with multiple meanings - I think they're called homonyms.

answers.answer: A homonym is a word that is spelt and sounds exactly the same in two completely different meanings.
Duck has three meanings - the aquatic mammal, the verb meaning to take evasive action, and in cricket (zero runs).

The word 'set' (S-E-T) has 17 meanings - concrete set, tennis set, a badger's house (sett), and many more. If you go in the dictionary it should be there. I like dictionaries and I love language. I learned this when I was about nine years old.

questions.question: You have a dozen (12) and a baker's dozen (13). If you have a mile, is a country mile a different measurement to a normal mile? Like when someone 'won by a country mile'?

answers.answer: I think it's similar but a companion piece to the 'as the crow flies' question. A country mile would be the opposite concept - accounting for actual roads and terrain. I don't know if we can go definitive on that though.

It's to do with road conditions being so awful in the country that it took you so much longer to get from place to place than in the city. A country mile is a deceptively long distance. For example, if you landed at Plymouth in the 1870s and wanted to get to London, the carrier's cart took three weeks. It means a journey that takes a very long time or a very long way.

questions.question: Why can you get a headache from glasses when your eyes hurt, not your head? How can glasses give you a headache when your eyes are the problem?

answers.answer: It's the muscles in your head connected to your eyes. Your whole face is connected. It's like getting a leg ache if you go for a long run - your eyes are straining. When you get the right prescription, you don't strain, so your eyes don't hurt.

questions.question: What's the minimum amount of people and instruments you can have to still be called an orchestra?

answers.answer: I don't know if there's a set definition of an orchestra. There's the ukulele orchestra of Great Britain which is all ukuleles and possibly a kettle drum. Is it one up from a quintet? If you have 40 trumpets with no drums, is that an orchestra? You have to have a set amount of instruments.

There isn't really a set answer. It depends. You can have as few as four or five in a theatre pit and it would still be called an orchestra. There's something called a symphonietta - I think that's five cellos and five violins - which is technically still an orchestra, though it might be called a symphonietta. There isn't any stipulation about multiplicity of instruments. My daughter plays in the NCO (National Children's Orchestra) and goes to Royal College of Music - I asked this question last Saturday.

questions.question: What is the youngest age you can be a monarch of Great Britain?

answers.answer: You just have to be alive. Prince Charles became next in line to the throne the second he was born. If he's under 18, you'd have a regent put in place - historically the Earl of Warwick or someone like Thomas Seymour would run things until Edward came of age. But he would still be the actual king. If anything happened to the first six people in line overnight, Archie would be king, though he wouldn't be able to do anything. There is no historical precedent for setting an age.

The monarch can technically be any age, but in the 1930s they passed a Regency Act which declared that if the monarch was under 18, the next person in line above 21 became the monarch and regent. Then in the 1950s they changed it so the regent could be over 18. So the monarch can be any age but regent provisions kick in under 18.

questions.question: What is the inner monologue that gets played when a deaf person who has never learned any language other than sign language is reading? Do they have an inner monologue?

answers.answer: I don't know who's going to be able to answer this. If you've never heard words being articulated, what could that internal voice be? It seems set the bar quite high for contributors.

Deaf people do not 'hear' anything when reading because people born deaf are notoriously bad readers - they don't know what the word sounds like. They have no contact with sound. A T sounds like T to us but to a deaf person it doesn't sound like anything - it's just two lines on a piece of paper. They can't distinguish sounds. It's effectively asking them to understand an abstract concept. That's why there's such a push for British Sign Language on TV and at conferences. Most deaf people have a reading age of about 11. I was asked to be an ambassador for the Harrow Deaf Society.

questions.question: When does a murder become an assassination? How far up the pecking order do you have to be before you get assassinated rather than murdered?

answers.answer: If it's done for political reasons, it's an assassination. When somebody is killed for political reasons - like air or the IRA killing Lord Mountbatten, or Jo Cox being killed by a terrorist - those are assassinations. It's about political motivation, not the status of the victim.

questions.question: When I'm sat in my car and look in my rearview mirror, objects seem further away. When I look in my wing mirrors, they seem closer. Which mirror is accurate? Why do we have two different perspectives?

answers.answer: Interior mirror is flat and gives a true reflection of distance. Exterior mirrors are convex and give a distorted distance to make things look nearer so that you act more safely.

questions.question: Why does crossing of fingers symbolise hopefulness?

answers.answer: It's a little prayer. In the Christian church, what is an item of worship? The cross. Ergo, crossing your fingers references the cross and prayer.

questions.question: Why do babies, and adults as well, stick their bottom lip out and quiver when they cry?

answers.answer: A midwife told me when my son was having vaccinations that the reason they curl their bottom lip when crying is because it helps the mother soothe them when she latches them on - it helps them latch onto their mother. If they didn't roll their bottom lip, they couldn't get soothed by a bottle or by mum and wouldn't be able to feed and relax.

questions.question: Me and my wife are big gin fans but we're annoyed that you can only get tonic water in one small one-litre size. Why is that when you can buy gin in larger bottles?

answers.answer: The idea is that a tonic bottle is a measure for one drink. If you poured a whole can of cola into your rum or Jack Daniels, you wouldn't be able to taste the spirit. Same with tonic and gin - you need to keep the proportions right so you can actually taste the gin. Also, tonic goes flat if you open a big bottle, so you get smaller bottles that stay fizzy. You can buy Fever-Tree in little six-packs - open a new bottle for every drink and you're guaranteed fizziness and perfect proportion.

questions.question: Why is a carpenter's pencil flat when a normal pencil is round?

answers.answer: Mainly to stop it rolling away. They can also be used as a measuring implement because their dimensions are the same no matter where you get them - they're half inch wide and a quarter inch thick. The lead is the same shape as the whole profile but smaller, so you can sharpen it blunt for use on rough surfaces like brick or concrete. The thick nib doesn't blunt as quickly as a normal pencil lead.

questions.question: Why do MPs have surgeries? Why is it called a surgery when it's a political meeting?

answers.answer: Surgery means any work done by hand - from the Greek 'cheir' (hand) and 'ergon' (work). It's just work done personally. That's why a personal meeting with your MP is called a surgery. Originally surgeons in this country were barbers who did all the stuff by hand. Doctors didn't do any surgery earlier on - the surgeons were the ones with the sore bones, literally doing the work by hand.

questions.question: Why does it smell when we cut the grass?

answers.answer: It's the plant releasing a chemical when it's cut that helps deter herbivores. The chemical that comes off is like a warning to other grass plants that it's being eaten, and it allows them to start building toxins up in their leaves. That's why you might see a herd of sheep grazing in a spot and all of a sudden they'll just walk across to another patch - the plants have released enough toxins to warn them away.

questions.question: Why are some church towers square and other churches have round spires?

answers.answer: Norman churches have square towers. Anything built before the Norman period generally has round towers because they were made of flint - it's very difficult to make corners out of flint if you mix it with mortar, but if you build something out of stone it's much easier to build a rectangular shape. So round towers are older than square towers.

I disagree slightly - many square towers used to have round wooden spires on top but these would frequently become damaged and fall over in storms. In rural areas where there wasn't the wealth to rebuild them, they stayed square. The church in Kibworth Beauchamp where I grew up had a spire that fell over in the 19th century - a young girl jumped over the spire on the floor on her way home from school and told her mum, who didn't believe her because she thought it was still on top of the church.

questions.question: Why are some villages and towns twinned with other villages and towns in different parts of the world? Who does it and are there any perks?

answers.answer: Councillors arrange twinning and they get to go on lovely jollies to the towns and cities they're twinned with, and they're reciprocated - so they get free holidays out of it. You also get a bit of cultural cooperation. It's arranged by local authorities, whether municipal or county councils.

questions.question: When I was doing my Duke of Edinburgh expedition, I learned bell ringing in church. At the end of the bell rope there's a piece of carpet called the 'sally'. Where does the word 'sally' come from?

answers.answer: The word originates from a French word meaning the action of jumping rope. The French word is 'salire' meaning to leap. One of our older bell ringers used to call it a 'fillet' as well, which is another rope term meaning something to do with a corded rope.

questions.question: When did we start sleeping in bed? When did we start sleeping with a duvet and fluffy pillow? What is the first recorded incident of a bed?
Why do mushy peas come in a smaller can compared to other canned products like beans?

answers.answer: Portion control - only one person in the household eats them, unlike beans which are shared
Mushed peas take up less space than unmushed peas because when you smash round things up they take up less volume
Rejected Pat's answer as speculation rather than knowledge-based, not giving a round of applause

questions.question: How do Thameslink trains detect how full each carriage is? The digital screens show carriages as green, yellow, or red to indicate fullness.

answers.answer: The carriages have weight sensors. When empty they know how much they weigh. When passengers get on, they've calculated the average weight per person. If the weight dictates around 150 people, it goes red or yellow. The suspension adjusts as people get on and off, and the whooshing sound at the platform is the air system adjusting.

questions.question: How long does food that you eat take to become fat or weight on your body? If you get weighed on Monday night and eat what you want after being weighed, when does that food actually become fat?
Why is it called a 'bill' when you pay for food in a restaurant? Why not call it something else?

answers.caller: Matt (Bromley) - trained in catering at Royal Festival Hall
answers.answer: Bill comes from French 'billet du' which literally means a little note or little love letter. In early days, they used to write the total on the back of the menu with pen or pencil and present it as a billet du.
Bill is named after William Pitt the Younger who introduced income tax. The demands on bits of paper became known as 'bills' after his Christian name William, colloquially shortened to Bill.

questions.question: Why does the number seven have a line through it? Is it a European thing to stop it looking like a one?

answers.answer: Yes, it's to stop the seven looking like a one when written in a hurry. If you're writing quickly, a one usually has a little tail and a seven might look like a one.

questions.question: Where do seagulls go in winter? In Brighton they vanish from October to around February. They're not hibernating or dying, but they're not at the coast or inland either.

answers.answer: Seagulls do migrate - they go after food sources. They don't go inland much because they're called sea gulls.
I've heard the answer is that seagulls go inland about 4-5 miles, but I don't believe it because everyone would know about it.

answers.caller: Jazz (Glasgow) - zoology student studying migration and behavioural ecology
answers.answer: Seagulls DO go inland in winter - about 30 kilometres from the shore. When weather turns cold, the warmest places are inland where they're shielded from harsh coastal conditions. Some gulls do migrate for breeding, and seagulls exhibit site fidelity - they return to the same locations. In winter they can be found on rooftops in cities like Glasgow.

questions.question: Follow-up observation about mushy peas: They're not green naturally, the tinned stuff has food colouring in it. The EU was trying to outlaw the colouring and mushy peas would be grey sludge without it.
What happened to John Stuart Mill's housemaid who burnt Thomas Carlyle's manuscript of The French Revolution? It's recorded that she did it but no one records what happened to her afterwards.

answers.caller: John (Eltham) - retired history lecturer fascinated by Victorian social history
answers.answer: The answer comes from Jane Carlyle's diaries and letters (published late 1880s). It wasn't actually Mill's maid - Mill had the manuscript from Carlyle to proofread, and his maid was laying the fires and needed kindling so she burnt it. Jane Carlyle couldn't keep servants - the average time a servant kept a job was 3-4 weeks. They had two servants: a cook and a maid of all work who slept in the kitchen. So the maid probably just left and got another job. Victorian servants had to get up at 4am to lay fires, wet down carpets with cold tea leaves for dust, and scrub front doorsteps.

questions.caller: Nicholas (Brighton) - insomniac who studies everything from heliodynamics to plasma
questions.question: Expanded answer about why sevens have lines through them - explained the origin of Arabic numerals

answers.answer: Arabic numerals were originally written with straight lines only - no curves. Each number represented the amount of angles contained within it. A one had no angles. A two had two angles. A three had three angles. A four was literally a triangle flag on top of a stick with one line going down. A seven originally had three angles without the line, but also had a line across the base in Arabic, giving it more angles. Adding the line through the seven added four more angles. An eight looked like an hourglass. A nine was like a box with a line going down and another little box on the end - which is where cursive nines originated from.

questions.question: Where did the counting method come from where you do four marks and then cross it out with the fifth to make five?

answers.answer: It's a way of counting on paper that you would have done with your hands. You would call in your tallyman to help with counting, whether it was bales of hay or barrels of beer or bushels. Your tallyman would do that and prove it to you, being numerate, farmer or barrel owner. Strike, strike, strike, strike, cross.
A sort of mathematics historian. It became a thing about the 1850s.

questions.question: When you use hand sanitizer and kill germs, where does the actual germs go? If your hands are dirty, where do the germs go?

answers.answer: The dead germs go the same way your skin goes because your skin turns over every 28 days. You wipe your hand with the sanitizer, it kills the germs, the alcohol evaporates and they leave. They create house dust. The dust in your house is 90% human skin and bacteria and flakes of dander. Some stay airborne, get breathed in, caught by mucus in your nose.
I'm the Professor of Public Understanding of Science at the University of Brighton.

questions.question: Where does the word 'lanky' come from?

answers.answer: Lanky, or Lang (L-A-N-G), is the original Old English or Anglo-Saxon word for long. Edward the Longshanks would have been Langshanka - Lang meaning long and shanka meaning leg, as in lambshank.

I read and translate Anglo-Saxon poetry. I've always been mad on history and I'm a huge fan of Bernard Cornwell's Saxon stories. I picked up a book and started learning it, read and speak it a little bit as a hobby.

questions.question: In old hot air balloons, they used sandbags inside the balloon and when landing, they would put sandbags on the outside of the basket. How does putting sandbags inside versus outside make any difference?

answers.answer: It would be more for balance - to make sure the balloon came down in a balanced fashion rather than the sandbags having a different mass inside or outside the basket. The more width you can get on your axis, the more balance you will achieve.

As the sand is supplied as ballast, the intention is that if you quickly eject it, you can gain altitude, which is useful in desperate situations or tricky wind conditions if you're low to the ground. If the sandbags are over the side, you can quickly cut the cords and release them and still keep an eye on what's going on outside of the basket. If the sandbags are inside, you can't see what's going on outside and you've then got to lift them outside and it takes longer.
Ex-private pilot, ex-Royal Air Force. I just put this one down to logic.

questions.question: When the universe formed, why is it that stars and planets tended to form into spherical shapes like a ball, but galaxies themselves have formed into flatter disk shapes? Why the difference?

answers.answer: The centre of the galaxy has a black hole spinning very fast and pulling matter towards it. Our solar system is spinning around that black hole and also travelling through space. The black hole is also moving through the universe. When matter is pulled to a centre of gravity and is spinning, it forms a disk shape - like putting five bricks in a washing machine and turning it on for ages, eventually they'd be spheres. Galaxies are made of stars and gas. Planets are solid matter. Gravity pulls everything towards its centre equally from each side, so it ends up round.
I'm a sort of amateur astrophysicist. I study in my own time. My day job is army officer.

questions.question: Why is the speaker dragged up to his chair when he is elected in the House of Commons?

answers.answer: In the olden days, if the king didn't like what the speaker said, he could have the speaker bumped off. He would quite often get rid of the speaker. So it was not seen as always a great, reluctant honour. That's why when a new speaker is elected, he has to be dragged from his chair because he shouldn't really want the honour of that. It's an old tradition.
I got this from a Geoffrey Archer novel, First Among Equals.

questions.question: Most modern phones use facial recognition. When you're wearing sunglasses, why can the phone still unlock? But if you're not wearing sunglasses and you look to the left or right with your eyes (not your face), why does the phone then refuse to unlock?

answers.answer: Facial recognition technology uses infrared light to make a 3D scan of your face and decide whether it's you or not. Some sunglasses actually block infrared light, and therefore the phone is not able to see a major part of your face and unable to tell if it's you or somebody else. The phone requires your attention and judges it by looking if your eyes are pointed exactly towards it. If it can't see your face and identify you, it won't unlock. If you're wearing glasses that don't block infrared and you're looking away, it also won't unlock to protect against accidental activation.
I'm an IT engineer. I like to read stuff.

questions.question: Where did the two ways of drawing the number four come from?
Why doesn't a bigger brain necessarily make you smarter? You can have people with big heads but they're not necessarily smarter than other people.
Does the Queen have a will?

answers.answer: Yes, the Queen has a will for her personal belongings. She'll leave Prince Charles a nice fountain pen, for example. But not palaces or crown jewels - those belong to the crown, not to her personally. She only possesses them as Queen. They would pass automatically to her heir. James admitted he's 99% certain but not 100%, and left it on the board.

questions.question: When a child is overdue, so the mother's pregnant and the baby's due... Is it the mother that initiates the chemical change that causes childbirth, or is it the baby?

answers.answer: It's a hormone called oxytocin released from the mum's brain. There are a couple of theories. One theory is that the lungs release a certain protein when they're ready. The other is cortisol, which is a hormone being released from the adrenal glands of the baby to say that everything's ready. So it's both. Anything in the baby has come from the mother anyway. So the answer to the original question is both.

questions.question: What is the most valuable liquid? We were having a conversation at work. I was speculating whether the most expensive wine was more expensive than perfume, melted gold or something.

answers.answer: It's a gene therapy treatment which is marketed as Glybera. It treats a genetic deficiency where the patient can't process fats. A single dose, which is about one millilitre, costs approximately £40,000. It was known as the million dollar drug. There are only about 30 people worldwide actually being treated with it because of the expense and the rarity of the condition.

Scorpion venom. There are only 25 species which actually produce that venom capable of killing a human. It's used for medicinal purposes and there are black market dealers in Southeast Asia and parts of the US. It's around $39 million per gallon, so around $8,670 per millilitre. Scorpion venom is second to the gene therapy. King cobra is second to scorpion venom.

questions.question: Why is it that when you look in the mirror, the image is reversed left-right, but not top-bottom? If you've got a wedding ring on your left finger and you look in the mirror, it's on your right finger.

answers.answer: Mirrors don't flip left-right. You hold your hand up in front of a mirror and there's no trickery. Stand in front of a mirror, lift up your right arm, and the reflection comes back at you. So it looks like it's your left arm but it's still your right. For it to make sense that you'd somehow be flipped upside down, there's no parallel or comparison. Your head is exactly where it would be. It's just that it's as if you're looking at yourself.

The person in the mirror is just like somebody standing in front of you, and it depends which side of that person you're on. If you were standing in front of them and lifted up your left arm, if you walked behind that person, it would be the opposite. It's not the brain. It just depends which way you're facing when you're looking left and right. She used the analogy of teaching people to reverse in a car - when you look at the front of the car, point left means curb; when you look out the back window, point left means roadside.

questions.question: Why is it much rarer for people to get cancer of the heart?

answers.caller: Jeremy (Bracknell) - GP with degrees in human physiology and biochemistry
answers.answer: Where you have a larger organ or an organ that has pairs, like a kidney where you've got a spare one, it's less likely to kill you. In evolutionary terms, those organs had less need to adapt to cancer. The heart is small, it's critical, slow cell turnover. It's the classic example of one that has the adaptive mechanisms because if it didn't, we'd all be dead. Cancer protective mechanisms are typically ways of stopping the cells dividing in an uncontrolled way. Skin gets quite a lot of cancer even though it's big because it's exposed a lot to UV. The liver is doubly affected because it's a big organ with less adaptive mechanisms and it has rapid cell turnover.

questions.question: When did egging become a form of political dissent? Who was the first politician to get egged?

Why do airfares change so constantly? Even on one airline, the flight today could be £46 and tomorrow the same day at £90. Then you look again and it's £80. They constantly change with no explanation.

answers.answer: The main driver is the amount of seats left. With scheduled airlines like British Airways, Lufthansa, Virgin - they sell the first 10 seats for the lowest price for marketing purposes, then the next 10 at a slightly higher price and so on until the last 10 which are the most expensive. If there's a cancellation and one of the first 10 seats comes back into the system, they can come down. The cheap tickets are 100% non-refundable and non-changeable, while the expensive ones allow free changes and cancellations. With chartered airlines like TUI, they work the other way around - they fill up seats as much as possible and if they've got any left over, they flog them off cheap.

questions.question: Why is a black box called a black box when it's usually orange? Were they black to start with? Is the orange case a design change? Is there a black box inside the orange box?

answers.answer: There's absolutely no reason why it's called a black box. It's international orange. It's got the flight data recorder in it, the cockpit voice recorder. It's painted that colour for searching. There's absolutely no reason. It's possible it was called a black box because internally it might be completely void of light. But that's it. When they started building them, someone called it a black box at some point. It's more a populist thing that found its way into the press. They've always been painted orange as far as I know. There are two parts to them, clearly labelled as a flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder.

answers.caller: Martin (Maidstone) - President of Cybernetics Society, retired professor of robotics
answers.answer: It goes back to the first days of cybernetics where scientists wanted to analyse closed systems. A closed system was called a black box and an open system was called a white box. You can analyse how a signal goes from the input to output, which is called a transfer function, by applying a standard clever known input and looking at the output. It's a technical term, not a physical one. It describes a technological phenomenon, not a physical entity. It was also used to describe electronic boxes, but cybernetics made it more general. There are lots of black boxes not confined to aeroplane flight recorders. They can be any colour at all.

questions.question: Where did dragons come from? Where did they get invented from? We've got a constellation named after dragons, we've got the Welsh flag with a dragon. Where and when did dragons come about? Because if everyone closes their eyes and thinks what a dragon is, we all come up with the same image.

answers.answer: The answer is in the Bible, the book of Job chapter 41, which has a description of Leviathan. It says 'its snorting throws out flashes of light. Its eyes are like the rays of dawn. Flames stream from its mouth. Smoke pours from its nostrils.' God is speaking to Job in the Old Testament. This appears to be one of the earliest written descriptions.

It's not just from the Bible. There are lots of different types of dragons in various cultures - Greek mythology, Chinese mythology. Chinese mythology would predate the Bible probably. There's the Hydra in Greek mythology, which is a snake-like being, though not technically a dragon. There are lizard-like creatures in mythology.

questions.question: Why in some sports do they change the number zero to nil, or in tennis to love? For example, why is it 'one nil' in football rather than 'one zero'? Nil means nothing, zero means nothing - they're synonyms. So why doesn't it stick to the numbers?
Why is fish course cutlery smaller than meat course cutlery?

answers.answer: Fish is fiddly and bony. You need slightly smaller implements to separate the fish from the skin and the bones and pop it in your mouth.

It was a visual aid for the serving staff in the 1500s-1600s. When everything was being laid out, they couldn't get the cutlery mixed up. The fish knife being smaller than the main course knife meant they knew where it would be placed. Also, different fish cut in different ways, so the shape of the blade helps identify which knife to use for which particular bit of fish.

questions.question: How was it first decided what colour football teams would take on as their team colour?

answers.answer: It's probably chronological. The first couple of clubs chose their colours because they liked them. There's no rules about duplication - Nottingham Forest and Kid and Minster Harriers both play in red, but they're not Arsenal or Man United.
Arsenal wear red because they got their shirts from Nottingham Forest at the beginning. A player called Fred Beardsley brought them with him.

Usually it's because the kits they had at the time was what they had lying around. They were associated with the industry, and that had a colour, so they used that. Over several hundred years, people have just nicked colours off other teams as a homage. Athletic Bilbao wear red and white stripes because that's what Sunderland wore when Sunderland went on tour to Bilbao. Managers sometimes chose colours because they wanted to emulate a particular team - Don Revy changed Leeds' kit from yellow and blue to all white because he wanted the players to feel like they were as good as Real Madrid.

questions.question: At what point does a plate become a bowl?

answers.answer: It might be the angle of the lip or the shape of it. A bowl has a curved bottom - it's bowled. But you can get a bowl with a flat bottom. Maybe it goes on width to depth ratio, or angle of lip, or whether the bottom is bowl-y or flat. If it has a flat bottom, it doesn't matter how high the sides go.

questions.question: Why do tractors have massive back wheels?

answers.answer: It's probably to do with the amount of bulk on the back of the tractor. But I don't really know.

The wheels are small on the front for the turning lock - if they had big ones on the front, you wouldn't have half the turning lock. The back ones are so big because it helps with traction and radius and imprint of the tread on the floor.

You need the massive back wheels for traction so the tractor can go through muddy fields in a way that smaller wheels couldn't. They provide weight and grip. But if you had massive wheels at the front as well, you wouldn't be able to steer.

questions.question: Why can't you put metal objects in a microwave if the inside of a microwave is made of metal?

answers.answer: I don't know. It sparks a lot, but some microwaves it doesn't even apply anymore. I'm going to find out for you.

Microwave ovens are powered by devices called magnetrons, and they're very sensitive to something called voltage standing wave ratio. If they transmit power and some of that power gets reflected, they're very sensitive to the voltage created when power is sent back up them, and they can be destroyed. If the energy comes off a metal object but is reflected at the wrong angle and back up the microwave into the magnetron, it'll be destroyed. The design and angle of the metal inside a microwave is such that energy doesn't get reflected back up into the magnetron.

questions.question: Why do trains blow their horn?

answers.answer: Trains blow their horns in case there's cattle on the track or to alert people. It's like a car horn, although drivers don't use it as frequently. A train can't just stop like a car can, so there's all the more reason to have a horn. Drivers can blow their horns at their own discretion, which is why children standing on railway bridges sometimes get a thrill.

It's a way of communicating between the train driver and workers on the tracks - they've seen each other. If a train driver sees workers on the tracks, he blows his horn, and if workers on the tracks see a train coming, they raise their hands towards the train, and the train driver honks in response to show he's seen them.

The three Norths - depending on where you are, it's something drivers do before they leave as pre-cab checks to make sure they do have a horn when they're out and about. There's no point getting to the time where you need to use it and finding out you don't have a horn because by then it's too late. The first answer was technically correct - you are allowed to use your horn at any time you feel it's necessary.

questions.question: Why do we say the word 'quid' instead of 'pound'?

answers.answer: I have no idea. Will it not come from 'quid pro quo'? I don't know. Which means something for something.
It's short for 'quid pro quo'. Which means something for something. As in, you give me a quid, I'll give you a quo.

questions.question: Why is there a gap in the roundabout road sign?

answers.answer: The junction is always at six o'clock - you always enter the bottom of the sign. The sign is a routing sign telling you the route to get to somewhere. They have the section missing at five o'clock to illustrate that you can't turn right - don't drive into the gap. You have to follow the route round to your junction.

questions.question: When does a bridge turn into a tunnel?

answers.answer: If you use them as verbs, you'll find your answer. A bridge is the result of bridging, and a tunnel is the result of tunnelling. You tunnel through something. If you had quite a thin sheet of rock on your route, even if after tunnelling through it it's turned into a natural bridge as wide as a footpath, it would still be a tunnel rather than a bridge. Bridging and tunnelling are two very different verbs.

questions.question: Why do MPs get more time off than the rest of the normal working class when they have more things to do than dinners?

answers.answer: Historically, MPs are supposed to do lots of work in their constituency when they're not in Westminster, so you wouldn't necessarily describe it as time off. They get roughly the same recesses as school holidays - summer off, Easter off. The answer will be they're supposed to do work in their constituency.

The reason they have such a long summer recess is because back in the day, raw sewage used to be thrown in the pens. So it stank all summer. The stench was overwhelming, so the politicians refused to sit in Parliament.

questions.question: What is the association between Sticks of Rock and the Seaside? Because you only seem to find Sticks of Rock at the seaside.

answers.answer: It's because of the wording running through the middle of it. You only want to buy a Stick of Rock because it's not actually a very efficient way of eating sweets. The answer will be the novelty value of having the words running right through it. The fact that you can put the name of the place you're visiting through the Stick of Rock is a quasi-souvenir. Places that are associated with destinations which are a treat to visit, i.e. places from which you would want to take a souvenir. Ergo, Sticks of Rock are routinely associated with seaside town destinations. Teddy Gray's in Bewdley is a famous rock maker, and Bewdley was a tourist destination because it nestles on the banks of the River Severn, so people would go there for a break.

questions.question: Why is a teddy bear called a teddy bear and not something like a soft bear or play bear or toy bear? Where does the 'teddy' bit come from?

answers.answer: It's something to do with Teddy Roosevelt. The American president. I think I've heard that it has something to do with when he was out hunting - there was a bear that he saved and the press reported it as Teddy's bear. That's how it's done.
You were right that it is to do with Teddy Roosevelt. It was to do with when he was out hunting. There was a bear that he saved and the press reported it as Teddy's bear. And that's how it's done.

questions.question: How far do ducks ordinarily stray from their home pond?
Why do women faint more than men?

answers.answer: Initial speculation - could be linked to going without food, or medical conditions involving fainting that are exclusive to women.

Vasovagal syncope affects both boys and girls equally. Historically women were thought to faint more due to swooning stereotypes from the corset era. Actually women do faint more between ages 15-30 due to menstruation causing iron deficiency, diet issues, and anxiety. Fainting is a physiological reaction to stress, fear of blood, claustrophobia, or fright.

questions.question: How do they decide how far apart to put bus stops? And is each bus stop the same length?

answers.answer: Local councils set minimum walking distances: 200 metres for majority in urban areas, 400 metres in rural areas, and 150 metres uphill (harder to walk). They use GIS (geographical information systems) with coloured pins to map coverage - green houses have bus stops nearby, red houses don't. Multiple buses on overlapping routes must coordinate stop placement.

questions.question: Why is the gum shield only covering the top teeth, not the bottom teeth?

answers.answer: Top teeth naturally cover bottom teeth when mouth is closed due to overbite. If you had to choose between protecting top or bottom jaw, you'd protect the top.

Mouthguard is to protect teeth from hitting each other and causing concussion. A rugby ball won't knock teeth out, but smashing upper and lower teeth together can knock you unconscious. In American football they cover both sets due to extreme head impacts.

Tongue naturally sits in the lower arch of teeth. The bulk of the mouthguard on the inside would make your tongue 'all over the place'. Upper-only placement allows better oxygen intake during prolonged activity like rugby. American football has short plays so they can cover both sets.

questions.question: Why is a toast called a toast? (referring to the drink toast, not bread toast)

answers.answer: Goes back to Elizabethan times. They put spiced toast at the bottom of the cup or glass before pouring drink. It improved the taste because ale and wine were often ropey, and it soaked up the dregs. The Tatler ran a story in early 1700s about the 'toast of the town' - a woman in Bath, a male admirer drank her bath water with toast in it. This is where the phrase 'toast of the town' originates.

questions.question: Why do we say a bomb has gone off or a fire alarm has gone off when it's actually gone on?

answers.answer: The alarm is constantly 'on'/set. Something triggers it to 'go off' (start), then it continues going off until it 'goes off' again (stops/finishes). You can't say 'gone on' because the alarm is always set/on. The alarm can't 'go on' because it's already on.

questions.question: Where did rock, paper, scissors originate?
Why in the UK does the telephone dial-in tone have a double trill compared to internationally where it's a single one?

answers.answer: Not unique to UK - Australia has exactly the same system. New Zealand is the same as well. Commonwealth colonial connection suggested but reason not confirmed.

questions.question: Who invented the electric toaster?

answers.answer: Alan McMasters. Guess around 1895-1900. Works in catering equipment sales so learned this along the way.
Confirmed: Alan McMasters, 1893. Later marketed by Stephen J. Cook & Co. as 'the Eclipse'. McMasters died Christmas Day 1927 living in Versailles.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'touch wood' come from in the context of good luck?

answers.answer: I've always presumed it's touching the wood of the cross. Jesus is calling. Of the cross.

The Druid one was that the Druids believed that if you touched a tree, you could implore the fairies living within or the spirits living within to come out and they would give you aid or protection. Dryads. He recited a poem by Nora Archibald Smith: 'They'd knock on a tree and would simply say to the spirits who might be within there that day, very fair, very fair, wish they me well, against evil which trees weave me a spell.'

questions.question: Can insects get fat? I don't mean just big, obviously to keep feeding them a bit bigger, but can they get fat?

answers.answer: Given that insects have exoskeletons, then they can't get fat because they'd explode like Monsieur Creosote. They've got an exoskeleton, so they can't get fat, can they? They literally burst.

Insects do get fat depending on whether they are subject to a large food supply. But it is in the larval stage that they tend to get fat. If you have, for example, a butterfly, a whole load of butterfly caterpillars on a plant, if there's plenty of plant, the caterpillars will get fat. They will molt because they go through a process of going through various instars. If a caterpillar is starved, you will finally get a butterfly when it pupates, which is a tiny little thing. But if you've got a caterpillar where there's masses of food, at the end of it, you get an outsize, a large specimen.

questions.question: If you are a child actor performing in a film which is an 18 plus, say if you're 12, are you able to go and watch the premiere of your film? Or do you have to wait, say, six years before you can actually go and see your own film?

answers.answer: I think it would be up to the parent, probably. If you showed an 18 film to your 12-year-old at home, it's not a crime, is it? You're not going to get prosecuted. I think it's only the selling of tickets that's prohibited by law.

They are definitely allowed to go to premieres, even if they are too young to legally have been allowed to go. However, if they then wanted to go again with their children, they would not be allowed because you're not allowed to buy a ticket. My son was in Juliet Naked with Rose Byrne and Ethan Hawke. It was a 15 and at the time of the premiere he was 10. He went to the premiere. They left it up to me.

questions.question: What happens to court sketches? Who keeps them? Do the media send their own court artist, or is the court artist employed by the court? Is there an archive?

answers.answer: They're only made for the media. If they've ended up on Michael Mansfield's wall, then they're obviously buyable, which means they either revert in copyright or ownership to the artist, or they revert to whoever's paying the artist.

The media, whether it be the BBC or ITV or Sky, commission the artist to go and sit in the courtroom all day to sketch the pictures, because cameras aren't allowed in. Nobody shares the pictures. Sometimes you have more than one court artist representing different broadcasters. The company that's commissioned them owns them. They can sell them because you get paid for your labour, not for your intellectual property. Michael Mansfield having them on his wall would be a gift from possibly the journalist covering that case, or a purchase.

questions.question: Why are they called Reddy Salted Crisps? Why do I need to know when they've been salted?

answers.answer: Crisps used to be sold with a little twist of wax paper in them containing salt, which means you would salt them. The salt and shake. They are Reddy Salted as opposed to self-saltable or salt and shake.

questions.question: Why is water taken as the sign of life, the definitive sign of life by astronomers or astronauts? Isn't it a bit blinkered to assume that just because we need water on Earth, we also need it on any other planet?

answers.answer: I bet it's got something to do with oxygen and hydrogen.

To have carbon-based life, which is what all life on this planet is, you have to have liquid water. Water has between 30 to 50 different functions. It's a solvent for all the reactions in our cells. It's a coolant. It's essential for our metabolic and catabolic processes. We burn sugar to give energy, and water is the ultimate product. When you breathe out, you're breathing out water. As for silicon-based life, if you ate silane and reacted it with oxygen, you'd breathe out silicon dioxide, which is sand. You can't breathe out a solid. For that one single reason, you cannot have silicon-based life. You have to have proteins and all those things have carbon as the backbone.

questions.question: Does antiseptic cream lose its antiseptic properties after the expiry date? If Savlon has an expiry date on it, what happens after that date?

answers.answer: I don't know whether it lost the answer. Most obviously, what happened to the graze? It probably by law has to have some sort of expiry date on it, otherwise some rascal would be selling you 50-year-old stuff out the back of a lorry at a car boot sale.

They're there for protection. They lose some of their efficacy. They still do the job, but not as well as a brand new tube. The active ingredients remain active but not as active. You mustn't get confused with a use-by date or a sell-by date. A use-by date is when a product should be used by. You can still sell it past its sell-by date. After opening, some medicines have a date of six months or twelve months or 24 months before they're no good.

questions.question: Is there any British manufactured car that's ever been manufactured, made and sold in Britain that is now extinct? No surviving examples anywhere?

answers.answer: We need to clarify slightly, because we won't know if there's one in a barn as yet undiscovered. What you want to know is a recognised marque with a Q at the end of a recognised marque of British manufactured motor car of which there are currently no known surviving examples. I shall do my level best to find out for you.

There was a car manufactured around here in Kent back in the 30s. I think it was called the Orpington car. There was only one model. They made more vehicles than one, but I think they only even made one model.

questions.question: Why do all the heads on coins face one way, and all the heads on stamps face the other way? Why must there be a reason?

answers.answer: Sometimes it just is. There doesn't have to be a reason for everything. However, on every coin, if it was random, you'd probably have some heads facing the other way.
Monarchs don't always face the same way on coins. It alternates with each monarch. So our next monarch will be facing the opposite way to that which the Queen currently faces on all coins.

questions.question: Is the sea less salty than it used to be, because we've taken salt out of it for cooking? If it's measurably less salty?

answers.answer: No. It's not a finite amount of salt that was in the sea once and stays there. Salt is arriving in the sea every day from rivers. For every salt that is taken out of a sea, it replenishes again with rain and rivers. The rain wouldn't bring any salt with it, but the rivers would. Rivers coming down through salty terrain, through rock salt. Even if the salt is under the sea in rock form and slowly dissolves into the sea over the millennia.

questions.question: Are crosswords copyrighted? Is there anything to stop someone taking a crossword from an obscure publication 10, 20, 30 years ago and just changing one or two of the clues?

answers.answer: It's not quite binary - you can't have complete copyright because that would involve copyrighting words that everybody's allowed to use. A crossword is like a story using words in a particular order which takes a long time to compile.

A crossword is intellectual property because it's been created, like a song or photograph. As soon as it's committed to physical form, it gets protected under copyright law. The law determines whether you've done enough work to make it your own. If someone changed just one word like 'knit' to 'snot' and left all the other work in place, they would be in breach because they haven't changed enough to make it their own. You'd go into arbitration or legal action.

questions.question: Why after you have a drink if you're really thirsty do you go 'ahhh' and make that noise?

answers.answer: You can't breathe while drinking. The longer the drink, the longer you've gone without breathing. At the end of a very long drink after being particularly thirsty, you need to breathe urgently. The exhalation is at greater speed than usual, which is what explains the sound so you can breathe in more quickly.

It's a natural bodily function. You can't breathe and drink at the same time otherwise you'd drown yourself. The longer the drink, the greater the need to take a deep breath after. The deeper the breath you need, the deeper the breath you take, and the more likely it is to make a noise. You're emptying out the lungs, getting ready for a lovely dose of oxygen.

questions.question: In the old days with ring pull cans of lager or fizzy pop like Iron Brew, if you shook them up before pulling the ring pull, you'd get a fountain everywhere. Now with modern cans where you just click the tab, if you shake it up and kick it around the floor, it doesn't spray anywhere. Why don't fizzy pop cans 'skoosh' anymore?

answers.answer: They changed the design of the tin because the ring pulls were detachable and sharp. It was a simple safety issue.

questions.question: Why do human beings across the globe respond to what they identify as a beat in music by dancing to it? Even if it's not an evolutionary explanation, why is it so core to human beings?

answers.answer: The beat replicates the heartbeat. The heartbeat reminds us of absolute security, and absolute security makes us want to dance.

Before we had verbal language, a beat created unity for people working or moving together - like Homo erectus or other predecessors. When walking as a group, feet would create a beat, which became an evolutionary thing where the beat creates unity. Any type of ritual or gathering would use a beat to create cohesion without language. This is theorized as one of the origins of language itself.

questions.question: What is the most expensive thing in the entire world, monetary-wise? Is it a piece of art, a vehicle, a possession, something out in space, a spaceship?

answers.answer: It's too vague. We need to confine it to 'what is the most expensive thing any human being has ever bought?' Also what about things sold a thousand years ago? And what's the relationship with priceless things like peace and love?
The International Space Station. Based on the cost and the amount of shuttle launches it took to build it, it's estimated at around $150 billion. It's general pub trivia knowledge.

questions.question: Why do cat scratches itch more than normal scratches? If you scratch your arm it doesn't itch, it might hurt but it doesn't itch. But cat scratches itch.

answers.answer: I suspect you're not comparing apples with apples. You're comparing scratches of two kinds, one of which is itchy because it's a deeper scratch. I will find out.

Cat scratches are inherently dirty wounds because cats run around the garden digging in soil. Dirty wounds result in localised inflammation. As part of the inflammatory process, mast cells are released, which also release histamine, and histamine causes itching and sneezing (which is why we take antihistamine tablets for hayfever). So a really itchy cat scratch could be helped by an antihistamine tablet.

questions.question: Are you more or less likely to win the lottery if you play the same numbers every week?

answers.answer: No difference at all. If you have a coin and toss it 19 times and it comes up heads every time, the chances of it being heads on the 20th is still 50-50. You have six numbers picked from 49 - the odds are identical to any other six numbers, regardless of what the last six numbers were.

questions.question: When was the first passport invented? Was it medieval or Roman times when you could just walk across borders?

answers.answer: I don't know but I wonder if it had something to do with the Crusades. I think I've addressed this or similar before, so hopefully we can get you an answer.

In Britain, the first passport was created by Henry V around 1414 during the Hundred Years' War against the French. 'Passport' comes from the French word for porter (gate) meaning passing through gates. An act of parliament was passed making it a crime to kill anyone who carried a passport signed by the king who was carrying out official business - essentially diplomatic protection.

questions.question: When we launch a satellite, what dictates whereabouts in Earth's orbit it goes? Do you have to get planning for it so it doesn't bump into another one?

answers.answer: Great question - I hope I can get you an answer.

A company called IntelSat decides where satellites can go based on demand and reach requirements. You can only reach certain parts of the globe from certain positions, so orbital placement depends on what coverage you need - Atlantic Ocean for US coverage, Indian Ocean for other regions. It's not a supranational organization everyone signs up to - even North Korea would have to coordinate through them. Gary worked for Brightstone, the first commercial satellite operation in Britain, involved in Lockerbie and the fall of the Berlin Wall.

questions.question: When football clubs buy or sell a player, who performs the medical - the selling club, the buying club, or an independent body?

answers.answer: The BUYING club does all the medicals - cardiac and musculoskeletal. You're in charge of the asset as the purchaser, so you get the survey done. If things are worse than represented, you pull out.

questions.question: Does the concaved bottom (punt) in wine bottles indicate better quality wine? Why do some bottles have punts and some don't?

answers.answer: The concave is called a PUNT. James said he'll find out but doesn't know the answer.

questions.question: Do trees clean the air in winter when they don't have any leaves? If there's no photosynthesis, how can they be doing anything?

answers.answer: No - photosynthesis needs chlorophyll present in green leaves. Without leaves, there's no transformation of carbon dioxide into oxygen.

Correct - trees don't photosynthesise in winter so they don't pull out oxygen. But for other pollution, trees like the London Plane catch particulates on their bark like a net - they're just catching pollution, not chemically processing it. That's why they were planted.

questions.question: Is there a plague burial pit that explains why the Piccadilly line does a big loop between South Kensington and Earl's Court? His brother told him this growing up but his brother 'didn't always tell the absolute truth'.

answers.answer: James mentioned there's a river in a pipe going over the platform at Sloane Square station, but doesn't know about the plague pit. He'll put it on the board.
Checked historic-uk.com - they have an interactive map of all plague pits. There is no plague pit in the South Kensington/Earl's Court area that would explain the Piccadilly line route.

questions.question: Is it true you have to moisturize upwards (not downwards) otherwise your skin will sag? And is the ring finger really necessary for the eye area?

answers.answer: James said he does vigorous circular motions and doesn't know. He mentioned it sounds like one of those modern tales. 'Instructions are for the birds.'
No, it doesn't matter which direction. Any direction would benefit the skin. You moisturize downwards first to withdraw blood from the skin and close the pores.

questions.question: How can underwater gas cutters/flames work if fire needs oxygen? The flame would be extinguished by the water, right?

answers.answer: James mentioned being in Marrakesh where there was a fountain with gas flames and water - suggested high pressure might be involved. Didn't know the actual answer.

answers.caller: Daniel from Huddersfield (gas blender for technical scuba divers)
answers.answer: The acetylene torch works underwater because it's oxyacetylene - it provides its own oxygen. The oxygen provides both the ignition heat source and the fuel, creating the fire triangle itself.

questions.question: How is a thermometer calibrated? There's a constant for size (a kilogram), but temperature is always moving - how do you know your thermometer is accurate?

answers.answer: They use test chambers - areas that keep very constant temperatures that can be monitored. They put thermocouple thermometers in at multiple temperatures and provide a certificate showing how far out the reading is (e.g., 'add 0.01 degrees to everything'). This is for industrial/commercial thermometers, not domestic ones.

questions.question: Why are barges square instead of having pointed edges like ships? It would be easier to go through the water - the energy required to pull them against the tide was massive. Why are they called barges?

answers.answer: James speculated it must be because barges are used to bang into other vessels - if you had a pointed front, you'd sink the thing you're barging into. 'It must be the answer. There can't be another answer.'

The bulges are actually LIGHTERS, not barges. They're built that way to maximise the amount of containers that go in them. The squareness is for containerisation of London's rubbish. Has nothing to do with smashing into ships.

questions.question: Why do men lose their hair (get bald patches) but women generally don't? Apart from alopecia.

answers.answer: Testosterone plays a part. The prominent hormone difference between men and women is testosterone, and there must be something about it that makes men lose their hair in a way women don't. Men with bald patches are demonstrably more manly than men without.

We suffer from a hormone called PGD2 more than women do. It's androgenetic alopecia and women don't have it as much. Women don't suffer from it like men do. Imran also mentioned he had a hair transplant.

questions.question: If alcohol is both colourless and tasteless, why do low alcohol and non-alcohol wines and beers taste rubbish?

answers.answer: Alcohol isn't tasteless. Pure alcohol has a pungent aroma and burns the back of your throat. The chemical reaction when making drinks creates flavour, and even if alcohol is colourless and flavourless, when it's not present in a drink, the chemical reaction can't take place the same way.

They taste poor because when they get rid of the alcohol, they boil it off during distillation, and the tasty compounds that taste nice also have low boiling points and boil off largely at the same time. So in the process of removing the alcohol, they inevitably also remove some of the flavoursome components.

questions.question: Why does 32-degree air feel really hot, but 32-degree bath water feel really cold?

answers.answer: It's similar to wind chill factor. The water takes away heat from your body and replaces it with cold water, which your body then reheats. And then that moves away and does it again and again. Like when you go in the sea with a wetsuit, it holds water inside that your body carries on heating.

Your core temperature is 37 degrees. Skin temperature varies - maybe 18-20 degrees on hands and lower arms. When you sit in a bath at 32 degrees, you're losing heat because water is a very good conductor. When you're in 32-degree air, you're not losing heat because air is a very poor conductor. That's why even in a convertible at 30 degrees, you feel cold - convection creates good conduction of heat away from your body.

questions.question: Why don't we run clockwise? Whether it's Olympic events, horse racing, or dog racing, everything is anti-clockwise. Is there a reason we can't run clockwise?

answers.answer: I think it's because of the Earth's rotation - you go faster running anti-clockwise. Historically we did run in both directions, but once digital technology delivered timing accurate to fractions of seconds, they noted running anti-clockwise shaved hundredths of a second off times. I can't prove this but I'm 99% sure.

The Olympics originated in ancient Greece whose philosophy was based on mythology, cosmology, and astrology. Running anti-clockwise was based on the planets moving anti-clockwise around the sun. All the original Olympic games were to do with spheres representing planetary motions and how planets and moons orbit. In ancient Greece, everything was done anti-clockwise.

We run anti-clockwise because our heart is on the left-hand side. For many years, students in halls and fields innately run anti-clockwise. It's a mixture of anatomy and tradition. Children on a field told to start running will go anti-clockwise - it's innate in us. We probably do run a bit faster when running anti-clockwise.

questions.question: Why are roses synonymous with love and Valentine's Day? Why not tulips or daisies?

answers.answer: Hearts, reds - they're the most obviously red flower. I don't know. I'm putting it on the board.

A rose would smell as sweet by any other name. Roses have lots of different meanings - the red rose symbolises love because of its colour, the colour of passion, war, bloodshed. It goes back to Greek mythology - Aphrodite was seen with a red rose. Yellow roses mean friendship. White roses symbolise sympathy.

questions.question: Why would she be 55 in Iran but 54 in England? In Iran they count life in the womb, so she would be entering her 55th year of life.

answers.answer: I was confused by the premise. If in Iran they say you're 55 on your birthday, then you should be entering your 56th year, not your 55th. I questioned the logic.

The same issue applies in Somali culture. They count the year of your birth as your first year of life, so they don't say you turn one after finishing a full year - they say you turn two. It has nothing to do with pregnancy or nine months in the womb. It's simply about how some cultures count age - the birth year is year one.

questions.question: What are the rules about horse riders having to pick up their horse's poo from the road? What's the difference between that and dog poo?

answers.answer: There aren't any rules - horse riders don't have to pick up horse poo. Horses are herbivores, so there's no diseases associated with it. You can put it on your roses. Dog excrement is poisonous and can harm people, but horse poo won't cause you harm if you tread in it.

questions.question: Why do we celebrate wedding anniversaries with items - first paper, then wood, lace, gold, silver, pearl? How did that come about?

answers.answer: The tradition goes back to medieval Germany and the Holy Roman Empire when men would present their wives with gifts on their anniversaries, crowning them in the tradition of Charlemagne, with silver wreaths on 25th anniversary and gold on 50th.
Lace evolved from giving bolts of exotic fabric as wedding gifts - lace was once handmade, and Nottingham was a great centre of lace.

questions.question: Who made the cigarette? What was he thinking? Where did the idea even come from? Who was the first person to actually light tobacco and smoke it?

answers.answer: Walter Raleigh brought tobacco to Britain, but the locals were already smoking it. No one knows who first smoked it - similar to who first ate a magic mushroom.

questions.question: How do they calculate box office receipts for films? Is it the full price of the ticket or a percentage? Also bonus question about unlimited cinema cards.

answers.answer: They just add up all the tickets sold at every cinema showing that film.

70 to 80% of box office take goes to the film company/producers/distributors. Cinemas make their money from popcorn and confectionery. In the 80s, cinemas would phone in their figures to a central person. Now it's all computerised.
Rejected the question as too complicated - nobody knows how unlimited card viewings get totalled up in box office receipts.

questions.question: Why does the first pancake always fail?

answers.answer: Wait until the batter starts bubbling and you can see air bubbles expanding before contemplating tossing. Only toss when you can see the whole pancake move on a light jiggle of the pan handle.

questions.question: With the Christmas Truce in 1914 and the football match that took place on Christmas Day, does anyone know the score?

answers.answer: The game happened but no one kept score - they just played for fun. They started by crossing into no man's land, chatting, cutting each other's hair, and someone threw a ball on and they just ran around.
answers.qualifications: Works in TV and film production, worked on the Sainsbury's Christmas ad about the truce and made a documentary about it.

questions.question: Where did the superstition 'seven years of bad luck for breaking a mirror' come from?

answers.answer: People who worked in mirror-making factories had mirrors deducted from their wages, and it took seven years to pay it off.
answers.qualifications: Told by his mate Dennis who is big on history.

answers.answer: It was actually deducted from wages of housemaids and chambermaids - if they broke a mirror, it was deducted from their wages and took seven years to pay back.

questions.question: How do we know where two seas meet? Like the English Channel and the Atlantic - how do we know where the border is?

answers.answer: It's just plotted on a map, similar to how land borders are.
[Call cut off - line went bad]

questions.question: If I was on a desert island, would I be able to catch a cold?

answers.answer: You could catch bird flu from birds.

questions.question: How many years after Christ was born was the actual Christian calendar established?

answers.answer: The Julian calendar was introduced around 46 BC, named after Julius Caesar. It was later refined into the Gregorian calendar in the Middle Ages.
The Julian calendar was introduced by Augustus around 40-50 BC. Later refined to the Gregorian calendar with leap years.

The Anno Domini system was introduced around the year 1000 or 1033 by a Pope as part of a push for papal supremacy - before that, historians dated things from local kings' reigns. This is from Tom Holland's book Millennium.
answers.qualifications: Reading Tom Holland's book Millennium.

questions.question: Why do some chefs have much taller hats than others?

answers.answer: Traditionally, the head chef wore the tallest hat (called a toque) so he could be spotted in busy kitchens. The tall hat was also thought to circulate air and prevent baldness, but that was proven false. Now people wear different sizes.
answers.qualifications: I'm a chef and work at Steve's Pie Place in Shardlow, just outside Derby.

questions.question: Why is clinker used between railway lines worldwide? I've seen these little stones between the railway lines wherever I've been.

answers.answer: It's there for ballast. It presses in against the sleepers, whether concrete or wood, to give a compact so the rails don't move and you get a nice smooth journey. The machine comes along every now and again, maybe once a week, lifts the tracks, supports the sleepers, pushes and compacts it all. Used to be done by men called navvies years and years ago.

questions.question: Why as human beings do we have only four main eye colours - blue, brown, green, and hazel? Why aren't there more vibrant colours like red?
Where did the expression 'knock ten bells out of this guy' come from?
Why are foam shrimp and bananas sold together as sweets? I've never actually seen a dish that uses those two ingredients.

answers.answer: It started being sold together only when sweets got packaged. They used to be sold loose in sweet shops. The reason they were paired is that they're both made of foam - it was about nice shapes. As for why shrimp shapes, why anything shapes? Candy cigarettes exist. They're just shapes.

questions.question: We hear about the watershed after 9pm for adult programmes, but when does the watershed finish in the morning?

answers.answer: I think it ends with the close-down. It's an odd anachronism from linear television days and is now meaningless with streaming.
The watershed finishes at 6am. I was watching a Bellator fight last year and just as it got to the main event, they cut it off on Channel 5 and put on Peppa Pig because 6am was the watershed.

questions.question: We have absolute zero - minus 273 degrees or so. Do we have an absolute hot? A temperature above which nothing can get hotter?

answers.answer: Yes. Every hot thing emits electromagnetic radiation, and the hotter the thing, the shorter the wavelength. At some point it reaches the Planck length, the smallest thing you can ever get to, which corresponds to about 10 to the power of 32 Celsius or Kelvin. Above that, you can't heat it anymore.

questions.question: Are there any other Christian countries that don't have a traditional Christmas meal? Holland doesn't have one.

answers.answer: Australians don't have a traditional Christmas meal. When I was in Australia on Christmas Day, we just did a barbie. It depends on the weather. If it's warm, you'll have fresh prawns and seafood. More traditionally, you go to your local chicken shop and get a rotisserie chicken to take home.

questions.question: Why don't they make beds longer than about six foot? I'm just over six foot and my feet hang over the edge.

answers.answer: Beds are made to a standard length based on average human heights and also for practical reasons - to fit in houses and for bedding standardization. If they made them shorter, people's feet would dangle. If longer, most people would have more bed than they need.

questions.question: What is the meaning of 'seven bells' in the expression 'knock seven bells out of someone'?

answers.answer: Seven bells is the last bell you hear before the end of your shift on a ship. A four-hour shift consists of eight half-hour bells, and when you hear the seventh bell, you know you're on the last bit before the end.
