To kick seven bells out of someone is to bring them pretty much to the end - nearly curtains, but not quite.

questions.question: Is it better to drive past a Gritter faster or slower to avoid damage to your car from the salt they spread?
What is the origin of 'ten bells'?

answers.answer: I heard this from a beef eater from the Tower of London on a Jack the Ripper tour. There's a pub in the East End called the Ten Bells, opposite a market. Workers used to come out, drink heavily, and beat each other up. That's how it got the nickname. I was also told that's where 'mind your feet' comes from.

questions.question: Why don't they test blood donors for ferritin levels? Ferritin is your iron stores.

answers.answer: Ferritin is a storage protein. It shows how much iron you have in your stores. They don't test for it because it's not what they're looking for - they're looking at haemoglobin. If you have low haemoglobin and give blood, you could get dizzy, lightheaded, or faint.

questions.question: What's the difference between a beef stew and a beef casserole? I've used exactly the same recipe but called it different things.

answers.answer: A casserole is just the name of a dish cooked in a casserole pot. There's no real difference. When we were kids we had stew, then when Mum moved up in the world we called it casseroles with the same recipe.
A stew is done on the hob, a casserole is done in the oven.

questions.question: Where does all the venison go after they've culled the deer in Richmond Park?

answers.answer: The deer or the venison was distributed amongst the estate workers and friends of the estate. None of it was sold, because they don't kill that many.

questions.question: Why does hair on your head grow forever but pubic hair or eyebrows only grow to a certain length?

answers.answer: The hair on your head falls out. But how does it know to fall out? That's the bit where I can't remember my answer.

questions.question: Do our taste buds change biologically as we get older, which would explain why things that were yucky when we were young can become delicious as we get older?

answers.answer: The word is ageusia - it's the loss of taste buds over a period of time. As you age, your taste buds become less sensitive, so you start to get more sensitive to stronger flavours. It's the same as losing eyesight, hearing, sense of touch and smell - it all goes together.

questions.question: When Big Ben chimes, how far away can you hear it? What's the furthest away anyone's ever heard?
Why do his fiancée's eyes water in cold windy weather but his don't?

answers.answer: It's when the eyes overflow. The small glands underneath in the lower lid of your eye called meibomian glands get blocked - especially by makeup remover and face cream. Then the tears can't escape so they overflow.

The tears are produced by the lacrimal gland and swept across the eye surface to keep it lubricated. They drain through two small holes called the puncti at the inner part of the eye. When it's windy, the wind causes evaporation of normal tears which induces more tears to be secreted. Some people have different sizes of those puncti and drainage ducts, so they can't cope with the increased secretion and it overflows onto the cheeks. Chris is probably in better nick than his fiancée. If the overflow is causing problems, she could see an ophthalmologist.

questions.question: Why can you pause live TV but not live radio?

answers.answer: It's because what would the presenter do while being paused? Some DABs have a pause function but most don't. It's a cost versus priority issue. Podcasts have done away with the need to pause live radio because they're recorded and easily pausable.

questions.question: When you open a bottle of red wine and let it breathe an hour before drinking, what gas comes out?

answers.answer: As part of the fermenting process, CO2 is given off and this sits on top of the wine in the bottle and helps preserve it. Letting it breathe is a myth - you just bring your wine up from your cellar long before you serve it so it reaches room temperature. Once the cork's out, the wine starts to go off due to oxidisation.

You let the wine breathe to let air and oxygen come into the wine - that's why you can buy aerators. The oxidation enhances the tannins. But there's a peak of oxidation after which the wine starts tasting vinegary and goes off.

questions.question: Why can you buy organic chicken breast but not organic chicken thighs or other parts of the chicken? What happens to the other organic parts?

answers.answer: It's demand. People who buy organic food tend to be rarefied consumers more likely to go for expensive cuts rather than cheaper thigh meat.

It really comes down to cultural consumer tastes. In the UK, people have a taste for lean cuts which is the breast. On the continent, they prefer the legs which are fattier and tastier - more for a stew. You flog your breasts in Blighty and you flog your thighs in France.

questions.question: How deep does a body have to be buried before a cadaver-sniffing dog cannot detect it?

answers.answer: The grave has to be six foot. That's the industry standard minimum.

Technically, there is no depth. The way cadaver dogs work is they probe the ground with a probe to a given depth, and the dog smells the hole. A body buried 20 feet down with an 18-foot probe would be detected if the decomposition fluids leak into the surrounding ground and the probe reaches that area. Foxes are not going to dig a body up from six feet down - that's what grave diggers worry about, not police dogs.

questions.question: How did they measure the milestones in the olden days? What did they use?

answers.answer: May 1731, William Warren, a professor of one of the Cambridge colleges, set out from Great St Mary's Church with a chain and an assistant, and between them they measured out the first set of milestones post-Roman era in the country.

questions.question: What came first, the wall or the wheel?

answers.answer: The wall can be dated back to the settlements around Jericho and the Temple of Urfa in Turkey, both dated from around 9000 BC. Whereas the first recorded example of a wheel was from around 3500 BC in Mesopotamia where it was used as a potter's wheel. They used the log technique to build walls without wheels.

questions.question: If you sever a limb and go to hospital and they can't reattach it, who actually owns the limb? Could you take it home?

answers.answer: The person owns the limb because my brother-in-law had his leg amputated and he was offered the choice whether he wanted to take the leg home with him and have it buried, or have it donated to science, and he said he would donate it to science. It was the person's choice.

questions.question: If I was a Brexiteer, can I put that on my census as a religion? What is the definition of religion for the purposes of the UK census?

answers.answer: If you could put Brexiteer down on your census as a religion, for it to be officially recognised as a religion on a census form, it would need 250,000 followers. That's how Jedi Knight became recognised - enough people put it down on the census.

questions.question: When you hear adverts on the radio, whether it's for insurance, capsules, or well-known Swedish furniture, why does it always say 'excludes NI'?

answers.answer: It's down to marketing distribution rights for products. The brand is owned by the Coca-Cola company based in Atlanta, Georgia, and the bottling rights are awarded to different partners in different countries. UK is Coca-Cola GB and for logistical reasons, Northern Ireland is often covered by companies who have the right for the island of Ireland rather than the British Isles.

questions.question: The bearskin hat that the horse guards wear, why does the chin strap go under their lip and not under their chin? It seems insecure.

answers.answer: It's regimental tradition. All the different regiments tend to wear them differently. The Blues and Royals wear their chin strap underneath their chin. The Lifeguards wear it underneath the lip. There's no real reason except difference and distinction - soldiers being soldiers try to push boundaries of what they're allowed to do. They've only been wearing bearskins since 1813-1814.

questions.question: Where does the term tongue-in-cheek come from?
When people shake up a can of drink and before opening it, they tap the lid because they think it's going to stop it fizzing up and get all over them. Does tapping a can actually work?

answers.answer: When they make fizzy drinks, they dissolve carbon dioxide into the liquid - the bubbles are undissolved CO2. When you shake it up, those little bubbles distribute all the way around the can, and when you open it, those bubbles expand rapidly with decreasing pressure, forcing the drink out. By tapping on the top, those little bubbles move gently to the top, and then you can open it safely.

questions.question: How do they calculate how many stars are in our galaxy and how many galaxies are in the universe? Brian Cox mentioned 200 billion stars in our galaxy and 200 trillion galaxies.

answers.answer: They use monster big telescopes which can see an enormous distance away using infrared. They take photographs and count all the stars in that image, then make an estimate of how many images you'd need of similar sort to cover the whole galaxy and multiply. The same with galaxies - Hubble has taken images almost every day. There are distributions because in the Milky Way stars go in long curving arms, so it's not uniform, but they can make a clever estimate.

questions.question: Answer about tapping ring pools - why do people tap the top of a ring pull can?

answers.answer: Poisonous insects hide themselves under ring pools and people used to tap the ring pool to dislodge the insects before opening, in case they fell into the drink and were ingested.

questions.question: If you add 33 and 45 RPM for records, you get 78. Is that a complete coincidence or is there some kind of maths behind the speed involved?

answers.answer: Absolute pure coincidence. Way back in the day, it was a needle traversing a groove in a wax cylinder and then on a shellac plate, and you needed to go really, really fast to get sound fidelity. They could fit more information in a longer groove in a shorter time. When they moved to diamond needles, it could slow down, allowing more playing time on one side of the disk.

questions.question: At the cinema or children's play area, there are signs saying you can't bring in your own food or drink. Is there any legal grounding to this?

answers.answer: Because it doesn't have a health and hygiene certificate, they aren't allowed to allow people to bring external food - they can't guarantee the food. If someone gets sick from food, they can't prove whether it's their food or yours. They have a legal right to refuse outside food and drink, though they don't police it closely.

questions.question: Why are there different types of light bulbs - bayonet one and the Edison screw type? Why don't they just make one standard?

answers.answer: It's due to historical precedents. The UK historically has always had bayonet type light fittings for ceiling fittings, while Europe and US have always used screw-in types. Now with European regulations standardising things, most table lamps come with screw-in fittings for export. Hopefully we'll harmonise to all screw-in bulbs in the future.

questions.question: Why are cash registers called tills?

answers.answer: A till is a draw. The cash register is the machine in which there is a draw called a till. They've become conflated over the years. A till is a money draw, and because every cash register has a till in it, a till has become a synonym for cash register.
A till is called a till because it comes from the French word till, which means compartment. A cash drawer is separated into different compartments.

questions.question: Why is it that when you're keeping a secret or someone tells you something they don't want you to tell others, they tap their nose twice?

answers.answer: It just means 'don't be nosy'. If you're tapping your nose to signal 'don't tell anyone', you're essentially saying 'don't be nosy, keep it to yourself'.

questions.question: There are counties called Essex, Sussex, Middlesex and Wessex which seem to mean south, east, middle and west. Why is there no north version like 'Nussex'? Why don't northern counties end in 'sex'?

answers.answer: It probably refers to the Saxons. The reason there are no northern counties with the 'sex' suffix is because they were never settled by Saxons. The Saxons hung out around London and the south. Northern counties weren't conquered or named by Saxons, which is why you don't find 'Nussex'.

questions.question: Why does cling film only stick once? If you put it over a bowl, it works fine, but once you've used it and taken it off, it won't stick properly afterward.

answers.answer: I think it's charged. Static electricity. The cling film on the roll has a static electric charge that isn't there after you've used it.

It's to do with surface tension. The thickness of the material is able to hold its own weight through surface tension alone. Once you've used it once, you've broken the surface tension, so it won't work the next time. It loses its ability to have effective surface tension because it only has a finite level of elasticity. Once you stretch it the first time, it doesn't go back.

questions.question: Why can't we convert landfill waste into usable energy?

answers.answer: We can, but it wouldn't be either economically or environmentally viable because we'd have to burn it.

It does happen on quite a large scale. They're called energy from waste or energy recovery facilities. They are large incinerators. Bin lorries from a wide area dump their refuse into a large sorting hall, the material is picked up by a large grabber and put into a large incinerator. The exhaust fumes are treated and controlled so that emissions to the atmosphere are minimal with no environmental consequences. It's something we should be looking to do more of.

questions.question: Why do we cry when we are touched or moved by something? What is the physiological or evolutionary reason behind crying?

answers.answer: The evolutionary reason it will be, probably. Communicating silently to the rest of the tribe that something frightening is happening? No, because you can cry at sweet stuff too.

We don't really know but we think it's to elicit an altruistic response from other people. Animals do it too - elephants do it as well. If you cry, you'll be looked after, therefore it does give you a sexual advantage, which is what evolution is all about. It's a visible show of emotional distress so others know you need care.

questions.question: What animal in general makes the best manure for growing things?

answers.answer: It would be a herbivore, wouldn't it? Because meat's got much more protein and much more interesting things in it, but that's only at this end. Not all of it's going to get absorbed. I'd go for a horse.

It's called guano, which is excrement from sea birds and bats. In the 19th century, it was so valuable that it was actually worth its weight in gold as a fertilizer. There's a South Sea island that is per capita one of the richest places in the world because it has so much guano. It's due to high levels of nitrogen.

questions.question: In cricket, why aren't the positions of the stumps marked permanently on the batting crease or popping crease? At the start of each batsman's innings, he has to ask the umpire to mark his crease. Given that position doesn't change, why aren't there permanent chalk marks?

answers.answer: It might be a remnant from before the middle stump was introduced. There was no middle stump originally - you had two stumps and one bail. A bowler called Lumpy Stevens was so accurate he kept putting the ball through the stumps without dislodging the bail. They only introduced a middle stump in the 18th century because of him. So having marks on the ground for which stump you were using would have been pointless before that was introduced. It's just a remnant of those days.

questions.question: If you're arrested, charged and denied bail, what happens to your mortgage payments, your bills and all that stuff with your house?

answers.answer: I'll find out for you. Presumably you have to find someone to take care of it for you. If you're on your own, you get your one telephone call - who do you phone? Do you phone your mortgage company and say it's not going to be around for a while? It's really interesting. How do you tell your mortgage? Do you get a break on your mortgage or do you have to sell your house?

questions.question: When were diamonds first discovered? And when were they first deemed valuable?

answers.answer: Gold is valuable because it's rare and shiny. I imagine the answer to your question will be the same for diamonds - rare and shiny. But you can show off a gold ring easily. A diamond is much more difficult to show off.

Diamonds became routinely valuable in the 1930s. They are not actually valuable - they're only valuable because the duopoly (De Beers and one other) put all the diamonds in a great big vault and dripped them onto the market. In the 1930s they started associating diamonds with engagements and said 'a diamond is forever' and suggested three months salary. Gold is valuable because it's a commodity. You try reselling a second-hand diamond - you can sell the gold from an engagement ring for scrap value but the diamond you can barely give away. Diamonds are one of the first examples of branding.

Diamonds were first used in manufacturing or polishing of other gemstones. We have evidence going back to almost Egyptian times - they were always in use then. In the 1400s they were first given as engagement rings. They've been seen as valuable for an awfully long time. The Koh-i-Noor was prized by princes and sultans for many years. Professor Howell was partially right about modern commerce and resale value, but historically diamonds have been valuable for millennia.

questions.question: When you go to a graveyard and there are loads of graves that haven't been touched for years, what do they do with them? Do they dig them up? Do they leave them?

answers.answer: There's no catch-all answer. It depends on circumstance. In some graveyards they dig new graves and put coffins on top of what was previously a coffin. But equally in some other graveyards, they stay untouched for two or three hundred years. Anyone who runs a graveyard, any priest with a graveyard attached to their church, will have had to make a decision at a parish or diocesan level about whether or not they start stacking. It's a decision made locally.

questions.question: Why don't adults get nosebleeds as much as children do?

answers.answer: Probably something to do with the size of your capillaries or a kind of manifestation of something akin to growing pains, but I haven't got a clue. My teacher used to tell us it was because our brains were growing faster than our bodies. Though I suspect that's wrong.
The scientific name is epistaxis, not peristalsis (which is what your gullet does when you swallow).

Kids have more nosebleeds because they have more blood vessels in the nasal plexus. They also pick their noses more. They're more active than adults so they fall over more and are more prone to bleeding. It's a developmental thing - kids develop differently from adults. Their bone structure is different, they have more cartilage rather than bone. They have bigger heads proportionally than adults so they have more blood vessels in the nasal plexus. When you're growing, you need to transport blood around your body at a different rate and quantity than when you stop growing. Pregnant women have about 150% of normal blood volume and are more prone to nosebleeds because they're more prone to hypertension. There are different reasons at different ages.

questions.question: Why are companies and stations called sister? Why not brother? Or if distant, why not cousin or second cousin thrice removed?

answers.answer: It's based on old maritime admiralty and law of water concepts. Companies are deemed as vessels and referred to as she or her. Ships were traditionally given female names and had figureheads of women. Maritime admiralty traditions explain why we use 'sister' - it's from the nautical tradition.

questions.question: The person who invented clockwise, why did he invent it right to left? Why not left to right? Where's the whole thing of clockwise come from?

answers.answer: It's based on the direction the shadow goes around on a sundial. When making clocks, they copied sundials and everybody was used to the shadow going around in that direction.
When you have a sundial, it goes from right to left - that's why clocks go clockwise. The time comes from the right-hand side and always turns around like that.

questions.question: What happens to all the old mobile phone numbers you no longer use? The number I used to have - what happens to it?

answers.answer: They stay dormant for a period and then may be reallocated at some subsequent time. James mentioned he once rang his old number and it rang out, noting he'd nearly said the number on air which would have caused problems for the new owner.

questions.question: Why does every door have six panels normally that look like they could be glass panels on a porch door, but they just have wooden panels? Is there a reason? Can you replace them and put glass into them? Is that why they do it, mass produce them so you can take them out?

answers.answer: It's about timber size and using all parts of trees to build things. If you split a door into three with styles and centre mullion and they're all six inches wide, you get rid of 18 inches of door and have your panels. You couldn't do that in one big plank because the plank would have to be massive. A panelled door is constructed from lots of skinny bits of timber rather than one great big piece. The original ones could have glass, timber, or anything. It's not about crosses and books being represented in the panels - that's nonsense.

questions.question: Can you turn the internet off? Is there one switch?

answers.caller: Mike (Haze) - Cisco Certified Internet Work Expert
answers.answer: Unfortunately, no, you can't switch off the internet. Everything converts to a phone number (IP address). When you go to google.com, you traverse 20-30 hops or different nodes. Even if you took down one data centre, it would route through another path - called open shortest route. You'd have to shut down all the nodes one by one, plus Google's domain name controllers, and that's just for one site. There's massive redundancy built in.

questions.question: Why does kissing attract cats? He makes that noise on calls and it attracts cats, but cats don't make kissing noises themselves - you hear them meow and hiss. Do cats associate it with something in the natural world?

answers.answer: The key is in the pitch. High-pitched noises - we're all programmed to react to high-pitched noises that babies, kittens, and puppies make, because mothers go and help when they hear that sound. So we're programmed to hear that, and that's why the cat reacts to the high-pitched noise. But also, the cat has actually conditioned the owner to make the kissing noise to make him come - so it's unclear who's been conditioning who.

questions.question: Why are bathroom lights so loud when switched on or off? It's the one light you need to be the quietest and it's the loudest. You can't even do it quietly when you're half-asleep.

answers.caller: James (Shoreditch) - Former electrician, now sound engineer
answers.answer: Two things: 1) Bathroom has hard surfaces, so acoustics reverberate the sound more. 2) With a pull switch, you're not directly touching it, so your body isn't absorbing some of the energy like it would with a rocker switch buried in the wall that you press. The pull switch has to spring more and exert more pressure. They could be the same in laboratory conditions, but the extraneous variables render one quieter than the other.

questions.question: Why does the radio not have a watershed moment like TV does? TV has colourful language allowed after 9pm, but radio never does. Clive Balle used to swear on his show - is that linked to the watershed?

answers.answer: He noted there are things he'd do at night that he wouldn't do during the day, but it's more about subject matter than language. Nick (producer) sometimes says if you have a child with you, you might want to turn the radio down, but that's just being well-mannered, not an actual rule in the broadcasting code. James said he'd find out more.

In children's wards, radios are all turned off at 9pm, but that's because it's bedtime, not because of content restrictions. They have a request show 8:30-10pm and they put a watershed on content-wise, playing radio edits rather than explicit versions.

questions.question: If you pull a white hair out of your beard, do you really get more white hairs? Is there science behind not pulling out white hairs?
The Chinese satellite landed on the dark side of the moon - how is it sending signals back to Earth? The moon is always in the way.

answers.answer: It sends a signal to a satellite that's within sight, then the satellite sends a signal to Earth.
They've got a special satellite specifically for the mission.

answers.caller: George (Redditch) - Retired physics teacher, keen amateur astronomer
answers.answer: The Chinese have sent up a separate satellite specifically for this mission, orbiting around the moon to relay signals back to Earth. They do this with Mars rovers too - relay satellites closer to Mars and possibly on the other side so they can get signals back to Earth.

questions.question: Why are due dates for babies so wildly inaccurate? Will we or can we ever get a more accurate prediction for a due date than that?

answers.answer: They do it differently in France already. They calculate it as a different number... They have to estimate the moment of conception by looking at how far gone they think you are, and then they extrapolate from that how long the average gestation period is. In France they work from a different average.

Actually it's unfair that at least in Western societies we tell women to expect their baby on the 40-week mark. That is a very small proportion of babies - 5% born on their expected due date. A term baby is born between 37 weeks and 42 weeks - a five-week window. At 37 weeks, from the perspective of lungs, heart, brain and guts, it should be absolutely fine. Delivering three weeks early is still on time. There's no way of doing it more accurately. We should be preparing women for delivering between 37 weeks and 42 weeks.

questions.question: How do they make cheese different strengths? Specifically cheddar from mild all the way up to extra mature.

answers.answer: As you just spotted yourself, you may have accidentally stumbled across the answer with the word 'mature'. They just leave it somewhere. [Later confirmed as wrong]
With blue cheese, they stick it in with a stick. No, they put copper wire through it.

Milk is put into a large vat and a starter culture is added. It's churned for about 12 hours and the cheese is scooped off into large blocks. After about three months when it's gone a bit hard, that's your mild cheese. After six months, your mature cheese. After a year, your extra mature cheese. The cultures inside the cheese are creaming up and making it into the cheese. Once it's taken out of a room at constant temperature and put in your fridge, it will no longer mature - that's how you get your mild cheese. For blue cheese: they put penicillin in it and then spike the edges. Air gets into the cheese and that's how you get the blue vein. You don't use copper wire anymore.

questions.question: How do the police track down the user of rogue drones?
Is a pepper a fruit or a vegetable?

answers.answer: The difference between fruit and vegetables is that fruit contain pips, seeds, or stones. You see this in lemon, apples, tomatoes. Peppers have little seeds inside them. Cucumbers have seeds. Butternut squash also has seeds - that makes it a fruit. Vegetable is not actually a scientific term. Chilli peppers are also classed as fruit because they have the little stones inside. As for potatoes - underground produce like carrots, beetroots don't have seeds and are dug up.

questions.question: Do animals, specifically domestic animals like dogs and cats, have voices that break like humans do at puberty?

answers.answer: Voices do change. There is a difference between male and female dogs - female dogs tend to sound not much different from adolescence to adults, but male dogs go through puberty in a much stronger way, like young male humans, and their voices change to a lower pitch. They actually get startled by their own voice breaking - suddenly really low and they notice it. This happens with all mammals except those underwater. The change is because of the growth and change of volume in the lungs and larynx.

questions.question: At what temperature would a lone emperor penguin freeze to death in the Antarctic?

answers.answer: Penguins could freeze to death at minus 45 degrees. If they're with their pack and huddle together, taking turns on being on the outside, even if temperature goes to minus 45 they survive because they're huddled together. It would have to go to minus 55 for prolonged periods for the whole pack to freeze. A lone penguin could freeze to death at a temperature he would otherwise survive at if with his mates.

questions.question: How did they program the first computer without a computer?

answers.answer: Computer was a glorified calculator that did really big sums. The way numbers were put in was by perforated cards with holes in them.

It wasn't the kind of computer you're thinking about. It was Babbage's computation machine which was all mechanical cogs and switches and dials. They changed the dials around to do a sum of things and press the button to get the result. It's all based on how the cogs interact, which maps onto modern instruction sets. Ada Lovelace worked with Babbage and deserves to be much more widely known.

questions.question: What was the first use of the word Brexit? Who coined it and when?

answers.answer: It was coined by a guy named Peter Wilding. He was on one of the news programs a couple of weeks ago. His biggest fear is that this is going to be his epitaph. He is Chairman of British Influence.

questions.question: Where does the tradition of pulling Christmas crackers come from?

answers.answer: The info was on a little info sheet inside a cracker instead of a joke. It was the 1800s. A gentleman called Tom Smith did it, and the first ones were made for royalty with sweets (bonbons) and paper crowns inside. Tom Smith invented the crackers and took them to the Queen - probably Queen Victoria and Prince Albert.
That was a good answer but there's room for more detail if others want to flesh it out. He was invented by a bloke called Tom Smith.

questions.question: How do ants always manage to find food in the middle of nowhere?

answers.answer: Ants use their antennae. They can pick up new odours - they can detect sugar smells and new food odours. They detect the food and then communicate back to the colony through their antennae.

questions.question: How will the police investigate rogue drone flyers? What technology is available?

answers.answer: Police won't do anything themselves - they'll outsource to a company with the correct equipment. It's quite easy to hack a drone with high-gain antenna and scanner. They find the frequencies, walk around in a circle until they find the direction. They can get serial numbers off the drone and track back where it was bought from through online accounts or shop CCTV. Drones are sometimes used as mobile hacking devices - Raspberry Pis are put onto them so if you can't physically access a site but they've got Wi-Fi, you fly the drone in and land it to access their network.

questions.question: Why do wine gums have 'wine' in the name? Were they ever actually alcoholic?

answers.answer: Back in the day, there was probably some wine in them. It's easier to believe than the fact there used to be cocaine in Coca-Cola.

Maynard wine gums were started in Stanford Hill. A Jewish guy whose dad wasn't happy he'd used the word 'wine'. They never had any wine in them. His dad was religious and disapproved. So no alcohol was ever in them.

questions.question: Why is flu season in winter and not summer? Why do we only get flu jabs in winter?

answers.answer: It must be something to do with the temperature.

It's not really known why incidence of flu increases in winter. The virus survives better in cold weather. In humid temperatures, droplets fall to the ground, making transmission less. The World Health Organization meets in February/March each year, pulls together public health data from various countries, decides which strains should be in the vaccine for the following year. It then takes 6-8 months to produce the vaccine, which is given from October to December.

questions.question: There's an old saying 'gentlemen prefer blondes'. And the opposite saying is 'women prefer their men tall, dark and handsome'. Are those sayings true? If so, why?

answers.answer: When women are pregnant, whatever colour their hair is, it naturally gets lighter. This triggers protective nurturing instincts in people. In males, it triggers the response that they're fertile and a good mate. So lighter hair gives a head start with anyone who's pregnant or prone to those responses.

questions.question: My medicine packaging says 'do not crush, take whole'. Why? Why can't we crush our medicine?

answers.answer: It probably has a coating to make it palatable. If you crush it, the flavour underneath would taste absolutely foul.

Several reasons: (1) Some drugs are designed for sustained release, the coating helps prevent all being absorbed too quickly to smooth out effects and prevent overdose. (2) Stomach acid can destroy some drugs, so coating protects it until it reaches the more alkaline areas of the gut where it can be absorbed effectively. (3) Some drugs like ibuprofen can cause stomach side effects like acid reflux or ulcers, so the coating stops release in the stomach. Sometimes the coating is made deliberately foul-tasting to prevent misuse, like paracetamol.

questions.question: How did the Royal Mint know how much money to make every day? How do they decide how much to produce?

answers.caller: Trevor (on way to Royal Mint) - Royal Mint supplier
answers.answer: The Royal Mint is an independent company with a contract with the Bank of England. The Bank of England tells them how much to produce each day. They manufacture and record in response to the amount ordered.

In terms of new money going into or being taken out of the economy, it's one of the measures used to manage inflation through the money supply. Cash and cash equivalents are called M0 and can be found on the Bank of England website. This changes to manage inflation. Decisions about cash would be made at MPC meetings on the third Thursday of every month.

answers.caller: Michael (Bromley) - Stock market trader, economics background
answers.answer: If the Bank wants to print a billion pounds, approximately 70% will be digital money, 20% banknotes, 10% coins. So they'd tell the Royal Mint to print 100 million pounds worth of coins. This gets allocated into coin types - 12.5% of coins would be two-pound coins, which is 12.5 million two-pound coins. Divided by 365 days, that's about 34,000-35,000 pounds worth of two-pound coins printed per day. The Monetary Policy Committee does the calculations regarding inflation, quantitative easing etc., and at the end of that process tells the Royal Mint what to produce.

questions.question: On a stapler, there's a little silver plate with two settings - one pushes staples outwards and one pushes them inwards. What is the other setting for?

answers.answer: I don't know.

When you don't want to staple something permanently, twist the plate so the prongs go outwards. The staple comes out flat like a letter 'I' instead of bent like a 'C'. Then you can pull at one end and the papers come apart without tearing. Useful for attaching checks to documents - you can remove the check without damaging either the check or the document.

questions.question: Wherever I go abroad, I always come back covered in mosquito bites. The rest of the people I go with aren't. Why are some people prone to mosquito bites?

answers.answer: Vinegar is good. Get some vinegar behind your ears before bed.
Everyone gets bitten. Some people react, some don't. It's not about whether you get bitten - it's about whether you react to the bites. My wife doesn't react so she doesn't know she's been bitten.

questions.question: In the Oval Office, are the pictures on the walls curved to fit the oval walls? They look flush with the walls.

answers.answer: I'll find out for you.

questions.question: How do they work out how many letters and tiles to have in Scrabble for different languages, like Polish which has lots of Ys, Zs, and Ws?

answers.answer: The scoring is based on word entropy - how often letters appear in a language. Monks 900 years ago counted letters in the Bible to find hidden meanings. Letters that appear less often score higher. The same principle applies to every language.
The answer is N-grams - a collection of statistics about frequency of letter uses in a language. Calculations based on letter frequency in any given language.

questions.question: Who estimates the number of people on a march or protest and how do they do it?
Why do some dogs tilt their heads when you talk to them in baby talk?

answers.answer: Dogs tilt their heads to pick up keywords like food, treat, ball, play, park, or let's go - it helps them concentrate. They're filtering sounds. Also, they seek attention from us, and when we find it cute and give them attention, we positively reinforce the behavior. Any dog can learn to do it - it's a conditioned reflex.

questions.question: What happens to the rubble when a building is demolished?

answers.answer: Rubble gets taken away in big eight-wheelers to a yard, put through a crushing machine, and goes back into construction projects as 'type one' - crushed concrete. Massive amounts become hills or fill marshland. It's a valuable commodity for recycling - nobody wants to landfill it.

questions.question: Why do passports have the photo page inside rather than on the front cover so you could move through customs faster?
Why does low frequency music in horror films work so well to create dread? Is it linked to evolutionary reasons like fingernails on a blackboard?

answers.answer: Sound in horror films amplifies what's on screen. Basic building patterns create tension over time. Lower keys work better than higher pitches for creating fear. Modern horror uses subsonic and infrasonic sounds tied to things like tiger calls. In films like Halloween, they use instruments like the theremin that produce very specific frequencies. It's all about frequencies.

questions.question: Why do car windows frost and freeze up more than home windows?

answers.answer: It's about surface area to volume ratio. Cars have more surface area for their given volume - they get rid of heat quicker than houses. Other examples: fingers get cold before the rest of your body, elephants with massive surface area and little volume need to get rid of heat differently.

questions.question: What flavor is 'Original' Doritos? What does original actually mean as a flavor?

answers.answer: It's Cool Ranch. In America it's called Cool Ranch - ranch dressing is garlicky and herby, white, not tomato-based. The plain Doritos are lightly salted and called original.

questions.question: Can you answer the crowd counting question? How do the police estimate crowd numbers?

answers.answer: For a march, you have a fixed point, count the number of people going past in a given time, then work out how long it takes for everyone to get past and multiply together. It's human counting with clickers. For a contained area, you take an aerial image with a grid, count people in one square, multiply by number of squares. The biggest crowd he counted was 75,000 at a Kurdish homeland demonstration in Trafalgar Square. Only a couple of dozen officers in the Met do this work.

questions.question: When you finish on the toilet and wash your hands, you want to exit but the door has a handle and you don't want to touch it because it's full of germs. Some have a wooden handle you push, some have metal. Which is better to touch? Does bacteria thrive better on metal or wood?

answers.answer: If there is the option of a natural wood part, go for that, because it's naturally antibacterial. When bacteria lands on plastic, it stays there and survives long, where natural wood will degrade it and decompose it and kill off bacteria.

The answer is it doesn't really matter. Every time you go in the bathroom, you get covered in fecal flora. If you brush your teeth, you get covered in fecal flora. So one needs to forget about the loo doors and just ensure that one washes one's hands regularly. Keep your hands as clean as possible. That's the real answer.

questions.question: At Prime Minister's Question Time, when the leader of the opposition or any of the opposition are clearly asking a question, why is it that everybody else stands up behind the Prime Minister who's obviously going to answer the question? Doesn't that disadvantage disabled people?

answers.answer: They're hoping to get picked next, aren't they? And yes, it probably does disadvantage disabled people, but I don't know what you would do if you struggled to get your feet.

Members of Parliament bob up and down because they're hoping to catch a speaker's eye, and they get called or not. If someone is disabled, what they do is they raise their order paper with their right hand high in the air, and the speaker will very nearly always call them. He sees them and keeps an eye out for people who he knows are disabled.

questions.question: Why do we have uppercase and lowercase letters in the alphabet?

answers.answer: Years ago, you had compositors that used to have like a John Ball printing outfit and put letters in to make a page up. The capitals were in the top case and the ordinary letters were in the bottom. So the capitals were uppercase and the ordinary ones were lowercase.

When your researcher asked me, I'd forgotten that a long time ago I'd actually done a course on Anglo-Saxon and looked at some manuscripts, and there it was all in lower case except for the first letter, which was illuminated and still in the Roman upper case. It was the monks that started that distinction. It was actually the monks that had invented the lower case letters because it was all in capitals previously, being the Roman alphabet. They developed it for frugality because they'd get more letters on a page, and time and space was money because all the material they wrote on was expensive to make.

questions.question: I bought a new electric toothbrush and when I went to charge it, it only had two prongs on the end of the plug. I don't have a plug in my bathroom either, so I had to buy an adapter. Why do we have two prong plugs in the bathroom and three everywhere else in the house?

answers.answer: It's to do with earthing. It must have something to do with not electrocuting yourself and presumably something to do with the water you would get in the bathroom.

It's half right, it's to do with safety. It boils down to what can kill you and what can't. In the bathroom, you have 110 volts which won't stop your heart. In a normal three prong which you plug in normally, it's 13 amp which will stop your heart. So if my electric device with a two-pronged plug falls into the water that I'm sitting in, I'll get a nasty shock but I'll survive.

It comes out at 230 volts. It's to do with what's called an isolating transformer. There are two coils in there and as long as they've got the same amount of winding from them, it produces the same voltage out. But there's electrical separation. There'll never be a route to Earth. So that's why it doesn't have the Earth pin. If there's no route to Earth, you can't get a shock.

questions.question: Agnieszka and I were coming back from Iceland and as we're descending altitude, there's a bottle of water we've been enjoying and it's decreasing in size. I know the cabin's pressurised. I know the water in the bottle does not match the pressure in the cabin. But the whole thing's shrunk like it had been squashed by hand. Why did the water bottle shrink when the plane was descending?

answers.answer: It's to do with differential cabin altitude in an airplane. You're typically cruising at 30,000 to 40,000 feet, and the cabin altitude inside is actually around 6,000 or 8,000 feet. As you descend, the airplane descends and the cabin altitude descends to sea level. The air in the bottle is around about 6,000 or 8,000 feet on the airplane. So then the ambient pressure around the bottle increases as the cabin altitude descends to sea level, around 14 pounds per square inch at sea level. So that then effectively crushes the bottle because you've got less pressurised air inside the bottle. They must have opened the bottle and closed it again before descending because you would need a gap of air.

questions.question: How cold does it need to be outside for water to freeze within one hour? In Home Alone, Kevin leaves the church at 8pm and the burglars arrive at 9pm. He pours water onto the steps and it freezes so they fall down. What temperature would water need to be to freeze in an hour?

answers.answer: It's not just a case of how cold it is, but how long it's been cold. If you've got something nice and heavy like a doorstop, that's going to really get cold and be a big energy sink. You pour some warm water on it, it's just going to draw the heat right out of the water to try and warm itself up, and that will cause the water to freeze very quickly, perhaps even instantly if it's cold enough. The water forms a nice thin layer so it could potentially freeze in seconds or minutes. It matters how long it's been cold, not just the temperature.

questions.question: Why is menswear never on the ground floor?

answers.answer: The short answer is that they never sell as much as women's wear, so you put your biggest sellers on the ground floor, and that's always going to be women's wear. Women will walk 5,000 miles to find a pair of shoes. The ground floor is your biggest sales area, so you put your most popular items down there. If it's a department store, you're going to have your perfumes downstairs, but if it's just a clothing store, you're going to have women's wear downstairs, men's wear upstairs.

questions.question: On deodorant bottles, it always says how long the antiperspirant lasts - 20 or 40 hours. How do they test that?
Why don't countries call other countries by their actual name? For instance, why don't the French call us England? Why don't we call Germany Deutschland? Where does that come from?

answers.answer: The word Germany actually came through Latin. It was used by Julius Caesar in the first century to describe the Germanic people. Germania in Latin was the people as much as a place. Deutsch actually means 'of the people' in Old High German, so when they say Deutschland, it means land of the people. The names for countries have evolved from a period of history where countries weren't formally formed and borders were a lot more fluid. So they're more likely to refer to people than to places.

questions.question: I walk past the Ministry of Defence every day and there are two large statues of women who are naked. Who are they? Why are they there?

answers.answer: Probably goddesses of war? You've got Mars, there's a bloke, probably goddesses.

The two that are there now are the Earth and Water statues, but originally there were going to be four, two at either end. It was originally the Air Ministry, so when it was finished in 1939, they just ran out of money and never got round to building Fire and Air. So we only have Earth, Wind and Fire's lesser-known cousins. Earth and Water.

questions.question: At what point did we become great, I think, Great Britain? Who, when and how?

answers.answer: The Great in Great Britain simply means that we're bigger than Brittany. After the Norman conquest, when the name of Britain and Brittany were so similar, they had to distinguish between them, so they went for Grande Britannia - to distinguish between our Britain and their Britain.

questions.question: When and why did American and UK English spellings diverge? (colour/flavor, realise/realize)

answers.answer: The Americans may be doing it the traditional way and we're the ones who changed.

questions.question: Do cockeyed people see straight?

answers.answer: Yes, I do see straight.
Ivan can't see 3D films even when he's got the glasses on.

questions.question: Are there any areas of Earth above sea level that have not been explored yet? Any unclimbed mountains or unexplored islands?
If we use a lot of hydroelectric power to harness the waves, tidal energy, will it affect the orbit of the moon over and above what it might already be changing by?

answers.answer: Not a stupid question. The tides work because the Moon tugs the water - there's a bulge towards it on both sides. Energy is transferred from the Earth to the Moon. Every year, the Moon moves away by about 4 centimetres. We lose a fraction of a second a day. But the tide thing is absolutely minor - it's so marginal you probably couldn't even measure it. It's a drop in the ocean.

questions.question: As inflation increases and numbers get bigger (million, billion, trillion), will calculators need to get bigger in the future?
Why are certain allergies so much more common than others? For example, peanuts or shellfish. Why not a Brazil nut? What is it about peanuts?
What happened to the signs/stickers on the back of buses that used to say 'Let the bus out first, please'? Where's it gone?

questions.answer: They used to have to let buses out by law. They changed the Highway Code - Rule 223 - so you only have to let buses out if it's safe to do so. Some buses still have the new sticker with Rule 223.

questions.question: Why are there so many blue-roofed buildings in Far East countries like Korea's and China? Also seen in North Korea within the DMZ.
What did the Romans call the years that we call B.C.?

questions.answer: All legumes contain something called lectins - proteins that bind carbohydrates together in your body so you can't release them and they're toxic. Cooking and fermenting for hours reduces lectins, but people don't do that. Peanuts and cashews are the worst for lectins. Actual nuts like Brazil nuts, walnuts, pecans have no lectins and are good for you.
Great Britain is just great because it's the biggest of the British Isles. Like Grand Canaria in the Canary Islands - it's called Grand because it's the biggest.

Most computers have 64-bit registers, which can store numbers up to 10 to the power of 19 - that's 10 with 19 noughts after it. Even for NASA looking at stars in the universe, computers have clever ways to deal with bigger numbers without having the whole number in memory. No one's going to make calculators bigger because it's all part of computers.

The Romans had three calendars. The first was religious, counting years from the founding of Rome (around 735 BC). Practically, people said 'the year of the consul' because they all knew the political system. Later, the Byzantine Empire determined the world was created around 5,500 BC and rewrote their calendars using that as year zero. In Britain at the time, people were 'too busy smearing ourselves in woad and dancing around Stonehenge.'

North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal. It's a protected island because the natives are incredibly hostile - everyone who has set foot on the island has been killed. There's an exclusion zone of about 4 kilometres around it, also to protect the natives from diseases since they've never had contact with the outside world.

questions.question: Why is green associated with fully charged or go, and red associated with stop or out of battery?

answers.answer: Red means stop and green means go. Red on a battery means not going, green means going. Probably stems from traffic lights.
Goes back to the Vienna Convention and international standardisation. In some countries green was blue, particularly Japan where a green light was a blue light.
It comes down to basic colors in nature. Red is the least dominant color in nature and is used to symbolize danger, alerting us quickly. Green is the most common color with trees and stuff.

questions.question: Why is it that shampoo lathers up in your hair and bubbles up, but conditioner doesn't?

answers.answer: Shampoo has soap in it which bubbles it up. Conditioner leaves stuff in your hair rather than washing everything out, so it doesn't have soap.

Shampoo has a detergent to dissolve oil, sweat, dead skin cells and products people put on hair. Conditioner is to put back oils stripped out by shampoo so you can get a comb through it. Shampoo needs the soap to foam, conditioner doesn't.

questions.question: Do dolphins, whales and porpoises have a sense of smell given they breathe through blowholes?

answers.answer: Probably don't have a sense of smell. May have taste buds in their mouth.
They don't have any nasal receptors. Dolphins living underwater don't have receptors so they do not have a sense of smell. They use sonar to find food.

questions.question: Where do all the olive stones (pits) go?

answers.answer: Historically they would have just chucked them away. They're turning olive stones into fuel, a renewable fuel. There's quite a growth area in Greece. Olive trees are generally in orchards and it's against the law to chop down olive trees in Greece.

They get made into what we call PIPs (P-I-P-S). They're used as fuel in solid fuel heaters, boilers and stuff for heating houses in Spain over the winter. In an olive growing area, it's cooperative so you help with olives and get free bags of PIPs delivered to your house over winter.

questions.question: In Back to the Future, when the DeLorean travels through time and comes back, it's freezing cold. Is there a science behind that?

answers.answer: We can't time travel so there isn't any science behind time travel. He put it on the board.

Time is a fourth dimension with one side and another side. They collapse in on each other where there is nothing, no particles, no energy, and therefore the temperature there is believed to be absolute zero, thus freezing cold. The film commentary mentions they stopped doing the ice effect in later films because it was too expensive with liquid nitrogen.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'first dibs'?

answers.answer: It comes from 'dibstones' - the game of knuckle bones played by tossing things up and catching them on the back of your hand. First dibs is the first person to go on that. It's apparently US in origin.

questions.question: When traveling from the States to the UK by plane, you change your watches five hours when you get on the plane. Friends are coming back on the Queen Mary 2 which takes five days. When do they change their clock? Is it one hour a day or five hours straight away?

answers.answer: One hour at one o'clock.

Generally if it's five days and five hours, you do it every day one hour. They do it at 1 o'clock in the morning. When you have more time, like going from Florida to Gibraltar over about two weeks, the captain chooses which day. You never go more than one hour simply because that messes up the body clock. You adjust your body clock without really noticing.

questions.question: On the London Underground, there's a pit under the rails at stations. When the train goes overground towards Heathrow, there's no pit - it's just level. What's the pit for and why isn't it there overground?

answers.answer: Should anyone fall onto the tracks or find themselves on the tracks and haven't got time to get back up onto the platform, they've got somewhere to shelter should a train be hurtling towards them. On the overground you could just roll into the meadow and have more space to get out of the way. The pit only exists on station platforms, not in tunnels.

questions.question: If road safety is so important, why are there not seatbelts on buses?
When were calories first discovered?

answers.answer: Calories were defined by French scientist Nicolas Clement in the 1830s or 40s. There are two types: the small calorie (gram calorie) is the amount of heat energy required to raise one gram of water by one degree centigrade at one atmosphere of pressure. The large calorie is used for food measurement.

questions.question: Why do I get less mashed potato from sweet potatoes than from white potatoes when using the same weight?

answers.answer: Sweet potatoes aren't actually potatoes - they're the roots of a bindweed plant. The tuber is made of fibrous material, which is completely different from white potatoes. When you mash it, it doesn't hold as much air. White potatoes are more like a honeycomb with holes that fill with water, butter or air. That's why you get more volume from white potatoes.

questions.question: How can you undercook beef but you can't undercook chicken or pork?

answers.answer: Salmonella. It's bacteria. Beef doesn't contain harmful bacteria in the same way raw chicken would.

With pork it's because pigs are omnivores and eat rodents which carry a parasite called trichinella. You have to cook pork thoroughly to kill the parasite. This also explains why ancient religions avoided pork.

questions.question: If a Carrington event happened today, how much warning would we have?

answers.answer: When the sun emits radiation, it takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. If we're watching the sun and see a flare expel from the surface, we'd have about 8 minutes to know it.

The photons from the sun take about 8 minutes to get here. But the protons and neutrons that actually do the damage take 5 to 8 days to reach Earth. It's like a sprinkler - you can see it turn on but the water takes time to reach you. We could see the photons coming and take precautions before the damaging particles hit.

questions.question: What do they do with all the soil when they build tunnels like Crossrail? And why can't tunnel soil be used to stop cliffs falling down on the coast?

answers.answer: Crossrail material went to Wallasey Island in the Thames to create wetland bird habitat. They make the island bigger with it. For why it can't be reused: it depends on the material and tunnel method. Slurry tunnel boring machines render material useless because they grind it up rather than dig it out, and additives are added that make it unusable. Earth pressure balance are different.

The short answer to the second bit is it would just wash away if you dropped loose soil somewhere. For the first bit, they generally try to relocate it somewhere beneficial. Example: St Catherine's Dock soil was taken by barge up the Thames to render Pimlico safe - Pimlico was marshland until they piled dry rocks and soil on it.

questions.question: Did the @ symbol exist before the computer age? And if so, what was it used for?

answers.answer: It's an accountancy symbol - it's been around as long as printing presses have, since Victorian times. 'At' means 'each at'. You'd write '10 apples at 4p' on an invoice or ledger. It's used for 'each at' specifically, so you know whether it's 10 apples for 4p total or 10 apples for 4p each.

questions.question: Who designed the dartboard? Why are the numbers arranged the way they are?
Why can't you smell your own breath if you breathe in through your mouth and then breathe out through your nose?

answers.answer: The olfactory receptors are on the roof of your nose - that's where you sense smells. When you breathe in, the air direction takes it to the roof of your nose where you do your smelling. When you breathe out, the air is humidified and heavier, and it goes straight out through your nostrils - it doesn't go to the roof where the olfactory epithelium is. So you can't smell your own breath through your nose.

questions.question: Why is a cowlick called a cowlick?

answers.answer: It's an unruly bit of hair that goes out of kilter with the grain of the rest of your hair
Could it be that if you were a little calf and your mum gave it a lick until it went down flat?
The rogue piece of hair resembles the lick of a cow. When a cow licks its own nose, it curls up long and curly. Cows have long tongues because they can't pick their nose in the normal fashion.

questions.question: Why is it always titled Indian tonic water?

answers.answer: Related to empire and malaria. British people in India needed to consume quinine to fight off malaria, and tonic water contained high levels of quinine.

Quinine is indeed a prophylactic against malaria. British people in India needed it, which is why it's called Indian. Same with India pale ale - it didn't survive the trip to India, so they made it slightly stronger.

questions.question: What is the newest language? I don't mean slang.

answers.answer: Esperanto - an international auxiliary language devised in 1887. It was designed as a European project for a language the whole of Europe could speak.
Serbian, Bosnian and Montenegrin when the Eastern European bloc was broken up in the late 80s. Bosnian was codified then. Serbo-Croat used to be one language.

questions.question: Why do human beings have the menopause when so few other animals do?

answers.answer: I don't know. I wonder if it's a proper question - if you can answer with 'why not' then it's not a proper question. But I like it. If there were a disadvantage, evolution would have sidelined it.

There are only five species on Earth that go through menopause - humans and four whales (killer whales, beluga whales, shortfin pilot whales, and narwhals). It's the effect of grandmothers. From a genetic point of view, an older female is better off investing in her grandchildren than having more children. When you have children, they carry half your genes. When they have children, those grandchildren carry a quarter of your genes. By the time you have four or more grandchildren, you're better off ensuring they survive. Evolution works on genes, not individuals.

questions.question: Why don't dogs squint?

answers.answer: Different ocular biology. They don't need to squint because their eyes are made differently.

Dogs squint very slightly. Their eyes are very different to human eyes - they don't see red and green but are very good at seeing movement. They have a reflective carpet on the back of their eye (tapetum lucidum), which is why you see their eyes shining in the dark. They see movement best but don't see sharply - on a scale of 1-10 where humans see 10, dogs see about 5-6. They're going through a foggy world, but their nose compensates. Dogs are specialized predators hunting in packs, so they need to identify anything that moves.

questions.question: Why do chefs wear silly trousers?

answers.answer: I like that. I've never thought about it either. They have a patterned trouser that's specific to chefing.

It's for hygiene reasons. When you are working in a kitchen, you shouldn't be wearing the same clothes that you sit on the sofa and cuddle your dog with. The trousers are designed to be very specific to the kitchen - something you wouldn't wear outside.

questions.question: Why do external doors open inwards?

answers.answer: One reason could be so that you don't clatter someone outside the door when you open it. But I don't know if it's building regulations or convention.

Fire flow times. If you imagine a building as a bucket of water, more holes means faster dispersal. A door opening outwards doesn't impede flow as much. In the early 1900s in Edinburgh, after a fire where everyone got out in two and a half minutes, that's been treated as gospel - everyone must get out of a building within two and a half minutes. If you have more than 60 people in a room, doors should open outwards. For flats in corridors, doors open inwards so they don't impede the corridor.

There's nothing in building regulations that stipulates fire doors must open out or in. Doors can work both ways. The 60 people rule is a recommendation used to fulfil functional requirements which are law, but not law itself. If you go home and rehang your front door to open outwards, you won't get into trouble.

questions.question: What is the evolutionary point of colour blindness? Why are people still colour blind?

answers.answer: There is no evolutionary benefit of any disability or colour blindness. Colour blindness passes through the population precisely because it conveys no reproductive dividend, but the opposite of no reproductive benefit is not that you don't get to reproduce. It is hereditary, coming from the female side.

questions.question: Why is it people that are allergic to eggs aren't allergic to chicken?

answers.answer: Eggs aren't chickens. They are two completely different chemical formulae. They come from a chicken and can turn into a chicken, but they're not the same thing.

The protein that causes egg allergy is found in the albumin (egg white). That protein is not present in a chicken. They are different foods, different chemical compositions. The protein is only in the egg white, but you can never entirely separate egg white from egg yolk without cross-contamination risk. A forensic amount that's not visible can kill someone severely allergic.

questions.question: Do emergency vehicles have their own speed restrictions? Could they do 120 in a 30?

answers.answer: No, they don't have to obey a speed limit. They just have to drive at whatever speed is sensible. They can be prosecuted if something happens and it's believed to be driver error, but that's not the same as a speed restriction.

Emergency vehicles have an exemption from the speed limit, red traffic lights, and certain directional arrows. There is no limit to the speed you can go, albeit subject to laws regarding reckless driving. In a 30, you're not limited to doing 50 - you could do 140 if it was a clear road. Bernie was a former police officer and Class 1 advanced driver.

Scottish fire engines have a 50% limit over the speed limit. In a 30 limit, they're limited at 45. Fire engines are limited at around 70-75 mph maximum. This was introduced about four or five years ago. Previously they drove as quick as a fire engine could go.

Ambulance driver based in Worcester. Stretcher ambulances are only allowed to do 20 over the speed limit. Rapid response vehicles are more like a state car and can do quite a lot faster - around 110 mph. It depends whether you have someone in the back or not.

Head of Driving Standards for the London Ambulance Service. There is no speed limit for emergency service vehicles. Section 87 of the Road Traffic Regulation Act gives the exemption. While local organisations might put policies in place according to training and vehicle type, there is no legal cap providing it's done safely with no intention of dangerous driving. This applies in England and Wales, but not Scotland.

questions.question: Multi-vitamins - if you get all your vitamins in one pill, shouldn't it be the size of a golf ball?

answers.answer: Most of an average vitamin pill is Kaolin, a clay-like binding agent used to bulk out the active ingredient. When you combine vitamins, you just reduce the amount of binding agent, so your multi-vitamin is not going to be the size of a golf ball because much of the pill would be non-active binding agent, not vitamins.

questions.question: At the Sochi Winter Olympics, why did they put salt on the snow to keep it firm for the cross-country event?

answers.answer: The melting point of salt water is lower than the freezing point of water, which is why we put down salt to de-ice pavements. The sea doesn't freeze for this reason. James wondered if it might be physics rather than chemistry, but couldn't provide a definitive answer.

Snowboarder. What the salt does is melt the top layer of the snow. Then because you've got a snowpack underneath, the water refreezes, creating a smoother, more skiable or snowboardable surface. This is why they did it at the Winter Olympics.

questions.question: If average body temperature is 36.5 degrees, why do we find it unbearably hot when it's 30 degrees outside?

answers.answer: This is about confusion between internal temperature and external temperature. James couldn't remember the answer and left it on the board.

Professor of Robotics at University of Middlesex. It's not so much a question of temperature as generating heat and getting it away quickly - the only way you can do that is by sweating. You need surface area to sweat enough to lose the heat you're generating in your brain and other body organs by metabolism. It depends not only on temperature but on humidity, whether there's a breeze, and for example in water you can get rid of heat more quickly because of the thermal conductivity of water. So the external temperature of 30 degrees combined with humidity and lack of breeze makes it hard to dissipate the heat your body is generating internally.

questions.question: What's happening scientifically in your brain when you get a song stuck in your head?

answers.answer: James acknowledged he didn't know the answer. This is why it's a mystery question.

Plays percussion in the Halle Orchestra. The brain can't really deal with complicated tunes. The reason songs get stuck is because they're the easiest bits to recall. When you're driving home after a concert, the brain is idling away and just pops up the easy-to-remember parts. Sometimes songs get stuck because two songs sound similar and one triggers the other. It's the brain just sort of idling away, almost like you'd be whistling if you were digging the garden.

questions.question: Does tea have some sort of preservative quality to milk? When he makes his four-year-old daughter a bottle of milk, if left overnight it goes cheesy and yoghurt-like. But if he puts milk in tea, it doesn't turn. Is there something in the tea preventing the milk from turning?

answers.answer: The hot water might be the factor, but it's not really enough to stop curdling. James couldn't determine if there was enough protein being affected.

Soap maker who uses green tea in soap because of its antioxidant properties. Tea is a powerful antioxidant, and when milk curdles it's being oxidised. Tea prevents the milk from oxidising and going off easily. Green tea and black tea come from the same plant, just picked at different times.

questions.question: I watched Pirates of the Caribbean last week and noticed that the CGI cost £150 million. Why does it cost so much if it's all computer generated? Is it not just a bunch of geeks on computers?

answers.answer: Computer graphics, whether we're talking about feature films or computer games, is highly specialised. If you look at the credits for the average animated film or even a computer game, they run just as long as any big blockbuster film production. You have set designers, specialists in animation of all kinds. So this all adds up. The actual time it takes to make really good computer animation is on a very similar level and timescale to a feature film, perhaps even longer. In Pirates of the Caribbean, you've got an entire fleet of ghostly pirate ships coming over the horizon and every single one of them is painstakingly realised and beautifully depicted. There are specialists in clothing animation. You've got lots of staff, hardware, software, engineers to look after the hardware and software, programmers and coders writing it. And they're going to be in a building where you've got to pay rent and they're going to need cleaners.

questions.question: Does she dream? Do puppies and dogs dream?

answers.answer: The answer is yes. They've stuck electrodes to dogs' heads while they're sleeping and concluded that they do dream. You'll get leg twitches, growls. They're doing in their dreams the same as we are. They might be chasing a rabbit.

questions.question: Is there a specific height or amount of floors that a building has to have to be considered a skyscraper?

answers.answer: The first skyscraper was the Flatiron Building in Union Square, New York. After that, any building that was higher was called a skyscraper. So it's not a function of feet and inches.

questions.question: What's the difference between water-resistant and waterproof?

answers.answer: Waterproof means you could essentially swim in it if it was tight enough. Waterproof will admit no water. Water-resistant will admit a lot less water than other stuff.

For a product to be waterproof, it needs to withstand 1.5 metres of water pressure directly to the actual fabric. That's called a hydrostatic head test. The legal definition is that you also need to tape the seams of the garment - any stitching or embroidery had to be taped on the inside. Water resistant means they waterproof the fabric but don't tape the seams because it's labour intensive and costs more money. You can waterproof up a jacket yourself for less money using seam sealant.

questions.question: Why do pedestrian traffic lights have grills over the green man that block your view, so you cannot actually see the green man unless you wiggle around?

answers.answer: They're called louvers. You only get them on multiple crossings - if you're at one side of a crossing and you can see another crossing which is on a different face, you won't get the read-through. So a driver might get a glimpse of green and think it's meant for him and then go. You put the grills there so you have to be quite near and specific to that light in order to see it.

questions.question: Why does an underwire bra not activate the metal detectors at the airport when they tell you to take everything else metallic off?

answers.answer: All machines have different settings. You can whack up the settings and it picks up absolutely everything like piercings, or you can whack it down and it passes through smaller objects. So depending where you are and what your needs are, you can have different settings. Airports, government buildings will have different settings. So yes, sometimes the bra would set off an alarm - it depends on the settings of the machine, how tight they want the security.

questions.question: How high does an aeroplane or spacecraft have to go off the Earth's surface before it can't use a compass anymore for navigation?

answers.answer: The point at which you leave the Earth's atmosphere and enter the stratosphere because there is no gravitational pull to give you the two poles. That's about five miles up.

It's nothing to do with gravity whatsoever. It's everything to do with two magnets lining up - the magnet of the compass and the magnet of the Earth internal iron-containing compounds going round. The further away you get, it decreases exponentially. It would decrease completely by the time you got to the outer reaches of our atmosphere. It's nothing to do with gravity - it's the magnetic force which is another fundamental force.

questions.question: Where did the nickname Tommy Atkins for British soldiers come from?

answers.answer: Tommy Atkins is just a generic term for a British soldier. Atkins is the surname he would have had. It's like Joe Bloggs except for soldiers. There's a Rudyard Kipling poem called Tommy, but it didn't originate from the poem.

questions.question: Why is a boxing ring called a ring if it's a square?

answers.answer: It used to be a ring. Go back to when boxing was first formalised in the 18th century or earlier, they'd draw a route on the ground into which fighters would go. But the ring would be made of people standing as the boundaries - they couldn't stand in a square. When they started doing it on a raised platform so they could sell tickets, it would have been almost impossible to do it in a ring because you'd have bars every couple of stages. So it simply morphed from a ring to a square, known as squaring the circle. That would have happened in the first half of the 19th century when boxing became increasingly popular, and that's where the phrase ringside seat came from.

questions.question: Why is it on advertisements for watches that the time is always ten to two?

answers.answer: It looks symmetrical and a smiley face. The human brain likes symmetry, and there's no danger of the branding or other bits on the watch face being obscured by the hands, but it is just pleasing to the human eye to see it at ten past ten or ten to two.

questions.question: Why are two juvenile squirrels burying conkers in my lawn and flower bed?

answers.answer: The most crucial word in your question was 'juvenile.' They will dig up a conker, have a little nibble, realise it is disgusting and never bury a conker again. Once their mums taught them properly, they know they're poisonous. You wouldn't catch an old squirrel doing that.

questions.caller: Deborah (Ascot) - on behalf of son Rory
questions.question: Who decides whose face or what is put on the face of a coin in circulation? As in the words and decorations and slogans?
Why doesn't our own snoring wake us up? It wakes up the person next to us but doesn't wake us up.

answers.answer: It's surprising that we don't wake ourselves up more often with our own snoring. James mentioned he sometimes wakes himself up with the snort rather than the snore.

questions.question: Was there less gravity in the past? Every year material from space gets deposited on Earth, making it bigger. Life in the past was much bigger (dinosaurs). Could the smaller Earth mean less gravity and explain why things were so big?

answers.answer: I don't think it's got anything to do with gravity. Evolution has decided that being that big doesn't make you more prone to survival and procreation.

There's an equilibrium - for every meteor that comes in, things like helium escape. The dinosaurs are a red herring - there is as much biomass on Earth as there ever has been or ever will be. The ecosystem is relatively a closed loop. No, gravity is not affected. The formula is F = GMm/R squared - we're a relatively closed system and gravity is constant.

questions.question: Can pilots use the seatbelt sign for reasons other than turbulence? On a recent flight with many kids running around, the seatbelt light came on with no announcement. Did the pilot put it on just to control the kids?

answers.answer: I'm pretty sure they can use it for issues within the plane.

Yes, for security - when cabin crew need to use the toilet, the seatbelt signs go on so everyone sits down. Also for drunk passengers causing trouble, the crew will ask us to put the seatbelt sign on because it's difficult to run trolleys up and down the aisle.

questions.question: Why have they called my place Bushfield Walk? There's no nice walk there. Why do they name places things like Rise, Avenue, Lane, Road, Walk, Path, Drive, Green? Who decides?
