answers.answer: The council decides, I think. It'd be a cool job. What's the difference between a lane and an avenue? Doesn't an avenue have trees on it?

Older street names come from what was originally there. Stables Street would have been backing onto big houses. A green would have been where the compter was, the watchman was, where they locked drunk people and petty criminals. In Islington, drovers would keep stray animals on the green. The Georgians were the ones who brought street naming in.

When there's a new road, the local councillor gets the privilege to name it. My dad was a councillor and he named our street Jenny Lee Drive after Jenny Lee, a Labour MP in the 1940s, one of the first women MPs. In Scotland they let the public name it - that's how you get Boaty McBoatface.

questions.question: Why do ice cream vans play Greensleeves?

answers.answer: Greensleeves is very catchy. Who wrote Greensleeves? Henry VIII.
It's licensing - Greensleeves is in the public domain, so no royalties, no public performance fees. It's cheerful and free.
It's a well-known misconception that Henry VIII wrote Greensleeves. It's Italian in style and didn't reach England until after Henry's death, making it more likely Elizabethan in origin.

questions.question: How much does electricity weigh? If electricity accumulates, there must be a weight to it. Does a charged phone weigh more than a flat one?

answers.answer: There must be some sort of difference in weight because there's something there - electrical energy.

The answer is no - electricity doesn't weigh anything. Electrons have mass, but if you apply voltage to a wire, electrons go in one end and come out the other, the wire won't get any heavier. A capacitor doesn't get heavier when charged. A battery is different - it's about chemical reaction, and mass stays constant. You don't introduce electrons to your phone when charging, you're changing the chemical construction of the battery.

questions.question: Why do certain perfumes and aftershaves smell different on different people?

answers.answer: Key reasons are temperature, body temperature, and your own scent - everyone has a different smell. It's a combination of the external scent with your inherent scent, so it's bound to smell slightly differently from person to person.

questions.question: When I'm watching TV and need to pop to the loo, I can pause it. If I don't understand something, I can rewind. Why can't I do that with my radio as easily?

answers.answer: You can - on digital radio, apps, websites. Some newer cars like Lexus have rewind and pause. You need digital technology. Regular DAB radios don't have it yet but it will come. Not every radio program is worth rewinding though.

questions.question: Does sign language have rhyming words? And do people born deaf understand the sound of rhyme?

answers.answer: Rhyming as a concept is an audio phenomenon. If someone was born profoundly deaf, their experience is going to be different from someone who lost hearing over time.

A lot of deaf people have a very low reading age because they don't learn the sounds, they never understand the sounds. Profoundly deaf from birth learn British Sign Language as their first language. Many have a reading age of about 11. They just can't hear that a T sounds like a T - it's an utterly alien concept. That's why BSL is important, not just subtitles.

questions.question: Sea level is given as an exact number for mountains etc. But sea level varies wildly at times at the beach. Is sea level taken from low tide, high tide, or average?
What happens to the roe when you buy scallops? It seems to always be removed, and you can't buy scallop roe by itself.

answers.answer: Scallop roe is dried and flaked as a seasoning in Chinese restaurants - you see it as that flaky orange powder on top of dishes. It's very umami and delicious. Chefy markets sell it. Nigella Lawson likes scallop roe on toast with streaky bacon.

questions.question: Why do we stand on the right on escalators but keep left in corridors on the London Underground? Why the difference?

answers.answer: The rule is always walk on the left. When walking in corridors, the obstacle hitting you is people on the right coming towards you. On escalators, the obstacle is people standing on the right as you walk up. Walk on the left and you can't go wrong - it's common sense to avoid the obstacle.

questions.question: Why does bread go stale and stiff when left out, but biscuits go soggy and absorb water? What is the science behind this difference?

answers.answer: Bread dough contains a lot of water. When it bakes, the starch absorbs the water (like making a roux). This process reverses very slowly after baking - the water emerges from the starch back into the surrounding air, causing staleness. Biscuits are made with lots of fat and sugar with very little water. Sugar is hygroscopic - it attracts water. So biscuits absorb moisture from the air, making them go limp.

questions.question: Why are those exercises called 'burpees'? It doesn't make you burp. And the gym instructor didn't know either.

answers.answer: It's named after Royal Burpee, an American physiologist who invented it as a fitness test. You lie on the floor, heart pumps blood down to feet, then you jump up and put hands above head, so heart has to pump blood all the way up to your head. It really works the heart.

questions.question: Why are new books released as hardcovers first, then you have to wait months and months for the paperback? Is it just about money?

answers.answer: Historically it's about money - people pay more for hardbacks. But the Kindle thing has messed that up.

It's about profit. Hardbacks are seen as more of a luxury item so publishers can charge more and get more profit. Since the rise of Kindle, there's been a move in publishing to put more money into production with nice cover effects to make the physical book a desirable object.

questions.question: Why does the sun fade things? Furniture, books, book spines - why does light from the sky bleach things?

answers.answer: It's not the visible light you see that's doing the damage. Imagine light as a layer cake - visible light is in the middle, surrounded on one side by ultraviolet energy and on the other by infrared energy. It's the ultraviolet end of the light spectrum that reacts with the dyes and inks, causing the fading.

questions.question: If an octopus has a heart attack, is it all three hearts affected, or can one heart have issues while the other two kick in to assist?
How has water remained on the surface of the Earth over millions of years? Why hasn't gravity drawn it underground or beneath the surface? Why isn't there just a ball of soggy soil in the middle?

answers.answer: The sand reaches saturation point. Beneath the seabed there's rock - water can't keep going forever.

Water cycle keeps water circulating - even if it did seep down and get hotter, it would evaporate and rejoin the water cycle. We drink water, we weird out, water evaporates, goes to clouds, rains back down, gets purified, we drink it again. It's like a bouncy castle where air leaks but is being replenished. Also the density of rock beneath the water is greater than the density of water, so it doesn't sink further.

questions.question: Why is there no gender distinction for cousin like there is for niece/nephew, uncle/aunt? Does French have different words for male and female cousin?

answers.answer: Originally 'cousin' meant relative, not specific to gender. Shakespeare used 'cuz' in this way. English didn't have a specific word for what we now call cousin, so we borrowed the French word 'cousin' which just meant relative - any relative, not gender specific.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'ripped off' come from? Like, if you go to a shop and you feel like it's too expensive, and you say 'I feel like I was ripped off', where are the origins of it?

answers.answer: It means you've paid over the odds. It doesn't mean you've been conned. If you bought a box and you'd been told it had a computer in it, and when you got it home it had bricks in it, that would also be ripped off - as well as being overcharged, it's not what you thought. But it probably only meant one of them originally.

I think it's to do with clipping coins - when coins were worth what they were worth according to their metal, people would clip a tiny bit off and melt it down to make money. That might be related to the phrase.

It's actually not that old - from the late 60s, African-American slang. 'Rip' was used since the early 1900s in America as prison slang to steal, and rip-off was an evolution of that. 'Rip' is actually Danish meaning to tear apart roughly - which is why you find it in rip tides and rip currents. In the 60s it moved on to 'rip off' meaning to steal from someone.

questions.question: Why do we in 2018 still use something as neolithic as water to put out large building fires? Why is nothing being developed which is more technical, more advanced?

answers.answer: Water's brilliant. It's the best thing you could use in terms of accessibility, efficacy, and cost. You're never going to find anything better than water. For liquid nitrogen or liquid helium, where would you get that from if you're trying to put out a big warehouse fire? You need something that's plugged into the mains.

The reason water is the main one is because the infrastructure is so easy to put in - all the air and water are readily available. But it's not just water - different fires have different flammability limits, and there are inert gas systems that flood rooms to take the oxygen below the flammability limit. Also, sprinklers wouldn't work in server rooms because they'd short-circuit everything.

questions.question: Where does the origin of basic tree tapping come from? If you're drilling into a tree and you install a tap into a tree and sap comes out, where does that practice come from?

answers.answer: Tree tapping has been around since indigenous Canadians did it with maple syrup, and it would have been in Europe for thousands of years.

The practice goes back several hundred years to Eastern European countries, Russia, Poland. You drill a hole about an inch diameter in the tree around March when the sap is running, draw off the sap, then plug the tree because otherwise it will bleed. Never take more than one gallon from a tree. Birch sap wine is similar to Sauvignon Blanc.

questions.question: Why are there no formal passport checks when you're leaving the UK, whereas when you're leaving Austria, France, Germany, Spain, they have immigration officers checking everyone's passports before you get on the plane?

answers.answer: I don't recognise what you describe. I've been to all those countries and I don't remember feeling more closely scrutinised. When you check in you have to show your passport. You can't get your boarding pass without showing it.

When you leave another country, as part of UK border control they check you more thoroughly than when you leave the UK where they just do a cursory check of your ticket. The person checking the ticket when you leave another country is UK border control. They're making sure you're not coming to Britain illegally. We're not worried about people leaving, but we're worried about people coming in.

questions.question: How do scallops multiply? How do more scallops get created? The French fishermen and English are waiting for the scallops.

answers.answer: They reproduce by a process known as spawning. The males release their sperm into the water at the same time as the females release their eggs, and the sperm floats through the water and fertilizes the eggs. That's how they do it.

questions.question: Why is scratching a remedy for an itch? Why specifically that?

answers.answer: An itch is to do with your nerve and a scratch is also to do with your nerves. When you've got an itch and you scratch it, the irritation to your nerves goes away.

questions.question: How long do spider webs stay sticky for? Do they all stay sticky? There's a web outside my house under a gutter that I've left for almost a couple of years and there's still things stuck to it.

answers.answer: I think they get their stickiness reapplied by the spider on a regular basis.

It would stay sticky for as long as the spider web is intact. The web can last for as long as it's not touched, basically. If someone doesn't hoover it up or move it, it should stay there for as long as it's there.

questions.question: Why do your toenails grow slower than your fingernails?

answers.answer: You're using your fingers more so you get natural wearing down on your fingers. You're not going to get natural filing on your toenails the way you would on your fingernails.

It's to do with vitamin D and sunshine. In winter toenails don't grow as fast as fingernails anyway because we wear socks and have feet covered up. In summer they grow much faster because toes are out in the sun benefiting from vitamin D. Fingernails tend to grow faster as well.

questions.question: Do babies suffer from travel sickness?
Why is it considered lucky crossing your fingers?

answers.answer: It's a little prayer, like doing the sign of the cross before taking a penalty. You're asking for God's help. It's the same way you do a sign of the cross.

questions.question: When the Olympics happened and North and South Korea had their combined flag, I wanted to know whether there's a name for the people who design flags. Back in the day when all nations were coming up with new flags, who actually made them, and is it a proper job?

answers.answer: Flags and insignia almost always have roots in fleets and navies, transmuting from fleets to nations. There's probably been a committee for something like the Korean flag. Every flag has probably got a slightly different story behind it.
The person who makes flags is a vexillologist. They study and design flags. In America where expensive fish are more popular, aquatic veterinarians are marine biologists and they're well paid.

questions.question: Why are all cereal packet characters male? Tony the Tiger, Cockerel, Snap Crackle and Pop?

answers.answer: If you're talking about the gender balance of 50 years ago, you'd be right - you would never have seen a woman in an advert unless it was for washing powder or Hoovers. The impression was that dad went out and worked and earned the money, so you have a hearty breakfast.

questions.question: Why do we call it the stiff upper lip when it's the bottom lip that tends to tremble?

answers.answer: The key bit of the figure of speech is the stiffness, not the upperness. You don't smile, frown, sneer, weep, or quiver. You keep it stiff, show nothing to Johnny Foreigner because if he can see into your soul he will know you're about to nick his country. Probably goes back to Dickens at least.
It comes from the war era - everyone had to make do and mend. (James noted this goes back further, at least to 19th century, so not a complete answer)

questions.question: Do animals suffer from irrational things? (phobias)

answers.answer: Cats fear cucumbers because they look like snakes - that's actually rational if they have genetic inheritance to be frightened of snakes. Rabies is hydrophobia - irrational fear of water. Dogs terrified of clowns might have been brutalised by a clown as a puppy.
Chocolate lab scared of heights - when crossing a steel footbridge with perforations, he lay on the floor and had to be dragged across. Also won't get on trains.
Had a pony with irrational fear of plastic bags - tried cognitive behavioural therapy with apple in plastic bag, pony bit it and had panic attack in stable.

As a canine behaviourist: Any animal that can experience pain or emotions such as fear is capable of developing a phobia through classical conditioning. If an animal experiences trauma in a particular situation, they get a negative association and that becomes a trigger for fight-or-flight. If you went back far enough into someone's subconscious you'd find a trigger. Also: dogs can be frightened of carrier bags because they get stuck in them, balloons, noise sensitivity. Horses can be afraid of drains.

questions.question: Do certain types of trees produce more or less oxygen than other types of trees? And could that inform which trees are planted in new housing developments?

answers.answer: Deciduous trees have a different relationship with photosynthesis than evergreen trees. Plane trees were popular with Victorians because they grew quicker and sturdier. Children are healthier if they live near lots of trees.

As an arborist: Oaks and redwoods produce more oxygen than other trees because they're more efficient at breaking down water to produce oxygen. Larger mature trees produce less oxygen but growing trees produce more. For reducing pollution you want plane trees (London planes) because they absorb a lot of pollution from streets. Conifers are rubbish for oxygen. Evergreen trees produce oxygen all year round while deciduous only during leaf months.

questions.question: Can you take fish to the vets? Like, is there a specific place that you need to go if your fish is poorly?

answers.answer: You probably could use a vet. Goldfish can go a bit white, fins go a funny colour, they look sluggish or won't get off the bottom of the tank.

In the UK we don't really take fish to the vet as it's not financially viable for goldfish. But for koi carp, vets will come to you. In America where fancy expensive fish are popular, there are aquatic veterinarians who are marine biologists - well paid. Big aquariums employ them too.
Yes, I took my fish to the vet - a lion-headed goldfish swimming on its side. The vet gave medicine and told me to quarantine the fish. I put it in a separate tank but then the whole tank died.

questions.question: Why do I feel more out of balance stepping onto an escalator that's not working than one that is moving? I stumble off by the time I get to the end.

answers.answer: Subconscious conditioning - your subconscious is preparing for the movement.

When running upstairs stairs are all the same height. On an escalator, your brain cannot correlate with your feet that you're walking on stairs but the stairs are getting shorter as you go down. That's why you fall. But you get wobbly before taking a step because your body automatically expects to move.

It's not subconscious conditioning - it's called classical conditioning. You expect the escalator to be moving (stimulus A), so you have a response (your body prepares to move). Summed up by Pavlov's dogs - ring a bell, feed them, after a while they salivate even without food. We're salivating metaphorically every time we step on an escalator.

questions.question: Me and my girlfriend went to a national heritage thing - it was a world-famous garden. I wondered what warrants being called a world-famous garden? Is there any criteria or referee for it?

answers.answer: There's no policing of the language - you could claim your garden was world-famous and if you tried to sell tickets you might get done for something else, but not for mislabelling it. You'd just need to find a few people in France who've heard of it to argue it's world-famous.

questions.question: I'm a Type 1 diabetic. I tested my blood sugar and got 5.2 in my left hand, then immediately tested my right hand and got 5.4. Why do I get two different readings from two different fingers?

answers.answer: Two reasons: One, the sticks you're using - if you've touched the stick it's got something on it that could read slightly differently. Two and more importantly, blood isn't totally uniform - it's like chicken soup. If you took two ladles you'd have five bits of carrot in one, two bits in another.

questions.question: Why, considering the new plastic banknotes have been in circulation for around a year or so, why is the Queen still depicted as considerably younger than she is now?

answers.answer: The monarch's head has only appeared on banknotes since 1960. Before that, notes like ten-shilling notes and five-pound notes were unprinted and showed nothing. They've stuck with the portrait from around 1960 when it started, and there's no real reason to change it since they'd need to update it constantly.
Speculated it might be the same picture from the 90s, and perhaps related to forgery prevention

questions.question: Why don't bra sizes just go A, B, C, D, E, F, G? They go double A, A, B, C, D, double D, E, F, G. Why not just use simple counting?

answers.answer: His wife is a lingerie designer. Women's bodies differ fundamentally from men's, so measurements need to be more precise. The sizing accounts for volume, not just proportions.

She worked in retail at a women's clothing store and learned this in training. The sizing system started in 1948 in the UK with just A, B, C, D. When they discovered there were different proportions, they tried to add sizes in. Double D was added because there was a significant gap between D and E where many women fell.

questions.question: Can you freeze your drinks or liquids to make them solid, then take them through airport security where you can't take liquids?

answers.answer: She works in airport security. If someone has a medical issue requiring something like insulin that needs to be kept cool, they ARE allowed to bring it through with ice - but they need a doctor's letter and the ice block must be tested in their machines to confirm it's actually water and not disguised contraband.

questions.question: Why is the longest day on June 21st, but the warmest months are July and August? And why is the shortest day December 21st but the coldest months are January and February?

answers.answer: Suggested it's because of our distance from the sun - our bit of the Earth is closer in July and August.

Corrected James. The Earth's distance from the sun oscillates around 93 million miles and has nothing to do with temperature. The North Pole in summer never gets dark (24-hour longest day) yet remains cold. What determines temperature is the angle to the sun - 90 degrees at the equator is hottest, shallower angles at poles are colder. The longest day is when Earth tilts toward the sun, but temperature depends on how long you're at the optimum angle to the sun's rays.

questions.question: What is the biggest number you can realistically make using Roman numerals?

answers.answer: Suggested you could keep putting Ms forever, making it infinite, but that M with a bar over it means 1,000, making MM a million - which is more efficient than Arabic numerals for very large numbers.

questions.question: Why do sheep only have teeth on the bottom jaw and not on the top? And why do they have no teeth as adults when lambs do?

answers.answer: Suggested evolution means if they needed top teeth, they'd have them - they don't need them because they tear grass out differently.

He's a sheep farmer. Sheep have a hard pad at the front of the top jaw instead of incisors, but they DO have molars (grinding teeth) further back inside the cheeks. They pluck grass by putting their mouth over it and nipping off at the bottom - like scissors between the hard pad and bottom teeth. Cows use their tongue to pluck instead. This is why they don't need top incisors.

questions.question: What is the origin of the term 'flagship'?

answers.answer: Her husband's guess: when you have a group of ships, the ship the commanding officer is on is called the flagship because it has the commanding flag.

He sails traditional ships. Before radio existed, they had to use flags to communicate with the rest of the fleet. Each flag meant a different letter. The ship that put the flags up was the flagship - the one with the commanding officer.

questions.question: Why, when you've settled down to watch TV and you're comfortable, do the adverts come on and boom really loudly and scare you?

answers.answer: Common sense answer is to grab your attention, but there might be a technological reason about different recording frequencies.

He's a broadcast engineer. When ads are made, they can't just be made louder or the TV station would turn them down to meet standard meter readings. So the audio is processed to make quiet bits louder and louder bits quieter, raising the average. This makes the LEDs on meters peak more often on ads than on programs, even though the maximum level is the same. On radio, there's constant audio processing that keeps everything the same loudness, which is why it doesn't happen on radio.

He mastered commercials for advertising agencies at Sky. The real reason is that advertisers use 'loudness walls' in old mastering techniques - they slice off peaks (which our ears don't really hear) and then turn everything up, making ads sound subjectively louder. UK rules using PPM meters allowed this. But European Broadcast Union rules are now changing with R128 metering.

questions.question: Why do we say we're heartbroken when something happens? Why is love associated with your heart when it's more of a feeling in your mind?

answers.answer: I think it's medieval art and medieval poetry, but I don't know for sure.

In history and literature, they always say people die of a broken heart. It's only in the last 10 years we know from modern technology that the heart actually, if it goes through a shock of some sort, good news or bad news, usually bad news, it affects the function of the heart and it can't pump as well. People present with chest pain and the surge in stress hormones, but the good news is it's only temporary. The mind, when you're emotional, releases different hormones. When you have bad news, you release other hormones which affects the heart's functioning. There's one called noradrenaline, so fight or flight. In evolutionary terms, when a big dinosaur is coming towards you or a bear, your blood vessels constrict.

questions.question: How come when we yawn, it doesn't seem to affect babies? My colleagues seem to yawn when I yawn, but whenever I try to put my baby to sleep, I can do whatever I want and she's immune against it.

answers.answer: There's a survival instinct that for some reason, if you yawn, I will yawn because you've told me that there's nothing behind me to be scared of. If there was, you'd not yawn. It's like a weird primal thing. If it's evolutionary, then baby should be born with it.

Babies can't fix and follow on a face. It's something they learn to do around about six to eight weeks of age. As soon as they can start to fix and follow with their eyes on a face, they'll stop and mimic facial expressions. So it's a question of focus. The evolutionary mechanism is in place, but the eyes aren't up to the job of triggering it.

questions.question: I saw the moon, which was like a half moon at the time, as the sun was coming up. I looked to the right and the moon was still there with a half moon. How can there be the moon at one side with the shadow of the Earth, but I can see the sun on the left-hand side? I can see both in the sky at the same time. If the shadow on the moon is the Earth, how can the sun be visible?

answers.answer: The moon goes around the Earth and the Earth goes around the sun, so there's no reason why you wouldn't be able to see both at the same time. The shadow on the moon isn't the Earth. There's no shadow at all. There's just the dark side of the moon. Get an apple and a torch. Shine the torch at the apple. The dark side behind it is no shadow, it's just the dark side, the bit of the moon that the light hasn't reached. It's nothing to do with the Earth. Move the torch so it's only shining on half the apple. You can still see the other half, but the half the torch is pointing at is much more illuminated than the dark side. If you look really carefully, you can actually see the other half of the moon. Because a tiny amount of light is reaching it, but nowhere near as much as the other bit because of where the sun is in the sky.

questions.caller: Holly and Oliver (child caller via phone)
questions.question: Where do flies go when it's raining?

answers.answer: They retreat to the underside of surfaces like leaves and eaves of buildings, anywhere where it's dark. If there's no sunlight, there's unlikely to be any rain. If the light can't reach it, the water can't.

questions.question: Why is 21st birthday a thing?

answers.answer: It's when you used to get the vote if you were a member of the landed gentry. I think it's probably linked to the vote. These things usually are. Why is 18 a big deal? In this country you leave school and you get the vote. You become more of an adult. Maybe it was when you were allowed to get married back in the day.

It used to be called the age of majority. Age 21 was the age you could vote, you could enter into contracts and things like that. In fact, when people could get married without their parents' consent. 21 is the new 18, 18 is the new 21.

questions.question: How did the sports sections get to the back of the newspaper? In France, the sports section is in the middle and the weather is at the back.

answers.answer: When you're trying to flog a paper, you want to use the front page as the tempter. That's why you put your best story on the front page. I imagine on a Saturday, you put the back page showing because people want to find out the latest sports news. So it's like two different ways of advertising what's inside the paper.

Some research was done. Most people are right-handed. If you pass them a paper or a magazine, something like nearly half people pick it up in their right hand and flick through it using their left thumb. In other words, they start at the back. If you are in a country that is fairly sport-obsessed, you're going to put your sport where it is the first thing that your regular fans will be reading. The inside back cover advertisement costs almost the same as the inside front cover for exactly that reason. A significant proportion of readers are going to go there first. In America, they're even more weather obsessed than sport obsessed because they have such extreme weather, so that's why they put sport in the middle and weather on the back.

questions.question: Why are certain musical scales more easy to digest? Major and minor scales are very widely used across popular music, but less popular styles like jazz and complex classical music use more complex scales. Why do we like some scales more than others?

answers.answer: Major and minor scales are dominant in Western culture, and it's simply a cultural thing. If I went somewhere else in the world, the more dominant popular music would be different scales. China is a very good example. There are types of gamelan music which use instruments that produce a different overtone series to our standard Western instruments. The scales are derived from mathematics at the end of the day. It's about the way the different frequencies of vibrations blend with each other. However, which one of those patterns sounds right to us is purely cultural. It's not that the music is suited to our ears, it's that our ears are suited to the music because of the level of exposure. The notes within the scale are determined by mathematical ratios. An octave is 2 to 1, a perfect fifth is 3 to 2, a perfect fourth is 4 to 5, and so on. In Western music we blur over some of those mathematical differences. There's a difference between a B-flat and an A-sharp which we ignore. But in India they have scales that very much recognize those differences and harmonize them.

questions.question: Why on the back of our car bottles do you not get typical nutritional value that on all other foods you do? It'll tell you what's in it in terms of sugar and fat and stuff, but it doesn't. I'm a diabetic and I was in a bar and I wanted to see how many carbohydrates were in a bottle of cider and there was nothing other than alcohol content. How does it break down?

answers.answer: This is an EU thing. The EU has allowed that the nutrition information on alcohol products should be voluntary and not imposed. Every couple of years they come up and suggest that the industry needs to shape up and start showing it, but the big wine industries in France and Italy resist it. So do the big spirit companies. If you see the amount of calories, the amount of carbohydrate on your bottle, it might put you off. But they are obliged to show things like alcohol content as well as allergens like sulfites. They don't do the breakdown of carbohydrates, fats and sugars. What you will notice is that the big retailers are more upfront - Sainsbury's, Tesco's, Waitrose insist on their own brands showing nutritional information. But the bigger brands don't do it.

questions.question: My son asked me why whales, the sea mammals, as big as they are, why can't they all be just as big? If it's a case of evolution, if one is bigger and therefore stronger, why aren't they all evolved to be the same size?

answers.answer: There are two types of whales - toothed whales and baleen whales. They all feed on different types of food. It's an environmental and behavioral constraint. They seek out different foods and they behave in a different way because they're living in different environments. In fact, there's some species that are even shrinking because they live on Madagascar, and there's a chameleon which is shrinking because it eats smaller food and isn't competing with other chameleons.

questions.question: How do they name buses? You see all the numbers near me, there's no letters, they're all numbers. But I've got an E3, an H91 and a 272. Is there a logic to how bus route numbers are allocated?
Why don't you fall out of bed?

answers.answer: When you're asleep, your consciousness is asleep. Your subconscious processes the day's events. Your subconscious knows where you're sleeping. As soon as you understand about what the bed is, about what happens when you fall down once or twice, your consciousness experiences it. You have to fall out of bed to learn not to fall out of bed.
When you fall into a deep sleep, your brain goes into an REM state which paralyses your body so you don't move around and hurt yourself.

questions.caller: Ryan from Swadling Cut in Derbyshire
questions.question: When people apply for a credit card or check their credit score, why does it affect their score? Why does their score always go down?

answers.answer: He speculated: Could it be that if you need to have a credit check, that means there's a possibility you'd fail it, and if there's a possibility you'd fail it, that's going to have a negative impact on your credit rating?

You're proving to everybody else that you've been turned down by a number of people, and therefore you're effectively looking more desperate. It's called a footprint, and certain mortgage lenders can now do a credit search where the footprint disappears within 48 hours so it can't harm your credit score.

questions.question: They say your brain weighs about a kilo to a kilo and a half but you don't feel the weight of it because it's kept in fluid in your skull and it floats to the top. I don't understand how that works because surely you would feel the weight of it on your neck, because the fluid counts as part of that weight as well.

answers.caller: Professor Hal (Professor of the Public Understanding of Science at University of Brighton)
answers.answer: It's not about liquid at all - it's about equilibrium. When we're in equilibrium with our surroundings, we don't feel our surroundings. We're used to having our brain weighing onto our neck, so we don't feel it. Also, the brain is the only part of your body that has no nerve cells for itself - you can cut your brain and not feel it.

questions.question: Why do men's bikes have the crossbar and women's bikes don't?

answers.answer: It was institutionalised misogyny. Women weren't allowed to part their legs in public, so they couldn't straddle a bike with a crossbar. The crossbar is part of the structural integrity making men's bikes actually superior.

questions.question: 21-gun salute. Why do we have it? Where did it originate from? When do we use it?

answers.answer: It's used at ceremonies, funerals, for heads of state. They have cannons and fire them when celebrating or at funerals.

answers.caller: Michael (British Shipbuilder, worked on Portsmouth and Devonport)
answers.answer: It originates with guns debriefing. As a naval ship enters a foreign harbour, it fires its guns to debrief. The fort would fire its guns to debrief and the ship would enter the harbour. It was later developed into a dignitary salute. Seven at sea, and on land because there's more ammunition, they times it by three to get 21.

questions.question: At the bottom of all UK bottles, there seems to be like a diameter embossed on them. I think it's to do with figuring out the volume of the bottle so you're not conned. It's only the UK - if you go drinking in France, none of them have it.

answers.answer: That's the distance from the top of the bottle, without its cap, to the surface of the liquid if the bottle is filled to the capacity it should be. The bottle itself becomes the measure. It's EU regulation under the Measuring Containers directive. Where you've got the reversed epsilon (back to E) on the base, that's where you get the distance in millimetres and a logo showing where the bottle was made. It's not UK-specific.

questions.question: Migrating geese fly in a V formation. How do they decide who goes at the front? Before they set off, does one of the ganders say 'I know the way, follow me'? Or do they take turns in going at the front?

answers.answer: He was 99% sure they take turns but had no idea why.

answers.caller: Susan (Studied evolutionary animal behaviour as part of degree)
answers.answer: There's a mathematical formula which applies to how animals behave in a group - geese, fish, any animals. It relates to survival of the fittest and natural selection. The stronger and fitter animals are more likely to be at the front and middle (safer positions), and the weakest will be at the edges (more risky, more likely to be killed by predators, more likely to get lost). There's constant jostling to get into the safer middle positions.

questions.question: How do moths know what colour they are? Because they always land where they're best camouflaged, but they can't see their wings.

answers.answer: Moths' eyes are almost 360 degrees - they probably can see their wings. Most insects have much broader peripheral vision than we do.

They don't actually know what colour they are, they just know what colour to land on. If they didn't land on the right colour, they'd be eaten. There's an evolutionary pressure for them to land on the right colour.

questions.question: The bigger animals in the zoo like giraffes and elephants, they don't stay past once they die. How does the zoo dispose of their bodies?

answers.answer: Incinerators.
A chap comes down to take the horse away and it is incinerated. He said they do it for farms and for zoos - they pick up the deceased animal and dispose of it by incineration.

questions.question: When does a heatwave become like a normal summer season? When do we stop calling it a heatwave and just call it summer?
What causes bags under the eyes?

answers.answer: Tiredness and dehydration can cause temporary bags under eyes, but not age-based bags. We'll find out about permanent bags.

questions.question: Why do different species of birds not interbreed? Like blackbirds and rooks, or different finches?

answers.answer: The definition of a species is an animal that can procreate and produce fertile offspring. Dogs are the same species (Pekingese, Labrador all one species) but different breeds. Birds like eagles and starlings are different species. Donkey and horse produce mules/hinnies but those offspring are sterile, so they're different species. That's why sparrows and starlings can't have babies - they might breed but offspring wouldn't be fertile.

questions.question: Why do UK rails always buckle in heat when countries that are much hotter don't have this problem?

answers.answer: It's all to do with the expansion of metal. In hotter countries, they have a wider gap between each rail (laid on sleepers). As the metal expands, it expands into the gap. In colder countries like the UK, the gap's a lot narrower. As we're getting hotter on average, we should start putting in bigger gaps.

questions.question: Why do flies circle round in an area in a room, like in the kitchen, not even under a light shade?

answers.answer: Possibly because the centre of the room is the furthest from all the walls, so they're less likely to fly into something. There's a tension between phototaxis (attraction to light) and wall avoidance.

They're attracted to lights when they're on because they think it's the moon. When they're off, they go to a big light as a landmark because they're looking for a mate. They fly around in circles to save energy and use the light to attract a mate - like saying 'hey, look what I found, come and mate with me.'

questions.question: In the 1920s and 30s, cartoonists portrayed spacemen wearing oxygen tanks and helmets before we went to space in 1961. How did they know we couldn't survive outside our atmosphere?

answers.answer: It's to do with knowing that in space the pressure would be vastly different, and humans would need a pressurized airtight suit, which therefore needs oxygen. Robert Boyle in the 17th century discovered Boyle's Law (gas under pressure). Through industrialization and building things like the Brooklyn Bridge, engineers discovered Caisson's disease (the bends) - when workers came up too quickly from high pressure, they felt sick. They realized air has weight (14.7 pounds per square inch) and that pressure was the issue. A pressurized suit that must be airtight would need oxygen.

questions.question: Celsius is the freezing point of water (32 degrees Fahrenheit). What made Fahrenheit pick his zero point? Is there an event that occurs at that temperature?

answers.answer: The zero point of Fahrenheit is the freezing point of mercury. (He was an ex-aircraft electrician in the Air Force who learned this during training.)

Actually, it's got nothing to do with mercury. The zero point is the lowest temperature Daniel Fahrenheit could produce in his lab - a slushy mixture of ice, water, and salt. He was trying to produce the lowest lab temperature to find a zero point. That's why Kelvin had to come up with a new temperature system to reach absolute zero.

questions.question: Why does computer memory go up in fours, eights, 16s, 32s rather than in fives and tens? And why when it gets to one gig is it actually 950 gig?

answers.answer: Computers address memory with binary numbers (one and zero). It's multiples of two, not fours specifically. You could use a 7 kilobyte chip but it would still take 8 kilobytes because of how binary works. As we get more access to power, they take bigger steps. With quantum computers, they're not restricted by binary - the first quantum computer was a 5 qubit computer because qubits can be one, zero, or neither/both.

A byte is eight bits of memory, each taking a positive/minus state. You stack bytes together - a kilobyte is 1000 bytes, but it's actually 1024, just rounded down and called a kilobyte. A terabyte isn't actually 1000 gigabytes but 1024 gigabytes. There's this slight divergence but it's so small no one really cares.

questions.question: On the Severn Bridge, when heading westbound into Wales, you only see the 'Welcome to Wales' sign once you get to the Welsh side. Heading eastbound, you only see 'Welcome to England' on the English side. When on the bridge, what country am I in?

answers.answer: My great-great-grandfather built the Victoria Falls Bridge and I was the first person to bungee jump off it. On both sides they had to get permission from both countries because there was a 'no man's land' - a join where the countries meet. There's a line somewhere on the bridge. If you look at a map, you'll see the red line across.

questions.question: With pound notes having the Queen's head on it, when she passes away, what will happen to all the notes? Will they change immediately or will they still be legal tender?

answers.answer: They'll still be legal tender. The new notes would have the new monarch on it, and the old stuff stays in circulation. The logistical requirements of taking everything with the Queen's head out of circulation doesn't merit contemplation - it would be far too huge. Old coins with previous monarchs were still legal tender in the 1960s.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'the world is your oyster' originate from?

answers.answer: It's from The Merry Wives of Windsor by Shakespeare. The problem with Shakespeare's coinages is you don't know whether he invented it, was just the first to write it down, or wasn't even the first but he's the only one who survived. The theory is he invented it because people who were first to write it down were going to use violent means to gain fortune. The violence is opening up the oyster and the fortune is the pearl.

questions.question: What causes bags under the eyes?

answers.answer: Several reasons: One is fluid build-up due to food intolerances (like wheat causing puffiness). Also, if you put skincare products like moisturizer or eye cream too close to the eye (especially with high oil content), it can cause puffy reactions. The skin around the eye is five times thinner than skin on the face, so you need less cream. It acts like blotting paper and draws product up, which can cause puffiness. Dark circles are something completely different.

questions.question: I was watching The Mohicans and they kissed - was that disgusting? What did they use before toothpaste? How did they manage personal hygiene?

answers.answer: If everybody stank, you wouldn't notice, so you could snog away to your heart's content because your breath would be just as rancid as theirs. They'd cancel each other out. They used just cloths and implements without having an actual paste, but they used salt and, oddly, charcoal, I think. Anything that could be an abrasive, you could use as a toothpaste.

questions.question: Why do the three most famous British nursery rhymes all have the same tune? ABC song, Baa Baa Black Sheep, and Twinkle Twinkle Little Star - and what came first?

answers.answer: The alphabet was set to the tune of a song that kids would recognise. It makes it easier to remember if you've just got a nice, memorable tune. And it's such a lovely tune that it's not that surprising that two different sets of words have been applied to it.

Twinkle Twinkle Little Star is a Mozart song. It's the opening bars of Eine Kleine Nachtmusik. The tune was French folk song even before Mozart arranged it. A clever teacher decided to put the alphabet to the tune of Twinkle Twinkle Little Star so that children would remember it better.

questions.question: Where does the term whistleblower come from? Was it the police or a safety thing in factories?

answers.answer: Deadline was from a prison system - there was a line around the prison that was literally the deadline that you'd get shot if you went past.
Whistleblower originates from the Victorian Royal Navy. The bosun's whistle was used to whistle orders around ships, including the captain's rounds.

Whistleblowing actually comes from 19th century police officers who used to run down the street blowing their whistles to notify the public that there was a criminal on the run. Ralph Nadar in the US coined the modern phrase in the 1960s and 70s from referees, which is probably why your last call thought it was to do with referees. Over the last 50 years it's actually been high-profile and been hyphenated and then converted into a word.

questions.question: If you get stung by a stinging nettle, you can always find a dock leaf nearby. How is that? Why would dock leaves and stinging nettles be in close proximity to each other?

answers.answer: That's the one. I love it, mate. I like that question. I'm amazed we haven't done it before. Explain the botanical explanation. I want to get botanical on this one.

It's basically just location. They like similar conditions, and that's why they're really close together. They self-seed really, really readily. They get into every nook and cranny. Dock leaves aren't specifically healing for stings - they're both quite acidic. The only reason why dock leaves help is it's the nearby leaf that you can use that isn't an irritant. It's cooling. The big leaf that's going to be near the nettles is cooling and removes the little hairs from your skin. You could do that with anything, but they're quite big and they're nearby.

questions.question: Why do we all use the same numbers? How did that come about? Chinese people don't use the same numbers as us, do they?

answers.answer: Trade is probably the answer. I can learn your language and we can coexist. So I can do trade with you verbally, even though we've raised possibly using different alphabets and different languages. But once we're paying each other for stuff, we have to have an agreed language, numerical language. It will be to do with trade and communication between different civilizations that had different languages and different alphabets. Because they were buying and selling each other stuff, they had to agree on numbers at some point. So it became like a lingua franca of international trade.

The Indians came up with it, and the Arabs adopted it. There's a logic behind it. If you look at the numbers, number one is just a straight line, one angle. You write number two in a certain way, two angles, three has three angles, and so on. It's the way the original sort of way it was drawn or written. And it spread around the world because of trade. Hindu-Arabic is the technical term of the numerical system. It spread through Baghdad in the 500, 600, 700s.

questions.question: Who invented the high five? Why would you randomly think to slap your palm against someone else's palm to congratulate them?

answers.answer: Probably sport, isn't it? It must be sport somewhere. It's probably baseball because they wear those big gloves. Because in baseball, they were wearing enormous gloves, they'd do a high-five with each other to avoid unseemly glove contact.

Although it is disputed, the high-five was invented by a baseball player called Glenn Burke. It was just a moment of exuberance. Glenn Burke was one of the first openly gay sportsmen in baseball. He came out in 1980. At the same time he was driven out of the game.

questions.question: If my six-year-old child fell off a high building, and I immediately jumped off after them - because I'm heavier, I would fall faster and could catch them. Then just before hitting the ground, if I threw him upwards, would that save him? Would I need to sacrifice myself?

answers.answer: Theoretically, you might be onto something, but whether, that's why I asked about your superpowers. I wouldn't want you to do it because I think in reality you wouldn't be able to undertake that manoeuvre.

Falling doesn't depend on mass - it all depends on air resistance. If Carlos is heavier and probably bigger than his six-year-old son, air resistance is likely to have a bigger effect. So he's going to fall slower actually. If they fall off together with the son in his arms and he keeps holding his son, they land at the same time because you could model Carlos and his son as being the same object. If he threw his son in the air just before impact, the reaction force back on Carlos would be stronger, so his son would feel less force because he would have been thrown up. If he landed on the corpse of Carlos, he would have absorbed less force because he wouldn't have been falling as far. In theory depending on when he threw the kid back up the kid might not actually be falling that far. In laboratory conditions you probably could save the child's life.

questions.question: Why do the clocks go back six weeks before the winter solstice, but go forward ten weeks after? Who picked the specific days on which clocks change?

answers.answer: I don't know. It could be Scottish hill farmers. I'll see if I can find out. Why do the clocks go back on the days that they do and indeed forward?

questions.question: Why are there only four different types of naturally coloured hair - brunette, blonde, ginger, and grey? Why can we never be born with green hair?

answers.answer: It's because it's genes. In your genetic cupboard, there are only the colors that you've described. There was no evolutionary advantage to having purple hair. We all originally would have been dark - every human being has their roots in Africa. As we progressed north, the melanin in our skin became less important because we're not going to burn the further north we go. So the paler we get. And the same thing happened to our hair. Gingers are a bit of an anomaly - they don't really fit into my theory.

questions.question: Were silent films silent by choice or were they unable to have sound? Did we manage to record pictures before we recorded sound?

answers.answer: I think it would have been too difficult to have a soundtrack running alongside. To get it bang on, it would have looked like an old Bruce Lee movie all the time. Recording video is harder than sound. Sound was recorded on discs originally, and you'd have had to change the record 100 times in the course of a film.

Photography was invented a long time after photography. Sound came in around 1920. The first problem was how do you record it? They already had the technology to take photographs - a film is just lots and lots of photographs. The second problem was how do you play it back? Playback of recorded sound was originally purely acoustic from cylinders and very early record players. It wasn't until magnetic tape was invented, which allowed recording to be put alongside the celluloid of the film, and you had electronic playback. You had to have all of those in order to be able to record and playback synchronized audio with the film to an audience.

questions.question: Where does the saying 'As happy as Larry' come from?

answers.answer: Larry Grayson was always very cheerful on the telly when we were growing up, but I think that the phrase was already in common parlance before Larry Grayson got the Generation Game gig

It comes from Lawrence Larry Foley, an Australian boxer who lived in Sydney. He was part of a gang called the Rocks Pushers, was a boxer, won a prize and $150,000. It was a headline in the 1890s - 'happy as Larry' after he won. He died in 1917.

questions.question: Why are some beaches sandy and some stony?

answers.answer: I don't know why some are sandy and some are stony

answers.caller: Ed (Plymouth) - civil and coastal engineering student
answers.answer: It's dependent on the strength of the waves and the profile of the beach. High-energy waves with a steep profile beach means less force spread over the beach, making a pebble beach. A flat profile beach with high-energy waves spreads the energy, making a sandy beach. Every beach would be sandy if it had the right waves.

questions.question: Why do we get a different, deeper and crisper tan abroad than we do in the UK?

answers.answer: I don't think it's true, but I'm not going to mock you in case I end up making an idiot of myself again

Skin colour is produced by melanin - skin pigment. Your skin colour is dictated by the amount of melanin and cells that produce it. When you increase UV light, you oxidise the melanin which gives an instant darker colour. It's all about the UV light - the closer you are to the equator, the more UV light passes through the thinner atmosphere, triggering a greater melanin response.

The amount of UV passing through the atmosphere depends on variables including thickness of atmosphere and location. So yes, you would tan differently but not more strongly - if you were exposed to the same amount of UV in a different place, you'd go the same colour.

questions.question: When does a pond become a lake?

answers.answer: I don't know. Is a lake naturally occurring and a pond is dug out? Or does a lake get fed by a river?
A pond is made where a spring comes up. A lake is a body of water fed by a river or stream. It's not about size - a very big pond would technically remain a pond even if we called it a lake.

questions.question: Can the Queen be prosecuted for crimes? Who would prosecute her if it would be the Crown versus the Crown?

answers.answer: I honestly don't know and it's something that does puzzle me

answers.caller: Andy (Milton Keynes) - law degree and 17.5 years in police
answers.answer: She can't be prosecuted because she's the prosecuting authority and is above the law. Even if she murdered someone, can't do anything about it.

questions.question: Why do people stick their tongue out when they're concentrating?

answers.answer: It focuses your mind and stops you from shaking, but I can't get the proper answer

answers.caller: Gemma (New York) - speech and language therapist
answers.answer: You stick your tongue out to keep your head as rigid as possible to minimise movement. That way your vision stays solid and your concentration improves. Your brain is mapped to your tongue - it's like a huge amount of data your brain is constantly dealing with, and when you cut down on that movement, you can increase concentration. Michael Jordan used to do it when concentrating.

questions.question: When we sneeze, what do we shout? Who first thought of 'achoo'?

answers.answer: The noise came before the word. Someone just wrote down the sound when someone sneezed. It's like 'cock-a-doodle-doo' - they just wrote down what it sounded like. You couldn't make a different noise naturally.

questions.question: Where and when was the very first embassy?

answers.answer: I love that question but I don't know the answer

The first embassies were in the 13th century in Northern Italy. Milan was one of the first - city-states sending embassies to each other. Before the 13th century in Greek and Roman times, countries sent representatives but didn't have embassies as such.

questions.question: Why do humans learn in threes?

answers.answer: I don't understand the premise of the question. Are you sure we learn in threes? I don't know why it is. It's a rhetorical device from ancient Greeks but that's more about public speaking than learning. I'll put it on the board.

It's called Pavlov's Count - it's about the way our brain is wired. If you go one, two, three, by the third you've tuned into someone's timing. In boxing, if I throw a jab then a cross, by the time I throw the third punch you've tuned into my timing and I'll never miss. In guitar, when you start a song you go one, two, three, and by three you're all tuned in.

questions.question: Do animals get hay fever?

answers.answer: Yes, dogs and cats definitely get hay fever. People have rung in before with dogs and cats that had hay fever. I don't know about farm animals like sheep and cows.

questions.question: What was the first movie sequel?

answers.answer: I don't know. Could be Amityville Horror or Jaws from the 70s/80s. High Society was a follow-on from Philadelphia Story but that was a remake not a sequel. Godfather Part II? Star Wars had Empire Strikes Back. James Bond films are separate self-contained stories with no narrative arc. I'll come back to that on another occasion.

questions.question: Why do we call the wheel in the middle of a table a lazy Susan? Who's Susie? And why is she lazy?

answers.answer: Thomas Jefferson invented the lazy Susan. He had five or six kids and the youngest one was always complaining that her food was getting cold. He built the rotating tray so she could reach everything without asking for help.

Traditionally, Susan is a generic name for a servant. The term comes from servant names like Susan Nipper in Dickens' Dombey and Son. It's called lazy because a servant doesn't have to be there - the lazy Susan does the serving work for you.

questions.question: Why are some people ticklish and others aren't? Is anyone completely unticklish?

answers.answer: He did yoga for many years and when anyone tries to tickle him, he just relaxes his body totally, so he's not ticklish.

questions.question: How can a baby have a different blood type to their mother when they were sharing blood during pregnancy?

answers.answer: The placenta acts as a filter. Oxygen, nutrients and antibodies pass through from mum to baby, but the baby's blood and mum's blood remain quite separate. The baby's blood type is determined by the genetics of both parents, not just the mother.

questions.question: People say it takes three hours at the gym to burn off a Mars bar. How many hours of doing Sudoku would do the same? Does your brain use more calories when you're thinking hard?

answers.answer: The brain uses about 40% of calories even when you're sleeping. However, the quality of calories matters - what goes in isn't the same as what goes out. Thinking harder (Sudoku vs watching Love Island) doesn't use significantly more calories.

questions.question: If a meteorite was heading for Earth like in Armageddon, just big enough to have catastrophic global effect, how much notice would we actually get?

answers.answer: All telescopes only look at a few percent of the sky. If we don't see it coming, it could hit us. We might only get warning when it's as far out as Mars - maybe two to three weeks.

questions.question: Why does putting an apple next to a banana keep the bananas fresh? Does this also work for avocados?

answers.answer: Plants produce a hormone called ethylene which ripens fruit. A ripening banana gives off ethylene gas, which actually speeds up ripening of nearby fruit (including apples) rather than keeping them fresh. To use this effect, put a ripening banana in a brown paper bag with unripe fruit like a hard pear.

questions.question: Why don't we talk louder when we've had alcohol? Is it just inhibitions going or something separate?

answers.caller: Ed (In St Albans, actually in Majorca)
answers.answer: When you drink alcohol, the auditory nerve shrinks. That's what transfers sound information from the cochlea to your brain. So you can't hear yourself as well, which is why you talk more loudly - not because of inhibitions.

questions.question: Why is the majority of the population right-handed? Is it something we're biologically predisposed to, or is it taught?

answers.answer: There are genetic links that give preference for left-handedness, but it's not predictable like eye colour. Evolutionary argument: on Stone Age implements, hand preference was divided fairly equally, but more sophisticated tools made consistent handedness an advantage - you didn't need to make two versions of everything. Theories include sun worship (moving left to right in Northern Hemisphere), heart position requiring shield in left hand, but nothing definitive.

questions.question: When you buy a house and garden, how much ground do you own beneath it? Is it three foot, six foot? Do we own down to the centre of the Earth?

answers.answer: His sister was paid when the Channel Tunnel was built under Bluebell Hill - they purchased the land underneath. Some people directly beneath the tunnel route got paid, others didn't. It was about property ownership, not just compensation for disruption.

In property law, whoever owns the soil holds title all the way up to the heavens and down to the depths of hell. However, if they found oil under your house, you wouldn't be allowed to keep it - the Crown owns mineral rights. If someone needs to drill through your property, they have to pay you for the rights.

questions.question: Has anybody ever had a star taken away from them on the Hollywood Walk of Fame?
Do snipers take the curvature of the Earth into consideration?

answers.answer: The book is Jack Reacher, who would crush you. Not definitive - might get someone who does long-distance shooting.

questions.question: Why does mint make you feel coldness when you blow on it?
Why is it called 'thin air'? What's the origin of the phrase 'vanish into thin air'?

answers.answer: If it was thick air, like cloudy, you could understand someone disappearing. But that's not definitive.

questions.question: ANSWER to sniper question

answers.answer: It's the rotation of the Earth they take into account, not the curvature. It's the Coriolis effect. The target moves while the projectile is in the air. If the record is two miles, it will have an effect. They aim slightly higher. Professional snipers have spotters who do calculations for them.

questions.question: What's the maximum number of pixels a TV can have where the human eye would no longer notice the difference?
Why do vans have a sign on the back saying they're limited to 70mph when the speed limit everywhere is 70mph anyway?

answers.answer: Company vans saying they're community-minded and safe, even if their drivers wanted to speed they can't go over 70. It's their way of showing they're safe and responsible.

questions.question: Do flies sweat?

answers.answer: Flies can't sweat because if they got soggy wings they'd fall out of the sky. They don't sweat. I'm not sure how they lose heat though.

questions.question: ANSWER - Why does mint make you cold?

answers.answer: Mint contains menthol, a cooling ingredient used in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics. When menthol is on your skin, it evaporates and draws heat from your skin, making it feel colder. Blowing on it makes you notice it even more.

questions.question: Why do people say 'and I turned around and said to him'? Why would you start a conversation with your back turned?

answers.answer: Possibly from heated arguments where you're walking away from someone and then you turn around to put them in their place. Also possibly related to taxi drivers. Not definitive.

questions.question: Do E numbers have an adverse effect on children's behaviour?

answers.answer: Some E numbers are harmful, some aren't. If they do have an effect, it's simply because they're chemicals and chemicals have effects on us. Not sure of the link or why it's more prevalent in children.

questions.question: Why do we get earwax? What's the purpose? Why don't we get it in our noses or other body parts?

answers.answer: Earwax cleans your ears. It's produced inside your body and comes out to clean your ears. Like oil. Though it wasn't entirely clear this was definitive.

questions.question: ANSWER - Why do we say 'I turned around and said to him'?

answers.answer: It's historical and to do with infectious disease. In medieval plague times, people would hold conversations deliberately facing away from each other because they knew disease was transmitted from human to human. They didn't know how, so they faced away. Then to make a final emphatic point, they would turn around and say...

questions.question: ANSWER - Challenging the menthol/mint answer

answers.answer: Cameron's answer was completely wrong. Evaporation only applies to liquids. Menthol is a solid. What menthol does is the opposite of chillies - it makes your thermoregulatory nerves less sensitive to heat, so you feel cold. Chillies work the opposite way, making nerves more sensitive to heat. It's about sensory nerves, not evaporation.
Earwax actually catches bits of dust and dirt. It acts like flypaper in your ear. It stops insects from living there too.

questions.question: ANSWER - TV pixel question

answers.answer: 4K is Ultra HD at 3,840 pixels across by 2,160 down. 8K is coming (7,680 by 4,320). He's seen 8K run and you really cannot tell the difference between real life and looking at the TV. You can tell the difference between 8K and 4K though - huge difference. 8K will be the maximum because you have to double up on pixels. The human eye won't be able to see any difference beyond that. He works for LG as a brand ambassador teaching people how to use and sell TVs.

questions.question: Using modern science, how close could you get to estimating someone's exact date of birth (not just age) if they couldn't tell you?
ANSWER - Origin of 'thin air' phrase

answers.answer: It originally comes from a Shakespeare play - he invented it, probably. Shakespeare made up many phrases and proverbs. In one fell swoop, budge an inch - these all go back to him. Either he made it up or his is the text that survived and is the first time it was written down. Regarding why 'thin air' specifically - it could be to do with air pressure or just the idea that thin air is really clear air, making someone disappear more completely.

questions.question: ANSWER - Do flies sweat?

answers.answer: Flies do not sweat because they've got to have skin to sweat, and flies have an exoskeleton, not skin. To have sweat glands you have to have skin. Some animals sweat but not many - cats and dogs only sweat where their skin is not covered by fur, through their paws. Qualifications: teacher of pottery and sailing instructor, always been interested in nature.

questions.question: ANSWER - Why do vans have 70mph signs?

answers.answer: Vans are limited to 70 on motorways but on dual carriageways vans can only do 60 (unlike cars which can do 70). There's a compliance issue in the van and logistics industry - they make it clear they can only do 70 to avoid frustration. Vehicles over 3.5 tonne on tachograph are regulated to 56mph. Also car-derived vans (Corsa van, Fiesta van) can do 70 on dual carriageways but larger vans can't. He's a driver trainer for a logistics company based in Ipswich.

questions.question: ANSWER - Do E numbers have adverse effects on children's behaviour?

answers.answer: The premise of the question is all wrong. All E numbers are a classification of food additives - they might be antioxidants or whatever. Within those there are lots of natural things and some not so natural. E numbers per se are not the problem - it's what sits behind the E number. Saffron is an E-number but it's naturally occurring. E just stands for Europe - in Australia the numbers are the same but there's no E in front. Qualifications: 30 years in the food business messing around with ingredients and putting things on supermarket shelves.

questions.question: Why don't scars on my arms tan even though I get a good tan?

answers.answer: There's no melanin in the scar tissue. If it was just skin, you wouldn't be able to see it next to the other skin. It's going to be something like that.
Scars are fibrous tissue and they can't produce melanin, so because they can't produce melanin, they can't tan.

questions.question: Do scars tan?

answers.answer: My scars do tan. I have skin grafts and they go darker than the rest of my skin.

questions.question: Why do we say 'par avion' on airmail stickers? Why French?

answers.answer: It's the lingua franca of international mail. French is the international language of diplomacy.

Par avion is originally where the airmail system was started by French people from Toulouse. They went along the African coast up to Senegal, and then as far as Brazil. This was the first airmail freight mail, and it became the standard.

questions.question: Where does the term 'silly sausage' come from?
Can you lose a Nobel Peace Prize? If Trump got one and started a war, could he lose it?

answers.answer: Aung San Suu Kyi had a petition to have hers removed over the Rohingya crisis. The head of the Nobel Institute said you can't take a prize away because the will of Alfred Nobel nor the rules of the foundation allow for it. It's never been done and you can't do it.

questions.question: Why is a baby kangaroo called a joey?

answers.answer: It originates from Aboriginal language meaning 'small animal'. Joey is the collective noun for any baby animal in Australia.

questions.question: Why do some daisies turn pink?
Why can't cars be manufactured with speed limiters at 70mph so we never go over the limit?
What are the origins of rock, paper, scissors?
What is the 1% of germs that Domestos doesn't kill?

answers.answer: It's to do with log reduction and the legal way they're tested. The law for cleaning products says they have to meet a three-log reduction, which is 99.9%. They can kill 100% but it would be dangerous to people and would damage surfaces.

questions.question: Why can't we grow blue roses?

answers.answer: There is a blue rose. It's a kind of bluey mauve, genetically modified in Japan or America, introducing a gene from delphiniums. It's sold as a blue rose but it's actually rather revolting looking.
It's called Rhapsody in Blue. It exists and I've got two of them growing in my backyard.

questions.question: Where does the origin of champagne bottle names come from? Why are they called Jeroboam, Methuselah, Nebuchadnezzar?

answers.answer: Champagne was popularized by monks at a monastery. Dom Perignon invented champagne and the abbot decreed that larger bottles should be named after key biblical characters - Jeroboam, Nebuchadnezzar, Methuselah.

questions.question: Why is the air that we breathe out of our nose colder than the air that comes out of our mouth?

answers.answer: Wind chill factor - when you breathe out of your nose, you're breathing harder so more air hits your skin, withdrawing heat faster.
It's about increased velocity. When you breathe out through a smaller hole (nose), the velocity is greater, so the temperature decreases. It follows the equations of fluid hydraulics.

There are three internal structures in your nose called turbinates. Their primary function is to warm the air we inhale. When exhaling, that same air from the lungs is being warmed up by those highly vascularised turbinates.

questions.question: Why are pandas black and white? Ones in the woods are brown. Over in Canada and stuff, polar bears are white. Just wondering why pandas are like that.

answers.answer: It actually is to do with camouflage. They live very high up in the mountains, so the white coloration is quite useful for camouflage. They do get predated on by things like tigers. The dark areas help them be camouflaged in the shades, but they also help with heat conservation. The evolutionary explanation is as it would be with other animals as well. It just promoted survival.

questions.question: Where does the phrase getting off scot-free come from?

answers.answer: Scott Free means tax-free. The Norse word for payment was scop. Scott, S-K-O-T, scop-free. No scop on it. It has evolved from there to mean getting away with it.

questions.question: Is there science behind boiling eggs? When you've boiled an egg, sometimes you peel it and there's a skin membrane inside that comes away easily. Other times it sticks and takes half an hour. Is it something to do with temperature or length of time?

answers.answer: The egg shell is porous. When the egg is fresh, the inside is against the shell. But through time, air gets in through the shell and pushes the egg a little bit more to the inside, so it's easier to peel.

There's a specific timing. In an egg factory making Scotch eggs, they found there's an optimum time to cool eggs before peeling. They don't plunge them into cold water - they leave them for a specific amount of time to cool down, which is the optimum time to peel whether it's five days old, one day old, or two days old. There's actually a sweet spot.

questions.question: Baby boys' clothes used to be pink back in the day - it was a Victorian thing. Why did it switch to girls now wearing pink? When did boys stop wearing pink?

answers.answer: Prior to the mid-late 19th century, there were no blue dyes. The German chemical industry had a big period of invention of different dyes and they became affordable. Someone just decided that boys were probably a member of the royal family or something, and then everybody else copied.

questions.question: Why do we clink glasses?

answers.answer: When you clink glasses, a bit of your drink goes into my drink and a bit of my drink goes into yours, which means we're not trying to poison each other.
Withdrew his earlier answer about pirates and poison - it's an urban myth, confirmed on Snopes.

Medieval times when people used to feud. When they got over their feud, they would drink together and clink with such force that the mead would share over into your neighbour's glass to prove you weren't there to poison them.

From the ancient Greeks - when drinking wine, it was about not leaving any of the senses feeling left out. You had the smell, taste, how it felt, and you wanted to hear it as well. You couldn't leave hearing out. So that was the one sense that had to be excited when drinking wine.

questions.question: On an aeroplane, why is the propeller called a propeller when it sucks and it doesn't blow? It should be an impeller because it sucks air, doesn't it, and pulls the plane forward.

answers.answer: You're looking through the wrong end of the telescope. You're looking at what the propeller does to the air rather than what it does to the plane. It still impels it forwards. It propels the plane. So it's a propeller.

questions.question: Do animals have moles on their skin? I was in the bath and found a mark on my dog which turned out to be a tick. How do I know if it's a mole or something more sinister?

answers.answer: Yes, dogs can get moles just like humans. Most moles on dogs are benign - just a darker patch of pigment. They tend to be flatter and darker. You tend to see more moles on darker-skinned dogs. As with humans, watch out for any changes with moles. Take them to the vet just to get them checked out. 80% will be benign but get them checked out.

questions.question: I've recently had a baby boy. Myself, my wife, and my daughter are all susceptible to hay fever. Do babies get hay fever? If not, at what point are you susceptible to

answers.answer: Hay fever is one of the atopic illnesses which also includes asthma and eczema. It's IgE-mediated - an antibody which our body produces. Babies have IgE passed on to them from their mother. That is attached to their mast cells, which break down when they come into contact with allergens, release histamine, and give you the allergic response.

questions.question: Bees typically fly in a straight line. If a bee flew into my house, my car, and I drove 10 miles and the bees flew out again, would it get lost?

answers.answer: If you move your hive more than three feet or more, the bees will try to go back to the pinpoint where they go entrance into their hive. If your bees are moved more than three miles, they won't go back home. So if a bee flew into your car and you drove ten miles, the bee will be lost. The good thing is the bee has got a life of 600 miles, so the closer he is to the source of his food, the more trips it can make. A lost bee could join another hive but would have to take some food or water as a present to enter. They might still have their queen's scent and the hive might kill them because they can smell a rival.

questions.question: How come when you stand under the shower and the water is cold, falling on your temple, if your mouth is closed, within a short time you begin to be breathless or gasping for air? As soon as you switch it to warm or hot water, it goes straight away. You could close your mouth and breathe freely under the water. What is the explanation?
What is the furthest man-made object from Earth and how far away is it?

answers.answer: Voyager 1. It left the solar system and moved into interstellar space in 2012.
