questions.question: Can you physically feel it when someone is looking at you?

answers.answer: You only register the times when someone IS looking at you. The other times you've looked up and no one was staring at you, you don't register.

There's an experiment called the double slit experiment. It concludes that all matter reacts differently when it's been observed to when it's not observed. If someone's really sensitive, maybe they can pick that up subconsciously.

questions.question: If a person committed a crime, got arrested, and refused to give their identity, what would eventually happen to them? Would they go to court? Could they serve a prison sentence without anyone ever knowing their identity?

answers.answer: I don't know.

They go on all documentation as 'name and address refused' and the system just keeps rolling on. DNA swipes taken, solicitor called. It happens remarkably frequently - drunk people, drugged people, sometimes organized criminals. Most sober up and give their details.

questions.question: Why does the bride always walk on the left-hand side when being walked down the aisle by her father? When did this start?

answers.answer: I don't know. Something to do with religion or the patriarchy maybe.

It's historical due to keeping his sword arm free. As he walks his daughter up the aisle, he needs his sword arm free should anyone object or leap out. The groom walks on the left so he also has his sword arm free.
As it says in the song, 'you have to pass the duchess upon the left-hand side.'

questions.question: Are opticians' charts all the same or do they differ? How do they change them between appointments? Could you memorise them?

answers.answer: I'll find out.

There are different types of charts from different manufacturers. Some are fixed and very old-fashioned. The newer ones are computer screens with remotes where you can randomise the letters quite often during each eye exam. Some practices just leave the old fixed ones up.

questions.question: Why is it that when you lose something, you keep going back to the same place time and time again even though you've already looked there?
Why do you never see any baby pigeons around?

answers.answer: They're all in the nest. They don't fly out of the nest until they look like grown-up pigeons.

questions.question: Are Brachiosaurus, Brontosaurus, and Diplodocus the same dinosaurs or different ones? Could it be a regional naming thing?

answers.answer: They're three different species of dinosaur. The Brachiosaurus has a thicker neck, the Diplodocus has a thinner neck, and the Brontosaurus is a different kettle of fish altogether.

They are all species of sauropods, which is a subset of herbivores, and they are different species. Asking if a brachiosaur is the same as a diplodocus is like asking if a rat is the same as a hamster. All three are distinct.

questions.question: Why do all the moons not rotate whereas the planets do? What stops them moving?

answers.answer: That premise is wrong - planets do rotate and moons are not planets, they orbit planets. The question may not be coherent.

The moon does rotate. The reason it doesn't appear to is that it rotates on its axis at roughly the same duration as it takes to go around the planet. This is called tidal locking or synchronous rotation - about 27 days for our moon.

questions.question: Why does a skin form on the top of certain liquid food items like gravy and custard?

answers.answer: Is it gelatine? Gelatine comes from bones.

There are two effects. Gravy, custard, milk are all colloids - droplets of fat suspended in water that never settle out. When you heat them up, the water near the top evaporates making it fattier. Also, proteins denature when heated - they change properties and become insoluble, rise to the top and make a skin.

questions.question: What's the door between number 10 and number 11 Downing Street?

answers.answer: I don't know but I will find out, mentioning Theo Usherwood should know
It's just part of Number 10, an extra door. They joined two houses together. Qualification: his girlfriend's mum is a cleaner at Downing Street

questions.question: If humans go really deep under the sea, they'll get crushed by the pressure. Why is it that deep-sea creatures don't get crushed by the same pressure?

answers.answer: It's about anatomy, different stuff, probably because we're full of air

Sea creatures are predominantly made of liquid, and liquids are incompressible at those pressures. Humans have air cavities (lungs) that get compressed. Jellyfish or tuna would be good examples. Qualification: PADI dive master

questions.question: Is there a correct way of saying H or H? Her son says 'haitch' and she says 'aitch'. The headmaster said it depends where you come from.

answers.answer: It's 'aitch'. The letter H begins with an A, it is A-I-T-C-H. 'Haitch' is an abomination. The world is full of ignoramuses. Look it up in a dictionary
Confirmed definitively it's H, not H. From Twitter correspondent who is a published author

questions.question: Why do pigs get sunburned?

answers.answer: I'll find out from a proper pig farmer. I want a proper answer

Yes, they do get sunburned. His sister owns Exmoor Zoo and she has put sun cream on the pigs to avoid sunburn. She's been in the national press for it. Two Vietnamese pot-bellied pigs. Qualification: my sister owns a zoo

questions.question: How deep is the desert? How far beneath the sand is there something solid?

answers.answer: I'll find out the average depth with the knowledge that when it's much deeper than average, that's when quicksand occurs

Antarctica is the deepest desert at roughly 2.1 kilometres deep (the ice). Deserts are defined by precipitation (less than 250mm annually). Sandy deserts like the Sahara are difficult to measure because aeolian environments are constantly shifting with wind. Qualification: PhD student in environmental science specializing in glacial environments

questions.question: Why do I get ear infections on holiday every time I go swimming in chlorinated pools? If chlorine is a cleaner, why am I getting infections from swimming in effectively pool soap?

answers.answer: You can buy spray or plugs for your ears. You'll have to pay for antibiotics otherwise

The chlorine keeps the water clean, but any dirt associated with people who haven't showered before getting in reacts to the chlorine and sits above the layer of water on the pool. That's also what gives people the stinging eye sensation. The infections come from the dirt staying at the surface. Qualification: former lifeguard and pool plant trained

questions.question: In Home Alone, in the scene where Michael Colton is in the kitchen eating pizza with a movie playing in the background, what's the name of that movie with the phrase 'keep your change, filthy animal'?

answers.answer: I'm pretty sure it's Jimmy Cagney, which means it would be a real film. You're on

The movie does not exist. It's a parody called 'Angels with Filthy Souls' made just for Home Alone. In Home Alone 2 they made 'Angels with Filthy Souls 2' as well. Qualification: comedian and magician, sees a movie nearly every day, seen Home Alone a billion times

questions.question: Why is it harder to open a freezer door the second time round? You open it, take something out, shut it, then try to open it again and it's almost impossible.

answers.answer: I'll find out by one o'clock or I'll give you the money myself

When you open the freezer door, cold air quickly comes out replaced by warm air. You close the door and that warm air condenses very quickly, creating a vacuum until it pressurizes. So the door is stuck to the seal. Qualification: studied refrigeration engineering about 20 years ago

questions.question: Why can't you make gravy with cold water? He tried using cold water with gravy granules and they didn't do anything, just sat there.

answers.answer: It's got fat in it, hasn't it? That might explain why it congeals as it gets colder. But I'm not taking that answer seriously

It's about starch, not fat. You need boiling water to break open the starch molecules to thicken the gravy. Cold water won't dissolve the granules properly and won't blow the starch open so you'll end up with thin gruel. He makes gravy from scratch with stock. Qualification: hotel and catering management, owns Whittington's Tea Barge in Reading

questions.question: Why are bath and basin overflow holes completely inadequate? If you leave a tap running, it overflows far too quickly to save you from damage.

answers.answer: If it was more efficient, taps could run forever and waste water indefinitely. The overflow gives you a window of grace to realize and turn off the tap. It won't stop overflow entirely but it gives you time to intervene

It's a misconception that it's an overflow. It's actually there to remove displacement - when you put your hands in the basin, the water level rises and the hole takes away that excess water. It's not designed to deal with taps overrunning. This corrects the premise of the question.

questions.question: Where does the term 'dole office' come from? Why do people say 'I'm on the dole'?

answers.answer: Department of Labour and Employment? I'm not sure if that's right. I'll leave it on the board

Dole is derived from a German word meaning 'to share'. You 'dole something out' - you're sharing it out. Has nothing to do with the Department of Labour. Qualification: plays a lot of Scrabble and was challenged by someone who said it was an acronym but turned out to be wrong

questions.question: Why is tinfoil shiny on one side but matte on the other?

answers.answer: It's the manufacturing process. Just like when melted chocolate is poured on a glass chopping board - the side touching the glass becomes smooth and shiny while the top goes matte when exposed to air. The same happens with molten aluminium during manufacturing.

When tinfoil is produced, the aluminium is rolled between consecutive narrower rollers. When it gets to its thinnest required thickness, the foil doubles over so it doesn't tear and the rollers don't need to be so accurate. The dull side is the inside of that doubled-over foil where it's been backed onto itself, and the shiny side is where it's been against the roller.

questions.question: If you woke up five light years away from Earth and had a telescope powerful enough to see Earth, would you be seeing Earth from five years ago?

answers.answer: Yes. The speed of light is 186,000 miles per second in a vacuum. Space is a vacuum, so when you're looking through a telescope at an object, the further away it is, the longer the delay. Stars billions of miles away show light that happened millions of years ago.

A light year is exactly what it says - the distance light travels at the speed of light in one year. You will only see light that's X years old. If you're looking at the moon, which is closer than a light year, you can't see what happened last week. Light takes finite time to travel.
Confirmed Jesse's answer was correct. The sun's light left 8 minutes ago. If someone was at Proxima Centauri (the closest star other than our sun, 4 light years away), they would see you 4 years ago.

questions.question: Why do newsreaders and weather presenters talk in a different way than normal conversation? Is there some sort of course that's taught?

answers.answer: I think it's just the difference between reading and talking. When I'm doing autocue, I try to make it sound natural and my voice changes immediately. It's not necessarily something that's taught.

When you read something, you're quoting someone else's writing and stuff you're not too familiar with. When you speak from your mind, it's different - it's coming from a different place. I did a course in radio speaking with someone named Geller from America who taught talk show hosts to speak conversationally, like ordering a drink at a bar.

questions.question: Why are beef burgers sometimes in the UK known as hamburgers?

answers.answer: Because they hail from Hamburg. The hamburger (minced meat in a patty) was probably first done in the German city of Hamburg and got exported from there. They wouldn't call it 'ham' in Germany though. Doner kebabs also come from Germany, oddly enough.

questions.question: How does city twinning work? Do councils just pick a town? Will Brexit affect twinnings?

answers.answer: Councils just hook up together - it's a bit like Tinder but for towns. Both sides have to agree to be twinned. If you go to the twinned town, you'll see a sign saying 'Twinned with [your town]'. Example: Kidderminster is twinned with Huesum (H-U-S-U-M) in Schleswig-Holstein, Germany. In my experience, it's often an excuse for councillors to go on jollies in both directions.

questions.question: Why is the snooze function on alarm clocks nine minutes?
Why is the snooze function on all timing devices limited to nine minutes?

answers.answer: Back in the day when clock radios had mechanical clocks, there was a limit to the size of cogs that would still mesh with other cogs. The options were about just over nine minutes or just over ten minutes. They thought ten minutes was too long to sleep, so they went with nine to fit the existing case size. We've kept it as tradition even with digital devices.

questions.question: Is it grammatically wrong to put a lowercase 'i' in the middle of a sentence? My son puts small 'i's and gets it wrong at school but I was always told never to put a capital letter in the middle of a sentence.

answers.answer: It's grammatically wrong NOT to put a capital 'I' in the middle of a sentence - 'I' is always capital. The teachers weren't saying you can't put an 'I' in the middle of a sentence; they were saying you can't put capital letters in the middle of words.

In medieval times, all writing was squashed together and hard to read. Lowercase 'i' blended in with other words and was very difficult to spot. Since 'I' is a personal pronoun representing a person, it needed to stand out and became capitalised. I heard this on The History of English podcast.

questions.question: Why don't you ever see a seagull in a tree?

answers.answer: Seagulls live on cliffs and try to replicate that environment when settling down - they'll stop on buildings or cliff-like structures rather than trees. Their feet are more like ducks - flat paddles designed for paddling on water. A paddle would be useless for gripping tree branches, unlike a sparrow's feet which have knuckles enabling them to grip twigs.

questions.question: How do fireworks create heart shapes or precision patterns in the sky?

answers.answer: Magic, mate.

The burst originates as a sphere with shapes inside. Stars (small balls of composition that burn in different colors) are carefully assembled by hand inside the firework in a pattern. When it explodes, the pattern shows. The larger the sphere, the more accurate the pattern.

questions.question: Why can't we farm expensive truffles like we can with mushrooms?

answers.answer: Nobody knows why truffles form where they form. Even Duke of Edinburgh tried to plant trees but it doesn't happen.
Steward's inquiry - the first UK truffle was cultivated in Leicestershire by someone who appeared on Dragon's Den. He harvested a 39-gram truffle in 2015. It HAS been done. The Dragons did invest.

questions.question: What's the most number of blue plaques on a single house?

answers.answer: I'm an anorak about blue plaques. There's a street near Russell Square with 6-7 plaques but not on one house. There's a street with Van Gogh and David Garrick plaques. There's a street with Mozart plaques. I don't know the definitive answer.
Two is the maximum.

questions.question: Do women suffer from midlife crisis?

answers.answer: Yes, women can have midlife crises. It's not medically recognized but behavioral changes happen.

Yes, I had one. It started when I wanted to go to France after Charlie Hebdo, my husband said no, and that kicked it off. I went to France for 4 weeks to help a friend with her B&B to sort my head out. It coincided with menopause.

questions.question: Who decided on the symbols for TV remotes (standby, pause, fast forward, rewind) and how did they become standardized?

answers.answer: Interesting question, I don't know.

Binary code - the standby is a mix of on and off signals. Whoever got first to market with a remote control (probably VHS video) set the standard that others copied. Fast forward uses arrows and double arrows for direction and skip.

questions.question: When surfaces get wet, why do they go darker in color?

answers.answer: Something to do with light - less light passes through or reflects.

Water on a surface traps light between the water layer and the surface, reflecting less light. For porous materials like clothes, water is absorbed and absorbs more light than it reflects, so it looks darker.

questions.question: Why are you allowed two serves in tennis but in table tennis and badminton you only get one?

answers.answer: To improve game quality so people try for amazing serves. If you only had one serve, you wouldn't try for aces.

Players try to serve a smash (hard one) on first serve which is difficult to control accuracy. Having a second serve allows control and makes the game more exciting. He's a former table tennis player.

questions.question: Why is stainless steel called stainless if it does stain?

answers.answer: It's about rust/corrosion resistance not actual staining. Stainless steel refers to not rusting.
Stainless steel is stain-resistant but WILL rust. Even 316 marine stainless steel can rust. James was wrong.

questions.question: Is there a link between having a musician's ear and the ability to learn languages and acquire accents accurately?

answers.answer: Might just be about how you learn the language rather than music. My Greek (learned by osmosis) is good, my French (learned in school with bad accents) was bad. It's about immersion and how you learn, not necessarily music.

questions.question: Why is it that when you mix two different alcoholic drinks, you get drunk quicker than just having the whiskey on its own or the beer on its own?

answers.answer: Yes, mixing drinks does increase intoxication speed. Alcohol is absorbed in the stomach, not the small intestine. Strong drinks like whiskey at 40% inhibit their own uptake - you won't feel intoxicated quickly. Weak drinks also don't absorb well. When you mix 40% whiskey with 4% beer, you get a resultant solution of 15-20%, which is the optimum level to get drunk. Port or sherry are the best drinks if you want to get drunk quickly. The stomach cells stop absorbing high concentrations, and only when diluted with water or beer does the concentration drop enough for absorption to resume.

questions.question: Is it possible to cry? I mean, really sob without emitting any tears?

Where do nuggets of gold come from? As in, they're created in supernova explosions, but how do they collect together to be nuggets of gold? Why don't they just stay as tiny particles spread throughout everything?

answers.answer: Originally gold is formed in veins, usually quartz veins, and it occurs in the veins in thin flakes. The larger thin flakes, as they're eroded out of the quartz vein, don't dissolve in water but get washed down the river with the quartz. The quartz breaks up into sand, but because gold is soft and malleable, instead of breaking up, it rolls itself up into a ball - like foil being squished. Then they get deposited in stream beds, usually on river bends, where they settle out. That's where you pan for gold. This applies particularly to gold because of its very soft nature and because it doesn't dissolve in water.

questions.question: If I was to get in my time machine, how far back in England or Great Britain could I go where people would understand me?

answers.answer: You can read the King James Bible with virtually no problem. Originally written 80% by William Tyndall 100 years earlier. Chaucer is 14th century - can read with difficulty. So broadly say 13th century for modern English. Even plebs were speaking English in the fields before that. King Alfred would have spoken Anglo-Saxon, a cross between German and Danish. Before the Vikings arrived, people west of the line (where Saxons were halted after Battle of Mount Badon around AD 500) would have spoken Welsh, more akin to Celtic. So it's all about that timeline - from Chaucer 14th century, back through Anglo-Saxon/Germanic/Danish, to Celtic/Welsh before that.

questions.question: I'm wondering what a male ballerina is called.

answers.answer: A male ballerina is a ballerino. It was a term which was first used in Italy, but it was dropped because the ballerino was deemed to be the star and ballerinas didn't like the fact that they didn't have their name, so the ballerino was dropped and the ballerinas took over.

questions.question: Why are clouds different colours? You get dark grey rainy clouds, or big white fluffy ones where it never rains.

answers.answer: It's the thickness. The thicker they are, the less light they'll emit, making them rainy grey clouds. If they're thin and wispy, lots of light comes through.

Clouds themselves don't glow - they only have colour from reflected light. Grey clouds are when there's not much light around, they're covering a lot of sky, very low down, or behind hills. In the evening when light goes through a lot of atmosphere and it's reddish, you get pink clouds. The orangey-green clouds last year were caused by fine dust from the Sahara reflecting light. When two clouds in the same sky are different colours, it's because they're picking up different lights - like a sunbeam through a hole making surrounding clouds brilliant white.

questions.question: Why does Grey's End pop up in the weather report so much? My cousin lives there and I often hear it's the hottest place in the country.

answers.answer: Gravesend will actually probably be the hottest place in the UK quite regularly. Gravesend has very sandy soil, so when the sun's out, the whole area heats up very quickly. My dad worked at the Met Office and confirmed that places with sandy soil heat up and cool down very quickly, giving them a much better chance of being the hottest place in the UK.

questions.question: Balloons. Why do we use balloons to celebrate with? I can't get my head around that.

answers.answer: Balloons first came in fashion with jesters way back in the Dark Ages for amusement. One of their tricks was to walk around with an inflated pig's bladder on the end of a stick. They'd go around tapping people on the head - something you could hit someone quite hard with without hurting them, which fits perfectly into a jester's modus operandi. As the jester evolved, the fool was the only person in court allowed to mock the monarch. The bladder became associated with fun and frolics, and then when latex came along, it became part of celebrations.

questions.question: On coins, the Queen faces to the right, but when I've looked at older coins I found in the shed, the monarch is facing to the left. Is this because she's a woman? I found a Victorian penny facing left too. Why does the Queen face right?

answers.answer: It's a tradition over hundreds and hundreds of years. The only one who broke the mould was Edward VIII because he didn't like his left profile, so he went on for his right profile. So it goes left, right, left, right, alternate monarchs. Edward VIII never got crowned but they did knock out some experimental coinage before he abdicated. He broke the mould due to vanity.

questions.question: Are saloon bar swing doors in Westerns real? If so, how do you secure the premises at night?

answers.answer: Swing doors were almost certainly not real. The Wild Bill Hickok was killed in The Gem pub in Deadwood which had regular doors. Swing doors were probably invented by film directors for dramatic effect. Very small bars might have had them, but big saloons almost certainly not.

questions.question: Where does the word 'gig' come from?

answers.answer: 1920s jazz terminology. It comes from the word 'engagement' - jazz musicians used their own lingo and called an engagement a gig.

questions.question: Who decides whether a word is feminine or masculine in foreign languages like French, Spanish, German? And are they the same in other languages?

answers.answer: It depends on the origin of the language. Latin has masculine, feminine, and neuter. Generally nouns that are feminine end with an E in French and A in Spanish, masculine elsewhere. But the very beginnings of why words got genders eludes us - nobody decides, it just happens through pronunciation and the way people have said things over the years.

questions.question: Why does the internet slow down when it rains?

answers.answer: The underground cable selects fine moisture in the air, and water acts as resistance on the copper cable, causing the slowdown.
When it's raining heavily, more people are at home using the internet, so it slows down.

questions.question: When you have a fever and your temperature shoots up, why do you feel cold and shiver?

answers.answer: You were radiating heat outwards, which left you cold inwards.

questions.question: What are moles (on skin) and why do we have them?

answers.answer: Melocytes (skin cells that determine skin color) cluster in one part of the body through accident of nature. They usually cluster in specific areas like backs and shoulders.

questions.question: How do apprentice tattooists learn without making permanent mistakes?

answers.answer: They practice on dead pig skin. When ready to pierce real skin with a tattoo needle, it's on a pig carcass first. Synthetic skin is now used for vegan tattooists.

questions.question: Why do UK bathrooms have European sockets/shavers with two prongs? Can you plug UK shavers into French walls?

answers.answer: The bathroom socket isn't exactly the same as a European one. It has an isolated transformer that isolates the mains from the supply so if you get a shock it won't kill you. There's no earth connection. All sockets aren't like that because it's expensive and you couldn't draw enough current.

questions.question: What does the P stand for that appears in the bottom right corner of Coronation Street and Emmerdale titles?

answers.answer: It denotes that the show has product placement within it - it's a pre-warning to viewers.

questions.question: When the Thames Barrier is closed during high tides, why doesn't the river build up and flood?

answers.answer: It's tidal, and the barrier is never shut for very long. They close it for the bit where tide and surge would combine to create flooding, but that passes quickly, then they open it up and everything gets flushed out.

questions.question: Why were people wearing high-vis jackets when counting votes in the Scottish referendum?
Where is there a land border between two countries where one drives on the right and the other drives on the left? What happens at that border?

answers.answer: Two answers. The boring one: between Cambodia and Thailand, there's a big gate where everyone gets off the bus, hands in passports, the bus drives through, and you walk through a DMZ-type space and get back on the other side. The cool one: China and Macau, which is a figure-eight bridge where you drive up on the right, do a swervy hoopy thing over water, and come out on the other side driving on the left.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'tight as old boots' come from?

answers.answer: Two explanations. First, old-fashioned leather boots would shrink and contract if you didn't wear them for a while, so they'd be tighter when you put them on. Second, when children's feet grow, their boots become too tight - hence 'tight as old boots' meaning mean.

questions.question: Do dreams run faster than reality? How can I have a really long dream in just 20 minutes of sleep?

answers.answer: When you're asleep, your body shuts down but your brain works really hard and very quickly to process data and information. In REM sleep, your brain is working at its highest capacity, so in one minute of real time, you can process enough to experience 200 minutes of dream time. Time is conveyed by your brain processing information - you can live three or four different lifetimes within a minute of REM sleep.

questions.question: Have animals developed better road sense over the last hundred years of cars through evolution?

answers.answer: Both learned behavior and actual evolution. Research shows frogs raised near roads get squashed less than frogs raised away from roads - that's learned behavior. But in 2013, research on cliff swallows found they've actually evolved longer wings when breeding next to roads because the high mortality rate from shorter wings drives rapid evolution. You can't pass on lessons genetically, only physical adaptations.

questions.question: Why does blood seep out of the bag when defrosting meat overnight, even though the bag is still sealed?

answers.answer: Two parts. First, the red liquid isn't actually blood - it's myoglobin, a protein in muscle tissue that looks like haemoglobin because it has iron in it. When cells freeze, they crack open and the myoglobin leaks out. Second, when you freeze meat in a plastic bag, the plastic freezes too and develops micro-tears that are big enough to let the myoglobin solution through - you'd need a microscope to see them but the plastic becomes porous.

questions.question: Why are champagne bottles named after ancient monarchs like Nebuchadnezzar, Methuselah, Jeroboam, and Rehoboam?

answers.answer: The only definitive answer is for Magnum - the first recorded naming was by Robert Burns in a poem as an abbreviation of the Latin 'Magnum Bonum' meaning a large good thing.

They're biblical characters, some of whom were also Babylonian kings. It's intertwined with how the church spread alcohol across Europe, including distillation. Monasteries had distilleries attached - like Dom Perignon - which explains the naming tradition.

questions.question: When was canned laughter first used and who invented it?
How do snails survive freezing temperatures? They only have thin shells and are made of gloopy gunk.

answers.answer: Snails secrete a layer of slime around the shell opening which effectively seals them in their shell for hibernation, which can last months.

It's to do with the saltiness of snails. When they hibernate, the salt in their bodies depresses the freezing point of the water, similar to antifreeze in a car engine. The water will only freeze at minus five, minus ten, or minus twenty degrees. It's both the slime seal and the saltiness.

questions.question: What makes a nut a nut? As opposed to anything else. If you look at a cashew and a Brazil nut, they seem to be totally different. What do they have in common?

answers.answer: All nuts are seeds. Not all seeds are nuts. It's the way that the fruit presents the item, the seed. If you get a single presentation that's not coming out of a fruit that's a nut. Hazelnut is the classic one. Brazil nuts are seeds. A peanut is called a ground nut but it's a legume.

questions.question: Why don't you get coffee as a percentage, like alcohol is? You can have 4% beer, 12% wine, 40% spirit. But with a coffee, there's no percentage. You can't get 90% coffee.

answers.answer: Caffeine is one of a class of natural products like nicotine, atropine, morphine. We're not comparing apples with apples because alcohol is a product of fermentation or brewing. When it reaches a maximum of 10%, the yeast gets killed by the alcohol, so from that point on you have to distill. You can't distill coffee because the caffeine is just naturally occurring. It's more or less the same, varying with small amounts by what coffee beans you're using. Arabica and Robusta are the two types of bean, and they vary slightly in the caffeine amount. But they vary so slightly that there's no point labeling it.

questions.question: Why don't Cadbury's flakes melt? When I put it in a bain-marie over a pan of boiling water, nothing. Microwave didn't work either. It stayed exactly the same texture and flakiness, would fall apart but not melt.

answers.answer: It's because it's made of dehydrated milk chocolate. When you try to melt a flake, the dehydrated milk molecules will sort of just shrivel, and the sugar will start burning. It goes harder and harder until the sugar burns.

questions.question: Wherever you go in the world, it's the Celtic faith, Celtic religion, Celtic people. You go to Boston, Stalabridge or Glasgow, and it's Celtic. Why?

answers.answer: It's a noun when you're talking about the Boston Celtics, Celtics or Celtic Football Club. It's an adjective when you're talking about the Celtic people or the Celtic language.

questions.question: Why was it decided to plot the London postal areas where they are, because they don't always make sense? You have Whitechapel with E1. The next step east is Mile End, which is E2. But E4 is way up north.

answers.answer: The postcodes are basically going alphabetically, not geographically. So E1 is not Whitechapel, it's Aldgate. Then you've got Bow, Bethnal Green, Chingford. Therefore, it's E4. E5 becomes Homerton, Hackney. The central areas ending in 1 are not alphabetical - N1, W1, E1, and S1. But everything else is alphabetical. Camden NW1, Hampstead NW3, Brixton SW2, Tooting SW17, Wimbledon SW19.

questions.question: Christmas Day, that date never changes. But why does Easter? Has to be on a Sunday. But that's it?

answers.answer: Easter is conveniently slid into a previously pagan festival, which depended upon the Spring Equinox. It's something like the X Sunday after the Spring Equinox.
Full moon after the spring equinox. I'm an astronomer and run an astronomy group in my town.

questions.question: Do pigeons have taste buds? I was standing at a bus stop and there's a pigeon eating a morsel on the street covered in dirt and crud and fag ash. If I put that in my mouth it wouldn't be pleasant. But also, if you put a discarded cigarette and a piece of bread next to each other, the pigeon will always peck at the bread and not at the cigarette.

answers.answer: Yes.

questions.question: Why do we still have ladies in waiting? Why do we have ladies in waiting? They're like paid friends for queens and princesses.

answers.answer: The reason is because most of the ladies at the time were single ladies and noble ladies as well. They were a friend and a cross between a friend and a servant. The reason is ladies want to go to court to find a suitable husband, so they were waiting for a husband, exactly or a lover, and the name stuck even after they got married. Some were already married and were ladies in waiting because they were the mistresses of somebody important in the court. In the Spanish court, in the French court, yes indeed.

questions.question: Why is the lint from a dryer always a shade of lilac regardless of the clothes you put in?
Some smells bring back horrible fears. One of them is the dentist smell. All dentists seem to smell the same. But I've never known what that smell actually is.

answers.answer: It smells of oil of cloves. Being a dentist of 37 summers tells me that the smell is because we use temporary filling material, which is a mixture of zinc oxide and some of your eugenol. And in the eugenol is oil of cloves. It's an all-pervading smell which makes every dentist smell the same. The good news is if you've done the job for 37 years, you don't smell it anymore.

questions.question: Where do bubbles come from when you boil water? If you get a pan of water and you boil it, where does the air come from? Because it's not in there to begin with.

answers.answer: When you boil water, water is hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen molecules get creakles, then they get hot because heat rises. The bubbles coming out of the water are pure oxygen. Until they reach the air when other molecules mix with them.

questions.question: Why do bobble hats have bobbles? Is it fashion, or has it got a reason?

answers.answer: The ease of removal - imagine trying to take your hat off without a bobble on it wearing big mittens, especially if it's icy or wet.
Sailors used to bump their heads on the low beams as they're walking through the boat, so they put a bobble on the hat so that would hit the beam first and be a warning to duck.

questions.question: How do new words like Brexit get into sign language?
Why don't we sneeze when we sleep? When we're asleep, we never sneeze.

answers.answer: He has seen his wife sneeze while she's asleep and she sneezes them both awake.

questions.question: Is there a formula to calculate how much snow would melt into how much water? If my garden's covered in four inches of snow, how much water is that going to melt down into?

answers.answer: The density of snow differs depending on how it's packed.

There are NOAA tables from the US - generally one inch of rain is equivalent to 10 inches of snow. This changes depending on location and proximity to waterways because that defines how much water is in the clouds.

questions.question: What happens to spacemen when they cut themselves? What colour is blood in space?

answers.answer: If they can breathe on the space station, the blood would still be red because there's oxygen there.

Blood is the same colour, whether you're in space or anywhere - it's red, it's never blue. The idea that blood is blue comes from olden days before science caught up with reality. You see veins on your arm and they look blue through the skin, but your blood when oxygenated is slightly lighter red, when deoxygenated is slightly darker red.
answers.qualifications: Retired consultant pathologist, fellow of the Royal College of Pathologists, over 30 years of autopsy experience

questions.question: Why is Stonehenge not lit at night time?

answers.answer: To prevent people from sneaking in to conduct Druid ceremonies and just faff about. If it was lit up, it would be a temptation and kids would be drinking cider there every night.

The Royal Astronomical Society and English Heritage/Historic England agreed together mutually that Stonehenge should not be illuminated. They said it would be against the unique interest of Stonehenge, which was more erected to study the stars. Illuminating it would go against that purpose and prevent people from looking at the sky properly.

questions.question: Why don't we eat turkey eggs?

answers.answer: Turkeys are bred solely for meat, not for eggs. There would be eggs that don't get fertilised, but there's no market for them.

A turkey will only lay about 100 eggs a year, and they're designed primarily for putting on meat for the table. A hybrid chicken is designed for minimum intake of food to lay maximum amount of eggs - about 235 per year. So cost-effectively, a chicken's egg is much cheaper than a turkey egg.
answers.qualifications: Keeps chickens; grandfather kept turkeys

questions.question: How and why did the naming of pubs come about? What prompted these unusual names like the Cross Keys and the Dog and Duck?

answers.answer: Pictograms - in days before widespread literacy, pub signs had to be recognizable images rather than written words. Pubs named after earls or dukes would have coats of arms that locals recognized. Pubs also developed reputations - some were better than others for ale, so you might go to the Cross Keys for good ale or somewhere cheaper for lesser quality.

questions.question: Where does the expression 'I'll be back in a jiffy' come from? Is there any connection to jiffy bags?

answers.answer: Jiffy bags are probably a trade name. No connection to the phrase 'in a jiffy'.
A jiffy is a unit of time equal to a hundredth of a second.
answers.qualifications: Has an app called 'A Thousand and One Interesting Facts'

questions.question: If you get a battery, how come if a human touches both ends, we don't get a shock off it? If you put a battery in a circuit it can power a light bulb, but if we touch both ends we don't get a shock.

answers.answer: If you lick a battery, particularly a PP3, you get a shock. The tingle on your tongue proves there's electrical activity, but the size of the circuit and conductivity matter.

Your body has internal resistance. Depending on the voltage of whatever you're touching, the internal resistance can cancel it out. Sometimes if you're feeling run down with a cold or flu and your resistance is down, you might get a tingle.
answers.qualifications: Electrical electronic engineer

questions.question: Sign language question - how does sign language accommodate new words like Brexit?

answers.answer: Sign language is a purely visual language. There's no centralised authority that registers new signs. For new things, someone creates a visual description - for Trump it's a flappy hair thing. It spreads through friends and the deaf community organically. Eventually it becomes standardised through teaching. For WhatsApp, it's a double tick sign. For Brexit, it's B-R then an exit sign. Signs can be linked to how the word is spelled or how something looks.
answers.qualifications: Trainee sign language interpreter

questions.question: Why does everyone always have salt and pepper on their table? Why not have two random spices like oregano and chilli pepper?

answers.answer: Catherine of the Medici, who married the French king, took her cooks and taught the French how to cook. The Medici controlled trade with the East, bringing pepper from Zanzibar and places like that. In Italian, there's a verb called saltimentare, meaning to add salt and pepper or season. The pepper was originally used to mask the flavour of rotten meat. The French don't have the word but just say du sel et du poivre. It's now just convention - salt and pepper are the most effective mode of seasoning. A good ratio is seven parts salt to one part pepper. Source: a brilliant video show by David De Jorge, a Basque chef with seven Michelin stars.

questions.question: Dollar capsules and washing machines - why do they work? Why doesn't the colour go onto other clothing? Why does it all go onto the colour catcher sheet?
On the back of a standard visa debit card, why are there seven digits when you're only ever asked for the last three?

answers.answer: The CBC code on the back of your card is not electronically saved. It's stored only on the print on the card. If your card gets cloned and someone tries to pay online using just the card number and expiry date, they won't have an electronic copy of the CBC code, so they won't be able to make most transactions. For telephone transactions like ordering pizza, they also ask for the last three digits because you need to physically see that code.
Some cards like American Express have a longer version of their own CBC code which includes the last four digits on the back of the card. Examples include Lloyd's and First Direct cards.

questions.question: Why is it impossible to contract HIV or AIDS from mosquito bites? If mosquitoes are drinking blood from someone with HIV and then biting someone else, why can't you contract it?

answers.answer: HIV cannot survive in the mosquito's gut, whereas malaria can mature there. HIV just dies in the mosquito and can't replicate, so it can't be transmitted. Also, there's just not enough HIV on the mosquito's beak to cause any significant infection. The same principle applies to needle stick injuries - if someone has a low viral count, there's a very small chance of infection.

questions.question: When you push two magnets together and they're repelling against each other, that force never seems to die out. It seems perpetual, which doesn't make sense because energy can't be created or destroyed. If you stuck them in a vice for ten years and then undid the vice, they'd ping apart. Where do magnets get their power from?

answers.caller: Professor Hal Howell (University of Brighton, Professor of Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: Using the analogy of springs - if someone pushes a spring in and it pushes back, they wouldn't bat an eyelid, but because it's an invisible force with magnets, they are. The answer is that you have atoms facing different ways in magnets, and they just don't like each other, so they use magnetic force to repel. When two magnets shoot together, there's kinetic energy that comes back when pulled apart. With a spring, you're putting in energy that comes back. With gravity, if you push a car up a hill, you get all that energy back when it rolls down. It's gravitational potential, spring potential, and magnetic potential - potential energy turning into kinetic energy.

questions.question: When you buy a suit or a jacket, the pockets are always sewn up. Why?

answers.answer: During transit, sewing up the pocket minimises the amount of movement of cloth. The pocket lining won't get scrunched up or moved around in a way that would make the jacket look more creased when you try it on. If the pocket is sewn shut, it can't get crammed onto a coat hanger in transit in a way that would have the pocket open and sticking out and getting all creased.

questions.question: When you're swimming, do you sweat? If you do sweat, how would you know?

answers.answer: From personal experience swimming a swim-a-thon many years ago at the Oasis in St Giles, he was sweating when he came out. People do sweat when they swim, especially in warmer water. The body will cool you down a bit, which might make sweating less likely than when working out on land, but there will still be sweat. We also lose weight swimming.

questions.question: When we have a national day, there's all sorts of national days, who actually dictates them?

answers.caller: Linda from Bromley (Secretary General for the National Edible Oil Distributors Association)
answers.answer: National Fish and Chip Day was introduced three years ago (2015). It came from a young fish fryer at the National Fish and Chip Shop of the Year competition, and the trade association took it forward with a fantastic PR company. It's on the first Friday in June every year. The answer to who dictates national days is basically nobody - it depends on how good your idea is and how good your PR is to get the message far and wide. They raise money for the Fishermen's Mission.

questions.question: When we had all the snow a couple of weeks ago, it happened every single time I got out of the car - I got a big static shock. Why does this happen in snow?

answers.caller: Terry from Croydon (trained geologist, worked as hydrogeologist)
answers.answer: When it snows, roads get gritted. Grit is basically salt. Once salt gets put into water, the conductivity, which isn't very high in pure water, rockets. This makes the conditions more conductive for static electricity.

questions.question: If a pregnant lady can have identical twins (where the egg is split), does this happen in the animal world as well? Can animals have identical twins?
Why don't ducks and swans and geese get frostbite on their feet when they stand on frozen lakes for hours at a time, when humans would?

answers.answer: Birds have a rete mirabile - a network of fine arteries that pumps warm blood from the heart quickly to warm up the cold blood in the veins in their feet, acting like a built-in blood conditioning system

There are two mechanisms: restricting blood flow to the feet when cold, and counter-current heat exchange where the warm artery blood transfers heat to the cold vein blood. By the time hot blood reaches the feet it's only 2-3 degrees, preventing freezing. He has a marine biology degree and recommended the book 'Why Don't Penguins' Feet Freeze?'

questions.question: What is the 10-11 digit number that randomly appears at the top of the TV screen during live football matches on Sky Sports or BT Sport?

answers.answer: It's your viewing card number. It appears to track and identify people who might be streaming content illegally online. If you posted footage online, they could trace it back to you immediately. This is why pubs can be prosecuted for using domestic subscriptions rather than business subscriptions for public viewing.

questions.question: Why do some people have bad breath in the morning even though they eat the same food and brush their teeth at the same time as their partner?

answers.answer: It's caused by VSC - volatile sulfur compounds. Brushing helps but mouthwash is better. You need a specialist mouthwash. It's not related to diet or dental hygiene - it's just bad luck if you have the condition. He also suffers from it himself. Specialist mouthwashes are now widely available at Boots and chemists.

questions.question: Why do humans instinctively hate the sound of fingernails on a chalkboard? Would someone who has never heard it before still react negatively to it?

answers.answer: The sound is at the same frequency as a human baby's cry or human scream. Evolutionarily, our most important task is reproduction, so we're hardwired to respond to sounds associated with babies. Everyone reacts the same way to it even for the first time because the frequency triggers our evolutionary programming, not learned experience.

questions.question: Why are the sinks smaller in disabled toilets than in regular toilets?

answers.answer: They get away with the smallest sinks according to building regulations. Left on the board for someone else to answer.
He's a plumber. The smaller sink allows wheelchairs to get around easier and the person can reach the taps. Sinks are also lower. The question assumes the disability requires wheelchair access.

questions.question: Where does the saying 'fast asleep' come from?

answers.answer: 'Fast' is an old English word meaning secure, sound, or strongly. 'Fast asleep' means very asleep or sound asleep. 'Stuck fast' means stuck securely. It's Anglo-Saxon in origin.

The root is 'fasten' - to make something secure. After it's fastened, it is fast. 'Hold fast' and 'stand fast' mean to hold or stand securely. He clarified that fast originally meant solid/secure, not 'very'.

The word comes from Norse/Viking influence, common in Yorkshire and North Lincolnshire areas. It means very or vigorously. The Old Norse root 'festa' means to make fast or secure, so 'hold fast' means hold securely. 'Fast' as in speed is a different word that became confused with 'fast' as in secure over time.

questions.question: Were musicians/soldiers given special protection in Napoleonic-era battles and not fired upon, similar to how flag bearers were protected?

answers.answer: Battlefield archaeology student. In reality, drummers were high-value military targets because they beat out commands - you'd actually try to take them out first to disrupt enemy communication. Pipers were stretcher bearers as well, so no special dispensation existed. At Waterloo, an 8-year-old French drummer boy was spared only because of his age, not military convention.

questions.question: If perspective drawing was discovered during the Renaissance, how did they build pyramids and ancient buildings before that?

answers.answer: She's a trained artist who teaches technical drawing. Architects don't need perspective drawing to build - they work with plans and elevations. Perspective is only used to sell an idea to a customer. Even in pyramid days they had plans and elevations, and they had bossy foremen who could read them. Perspective in art was formalized during the Renaissance, but functional architectural planning never required it.

questions.question: Why do movies and TV shows take so long to put onto DVD after the cinema run ends?

answers.answer: It's about incentivizing cinema attendance. The longer the gap between cinema release and DVD, the more likely people are to pay for cinema tickets rather than wait.

questions.question: Where do we get the term 'square meals'? Is it something to do with the Navy and square plates?

answers.answer: Speculated it might be related to square plates on ships, where round plates were stacked sideways to prevent rolling, making them appear square. It was an inducement to join the Navy.
On ships from the 1600s-1800s, round plates were stacked sideways on racks. Because they were stacked this way, they appeared square and didn't roll about in rough seas.

'Square' entered the language in 1856 meaning an honest meal. It's not about the shape of the plate but the type of meal - like a 'square deal'. He found no references to square meals in Navy literature from that era.

questions.question: Why can some people float on their backs in water while others sink like a stone?

answers.answer: Technique: Go on back, arms out, ankles up (toes poking out of water), take a deep breath and hold it. Also mentioned saltier water helps.

Body fat percentage is key. Fat floats. Women have higher body fat percentage so float more easily than men. She was a swimming teacher and lifeguard. Even with lungs full of air, very lean people struggle to float and need to be actively moving.

questions.question: Where do the names of seasons come from - Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter?

answers.answer: Couldn't give definitive answer. Suggested it's likely pagan and druidic in origin.
Spring, summer, and winter are all Anglo-Saxon in origin. Autumn is actually Latin ('autumnam') adopted after Christianity. Americans still call it 'fall'.

questions.question: How did we get the boundaries that form the borders, regions and shires? They seem so random.

answers.answer: Goes back to topography - streams, mountains, woodland. Also ownership of estates and defensibility. People would draw borders around mountains and along streams. The USA has straight lines because it was a new country drawn on maps by colonists. The Sykes-Picot agreement in the Middle East shows what happens when diplomats draw lines with rulers.

As an intern in digital cartography, he worked with maps that flipped between satellite images and official maps. The official border lines actually map streams and the shapes of fields. Borders follow natural geography on the ground.

questions.question: What's the origin of calling a 50th wedding anniversary 'golden'? Why gold?

answers.answer: Couldn't provide a definitive answer. Speculated it might be because gold was the most valuable/achievable metal and 50 years was an ambitious goal for a marriage.

questions.question: Why doesn't snow short-circuit the electricity between the third rail and negative rail on the London Underground? Rainwater should soak into ground, but snow sits on top.

answers.answer: Couldn't answer. Acknowledged he didn't understand the question properly.
Water doesn't conduct - dirty water does because of electrolytes that need to move. Snow has water molecules held in a rigid lattice, and until they can melt and move, it can't conduct electricity.

questions.question: Why is it that increasingly people speak with higher intonation at the end of their statements, as if asking a question, when they're not? Is it influenced by Australian culture like Neighbours?

answers.answer: Suggested it was cultural influence from Neighbours and Home and Away in formative years, which introduced Australian pronunciation patterns.

It's called 'high-rising terminal' or 'Antipodean inquisitive inflection'. But it's actually a 'conventionalised politeness strategy' - animals use higher pitch to show they're lesser/non-threatening, so people go up at the end to seem less assertive and more polite. He studies linguistics at Cambridge.

questions.question: When and why did men first start shaving?

answers.answer: Originally to repel lice. People used to shave their heads and beards. The aristocracy wore big wigs because they were all bald underneath due to vermin and lice living in their wigs.

Prehistoric man used razor clams to shave. Razor clams have long rectangular shells with a natural sharp edge that prehistoric man used. They even carved handles into them - like a razor shell with a handle. The reason was parasites - to get rid of nits.
Stone Age man was napping shards of flint and using them to scrape fur off animal pelts to get at the proper leather underneath.

questions.question: Why is Humpty Dumpty depicted as an egg when there's nothing in the rhyme that mentions him being an egg?

answers.answer: Humpty Dumpty was actually a cannon or gun that fell off a wall. The egg depiction comes from Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass. Some think it's a riddle where egg was the answer.
It was originally written as a riddle, so the answer (egg) wouldn't be in the riddle itself. But James strongly rejected this interpretation, insisting it is not a riddle.

questions.question: What does 'daft apis' mean?

answers.answer: Apis is a halfpenny. So 'daft apis' is a Yorkshire term meaning a halfpenny of little worth - essentially calling someone worthless or silly.

questions.question: How do we know how animals see? Dogs see in black and white, horses see differently - how can we definitively know what they see when we can't see through their eyes?

answers.caller: Professor Hal (University of Brighton - Professor of Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: Two methods: First, you can dissect an eye and look at rods and cones in the retina - cones deal with colour, rods deal with light/dark. By comparing animal eyes to human eyes where we understand the rod/cone relationship, we can determine their vision. Second, you can use PET scans - show an animal different stimuli and see which areas of their brain light up. Horses don't see well in 3D because they're prey animals with eyes on the side of their head, giving wide peripheral vision. Predators have eyes at the front for 3D depth perception. Stars twinkle because a single point of light touches a single rod, and as air moves, it shifts to the next rod.

questions.question: How many lumens is the sun?

answers.answer: The sun emits 10,000 lumens per square foot. If you multiply that by the square footage of the sun, you get the full amount.

questions.question: Why does time seem to speed up as we get older? When you're one year old, a year is double your age and feels forever. As you age, years feel shorter. Also, why can't we measure time differently to reflect this relative experience?

answers.answer: When you're ten years old, one year is 10% of your life. When you're 100, one year is only 1% of your life. So time appears to speed up because each year represents a smaller percentage of your total experience.

When you're younger, you're experiencing things for the first or second time, so your brain logs them differently. As you get older and experience things repeatedly, your brain files them differently. You remember new experiences vividly but routine repeated experiences don't get logged the same way. To slow down perceived time, you should put yourself in situations doing new things.

questions.question: With 30 million vehicles on UK roads and 120 million tyres, where does all the rubber go? Roads aren't building up with it.

answers.answer: It becomes dust. It behaves like all other dust - gets blown away by wind and dispersed by rain. We're breathing it in. Approximately 38.4 million kilograms of rubber are in the atmosphere.

questions.question: Why do national anthems from different countries all sound similar with a European orchestral sound? Why doesn't the Japanese anthem sound Eastern, South American sound Salsa-like, or Middle Eastern sound Arab?
Why are UK country lanes bendy and windy, while roads in America and Australia are straight?

answers.answer: Because farmers established the tracks. They went around fields, streams, and obstacles rather than through them. There was no central government organizing road-building. The Romans built straight roads, but post-Roman roads were made by individuals needing access to their property.

We probably followed the paths made by animals. On farms, cattle make their own paths between areas and they're clever at weaving around hills to find the flattest route. Humans likely followed these animal tracks.

questions.question: Why are all racers anti-clockwise? I've been watching the speed skating in the Olympics, and they go flying out when they crash. Is it to do with balance? Is it something to do with where the heart is? The heart isn't smacking the middle of your chest, it's slightly to the left.

answers.answer: It's to favour right-handed people. Most people are right-handed. It's like because knights traditionally were always right-handed people. That's why we travel on the left on roads, so you've got your sword hand ready to attack. Stairways and castles are anti-clockwise because it favours the defender with the sword.

The original Olympic Games in Greece were run anti-clockwise, but it was never for medical benefit. Horses are stronger on their right-hand side, so when training horses in horse races they did use to run them anti-clockwise. Humans just followed that.

questions.question: Why do escalator handrails always move slightly faster than the two-wheeled wheels? Because they're not able to move the treads themselves.

answers.answer: There is a roller that pulls the handrail round. Typically that's the bit that fails first. Friction wears it out so it gets smaller. So what they do is they make it larger when they install it. Which obviously increases the distance the handrail has to travel, which means it travels quicker. So as an escalator goes through its life, the handrail will slowly get slower and slower.

It's a safety mechanism. The reason why the hand part moves faster is so that it pulls you forward. You're leaning forward all the time. If you were moving at the same speed, you'd be leaning backwards.

questions.question: Why can't you eat your cake? The expression is 'he wants to have his cake and eat it.' Why can't you eat your cake?

answers.answer: You can't keep your cake and eat it. Think of it that way. It is binary cake. It's a one or a zero. It is either in your gob or on your plate. It cannot simultaneously be on your plate and in your gob.

The reason it doesn't make any sense is that it's been misquoted since the 16th century. Originally it was 'you can't eat your cake and have it too.' The Unabomber quoted it correctly in one of his letters, which led to forensic linguistics catching him.

questions.question: You've got Bob Sly and you've got the skeleton Bob. What does the Bob actually mean in bobsled?

answers.answer: When they first started the bobsleigh race, someone said it looked like they were bobbing up and down to move the sleigh. That's why it's called bobsleigh.

questions.question: Can you tell the age of an ancient woodland by the spread of the bluebell? The older it is, the more the carpet of bluebells would have extended across the canopy floor.
Why is a French kiss called a French kiss? A full-on snog with tongues and all.

answers.answer: It was originally called the Florentine Kiss. It was brought back by American and British soldiers from World War I. When they greeted their wives and girlfriends and started kissing that way, their women said 'what's going on?' And they said 'this is the way the French men kiss their women.' And that became known as the French Kiss.

questions.question: Where does the term 'rasher of bacon' come from? When all other meat is served in slices, why is bacon a rasher?

answers.answer: Rasare. R-A-S-A-R-E. Rasare means to shave in Italian. So a shaving of bacon is a rasher.

questions.question: Why do we boo people as a sign of disapproval, and where does it come from?
How does the phone or the health app know how many steps you're taking? My husband is 6 foot 3 and takes whopping great steps. I'm only 5 foot 7 and take lots of little steps.

answers.answer: It counts the bounces. You bounce more than you realise when you're walking.

questions.question: Why is so much faith given to a hallmark on a piece of jewellery? What has stopped a rogue jeweller stamping a nine carat gold ring with a 24 carat gold hallmark to make it worth ten times more? Why do they trust the hallmark?

answers.answer: The hallmark stamps are the legal stamp of purity on the gold done by the assay office in London. But you can't fake it because if anybody's going to buy a lump of gold jewellery, you'd look at the quality first. And then you do a slight acid test on the gold, and the acid test will determine whether it's 9, 14 or 22 carat gold.

questions.question: What's the origin of a testimonial match in sport?

answers.answer: Testimonials were awarded for service, generally after ten years back in the day. They were also given to groundsmen and people like that. Now they're based more on charity.

questions.question: Why are some berries that plants produce toxic?

answers.answer: I think you've got your toxicity back upside down. They're not toxic to everything. Brightly coloured berries are warnings to animals that they don't eat me, because you'll get sick.

Some berries have evolved to have higher areas of dispersal. If a berry is toxic and a human or mammal eats it, they won't travel as far as say a bird, and the bird will travel and spread the seeds further. Good example: chilies - mammals can taste the heat in chilies but birds can't, so birds spread the seeds for miles and miles and help the plant propagate.

questions.question: What's the largest number that's ever been on the back of a football shirt? Are there maximum limits on squad numbers for Premier League teams? Could you have a three-digit number?

answers.answer: Highest numbered shirts could potentially be Michael Foot, who for his 90th birthday was registered as an official player by Plymouth Argyle and given a shirt with number 90.
Ronaldo (Brazilian) had number 99 when he played for AC Milan.

The Premier League rule is that squad numbers must be consecutive and close to the current highest number. When Swansea signed Renato Sanchez in the summer, they gave him number 85 but it was rejected due to that rule by the Premier League. He ended up with number 35.

Manchester City have such a large squad they register their reserves as well as their youth teams, so their numbers go into the 70s. They registered Iannaccio as 72 because their squad is so huge. The rule still applies - numbers must be consecutive and close to the largest one currently there.

questions.question: Why is it that when you've had a deep sleep, you wake up with really puffy eyes and puffy face, yet if you've had a light sleep you don't?

answers.answer: Is it something to do with lymph nodes and water?

Your body regenerates and cleans out a lot of toxins while you're sleeping. The deeper you sleep, the more toxins you'll release. Your eyes go puffy because that's where your body releases a lot of toxins. That little bit of grit you get sometimes comes out a lot more the next morning after a good night's sleep.

questions.question: Why do you urinate when you're nervous?

answers.answer: Is it to do with adrenaline, fight or flight?

You were partly right about the adrenaline - it can make the kidneys produce more urine. But think about the bladder. The muscle, the detrusor muscle, is the bladder bag. Then you've got the sphincter. Normally the sphincter's tight and the detrusor muscle is relaxed. When you're nervous, think about your body getting all rigid, the detrusor muscle will be tight and presses on the sphincter, and then you want to pee.

questions.question: Why are some of us squeamish and some of us aren't squeamish?
What beans are beans on toast made of? They're not kidney beans, not borlotti beans... what kind of beans are they?

answers.answer: It's a borlotti bean, isn't it? The little borlotti beans, mini borlotti, borlottinis.
Beans means haricot beans. That's where you get it from - haricot beans.

questions.question: When you feel a sneeze coming on and usually you sneeze, but sometimes it just fades away. What is going on that that sneeze disappears?

answers.answer: Presumably it's a nerve ending that's being manipulated, tickled. And whatever is doing the tickling decreases in ticklishness. There are theories involving lights as well - if you want to sneeze or want to make the sneeze go away, you look at a bright light, but I can't remember which way around it is.

Your body's reaction to something being in your nose is sneezing - it's trying to eject that from the nose, such as bacteria, bits of dirt. When that's no longer in the nose, you no longer need the reaction to sneeze. Therefore the sneerly happens - when the thing that was aggravating your nasal membrane has stopped aggravating it.

questions.question: Who invented the weekends and why?

answers.answer: God. On the seventh day he rested.
It was actually Henry Ford when he created the whole production line. He also created the five-day working week. People used to work six, seven days before that.

questions.question: About moths using the moon to navigate - they don't want to get to the moon necessarily, they are using the moon to navigate
Can anyone prove that animals, or pets specifically, are homosexual? How would you prove? What would proof involve?
Does mashing the buttons harder on a remote control when the batteries are dying actually make it work?

answers.answer: In very rare cases you can make things work because the contacts get corroded and you can force your way through the corrosion with pressure. If you have a slightly low battery and a slightly poor contact with resistance, you can break through. Once you replace the battery, the poor contact doesn't matter anymore because the low resistance doesn't matter.

questions.question: If you go to private school, why are you referred to as a public school boy?

answers.answer: The original public schools were opened by wealthy benefactors for the public, and rich kids would have private tutors. When Henry founded Eton and King's College, he saw it as a way to educate poorer kids. It's evolved into places you pay for because they're not government-run, but the language has remained.

questions.question: How is it that they get the smell onto the paper in scratch and sniff books, but then that smell isn't released until someone scratches it?

answers.answer: It's done by microcapsules. The paper is coated with an emulsion containing microcapsules. The perfume is encapsulated in tiny pods wrapped in a thin coating of gelatin. When you scratch it, the capsules break and the perfume is released. Something made 20 years ago would still work unless someone had scratched it vigorously.

questions.question: Why have radiator keys always been square? Why did they become square and not hexagon?

answers.answer: Most radiator bleed valves are made of brass, which is quite a soft metal. It makes sense to have a square because it's equal on all sides so it doesn't wear down. You can also use your radiator keys on old boilers because they have the same system.

questions.question: Will my fingerprint come back the same as it was before? I cut through my fingerprint using a standing knife to open a box.

answers.answer: Fingerprints look at a much smaller section than we realise. He should try unlocking with numbers then reset with his new thumb. The computers can analyze a relatively small portion.

questions.question: Why are senior members of the government in the cabinet, and where does that come from?

answers.answer: It's French. Short for Cabinet de Toilette. Louis XIV was absolutely not interested in politics, he was above it all. While he performed his ablutions in his Cabinet de Toilette, his ministers would present the latest news and he would give short yes or no answers, sometimes just grunts.

It's terms from how we used to live in our homes, when families all lived in one room centuries ago. It was a name for an additional room within a property where families kept their more prized possessions, things that were shiny and valuable.

questions.question: What would happen if we didn't register our baby after three months? Would we have to go back and look for a new name? What would happen to us?

answers.answer: You'll get fined, and if you don't pay your fine, you'll get taken to court. It's a census thing, they need to know for schools planning. They can track you through doctor visits and hospital scans. If you don't register and they've got you on their system, they might think something sinister has happened.

questions.question: Why are apartments called flats in the UK when everywhere else in the world they're called houses and apartments?

answers.answer: They're called flats because they're all on one level and they're effectively flat. It comes from a German word meaning flat or level ground. It's because they don't have an upstairs.

questions.question: Why is shampoo and shower gel always white regardless of the color of the bottle, but the bubbles are always white too?

answers.answer: When shampoo is in its unfrothed state, light interacts with the electrons on the surface and reflects back a certain wavelength, which is why colored shampoo appears colored. When you froth it up, you make lots of tiny bubbles. The white light refracts into all its different parts - red, yellow, green, orange. These reflect off the back of the bubble and come back to you as white light.

questions.question: Why does facial hair grow slower when you're in a warmer country?

answers.answer: It's a physiological reaction to temperature. In hot weather, beard growth slows because you don't need the warmth. You value a pelt when it's cold. It doesn't turn off completely in warm weather in the UK because it's cooler here, so you still have to shave.

questions.question: Is there a direct correlation between altitude and weight? If you weigh 12 stone at sea level, how much less would you weigh at 30,000 feet in an airliner? And if you went down into the Grand Canyon, would you weigh more?

answers.answer: What he defined as weight is incorrect - he was talking about mass. Mass is how much material you're made of and that won't change. Weight is the force at which you and Earth are pulling each other together. The formula is inversely proportional to the square of your distance. At 30,000 feet compared to Earth's surface, it won't make an observable difference. But the further away you get, the less gravitational pull you feel.

questions.question: Why is the small plate that you have when you serve tea or coffee called a saucer?

answers.answer: Back in Tudor times, people had a plate called a trencher to eat from, and they had an additional plate on the side for their sauce. They would dip their food in the sauce before placing it on their trencher. So it was literally the dish for their sauce - the saucier.

questions.question: Why are sea snails not affected by the salt in water like a normal snail would be on land?

answers.answer: Because they're sea snails, so they're going to be biologically different. There's going to be an evolutionary reason that explains one or the other.

answers.caller: Professor Hal (Professor of Public Understanding of Science, University of Brighton)
answers.answer: It's all to do with environment and evolution and osmosis. Sea snails and marine animals have a different mechanism. When you put salt on slugs, that kills them because of osmosis. Marine animals have a different mechanism for osmotic strength in different environments, similar to how desert animals have a longer loop of henle in their kidneys.

questions.question: Is it true that you swallow spiders in your sleep?

answers.answer: It's true.

answers.caller: Mike (Twickenham) - Arachnologist who keeps tarantulas and gives talks on UK spiders
answers.answer: We don't eat them in our sleep. It would be a really bad evolutionary trait for spiders to crawl into big carbon dioxide-spewing holes. The myth was originally seeded by somebody studying urban myths just to show how easy it was to spread misinformation.

questions.question: Why do we have chins?

answers.caller: Andy (Sutton) - Former sports therapist, now garden maintenance and horticulturist
answers.answer: The chin is not really an anatomical place. It's the end of the mandible, the bottom of the jaw. It acts as an anchor for your musculature like your mastoid to eat with. It's part of the jaw rather than a separate entity. So if we didn't have a chin, all our food would fall out of our mouth while we eat.

Bruce Forsythe and Jimmy Hill had very pronounced chins but no better chewing ability or ability to keep food in their mouth because the muscles around the mouth called the orbicularis oris are not attached to the chin. The masseter muscle is attached to the angle of the jaw, not the chin. Chins are developmental, not functional.

questions.question: Is the energy used in making a battery greater than the energy that the battery supplies?

answers.answer: You can't take more energy out of something than you put into it. If the answer was no, then there would be energy being created out of nothing, which is one of the first laws of physics.

You can't possibly end up with more coming out than you put in. But you can't even have the same coming out because of energy losses. The battery has resistance, and you have energy drops inside the battery before you get anything electrical out. That's why the battery warms up. You'll never get anything approaching exactly what you put in.

questions.question: Why can't I smile in a passport photo?

answers.answer: It only came in the last 15-20 years. It's to do with facial recognition software. When you smile, it changes the points where the camera's looking, so you could mistake somebody at airport security control.

questions.question: Why do moths come out at night when it's dark and head for the nearest source of light?

answers.answer: They think it's the moon.
They use the moon to navigate. When they see a bright light that's up close, they get distracted by that and use the light instead to navigate.

questions.question: Why on American military uniforms do they have the flag back to front on the arm, with the stars on the right-hand side?

answers.caller: Damien (Seven Sisters) - Retired United States Marine
answers.answer: The reason the flag on the right shoulder is faced backwards is because it appears as though, looking on either side of the soldier, they're always going forward. They're never going to retreat. They're always moving forward.

questions.question: Why are people considered stupid or lacking intelligence called a lemon? What's the association between intelligence and food?

answers.answer: Like wincing when you lick a lemon?
Lemon Cherbet Herbert - it's rhyming slang. 'Lemon' rhymes with 'Cherbet' which rhymes with 'Herbert', and Herbert is the insult. It's double rhyming slang which doesn't happen very often.

questions.question: Why do we say 'bless you' when somebody sneezes?

answers.answer: Ring-a-ring-a-roses, a pocket full of posies. The nursery rhyme is about the bubonic plague. The idea was that you could fend off the spores that would give you the plague by having a pocket full of posies made of roses. If the spores did infect you, the first symptom would be sneezing. So when you sneeze, people say 'bless you' either as bad luck (looks like you've got a sneeze, maybe you're dying) or as a way of hoping that's just a sneeze and not the bubonic plague.

questions.question: If our brain was a hard drive, how big would it be?
How do they work out TV viewing figures so quickly after a programme airs?
