answers.answer: BARB (Broadcasters' Audience Research Board) sends electronic boxes to a representative sample of homes. If you put a box in ten houses representing a hundred, you multiply up. So if eight of ten were watching, you'd conclude eighty out of a hundred were watching.

The box is attached to the person. You're given one per household member and you have to carry it with you wherever you go. If you're in a coffee shop, you are deemed to be listening to whatever they're playing. They used to give vouchers as reward. Both TV and radio are measured this way.

questions.question: [From last week] Why do ears and nose appear to carry on growing long after the rest of the body has stopped?

answers.answer: They don't carry on growing. What it is is gravity. As you get older, the cartilage in your ears and nose breaks down. As they break down, gravity has more of an effect and pulls them down your face. It's the collagen and elastic fibres and the supporting tissue stops supporting those parts. So they appear to grow but actually it's just sagging. It's age and gravity.

questions.question: Can spiders use other spiders' webs? Different species, can they walk across it without getting caught?
How can you still have the option to call emergency services when you have no signal on your phone? What systems are in place that allow that?

answers.answer: Your phone is receiving a mobile signal, but it's from a different network and not the one you're subscribed to. If you're with O2 and you can't get a signal but you could get an EE one, then you're away. Theoretically, there are places where you'd have no option to ring emergency services because there was genuinely no service from any provider.

questions.question: If you employ a girl, you call her a nanny. If you employ a man capable of doing the same job, what would he be called?

answers.answer: Nanny has been accepted into common parlance to a degree where I wouldn't be surprised if it was in the dictionary. You could use the word nanny for a man. Nanny isn't necessarily feminine, even though its applications in other contexts are feminine (female grandmother or female goat).

questions.question: What are the meteorological circumstances needed for a cloud to dump its rain? Why does a cloud sometimes drop its rain and sometimes pass without raining?

answers.answer: When you breathe on a cold window, you get condensation. Warm air with water vapour hits cold air and precipitates through condensation. It has to be cold enough to cause the water vapour to condense. The cloud is warm air. Hits cold air and rain ensues. In this country, the wind comes from the south-west off the Atlantic which is relatively warm. If it hits cold air coming from the east or north, you get rain.

It's to do with the clouds being full of moisture, and as the moisture is lifted up, it condenses out and falls as rain. With fronts, it's pushed up by cold or warm air. You get lumpy clouds off cold fronts and flat-layered clouds off warm fronts. During summer with large cumulonimbus clouds, air is heated underneath by the sun and rises through the cloud, taking moisture to very high altitudes where it condenses out, helped by dust particles in the air. With very big clouds, raindrops go round and round within the cloud, get very big, can freeze into hailstones.

questions.question: How are earthworms getting up into trees? Found worms 15 feet up in beech trees, at branch junctions where leaf mould collects

answers.answer: Birds do drop worms in trees, but also when birds build nests they collect mud and there'll be worms inside that they maybe miss. On old pollard points, if they make a nest, as the mud disintegrates it sits inside and water gets in so they can survive there. Also insects can get blown into it.

Worms do climb trees. They don't climb on the outside like a squirrel, but they climb up through the inside through the decay. You've got heartwood decay in some trees and worms can climb up through the rotten wood. At the top of the tree, birds will take them out when they're hungry. Heartwood decay is fairly commonplace and there's nothing to worry about.

questions.question: Why on the underground escalator do you always have to stand to the right rather than on the left? Why can't it be on the left?

answers.answer: Because the massive majority of us are right-handed, so you'd have your stronger hand on the handrail for stabilising.

questions.question: If you stand in a field with a mirror 10 feet in front of you, you see your reflection. If the mirror is a mile away, you can't see yourself. But if you look at yourself through a telescope into that mirror, would you see yourself?

answers.caller: Professor Howell with Wayne from Basildon (University of Brighton)
answers.answer: It's all about the resolution. The Hubble telescope works with mirrors. If you had the right telescope and the right mirror, you could see yourself in a mirror a mile away through the telescope.

questions.question: Do spiders share webs? Can one spider use another spider's web?

answers.answer: In foreign countries they do, but in this country they tend to have their own web. You will see a spider in another spider's web when it's either preying on the other spider, or stealing the captured flies from the other spider's web. Some spiders can have eight different kinds of silk for the frame and different kinds for the sticky circles, but the spider still wants to avoid getting stuck.

questions.question: What is the origin of star signs? Who invented them, where did they come from and how were they done?

answers.answer: Astrology originated in Babylonia - the oldest written texts on it are from ancient Babylonia. It was influenced through Hellenistic periods, Mediterranean and Egyptian cultures. The Babylonians divided the ecliptic into 12 sectors based on Earth going round the Sun (seen from geocentric perspective). They were interested in omens and eclipses - noting when certain celestial events happened in particular parts of the zodiac, certain earthly events followed (floods, storms, droughts). This was then applied to human beings and evolved into today's astrological signs. Seasons were defined by symbols and if you were born under that season/symbol, it would denote certain characteristics.

questions.question: Why is Scotland Yard called Scotland Yard?

answers.answer: Scotland Yard wasn't originally where it is now. Great Scotland Yard was the back door of the original headquarters of the Metropolitan Police.

Scotland Yard was called that because the original headquarters of the Metropolitan Police was at Great Scotland Yard. It was quite literally Scotland's Yard. It was embassy ground - Scottish representation in Whitehall before the United Kingdom.

questions.question: Why are traditional dusters coloured yellow?

answers.answer: When boats were sailing from the high seas, sailors coming into port were riddled with disease. They used to stand off port with a yellow flag displaying that they were clean and could come into port. The yellow flag became a byword for clean - and dusters became yellow as a result. Lee's qualification: cleaning contractor for 30 years, member of Environmental Cleaning Association.

questions.question: Why are cucumbers wrapped in plastic when apples and other things with tough skin aren't?

answers.answer: In the majority of places, whole cucumbers are sold unwrapped. It's the portioned cucumbers that are wrapped because they're classed as prepared fruit and veg, and once a veg becomes prepared, it must be wrapped by law. If whole cucumbers are wrapped, it's usually for cosmetic purposes - the retailer chooses to do it. There's no requirement. Andreas (green grocer advisor) concurs - he blames it on the Spanish, saying they're obsessed with wrapping up all veg and fruits. Andreas also says the cellophane actually contributes to over-wateriness and bitter tastes because the cucumber sweats in a watertight container.

questions.question: Why does a row of Z's represent sleep, like in an emoji when you're texting?

answers.answer: It's a rough representation of the noise you make when you're asleep - like 'buzz' is a rough representation of the noise a bee makes. It became a catch-all term for sleeping because everyone recognises it. Liz: But you don't make that noise. James: You don't go... but you do arguably go... No one ever queries that bees make a buzz sound either, and that's not objectively true of all bees.

questions.question: Do fish consciously become thirsty or get thirsty?

answers.answer: No. Fish breathe by ingesting water. They've never not got water in their mouth.

It depends whether it's a freshwater fish or a saltwater fish. A freshwater fish's skin is a semipermeable membrane - the fish is constantly gaining water through its skin, so it doesn't need to drink. But a saltwater fish is the reverse: seawater is more concentrated than its tissues, so it's constantly losing water to the sea. It has to drink all the time and excrete the excess salt through its kidneys. So a saltwater fish could get thirsty and would have to drink all the time. Robin's qualification: O level and S level biology.

questions.question: Why do men's ears and noses get bigger as they get older? Is it just men?

answers.answer: I think the ears haven't grown - the skin and flesh has contracted around the skull which makes the ears look bigger.

If you look at somebody like Kirk Douglas, when he was younger his ears weren't that size and now they're massive. James: Are you sure his head hasn't shrunk? Tracy: I'm just looking at Kirk Douglas. His ears and lobes are massive. Maybe he had really heavy earrings. But that's just ears. You need another example for noses. James: What was his nose like before? Tracy: Tiny, still is. Got a lovely little nose, Kirk Douglas.

questions.question: On a conventional dartboard, who and why designed where the numbers go?

answers.answer: It was the Earl of Dartmouth. Just like the Earl of Sandwich invented the sandwich. (James admits he made this up)

It came up before - definitely the Earl of Dartmouth invented darts. He was a big fan of archery and couldn't go out arching because it was raining, so he came up with a way of doing archery indoors and arranged all the numbers.

questions.question: Why do you drive on the left side of the road in the UK?

answers.answer: In feudal times, right-handed people would carry swords on the left. You would want to be on the left-hand side of the road so as a right-handed person you could unsheathe your blade and face oncoming traffic. London Bridge in the 17th century got so busy and congested it was the first thoroughfare to have a rule to go on the left. I don't know why the rest of the world abandoned this sword-based scheme - probably Napoleon.

questions.question: Why do they still produce flat-head screws when cross-head/Pozidriv screws are easier to use and more efficient?

answers.answer: If you haven't got a Phillips screwdriver at home, you'd use a flat-head. James: That's clucking at the straws. Bradley: Or if you don't have any screwdriver - you could use a knife on a flat-head screw.

The single-slot screws look better. Philips and PosiDrive work much more efficiently, but they're ugly. If you get a brass door handle, they'll always be single-slot. It's purely aesthetic. Try finding a Posidrive brass screw - you won't. John's qualifications: tries to find fixings for lots of different things, has a builder in the family.

questions.question: With regards to football clubs, what does the word Albion mean? As in like Brighton and Hove Albion, Burton Albion, West Bromwich Albion, Albion Rovers.

answers.answer: Albion is the oldest name for England, or Great Britain. It's the oldest known name of the island of Great Britain.

It first appeared with Brighton and Hove. And the Albion, you were kind of right with the old name for Britain. Then the name was reserved for areas of coastal Britain with white cliffs. It began in Brighton, and then it got copied by West Bromwich and others.

questions.question: Does the Queen use her handbag to signal her staff with different messages, like a bit like a semaphore?
Where did accents come from? Why does someone from Wales sound different than someone from England?

answers.answer: I think there are a million different answers. My favourite is the idea that where I come from in the Black Country, the part of the reason they talk like this is because there was so much pollution that everyone's nose was permanently blocked. And that's where the Birmingham accent comes from. But I don't know if that's true. I suppose you've got proximity. So Liverpool probably has a large Irish contingent. The answer is something to do with environment and climate.

questions.question: At what viscosity does fluid become solid?

answers.answer: A liquid becomes a solid at the point when viscosity doesn't exist for that. When the structure becomes crystalline in a solid, viscosity disappears because what viscosity is, if we talk about kinematic viscosity, it's a ratio of absolute viscosity which is a sheer stress inside the material, as a ratio of the sheer rate of that material, over a density which is obviously variable with temperature and pressure. There's no answer. The answer is that there isn't an answer. Prior to that, there's no increase in viscosity that would hold true across all liquids.

questions.question: Do small insects see us coming in slow motion? Why do they get away really quickly?

answers.answer: It's about the speed with which insects process light. When you look at a wheel going round, it starts looking like it's going backwards. That's because your eyes and your brain, the journey from eye to brain is finite. It goes at a certain speed, and it would need to go faster. The fly is processing images quicker than what we can.
It's to do with flicker frequency. They perceive light much, much quicker than we can because their metabolism is higher.

questions.question: Do babies cry in the womb?

answers.answer: Yes, they believe babies cry from 28 weeks onwards. We found this out at Christmas when my daughter-in-law was pregnant and our dog would not take the size of her stomach.

They do cry in the womb. Some of it is when you do a massive stretch, you sort of feel like shaking. But some of it is babies practising crying in the womb. 28 weeks seems a reasonable cut-off point for that.

questions.question: Considering how many millions of pigeons and birds there are flying around the skies, why do you never see a dead pigeon anywhere?

answers.answer: You hardly ever see dead ones because of foxes and scavengers and things like that.

I'm a tree surgeon. All the pigeons are stuck in the trees, in massive conifers. Whenever we take conifers down, they're all stuck in the trees. Like squirrels. They're all flat as pancakes. They're stuck in shrubs and stuck in trees. Some pigeons can die mid-flight, and it just lands in a conifer. In Reading, there's a large red kite population. So the scavengers pick them up and eat them. In a massive conifer, average would be about one, sometimes a couple.

questions.question: Where do butterflies go in the winter?

answers.answer: They're all dead. They mate and lay an egg, and then that doesn't hatch until spring. It stays dormant throughout winter. The butterflies die. The egg turns into a wotsit, and the wotsit turns into a witsit, and the witsit turns into a butterfly, and everyone's happy except you.

questions.question: Who decided which words were acceptable and non-acceptable as swear words? At what point did something become offensive?

answers.answer: The Victorian times likely had a lot to do with it, though James admitted this was just off the top of his head. He noted it seems arbitrary - like how giving the thumbs up in Iran is like giving the finger.
It has to do with the Norman conquest of England. When the Normans invaded, French words became more high class and the original English words became the swear words we have now.

questions.caller: James from North Tuddenham in Norfolk
questions.question: What are growing pains? If they are actually you growing, do you feel yourself growing?

answers.answer: Yes, there are conditions specific to growth periods. Osgood-Schlatter's is where tendons pull on the bone of the shin - bones grow about six months faster than the muscles attached to them. Similar phenomena occur in the heel (Sever's disease) and knees. There are also referrals for growing pains when they're less specific, more to do with wear and tear and muscle imbalances.

questions.question: How many people have to be afraid of something before it's considered a phobia and documented as a physical phobia?

answers.answer: The short answer is one person. If you have an irrational fear of something, that's a phobia. But to be documented and given a name, there's not going to be a rule. The more prevalent the problem, the more likely something gets named and classified, but there's no specific number attached to the definition.

The general classification is that everything can be classified using the Greek root 'phobia' for fear plus the object of fear. So trees would be dendrophobia (from dendros for trees). Theoretically it could be anything - you just have to wait until it gets into the dictionary. But the actual classification criteria are less clear.

questions.question: Where do currency signs like pound signs and euro signs come from? Were they just thought up and designed?

answers.answer: The pound sign comes from the Romans and Libra. There were machines that demonstrated weighing of silver and gold, with little scales that had a balance on each end hanging from a chain.

The dollar sign used to be a P with an S through it for peso, because early trading was mostly with Mexicans when people moved west. Eventually it simply became an S with two sticks through it. The original word 'dollar' comes from 15th century Bohemia - 'thalor' meaning a single unit of currency.

questions.question: What does the apostrophe in O'Brien stand for? Apostrophes always stand for something.

answers.answer: It stands for 'son of' or 'member of'. O'Brien goes back to the King of Ireland, Brian Boru. Similar to 'Mac' in Scotland meaning belonging to a clan. Fitz means illegitimate child of, which applied often to aristocracy and royalty.

The apostrophe is an English way of writing the original name and represents an accent over the O. There are actually four forms: O (father, married man), Mac (father, unmarried), Ni (father, unmarried woman), and Ui (father, married woman). TV presenter Darrell O'Brien writes his name in the traditional way.

questions.question: Why do Scandinavian/Germanic/Northern European countries have an evil Santa?

answers.caller: Isabel from Portsmouth (lived in Belgium and Austria, interested in European cultures)
answers.answer: His name is Krampus. He's a half-demon, half-goat figure who is the opposite of European Saint Nicholas. While British Santa lives at the North Pole surrounded by elves, Saint Nicholas is a Turkish guy who travels by boat with helpers called Black Peters (naughty kids who've been dyed black through coal). When Saint Nicholas visits, if a child has been good they get a gift; if bad, they get coal as a signal for Krampus to come, abduct them in his sack and dye them to become servants. People have been dressing up as Krampus since the 16th century.

Krampus comes from ancient northern mythology - he was meant to be the goddess of the underworld's son. He would go around kidnap bad kids and whip them with birch twigs as a counter to Odin. During the wild hunt he tried giving gifts. This is an example of Christian tradition co-opting pagan traditions - like mistletoe which is also pagan.

questions.question: Why is there no such thing as a size B battery? Why does it go straight from A to C?

answers.answer: There used to be B batteries. They were probably just a bit rubbish and withdrawn from service. They might have been used in bicycle lamps.

answers.caller: Bob from Risely (engineer, started apprenticeship with old radios)
answers.answer: Many years ago, most houses didn't have mains electricity and radios required three batteries: a valve heater battery, an HT battery, and a grid bias battery. Grid bias batteries had six cells in. Slowly, the system was rationalized and reduced over the years. B batteries started around the 1920s and fell out of usage in the 1950s as technology overtook them. They were used in bicycle lamps and various configurations.

questions.caller: Tim from Clapham (question for his friend Fred)
questions.question: Why do nuclear explosions create mushroom clouds? Why that specific shape?

answers.answer: It must have something to do with different things travelling at different speeds - water and debris go faster than other bits, some go up and some go out. Probably something to do with pressure.

answers.caller: Professor Hallis (Professor of Public Understanding of Science at University of Brighton)
answers.answer: In a hydrogen bomb, fusion bomb, it reaches the temperature of 100 million degrees at ground level. Hot air rises - and it doesn't just rise, it rockets. The hot air shoots up carrying all the debris and even gaseous rock with it. At some point as you go up, the density of air gets thinner. When the rising air reaches the same density as the air at the top, it starts flattening out. That's where the cap of the mushroom comes from. The hot air separates almost like a plasma due to density differences.

questions.question: Why is a doornail dead in the phrase 'dead as a doornail'? Why did Dickens describe it that way?
Why do cigarettes have a cork effect on them?

answers.answer: They used to be made of some sort of cork

questions.question: Why is a dog called a canine?

answers.answer: Canus, Latin for dog

questions.question: How many commoners marrying into the royal family before it ceases to become a royal family?

answers.answer: There is no answer - there is no such thing as a royal bloodline. Royalty is by dint of birth, not bloodline. Prince George is just as royal as his father even though his mother was a commoner

questions.question: Is the sun moving while we're all following it in orbit?

answers.answer: Yes, the sun and everything in our solar system is revolving around the middle of the Milky Way galaxy

questions.question: Why is a female calf born as twin with a male calf always infertile?

answers.answer: Called a free martin. When twins share placental membranes, blood vessels get close and share antigens and proteins across them. The female twin develops some characteristics of the opposite gender and is infertile (90% of cases). The male twin has reduced fertility but is less affected. This involves diffusion across blood vessels

questions.question: How do they determine safe speed limits for pedestrians? How did they arrive at 30mph?

answers.answer: Can't be objective - there's no algorithm. Speed limits in pedestrian areas are 30mph, and there's been calls to reduce to 20 in residential areas

Two parts: 1) F=MA equation determines what speed causes harm to the human body - in built-up areas it's 30, around schools 20. 2) Average reaction rate of a driver versus risk of someone stepping out, combined with deceleration rates - slower speeds allow quicker percentage deceleration per second. Motorway is 70 because you might be further behind the car in front

questions.question: Why doesn't ink leak out of a biro when you take it apart?

answers.answer: It's the viscosity - the ink is so thick it doesn't leak. The ball pen design means the back gets coated in ink, and as you write, the ball turns and brings ink from above

Atmospheric pressure pushes into the pen to keep ink in place because it's airtight at the top with no pressure from the other side to push it out. The straw-with-thumb analogy - when he stuck the toothpick down, it pushed ink aside allowing air to come in from the side, which pushed it down and it all spilled out. The thickness of the ink helps but even watery ink would hold due to atmospheric pressure

questions.question: What are the huge bulbous growths on the sides of trees in Richmond Park?

answers.answer: Known as burrs in England, burls in America. It's a deformation in the grain when the tree is growing - can be caused by trauma or fungus. Like a scab that never heals

questions.question: Why do dogs roll in fox poo?

answers.answer: Working dogs that hunt and flush out game do this primarily to mask their scent - they roll in fox or badger mess. The smell won't scare away potential prey because wild animals don't fear domestic dogs in the same way. Dogs won't roll in their own territory because they don't feel the need to hunt and flush out there. It's evolutionary

questions.question: When did people start smiling in photographs?

answers.answer: Shutter speeds and exposures - back in the day you had to stand still for a long time so a stern/resting face was best. As technology advanced and photos could capture moments rather than formal portraits, people could smile. The shift from formal to informal smiling came from camera availability

questions.question: Sometimes when I'm listening to music on my headphones, if I yawn, it sounds like the BPM is increasing. I spoke to a music producer friend who says when he wakes up in the morning and is working on music, it sounds like the BPM is faster and changes throughout the day.

answers.answer: It's the change of air pressure in the eustachian tubes that run from your ear drums through to the back of your throat. It sort of bends the note. It distorts it. The impression Roland gets is that it's speeded up but his brain is processing the information his ears deliver and telling him it's getting faster but actually it's just getting different.

questions.question: My kids want to know why cows poo pats and sheep poo pellets, given that they have identical diet.

answers.answer: Four stomachs. Therefore cows process the grass a lot more efficiently than sheep. Because it's just been processed in four different stomachs and all the... There's nothing left. You're talking about a pat. There's no fibre, no roughage, it's all been absorbed.

It's how they evolved, because cows evolved on lowlands and forests, whereas sheep and goats evolved in the mountains where there's a lot less moisture and also a lot less green foods. So when they excrete their droppings, they have taken all the moisture out of the food.

questions.question: How do forensic pathologists know who the dentist is of an unidentified victim, given that I presume there is no national database for dental records? And what about foreign visitors?

answers.answer: If you find an unidentified body you can't identify them from their dental records - you can confirm an identity that you suspect. There's a national database of dentists if you're an NHS dentist. You look at what teeth are present, what teeth are missing, which teeth have got what kind of fillings in. It creates a unique fingerprint. I had to do this once - I had a colleague read out the map and I would just nod or shake my head while clearing away maggots.

questions.question: Where do you draw the line between grave robbing and archaeology? How long does a grave have to be before you can dig it up and count yourself as an archaeologist?

answers.answer: Anytime, really, but they've actually got to get permission from a data analyst. It depends if the site's protected, or if it's recent, the family. So a marked grave, you can't dig it up without permission, but you can get permission if your case is strong enough. There's no distinction between archaeology and grave robbing because the rules are the same whether the grave is 500 years old or five years old.

questions.question: When you delete a file or information off your laptop computer, say you send it to the bin and then you empty the bin, where does that information go from then on?

answers.answer: On a computer system, when it writes a file, it accesses the index file which contains information about where the file is physically located on the disk. When you delete a file, the computer just deletes the entry in the index file so it no longer knows where the physical location of the parts of your file are. The old file is still there physically on the disk until it's overwritten by a new file. Unless you completely format the disk and degauss it (pass it through a massive magnetic field), then it could still be available even after you've overwritten it.

questions.question: When you see car adverts on television, the cars always have funny registration plates like FB006. I'm wondering where these come from and how they come up with those registration plate numbers?

answers.answer: They look funny because they use letters like A, H, 0, 1, M - anything that reads forwards the same as it reads backwards. They do this because when you want to advertise the same car in Europe, you just flip the image, and the registration plate reads correctly in reverse.
Palindromes - the registration plates are palindromes so they read the same backwards as forwards.

questions.question: How come dice have dots and not numbers? You can count dots but you might not know numbers if you were illiterate.
What is a country mile and is it a recognised distance?

answers.answer: If you're out in the country, you're walking uphill and down dale. If you stretched that out and flattened it, it would be a good quarter or half a mile longer than what it actually is. The opposite of 'as the crow flies' - when you're walking over the downs, up and down hills, you might have only covered a quarter of a mile as the crow flies but you've gone a mile up and a mile down. So it feels like a lot longer.

questions.question: Why is a tea towel called a tea towel? A bath towel is for when you're in and out of the bath, but a tea towel is just for about the chin, not necessarily to do with tea.

answers.answer: When they first started appearing in kitchens, they probably were what you picked up the teapot with. It's your towel for picking up the teapot.
Years ago, when you made a pot of tea, you used to put the tea towel over the pot to keep it warm. And then you'd use a tea towel to wipe the dishes up because it's nice and warm.

questions.question: Why does everything stop growing but your wisdom teeth start growing so many years later? And your ear hair and nose hair?

answers.answer: Evolutionarily, our diet used to be unprocessed, uncooked foods. Teeth would rot away over time, so we needed new teeth. Wisdom teeth came with age, hence 'wisdom'.

questions.question: Who and when was it decided that Number 10 Downing Street was going to be the home of the Prime Minister?

answers.answer: Donated to Robert Walpole by George II in the early 1700s. George II spoke little or no English. Robert Walpole was First Lord of the Treasury, de facto first Prime Minister. George Downing built it but was an 'absolute cowboy'.

questions.question: How come when you drink too much beer (90-95% water), you get dehydrated?

answers.answer: Alcohol in beer is a diuretic. It doesn't matter how much you drink, you'll still be dehydrated. A diuretic makes you urinate more than your body wants. You're excreting more liquid than you're taking in.

questions.question: Why do people say 'brass monkey' when it's cold? Why does it have to be a monkey?

answers.answer: The figure of speech refers to the bits of a brass monkey.
The cannonballs are stacked on triangular brass monkeys. When it got very cold, the brass contracted, allowing the cannonballs to slide off on Royal Navy ships.

questions.question: How does my hair maintain its thickness? Every time I wash it, hair comes out. I've been doing this for four years.

answers.answer: The longer it is, the more you're going to notice when it falls out. It's not falling out more than short hair does. It's just more noticeable. Hair length has no bearing on how much falls out - it just affects how noticeable the fallout is.

The quality of hair is determined by what you eat - protein, amino acids, good fats. The hair isn't falling out, it's just dying. Every time hair dies, hair grows back. He's only noticing because it's long.

questions.question: Why is a boxing ring square?

answers.answer: Originally it was a circle defined by the crowd. When it became formalized and raised onto a platform, it made more sense to have corners so boxers had somewhere to go between rounds.

It's the 'squared circle'. The ring was originally a circle. You couldn't square off a circle in a perfect circle. So you put four posts in to separate punters from wrestlers or boxers, and as soon as you put the posts in, you've got a square.

questions.question: What's the manufacturing difference between paper you write on and tissue paper? How do they create different densities?

answers.answer: Paper is made from wood. You dissolve wood in water, apply the slurry onto a moving belt which sucks the water out, leaving blotting paper. All paper starts like that. Then you apply pressure, heat, or coating to make it stronger, shinier, or whatever end result you want. For wood-free paper, you dissolve with chemicals instead of chopping with blades.

questions.question: What does a 'wake' mean in Ireland? Where did it originate?

answers.answer: Speculates: originally a vigil where you'd sit up all night observing the body.
Back in medieval times, medicine wasn't accurate as it is now. When somebody died, they would lay them out for 24 hours or so to see if they came round.

questions.question: Where is the proof that we're revolving around the sun? There's something called vortex theory where we're running around the tail of the sun.
If you were in a hot air balloon, at what height would you notice the Earth starting to rotate?

answers.answer: It's not a question of height, it's a question of time. You need a moving picture to see the rotation - time to judge it. If you leave a camera shutter open at night for 30 seconds, stars blur slightly. Leave it open for 10 minutes, and you'll see the blur from Earth's rotation. To see with naked eye, it's about time, not place. You could be anywhere - it's just about time.

questions.question: Where does the thumbs up or down meaning good or bad originate from?

answers.answer: Roman emperors in gladiator fights. The emperor looks down at the defeated gladiator and if he puts his thumb up, you're dead. If he puts it down, you live to fight another day.

You're almost right. In ancient Rome (thought to predate Rome), in gladiatorial context they used thumbs up which actually meant 'raise the sword to finish the guy off'. It was in much later paintings in the classical era that artists showed thumbs up and thumbs down meaning life or death.

questions.question: What's the process in your mind where you know something but can't access that information? Like recognizing music but not being able to pinpoint it?
Why does your nose run when you cry?

answers.answer: Salt water from the tear ducts moves downwards due to gravity and some comes down the nose

questions.question: Why do commercial microwaves not have the spinning platey thing in them?

answers.answer: Commercial microwaves have a mode stirrer underneath instead of a spinning plate. The ceramic plate at the bottom allows microwaves through and the stirrer moves the microwaves around for even heating. Domestic microwaves can also come without spinning plates.

questions.question: Why don't eyelashes go grey like all other body hair?

answers.answer: Eyelashes DO go grey - she has black hair and her eyelashes are going grey

questions.question: Is sand called sand because it's between the sea and the land?

questions.caller: Steve from Cheam (spelled with two E's)
questions.question: When you have a blood transfusion, how long does it take before the donor's DNA is gone from your system?

answers.answer: They take out anything that isn't a red blood cell with some kind of solution. They clean out all the DNA-related stuff.

Red blood cells don't have DNA to begin with. Your red blood cells have a life cycle and only live in your body for about 100 days. They separate the red blood cells from plasma and platelets. Some blood is used whole, some is separated depending on what the patient needs. They test it all for compatibility first.

questions.question: Why do corned beef tins still have that stupid key on top?

answers.answer: The tin is opened from the top with the key so there's no lip left around the edge. If you opened it normally with a tin opener, the lip would break up the meat when you try to get it out. The tapered shape also helps slide the corned beef out in one piece.
The key is for when you're at sea and bobbing about - you peel the middle of the tin. It's easier on a boat and you can slide it out because it's tapered. The top doesn't have a lip on it.

questions.question: Why do all expiry dates on crisps appear to be on a Saturday?

answers.answer: It's largely true but it's just because it's easier to print one date. They choose the end of the week, the last day of the week.

questions.question: What is the origin of 'wolf whistling'? Why is it called that when it doesn't sound like a wolf howl?

answers.answer: Looney Tunes cartoon characters of wolves would whistle at attractive female characters and it became known as a wolf whistle. They gave us so much at the turn of the century that got into society.

Going further back, the wolf in fairy tales was always a predatory male. Looney Tunes picked up on this fairy tale mythology. Men have always wolf whistled - it's a certain type of predatory man. The fairy tales have fed into everything from the beginning.

questions.question: What happens to the turkeys that are pardoned by the US President every Thanksgiving?

answers.answer: They all live on a farm in Connecticut.

questions.question: I've been watching Blue Planet and all that, and I was just wondering if all the dolphins can all speak the same language, or squeak the same language, I should say. So you mean if a dolphin got transported from the Great Barrier Reef to the coast just off Scotland, would they understand each other?

answers.answer: I just don't know. I don't know. One click might mean something else in Scotland as it does in Australia.

My partner used to work at SeaWorld in Miami. Whales and dolphins are known to have different dialects with completely separate clicks and pitch. Different pods of dolphins would communicate just as different pods of orcas would communicate differently. So no, they don't all speak the same language.

questions.question: Why, when we see something that makes us shocked or startled, do we raise our hands to our mouths? Is it the same reason why we cover our mouths when we yawn?

answers.answer: What you're actually doing is covering the gaping maw caused by your gasp. You're not using the hand as a reaction to the shock. You're using it as a camouflage of the mouth's reaction to the shock.

When you are completely shocked, you would normally just scream or something, so covering your mouth is a secondary reaction to prevent yourself from verbalizing it, and probably the evolutionary thing would be to prevent from panicking people. So you're preventing yourself from screaming or swearing at a very high volume by the hand being inexorably drawn up towards the orifice whence that exclamation would emerge.

questions.question: Do all mammals itch? And if they do, why?

answers.answer: What provokes an itch... it could be a flea or a mosquito that might be giving you malaria. So we have sensors in our skin that tell us that something has landed on us. And we then move our fingers towards that area to scratch and ideally kill the potential parasite.

There are two sort of reasons why mammals may itch. First, if you get an injury, you need your immune cells to get to that injury to fix it. There's a chemical called histamine that encourages your blood to flow to that area. The side effect of that is itching - it's not evolutionarily useful exactly, apart from alerting you to the fact there's something wrong. The other way is that certain lights or bugs, bacteria, viruses cause you to itch. For example, if it was a skin condition, you itch the skin, you can cause the skin to break down and actually release the material that can be caught by others. So it's actually a way of the bug essentially spreading itself through hacking your body.

questions.question: Is there any biological or chemical difference between people who are morning people and people who are evening people?

answers.answer: It must have something to do with the chemicals that you're producing in your sleep, mustn't it?

Melatonin. The light that your eyes collect is transferred to the brain by the optic nerves to the pineal gland. And the pineal gland is where the hormone melatonin is created to regulate your sleep-wake cycle.

questions.question: Why do petrol stations charge a decimal per litre of petrol that is not legal tender in the UK? Like 119.9p when the 0.9 is not legal tender?

answers.answer: The way it works is it means you can see the small fluctuations in the price of a litre of petrol, but the way that the pump works, it's never going to end on a fraction that can't be paid. It's like when vodka is advertised per unit price - you see a bottle is £14.99, you're charging per unit a sum of money that is not legal tender. It's just where they've done the dividing.

questions.question: If we live in the living room, we bathe in the bathroom, and we go to bed in the bedroom, what's the etymology of kitchen?

answers.answer: It'll come from the Latin, won't it? Cucina. I think it's probably a bit of both - French, Latinate roots.

The Anglo-Saxons used to cook on kuchen. It's basically Old English for cooking place. In Old English it's k-y-c-e-n (kuchen), which is related to Latin cucina. The Romans influencing the Germans influencing the Angles. All European languages have got a common ancestor, Indo-European.

questions.question: How close does lightning have to be to her swimming in the gulf to be dangerous? The gulf is about 30 kilometers wide.

How did four guys manage to pick me up using just the tips of their fingers? I weigh 25 stone. They held their hand above my head for five seconds, then did it again and I went right up to the ceiling.
Why does washing dishes (by hand or dishwasher) leave a horrible wet dog smell? I smell it in restaurants and bars too. I don't have a dog.

answers.answer: It's your drains, mate. You've got a blockage in your drain. You've got some gunk in your drain. When the water goes down, it reinvigorates it, and it wafts back up the pipes. You need to go to Robert Dyess and get bathroom blocker, or sodium peroxide. Put it down your kitchen sink. If it hasn't gone away, it's something to do with your dishwasher waste pipe. You just have bad drains.

questions.question: Answer to the chair lifting question - how do four people with just the tips of their fingers lift someone?

answers.answer: The seven chakras in a human body. When you put the hands above the head in the formation, you're transferring the energy from the human body into those hands, ever so temporarily. Then you have to quickly put the fingers in to the positions which were under the knees, or under the armpits. When you lift all together, you can lift the human body. It's all to do with energy transfer, and it's more of a spiritual energy.

Sizing came into commercial realm in early 19th century for military uniforms during Napoleonic era. Men's sizing came with chest measurements. Women's sizing was based on American government studies in the 1950s on volunteers, which weren't representative of the whole population. The numbers 2, 4, 6, 8 were just put onto categories. The American government came up with the dress sizes now used by retailers.

questions.question: Where does the term 'part and parcel' originate from?
Where does the term 'spam' come from in the context of computers and emails?
How can you start your own country? (and would Grimsby get an exemption because of their fishing industry?)
Can you be addicted to heroin if you don't know you've taken it?

answers.answer: The term spam comes from the Monty Python sketch - the one with 'spam spam spam spam spam spam spam' because it goes on endlessly and never goes away. This was adopted by people in the tech industry as an in-joke that's stuck. It's received wisdom in the tech community that it comes from Monty Python.

questions.question: What is the definition of an island? When is an island an island and when is it not?
If twins are born at 1:59am and the second twin is born 10 minutes later when the clocks go back (making it 1:09am), would the second twin be recorded as older?

answers.answer: If you find unclaimed land, you go to another country and ask them to propose you as a member of the United Nations. All countries vote on it - if they pass, you're an independent country. However, five countries have veto power (Britain, France, Germany, China, America/Russia). If it's under UK monarchy, you could never declare independence because Brits have veto at UN. He's worked 30 years on Kashmir independence.

questions.question: Do nose burps smell?

answers.answer: It all goes back to the French Revolution. In Parliament, anti-monarchists (the third estate, Jacobins) sat to the left, and those with links to the old aristocracy and monarchy sat to the right.

All notes in hospital maternity wards are handwritten. They make a note specifying whether it's BST or GMT. The only time this would matter is if there's something like a title to be inherited. The one biologically born first gets it. Birth certificates used to be handwritten so notes could be passed on. Digital birth certificates should have a process for recording this.

questions.question: Why is it called an English breakfast?

answers.answer: It's legal terminology referring to land. If you're going to sell or annex a piece of land, you refer to it as part and parcel of the new land. It means the entirety of something - similar to 'lock, stock and barrel'.

questions.question: Why don't we charge people with treason anymore?

answers.answer: According to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), specifically Part 8 called the 'Regime of Islands' - an island is a naturally formed area of land surrounded by water, which is above water at high tide. So technically Australia is an island, and the American continent is too since it's continuously surrounded by water.
An island has to be subcontinental. The largest island in the world is Greenland.

questions.question: Is dreaming the only time you dream? I wake up with dreams every morning, so I was wondering if that might be the only time you dream.

answers.answer: I believe so, because every time I dream and I'm halfway into my dream, the alarm goes off. But that's just the dream you can remember.

We always dream when we have REM sleep, what they call rapid eye movement. During the night we have two, three or even more periods of REM sleep depending on how long we sleep. If we wake up close to the REM sleep because the alarm goes off, then we remember it much better. Most of us actually dream multiple times during the night. We just don't remember it all.

questions.question: Does green tea evaporate faster than black tea? When I make tea, my green tea seems to evaporate much faster than my wife's black tea.

answers.answer: How long would they watch the tea for? Seriously, how long would you watch it to establish that one liquid was evaporating faster than another?
He probably pours the water into his tea first, so the green tea would be hotter and therefore evaporate a little bit more.
Black tea should evaporate faster than green tea because black tea should be made with boiling water, green tea at about 85 degrees.

I've run an experiment using two identical mugs with black tea and green tea, filled to the same line with water at the same temperature, and set a timer for five minutes. To the human eye, there's absolutely no difference whatsoever. If they're the same temperature, there's not going to be any difference at all.

questions.question: What are the small yellow signs on buildings? They look like 50p-sized yellow discs with crosshairs, always on the side of buildings at ground floor/first floor level.

answers.answer: They're there for construction, for tunnelling mainly. The engineers go around and monitor the buildings to make sure there's no sediment in the tunnels and that the buildings are not moving. They use a theodolite.

questions.question: What does the number in women's dress sizes represent? A size 12, size 14 - what does that number actually represent?
Why is hot on the left and cold on the right when it comes to taps? Every manufacturer, every tap is always hot on the left, cold on the right. Why?

answers.answer: It's internationally for the blind. So that people who can't see will know it's always in the same place, and even people who can see but can't anymore see the H and C or the red and blue.

It goes back to Victorian times when you had to pump water into the house by hand. Most people were right-handed, so the cold water hand pump went on the right. When we started using hot water heaters, the tap went on the left. It then got enshrined into regulations when regulations were introduced. The blind can tell the difference without burning themselves.

questions.question: How much power do the Queen's Guards at Buckingham Palace and Tower Bridge actually have? Are they the same as police or do they have legit military power?

answers.answer: I'm a former Coldstream guardsman. The guardsmen (red uniforms, bearskins) are actual soldiers. There are five regiments: Grenadier, Coldstream, Scots, Irish, Welsh guards. Within each palace, they're there in combat with weapons and ammunition and serve as a reaction force (QRF). During 7/7, the guard was stepped up in case anyone was targeting royal palaces. At the Tower of London, they patrol overnight and pick up drunkards. They just march through you if you're in the way - you don't stop for anyone.

questions.question: Why don't Americans have blackcurrant? Not as a drink, fruit, jam, or squash.

answers.answer: Blackcurrants were grown in North America but they damaged the timber and the fungus would have destroyed a lot of their manufacturing industry, so they got rid of everything that might carry the fungus.
Blackcurrants are actually banned in America.

questions.question: Does the movement of liquid against other liquid create friction and therefore heat? When water falls from a waterfall and hits water at the bottom, do the molecules rubbing against each other create heat?

answers.answer: Yes, anything moving against another object creates heat. That's the reason why rivers steam when it's cold and the breeze over will slow them down.

questions.question: What should I do about my smelly drain? The waste pipe is boxed in from a kitchen extension.

answers.answer: Get a plumber. You can buy that acid that's in the news at the moment. You pour it after the U-bend at the first connection. But if the pipe is boxed in, you'd need to undo it from the U-bend. That's why you need to get a plumber.

questions.question: Why don't squirrels eat conkers?

answers.answer: They're semi-poisonous to many mammals, including humans. Squirrels historically have eaten conkers and died, so all the other squirrels retained a sense memory not to eat the conkers.

questions.question: Why are buildings called buildings when they're already built?
Why does the TB jab leave such a horrendous scar when other jabs don't?

answers.answer: If your genetics or family bloodline have come into contact with tuberculosis in the past, you will have some antibodies to it. Therefore you will react to the antibodies being injected in the vaccine. That's why some people get a nasty infection and some people don't. The people that don't, their genetic line has not been subjected to TB in the past.

The BCG is given under the skin, literally just under your skin, and it creates a bubble. Most other injections go into the muscle so you don't get a scar. It's about how much antibody your body makes.

questions.question: What are the perfect circles of trees on top of hills in Cornwall?

answers.answer: They're old sacred sites, English heritage sites, burial mounds. Farmers aren't allowed to plough them so vegetation grows naturally. Because they're often circular, the trees form in a circle.

questions.question: Why are royals known as blue-blooded?

answers.answer: Back in the day, having darker skin meant you spent a lot of time in the fields (a peasant/pleb). If you were wealthy or aristocratic, you stayed indoors. This is why people powdered their faces to look paler. The paler you are, the more pronounced your veins are on your skin. Veins are blue. Ergo, blue-blooded means posh/royal - not spending time outside in the fields.

The expression comes from royalty ingesting silver as medicine (antibacterial) and using silver cutlery. Too much silver leads to a condition (name starting with ARG from argent meaning silver in French) that causes bluish skin.

questions.question: Where do drosophila (fruit flies) come from?

answers.answer: I don't know where they come from is the short answer.

questions.question: Why is the sky between the two rainbows of a double rainbow darker than the surrounding sky?

answers.answer: It's called Alexander's Dark Band. The light reflected off the first rainbow lightens the sky below it. The second rainbow is caused by light that's reflected twice off a raindrop and lightens the sky above it. The space in between the two rainbows, the light can't be reflected directly to you, so it appears darker.

questions.question: When and where does throwing pennies into wishing wells originate?

answers.answer: In old days water was precious and not available on taps. Any spring or well was often blessed with precious metal, usually silver (hence throwing silver coins today). It was a form of sacrifice - an offering to the spirit that made the water flow from the ground, giving everybody the means to live. It evolved into throwing a coin down a well and making a wish - essentially saying a prayer.

questions.question: Can somebody copyright their voice?

answers.answer: Radio and TV ads must be submitted and approved by an independent body. They won't let you use a voice that sounds like anyone unless you have their permission or their estate's permission. Parodies are allowed (like a cartoon Queen voice) but generally if you use someone famous's voice, you're implying they endorse the product. That's why they paid Morgan Freeman even though he didn't do the voice himself - they're paying for his name and association with the brand. A sound-alike would be sued.

questions.question: Why do toilet seats in this country have no gap at the front while in Mexico and the States they have a gap (horseshoe shape)?

answers.answer: The gap precludes tinkle from happening for three or four inches, it's an improvement on a gapless scenario
When a gentleman sits down, no chance of private parts touching the seat - it's pure hygiene
To give women room to wipe
Boyfriend owned a plumbing and heating supplies company - it's for women, found in public toilets in this country, hotel rooms are unisex

questions.question: Does anyone actually live in gatekeeper's lodges in parks permanently?

answers.answer: Some lodges are inhabited, some are storage facilities disguised as dwellings. Hard to say specifically.
I actually lived in New Lodge in Hyde Park near the Serpentine and police station for a while, working with someone who was in charge of the New Bridge Theatre

questions.question: Do astronauts on the International Space Station get to vote in elections?

answers.answer: Yes, it's more about logistics - can't do a postal vote from space

Since late 90s, Americans have been allowed to vote in space via email. A NASA astronaut's wife pushed for him to be able to vote and now they send encrypted emails or PDFs. British astronauts like Tim Peake can do a proxy vote.

questions.question: Where does the term 'dog tag' come from as regards ID tags worn by soldiers?

answers.answer: They were tags put on dogs, and when the military needed to identify dead bodies, similar tags were used and someone pointed out the similarity
Amateur historian - dog tags go back to Roman days when they stamped lead discs with basic information for new recruits. Those tags resembled animal registration discs and got cut down to dog tags.

questions.question: In 2,000 years' time, what will our era be referred to as? (like Vikings, Saxons, Victorians)

answers.answer: British

questions.question: Are dogs handed? Do they have a preference to left or right side of the body?

answers.answer: Maybe - if one dog goes right and another goes left, that would suggest they are handed. Though it might depend on direction of travel and lamppost placement.
Mine has recently started doing handstands when peeing by the river, she cocks both legs and supports herself on front paws

Yes, dogs do have hand preference. Universities and pet therapists have done research. The easiest way to tell is what paw they put forward first when starting a walk, and what paw they use to hold down a toy or bone. The leg-cocking is more for comfort, not related to handedness.

questions.question: Why in algebra is the unknown known as X? The alphabet has 26 letters, X already has a job as a multiplier, so why use it?

answers.answer: Speculated it might be an Arabic word for 'I don't know' or that unknown people who couldn't write would put an X

questions.question: What came first, the orange or the colour orange? There was a time when oranges were naturally green, and when the orange colour didn't exist, we would have called it red-yellow

answers.answer: Green oranges are unripe - the orange colour is a sign of going over. We've now bred them to be orange sooner because that's the colour we like.

The fruit came first. It was called a norringe from Narancia in Spain. People with red hair used to be called red-headed because orange was a type of red. Until the orange came along, we didn't have that word. The Dutch bred carrots to be orange - they used to be purple.

The colour came first. Humans evolved to see the electromagnetic spectrum, orange is well within that spectrum. We would have seen the colour before the fruit existed. Oranges were cultivated about 2,500 years BC and were named after the colour.

questions.question: Why do you have a checkered flag to finish a race? We have green to start, yellow for caution, red to stop, so why checkered for finish?

answers.answer: Rejected the tarmac suggestion - not having it

questions.question: If it's zero degrees outside today, what will it be tomorrow if it's twice as cold?

answers.answer: The question is invalid. Cold isn't a concept - it's the absence of heat. The centigrade scale is arbitrary based on water's properties (ice melts at 0, water boils at 100). Zero degrees centigrade is 32 degrees Fahrenheit. You can't say 'twice as cold'. If the question was about molecular movement rate, there are too many variables.

questions.question: Why do burglars in cartoons and comics always wear black and white stripes?

answers.answer: Possibly something to do with silent performance and pantomime, like Punch and Judy. Maybe related to Commedia dell'arte from 14th century Florence.
It might be something to do with prison jumpsuits - years ago they used to be black and white, like escaped convicts.

Back in the early 1800s, the Auburn system was introduced in America. Striped jumpsuits were introduced so prisoners were instantly recognisable, both in prisons and if they escaped. This then got picked up in films and translated into popular culture in other countries.

questions.question: Does hair have a finite lifespan? If you pull it out enough times, does it eventually stop growing?

answers.answer: It's the follicle, not the hair. If you get the follicle out, it won't grow back - like a hedge where you can cut it a million times but it never goes away unless you dig up the roots. It's very hard to get the follicle out though.

Hairs will not grow back from just plucking. They have to be caught when they're in their growing stage, and can only be killed by laser or electrolysis. The reason hairs feel softer on legs from waxing is because they've got tapered ends, not because they've changed. You just get lucky with timing.

questions.question: What is a 'click' when soldiers say 'seven clicks west' in military films?

answers.answer: It's a kilometre.
Military radios used to have poor quality sound, so 'kilometre' could be misheard as 'metre'. So they shortened it to 'clicks' so there was no confusion about distance.

questions.question: Why do we change the name of some animals to meat (cow to beef, pig to pork) but not others (chicken stays chicken)?

answers.answer: It's something to do with the Normans and when we started serving banquets in French.

It's French words for the meat on the table. The aristocracy spoke French and the peasants spoke English. So the meat was called what the French called it - beef, pork, mutton - while the animals kept their English names. Poor people didn't have meat on the table and couldn't speak French.

questions.question: Why are dusters traditionally yellow?

answers.answer: Ships used to fly yellow flags to indicate they were disease-free - a way of communicating to shore that the ship had been quarantined. The yellow colour became associated with being clean, hence yellow dusters.

questions.question: Why don't irons have an off switch? You always have to unplug them from the wall.

answers.answer: Because it's potentially hazardous, so it has a built-in encouragement to make sure you unplug it properly.
When you rotate the thermostat dial down to zero, there's a light that goes off, but there's no actual power switch. And yes, the safety reason is correct - to encourage people to unplug it.

questions.question: What is the most expensive thing ever put up for sale but never sold?

answers.answer: My half-drunk mug of green tea that I just put on the market for £10 billion.

NASA discovered an asteroid floating near Earth worth over $100 quadrillion. It's made of precious metals and titanium. If we could mine it, it would crash the global economy. It's never been for sale though.

Ibiza. Back in the 1980s, the Germans negotiated for three or four years to buy Ibiza from the Spanish. The offer went into the billions, possibly early trillions. But the deal fell through at the last moment because the Spanish people didn't like it.

questions.caller: Wayne (Basildon - calling from Spain on holiday)
questions.question: What is that noise you hear when you yawn? Like a white noise that diminishes what you can hear around you.

answers.answer: It's blood in your ears - the rushing blood through your veins. When you yawn, the extension of the jaw brings the part of your ear that hears closer to the vein.
It's muscles vibrating when they contract in the head. It's the same noise you hear when you squat.

questions.question: Can the heart develop cancer?

answers.answer: Yes, you can get cardiac tumours. It's incredibly rare because heart cells don't split like cells elsewhere in the body do. Because the cells don't split, it's hard for cancer to spread, but it is possible.

questions.question: Did William Shakespeare have any relatives who still benefit from royalties on his works? I saw he's still one of the top ten best-selling authors.

answers.answer: Copyright lasts about 70 years after an author's death. Shakespeare's been dead a very long time, so there's no estate getting royalties. That's why you can get his works free on Kindle.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'pardon my French' come from? You said it this morning when you swore.

answers.answer: I think after the Norman invasion, we did our swearing in French. All rude words were French.
It goes back to just after the Norman invasion. English were unhappy about it. When Normans would wander around speaking French, they'd say 'pardon my French' and try to speak in pidgin English.

French became a derogatory term for things considered dodgy - French disease, French leave, French letter (condom), French practices (shoddy work). If you spoke French in company where it wasn't expected, you'd apologize. Royalty spoke French well into the Regency period, so if you dropped into French with the wrong crowd, you'd say pardon my French.

questions.question: Are surgeons allowed to chat during surgery? Not just asking for equipment, but about love life, finances, football?

answers.answer: Yes, they do chat. The consultant sets the tone entirely. Some surgeons love a bit of chit-chat, some play classical music, some put on Monty Python. During the really tricky bits, they won't be chatting, but when they're just mopping up, they talk a lot. It's a very deferential hierarchy in surgical theatres.

questions.question: What do astronomers see when they look through a radio telescope? We have an optical telescope at home and discuss this around the dinner table.

answers.answer: I don't know the answer to that.

Radio telescopes see invisible light - radio waves from deep space - and transform them into something visible on a screen, like a thermal imaging camera. You can see the shape of the universe, electromagnetic fields, black holes, pulsars, quasars, rather than just visible light.

questions.question: Where do wagon wheels outside pubs come from? You often see them but I don't know the origin.

answers.answer: Historically, pubs were often trading posts or stopping points. If you needed a new wagon wheel, there'd be a blacksmith or stabling facility attached to a pub. So there was a practical reason. But now the only reason to have one is decoration.
[Answer received via Twitter but full text not shared on air]

questions.question: What's the relationship between cinemas and popcorn? We went at quarter to ten in the morning and everyone was having popcorn, but you never see it anywhere else.

answers.answer: I know the beginnings of the answer - in this country you don't see it anywhere else, but in other countries you might. But I'm not going to answer fully.

It was discovered in America where corn was everywhere. It was used as confetti because it was so abundant. Then in the early 20th century cinemas started using it because it was cheap to make and they could hike up the price. And it makes you thirsty so you buy more drinks.

questions.question: Does scratching a coin make it work in a pay and display machine? I put 50p in and it doesn't work, then scratch it on the side and it does.

answers.answer: It's an urban myth, categorically not true. We've done this before and a bloke who makes pay and display machines rang in. Correlation does not equal causation - eventually it would have worked anyway.

answers.caller: Martin from St. Albans (vending machine engineer)
answers.answer: I'm a vending machine engineer with 30 years of experience. In the coin mechanism there are sensors that photograph and analyze the metal. If you have a dirty coin and scratch it, it allows the sensor to work better. It doesn't always work but it CAN work. Licking would clean it the same way.

questions.question: Why are hairdressers and barbers never open on Mondays? They seem to be Tuesday to Saturday.

answers.answer: It's a staff rota issue - you don't have enough skilled people to run a rota like a shop. You can't just get someone in like a cashier. It's like fishmongers - fishermen aren't out on Sundays so there's no fish on Mondays, historically. It's a slightly old-fashioned piece of knowledge that doesn't apply anymore with refrigeration.

questions.question: Why do women in Peru and Bolivia traditionally wear bowler hats as part of their traditional dress?

answers.answer: I didn't know this was true but you're right, there are loads of pictures. I think the answer might just be that it's tradition, like why cowboys wear cowboy hats or people in boats wear boaters.
The brim protects from the sun and acts like a chef's hat to cool their heads. They came from European travellers, probably railway workers who built railways into South America.

questions.question: When were the first cremations recorded by mankind? I know the Vikings did it but were there earlier?

answers.answer: I think it goes back to early ceremonial burial with early religion. The Ganges is on fire - Indians have done it for centuries.
It was Neolithic. They've found burnt remains at Stonehenge - pots full of charred bones.

questions.question: Why do dogs' noses get wet when they're awake but dry when they're asleep?

answers.answer: Dogs don't have sweat glands in their skin, so they cool themselves through evaporation in the nose area via panting and breathing. During the day when the dog is active and hot, there's a lot of cooling going on, so the nose will be cold and wet. At night when less active, the cooling effect is reduced and the nose dries out.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'big cheese' come from? Why is the main person in a company called the big cheese?

answers.answer: It comes from Elizabeth I's reign. She cranked up the number of high days and holy days. On these days, you could only eat fish or cheese (called 'white meat' at the time). If you were rich, you could afford to buy a lot of cheese, so 'big cheese' meant someone with money and status.

questions.question: How do they cull deer in Richmond Park?

answers.answer: They shut the park and send in marksmen.

The park keepers do it themselves very professionally. They send in marksmen at night time with very good quality equipment. They cull young bucks and yearling stags (called knobbers or prickets). Too many bucks causes spiking injuries from bigger stags competing for mates. The venison is the most humane way to do it.

questions.question: Why do some remote controls allow you to put batteries in with both positive terminals facing the same direction, when normally one battery goes positive up and the next goes positive down?

answers.answer: Batteries can be put in series or parallel. When batteries are nipple up and nipple down, that's series (like in a long skinny torch) - the voltages add up. When all the nipples face the same direction, that's parallel - you get the same voltage from each battery but more power for a longer period. Remote controls are designed with batteries parallel because they don't need as much power.

questions.question: Why is Wales next to the sea such a good place to go to?

answers.answer: It's old-fashioned seaside and reminds him of his childhood. It's proper old-fashioned British seaside with penny arcades, good fish and chip shops, a pub on the corner, and beautiful beach huts with tea-making facilities. It's a bit like going back in time.

questions.question: Why can you cook on a cooker with a naked flame without producing carbon monoxide, but the same gas in a boiler can produce carbon monoxide?

answers.answer: It's about context and environment. A cooker is usually in a well-ventilated room, so any carbon monoxide dissipates. A boiler is in an enclosed space and runs for hours, so needs an exhaust. Chefs in hotels have massive ventilation shafts because they're cooking for hours. If you only had a boiler on for half an hour a day, you wouldn't have a carbon monoxide problem.

questions.question: What do passport control officers look at on their screens? Why does it take 10-20 seconds per person?

answers.answer: They're checking whether there's anything attached to your name and passport number - your identity, immigration history, whether you've done anything dodgy, whether authorities are looking for you. It would come up as an itemized list on the computer screen.

answers.caller: Chris from Croydon (20 years in Home Office)
answers.answer: What James said was pretty much right. You check whether the person is clean or has any issues on their record.

questions.question: Why do people always mount horses on the left side?

answers.answer: It's about which leg you swing. Almost everybody is right-footed, so they put their left foot in the stirrup and swing their right leg over.

It probably goes back to ancient times when soldiers had swords hanging on the left of their bodies to draw with their right hand. It was easier to put the left foot into the stirrup first. Left-handed people would have swords on the right and mount the other way.

questions.question: When did mankind first start mechanically refrigerating food? How did we get to making ice blocks before electricity?
Do conkers really keep spiders away?

answers.answer: The received wisdom is that conkers give off some sort of gas that spiders find repellent, which is why you put them in corners. About ten years ago, the Royal Society of Chemistry started investigating whether there's scientific basis to this belief. He can't remember if they've reported back. There was even a cash prize on offer for someone who could prove it.
You have to drill a hole in them and the smell puts spiders off - they won't come through the window.
He's tried it in his son's room and there are no spider webs or spiders. They don't like the smell, but there's no scientific proof - just anecdotal evidence that it works.

questions.question: Why do tennis balls come in a cheap plastic tube where they have a metal ring like on a can of cashews?

answers.answer: It's air pressure, not gravity. You have to keep them fresh. A tennis ball becomes softer over the years due to gas moving from high concentration to low concentration through the semi-permeable membrane. James called this osmosis but later corrected himself noting it may be diffusion for gases.

Pressurized balls are in a can sealed with air pressure. If left out of the can, pressurized ones go flat as pancakes. Pressurless ones also come sealed but aren't dependent on air pressure - they can be left for a year and still bounce, though the fluff wears off and they get smaller and faster.

questions.question: If one was to drop a small nuclear bomb in the eye of a storm, would it vaporise all the water and just kill off the hurricane?

answers.answer: He doesn't know. Nuclear bombs have side effects most people wouldn't consider positive.

A hurricane releases 50 or more terawatts of heat energy at any given moment, only 1% converted to wind, equivalent to 10 megaton nuclear bombs exploding every 20 minutes. Dropping a bomb would just turn it into a radioactive hurricane - the effect would be negated.

questions.question: Why do we go 'wee' when we push our children on swings?

answers.answer: He doesn't know. Suggested it might have come from a book, nursery rhyme, or just someone started it and everyone copied.
The first time a child gets on a swing they don't know what to expect and it can be quite scary. 'Wee' is a simple way of reassuring them that it's fun.

It's part of teaching children to enjoy the sounds that words make, as a build-up to phonics and reading. When you read Peppa Pig books with repetition like 'tee-hee-hee' or 'grunt grunt grunt', it's teaching children to play with sounds. When you have a newborn, you burble nonsense to them, playing with sounds. That's how they learn to read - by thinking about the sounds letters make. The 'wee' is a smiley noise associated with happiness.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'close but no cigar'?

answers.answer: If you did something good, your boss would give you a cigar. A cigar is a mark of success and reward. If you did something pretty good but not good enough, you'd be told 'close but no cigar.'

questions.question: If I run in the rain, will I get wetter than if I walk the same distance?

answers.answer: It depends on variables - how big you are, how hard the rain is falling, how fast you're moving. You would get less wet running than walking.
Running gets you less wet than walking. Formula given: W = P(A.V_R/V_F + A/D)

You're better to walk. Unless there's wind blowing rain, rain falls vertically and you're a small target. If you run, you run into rain as it's falling in front of you, which far outweighs the time you save by travelling quicker. It's about whether the water is going down or standing up.

questions.question: Why don't we recognize our own voice when recorded and played back to us?

answers.answer: Your head is a sounding bell - your skull. When you speak, the sound resonates through your skull to your ears (traveling backwards) as well as traveling forwards to everyone else's ears. When you record and play it, you're listening to what everybody else hears rather than what you hear. It's like when you have a cold in your ears - you think your voice has gone funny but it hasn't. Your skull is a resonant body.

questions.question: When you stroke a cat, why does it extend its back legs and stick its bum in the air?

answers.answer: The cat is magnifying the pleasurable sensation from the stroke, kind of like when you get tingles and you stretch it out.

It's a reflex reaction. If you touch them along the back near the spine, there's a nerve response and the leg will pick up in the air involuntarily. He has dogs that do the same - if you put your hand on their back in a certain place, they walk across the room on three legs.

questions.question: Why do golfers shout 'four' when a ball goes astray? Why not one, two, three, or 'we all woo'?

answers.answer: The origins aren't entirely clear but they think it's Australian and military. It's an abbreviation of 'beware before' - you'd be on the shooting range and need everybody to get out of the way, so you'd go 'Beware before!' and they'd get out of the way and you'd go boom boom boom boom.

Back in the day, you had a caddy to carry your bag and didn't really know where the ball was going. You had two men ahead of you who would watch where your ball landed, and you would call 'four left' or 'four right' to make them aware the ball was coming their way.

Golf originated in Scotland sooner than in Australia. There was a 'four caddy' in golf whose job was to find the ball in the grass. The phrase 'four' comes from the caddies. The military 'beware before' phrase is separate but both are right.

questions.question: Does anyone own the rights to the Big Ben bongs?

answers.answer: He doesn't think anyone could own the rights because the copyright would have expired so long ago. There's definitely an expiry date on copyright, and there's no way the Big Ben bongs are younger than that.

questions.question: Why does a ping pong racket have one red side and one black side?

answers.answer: The color denotes different surfaces - one is pimply, one is smooth. When he was a kid, he had a Schlesinger bat, black on both sides with different surfaces. You could put different spin on a ball depending on which side you used. The rule came in so opponents could see which side you were using. You couldn't flip it quickly to disguise your spin.

questions.question: Why do we say 'I'm on cloud nine'? Where does the phrase come from?
