answers.answer: The atmosphere is measured in levels and cloud nine is the highest level. When you're on cloud nine, that's as happy as you can be.
Zero cumulus is the highest of all nine types of clouds. Hence cloud nine, you're at the peak.
Cumulus is actually the lowest cloud in the sky. It's the big, fluffy ones. That may have been James leading him down the wrong path. Cloud 9 is actually the lowest cloud.
I was a seafarer for about 15 years and we used to report cloud types in weather observations. The book 'Cloud Types for Observers' explains this.

questions.question: Why do I assign the most difficult job to my left hand when making chord shapes on guitar? I strum with my right hand. Why does the less good hand do the trickiest bits?
Why is it that in cricket, only the wicket-keeper wears gloves among fielders? Why can't they all wear gloves like baseball catchers?

answers.answer: Because we're English and we set ourselves challenges. Also: wicket-keeper needs gloves for efficiency - easier to catch fast balls, essential for stumpings (can't do with bare hands), and they don't have to throw long distances like other fielders.

Just historical development. A keeper gets the ball more often than anyone else in the field. It makes him better. There's a difference between laws and rules - gentleman used to use hats to catch but it was made against the laws.
Qualifications: played cricket for 45 years, biggest innings 135 in Sunday 2s league.

questions.question: When does a hill become a mountain?

answers.answer: I know it in America - 1,000 feet (about 300 metres). But not sure if it's still true or applies to Britain.
It's to do with underlying composition - a hill is earth, a mountain is rock. Goes back to geography O-level.

Anything above 300 metres above sea level. I saw this in a film with Hugh Grant called 'The Man That Went Up A Hill And Came Down A Mountain.' He was a topographer deciding what were mountains and hills.

questions.question: Answer to guitar question - why does the less dexterous hand do the fretwork?

answers.answer: It's actually quite difficult with both hands when you start. The rhythm thing is the bigger part of the answer. It's harder to keep a sense of rhythm with your non-dominant hand. You're keeping the rhythm with your right hand and teaching your left hand to keep up with it. The rhythm is the most underestimated part of being a decent player.

questions.question: At what point does breathing in pollution while exercising outdoors become more harmful than the exercise itself doing you good?
How do they measure the height of waves? How do they know a wave is 20 feet?

answers.answer: Take a picture and measure with a ruler, times by the scale your camera works on.
Two methods: fixed buoys with chains and elastic bands that stretch as waves hit - computers calculate the measurements. Also LADA radar on offshore drilling rigs.
Qualifications: master on a wind farm vessel servicing turbines near Yarmouth.

questions.question: Why is the top of my shin bone on both legs so jagged when all my other bones are smooth? Was I born with it or is it from falling as a child?

answers.answer: It's actually fluid that builds up as you get older in order to protect the front of your shin. Nothing to do with getting kicked as a child.
Qualifications: played rugby for 12 years and is absolutely riddled with rumour.

questions.question: Why are parrots and budgerigars the only birds you can teach to speak? What do they have that other birds don't?
In what year will a 2003 calendar work again? I had 300 calendars printed by my agent in 2002 for a modelling career. My mum bought about 300 of them.

answers.answer: The last time it would have worked was 2014. He missed it. Next time will be 2025. It's an 11-year cycle. There's a handy website.
The next year matching 2003 is 2020. Wednesday is the first of January, and that was right in 2003.

2020 is wrong because it only works for January and February. 2003 wasn't a leap year but 2020 is. Because of leap years, it's not a simple cycle. For 2003, the calendar will be the same again in 2014, 2025, 2031. Bingo - 2025.

questions.question: Why in deathbed scenes in films does someone lean over and close the eyelids of the deceased? Why wouldn't the eyes naturally close like when you're sleeping?

answers.answer: I think it takes effort to close your eyes. The natural state doesn't involve closing them.

When a person takes their last breath, they get a bit of a shock, gasping for air. They open their eyes and that's how they pass. If you've died with your eyes open, they're not going to naturally close because there's no muscle control. When you're asleep and hear a plate fall, you open your eyes immediately - same thing with the last breath shock.

questions.question: Why is it called an Indian summer?

answers.answer: Nothing to do with the country India. It's about Native Americans. It means the Native Americans' hunting season was longer.

questions.question: How much force measured in a unit of measurement would it take to knock someone unconscious? For an average bloke, five foot nine.

answers.answer: Roughly about six pounds of pressure square on would knock out an average-sized man.

An untrained person is about 110 pounds. A professional boxer needs a lot less than that. A person gets knocked out by heavy contact with the jaw or temple - it's the cranial nerve in the jaw that doesn't like being hit, which switches the brain off. The temple is more to do with brain rattle.

questions.question: Why do coins have dates on them but banknotes don't?

answers.answer: Banknotes don't need dates because they have serial numbers, from which you can tell how old the note is.

Historically, coins had innate value (gold or silver), so the date affected the coin's value - older or younger coins had different values. With banknotes, they have serial numbers for counterfeiting purposes, but banknotes can't garner more value if they're young or old, unlike coins.

questions.question: Where does 'mm-hmm' come from as a yes or no answer? Is it just learned behavior or did someone come up with it?

answers.answer: It's learned behavior, just like nodding and shaking your head. In other cultures you wouldn't use them in quite the same way.

questions.question: How are the numbers arranged on a roulette wheel? Is there a system?

answers.answer: It's to skew it in the house's favour. You get odd/even, red/black, and high/low numbers separated as much as possible. So when you look at a roulette wheel, you never know what to bet on because any combination of high numbers isn't placed next to each other - that would let you bet on multiple adjacent numbers and have a better chance.

questions.question: Why do we use the letter X for kisses in texts, Christmas cards, birthday cards?

answers.answer: They used to put a cross on letters to confirm honesty. Then the person signing would put a cross, like a kiss, across the top of that cross to confirm what they were sending was indeed their honest part of the letter. So it was a confirmation of truth that evolved into meaning a kiss.

questions.question: When archaeologists dig down to see where people used to live, does that mean the Earth is always getting bigger?

answers.answer: No, because stuff sinks. Built on the surface, 20 years later it's 20 metres below. Worms bring soil to the surface, we shed skin creating dust. But the Earth isn't getting bigger because of the finite nature of matter - just redistribution.

questions.question: Why is an ice cream with a flake stuck in it called a 99?

answers.answer: 99 centimetres tall - industry standard length from the cone to the tip of the ice cream.
It was all to do with the Italian Royal Family. They had an elite guard of 99 soldiers. Anything that's elite or good is called a 99.

questions.question: Why do we get large raindrops and small raindrops? What causes the difference?

answers.answer: It's to do with updraft. On unstable days with big clouds, the clouds push rain higher and the raindrop grows collecting more water. If there's not a lot of updraft, you get drizzle - small fine rain. Thunderstorms have large updrafts because of the heat.

questions.question: Why did 3D glasses change from red and blue lenses to the grey polarized ones? What changed in the technology?

answers.answer: Two completely different ways of creating a 3D image. The old red/green was done with colour separation - green and red fringes created the 3D effect on paper and screen. The new way is different.

The newer glasses use more sophisticated technology. What's projected on screen is an image for the left eye and an image for the right eye, and the glasses split them properly. The old red/green system split it just in two dimensions, but nowadays with proper left and right cameras for animation, you can go further back and it looks more convincing. That's why the red/green worked on paper too - it was just two dimensions.

questions.question: How do they tunnel under the sea? How do they keep the water back when putting sections of tunnel in?

answers.answer: When they built the Channel Tunnel, they dig down well below the level at the bottom of the sea - probably about 100 feet below. The boring machine takes away the earth, then they put concrete segments in place and bolt them together. You're going along under the sea, surrounded by soil, not water.

questions.question: If all plants and plankton stopped producing oxygen tomorrow, how long would we have left? How long would the existing oxygen last?

answers.answer: About three quarters of the oxygen in the atmosphere is from algae in the water, not plants. So if all plants stopped, we'd still have a lot of oxygen from algae.

questions.question: Why does the academic year start in September?

answers.answer: Back in 1899, the Education Act made school compulsory for all children. There was big uproar from families who needed their children to work on farms during harvest. The concession was a long summer holiday so they could work the fields, then school started in September. Qualifications: university lecturer in education history and education policy.

questions.question: Does cheese before bed really give you nightmares, or is it just a myth?

answers.answer: Cheese does make you have more vivid dreams, but I can't remember why.

There's tons of anecdotal evidence, but scientific studies have been inconclusive. Cheese contains amino acids that might affect the brain, but no direct cause has been proven. The best explanation is that cheese causes indigestion, which interrupts sleep, and when you're in the threshold space between wake and sleep, that's when you remember your dreams. We're not having more dreams - we just remember them better. The association with Ebenezer Scrooge may be where the myth originates.

questions.question: Is it true that Disney owns the rights to Happy Birthday?

answers.answer: Disney does not own the rights to Happy Birthday.

Happy Birthday was owned by Warner Chapel Music until about a year ago when a film director took a case against them. She was making a documentary about the song and was ordered to pay $1,500 to use it. She sued to stop them charging people, and the judge ruled the song should be in the public domain. Warner Chapel was ordered to repay $14 million in royalties. Qualifications: music teacher who taught about copyright law in college.

questions.question: Why do they say a building was 'razed to the ground' when 'razed' means raised?

answers.answer: It's spelled R-A-Z-E-D, which is a different word from raised (R-A-I-S-E-D). Think of it as raised meaning removal, like a razor or eraser. They're raising the building to the ground.

questions.question: Why don't animals like lions or silverback gorillas get sexually transmitted diseases?

answers.answer: Yes, animals can get STDs. Koalas can famously contract chlamydia. There's a story in the paper about One Direction going to Australia Zoo, holding koalas, and some urinated on the band members, who then had to get sexual health checks. If koalas as a mammal can get STDs, other mammals should be able to contract similar diseases.

questions.question: Why does your ability to control your bladder completely disappear at the end of a journey when you've been controlling it all along?

answers.answer: It's psychology - your brain sends a message saying you're nearly there.

It's all tied up with the autonomic nervous system and its relationship to the sacral anterior root which controls the muscles in your bladder neck. It's a learned behaviour - babies don't have it at first. When the bladder fills up, it sends a message to the brain that it needs emptying, and as adults we can override that, but at a cost (raise of blood pressure and pulse). When you see a visual cue like a bathroom stall, your brain says 'enough messing around, go and relieve yourself.' Qualifications: spinal injuries nurse who worked with a urologist who did implants for spinal injured people.

questions.question: If there are 365 days in a year and 52 weeks in a year (52 × 7 = 364), where does the extra day come from?
Do any other animals have pets?

answers.answer: No is the sad answer. They have symbiotic relationships but not pets in the sense of keeping another animal around for fun and frolics.
Monkeys do keep pets. Bigger predatory monkeys sometimes catch young smaller monkeys and keep them as pets, protecting them from the rest of the group. He saw this on a programme before Christmas.

questions.question: How much closer to the sun would the Earth have to be for life not to be viable?

answers.answer: It's all about the Goldilocks zone and liquid water. For life to exist, you need water in a liquid state, which depends on the star size and planet distance. The original question went on a red herring - the North Pole is cold not because it's further from the sun but because the sun's rays hit at a steep angle. We exist because we're in the Goldilocks zone - neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water. Closer to the sun and water would be gas; further and it would be ice. You could calculate this but there are too many variables for a precise answer.

questions.question: If you fly in the direction the Earth is rotating, do you get there faster? If two planes fly the same route in opposite directions around the globe, which arrives first and by how much?
Why does it take longer to fly back from New York (9 hours) than to fly there (7.5 hours)?

answers.answer: That's a load of rubbish. If you're exactly the same mileage from London and you're on the other side of the Earth, it doesn't matter which way around you go - it's exactly the same distance. Travel time would be the same with no headwinds or tailwinds. Qualifications: training to be a private pilot.

questions.question: Why do we all laugh in the same way? Someone in Japan laughs the same way as us.

answers.answer: Laughter isn't a language - it's a physical reflex action, like yawning. It's not a learned behaviour like nodding or shaking your head. Babies laugh as a reflex.

questions.question: How does my body know when a hair is detached? If I'm walking around with shoulder-length hair and it sometimes tickles me, when I find it to pull it away, it's actually detached from my head.

answers.answer: Your body can't distinguish between attached and detached hair. It just knows you're being tickled. The difference is that a single detached strand tickles differently than when hairs are touching en masse as part of a whole (like a ponytail or head of hair). It's like how you can't be tickled with a brush, but a single bristle will make you giggle.

questions.question: How do they grow seedless grapes?

answers.answer: They're not actually seedless - they just have very soft seeds that are malleable. The seeds exist but are barely noticeable.

questions.question: Where does the extra day come from if 52 weeks × 7 days = 364? (Answering Alan from Perthly's question)
Who is Pete in 'For Pete's sake'? Who was he for Pete's sake?

answers.answer: Saint Peter. It's a way of swearing without swearing - taking a saint's name in vain. Instead of saying God's sake, you say Pete's sake.
Probably the old St. Peter. We'll find out for you.

questions.question: Why are the home counties called the home counties? Why isn't Worcestershire a home county?

answers.answer: It comes from the Army and Navy personnel coming home from various world tours and European tours, particularly during the 18th and 19th centuries. They needed places to live in those counties so they could embark quickly when needed.

It has to do with judges' circuits when they were going around presiding over Assize courts. The London circuit was around the home counties, and since London was 'home', they were called the home counties.

questions.question: If I've got two items the same size but different weights and I drop them from a height, they'll both hit the floor at the same time. Why is that?

answers.answer: Everything falls at the same rate. Light things appear to fall slower than heavy things because of the density of air and resistance. If you imagine a feather floating down, it's resistance causing that, not velocity. If you put a feather and a cannonball in a vacuum, they would fall at the same rate. This was proven by Galileo at the Leaning Tower of Pisa.
It's not true. If you're high up enough, I guess they might both reach terminal velocity.

questions.question: How fast can a mouse run? If a mouse was the size of a car, what speed would it go? If a mouse was the size of a human, would it be faster than Usain Bolt?

answers.answer: Her son looked this up about 10-12 years ago. He calculated that a mouse the size of a human would be able to run at 150 miles per hour, and at his height about 120 miles per hour.

questions.question: On TV programs and movies where they have a completely made-up language, like Game of Thrones, is that language a proper language? Do they actually spend the time to create structure and verbs and nouns?

answers.answer: In the books, Martin only had a few words and phrases for Dothraki. But for the TV series, they hired a linguist called David Peterson who constructed the entire language from the small bits in the books. It needed consistency so actors could actually speak it.
Tolkien was a linguistics professor and constructed incredibly detailed languages for Lord of the Rings. George R.R. Martin probably didn't undertake similar work for Game of Thrones.

questions.question: Is sticking your tongue out to touch food before you bite it a sign of getting old? Billy Connolly made a joke about this.
What are those little colored squares or circles at the bottom of newspaper pages for? On the sports page they're green but there's no green on the marks.

answers.answer: They're called registration marks. All colour printing is four-colour printing: cyan, magenta, yellow, and black. Every photo is made up of a density of dots of these four colours. Even if a photo has no red in it, the red marks will still be there. If it's a red shirt, the magenta dot will be heavy; if it's a white shirt, it will be almost non-existent.
It's almost certainly a printing thing linked to printing.

questions.question: Is it possible to get 100% pure water? A window cleaner told me he uses 100% pure water, and I don't believe him.

answers.answer: Reverse osmosis. It goes through a semi-permeable membrane at pressure, rejects the impure water, and only pure water gets through. Window cleaners use this process to get pure water - it takes out all the minerals and limescale so it doesn't leave residue when it dries.
No, because water is the universal solvent. Whatever you put it in, it will pick up some kind of chemical. Even if you boil it, it has minerals, fluoride, chlorine.
You could create pure water by firing hydrogen and oxygen at each other in a vacuum.

questions.question: Aerosol cans - when you get to the bottom and give them a violent shake to try and get that little bit more out, does that make any difference? Is there any reason for shaking it or is it just a habit?

answers.answer: When you get to the last part of the contents, they settle on the bottom of the canister. The compressed air within becomes more dense and needs to expel those particles. The only way to get them to the top of the canister is to give it a shake. So it completely works.

questions.question: Why is the leap day in February? Why did we choose to have it in that month and not any other month?

answers.answer: Because it's the shortest month. If you need to stick an extra day somewhere, it makes sense to put it on the shortest month. The reason February is short is because Augustus Caesar took a day off February and stuck it on August to make his month longer.

questions.question: Where does the knock-knock-knock-knock-knock-knock sequence come from?

answers.answer: Shave and a haircut, two bits. It comes from people going door-to-door, and it's American.

questions.question: Why is a dry volley called a dry volley and a wet volley called a wet volley in tennis?

answers.answer: A dry volley is when they take it in the air and carry on the swing through. There's no such thing as a wet volley - Christian misheard 'drive volley' as 'dry volley' and invented the existence of a wet volley.

questions.question: Is body scent hereditary? I smelt like my dad when I took off my T-shirt - is it in your jeans/your smell?

answers.answer: Mammals have the same genetic scent as a mother until early adolescence when puberty kicks in. It's a survival mechanism so parent animals know the scent of their own animals and know when to feed them. When they reach adolescence and become more independent, things change. Environment, food, clothes, washing towels, perfumes have an effect, but stripped down to basics it's the same as your mum up until 11, 12, 13.

questions.question: Why are bumblebees particularly attracted to lavender? Is it a scent thing or the quality of the pollen? I don't see honeybees visiting and don't see bumblebees visiting other flowers like roses or poppies.

answers.answer: Bees see plants in ultraviolet light, different to how humans see the colours. Lavender attracts bees. There's also been a huge decline in pollinator habitat - 75% lost - so when suitable plants appear, all pollinators condense there. Different species of bumblebees have different tongue lengths - some can access deep flowers, others only flatter ones. In the questioner's neighbour's garden it could be a combination of lavender species, bee species, and geography - there might not be any honeybees in the district.

questions.question: Why do boats steer from the back? Cars steer from the front. Why haven't boats evolved?

answers.answer: Turning circle - if you steer from the back, you've got a much tighter turning circle than if you're steering from the front. Also, if you had the engine at the front, the back of the boat would be up in the air.

Works for London Duck Tours. The real reason is about sailing ships - with the tide, if you tried to turn with a front rudder, your back would be swung right round. You can compensate from the rear but not from the front.

questions.question: Why do doctors sign prescriptions when no one can verify the signature?

answers.answer: If you wanted to investigate whether a prescription had been falsely issued, you would go back to the issuing doctor and ask, is this your signature? The signature's impenetrability doesn't prevent identification by the author.

questions.question: Why do women like hotter temperatures than men? (e.g. shower too hot for men after women)

answers.answer: Women carry more body fat than men, so they take longer to warm up. That's why they want the heat turned up - the same as the central heating argument.

questions.question: How do bakeries cut a giant custard slice into individual pieces without squashing all the custard out?

answers.answer: Different bakeries use different methods: 1) Sharp serrated knife for thin pastry so you don't need much pressure, 2) Mould/guillotine type tool that cuts perfect lines, 3) Fridge the slices first so the cream firms up and is easier to cut without it squeezing out.

questions.question: Can you have thunder, lightning and snow at the same time?

answers.answer: Yes - it's also known as thundersnow or a winter thunderstorm. It's very rare to get lightning with it, but it is possible, only in the strongest weather conditions.

questions.question: Do butterflies have memories of when they were caterpillars?

answers.answer: Exposed caterpillars to a noxious stimulus plus something they'd associate with it in a conditioning experiment. Then let them pupate and hatch as butterflies, then exposed the butterflies to the same conditioning trigger and they responded the same way. So yes, butterflies can remember stuff from when they were caterpillars. But whether they could articulate the difference between being a butterfly and a caterpillar is impossible to know since any scientific experiment can only observe from the outside and manipulate and observe, never get into subjective experience.

questions.question: What's the origin of the phrase 'throwing a paddy'?

answers.answer: It's a slightly rude reference to Irishness, a derogatory term for Irish people. Historical rationale based on Irish complaints about English oppression - throwing a paddy like moaning about William of Orange's troops coming over and killing loads of Catholics.

Paddywhack is another name for the nuchal ligament in animals - the ligament that helps big animals like cows, sheep and goats hold their necks up. When slaughtering an animal, that ligament is called the paddywhack.

questions.question: What were smelling salts made of, and are they still used?

answers.answer: Ammonium carbonate. Yes, you can still buy them - Holland and Barrett sell them. It sublimates and releases ammonia - a pungent ammonia waft that goes right out of your nostrils and kicks you back into animated form if you're unconscious.

questions.question: Why do killer whales in captivity have flopped dorsal fins but in the wild they don't?

answers.answer: Because they are depressed and anxious. Referenced the Netflix documentary Blackfish about killer whale Tilikum - it goes into detail about the biology behind it. Like humans who hunch over and look down when sad, killer whales' dorsal fins go flaccid when they're sad.

questions.question: Why do tennis players bounce the ball every time they're about to serve?

answers.answer: Twofold answer: 1) Physically, it helps get your body in the right position for the serve - the left arm for a right-handed player goes through an arc when you throw the ball, and bouncing the ball helps describe that arc in reverse to get your body in position for an over-arm serve. 2) Psychologically, it's ritualistic - like Rafael Nadal who goes through an identical set of voluntary but involuntary-looking movements including bouncing. It's about clearing your mind and getting in the zone because if you imagine missing your first serve, you will miss it.

questions.question: Does having the air conditioning on use more petrol than having the windows down?

answers.answer: The claim about drag from open windows is wrong - there's not that much drag from open windows, and the car's aerodynamic whether windows are open or shut.
On Top Gear they said if you switch off the air conditioning you save about 10% power.

Helen's partner is absolutely right. The air conditioning takes quite a lot of power - a big compressor (used to be Freon), an electric clutch that takes a lot of current. If you're stationary in traffic and press the AC on, your voltage drops and engine speed drops. It takes about 3 kilowatts, which is around 4 horsepower. On a 200 horsepower average car engine, that's about 2% reduction in power. Every time she turns the air conditioning on, they're throwing pound notes out the window.

questions.question: Why are cream crackers called cream crackers when there's no cream in them? And why are water biscuits called water biscuits?

answers.answer: It's about the creaming process in how they add the oil to the flour and water mixture - they cream it. Water biscuits are exactly what they say on the box - made just with water and no oil. They were designed because cream crackers couldn't stand long journeys on ships - they'd perish more because of the oil content in them.

questions.question: What's the origin of flying the Union Jack upside down being a sign of maritime distress?

answers.answer: Any flag that's not fully symmetrical can be flown upside down as a separate signal. If you've only got one flag on your boat and you want to send a message different from everything's hunky-dory, how can you do it with a flag except by turning it upside down?

questions.question: Why do we brush our teeth with cold water when hot water is better for washing up? And would warm water improve tooth cleaning?

answers.answer: Historically, hot water tanks were in the loft and could be susceptible to pollution - his mother remembered her dad finding a dead rat in the water tank in Sheffield in the 1950s. That's why you wouldn't use hot water to brush teeth. Now with combi boilers, hot and cold come from the same source so nothing to stop you using warm water.
Hot water would soften the bristles on the toothbrush, making it less effective at cleaning - you'd want stiffer bristles, hence cold water.

questions.question: Why does the woman on toilet signs appear to have one leg while the man has two?

answers.answer: It's not one leg - she's got two legs held close together. The point of the signs is to highlight the differences between men and women to avoid people going through the wrong door. If the woman had her legs apart like the man, you'd need a much bigger skirt to distinguish them. The more differences you can get on the sign, the less likely anyone is to go through the wrong room.

questions.question: Is Andy Murray still officially Wimbledon champion even though he's been knocked out?

answers.answer: Yes - he's the reigning champion until someone else wins it. Like golf when they hand over the blazer - you are the reigning champion until the next tournament. Even if Andy Murray had passed away, he'd still be Wimbledon champion until someone else wins it.

questions.question: Why do newborns' first words typically end up being mum or dad rather than their own name? They hear their own name the most, so shouldn't that be the first word?

answers.answer: The professor will probably call up. I think the answer is the simplicity of the words mum and dad. Even if his son was called Doug, he'd still say mama or dada first, not Doug.
They're the easiest words to say.

Babies' first sounds are ma-ma and da-da because they're the easiest sounds to make developmentally. In different countries we interpret these sounds differently - in Norway 'da' means 'look at that' not father. It's a self-reinforcing thing. The baby makes the sound, we interpret it as meaning mummy or daddy, then we reinforce it by saying 'yes, mummy' etc.

questions.question: How do they measure blood loss during childbirth? When she was discharged she got a paper showing she lost 800mls, but nobody was standing there with a bucket.

answers.answer: The only circumstances in which people collect blood in a bucket is if they are making black pudding.

Former midwife. Big blood loss or after operations: they weigh everything soaked by blood (knowing weight beforehand, then subtraction). In delivery room or home birth: staff are trained on estimation, proven 98% accurate. For water births: very vague estimation.

questions.question: Why is rugby popular in Argentina but not in the rest of South America? Rugby is only really big in Argentina and Chile (because of the famous plane crash).

answers.answer: Welsh emigration - lots of Welsh sheep farmers moved to Patagonia and they took rugby with them.
Confirmed James was right. He went to a Welsh language high school where Welsh history including Patagonia emigration was taught.
Many football clubs were set up by English settlers: Boca Juniors, River Plate, Newell's Old Boys, and even Arsenal.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'break your duck' come from? You've been wondering for five years.

answers.answer: From cricket. Zero in cricket is called a duck. Bowled out on first ball is a golden duck, first ball of innings is a diamond duck. It's called a duck because when you write zero in the scorebook it's the same shape as a duck's egg.

questions.question: What happens to DNA in blood once you donate it? Will the donor have different DNA from the recipient?

answers.answer: There's no way that receiving a blood donation changes your DNA.

answers.caller: Professor Hall (University of Brighton, Professor of Public Understanding Science) - Answer
answers.answer: Red blood cells don't have a nucleus at all, so no DNA. They last about three months then die and are replaced. White blood cells do have DNA and last days, so theoretically donor DNA could be found for about 24 hours after donation. But if you have an organ transplant, you permanently have donor DNA.

questions.question: How do you find what you're looking for in a Chinese library? Their alphabet has 20,000+ characters, not 26 like ours.

answers.answer: Surnames - there's a much smaller number of characters that can appear at the beginning of Chinese surnames. The anglicised version of Chinese names (Mr Li, Mr Wong, Mr Wang) would work alphabetically.
Chinese libraries use pinyin - Romanised alphabet version of Chinese characters - to organise their library. The anglicised version of the author's surname is used to arrange the books.

questions.question: Why don't hotel rooms have big ceiling lights like residential homes do? You always have to use lampshades and spotlights.

answers.answer: Lower ceilings in hotel rooms than at home, so you'd bang your head on a pendant light.
American culture - in California, no bedroom lights in ceiling because if there's an earthquake, the light doesn't fall on the sleeping person. That's why 99% of hotel rooms follow this pattern.
Nonsense about earthquakes. Down lights can fit emergency lighting packs for power cuts. Also easier for chambermaids to change bulbs without calling maintenance.

questions.question: Are humans the only animals that cry tears when sad? His seven-year-old son George asked after watching his four-year-old brother have a meltdown.

answers.answer: Only elephants can cry. David Attenborough documentary - elephants have the same memory as humans and they cry. When a lion kills a cow, they gather round and cry real tears.
Camels cry tears. He watched a documentary (given by Rosemary Duffy) showing a baby camel separated from its mother, and tears came down.
I'm not buying the camel or the elephant. I'll get you one next week, George. Get your dad to remind me.

questions.question: How come space is so cold when the sun is so hot? If you're ejected from a spaceship you freeze, but the planet is heated by the sun. What happens to the heat energy traveling through the gap?

answers.caller: Professor Martin (Manor Park, Professor of Robotics and former physicist) - Answer
answers.answer: Heat gets absorbed by anything it lands on. In a vacuum there's nothing for it to land on, so it keeps travelling until it lands on something. You will feel it as soon as you stand in the way.

questions.question: Why do you have names like John Brown, John Black, John White, but not red, yellow, blue? Why don't you know anyone called Johnny Red or Peter Purple?

answers.answer: It comes from the time when people didn't really have surnames. They got named after their jobs or where they lived or their hair colour. Brown for brown hair, black for blacksmith, green for green grocer or living near the green. But there weren't jobs that fitted yellow or purple.
answers.qualifications: Excellent book Mothertongue by Bill Bryce

questions.question: Why don't babies get hay fever? I have a 13-month-old, and my wife and I have really bad hay fever, but the baby doesn't. From everybody I've asked, nobody has babies with hay fever.

answers.answer: Yes, babies do get hay fever. My son, born August 2015, has hay fever because in summer 2016 his eyes were red and watering and he was sneezing. He actually says 'hay fever bad' and pretends to ring the doctor saying 'doctor, hay fever, bad medicine please.'

questions.question: When we have a nap, why do we say have 40 winks?

answers.answer: A doctor wrote a book in the early 19th century about the well-being of life and referred to 40 winks as being the best kind of quick rest if you need to do some work later on in the evening. He meant 40 minutes is the optimal nap time. People went to work in the fields but then had to get up again to bring cows in, so they'd have a quick nap.

questions.question: My toothpaste is stripey, my bubble bath is purple, and my shower gel is green, but why are the bubbles always white?
When it's very hot and you fan yourself, the air feels cooler, but it's actually still hot. So why does air feel cooler when it's moving?

answers.answer: As the breeze hits your skin, the evaporation from sweat makes it cooler. Obviously the heat's evaporated so your skin is cooler because of the wind. Each molecule of air that hits your skin has less energy because it's a lower temperature than your skin, so energy is transferred from your skin to the air. If the air's moving faster, in a given amount of time more particles hit your skin, transferring energy quicker and cooling you down faster.
answers.qualifications: Teacher, now works in aviation

questions.question: I was doing my nails a few months ago and I noticed that on the pad of my thumb, my skin was peeling. And then when I got to the other hand, I noticed that the skin was peeling in the exact same place on my other thumb. Why?

answers.answer: You use your thumbs equally when playing video games, and that is why they are both peeling in the same place. It can go back months, skin peeling. It died when you were playing video games and is now being shed weeks subsequently.

She almost certainly has a condition called pompholyx eczema - Greek for bubble. It's a type of eczema that creates bubbles on the hands which form blisters and peel. They're almost exactly symmetrical on both hands at the same time. It's not serious, comes and goes, supposedly related to stress and hands sweating more triggering the reaction. Lots of moisturising cream when hands start peeling is about all you can do.
answers.qualifications: GP

questions.question: Greensleeves - who gives the royalties for that? Does somebody own the rights to it now, or does it filter back to the original rights of the family?

answers.answer: It was written in Tudor times, possibly by Henry VIII or one of his top courtiers like Sir Thomas More, and passed off as the work of Henry VIII because it was about Anne Boleyn. There are no modern rights to it because it's out of copyright. The song is about Anne Boleyn wearing her green sleeves and how it gave Henry VIII the horn.

questions.question: My son asked me: in a football game, if you score a hat-trick, you keep the ball, but what happens if two players score a hat-trick?

answers.answer: Probably the one who finishes the hat-trick first would get the ball.

Gary Lineker just tweeted me: two hat-tricks in the same game, you get a ball each. It's simple. At professional level, you get a ball each. If it's a Sunday league team with only one ball, you've probably only got one ball, so you'd have to share or the one who's never scored one before gets to keep it.

questions.question: Just before my mother closed her eyes and passed away, she went really wide eyed - as if she'd seen a ghost or been really surprised, super wide eyed just before closing her eyes, grimacing and dying. Is there any medical explanation for why that happens?

answers.answer: It may be to do with that in the process shortly before dying there's a change in heart rhythm and so on, you may get a big surge of adrenaline into the bloodstream and that can cause changes in eyes. But to be honest, it's so variable with different scenarios when someone does die that it's quite difficult to pin it down.

I agree with my GP colleague who called earlier. Part of it is release of hormones, release of neurotransmitters like adrenaline that he mentioned. Any person that dies in a different way will experience it slightly differently. That's a relatively common thing to happen. Unfortunately I deal with a lot of that in my work.

questions.question: I enjoy reading books but I've noticed every now and then you get three or two stars at the bottom of a page. It's not the end of a chapter or the end of a paragraph. What do those stars symbolise?

answers.answer: They denote a scene break. Normally what you'd have if you had continuous text on a page is you'd have a line break - just a blank space - and then you'd start a new scene. But when that break falls at the end of a page, you put the asterisks there to make it clear that's the end of that scene. When you turn over the page, the next line will not be indented, it'll be right out to the margin, indicating a new scene.
answers.qualifications: Worked in publishing for ten years and has typeset books

questions.question: My friend's name is Jack Pink. Where does the name Pink come from? His dad had a band called John Pink and the Pinkertons.
When you tee off in golf, I know you put the ball on the tee. Did you have a kicking tee? Where does the word tee come from? Why do they call a tee a tee?

answers.answer: It's T-shaped, isn't it? If you hold it up and look across it, it looks like a tee.

It comes from Scottish Gaelic words meaning house, believe it or not. It's called a tay - T-A-I-G-H. When golf was first played, the ball was set up within a club's length of the hole you just played, and that was known as the house, which is tay in Scottish.
answers.qualifications: Played golf for 50 years and is Scottish

questions.question: The constituents of stomach acid - the main one from my GCSEs is hydrochloric acid. How does any food survive going through digestion? But how does the goodness get through? If my organic apple has gone down through a small vat of hydrochloric acid, how am I benefiting?

answers.answer: The acid just breaks down the food in the stomach, and all the vitamins, the nutrients, are actually absorbed in the smallest intestine, which is the villi. The confusion is that he presumed the acid destroys everything, but it doesn't - it's quite mild, it just breaks things down so the constituent parts then get absorbed. The stomach acid is quite weak compared to normal hydrochloric acid you would use out in the real world, otherwise we'd all burn up from the inside.

questions.question: Why is it a milliner makes a woman's hat and a hatter makes a man's hat?

answers.answer: It's just the French word and the English word for the same thing.

questions.question: Answer about bubbles

answers.answer: It's to do with the molecules - they're broken up and separated by the air.

questions.question: How high can a garden frog jump?

answers.answer: Frogs can climb fences, not just jump. They find gaps where fences connect to walls and will climb up there. There's not much you can do. They also spawn in gardens, so tadpoles can appear in mud.

questions.question: Does alcohol evaporate from a mixed drink like gin and tonic or whisky and soda left overnight?

answers.answer: Alcohol evaporates a lot quicker than water. If you work in a bar, bottles must have caps on at the end of the night, otherwise the alcohol content changes and you can't sell that.

The word is volatility. Alcohol is volatile, much more volatile than water. It will evaporate from a mixture. More importantly, the juniper berries in gin are also volatile, which is why you can smell gin. If you can smell it, it's volatile and evaporating.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'getting down off your high horse' come from?

answers.answer: Rich people in medieval times had bigger, higher horses than commoners. As they rode in, they'd be looking down on people less fortunate than themselves. High and mighty and get off your high horse come from this association between aristocrats and large horses.

questions.question: Why do microwave ovens have dark tinted glass instead of clear glass so you can see through easily?

answers.answer: The glass isn't actually tinted. There's a sheet of metal on the inside of the glass with lots of little holes in it. The holes are smaller than the wavelength of microwaves, so the radiation can't escape through the door.

questions.question: Why do people with black hair grow ginger beards?

answers.answer: All body hair has a colored sheath over it. Ginger hair is the actual follicle underneath. Everyone has ginger hair with various coloring over the top. Sometimes a genetic throw-up in a hair follicle means it comes out without its sheath, producing ginger hair. This was discovered when police wanted to get photo fits from DNA evidence - the first hair color they could determine from DNA was whether someone was ginger.

The body has recessive and dominant genes. Some people have recessive ginger genes that could have been passed down through generations for years. They don't know what to do with themselves so they pop out in different parts of the body, sometimes as a full ginger beard.

questions.question: Is gruntled a real word? Are there other words like disgruntled where you only know the 'dis' version?

answers.answer: Dis from Latin means opposite, but sometimes goes back to Middle English meaning 'very' - like disheveled meaning very heavy. Gruntled in Middle English meant someone of a lower class, a dirty pleb. In the 1930s, people started jokingly using gruntled to mean happy, playing on the idea that dis means opposite. It appears in P.G. Wodehouse books.

questions.question: Why is it 7 dog years = 1 human year? Who made that up? Can it apply to other animals?

answers.answer: Vets have charts for dog years but the formula varies by breed size. A 7-year-old black lab is equivalent to 52 human years, a Jack Russell is 40, and a Great Dane would be 70. Smaller dogs live longer (labs 13-14 years, Jack Russells into teens) while larger dogs have shorter lives. The seven-years-per-year formula is completely made up and has no scientific basis.

questions.question: If you've ever been detained at Her Majesty's pleasure, do you actually receive a telegram from the Queen when you turn 100?
Why does a hot cup of tea cool you down in hot weather?

answers.answer: If you make yourself feel hotter internally, it makes the hot weather feel relatively colder. The temperature difference between your body and the outside becomes less, so you don't feel the heat as much. It raises your core temperature temporarily, reducing the contrast with the external temperature.

questions.question: Why is plant hire called plant hire? I mean green plants. I mean plant machinery. Why is it called plant machinery?

answers.answer: It comes from the verb to plant - heavy stuff is planted on the ground before you can use it. Goes back to the 18th century. The other theory is it's an abbreviation of plantation as in working on the plant. But nobody really knows for sure.

questions.question: My friend is pregnant and past her due date. She wants the baby out. We've been discussing inducing labour. One that keeps cropping up is having a very hot, spicy curry. Is it true? And if it is true, how does it work?

answers.answer: I know that it's true but I can't remember why. I think with our eldest, she had a spoonful of my spicy curry and we were at the hospital within 12 hours. But it might have happened anyway - it's correlation not causation.

There is some truth behind it. The theory is a woman's body preparing for labour often gets an upset tummy beforehand - getting everything out of the system before focus goes on pushing the baby out. Spicy food can irritate the bowel and trigger things. It's not scientific but many midwives say having that upset tummy will get things going.

questions.question: Boxes of chocolates - sometimes one chocolate will be wrapped in foil, sometimes it's a strawberry one or orange one. But sometimes the strawberry one has foil and the orange one doesn't. Why are some wrapped and some aren't?

answers.answer: I think it's just to make them look smarter - the foil makes them look more expensive. That's all it is.

Chocolates with foil normally have a liquid caramel or ganache centre. The outside is only a thin layer of chocolate holding it in shape. The foil protects it from heat sources and keeps the shape of the chocolate. The strawberry cream had foil because it had a thinner chocolate shell with a higher melting temperature than the orange cream.

questions.question: Avocados go brown when you cut them and leave them in the air. But if you take out the pit and put it in a cup of water, the avocado stays green. How does that work?

answers.answer: It can't be true. There's no way an avocado stone can communicate with an avocado pear from the other side of the room when in a glass of water. Your premises are false.
Leaving your avocado stone with a salad - if you just cut your avocado and leave the stone in it will prevent it from going brown because they're touching.

questions.question: Why do cats have cat litter and dogs don't?

answers.answer: Because you can't take your cat for a walk and dog poo really stinks worse than cat poo. Cat litter might be for training the cat to know where it's home, or they lock the cat in at night.
Cats bury their poo - it's their instinct. Dogs don't bury their poo. That's why cats need litter trays and dogs don't.

questions.question: When I was young I fell off a wall and clipped a little bit of my ear off. When my son was born he's got the same bit of ear missing. Is there any kind of genetic thing or is it just coincidence?

answers.answer: Definitely coincidence. It's one sperm that is somehow containing the knowledge that you've had a chunk taken out of your ear during your childhood. There's no way a sperm can know what your ear looks like after it's been changed.

questions.question: How do they install high power pylons on mountains, and how do they pull the wires across the gorges and mountains to connect the pylons?

answers.answer: They do it at ground level and then lift it up to the top. For big gorges they use helicopters. For really tough terrain they use donkeys. Or they drop it from above using a helicopter.

If there's a ravine, helicopters will deliver the pylons in sections and if it's a long span they'll deliver the cables by helicopter as well. There'll be people on the ground but only to deal with the stuff coming down from the sky.

questions.question: Do rechargeable batteries leach power if the power isn't actually being used? My radio had full batteries on Sunday night but was dead by Wednesday and I couldn't listen because I'd been sick Monday and Tuesday.

answers.answer: Maybe you bought some duds, or maybe you left your radio on with the volume on zero. The only explanation is that the batteries have reached the end of their life.

If it's an alkaline rechargeable battery, they'll hold their charge for a lot longer. If it's a nickel-metal hydride battery, they will self-discharge anyway. If you continuously try and recharge a rechargeable battery, you will eventually kill the cells - like with your mobile phone if you charge it every night, you will lose battery life the longer you do it.

questions.question: If you are swimming in the sea on holiday, is it bad for you to drink too much salt water accidentally? We were on holiday recently and my wife made us swallow an awful lot of salt water.

answers.answer: Your kidneys make urine that is salty and it can only make urine that's saltier than salt water. So the more salt in your system, the more fluid you're going to retain. If you keep weeing you should be all right but you need to keep drinking non-sea water to dilute. If you go over your recommended daily allowance then you move into troubling territory.

It won't do you any harm unless you drink it every day. The reason is because your hormone regulation for salt and water retention will reset to retain more water and then raise your blood pressure. Having too much salt for one day is not a problem but exceeding your recommended daily allowance every day, whether it's salt water or any other source of salt, that will be bad for you.

questions.question: What's the link between shoesmiths and locksmiths? Whenever you drive past a shoe repair shop they also cut keys. Is it something to do with the machine they use?

answers.answer: Maybe it's the same machine - you change something on it like on a food mixer when you move from balloon whisk to dough kneader. It would be a grinding wheel for keys and a polish brush for shoes.

There's no link between cutting keys and repairing shoes. It's just another way for a cobbler to make money. They use completely separate machines - one is a tiny little machine that sits on the bench and one is a huge machine for repairing shoes. Cobblers didn't start cutting keys until the 70s when shoe repair started dropping off so they needed another way to make money.

questions.question: What is the difference between a cobweb and a spider's web?

answers.answer: A cob is just an old English word for a spider. So a cobweb is just an old word for a spider's web - there's no difference.

questions.question: When Her Majesty eventually makes way for King Charles, will those royal appointments for products like mustard from Norwich or sauce from Worcester have to be reapplied for or reassigned by His Majesty?

answers.answer: Yes, King Charles already has his own royal appointments. The companies would need to reapply for the new king's approval. They'd get given a list of the ones his mum had and he'd say which ones he doesn't like. So there might be a bit of negotiation but it needs a new royal bump stamp.

questions.question: Why did men evolve to have beards and women didn't?

answers.answer: Women don't have beards because of sex hormones. They have lower levels of testosterone than men and more estrogen, which also explains why women have longer, more luxuriant head hair. Testosterone causes thick, coarse hair growth on faces. Women do have facial hair but it's soft and downy.

questions.question: Why are pirates portrayed as having a West Country accent?

answers.answer: Robert Newton played Long John Silver in Treasure Island. That performance was so seminal that all subsequent pirate characters used his accent. Before that, pirates weren't portrayed that way. The South West, particularly Bristol, was connected to both the slave trade and smuggling, which may have informed his choice of accent.

questions.question: How do insects sleep with compound eyes that they can't close?

answers.answer: Insects do sleep - it's called torpor. They evolved without eyelids so they shut down various parts of their brain to rest. Even when it's light, they can sleep by shutting down relevant parts of their brain, like fish. Flies can sense pressure changes in the air which wake them up. When insects are asleep, the color of their eyes darkens and they get startled if woken up, similar to humans.

questions.question: Why does scratching a mosquito bite feel so good if it's bad for you? Is there anything in it for the insect - does scratching alert other insects?

answers.answer: When insects feed on blood, they inject a chemical that serves two purposes: it numbs the area and prevents blood from coagulating so they can continue feeding. The itch is an accidental side effect of these chemicals - the chemicals are there for the insect's benefit, not yours. Scratching can cause secondary infection. The caller noted that Keith got it partially wrong and there may have been corrections.

questions.question: Has anyone ever lost a sainthood?

answers.answer: No pope has ever rescinded or revoked a sainthood. The process requires evidence of miracles and involves the pope speaking ex cathedra (from his throne), which by Catholic doctrine makes it absolutely impossible for a pope to be wrong. Therefore it would be impossible to admit a mistake in bestowing sainthood.

In 1969, Pope Paul VI did review and removed feast days from some saints beatified prior to the 13th century. They were demoted but not technically desainted. Saints like St. Christopher, St. Nicholas, and possibly St. George may not have actually existed historically.

questions.question: At what age and how do children stop falling out of bed?

answers.answer: When we're babies, we learn that rolling over on our face obstructs the airwaves because it's harder to breathe. So when we're older and sleeping near the edge of a bed, if we start rolling over, we automatically roll back because we've learned as babies that rolling on your nose is dangerous. It's learned behavior that continues into adulthood and prevents us from falling out of bed.

questions.question: Why are orchestras described as philharmonic rather than just harmonic? Where does the word 'phil' come from?

answers.answer: Philo means love or affection. Philharmonic means an affection for harmony or music - it's about love of music. Similar to bibliophile (someone who loves books) or francophile (someone who loves France). So a philharmonic orchestra is literally an orchestra for music lovers.

questions.question: Why can't great white sharks be held in captivity?

answers.answer: Great white sharks get very stressed and depressed in captivity and just die. It's similar to how dolphins and orcas don't do well in captivity - it's very rare they breed successfully. The bigger the territory an animal is used to roaming, the more stressful confinement is. Great whites feel this even more keenly and waste away.

questions.question: When they dig new tubes and high-speed rail tunnels, what happens to all the earth they dig out?

answers.answer: The soil from tunnel digging is used to fill up and create hills on golf courses in the local area. They sell it or give it to golf courses who design their courses around the new terrain. There's a visible example on the M25 and in Essex where massive hills appeared that weren't there five or six years ago, built from tunnel excavation material.

questions.question: Why are cans like Coke and Fanta measured in 330ml specifically?

answers.answer: 330ml is roughly one third of a litre (333ml would be exactly one third). The filling machines aren't precise enough to fill to exactly one third litre, so they round to 330ml. There's also a connection to 12 ounces. The machines fill so quickly with some dribble involved that they can't be more precise, and 330ml is the manageable, rounded result.

questions.question: Why can newspapers tell people who and not to vote for, but commercial radio stations and TV stations have got all these restrictions? When did it happen and who made that decision?

answers.answer: Short answer: I haven't got a Scooby Doo.
The government give out the licences for radio and broadcasting, and they're not allowed to let broadcasters be partial in any way, because it might influence the awarding of a licence.

questions.question: Why do ladies have a different sort frame to guys on push bikes? Why do women have a horizontal crossbar while men have a diagonal one?

answers.answer: Historically, women rode horses side saddle for reasons of modesty - it was considered indelicate and vulgar for a woman to have her legs wide apart. At the turn of the last century when bicycles became popular, the ladies bicycle was designed so she could get on and off without exposing herself, especially since they were wearing skirts. It's all about how you mount the bike.

questions.question: Medieval paintings and drawings of faces - why are they so terrible? Why can't people draw faces properly in medieval art, and what changed to make them better?

answers.answer: It's all to do with perspective. Medieval paintings like the Bayeux Tapestry are all two-dimensional, flat images - same with the heads. Botticelli in the 14th century came up with three-dimensional perspective. Prior to Botticelli, they did it flat instead of trying to paint 3D. That's why statues would work but paintings wouldn't.

questions.question: What is the physiology behind brain freeze when we eat ice cream?

answers.answer: The top of your mouth is quite sensitive, so when the cold touches it, it can stimulate up to your brain, which makes the pain, which panics you into saying that it's really cold in your mouth.

It's all to do with the density of nerve endings on the roof of the mouth. The nerve endings are numbed by the cold - it's not actually pain itself. The blood vessels contract from the cold, the brain receives signals and conducts it as pain because the blood flow is constricted around the nerve endings. The tongue placed to the roof of the mouth reheats the blood vessels and takes away the brain freeze.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'to grass somebody up' come from? Why do we call somebody a grass when they're dobbing someone into the authorities?

answers.answer: Rhyming slang - grass hopper rhymes with copper. If you're on the same side as the coppers, you're a grass hopper, you're a grass. That's the widely accepted belief.
Grass comes from 'snake in the grass' - someone who tells on you. A grass is someone who informs on people, hiding their back.

questions.question: Why do some planes leave a big cloud of smoke behind them while others just leave a trail that disappears within a couple of seconds?

answers.answer: It's the same as why you can see your breath sometimes and other times you can't - it's about temperature and atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: Why do books come in hardback first?

answers.answer: If there's enough desire to read it right now rather than waiting for a paperback, they make more money out of it. The markup's bigger on a hardback than on a paperback.

Originally books were only available in hardback. When the technology became available to bind them in paperback, they retained the hardback for people like public libraries because a paperback book would not stand the stress and hassle of being moved in and out of the library. Now it's partly tradition and for readers who prefer them, but from a publisher's point of view, they can trouser a few more quid six months prior to the paperback release.

questions.caller: Mark from Bromley (on behalf of Sonny, age 8)
questions.question: Is there such a thing as a perfectly straight line? Sonny's claim: 'There is no such thing as a straight line, Dad.'

answers.answer: In geometry, a straight line is a theoretical abstract perfection - it must have no thickness and be drawn on a perfectly flat surface. In reality, a line has to have some thickness or you wouldn't be able to see it, and it's very difficult to draw on a perfect flat surface. Any line drawn on the surface of the Earth would automatically be curved. A perfectly straight line is impossible in reality - if there were one, you wouldn't be able to see it by definition.
Yes, you can have a perfectly straight line. Two points define a line. Theoretically.

questions.question: Does blood get old? His wife is 64 and has just made her 73rd blood donation. The transfusion nurse said they love her blood and it's perfect for tiny babies. Why?

answers.answer: Blood gets old - about 100 to 120 days depending on what component of blood you're talking about. It's a regenerative process. Red blood cells have an average lifespan of about 120 days. They're destroyed by a body process called hemolysis. Then the body produces another set of red blood cells through hemopoiesis, via the bone marrow. It's a cycle. As for why his wife's blood is good for babies - it depends on what kind of antibodies she's got in her body. If she's got really clean blood with good antibodies, it would be good for babies because she would be carrying less foreign bodies into the baby. She probably leads quite a healthy lifestyle.

questions.question: Why is it okay for your heart rate to increase with exercise but not advised to make your heart rate increase through drinking caffeinated drinks?

answers.answer: With cardio, you're getting good oxygen into the lungs and body, building up internal organs. But caffeine gets the heart rate up just purely because of sugars and bad content. The reason cardio is good is to improve and strengthen your body - your heart gets stronger, your lungs get stronger, everything gets stronger. But caffeine is just raising heart rate without those benefits - it's basically bad for you.

questions.question: What is the difference between olive oil, virgin olive oil, and extra virgin olive oil?

answers.answer: You put olives in a press, either industrial or manual. The first stuff to come off is extra virgin, then virgin, and the stuff they extract from all the pulp and leftover is your bulk standard olive oil.
In Greece, everyone takes their olives to the mill to be pressed and they keep some as payment. That confirms it's about the pressing - the first pressing is the best quality.

questions.question: Why don't alcoholic drinks have nutritional information (calories, sugar content, ingredients) like other foodstuffs? Why no health warnings with calorie information?

answers.answer: Alcohol isn't considered a food product, whereas fizzy drinks and food are. They're regulated by the EU Food Agency. There was a vote on it in 2015 in the European Parliament, but it wasn't passed as legislation, so hopefully that happens at some point.

questions.question: Why is MCR the symbol for Manchester? Some friends have started getting MCR tattoos following the events of the week.

answers.answer: It's all about the Industrial Revolution. MCR stands for 'Worker B'. Mancunians are the Worker Bs of Britain. You can see the Bs all over the shop - there's the mosaic at the town hall and in some of the civic buildings.

questions.question: What causes the change of accents? Does the change of accents have anything to do with global positioning? As you travel west, the accent seems to become more and more American-like.

answers.answer: I don't know that anyone's come up with a definitive answer to that. There's a theory that the American accent is the sort of English-Irish accent from the period of the Mayflower, but I don't know how anyone would go about proving that. The way people speaking English in other countries is going to have an awful lot to do with how they were taught. It's not going to have anything to do with geographical positioning.

Think of the English language as a tree. The trunk is the base root, and as the tree expands, all the branches develop into different dialects. This is generally down to isolation - people that develop in isolation start to pick up habits within their own little dialects. There's also foreign influence - the English tree touches branches with a French tree next door, and we pick up French words into our dialect. The main reason most English speakers don't understand each other today is because we're saturated with American media. Accents are disappearing because of the Americanisation of every corner of the country.

questions.question: This relationship with feelings and colours, like I'm feeling blue, I'm green with envy, I'm red with rage, yellow is a sign of madness. How did that all come about?

answers.answer: Probably before we could all read and write, it was used as a sort of pictogrammer-type way of conveying emotion.

questions.question: How thick does normal window glass, the gap before you can't see through it?

answers.answer: I don't know. We'll find out for Greg.
Hundreds of miles. If you think of fibre optic transmission cable that sends light down very, very, very long cables - hundreds of miles long.
You said 100 miles, then 75 miles, then 1 mile. You're just making up numbers.

If the glass is optically pure, you can see through it for miles and miles and miles. The thing is, it's your eyesight that can't go that far. With ordinary glass, there are imperfections, and the manufacturers make it just perfect enough so you can see through it for three or four miles. But if you use the same molten glass and try to make something thicker, it would actually become opaque quite quickly because of all the imperfections and impurities. Green light travels through glass slightly better, which is why when you look at glass through the thick side of things, it always looks green. There's actually a museum somewhere that's got a massively thick pane of glass that's optically pure, and you can look through it.

questions.question: Why are all the planets completely round or globe type?

answers.answer: I think it's like if you put bricks in your washing machine. Over millions of years, they've bumped into so much stuff that they've ended up getting rounded off.

It's all down to gravity, James. When a large amount of mass comes together, it collapses in on its own gravity. Imagine you're building a pile of sand - that pile of sand will stand on its own only up to a certain point, and as you put more sand on, it will eventually collapse and flatten itself out. When massive amounts of matter come together, gravity pulls in everything at the same rate, and it's inevitable that it becomes spherical. So there is a threshold of how something has to be before it collapses in on itself and becomes spherical.

The explanation was apposite and accurate. The only thing I'd add is that most planets aren't perfectly round - the spin causes the middle to bulge out more than the poles. As the gravity increases, everything gets pulled in equally from all directions, so it would inevitably end up being circular.

questions.question: Why is a piggyback actually called a piggyback? Because I've never sort of thought pigs carrying anything.

answers.answer: You used to carry pigs to market on your back? You would get it on your back and hold it by the little trotters, wouldn't you? Up on your shoulders. It'd be great. Like a scarf, but not wrapped. So you've got a trotter over each shoulder, and the pig's head just behind your head.

This dates back a few centuries and started out as a phrase 'pick back'. What it meant was you just carried something on the back of the shoulders, and then later on the term 'pick pack' meant to jump on and have a ride on somebody's back or on the shoulders. The word pig has got nothing to do with it. A load or something to be pitched onto someone's shoulders or their back. It was a medieval term. Then human error came in and people started calling it piggyback, like when we say now 'he did it off his own bat' - the correct pronunciation is 'off his own back'.

questions.question: Is jelly a liquid or a solid? And what about toothpaste?

answers.answer: Solid. If you can pour it, it's a liquid. You can't pour toothpaste. The definition of a liquid for the purposes of security clearances at airports may be different from the semantic definition of a liquid, which is something that can be poured.

I believe it could be a non-Newtonian liquid. The definition of a liquid is its pourability, or some people have suggested it will expand to fit in the container - that's the viscosity of a liquid. However, viscosity can change under pressure, and that's the difference. Toothpaste, ketchup and jelly - when you squeeze them, they come out. They've got different molecular bonds to solids. Solids have got more stable molecular bonds. A non-Newtonian liquid sits in between a liquid and a solid, doesn't follow Newton's law of pourability.

questions.question: When you snap a piece of spaghetti, why does it break into three pieces and not two, or splinter like a pencil does?

answers.answer: It's because it's so long, so when you bend it at the two ends, the pressure is different. That would be the answer. It might not be right or even remotely relevant to the question.
I tested it live during the call. The first one I did went straight into four pieces. And then I picked up one of the small bits, and it went into two. So it doesn't always break into three.

questions.question: Why do tennis scores go up 15, 30 and 40 and not 15, 30 and 45? Why are they uneven?

answers.answer: They used to use a clock face to keep score. If you've got four points - 15, 30, 40, game - you need another one for deuce, so that's probably why it doesn't go to 45.

It was 15, 30 and 45 originally. That's an o'clock. But they found 45 a bit too cumbersome, so they changed it to 40 for some reason. I found this out from an old gentleman who came to see me for treatment in my chiropractic clinic. He played Fred Perry at Wimbledon before the war and was giving me a lesson in the history of tennis.

questions.question: Why are there so many villages and towns in Cornwall that begin with TR? Every time I go to Cornwall I seem to come across a new village that begins with TR.
Why is a dartboard separated into 20 segments? Who was it that came up with that?
Why is it that so many sports trophies, and I guess probably other trophies too, are in the shape of big cups?

answers.answer: Perhaps champagne would be put in it. They'd all have a swig of something after they won.

It goes back to classical times and pagan religions when people were involved in ancient sports and would make an offering to their gods. The animals they'd sacrificed would be used as offerings - in some cases they would drink their blood in order to take on the characteristics of those animals to help them in their sportive endeavours.

questions.question: Why do we call a kitty a kitty? (referring to a pool of shared money for children's expenses)

answers.answer: I don't know. If it had a Latin root or something like that, I'd have a go at it. But there's nothing there.

It comes from the old version of Cockney rhyming slang for hat - 'kitty cat' hat. Back in the days when you could gamble in a pub without being frogmarched out, they used to put a hat in the middle of the table and you'd throw your money in the kitty.

questions.question: Is there an ergonomic reason why the numbers on my telephone are the opposite way round to the numbers on a calculator or on my keyboard?

answers.answer: So if you look at your calculator, it's got seven, eight, nine across the top row. Before touch-tone phones were invented, when it was all click phones, people who were using calculators more than computer keyboards were so quick at the way the pad was laid out that they were faster than the touch-tone phone technology could keep up with. So one way of slowing down the speed at which people operated these new keypads was to turn it upside down, so they weren't able to type as quickly.

questions.question: If we were in caveman times with bad eyesight, we wouldn't be able to hunt for food. So has bad eyesight always been around or have we evolved? What did cavemen do before glasses?

answers.answer: The further back you go, the more likely bad eyesight would threaten your life. But you would rely upon your fellow citizens to look after you. The answer is squint. The first pair of spectacles were simple magnifiers.

In Roman or Norman times, people that were short-sighted would do things like etching, needlework, masonry. They'd find a way for you to contribute that accommodated your short-sightedness - like doing close work making arrows or being a fletcher. If you were completely blind, you'd do jobs that allowed you to accommodate your condition, like piano tuner.

questions.question: I was on holiday in Indonesia and the people there said time moves much more slowly there than in European countries. Does time around the equator actually move slower than where we are?

answers.answer: When they told you that time moves slower in Indonesia, that just meant it was a more relaxed lifestyle. You're not suggesting that if you go to the equator your watch literally runs slower?

Time slows down as you approach the speed of light. The Earth is toroidal - slightly ovoid rather than perfectly spherical. If you're near the equator, you're going faster than you are if you're further north or south. They put special clocks in the nose of the space shuttle, and because that went dead fast, when it got back to Earth it showed a difference in time.

It's not only speed, it's also gravity. Three years ago Richard Feynman was proved right that the inside of the Earth is about three years younger than the outside because there's less gravity at the core. Your perception of time changes with both speed and with gravity - as seen in the film Interstellar.

questions.question: In England, the title on book spines goes down the spine, whereas in France it's the opposite - it goes up the spine. Why are French and British book spines designed differently?
Why don't babies have nasal hairs? Babies don't have an advanced immune system, and nasal hairs are a filter for adults to prevent infections.

answers.answer: Their little baby nostrils are so tiny. If they had nostril hair or anything like mine, they wouldn't be able to breathe. Oxygen is more important than germ repulsion. Also, the baby needs to smell her mother for bonding.
They do have nasal hairs, they're just very, very microscopic so you can't see them with the naked eye. If you took a sample of it or looked under a microscope you'd be able to see some.

questions.question: When we get cold and shiver, why do our nipples go hard?

answers.answer: It's goose bumps. When you get cold, goose bumps make the hairs on your body stand up and that provides some form of insulation against the cold. The nipple is just the most prominent manifestation of that physical phenomenon.
The skin tenses up to lift the hair. The skin on the nipple is tensing to lift the small tiny hairs on your nipple, which helps keep you warmer.

questions.question: How do ducks know how many ducklings they have? They can't count and they don't have language, so how do they check they've got all their chicks with them?

answers.answer: Mothers don't actually feed ducks like mammals - they're not just looking after their own exclusively and will let others join them. Little baby ducklings will go to any mum that's got a clutch and looks affable and friendly. So the mum isn't checking - it's a community thing. It's imprinting.

questions.question: Why don't we have bones in our ears?

answers.answer: You don't need a bone in your ear. Otherwise we'd have one. There are body parts that don't contain bones.
When the baby is born, it would break when it came out. It wouldn't be able to fit.

questions.question: Why has my foil helium balloon (an emoji face with a wink) stayed on my lounge ceiling for almost three months?

answers.answer: Is it because it's foil?
A foil balloon is pretty close to hermetically sealed. The helium can't get out and the air can't get in to dilute the helium. A latex balloon is semi-permeable - the air slowly seeps out.
The latex balloon is small and when you have inflated it, it has to be pressurised to inflate it. The foil balloon is not pressurised, so the air doesn't seep out.
