questions.question: What's the physiological explanation for the feeling in your stomach when you suddenly drop, like going over a humpback bridge or on a ride? Your tummy turns over and it makes you make a noise.

answers.answer: It's because the organs inside are floating in space until gravity kicks in.

questions.question: How did hat measurements like 7 3/8 come about?

answers.answer: It's the circumference of your head divided by pi (3.1415927). And it's because our heads aren't perfect circles, so to get a perfect circle in a hat, that's how they measure it.

questions.question: Where did the superstition of throwing salt over your left shoulder come from?

answers.answer: It's the devil looking over your left shoulder and Jesus is on your right. So if you do something wrong, you throw the salt into the devil on your left shoulder and he can't see you. You put him off.
Got something to do with Judas Iscariot and the Last Supper.

questions.question: Why are there only numbers 10 and 11 on Downing Street? Are there any other houses?

answers.answer: There's number 10, 11 and 12. They're all interlinked. They knocked down the ones up to nine back in the Victorian times. It's owned by the church. If you walk through number 10, you can get into number 11 and number 12.

questions.question: Why are guitars informally referred to as axes?

answers.answer: Typically of the age of Jimi Hendrix, the SG guitar came out which was similar in shape to a double-headed axe. And the term came from when they used to do sort of music battles against saxophones. So they were known as sax-axe battles.

questions.question: Why are sturgeon eggs called caviar? Why not just sturgeon eggs?

answers.answer: It's actually a Persian word. The word for caviar in Persian is khaviar. The fish that it comes from is a sturgeon, which is indigenous to Iran, so they coined the term caviar.

questions.question: Why can't you buy wholemeal crumpets?

answers.answer: There's a five-grain crumpet in Marks and Spencer's. Otherwise the answer would be supply and demand - there isn't enough demand for wholemeal crumpets.
You can get wholemeal crumpets in Whole Foods supermarkets.

questions.question: Who is the president of North Korea?
When a new pope has been elected, why does he take the name of a previous pope plus a number like Pope Innocent 12th or 13th?

answers.answer: When you're baptised as an infant, your parents choose your Christian name. When you get to confirmation, you also get to choose your own name - a saint's name. The idea is so that you look at the saint's life and say 'I would like to live my life in a similar fashion as he did' or 'I would like that saint to watch over me.' In that similar way, when cardinals become popes, they say 'I'd like to live my life in a similar way as this saint' or 'I'd like this saint to watch over me.' Francis I cited St Francis of Assisi.

questions.question: How can you tell if sour cream has gone off?

answers.answer: Three ways to tell: 1) When it's properly gone off, it gets mold - green and black spots on the surface. 2) When you taste it and it's fizzy and effervescent - that happens because the bacteria have run out and bad spoilage bacteria start dissolving the protein and giving off gases. 3) Sour cream's meant to be creamy in texture, so if it starts to go off, there's whey collecting on top and it becomes quite runny.

Sour cream is cream that's gone off literally - it's bacterial acid cream. The tart taste is caused by two acids: lactic acid and butyric acid. All things like cheese are insoluble protein. As the bacteria metabolise, they produce these acids which drop the pH. There's a protein in milk called casein which becomes insoluble at low pH, which is why you get the curds and whey. The fizziness comes from carbon dioxide which is a product of the same thing.

questions.question: Why can't you fold a piece of paper in half more than seven times?

answers.answer: You actually can. Brittany Gallivant was an American schoolgirl who demonstrated you could fold paper twelve times. She got some enormously long piece of paper and folded it twelve times. She also came up with an equation which tells you exactly how long a strip of paper needs to be in order to fold it X number of times.

questions.question: Why when you get hit on the head in cartoons you see stars? And why does he see stars when he has a sneezing fit?

answers.answer: It's a lack of oxygen to the brain.

questions.question: Why is a gentleman's prophylactic called a French letter?

answers.answer: It's linked because the French letter is associated with a love letter. The French have a reputation for being lovers, and the idea of a love letter comes from the French.

questions.question: Why do you drink a drink but you don't food a food?

answers.answer: You've got it in the wrong context. You eat food and you drink fluids. It's not a drink, it's a fluid.

You can 'food' food, it just depends where in the world you are. If you go to Zurich in Switzerland, in Swiss German you would say 'ich esse' - esse is the German for to eat and for food. So in Swiss German you say 'ich esse' (I food). The answer is it depends where in the world you are - it's just linguistic. English is a Germanic language, food doesn't have a Germanic root, eat does.

questions.question: My partner is celiac and has a gluten allergy. She has to be very careful about things like soy sauce which contains gluten. Why can she kiss me when I've been drinking beer without getting ill?

answers.answer: The amount of gluten on your lips after supping a pint would be so negligible that it just doesn't impact. It'd be like a droplet.
Beer has very little gluten, both in terms of quantity and thanks to the presence of the alcohol which negates the protein, the quality as well.
Celiac disease is not an allergy. It's a digestive disorder. Skin contact, even lips, will not necessarily cause a reaction as it doesn't affect your digestive system.

questions.question: When I buy stones, cement or sand at the garden centre, they always come in kilos (a weight measurement), but when I buy compost it comes in litres (a volume measurement). Why is that?

answers.answer: Compost is sold by volume not by weight because even in a bag, if it's wet when put in, it weighs more than if dry. The volume would become less as it settles.

Compost has large water content which varies. Wet compost weighs considerably more but takes roughly the same space as dry compost. Weight fluctuates a lot more than volume, so they sell by volume. Stones and pebbles don't vary in weight, so they can be sold by weight.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'like it or lump it'?

answers.answer: I don't know - possibly related to porridge.

The phrase came from America originally and was brought to Britain by Charles Dickens. 'Lump' in the 1800s meant moody or grumpy. So it means 'like it or be miserable' rather than referring to a physical lump.

questions.question: When listening to an LP on vinyl, in the quiet between the tracks, if you turn the sound right up, you can hear a faint echo of what's about to play - about five seconds before. How does this happen?

answers.answer: That's because you're stoned - joking! I don't know but I'll find out.

The record has grooves that the stylus runs in and extracts the music. When coming up to the next track, you're one side of a set of grooves, so it picks up what's on the other side. It's like being able to look through the wall of a tunnel - you can hear what's on the other side.

It's called pre- or post-code and comes from stress in the cutting process during production. It's in the master copy - the original copy all pressings are made from. You can adjust the frequency when producing to lessen the echo.

questions.question: From my granddaughter who is learning to be a lawyer: What is the difference between 'unlawful' and 'illegal'?

answers.answer: Illegal means forbidden by law. Unlawful means not authorized - there isn't a law that's been passed to make it permissible. So illegal is against a law that has been passed, unlawful means no law allows it.
Illegal refers to criminal acts. Unlawful refers to acts which are unlawful but not criminal - civil law. She cited Black's Dictionary of Law as backing James's original explanation.

questions.question: Is there a specific time of day when afternoon becomes evening, evening becomes night, and then night becomes morning?

answers.answer: It's all about the sun. As soon as the sun starts going down, it's evening. When it's gone down, it's night. When it starts coming up, it's dawn. When it's up, it's morning. So it varies every day according to sunset and sunrise.

questions.question: Why can't you hear the baby while pregnant? When you go underwater you can hear whales. I'm six weeks away from giving birth and I can feel the kicks but can't hear any noise.

answers.answer: The fetus doesn't have any functioning lungs. All noise needs air - air passes over the voice box. Your baby's lungs are full of amniotic fluid. There's no physical way it could make a noise. Whales have air - that's why they have blowholes. Nothing in a womb can make noise because there's no air.

questions.question: What's the difference between a chicken and a hen?

answers.answer: Chicken is the genus - the general term. A hen is a female chicken. A cockerel is a male chicken. You wouldn't be eating a cockerel - you'd be eating a hen, most likely.

questions.question: Does plutonium have a commercial value? If so, how much would it cost?

answers.answer: It must have a commercial value - when building missiles, you'd cost out the plutonium. But I don't know enough about this subject to give a proper answer.

questions.question: Why when you lick a lemon or grapefruit does your face contort on the LEFT side specifically? Why is it always the left side of the face that does the citrus wince?

answers.answer: I don't know why it would specifically be the left side. I don't have that information.

In school they mapped out the tongue into different zones for taste - sweet at the bottom, bitter at the top, sour and salty on the sides. Citrus triggers the sour receptors on the sides of the tongue, causing the wince.

questions.question: Why do humans get morning sickness during pregnancy but other animals like dogs and cats don't seem to?

answers.answer: Animals do get morning sickness. As a zookeeper with over 20 years experience breeding creatures including primates (gorillas, chimps, monkeys), females can get morning sickness just as bad as humans. It's just not as noticeable in some species because of different gestation periods.

questions.question: Why does it feel like you run faster at night than during the day?

answers.answer: It's called 'optic flow'. When you're in daylight, you can see miles ahead so distant objects take ages to approach. Objects immediately surrounding you move faster. At night, because you can't see as far, your brain perceives how fast you're going by the objects you're passing nearby - which makes you feel faster.

questions.question: If your skin sheds every 7 years, why do tattoos stay?

answers.answer: The ink is below the skin - it's subcutaneous. The normal shedding of skin doesn't reach the ink that's embedded deeper.
The word is 'subcutaneous' - under the skin. That's why.

questions.question: When pupils get smaller in bright light, how come we don't lose any of our vision field?

answers.answer: The pupil controls how much light enters the eye, not the angle of vision. The field of view is controlled by the width of the retina and distance from the pupil to the retina. A smaller pupil means less light but the same field of view. However, when the pupil is wider, you get chromatic aberration - all the different colors trying to land in different places makes it more blurred. So it's a compromise between light amount and image quality.

Professor Martin failed to mention depth of field. When the pupil is tiny (daylight), you can focus on things far away and close up simultaneously. When the pupil is wider (night), depth of field is less, so only one distance is in focus at a time. That's why.

questions.question: In a nuclear war, how far underground would you need to be to survive? Could the tube be used as a bunker?

answers.answer: Modern nuclear weapons aren't detonated on the ground - they're air bursts to cause the EMP effect that disrupts electronics. There's no definitive answer as it depends on the bomb type and detonation circumstances. Distance matters less than what you're inside of. You need something that will withstand the shockwave and block radiation. The tube isn't deep enough and has too much ventilation.

questions.question: Who is Larry and why is he 'happy as Larry'?

answers.answer: Two possible theories: 1) A boxer called Larry (possibly Larry Foley) who never lost a fight and made money in the late 19th century. 2) It comes from the word 'larrikin' which describes a layabout who sits around boozing - popular in Australia, derived from Devon/Cornwall origins. So 'happy as a larrikin' became 'happy as Larry'.

questions.question: When did we stop giving out new surnames?

answers.answer: Most surnames came from hundreds of years ago in villages where you might have multiple Johns, so they took job descriptors like John the Blacksmith becoming John Black or Smith. It was a practical solution to distinguish people. The practice died out once literacy became widespread, though you can technically still register a new surname.

questions.question: Do you continue swallowing when you're asleep?

answers.answer: You do swallow when you're sleeping, just not as much. Normal resting swallowing is about every 12 minutes, dropping to about twice an hour during sleep. People with apnea swallow more.

questions.question: Where does all the boogies/mucus come from when you have a cold?

answers.answer: The increase in green mucus is due to white blood cells attacking bacteria and viruses - it's their dead bodies and breakdown products. You also have goblet cells lining airways that produce mucus to catch foreign particles. During infection, your immune system produces excess mucus as part of the fighting process.

questions.question: Why do we call cats 'pussycats' instead of just cats? Where does 'pussy' come from?

answers.answer: It comes from the Dutch word 'pus' which means cat. This exists in several Germanic languages and with migration of people and language, we got 'pussycat' in English.
An alternative explanation: there was an Egyptian cat goddess called Pasht, and that's where 'puss/pussy' comes from.

questions.question: Why do trams use bells everywhere instead of horns like cars and buses?
Why is it easier to balance on a bicycle when it's moving compared to when it's stationary?

answers.answer: Gyroscopic effect - a spinning wheel wants to keep going in a straight line and resists being turned left or right. The momentum of the spinning wheels keeps the bike upright.

questions.question: What makes camels run in camel racing in Abu Dhabi? There's no jockey on them and no hare to chase, so what inspires the camels to run?

answers.answer: The camels have a little pack on their back with a mini robot that whips the camel. It's like a little robot with an arm that whips the camel.
I can confirm it's true - I have a still photograph and some video footage of camel racing featuring robot jockeys on my Twitter account.

answers.caller: Ibrahim (Camden, formerly a camel race organiser in Doha and Qatar)
answers.answer: They used to put Vic's Vaporub on the camel's bum to make them go faster.

questions.question: Why does the Queen's guards wear bearskins on their heads? Why does it have to be a bearskin?

answers.answer: The guards were fighting for Wellington at the Battle of Fuentes de Oñoro in Portugal in 1811. Napoleon's Imperial Guard wore the bearskin hats and the British guards destroyed them and took the hats as trophies. They've worn them ever since.

The bearskin caps were captured at the Battle of Waterloo in Flanders, not Portugal. Every grenadier regiment in both British and French military wore bearskin caps to make them look taller and more intimidating. Napoleon's Imperial Guard wore them and we captured them as trophies. It probably happened at more than one battle.

questions.question: At what point does an egg become meat? My vegetarian ex-girlfriend wouldn't touch meat but ate eggs, and if eggs aren't meat, when do they become meat? My boys asked me this daddy question.

answers.answer: Most eggs you eat are unfertilised. A fertilised egg is still edible even if being fertilised. Most of the yolk is food for the embryo. At what point does a fertilised egg become meat? That question is just not right.

answers.caller: Professor Howell (Professor of the Public Understanding of Science, University of Brighton)
answers.answer: Use human physiology as an analogy. A human egg has 23 chromosomes (haploid number). When a sperm fertilises it, it becomes a diploid number. At that moment of fertilisation, it ceases to become an egg and becomes a zygote. We can draw exactly the same analogy with chicken's eggs - as soon as it's fertilised, it's technically no longer an egg, it's a zygote. In the Philippines, there's a delicacy of well-developed fertilised duck's eggs where you crack open the egg and there's a little baby duck inside.

questions.question: Why do people put candles on a birthday cake and not anything else?

answers.answer: There are two theories. First, it's sweet - when you make a wish and blow out the candles, the idea is that when it was a prayer, the smoke would carry your prayer or wish up to heaven where God would be more likely to hear it. Second, a very rich German named Ludwig von Zinzendorf about three or four hundred years ago wanted the best birthday party ever, so he came up with sticking candles on a cake and lighting them.

questions.question: What is the burdock in Dandelion and Burdock drink?

answers.caller: Vince (Adelston, National Trust guided walks on Edible and Medicinal Plants)
answers.answer: Burdock is a biannual weed you'll see in the countryside. The root is what they use for Dandelion and Burdock drink. The little prickly balls children used to throw at each other are the burrs of the burdock plant. The root is like a potato - you can dig it up and roast it. There's definitely a similarity between root beer and dandelion and burdock.

questions.question: Where did the playground game Bulldog originate from?

answers.answer: British Bulldog dates back to Spartan times when kids went into the agogos every year for a kind of sports day to find the champion of that year. One of the games was a version of British Bulldog where kids had a little red rag hanging out of their pants at the back, and the idea was to grab that.

questions.question: Why are all watch faces set to 10 minutes past 10?

answers.answer: It's just because it looks like a smile. It's the most primitive form of marketing - there's some subconscious communication of happiness to make you more likely to buy the watch.

The main reason is to show the brand name. On most watches and clocks, the brand name is in the middle at the top, and this position allows the hands to not cover the brand name while still looking aesthetically pleasing.

questions.question: When did the tradition of shaving off beards start and why did it come about?

answers.answer: It came about because of the Romans. They were the warrior class and had to be clean-shaven so that their beard couldn't be grabbed in battle. That spread to everyone. It only switched in the Victorian age with the Crimean War when they couldn't get shaved, and therefore growing a beard became a sign of nobility.
The ancient Egyptians were also big fans of shaving, so it might not have originated with the Romans - that was more for religious reasons.

questions.question: Why is a third world country called a third world country?

answers.answer: Third world country refers to how a country was aligned during the Cold War. A third world country was one not aligned to anyone, a second world country was aligned with Russia, and a first world country was aligned with the USA. It originally had nothing to do with comparative wealth. Ireland was technically a third world country because of its historical neutrality.

questions.question: What was the purpose of the leather strip people used to hang from car rear bumpers to prevent car sickness? Was there any science behind it?

answers.answer: It was absolute hogwash. It was supposed to take some form of disruption out of the car and leave it on the road. It didn't work. Someone was selling them and they had good marketing, and mugs like your dad fell for it.

The earth straps on cars were to do with positive and negative earth systems. Up until the early 1970s, all cars had a positive earth system where the live was earthed onto the chassis. When alternators came along, they changed to negative earth, so the body of the car was no longer live. It became an urban myth that they helped cure car sickness.

questions.question: My son threw a Victor's Go Park to school every day, and within 24 hours the grass (the size of 4-5 football pitches) was completely covered in spider's webs. Was it one spider or many spiders? What breed of spider did it? Why did they do it on the grass? How did they do it so quickly in 24 hours?
Why haven't the batteries in my Sharp calculator (model EL8146) that I bought in 1983 run out? I've only used it about five minutes a month for my bank statement.

answers.answer: Because you haven't used it enough.

It must be an LCD display because LED takes too much current. LCDs take very tiny amounts of current. The odd thing about batteries is if you take a little current, they last longer than if you take no current - longer than shelf life. If kept in low humidity, low temperature, self-discharge is very low. Original equipment batteries are also higher quality than replacement batteries. If he'd left it in his drawer unused, it probably would have run out by now. Five minutes a month actually keeps it ticking over better than no current taken.

questions.question: Is David's calculator solar-powered?
Why does the devil have the number 666? Why six? Why three sixes?

answers.answer: Seven is the perfect number, so short of perfection is the reason why six. The triple six is emphasis.
You were right with six being short of perfection, and it's simply three times the emphasis. The Bible says something is said three times for emphasis.
Some recent research was done about it. Apparently it's the phonetic way of writing down the name of Julius Caesar as well. It was supposed to be some Jewish riddle or something.

In Bible numerology, the number six stands for man - God created man on the sixth day, you could only work for six days as a man, Hebrew servant freed after six years. The triple six is the personification of evil because man is referred to as evil. The devil is the personification of evil, hence 666. Seven is the perfecting number of God.
The Revelations is in the New Testament which was written in Greek. That's where 666 comes from - Greek translation.

questions.question: Why are there jokers in a pack of playing cards?

answers.answer: It has to do with tarot - from when cards were used for fortune telling as well as games.

It's not to do with Tarot. It was a game introduced during the Civil War where jokers served as a trump card - your winning card. Though it does have a comparison to tarot, so maybe that's why people think that. But it's purely down to the Civil War game.

questions.question: Why are all crosswords symmetrical?

answers.answer: Crosswords aren't all symmetrical. Some are vertical only or diagonal.

They were originally called word crosses and appeared in New York in the early 1900s. They felt it was elegant to have symmetry and convention stuck. An immigrant passed it from the UK to America. In America and UK, all crosswords have symmetry, but everywhere else in Europe they don't.

questions.question: Where did the phrase 'penny dropped' come from?

answers.answer: Almost certainly when you put a penny in a slot machine and when it drops, the machine starts working.

When they first excavated the caves in Cheddar Gorge, they weren't sure which seams would open during excavation. So they pushed pennies into the seams in the roof, which are still there to this day. Because the caves were completely silent, you would hear the penny drop when a seam opened. This told them to stop excavating that area.

questions.question: Why can't multi-pack items like bags of crisps or drinks be sold individually?

answers.answer: It's because if you buy in bulk, it's cheaper per item. Distributors and outlets buy in bulk whether individually wrapped or multi-pack wrapped.

The outer packaging has a barcode but the individual items inside do not. It's not actually a rule or law, it's just that there's no barcode on individual packs to help retailers scan and price them. The retailers who don't do it are the ones that still operate without barcodes.

questions.question: Can unexploded bombs from WWII go off on their own years later without being discovered or disturbed?

answers.answer: Bombs that didn't go off originally didn't explode because their fuse didn't work. If it degraded enough, could it suddenly blow up? We're looking for callers with knowledge of this.

The majority of Luftwaffe bombs on Coventry, Sheffield, London were propeller-triggered. As they went through the air, the propeller created a corkscrew effect completing a circuit. They only blew up on impact because they were timed by altitude. Incendiary bombs blew up immediately. But mines could lay dormant for years and remain active. However, with a chemical fuse or propeller screw, if the circuit isn't completed, it won't go off - you could hit it with a hammer and it wouldn't detonate.

questions.question: Unasked question - caller hung up before asking
Why are disc jockeys called disc jockeys? I understand the disc bit, but I don't understand the jockey bit.

answers.answer: It was Walter Winchell in the 1930s who coined the term. Radio was new and when presenters started playing records (discs), he just started calling them disc jockeys. The jockey part comes from riding a desk or riding the microphone. You're riding the discs while they do the work.

questions.question: Why does the Italian football team play in blue when there's no blue on the Italian flag? And the Dutch play in orange when there's no orange on the Dutch flag either.

answers.answer: Your question assumes teams SHOULD play in flag colors, but that's not a rule. Italy are called the Azzurri (the Blues) and wear blue. The Netherlands wear orange due to the House of Orange.

Dutch play in orange because of the House of Orange. Italy play in blue because of the House of Savoy who used to be their rulers. Germany in black and white is the colours of Prussia. When the first football association was formed in what is now Germany, the dominant state was Prussia. There's no requirement that your football strip should reflect your flag, but tradition suggests it usually does. In Oliver's anomalous examples, if you go back far enough, there's always a historical association with that colour even though it's not on the modern flag.

questions.question: Where did the tradition come from where MPs talk about 'the other place' and Lords say 'the other place' but never mention the actual names of the chambers?

answers.answer: I heard something was to do with Charles I, when you didn't want to be seen as a royalist or commoner by talking about the other house. But that's a bit spurious.

It comes from the mid-17th century, during Oliver Cromwell's time when there was so much animosity between the House of Lords and the House of Commons that they refused to refer to either chamber by their actual names. It was a way of being polite in Parliament while not having to say the words of the place full of people you didn't like.

questions.question: When you've quit smoking, do your lungs ever fully recover to pre-smoking days before you ever started smoking?

answers.answer: Cancer risk stops fairly soon after you've given up. That might be what I'm thinking of - the top-level cancer-inducing things disappear. But the other damage you've done, all the tar in the lungs, I'm not sure if that goes.

I had to go for asthma check-ups and asked the nurse this exact question. She said if you've smoked 20 cigarettes or more for over 20 years (a '20/20' smoker), your lungs will never return to fully perfect and functional condition, even though you've done yourself a lot of good by giving up.

questions.question: Given the vast volumes of rats that must be around and how few dead bodies we see, do rats eat dead rats?

When I put my son to bed in the evening, we read books and he's fine. Then lights go out, he falls asleep, and I have to go back to take his cover off because he is dripping in sweat. What is going on in his body?

answers.answer: It's called sleep apnea. It starts off with sweating in some people and then affects breathing. It can display in children as young as two. She should get it checked - go to the GP and get an ENT referral to see if it's sleep apnea. In extreme cases, it's serious.

questions.question: What is the collective noun for a group of solar panels?

answers.answer: A single solar panel is just a solar panel. A collection of solar panels is a solar array. And a collection of solar arrays is a solar farm. The word to know is 'array'.

questions.question: Yesterday, the Queen gave approval for Brexit. What would happen if she had refused to sign it?

answers.answer: The Queen's approval is largely ceremonial - no monarch has refused to sign since Queen Victoria. If she refused, it would cause a huge crisis.

Any monarch can technically refuse to sign a bill into law - they're perfectly allowed to do so. However, they never will. It's a constitutional convention, like the Queen being allowed to vote but choosing not to. If she ever did refuse, the constitutional crisis would be so huge that there would either be a civil war or they'd have to accept that she didn't sign. The only time it came close was during the civil war. It's a convention they won't refuse, not a law.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'mum's the word'?

answers.answer: Originally the phrase was simply 'mmm's the word', and it's got changed to 'mum'. When you say the word 'mmm', you keep your lips together, you don't say anything. So that's why keeping mum is like being silent. I was doing a classroom observation and the teacher said to the kids, she put her finger over her lips and said, mmm, keep mum. She wants them to be quiet. And one of the kids said, why did you say that? And she explained it.
For 'mum', it actually comes from old pantomimes when women didn't talk and they kept silent. They were called mums. They were miming in a pantomime, didn't speak. And I was told it means silent.
That mums the word answer is absolutely poppycock.

questions.question: Which airport has the worst reputation for landing - Madeira, Santorini, or somewhere else?

answers.answer: It's the Lukla Airport in Nepal. You land on a very short runway which slopes up by something like 35 degrees.

Madeira, Gibraltar and Innsbruck in Europe are the scariest, but Madeira out of all of them. What makes an airport scary is the length of the runway, the shorter the runway the more higher risk, the narrower the runway, airport shades, air traffic control. Madeira is probably as high risk as it could be. There is special training required to land at Madeira.

questions.question: What happens to the fleet of state cars - Rolls Royces, Bentleys - when every few years the state provides a new car to the Prime Minister or Royal Family? Where are the old ones?

answers.answer: My dad's always had interesting cars, and once I saw a picture of this stretched Mercedes E-Class, and it was white. It was bulletproof. My dad said it was to put your cot in the back when you were a kid. He bought it from Princess Margaret, and she had the bulletproof, stretched Mercedes E-Class. My dad said you couldn't open the windows. Once they lost the keys and it had to wait about a month before they got the keys back. So the answer is, they do sell them on.

answers.caller: Chris Evans via Twitter (mentioned by James)
answers.answer: You can buy the Queen's last Bentley Mulsanne. It's currently for sale, complete with handbag holder. Bramley Motors in Bramley have it up for sale. Even people like us can buy royal vehicles.

questions.question: Why is the height of buildings referred to as 'stories'? If it was a unit of height, then an aircraft hangar with only one floor would have the same height as any other building.

answers.answer: Go back into the days of King Arthur and castles. When under siege, or whenever, they used to use the different floors as storages, and like, there'd be a grain store on the first floor. On the top floor there would be arrows and weapons and stuff like that.

questions.question: Why are there magnets in speakers? I used to take magnets out of speakers and hang them on a fishing rod to see what I could find in the river.

answers.caller: Professor Martin (Professor of Robotics at Middlesex University)
answers.answer: Coming out of the amplifier down the speaker cable is an electric current. And an electric current, when it's changing, produces magnetic field. Inside the speaker is a coil of wire, which produces a big magnetic field. To make the cone of the speaker move, you have an opposing magnetic field. The reason they want the most powerful magnets they can get is because you want the loudest sound. The more stronger the magnetic field, the more movement of the cone and the more sound you'll get.

questions.question: Is there any currency system left in the world which isn't under the control of a central bank? If there isn't, which one was the last currency system to adopt a central bank?

answers.answer: There are only three countries that are left without a central bank being owned or anything. That's Cuba, North Korea and Iran. They're in control of it, they run all their own affairs.

questions.question: Why do women's dress sizes go up in twos, not ones?

answers.answer: It's to do with mass manufacturing. The difference between a size 8 and a size 9 just wouldn't be enough to justify making two lots of. They go up in twos because the manufacturing process costs a lot of money to reset and do it, so even though you could have something that fills in the gap, they just don't make it.

questions.question: When a fetus is forming in the womb, how does the heart start for the very first time? Does it get jump leads from the mum's heart via the umbilical cord?

answers.answer: Cardiac cells are intrinsically myogenic and can initiate contractions on their own.

questions.question: Why does a cooked potato have more calories than a raw potato? Even if you bake it or boil it. Even oven chips have more calories than a raw potato.

answers.answer: It's just about weight. The calories are given to you generally in 100 grams on whatever you look at. When you cook a potato, it loses water, so it loses weight, and the calories are concentrated in a smaller amount of weight. So it's calories per 100 grams that goes down, not the total number of calories that you consume.

questions.question: During the six hours it takes from low tide to high tide, does the tide come in at an equal rate, or does it start off slow and then speed up? The Bristol Channel has about a 10 metre average tide.

answers.answer: The tide comes in due to the rotation of the gravitational force of the Moon around the Earth, you get a high tide and a low tide every 12 hours. It comes in, it builds up slowly, slowly.

questions.question: How come he can throw an egg over his house without it breaking? He threw an egg over his house and it didn't break. It landed on the lawn. How come?

answers.answer: If you cup your hands together with your fingers interlocked, you put the egg in long ways between your palm, where the bone is, and if you try and squeeze that egg, as long as it doesn't slip, you'll never break that egg. It doesn't matter how strong you are. The egg is a shape of an arch, which is very strong. That's why a lot of railway bridges are that shape, because the actual force itself won't break.

The egg is a shape of an arch, which is very strong. So that's why a lot of railway bridges and different shapes are that shape, because the actual force itself won't break. If it lands on the arch, it'll be all right. I learned it at school.

questions.question: Under globalised capitalism, is it inevitable that one person is going to end up owning everything? Because all of the trends move in the direction of wealth moving from the many to the few. Does the few eventually become the one?

answers.answer: It's never going to be one. But when you look at the amount of wealth that is held by the 0.01%, or half of the world's wealth is held by 80 people, that's where your suspicion comes from, right? That eventually, 100 years down the line, it may just be one, or one organisation.

It is possible, as illustrated by the game Monopoly. Unless the government was to intervene, eventually one company would own everything. People could boycott companies before they got so massive. But technically, yes, it could happen. You always end up with one person having everything when you play Monopoly.

questions.question: Can you have a one-letter word in Scrabble?

answers.answer: Of course you can. Why wouldn't you be able to put down A?

You can't have a one-letter word. Because you have to start with at least two letters, and every time you play a letter on the board, you're putting one letter down. You have to join it to at least another letter, so it has to be a two-letter word.

questions.question: Are bogeys nutritious? My friend likes to pick his nose a lot and I was wondering whether there's any nutritional content.

answers.answer: My firm belief is that picking your nose and eating it builds up your immunity to diseases and viruses because the small amount of germs that you're ingesting will build up your immunity to other germs. About six years after doing it on Mystery Hour, there was some research published in Scandinavia that proved that it was true.

Your nasal contents are basically a form of excretion of the body. By definition, it can't be nutritious, otherwise the body wouldn't excrete it. Your body keeps the stuff that's nutritious and uses it and gets rid of the stuff that isn't. It's also stuff that you've inhaled that's been caught in your nostril hairs. If you worked in a custard factory and breathed in custard powder, you'd end up with custard bogeys and they would be nutritious. Your body would keep that.

questions.question: When I tune up my guitar, sometimes it's gone flat, which I understand because the strings have slackened off. But what I don't understand is that so often it's gone sharp. I've asked many musicians and no one can give me an answer.

answers.answer: Every natural note has sharp above it and flat below it. You've got it tuned to natural, and you leave it for a while, and then it goes to flat, and you leave it for a bit longer, and it gets even looser, and it goes to the sharp of the note below.

The reason they go sharp is because they're cold. It's expansion and shrinking of guitar strings. He probably keeps it in the spare room where he doesn't have the radiator on, and when he goes in after a while to have a bit of a strum, it'll be sharp.

questions.question: Why is it that white people are the only race that's got so many different colours of hair? They've got ginger, brunette, blonde, mouse brown. You don't see that variety in black people or Asian people.

answers.answer: It's obviously to do with Northern European pigmentation. That's possibly the same answer to why some people have ended up with white skin despite the fact we all started off black.

It's all to do with the agricultural revolution that happened between 15,000 and 12,000 years ago in Northern Europe. Hair colour and eye colour is controlled by melanin production, just like our skin. In Northern Europe you get this warm, humid climate combined with lower sunlight. That went with the farming of grain, which led to a diet that lowered the amount of vitamin D that could be absorbed. That meant that skin colour had to get lighter to absorb more sunlight and create more vitamin D.

questions.question: Where does the expression 'a bit of how's your father' come from? It's probably a music hall song, don't you think?

answers.answer: I got my call from QI. It was a code during wartime. A young boy would come and pay a visit to his paramour. After a few pleasantries, he'd say 'oh, how's your father?' It was an innocent sounding expression, but basically he's saying 'is your father in?' If he wasn't, some illicit assignation might be in order. You'd go round, your girlfriend would open the door and you'd say 'how's your father' to establish whether he was in or not.

questions.question: Does meat that we eat get rigor mortis?

answers.answer: It does and then it passes and then you eat it. That's why you know you hang beef for a long time. The best beef is hung. Anything that's dead would get rigor mortis, but it wouldn't be a permanent condition. It passes after a while.

The food we eat does go to rigor mortis. It takes about 12 to 24 hours for it to happen. The way it goes away is the hanging process, which develops flavour and makes the meat more tender. A chicken takes much quicker, a couple of hours. In India, when you get meat that's been freshly slaughtered, you need to really pressure cook it or cook it for longer to get it tender.

questions.question: Will they ever reach a point where we've exhausted the maximum amount of music combinations or the maximum permutations of music?

answers.answer: The answer is no. If there's no maximum number of notes, there can't be a maximum number of combinations. Think of the highest note imaginable, and now go one note higher. It's like halving a number - will it ever be zero? It will never be zero because you can halve it again and again. It's the same with notes - it goes on forever.

Not infinite, because the human ear is limited to low sounds and high sounds. If you designate note A as 440 hertz, then you've got a finite number of notes in your musical scale. And there's a finite amount of combinations you can make with those notes.

questions.question: Why should something as innocuous as a draft through a window result in you waking up with a really stiff, painful neck? It's just a bit of air. How can it have such a painful effect?

answers.answer: If you go outside and it's freezing cold, what does your body do? It tenses up, and when you tense up, your muscles spasm. So if your neck is exposed to cold air, your muscles spasm and you get a stiff neck.

questions.question: In adult relationships, why do we still label ourselves boyfriend and girlfriend and not man-friend and woman-friend?

answers.answer: You would never have had a romantic relationship until the post-60s where you didn't have to get married. You would be boyfriend and girlfriend until you got married. Post-60s, we've gone to a place where you don't have to get married at all, you can shack up and stay together. And we just haven't, the language hasn't caught up with the generational change. If you feel self-conscious about your age when you introduce your girlfriend or boyfriend, then you just introduce your partner.

questions.question: When we listen to the radio, we hear Nick Ferrari's had one million viewers this month and you've had 500 viewers this month. How do you know that? Every time I turn my radio on, how do you know that I'm listening?

answers.answer: A bunch of people get sent diaries, some online, some on paper. They fill in what they're listening to at 10 o'clock on every weekday morning. Then they extrapolate from the sample of people who've been sent the diaries the broader population. It's not exactly the most reliable measurement on the planet, but it's the only one we've got. TV's the same, except you've got an electric box on your telly that sends the information to Barb. On radio, that's not a person called Barbara, it's an organisation called Barb. Radio doesn't have that. With digital it might be easier to get a bigger sample.

questions.question: Why does brown toast go cold quicker than white toast?

answers.answer: Dark colours absorb heat and cold faster than light colours. It's why Bedouins wear dark robes. The brown toast should absorb cold quicker than white toast. I can have it both ways - dark colour both absorbs heat and cold faster than light colour.

It's the blackbody radiation. A blackbody will not only absorb heat very well, it will radiate heat well. So brown toast absorbs heat better but also radiates heat better, so it goes cold quicker than white toast which reflects heat better.

questions.question: Why is it that a son born to mum and dad and named after the father will be referred to as junior? But a girl named after her mother won't be referred to as junior.

answers.answer: It's about passing on the family name. In Anglo-Saxon tradition, you pass on the surname through the father. So even if the Queen was named after her mum, she can't be Elizabeth Windsor Jr. because her mum was born Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon.

questions.question: How strong do winds have to be in order for planes to be diverted?

answers.answer: When each plane is built for the first time by Airbus or Boeing, they undergo maximum crosswind tests and are rated up to a maximum wind. For a jumbo jet, the maximum crosswind is 38 knots. An Airbus A380 is 53 miles an hour.

It's not to do with ultimate wind speed but with the crosswind component. For example, at Stansted they were landing 737s in 46-48 knot gusts even though the 737-800 rating is 38 knots, because the wind direction relative to the runway means the crosswind component on a 40 knot gust is about 12 knots. Airlines like Ryanair have their own standard operating procedures - they use 33 knots even though the aircraft can take 38 knots.

questions.question: Can you tell someone's race or ethnicity by their voice on the phone?

answers.answer: No, you can't tell someone's ethnicity by their voice. James demonstrated by having Sadiq pronounce 'air, hair, lair, there' to show how regional accent can be mistaken for ethnicity.

questions.question: Why do working dogs have their tails docked? Does it affect their ability to communicate?

answers.answer: Dog tail docking is illegal in the UK except for working dogs where a vet is allowed to dock. The reason is that when dogs are running through brush working heavily, they don't want to get a broken tail which can cause big complications. Another possible reason is so that rats can't bite the dog's tail.

questions.question: Why in the UK is 18 the legal age to be an adult? Is it a biological thing or a socially constructed thing?

answers.answer: It's socially constructed. Politicians decided that 18 is a reasonable age. However, you can get married at 16 with parents' permission, so even that's a movable feast.

It used to be 21 years of age for coming of age. After the war finished, people complained that they could send their lads to war at 18 to be killed, but they couldn't vote until they were 21. That's why it was changed to 18.

questions.question: Why is it that shirts have tails?
Do penguins have knees?

answers.answer: Penguins have knees and they have femurs. It's basic anatomy. They stand up and transfer from mother to father on their knees. He watched it on David Attenborough. They tiptoe.

questions.question: Answer to Bill's question about why women aren't called junior

answers.answer: It's got something to do with lineage and passing on the family name. Historically lineage has always been male-dominated. In Anglo-Saxon tradition, you pass on the surname determined by the father, not by the mother. Even if the Queen was named after her mum, she can't be Elizabeth Windsor Jr. because her mum's name was Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon.

questions.question: Why does beer from a bottle taste fizzier than the same product from a cask, even though it's the same ingredients?

answers.answer: At the brewery, they add more CO2 primarily because PET bottles lose gas through them over time.

answers.caller: Charles from Stockport (campaign for real ale member for 40 years)
answers.answer: Cask-conditioned beer has only a small amount of secondary fermentation that takes place. It doesn't really pressurise the cask, so when you pull it there's just a bit of sparkle. Bottled beers have a lot more pressure. It's not about plastic bottles - they were fizzier before plastic was used. Some beers like Brewdog in bottles don't have that level of pressurisation so they taste more like cask-conditioned beer.

questions.question: Is the sun the same size now as it was when dinosaurs were around? Is it getting bigger or smaller?
Do UK prison walls have to be a minimum height? And if so, how is it calculated?

answers.answer: There is a national standard for prisons - medium secure, low secure, rehabilitation units - governing the size of walls and fencing and what you can have going over the top. Sometimes walls are curved so people can't climb over them. It's all governed. Paul works as a nurse in an intensive care unit and is governed by similar rules for fences. It would be the Home Office that covers this.

questions.question: Answer about shirt tails

answers.answer: In the early 1300s, shirts were made that length so people could pull them between their legs and use them as a nappy when eating at tables and throwing food to dogs.

questions.question: What's the origin of the word watershed?

answers.answer: So it's not actually a lake, it's a drainage, it's a drainage basin. So it's something into which water has been dug to irrigate land. And for reasons I don't fully understand, you separate drainage basins and the thing that separates them, like a sort of wall, is called a watershed.

questions.question: Is there a connection between my birthmark on my inner thigh and my mum being kicked by a horse on her inner thigh when she was pregnant with me?

answers.answer: They're not related. They've been kicked by Arsenal. They're not related. Because I've got one, and my auntie's got one, and neither of our mums were kicked by a horse.

questions.question: If we as a species stop polluting, would the ozone layer be able to repair itself?

answers.answer: I thought it had worked. I thought that the ozone layer had kind of repaired itself. Or, you know, the layers of gas in that part of the atmosphere had kind of replenished.

So you're kind of right, basically, because the CFC gas has got banned and they won't be used, the ozone layer is repairing itself. It isn't repaired yet, but if you can guess the year that it will be repaired by, you can share the applause with me. 2050.

questions.question: Why are all eggs in supermarkets brown now, when they used to be white and brown?

answers.answer: It's the breeds of chicken that have proliferated in the commercial production of eggs have been selected because of their regular laying, their longevity, and probably partly because of the size of the eggs that they lay. And because it's the breed of chicken that determines the color of the egg, the predominance of the brown eggs that you're receiving is down to the predominance of the breeds of chicken that are now part of industrial chicken and egg farming.

It's to do with the ears on the chicken. Some chickens have brown ears. Some have white. And depending upon the colour of the ears, here, depends upon the colour of the egg. And the reason we have brown in this country is purely aesthetics, because in America they have white eggs, and over here we have brown, and it's purely just for the look.

questions.question: Why do we wear our wedding ring on the ring finger of our left hand?

answers.answer: It's to do with a vein that goes straight to your heart. The reason why the tradition started is because people believed that a vein ran directly from that finger to the heart. You put your wedding ring on the finger that's linked to your heart as a pledge of your eternal devotion to whoever it is that you got wed to.

questions.question: Can scientists determine the time or date of a person's conception from their DNA?

answers.caller: Professor Hall (University of Brighton - Professor of the Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: You can't use DNA to age someone in any way, shape or form. It hasn't got a time stamp to say, this was used today. A sperm is half a blueprint for a human being. You can't look at DNA and say when it was used. You could look at evolutionary trends and say this came from that era, to the nearest million or so years. It's not like a little barcode that you can read.

questions.question: Why do we eat bacon for breakfast? Why is that the essential breakfast meat?

answers.answer: It's because it's cured. Because bacon is cured, so it lasts a lot longer than other meats. So that's the reason why you'd eat bacon and not uncured meat.

Bacon and eggs came around through Edward Bernays, Sigmund Freud's nephew, who used a lot of Freud's techniques in advertising. He was hired by a packaging firm that mainly did meat products. He went to a doctor who worked for the firm and got him to write to 5,000 doctor colleagues confirming that protein-rich breakfast is good for you. He used that in advertising to say all these doctors say a protein-rich diet is good for you. Have bacon and eggs. This was the birth of modern PR propaganda.

questions.question: How do they get the massive concrete counterweights up to the top of tower cranes without building another crane?

answers.answer: They start off with a mobile crane to build the first crane. On really big sites like the Shard, you normally have two cranes. The mobile crane doesn't have the ballast in the same way a stationary crane does - it has big, huge legs that come out. And that's where you start. And the big sites like the Shard, they're two cranes, so they build each other up as they go up. Once you get the first section going, depending on how high you're building, you can use the crane you've already got to bish-bosh the new one.

questions.question: Why do we lose our appetite when we get bad news?

answers.answer: Bad news triggers the flight or fight situation in evolutionary terms. Your body releases the hormone cortisol, which is the stress hormone. What it does is it aids metabolism of fats and proteins in your body to increase your blood sugar levels in order for you to either fight or to run away. And what this then does is it suppresses other systems in your body so your immune system is suppressed and so is your digestive system as well, in order to basically pull all your resources into either fighting or running away.

questions.question: What happens to the empty space inside the body when an organ like the bladder is removed?

answers.answer: Connective tissue is what keeps all the organs in place so you don't have a hole inside you that gets filled up by all your other organs. Connective tissue is all around you, inside you. All your organs are held in place by connective tissue to the walls of your abdomen and the other organs. It looks like a white film when you open someone up, and it's made of fat. That's what holds everything in place. Obviously there will be some slippage, but essentially you will have some sort of cavity where the bladder was. There'll be a little gap there, but nothing to worry about because there'll be enough floppage to sort of hold things in place.

questions.question: Why do some bacteria have an odour and others don't?

answers.answer: It's all just the odours produced by by-products of whatever it is that the bacteria are breaking down. If you get meat starting to go off in the fridge, bacteria are breaking down various molecules in the meat and you get gases that smell like methane or sulfurous stuff. There must be things that break down without giving off particularly pungent aromas. Body odour is bacteria feeding on your sweat and dead skin.

questions.question: Do donkeys sleep standing up?

answers.answer: Horses and donkeys do tend to sleep standing up, and the reason being it's hereditary because in the wild they stand up and doze or sleep very lightly in case predators come because they want to leg it. When they get used to the fact that they're in comfort and security, they will lay down to sleep.

questions.question: Why is it more dangerous for adults to get chicken pox?

answers.answer: It's shingles when an adult gets it, but it's the same virus, so why is it more dangerous?

Adults need a larger dose of the virus to be affected because their immune system has built up against it. If adults get chicken pox, their immune system is already suppressed, making it worse. Adults generally won't catch it unless they're already ill with something like flu.

questions.question: Why do pigeons bob their heads?

answers.answer: Commented it was a rubbish question but said he'd apologise if there was a clever answer.

Pigeons bob their heads to keep their eyes still relative to the scene as they move forward, like a series of still images in a film. They have relatively long necks but small brains and are trying to avoid blurred vision. Chickens do it too.

questions.question: Why isn't Westminster our official capital city? Why is it London when none of those buildings are in London?

answers.answer: Discussed that the City of London is just a square mile, Greater London is a metropolitan county, and the capital is officially London.

You're sitting in the historic county of Middlesex but in the unitary authority of the City of Westminster. The notion of London being the capital is more emotional than factual. Local government only came into being in 1889, and before that there were historic counties. Westminster was actually the capital of Middlesex County Council.

questions.question: If we evolved from apes, why do apes still exist?

answers.answer: Rejected this as a daft question, similar to 'If we're through history, if we're meant to evolve from apes, why are they still around?'

questions.question: Why is the euro exchange rate on the news so different from what banks and post offices offer?

answers.answer: The person changing your money gets to keep a bit - they have to make a margin.

Profit is secondary. First is bid-ask spreads. When interbank rates are quoted, they go to four digits (e.g., 1.2556). But when it goes to retailers doing individual amounts of £100-£1,000, they quote rates that won't move too much by end of day. Banks make money through bid-ask spreads, not just margin.

questions.question: My dog barks at the bottom of the garden all morning and only comes back when I say 'sausage'. Do dogs get sore throats?

answers.answer: Suggested dogs might not have throats like humans, or asked whether dogs can lose their voice.
Dogs bark using their diaphragm pushing air through their lungs without stress on vocal cords, similar to how babies cry. Unlike humans shouting, this doesn't cause hoarseness or soreness.

As a former vet rep, he put three dogs in kennels for three days and the golden cocker lost its voice by the first night. The kennels had to take them inside and they needed penicillin and paracetamol for a week to recover. Dogs CAN get sore throats from barking.

questions.question: Why does herring become a kipper when smoked, but all other smoked fish keep their original names?

answers.answer: Discussed that smoked salmon stays salmon, gravadlax is still salmon. Asked why herring doesn't stay herring.

Originally 'kipper' was the name for a male salmon during spawning season. The name came from how it was cooked - split down the middle, head off, flattened like a butterfly, and hung to be smoked. When herring started being smoked the same way, it also became a kipper. A kipper is a cold-smoked herring. Other smoked fish: haddock is hot-smoked, bloater is whole cold-smoked herring, buckling is whole hot-smoked herring.

questions.question: What is the origin of the heart shape on Valentine's cards, given that an actual heart doesn't look like that?

answers.answer: Admitted he had no idea.
The Valentine heart shape is an approximation of what two real hearts would look like stitched together and cartoonised to look less grisly.

The heart shape originally appeared on medieval armour and playing cards. It was actually the other way around - the humps were underneath - and it was meant to signify a lady's bottom and waist. It's all about buttocks.

questions.question: What is the measure of when something has 'gone viral'? How many views, shares or hits does it need?

answers.answer: There is no official measure. PR departments and media decide. It's like asking what 'popular' means. It just means popular. It originated with viral marketing when the internet was young. Adrian (the producer) decides on LBC what's viral. Anyone can claim anything's viral with 100 hits but people might laugh.

questions.question: How do snowflakes know to be symmetrical? How does each arm know what the other arm's doing?

answers.answer: A snowflake has no other choice but to be symmetrical. As it's falling, it has pressures that work on it equally on all sides. The temperature that affects it is going to affect it equally as it falls and the air pressure against it. So as one arm forms, the same pressure that's making that arm form is affecting the opposing side in the exact same way so it has no other choice but to form in a symmetrical pattern.

Snowflakes form through thermodynamics and crystal formation. A snowflake starts with a seed - a little bit of dust or ice upon which subsequent bits of water molecules will fit in where they fit in best. It's like tessellations - patterns which expand making ever greater patterns but always the same repeating patterns. Thermodynamics says a system will always try and find the lowest order and each subsequent particle of ice will fit in the same way.

questions.question: Can kangaroos swim?

answers.answer: Yes, kangaroos can swim. In 1989 I was hitchhiking all over Australia. Down the side of Western Australia there was a tropical storm and at night all the kangaroos tend to huddle up on the road because it's warmer - absorbed the heat during the day onto the Tarmacadam. There was a massive downpour and we came over a hill into a dip full of water and there were kangaroos swimming all over the place trying to get out of the water.

questions.caller: Helen (Harrow) - on behalf of daughter Zoe, 14
questions.question: If you have two identical girl twins marry two identical boy twins, will their children be identical? Will the cousins be identical?

answers.answer: No, they wouldn't be identical. The answer is no. Your three boys have got the same mum and dad but they're not identical to each other. When those two chromatids, when the X and the Y mix, if identical twins were going to have identical children, then all of your children would be identical - and that is the answer.

Technically, children of identical twins that get married are siblings genetically. Your cousin would be your brother. They'd have the same DNA. But they're not going to look identical unless the egg splits. They can never be identical because that would involve two eggs splitting in two different people. Your cousins would look similar but not identical.

Two brothers and a sister married two sisters and a brother on the other side. They had seven children and all cousins have exactly the same bloodlines and they all look completely different. However, all seven have a really gummy smile.

James was 99.9% right. All genes come with alleles - variations. Like eye colour - blue eyes are recessive, brown is dominant. Even though you will have the same genes, you will not look the same because all genes have variations called alleles. The caveat is there is actually a vanishing chance, smaller than Jeremy Corbyn's chances of being voted Tory of the Year, that you could get identical children from two sets of twins marrying each other. But there's no recorded case of it ever happening.

questions.question: Why is it that light bulbs only seem to blow when you turn them on, not while they are on?

answers.answer: An ordinary standard light bulb consists of a little coil of wire inside the glass bulb. When you switch it on, an electric current passes through it and it heats up and it glows. Because there's no air inside the globe, it doesn't burn away - it just glows. When you heat that little coil of wire up, the first thing it does is it expands. It's metal. With heat it expands. If there's anything wrong with it or it's a bit old or faulty, that movement is when it's going to fracture. After a while, all the heating and cooling and expanding and contracting makes it brittle and sooner or later you'll switch it on and the fracture in the filament will break only when it begins the process of expansion.

questions.question: When they made musical instruments like harpsichords and they tuned things, how do they agree that the C major or C minor is the same note around the world? Who came up with the musical notation system?

answers.answer: J.S. Bach standardized all notation and published The Well-Tempered Clavier - evenly tuned keyboard. He published two sets of preludes and fugues in every key. At an orchestral concert, every note has a different resonance. The orchestra tunes up to an A and the note A in the middle of the stave beats at 440 beats per second, and that is the standard from which all other notes are related by tone or semitone.

questions.question: Do seagulls send out scouts looking for food? Because I have one circling around. If I throw bread on the garage roof, within 15 minutes I get about 20-odd.

answers.answer: Occam's razor would suggest that you've already answered your own question but you want it confirmed by a naturalist or ornithologist.

Yes they do send out scouts. The one flying around in 360 degrees is called a dodman. Right up above, out of eyesight, are most of the female birds. The dodman sends a signal back - a sort of cry - to the others.

questions.question: Why does the financial year begin and end in April?

answers.answer: It actually used to be at the beginning of January. It moved when our calendars went into line with the Gregorian calendar with Rome. The crown didn't want to lose tax revenues for a three or four month discrepancy. Instead of shifting three months and losing revenue, they shifted the tax year to the beginning of April. Subsequently leap years got in the way and they moved it until eventually it was fixed at April 5th.

Rent was paid on quarter days - 25th March, 25th June, 25th September, 25th December. When they changed from the Julian to Gregorian calendar, they lost 11 days. So the 25th of March became the 6th of April to protect the revenue for those 11 days.

questions.question: What is a tog in terms of duvets?

answers.answer: It's a unit of measurement - like an amp or a degree centigrade. I think it's thermal insulence.

A tog is the rate of thermal resistance between one side of the duvet and the other - the amount of time it takes for heat to dissipate. I read it in the duvet section at IKEA. It actually says it on the side of the packaging.

questions.question: Ships are female and planes are female. What are buildings? Do they have a gender in the way that some vehicles do?
Why have I never seen a dead squirrel in all my years of walking through parks three times a day with my dog?

answers.answer: Theories included: squirrels die in their nests/drays and birds eat them, or other squirrels bury them. Or the person hasn't walked under enough trees.
He was hit on the head by a dead squirrel falling out of a tree while cycling - proof that dead squirrels do fall. By the time they're scavenged, they look like rats anyway.

questions.question: How do you measure the brightness of something?

answers.answer: It's measured in lumens. Volume is measured in decibels, light is measured in lumens.
Lumens are based on the brightness of a single candle. A 100 lumen torch is the brightness of 100 candles. Measured with some kind of scientific equipment.

One lumen is the amount of light to light one square metre at a distance of one metre. It used to be called candle foot. A light meter is used to measure it. Qualifications: helped son with GCSE physics.

questions.question: Why is there a use-by date on a bottle of water?

answers.answer: Molecular disintegration - plastic molecules leach into the water over time. Also commercial reasons: if it was infinite, people would buy less. Glass bottles probably less likely to leach.

Water acts like a sponge, so plastic will leach its nasties into the water over time and make it unsafe to drink. Glass doesn't leach as much because it's a more solid material. Qualifications: worked in the potable water industry.

questions.question: What does 'SIC' mean when seen in brackets in newspaper articles?

answers.answer: SIC means 'thus' - from the Latin 'sic erat scriptum' (thus was it written). It's used when reproducing text verbatim, typically to indicate an error in the original that you're copying faithfully.

questions.question: In the Battle of the Bulge, why did American soldiers reply 'Nuts' to German demands for surrender? Where did this come from?

answers.answer: Pondered whether it meant they were 'nuts' (crazy) to expect surrender, or if it was a euphemism for something rude.

In the 1940s, 'nuts' was intended as a swear word pertaining to male testicles, which had stronger impact than current language. During the Ardennes Offensive Christmas 1944, two Belgian towns (Bastogne mentioned) were surrounded by German Panzers. Americans were in a hopeless position. Germans sent white flag demanding surrender; commander replied 'Nuts' meaning 'no way.' The Germans couldn't understand it. Qualifications: relatives in WWII army on Western Front, seen the film Battle of the Bulge multiple times.

questions.question: Why is absolute zero the lowest possible temperature? Why can't we get colder than that?

answers.answer: Speculated that perhaps you can go below absolute zero and we just haven't discovered it yet. Mentioned Kelvin and Celsius scales.

Absolute zero is minus 273 degrees Kelvin. Matter stops moving at that temperature - absolutely everything stops moving. Temperature requires physical movement, and at absolute zero, movement ceases completely. Qualifications: refrigeration engineer.

questions.question: Do advertisers have to pay royalties to use characters like Batman or Superman in radio or TV adverts?

answers.answer: Didn't know for certain. Guessed yes - if you said 'I am James Bond' you'd have to pay the estate of Ian Fleming. Otherwise everyone would use famous characters without paying.

Depends. For parody, you don't need to pay. But for commercial use, you need permission from whoever owns the rights. Bob Kane and Bill Finger created Batman; there's been a big US court case about Bill Finger's estate trying to get DC Comics to acknowledge their party. DC Comics own the rights. Similar situation with Hulk Hogan and WWF - had to pay Marvel Comics for 'Hulk' name. It's about copyright/trademark law. Qualifications: comic book reader.

questions.question: Why do pregnant women get stretch marks but children who are growing don't? Is there a limit on how much skin can grow?

answers.answer: Stretch marks happen when you've stopped growing and then start expanding (baby in belly or weight gain). Children's skin grows alongside their body proportionally, so they don't get stretch marks.

It's about the rate of growth. Pregnant belly grows quite quickly; some people's skin doesn't have enough elasticity to keep up, so it cracks - those cracks are stretch marks. Children grow internally in sync with their skin, so no cracks form. Some teenagers get stretch marks during growth spurts. You can also get them from rapid weight loss. Qualifications: serial researcher who had a baby last year and researched this extensively to avoid stretch marks.

questions.question: Why are LP records 33 and a third RPM? Why not 30 or 40?
When companies get fined (like 30 million for PPI mis-selling), where does the money actually go? Does it go to the Treasury?

answers.answer: Didn't know where the money goes.

When UK banks are fined, money goes to Serious Fraud Office and various authorities. Example: RBS got fined billions - much went to US Serious Fraud Office, UK got about 50 million. Qualifications: learns about it at university.

questions.question: Why do girls develop things earlier than boys? My 5-month-old daughter started teething at 4 months and rolling over early, and everyone says it's because she's a girl. What's the reason behind this?

answers.answer: It's to do with the growth of the baby inside the womb of the mother and the fact that the male child is trying to grow with different hormones to the host, creating a state of conflict. This is why some boys are at more risk of diseases and illnesses at a young age - they're still developing that hormonal balance after leaving the womb. Boys will always be behind female children until they pass puberty, when they catch up. By adulthood, it's all even. I studied this for my Masters, reading 'Pink Brain, Blue Brain' by Eliot. The answer involves testosterone and the different developmental paths.

questions.question: When you're hungry, why does your stomach make a noise?

answers.answer: Acid! The acid that is there to digest your food doesn't have anything to digest, but it's still bubbling away. It's having a little pop at the mucus that lines the stomach wall. It's just a chemical reaction that food stops.

It's not linked to acid at all. When your intestines are full and you've got lots of food in your stomach, there's no room for echoing or vibration because food absorbs the sounds within the bowel and gut. When your stomach is empty, that's when you hear all the noise because there's no absorption. The noise is actually always happening, but you only hear it when the stomach is empty. It's like insulation or soundproofing - when food is present, it dampens the sounds of the acid and digestion.

questions.question: How do scientists calculate that there are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on Earth? My physics teacher told me they knew this, and I'm wondering how they worked it out.

answers.answer: Scientists count how many stars there are in a relatively small part of the universe and then multiply it by the scale of the known universe. There are thought to be 10 to the power of 11 galaxies, and 10 to the power of 22 stars. The scale of the universe is immense - far larger than any earthly comparison could account for.

The claim is true. The universe is not unlimited - we live in a closed universe which has been expanding since the Big Bang, which had a beginning. One proof is that when you tune your analog TV and see static, some of that static is radiation from the echo of the Big Bang. The Hubble telescope, launched about 30 years ago, opened up our knowledge of what's out there. Scientists pointed it at a patch of apparently empty sky, saw galaxies within that tiny patch, extrapolated across the entire universe, and clearly blew sand grains out of the water. There are infinitely more stars and galaxies than there could possibly be grains of sand.

questions.question: Can somebody definitively tell me whether cooking with microwaves actually damages food? Some people are adamant you shouldn't do it, and others say it's perfectly fine. I'd also like to know why.

answers.answer: Microwaves are actually really good for food. They cause intense heat within the food by moving molecules at great speed, which releases moisture. If you put pancakes in the microwave, it makes them steam, softer and fluffier. If you put broccoli in the microwave, it makes it extremely green - green is from the superfood part which holds all the nutrients. If you boil broccoli, you'd boil out the goodness into the water. So in some cases, microwaving makes food better for you than boiling. Microwaves are not bad for you at all.

questions.question: At what point does meat start making you hungry? I saw a picture of a cow in a field and felt nothing, but saw a picture of a steak and started salivating. I've seen uncooked seafood and it makes me hungry. Why does that happen?

answers.answer: It's your memory and sense memory. You see a picture of a big juicy steak and you have a sense memory of the last time you ate a big juicy steak. You see a picture of a big cow - you've never had an encounter with a cow that left you feeling satisfied and full of delicious food. It's like Proust with madeleines - when you get a smell or sight that reminds you of a past experience, it triggers that response.

You're wrong on this one. If you look at a cow, a longhorn cow, and you know that's beef and you're going to slaughter it, cook it and eat it, you'll salivate. Eastern European cultures slaughter animals, hang the meat and cook it - people there will salivate at the sight of live animals. It's about your cultural experience and whether you have the mental association between the live animal and the meal you'll make from it.

I had a personal experience during a marathon where I forgot to take energy bars and got hypoglycemic. I was shaking and saw a field of sheep. It was like Tom and Jerry - the sheep morphed in my head into a beautifully prepared joint of meat. I wanted to eat that sheep right then and there. I was actually salivating at the sight of a live animal.

questions.question: Why do I sneeze when I have sexual thoughts? Not all the time, but sometimes more often than normal sneezing, so there seems to be a link.

answers.answer: It's called sexually induced sneezing. It's a real thing. The parasympathetic nervous system - the one that makes your heart rate straight or sweat when you're excited - can be cross-linked to your sneezing reflex. It mainly happens during orgasm but can occur with sexual thoughts. The advice is to never tell anyone you have this condition; just say you have hay fever, otherwise people will call you out every time you're excited.

questions.question: Is sign language universal around the world? Braille seems to be universal, so is sign language too?

answers.answer: No, sign language is absolutely not universal. There are about 130 different sign languages in the world. Someone from China wouldn't have the same signs as someone from England. Deaf people are just like hearing people in that they speak different languages depending on where they're from. We all speak different languages - why would deaf people be any different?

questions.question: Why do some people stick their tongue out when they concentrate? Like when playing pool, threading a needle, or ladies putting on mascara.
