answers.answer: The amount of brain power required to look after your tongue is significant - it's constantly moving in your mouth whether you're talking or not. When you're concentrating on something really difficult, even just drawing a circle, your brain wants to stop thinking about your tongue to prevent it from choking you or going to the back of your throat. It's like allocating mental resources - the brain has to focus on the difficult task and stops worrying about tongue control. I know this because my son, who has cerebral palsy, sticks his tongue out all the time when he's writing as he finds it difficult, and we asked the doctor about it.

questions.question: Why is there a watershed on TV but not on radio? Why can you hear swearing after 9pm on TV but not necessarily on radio?
Why do dogs lick humans? Is it just because they like us or affection, or is there another reason?

answers.answer: It's an inherent thing from when dogs are pups. Pups would lick their parent's face to signal they're hungry. With dogs now, when they lick our face, they get a good reaction from humans - it's a learned behaviour through something they've always done inherently. Some people mention salt in this context, but the answer is that it encourages the adults to regurgitate half-digested meat to feed the puppy. So you lick the chin in particular and you get a lovely meal back.

questions.question: How do washers work on screws and bolts?

answers.answer: Washers have two different functions. First, they spread the load when bolting to soft materials like plastic, preventing the bolt from pulling through. Second, they work as a sealing mechanism, like the copper washer on a sump plug which is deformable and designed for single use. Third, there are split washers.
The spring washer is another type that was missed - it provides tension.

questions.question: Why did Michael's glass flask break when he stirred his coffee with a metal spoon?

answers.answer: He smashed it with his spoon - you should put the lid on and shake it instead.

Vacuum flasks have two pieces of glass separated by a vacuum to prevent convection and conduction. Glass is unforgiving with temperature extremes - the cold milk cooled a section which contracted, causing it to break. The vacuum makes the glass under tension like a balloon, so a tap from the spoon could be the final straw.

Manufacturers make the glass as thin as possible to avoid heat conduction. Because there's a vacuum on one side and atmospheric pressure on the other, the glass is under tension like a balloon - a tiny pinprick shatters it. It's the combination of the spoon tap, the vacuum, and the extremely thin glass.

questions.question: Why are long johns called long johns? Who was John?

answers.answer: Named after the 19th-century heavyweight boxer John L Sullivan, who was one of the first to wear them publicly as his ring attire. His mother-in-law always called them 'John L's' - Short for John L. Sullivan.

questions.question: How do you grow seedless plants if they have no seeds?

answers.answer: They're not grown from seeds but from cuttings - you clone them from the vine. They cut a flower and place the vine into soil to grow.

questions.question: Why do ducks walk in a line?

answers.answer: From 7 days of observation feeding ducks at Centre Park - ducks land 20-30 feet away, get in a group, then march in a straight line into the food area. The straight line is tactical: it disperses rivals for food, minimizes target size for predators, like Star Wars stormtroopers.

questions.question: If you bang yourself really hard on the temple, will you die?

answers.answer: There is a very dangerous spot at the temple - the bone is quite thin and underneath is the middle meningeal artery which is quite vulnerable. A blow there can damage the artery and cause a brain bleed. It's not a pressure point but a vulnerable area where thin bone covers a superficial artery. Qualifications: Trevor is an osteopath who teaches at the British School of Osteopathy.

questions.question: What is the potential lifespan of a transplanted human organ if it keeps getting transplanted to new recipients?

answers.answer: Transplanted organs cannot be re-transplanted because they undergo trauma and sclerosis during transplantation. Hearts have a limited life - usually a maximum of about 30 years, often much less. Qualifications: Diana is mother of a double transplant recipient and also a kidney donor herself.

questions.question: Why are DVD cases bigger than CD cases when the discs are exactly the same dimensions?

answers.answer: So you don't get your DVDs mixed up with your CDs.
DVDs replaced VHS tapes, so DVD cases were made the same size as VHS cases. This meant people could use their existing VHS storage solutions for their new DVD collection.

questions.question: What does the X stand for in LAX? I went to the States last year and was told to get on the, when I was leaving, the airport will be on the motorway and I got totally lost because I had no idea what LAX was.

answers.answer: Los Angeles airport. Isn't it just to distinguish it from somewhere else? I've no idea.

Three-letter airport identifier. Airport code. It used to be two letters and then it went up to three, so they had to stick something on the end of it. The X doesn't mean anything. For example, Dubai's DUX, Toronto's YYZ. It's just a three-letter identifier. Probably they chose X because not many cities have loads of X's in them.

questions.question: Why do we get knocked out? There must be some kind of reason for it but I just have no idea what it would be. What's the evolutionary explanation for unconsciousness?

answers.answer: If you don't get knocked out, but you might have sustained a concussion, they tell you to stay still, don't they? So it's probably to do with keeping your brain stationary.

The brain is a bit like a computer, and if you dropped your computer, it would freeze up and reboot itself. The brain is exactly the same way. It's a self-preservation mechanism in order to stop any kind of bruising or contusions to the outside of the brain as it smacks into the skull. Fighters like Mike Tyson, who had incredibly thick necks, were almost impossible to knock out because their brain did not move in their skull when they got hit. By being unconscious, you stop any additional trauma being created. Your body reacts to stop any further damage being created to it.

questions.question: When you make a beeline to something, where did the word or the term beeline come from?

answers.answer: Once a bee's got the honey and it's coming back to the hive, straight line, boom, beeline.

The bee flies out, finds some nectar. Find some nectar and then straight back to the hive. Straight back to the hive. If you want to prove that, if you move a hive a couple of feet left or right, you'll just see the bee fly around and around in circles because it knows the entrance, but you've now moved it and it won't fly. Whatever way it flies out, it'll fly back in exactly the same line. When it leaves the hive, it can fly in any direction, but it will always fly back in the same direction as it flew out.

questions.question: Sometimes when you watch these fishing programs or a ferry going somewhere, why do you always have seagulls literally there waiting for fish or food? Sometimes you're in the middle of the Atlantic. The North Sea, and you've got seagulls there with a fishing trawler waiting for fish. How are there always seagulls there?

answers.answer: They can land on water. They can stop for a kip. They can kip on the water. They're not monogamous. They don't have an exclusive relationship with one fishing trawler.

They get used to the trawlers, the smell, and the fact that they're throwing things over the side. They stay with the trawler. The birds will rest on the water, but they will also rest on vessels. Especially at night time when there's no one on the upper deck to shoo them away. When it's really rough weather and they have difficulty resting on a surface, they tend to go further inland. So the more further inland you see seagulls, it means it's rougher at sea. They learn. The seagull follows the trawler because they think the sardines will be in the sea.

questions.question: Why do you remove the back cover, twiddle the batteries around, and it seems to work? It doesn't work, and then it does work. Just with a wiggle.

answers.answer: The connection had broken, and then you just remade the connection, surely?

On the batteries, the internal resistance goes up as you use it. By actually either heating the batteries up or moving the batteries around, you're actually changing the resistance of the circuit. You will get a bit more extra use. Think of it as water flow - if you put any restriction in the way, like a dam, then the amount of water flowing will slow down. The more resistance in the circuit, the less flow you're going to get, less amperage.

questions.question: You mentioned beak, as in referring to a judge. Where does that come from?

answers.answer: During Victorian times, when they went into stinky prisons, they'd have a kind of nose bag. Isn't it because when they go into stinky prisons they'd have a kind of... I think it's got something to do with having smelling salts strapped to your face. I'm making it up as I go along.

During the time of the Great Plague, especially in 1666, they thought the plague was disseminated by germs and by the air. The posh people, people with a lot of money, could afford to have masks. The masks were frequently the shape of a beak. Inside the bill, there were herbs and so forth, which they thought would freshen the air. So if a magistrate or a judge had to go into a closed courtroom, they thought there was going to be much more chance of contracting this disease. Because it's full of plebs. And so they kept the mask on all the time. And they could also have fun of looking down the mask and seeing the nasty people below. So they were then called the beaks.

questions.question: Why does your hair and eyes change colour as you grow older? When you're a child you have a certain colour hair, and when you get over a toddler, you have a certain colour hair that changes sometimes. Why does that happen?

answers.answer: Every seven years, I think, your hair changes, can change colour.

It's all to do with a protein called melanin. And your genes. You'll get a bit from your mum and a bit from your dad. And they might be different colours. And then your genes will kind of turn on and off. A bit of your mum's, a bit of your dad's. And then as you're getting older, it'll constantly change. Eventually you'll go grey. It'll just keep going on and going on. Genes getting turned on and off. It's the same reason why you don't have exactly the same hair colour as your brother, even though you've got exactly the same parents. Because things are turning on and off at different times.

questions.question: If literally everyone that I've ever met can whistle in tune, surely if the brain has the power to put everyone's mouth in the correct positions for that song to be in tune, why can't the brain do the same thing for singing?

answers.answer: It's either you can whistle or you can't. You can't sort of not. So you can't go in the middle.

Recognising whether something is in tune or not is part of the oral mechanism of singing and music and musicianship. So that's done through hearing and in your brain. And the physical mechanisms to whistle in tune are considerably less complex than the physical mechanisms needed to sing in tune. Whistling in tune is just the tightening of the lips and the opening and closing. Singing involves considerable more control over how you compress the air through your vocal valves to make them vibrate at the right frequency that you want to produce the notes and the sound.

questions.question: How does the Heimlich manoeuvre work? What's actually occurring inside the body that causes the expulsion of the matter that's caught in the airway?

answers.answer: Think of a balloon with a marble in the neck. But there's some air in the balloon. And you squeeze it really hard, really quickly. What happens to the marble? It shoots out. That is the Heimlich manoeuvre. His windpipe is blocked by the food. Someone else grabs and gets the balloon that is their abdomen, squeezes it really quickly, sends a bolt of air up their windpipe, and knocks the food out.

You're basically right. It is air. When you're doing the Heimlich maneuver, you put pressure on the top of your abdomen, just where your diaphragm is, and you compress the lungs and out pops the foreign body with lots of air. It's pressure. You need pressure there. You squeeze the balloon and the air shoots up the spout and the marble flies out the end.

questions.question: Why a standoff is Mexican? Why is it called a Mexican standoff?
When I was a kid growing up in London, we used to have a rag and bone man come round quite regularly. I get the rag part. Why bone? Why is it called bone?

answers.answer: They used to take bones. It really is as simple as it sounds. They used to take bones away, and there was some recycled... It was the first form of recycling, you know, the rag and bone man. We think of recycling as being something quite new, don't we? But that's what he was doing. He was recycling stuff.

questions.question: Do flashing Christmas lights use up half the electricity compared to static Christmas lights? How do they work?

answers.answer: Flashing lights used to work using a bimetal strip that flicked on and off.

Flashing lights use exactly the same amount of electricity. It's done with a capacitor and 555 timer chip. The capacitor fills up and empties out - current is always flowing, never actually off. So you don't save any electricity.

questions.question: How long can hair grow? If you never cut it, would it grow and grow like Rapunzel's?

answers.answer: Hair never stops growing - it keeps going even after death.

Each individual hair has its own growth cycle. For some people, their genetic cycle means they can only grow 7-8 inches before that hair falls out. So not everyone can grow hair forever - that's why some people can have really long hair and others can't.

questions.caller: Tom from Crawley (on behalf of his 8-year-old son Joey)
questions.question: How does your stomach acid not digest your body? Why doesn't it eat your stomach?

answers.answer: The stomach has a mucus-alkaline lining that keeps the acid away from the actual flesh. It creates a barrier so the acid doesn't touch the body tissues it would break down.

questions.question: When does long haul become short haul? Is it based on time zone, distance, or flight time?

answers.answer: Historically, it was based on whether you could do it in a day. BEA used to say Back Every Afternoon. Short haul was anything that couldn't fly further than the eastern Mediterranean (about 4-5 hours). If you had to stay overnight, it was long haul.

questions.question: Is there anything besides light that moves at the speed of light?

answers.answer: Darkness
Darkness is an absence of light. By definition, it's nothing, so it can't have properties. Any answer involving darkness is rejected.

questions.question: Is there a correlation between climate change and the number of large earthquakes? The Japan earthquake was so massive it changed the Earth's axis - could that affect climate?

answers.caller: Chris from Market Harbour (married to a scientist who researched it)
answers.answer: There's a connection. Research established that the geographical North Pole changed direction - it was moving towards Greenland but started moving towards the UK. The ice melting has redistributed water masses which changes the wobble. If you can change the North Pole's direction by redistributing water, it could affect tectonic plate movement and potentially generate or exacerbate earthquakes.

questions.question: Where does the saying 'Stick it in your pipe and smoke it' come from?

answers.answer: The first recording is in an American play from the 1800s. It comes from when people used to sit around smoking pipes as a meditation thing - old men would smoke pipes. It's symbolic meaning is acceptance: just accept it.

questions.question: Why do people kiss under the mistletoe? Where does that tradition come from?

answers.answer: It's a pagan fertility rite to encourage 'shenanigans in the dark months' to get 'fruity' when everyone's bored in winter. James thought he was on to something.

It goes back to the Norse goddess of love, Frigga. She loved this plant and carried it everywhere. (James adds: Frigga's son died and she cried over him - he was brought back to life by her white berry tears. People who walk under the mistletoe are blessed with Frigga's kiss.)

questions.question: Why do we put wreaths on Christmas trees AND on coffins? What's the connection? Is the Christmas wreath more about the end of the year than the birth of Jesus?

answers.answer: We put wreaths to mark the end of stuff. It's the end - of the year at Christmas, of a life at funerals.

The circle represents eternity - no beginning and no end. It's a Christian symbol meaning life and growth. At Christmas it's about new life (the birth of Jesus), at funerals it's about going to the next life, so you're not really dead. Circle of life - Hakuna Matata.

questions.caller: Jake from East Grinstead (worked in pantomime for 30 years)
questions.question: Why do ladies play the male roles (Principal Boy) in pantomimes? Like Peter Pan and Dick Whittington.

answers.caller: Zoe from Chessington (descended from Victorian actors, researches pantomime history)
answers.answer: In the early 1800s, new laws restricted child actors on stage. All roles were written as young men, so the closest representation was young female actresses in boy costumes. When they realized it was popular to have young girls on stage in tight costumes where audiences could 'ogle' their forms, it became very popular and spread.

questions.question: Why do prawns and lobsters go pink when you cook them? They're bluey-grey before cooking but turn bright pink.

answers.answer: It's a chemical reaction of some sort when heat hits them, but he doesn't know the details.

Their diet includes plantains and bacteria that are that colour. When you kill the bacteria (by heat or digestion in flamingos), the colour comes out. That's also why flamingos are pink - from eating shrimp.

questions.question: Why do humans nod up and down for yes and shake side to side for no? Why don't more people do it the other way around?

answers.answer: It stems from when you're a baby being spoon-fed. If you don't want the food, you automatically move your head away from the spoon - and it's easier to do side to side. That's how the symbol became associated with 'no'.

In some Middle Eastern countries, parts of India, Bulgaria and Greece, the nodding/shaking conventions are completely different. A shake of the head means yes in parts of India and Bulgaria. In Greece, you do a tut and move your head upwards - and 'ne' means yes.

questions.caller: Zach from Richmond (on behalf of his 10-year-old son Armani)
questions.question: Is it possible that one key could unlock another person's door or car? How many combinations of locks are there?

answers.answer: It depends on the lock. A tibbe lock (used on old Fords) has 5 possible positions per cut with 4 rows of discs - so combinations are calculated as 5x5x5x5. A Chubb mortis lock has fewer possibilities than a 7-lever lock. Yes, there will be duplication - insurance requirements mean you need at least a 5-lever mortise lock on external doors. A 3-lever lock doesn't have enough possibilities for security.
I had a car key for my Metro in the 90s that opened a friend's Metro door, but it wouldn't work in the ignition.

questions.question: Do dogs ever completely empty their bladder?

answers.answer: Dogs never completely empty their bladder because they keep some urine to mark territory. When a dog goes to the toilet, they'll keep some back for marking trees and lamp posts.

questions.question: How fast does blood move around your veins? It was a medical procedure where a drug was injected and the effect was instantaneous - how fast does blood travel?
How does the live traffic system on satnavs and in Google Maps work? How does it know there's traffic ahead or how fast it's moving?

answers.answer: Mobile phone networks (TomTom and Vodafone) track phones that aren't moving via triangulation. If a lot of phones from one network are stationary, it indicates a traffic jam. The GPS tells you where roads are, but traffic data comes from tracking mobile phones. If everyone left their phone at home, sat-nav would have no knowledge of traffic conditions.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'a load of cobblers' come from?

answers.answer: It's company rhyming slang from 'cobbler's awls'. An awl is a pointy tool that cobblers use to put holes in shoes. Cobbler's awls rhymes with balls - so it's a load of balls.

questions.question: Why does the pitch go up when you speed up a video or tape, and go down when you slow it down?

answers.answer: Sound is a waveform with peaks and troughs. If you speed up the tape, you receive more peaks per second at your ear, making the pitch higher. If you slow it down, you get fewer peaks per second, lowering the pitch. This is the Doppler effect. It also works with light - the red shift in stars shows the universe is expanding.

questions.question: Why 70 miles per hour as the national speed limit? Who decided that and was it random?

answers.answer: Around 1965, car manufacturers like Jaguar, Aston Martin and Cobra were speed testing on UK motorways with no restrictions. Barbara Castle as Transport Secretary introduced the 70mph limit along with a research centre, originally as a temporary measure for three to four years. It was also introduced because 1965 had the highest road deaths ever recorded - 8,000 fatalities.

questions.question: Why do you never see sheep and cows in the same field?

answers.answer: It's to do with different mouth actions for eating grass. Sheep chew grass low to the ground, while cows use their tongues to pull grass up and chew the cud. Sheep cope with short grass but cows want long grass, so they wouldn't be in the same field.

questions.question: Where did the universal knock come from? Is it Morph code related? Why does everyone do it worldwide?

answers.answer: It's 'shave and a haircut two bits'. Tommy Steele did it. The American version is 'shave and a haircut two cents'. Two bits is American for quarters.

questions.question: What is the chemical reaction in your body that makes your head perspire when you eat strong or mature cheese? Where does cheese sweat come out from?
Why does sugar seal a deep cut very well? Her son cut his finger at a fish and chippy and someone said to put sugar on it and it worked.

answers.answer: Sugar makes a bridge between the wound so blood can coagulate. Blood itself can't bridge the gap between two sides of a wound, but it can bond to sugar molecules and then to the other side of the wound. The sugar accelerates scabbing and makes a firmer scab. Italians do similar with the rough edge of leather from a belt.

questions.question: Is the female of the human species the only one to have an orgasm, or do animal females have orgasms too?

answers.answer: Certain members of the animal kingdom do have orgasms - female members of the animal kingdom do have orgasms.

questions.question: When, who, and why did we start clapping to show appreciation? Is it primeval and pre-verbal?

answers.answer: From the Mystery Hour archive - from Greek days when people imparted knowledge to large rooms. At the end, people would come up and slap them on the back to say thank you. People who couldn't reach the person would clap.

questions.question: Why, as a man gets older, do eyebrows grow thicker and faster? Why do old men have dense, thick eyebrows?
What is the speed of blood through the human body?
Why do we learn times tables up to 12?

answers.answer: It's because 12 was a crucial number going back to imperial measurements. 12 inches in a foot, 12 hours on a clock, 12 old pennies in a shilling, 12 shillings in a pound. It goes back to the Bible and beyond. That's why you need the 12 times table even though we now live in a more metric world.

questions.question: Why do we say Roger on the radio instead of Trevor?

answers.answer: Roger comes from military radio communication. R stands for 'received' - it means the message was received and understood. They chose a word that can't be mistaken. It's been used since around the First World War.

Roger used to represent R in the phonetic alphabet way back when the first invention of radios in the First World War. But before Romeo, it was cheers to Romeo, and it was the first letter of the word received. So people just said Roger.

questions.question: Who decided what colors the snooker balls would be?

answers.answer: Snooker as we know it is a derivative of a game called Pyramid Pool, which came from bar billiards popular in the British Army in India. The regiments that played it in Jalalpur had cadets known as snookers. It came to the UK in the late 18th/early 19th century, probably in officers' messes. Joe Davis was instrumental in introducing it as a sport and started the first world championship in 1927. Nobody knows for certain who decided the specific colors.

questions.question: Does the Official Secrets Act ever run out or need to be renewed? Am I still covered?

answers.answer: There is no statute of limitations on the Official Secrets Act. If you wish to go public, i.e. writing a book, you need to seek the permission of the Attorney General. And if you don't, even if it's been 25 years and they consider that information to be damaging to the country, they will prosecute. It's the documents and information being published that they're governing, not a person telling the story.

questions.question: What's the difference between an American cup and a British cup?

answers.answer: Each of them is a half pint measuring cup. But an American pint is 16 fluid ounces and a British pint is 20 fluid ounces. So a half pint measuring cup is 8 fluid ounces in America and 10 fluid ounces in Britain. Not enough to massively mess up most recipes but enough to merit knowledge of the distinction.

questions.question: What's the first recorded evidence of humans making jokes? Is there evidence on hieroglyphics or Mayan writings or cave paintings?

answers.answer: The earliest recorded joke is about 2,000 years old, from ancient Sumer around 1900 BC. It's a proverb that says 'Something which has never occurred since time immemorial, a young woman did not break wind fart in her husband's lap.' I read it on the BBC website years ago.

questions.question: A fighter pilot, how loud do they hear a sonic boom? They travel faster than the speed of sound, so the sound would be behind them.

answers.answer: He never hears the sonic boom because he's traveling faster than the speed of sound. He would never reach his own ears because he's going faster than the speed of sound, which is why he's caused a sonic boom in the first place.

questions.question: Why is there a three-minute delay before you can open the washing machine door once the cycle's finished?

answers.answer: It's a safety lock from the 1950s and 60s when people could open the lid while it was still spinning and get their arms broken. It needs to wait until the drum completely stops spinning before the lock releases. That's why there's a delay.

questions.question: When skyscrapers are built and cranes are put on top, when the building's done, how do they get the crane back down? They use another crane?

answers.answer: They're big Meccano sets built in situ. When finished, they take them down piece by piece. You use steeplejacks to physically unbolt sections and lower them down using the remaining crane structure and winches. It's like getting them up but in reverse. You don't necessarily need a bigger crane.

questions.question: Why do we serve pigs in blankets with turkey at Christmas?
If I want to buy a Banksy, then how on earth do I get it home?

answers.answer: You can buy canvas-based ones, or some people have chipped all the plaster off the wall. Some people have knocked walls down. I mean, there's all sorts of circumstances in which people have tried to transport the street art that has obviously been put onto street furniture.

questions.question: When you hear American radio stations and their names and their titles, so many of them have the letter K in there. What's the letter K mean? Why are there so many Ks and Ws in American radio station titles?

answers.answer: It's issued by the FCC in the States. They're given the numbers. Ws are east of the Mississippi. Ks are west of Mississippi for some reason. And it's just like an identification thing for radio stations rather than giving it names like LBC or Capital World.

questions.question: The expression 'someone walked over my grave', when you get a shiver. Anyone know where that comes from? Why would we say someone's walked over my grave?
Why are certain drinks like brandy, whisky, vodka, why are they called spirits?

answers.answer: If you take a glass of water on a hot day and look just above the glass, you just see normal stuff. If you took a glass of, say, petroleum spirits, or diethyl ether, or even alcohol, and looked just above the glass, you'd see a weird shimmery effect, just like on a hot day when you fill your glass in your car. Because water's got lots of surface tension, and spirits don't have. And the kind of entomology was it looked a little bit ghostly, and therefore that's why they're called spirits. And methylated spirit is alcohol, ethanol, with a little bit of methane to make you throw up if you drink it. And if it reached a certain point of dilution, it would be a spirit. It ceases to be shimmery, and at that point, it's not a spirit anymore, so to speak.

questions.question: My eight-year-old son asked me - if your stomach acid was on your hands, would it burn you? And if that's the case, why doesn't it burn your stomach?

answers.answer: Probably would burn your hands. And why doesn't it burn you? Because on your stomach, saliva, mucus, membranes.

When a little bit of stomach acid follows your number two out... and that stinging that you get is because the stomach acid burns. So, if it came in contact with your hand, it would burn. Maybe not as much as down there because it's a bit more sensitive. And obviously it doesn't burn your stomach because your stomach's built to house it. It's lined with a very... The stomach lining is very alkaline.

questions.question: If a market is completely illegal and therefore unregulated, how can you know how much money is passing through that? How do they even get to a ballpark figure for drug industry valuations?

answers.answer: They estimate several variables and extrapolate a number from them. So, how much product is created? Average sale price of product. Combine the two and you come up with an average size of market. The price is not unknown. You can extrapolate from street value down to wholesale value quite easily. And then the scale of production would be probably more of an estimate than the price, but still a pretty good estimate. You'd get a fairly clear idea through convictions and capture and then extrapolate from that all the people who are in the market. So, you can estimate the number of people who haven't been convicted or captured and roughly estimate how big the production annually is. They estimate how much cocaine comes out of that part of the world in a given year, and they do that by looking at what they know and then estimating what they don't know and coming up with a figure. That's why they said estimated.

questions.question: Why can't you massage yourself?

answers.answer: You can massage yourself but it's not the same sensation. If you're squeezing your own shoulder, you've got your arm all bent and stressed. When someone else does it, you're all relaxed. The reason why you can't apply a massage to your own muscles as effectively as someone else is that you need to use your muscles to apply the pressure to the massaged area. Also, part of the point is expectation - you know it's coming when you're doing it, but when someone else is doing it, you're taken by surprise. You don't know whether they're going to go left or go right.

It's simply a matter of angle, what angle you can have and the fact that you'd probably be using two hands. When she was massaging his shoulders, she was probably using two hands and not one. It's a combination of unexpectedness of touch and your own discomfort in having to reach the relevant area.

questions.question: Who decided on the length of a cigarette?

answers.answer: They decided to sell a cigarette with X ounces of tobacco in it and once they'd rolled it up in a satisfactory fashion, it turned out to be a certain length and then they made a machine and it was all uniform. Someone decided on the length of everything.

It's all to do with the rate of flow of the smoke that you inhale because it's about balancing the amount of tobacco to the length and the rate of flow so that's why it's got to be a certain length as well. If it was too long, you'd be like not getting anything out of it and if it was too short, it'd be gone in a flash. You have to have a certain amount of tobacco within a cigarette to make it satisfied and if it was too short and you wanted the same amount of tobacco then it would be too wide and it would burn too quickly.

questions.question: Why is it that when you see a wheel on a bike in the park going, it looks like it's going backwards when you focus on it?

answers.answer: It's to do with how quickly your eyes can process information. Like a frame rate on your eyes, you get a frame rate on a film or a camera. Your eyes are taking lots and lots of tiny little photographs and your brain is turning it into a moving picture and the wheel is turning around faster than your eyes can process the information. So the pictures they're taking are spaced apart in such a way that it makes it look as if the wheel is going backwards.

questions.question: How long after Queen Elizabeth died will we see Prince Charles's ears on some coins? How long after becoming king will Prince Charles's face appear on our coinage?
[Answering: Where does 'walking over my grave' come from?]

answers.answer: I believe it's from Newgate Jail where the prisoners were taken out to be hung. They had to walk over the burial area because the prisoners were buried within the confines of the prison. So they would genuinely walk over their own graves on the way to be hanged. I heard it on the History Channel and I've got various books on London's prisons and executions and it's come up in those as well.

questions.question: [Answering: How long after the queen passes will Prince Charles's face appear on coins?]

answers.answer: They start making them when the queen passes away but they don't issue them until he's got the crown on his head. I'd say about three months before he gets crowned. Like when the queen passed away on December 23rd or something, it won't be for about another year before Charlie gets put on the throne and crowned. So the coins would normally come out approximately the time of the coronation because he will be then the crowned sovereign.

questions.question: Why do coffins go into the hearse and church feet first?

answers.answer: It goes back to biblical reference about resurrection - when Jesus resurrects, everyone is risen facing the altar. So the head should be closest to the altar. Also the head end is generally heavier so feet first provides better balance when carrying.

questions.question: What is the complete opposite of a supermoon? When it's furthest away and smallest?

answers.answer: It's a micromoon. The supermoon is a perigee syzygy, and the micromoon is an apogee syzygy.

questions.question: What's the difference between a secretary and a minister, like a Secretary of State and a Minister for something like Fisheries?

answers.answer: The Secretary of State is the most senior minister in a department. So the Secretary of State for the Environment will have other ministers, but there's only one Secretary of State. It's like asking what's the difference between a headmaster and all the other teachers.

questions.question: Why do we say you've been 'sent to Coventry' when someone's not speaking to you? Is it to do with Lady Godiva?

answers.answer: The Germans bombed Coventry in WWII and completely obliterated it.
It refers to the English Civil War when Royalist prisoners of war were sent to Coventry jail and were summarily forgotten by Cromwell's forces - written out Stalin-esque style.
In medieval times, guild members who upset the guild or were found not trading fairly were expelled and couldn't work in London. Coventry was the nearest city where they were allowed to work.

questions.question: What is it with conkers that keeps spiders away? Is it gas?
How does paracetamol know which part of your body is in pain? And how do Feminax and things know it's period pains?

answers.answer: Ibuprofen and paracetamol as anti-inflammatories enter the bloodstream and don't actually know where the pain is - they go around the whole body. All pain involves inflammation of some part of the body, so anti-inflammatory drugs will only act on the bits that are inflamed.

questions.question: What was the first-ever country in the world?

answers.answer: The Republic of San Marino, founded on September 3, 301. It was a part of the Roman Empire that seceded when the barbarians came along to invade Rome. It's been going for 1,700 years and is the longest surviving country with an actual recorded founding date.

questions.question: Why do I get travel sick when reading a book as a passenger in a car but not on trains, underground, or planes? Also got travel sick go-karting.

answers.answer: It's about eye movement - on trains and planes your eyes move in a horizontal or vertical direction. In a car they turn at certain angles which causes the problem. That's why you also get it go-karting - it's the turning. If you drove the car you wouldn't get sick because you're looking straight ahead. As a passenger reading, your eyes are lagging from side to side.

questions.question: Why don't seeds from the previous year's crops grow in fields the next year? After harvesting wheat, why don't those seeds germinate among the new cabbages?

answers.answer: Each seed can only germinate once. Also, modern combines have very little waste so hardly any seeds drop. Farmers also use selective sprays to kill off anything they don't want and keep what they do.

questions.question: What happened to MI-1, 2, 3, and 4? Why do we only have MI-5 and MI-6?

answers.answer: They all existed. MI-1 was part of the War Office during World War I. As society changed and history unfolded, the breakdown really became between domestic affairs (MI-5) and foreign security (MI-6).
There was also an MI-9 during WWII which took care of downed flyers and escaping prisoners - their whole job was to repatriate RAF flyers back to England through France and Italy.

questions.question: You said you can't bring people back to life after freezing them. But how can embryos be brought back? They're frozen and then revived in IVF.

answers.answer: It's all about water. An embryo is a relatively small number of cells. They remove the water from the cells and replace it with something loosely described as antifreeze. Then when they bring them back, they revivify the cells with water and the cells resume life. Removing all water from every cell in a fully grown human is rather different.

questions.question: Are there any other animals in the world that sleepwalk, apart from humans?

answers.answer: Dogs sleepwalk or sleeprun. I saw it on YouTube. A dog was asleep in its bed, dreaming, and its legs started to go running. They get traction and one of them actually runs up a wall. They're asleep because when they get up the wall, they wake up quite drastically.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase clever clogs?

answers.answer: Clever boots was the original phrase. In the 17th century, men were referred to as 'boots' as slang for fellow or man. The phrase then got changed to clever clogs because of the neater alliteration.
It's the etymology from Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable. Boots meant fellow back in the day.

questions.question: Why is a bust called a bust?
If we sweat when we're hot, do we sweat in hot water? Does the body know we're submerged in water so there's no point in sweating?

answers.caller: Professor Howe (Professor of the Public Understanding of Science at University of Brighton)
answers.answer: We sweat all the time because we're heat generators. Our body's core is oxidising glucose and making heat. When overheating, we divert blood to extremities (fingers and toes) which are excellent radiators. We also exude water and as it evaporates, it takes heat away (latent heat of vaporization). The body would sweat in warm water because it doesn't know whether you're surrounded by hot air or hot water. We would sweat in hot water. That's why if someone's overheating, you use cold water not cold air to cool them down.

questions.question: Why do people get given the same medication dosage regardless of their weight? I'm quite small and larger women were given the same dosage. Why?

answers.caller: Zaid in Nottingham (with gardening lady also contributing)
answers.answer: For most drugs, one dose works fine regardless of body size because they metabolise the same way. Some drugs do require weighing because it depends on how the body metabolises and gets rid of the drug. When we give people a drug, there's always the risk of side effects, and we don't want to precipitate a side effect unnecessarily. We give a standardised dose and can increase it later if needed, rather than give a big dose and cause unnecessary side effects. Some drugs dissolve in fat, so body fat affects dose for those specific drugs, but for most drugs it doesn't really matter.

questions.question: Why do younger people speak with their sentences going up at the end, making everything sound like a question?

answers.answer: HRT (High Rising Terminal) is also known as Australian Question Inflection or 'Moronic Interrogative'. There's a Guardian article about this. The suggested rationale is that Australia has a massive chip on shoulder as a result of cultural inheritance/imperialist inheritance, so they're insecure in their position and always end sentences with a question rather than a definitive statement.

questions.question: Why are there more white keys than black keys on a piano keyboard? If all notes have a sharp and a flat, shouldn't there be as many black keys as white keys?

answers.answer: The white keys give you a major scale starting on C and an A minor scale - the two most dominant scales of Western music - immediately available on white keys alone. If someone is singing and can't sing as low or high as the tune, you need to start on a different note. If you want to start a major scale on D or E, for example, you need to include black notes for the scale to sound correct with the right gaps between notes. The distribution of notes is about making music sound nice with harmonising notes.

questions.question: How did we synchronise the world to the exact minute? How come time zones are to the hour (or half hour) rather than arbitrary minute differences?

answers.answer: India is 5 and a half hours ahead of UTC. When we were over there in Victorian times, turning your watch upside down would tell you what time it was in England.

answers.caller: Professor Martinex (Professor of Robotics, University of Middlesex)
answers.answer: Time zones started with trains. People leaving London by train to go to Bristol would leave London at 12 and arrive at Bristol at 1 o'clock when the journey was only 45 minutes. They decided to have one time zone for the whole of the UK instead of setting time by the sun. That spread around the rest of the world. There are 24 possible time zones (or 48 including half hours). It's a matter of convenience - it would be daft having one minute or two minute differences.

questions.question: What is the theoretical limit of the human lifespan? In the absence of disease, what actually causes death?

answers.answer: When you're born, your cells regenerate. There's some kind of master brain/regulator in each person that predetermines when you're going to run out of ability to regenerate. When you've used up your quota of regeneration, that's it.

questions.question: When was the very first university opened?

answers.answer: Bologna in Italy, founded end of 11th century, set up to study law
El Karawin in Morocco in Fez is older, founded in the 800s or 900s. It's still granting degrees today

questions.question: Why do you get that intensive pain for about three or four seconds when you get water up your nose?
Why do some people get really badly mosquito bites and others don't?

answers.answer: Pheromones. Mosquitoes are attracted to the pheromones you give off. The more pheromones, the more attracted they are. Mosquito spray creates a mask over your pheromones

questions.question: At what point will TVs outgrow what the human eye can actually take in? When will they reach maximum that the eye can cope with?

answers.answer: There's a point where your eyes won't keep up and to an extent it's already happened. With 4K TVs, unless you're sitting less than around two metres from a 50-inch screen, the difference from 1080p HD to 4K isn't perceptible. It depends on screen size and how close you sit. For average living rooms, that point has probably already come for many people

questions.question: Why do nursery rhymes always end in tragedies?

answers.answer: It's more children's literature in general and it used to be a lot worse than now. The idea is to introduce children to the tragedies of the world and keep it at a safe distance. So when they're younger they're still happy but they know about tragedy at a distance, and then they can take on board the tragedies as they grow older and learn how to manage it better

questions.question: How long did giant house spiders live for?

answers.answer: Giant house spiders can live for several years. They breed rapidly and a female can produce multiple egg sacs per year, each containing hundreds of babies. They're not dangerous and actually do a good service eating other crawling things

questions.question: Why the term Cloud Nine?

answers.answer: Cloud atlases are a thing with different types of clouds described. The highest cloud is the ninth, either Nimbostratus or Cumulonimbus. Being on the ninth cloud means you're the highest and happiest you can be

questions.question: Who has the final say on the colour and design of a goalkeeper's kit? Is it the manufacturer or the goalkeeper? Do second and third choice keepers have to wear what's given?

answers.answer: Outfield players don't get a choice either - it's made up for them. Goalkeeper shirts used to be plain yellow or green. Then a company in the Midlands started designing more flamboyant kits in the 70s. When big manufacturers got involved, they did a study on colours and noticed fluorescent colours attract attention, so they introduced those

questions.question: Why is the BCG mark the only injection that leaves a scar on our arms?

answers.answer: BCG is a live attenuated vaccine (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin). Most vaccines are given intramuscular, but BCG is given intradermal (under the skin), which causes a reaction that leads to scar tissue. It has an advantage - in countries like India, they can check if people are vaccinated because the scar is visible. It's always given on the same arm so they can verify the vaccination was done

questions.question: Why do I get goosebumps when I listen to certain music?

answers.answer: The technical term is 'frisson' - a French term meaning aesthetic chills. It's a neurological response where blood rushes towards the brain, leaving your body and cooling you down, which causes goosebumps. It's related to pleasure centres in the brain. It's personal - different music affects different people differently

questions.question: If you lost both legs and got artificial legs, could you make yourself taller? Like if you were previously 5'4", could you be 5'12"?

answers.answer: Yes, you could. Referenced Oscar Pistorius - when he was beaten at the Paralympics, there was an accusation that the winner had used extra long legs that he hadn't used in practice

questions.question: What is the smallest population the Earth needs to sustain a modern level of civilisation?
Why do cats have the knowledge or decency to bury their own waste?
Why do we not get goosebumps on our face?
Why are bullets made of lead, as opposed to any other metal?

answers.answer: Lead has a very low melting temperature so soldiers could melt it in a field fire with their own musket moulds. Iron would be too heavy and require blast furnace. Modern bullets are still lead but coated with metal jackets for malleability and stopping power.

questions.question: Do we actually ever forget anything? Is everything we've ever learned somewhere in our mind?

answers.answer: Difference between short-term and long-term memory. If memories in short-term don't get filed into long-term, they might be lost.

Memory has many components: episodic, categorical, procedural memory (like riding a bike). Neurons and connections break down with age. The more often you recall and store again, the more likely to remember. In dementia, things recalled often spread around the brain are remembered while recent events aren't.

It's a predator-avoidance thing. If cats bury their waste, larger predators can't track them. Dogs also try to do the kick-leave thing but aren't as sophisticated. First cats that buried did better and passed genes down. Animals that don't do it simply haven't found evolutionary advantage. Top of food chain (like bears) don't need to hide.

questions.question: How far can a bird fly before it has to sit down?

answers.answer: Swifts, once they leave the nest, will fly for the first two to three years of their life. They eat, sleep, and do everything on the wing. They only land when they get the urge to mate after three years.
The wandering albatross can fly for two to three months without landing. They live to be 60-70 years old and are completely monogamous, always returning to the same partner and same place.

questions.question: Why is it that marmalade doesn't go moldy when you leave it in the cupboard but most jams do?
What is the difference between magma and lava?
Why do people spit on their hands when they shake on an agreement?

answers.answer: He has a jar of marmalade in his cupboard with mould on top - over a year old. Reframes the question: why does jam get mouldier than marmalade? He eats marmalade quickly but keeps jam for cooking glazes.
Magma and lava are both the same substance - when it's below the Earth's crust it's classed as magma, once it breaks through and erupts it's classed as lava. It's simply about location.

questions.question: Why don't British banknotes have a date on them unlike British coins?

answers.answer: On the back of the 20 pound note (with Adam Smith 1723-1790) there's a copyright symbol next to it saying 'the governor and the company of the Bank of England 2006' - that's the date the copyright of the design was registered. Notes could have been made any time after 2006.

questions.question: Why do wind turbines have to be shut down when it's too windy? Why can't they just add more restrictors to create more energy or turn the blades?
Where does the superstition that the groom can't see the bride before the wedding come from? Is it the bride or just the dress?

answers.answer: It's because he was feared that if the groom met the bride before the wedding and he thought she wasn't attractive, he'd call off the wedding, which would cast shame onto the bride and her family. The original purpose was also to keep the groom from finding out what the bride looked like until the last possible minute with regard to the veil. It's a tradition where you're only allowed to meet at the wedding ceremony, going back to arranged marriages.

questions.question: Why does white noise help us sleep?

answers.answer: When you put the baby in the womb, the sound of the blood rushing through the mother's system makes a similar noise. I researched it and asked the midwife. In the womb, it's absolutely deafening. Having background noise mimics that constant noise.

questions.question: Where does the term kettle of fish come from? And what does it mean? As in a different kettle of fish?

answers.answer: A kettle is a kettle net - a type of net stretched on the shore. When the tide came in, fish came in with it. When the tide went out, it left the fish behind. An old fishing method used along the Kent-Sussex coast.

The kettle was a trap shaped with a small hole like a bottleneck - similar to a lobster trap. Fish swam in but couldn't get out. The kettle trap was used to catch salmon in Scottish rivers. They named the fish kettle after the trap because it looked very similar. They used bigger and smaller kettles for salmon and for trout, hence 'a different kettle of fish.'

questions.question: What does AM and PM stand for?

answers.answer: It's Latin for ante meridiem and post meridiem, with meridiem being midday. Ante means before and post means after.

questions.question: Why do eyelids twitch?

answers.answer: They twitch when you're tired. My friend and I used to suffer from this and we called it flicky eye syndrome.
Sometimes it's psychological, people get a twitch that's almost an anxiety disorder.

questions.question: When you say cheers, when you're having a drink, why do you click your glasses together?

answers.answer: When we clink glasses, originally a little bit of drink out of my glass went into your glass and a little bit out of yours went into mine. That would prove we weren't trying to poison each other.
It's to do with wine and the five senses - touch, smell, swirl, look for impurities, taste, and the last one is sound.
The original clinking of glasses goes back to poison.

questions.question: When I'm doing online banking and I'm paying someone money, how does the bank know that's correct? The pin-sensory machine isn't attached to the banking system.

answers.answer: It works on an algorithm. The bank has two pieces of information - account number and amount or card details. On your end you have the account number and card. When you mix those, the bank knows that one and two equals three, your card knows one and two equals three, and when you create the algorithm it gives a specific answer. The bank knows the answer it's expecting so it lets you go through.

questions.question: DNA. Is it exactly 50-50 for the parents of a child? Or is it 80-20, 60-40?

answers.answer: Yes, it's 50-50. It's 23 pairs of chromosomes, one of each pair comes from dad and one from mum. In spermatogenesis when sperm are produced, you get a shuffling - each sperm is different and contains different attributes. So things like eye colour and hair colour can be dominant or recessive and in different combinations, different attributes come out. Also, all eggs are X, and sperm are X or Y - sperm determine the gender.

questions.question: Why does the wake behind a ship stay visible for so long? The Med is 700 metres deep so sediment can't be the cause.

answers.answer: It's the excitement of the molecules and there's a feedback loop. When one molecule excites another molecule, that molecule excites the molecules around it, and they feed back on each other, which is why the wave carries.

It's caused by plankton being damaged by the revolution of the propeller, which smashes the plankton to pieces and releases the gases. What you're seeing is the tiny little bubbles of damaged plankton combined with their broken up bodies.

questions.question: Why does tying shoelaces with the opposite hand work better?

answers.answer: It's because the knot you're tying is based on a reef knot rather than a granny knot. When you do the first knot where you overlap the two strings, when you then tie the bow right-handed you're basing that on a granny knot. If you swap either of them round, you're doing it on a secure reef knot, so it doesn't come undone. Qualifications: fan of Professor Shoelace on YouTube.

questions.question: Why do we salute magpies?

answers.answer: Magpies are famous for making good life with a partner. If you see one on its own, it meant the partner had passed away or died - one for sorrow. Usually they come in twos. You salute a lone magpie because people used to think it had lost a partner and it was a sign of respect.

questions.question: In what circumstances would you imagine a fish getting thirsty?

answers.answer: Fish, like any living being, need water in their tissues. They absorb it through osmosis - through the skin and gills. When you have to top up a fish tank, it's mostly due to evaporation, not the fish drinking all the water.

questions.question: Why do we in the UK and US use a dot for decimal numbers, whereas in Europe like Italy they use a comma? (e.g., 50.50 vs 50,50)

answers.answer: A lot of this came out of India and subsequently Arabia. An Indian mathematician discovered the decimal point system and used a dot. Arabian mathematicians later used a small diagonal line. When European printing came in, the comma became the obvious analogy to the little line, and other countries stuck with a full stop for the dot. The divergence happened sometime before the Middle Ages.

questions.question: Where do we get the phrase 'hunky-dory'?

answers.answer: The 'hunky' from hunky-dory refers to 'home' - a Dutch word. It was used in 19th century America, fitting with Dutch colonization. It connects to 'hunker down'. It was also used in baseball terminology. Hunky-dory means everything's great, like tickety-boo which comes from Hindi meaning satisfactory.

questions.question: Why is it when you mix alcohol, you get drunker than when you stick to the same kind of alcohol all night? Why do different drinks make you feel different types of intoxication?

answers.answer: Different drinks affect the body's ability to absorb alcohol due to things called congeners. They block the body's ability to absorb alcohol. Doctors calculate absorption assuming 100% pure laboratory-grade alcohol, which drinks never are. Whiskey has more congeners than vodka, red wine more than white wine. The darker the drink, the more difficulty the body has absorbing the alcohol. This explains why mixing drinks gives different reactions - your congener levels are inconsistent.

Mixing alcohol doesn't actually make you any more drunk. The only difference might be that it upsets your stomach. The answer is the congeners - different drinks have different levels of these catalysts which affect how your body processes the alcohol and how you feel during intoxication.

questions.question: Why is it that when people scrape fingernails down a blackboard, that really has the same effect on most people? What is it we really dislike about that sound?

answers.answer: It's not the same sound as a human scream, but it is at exactly the same pitch as a human scream of pain. It's an evolutionary response, the same way a baby scream goes through you.

questions.question: What's the origin of a judge's wig? Why do lawyers and judges wear wigs?

answers.answer: It's all a disguise so you can't recognize the lawyer in the street if you got sent down.

It's not a disguise - you'd wear a balaclava for disguise. It came from the Restoration when Charles II brought wigs over. Lawyers started wearing them after the rest of the population and never stopped. After the French Revolution, because of the powder tax, people stopped wearing powdered wigs, but barristers and judges continued.

questions.question: Why do mouth ulcers hurt so much when you bite your mouth?

answers.answer: You've punctured the skin, it's more like a scar or lesion than an ulcer. The mouth has a lot of nerve endings.

It's bacteria. Your mouth has a lot of bacteria. When you bite it, it gets infected, which causes the pain. The body creates pain to tell you something's wrong, giving it a chance to heal. A human bite is actually lethal because of all the bacteria.

questions.question: Do chickens have taste buds?
As humans get faster (running records broken), do animals like greyhounds and racehorses get faster too?

answers.answer: It depends on whether speed will promote survival. With cheetahs, when they get faster, they also get weaker ankles, which can cause damage. If there's an evolutionary advantage in speed, it gets passed on over generations. But animals won't just get faster forever because there are consequences.

questions.question: Why is the play button a triangle, stop button a square, and pause button two vertical lines? Where did these symbols come from?
Why do we generally only feel ticklish in certain parts of our body like our neck and under our arms?

answers.answer: It's where your nerve endings are. You've got more nerve endings in certain parts. The more nerve endings in a part of your body, the more ticklish you'll be. There's a lot going on in your neck, much more than in your knee. Also bones play a part.

questions.question: What did T-Rex use its arms for?

answers.answer: They're not useless, they're like cutlery. If you're a T-Rex and you've killed prey, you need something to tear out entrails with - the small grippy claws would be helpful.

Scorpions have very small claws when they're really poisonous because they no longer need big claws to be dangerous. The T-Rex developed a very large head and very small arms because it no longer used them as a weapon - it developed a powerful bite as its primary means of catching prey.

questions.question: When you open a door or window, does the heat escape or does the cold come in?

answers.answer: Temperature and pressure are related. Hotter air is at higher pressure, so when the window is open, the heat transfers to the outside where it's colder because there's less pressure. Cold is just an absence of heat rather than something in and of itself. This is basic thermodynamics.

questions.question: Why do golf courses usually have 18 holes and not 20 or 15?

answers.answer: In Scotland, between the village and the ships/boats that went fishing, they only had enough room to build nine holes. They played nine on the way to work and nine on the way home after work. Hence, 18 holes.

questions.question: Why is the number one at the bottom left on a calculator but at the top left on a telephone keypad?

answers.answer: The telephone keypad evolved from when the dial was round and one was the first number you'd dial. Actually, zero would take the longest to dial around, so it might have been first. It used to be clicks based on the number (down to nine).

questions.question: How come Mystery Hour is on a Thursday when it feels like a Friday kind of thing?

answers.answer: The Friday quiz was on Fridays, so Mystery Hour had to be on a Thursday because you couldn't do the Friday quiz on a Friday. It started on a Thursday. Later, management changes nearly killed it, but it survived because the podcast became the most popular thing on the whole station.

questions.question: Why does a men's shirt button left to right and a woman's shirt button right to left?

answers.answer: Ladies would be dressed by their maid, and because most maids were right-handed, it was easier to button the woman's way (button on right, hole on left). The aristocracy that had buttons, the rest wore smocks. Men's buttons went the other way because men dressed themselves.

questions.question: If you were on the International Space Station and you hit a golf ball out into space, would it ever stop? How far would it get? And if it didn't stop, would it stay at a constant speed?

answers.answer: If you hit the golf ball with speed equal to escape velocity (11 km/s at Earth's surface, less in orbit), it will forever leave Earth. Even the Moon is still gripped by Earth's gravity.

answers.caller: Mike from Hemel Hempstead (British Interplanetary Society)
answers.answer: Space station travels at 17,000 mph, escape velocity is 25,000 mph, so you'd need to hit the ball at 8,000+ mph. If you hit it backwards from the space station, it would travel slower than the station and sink towards Earth, then catch back up. Over time, colliding with air molecules would slow it down and it would burn up as a meteorite.
Confirming Bob's answer - if you hit it away from Earth it heads off, towards Earth it shoots down as a meteor, and in the direction of travel it slowly crashes down.

questions.question: Why is a purse for a woman and a wallet for a man?

answers.answer: Men have pockets. Women don't have pockets. Ergo, they need something that shuts with a clasp to keep their coins in. Coins in pockets, so men don't need a sealable receptacle for coinage.

questions.question: Why do British passports still have French writing next to the details?

answers.answer: French is the international language of diplomacy. Rules are set by the International Civil Aviation Authority for getting in and out of customs.

questions.question: Why do film and TV credits at the end show the date in Roman numerals? Why not just use regular numbers?

answers.answer: The theory is that it's done deliberately to deceive you so you won't be able to tell how old something is. It stays there forever and doesn't date, so you won't realize you're watching something 30 years old.

questions.question: Why does witnessing someone yawn cause you to yawn?

answers.answer: The theory is evolutionary. When you yawn and I can see behind you (nothing there), it communicates that we are both safe. If there was a lion behind me, you wouldn't yawn. So when you yawn, I'll yawn too because it's good to suck in oxygen. Everyone's a winner.

questions.question: I have two identical DAB radios, one upstairs and one downstairs. When I have them both on at the same time, why aren't they in sync?

answers.answer: There is a large delay on DAB compared to FM - up to about a minute. If he's on the border between two regions, one radio picks up one region and the other picks up the other.

Although the radios are identical, the components (resistors, transistors) have tolerances and will vary slightly. The signal reaches each radio at slightly different times, and without circuits to synchronize them, they will never be in sync.

questions.question: Why do we have to have two different types of screw heads? Why can't we just get rid of slot top screws?

answers.answer: Slot screws slip more easily, can scratch the hinge. Cross-head screws (Phillips or PosiDrive) have better grip. However, for soft metals like brass, the cross-head rounds off the end because you can't get enough purchase - you need the wider slot for torque.

questions.question: Why is dentistry not an 'ology' like cardiology, neurology, oncology, ophthalmology?

answers.answer: An ology is the study of something, not the mending or repairing of it.
The correct answer is odontology - the study of teeth and the diseases of teeth.

questions.question: When farmers are ploughing a field in the middle of the country miles from anywhere, within 20-30 minutes there are 50 seagulls behind every tractor. How do seagulls know about the tractors?
When trees absorb CO2, and we cut them down, is all that good work wasted? If you make a table out of wood, does it retain the CO2?

answers.answer: When the Earth was formed, CO2 made up one-third of the atmosphere (300,000 parts per million). As life evolved, carbon was sequestered from the atmosphere. Your piece of wood is carbon (lignite). There's no CO2 in it - the carbon is locked in. If you burn it, it reacts with oxygen to create CO2. Fossil fuels are called fossilised sunlight.

questions.question: Is going to Wales from England a foreign holiday?

answers.answer: It is categorically not a foreign holiday. Wales is part of the United Kingdom.

questions.question: Why is it traditionally we always wear black at funerals? We associate it with darkness, the end of the day. But why does it have to be black?

answers.answer: It goes back to the Roman Empire where they wore a dark-coloured toga called a toga puller to show mourning. Purple was half mourning - when you went into half mourning, you could wear purple. Africa and Asian cultures mainly wear white for funerals. The theory is that our roads were muddy and theirs were sandy, so our whites would have got dirty. In Victorian days, the higher up in social standing you were, the longer you were expected to wear black. For nobility, it was four years.

questions.question: What's happening when I rub my tube barb on a paint machine? Why does it seem to work when it didn't work before?

answers.answer: It's law of averages. When you rub it, it sometimes works, but three times out of ten it might work anyway without the rubbing. It's just confirmation bias - you're remembering the times it worked after rubbing but forgetting all the times it didn't work even with rubbing.

questions.question: Where did the saying 'diggs' come from? When my dad was younger and he moved to London from up north, he used to say 'I stayed in digs'. Where does the phrase come from?

answers.answer: There were lodgings and boarding houses for the guys that were building the canals in the Midlands. You get 'navigational diggers' so you end up with 'navvies' and 'digs'. The navvies were the name given to the people building the canals (usually Irish), and the digs was the name given to where they stayed. This came from a book he read years ago.

questions.question: Why does colour variation in cats and dogs seem confined to paws and faces? The pigmentation is roughly equal, isn't it? You never see a cat that looks like a Friesian cow. Why is it always the paws and tail that get white?

answers.answer: It's epigenetics - how your genes interact with the environment. When kittens and puppies are young, the extremities (paws, ears, tail) are the bits that get colder. When they get colder, the amount of blood that's there changes, and from that point on, the fur is a different colour. It's about how environment affects gene expression.

questions.question: What is the recording system that is used in courts where you see a lady sitting with a tiny machine? It's stenography, isn't it? She keeps up word for word exactly in time. So what is actually being recorded? What's the system that allows you to keep up verbatim?

answers.answer: It's like a changed typewriter where combinations of keys make a word, phrase or saying. When pressing three keys it would do a word rather than having to type out a word - so combinations of keys do words and they can type up to 200 words per minute.

I'm a palantypist - same as a stenographer, one is the American machine and one is the French machine. Mademoiselle Palanc invented it because she helped people who stuttered. She worked out that if you use both hands equally, both sides of the brain will respond equally. Nothing is written on the keys - you press them as chords, like playing a piano. What we're taking down is phonetics.

questions.question: Why have Disney never built a theme park in the United Kingdom? We all go all over the world to Disney - they have one in China, Japan, America, Europe. Why not England where we'd have to travel everywhere to get to one?

answers.answer: The only answer is because they didn't want to. When they built Euro Disney, they considered a few sites in Europe and we were among them. But the French government rolled out the red carpet with a good price deal. It's about government incentives and economics.

Disney did a survey in England and found the only site they'd like to build on was Rainham Marshes in Essex. When they were doing CTRL (Channel Tunnel Rail Link), they were going to build a station there for Disney. But Disney pulled out because of how much money it would cost to firm up the marshland. They pulled out, so they scrapped the train station and let it go straight through to St Pancras.

questions.question: In life, in general, you can do most things left-handed. However, why can't you conduct an orchestra left-handed? I have friends who are Royal Marine musicians and they tell me you can't conduct an orchestra left-handed.

answers.answer: Actually you can conduct an orchestra with your left hand - if you can keep the beat with your left hand, you can conduct. He had seen conductors conduct with just their left hand.

There are left-hand conductors out there, and it does drive the orchestra a bit potty. The way orchestral musicians train is: four beats in a bar - down for beat one, across to the left for beat two, back to the right for beat three, diagonally up for beat four. If you have a left-hand conductor, it's completely opposite to what they're used to. It's like driving on the other side of the road when you go on holiday - you can do it but it's hard and discombobulating.

questions.question: Why are motorcycles advertised on TV when cars aren't? There aren't enough motorbikes sold in a year to justify an advertising campaign on TV, so why advertise?

answers.answer: The cost-benefit ratio wouldn't be justified. Car adverts have the budget of a Hollywood movie. Motorbike advertising would need to be similarly high quality - it couldn't be cheap Sky during the day adverts. The return on that investment wouldn't be justified by the number of motorbikes sold.

questions.question: I was cooking and dropped a spoon just a few inches away from the flame. The flame changed from blue to orange in time with the sound of the spoon falling and hitting the counter. Why did the flame change colour? I put my hand and a tray between the flame but it still changed. When you blow on a flame it also goes orange.

answers.answer: It's a draft. When you blow on a flame you're interacting with it with air - it's the oxygen/draft affecting it. The sound of the spoon falling creates air movement that affects the flame.

questions.question: Why do headphones get tangled in your pocket?

answers.answer: There's no electricity going through headphones when they're in your pocket. They're not staying still - they're being gently agitated every time you take a step, like duvet covers in a washing machine.

Not electromagnetic. You're more likely to get tangles if the cable is long and flexible. There's weight at the end of the headphones exerting gravitational pull, so in the context of a moving pocket, there's no such thing as still. Also, there's only one way it can be untangled but infinite ways it can be tangled.

questions.question: Why do you get that lovely curly curl on the end of ribbon when you scrape scissors along it?

answers.answer: It's similar to when something knitted unravels and goes all curly because the tension is in the core fibre and its natural state is curliness.

When you're stretching the ribbon over the edge of scissors or a metal ruler, you're making the outside edge slightly longer than the inside edge, and that's why it curls round. Same principle as pipes being curved - the outside circumference is longer than the inside. You make one side longer than the other and physics dictates it must curl.

questions.question: What's the difference between runny honey and set honey? How do they make honey set?
What was the blue bit on pencil erasers actually for? It never seemed to rub out ink properly.

answers.answer: It genuinely was there so you could rub off ink. It was made of sand and actually removed the page from the page, leaving a papery scab.
It's not for ink. It's for erasing pencil from card and heavy paper - when you'd be there for ages with the soft end trying to get it off, the hard end takes it off straight away.

questions.question: Why does my dad have a beer belly when he hasn't drunk a proper drink in about 20 years?

answers.answer: Hard bellies are the bad kind - they have that medicine ball effect. The fat is near the surface. Beer bellies are hard. (But then contradicted himself)

There are four reasons for putting fat on: calorie deficit, liver detoxification (toxic liver shunts toxins into fat cells), hormone imbalances, and insulin sensitivity. Beer is toxic to the liver. Cortisol stores fat near the stomach area because it's closest to the liver to process. This is also why men have more bellies - excess estrogen in women tends to put fat on around thighs and bum. Once you damage your liver with beer, you create insulin sensitivity and it becomes a self-reinforcing cycle that's hard to get rid of.

The hard belly is the bad belly because it's around your organs. The soft belly is a good belly because it's just under the skin. As you get older, you exercise less but still eat the same amount, so you store it. Fat starts from the stomach and spreads out.

questions.question: Why is pink always associated with girls and blue with boys? Why not green or yellow?

answers.answer: It didn't used to be like this. Boys in Victorian times were dressed in pink. Purple denoted wealth in ancient times.

This changed around the 19th century. Originally girls wore blue and boys wore pink. It changed after the First World War when department stores and the feminist movement got involved - they didn't want children to be gendered in that way. But the call dropped.

questions.question: How can herbivores like hippos, horses, cows get so big without eating any fat or protein - just grass?

answers.answer: There's fat in grass. There's sugar in grass. There's more in herbage than we might think.

It's a simple matter of calories - if you eat more calories than you use, you grow. But there's also bacteria involved. The grass goes into the stomach and bacteria turn it into protein, which the animal absorbs. They chew the cud - it comes around twice like rabbit food. The food goes through the whole system twice.

questions.question: Why don't we sneeze when we're asleep? I sneeze multiple times during the day but never at night.

answers.answer: Is it not that all our muscles are relaxed when we're asleep, so the reflex wouldn't happen?

He asked a doctor about 30 years ago. The explanation is that whatever's in the nose that makes us sneeze swells up when we're sleeping, but the motor neurons that send the signal to the brain turn themselves off when you're asleep. So when you wake up, you're very susceptible to sneezing and your nose immediately goes 'oh hello what's going on here' and you have a massive sneezing fit.

questions.question: Why do actors in TV and films always have a bright green reflection in their glasses?

answers.answer: It's the anti-reflection coating on the spectacles that gives the green colour. Opticians try to persuade you to have anti-reflection coating in glasses - it allows much more light to pass through and has a green tinge when light hits the lens at an oblique angle. He clarified it wasn't green screen because Coronation Street wouldn't have used that technology back in the day.
