questions.question: Where does the phrase 'blue murder' come from? Was there a point when we went around killing blue people or Smurfs?
What's the deal with reheating rice? Can you eat curry rice the next day? Can you microwave it? What are the rules?

answers.answer: It increases the likelihood of food poisoning. The longer it's left at room temperature, the more likely bacteria will multiply. All rice has got bacteria - you cook it and kill most of it, you eat the rice, then you let it cool. When it's not hot, the bacteria starts multiplying. So if you let your takeaway cool and then stick it in the fridge, it doesn't really matter about reheating - it's about the time at room temperature.

He's a microbiologist. The problem with rice is a bacteria called Bacillus cereus. At room temperature, this bacteria releases a toxin. This toxin cannot be killed when reheated. It's this toxin that makes you violently ill, probably within about half an hour of eating it. The longer rice is at room temperature, the greater the likelihood of getting food poisoning.

questions.question: Why do the bride's family traditionally pay for the wedding?

answers.answer: It's linked to the dowry and the idea that back in the day, your daughter would have been moving in with her husband's family after getting married. They would have been assuming responsibility for the cost of her life - feeding her, clothing her, housing her. So as part of the dowry, you pay for the wedding, because they're paying for everything else subsequently.

A woman was a chattel, a possession, a burden. If she wasn't owned by the father, the brother was her owner. If there were no brothers, then her uncle was her owner. So she was available to be sold, basically. The wedding was paid for to get rid of her.

questions.question: How do they measure time in space?

answers.answer: It's the same as at sea. All shipping obeys the same time. I think it's Greenwich Mean Time, so space will be the same. They're just following Greenwich Mean Time, and they've got a clock to tell them.

A day is the time it takes for the Earth to go through one rotation. As soon as you can rely on a clock to emulate Earth rotating, you don't need the Earth rotating anymore. We have atomic clocks - they supersede quartz-based clocks and are based on the vibrations of cesium atoms. Wherever you are, you know that one day is one day. Greenwich Mean Time is effectively the universal standard. Wherever you are, as long as the clock is based on one rotation of the Earth, then you can tell the time. It's GMT that they're subscribing to, UTC.

questions.question: Why are dogs at their most fertile when in season, but humans are at their least fertile when menstruating?

answers.answer: A dog, when it's on heat, is ovulating. The human, when they're menstruating, is the exact opposite of the cycle - it's breaking down. Ovulation and menstruation are two completely different things. They're the polar opposite of each other. Women give off pheromones, hormones, when they're ovulating that increase the likelihood of them being impregnated. And that's what dogs do when in season, so it's the same thing - it's just not as stark.

questions.question: Why do bus stops have letters on the top and what do they mean?

answers.answer: It's the name of the bus stop. You can't do it alphabetically because you never know where new ones are going to appear. You call it KP or PK or K, and it means that the driver can report to base which one he's at, where he is. Because you might have two streets with the same name on different bus routes at opposite ends of town. You might have the Acacia Avenue stop for the number 37 and the number 44. So they can't call it the Acacia Avenue stop because there are two. So they have to give it a name that's unlinked to its geographical location.

answers.caller: Peter from Thornton Heath (30 years bus driver)
answers.answer: They're basically just map references for the public and emergency services. If you look on the map at the bus stop, you'll see that normally in a busy area where there are numerous stops, like Elephant and Castle, just so you can get your bearings, and also if the bus driver has to call the emergency services out. It's a reference point. They're totally random - they use the alphabet. Where you get lots of bus stops, the next one is PN or PA. It's just a reference point for the emergency services and public.

They are random, but it actually has nothing to do with the bus shelter itself. The shelter itself has its own determined 10-digit number. The letters actually determine the post that they're sitting on top of. It's got nothing to do with the bus shelter whatsoever. If the post's been damaged, it identifies that post along that street, or if you're going to suspend the bus stop, that's where they'll put it.

questions.question: Why are some islands called 'something Island' and others called 'Isle of something'?

answers.answer: There is no difference. Isles predates islands by about 300 years. It was an older English term.

questions.question: Where did the phrase 'man alive' come from?

answers.answer: It's a maritime saying. It was at shipwrecks when they'd gone to rescue people. They'd shout it when they found someone floating in the water still alive. 'Man alive! Man alive!' And it just carried on from there.

questions.question: Why can you wake up your spouse, kids, pets, and neighbours when you snore, but you can't wake yourself up?

answers.answer: You can wake yourself up. You're only going to wake up the spouse when she's at a different point in her sleep cycle - she's going to be in the kind of not the deep sleep bit, and you're going to be in the deep sleep bit when you're snoring. If you weren't in the deep sleep bit, you wouldn't have snored, because the first time you snored, you'd have stopped, because you heard it. It's the depth of sleep that you're in.

questions.question: How long do I have to listen to your show before I become a listener?

answers.answer: You never become a listener in terms of the ratings unless you get sent a diary, unless you're put on a list of people whose listening habits are tracked by the central body called RAJAR, and then they extrapolate from a sample the broader population. They break them down into 15-minute groupings. So technically, the answer is 15 minutes.

questions.question: Why do houses need skirting boards? What would happen if a house didn't have them?

answers.answer: You can't plaster down to the floor. It's very, very difficult to do a neat job down to floor level. Not least because your floorboards are made of wood, therefore they are prone to warping. They will bend a bit and absorb and move. So the gap between the bottom of the plastered wall and the wooden floorboard, whether you've got carpet or not, would be unsightly. So you stick your skirting board in and it covers up the unsightly gap. It's essentially a cosmetic decision. Also, it stops mice - that's the seal on the wall that you can't really do with just wood and plaster.

The skirting board is there to cover the plaster. But the reason it's there to cover the plaster has nothing to do with it being difficult to plaster down to the floor. You can't plaster down to the floor because you get damp. The floor wicks up, so if you plaster down to the floor, the moisture would travel up the wall. It's a construction rule that you have to leave a gap and that's what the skirting board covers.

questions.question: Did Germany have an equivalent of Bletchley Park and did they ever break British codes?
How come my hand didn't go numb when I was rubbing analgesic cream into my wife's back?

answers.answer: Because of the thickness of your hand being much greater than the epidermis on your hand. It takes longer to get to the nerve, so your hand doesn't go numb.

Most creams contain diclofenac, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory that doesn't contain numbing properties. The active ingredient targets inflammation, not numbness. Your hand didn't go numb because your hand had no inflammation to be treated.

questions.question: Would inflation be a result of all the new plastic five pound notes being released?

answers.answer: I don't think either of us are qualified to deal with this question, but I'm going to put it on the board.
No, because the banks just swap them. As you pay an old one in, they give out new ones. Your mum worked in a bank, so it's pretty obvious.

questions.question: What would happen if one of the presidential candidates croaks before the election?

answers.answer: If they die, it's by the vice presidential candidate. If they pull out, there's no formal mechanism in place, but the presumption is the vice presidential candidate would step up to the plate. If they didn't want to, the party management gets to make an appointment.

questions.question: What will we use for all the things we use newspapers for when there aren't newspapers anymore?

answers.answer: That's not a mystery. It's a different question for a different day. It's Amateur Hour, not mystery.

questions.question: When funeral directors are preparing a body, what happens to the blood? Does it go in the main sewer? Do they sell it for fertiliser?

answers.answer: Oh, God. I don't know. Well, that's a mystery then, isn't it? You've quite a sick mind, Maureen, if you don't mind me saying so.

Bodily fluids are disinfected and then placed down the drain. It's collected in a vessel that we disinfect before we actually throw it straight down to the sink. No special pipes or anything like that. I'm a qualified embalmer and funeral director.

questions.question: How do the police name their operations?

answers.answer: I'm quite confident the original answer is that there's an approved list with a bunch of words on it, and the police officer in charge of the operation just picks one. But for something like Operation Lenore at Fabric Nightclub, that's too much of a coincidence. We need a copper and we will find out.

There's a computer at Scotland Yard that throws out these names randomly from an approved list. Previously it was up to the senior investigating officer to pick a name, and sometimes they were inappropriate, like Operation Money Spinner because everyone was earning overtime. So they set up a computer to do it randomly. But for local operations dealing with specific local problems, someone locally might think of a name. It depends on the scale of the operation.

questions.question: How do circus posters get inside shops that are closed?

answers.answer: I don't know. I presume it's got something to do with the estate agent. It doesn't happen very often, but it certainly happens. And it is usually a select few posters that manage to breach the defences.

They basically stick a poster onto a poster with sellotape, and they push it in through the slot at the top of the door, and they dangle them down until they've got them far enough inside, and then they just sellotape them onto the inside of the top of the door. I'm a taxi driver, I watched a bloke do it. Many people on Twitter confirmed this.

questions.question: Why is it when we're looking for good luck, we tap our heads and say 'touch wood'?

answers.answer: We're tapping our heads is a later development. Originally, we would have touched actual wood. The cross is the symbol of Christianity and what is the cross made of? Wood. When we touch wood, we're basically acknowledging that, or it's a prayer or something. We don't touch metal or glass because we're not saying a little prayer.

questions.question: How do they distinguish a large town from a small city in America? In the UK it's by having a cathedral, does that rule work in other countries?

answers.answer: I haven't got a clue. It's a lovely question though. Definition of a city in America, please. Actually, it could be that they do just call it a city. Some places with cathedrals qualify as cities even if they're small. It might be a decision rather than a rule.

In America, it goes back to the pioneer days when they had little one-horse towns and they wanted to attract more people to come and live there. So they called it a city to sound bigger and more important than it was. It's just legislation, a decision. We have cities in the UK that don't have cathedrals too, like Sunderland and Brighton. I read it in a book, probably Bill Bryson.

questions.question: Does the mass of the Earth change as a result of more people being on the planet? Does the weight of the world go up?

answers.answer: No, the mass stays the same. You can't create or destroy matter other than with a nuclear reaction. Everything else is chemical reactions. Humans and all animals are made out of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen - that's had to come from somewhere. It's come from the earth, trees, whatever, and carbon dioxide in the air. The overall mass remains the same. It's just chemistry.

questions.question: How did the Victorians navigate when building Underground tunnels? They didn't have GPS, were hundreds of feet underground with no landmarks, how did they connect one point to another so exactly?

answers.answer: I don't know, but compasses work underground as well, so that's one way. There is a station on the Circle Line that has a river going through it above the level of the railway track - Sloane Square, the River Westbourne. They had to pipe it because they couldn't change its course.

They use similar surveying equipment to what engineers use in construction. They use lasers to find points and set lasers up to direct the line - keep the laser in the centre where they need to be going. Then the next point will be two metres left of centre when it needs to turn. Set up on an angle and that becomes the new centre. I was an underground miner for eight years, so I used similar equipment.

The Victorians excavated all the ground and then built it from scratch from the bottom up. It's called 'cut and cover'. They just took all the ground out and built it from there. It's the same way you build a building - you get the foundations in and then build it.

questions.question: There's a massive asteroid crater in Mexico that took out the dinosaurs. Where's the asteroid? If it broke up, why is there still a six-mile crater there? Shouldn't there be a great big mountain?

answers.answer: Your answer is someone's taken the asteroid away, probably in pieces. It probably broke into loads of pieces when it hit. Scientists have only worked this out in the last few years. They didn't know how space worked before.
The forces of the impact and energies released at the speed and pressure caused the stone or whatever the contents of the asteroid were to evaporate. It basically exploded on impact.

questions.question: Why does all rubbish always smell the same? Whether it's from my girlfriend's flat or a tip, the smell is always identical.

answers.answer: It's bacteria flatulence - the bacteria decomposing the rubbish is giving off the aroma. All rubbish has in common that it's all rotting.

Common denominator is food and protein sources. Bad smells contain sulphur compounds (hydrogen sulphide). The smell is cadaverine and putrescine - amines produced by breakdown of flesh. Bacterial breakdown of protein compounds makes all rubbish smell the same - bacterial flatulence.

questions.question: Are nuns allowed to go swimming and if so, what would they wear?

answers.answer: Yes, nuns are allowed to go swimming and they can wear whatever they want.

questions.question: Why is 'Master' used as a form of address for young boys (like on birthday cards) when it's also used to denote superiority/excellence (MasterChef, Master Builder)?

answers.answer: Comes from Latin 'magister' (where we get magistrate). Used to distinguish from Mr. - to denote childhood rather than adulthood. James admits he cannot explain why the same word is used for young males and expert older males.

questions.question: Why when swimming in the sea are there warm pockets of water that feel like someone has urinated in them?

answers.answer: Hot pockets - warm water from the sun heating up pockets of water that haven't mixed with the colder water yet. Like when you run the hot tap in a bath - you need to swirl it around.

These are called thermoclines - underwater hot springs. Water of different temperatures and salinity won't mix straight away, causing temperature differences. Also caused by the sun heating surface water.

questions.question: Why do defendants in court confirm their name and address and then apparently just leave? If police already know their details, what's the point?

answers.answer: The question is wrong - they don't just go to court and leave. They confirm name and address, then are remanded either in custody or on bail. The remand is the important part - it gives authorities judicial power to detain them. Police can only detain under certain circumstances and for certain lengths of time. The magistrate can detain and remand for trial, making the detention lawful.

questions.question: Can moths eat the fur of living animals? I'm worried about my cats who have been moulting more than usual.

answers.answer: I don't think so, but I can't claim any expertise in this area. Will leave it on the board.

Moths won't lay eggs on a moving live animal because the eggs would fall off and there's no food source. They only eat from dead animal fur/hair. Moths feed on keratin - fur, wool, even human hair. If the gentleman hoovers wall floor junctions thoroughly weekly (and throws away the bag because eggs might still hatch in the hoover), that would help prevent the moths.

questions.question: Why is my beard bright red while all the other hair on my body (including everywhere else) is dark brown?
Why is my belly soft and wobbly when my mate's belly is solid (like a medicine ball) even though we both have similar sized bellies?

answers.answer: The soft belly (wobbler) is actually healthier - the fat is just under the skin (subcutaneous). The solid belly is visceral fat - fat around the organs, which is more dangerous. It's just how different people lay down fat - genetic inheritance.

questions.question: Why is the King of Hearts the only playing card king without a moustache? (Asked by her six-year-old daughter)

answers.answer: The King of Hearts was originally based on Charles VII of France, who had no facial hair.

questions.question: Answering question about Mister and Master (confused response about maritime law, legalese, corporations)

answers.answer: Claimed Master comes from maritime law/legalese, and at age seven children are considered 'lost at sea' in legal terminology. Mr. comes from 'Mister' as in Mr. Christian who set sail. James was unable to extract a coherent answer.

questions.question: If I'm swimming in the sea and lightning strikes, how far away do I need to be to not be electrocuted?
What makes sweetcorn survive the digestive system?

answers.answer: The husk on the outside of the corn niblet is so thick that stomach acid cannot break down the cellulose. It's like swallowing an apple whole - if you don't chew it properly, the acid can't penetrate the thick skin.

questions.question: Why are all garden centres called nurseries?

answers.answer: Probably to do with nurturing plants for a while from birth before selling them to customers.

questions.question: Why are most hairdressers closed on a Monday?

answers.answer: Five-day week - hairdressers work Saturdays so take Mondays off. Historically barbers could rent chairs so some would work Saturday but not Monday, allowing continuous business. James mentioned patron of Arthur Razor in Acton.

questions.question: Why is the emotional feeling called Cloud 9? Why not Cloud 8 or 7?
In old films, when someone got a fright their hair turned white overnight - is there any scientific basis for this?

answers.answer: There is some truth about stress for greyness. James noted their boss came in with black hair and is now completely grey. Suggests a trichologist might be qualified to comment.

questions.question: If caffeine is naturally occurring in coffee beans, how do they take the caffeine out to make decaf coffee?

answers.answer: The American Meteorological Society has nine categories of clouds. Cloud 9 is cumulonimbus, the biggest kind of cloud. Saying you're on Cloud 9 means you're at the highest possible point - on top of the world. Reference: Brewer's Dictionary of Phrasing and Fable.

questions.answer to question: Why are garden centres called nurseries?

answers.answer: Garden centres were fundamentally correct. Production nurseries grew plants before the 1950s but could only sell in dormant season. The invention of the plastic plant pot meant plants could be grown and sold year-round. Many production nurseries developed into garden centres with coffee shops and gift shops. Some purpose-built garden centres were never actually nurseries. Qualifications: professional horticulturist who went to Pershaw College of Horticulture.

questions.answer to question: How do they remove caffeine from coffee?

answers.answer: Two methods: 1) Green coffee beans are immersed in a solvent which dissolves and extracts the caffeine. 2) Swiss Water method uses heat and osmosis to remove caffeine. Dave researched this after getting palpitations from too much strong coffee on holiday in Italy.

questions.question: When seawater comes up the Thames estuary, how does it become fresh water in central London? Where does the salt end?
Why do eyebrows only grow to a certain length, while head hair keeps growing?

answers.answer: They fall out and replenish. Same as all body hair - they have a growth cycle and then fall out. Head hair is different because it grows for longer periods before falling out.

questions.question: What is the origin of the word 'chuffed' when we say we're really chuffed with something?

answers.answer: Thought it might be linked to steam trains - 'chuff' is the sound they make. James was happy to see steam trains and mentioned Kidderminster Harriers football ground where you can hear them passing.

questions.question: Do ants ever sleep? They seem to be about 24/7 in the garden.

questions.answer to question: Where does the Thames cease to be salty?

answers.answer: The Thames is tidal up to Teddington Lock. Fresh water flows down from the land, while tidal water comes back from the sea. Where they meet it's brackish - a mixture of salt and fresh water. The sheer volume of water from tributaries stops the tides going further. Recommendations: book about the Thames, Kew Bridge has bullet holes from WWII target practice.

questions.question: How do colour catchers work in the washing machine?

questions.answer to question: Can hair go white with fright?

answers.answer: When scared, blood is drawn from skin to essential organs for fight or flight mode, making skin paler. Less blood in skin accelerates ageing and stress, causing long-term ageing in skin and hair over time.

questions.answer to question: Can hair go white with fright? (counter to Harley)

answers.answer: Harley is totally wrong. Hair is dead tissue so it cannot change colour through blood flow. However, stress could kill pigment cells in hair roots over weeks, so hair could go grey as it grows out. Hair cannot change colour instantly - it would only show as new growth comes through. Reference: Marie Antoinette legend - hair may have gone white under prison stress but would only become visible as it grew, not overnight. Heard answer 30 years ago on radio.

Dyes bond to fabric through polar bonds - they're weak bonds. In the wash, dyes come off and colour catchers have lots of polar groups, making them much more attractive to dyes than clothes. So all the dyes attach to the colour catcher instead. Qualifications: Chemistry student at university. Additional terms: hydrogen bonding, basic groups on fabrics, acidic groups.
One theory from 16th century means 'bloated out' or 'puffed up' - he was cut off before giving the happiness theory.
Yes, ants do sleep. Saw a documentary 4-5 months ago showing ants in a set-up taking it in turns to sleep.

questions.question: Why are foxes the only wild animals that won't go in water?

answers.answer: The premise may be flawed - foxes are not the only wild animals that don't go in water, and foxes may actually go in water.
The only time foxes go into water is to get rid of their fleas. They walk in slowly, fleas gather on their head, then the fox dips under and leaves all the fleas in the water.

questions.question: Why does paper rise up to meet sellotape before contact, like a magnet?

answers.answer: Static electricity. When you pull sellotape apart, you're applying energy and electrons (negative charges) are attracted to one surface while protons are attracted to the other surface, creating an electrically charged static effect.

questions.question: What do the 'arms' in pub names like Joiner's Arms or King's Arms refer to?

answers.answer: Pub names used to be pictograms when literacy was rare - you would recognise the sign depicting a coat of arms linked to trades or professions.

The arms refer to coats of arms for guilds (carpenters, coopers etc). Also, during the Civil War, pubs changed their signs quickly - King's Arms for Royalist areas, King's Head for Parliamentarian areas - to show allegiance and avoid having goods stolen.

questions.question: Do animals get jet lag?
Do animals get jet lag?

answers.answer: Yes, animals do get jet lag. On BBC television, Ben Shepard asked the dressage gold medalists about this, and they confirmed horses do get jet lag, with one horse ending up with swollen legs.

questions.question: When was the first puzzle created or discovered? What was the very first puzzle?

answers.answer: The oldest puzzle was the Egyptian pyramids. When they built the tombs with forced entrances and labyrinths, once completed, everyone wondered how they'd get in - that was the puzzle.

questions.question: Why did thousands of tiny fish jump out of the sea in an arc, bouncing off people in the water?

answers.answer: It's likely a predatory fish chasing bait fish. Bait fish leap out of the water to evade being eaten - it gives them an edge since predatory fish usually don't follow them out of the water. It's not that rare if you're in the right place.

questions.question: What is the tradition of birthday candles on cakes? Why do we put them on cakes?
Can a swan actually break a human arm with its wings?

answers.answer: A man on the Thames got too near rushes and a swan attacked him, breaking his arm with its beak, not its wings.
A swan cannot break the bones of a human with its wing - it's a myth. Seen on a wildlife programme.
A swan broke my mum's arm some years back by grabbing her arm, and she has suffered damage ever since.
A swan probably could break your arm with its wings. I have 15 years experience rescuing swans at a swan sanctuary and have been hit by many swans.

questions.question: Why does light change the flavour of beer in clear bottles?

answers.answer: It's because of the yeast. Yeast is used in making beer and is affected by light - that's why Marmite comes in dark jars. The same applies to beer.

questions.question: What is the origin of the thumbs-up sign?

answers.answer: Roman gladiators - thumbs up meant you live, thumbs down meant you die. That's probably where it started.
It's used in scuba diving to mean let's go up, and water sports were used long before aircraft.

questions.question: What was the first puzzle ever invented?

answers.answer: Jigsaws were the first puzzle, created by cartographers during King George III's reign who cut around country boundaries as teaching aids.

questions.question: Why does a vacuum cleaner motor run faster when the tube gets blocked?
How did the actual horses get to the Olympics? Did they fly or how did they get there?

answers.answer: They fly on planes. It's absolutely impossible to get a horse to Brazil in the timescales relevant to an Olympic Games without sticking them on a plane.
They go via aeroplane. They have their own individual passports and go through their own customs. They also have a hay allowance because of the weight on the plane.

questions.question: Why the hell do we put lead on windows?

answers.answer: It's done for aesthetic reasons by people who are quite naff. Leaded windows have got something to do with trying to make your house look like the windows back in the day when they needed to be leaded because the technology hadn't tackled creating big pieces of glass yet.

In the modern world, the leaded windows are just sort of mock Tudor fake attempts. They're just for the look. Mum and Dad had some lead-lighted windows that were made of small panes. The glazer told me it's quite an old idea anymore and you can't buy these anymore because they're very expensive to do and maintain.
Lead lights are, indeed, just for the look. In the really old windows, it's separate panes.

questions.question: When you look rough when you come in the door to work and you said 'I had a few sherbets last night', what's a sherbet got to do with beer?

answers.answer: A sherbet originally was a drink, Lucy. You've just grown up in an era where you associate it with fountains and liquorice. But originally, a sherbet was a drink. Like a sorbet, but liquidy.

It's from Cockney rhyming slang - Sherbet Dib Dib equals sick. Having a Sherbert means having a drink. Also told there's an Australian theory that it means the frothy head of a newly poured glass of beer.

questions.question: How do food fads happen? Like cider, coconut oil - did somebody pre-plan these things 20 years ago?

answers.answer: One company breaks through and then the other company, due to commercial considerations and advertising and a change in style, pile in with their own attempt to get a piece of the action and it means they have to pay a premium for their apples. With coconuts, huge amounts were previously thrown away so they've just found ways to use byproducts.

If you're an apple producer or a potato producer, you'll look at making crisps or cider because it'll give you higher margins. And then if one company's successful, a load of other companies will follow. But the cider resurgence wasn't prompted by apple producers - it was prompted by cider producers who contacted advertising agents.

questions.question: Why don't people eat seagulls? Why don't people eat pigeons? There's loads of them.

answers.answer: They don't taste very nice and they're quite hard to catch. And a lot of them will be protected - that's RSPB territory.

Seagulls are a protected species. Britain has more than the whole of the rest of the world put together, and it's mankind's behaviour that's driving them out of their natural habitat. You can eat some gulls eggs, but you need all sorts of licences to do so.

questions.question: We can eat red meat raw almost, but we can't do the same with chicken - why?

answers.answer: Salmonella. But the farmer and the chicken live on the same farm, eat the same grass - so it must be something more specific to chicken. James wasn't fully satisfied with the answer and left the question on the board.

questions.question: Why aren't all plastic bags sold biodegradable? Surely that's better for the environment?

answers.answer: It would cost too much. The biodegradable bags you get aren't as sturdy as normal bags.

Co-op provides a choice of biodegradable shopping bags - you have to ask for it at the counter. It's about consumer demand and profit incentives. If there was enough demand, other big names would provide the option too.

questions.question: If Hillary Clinton becomes president, what are we going to call her husband? Because 'First Man' just sounds a bit weird.

answers.answer: It would probably be 'First Gentleman'. Bill Clinton is reportedly said he wants it to be 'First Guy'. But because he is a previous president himself, the chances are he'll carry on being addressed as Mr. President, because ex-presidents still are.

questions.question: Why do some houses have a sparkling little metal thing on their chimneys that looks like an upside-down colander?

answers.answer: To stop pigeons falling down their chimneys. The shiny, spinny ones make them less likely to land at all.

They're called revolving chimney cowls. They spin in the breeze and eradicate the downdraft - they draw the air up and out. So yes, they'll stop pigeons coming down, but that's not what they are - they're to stop that cold, biting wind that comes down Victorian chimneys into the fireplace.

questions.question: Why do some houses have those metal upside-down colander things on their chimneys?

answers.answer: To stop pigeons falling down their chimneys - the shiny, spinny ones make them less likely to land.

questions.question: Why do athletes run around the track anti-clockwise?

answers.answer: This is in the Mystery Hour archive - was actually tweeted by the Internet Department yesterday as a great example of Mystery Hour. But Paul cut him off before he could give the answer.

questions.question: Can insects get drunk? When an insect lands in your drink, does it get drunk?

answers.answer: Bees can get drunk. They'll sometimes find fermented nectar and get drunk, and certain bees seek out fermented nectar - they have similar rates of alcoholism as humans. They have guard bees at the door like bouncers. If a bee has had too many, they'll be pushed away. If they do too much, they'll get a leg pulled off. Bees can metabolize alcohol in fermented nectar so they could probably metabolize it in lager and cider and wine.
Getting drunk is pretty common across all animals. If a goat or a pig eats apples that have fallen and gone a bit rotten, they can get plastered as well.

questions.question: Why are there all these big stones on the railway tracks?

answers.answer: To stop the trains from falling off the tracks (wrong answer)

The stones are there because when trains go over the railway tracks, they create a lot of down pressure. The random shapes of the stones help spread that pressure out. If you had smaller, more uniform stones, they would just break up and create dips and tracks in the railway.

questions.question: Why can't we collect lightning energy? It's an incredible resource that we don't do anything about. Also about collecting solar energy from the moon.

answers.answer: For lightning - the answer is probably similar to the biodegradable bags question: it's not been worth anybody's while yet. The rewards aren't big enough and the investment would be too huge. If it is technologically feasible, you need someone to be making a fortune out of it.

questions.question: Answer about why we can eat raw beef but not raw chicken
What happens to the internal part of the umbilical cord? We know it gets cut at birth and shrivels to form the belly button on the outside, but what goes on inside?

answers.answer: The placenta attaches to the mother's womb, the umbilical cord comes from that and attaches to the baby's belly button. On the other side of the belly button is the umbilical vein going into the baby's heart. When the baby is born, it withers and becomes part of the structure linked to the liver.

questions.question: How far down the line of succession are royals allowed to vote in elections? Does it affect the Queen?

answers.answer: Everyone in the royal family is allowed to vote, including the Queen. They just choose not to by convention to remain politically neutral.
All members of the royal family cannot vote because they are potential members of the House of Lords.

questions.question: Why don't some clams in paella open even though they look fine? My girlfriend said not to eat them.

answers.answer: It's a muscle that opens the shell, and if it's dead, the muscle won't work so the shell won't open.
When mussels arrive at restaurants, kitchen porters put them in water. The ones that don't open are thrown away because they're dead.

Mussels work with actin and myosin, two proteins that allow movement using ATP (adenotriphosphate). When alive, you can tap them and they close. Warm them in water and if they open they're alive. If they don't open at all, they're dead. Eating a dead mussel causes food poisoning.

questions.question: How did the first person work out how to make popcorn?

answers.answer: They were making bread, grinding corn and wheat to make flour for tortillas or flatbreads. One day a kernel got heated by the sun through something like glass or magnifying material, it popped, they tasted it, it was delicious, so they decided to heat more on purpose.
The kernel is naturally dry, you don't have to dry it out. It's not sweet corn, it's corn corn from fields. It's not off a cob like sweet corn is.
The corn for popping is from a cob, it's just a different variety of maize. They dry the kernel and put it on hot stones where it pops. Sweet corn is cooked differently and put in brine for tins.

questions.question: What causes homesickness? Even when on holiday with family, after a couple of days you sometimes get a funny tummy. Is there a biological or physiological hormone involved?
Why are soap bubbles always white regardless of the colour of the soap? Why don't they reflect the soap's colour?

answers.answer: The soap film is too thin to absorb colour, so it reflects the light around it. That's why you often see rainbow colours. But collectively with house lights or sunlight, it reflects white, which is why bubbles appear white.

questions.question: Why do fridge egg shelves have 8 or 10 spaces when eggs only come in sixes or dozens?

answers.answer: You shouldn't keep eggs in the fridge anyway - it's a bad habit from when fridges became popular. Eggs are like tomatoes, better kept out. As for the gap mismatch, you don't want exactly the right number of egg holders or you'd run out more. Replace eggs when you're down to your last one or two.

questions.question: A bird in my willow tree has been chirping continuously for weeks, morning to night. Do birds get sore throats? If you or I did that, we'd have a sore throat.

answers.answer: Birds don't get sore throats because they have a gizzard with stones in their throat. That's why chickens peck gravel - the stones aid digestion. Having stones in your gizzard means you're unlikely to get a sore throat.

questions.question: Body hair like underarms stops at a certain length but head hair keeps growing. How does the body know when it's reached that length and should stop?

answers.answer: Hair doesn't stop growing, it falls out at full length. Body hair is in a different phase from head hair. It's about blood supply during the growing period. The phase for head hair can be up to six years before it reaches its extension and drops out. They all come out in the shower, bath, swimming pool - that's why they appear to be all the same length.

questions.question: Olympic divers carry around a small brightly coloured square of material and hold onto it, put it in the water, take it in jacuzzis. What is it?

answers.answer: It's a towel, a chamois made of special fibre that dries really quickly. Just to get the excess water off the surface.
It's a shammy cloth, like microfiber. They wet it and wring it out because it dries better when wet - same as the cloths used to dry cars after washing.
Confirmed Stuart is dead right. He's a diver and world master champion.

questions.question: What are those boards you stick your head through on Brighton Pier called?

answers.answer: It's called a peep-through board

It's also known as a carnival cut-out, festival cut-out, beach cut-out, festival amusement cut-out, and if ordering today you'd ask for a stand-in. They originated from American carnivals and Barnum Circuses where you'd have the strongman pose with an empty head slot.

questions.question: Why is it rude to put your elbows on the dining room table?

answers.answer: It goes back to the days when not many people could afford tables. Tables were on trestles and you would bring them out at mealtimes. If you put your elbows on the table, you'd tip the trestles up. The table wouldn't be permanent.

questions.question: Where did the four suits of playing cards come from?

answers.answer: Something to do with French cards before the French Revolution. The French used to play cards and named them after different areas of public life. He mentioned it was pre-revolution and the French were involved but couldn't remember details about what groups the suits represented.

questions.question: Why is the fourth and seventh wave always bigger?

answers.answer: It's to do with the natural frequency of water. If you tap water at a certain frequency, the water will vibrate at a maximum. Every particle has a natural frequency. The seventh and fourth wave are just the maximum caused by the vibration. It's about maximum oscillation. It's not just waves - it's also cups of tea; if you walk with a cup of tea on the seventh step, it's most likely to go the highest.

He's a surfer with 25 years experience. It's about wave sets that come in pulses. You'd sit on your board during lulls and wait for the set to come. The bigger waves in a set are typically the third or fourth in the set, not prescriptively fourth and seventh. He never heard of it being prescriptively fourth and seventh.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'pull your finger out' come from?

answers.answer: In the old days with cannons, one person would stuff gunpowder and the cannonball into the cannon, another would stick the ignition wick in (which was sticky), and another would want to light it. Someone would say 'come on, pull your finger out' so they could light the cannon without losing a finger.

questions.question: Did humans invent maths or discover it?

answers.answer: Maths is numbers, and numbers are a human invention to describe something that already existed. It's like words - an apple is an apple but it's only called that because we decided. We invented numbers to describe eternal truths, universal truths.
The fundamental concept of maths has to start with the concept of zero, and that had to be invented. There are tribes in Africa that still can't count beyond three. Maths was invented by the Arabs.
A bit of both. Math is a language which tries to represent the universe. Mathematicians invent a way around it to explain something. They invent the language to describe stuff that was already there.

questions.question: Are smells (good and bad) learned?

answers.answer: Yes, we learn smells. When we're born as babies, we're a complete blank canvas. The only innate fears are falling and loud noises. Everything else is learned through experience, peers, parents. We don't have automatic dislikes until someone tells us - like children not disliking spiders until someone tells them to. Smell is a sense we learn.
I was born and brought up on a dairy farm and lived with the smell of cow poo. I'm now 57 and I absolutely love the smell of cow poo - it reminds me of carefree summer days as a kid.

questions.question: Why do veins appear bluey-green on skin when the blood inside is red?

answers.answer: It's something to do with oxygen - when there's no oxygen present they're blue, and when they get out of your veins they turn red. (Later admitted he might have made this up.)

It's actually to do with light passing through your skin. The light reacts with your skin and causes the blood to appear blue. The hemoglobin is the coloured part in your blood and it never actually becomes blue inside the body. The blood is always red - different shades of red according to whether it's making its way into or out of the lungs or heart. It's the properties of the skin that make it look blue, not the actual colour of the blood.

questions.question: Can a giraffe cough?

answers.answer: Yes, giraffes can cough. I used to be an elephant keeper and the giraffe house was next door. The giraffes would lean over quite often and sneeze and cough.

questions.question: Why is it that some newborn babies stay absolutely still and others constantly kick around?

answers.answer: Some people sit still and some people don't. It's a sign of a creative mind. Some adults fidget all the time and some can't sit still.

questions.question: Why do chickens lay eggs every day and no other birds do?

answers.answer: We've bred them that way.

It's down to breeding. Birds in captivity are bred to lay eggs for 18 months to two years on a regular basis, as long as they're fed well with layers pellets. Over generations, chickens that laid well were bred from. Naturally, hens will lay up to 10 eggs one after another every day, then sit on them for 3 weeks. We've bred out the sitting behavior generally.

questions.question: Are advertising stories always real life and true?

answers.answer: If it's not, they'd have to say so. Under ASA rules, they wouldn't be allowed to invent stories - it must be based on real life. But they will be professional actors telling real stories.

questions.question: Why do toenails grow so much slower than fingernails?

answers.answer: Sunlight - because toenails don't get any sunlight.

It's about blood supply. We've got a better blood supply to our hands - arteries are slightly larger. Better level of nutrients coming in and nastier stuff getting carried away. Also, fingernails experience more friction and damage so they grow faster to replace it. Skin and nails are both made of keratin. The toenail is thicker because of this.

questions.question: Will there come a time when the sewers of London are absolutely chunk-a-block with cigarette butts?

answers.answer: They clear the sewers routinely. In Sydney, there was a mesh over an outlet pipe catching piles of cigarette butts before they reached the beach.

Inside the gully, there's a pot - a big bucket which collects all the debris including butts before it goes out to the outlet. The pot gets emptied every six months. Butts shouldn't be going out through to the sewer.

questions.question: Why did a bottle of water from a hotel fridge in Goa turn to ice when poured into a glass?

answers.answer: He couldn't answer, said he'd try to get Professor Howell to explain.

It's called super freezing. If you put something in the freezer and it gets close to freezing but not quite goes over, the molecules are ready to freeze. As soon as you disturb it by squeezing, picking up, or jostling it, it immediately freezes.

The water was under pressure. As soon as the pressure dropped, it freezes. The melting point of water is pressure-dependent. Referenced the physics experiment of hanging weighted wire across ice - it cuts through because it melts under pressure.

Anti-freeze principle - impurities lower the freezing point. This is why we put anti-freeze in car radiators and salt on roads. Carbon dioxide in fizzy drinks keeps them liquid. When you take the top off, pressure is released, CO2 comes out of solution, freezing point goes up, and it freezes. The pressure explanation is correct.

questions.question: Can giraffes cough?

answers.answer: Couldn't answer. Promised to try to find out. Said he might break the habit of a lifetime and put it on the list next week.

questions.question: Why when going over a Humpback Bridge does the driver not lose his stomach but all passengers do, even if they're watching?

answers.answer: The driver can prepare with his core muscles. He knows what's coming. The passenger can't prepare for the exact point of the apex. New bridges catch people more because they don't realize it's a humpback. The more you concentrate, the more likely you would be to brace.

questions.question: What do you call a collective group of aunts and uncles? There isn't one. Why not?

answers.answer: Aunts and uncles aren't united by anything in the same sense. Siblings are united by biology. Parents are united by having children. Aunts and uncles aren't united by anything in the same way. That's why they don't have a collective noun.

questions.question: Why do you get brain freeze when you eat something very cold? And it's sporadic - sometimes you get it, sometimes you don't.

answers.answer: Push your tongue into the roof of your mouth, it takes the pain away.

Cold is a vasoconstrictor - when you get cold, your blood vessels constrict. When you put ice cream in your mouth, the blood vessels constrict and your body tries to warm them up again, and they effectively throb. Anything that causes throbbing or increase and decrease in local blood pressure gives you a headache. The cure of putting your tongue to the roof of your mouth just warms you up and the throbbing goes away.

questions.question: Did the occupying German soldiers in the Second World War respect the memorials and graves left behind for the Allied soldiers after the First World War?

answers.answer: Yes. There was a film called Rome Open City and they made an agreement where historical sites would be left untouched and undamaged. Also memorials, gravestones and things like that were part of that. The general observation would have been that the Germans abided by that agreement.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'look at you for the price of eggs' come from? My grandparents used to say it, my parents would say it.

answers.answer: It's said when someone is really messy, in the same way you might say 'look at the state of you'. It seems like Kent and Kidderminster have different dialects.

It seems to be a combination of two different phrases. There's no 'price of eggs' version, but there is 'look at you and the price of fish', which is related to some event where fish shot up in price. So if you come home looking an absolute mess, they'd say 'God, look at you and the price of fish.' I think you've jumbled it up with 'what's that got to do with the price of eggs?'

questions.question: Why is the pound worth more than the dollar or yen even though their economies are stronger? We get 1.4 dollars or 147 yen for one pound. It seems like stronger economies should have more valuable currencies.

answers.answer: It's all to do with when we started trading currencies. I think she's too clever for both of us.

Imagine a big economy or big country is like a branch of a big chain of supermarkets, as opposed to a small grocery shop further down the road. Once a small grocery starts its trading, the way they decide on prices is based on a wide range of factors - for example, to attract customers. So it's not a straight comparison on a level playing field. A pint of milk might be sold in the big shop as 95p, whereas in the grocery shop it's different. They're trying to make their currency more or less attractive.

questions.question: Why do snails bubble when you pick them up? Sometimes they bubble from the hole that the slime normally comes out of.
Why in the Olympics is it Team GB and not Team UK? Northern Ireland is part of UK, not Great Britain.

answers.answer: GB stands for Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland is part of United Kingdom, not part of Great Britain. But I'm going to try and find out for you why it's Team GB and not Team UK.

If you drive anywhere in Europe, you have a GB plate. It's the internationally recognised abbreviated symbol for the UK. A while ago, it was all agreed what our internationally agreed abbreviations were for our various nations, and it is GB.

On the athletics vests, they've got GBR - that's the code teams have like Germany's GER, Netherlands NED. But if it was to do with GBR, it should actually be Team GBR. If they said Team UK, it would confuse the Americans who don't really know the difference between Great Britain and England.

questions.question: Once Article 50 is invoked, can we withdraw it? If so, is it unilateral or do we need something?

answers.answer: Once you press the button, you can't withdraw it.

questions.question: Yesterday they were saying Theresa May is either the 74th or 75th Prime Minister. Who was the first and how far back do we go to say when we had our first Prime Minister?

answers.answer: It doesn't go back to 1066. It goes back to 1721, and it was Sir Robert Walpole - our first Prime Minister in the modern sense of the word. He was the MP for King's Lynn.

questions.question: Is who decides what is a weed and what is a flower? I can't decide what is which.

answers.answer: You do. There's absolutely no biological distinction between a plant that you want and a plant that you don't. It's entirely in the eye of the beholder. If you were landscaping something ten times the size of an average garden, stuff you'd pull out of your front garden you'd plant in your back meadow. A weed is a flower that's in the wrong place.

questions.question: What if something epic happened during the 26-second handover between PMs? Cameron was already out and May hadn't been sworn in yet. Who would decide and take charge?

answers.answer: You'd have a Deputy Prime Minister. Cameron didn't have a Deputy PM in recent times. The only person who really had a Deputy PM was Tony Blair. Back in the day, the Chancellor was technically the second-in-command. So who is in charge when you can't get hold of the Prime Minister is the question.

questions.question: Why is the CPR doll called Annie?

answers.caller: Matt (Bristol) - Former military first aid instructor
answers.answer: There was an American guy whose daughter drowned. If he'd known CPR, he could have saved her. He dedicated his life to producing these dolls, and the doll is named after his daughter, Annie.
Recess Annie was developed by a Norwegian toy maker. They're called Asmund Lerdal and Dr. Peter Safar. It was named after one of the manufacturer's existing toys.

questions.question: What is the origin of 'pinch, punch, first day of the month' (and white rabbits)?

answers.answer: From Middle England when they believed in witches. The pinch is actually a pinch of salt because they thought it weakened witches. Then they'd punch them to banish them. (Could not explain why specifically the first day of the month.)

questions.question: In Harlan Coburn's book 'The Woods', they say a scream can last forever. Is that true? Does sound ever stop?

answers.answer: Sound is a wave and never stops completely. It just gets bigger and thinner until almost nothing, but never actually nothing. Like chopping chocolate in half repeatedly - you'll never actually get to nothing.

Sound won't travel very far because it needs energy to make air molecules bounce up and down. Eventually the molecules are too heavy to move - the energy disappears to nothing. Unlike chocolate which is a particle, sound waves dissipate completely.

questions.question: Why does my left nipple become erect whenever I eat spicy food, even the smallest amount like peri sauce at Nando's?

answers.answer: When you eat spicy food or something enjoyable, your body produces hormones linked to excitement and also to sexual arousal. You can't get as sexually attracted to a chilli as to other things, but you can get a limited amount that can cause certain body parts to become aroused/turgid. Why only the left one - who knows?

questions.question: Why does the Wimbledon men's trophy have a pineapple on top?

answers.answer: From seafaring terminology. When captains used to come home, they put pine cones on the pillars of their driveways as air fresheners because they'd been at sea. There's dispute - some say it's a pineapple, some say it's a pine cone. The captain normally was the umpire.
Same theory - naval tradition. When captains came home from sea, they'd put pine cones on pillars as a smell/tradition. That's where it came from.

questions.question: Why don't horses slip and fall over on roads like we would if we had metal horseshoes on tarmac?

answers.answer: It's about surface area. A horse's weight on four relatively small hooves exerts enormous pressure, giving epic grip - like a stiletto heel. Horses are more likely to fall on grass because their foot sinks slightly, increasing surface area.

Horses wear road nails - one single pointed nail hammered into each shoe that grips into concrete. Horses are shod every five to six weeks and these nails last about that long. By the fourth, fifth or sixth week, they've worn down or snapped off, and then horses will skid, especially going down hills. Racehorses and those on soft ground don't need them.

questions.question: Do birds ever fly just for fun, or are they always after food or mating? How would we ever know?

answers.answer: If you gave a bird all the food, water and mating it could ever want, and it still went for occasional little flights just because it's a nice day - that would be flying for fun. Like humans who walk even when they don't need to.

answers.caller: Steve (Bristol) - Falconer and pest control operator
answers.answer: Yes, definitely. His hawk goes up on buildings and soars around on thermals just for fun, not looking for food, mates or anything. He can hear them singing while they fly which also suggests they're enjoying it.
Birds do fly for fun - you can hear them singing while they fly.

questions.question: If Teflon is non-stick, how do they stick it to the pan?

answers.answer: Teflon is non-stick to food, but it doesn't mean it's non-stick to metal at very high temperatures. Otherwise you wouldn't have a Teflon pan in the first place.

In the old days they made the metal very rough and sprayed Teflon on, hoping the nooks and crannies would provide hooks so it would stick. That's why you couldn't use a metal spatula. Now they spray with glue containing a tiny bit of Teflon, let it dry, then spray more glue with more Teflon, gradually increasing the ratio. This allows thicker coating that sticks and doesn't scratch.

questions.question: We have lamb chops and pork chops - why don't we have beef chops?

answers.answer: A chop looks like a little axe. The beef equivalent is a rib. Because beef is bigger, you don't need the riblet - you can serve just the rib. If you include the riblet, it becomes a T-bone steak which is much bigger than a chop.

A cow is so heavy that cutting through the flesh to the bone requires a saw, not a cleaver. That's why beef is sawn (becoming rib, T-bone, etc.) rather than chopped. Lamb and pork can be chopped with a cleaver. A chop is called a chop because you chop it - you can't chop beef, so it's not a beef chop.

questions.question: Eagles and tigers have beautiful orange/amber/terracotta eyes. Why can't humans have that eye colour?

answers.answer: It's not in our genes. Eye colour is genetically predetermined, and amber/orange eyes simply aren't an option for humans.

questions.question: Why don't zombies eat each other?

answers.answer: It's fiction - zombies aren't real.

questions.question: Can I legally leave my skin to a friend or relative after I die so they can have my tattoos framed?

answers.answer: I can't see why you wouldn't be able to. I know you have to have a licence to keep human remains.
There was an aristocrat who wanted to leave his body to Battersea Dogs Home as food. He was legally allowed to, but Battersea Dogs Home decided they didn't want to get involved.

In September 2015, an organization launched in the USA that preserves people's tattoos. The owner paid about $10,000 for all the tattoos on his back. You have to be a member and register exactly what you want done prior to death. It must be done within 18 hours after death. They work with embalmers to remove the skin and provide it in frames. The service is available worldwide.

questions.question: Why do Americans drop the H in 'herb' when they don't do this with other words like helicopter, hospital, etc.?

answers.answer: Herb is one of those words that hasn't evolved from the shared base pre-Mayflower. It has evolved separately in America. This is why Americans drop the H - it's a pronunciation that developed after the split.

Herb is associated with the French and cooking, and the French stopped using the aspirated H a long time ago. American English has lots of old English terms that stayed there. Herbs is a word that would have been in common parlance at the time of the Mayflower, unlike helicopter. It would have come from Norman French.

questions.question: Why do we say 'raining cats and dogs'?

answers.answer: Back in the day, when we all slept under one roof with pets, the cats and dogs would be sleeping in the roof area. If the rain started coming down heavily, they'd come down from the roof inside, and that meant it was really pelting it down outside.

In olden days when roofs were made of thatch, dogs and cats used to huddle in there to keep warm. Then as rain came down, it made it slippery and they used to fall down. People would see cats and dogs falling down from the roof onto the floor past the window, so they knew it was raining quite heavy.
Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable specifically says both these theories are false. A properly maintained thatch is naturally water resistant and slanted to allow water to run off.

questions.question: Why do seagulls stand on one leg?

answers.answer: You can swap legs when it gets cold, so it doubles the amount of time you can stay in the water on your leg hunting.
Birds can shut off one side of their body from the other - they put one side to sleep while the other side's awake. That's why flamingos do it.
Semi-hemispheric sleep will be part of the answer, but it may hold true for flamingos only. Does it hold true for seagulls and ducks?
Flamingos live in an acoustic environment and lift their legs up to stop sediment like rock and minerals building up on their feet. It might be the same for seabirds.

questions.question: Can salt dissolve in salt water?

answers.answer: Yes, you can dissolve salt in salt water. Take salt water, add more salt, it dissolves.

questions.question: Is there a point at which you can't dissolve any more salt in salt water?

answers.answer: Yes, it's called the saturation point. The Dead Sea would be closer to this point because it's so much more salty than other seas, which is why you can float in it.

questions.question: Why do Americans drop the H for herb but not for hotel, hospital, and helicopter?

answers.answer: Some words have a French origin like hotel, herb, or hospital. The question is why do Americans drop the H for herb and not for the others?

questions.question: Can a sauna help you lose weight?

answers.answer: Yes, it does help you lose weight. Jockeys use saunas before races to get their weight down under the limit. But it's not a dietary substitute - eat less and exercise more.

questions.question: Is it true that when a new Pope is elected, they are given a piece of parchment with information that only the previous Pope knew, and it takes them days to read it because it's so shocking?

answers.answer: Only Popes would know. It sounds like something out of a Dan Brown book rather than a history book. I don't know who would know the answer.
This stems from the apparition of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Sattava. She passed on information or gave them something to go to every single Pope, and it's due with the apocalypse.
There is a reason only the Pope can see it. The words written on it are the reason they all look so unhappy. (Phone cut off before he could finish)

From a Discovery Channel programme, the Pope receives an envelope which has whatever the mysterious items are. He reads it and reseals it with his personal seal and candle wax, and it's kept in the vault. He only reads it once. If anyone tampers with it, you'd know from the seal.

questions.question: How much cash does a street sweeper find on average in a year?

answers.answer: I am a street sweeper. Last year I found about £16. If you find any significant amount, you'd have to hand it in because it would be theft by finding if you didn't.

Not a lot is the answer. People tend to drop coppers. If they drop silver money or paper money, they pick them up. Today I found 11p. That's an average day. My best day was finding £3.50 in Nigerian money, which worked out at about £9.

questions.question: What's the most cash a street sweeper would find?
Why do football referees whistle in a specific tone at the end of games?

answers.answer: The whistle is blown at a lower pitch so it travels further and gets through all the players on the pitch. For a foul, it's a higher pitch so only the nearby players need to hear it.

questions.question: How does cold spray stay cold when it's left in a warm room, whereas deodorant and air freshener don't?

answers.answer: It's got different gas in the bottles. As soon as you introduce it to the atmosphere, it starts withdrawing heat from your skin.

questions.question: Why do they put a chemical that can be considered laxative in chewing gum?

answers.answer: It's the shiny outside shell. It only becomes a laxative if you take it on a scale that you're not really supposed to consume chewing gum.
It's sugar-free gum they're talking about. The artificial sweetener has that side effect. If you use it in cakes, it has the same effect.
Sorbitol is the correct answer. It's used as a humectant which retains moisture in the product and extends shelf life.
The word is sorbitol. Cool mints when we were kids had sorbitol which caused the laxative effect.

questions.question: When Henry VI became king, he was eight months old. Who makes the decisions for child kings of that age?

answers.answer: Whoever is most powerful in the court. It might be a cousin, a brother, or the widow of the recently dead king. It will be all about power play and politicking. You'd think when he reaches his majority, 16 or 18.

questions.question: Is it possible that my Labrador could be gay?

answers.answer: You might have a gay Labrador. There are examples of homosexuality right across the animal kingdom.

At a Richard Dawkins lecture, he explained that 10% of all animals are gay. The speculation is that it has a survival mechanism within our genes - masculine males are less threatened by gay males and leave them back with the pride. They play a role in nurturing and child-rearing rather than hunting and gathering.

questions.question: Why do we never fall out of bed at night? Why do we worry about babies falling out of beds but not adults?

answers.answer: He had a vague theory about sleeping in trees evolutionarily, but he wasn't sure.

It's to do with proprioception - your body's awareness of itself in relation to its environment. It's how you're able to move without having to think about it. In babies it probably isn't as developed as it is as you get older. When you're asleep, you have a subliminal understanding of where the boundaries of the bed are. Athletes have very refined proprioception.

questions.question: If a future monarch has their birthday in the summer months, when do we celebrate the Trooping in the Colour? On the actual birthday or on another day?

answers.answer: The official Trooping in the Colour will always be on the official birthday. George II had his birthday in November and it always rained, so he wanted the parade in summer. Also, if the king dies just before his party, you still need a Trooping for the new king on the new monarch's official birthday.

questions.question: Why do we vote in pencil? For any other legal documentation, you would never do anything in pencil.

answers.answer: Two reasons. First, operational: pencils are kept in boxes for one year or even five-year intervals. By the time you took them out, nothing else would work. They use pencils because they never run out and you can see whether they work. Second: so if you don't win, you can claim it was a conspiracy and they were rubbing out votes. But you are allowed to bring your own pen if you want.

questions.question: Why is it called plastic surgery? There's no plastic involved.

answers.answer: In its earliest days, a plastic was used to cover scarring from WWII injuries. But it's close but not quite right.

The word plastic existed way before the substance we call plastic. Plastic means able to be bent or moulded. Plastic surgery is to do with making the contours of the face as good as they can be - you're not curing a disease, you're remoulding a body. That is plastic. Malleable.

questions.question: Why is Vic short for Richard? Why is Jack short for John? Why is Jim short for James? They have the same number of letters.

answers.answer: Bill is short for William, Dick is short for Rickard (the original Norman pronunciation). If you go with Rickard instead of Richard, then you might have a better answer. When they were talking French in the time of Richard III, it might make more sense.

In Victorian times and earlier, generations of the same family would live in the same house and children were always named after their parents. So they'd have granddad, dad, and son all called John or Richard. They needed ways of distinguishing them. So John would become Jack, Richard would become Rick and then Dick, Mary would become Molly and then Polly. You distinguish whether you're talking about the gran or the mother or the little daughter.

questions.question: When a new film comes out and it says it took how many millions in box office sales, do they take into account that it's more expensive now to go to the cinema than it was 40 years ago?

answers.answer: No, they don't take that into account. That's why Avatar and films from the last ten years dominate the top ten. You're paying 10 or 15 quid a ticket now, so they're bound to have better box office receipts. All the older films will just drop off. To know the actual number of tickets sold, you'd have to divide the total box office receipt by the ticket price.

questions.question: April, May and June are all girls' names. Why not the other months?

answers.answer: Because no parents have called their daughters the other months. There's January Jones, and we've heard from listeners with daughters called December and October. You can call your daughter whatever you want - nobody's stopped you. The answer is simply that not enough parents have chosen those names.

questions.question: Trouser measurements don't match up - I'm a 32 in some shops, 34 in others, 36 in others. Why would we have a measurement if it's such a vast difference? Why is there so much disparity in sizing from one brand to the next?

answers.answer: The sizing system probably started because retailers would change their sizes to make customers feel thinner - a 14 would become a 12 to attract buyers. It may have become a race to the bottom.

Most clothes are made by the same manufacturers. When retailers give manufacturers the breakdown of sizes they want, if they've made a mistake on the cut and haven't got enough of one size, they just label it with a different size. The clothes go to different retailers with different labels. This is why sizing is so inconsistent.

questions.question: Why do we have stag and hen parties, not stag and doe or cock and hen? Why have we got two different species, not male and female of same species?
Why are petrol stations allowed to charge decimals of pence that they can't give change to? No other retailer does this.

answers.answer: The pumps are calibrated so you never end up with a fraction of a penny cost. Anyone could advertise a fraction of a penny but they don't because it's not the unit we're used to dealing in.
It's psychological pricing to get you onto the forecourt. The pumps only dispense in full pennies but dispense in fractions of litres, so it's balanced out that way.

questions.question: Why is it that if you hit puberty younger, you end up shorter, and late bloomers always end up taller?

answers.answer: The long bones have cells at the ends underneath the joints that generate bone. If you start puberty earlier, those cells cease functioning sooner. If you start later, those cells are busier for longer, making the long bones longer. There's a finite length to the bone that grows in direct proportion to the activity of the bone-generating cells.

questions.question: Where does the term 'going commando' come from?

answers.answer: Before going on a mission, you had to take off your undercrackers. In the moist and humid conditions of warmth, undercarriage chafing incidents increase, and going commando provides more ventilation. This became commonplace among American soldiers in Vietnam.

questions.question: Why do parents have the two-second rule for dropped food?

answers.answer: Parents introduced the two-second rule so children don't labour under the illusion it's alright to pick up stuff they didn't drop. You can pick up a sweet you've dropped yourself, but not a sweet found under a bench at the bus stop that could have been there half-sucked for weeks.

questions.question: Which bin does a Pringles tube go in? The top is plastic, middle cardboard, bottom metal.

answers.answer: You have to dismantle the Pringles tube and separate the materials.

questions.question: Why can we say 'badly' but not 'bigly'? We used to say 'goodly'.

answers.answer: Linguistic evolution - some words stayed in common parlance, others dropped when we didn't use them enough.

Words ending in -ly are adverbs that describe process. If you say Trump is going to win bigly, you're forcing the language to describe the process as grand. Big describes the result. Some words can be both adjective and adverb, some can't.

questions.question: My daughter asked - like Edwardians, Elizabethans, Victorians - what will happen when this era pops its claws? What will this age be called?
Why do I look good in the mirror but look a mess in photographs? The reflection in the mirror is completely different to the photographic image.

answers.answer: When looking in the mirror, you pose yourself in a way that looks good. When you're unaware someone's taking a photo, you're not posing. People think holding their head up stretches their neck and gets rid of double chins, but actually you should put your head down and stretch it forward. Stand slightly angular to the picture. Also, people who are less expressive in real life don't get wrinkles and always look the same in photos.

questions.question: Who picks up guide dog poo?

answers.answer: Guide dogs are trained to spend in a particular area, like a corner of the garden. When out and about, the dog will do an anti-clockwise spin then adopt posture. The technique is: keep your right leg beside the dog's back right leg. When finished, keep hold of the lead, your foot hasn't moved so you know where the poo is. Put a plastic bag over your hand, reach down, scrabble for the poo, pull the bag inside out, tie it in a knot, then either leave it at the curb or put it in a bin.
Thinks James was wrong about the commando origin involving Churchill.

questions.question: Why did I get an electric shock when my son took a picture with his iPhone through a black square drawn on my hand with a Sharpie pen?

answers.answer: Ink from pens is very dense in electrons. When the phone is placed upon it, the battery is in close contact with those electrons. When a picture is taken, there's a sudden discharge of the battery which causes a sudden movement of electrons from the electron-rich area in the palm to the battery. You need to color in the square completely - a hollow square doesn't work.

You're about two-thirds right. Cyanoacrylate glue polymerizes when it comes into contact with water - the minute amounts of water in the air and on surfaces catalyze the reaction. Water is the catalyst, not oxygen.

questions.question: Do your irises change colour as you get older?
Why in the poem 'It's Raining, It's Pouring' does the old man not wake up?

answers.answer: Because he went to bed with a bump on his head. The lad's concussed, he's got concussion, he's out cold, he's unconscious - he's been knocked out by the bump on his head.

questions.question: If there's a street name sign attached to the side of my house, who owns it? Can I take it down if I don't want it there?

answers.answer: In land law, there's something called an easement which gives someone the right to do something over your land or vice versa. The local council likely has an easement dating back many years, meaning the sign belongs to them but they have a right to display it on your property. It's very complicated to remove them as many date back hundreds of years.

questions.question: Where do moles (skin marks) come from? Are they genetic?
Why do older people grunt when they sit down or get up?

answers.answer: Your muscles are nowhere near as elastic as you get older. Your muscles get less elastic, so when they've been in the same position for a long time they seize up a bit. When you get up you feel discomfort which translates into an exhalation of breath or expression of pain.

It's not just elasticity - it's strength. The glutes in particular atrophy over time, especially for people with sedentary lifestyles. The gluteus maximus is one of the largest muscles in the body and helps you sit down and stand up. When you move, you need to exhale and engage your abdominals to make the movement smoother and more effective. It's effort, not just pain.

questions.question: Why are professional golfers not allowed to wear shorts when they're playing in a tournament?

answers.answer: Yes, it's entirely true - professional golfers are not allowed to wear shorts on the course. It's a long-standing traditional rule because it doesn't look professional enough. However, the European Tour changed this at the end of last year to allow shorts in practice rounds and pro-am tournaments. It's just tradition.

questions.question: When we say food or drink has 'gone down the wrong hole' and we start spluttering, does it actually go down the wrong hole or is it just a phrase?

answers.answer: Something that's supposed to go to your tummy temporarily heads towards your windpipe, and that's where you cough, which sends it back in the right direction. So it has flirted with the wrong hole.

There are two holes in your throat - one going to your lungs and one going to your food passage. When something foreign goes there besides air, you start coughing to disperse it. This is the gag reflex. From personal experience, a spring onion got stuck hovering over both holes and I had to go to hospital. In the end they gave me a sandwich which dislodged it.

The windpipe is called the esophagus. The top has a flappy bit of skin called the epiglottis which stops food going into the windpipe - if food goes down there you will die. Food can't actually go down there, which is why you start coughing and sputtering because it's extremely dangerous. The chugging a pint technique works by suppressing the gag reflex and opening your gullet so you don't need to swallow - you just pour it straight into your tummy.

questions.question: Why do lions have cubs but cats have kittens?

answers.answer: Kitten comes from the French word for baby cat - chitoun (old French, 15th/16th century). We took that word and anglicized it because we kept cats as pets and had that domestic experience. We adopted the French words. Cubs would be the word applied to wild animals. When we encountered young big cats, we used terminology more associated with wild animals - ergo cubs.
Correction - the French word for kitten is chaton (c-h-a-t-o-n), not chitoun. I'm French.
Cats are feline genus, and lions have cubs because they are panthera genus. It's a taxonomy issue - they're different species, hence different terminology.

questions.question: Why doesn't superglue stick to the inside of the container?
