answers.answer: It's to do with the air and oxygen. It doesn't become sticky until it comes into contact with air. There's a chemical reaction that occurs when it meets air that makes it really sticky.

You're about two-thirds right. The correct answer is water - minute amounts of water in the air and on surfaces catalyze the polymerization reaction of cyanoacrylate. This also explains why the more empty the tube gets, the more likely the last bit hardens by itself. Water is a reagent in this reaction, not just a catalyst.

questions.question: What did people say before sliced bread was invented? What was the phrase before 'best thing since sliced bread'?
Can you do a wheelie on a tandem bike with two people?

answers.answer: No. To do a wheelie, you'd need to be pedalling at the back for ballast but pulling up the handlebars at the front for leverage, which is a physical impossibility. Unless you're Mr Tickle, you wouldn't be strong enough to both reach and lift.

questions.question: What did people say before 'best thing since sliced bread'?

answers.answer: Best thing since the wheel.

It came from the Wonder Bread Company advertising campaign. Before sliced bread existed, unsliced bread was the standard, then sliced bread came in and they marketed it as the best thing since sliced bread.

questions.question: Why do I always get absolutely famished and starving beyond belief when I'm in the swimming pool, even when I'm not swimming and just watching the kids?
Why do we call her a mother-in-law? What has the law got to do with it? Why is she not just your wife's mother?

answers.answer: It comes from church law, ecclesiastical law. That's the law you're married under. The law of the church, not the law of the land.

It's a way of identifying how you're related to someone in the church. The church is a big family and everyone is our brothers, sisters, mothers and fathers. If you're related to someone by blood they're just your brother, sister, mother or father. If you're not a relative they're your brother, sister, mother or father in Christ. If you're related by marriage they're your brother, sister, mother or father in the church law.

questions.question: Is sea air good for you? And if so, why?

answers.caller: Professor Hall (University of Brighton - The Professor of Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: Sea air is not specifically better for you - it's more the absence of bad rather than the presence of particular good. Urban/inland air has pollutants from traffic and industry (nitrous oxide, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide). Sea air is cooler because water has high thermal inertia and takes time to change temperature. It dilutes pollutants with onshore winds and you don't have industry or traffic at sea. Regarding ozone - it's actually bad for you, a carcinogen that breaks down into oxygen radicals. The seaside smell is to do with particular seaweed we have around our coasts.

questions.question: Why when you use a vending machine, if it doesn't take the coin, but when you scratch the metal, it then works?

answers.answer: It's a total fallacy that scratching coins works at all or licking coins. They had to design and develop coin scratch plates to protect vending machines from damage because kids scratch the machines right back to the bare metal. If you put the same coin through the machine ten times, you wouldn't get rejected or accepted ten times - there's an equal chance it will be accepted whether you scratch it or not. The whole thing is apocryphal.

questions.question: About 10 years ago I flew from Stansted to Texas. The TV screen showed the route going up to New York and then back down to Texas - a horseshoe shape. Why do flights take such a long route instead of flying in a straight line?

answers.answer: It's because the planet isn't flat. If the world was flat, you'd fly in a direct straight line. But because you're flying around a ball-shaped planet, you go in a horseshoe shape. The flight might still arrive on time because the actual distance is less going around the curve of a sphere than trying to go straight would be. The Earth is also turning while you're flying which might be relevant.

questions.question: Why doesn't a tattoo just grow out? You're always told your skin sheds daily, so after 20 years why can you still see a tattoo? Same question applies to scars.

answers.answer: The ink goes below all the layers of skin that are subject to the shedding processes you described. The tattoo is in the deeper layers of skin that don't shed.

The tattoo goes into the epidermis of the skin which is part of you and will be forever until you've got away. It fades over time but doesn't disappear - everything fades even the paint on your car fades over the years due to the sun.

questions.question: Why do we have two nostrils? Two eyes give us depth perception, two ears let us locate sounds, but what benefit does having two nostrils give us?

answers.answer: It doubles your chances of being able to breathe when you've got one blocked nostril.

They're linked to the ears. The Eustachian tube joins the nostril to the ear and air goes down the Eustachian tube to equalize the pressure in the middle ear. If you only had one nostril, you could only equalize one ear. Having two nostrils means having two Eustachian tubes so both ears can equalize properly. This is especially important when diving - as water pressure increases, you have to put air through the Eustachian tube into your middle ear to stop damaging your eardrum.

questions.question: The Queen's 90th birthday celebrations - all those people giving her flowers. What happens to all the flowers given to the Queen? Does she take them home? Does she eat them? Does she put them in a vase? Do they go to hospitals?

answers.answer: Depending where she is, they get distributed towards hospitals, hospices, elderly care homes. They're presented at the entrance of the establishment. Probably more hospices and care homes than actual hospitals because of pollen and health and safety - a lot of hospitals these days won't allow you to bring flowers in.

questions.question: On the back of every single bottle of toiletries - shampoo, shower gel, even hair gel - there is a little circular box that says 12M. What does that mean?

answers.answer: It is the expiration of the product. Once it's opened, that's how long it will last before - 12 months after opening it is the use by date. It actually looks like a little pot with an open lid with 12M written on it.

questions.question: Why is it that when you're on a roller coaster, or maybe driving really fast downhill, you get that stomach drop feeling?

answers.answer: It's a small release of adrenaline in your body. It comes back to your fight or flight mechanism, which is governed by adrenaline. The shock of the sudden fall brings the adrenaline subconsciously to the fore. You feel it in your stomach and around your kidneys because your adrenal glands are on top of your kidneys. The reason they call it butterflies in your stomach is because your adrenal glands, which are on top of your kidneys, are a butterfly shape.

questions.question: What is the most expensive metal that doesn't need a hallmark? At what point do they start putting hallmarks on things? How do they qualify the purity of cheaper metals?

answers.answer: Metals more precious than gold that don't get hallmarked include rhodium, tantalum, niobium, and promethium. Tantalum and niobium became very expensive when mobile phones started becoming popular - Rwanda has the biggest reserves of coltan which is the ore for those things. The only stuff that gets hallmarked is stuff that gets turned into jewelry or used as a store of value, like the noble metals in the periodic table - platinum, palladium, gold, and silver. Commodity metals which are used in industry can't have a hallmark because they're melted and used as various components. They go up and down in price with demand. Iridium was the closest to overtaking gold because it's used in satellite phones. Rhodium made gold look cheap at $10,000 an ounce versus gold at $700.

questions.question: A panda bear weighs about the weight of a human male. A human child is born at 2-3 kilos (7 pounds). But a panda bear cub weighs only 5 ounces. Why is a human baby born weighing 6-7 pounds where the parent is the same sort of weight as a panda, but a panda cub is only 5 ounces?

answers.answer: It's probably evolution. It's quite hard to protect a panda cub in the wild from predators. So they don't predate themselves. It's easier to protect a five-ounce panda until it's big enough to protect itself than it would be to protect a 2-3 kilo-sized panda. Historically, going back through the millennia, as the panda evolved, the likelihood of the baby surviving was increased by the baby being small.

It has to do with food that pandas eat - bamboo. Bamboo has so little nutrition that if pandas had big babies, it would take too much strain for the moms to feed the babies. It protects the mom. They couldn't gestate even a bigger baby without having more nourishment in the womb.

questions.question: Why is it MI5 and MI6? Is there a 1, 2, 3, and 4? What does MI stand for?

answers.answer: MI stands for Military Intelligence. They were set up chronologically. MI5 is domestic, MI6 is international. Numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 were superseded or absorbed into MIs 5 and 6. They had specific purposes that maybe no longer exist, like infiltrating Nazi Germany.

questions.question: Memory sticks - we all use them. Do they have a lifespan? And if so, how do you know when they're about to die?

answers.answer: They do fail. But it's not to do with lifetime - it's to do with the amount of uses. The more you use it, the more likely it is to fail because it works on electrical charges. Every time you save data or copy data, it runs an electrical charge to it and the memory cells get a little bit weaker over time. A standard USB stick probably lasts about 10 years and 100,000 read-writes. That also applies to hard disks, but hard disks die a lot quicker because they have a spinning platter like a record player.

questions.question: Why do children open their mouths when they're trying to catch something?

answers.answer: It might be to do with concentration. If you are concentrating, it's easier to concentrate when your mouth is open. I don't know why.

If you're catching a ball, you look up and it pulls on the muscles and stuff in your jaw and it opens your mouth. Maybe it's an anticipation of something going wrong - you're getting ready, based on the fight or flight thing.

questions.question: Do tower cranes have toilets up there? Because it must take the crane driver at least 10 or 15 minutes to get up there. And then if he wants to go to the toilet, do they have toilets up on there?

answers.answer: No, they don't have toilets up the tower cranes. For one quite obvious reason - the plumbing would be a problem. They go before they go up. And then if they need to do a wee, they do it in a bottle.

questions.question: I put a fitted sheet with a very high thread count (600, Egyptian cotton) on my daughter's bed. It shrank a bit in the tumble dryer, which was actually good because it was a bit too big. I don't want it to shrink again. When you shrink something in the tumble dryer, does it only shrink once? Or is there future shrinkage? If you keep the test at the same temperature, will it shrink again?

answers.answer: It's to do with moisture content. If you leave cotton in a drawer for a long time, it actually will just shrink because it loses moisture. So if you put your pants in a tumble dryer and leave them in too long, they will shrink to the point where there's no moisture left in it for them to contract anymore. If it's already shrunk once, it won't shrink again under identical conditions because the moisture has evaporated to a point where there's none left to evaporate. The first time around it shrinks because there's moisture to lose, but once all the moisture is gone, there's nothing left to shrink.

questions.question: When you want to cook chicken from the freezer, you have to defrost it first. But if you were to just put it in the oven, it will defrost while it's cooking anyway. Why do you have to let it defrost first when it's going to defrost anyway while you're cooking it?

answers.answer: You can cook a chicken from frozen. But they cannot put the correct cooking instructions on it because they don't know how frozen it is. It makes cooking too variable. Some freezers are colder than others. Different drawers have different temperatures. The top shelf of your freezer is colder than the bottom shelf. If you undercook it, it will make you ill. They can't give precise cooking instructions if they don't know how frozen it is.

questions.question: Why can't you tickle yourself?
Why isn't the British Army called the Royal Army when we have the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force?

answers.answer: Regiments have royal patronage individually, so you don't need royal patronage for the collective noun 'army'.

The British Army couldn't be royal because there was no standing army until Cromwell raised one, and he wasn't about to make it royal given he was cutting the royals' heads off. Individual regiments answered to local earls and dukes. By the time the Navy and Air Force came about, they were national bodies under the authority of the crown, hence 'Royal'. But regiments only came into existence after the Civil War.

questions.question: Where did the term 'wolf whistle' come from? Why do we call it that?
Why do birds come down and drink my dog's urine from the patio?

answers.answer: Birds need the salt from the urine. All animals (dogs, horses, cows) get salt licks on farms, but birds can't access that. The nitrogen/minerals/salt in diluted urea provides something birds need that isn't present in plain water.

questions.question: Why do we cry? Why do we produce tears as a physical manifestation of emotion?

answers.answer: Tears maintain the balance of serotonin in the brain. When upset, negative chemicals build up and tears flush them away - which is why you feel better after crying. Same with happy tears - flushing excess happy chemicals. It's about keeping hormones in balance.

The limbic system in the middle of your brain processes emotions and feeds into the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus releases hormones including prolactin, which causes tears. This works for both happy and sad emotions. Abbas is a doctor who did a thesis on the psychophysiology of crying.

questions.question: Why do we stumble when stepping onto a broken or stationary escalator, even though we know it's not moving?

answers.answer: It's your brain thinking the escalator is still moving.

answers.caller: Professor Hal Sosabowski, University of Brighton
answers.answer: It's operant conditioning, as suggested by Pavlov. We're conditioned to step onto escalators in a certain way because they move most of the time. Just like Pavlov's dogs associated the bell with food and would salivate even without food, we associate escalators with moving and adjust our steps accordingly.

questions.question: Why is a hard shoulder called a hard shoulder?

answers.answer: It's the shoulder of the road - the left and right extremities. It's 'hard' because it's covered in tarmac. Soft ground on the edge would be the soft shoulder, but that's just grass/dirt.

questions.question: Could a pigeon commit suicide if it wanted to? If it jumped off a multi-story car park, would it fly or just fall?

answers.answer: There are evolutionary behaviors among some mammals involving older members of herds jumping off cliffs for population control, but pigeons aren't known for suicidal behavior.

I saw a pigeon commit suicide once in Leeds. It had a broken wing, was injured, and edged to the pavement edge where traffic was stopped at red lights. A double-decker bus was there. It dropped off the curb and went under/by the wheels, waited for lights to change, and the wheels turned over it. It could have gone anywhere but chose to end its life. It took a quicker route because it was injured.

questions.question: Why has the wolf whistle become a sign of appreciation? (Answer to Mark's question)

answers.answer: The wolf whistle is derived from the boatswain's call used in the Navy to get people's attention before piping. It's a specific whistle to say 'pay attention, everybody'. Getting someone's attention transmutes into appreciation.

questions.question: What qualifications do you need to be a slaughterman in an abattoir?

answers.answer: It depends on where the meat is going. For halal exports (like Silver Fern Farms in New Zealand), you'd need to be of Muslim faith. But generally, no formal qualifications are needed - it's all experience-based. You work your way around the abattoir from chopping shoulders, boning out legs on the bandsaw, eventually reaching 100% competence, then you can become a slaughterman or bandsawman.

questions.question: What are the three little buttons on the end of men's jacket sleeves for?

answers.answer: It's called a surgeon's cuff or working cuff. Originally, surgeons would unbutton and roll up their jacket sleeves to operate, hence the name. Now it's purely decorative on cheaper suits. On genuinely bespoke or designer continental European suits, the cuff can actually work - you can unbutton it and roll up the sleeve. Three buttons indicates a cheaper off-the-peg garment, whereas four or five buttons indicate a better-quality suit.

questions.question: When I bathed my daughter and put a ship in the bath, the water level rose. Does that mean every time a ship is launched into the ocean, the sea level rises slightly?

answers.answer: Yes, negligibly. It's Archimedes' principle - the Eureka moment. The ship displaces water, causing the level to rise.

questions.question: How do we know the stars and planets we can see are still there? If some blew up half a million years ago, we'd still see them because the light takes that long to reach us.

answers.answer: We don't. We have no way of knowing. Many of the stars we can see died millennia ago - the light just hasn't reached us yet. The universe could be virtually empty and we'd think it's full because the light of dead stars is still traveling toward us. You could say half the stars might not even be there anymore.

questions.question: Why do jackets have buttons on the cuffs? (Alternative answer to Joe's question)

answers.answer: In the Royal Navy, midshipmen were called snotties because they always had snotty noses. They used to wipe their noses on their sleeves, so the buttons were put on cuffs to stop them wiping their noses on their sleeves.

questions.question: Why do clothes get dark when they're wet, even though water is clear?

answers.answer: It's to do with light, but he admitted he can't get close to a proper answer and threw open phone lines
It's to do with absorption - wet fabric absorbs more light than dry fabric. Light frequencies absorbed by an object determine its color. James argued it's refraction, Roman insisted it's absorption.
Refraction is the reason clothes get darker when wet

questions.question: Is there a clinical difference between a psychopath and a sociopath? If so, what is it?

answers.answer: Neither have empathy. Suggested reading 'The Psychopath Test' by John Ronson. Said he thought all psychopaths are sociopaths. Didn't give definitive answer - promised to find out.
A sociopath has extreme antisocial attitudes but a psychopath has violent social behaviour. One will hurt you, one just won't care that you're hurt.

questions.caller: David (Forest Hill, age 9, with dad Stuart)
questions.question: If you dug a hole through the centre of the earth and dropped a ball through it, what would happen? Would it stop in the middle because of gravity?

answers.answer: The momentum of the ball would be big enough to defeat gravity, which isn't actually very strong on this planet - you can jump in the air, proving gravity isn't that strong.

answers.caller: Professor Hal (University of Brighton, Professor of Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: Ignoring air friction, the ball would drop and accelerate but reach terminal velocity. It would go through to the centre, then effectively up the other side, nearly reaching the height it started, then fall back down. It would oscillate like a pendulum, eventually coming to rest at the centre of the earth because energy is slowly being lost.

The ball wouldn't go any further than the centre of the earth - it probably wouldn't even get there depending on what it was made of. If you actually made the hole, the ball would catch fire. James dismissed this as being practical when a theoretical answer was requested.

questions.question: Do animals have a natural sense of rhythm?

answers.answer: Yes, animals do have rhythm - cited his own dog raising her paw up and down in time with music. Promised to find more authoritative answer.

questions.question: Who discovered England? As Captain Cook discovered Hawaii and Columbus discovered various countries, who discovered England?

answers.answer: Nobody. There's no discoverer of England. The only reason you know about other places being discovered is because the civilization that discovered them had history and writing and recorded these things. Plus there were indigenous people in these countries we 'discovered'. It's a post-imperial worldview.

questions.question: Answer: Why is Jordan Vertout arguably the unluckiest footballer in the world?

answers.answer: Vertout had the choice of choosing between Aston Villa and Leicester City, both with contracts agreed and same salary. He chose Villa, who were garbage and got relegated. Leicester did fairly well. His mate was the agent who tried to convince him to pick Leicester.

questions.question: Why is toilet paper made up of two parts? Why not one sheet that's twice as thick?

answers.answer: If you made one sheet twice as thick, it would be half as soft. Softness is the crucial factor. Thick toilet roll is essentially kitchen roll. Proposed the three-ply idea to the razor blade model.

It's about trade-off between flushability, comfort, and roll longevity. More plies = more comfort but fewer sheets per roll. If you made it thicker like kitchen roll, it wouldn't break down in the toilet system and would block it. That's why you don't throw kitchen towel in the sink.

questions.question: Why does your own crossed leg feel weightless, but if someone else puts their leg on you, it feels really heavy?

answers.answer: When you cross your own leg, your thigh takes a lot of the strain. But when someone else puts their leg on you, they've got no tension in their thigh, so there's more pressure on a smaller area. Made up answer about an 'elastic muscle' in the leg.

answers.caller: Professor Martin Smith (University of Middlesex, Professor of Robotics)
answers.answer: The weight is the same but discomfort differs due to contact area. If your ankle is over your knee, you have a very small contact area so the same weight feels very uncomfortable. When you cross your own legs normally, weight is spread over the whole length. Someone else typically puts just their ankle on you - small area, high pressure, like a stiletto heel vs Wellington boot.

questions.question: Who makes morals? Historically it's religious leaders, but with religion dying, who's making them up now?

answers.answer: Everyone - politicians, philosophers. Referenced classic traditions: John Stuart Mill's utilitarianism (do what's best for majority even if bad for minority), Kant's categorical imperative (do unto others as you'd have done unto yourself), John Rawls' veil of justice (everyone decides what they'd want without knowing their position in society). Morality is determined by what's best for the population. When looking at questionable internet activities, the moral question is: are you doing harm?

questions.question: Why do we never see baby pigeons?

answers.answer: When pigeons are in the nest, they're babies and don't leave until they can fly. Same reason you don't see other chicks from tree-nesting birds. Pigeons originally nested on cliffs so they nest higher than other birds - on balconies etc.

questions.question: Why did mods choose the Lambretta/scooter as their iconic bike instead of a motorcycle like rockers? Who decided this?

answers.answer: The scooter thing didn't really come in until about 1962. The original mod movement started around 1958. The origin of the scooter was Italian waiters in Soho who used to dart about from restaurant to restaurant on scooters. The whole movement is based on the continental look of the French and Italians, and that's why they chose to drive scooters. It starts with the sartorial style and then expands. I'm a mod - 44 years old, I still dress smart and listen to decent music. The movement evolved out of North London with a Jewish community - Jewish tailors making clothes for their sons, listening to traditional jazz.

You can't ride a motorbike with a suit on because you'd get too messy. The rockers would wear leather jackets, leather trousers or jeans and they didn't really care. But mods wore suits, Winkle Pickers, and little Berries. So you chose the scooter because of the look - it was part of the Italian aesthetic tradition of modernism.

questions.question: Where does the word 'bloke' come from?

answers.answer: The word comes from Bengali. 'Bloke' in Bengali - actually 'loke'. It got brought back from the subcontinent along with other words like 'pucker' which are mainly Hindi. Brought back from the subcontinent by the British. I did a college linguistics course so I have some qualifications here.

questions.question: How much weight would it take for an underground tube train to be unable to move? Is there a maximum capacity like lifts have?

answers.caller: James (Crystal Palace) - National Rail train driver
answers.answer: Technically, no, it cannot be too full to run. To operate a train, you need two things: air and amps (electricity). Providing the train's got a compressor on it, it can keep the necessary air within its system for brakes, doors, and things like that. You could keep packing people in and the compressor would keep filling up with air - it would never stop running. The only time you wouldn't be able to move the train is if there are too many people and they jam the doors open. In terms of burden and weight, you could just keep filling it up.

questions.question: What happens if another female bee is growing to become a queen? Is she kicked out or assassinated?

answers.answer: If the bees aren't happy with the queen for some reason, they'll start to create what's called a queen cell. And as a beekeeper, you have to take those away if you don't want a new queen. If they want to swarm - meaning leave the hive and go off in search of a new home - they'll start creating a queen cell because they need more space. As a honey producer, you don't want to lose half your bees. The other thing is that if the queen were to suddenly die, if there are eggs in the hive that are less than three days old, they can change that into a queen by feeding it different food - royal jelly. And then the hive itself will make that decision based on what they feed that cell. If she's not letting off enough pheromones, worker bees can then become layers themselves because her pheromones suppress their system. So it's the hive that decides when to replace the queen.

questions.question: How do you make fluorescent colours? Why is it different from any other colour?

answers.answer: There's a chemical put in any fluorescent dye or paint. The chemical absorbs ultraviolet light which causes the electrons to momentarily jump up an energy level, but it's only temporary. When they drop back down again, they emit a lot of visible light. So effectively they convert invisible ultraviolet light to visible light, which is why they look brighter. It became popular in the 80s with disco ultraviolet lights. White shirts would fluoresce under those lights to look whiter than white.

questions.question: When do you use 'a' versus 'an'? People have started using 'a' before words starting with vowels (like 'a accident') - is that correct?

answers.answer: It all depends on what the word is that's following it. If the word begins with a vowel sound like 'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u', then you would put 'an'. And if it begins with a consonant sound, it would be 'a'. The reason is because it just sounds nicer and is easier to say. We have to insert something called a glottal stop otherwise which sounds quite unpleasant to say. It's less effort to do it that way.

It's the indefinite article. The rule depends on whether the word sounds like it begins with a vowel or a consonant. So it wouldn't work on 'unicorn' - you'd say 'a unicorn' because the 'u' sound acts as a consonant in that word. But you'd say 'an honest man' because the 'h' is silent and it begins with a vowel sound. It's the sound, not the letter.

questions.question: Why do we have an East End and a West End in London, but no North End or South End?

answers.answer: It relates to the River Thames. The river runs from east to west and that's why we have an East End and West End. There isn't a river that does that north to south in the same way, and that's why we don't have a North End or South End in London.

In every town, the posh people wanted to live in the west end because when they had smoke coming out of chimneys, they wouldn't get the bad air. With the wind, the prevailing wind blowing west to east, generally the west end is the posh end and the east end is the less posh end. This works for industrial towns, though for London specifically the river explanation is also valid.

questions.question: Do 3D contact lenses exist that would let you watch 3D films without wearing glasses?

answers.caller: Will Guy - LBC tech and gadget expert
answers.answer: They don't exist at the moment, and I don't think they ever will get developed because 3D films are dying off - they're just going to be a cinematic thing. However, Google is developing a lens that can beam a video picture directly to your eye. So eventually your mobile phone will probably be almost like a Terminator-style overlay which you wear as a contact lens on your eye. That technology is probably five to ten years away.

questions.question: When women dye their hair, it looks normal. When men do it, it looks ridiculous. Why do we notice men's hair dye more than women's?

answers.answer: Women dye their hair according to what looks best all the time. So they're not trying to make it look like it looked before they started going grey - they're dyeing their hair a new colour. A man tries to camouflage his grey by making his hair dark again, and it often ends up looking purple. He's not embracing the colour, he's just trying to hide the grey. So the woman goes to a colourist and she's not trying to cover up the grey, she's choosing a new look. Additionally, we expect women to dye their hair more socially and culturally, so we're not shocked by it. You see a bloke with implausibly black hair and it looks like odd behaviour. It's partly camouflage versus camouflage - men are usually camouflaging where women are camouflaging - but also we don't notice women who've dyed their hair whereas we do notice men because it's unexpected behaviour.

questions.question: If you're adopted, can you take on the passports of all four people involved (adoptive and biological parents)?

answers.answer: No. At the point of adoption, your biological parents cease to be your parents. That's the whole point of adoption. You can't take on all four passports because legally you only have two parents after adoption.

questions.question: What are the origins of the word 'ambulance'?

answers.answer: It comes from the French 'ambulant', meaning walking or more pertinently mobile. In the 17th or 18th century, 'ambulant' combined with 'hospital' created the term for the first battlefield-based hospitals - mobile hospitals. The word evolved in English to drop the 'hospital' part and 'ambulance' came to mean a mobile hospital, and today in English it's simply the word for the vehicle that carries the injured.

questions.question: What's the significance of the 21 gun salute? And why 41 guns today for the Queen's birthday?

answers.answer: It's to do with man-of-war ships returning to port after a battle. They fire the remaining load from the ship, and the port fires three for every one they fire, which adds up to 21. The number increases depending on rank - hence the Queen got an extra 20.

questions.question: Are there any other mammals in the animal kingdom, apart from the polar bear, that don't drink water?

answers.answer: Dolphins and whales don't drink water - they live in salt water and can't drink it, so they get all the moisture they need from the food they eat. The same might be true of polar bears.
He sent a picture of a baby polar bear drinking water, challenging the poster's claim

questions.question: On the Queen's Birthday Honours List or New Year's Honours List, how do they decide who gets what? What's the difference between an MBE and an OBE?
What was the first recording of people clapping to show appreciation? When did we start clapping to show appreciation?

answers.answer: In the Roman Senate, when they had a very good speaker, people used to pat him on the back. Those who couldn't reach the speaker used to clap their hands instead to make the same sort of noise.

questions.question: How do they measure the heat of chillies? There's a scale, isn't there? What's the name of it and how does it work?

answers.answer: The Scoville scale. You mix the weighed amount of chilli with water (and possibly salt or sugar), then dilute it and have a panel taste it repeatedly until they can't detect the chilli anymore. The amount of dilution needed determines the Scoville units.
Confirmed the Scoville heat scale explanation. Owns two Thai restaurants and uses a lot of chillies.

questions.question: Why was the mechanical shark in Jaws called Bruce?

answers.answer: The mechanical shark is nicknamed Bruce because it's named after Steven Spielberg's accountant. During filming they had terrible problems with the shark not working, and the production accountant named Bruce kept telling Spielberg he couldn't spend any more money. They named the shark after him when the film succeeded.

questions.question: Where does the term 'the real McCoy' come from?

answers.answer: They were a manufacturer of distillers in Canada. During Prohibition they shipped proper stuff across the border, which was much better than the bathtub gin made in the States. So people started saying 'that's the real McCoy' meaning good stuff.

Elijah McCoy was an American engineer who invented a lubricating device for train engines called the oil-dripping cup. Because he was poor, there were lots of knock-offs. When people got one that actually worked, they called it the Real McCoy.

questions.question: Would a nuclear missile destroy a meteorite in the vacuum of space?

answers.answer: Nuclear explosions don't need oxygen - they use splitting of heavy metals like plutonium/uranium or fusion of hydrogen nuclei. So a nuclear explosion will work in space.

Nuclear explosions create superheated air that causes a massive wind blowing everything out - that's what you won't get in space. A nuclear blast in space won't have the same blasting effect. Instead of one big meteorite you'd have lots of smaller ones scattering damage across Earth.

questions.question: How did the X become the symbol for kisses?

answers.answer: The Saxons and Vikings used runes carved onto sticks and stones. Their letter X was a love rune called Gifu (meaning gift). If you were carving a love rune for someone, you'd put Xs on it. That's how we got using X for kisses.

questions.question: Why do snails climb up windows and die? Is it like elephants going to the graveyard, or do they have no sense of direction and keep going until they find vegetation?

answers.answer: Insects and snails can suffer from fungal, bacterial or viral entomopathogens. Fungal entomopathogens reproduce via spores and can reprogram insects to crawl to a high place, so when they die the spores spread on the wind. This is likely what's happening to the snails.

questions.question: What happens to valuable items like bracelets that get dropped down drains and into sewers? Is there a sewer lost property office?

answers.answer: It depends on the catchment area. In a small catchment with a pumping station, heavy metals like rings can sink to the bottom and occasionally be found in the manhole or at the screens of treatment works. Workers might spot watches or rings and set them aside. But in a big city network, it's unlikely to be found. There are no official rules - if someone calls to report a lost item, they might make an effort to look, but generally the answer is 'not a lot happens'. If a worker finds something valuable they usually keep it.

questions.question: If Hillary Clinton wins the US presidential election, what will her husband Bill be called?

answers.answer: He'll still be called Mr. President.
The answer is 'the first gentleman'. That's the convention used in books with fictional female presidents. First lady, first gentleman.

questions.question: Can a baby break any bones while they're in the womb?

answers.answer: Yes. My son was born with a broken clavicle. He was nearly nine pounds and it was a quick, non-traumatic birth, so the doctors couldn't confirm whether it happened in the womb or during birth. He recovered fully and is now 20.

questions.question: What are the odds of finding a four-leaf clover?

answers.answer: It depends very much on where you are. A friend from France gave him 10 four-leaf clovers as a Christmas gift. They came from a corner of France where they're very common. In most places the odds are very slim, but in certain locations they're more prevalent.

questions.question: Is porridge a cereal? Even after it's cooked and changes state?
Will Britain eventually disappear entirely due to coastal erosion? Not from rising sea levels, but from the land itself being eroded away until there's nothing left?

answers.answer: Years ago the Isle of Wight was connected to mainland Britain. Over millions of years it eroded away, which is why the Needles are still there - they're part of where the island used to be connected. Similarly, pebbles on beaches have eroded from rocks, so water will eventually erode everything. Britain will get smaller and smaller, and in millions of years there may be very little left.

questions.question: Why does breath come out warm when you breathe with your mouth open, but cold when you purse your lips and blow?

answers.answer: It's called the Venturi effect. When your mouth is open the air comes out at body temperature. When you purse your lips the air is compressed and comes out colder. This was observed in the 18th century by Venturi in Italy.

questions.question: Why do we use silent letters in words? They didn't used to be silent - for example pterodactyl was originally spelt without the P.
Why is it bad manners to lean your elbows on the table while eating dinner?

answers.answer: Back in the old days before tables were joined together, they were placed on top of a log. If you put your elbows on the table it would flip up. That's how it became bad manners - it's from trestle table days.

questions.question: How do they project black light onto buildings? I saw them projecting the Belgian flag colors (orange, red and black) onto the London Eye and Big Ben, but I can't understand how black can be projected as light.

answers.caller: Professor Martin Smith (University of Middlesex, Professor of Robotics)
answers.answer: There's no such thing as black light. What you're seeing is about contrast. If the areas around are bright, the eye adjusts its aperture so everything else looks darker. With very good lenses and reflectors that approximate a point source of light, you get very sharp cutoffs in the projection.

You can't project black light. From a distance, the effect works and you see the black. Up close, you can see the red and yellow mixing in with the ambient light. It's about distance and quality of projection.

questions.question: What is the difference between peas and beans? My 10-year-old daughter asked while we were eating Sunday dinner with traditional West Indian rice and peas.

answers.answer: There is no difference. They're both from the same family called legumes. A pea is a bean and a bean is a pea - they're all seeds of vegetables in pods. In America, what we call a black-eyed bean, they call a black-eyed pea.

questions.question: Why is Easter so early this year? Who decided to bring it back a week?

answers.answer: Easter is the first Sunday following the first full moon after the 21st of March. It's set by the lunar calendar.

questions.question: Why do Scottish football results always seem to come in before English ones on Saturdays? Scottish games kick off at the same time but finish earlier by minutes.

answers.answer: It's all down to television. Halftime used to be ten minutes across the board. But once television got involved and started showing live matches, they introduced 15-minute halftimes. Scottish games in the lower three divisions are never on television, so they still have ten minutes, as do non-league games in England.
Because the stadia are much smaller in Scotland, the distance from the dressing room to the pitch is smaller.

questions.question: At what point does it become unprofitable for the rich to keep taking wealth from the poor? When does capitalism fail because the rich have got everything?

answers.answer: This is called secular stagnation where there's no organic growth - all growth is just speculative asset prices. Some rich have already stopped making money. The investment banks make money off credit, creating instruments and selling them. Companies can only grow by buying other companies. Meanwhile, pensions and buy-side investors are losing money. The only way capitalism resets is through credit crunches, then it restarts. It won't look the same in 10 years - the platform economy like Uber and Airbnb is already changing it. Also, if the top 20% income goes up by 1%, GDP goes down by 0.16%, but if the other 80% income goes up, GDP goes up.

questions.question: If I post two letters, one with a first class stamp and one with a second class stamp, what happens to the second class one? Does it just sit in a pile for days? My second class letters have arrived at the same time as first class.

answers.caller: Lewis (Surbiton) - Works with someone who used to work in a sorting office
answers.answer: There's genuinely no difference. Postmen take all the post together. If they have space in their bag, they take second class with them at the same time as first class.

That's rubbish. The machines recognise the phosphor on the stamps. First class mail is prioritised in the evening sorting process. Second class gets stored and sorted the following morning. The discrimination takes place during sorting, not when putting mail into bags.

questions.question: How does pita bread end up as two layers with a perfect seal? It starts as flat dough like a pizza base but ends up with a pocket.

answers.answer: It's cooked on a hot surface and turned over. That's how you get the two layers hardening. If you cooked pizza dough on a hot surface and turned it over, you'd get something akin to a pocket, more like pita.

questions.question: How do worms get through the earth? My 8-year-old son found it hard to believe they're strong enough to wiggle through compacted, hard ground.

answers.answer: Worms have bristles on their bodies. When they go in the earth, it grips the dirt and passes it under their head. They eat dead plant stuff to get through.

Worms don't get through hard soil. They excrete as they go - what comes out is called worm cast. If you lay plastic on your lawn for a few days and lift it, there'll be worms underneath because they come up to soft soil. They eat soil and excrete it, aerating the soil. The worm casts you see between flagstones are the evidence of this.

questions.question: My girlfriend called me from her car using factory-fitted Bluetooth from her iPhone. She was listening to Justin Bieber on CD. When I answered on my landline, the Justin Bieber music started coming through my TV soundbar, even though I had muted it. How did that happen?
Where do new words come from? My teenage daughter uses words like 'leng', 'peng', and 'peak' (which means bad, not good). Who makes these words official?
Is it possible to have two colds at once?

answers.answer: Yes, you can have two infections at once. My son had croup and pneumonia simultaneously when he was four.

questions.question: Why is a horse's height measured in hands and where does that come from?

answers.answer: It originated in ancient Egypt. A hand's breadth was used before literacy to communicate size verbally. There's some dispute over whether it included the thumb or was just the fist, but men's hands are surprisingly similar in size. It's mentioned in the Bible as well.

questions.question: What happens when there's a fire in a prison? If everyone evacuates over the road, won't they all run away?

answers.answer: The main job is preservation of life. They have contingency plans - if there's a fire throughout the jail, they'd either take prisoners to the football yard, or if that's also on fire, they'd take them outside through the gates with police assistance. If prisoners escape, at least their lives are saved and they can work to recapture them.
Police would turn up mob-handed and help shepherd prisoners. They would get them into custody, using cells in custody suites or opening old police station custody suites for this operation.

questions.question: Why can't you see your eyes move when you look in a mirror?

answers.answer: The brain samples what we see rather than working like a video camera continuously. There's only a very narrow sharp focus range, and the brain infills from what it already knows or has already seen, editing between the very short gaps between sampling. It's like a refresh rate.

The brain momentarily hangs onto the previous image and stitches it onto the next image. This is how films work - a series of different pictures blended together so you don't see them jerk. Similar to how the What the Butler Saw fairground apparatus worked.

questions.question: Why do large crowds in football stadiums sound like they're singing in tune when individually they probably can't sing in tune?

answers.answer: It's like audio feedback. If you can hear a sound you know is right, you can bring your voice onto that same pitch, which is very difficult from memory alone. That's why people who can't sing well alone enjoy singing in choirs. It's a cocktail party phenomenon where you can pick out one conversation. What we get with crowds is negative feedback - the opposite of the whistle you get when a microphone is near a speaker.

questions.question: Why do they call it a boxing ring when it's square?
If you draw a continuous line with a biro until it runs out of ink, how long would the line be?

answers.answer: About two miles. I worked in a pen shop and we had five days of training on all different types of pens.
It's two kilometers, not two miles. I worked in the pen industry for 19 years.

questions.question: Before we built cities, the ground must have been much lower. How much taller is the ground now? For example, when cobbles are visible beneath tarmac?

answers.answer: It varies enormously by location and age of settlement. For Roman London specifically, the streets are about 20 feet below modern pavement level. At the Grange Hotel near Tower Hill, you can stand on the patio and look down at the base of the Roman wall.

questions.question: Why do some occupations end in 'er' (farmer, presenter) and others in 'ist' (dentist, stylist, pharmacist)? Is there a difference?
Why do we blow on dice for good luck before rolling them?

answers.answer: Nobody knows for certain, but there are two theories. One is that bad gamblers had doctored dice with a substance that became sticky when blown on, so blowing was a way to check for cheating. The other is simply to clean the dice. Like most superstitions, it has no root in rationality.

questions.question: Why are champagne bottle sizes named after Old Testament kings like Jeroboam, Nebuchadnezzar, and Methuselah?
What is the origin of the phrase 'honeymoon'?

answers.answer: The phrase honeymoon comes from the length of period that you would be able to get off work after getting married and the fact that honey would be involved in your dowry or your marriage gift.

questions.question: Did they eat the pigs used in the filming of Babe at the wrap party?
Is there any link between the type of fingerprint you have (swirls, curves) and your ethnicity?
Why do drummers say 1-2-3-4 before starting but dancers say 5-6-7-8?

answers.answer: Because if dancers go on 1-2-3-4 at the same time as the drummer calls it, they'd all start at the same time and you wouldn't have any synchronicity. 5-6-7-8 allows dancers to start at a different time than musicians.

questions.question: Why do dancers have to wait for four seconds before they start dancing?

answers.answer: The drummer shouts out 1, 2, 3, 4 at the tempo he's going to start the tune at so the rest of the musicians know the tempo. Dancers catch on to the tail of the rhythm on the second or fourth bar with 5, 6, 7, 8 and then go into it. The drummers set the pace of the tune.

questions.question: What criteria have to be met before a snowfall on a hill can be described as an avalanche?

answers.answer: Avalanches can only happen in mountainous or hilly areas where there's a lot of snow that's already been there for several days or weeks. Another snowfall or rain can set off some of the previously settled snow.
An avalanche is an action. It's a layer of snow sliding down another layer of snow. It doesn't matter about the quantity - it's the action that creates it.

questions.question: Why didn't dinosaurs evolve to be like us, using tools and being intelligent?

answers.answer: Genetic mutations occur that provide evolutionary advantages. The reason dinosaurs didn't evolve to use tools is that no dinosaur was ever born with a genetic mutation involving opposable thumbs. It's just a fluke - like how no human has been born with 18 heads.

questions.caller: Tom in Sutton (answer to previous dinosaur question)
questions.question: How do we know that dinosaurs didn't use tools like sticks or branches?

answers.answer: Maybe dinosaurs did evolve to use things which we wouldn't think of as tools. We think of power drills or spades, whereas a dinosaur might have used a twig or a bit of branch.

questions.question: If a person is deaf in one ear, can they hear stereo sounds?

answers.answer: No, you can't hear stereo if you've only got one ear. It's mono.

answers.caller: Scott in Southend (deaf in one ear since birth)
answers.answer: I can definitely hear stereo. I've got a hi-fi with a mono button and a stereo button and I can tell the difference. I can tell where stereo's coming from, even in one ear.

questions.question: Does it cost more to produce a penny than it actually worth?

answers.answer: The only coin that has more value than its face value is a 2p piece because it has more than 2p worth of money in it. A penny has less than 1p worth of copper in it.

questions.question: When does a religion become an official religion, particularly regarding animal sacrifice and animal cruelty laws?

answers.answer: I believe it's 250,000 followers for which we recognise something as a religion. It goes back to the census form - there were more than 250,000 Jedi Knights who claimed that as their faith, so if they all cite that as their faith, it gets afforded official religious status.

questions.question: Since the introduction of same-sex marriage, have they updated the Book of Common Prayer's table of prohibited marriages?

At the end of a lot of commercials, there's a terms and conditions guy who speaks really fast - are there actually people who need to speak that fast, or do they just record it at normal speed and speed it up?

answers.answer: A bit of both - you do it as fast as you can, but they can speed it up even more in post-production.

questions.question: When someone says someone blackmails me, why do they use the word blackmail? What's the origin of that word?
Fuel is charged at an illegal price of 0.9p - why do petrol stations charge this amount?
Can humans pass on diseases to animals? Can I give my dog my flu?

answers.answer: I presume that they can. I mean, if it's blood carried or something like that.

Yes, humans can pass on illnesses to animals. When I used to have hamsters as a kid, you're not allowed to pick them up and play with them when you've got a cold, because they can get the sickness from it as well.

questions.question: Why is anything below the waist called 'a pair' (pants, knickers, shorts, trousers) but anything above the waist is singular (shirt, vest, jumper)?

answers.answer: The reason is to do with cod pieces. Back in the day, the two parts of our trousers were not joined together. So the cod piece would protect your modesty in the absence of a needle and thread. So you had two separate garments that you would pull on as trousers, or pantaloons, or socks, or stockings. Now that they're joined together at the crotch, the language has simply stayed where it was before, where you would have two stockings, two trouser rings, two undercracker rings. Ergo, whenever it was involved in covering your legs, you would have a pair of them.

questions.question: Why do we have three cheers? Why not one, two, four, or five? Why specifically three?
How much cash does the average cash machine hold?

answers.answer: I've got 30 grand in the back of my mind for some reason, and it gets refilled quite regularly because you very rarely find empty ones, except at chucking out time on a Saturday night.

Your average cash machine will have £60,000 in it. You've normally got four cassettes in there which are full up with notes - two lots of cash. Two cassettes are made up with £20 notes which have £20,000 in each and two cassettes with £10 notes in which have £10,000 in each, making £60,000.
I heard that it was £25,000 per cassette and there could be up to seven cassettes depending on the location. In a very popular area, say in the West End, it might go up more.

questions.question: Who wrote the wedding vows? Because they seem to be the same everywhere.

answers.answer: Geoffrey Archer. No, I'm teasing you. If it's a Christian wedding, I'd go out and suggest it was the Book of Common Prayer. But I don't know that, so it's a good question.
Thomas Cranmer. Book of Common Prayer.

questions.question: If the body gets damaged externally (cut skin) or internally (operation, bite tongue), how does the body know what trigger mechanism is involved to send the right cell to repair the damage? You wouldn't use emulsion paint on the outside of your house.

answers.answer: I suspect that a proper scientist would be sniggering at our ignorance. In my mind, I'm wondering whether stem cells are relevant to this, because they're cells that can become anything. It must be a chemical.

First of all, it doesn't. The body releases histamines. When damage is made to any part of the body, it releases histamines. The histamines go through the nervous system and it tells you where extra blood is needed. A mesh is created by red blood cells, white blood cells, and plasma to make up the actual replication. All cells in the body are exactly the same. They have the same DNA in them. They just replicate. So if we take Jason's example - he's cut his knee - it won't grow an ear cell. It's going to grow whatever cells it's found itself in the middle of.

questions.question: Why do mammals have a deciduous set of teeth? Why don't our teeth grow like our other bones grow?

answers.answer: The answer is evolution. There has been no evolutionary glitch whereby we would have been... Teeth are one of the most interesting elements of evolution. I think we should have evolved not to have teeth. We should have evolved to have fantastic blades in our mouth or something completely immune to decay and almost made of metal, but we haven't. The answer is because there's no advantage in it being the other way around that's been discovered evolutionarily.

We are actually born with our teeth developed, mostly developed in our skull. They develop when we're a fetus at about four or five weeks. If you Google x-rays or images of skulls of children, you can see the teeth sitting in around the jaw, the adult teeth packed in underneath the non-adult teeth.

If you were a rabbit, you would continually grow your teeth because at the other end of the tooth, the bit that sticks out of the gum, that's below is an open apex where the tooth continues to grow. Same with rats. Your two girls are shedding teeth. When they were born, they had things called tooth germs in their skulls, not fully formed teeth. As they get older, the calcium is laid down in the epithelium of the tooth germ, and therefore, when they're six months, the first two teeth come through. When they're older, about six or seven, the deciduous teeth are pressed underneath by the ensuing tooth germs of the permanent teeth, and therefore, the root gets dissolved.

questions.question: Why do we say 'chop-chop' to hurry children along? Is it from cooking or karate?

answers.answer: I was thinking maybe cooking, but that doesn't really make sense. Karate? Potentially unlikely though.
It's from English seamen that picked it up from Chinese Cantonese-speaking workers back in the 1800s. There was a Cantonese phrase that basically translated to 'hurry hurry' - chop chop.

questions.question: Are humans capable of using 100% of our strength? Is our bone structure strong enough to withstand the sort of strength our muscles could exert?

answers.answer: I'd say that the mind limits are the most important thing in the human's life. They are capable of using 100% of their strength. But I don't know that we've nailed it.

I'm a visual effects artist and we did a TV show about people that have survived horrible situations. A rock climber was climbing up a rock face and a rock fell on him that weighed about a ton and a half. He was sliding off the cliff and he managed to push it off him. He essentially fired all of his body muscles at the same time to lift it. The result was that everything tore away from the bone. Your muscles are stronger than your tendons. So he tore himself to pieces - everywhere was bruised, his pectoral muscles had detached from his ribs. That's why your brain limits it - better than being dead. They call it hysterical strength and it's not good for you. The body dials it down. The flood of adrenaline causes huge stress but beyond the chemical stress it actually can cause you to effectively rupture yourself.

questions.question: Why is scratching your back more satisfying than scratching any other part of your body?

answers.answer: When you're in your mid-40s, Christy, you may discover that there is a part of your anatomy that delivers a scratch-based satisfaction that at your tender time of life you will find impossible to believe. I'm saying no more than that.

questions.question: When you see a car on TV, the wheels appear to be going backwards. Does this happen in real life on the motorway too, or is it just on TV?

answers.answer: If it's just on TV, it'll be the frame rates of the camera. I think the wheel is moving fast. I want it to go backwards. It would just look a little bit stuttered in its movement, but not to actually look like it's going the other direction.

It's to do with frame rate per second rate of film, which is 24 per second traditionally. So because it oscillates, it picks up the spokes depending on how fast you're going. That's why sometimes it looks like it's rotating forward, sometimes it looks like it's rotating backwards. Same with helicopter and aeroplane propellers - they look like they're rotating really slowly but they're not. That's why you can't film TV screens - they always used to look really bad.

questions.question: Why do we do three cheers? (Answer: from three Hail Marys)

answers.answer: No, it isn't. Three Hail Marys isn't a traditional Roman Catholic thing. Saying it once is. Saying it three times doesn't carry any special weight. You might get it as a penance in confession, but that's not something you'd cheer to - you'd hang your head in shame and look forward to the eternal fires of damnation. That's not the reason you do it three times.

questions.question: Why is a tent called a tent?

answers.answer: Tents are called tents because it comes from Latin tendere, which is to stretch. Various Latin words beginning T-E-N-T are all about stretched things. It came down through French into English from about the Middle Ages.

questions.question: Is chewing gum a good way of losing weight?

answers.answer: An average stick of gum is 11 calories. It takes one hour to chew 11 calories, so it's absolutely pointless.
You would end up putting weight on. The act of chewing gum would make you hungry because your stomach would get ready for food.

questions.question: Are there any Down Syndrome animals, or does nature have a way of dealing with that?

answers.answer: There's actually a white tiger in the United States by the name of Kenny who was born with Down syndrome. It was to do with the limited gene pool that goes along with the rarity of white tigers.

questions.question: Why does a golf ball have dimples?

answers.answer: If you get exactly the right amount of roughness, the air molecules will stick to the ball, which will make it appear as it goes through the air smoother. Because there's this little thin layer of air around it, and molecules of air are very smooth, it will go through the air with less drag, so it will go further.

questions.question: Are all large apes ambidextrous or do they have a predominant right or left hand?

answers.answer: All animals tend to have laterality preference. They do tend to be left-handed. It's to do with something with embryonic development, so it's definitely within the womb. However, there is a factor of environment as well.

questions.question: Why do we refer to awards as 'gongs'?

answers.answer: It's because of medals. A medal looks like a miniature gong, so a medal became known as a gong, and then other awards given out by juries or panels have become known as gongs as well.

questions.question: Is the lethal injection for death row the same as for assisted death/mercy killing at places like Dignitas?

answers.answer: They are completely different. The one used mainly for euthanasia is called eubutanol, which stops the cardiac system working - it paralyzes the diaphragm and brings on cardiac arrest. But it's not painful. In the penal system, they use three drugs: one to sedate, one to paralyze, and a third to kill, which is a very painful drug. The chemicals are different and they continuously change the chemicals used in prisons because companies stop selling them based on rights issues.

questions.question: Why do we call painters and decorators 'cowboys'?

answers.answer: If you were a cowboy on the plains with your herd and had to cover a lot of ground, you might stop off on the way and have a kip. Or if you were part of a gold rush and arrived at a town, it's about throwing up a residence quickly without paying proper attention to permanence.

questions.question: If a knighted man is married to another man, does his husband get a title like a wife would?

answers.answer: If a Lord marries a gentleman, the Lady that was his wife and is now a man remains a man. He doesn't acquire any ennoblement of any kind. This doesn't apply in the case of a Baroness like Mrs Thatcher. She became Lady Thatcher - that was a life peerage, and at the time Dennis was not entitled to anything.

questions.question: Why do we use the tick symbol for correct and X for incorrect?

answers.answer: It's from Greek. 'Ochi' is no in Greek, which gives us the X. And 'Ne' is yes in Greek, which looks like an N, the shape of the tick.

questions.question: Why can't we pause the radio the way we can pause our TVs?

answers.answer: On digital radios, you can pause them, but they cost over a hundred pounds as opposed to a normal radio.

questions.question: Why is an American gallon different in size to a British gallon?

answers.answer: An American pint is only 16 fluid ounces compared to our 20. It's something to do with the fact that once upon a time in this country we had two units of measure. One to do with the West country was 16 ounces to a pint. One got exported on the Mayflower and one didn't. That's why Americans have gone down the other road and why an American gallon is smaller than ours.

questions.question: Why is it called Russian roulette and not Greek or Chinese roulette?
Why is an American gallon smaller than a British gallon?

answers.answer: His grandfather told him they were selling oil or something to America during the war and were pinching it out of the top of the barrel and selling it to them as the same amount of gallons.

questions.question: Why are piggy banks called piggy banks? Where is the origin? Pigs don't have anything to do with money. Why is it not a doggy bank or a monkey bank?

answers.answer: It's from the 15th century. The material they used to make piggy banks was called pygg (P-G-Y). So there was pygg clay. And then potters over the years made it look like a pig. Nothing to do with the animal whatsoever.

questions.caller: Sully (Chislehurst) - on behalf of son Talon
questions.question: The very first leaf to fall off a tree in autumn - will that be the first leaf to grow back in spring?

answers.answer: No. When you observe in spring, you will see the buds at the tip of the branch, and the first leaf to fall is at the bottom of the branch in autumn. So it's not the same leaf that fell in autumn that goes first into spring.

questions.question: Why do I sneeze when I look into the sun?

answers.answer: It's genetic - same way that curling your tongue is a genetic ability. Some people can sneeze when looking at bright lights and some people can't. It's a genetic condition that bright lights can trigger sneezing.

questions.question: Why don't bats get head rushes when they hang upside down to rest? If you hang upside down for even 10 seconds, you'd want to die because all the blood rushes to your head. What is it about bats that means that doesn't happen?

answers.answer: They've got one-way valves in their arteries which stop the blood rushing back to their heads.

questions.question: What's the relevance of the term Roger and why is it used on the radio? Roger is for Romeo in the phonetic alphabet but that doesn't seem right. Why roger?

answers.answer: The difference is that Romeo is part of the phonetic alphabet you use to spell words. Roger, over, out - that's shorthand. Roger means I understand your last transmission. It's not the phonetic alphabet. When talking to another ship or ham operator, if they gave a command, you would just say Roger because it means understood.
It actually stands for something: Reference Orders Given Everything Received.

questions.question: If you could drink petrol, how many calories would there be in a litre of petrol?

answers.answer: I can tell you how to work it out. One calorie is the amount of energy required to heat one kilogram of water by one degree Celsius.

Petrol has carbon-carbon bonds and carbon-hydrogen bonds. When these break and form bonds with oxygen to create carbon dioxide and water, that gives the energy. Fats, proteins, wood, sugar all have more or less the same amount of energy. You'd need to look up the calorific value.

There are 32.4 calories per litre on the energy density scale (megajoules per litre). On the specific energy scale (megajoules per kilogram), it's 44.4. There are four or five different ways of working it out.

questions.question: In films, when someone is having a heart attack, people strip out a lamp, get two of the leads, live and earth, and shove it on their chest like a defibrillator. Would that work in real life?

answers.answer: Story about trying to revive wife's shocked rabbit with car ignition lead - high voltage about 50,000 volts. The rabbit was jumping around but didn't come back to life. Not conclusive proof.

A defibrillator works with very high voltage, very low current. A gas cooker spark is about 25,000 volts - that's low current. The correct voltage to start a heart is about 50,000 volts. If you use mains electricity, it would fry them. A car battery might work but you couldn't safely adapt it. What you see in films with lamps is rubbish - it would kill you.

questions.question: What is the difference between illegal and unlawful? Sometimes on the news they say unlawful killing, sometimes illegal war. If they're the same, why don't they just use one word consistently?

answers.answer: Fielded calls saying unlawful means against the law and illegal is a poorly bird - callers were joking.

Things that are illegal are defined by Acts of Parliament, and things that are unlawful are defined by common law which involves loss or damage. Acts of Parliament can change over time, common law can't. An example: migrants going to certain countries may go illegally but it might be lawful.

questions.question: What time do astronauts use when they're in the ISS?

answers.answer: It's GMT on the ISS.
It's actually called Zulu time, which is exactly the same as GMT. One hour behind BST. It's used by aviation, naval, and space exploration. 15 years in the aviation industry.

questions.question: If you have a laser torch pen and point it at a television, can you do any damage to the television?
Can I get a suntan through my conservatory glass? Will I get the same vitamin D benefits as standing outside?

answers.answer: Yes, you can tan in a conservatory. Plain glass doesn't block UV rays. But car windscreens do block UV light, which is why photochromic glasses don't change colour behind a windscreen. In conservatories, unless the glass is treated, you'll be fine.

Vitamin D is made from UVB rays specifically, and ALL glass blocks UVB rays - both car and conservatory glass. So you can't make vitamin D in a conservatory or car. However, car side windows let through UVA, while windscreens (which are laminated) block UVA too. So Shams was wrong but not completely wrong.

questions.question: How many countries does it take for a war to become a world war?

answers.answer: Nothing to do with the number of countries. The Seven Years' War and Napoleonic Wars ranged all over the globe but weren't called world wars. It was just academics in the 1920s who decided to call WWI 'The First World War.' It's just words.

The US always says WWII began at Pearl Harbor, but that's only because Germany declared war on the US later that day. Whether belligerent parties are separated by a large body of water or a continent, the Americans stipulate it began at Pearl Harbor.

questions.question: Why does water run out in a clockwise direction in a sink or bath plughole? It doesn't in Australia.

answers.answer: It's because of the Earth's rotation. The northern hemisphere drains clockwise, the southern hemisphere drains anticlockwise.
It doesn't matter about hemisphere. Mythbusters tested this and found it's the design of the bowl that determines which way water drains, not the Earth's rotation.
It doesn't matter about hemisphere - it's centripetal force. Like a penny spiralling to the centre of those penny-farthing rides. The direction depends on how you orient the bowl.
I tested this in my basin. Left tap on: anticlockwise. Right tap on: clockwise. It depends entirely on the plughole design, not hemisphere.

questions.question: In pre-decimalisation prices written as 'one shilling and sixpence' (1S 6D), why was a penny denoted by 'D' and not 'P'?

answers.answer: It's Latin, isn't it? Something from denarius?

The pound comes from Latin 'libra'. The 'S' for shilling is 'solidus', invented by Constantine in the 4th century to stem inflation. The 'D' comes from 'dinarius' - the Roman coin mentioned in the Bible when Mary Magdalene poured perfume worth a year's pay (300 dinari) over Jesus' feet. So 'LSD' = libra, solidus, dinarius. Written Latin was never changed because it would be too confusing.

questions.question: Why is it called 'mincemeat' when there's no mince or meat in it?

answers.answer: It originally did contain meat. People put fruit into meat pies because it helped preserve the meat and made it tastier. Over time, the fruit content went up and meat content went down. All that remains now is suet in the mincemeat, though you can buy vegetarian versions without meat suet.

questions.question: What's the difference between a lake and a pond?

answers.answer: I think lakes get rivers or streams going into them, but ponds don't. Ponds just fill from rain.
A pond can sustain life anywhere in it, but a lake has areas where nothing can live.
A pond is man-made and a lake is natural.

questions.question: Has any artist or band ever deliberately set out to have only one hit and then walked away?

answers.answer: In 1988, A Tribe of Toffs had a hit with 'John Kettley as a Weatherman'. They were just students between school and university who wrote a silly song as a laugh. To my knowledge, they only released that one single.

The Tribe of Toffs actually tried to release more serious songs but couldn't get a recording contract. They released another single in 1989 called 'Terry Wogan's On TV' again. So they weren't one-hit wonders by choice.

The 'Suicide is Painless' theme from M*A*S*H was a number one hit in 1980. It wasn't a real group called The Mash - it was session singers called The Ron Hickman Singers. They recorded the theme and then went off and did their own things. That was truly a one-hit wonder.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'Bob's your uncle' come from?
Is the diameter of your index finger directly proportional to the aperture of your nostrils and ear canals? Is there a genetic or evolutionary relationship?

answers.answer: I think the answer's no. All your fingers seem to fit snugly in your nose.

questions.question: What is the strongest substance made by animals? Is it spider silk or something else?

answers.answer: He considers whether silkworms make the strongest silk but doesn't give a definitive answer. Says 'Let's find out' about the strongest man-made fibre, but the question was about animal-made substances.

questions.question: If you found an island that was previously uninhabited, how many generations of the peoples that then inhabited the island would it take for them to be considered indigenous?

answers.answer: Suggests children would be indigenous immediately if their parents were the first people on an uninhabited land. Notes that only African people (who evolved there) would truly be indigenous. Says it's a brilliant question that may not have an answer and offers money if there's a definitive solution.

questions.question: Why do flammable and inflammable mean exactly the same thing, when similar word pairs like visible/invisible are opposites?

answers.answer: Suggests it might be related to 'flamed' and 'inflamed' meaning the same thing. Admits he doesn't know and says there's probably no answer - just an accident of verbal etymological evolution.
Proposes it's about proximity to flame - when flame is close, it's flammable; further away, it's inflammable; even further, it's highly inflammable - different degrees of flammability.

Old enough to remember when 'inflammable' was the only word used. When people started misunderstanding 'inflammable' to mean 'can't be set on fire', labels were changed to 'flammable' to make people understand the danger. Both words mean the same thing with 'inflammable' predating 'flammable'.
Argues flammable means something you can set alight, while inflammable means something that will light itself and is volatile.

questions.answer: The hardest naturally occurring substance in nature is limpet teeth. He saw this on nature programmes.

questions.question: When I die, I want to be cremated. Is it obligatory or is there a law that I have to have a coffin? Couldn't I not just have a body bag? It's a lot cheaper.

answers.answer: You need a really flammable container for cremation so it goes quickly, like kindling. A paper bag would work. The temperature is so huge, she can't believe wood is necessary to the combustion process.

Cremation bags aren't allowed for hygiene and environmental reasons. Crematoriums are regulated on gases released. Wood doesn't cause as much impact as burning rubber or plastic. If an eco-friendly, sustainable, sturdy bag could be invented, it might work.

questions.question: Who designed the layout of a QWERTY keyboard? And when they were doing it, did they realise that you could spell the word typewriter on the top line?

answers.answer: Explains the QWERTY layout is linked to typewriter hammers - frequently used letters need to be spaced apart to minimise the likelihood of hammers sticking. Doesn't know who designed it. Thinks the 'typewriter' coincidence on the top row is just that - a coincidence.

questions.answer: His boss said £25,000 gets dropped on the street in loose change every day. He calculated this equals roughly £9 million per year.

questions.question: Should vinyl albums be stored vertically or laid flat to prevent warping?

answers.answer: A record producer neighbor stored thousands of albums vertically on shelves. When stored horizontally on the floor, they warp. Vertically, with bookends holding them tightly, prevents warping. Also keeps album names visible for easy retrieval.

questions.question: When you drop a fizzy drink can and it fizzes up, why do we tap the top of it? Does that actually work?

answers.answer: Tapping encourages bubbles to the top of the liquid so when opened, gas escapes gradually. If gas remains within the liquid, it rushes to the surface taking the liquid with it, causing the cup to runneth over.

questions.question: Neptune is completely made up of gas. How can it orbit around the sun if it's just a big ball of gas?

answers.answer: Neptune probably has a small rocky nickel-iron core but is surrounded by ice thousands of miles thick. Gravitational pull holds all molecules and atoms together in spherical construction. Everything larger than a certain mass goes spherical due to gravity. While Neptune is called a gas or ice giant, most of it is water, frozen methane or carbon dioxide. It may have a core like Uranus.

questions.question: Why is water temperature called "lukewarm"? Why use "luke" specifically?

answers.answer: L-E-W-K in Old English meant tepid or mild. It probably came from Old English or Scandinavian origins, and over the years the spelling changed from L-E-W-K to just Luke, as we say in the name.

questions.question: Is saying "ouch" when we hurt ourselves learned behaviour or was it made up? Did someone write it down first?
