answers.answer: The 'ch' is likely a human invention, but the 'ow' is probably reflex. The cartoon sound effects like 'kapow' may have come from naturally saying ouch, then writing it down rather than vice versa.

questions.question: Why is the musical instrument called a recorder? It doesn't record anything.

answers.answer: It's probably 'reed recorder' - they needed reeds like on an oboe or clarinet.

The recorder is one of the few woodwind instruments that doesn't have a reed. It has a whistle mouthpiece like a school playground whistle. The name comes from Latin 'ricordare' - 're' means to play again, 'cord' means by heart, so you're recording music in your memory by playing it over and over without sheet music.

questions.question: Why do all the numbers on a roulette wheel add up to 666, the number of the beast?

answers.answer: Pascal invented probability and roulette. 36 times 37 divided by 2 gives 666 - it's the sum of the sequence of numbers. He was a mathematical genius and it was a joke.

questions.question: How can I tell the age of a tree without sawing it down and counting the rings?

answers.answer: They use a serrated metal tool attached to a hand drill, insert it to halfway through the tree, and pull out a core sample showing the rings - similar to how cheesemakers take samples.

A tree preservation officer used a special tape measure wrapped around the thickest part of the tree, divided by 2.4 inches or 2 centimeters, which estimated his oak at 450 years old. But James pointed out this wouldn't work for all trees as they grow at different rates.

questions.question: If someone is blind from birth, do they perceive images in their dreams?

answers.answer: No, they cannot physically see images because if they've never seen anything, they can't know what anything physically looks like. But they feel things, smell things, taste things, and use all their other senses in dreams.

questions.question: Has human evolution slowed or stopped because medicine and technology now keep weaker people alive who would have died and not reproduced in the past?

answers.answer: Medicine has not stopped evolution. By obviating the need to overcome nature's hostility through medicine, we are preventing natural selection - any mutation causing disease that previously gave an advantage has been leveled. Evolution is passive, happens by chance, and changes are incremental over generations. Darwin never coined 'survival of the fittest' himself.

questions.question: How are postcodes linked or organized? Why isn't South West 1 next to South West 2? Why is SW10 (Chelsea) not near SW11 (Battersea)?

answers.answer: Postcodes in London are alphabetical - E3 is Bow, E4 is Chingford, E5 is Clapton, etc. Areas were developed and added later, which is why SW10 (West Brompton) isn't next to SW11 (Fulham area).

questions.question: Can you fire a handgun on the moon or in space?

answers.answer: Yes, you can fire a handgun on the moon. You don't need air because the gunpowder inside the cartridge case already contains all the oxygen it needs in the potassium nitrate (nitrogen and three molecules of oxygen). This also explains why you can fire a gun underwater if you keep the powder dry.

questions.question: Why does déjà vu make you feel uneasy?

answers.answer: Suggested it would be a mystery if it didn't make you feel uneasy since you're experiencing something that seems to have happened before.

It's almost like having a mini seizure - a very quick rewiring of your brain, almost like an electrical misfiring that triggers the part of your brain where memories are made. So it feels like a memory but isn't, which makes you feel disoriented.

questions.question: Why aren't sloths extinct? They move in slow motion, sleep all day, must be sitting ducks for predators.

answers.answer: Sloths live really high up. They allow mould to grow on their fur making them stinky and horrible, so most animals won't want to eat them. Their only predator is eagles and there just aren't many eagles around. (Learned from David Attenborough)

Sloths eat a particularly poisonous plant, making them poisonous to other animals themselves. They move slowly because if they moved any faster, their metabolism would speed up and their main food would actually kill them. Nothing else will touch them except eagles, making them incredibly successful.

questions.question: Is there any logic to the alphabetical order of the alphabet? Why are the letters in the order they are?

answers.answer: Alphabet comes from Greek alpha and beta. Greeks took letters from their invasions (Alexander the Great brought the X from Persia). Roman culture adapted Greek letters. But this only explains the letters' presence, not their ORDER.

The alphabetical order has only been rearranged since medieval times. Before printing, words were organized by first letter into lists. Since the advent of printing, they've strictly organized into ABC order. But the original ORDER question wasn't fully answered.
Claims it's all to do with phonetics (offered as educated guess).

questions.question: How fast do you have to go through a speed camera before it can't pick you up?

answers.answer: 172 miles per hour. Top Gear tested this - they set up a gas hole in a runway and got progressively faster cars to go through the camera until they could get the car through. James gave him a round of applause.

questions.question: Where does the term 'swan song' come from? Do swans sing when their partner dies?

answers.answer: Goes back to 3rd century Greek mythology. The swan was Apollo's favourite bird and was supposed to sing beautifully before it died. It appears in Aesop's fable 'The Swan and the Goose' where they caught a goose but it proved to be a swan when it started singing before they killed it.

The most common swan in the country is the mute swan, which doesn't really sing. But common folklore had it that the only time it ever sang was just before it died. That myth started in ancient Greece where the swan is sacred to Apollo. It also appears in Aesop's fables.

questions.question: If you're in a coma, do you still have bowel movements and do you still menstruate?

answers.answer: Yes, people in comas definitely still have bodily functions. Nurses change colostomy bags, catheters, bedding, give bed baths - it's a difficult job.

questions.question: How many trains are on the Tube network during rush hour in London?
Can you yawn when you're sleeping?

answers.answer: No, probably not. A yawn is about bringing in more oxygen when you're tired and need energy. If you're asleep, you wouldn't need that boost. The show gave a round of applause.

questions.question: What's the purpose of the semicircle at the edge of a football pitch's 18-yard box?

answers.answer: Players aren't allowed into the arc when a penalty is being taken.
So that people not taking the penalty maintain a certain distance (about 12 metres) from the penalty spot. The arc ensures everyone stays back.

questions.question: What keeps sound on a record or CD? What stops it from fading or disappearing over time?
Why do I sometimes have a bit of a shiver when I'm urinating?

answers.answer: It's the rapid loss of heat from the bladder. Urine is stored at body temperature. The more pressure you exert, the faster you lose heat, hence the shiver. Same reason you shiver in any other circumstance - it's about heat transfer.

questions.question: Who is Riley in the phrase 'living the life of Riley'?

answers.answer: Riley was a double agent for the Allies and for the enemy.
Sir Walter Riley who was having an affair with the Queen, travelled on expeditions bringing back tobacco, potatoes, tomatoes, tea. When he committed a crime, the Queen pardoned him.

It goes back to the early 1900s. It was a character in musical songs. It's an allusion to a comic song by Pat Rooney popular in America in the 1880s about a bloke who came into an awful lot of money to live luxuriously.

questions.question: What's happening in the brain when you laugh vs smile? Why is laughter more debilitating than smiling?

answers.answer: Laughter is a primitive primate response that's an empathic response halfway towards crying. It's based on looking at the downfall of others and expressing a cry to warn people, with some nervousness about yourself enduring the same downfall. It's seen in primates as well. If a chimp falls out of a tree, other chimps laugh - it's an expression of fear. When a comedian tells a joke about someone's downfall, the audience laughs because they have an empathic response and are relieved they're not having that downfall.

questions.question: What's the origin of the word 'lap'? Where did it come from when we say 'sit on my lap'?

answers.answer: 'Lap' comes from a German high German word. English has German origins. It comes from a garment worn around the waist called a 'labber' or 'labben' - common in high German languages, Dutch, Frisian. In the 17th century it developed a figurative meaning to envelop or surround - 'lap of luxury,' to lap someone on a track, or animals lapping up water.

questions.question: Can a fish sneeze?

answers.answer: Fish cannot sneeze. To sneeze you need lungs and nasal passages which fish don't have - they have an oxygen transference thing in their gills. What Kirk saw was probably a jet of water from the gills - cleaning his gills which looked like a sneeze.

questions.question: What's the association between theatres and serving ice cream in the interval?

answers.answer: Ice cream in theatres started in the 19th century with large Italian migration. The Italians had it in their theatre halls and operas. It was a Victorian craze that caught on, starting in concert halls and seaside piers before making its way to London theatres.

questions.question: How cold does it have to be in London for the Thames to freeze over?

answers.answer: The Thames would not freeze over now, but in Victorian times it did because the bridges had very narrow arches so water ran slower and could freeze. They held parties with fires actually on the Thames. Also mentioned volcanic eruptions causing overall cooling.

questions.question: Why is a green room called a green room?

answers.answer: It's from Stratford-upon-Avon. In medieval times they put on plays and actors got changed in the room next to the main hall where the council used to meet. It was known as the 'agreeing room.' With a Warwickshire accent, 'agreeing room' became 'green room.'

questions.question: Why do we lose hair on the top of our head (male pattern baldness) but not on the sides?

answers.answer: The hair at the top of the head is genetically different from hair elsewhere on the body. It's more susceptible to testosterone, which makes it fall out. As hair gets further from the top of the head, it gets more curly and thicker - genetically different even before it falls out.

questions.question: Are humans going to keep getting taller as time goes on? We've gotten taller over the years, doorways were smaller in the 16th century, suits of armour at the Tower of London are tiny.

answers.answer: It's to do with nutrition partly, and evolution. Evolution's not finite, nutrition might be. There's an evolutionary advantage in being taller, but I don't know if we'll continue getting taller indefinitely.

People are not getting taller - it's just nutrition. Henry VIII was over six foot. The average human height has gone up by about 10 centimetres in 150 years in industrialised countries, and Dutch men are 19cm taller than their mid-19th century counterparts. But this is only nutrition, not evolution. There's no advantage to being taller. If people were getting taller every generation over 10,000 years, we'd be 10-13 feet high by now.

questions.question: What was the difference between a duvet and an eiderdown? (From earlier in the week - staff at Windsor Castle were sniffy about duvets being common and preferred eiderdowns)

answers.answer: Eiderdowns were originally stuffed with feathers from the eiderduck. They changed the name to duvet around the time cookery changed to nouveau cuisine - it's gentrification. An eiderdown is a quilt filled with feathers, a duvet is similar with man-made stuff. An eiderdown is a type of duvet.
You do not use sheets with a duvet, but you do with an eiderdown. They are not used the same way - it's just a tradition.

An eiderdown was used to cover the bed and make it look nice. It was made of down feathers but used as a coverlet on top of blankets. A duvet replaced the need for an eiderdown. An eiderdown is like a thick bedspread, not a duvet.

Duvets have a removable, washable cover. Eiderdowns don't have a washable cover and usually have to be dry-cleaned. An eiderdown is a self-contained piece of linen with no removable parts. If you have feathers inside and put it in a washing machine, it's ruined.

questions.question: Does putting a spoon in Prosecco keep the bubbles, and if so, why? We had bottles over Christmas and one stayed fizzy overnight.

answers.answer: It could be an urban myth. Professor Hal might know the science.
It keeps you colder. In the old days when they didn't have fridges, if you stuck a big metal spoon in it, it would keep it colder so it would stay fizzy longer.

It's a myth. The solubility of carbon dioxide is what matters. If you put a half-open bottle in the fridge and pour it the next day, it'll still be fizzy because colder temperature increases solubility. The colder it is, the more soluble the CO2. Putting a spoon in doesn't make it colder - it would have been fizzy anyway. People put a spoon in, it was fizzy, and they assumed cause and effect but it was just the temperature.

questions.question: How do they get the white for white paint? White is a colour that's absorbed by every other colour, so I don't understand where the base of the white comes from.

answers.answer: Chalk, wouldn't it? Calcium carbonate base? You get something white and solid, then you find a colourless solvent which can turn it into a paint.

questions.question: Why does the Sky Digibox fast-forward go 3, 6, 12, 30? 3, 6, 12 are all units of 3, but where does 30 come from? It seems arbitrary and I'd prefer 24 to make it more symmetrical.

answers.answer: 30 is probably about the fastest they could go while still being able to track visually what was happening. Any faster would be a pointless blur. The difference between 12 and 30 - there was no significant increase in between that was worthwhile having an extra speed for.
Those are all divisible - 60 seconds in a minute. 30 is half a minute, so you can fast forward five minutes by going at 30x for 10 seconds. That's why they go to 30 and not 24.

questions.question: Why do puppies when eating sometimes lift their back legs up and fall tail over head into their bowl of food?

answers.answer: Imagine eating a sausage that's clamped at one end. Your head moves towards the clamp as you eat. The puppy starts eating the food nearest to it, then carries on eating without realising it has to move its feet forward. It's a baby puppy that hasn't learned that lesson yet, so it loses balance and topples over. It won't happen more than two or three times after they learn.

questions.question: Where does Tim Peake pay his taxes now he's in space for six months? If you work overseas, you don't pay UK taxes.

answers.answer: I don't know. I think you need to be more than six months out of the country for tax purposes. He's gone for six months exactly. If he commits a crime up there, like International Waters, whose jurisdiction? That could be a thriller plot.

He pays tax where he's paid. If he's paid in the UK, he pays it direct from his salary to the UK. He's clearly not paid by an alien spaceship, so he wouldn't pay tax there. Someone working on a cruise liner for a UK holiday company wouldn't pay taxes in all the different countries they visit - they pay to the UK because that's where their base is.

questions.question: On a map, where land meets sea, is the boundary drawn at high tide or low tide? This would impact big estuary areas where huge expanses of sand emerge at low tide.

answers.answer: The high tide isn't always the same high tide - it depends on the time of year. Some low tides go much further out at certain times. What they do is take the average midpoint of the tide over the year to work out ownership. Above the midpoint is owned by whoever owns the land (council, Duchy of Cornwall etc), below that is maritime law. This is how maps work too - the boundary has to be on ownership.

questions.question: If the Queen gets to 100, does she get a telegram, and if so, who sends it? She can't send herself one, can she?

answers.answer: You're right, nobody sends her a telegram because she is the Queen - she's the person that sends telegrams to others when they reach 100. It's a great question - nobody sends her one.

questions.question: Can you melt a diamond?

answers.answer: You cannot melt a diamond in the strictest sense. Diamond is carbon bonded to four other carbons - there are no individual diamond molecules. If you heat it to several thousand degrees, you'll liberate all the carbon and turn it into charcoal. You can burn diamonds (oxidize them) in liquid oxygen, but you cannot melt them. There is no such thing as liquid diamond.
You can break it down but not actually melt a diamond in the strict sense of turning from solid to liquid.

questions.question: Is there a finite/statutory limit on the number of dimples you can have on a golf ball?

answers.answer: There are 376 dimples on a golf ball. She read this from a fact sheet that came with golf balls she bought for her dad.
The maximum number is between 300 and 500 dimples. This came from his brother-in-law who is a greenkeeper.

questions.question: Why is a priest's neckwear called a dog collar?
Why is there a hole in a bagel?

answers.answer: Bagels are boiled before they're baked (in hot fat, not actually boiling). The hole serves several purposes: it allows maximum surface area for the crust, makes them chewier, helps them stay fresh longer than a bap or barm cake, and allows the boiling process to work properly through the center. The hole also helps with cooking the middle of the bagel. It's not just about looking like a donut.

questions.question: How important do you have to be to be assassinated instead of murdered?

answers.answer: Three elements must be present for it to be an assassination: First, the victim must be someone famous or of some notoriety. Second, the perpetrator must be politically or ideologically opposed to the victim (like a revolutionary or Republican). Third, there must be a specific political or gangland motive. If those elements are present, it's assassination; otherwise it's murder.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'Oh my giddy aunt'?

answers.answer: 'Giddy' comes from being possessed by God. It was used as a way to swear without swearing (like 'OMG'). When people didn't want to say 'Oh my God,' they said 'Oh my giddy' instead. The 'aunt' was added at the beginning of the century.

questions.question: Why do crabs walk sideways?

answers.answer: It's all to do with the joints in their legs. The joints can only move in one direction, and because the legs are on the sides of the crab, they can only move in a sideways motion. This is evolutionarily beneficial for scurrying around the sea floor and hopping off the beach.

questions.question: What time is it in space? What time do they work on the space station?

answers.answer: He learned the answer from watching Stargazers where Brian Cox and Derek Green discussed what time the space station uses.

questions.question: Do celebrities have two different signatures - one for autographs and one for official documents?

answers.answer: He used to do two different signatures when he was on Big Brother - one for fans and one for official documents. He thought if he ever had to give a signature, he could differentiate between them. However, he notes that autographs have been replaced by selfies - he hasn't given an autograph since 2004.

questions.question: Why am I so happy? (What is the origin of the phrase 'happy as Larry'?)

answers.answer: It was a boxer named Larry Foley from Australia or New Zealand from the 1890s. He won a fight and the headline the next day was 'Happy as Larry'.

questions.question: If you put a wooden spoon across boiling pasta, the water will never overflow the pot. Why is that?

answers.answer: The bubbles of the water hit the spoon and they condense and turn back into water. The spoon pops all the bubbles so they can't build up into a foam. Wooden spoons don't conduct heat as quickly as metal spoons, which is why you use a wooden one.

questions.question: What does horsepower mean? Does it mean the car has the equivalent strength of being towed by 270 horses? Are there other vehicles labeled with horsepower?

answers.answer: James Watt invented steam engines and needed to compare them to something people understood. He worked out what effort a draft horse could supply to pull a certain amount of weight over a certain distance in a minute, then said his engines could do more than that.
746 watts equals one horsepower.

questions.question: Why are there warm pockets of water in the sea at Westgate in Kent, near Margate?

answers.answer: They're called thermoclines. The sun warms up the surface water and during movement, pockets of warm water form. It can also work in reverse with cold water from the bottom. Water is not homogenous - it's lots of different pockets.

questions.question: Who first put a candle on a cake and called it a birthday cake?
Do animals have rhythm? My little girl asked if the cat she was playing with could dance to music.

answers.answer: Animals do have rhythm. Snakes dance to the movement of the flute from snake charmers.
Snake charmers tap their feet, which is why the snake moves. Cockatiels dance to heavy metal on Facebook and there's a great film of a nodding cat - they have rhythm.

questions.question: When does a pond become a lake? At what size does a puddle become a pond?

answers.answer: A pond occurs naturally because of the water table in an area - dig a hole and it fills up naturally. A lake is fed by a stream - it has an inlet, the body of water, and an outlet. A reservoir is a man-made lake.

questions.question: Why do we kiss underneath the mistletoe?

answers.answer: It has nothing to do with Christian festivals - it's a hangover from pagan times with fertility relevance.
Mistletoe is a parasite in a tree - it blooms when the rest of the tree doesn't. It's to do with fertility and winter.

questions.question: Why do we call the zip at the front of trousers the 'flies'?
What's the difference between a robbery and a heist? (Great Train Robbery vs Hatton Garden Heist)

answers.answer: A heist is a big robbery undertaken by a gang with planning. The Great Train Robbery was a heist, as was Hatton Garden. The planning aspect is key.

Robbery is theft with violence or threat of violence. The Great Train Robbery was a robbery because they hit the driver. Hatton Garden involved no violence, so it couldn't be a robbery - it must be a burglary.

questions.answer: Why do we call it the flies?

answers.answer: It's actually Cockney rhyming slang - 'fly tip' rhymes with 'zip'.

questions.question: If you speak in a foreign language and you have a stutter in English, will you stutter in the foreign language?

answers.answer: It depends on the trigger factors for the stammer. Some people stutter more when speaking quickly, so in a foreign language where you're naturally slowing down and thinking things through, it might be less noticeable. But others have issues around confidence and anxiety finding the right words, which would be even more challenging in a foreign language. There's no set pattern - it's different for each person.

questions.question: Red sky at night, shepherd's delight. Red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning. Why does that always seem to work? What's the science behind it?

answers.answer: It's to do with where the sun sets and where weather fronts come from to the UK. Weather fronts approach the UK from the west and the sun also sets in the west. If the sun's setting and it's obscured by cloud which is approaching, you won't get a red sky at night. If there's no cloud obscuring the sun as it sets in the west, it means there isn't a weather front on its way and we should have nice weather in the morning. From a shepherd's point of view, rain is the worst thing because you get soggy sheep.

questions.question: Does it make a difference to the efficiency of the body at what time you sleep? If you have an hour's nap during the day, that seems to be more efficient because you can stay up a lot later at night. If he naps for half an hour at two o'clock, that would cancel out about three hours at night.

answers.answer: It's all to do with rapid eye movement (REM), which is the period of sleep when you dream and the most refreshing bit. You go into REM very shortly after you fall asleep and generally have REM just before you naturally awake, which is why you remember dreams first thing in the morning. Scientists in America in the 70s tested people by waking them up as soon as they went into REM sleep - they got 8-9-10 hours sleep but none of it was REM sleep, and they were like victims of sleep deprivation. A nap is more refreshing because you reach REM quickly. The ideal nap is between 20 minutes and 2 hours - anything in between can be more disturbing than nothing at all.

questions.question: When books are published, why are they first published as hardbacks and then later published as paperbacks?

answers.answer: It's all about the Benjamins. The idea is that the original market of people who have to have it the minute it comes out will pay £15. They won't wait seven months and then pay £6. So you might as well fill your boots with that market and then go after everybody else. Hardbacks are more costly to produce but the markup is much bigger than on a paperback.

questions.question: Has anyone paid with an arm and a leg? It must have a proper origin, that, mustn't it?

answers.answer: Pirates were paid compensation if they lost limbs and eyes and ears and noses. I think you got paid more for an arm than a leg.

It's to do with portrait painters. A lot of portraits used to be done from the side profile because it was cheaper to just paint one limb on either side. If you did a full-on frontal portrait, it would cost more - it would cost an arm and a leg more.

The phrase is not recorded until about the 19th century. The French have an identical phrase - ça coûte les yeux de la tête (costs the eyes out of your head) - which has nothing to do with portrait painters or pirates. So it literally just means it costs an awful lot.

questions.question: Why are number plates white at the front and yellow at the back, as opposed to other number places?

answers.answer: It's so that you can tell at distance or during times of reduced visibility whether or not you're approaching the front of the car or the back of the car, which provides a fairly reliable guide to whether the car is coming towards you or going away from you.

You're not allowed a white light on the back of a vehicle (with exception to reverse lights). A white number plate can be dazzling due to the rear number plates. The front one is white because you've got white lights to the front of the vehicle. They're also reflective.

questions.question: Why does February only have 28 days when all the other months have 31 or 30? Why are July and August different from all the other months?

answers.answer: There were originally only 10 months in the Roman calendar. You can trace the names back by numbers - decem for 10 (December), novem for 9 (November), octo for 8 (October). July and August stick out because two emperors, Julius and Augustus, wanted to be remembered forever, so they had months named after them. They both stole a day off February and stuck it on July and August to make their months longer than the others.

questions.question: How come the hairs on your head grow a lot longer than your eyebrows, but they're on the same part of your body and only a few inches different? How come your eyebrows don't grow as long as your hair?
Why, when you're on an aeroplane, during take-off, do the blinds have to be up?

answers.answer: The worst thing that could happen to an aeroplane during take-off is an engine fire or explosion. If the engine catches fire, you need to know about it so the pilot can shut it down. The reason you have the door blinds open is so before you open the door to evacuate, you can check outside for hazards like a burning engine. The cabin blinds don't have to be up - passengers can do what they want with those.

You don't actually have to have the blinds up on the doors - only on the doors if you're sitting in the first row. Throughout the cabin, passengers can do what they want. The only reason you have to have the blinds on the doors open is if there is an aborted take-off and you have to evacuate - you need to check outside for hazards before opening the door. It has nothing to do with engines catching fire on the cabin blinds, but it does relate to the door blinds because you wouldn't open the door and evacuate people if an engine was on fire.

questions.question: We went to Stonehenge and saw the missing stones - where are all the missing stones? The top bits are missing. Did they not finish it?

answers.answer: Stonehenge is old - if you lived in that part of the world and needed a whopping great big stone, you'd go to the weird circle of stones around the corner and take some. Once you eliminate the impossible, whatever you are left with, however improbable, must be the truth. There's probably a corner of a barn somewhere with a Stonehenge stone in it, or a cottage built on a foundation made of Stonehenge stone.
It's about people robbing the stones. From every session of Time Team, they're always nicking Stonehenge stones - those pesky peasants from the Middle Ages. It was often the Romans.

questions.question: Where's a bird? We have seabirds and birds that migrate thousands of miles over oceans. When it's night time, where do they go? What do they do? They don't sit on a wave and have a float around. There's no nest out there.

answers.answer: I can only do one seabird at a time. Either they find somewhere to perch or they sleep on the sea.

Some migrating seabirds like geese will fly in skeins (like the tip of an arrow formation), which gives them a lift from the bird in front, so they take it in turns and can catnap. Other birds like migrating swifts will fly very, very high and then have brief sleep periods while they drop, then wake and fly up again. Swifts never land.

questions.question: When banks and bankers get fined millions of pounds, who gets it? And when boats drop oil on the coast and get fined billions of pounds, does that go to the Treasury as well?

answers.answer: Treasury gets all the fines from banks. In this country, if a bank does something wrong, the money goes to the Treasury, goes to the government.

questions.question: How does our brain decide what memories to keep? Some of my most vivid memories are trivial little things like being chased around the playground, but I can't really remember my eldest daughter being born.

answers.answer: The more you think about something, the more you remember it. The analogy is that it's like a pathway. If you walk down a path once or twice, you leave a small path. If you go down hundreds of times, it becomes a very established path and eventually a road. Even though some memories are insignificant, we've thought about them many times in our life, which establishes them as strong. Whereas things that may emotionally appear more significant, like your wedding day, you haven't thought about the specific aspects of it because you were so busy.

I'll explain shivering - we shiver because we're trying to retain body core temperature. If it's an emotional response, which is adrenaline, fight or flight. For example, if you go to the loo and do a wee, you'll shiver afterwards because you're lowering your body core temperature. A shiver is a physiological response to either an emotional or physical action linked to core temperature. Nothing to do with electricity. If you get a fright, it will increase adrenaline because you're going into fight or flight, and your body needs to maintain temperature.

questions.question: How do you get the gas into a ping-pong ball? It's a very pressurized ball and it smells when it's punctured.

answers.answer: The ping pong ball is made in two sides, pushed together and electronically sealed with heat. The actual smell is not a gas - it's the smell from the burning of the inside, it stays on the inside of the ball. It's just air inside. The bounce you get is from the stress on the ball because it's actually plastic.

The ball is made of two plastic communion wafers heated, formed into hemispheres, then glue heat welded together. They get tossed in grainy powder which sticks to the outside giving the ball grip. There's no gas - it's just air.

questions.question: I used to work at a pub called The Red Lion and I noticed there are loads and loads of Red Lions in the UK. Why is it called The Red Lion? What's the origins? Why not The Red Sheep?

answers.answer: The Red Lion is linked to the Crusades and Richard the Lionheart. Pub signs go back to the days before we could all read and write. The lion is more eye-catching than a sheep, and you'd know you'd found The Red Lion because there would be a lion there painted red.

The answer you gave earlier is complete bunkum. How would an illiterate person who couldn't read know what a lion was? The real answer is that pubs are called The Red Lion because it's recognisable to people going there in the days before literacy was widespread. There's dispute over whether it's Richard the Lionheart or James I of England, James VI of Scotland, but that's the real answer.

questions.question: Why does the moon affect things like your menstrual cycle and your dreams?

How is it that ladybirds can walk straight out of spider's webs when flies definitely can't? I saw two ladybirds walking on my kitchen window going into webs and walking straight out again. One flew into a hanging web and flew straight out.

answers.answer: A ladybird is a type of beetle and they've got a shell that's quite smooth. If you look at flies and bumblebees under a microscope, they have tiny tiny hairs. When a fly goes into a spider's web, it gets stuck because of all its little appendages. But ladybirds are smooth, so nothing's going to stick to the web.

questions.question: What's the meaning of when you get a chill down your spine and someone says 'someone just walked over my grave'? Why would that be a suitable response to a shivery feeling?

answers.answer: We shiver because we're trying to retain body core temperature. If it's an emotional response, which is adrenaline, fight or flight. If you get a fright, you'll shiver. The phrase 'someone's just walked over my grave' is just a way of describing the shiver - if you're going in a grave, you'd be cold and emotional.

questions.question: Why do the planets in our solar system rotate and what causes them to rotate? Why do some things not rotate like our moon? Why do we spin?

answers.answer: When the solar system forms, all the gas formed from a nebula - a cloud. This cloud began to contract at the centre and all the gas and dust began to spiral in towards it like a whirlpool. As the dust and gas and metal accretes, forming planets, these planets rotate at different velocities. The sun does rotate but because it's not a solid object, it rotates at different velocities depending on where you are on the surface. All the ones in the solar system rotate. They continue to spin because of inertia. They're slowing down - the Earth is slowing down partly because of the drag of the Moon. In a billion years' time, an Earth day will be about 40 hours long. Venus rotates in the other direction, west to east, and a Venusian day is 222 Earth days.

Correcting himself - of course the moon rotates! We only ever see the same side of the moon because we're rotating as well. If the moon wasn't rotating, we'd see all different sides of it. The original question was why do some heavenly bodies rotate and others don't - although I can't think of any that don't.

questions.question: December should actually be the 10th month, September should be the 7th, October the 8th, November the 9th. They are all shifted too long. Which two months have been inserted and why?

answers.answer: July is named after Julius Caesar - he named a month after himself. And August is named after Augustus Caesar. The two months were inserted by Roman emperors in honour of themselves.

questions.question: In the French language, some things are masculine and some things are feminine. Why do they have masculine and feminine in French? For example, a masculine gate and a feminine fence.

answers.answer: Before the French Revolution, women were the property of their husbands and had no rights. But after the Egalites Fraternite set-up came along, they decided to have equal everything, including the same personal rights and the same personage in language.
It's because it's the Latin language. Every Latin language has masculine and feminine. It's for Latin. Also if you're Latin, you have to know what you're saying - you have masculine and feminine.

French, Spanish and Italian are all derived mainly from Latin, but also from ancient Greek. Ancient Greek had masculine, feminine and neuter. German still has it. English is the anomaly - we don't have genders. Romance languages having genders is completely normal.

questions.question: How do they work out that there is seven dog years to one human year?

answers.answer: Dogs live roughly a seventh of how long humans do. Once you've eliminated the impossible, however improbable, must be the truth. Someone realized dogs lived about a seventh of how long humans lived and that's where the seven dog years idea came from. But there might be a more comprehensive answer.

Different species of dogs have different lifespans. Big dogs actually deteriorate faster than small dogs. The seven years is a broad average but there's a study showing it's actually species-dependent.

questions.question: How do they get fizzy drinks into cans? My son asked me this and I didn't know the answer.

answers.answer: The bottom section is filled first and then the top is crimped on. This is all done at very high speed, about 1500 per minute. The drink goes into the bottom container that has a lip and the lid is crimped on at high speed. The metal folds over the lid to make a hermetic seal. The lid with the ring pull is preformed before being put on.

Qualifications: I have an invention designed to go down a filling line, but the bottom section isn't aluminium, it's plastic. It's called the Bevy Pack. Designed for the events market where you have to serve in paper or plastic cups. You twist the top off instead of a ring pull. Takes about two seconds to serve instead of 14.

questions.question: What is happening when you bash your funny bone? Why do funny bones work? Why does it cause that tingling sensation?

answers.answer: When you hit that small area on your elbow, you're hitting the ulnar nerve against the end of the humerus, hence the name funny bone. It's the ulnar nerve that supplies feeling to the little finger and the ring finger, and that's where you get the funny pins and needles feeling.
Qualifications: I'm a nurse. I phoned in a couple of weeks ago about the elbow - the question was what's the inside of the elbow called.

questions.question: How do you navigate in space? I've watched lots of sci-fi films and wondered how on earth you navigate.

answers.answer: NASA especially have a deep space network. They ping a transmitting signal to a probe from the spaceship. The probe picks it up and pings the signal back to Earth. Then people on the ground calculate speed, distance over time, to work out how fast they're moving, what direction, the trajectory. You can't navigate without Earth. All you need is a reference point. You could pick something really far away - like another galaxy - and use that as a reference point to navigate around the local area. But that would be difficult because the signal takes such a long time to get back and forth.
Qualifications: Degree in geology.

questions.question: Given optimum conditions, can a plant like a redwood tree die of simply old age? If you provide conditions where no harm is being done to the tree, can it live forever?

answers.answer: Even if you were to feed a tree hydroponically and have it in a low gravity situation with the perfect light set up, eventually it will die because of cell replication. Cells can only replicate a certain amount of times. There's a chemical attached to the ends of each strand of DNA. On a DNA level, eventually cell replication will cease.
Qualifications: I've grown things with those kind of conditions. I have experience with growing trees.
Not entirely happy with the answer.

questions.question: Why do male seahorses carry the babies and give birth instead of the female?

answers.answer: Nobody knows why from an academically qualified perspective. I'll give a round of applause for someone who confirms that nobody knows why.

The male seahorse doesn't actually give birth or lay eggs. The female produces the eggs. He takes them off the female and protects them from predation for a period until they hatch, and then he just releases them.
Nobody knows the 'why' - why is it the male that does it rather than the female? Don't know, don't need to know, nobody knows.

questions.question: When a body dies, rigor mortis sets in after a few hours and everything stiffens up. How do we get juicy, soft chicken breasts, lamb legs and beef within hours? How is meat not affected by rigor mortis?

answers.answer: Possibly because we drain the blood from the carcasses so they don't stiffen up? But do we drain all the blood? If I cook a rare piece of steak, it still has blood in it.

The basic premise is that you have two chemicals in your body in muscles - one called actin and one called myosin. When you activate a muscle, they form a breakable bond and pull each other along like a rower rowing through a river. That's what makes muscles contract. You have an enzyme which breaks that bond down and it continually keeps reforming. When you die, that enzyme is no longer produced, so the bond goes into continuous mode. It sticks and becomes firm. Then after a period of decomposition, that bond begins to break down and you loosen back up again. So the stuff we eat did go through rigor mortis and then it just softened up again. You kill a cow and within half an hour to an hour it'll be stiff as a board.
Qualifications: BSc in Human Biology.

questions.question: Why is Mystery Hour always on a Thursday? Weekend would make more sense because I don't have time to think about things during weekdays.

answers.answer: I'm not on air at the weekends. We do it on a Thursday because the very first time we did it happened to be a Thursday and it went so well it stuck. That's my round of applause.

Tuesday was the Tuesday Free-for-All, Wednesday was Prime Time, Thursday was Mystery Hour, Friday was John Cushing's World of Sport. Mystery Hour is a long line of additions that eventually went by the wayside but managed to stay.
I can't believe you've just corrected me on a fact about my own programme.

questions.question: Why haven't we evolved so that giving birth is anything more than painful and complicated and excruciating? Bearing in mind we all have to do it to bring a baby into the world, shouldn't nature have made it easier?

answers.answer: The obvious answer is that the aperture is a lot smaller than that which needs to pass through it. You need a lot of nerves in that area for various reasons. The ultimate answer is because people still want to do it even though it hurts. The only circumstances in which evolution plays a role in gene replication is when the gene's replication increases the likelihood of further replication.

Human birth is actually very painful because our head size has increased whereas the gap in the pelvic girdle hasn't - which is why we've had to opt for C-sections. There's an evolutionary advantage to having a bigger brain so that increases the likelihood of passing on genes. The notion that evolution would do this and do that is wrong - evolution doesn't do anything. It's a process which hasn't got a strategy. It happens by chance - point mutations cause a difference which may be good or bad. Those who inherit the good difference have an advantage and procreate. The giraffes with longer necks could reach higher leaves - they didn't stretch their necks, it was just chance. Also, teeth are actually very good - enamel is the hardest natural known substance. It's only in the last 500 years since Elizabethan times that our sugar diet has caused these issues.
Qualifications: I'm the Professor of Public Understanding of Science at the University of Brighton.

questions.question: Why isn't pasteurised egg yolk cooked and hard? Why is it in liquid form?

answers.answer: Because they use really low temperatures. That's the answer.

questions.question: Why do we have orgasms?

answers.answer: The orgasm is a psychological reward for doing something necessary for the continuation of the species. The hope of getting one is what makes you pursue the act that leads to reproduction. It encourages you to have sex which keeps the species alive.

questions.question: Why are storms named after people? (for his daughter Abigail)

answers.answer: There's a list put together by the World Meteorological Organization that goes in alphabetical order.

The World Meteorological Organization started naming storms in the 1970s. Names go in alphabetical cycles every six years. Letters Q, X, Y, Z are never used. Particularly intense or historic hurricanes have their names retired and never used again (like Katrina in 2005). If there are too many storms to fit the alphabet, Greek letters are used (Alpha, Beta, Gamma, etc.)

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'the penny drops' originate from?

answers.answer: It must be from those fairground penny push machines where dropping the penny means you've won.

questions.question: What happens to radio waves? Do they go on forever?

answers.answer: Radio waves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum - same as light waves, microwaves, TV waves, UV, infrared. They differ only in frequency and wavelength but all travel at the speed of light. As you get further from the source, the intensity weakens, proportional to one over R cubed. They don't go on forever but become infinitesimally small. Some static on TVs is actually the echo of the Big Bang from 14 billion years ago.

questions.question: Where is the rest of the ox? If we eat oxtail, are there tailless oxes running around?

answers.answer: An oxtail is indeed the culinary name for the tail of cattle. A butcher will tell you that in this context, 'ox' and 'cow' are the same thing.

questions.question: Why are men hairier than women when other mammals (dogs, cats) don't show this difference between sexes?

answers.answer: The theory is that men stayed in caves while women went out hunting. Men needed fur and a pelt while women were always indoors so didn't need as much hair. (This was James's unscientific theory)

It's to do with testosterone. But the deeper theory is natural selection - men preferred women who appeared younger (less hairy), so genes for less body hair in women got passed on more frequently over generations. Testosterone at the molecular level determines hairiness.

questions.question: Why are some hay bales round and some square? Is there a reason or just the machinery they use?

answers.answer: Round bales are made by cheaper machinery. Square/rectangular bales cost more but stack better and save more space because you don't get gaps between them. The type depends on what machinery farmers have and whether they need to store them efficiently in barns.

questions.question: Why do migrating birds fly in V formation?

answers.answer: It's aerodynamics - like cyclists. The slipstream behind the lead bird means less energy is needed to fly. They take turns being the leader and the one in back conserves energy.

The birds are actually sleeping while flying - it's called unihemispherical sleep, where half the brain is asleep. The leader does all the work while the others rest. This is how they can maintain the formation while sleeping.

questions.question: Why is sadness called 'the blues' and the music called 'the blues'? Why not 'black mood' or 'grey mood'?

answers.answer: The phrase 'blue devils' comes to mind - 19th century expression. (James was unsure but mentioned this as the extent of his knowledge)

questions.answer: Origin of 'the penny drops'

answers.answer: Press gangs in pubs would get someone drunk and drop a penny in their drink. When the penny dropped, they realized they'd been signed up for the Navy. Old pubs have glass-bottom tankards so you could see if a penny had landed. Taking the king's shilling was the signing of the contract. This is also where 'hoodwinked' comes from - throwing something over someone's head to take them aboard.

questions.answer: Challenge to William's answer about 'the penny drops'

answers.answer: William was right about press gangs and glass-bottom tankards, but it couldn't have been a penny - it was the King's shilling. The phrase 'taken for a mug' is linked to seeing the shilling land in the glass, but not 'penny drops'.

questions.answer: Origin of 'the penny drops'

answers.answer: A guide in Cheddar caves told him that early explorers wedged pennies in cave fish. If there was movement in the cave, the penny would drop and warn them to leave. He heard this on a family visit.

questions.answer: Origin of 'the penny drops'

answers.answer: In Victorian times, on piers and arcades, the most popular slot machine was 'What the Butler Saw.' When you put your penny in, the penny drops and all is revealed - you get your result. That's where the phrase comes from - when the penny drops, you get what you're paying for.

questions.answer: Why is it called 'the blues'?

answers.answer: Picasso went through different painting phases. His girlfriend or wife passed away, he got upset, and everything he painted was in blue tones - that's where the term originates from, the blues period.

questions.question: What are the little gravestones visible from the top deck of the 148 bus travelling from Marble Arch past Lancaster Gate near Hyde Park?

answers.answer: It's the Pet Cemetery of Hyde Park. Started in 1881 by accident when the lodgekeeper Mr. Winbridge let someone bury a pet there. There are about 300 graves. The little building at the exit to Hyde Park has someone who lives there who will show you around their garden. There's also a royal connection - a dog belonging to Prince George's wife Louisa Fairbrother is buried there.

questions.question: Why is it actually called a honeymoon?

answers.answer: If you go back to pre-Norman times, the groom would receive an exemption from work for the duration of an entire lunar cycle. Because honey is the only foodstuff known to man that doesn't decay, it has historically been a great sign of longevity and commitment. You would give honey to a newly married couple because it never rots (they found some in Tutankhamen's tomb that was still edible). Ergo, honeymoon - it's about the break from work you got and the fact that honey never rots.

questions.question: Do dogs have the same blood as humans? If not, do they have different blood groups? Could you get a transfusion from a dog?

answers.answer: No, dog blood is not the same as human blood. And yes, dogs have different blood groups (just like humans do). You can't top up your dog with your own blood. The reason you know this is because pet blood banks exist - when operating on a dog, like when Paul's cat had a hernia operation that took six or seven hours, you need blood products.

Any dog can give blood to any other dog because they all originate from one species, the wolf. All dog blood is compatible - there's no A, B, O system like in humans. The blood groups you might hear about in dogs work differently than in humans.

questions.question: Where does the @ symbol come from? Why that symbol in particular?

answers.answer: The correct term is 'commercial A'. It was used in the printing industry when producing ledgers. If you had five scarves at a pound, you would itemize: five scarves, then the commercial A, then one pound, then you'd go across with leaders to show the total. It tracks back to the 16th or 17th century. Steve knew this as a hot metal compositor and proofreader.

It stems from a misunderstanding of the word 'at'. It means 'each', not a position of a website or person online. It comes from Latin where 'at' means 'each'. It was used by accountants (and probably monks) as shorthand because writing with quill pens was difficult. So originally it meant 'at each', not 'at' in the sense of a place.

questions.question: Why do they roll out the red carpet for premieres? What's so significant about the red?

answers.answer: The colour purple is actually red. It was originally red, made from crushing Murex shells by the Phoenicians, and was called 'the colour of kings'. The Romans when they said they wore purple, it was actually red. That's why the Pope wears red shoes and red socks - because actual purple is red.
In ancient times, purple was the colour of gods and everyone special. The first mention was in the Agamemnon (a Greek tragedy) where Clytemnestra was preparing Agamemnon's arrival.

questions.question: Why is Bubble and Squeak called Bubble and Squeak?

answers.answer: It's potatoes and cabbage and maybe a bit of bacon if you're rich. It bubbles and squeaks when you cook it. It really is that simple.
Confirmed James was right - it's the noise it makes while you're cooking. You are frying carbohydrates essentially, and maybe some bacon and Brussels sprouts.

questions.question: Why don't dolphins get the bends? They dive deep and surface to breathe, why don't they get the bends like divers?

answers.caller: Professor Hal (Professor of the Public Understanding of Science, University of Brighton)
answers.answer: The reason you get the bends is: as you go deeper in water, pressure increases and nitrogen dissolves in your blood plasma. The deeper you go, the more nitrogen dissolves. If you come up too quickly, it undissolves (like when you open a champagne bottle or cola bottle) and appears in your brain, heart, and joints causing the bends. Because you're breathing all the time, more and more nitrogen dissolves. Dolphins hold their breath - they've only got one breath's worth of nitrogen dissolving in their plasma, so they can go up and down as they please.

questions.question: How do they get champagne corks into a bottle? The pressure would make it difficult to shove in.

answers.answer: There are two processes involved. At the end of the process, they reopen the bottle, pour some out, put some stuff in, and put the cork back on. The pressure builds up inside the bottle after it's been corked, so you just shove it in - that's what you use the cage for.

It's a two-stage process developed by Madame Tico (not Dom Perignon). When wine is being produced, fermentation produces carbon dioxide. In normal wine production that is released, but for champagne it's fermented in the bottle capped with no cork, so CO2 has nowhere to go and creates bubbles, but there's also sediment. They tip it upside down, freeze the head so the sediment freezes into an ice cube, take the top off (there's a burst of champagne that draws out the sediment), put in more wine and yeast, then put the cork in with the metal cage. Damien saw this in the champagne cellars in France.

questions.question: What is a juke and why is it called a jukebox?

answers.caller: Brian (caller, location unclear - phone line cut off)
answers.answer: It was about plantations in America and the slaves working on them at the end of the slave trade. They used to play a lot of blues music and had entertainment.

'Juke' was an abbreviation for bordello (a lady's working house). It was a place where they started playing music inside. When they made the actual instruments in the 1930s and 1940s, they had them in bars and brothels, and it just took on the name jukebox.

It's a juke joint - which doesn't have to be a brothel. It was just an informal, possibly not properly regulated African-American music place. It started on plantations where slaves were, and the music that became was the blues. So both Brian and Joseph are right - it did originate in that context.

questions.question: Why are mountain lion babies called kittens when lion and tiger babies are called cubs?

answers.answer: The mountain lion is not actually a lion. It's the largest of the cat family (felines), sometimes called a cougar or puma. Lions and tigers are of the genus Panthera, but the mountain lion is of the genus Felis. Different genera get called different things.

questions.question: Why do we put cold water in a kettle when it probably makes more sense to put hot water in?

answers.answer: When you had a hot water tank in the loft (old houses), the hot water tank wouldn't be clean in the same way a cold water tank would be. The hot water tank feeds the immersion heater and water sits in the loft for a month or however long since you last had a bath. The cold water came in fresh. Now with combi boilers, water comes out of the same combi boiler, so you can put hot water straight in the kettle, it takes less time to boil, and you save money. If you have an old tank system, you should still use cold water.

questions.question: Why can't I put 'single' on official forms after divorce? Why must I put 'divorced'?

answers.answer: It's probably to alert whoever you're filling the form in for to the possibility that you might have other financial responsibilities that you wouldn't have if you were single.

As a widow receiving a widow's pension with children, you have to put widow because it's a legal requirement. It highlights the possibility of financial and legal responsibilities that do not apply to single people, like maintenance payments for ex-spouses.

questions.question: Why can humans only access certain parts of their brain?

answers.answer: We actually do use all of our brain. The idea that we only use 10-16% at once is about energy - we can't send enough sugar/power to all parts of the brain simultaneously, which is why multitasking is physically impossible.

questions.question: What is the inside of the elbow called?

answers.answer: The antecubital fossa (A-N-T-E-C-U-B-I-T-A-L F-O-S-S-A).
The crook of your arm/elbow.

questions.question: Why are the wheels beneath a carriage of a train called 'bogeys'?
Is there a specific number/threshold for when an animal becomes officially endangered?

answers.answer: An animal is endangered at the point when they are dying off quicker than they are reproducing.

questions.question: Why is Wales not called 'Walesland'? And why is Welsh not called 'Welshish' (like English, Scottish, Irish)?

answers.answer: When the Anglo-Saxons invaded, they weren't a united people, and England was divided into kingdoms. Not all kingdoms had 'land' in the name. The Welsh were called 'Wealh' or 'Walas' (foreigners in Anglo-Saxon), which evolved into 'Wales'. The Welsh themselves call themselves 'Cymru' meaning comrades. 'Welsh' is purely the Anglo-Saxon word we gave them. Cornwall is also from the same origin - Corn-walas meaning Welsh of the peninsula.

questions.question: How do our ears locate sound if it's not coming from left or right (e.g., directly in front or behind)?

answers.answer: The ear itself - the pinna (outer ear) has cartilage that funnels sound into the ear canal. The brain learns differences in tone and compares sounds between the two ears in about three thousandths of a second. For sounds directly in front, both ears hear at the same time. The brain uses expected volume and how sound is funnelled to distinguish front from back. Mistakes are possible but rare.

questions.question: Why are there so many fur shops on Rhodes (a hot Greek island)?

answers.answer: Rhodes is part of the Dodecanese islands. It's about targeting tourists, particularly cruise ship passengers. The shops proliferate along tourist routes like Lindos Road. This also explains the jewelry shops on Santorini.

As someone who lived in Crete for five years and knows Greeks with these shops - they purely target Russians on holiday because fur coats are cheaper in Greece than in Russia. The shops even employ attractive young Russian girls.

questions.question: How long exactly is a generation?

answers.answer: A generation is the distance between being born and becoming a parent - roughly 25 years in modern society. When life expectancy was shorter and people had families younger, it was closer to 20 years. Generations are now getting longer because the gap between being born and becoming a parent is the biggest it's ever been in human history.

questions.question: Why are apples and pears sold in plastic bags at the supermarket, but oranges and lemons are sold in netted bags?

answers.answer: Apples and pears are in plastic bags because you eat the skin. Oranges and lemons are in netting because you don't eat the skin, so handling the netting won't affect the fruit.

questions.question: Why do fingers and toes go wrinkly in the bath but not other parts of the body?

answers.answer: It's an evolutionary thing so we can have more grip underwater. Also, someone told me babies can grip their parents' hair in water.

questions.question: What happens to the DNA in donor blood during a blood transfusion? If you take a pint of someone's blood and put it in me, does it become absorbed or maintain its original DNA?

answers.answer: Red blood cells don't contain DNA. White blood cells do, but it's never going to be a big enough proportion to cause problems.

answers.caller: Professor Hal (Professor of Public Understanding of Science, University of Brighton)
answers.answer: Red blood cells don't have nuclei and can't reproduce themselves - that's why they're made in the bone marrow. They last about 120 days. Rejection is caused by proteins on the outside of cells, not DNA on the inside. You'd find donor DNA from white blood cells for about 120 days until everything is replaced.

questions.question: How do spiders build initial webs spanning 5 feet between two wooden frames with nothing above them to swing from?

answers.answer: Spiders wait for the wind to start blowing, then let the breeze carry them over to the other side, and then start spinning the web.

Spiders let a thread out with glue on the end and let the breeze take that gossamer thread across to the desired location. They sit downwind and once that single thread is attached, they crawl across it and start building the web.

questions.question: Why do African elephants have bigger ears than Asian elephants?

answers.answer: It'll be something to do with evolution, but I can't think of what the evolutionary answer might be.

African elephants live in open savannah with lots of heat. They keep cool by wafting their ears - there's a cobweb of veins running through them that cools the blood and keeps the body cool through heat dissipation. Asian elephants are mostly in shade under trees.

questions.question: Why is the score over the line in rugby known as a 'try'?

answers.answer: Based on the legend of Webb Ellis at Rugby School. He was playing football, picked up the ball and ran down the pitch, plonked it over the goal line. He asked the teacher if he'd scored and was told no, but he could have a try at kicking a goal. So by carrying the ball over the line, he earned the right to have a try at the conversion.

questions.question: Is it theoretically possible to generate electricity using electric eels? Could a family power their home with a pond of electric eels?

answers.caller: Professor Martin Smith (Professor of Robotics, University of Middlesex)
answers.answer: You could harness it, but it would be difficult. Eels produce hundreds of pulses per second, very short pulses at hundreds of volts. Converting to 240V AC would involve pretty grim power loss. They don't produce much power. You could hook it to a light bulb, but you'd probably need to frighten the eel for an hour to get half a minute of light.

questions.question: Where did the similarity between English 'nan' for grandmother and Bengali 'nani' for maternal grandmother come from? Did we get it off you or did you get it off us?
When TV competitions say you can win £50,000 in cash, can you insist they pay you in actual banknotes and coins?

answers.answer: They say 'cash' because it's cash as opposed to credit. But also because competitions are usually sponsored by manufacturers - if it didn't say cash, they could give you £50,000 worth of their product. So they say cash to make clear it's real money and not Corn Flakes or Pringles.

questions.question: Why is a ship's figurehead called an Aunt Sally?

answers.answer: Aunt Sally was from a fairground, and that's what the figurehead was called - there was a connection to the game.

questions.question: What condiment goes specifically with chicken? Beef has horseradish, pork has apple, duck has orange, lamb has mint, turkey has cranberry - but what's the chicken equivalent?

answers.answer: Bread sauce goes with chicken, especially white poultry.
Bread sauce - but you can't buy that in a jar in Tesco's, you'd have to make it.
Cranberry sauce with chicken works well - I've served it to people and they liked it.

questions.question: Why is a piece of turf called a sod?

answers.answer: Kidderminster Harriers pies are so expensive because they weigh about a pound - it's a huge portion.
Sod comes from Middle Germanic 'soda' meaning a clump of earth or turf.

questions.question: Where do honeybees go in the winter? There are no flowers, so how do they survive and what happens?

answers.answer: They hibernate. My parents had a bees nest in their lawn and they've gone - they're hibernating.

questions.question: Can someone recommend a good shop in London where I can take my teddy bear and get it valued?

answers.answer: There's a dolls hospital and teddy bear hospital in Hammersmith.
There's a fantastic old shop called Asquith in Henley that's been there for centuries. They specialize in teddy bears, including antique and vintage ones worth thousands of pounds.

questions.question: How high can an ant fall from before getting hurt?

answers.answer: Ants can fall from anywhere - even out of the space shuttle - and not hurt themselves. They have a very low terminal velocity due to their small mass and buoyancy. They reach terminal velocity so quickly that they won't build up enough kinetic energy to cause damage. They also have a robust exoskeleton with bones on the outside. The ant could have fallen off a ten-story house and landed unscathed.

questions.question: Why are guide dogs almost exclusively Labradors?

answers.answer: Labradors have the best combination of attributes - best at learning, best size, best temperament. You could train any dog to be a guide dog but they wouldn't be as good at it.
Labradors are genetically fairly robust, whereas most other large dogs have genetic defaults - for example, Alsatians have clicky hips.

questions.question: Why does the poodle part of the name always come first when naming poodle mixed breeds?
What is the origin of the word 'nickname'?

answers.answer: The word comes from Anglo-Saxon times when people didn't have surnames. They introduced an additional name to make people stand out more - like 'Stubbly Chin' or 'Red Beard'. In Anglo-Saxon, that was called an 'Eek name' (spelled E-E-K). As English evolved, it turned into 'Neek name' and eventually 'nickname'. For example, Ethelred the Unready would have had 'the Unready' as his Eek name.

questions.question: Why does ice float in water?

answers.answer: Ice is less dense than water. This is because of how hydrogen bonds work in water molecules (H2O). When water freezes, the hydrogen bonding causes a crystalline structure that actually takes up more space than liquid water, making it less dense. This is an exception to the general rule that things become more dense when they solidify.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'when pigs fly'?
Where does the phrase 'Shanks's pony' come from?

answers.answer: Shanks just means legs. So 'Shanks's pony' means your legs - it's a reference to walking as opposed to travelling by car or train. James referenced Edward Longshanks (Edward I) as a potential origin.

questions.question: How can you tell which is the front and which is the back of a pair of tights before putting them on?
Why are unidentified male bodies in America called 'John Doe' and females called 'Jane Doe' instead of just 'unidentified male/female'?
How does a helicopter fly?
Why does the planet actually move on its axis? What makes the planet tilt? Do all planets in the solar system have seasons too?

answers.answer: When the Earth formed four billion years ago, the day length was ten hours, rotating very fast and couldn't wobble much. The Moon is slowing the Earth down, lengthening the day and increasing the wobble. 450 million years ago, the day was about 21 hours, today it's 24 hours, and in a billion years it'll be 40 hours. The seasons are because the Earth wobbles more on its axis, and the British Isles move away from or toward the Sun. Yes, other planets have seasons too.

questions.question: How do they check in the specialist rounds that the questions are of equal difficulty? You can't equate a Catherine of Aragon specialist subject with a Rush specialist subject.

questions.caller: Doris (not Emma, actually from Dagenham, not Hammersmith)
questions.question: How do you know for certain there's a nuclear weapon heading towards you? How do you know if someone has actually pushed the button or if they're lying about having pushed it?

answers.answer: Land-based nuclear weapons: satellites circle the Earth, monitor heat signatures and seismic events because a rocket launch creates a mini earthquake. You could never know for absolute certain a warhead was on it, but you use intelligence. With Trident from submarines, it's harder to detect the launch. Countries pay trillions for the advantage of maybe an hour or two. Eventually the missile would be picked up by satellites or land-based air traffic control systems. You just presume there's a warhead because they've told you.

questions.question: Why do people drink tomato juice on aeroplanes when we very rarely drink it anywhere else? I work behind bars and it collects dust on shelves.

answers.answer: It's a domino effect. When one person orders tomato juice, everyone else sees the drinks cart coming and thinks 'what should I have?' - they end up ordering the same. It's also about availability - all the condiments like Worcestershire sauce are there on the plane.

questions.question: Where does the saying 'nickname' come from? And who's Nick?

answers.answer: It comes from Father Christmas - St. Nicholas. They used to call him a variation of Nicholas, some called him Nick, and it became a shortened version of someone's name, hence 'nickname'.
Through farting on someone.

questions.question: Why are numbers on a telephone keypad arranged 1-2-3 at the top and 7-8-9 at the bottom, while on a calculator it's the opposite - 7-8-9 at the top and 1-2-3 at the bottom?

answers.answer: Calculators were invented first for accountants, so lower numbers were at the bottom. Telephones came later and needed letters, so the arrangement was different. (James rejected this answer as telephones predate calculators.)
It's to do with dial phones. The one would be first on a dial phone, and nine was at the bottom so you could dial 999 in the dark. The modern keypad replicated this arrangement.

questions.question: How do things glow in the dark? He has glow-in-the-dark stars and moons on his ceiling.

answers.answer: Glow-in-the-dark things contain chemicals called phosphors. They are energized by UV light during the day, absorb all that UV light, and at night time emit that energy as visible light. It's naturally occurring - you can see it in jellyfish. When they look tired, leave the lights on to recharge them.

questions.question: What causes eyelid twitching and sometimes leg twitching when you're tired? It feels like veins flickering.

answers.answer: It's called hypocalcemic tetany. It happens with vitamin D deficiency, which is common in the UK. When you have low vitamin D and low calcium, you can get twitching all over the body.

questions.question: Why do human beings have different blood types? Is there an evolutionary reason for it?

answers.answer: Health and safety. They have a legal requirement to put the ashtray in the toilets. Even though smoking is banned, some people will still do it, and you need a safe place for them to put a cigarette out - you don't want someone trying to dispose of a burning cigarette on a flying fuel tank.

There is no particular evolutionary benefit to different blood types. It's the same reason we have different eye colours and hair colours - genetic variation. There are about 35 different blood typing systems. Someone with blood group AB is a universal recipient, and group O is a universal donor. If blood transfusions were affecting evolution, we'd all eventually end up as AB because those people would be most likely to survive and procreate.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'cut the mustard' come from?

answers.answer: Before machinery, people had to cut mustard seeds to different sizes by hand with extremely sharp knives. It was very valuable work and you had to really know what you were doing because the seeds are incredibly small and hard to cut to the right size. To 'cut the mustard' meant to know what you were doing.

questions.question: Why do planes still have ashtrays on the inside and outside of toilet doors, even though smoking is banned on planes?

answers.answer: Health and safety. Legal requirement to put the ashtray in the toilets. Even though smoking is banned, some people still do it and you need a safe place for them to put the cigarette out - you don't want someone disposing of a burning cigarette on what is effectively a flying fuel tank.

questions.question: Why does eating a grapefruit make his wife's nose run?

answers.answer: The lady is showing an allergic response similar to hay fever. When she bites into the grapefruit, chemicals hit the back of her nose and cells release histamine, making her nose run. It's the same mechanism as eyes watering when chopping onions. I used to sell antihistamines and once encountered someone in a chemist shop who was allergic to grapefruit. I told them to try antihistamines and it worked.

questions.question: Why do we learn the 11 and 12 times tables when everything else in our system is decimal and we work in tens?

answers.answer: There are many things that go higher than 10 in our culture - like a clock having 12 hours, pre-decimal currency (12 pennies in a shilling), and 12 inches in a foot. That's why we still learn the 12 times table.

questions.question: If light has no mass, why does mass bend light?

answers.answer: Light has momentum and movement. Even though it has no rest mass, it has movement. If you interrupt a beam, it goes around it or gets distorted. Space is bent, and that's why light is bent.

Einstein's general theory of relativity says that space and time are in four dimensions, and space is bent by gravity. Light thinks it's going in a straight line, but it's actually going through curved space because space itself is bent by gravity. This is gravitational lensing. Light going straight through something bent doesn't go in a straight line.

questions.question: Why is aluminium foil shiny on one side and dull on the other?

answers.answer: They start with a great big block of aluminium and roll it through a press to get it thinner and thinner. When it gets to a certain point where the rollers can't get it thin enough, they use two different rolls of foil and roll them together like a sandwich. The dull layer is the one where it's been up against the other sheet of aluminium. The shiny side is the side that was exposed.
The shiny side is to reflect heat and the non-shiny side doesn't reflect heat as much.

questions.question: Why does Royal Mail never deliver on the one day everyone's home?

answers.answer: Historically, no-one worked on the Sabbath. It was a day of religious observation. Plus, the massive majority of what they deliver only needs a letterbox, not a human to receive it. It will probably change now it's been privatised eventually.

questions.question: Why don't glasses burn people's eyes or skin around swimming pools like they can burn paper?

answers.answer: You move if you feel yourself getting hot. Your eye won't let you align precisely on the axis where it would focus enough to provide that pinpoint of heat.

Glasses don't have the focal length needed to focus the sun's rays. You'd need a relatively thick, pebbly convex lens because the focal length would be about 4 to 5 inches. Spectacle lenses are nowhere near that strong. They don't have anything like the strength that a magnifying glass has.

questions.question: Why are people with Tourette's compelled to say something shocking rather than nice things like fluffy kittens or candy floss?

answers.answer: It's not always unpleasant things - people with Tourette's can say completely random things like chocolate biscuits. Tourette's involves articulation of uncomfortable thoughts, not necessarily unpleasant ones. It's an element of the condition but not exclusive.

questions.question: How does my sat-nav know there's a traffic jam 25 miles away?

answers.answer: Mentioned cameras all over the place feeding data into sat-nav devices

questions.question: Why is a circle made up of 360 degrees? Why wouldn't it be a nicer round number like 100?
Why are knives and forks weighted at the handle instead of at the fork/blade end so they stay on the plate when picking it up?
Answer to: Why are there 360 degrees in a circle?

answers.answer: Linked 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour - said 360 degrees is relative to time. He linked it to Copernicus (incorrectly mentioned astrology, then corrected to astronomy).
His sums were wrong - 60x60x24 doesn't equal 360. Rejected his answer.

questions.question: Why are some beaches half pebbles and half sand? What caused the sea to do one half and not the other?

answers.answer: Different hardness of rocks - harder rocks remained as pebbles, softer ones eroded into sand. All sand was pebbles once, all pebbles were rocks, all rocks were cliffs.

questions.question: Answer to: How does sat-nav know about traffic jams?
