answers.answer: Traffic Master system monitors traffic flow using induction loops in roads, mobile phones detect when people stand still in certain places, cameras provide visual data. All connected systems feed into the sat-nav.

questions.question: What is the origin of 'spick and span'?
Answer to: Why are there 360 degrees in a circle?

answers.answer: The Sumerians tracked the sun using obelisks and noticed it took 360 days for the shadow to return to the right position. They used a base-60 number system (from Babylonians). 360 is highly divisible by many numbers which is practical for calculations.

questions.question: Why does the wind always die down at night even after a windy day?

answers.answer: Wind is caused by movement of air from high pressure to low pressure areas. The sun creates heat which creates differences in pressure. When the sun goes down, the source of heat is removed, pressure differences shrink, and wind dies down.

As a flying instructor: During the day, the sun creates thermal mixing of the lower atmosphere which brings faster-moving winds down to the surface. Once the sun disappears, this mixing ceases and surface winds slow down due to friction with buildings and terrain.

questions.question: Why do you go deaf when you yawn?

answers.answer: Compared ear canal to a straw - when you yawn you squeeze it shut like pinching a drinking straw, cutting off sound.

As an audiologist: When you yawn, your eustachian tube (which connects middle ear to nasopharynx and is normally closed) opens to equalize air pressure in your middle ear cavity. This change in air pressure affects hearing.

questions.question: How do I get rid of the musty odor from antique books?

answers.answer: Suggested putting books in a plastic bag with lavender oil for a month - though he acknowledged this might just add a lavender top note to the musty smell.
She sun-dries old clothes to eliminate musty/mildewy smells - UVA/UVB rays react to bacteria. Suggested it might work on books too, but acknowledged she hasn't tried it on paper books.

questions.question: Answer to: Why is cutlery weighted at the handle?

answers.answer: Knives and forks need to be fit for purpose - when cutting meat you're using the weight of your arm and hand for leverage. Also for balance - if weighted at the business end things would drop out of your hand. The handle end is heavier because there's more metal needed there compared to the thinner prongs/blades.

questions.question: Why are stamps always placed in the top right-hand corner of an envelope or postcard?
What is short about short crust pastry? Why is the short in short crust pastry?

answers.answer: Shortcrust pastry is made with fat, which used to be called shortening. The reason it used to be called shortening is because if you put fat into flour, it lubricates the flour so that the gluten don't stretch. Pastry is then short and not long, which is stretchy pastry.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'hunky dory' originate from and what does it mean?
Why do I get white flashes in front of my eyes just for a split second when I close my eyes in a dark room before nodding off to sleep?

answers.answer: It's caused by either a detachment of the retina or a detachment of the membrane that surrounds the jelly within the eye. It's better to have the detachment of the membrane around the jelly rather than a detached retina because a detached retina can cause loss of some vision. If he had a detached retina, he'd probably know about it. Best thing is to go to his local eye clinic very quickly.

questions.question: When you eat chicken you eat breast, leg, thigh. When you eat beef you have loin, rump, leg, thigh. When you eat pork you've got gammon, ham, bacon. Why don't we give parts of the pork different names? Why don't we just call it pork leg?

answers.answer: Everything you've described has been cured in some way. Bacon has been cured or salted or smoked. Ham has been cooked. Gammon is uncooked ham. It's about the treatment of the meat rather than where it's come from. You need different names because if you said 'six slices of pork' and I wanted bacon, we'd have a problem.

questions.question: Where does this money come from? Like, some nation must be doing really well that's holding all this money that's lent out. To whom is a national debt owed when a country is in debt?

answers.answer: Government bonds. It's owned by great big fund managers, great big pension funds, great big financial institutions, who are holding it for what's known as the coupon, or the interest rate that attaches to it. You buy a bond because you've got capital, and a government bond pays a guaranteed interest rate while you still owe me the capital. That's where you get your triple A's and double A ratings on sovereign debt. The Church of England has billions in pension funds and that will include national bonds. It's a nice solid investment that gives them a nice return.

questions.question: You know people have been on death row in the United States for decades. The longest post is over 30 years. Why is that? Why do people spend decades on death row once a sentence has been handed down?

My local evening news is London but very occasionally I'll get it from Worcestershire, Birmingham, and then being a kid of the 70s it's really disconcerting when sometimes it's Meridian and it's Fred Dynage. How is it that my local news varies? Is this a widespread phenomenon?

answers.answer: When she first tuned her box in, depending where you live, you may pick up two different transmitters. When the weather goes poor, it won't automatically change - she must be changing the channel. A few years ago ITV changed their regional news, grouping them together to make them more cost effective, so different transmitters can pick up news from different regions. It's impossible to do it on the same channel automatically - I think she must be slightly misled on that.

It is possible that the lady's TV occasionally picks up another regional news programme. Her neighbours will be having the same issue at the same time. If there's a technical problem in your area - most likely in the studio, or a problem with the feeds - I've even known power cuts and fires and presenters not turning up - then the next closest regional news programme will be sent to you.

questions.question: If gravity is such a powerful thing, how can little limbs or branches and leaves of plants not be pulled to the ground? Why don't delicate plants get pushed down towards earth?

answers.answer: The Earth is rotating, so it's being pulled in 360 degrees at every different moment in time.

Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces. The only reason we feel the effect of the Earth's gravity is because the Earth is huge - seven times ten to the power of 24 kilos. It takes all of that just to make you weigh 79 kilos and keep you down to the Earth. That's why something very light and delicate doesn't bow. You have to have massive, massive amount of mass to have a significant amount of gravity. Everything exerts gravitational field - you are pulling the Earth up as much as it's pulling you down.

questions.question: If I were to levitate long enough, would I land in a different spot because the Earth is spinning?
Why is the keyboard arranged the way it is? Why the QWERTY layout?

answers.answer: It was researched into the frequency of the use of letters.

It is partly to do with being more efficient to have the letters lined up using two hands. But the main reason is remember the old keyboards of the old typewriters? They had hammers. When you pressed them, the hammer would go across and hit the paper. They would just jam. The QWERTY keyboard was designed so that when you hit the hammers, they don't get stuck. They keep the keys separate from each other. They must have done some quite complicated calculations to work out the incidence of letters being next to each other on the page and making sure they were nowhere near each other on the keyboard. If you did it alphabetically, you'd have had a lot more jams.

questions.question: Do flies sleep? And if so, where?

answers.answer: Of course flies blimmin' sleep. And they sleep anywhere.

questions.question: Why do you not get the effects of carbon monoxide poisoning when you're cooking on gas?

answers.answer: Natural gas is methane, CH4. When it combusts with oxygen, you get carbon dioxide and water vapor. If you don't have enough oxygen, i.e. enough air, with it, you get carbon monoxide. So theoretically you shouldn't get any carbon monoxide from a proper burn. If it's burning properly, you won't get any carbon monoxide, which is why it's a faulty boiler that creates the problems that have been so well documented. You might get a small amount but you can have flueless gas heat which has a catalytic converter to make sure that even if there is a small amount of carbon monoxide, you get it converted to carbon dioxide.

questions.question: How did everyone years ago agree what the price of gold should be? Was the price the same around the world in Elizabethan times?

answers.answer: Gold is valuable simply because it's shiny and rare and people decided to make it valuable. It's not really that useful. So the price was never set internationally back in the day - it was set solely by how much you could sell it for. If you had a lump of gold and you hawked it around the village, that gold is worth whatever anyone is prepared to pay for it. Whoever paid X established what it was worth in that environment. On the other side of the world, someone might have been paying a fraction of X for a lump of gold. As the world became increasingly connected, the Elizabethan era was a crucial milestone, and there'd be a more international standard imposed.
You're correct on the gold. Gold is only valuable because it's shiny and rare, which means the price was never set internationally back in the day. It was just set by how much people would pay.

questions.question: Is there ever going to be a 30th of February? The year is 365.2 something days. Every four years they add another day. Sooner or later won't the calendar go off a bit?

When you build a wall and stagger the joints, when you get to the end you cut a brick down the middle and that's called a queen closure. And when you cut just a quarter off, that's called a king closure. Why do we call it queen closure and king closure?
Why are the bottoms of clouds always flat?

answers.answer: As you increase in height, temperature and pressure go down until water vapor condenses into droplets. The bottom of the cloud is where condensation occurs at a constant level across the sky. However, if it's windy, clouds won't be flat.

questions.question: Why does salt water taste so foul when salty chips taste so delicious?

answers.answer: It's the minerals in the water that intensifies the taste of salt. When you fry potatoes, the water is taken out, so the salt doesn't hit as much water. But on raw vegetables with more water content, or in salt water, it tastes worse because of the minerals.

questions.question: If an anchor is wedged under a rock or the seabed, how do you get it back on board?

answers.answer: Before putting the anchor overboard, a secondary line goes to a shackle near the bottom of the anchor, with a buoy at the surface. To retrieve, you pick up the buoy and pull from that direction, extracting the anchor backwards so however the flukes went in, they come out backwards.

questions.question: Why is there often a depiction of a snake or serpent on medical institutions such as pharmacies and ambulances?

answers.answer: It goes back to Greek mythology - Rodos Asclepius, son of Apollo, who was the god of healing. The snake shedding its skin represents rebirth/renewal, which became associated with healing.

questions.question: In the olden days, how did people cut their toenails if they didn't have scissors or nail cutters?

answers.answer: They could use stones to file them down, or more supple people could reach their feet with their mouths.

questions.question: How can an avalanche go faster than terminal velocity? David Attenborough said 250mph for avalanches but skydivers only reach 122mph.

answers.answer: An avalanche is tons of tiny bits of snow acting like a liquid, with less air resistance so it can move quicker.

Terminal velocity is when upthrust balances gravity. An avalanche is not like a liquid - it's a solid lump going down a 45-degree angle, subject to gravity. An avalanche cannot go faster than 122mph. The caller likely misheard or misremembered the numbers.

questions.question: When people grunt in the gym, does it actually help with physical performance or is it just an expression of fatigue?

answers.answer: When you exhale forcefully during exertion, you generate more power through your core muscles (transverse abdominal muscles), giving more stability and strength. It's like martial arts - forceful exhalation braces your core. The noise becomes a habit and can also be intimidating to opponents.
A grunt is just a big exhale that helps with muscle movement - from an ex-professional tennis player.
The hydraulic amplifier effect - strain on your trunk and diaphragm means you need forceful exhalation to replace breath quickly.

questions.question: Is the cash on Dragon's Den real?

answers.answer: The top note is real, the rest is not.

I was on Dragon's Den three years ago pitching Bionic Gloves. During filming I picked up some notes from Peter Jones's pile - the top note was real, but the rest is good forgery. For the purposes of the camera it looks real, and they're probably only printed on one side to avoid legal issues.

questions.question: Why does NASA still use so many black and white cameras when they have billions to spend? Curiosity rover has some color cameras but still uses black and white.

answers.answer: Black and white shows a true image with minimum distortion. Color and the way it's perceived through the spectrum can cause problems - we saw this with the dress debate a few months ago where people argued over colors in the same picture. Similar to how we still x-ray humans and engineering in black and white.

questions.question: What is the origin of Britannia? As in 'Rule Britannia.' Is she real? Is she a mythical figure? Who dreamt her up?

answers.answer: Old English coins going back to the 1500s bore the insignia of Britannia. It was on the groat. Britannia was on the ships they used for trading across the ocean, which is where 'rule the waves' comes from.

questions.question: Why do they call doctors quacks?

answers.answer: During the Great Plague, doctors wore big capes with hoods covering their heads and had big filters in their noses to try and stop the spores. They looked like ducks walking around, and that's why they got called quacks.

questions.question: If I stood in the centre of London, where would I be?

answers.answer: Charing Cross. That's the dead centre of London - when driving on the motorway it says London is 37 miles away, it's 37 miles to Charing Cross.

questions.question: If I bought an island in the middle of the ocean, would I be able to make up my own laws?

answers.answer: Just off the coast of Suffolk there's a WWII gun emplacement called the Principality of Sealand. It was sold to the Bates family in the 1970s. It's a man-made structure in international waters. They've got their own constitution, their own international football team, and a half marathon every year. They've even been invaded by Dutch and German mercenaries. It's an unrecognised micronation - they declared independence from the UK.

questions.question: Why is it that when women put on mascara, they always open their mouth at the same time?

answers.answer: When you're putting mascara on, you have to tilt your head upwards so your eyelids go down to get to your eyelashes. If you put your head upwards, it's automatic for your jaw to rest downwards - it's gravity. If you try it in the mirror, you'll see there's pressure on your jaw if you look up.

questions.question: Can a religious group become a political party and rule England? Is there anything to stop the Catholic Church, Jewish faith, or Muslim faith just setting up a party?

answers.answer: There's nothing in Magna Carta to stop it. You'd just have to get enough votes. You'd have to win a majority of seats in Parliament to form a government. There was a Christian Party around at the time of the last election. So yes, you can.

questions.question: Why don't penguins' feet freeze?

answers.answer: Penguins can control the flow of blood to their feet like we can - when cold, fingers go white, when warm, pink. But they also have something humans haven't got at the top of their legs that allows arteries full of hot blood to split into loads of tiny little bits to keep the feet warm. They can control both the quantity and the heat of the blood going into their feet. The blood flow regulates the temperature and keeps their feet above freezing - about 40 degrees centigrade.

questions.question: Why do we still feel like we're on the boat even after we've stepped onto dry land?

answers.answer: It's got to do with the liquid in your ears. When you've been on the boat for several hours and you step onto dry land, the liquid is still moving in your ear, so you're actually still rocking from side to side. That's why it's also known as 'sea legs'. You can always tell when a sailor's just got off a ship because they waddle - their brain is expecting the ground to be moving.

questions.question: How can you help a toddler who is screaming on an aircraft, especially during landing and take-off?

answers.answer: Give their ears a good rub - massage quite firmly where the pain is (where you feel pain when your ears hurt on a plane). Copy it on the child. A dummy also helps because sucking and swallowing clears the ear. So a dummy coupled with ear rubs works best.

questions.question: Why do the first lines of chapters in books often appear in capitals, two-thirds of the way across the page?
When you crack an egg and shell falls into the white, why can you get it out easily with another piece of shell but not with your finger?

answers.answer: Egg white is a protein - a viscous liquid. Your fingers don't have any corners on them. So if you try to pinch a bit of egg shell out, it just slips because it gets caught between your finger and the shell. If you put a shell in, you can use the corner to scoop it out. It's about purchase - having a corner.

questions.question: Who monitors all the barcodes? Who decides what barcode a product gets? If I invented a product tomorrow, who gives it a barcode?

answers.answer: There is one organisation in each country in charge of barcodes. In the UK, it's called GS1 and you have to buy barcodes only from them - they're the only ones who distribute them. The manufacturer buys them rather than the retailer. They give you a whole range of barcodes and you're the only one that gets that barcode range.

questions.question: How do we know when meteor showers are coming? Do we have some sort of intergalactic radar to tell us that we've got some meteors coming our way?

answers.answer: A meteor is just a bit of rock randomly flying through space. It'd be tracked the same way as anything else flying through space - you'd see bleeps on a screen and know something was set to enter your orbit.

It's thanks to Isaac Newton. He formulated his laws of motion - objects will continue in uniform motion or stay at rest unless a force is acting on them. If you have a photograph of an object and then take another photograph later, you can plot its path, and Newton tells us it will continue on that path forevermore. The more photographs astronomers have over time, the better they can determine speed and direction, and predict when it will be visible above Earth.

questions.question: Where does the expression 'bowling a maiden over' or 'scoring his maiden century' come from? Where does the word maiden fit in?

answers.answer: A maiden is a description of an over where no runs have been scored.

The English 'maiden' has equivalents in German 'Frau', French 'mademoiselle', and Spanish 'senorita'. They all mean unmarried/untouched/unsullied. If an over is bowled with no score, the over is virginal - no score describes a virgin. No score describes a runless cricket over.

questions.question: Why do we apportion emotional pain to our heart and not to our brain? It also rhymes.

answers.answer: We think of our brain as being logical and when our emotions (which are often illogical) kick in, we need to make sense of that by putting them somewhere that isn't logical - therefore the heart.

The answer is romantic. It was probably medieval poets, or the Greeks, or Sappho who first came up with the idea of the heart being the repository of feelings and the head being the repository of thoughts.

The heart produces an electromagnetic field 5,000 times stronger than the brain. The heart also contains neurons (brain cells) and produces hormones as part of the endocrine system. Even before we had medicine, people could see that the beating of the heart determined whether someone stayed alive, so they pointed to the heart as the center of consciousness and feeling.

questions.question: Why does our broadband never work when it's raining?

answers.answer: Really bad rain plays all sorts of havoc with electrical signals. Though you would expect by now the technology to have reached a place where it doesn't.

It's called 'rain fade'. Your broadband router connects via cable to a main up and down link position, which connects via satellite to the main server. When it rains, water is a physical obstruction between the two points of the satellite, weakening the signal. The only solution is to move closer to a substation.

questions.question: Can you feed bees like you feed birds? Is there something you can do immediately - like putting out nuts or seeds? Or can you buy a bee feeder?

answers.answer: Bees eat pollen naturally, so planting more flowers would help. But he doesn't know if there's a direct equivalent to bird feeders for bees.

You can feed bees. Certain times of the year when you see bees crawling on the floor looking like they're dying, it's just because they're tired and run out of energy. Get some white sugar and warm water, mix it into a syrup, put it on a spoon in front of them, and they'll drink it. After a couple of minutes, they'll recover and fly away.

questions.question: Why is the British National Anthem about the Queen and not about the country? (Why is it about the monarch rather than the nation?)

answers.answer: Because you could have had 'Land of Hope and Glory' which is much more rousing, but that's not what we have.

It was never originally designed to be a National Anthem. It was composed after a king was attacked on the way to a theatre in the 1700s (probably George IV). A member of the orchestra composed it in a hurry, and it only had one verse. That's why the words are so rubbish - it was done on the hoof. It proved so popular at the end of the performance that they did it after every performance. It was never meant to be a national anthem, just a royal salute.

questions.question: Why does a cement mixer rotate anti-clockwise? Everything else rotates clockwise.

answers.answer: If you look at a cement mixer from the front (where you empty it), it's rotating clockwise. If you're standing behind it, it's rotating anti-clockwise. But other things like washing machines and tumble dryers rotate clockwise when viewed from the front.

When loading sand and cement with a shovel, most people stand to the right of it. If it spun clockwise, the shovel would catch and pull you toward it, risking your head ending up in the cement mixer. Spinning anti-clockwise pushes your shovel away and keeps you safe. When you're emptying it from behind where the handles are, it appears to spin clockwise.

questions.question: Why do we say 'water cannon' (singular) rather than 'water cannons' (plural) when referring to multiple cannons?

answers.answer: It's like the word 'fish' - cannon is both singular and plural. Just as you'd say '12 fish', you say '12 cannon'.
Fishes is for multiple fish of different species. Fish for single or multiple of the same type.
The plural of fish is only 'fish' if they're all the same species. If more than one type is present, the plural would be 'fishes'.

questions.question: Why when cycling downhill fast on a hot day, does the air feel colder than it actually is? What is wind chill factor?

answers.answer: The air closest to your skin gets warmed up by your skin, and when there's a breeze, it gets blown off you. Your body is trying to warm up the new cold air, which makes you feel cold. It's like when you lick your finger and blow on it - it's colder than when you haven't licked it.

The cold air is constantly being replaced by other cold air. Each bit of cold air that goes past you is warmed up slightly by your skin, and the faster it's replaced, the more heat is taken away. The gap in the earlier answer was sweat - sweat evaporates and takes away heat (4.2 joules per gram). In hot, dry air, sweat evaporates even faster, which paradoxically makes you hotter. There's a temperature equilibrium point around 37 degrees where sweating doesn't cool you down.

questions.question: Why do the characters in Coronation Street drink out of empty cups? When you look at the camera angle, the cups are clearly empty - no meniscus, nothing there.
What were hashtags originally meant for before Twitter? They were invented long before Twitter.

answers.answer: The correct name for a hashtag is 'octothorpe'. An old geography teacher told him it was a map maker's symbol for a village, representing the village square surrounded by eight fields. 'Thorpe' is an old name for a village, and 'octo' is for eight.

questions.question: What would happen if we nuked a desert? Would there be an enormous cloud of sand or would it turn into a lake of glass because of the heat and sand being a constituent part of the ocean?

answers.answer: You get a big glass crater because the temperature of a thermonuclear device (a hydrogen bomb/fusion bomb) is 100 million degrees, well above the melting point and probably above the boiling point of sand. It would be like a dirty glass crater, an ice rink almost in shape - dirty because it would have pockets of non-homogeneous sand. The 100 million degrees creates a column of very hot air which is much less dense than surrounding air, creating the stem of the mushroom cloud. At some point the rising air's density equals the surrounding air's density so it spreads out to form the top, and that's when all the sand would be scattered as particulates (fallout).

questions.question: What is the origin of kissing? Why is it that when I put my lips on someone else's cheek it's a sign of affection? Where does that come from?

answers.answer: It's part of an animal instinct where animals pass food by their parents and they chew it up. Young animals are always around their parents' mouth, licking and trying to get affection for food. Birds still do it - they chew food and then deliver it mouth to mouth to their child. So we had this in us for millions of years. Then when we started communicating verbally, we said 'I don't want the food, just give us a snog' and the affection transferred from food to just affection.

questions.question: Why is it that dead people are referred to as 'late'? Why do we say 'late' for someone who has passed instead of dead?

answers.answer: It comes from 'latter' meaning to remember someone second. You would say 'late' instead of 'latter'. So 'late of this parish' rather than 'latter of this parish' - remembering someone second/latterly.

questions.question: Why do we use the term 'copycat' for someone who copies something? Why cat instead of just 'copier' or 'copy-parrot'?

answers.answer: She saw it in a book where ancient Egyptian women copied the shape and style of cats' eyes in their make-up, hence the saying 'copycat'. She has a picture at home of an Egyptian queen with a cat peeping behind the mirror where the queen is copying the shape of the cat's eyes, and the caption explained this origin.

questions.question: Are there any instances of genuine, deliberate humor in the Bible? Not unintentional humor, but what the writers intended to be funny?

answers.answer: The story of Elijah and the prophets of Baal from 1 Kings Chapter 18. When the Baal prophets were calling on their god and nothing was happening, Elijah mocked them saying 'cry aloud, because he's a god - either he's talking, or he's pursuing a journey, or sometimes he's sleeping and you got to wake him.' The idea that an omniscient God would somehow be unable to hear his priests shouting, maybe he's popped out for a pint of milk, is deliberate humor by whoever wrote the book of Kings.

questions.question: Why do some clocks show four as IIII (four ones) and some show IV? Why don't they put two V's next to each other on a clock?

answers.answer: It's about aesthetics and simplicity. On one side (8,9,10,11,12) there are 17 strokes, on the other (1,2,3,4,5) there are only 11 strokes. Using IIII instead of IV adds 2 strokes to the lighter side, making it more balanced. Also having VVV would be confusing, and the traditional smile position (10:10) looks nicer.

questions.question: What comes out of the nozzle of a 3D printer? Is it always the same stuff? They read about one printing a steel bridge which suggests steel comes out.

answers.answer: Molten plastic - on a roll of filament like a roll of wire. The printer sucks in the filament and pushes it through a hot nozzle, melting it, and the model is created in layers of melted plastic. But you can also get polymer mixtures with copper and glue to print metal. You can even print with a wood and glue mixture like liquid wood, which is resiny.

questions.question: Why is Los Angeles known as LAX? What does the X stand for?

answers.answer: Probably to distinguish Los Angeles from other cities like Lagos that came later and bagged shorter codes. The X was just the most obvious way to make it different. Portland, Oregon is PDX because PD was already taken.

questions.question: Are olive stones used for anything other than planting and growing more olives?

answers.answer: When you've pressed the olives and got the oil, extracted all the oil, and the pips and nuts and stones are left, they dry them and put them into an auger and heat their houses through the winter with them. It's classic biofuel. My brother is buying a place in Puglia and looking into this as a way of heating the house during winter.

questions.question: Can dogs actually sense a human's fear through smell?

answers.answer: Dogs can't smell fear. There are no scientific tests at the moment to prove unquestionably that dogs can smell fear. A lot of people think they can, but I don't believe they can. A terrified human being will have no impact whatsoever upon a dog's likelihood to attack. I think dogs react to body language, not the smell. If someone is scared of a dog, they put their hand above the dog's head in a certain way, and the dog reacts to that.

Yes, it's all to do with pheromones. There's an evolutionary basis for exuding a smell of fear - there's a benefit in being able to communicate to others unease or danger without actually making them feel fear. Dogs can detect things like diabetes, cancer by someone's breath, so it's not a great stretch to say they can smell fear. Humans can detect the smell of fear themselves.

questions.question: Why is it that the title of a book on the spine of the book in English is written from top to bottom and for foreign books (French, German, etc.) they're written from bottom to top?

answers.answer: As a former typographer who worked for Cambridge University Press, I can tell you that books go both ways - top to bottom, bottom to top. There's no rule. Rupert's observations were unscientific.

questions.question: Why do golfers shout 'Four!' when the ball goes left or right onto another fairway?

answers.answer: Shortened from 'Look out before' from the Napoleonic Wars. Two rows of soldiers - first rank would duck, second rank would fire their guns. Rear rank would then shoot and shout the warning so they didn't stand up and get shot in the back of the head. A four. Look a four.

Four caddies - in the old days in golf, there were two types of caddy. One was a caddy caddy that would carry the bag. The other was a four caddy that would go ahead to find the golf ball in bushes and heather and gorse. When golfers hit it offline, they would shout 'Four!' to get the four caddy's attention to tell him to start looking because the ball had gone over towards him. It's not about soldiers - it's about getting the attention of the four caddy to find the ball.

questions.question: Who's the Seven Sisters?

answers.answer: There were seven trees located there. They had to cut those seven trees down to build the station. The trees were called the Seven Sisters, and the name was transferred onto the station and the road.

questions.question: Why don't bus drivers have to wear seatbelts?

answers.answer: Older buses don't have seatbelts, newer ones do because of recent safety laws. Drivers only have seatbelts for passengers if the buses are on for hire.
They don't have to wear a seatbelt because they're travelling less than 500 metres per stop.

questions.question: Where have all these bats come from? Why so many flying around the window?
How come I have dyslexia problems with English but when speaking or writing Arabic, I don't have any problems? Is dyslexia just an English thing?

answers.answer: It's not dyslexia, it's dyslexias. There are lots of different kinds caused by different things - lesions on the brain, problems in different parts of the brain. With a pictorial language different from our language, someone who had problems reading English wouldn't have problems reading Chinese. Character-based instead of letter-based would explain why the brain struggles with one of them and not with the other.

questions.question: Why do we dance? What is the evolutionary reason why humans dance?

answers.answer: The fetus reacts to the heartbeat of the mother. And that's why little kids basically dance. It's about responding to the beat, learned in the womb.

questions.question: Why can I grow a full beard while going bald at the same time? It feels unfair.

answers.answer: Hair follicles on the bottom of your face are overactive in cell division and cell growth, so they grow exceedingly quickly. The ones on your head are either dead or very inactive, so they divide slowly.

questions.question: Has Robert De Niro ever died in any film? Does he have a policy not to die?

answers.answer: Heat - Robert De Niro is a bank robber and Al Pacino (a cop) kills him at the end.

questions.question: How do fish (minnows and sticklebacks) get into a newly constructed canal that only has rainwater and no connection to any other water course?

answers.answer: When water gets heated it evaporates and gets drawn up into the clouds with whatever particles are in it. The clouds move and rain elsewhere, dropping whatever was in the water. Fish eggs are so minuscule and tiny they could easily get pulled up - like sand from the Sahara.
It comes from the birds. Foreign birds come over here, nick eggs, land on lakes. The eggs end up in the water.

questions.question: When/where did punctuation first come about? Who decided we need a full stop or a comma?

answers.caller: Mark from Barrow-in-Furness (linguistics researcher and lecturer)
answers.answer: Punctuation as we know it goes to the late Middle Ages/early modern times, especially with printing (Caxton). But there's earlier punctuation - the Festus Disc from Crete (c. 1700 BC) has symbols divided by lines, possibly like commas. Middle Eastern steles have markers separating words/paragraphs. But modern punctuation developed much later with printing presses.

questions.question: Why is a mistake called a 'boo-boo'?

answers.answer: Might be military in origin? Could be from Yogi Bear ('smarter than the average bear' - smaller than the average bear = boo-boo?)

questions.question: Why is red wine kept in green bottles, and why is white wine sometimes kept in white/clear bottles?

answers.caller: David from Brentwood (makes his own wine)
answers.answer: It's to do with light - to stop the colour fading or bleaching inside the bottle. Dark bottles don't admit light. When he first started making wine, a kit came with white bottles, so he looked it up.
It's cost efficient - dark glass is slightly cheaper than clear glass. Also reflects light.

questions.caller: Caller from Raising Great Portland Street
questions.question: Why do we talk to ourselves out loud?

answers.answer: It's just thoughts coming out. Thinking squared. There's nothing special going on.

questions.question: If you turn off the switch on your TV or kettle but don't pull the plug out, are you still using electricity? Someone from British Gas told me this.

answers.caller: Professor Martin Smith (Manor Park, professor of robotics at University of Middlesex)
answers.answer: It depends. If you switch off at the wall socket, no current is being used - electricity is definitely off. However, many devices (TVs, computers, printers, video recorders) have a separate box in the cable and may have a separate on-off switch. In those cases, if you only switch off at the device but not at the wall, it will still use electricity.

questions.question: How many different types of 50p coins have been issued since decimalisation? There are commemorative ones, some worth thousands (like Kew Gardens).
How do crane operators go to the toilet when they're at the top of their crane? What about number twos?

answers.answer: They do it in a bottle. If they need a number two, they'd have to come down.
Dear James, I am a tower crane operator, and I absolutely do not poo in a bucket.

questions.question: Why doesn't meat hanging in the butchers' window (with '14 days' and '28 days' labels) ever get fly-blown and maggoty? It must be fly-blown but it never seems to be.
Why is there a cat flap inside an ambulance and where does it lead?

answers.answer: They're actually cat flaps, but not for cats - they're for clinical waste bins. You push clinical waste through the cat flap and it goes into a bag at the bottom of the bin. The bag gets emptied when you're back at base. Needles go in a separate bin in a separate cupboard.

questions.question: When an elephant makes that trumpeting noise, is he making it with his voice or with his trunk?
How did countries get their names? Who named countries?

answers.answer: You give a name to your tribe to distinguish it from other tribes, then you name the bit you've taken over after your tribe. If you're a Frank, you call the area France or Frankland. If you're Norman, you call it Normandy. If you're a Saxon, you call it Saxony. But there's no catch-all answer that works for every country. Liberia in Africa was named because it's where freed slaves were sent - derived from the Latin word for freedom.

questions.question: Why are planets round?

answers.answer: Over millennia, billions of years while orbiting around the sun, they had their rough edges knocked off by space debris, asteroids, comets - just like pebbles on a beach getting polished.
Planets are formed from stars, and when they form they're all molten, so they're liquid. They form little spheres. Then they cool down, and when solid, they're round.

The core is heavier than everywhere else, so that's where everything gravitates to. This acts evenly across the surface, which causes it to form a sphere. The centrifugal force of the Earth spinning means it bulges around the equator, so it's not a perfect sphere.

questions.question: Where did the phrase 'I'll be there in a jiffy' come from? What does jiffy mean?

answers.answer: It's a scientific term for a very short period of time, like a nanosecond or millisecond. Source: book called 'Red Herrings and White Elephants' about riddles and mysteries.

questions.question: What was the time period called when Jesus was alive? If BC is before Christ and AD is after, what do you call during his life?

answers.answer: It would be A.D., because A.D. starts when he was born. The exact date of birth is disputed, but for purposes of the dating system, his lifetime would be covered by Anno Domini - the year of our Lord.
At the time, they would have been using the Roman calendar founded by Romulus and Remus, not BC or AD. The BC/AD system came later and was set up by the Roman Catholic Church with their own date.

questions.question: What's the purpose of a toenail? We use fingernails to pick up stuff, but what do toenails do?

answers.answer: It's an evolutionary hangover like your appendix or tonsils. We used to have claws which helped us climb trees or dig underground, and they've evolved into nails. We don't really need them anymore.
Toenails are for protection. The toes are the pointiest parts of our body that get touched the most, so we have protection so we don't get bruised and battered.
Nails were claws, and over evolution they didn't get rid of them - they developed them into new hands that we developed after millions of years for more dexterous usage.

questions.question: Why don't dogs get stung by stinging nettles? Even on their noses and underneath their private parts where they have hardly any hair?

answers.caller: Alex from Hertfordshire (dog walker with doggy hotel)
answers.answer: Dogs do get stung by stinging nettles - in between their paws. They won't get stung through their fur, but their paws can get stung. They hate it and lick it for about half an hour after. They have some antiseptic in their saliva.

questions.question: Where do palm hearts (the vegetable) come from?

answers.answer: They come from the center of palm trees. Palm trees don't have rings like other trees - they have a white stick through the middle. Now they cultivate palm trees specially so they can take the heart out without the tree dying. You chop it up and put it in tins.

questions.question: If the Queen were to pass away tomorrow, would the National Anthem change from 'God Save the Queen' to 'God Save the King'? Whose job would it be to change it?
What causes the dropping/falling sensation that sometimes wakes us up in the middle of the night? And what is our internal alarm clock?

answers.answer: It's a throwback to when we slept in trees. When you're sleeping in a tree, the worst thing that could happen is falling out.
(Later admitted he was playing with Ollie - this wasn't a real answer)

It's called a myoclastic jerk. It's the point when you're between consciousness and unconsciousness, just about to fall asleep. The unconscious part of the brain is taking over and doesn't know if you're dying or alive, so it sends a pulse through your body making your feet jerk.

questions.question: Where do they measure the speed of a tennis serve at Wimbledon? Is it as the ball leaves the racket head, as it crosses the net, or when it lands?

answers.answer: They need to measure it from A to B like a speed camera on the motorway - how long it takes to pass between points X and Y.
They measure the speed from the racket, because by the time it gets to the other side, it's slowed down a lot due to air resistance on the ball.

They use radar in the same way as a police officer uses radar to catch a speeding motorist. It measures the change in frequency of reflected radar using the Doppler effect. There's no need to have a fixed point A and point B - it can be a journey consisting of only one or two radar wavelengths, about 5 centimetres maximum.

questions.question: What is the story of the first passport? How did it start and which countries is it from?

answers.answer: The first passports were recorded 450 BC by a Persian king (possibly Darius). It was basically a letter on papyrus given to people crossing rivers so they were given good passage, and if they weren't, there would be repercussions for attacking the king's emissary. The first official passport was under King Henry V, written on gold tablets, so British citizens could travel. No one would have left the country until relatively recently - everyone would have recognised a King of England.

questions.question: Why do men always get through to the show more than women?
Why aren't lie detectors used on all criminals to find out if they've done it? Wouldn't it make life simple?

answers.answer: They're not completely foolproof. They do use them sometimes in some jurisdictions and the technology improves all the time, but it can never be conclusive evidence in a court of law. They measure things like fluid on the skin or heart rate, and you can train yourself to control these physiological responses.

questions.question: If emotions are simply chemicals in our body reacting, can we control the chemicals in our body?

answers.answer: You can control some of them some of the time, but you can never be in complete control of your hormonal or chemical composition. Taking drugs is the most obvious way to affect your chemical balance, but it wears off and you get a hangover - you can't affect it permanently.

There are some emotional physiological things we can't control, like the fight or flight response and adrenaline. However, you can learn to adapt your cognitive reaction to those chemicals through CBT, anger management, stress management, and mindfulness, which can lead to neurological changes in the brain. So it's a big circle - if you have a problem with anger management, you can learn to control the adrenaline response, and that in turn can impact your adrenaline production.

questions.question: What does the 'O' signify in Irish surnames like O'Brien, O'Malley, O'Neill? What are its origins?

answers.answer: It denotes Sonov - son of. So O'Brien means son of Brian Baru, the last king of Ireland. All the O'Briens were members of his clan. Mac is the same (son of), and Fitz means illegitimate son of.

questions.question: Which came first - property addresses or the postal service? Did properties always have addresses, or were addresses created because of the postal service?

answers.answer: Houses had names - like Green House or Red House, or house next to pub. That is essentially an address. The question is not a mystery, it's just not understanding that houses had identifying features before numerical addresses were invented.

questions.question: Where have all the swallows gone? I grew up in Kent and used to see swallow nests under eaves everywhere, but haven't seen a single swallow this summer.

questions.answer: Where does the phrase 'fill your boots' come from?

answers.answer: During the roundhead and cavalier era, soldiers going to the front would stop at watering holes and the captain of the guard would say 'fill your boots.' The boots were actually leather water bottles, so it meant carry as much water as you can.
Alternative suggestion: pirates, when they couldn't carry any more booty, would put it in their boots. But I think the leather water bottle answer is more plausible.

questions.question: How does a tattooist learn how to use the tattoo gun? What do they practice on with the actual needle gun before they obviously... You can't just walk in and go, he's the apprentice, he'll be doing your tattoo.

answers.answer: They practice on pigs.

They do practice on pigs, but not actually a pig. You buy strips of pig skin, and they practice on that. My son's going through this and he's been doing it a year and a half. He buys pig skin strips from Morrison's in the meat section.

questions.question: Why is it that when you pull a nose hair, your eye waters? The eye that waters is dependent on what side you pull. Why?
We have chicken eggs, duck eggs, quail eggs, goose eggs, and we eat all the meat. Well, why don't we have turkey eggs?

answers.answer: Because turkey's a very seasonal bird. It's very carefully controlled so that you've got loads to eat at Christmas. Very little demand for it for the rest of the year. So half of the answer is that they fertilise all of the eggs that they need to create turkeys. And the other half of the answer is that nobody wants turkey eggs.

questions.question: What is the evolutionary purpose of anger, because evolution has a way of phasing out things that make us do stupid things but yet whenever we get angry we do stupid things?

answers.answer: It's fight or flight isn't it? The adrenaline comes into you and it gives you either the strength to have a scrap or the strength to run away. That's why you're successful. The adrenaline is what you're asking about - why do we get adrenaline pumping through our system when we're angry, and the answer is to give you the wherewithal to fight or flight more effectively than you can when you haven't got the adrenaline in your system.

I concur with your answer. There are two things - there's physiological response to adrenaline, and the emotional response to adrenaline, which is the flight-or-flight hormone. The physiological response is your breathing goes up, your heart rate goes up, you get vasodilation and constriction, blood's diverted to your limbs, and your blood sugar goes up. The blood goes to your limbs so that you can use them. Anger is the motivation to fight, and fear is the motivation to flight. You can't fight if you're not angry. The other thing is sometimes it's better to avoid a fight but still get what you want - that's why you have mock charges with gorillas, or teeth-bearing, or chest-beating. If you have a fight, you both lose resource, you both run the risk of injury.

questions.question: What is the difference between a screw and a bolt? I need the answer for my product design exam.

answers.answer: A bolt requires a nut to make it captive, to join two pieces together, but a screw doesn't.

Screws are tapered, and with a point on the end, normally designed for joining two pieces of wood together with no other fixings. They just draw themselves in until the head pinches the two pieces. The bolt requires a nut to make it captive.

A screw is threaded its entire length, whereas a bolt only has a thread part way up. A bolt should be called a set screw, which is a correct term. Bolts have a part that isn't threaded which is the exact size, so you don't get any lateral movement when you tighten things up. You can thread a bolt into a threaded hole, it doesn't need a nut.

questions.question: Bicentennial of the Battle of Waterloo today. I was wondering what was the bloodiest battle in history?

answers.answer: The Battle of Stalingrad, which I believe was something like 1.9 million casualties. I have a history A-level and some history as part of my degree. The populations in ancient times were tiny, so it's not them.

questions.question: Do ostriches actually stick their head in the sand? Because I've never seen it or photographs or zoos.

answers.answer: An ostrich would have been a tall animal, and it's a plains animal in Africa. They don't bury their heads in the sand. What they actually do is they put their heads very low to the ground, so they can spot predators against the horizon.

questions.question: For those who believe in evolution, if humans did evolve from monkeys, why are there still monkeys?

answers.answer: To explain how evolution works, you have a genetic defect, or a genetic difference that one member of a species is born with. And that, by accident, provides them with an attribute that means they're going to breed more effectively than all the other members of that species that don't have the genetic difference, right? And that genetic difference gets passed on to their progeny, and their progeny, and their progeny. So you have an entirely separate branch, if you will, of the monkey family tree going off in that direction. And your question is, why aren't all the monkeys on that new branch of the family tree? Can you see now how silly this question is?

questions.question: TV soaps - when they kill somebody off, or somebody gets married on a TV soap, a day or so later they come out saying 7.5 million people watched that. How do they come to that conclusion? How do they count TV views?

answers.answer: They do it through samples. They put a box on X number of televisions right across the country, and that records what everybody's watching, and then they multiply it to get the total population. It's called BARB, and they do it overnight. On TV they do it overnight. They can tell you now how many people were watching telly last night. It's a reliable estimate - it's not scientifically accurate, no, but it's widely considered to be a highly reliable estimate.

questions.question: Is there any relation between the moon cycle and our sanity? Does the full moon affect human beings and make them extra emotional?

answers.answer: I read in an Asian Sumerian text, tablet, called the story of Luna. It talks about a deity called Luna who ruled a part of the Earth, which you can scientifically prove the moon was a part of this planet Earth. He wanted to rule the whole planet and wasn't allowed, and his followers were called Lunatic. After the moon was broken up from the Earth, he became angry and wanted to destroy the rest of the Earth. Because the moon affects the wave of the sea, they always said that when there is a full moon, people in mental institution really act.
Do we know whether it's actually true or not?

questions.question: When they build new roads, or the existing roads that we have, where do they get the names from? If you've got a road name called Fisher Way, where do they get the name Fisher Way from? If there's a road called Norman Road, is it someone called Norman that built the road?

answers.answer: The really old ones will have a whole variety of explanations. I think the answer will be different according to almost every council. There's an estate in Kidderminster named after 19th century poets and authors like Byron, Wordsworth, Shelley, Coleridge. Some places are named after local councillors. I think it's just whimsy and humanity.

The name road goes to the planning committee. As an elected councillor, I had to sit on a committee where we were deciding the name of a road. The developer put forward their proposed name, and we decided we didn't like that. We were going to put it in the name of a local person that was sorely missed.

questions.question: Most of the pots on the top of the chimneys are open-ended, so why, when it rains, don't you get water in your fireplace?

answers.answer: The pot's aperture is much smaller than the bottom of the chimney. And they get quite hot, so the likelihood of rain actually reaching the fireplace is zero. Think - you go out in a thunderstorm holding a pint pot and see how long it takes you to fill up the pot.

questions.question: Why does milk not go off inside the cow?

answers.answer: The body controls the temperature and that's why milk doesn't go off inside. It's the same with blood - the body is sensitive enough to hold it for the period required.

The inside of our bodies is a sterile environment. Our immune system kills off bacteria and viruses. Once you extract milk from the cow, you expose it to bacteria in the environment outside, and that is what makes milk go off. Pasteurization is designed to kill off whatever bacteria gets in.

questions.question: How do spiders see the world? When they're upside down on a ceiling vs right way up on a floor, do they see things differently?

answers.answer: Most spiders don't actually have good vision - they sense through vibrations. Jumping spiders are an exception and have better vision. If they're using vibrations, they're using the same senses regardless of their physical position. The ones that do see more clearly have multiple eyes.

questions.question: Why do I look better in the mirror than in selfies? Is it just about light or does my face actually look different?

answers.answer: Cameras on phones have wide angle lenses, and because of the proximity when you take a selfie, it distorts your face. Selfie sticks were invented to get further away for a better look.

Your face is never symmetrical. The more symmetrical your face, the more attractive you are. When you look in a mirror, you see the inverse of what everyone else sees (like ambulance writing backed up). A photograph shows what people actually see. People are just more used to seeing themselves in mirrors than in photographs.

questions.question: Do different sized heads mean different sized brains? Does brain size determine intelligence?

answers.answer: There's no relationship between head size and brain size. In Victorian times they tried to answer this through phrenology by measuring skulls, but it doesn't work. All brains are around 8 ounces, plus or minus 2. Intelligence is a mixture of nature and nurture. Einstein had quite a small brain but it had lots and lots of folds.

questions.question: Did Marco Polo take spaghetti to China or pick up noodles from China and take them to Italy? Or is it just coincidence?

answers.answer: The Chinese were masters of invention and came up with it first. It is believed that through trade - possibly Marco Polo (though that may be apocryphal) - it was traded back to Europe. The Germans call spaghetti 'Nudeln' which is like noodles.

questions.question: Where does the sea go when the tide goes out? Does it go to the other side of the ocean?

answers.answer: Think of it like a bath - the water wobbles, goes up at one end and down at the other. The amount of water remains the same, distribution changes with the tides. So in Spain the tide comes in while in England it goes out.

The moon has a gravitational pull. It pulls the water that's closest to it towards the moon. As the moon rotates around the Earth, there are high tides on the side facing the moon AND on the opposite side of the Earth (because the water at the bottom isn't pulled while the Earth is pulled). So when tide goes out on one side of an ocean, it may also be going out on the other side.

questions.question: How do you know if there's a chick in an egg or not? When you get an egg, how do you know it might not have a baby chick in it?

answers.answer: If there's a daddy chicken and a mummy chicken around, the eggs may be fertilized and could have a chick. But if you only have hen chickens with no rooster, all eggs will be eatable eggs. Farms use powerful lights that shine through the shell to see if a chick is forming inside.

questions.question: Why do police ride on horses? I was stuck behind two police on horses in Lewisham and wondered why.

answers.answer: The horse gives height to see over crowds and get a good view. It's mobile - not a vehicle. It acts as a mobile barrier to shepherd people in certain directions. They need to get from A to B and give horses exercise.

questions.question: If the sun is essentially a big ball of flames, why don't I get a suntan lying next to a fire?

answers.answer: It's ultraviolet light that gives you a suntan, not a flame. The sun isn't a ball of flames - it's a nuclear explosion. Normal fires don't produce ultraviolet light.

questions.question: Why don't trains have seatbelts?

answers.answer: It's a cost-benefit analysis. Installing seatbelts would be extremely expensive, and train crashes are relatively rare. There's no law requiring them. This is similar to why we don't have platform screen doors at every Underground station - the cost outweighs the benefit given the few deaths per year.

questions.question: How do you know that two people are seeing the exact same colour? When someone brings you a 'red' top, they've assigned a word to a shade, but how can you verify you're both seeing the same red?

answers.answer: There's no way to prove that two people both seeing and saying 'red' are actually seeing exactly the same colour. This is a philosophical conundrum - you could be seeing what I call green and calling it red. Wittgenstein wrote about this. All you know for certain is that your own mind exists (Descartes). You don't even know if your boyfriend exists or if you're just a brain in a vat imagining everything.

questions.question: Where does the word 'punter' come from? Why is a customer called a punter?

answers.answer: It's a horse racing term. The Irish word for pound is punt, and to have a punt on a horse is to put a pound on a horse, so therefore you become a punter.

questions.question: Where does acid come from? How is sulfuric acid manufactured?

answers.answer: To make sulfuric acid, you dissolve sulfur dioxide in water. SO2 plus H2O equals H2SO4. You can burn sulfur (brimstone dug from the ground) in oxygen to create sulfur dioxide - that's what causes acid rain.

questions.question: What determines people to be left or right-handed, and why does it differ during different activities?

answers.answer: It's a genetic predisposition, like the colour of your eyes. It's determined by DNA, passed down through family lines. Used to try and train kids out of it in Victorian times by strapping their hand behind them.

questions.question: Why can you no longer buy tomato olive oil in the shops?

answers.answer: Flavoured oils were more popular a few years ago, gastropubby. Can probably still get it online or in some specialist shops.

questions.question: Why are heavy industrial machines called 'plants'?
How do babies know how to scratch an itch?

answers.answer: They did it once and it worked, so they keep doing it. It's like a reflex - a baby touches an itch, feels better, next time it happens they reach for it again.

questions.question: Did Ian Fleming get the idea for James Bond's code name 007 from a bus route between St Margaret's Bay and Canterbury?

answers.answer: 00 is the prefix for agents licensed to kill. Seven is his agent number. The prefix distinguishes agents - they may not want to write it down in case it's intercepted.

questions.question: Why are towns twinned with other towns, and is there any relationship between twinned towns?

answers.answer: It's just councils who decide, they get free trips. The original idea was to expand understanding of other cultures, to recognise the single uniting nature of humanity, a window on the world when travelling wasn't commonplace. Now it's mostly just a jolly for councillors.

questions.question: Why is the kitchen not called the cooking room, when every other room is named after its function (bedroom, bathroom, dining room, sitting room)?

answers.answer: Kitchen comes from German 'kuchen' meaning to cook.

questions.answer_to: What is the origin of the name James Bond?

answers.answer: James Bond was the name of an ornithologist who was friends with Ian Fleming, author of The Birds of Jamaica.

questions.question: Can a venomous animal poison itself or another of the same species?

answers.answer: Yes, they can. Honeybees: two queens born in a colony fight by stinging each other to death. Scorpions stab each other until one dies. Adders do as well.

questions.question: Who looks after pets and household things if someone is arrested in a dawn raid?

answers.answer: Any animals are usually contacted with animal wardens from whichever council controls the area. If they kick the door in, they have to contact the local council to come out and seal the door up. Bills can be dealt with from prison.

questions.question: Why do pyjama tops always have a top pocket?

answers.answer: To keep your handkerchief in (or a condom as a joke).

questions.question: How does suction work when the bag covers up the nozzle of the vacuum cleaner?

answers.answer: The bag is just a porous paper membrane. The motor creates suction in the chamber, pulling air through the paper bag. Air passes through but debris doesn't. That's why they're made out of paper, not plastic.

questions.question: Why do women squeeze toothpaste tubes in the middle and men squeeze from the end?
What's the difference between ginger beer and ginger ale?

answers.answer: Ginger beer is fermented with yeast (like his neighbour used to make in the airing cupboard). Ginger ale is just carbonated water with ginger flavouring added (like from a SodaStream). Ginger ale has less depth and is less pungent/spicy.

questions.question: Was the Big Bang called 'big' because of the size of the explosion or because it was a big event in history?

answers.caller: Professor Howell (University of Brighton, Professor of Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: It was coined by Fred Hoyle, who didn't believe in the Big Bang theory - he believed in a steady-state universe. He used the term slightly ironically/sarcastically. The 'big' refers to the scale of the event, not a sound. There was no noise because sound doesn't travel in a vacuum - you need a medium/atmospheric pressure. The bang itself is a misnomer; the big was bang on the money. It went from the micro (point mass of 10 to the power of 78 particles) to the macro (expanding universe).

questions.question: Where do seagulls come from? Do they have two homes - one in France and one in England?

answers.answer: The real question is how far from home can a seagull roam?
She sees seagulls on cruise ships days out from land across the Caribbean and Atlantic. She thinks they must have more than one home and live on top of ships.

questions.question: Why do cartoon characters only have three fingers and a thumb?

answers.caller: Robert (creator of children's TV show, caller from M25 near Rickmansworth)
answers.answer: It looks better visually and is more natural. Four fingers can look scary for young children. Also, it's easier to draw (historically).
Cartoonists have said before that they're easier to draw that way. It might even be part of Disney folklore.

questions.question: Why is it called the 'periodic' table? What's periodic about it?

answers.answer: The elements are organised by atomic number. The periods are the horizontal rows and groups are the vertical columns. The periods show recurring trends and characteristics of the different elements. It's a way of making sure elements go with their like ones, the similar ones.

questions.question: What is the tune that ice cream vans play?

answers.answer: Greensleeves - written by Sir Thomas More as a tribute to Anne Boleyn (or possibly Henry VIII claimed to write it).
It's definitely Greensleeves - also heard it on ice cream trucks.

questions.question: Are we the only country in the Western world that has a national anthem focused on one person (the monarch)?
What happens if you win the lottery? Where does the money physically reside?

answers.answer: There are lottery stewards around the country who present shows and can help. Camelot also have financial advisors to help winners. You can actually pay millions into your normal bank account.

questions.question: Why is a spider web also known as a cobweb? What does the cob part mean?
Do people sneeze and laugh in a different language according to where they live? Would it be the same with birds? Do they tweet in a different language?

answers.answer: Well of course they don't... Until I remember... No, anyway, you tell me.

I'm from India. My dad, rest his soul, when he sneezes, he'd go 'huh-cheh'. So people from different places do sneeze differently. The sneeze sound is not universal - it's culturally learned and reproduced.

questions.question: Why does milk have a skin on top when you boil it? Is there anything you can do to stop it?

answers.answer: The fat in the milk is more buoyant than the other parts, so it rises to the surface. That's why you get more skin on cream and custard than on skim milk. The fat rises to the surface and sticks together, binds.

Water can only evaporate from the top. So what's left gets more concentrated. At higher temperatures, chemical reactions work faster. The fats and proteins mix together better and form this gelatinous skin. To prevent it, put a lid on it - cling film or a plate.

questions.question: What's the difference between a duke and a prince?

answers.answer: Prince means you're either married to or descended from the monarch. Dukedoms are in the gift of the Queen - some are hereditary, some are not. Prince of Wales and Duke of Cornwall are titles in the gift of the monarch.

questions.question: How is the caffeine abstracted from decaffeinated coffee?

answers.answer: It's all about solvents. Sometimes they use hot water to make strong coffee then extract the caffeine using dichloromethane (used to be dry cleaning solvent). Caffeine is more soluble in the solvent than water, so it migrates to the solvent layer. Then they freeze-dry the remaining liquid for instant decaf. Sometimes they use water saturated with caffeine so beans don't lose their aromatic things - those beans can be used again.

questions.question: Do big cats (lions, tigers, lynxes) react to catnip like domesticated cats do?
Where does the silent K in English language come from? (knife, knee, etc.)

answers.answer: In Old English, the K wasn't silent. You can see this in German words where K is still pronounced at the start. They're called cognates - words in foreign languages that correspond with English ones. In the Germanic languages, they were still announced. It's not just K - the G in words like 'gnome' is similar.

questions.question: What is the storage capacity of our brain? Can it be compared to computer memory in gigabytes?

answers.answer: We don't know - scientists describe it as unlimited. Memory is very difficult to study because there are many factors affecting what goes in and what we can retrieve. Example: eyewitness testimony - different people see the same car accident and remember different colours. Memory is affected by attention paid, past experience. Things can be in there but we can't get them out - that's why hypnosis is used in serious cases.

questions.question: Why does washing always end up inside the duvet cover when you put them in the dryer? Even when she puts two duvet covers in, everything ends up in one.

answers.answer: Because your duvet cover's got a whopping great hole in it. It bangs about all over the place. It's easier to get in than it is to get out.

Combination of lobster pot theory and centrifugal force. Like when a lobster goes into a lobster pot - it's got a hole but it can't get out because the hole is smaller. Centrifugal force means anything that's in there will never come out.

questions.question: Why do our stomachs rumble? What is physiologically happening?

answers.answer: It's the acids, the stomach acids breaking down food. If there's not as much food, they're still bubbling away.

The digestive system from gullet to anus is all linked. It moves food in waves - peristalsis. Once it starts at the top it goes all the way down. That's why when you eat breakfast, soon after you need the loo - it starts that process pushing yesterday's food out. The rumbling is just movement. The acidic argument is part of it because some sounds are bubbles, but it only happens because the food is moving - either because you've eaten or you're in anticipation of eating.

questions.question: What statement is contained in: J M O T D I B (with J, M, T, D, P as capitals and 'in' underlined)?

answers.answer: Jim Morrison of The Doors is buried in Paris.

questions.question: What does each point represent in the FTSE 100? When it goes up or down by points, what does that actually mean in monetary value?

answers.answer: Admitted he didn't know the answer
Explained that the index was started at 1,000 points, and when looking at derivatives, each point is worth about £10. He was a futures options broker for 19 years.

In the early 80s, the FTSE 100 index was divided into 1,000 pieces when it started. Each day, the value of the market is divided into the new closing number of pieces. He was in financial services for 15 years.

questions.question: Why does the American military keep saying 'affirmative' for yes and 'negative' for no? In situations like a sniper waiting for a shot, wouldn't it be faster to just say yes or no?

answers.answer: You can't mix them up in a sentence. They're very definitive words that sound dissimilar to everything else, don't rhyme, so you can't make a mistake over the radio where a lot of conversation can be lost. Andy had 6 years in the military.

questions.question: On the day of a flight, if one of the pilots doesn't turn up due to sickness, how does the airline get another pilot? It's not like they have pilots hanging around the airport.

answers.answer: They don't need 101 pilots, just someone on standby.

As part of monthly rosters, crew have standby duties. Three types: home standby (you must be at the airport within a couple of hours when called), airport standby (wait in airport lounges), and quick response standby (stay at airport hotel, car picks you up quickly). Wendy had 35 years as airline crew.

questions.question: Tomorrow the moon is in perigee, its closest approach to Earth. Which part of Earth's surface will be closest to the moon?

answers.answer: It's also called a supermoon. Due to the axis of Earth and how the moon rotates around it, the closest point would be somewhere in the northern hemisphere - probably Scotland and Norway latitude. His sister was into astrology and astronomy. Also depends on height above sea level.

questions.question: Why do diplomatic cars in London have number plates in a different font to normal number plates? You can already tell they're diplomatic by the arrangement, so why the unique font?

answers.answer: So that everybody knows it's a diplomatic plate - belt and braces.

Plates are issued by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. Three numbers, D (diplomatic) or X (consulate), then three numbers. First three numbers denote the embassy, last three denote which person. The unique font makes them harder to fake, and the FCO has its own specific supplier. Also, diplomats can use standard DVLA plates but won't get treated specially. Steve was in the diplomatic protection group of police for 20 years.

questions.question: Why do flies come in every summer and circle underneath light fixtures that aren't even on? They go straight back if you shoo them away.

answers.answer: Maybe because it's the dead centre of the room and safest from predators.
Flies and moths work on the same principle - they navigate by natural light sources. They circle lights trying to orient themselves.

questions.question: Why do you have to send your birth certificate to get a new passport if it clearly says on the bottom of the birth certificate 'This document cannot be used for identification'?
Why do we vote in elections using a pencil and not a pen? Why not a permanent marker?

answers.answer: You can take a pen if you want, but pencils last forever. Equipment gets stored for years between elections. Pencils still work after five years in a cupboard; pens dry out. You could use a pencil for 20 years across multiple elections.
You can sharpen pencils. You can't sharpen pens. They last forever.

questions.question: Why is it called a 'spelling bee'? My son asked on the school run.
What makes our toes curl? What's the message from the brain to tell our toes to curl if we see somebody getting hurt or an accident?

answers.answer: It's like getting you ready. You sort of go... (Technical turn)

It's an automatic reflex of protection in the same way as a cat's claws flex out and curl inwards when they're in danger and the chicken will bend its talons round and such. It's a protective thing. It's to give us a stable base more grip more purchase on whatever we're standing on.
answers.qualifications: Discussed with her vet after noticing her cat's and chickens' claw behaviors

questions.question: Are the birds outside my window actually speaking to each other? The utterances are highly complex, non-repeating, and seem like a conversation back and forth.

answers.answer: They're actually having a conversation. The dawn chorus isn't all sweetness and light - they're marking out their territory saying keep off this branch, get out of my airspace. Different species of birds must be like different races of people - they're all speaking the same language.
answers.qualifications: His brother-in-law works for Norfolk Council and knows a lot about birds and animals

questions.question: Where do Savaloys stop being available geographically? I can't get them north of London but you can get them everywhere in London. What's the best way to get a Savaloy? Is there a Savaloy Gap like the Watford Gap?

answers.answer: You get them in the Midlands. If it does chips and fish, then it will do a Savaloy. You'd struggle not to see a Savaloy. And a proper chippy.

Savaloys are available in Inverness (Mr. Chip's with batter, Harry Ramsden's without), South Shields (Dickinson's and Dixon's Butchers), Newcastle, Peterborough, and East Anglia. The geographical split appears to be east-west rather than north-south. Savaloys have not crossed the Irish Sea (Irish correspondent horrified at seeing one in Crawley).
I work at Walk and Roll (a Chinese and fish and chip shop combined) and we sell Savaloys for £1.10. They're mainly pork.
answers.qualifications: Works in a fish and chip shop

questions.question: Why does hot water make a completely different sound than cold water when poured into a cup? I can tell straight away when water isn't hot just by the sound, and it's not because of the absence of steam.

answers.answer: The viscosity of boiling water is greater or lower than the viscosity of cold water.

The density of water changes with temperature. When you pour very hot water, it's less dense, so a given volume is lighter and sounds different. Plus, when it's nearly boiling with dust in the cup, there are small nucleation sites causing micro-boiling, making the sound different. Cold water's more dense, hot water's less dense.
answers.qualifications: Professor of the Public Understanding of Science at University of Brighton

questions.question: Why did ancient Greeks have lions in their war paintings when lions weren't native to Greece? How did they manage to capture them and bring them back home?

answers.answer: They went and got them from Africa. Same reason the Tudors brought giraffes and elephants to court at the time of Henry VIII. Because they were amazing and exotic and no one had seen them. Wealth on a scale hard to contemplate.

There were lots of lions in the Near East. The Egyptians used to mummify them and breed them because although they worshipped them, they hunted them to extinction. The Greeks had lots of trading posts in the Near East pre-Alexander the Great, so they would have had contact with lions. The Persians used to hunt them in game parks. Xerxes proved his bravery by killing lions. They were imported and used as symbols of power and strength.
answers.qualifications: Just loves Greek history

questions.question: Is there a rate by which the sea and its tidal flow turn stones into sand? Is there a general rule or level of friction that has to be achieved before a rock turns into sand?
If there's an explosion underwater, would the water nullify the explosion (cushion the diver) or would the shockwave be magnified by the water (injuring the diver worse)?

answers.answer: If I came round with a hand grenade, would you rather I put it in your pocket or in the bath?
