answers.answer: There's a very heavy metal plate at floor level, covered perhaps with a blanket or a Yoda-style landscape, but underneath is a very heavy metal plate from which extends a pole with a platform for you to sit on. The actual heavy metal plate is invisible but provides the stability. For the ones with walking sticks - the stick is resting on the same thing, the heavy plate provides the counterweight so you can stand perfectly still.

questions.question: What are the limits of diplomatic immunity? Can they steal sweets or do worse things? Where's the limit?

answers.answer: I think it goes all the way to the wire... I was listening to something on the radio the other day about diplomatic immunity and it certainly goes a lot more seriously than stealing sweets. I mean, it was a sexual assault... murder, extreme things like terrorism.

Strictly speaking, diplomatic immunity would apply to anything anybody does. However, if somebody does something really serious, the Foreign Office can approach the embassy or the government of that particular country and ask them to lift the diplomatic immunity, which sometimes they do. So if somebody commits murder, for example, or is suspected of murder... They can approach the embassy. You're not talking to our cultural attache about the disappearance of that person on such and such a day because our cultural attache is a spy. So you could commit a murder with the diplomatic immunity? You could do. The other thing the government can do is they can ask for that diplomat to be removed. You can expel them. But sometimes the government of that particular country will lift the diplomatic immunity so that the person can be prosecuted in this country.

questions.question: How are hallmarks dated? They have fancy stamps and letters instead of dates. Why don't they just put the date? Why is it called a skip?

answers.answer: I don't understand the question. I've got no idea what you're so cross about... Are you talking about hallmarks?... That little rule about dullness, a question to which only you will be interested in the answer, has rarely been as well fulfilled as it just has by you. It's just incredibly boring, isn't it?

Firstly, if you've got to stamp four letters or four numbers onto something that's very small and delicate, it's going to be far more problematic than stamping a single letter. Absolutely. Second part of the answer is that Hallmarks are the oldest protection in the world. They're getting on for a thousand years old. And if you go back seven, eight hundred years, you've got to do one little stamp. They used to stamp the letter because the date used to change every year, and it was different for each assay office. So one assay office might change it on the 5th of January, and the other one might change it on the 28th of July. But going back seven or eight hundred years, not everybody knew when the date was. It was only since the unification of the Hallmarking Act in 1975 that they changed all the hallmarks on the same day every year, and they changed the font and the surround and the style of lettering on the same day every year.

questions.question: Why did they change larboard to port? When did it change?

answers.answer: I don't know... The port changed to port so that everyone would know that's the side that's supposed to go into the port.

The two sides of a ship, one was called starboard because it's where the steering board was where they used to have, like on a Viking ship where they have a larboard and they had a large paddle on the side to steer it. So they couldn't put that side to the port. So the other side was the lading board and as usual things get slightly corrupted and it became larboard or loading board. So that would be port side. But, of course, you had rudders later on so that you didn't have a steering board. So either side could pull up alongside the other. But the name stuck. Larboard and starboard are so similar that in a gale or anything else, so people started to call it the port side. The side that you pulled up to the port because it was traditionally that was the side. And so that's why it became.

questions.question: I discovered last week that the warmth of LED light bulbs is measured in Kelvins. Who's Kelvin and what's he got to do with the warmth of a light bulb?

answers.answer: Kelvin was a scientist who invented the temperature scale that we used before Mr. Centigrade came along and invented a new one, Mr. Celsius. He's a British physicist, probably Scottish, from that era. He invented a measurement of temperatures that was in place before Celsius.

questions.question: Where does the word 'skip' come from? Why is it called a skip? It's like a giant bin. Why is it called a skip?

answers.answer: I can't think of any sort of even starting point on that.

I was a skip driver for years and I asked why it was a skip and he said it's all to do with the motions of skipping. When you have your arms, you've got two arms, right? And a chain. You've got two chains on each side of the arms and then you attach it to a drum or a skip. We have to call it a skip. It's the same as using a skipping rope. It goes up and it goes down. It's a quick form of when you're skipping and that's with the lorry using the arms. The lorry is the skip. The arms with the chain to attach it to the... It goes fast and it goes forward. It does, it skips. The actual motion of the lorry.

The actual answer is it's just a corruption of a skip. S-K-E-P. And that's Norse, Danish. It is Norse, yeah. It sounds Scandinavian. A skip was actually a... I had it in a crossword once. It was a boat of some sort. No, it's from the size, I believe. It's something to do with about the size of a bushel or something like that.

questions.question: Why aren't the trees in Chernobyl dead? I thought radiation kills, and why are the trees very green and luscious?

answers.answer: I don't know. I've never been there. Well, no, because you've got the stories about mutations. I don't know that it killed everything. But surely after a number of years, radiation kills you over a period of time.

Basically, trees grow very slowly. So you would see effects if you were looking at a shoot coming out of the ground because it's a lot of cell division, and that's where the radiation will affect the plant itself. It will actually sort of hit the chromosomal level and make the cell abnormal, like a cancer-type thing. And that's why with humans, because we have high rates of cell division, we get hit with it. But with a tree that grows, some of them live for a thousand years? It's a very, very slow process. So it will happen, but it will take a long time before you start to see any obvious issues with the tree.

questions.question: Why do regional accents disappear when singing? Andreas on X Factor has a strong Italian accent when talking but none when singing.

answers.answer: Most regional accents disappear when you sing. Because you're hitting a musical note, which automatically affects the cadences. It's not the same as speech. You don't want an accent when you're singing. It's deliberately... When Sting talks, he's a Geordie, but when he sings, you wouldn't know he was from Newcastle. Some do. I mean, have you ever heard Charles Aznavour sing, or Edith Piaf? If you listen to them singing in English, you can tell that they're French. So it does happen, but generally speaking, you're more likely to put off a listener if you've got an accent than if you haven't. Chaz and Dave are the only ones I can think of whose regional accents stay in place.

If you listen to people like Paul Weller and Lily Allen, and Chas and Dave, they all sing purposely in an English accent. But when people have singing lessons, they're all taught to sing American. If you look at the great works of the boy band Five, they all sing with an American accent. He's mimicking the songs that he's singing, he's mimicking the American version or the English version, which is sung in the American accent. It would be odd to listen to a song, learn it, and then sing the word differently from how you heard it.
[Answer about the singing question, but response was cut off]

questions.question: Why do Americans put the month before the day when they write the date? Why do they do their own thing?

answers.answer: I like that. What are you doing in Spain? You're living the dream.

I believe it goes back to sort of pilgrim days, whereas we say the 4th of December, they say December the 4th. I had to ask myself. They do... So if it was linked to the Mayflower, then that means probably we used to do it the way they do it now, but we've changed for some reason, probably because of links to Europe. So we've probably adopted the continental European way of doing it, and America has clung on to the old Anglo-Saxon way of doing it because they took it over with them on the Mayflower, and it stuck.

questions.question: What would Prince William's reign be called? Like Elizabethan, Victorian - what would Williamian or whatever be?

answers.answer: Wouldn't it be Carolingian, actually, to get the Latin right? It'd be Carolingian... What will Prince William's reign be known as? What will that era be for historians of the future? We'd have to be able to see into the future... I don't know, mate.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'more power to your elbow' come from and why?

answers.answer: That's a good question, actually. Well, I don't know. It would have been worth waiting for, but we're not going to get over the line with an answer. Quickly, I've got some phone lines free on this. If you know the answer to... the origins of the phrase more power to your elbow, it's quite literal, but why is it a phrase? The Willingian? The Willies.

questions.question: How long would it take a modern household computer to crack the Enigma code that Alan Turing's machine took so long to break?

answers.answer: The computer is simply the compute medium, and you'd need an application sitting on that computer to decipher the code. So it would depend on the efficiency of the application. Given modern-day technology, it would literally be half a second, if that. The hard work is the application - you'd have developers building it for months, but once in place, it's running.
It took a few hours with Alan Turing's machine. It'd take less than a second, almost certainly with modern computers.

questions.question: How could you tell that there's no oxygen in space just by looking at the sky? And how does the sun burn if there's no oxygen?

answers.answer: The original quote is quite right that most combustion reactions require oxygen. But the sun is not a chemical reaction - it's a nuclear reaction. It's nuclear fusion. In fusion, you're taking tritium and deuterium (forms of hydrogen) and squashing them together to form helium. That's why Helios is the god of the sun, and why helium is called helium. When you fuse something, you push them together - two becomes one. You get energy out of that. The sun is a giant nuclear reactor, rather than a ball of burning flame. The bad news is that sooner or later the sun's going to run out of hydrogen and start squashing helium, expanding into a red giant and swallowing us all up in about four billion years.

questions.question: Regarding Harry Roberts getting out of jail after shooting the three policemen - he's been in jail so long, he's 78. Do prisoners get a pension? Does he come out with quite a lot of money? Would he have accrued his pension over the years he was in prison? Does he not have to pay for lodgings?

answers.answer: He won't get any pension while he was in prison. If you were getting your pension during your sentence, the longer the sentence, the bigger the jackpot. Also, why would you spend half your life knitting mail sacks for 20p an hour if you're still getting a state pension? If criminals were accruing state pension payments while serving lengthy sentences, some of our friends at the less thoughtful end of the British media would have brought it to our attention and invited us to get furious about it.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'perfect stranger' come from? Perfect means without flaw, so why would you call someone a perfect stranger?

answers.answer: Perfect in that context simply means complete, absolute. As in a perfect circle or a perfect storm. A perfect stranger is a stranger of absolute strangeness - maximum strangeness. You're familiar with 'a perfect example' - it just means an unchallengeable example. And in the context of a perfect stranger, it highlights the extent of the strangeness - someone you don't recognise at all.

questions.question: Why do you have people of different hair colour, yet everyone's nail colour is the same? And they are made of the same stuff - keratin.

answers.answer: The keratin thing is a slight red herring. The answer comes down to our evolutionary roots. We evolved from small mammals. Our nails are descendants of the claws that our ancestors had, whereas our hair descends from the fur. Our nails, as the claws of all vertebrates, are formed from skin cells that get squashed down and filled with keratin. The cells are left with just a block of keratin, designed purely to be hard - either armour or to help our ancestors grab things. Our hair, on the other hand, is descended from fur that had an entirely different function - to camouflage us from predators. Fur is a solid block of keratin with certain pigments that go into it to make it a certain colour. Since we became primates, fur has sort of lost that function. There are different forms of chemicals called melanin that give the slightly different pigments that people have. You might as well have asked why rhinoceros horns aren't all different colours.

questions.question: Why are some people more ticklish than other people? Why are some parts of our bodies ticklish and others aren't?

answers.answer: I don't know if it's a neurological thing or something else.
Line was lost before the answer could be given.

questions.question: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen - can we manufacture water? If so, why don't we use it to solve drought?

answers.answer: It's really expensive to manufacture water. You'd need a rocket on such a grand scale to make enough water to solve a drought that it wouldn't be cost effective. As for why they say the amount of water in the planet remains constant - the amount of hydrogen and oxygen atoms is constant since creation, but they might be split and joined together at different points. Hal mentioned that rockets burn hydrogen and oxygen and create water.

questions.question: What determines if a child is left-handed or right-handed?

answers.answer: It's to do with your eyes. If you hold your index finger out about a foot away from your nose, and shut one eye, it won't move. If you shut the other eye, it will move. The eye that it doesn't move in is your dominant eye. Because that takes less time for that signal to reach your brain, that denotes whether you're left or right-handed. What determines the dominant eye is genetic inheritance.

questions.question: Why do you tend to refer to black people as 'people of colour' rather than 'a black person'?

answers.answer: I asked Oprah Winfrey's advice. She spent a lot more time worrying about these issues than I have. She said if in doubt, use that phrase and it won't upset anyone. The phrase 'colored' has become objected to by many, even though the NAACP is still the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. There's an awful lot of confusion. If you care about other people's sensibilities, there's a danger of tying yourself in knots. It's what people who resent not being able to be obnoxious and prejudiced usually call political correctness. But those of us who are very keen not to be obnoxious and prejudiced generally call it good manners.

questions.question: Why do we only see one rainbow when it rains?

answers.answer: You're only standing in one place. There are lots of water droplets and lots of sun. You can see more than one rainbow in more than one place - one to the east and another to the west if the circumstances are right. The likelihood of seeing one rainbow is already rare, and squared is the likelihood of seeing two.

questions.question: What is the male equivalent of the First Lady? If America gets a female president, what will be the status of her husband?

answers.answer: He'd be the First Gentleman of the United States. It's never happened, but the convention is in place. In fiction where there's a fictional First Lady, they all use that. Ladies and gentlemen - you say the opposite number of a lady is a gentleman.
Ex-presidents are still called Mr. President. So Bill Clinton would continue to be Mr. President.

questions.question: If I threw a stone in space, would it stop? And part about the Big Bang - what caused the Earth to stop?

answers.answer: The Earth is in orbit around the sun, so the solar system, gravity... The answer to the first question is yes, the stone would carry on forever. These spaceships now taking pictures of Mars ran out of fuel decades ago and they're still going. It's the Voyager thing that's just gone past Mars.

According to Newton's laws of motion, a body will not change its motion unless it's acted upon by another force. So if you throw a stone in space, it will fall towards anything that's got gravity, but it's not got any air resistance or friction to stop it. So it just carries on until it hits something. The Earth is hurtling through space. It's falling towards the Sun continuously. The Sun's gravity is pulling the Earth towards it.

questions.question: Where do double-barrelled surnames come from? I've never understood what the barrel is to do with it.

answers.answer: They're made up. Mine was. They're just invented by people who want to sound posher than they really are. Unless you've got four or five names, and then you're probably related to royalty.

questions.question: With all the foreign exchange premises throughout the world, how much at any point of a country's currency is held outside of that country?

answers.answer: I used to work in the city, and the Bank of England used to publish money supply figures every month. Part of that figure was notes in circulation. As certain notes expire and they're burnt, they issue new ones. So they know the total amount of notes in circulation. But to actually quantify the amount that is in any one country or... circulation possible, location impossible.

questions.question: How do they farm maggots? How do they get them on such mass?

answers.answer: The commercial producers of maggots have huge sheds with trays going the length of the shed, and underneath there's another tray to collect the maggots. They use rotten meat, fallen stock, animals. They slit the animals so blue bottles can land on them and lay their eggs. The eggs turn into maggots, and when the maggots fall, they drop down into these huge trays and are collected.

questions.question: Why don't birds eat worms that come out in the rain? The worms come out of the ground but birds don't seem to take any notice. Why is there not a feeding frenzy?

answers.answer: Maybe they're not hungry. Maybe they've had their fill.
They do eat worms - James later mentions callers are telling him that birds do eat worms.

questions.question: Why don't seagulls sit in trees?

answers.answer: A seagull is a cliff-dwelling creature, which is why they're drawn to skyscrapers. The perspective they enjoy from a cliff or a building makes it easier to spot any predators in the vicinity. If they're in a tree, they could get attacked from behind.
A seagull is a seabird and they have webbed feet. Webbed feet don't have claws, so they can't grip a branch. They could sit on a plank of wood, but couldn't grip a twig.

questions.question: Is a rainbow the same size wherever you are in the world?

answers.answer: No, they're not always the same size.

The rain falling from the cloud acts like a prism. It slows down certain wavelengths of light more than others, creating the rainbow effect. A small cloud with a small amount of water falling creates a small rainbow. A large cloud with more water falling creates a bigger rainbow.

questions.question: Why do we translate some foreign place names, but not all of them? For example, München/Munich, Marseille but Paris stays Paris.

answers.answer: I don't know, mate. That's a really good question. Perhaps München became Munich because everyone thought they were saying Munchies.

questions.question: What was the original time? Because clocks go forward and clocks go back, but the position had to start somewhere. Whichever one went first would be the original time, and the other one would be this made-up mythical time.

answers.answer: It started in the First World War. The clocks were put forward during WWI as a daylight saving exercise to try and save energy. In WWII, clocks went forward all the time - there was British Summer Time the whole year round. And in summer, there was double summer time when clocks went forward two hours from GMT.

Daylight saving was invented by William Willett, who lived in Chislehurst. He used to ride a horse in Petts Wood in the late 19th century and wanted more daylight time to ride his horse in the morning. He was an MP and had a bill passed in Parliament. There is a monument to Mr Willett in the middle of Petts Wood.

questions.question: If you have a little bit too much to drink, the next day you can't remember what you've done. Why does alcohol make you lose your memory?

answers.caller: Marenika (Kensal Green) - conducted research at university
answers.answer: Once you've had too much to drink, it stops the part of your brain that forms short-term memory. The alcohol affects the part of the brain that stores short-term memory, and that's called a blackout.

questions.question: What colour is a mirror? I'm looking at a mirror now and it's doing my head in. I can't work out what colour it is.

answers.answer: The mirror is silver. If you smash a mirror and all the glass falls off it, you're left with a plate of polished silver. You're seeing your reflection, not the colour of the mirror.

questions.question: Why are rain gauges narrow at the top when more rain falls across a wider area? It seems like more rain is falling in those five inches across than actually collects at the bottom.

answers.answer: You have a broader area which funnels down, and then you divide the width of the funnel by the amount of water in the bottom to get an idea of how much rain has fallen on a smaller space like an inch. It's measured per square inch or square foot.

questions.question: What is a lovebird? Is it true that they should be in pairs, or can they live on their own?

answers.answer: Lovebirds can live alone. The person telling this story had a pair of lovebirds, one died, and the other one lived fine for over two years after that.

questions.question: Where does the term 'get in cold feet' when getting married come from?

answers.answer: I think that cold feet relates to cold sweats when you get nervous. If you were getting married against your will, you'd come out in a cold sweat. The sweat drains to the bottom of your body.

questions.question: How many beans make five? My mum always used to say this to us as children and we never knew the answer. I'm 42 and I still don't know.

answers.answer: The only answer people have come up with is: a bean, a bean, a half a bean, a half a bean, a bean, a half a bean, a half a bean, which adds up to five. But it's a riddle with no definitive answer.

questions.question: What is the point in having white gold? Because if you like gold, you want it to show gold colour, not a silvery colour like platinum or silver.

answers.answer: White gold is more expensive than silver, but not as expensive as platinum, as platinum has natural rhodium in it, and white gold is plated by rhodium.

White gold is an alloy. Pure gold is 24 carat, which is yellow and too soft for jewelry. You mix it with silver and other metals. You can colour the gold by adding different metals. White gold became fashionable because platinum is so expensive. White gold is dipped in rhodium to stop it tarnishing, but the rhodium is not the white gold - that's what protects the white gold.

questions.question: Why is it traditionally good manners for men to take their hats off when they come indoors?

If you drink a cold drink, do you need more calories to consume that? Because it's a lower temperature than your body. So does it take so many calories just to heat that drink up to your body temperature?

answers.answer: Yes, technically. A calorie is the energy required to raise 1kg of water by 1 degree C. If you drink beer at 5 degrees (33 degrees below body temperature), you consume about 33 calories heating it up - about a biscuit or half a biscuit. However, it's a red herring - cold beer is technically marginally less fattening but not enough to make any real difference.

questions.question: Why is it when on my washing machine, on my dry cleaning machine, it's always in pounds, abbreviated LB?

answers.answer: LB stands for Libra - the Latin word for scales. A weight is a pound, so it goes back to Roman times.

questions.question: If you've got bigger ears, can you hear better?

answers.answer: In order to capture the most sound, the bigger the ears, the better. You capture more of the wave front of the sound coming towards you. It depends on the shape and direction of your ears - it's like an ear trumpet.

Theoretically correct, but in 15 years as an audiologist, he has never encountered a patient who was hearing better because they had larger ears. The difference between no ear and a standard-sized ear is huge, but the difference between a small pinna and a large pinna is not enough to actually affect hearing.

questions.question: When it's cold, why do we need to go to a toilet more often?

answers.answer: When it's cold and you shrink, your bladder shrinks, it can hold less water, so you need to get rid of it more often.

In the summer when you're hot, you perspire so you're emitting fluid via other routes, so you don't need to go to the toilet as much. In the winter, there's no perspiration, so you have to drink more fluid, which means you need to urinate more.

questions.question: Do animals have a preference for using either left or right paws? Like if a cat is playing with a mouse, would it favour its right paw?

answers.answer: At Center Parks, a nature expert showed that squirrels are left or right-handed - some strip pine cones in an anti-clockwise direction, others clockwise. This demonstrates that squirrels have a preference and other animals must as well.

questions.question: Why do men remove their hats when they come into a house? Why is it good manners?

answers.answer: Chivalry comes from the knights of old, and they would remove their helmets and armour when entering somewhere peacefully to show they're not going to attack you. They'd unveil as it were.

questions.question: What determines the colour of an egg?

answers.answer: It's all to do with the breed of the chicken, not the colour of the chicken. A Dutch chicken lays blue eggs, a South African black chicken lays tiny brown eggs about an inch long, other breeds lay normal brown or white eggs.

questions.question: Why do they dim the cabin lights in aircraft during the hours of darkness to take off and landing?

answers.answer: It's to allow your eyes to adjust to the darkness just in case you need to evacuate the plane - so you won't be blind coming out of the light into the dark.

questions.question: What determines the colour of an egg?
Why do they dim the cabin lights in aircraft during the hours of darkness to take off and landing?
What would happen if a party won an overall majority, but the leader of that party lost his or her seat? Who would be Prime Minister?

answers.answer: The parties have deputy leaders. The deputy leader would go to the palace and form a government. In due course, the leader himself would get a seat. Somebody would fall on his sword, go to the laws or whatever. The man would be re-elected and then would take over.

questions.question: Where does wind come from?

answers.answer: You've seen the isobars on a weather map. That is a measure of atmospheric pressure. Wind is merely air molecules moving across the gradient or differential of atmospheric pressure.

The air is surrounded by atmosphere, air. That atmosphere, that air is heated in different degrees, some parts of daytime, sometimes at night. The areas that heat expand, and the areas that are colder are compressed. So those different areas of heating and cooling create movement of air molecules - that's wind.

questions.question: What are the origins of the red carpets? Why do we have this tradition of anyone from celebrities to royalty walking up a red carpet?

answers.answer: The record comes from Greek times where it was used for dignitaries and heroes. It is mentioned in Agamemnon, which is a play by Aeschylus.

questions.question: What would you call a male sister in a hospital environment? If a man was a sister on a ward, would he be called a brother?

answers.answer: The male equivalent to a sister is called a charge nurse. All male members of staff are called charge nurses. And a male matron is called matron.

questions.question: Why is it that monks have a bald spot on the top of their head?

answers.answer: He refers to the tonsure. It may be a sign of religious devotion. The original origin probably goes back to the Torah, where you weren't allowed to shave the sides of your head. And that would have evolved over the years with male pattern baldness into deliberately shaving the top of your head and having hair on the side.

questions.question: Why does every answer have French after it on a passport and not any other language?

answers.answer: For centuries, before English became the predominant language, French was the international language for diplomacy - the lingua franca. So all diplomats on all diplomatic documents across the world were exchanged in French language.

questions.question: Where we can crack the Enigma codes and decipher encoded messages, why have we never managed to crack another species' language, even dolphins or dogs?

answers.answer: You're looking at the wrong end of the telescope. Animals don't have a language as sophisticated as ours. When you listen to recordings of whales or dolphins, there are clicks and words that must mean something, but they communicate about food and danger, not chats about what they did last night. We've learned how they communicate - horse whisperers, people who spend time with gorillas, dog trainers. We've learned how they communicate with each other, just not in a way that would allow them to communicate back in our language. There is a chance dolphins are having more sophisticated conversations than we realize, but I don't know how we'd ever work that out.

questions.question: How do I explain to a seven-year-old where wind comes from?

answers.answer: All the air is made up of tiny, tiny molecules. Imagine the smallest thing you can imagine - that's what the whole world is made of. Like tiny invisible Lego bricks. When they get hot, they get bigger. When they get cold, they get smaller. When they're all expanding in one place getting heated up by the sun, that's a big movement. Imagine a balloon being blown up really, really quickly - it's going to create a waft. Imagine that on a really big scale - there's wind.

questions.question: If the care of young children is paediatric and care for older folk is geriatric, what's the care of people in between called?

answers.answer: Paediatrics runs to 16. Geriatrics - you're no longer allowed to call people geriatric now, you call it care of the elderly, and that starts at 55. The lump in the middle is general medicine. Everything that a doctor does for you, he could also do for a child or an old person, but there are things specific to children or old people that don't apply to adults in between.

questions.question: Where on earth do flies disappear to at winter?

answers.answer: Flies don't have a very long life. They all die towards the end of summer, but they've laid eggs that in the cold winter don't hatch. And when it warms up again, the eggs hatch. You've got maggots and then you've got flies.

If flies seek refuge in warm places like light shades, they can still come out in winter. The eggs can stay dormant for ages - it's only when they get hot that they hatch. Sometimes you get an infestation of flies in winter and when you trace it, there's someone who's laid eggs in your light fitting.

questions.question: Why is it traditional for people to have grapes as visitors in hospital?
What are the origins of the red carpet tradition?

answers.answer: It originates from Greek times in the 5th century. The Greek king's wife set him up to be killed using a red carpet. In the play Agamemnon, she puts down the red carpet for him to walk on. In those days, carpets were laid out as a way to honor gods. He walks on the carpet and she whacks him over the head as he steps in the house.

questions.question: How does my nan and granddad's apple tree grow pears when there's no pear tree around it anywhere in sight?
Why is it when you go for a meal, you put your knife and fork together after you've finished your meal and not to the other side of the plate?

answers.answer: So the waiting staff knows that you've finished. Often the waiting staff might have been speaking Anglo-Saxon and they'd be serving nobles who only spoke French, so they wouldn't be able to say 'Oi, John, I've finished.' You'd put your knife and fork together and that would deliver the message to the waiting staff that they wanted their plate taken away. The reason you don't put the cutlery to the side is because you want the cutlery taken away as well.

questions.question: Do horses ever get tired of standing up? Because I've never seen one sitting down.

answers.answer: Horses do sleep standing up. They have a ligament in the back of their leg called a check ligament, which locks, which prevents them from falling over when they sleep. So it's not putting any stress on their legs. They do lay down and go to sleep, but only for short periods of time. They will lay down more if they're out in the field surrounded by friends - it's a security thing. You'll have some standing up, some laying down sleeping. But there'll always be one on the lookout.

questions.question: Why do cats get fur balls but dogs don't? Dogs are always molting, there's hair all over my house, but it doesn't coagulate in the same way that softer cat fur does.

answers.answer: A cat's tongue is rougher, like little needles sticking up, so when it licks its fur it pulls the hairs out. A dog's tongue is smoother. There's simply more hair going down a cat's throat than a dog's.

questions.question: Why are people's heads so shiny when they're bald?

answers.answer: Because of the oils being secreted - it's called sebum. You have to wash your hair once a week because of the oils. If you haven't got any hair, the oil that would normally end up on your hairs just gives your head a lovely polish.

The essential shininess is caused by the grease coming out of the pores - the sebum. Bald heads are a bit more matte or gloss depending on how much sebum you're producing. Some people produce less sebum than others, hence some bald heads are shinier than others.

questions.question: Why does frosted glass go clear when you make it wet?

answers.answer: The water fills in all the sort of points of diffraction.

Frosted glass is created by roughly sanding the top surface. When you introduce water to that sanded surface, it takes away the impurities and it takes on the transparency of the water. That's why it goes transparent when you put water on it.

questions.question: Is there any naturally occurring blue food? Not blueberries because they're not blue - they're more purple black.

answers.answer: If you eat blue ice cream in Baskin and Robbins, it turns your poo blue - but that's synthetically created and doesn't count.
Some species of lobster and prawns are blue when uncooked - you'd have them in sushi.

The inside of blue ring ginger has a blue ring, which is naturally occurring. It's called blue ring ginger. At a local Sainsbury's, nine times out of ten you'd be getting blue ring ginger. Also, most carrots originally are purple, and some salad potatoes are purple too.
Stilton or any other type of blue cheese - the edible mould is blue and it's a food.
There's a blue mushroom popular in China that's edible, and lingcod is naturally blue.

questions.question: Who has the final say on how a word is spelt in dictionaries? Who at the Oxford Dictionary decides?

answers.answer: There's a committee of people who decide what gets in and how it's spelt. Susie Dent from Countdown also works for the Oxford English Dictionary - she might be part of that.

There's an international body called the Oxford English Corpus that monitors all spoken and written English. They get together once a year, discuss what they've heard and read, and put forward suggestions for new words. Those are decided by a small group within the body.

questions.question: If all cells renew themselves except brain cells, how do tattoos last?

answers.answer: When you get a tattoo, the ink goes beneath the first layer of skin - between the epidermis and dermis. Your body thinks it's a foreign object, so white blood cells come along and try to absorb it. But the ink particles are too big, so they get stuck and suspended and can't go anywhere. That's why tattoos don't disappear - the ink is trapped under the skin by your white blood cells.

questions.question: If people started flapping their arms about now, over time, would they gain the ability to fly?

answers.answer: No - evolution can't work that way.

answers.caller: Professor Smith (University of Middlesex - Professor of Robotics)
answers.answer: No, absolutely not. You can only have small changes in evolution - incremental. And if that tiny change helps you survive and reproduce, then it's going to stay in the DNA. But if it doesn't help you reproduce or live longer, then you will die out. It can't stay there because you want it to - it has to provide a demonstrable reproductive advantage.

questions.question: Why do menstrual cycles synchronise when women are in close proximity with each other?
Why do buses not have seatbelts when all other modes of transport have them?

answers.answer: Buses are exempt from seatbelt regulations. When I was training as a bus driver, I recall reading that if a vehicle stops more than 10 times within a mile, it's exempt from seatbelts. Postal vans have the same exemption.

questions.question: How many humans does it take to actually start the human race as we know it?

answers.answer: The fundamental basis of evolution is a tiny change that gives you an advantage over every other creature you're competing with. Humanity as a species began when one individual developed a genetic mutation that gave them an advantage. That mutation was passed to every child, grandchild, and great-grandchild. One genetic improvement can constitute a change of species if it's big enough. Evolution is a genetic accident that gives you an advantage in the reproductive stakes.

questions.question: If humans evolved from apes, why are apes still around?

answers.answer: The improvement from ape to human was only undertaken by a tiny, tiny, tiny fraction of the ape population. The rest of the ape population stays put, still lives in the trees, still breeds, still has baby apes. Ergo, apes are still around.

questions.question: How do they know what flu vaccine to develop before the flu season even arrives? How do they know what type of flu you're going to get?

answers.answer: They look at the World Health Organization statistics for flu viruses across the world, and they choose from that which they think is going to be the most likely to make it to Britain. And then on the back of that, choose to play with a vaccine. It's educated guesswork.

questions.question: Who put the camera there? Neil Armstrong was supposed to be the first man to ever arrive on the moon, and you see the camera focused on the steps with him coming down.

answers.answer: It was just a remote control camera.

questions.question: Why is pet food not fit for human consumption? I'm standing here with a tin of cat food containing tuna, fish, shrimp, omega-3 and omega-6, rice. Nothing else. No preservatives. This tin was made at the same tuna canning factory that human consumption tuna is.

answers.answer: They stick it in the pet food and they've worked out the maximum you're prepared to pay for pet food. They bung it in that tin, stick 'not fit for human consumption' on it. Otherwise, you'd never buy the expensive tuna again.

The laws governing what you put on the ingredients for pet food are probably laxer than food for human consumption. When you put 'not for human consumption' on it, it probably means this is indeed the sweepings off the abattoir floor, and if we were trying to flog it to humans, we'd have to say so, and no one would buy it. So by calling it pet food, we don't have to go into the same amount of detail.

questions.question: Why is toad in the hole called toad? It doesn't make any sense. You've got a hole. You'd much rather have a sausage in the hole.

What makes us left or right handed? I want a proper answer. I don't want scientific facts. I don't want scientists to think there's a chance. I want a proper definitive answer. If there's facts, there's facts.
The Queen left Buckingham Palace today and her colours have split. How long has she got to be gone before her colours get taken down and the union jacket is put back on?

answers.answer: If she's staying there tonight, they won't bring it down again. They can't be doing it. If she went out tonight, went to the shops, had a quick browse around Budgins and got back home, they couldn't be bringing the flag up and down again.

It's when the flag flies that she is in residence. So when she goes to Balmoral, Sandringham, Windsor, the flag is taken down. It doesn't fly when she's indoors. If she's kipping there that night, the flag is flying from the palace.

questions.question: On an aeroplane, how come the passengers sit facing the cockpit and the cabin crew is the other way, facing the passengers?

answers.answer: It's a lot nicer to face in the direction of travel, and the staff and the crew have to keep an eye on the passengers. You wouldn't want to travel backwards, would you? You want to face the direction of travel.

They're called jump seats. They don't all face backwards for a start. They can face sideways. The reason they're in the places they are is because they're flat folding. They have to be fixed to a bulkhead. That's purely why they are where they are. On a jumbo, you've got 14 cabin crew.

There's a Civil Aviation Authority rule - you need to be able to see the customers in the cabin. Also, on military transport aircraft in the UK, up until recently, all Royal Air Force passenger transport aircraft had their seats facing backwards because it's safer if you crash and your back will absorb the impact and the chair will absorb it.

questions.question: How on earth can anyone decaffeinate a coffee bean? My carer says it's all a big scam, there's no such thing.

answers.answer: It is not the bean that one decaffeinates. It is the drink. Caffeine is pretty tasteless. They've put it in shampoo now.

The problem with trying to take anything out of coffee beans is if you take one thing out, you're likely to take other things out like the oils that make it smell nice. They use a particular solvent called dichloromethane, which used to be used as dry-cleaning fluid. That removes most of the caffeine, which is quite bitter. There's also another method where they use water pre-loaded with some of these oils so they don't dissolve.

questions.question: How come people riding on a bike when it's raining don't need windscreen wipers on their helmet? Surely it's a safety hazard.

answers.answer: Aerodynamics - you're going fast enough for it all to blow off, and if you're going slowly, you give it a wipe. You wouldn't want a windscreen wiper on your helmet. You'd have to have a battery in it. It'd be flashing in front of your eyes.

questions.question: Why do most chairs have a hole in the back of them?

answers.answer: It's simply because it's cheaper. You need less plastic.

questions.question: How did people born before the birth of Christ know what year it was?

answers.answer: There were very many different calendars. The Egyptians, the Mesopotamians, the Jews, the Greeks. The Romans had a different calendar. It's only the Christians who do the BC/AD distinctions. Other parts of the world still count the years differently as well, religiously.

questions.question: Why are partner companies known as sister companies? Why aren't they known as brother companies or uncles? When we say our sister station, Capital Radio, Heart FM, Classic FM, why is it not brother?
If you take a normal carrot and cut it long ways rather than chopping it, and then cook it, why does it always taste better?

answers.answer: The inner part of the carrot is sweeter than the outer part. So when you cut them into batons, you'll get more of the sweeter inner part.

questions.question: If the Earth didn't have a moon, would we still have tidal seas?

answers.answer: No. It's the gravity of the moon that is responsible for the tides.

questions.question: Why are things like boats called 'she'?

answers.answer: Because they carry life.

questions.question: Why is the watershed called a watershed? It clearly has nothing to do with water.

answers.answer: The watershed is the level at which water endangers a craft. Like a pencil line.

In geography, a watershed is where the water hits a cliff or mountain. Half falls one way, half the other. It applies because one side of the watershed has guided content, the other has adult content.

questions.question: How does a spider get the initial string from one tree to another tree without going down the trunk? Does it lasso it?

answers.answer: The spider spins a line and allows the wind to carry the web to the article it wants to go to. The spider dangles on the end of the line like a pendulum, and the wind blows the spider pendulum, and it grabs another bit where it starts webbing from.

questions.question: Why does runny honey start to solidify at the bottom of the jar?

answers.answer: Unless you regularly shake your honey, the heavier honey particles sink to the bottom and the lighter particles float at the top. You squeeze out the runniest bits first until you get to the very bottom where you've got the least runny bits.

Honey is a super-saturated solution of sugar and water. As you keep using it and introducing impurities (crumbs, butter), the sugar crystallises out. To return it to its original state, stand it in hot water or microwave for 20 seconds and the sugar re-dissolves.

questions.question: If I've got an open bottle of champagne I want to keep fizzy for the next day, why does putting a fork handle down in the neck work?

answers.caller: Professor Hal (Professor of Public Understanding of Science, Brighton, calling from Moscow)
answers.answer: It's a MYTH! If you put a bottle in the fridge without a spoon and a bottle with a spoon, they will be equally fizzy the day after. The solubility of carbon dioxide in cold water is a constant. It's the cold fridge that makes it more soluble, not the fork.

questions.question: Why do people applaud to show their appreciation of something? As opposed to shaking their heads or not doing anything?

answers.answer: In the olden days, they used to pat the actors on the back on their way out. Because not everyone could get to the actor, people started clapping their hands instead.
It's evolutionary. Monkeys clap and laugh in exactly the same way. It dates back to our days as apes in the trees.

questions.question: Can a blind person from birth dream? And if they can, what do they see?

answers.answer: They obviously dream, but quite what they see or experience during the night is something we need to hear from someone who is blind to be 100% clear on.
They have feelings instead of pictures. They touch and sound and sense. They have echoes like we do of whatever their sensory experiences were during their waking hours.

questions.question: What does Regis mean in place names like Lyme Regis, Bognor Regis, and Hulton Regis?

answers.answer: Regis refers to the monarch. It’s a gift from the monarch to a town that he or she liked. Bognor Regis and Lyme Regis were popularised by George III as holiday destinations, and he allowed them to call themselves Regis as a mark of kingly affection. It’s like how Kensington can call itself the Royal Borough.

questions.question: Why do we follow the male lineage on our family tree? Why do we keep the name of the father as opposed to the mother?

answers.answer: In olden days, the man was the breadwinner, doing business with the outside world. He was the recognisable face of the family. Carrying the mum’s name would have been meaningless in the marketplace or in the next village along. Also, men care about stuff like that.
We follow the male line in genealogy because the surname never really changes, as opposed to the female where the surname changes through marriage.

questions.question: Why do salt pots have one hole and pepper pots have multiple holes when traditionally pepper as a spice was more expensive?

answers.answer: Salt was so precious you'd keep it in a small pile on the side of your plate, and one hole helps you make a pile as opposed to a general sprinkle.
Salt attracts water and clumps very easily, so having a bigger hole means you can get the salt out very quickly. In drier continental European countries it's the other way around because of humidity.
In France they do have it the other way around - it's true.

questions.question: What's the mechanism for the brain that decides what goes into short-term memory vs long-term memory? And how do I get things from short-term to long-term?

answers.answer: Short-term memory lasts about 18 seconds and has capacity of 7 plus or minus 2 chunks. Long-term is indefinite. You get information from short to long-term by depth of processing and rehearsal - repeating the information to yourself. Also meaning attached to memories helps, things of particular importance are processed deeper.

questions.question: Why do we say 'step' in stepdaughter, stepson, stepmother, stepfather? What does 'step' mean?

answers.answer: You step up into the role of a surrogate parent.

It's a corruption of old German/old English word for orphan or bereaved. 'Stufen' means bereave or bereavement. A child without a parent becomes a stepchild, and the step-parent is the step-parent of that stepchild.

questions.question: Why did the foot department change from 'chiropody' to 'podiatry'? What's the difference?

answers.answer: There is no difference. Podiatry is an Americanism, and a few years ago they changed over to podiatry to avoid confusion. On his training course, the podiatrist confirmed they do the same things.

questions.question: Where does the name 'Undertaker' come from for funeral directors?

answers.caller: Tom from Hornchurch (professional organist at crematorium for 10 years)
answers.answer: Historically there were no professional undertakers. They were members of other professions - often carpenters - who would undertake to conduct funerals and make coffins. They branched out into doing the whole funeral service.

questions.question: Why is Africa called a subcontinent? What does 'sub' mean here?

answers.answer: Sub means under, like in submarine. Africa is a continent but the Indian subcontinent is part of the Asian continent - if you have a landmass that's big enough and part of another continent, it's called a subcontinent.

questions.question: Why does the moon look so bright from Earth but when you see it on TV it looks dull and grey?

answers.answer: The camera has a dichoric coating developed by NASA on the lens that reflects radiation and sunlight away - like expensive Ray-Bans for the camera. That's what astronauts have on their gold visors too.

questions.question: Why do mushrooms and toadstools grow in crescent or horseshoe shapes in the grass, not straight lines or randomly?

answers.answer: Mushrooms aren't individuals - they're the fruiting body of one organism growing underground called mycelium. They grow from one spore evenly around the ground and when they fruit, they do so at the same sort of distance, creating a circular effect.

questions.question: Why isn't the time we spend in the womb counted after we're born? Why don't we count from conception?

answers.answer: You can't know when you were conceived. Even with modern science, gestation periods vary - James's eldest was two weeks late, neighbors were two weeks early, supposed to be born the same day. It would have been historically impossible to start the clock at conception.

questions.question: Do animals ever have identical twins like humans do?
Why are some people naturally hot and others naturally cold? Not due to illness or body size, but two similarly built people in the same room where one is warm and one is cold.

answers.caller: Judy from Chingford (obesity and diabetes specialist)
answers.answer: It's metabolism and thyroid. Someone with a fast metabolism has their body clock working quickly, warming internal organs, so their body cools down through sweat. People with slower thyroid don't need extra warming because internal organs stay warmer.

questions.question: Why do I not sink when I'm in the swimming pool? I just bob about on the top vertically, not on my back. I don't have to hold on the side or tread water. I can do it indefinitely.

answers.answer: It's all to do with body fat composition and distribution over your body. Women tend to float much higher in water than men because of higher distribution of fat over the stomach, hips and chest. Men have a much higher distribution of muscle from the waist down so they tend to sink.

questions.question: Why are doughnuts called doughnuts when there's no nuts in them?

answers.answer: The ring doughnut looks like a nut as in a nut and bolt. The shape has a hole in the middle.

It's dough-naught. Like adding a zero. Not N-O-U-G-H-T. Doughnaught. As in a naught shape made of dough. A jammy doughnut is not a real doughnut - it's masquerading as a doughnut, it's really just a jam-filled ball. In France they call it a boule de Berlin.

questions.question: How comes skin doesn't let moisture in from the outside when it lets sweat out? If you stood in a swimming pool, your whole skin wouldn't fill up with water, would it?

answers.answer: I don't think it's one-way traffic. I think fluid can pass into your body. It's osmosis.

Actually, you can let moisture in. Sweat glands pump water out because water has a high specific heat capacity - it evaporates and cools you down. But we do take in water when you're in the bath. We are basically a salty bag of liquid. There's a semi-permeable membrane called your skin, and water passes through it via osmosis to try and counterbalance the concentration of the bath water with your plasma. The pruning of skin when you've been in the bath does NOT have anything to do with osmosis - apparently it's an evolutionary trait caused by the brain to enhance the grip of your fingers underwater.

questions.question: Where did the phrase 'over the moon' come from?
Why do I get bags under my eyes when I'm tired? Why does tiredness cause them to puff up and go dark?

answers.answer: It's actually a condition called omasis. It's more common with ageing. The muscles supporting your eyelids weaken, and the normal fat cells that help support the eyes migrate forward into the lower eyelids, causing the lids to appear puffy and dark. The temporary instances of it are to do with lifestyle and tiredness and alcohol - when you're dehydrated, fluid builds up in the space below your eyes. It can come and go depending on fluid retention. There's no house remedy for it - the only treatment is cosmetic surgery to tighten the muscles under the eyelid. My partner is an optometrist and I suffered really badly from it from age 16.

questions.question: What would be the eyeball's equivalent resolution to a TV? A normal HD TV has a resolution of 1080 pixels by 1920 pixels. What is the resolution of a human eye?

answers.answer: When light comes into your eye, it's focused on the retina at the back, and there are lots of dots there called rods and cones. You've got about 100 million rods and about 10 million cones. The rods see black and white light, and the cones see coloured light.

The rods and cones answer was totally out of the game - that's not really answering the question. Pixelation only started when digital came into being. Previous to digital, when we used cameras with lenses, everything worked on a lens basis. It's more to do with lenses and visual acuity, not counting rods and cones.
576 megapixels. That's how good your camera phone or camera has to be to be as good as a human eye. Professor of robotics, and a keen photographer for many years.

questions.question: I know DEFCON is a level of alert, but what does DEFCON actually stand for?

answers.answer: Defence Readiness Condition. His qualification was video games.

questions.question: If James were knighted by the Queen and became Sir James O'Brien, his wife would become Lady O'Brien. What happens with gay marriage and civil partnerships? Will it just be two sirs and two ladies? If Mrs O'Brien gets ennobled, what does James become?
Does a bee know it will die when it stings?

answers.answer: No, they don't know they'll die. Their intention is not to sacrifice their life. Human skin is quite tough and leathery to the sting of a bee, so the sting gets caught in the skin. When the bee tries to make its escape, it leaves a little bit of itself behind - it essentially disembowels itself. It would never do it deliberately.

questions.question: Why is a cheesecake called a cheesecake when all that is on it is coconut? I bought one from Greggs and it was just biscuit-based with pastry and shredded coconut on top - there's no cheese on it whatsoever.

answers.answer: What he's talking about is a London cheesecake - flaky pastry, icing sugar, and shredded coconut. They've been around since before cheesecake came to England from America. The coconut on top looks like grated cheese.

questions.question: What is a blue moon? As in 'once in a blue moon.' If there is one, how can I see one and what causes it?

answers.answer: A blue moon is when you get two full moons in the same calendar month. The second full moon in the month is called a blue moon. It's not actually blue - it's just the terminology for two full moons in one calendar month.

questions.question: What determines the arc or size of a rainbow? My four-year-old daughter asked why a rainbow is so big.

answers.answer: A rainbow happens when light is broken up because different colours of light get slowed down by different amounts. It's to do with refraction, like a prism splitting light.

questions.question: Where does the term medicine ball come from? Why is it called medicine when they're just leather balls used in gyms?

answers.answer: They used to build up muscle. If you were recovering from tuberculosis, you would go to the gymnasium which literally means something to do with health, and the medicine ball would be part of your prescription.

The medicine ball has been around for thousands of years before Christ, used for exercise, health, sport and building muscles. The word 'medicine' used to mean health or exercise, not just doctors and pills. It's just the change in the meaning of medicine over time.

questions.question: What are the little rooms with doors along the harbour wall at Dover? There must have been 30 little rooms all along it.

answers.answer: The doors on the harbour wall are storage units built during the war. They're now storing life-saving equipment and navigation buoys. Further up in the cliffs are doors to listed buildings containing diesel tanks for the Royal Navy during the war, dug out by Cornish tin miners, about 30 foot high and 80 foot wide. There were tunnels coming off either side with big pipes leading to separate places.

questions.question: What is the scientific reason for dreams? What makes them happen - what's the brain chemistry?
Do any creatures other than humans combine ingredients to make food or make it nicer? Like a monkey eating a nut then licking a leaf?

answers.answer: Honeybees combine nectar with enzymes to produce honey. They leave it until it's dehydrated so there's only 16% liquid. But the enzymes come from within the bee so it may not count as combining two foodstuffs.

Japanese macaques collect sweet potatoes and wash them in saltwater to impart saltiness which they find preferable. Chimpanzees put eggs in one side of their mouth with leaves in the other and chew them together. Monkeys also put bitter nuts in the sun for weeks to dry them out, then crack them on their own anvils which takes nine years to learn - it makes them sweet instead of bitter.

Horses and other grazing animals mix grasses, berries and things in their mouths. They pick a bit of one and a bit of another, and some horses will consciously mix their food if given sugar beet in dry food.

questions.caller: Nick Shule in Toronto (Twitter Mystery Hour)
questions.question: Does catnip affect large jungle cats the same way it does domesticated cats? Does it work on lions, tigers and leopards?

answers.answer: Yes it works, but whereas you need only a small pouch for a domestic cat, for a lion or tiger you need like a builder's bag full of it. I watched an Animal Planet programme at Ripsnade where someone threw balls of it into a lion enclosure and the lions were purring and rolling around like overgrown kittens, going absolutely crazy.

questions.question: Why are human bodies symmetrical? Why are all mammals and animals symmetrical?

answers.answer: There's no evolutionary advantage to being asymmetrical. We developed symmetry because it's advantageous - you'd be wobbling and falling over all the time if you were wonky.

Human beings actually aren't symmetrical. Your heart is slightly to the left, liver to the right, stomach and bowels go round in a circle. Our external view has evolved to appear symmetrical because in evolutionary terms, the more symmetrical something is, the more attractive it's perceived to be. If you Photoshop someone so the two sides were identical, they'd look quite different. So externally we appear symmetrical but internally we're totally not.

questions.question: Why is a meal called a square meal when most people eat off round plates?

answers.answer: A square meal is one that's got everything represented - proteins, carbohydrates, all the nutrients.

It's a historical naval term. When people were gang-pressed into the Navy, they were often malnourished. The one advantage was they got three meals a day on board ship. The place where the boards were on the ship was square (not round) because it's easier to make square wood boards that don't fall about. 'Bed and board' comes from this - board meaning food. The square board where they ate became 'square meal'.

questions.question: Why do we not eat turkey eggs? Are they poisonous?

answers.answer: We don't eat them because we want them all to hatch so we can eat the turkey at Christmas. They're not poisonous at all.

questions.question: Why do pot noodles/instant noodles have more calories when you add water than when you don't? Water has no calories.
Is it normal for a 13/14-year-old boy to have hair under one armpit but none under the other?
Why is it 'being sent to Coventry' when colleagues refuse to talk to you, rather than 'sent to London' or somewhere else?

answers.answer: Coventry during the English Civil War was a Royalist stronghold, never actually taken, completely walled and fortified. More importantly, it was a place where very important Parliamentarian prisoners were sent. They were allowed absolutely no communication with anyone from outside, or even minimal contact from the guards. Being sent to Coventry means being put in a place where no one could communicate with you. Low-ranking prisoners would have been allowed visits, but the senior ones were allowed nothing at all.

questions.question: How do police operations get their names? (Context: She heard about 'Operation Biscotti' in relation to a murder case in the New Forest and thought it sounded flippant for a serious crime)

answers.answer: There's no science to it. Various departments in the police use code words. The officer in charge of a particular part of an investigation would decide. The senior investigating officer (SIO) would judge whether it was ridiculous or offensive. If the answer was no, then it would probably be okay.

questions.question: Why is the speed of light (c) squared in E=mc²? What's the physical reason for it being squared, not just the mathematical one?

answers.answer: The equation says mass and energy can be converted from one to the other. To get a certain amount of energy (E) from mass, you multiply the mass by c squared, which is a large number squared, making a massive number. This explains why a tiny bit of plutonium causes a massive explosion. You get an awful lot of energy from a very tiny amount of mass. Einstein found that relationship. The answer is essentially 'because it is' - that's the relationship.

questions.question: What is a rasher? Where does the word come from? Why is it only used for bacon? Is there anything else that is considered a rasher?

answers.answer: In his father's transport company, 'Russia' was a nickname for thin people. At David Gregg's company, when you asked for bacon they'd say 'how many russias do you want?' It was a measurement of thin. He thinks it might be Saxon or French in origin.

The Italian verb 'rasolare' means to shave thin. It's spelled raso, rasa, rasher. So rasher means a shaving. The French also has 'rasage' which likely influenced English with the Norman invasion. A rasher is a shaving - a thin slice of something.

questions.question: Are all mammals born with umbilical cords?

answers.answer: The duck-billed platypus is a mammal but lays eggs.
The infant platypus has an umbilical cord attached to the yolk in the egg. Like baby birds, it has an umbilical cord connecting to the food store in the egg. Wayne's answer was incorrect.

questions.question: The dollar sign used to have two lines through it but now has one. When did it change and why?
What is the difference between an android and a robot?

answers.answer: An android has a degree of autonomy and a brain, and is more humanoid looking.

answers.caller: Professor Smith (Middlesex University, Professor of Robotics)
answers.answer: A robot can be something like a robot arm in a factory or a robot car. It comes from the word 'Rossum's Universal Robots,' a play written by Czech writer Karel Čapek. An android is derived from 'andros,' meaning man, so it's a humanoid-looking robot. There are already androids in existence, even though there aren't any robots with brains.

questions.question: How do companies ensure they don't have the same barcode on products as other products?

answers.answer: There's a centralized database of barcodes. There's an organization that runs barcodes and they ensure there's no duplication. You have to apply to get a barcode and it's given to you. You can't just draw your own.

questions.question: Why is it that one minute past midnight is considered the next morning? If midnight means the middle of the night, shouldn't it still be night time?

answers.answer: It's actually the middle of the night because the night doesn't actually end until sunrise. One minute past midnight is still night time. The next day begins on the morrow, at sunrise.

questions.question: If Scotland votes yes for independence, what will be the most northerly point in the United Kingdom? What will replace Land's End to John O'Groats?

answers.answer: Marshall Meadows Bay is the northernmost point in England, just outside Berwick-upon-Tweed. There's a first and last pub in England there called the First and Last, which marks the border.

questions.question: When you suck the juice out of an ice lolly and only have the ice left, does that mean the juice has a lower melting point?
Why is the zip up the back of a wetsuit and not up the front?

answers.answer: Two reasons: comfort and logistics. The back is a fixed point with the least flexibility, so the zip stretches and moves less there. On the front, you'd get uncomfortable welts on your chest and stomach, and the rigid zip would cause terrible chafing. Also, when waves pound you, a front zip would get ripped open. That's why they're on the back.

questions.question: Why is the Ace of Spades more decorative than all the other aces?
Why does lamb have a B at the end? (silent B in lamb)

answers.answer: Lamb is a very old word from Anglo-Saxon/Old English, which was the Old English word for a young sheep. Most silent letters come from either Old Danish or Old English. The word was lamba in Anglo-Saxon.

questions.question: Why do we have birthmarks? What causes them?

answers.answer: There are two types. One is caused by too much skin pigment (melanin), like moles - brown marks where pigment is trying to protect skin from ultraviolet. This is more common near the equator. The other type is reddish birthmarks, caused by too many small blood vessels near the skin or poor nerve supply to those blood vessels. It's genetic variation, a random mistake rather than design - no reason for them.

questions.question: Can chickens have twins? If you get a double yolker egg, why don't you get two chicks hatching?

answers.answer: Twin chicks don't hatch. The shell isn't big enough for both of them. They stay tiny and undersized, and if you try to break the shell, they bleed and you lose them. Over 40 years of keeping chickens (mainly silkies), she's had about three eggs with twin chicks, and they always die. She now shines a light through eggs and if she sees two yolks, she doesn't put them in the incubator - just has them for breakfast.

questions.question: Do emergency services vehicles have different sirens? And why?

answers.answer: There is no difference between fire, police and ambulance as in different tones. The only difference is the supplier of the unit and speaker, which may give a slight tone difference. All vehicles are fitted with whale (whoop), yelp and two-tone settings. When two fire engines go together in tandem, they use different settings so motorists know two vehicles are coming - you don't want both on the same setting or a car pulls out and gets wiped out.

questions.question: Why is 666 the number of the beast? What is the relevance?
Why don't we sneeze in our sleep?

answers.answer: Two reasons: 1) When you're lying still, you're breathing in recycled air in your room, so there's not much to cause you to sneeze. 2) As you go into REM sleep, your brain actually paralyzes your voluntary muscles so you don't act out your dreams (so you don't jump off buildings or fight superheroes). You're essentially paralyzed, so you can't sneeze.

questions.question: In the cockpit of an aeroplane, if you've got the captain on the left and the co-pilot on the right, if the controls are the same or more or less the same on both sides, why does the captain always sit on the left? Is there an operational reason why it's better off for the captain? Is it a tradition?

answers.answer: It goes back to the first side-by-side planes in the 1930s. The early engines had propellers that went anti-clockwise, and that creates a force called propeller torque that makes the plane want to go clockwise. They stuck the pilot on the left-hand side to slightly counteract that force. But if you're flying with a co-pilot, it makes no difference. And on a jet aircraft, it's completely irrelevant, but the tradition has sustained. A lot of planes now have propellers going the other way, but it's just become a tradition.

questions.question: What is the difference between a chemist and a pharmacy? They sell the same thing. Drugs. Why can't they just mean the same thing?

answers.answer: A pharmacist is a subset of a scientist we call chemist. All pharmacists are chemists to a greater or lesser degree, but not all chemists are pharmacists. Chemistry is the study of how matter interacts. Pharmacy is particularly the chemistry of medicines, but nowadays also includes things like microbiology. To define a pharmacist properly, they have to pass a degree accredited by the Royal Pharmaceutical Society and done a pre-registration degree. In years gone by when barbers did surgery and so forth, the chemist would also do the chemistry of medicines and other stuff. They were a sort of jack of all trades. But nowadays it's much more regulated. In terms of what the shops do, the answer is there is no difference at all. Boots the chemist could as well be Boots the pharmacist. Sometimes when a pharmacist goes to their lunch break, they're not allowed to dispense medicines. So then it's designated as a chemist without a pharmacy in it, because they cannot give certain prescription-only medicines without the pharmacist being present.

questions.question: Can we actually see the American flag that was planted on the moon when the Americans went to the moon, from a telescope from the ground? Has it ever been proven to be actually up there?

answers.answer: Sent a picture suggesting the flag can be seen from Earth with a telescope

Mythbusters did an episode that refuted all the conspiracy claims about the moon landing. They said there's no way you can see the flag with a telescope from Earth. But what they did leave out was the huge reflective mirror they placed on the Moon. You can fire a laser to the right coordinates from Earth and have the laser bounce back to you - that's proof we are standing on the Moon. There was more than one flag as well. The first one fell down - Buzz Aldrin said it was knocked down by an engine exhaust as Apollo 11 lifted off.

questions.question: Are there any Concorde concourses that could be made to fly again? Could they be made airworthy? Are any of them actually air-ready?

answers.answer: My father-in-law, who's an aircraft engineer, said whilst you may be able to get the parts and get it flyable again, it lacks something called an airworthiness certificate, which is basically its permit to fly. Unless you owned a massive plot of land where you owned the airspace as well, you can't actually get one off the ground. They can make parts for classic vehicles and could remake the parts for Concorde if needed. But they wouldn't be allowed to fly it anyway. It was mothballed for economic reasons - too expensive to run.

questions.question: What's the difference between a house and a cottage? Can you get a cottage in town? Is it a size thing? Is it an age thing?

answers.answer: The difference is houses have slated roofs and cottages have thatched roofs.
You can tell if it's a cottage if you open your front door and you're immediately in your living room. If you open your front door and there's a form of hallway or segregated area, that's a house.

questions.question: What happened to sheep before humans sheared them? Did they just run around as big, fluffy balls of wool? Does wool keep growing if you don't shear a sheep? Does it grow infinitely?
How old is the average glass of water? Is the water we're drinking the same water that the stone cavemen were drinking? Does water just keep getting recycled?

answers.caller: Professor Martin (Middlesex University, Professor of Robotics)
answers.answer: Yes, it is. It hasn't always been here in liquid form - water was only here in liquid form when the Earth had cooled sufficiently, which was about 4.6 billion years ago. You can tag water using radioactive elements in it which you can detect. At very extreme dilution levels, you could have drunk the sweat of Socrates. It's constantly being redeployed and recycled continuously all the time.

questions.question: How does a shark smell blood so quickly from such a great distance through water? Like if a couple of drops go in the water over a mile away, they almost turn and head towards it straight away. How does it travel so quickly?

answers.answer: They can't actually detect a drop of blood in a mile of water - that's a myth. They can detect blood in the water and are highly sensitive to it, better than any other fish. But the myth that they can detect it that quickly from that distance is wrong. If there was a big tuna or something over that distance, they would pick it up after probably half an hour, but the myth that they can pick it up that quickly is wrong.

questions.question: If you can't see, you're blind, and if you can't hear, you're deaf, is there a word for if you can't smell? If you have no sense of smell?

answers.answer: The answer is anosmia. You're anosmiac if you have it. Graham himself has it and says it's not debilitating in the sense that if you're deaf or blind you can't engage with so much of the outside world. Most of our sense of taste is smell when we eat, so eating becomes less exciting - you get excited about texture, but it's mostly just refuelling. It can be common after head injury - James Cracknell got it after his head injury.

questions.question: Why aren't there any solar panels on houses in Tenerife? I noticed on holiday in Grand Canary there were no solar panels on houses, but there are loads of wind turbines. It's quite sunny there, so there should be a proliferation of solar panels as well.
Why aren't there any solar panels on Tenerife?
If we produce saliva while we're sleeping, and if we do, do we still swallow it whilst we're asleep?

answers.answer: You do swallow when you're asleep because the swallow is a reflex. You don't actually think about swallowing your saliva. It just happens. While you're in the show, for example, it just happens. It just also happens when you're asleep and saliva is produced, obviously, much less because you're sleeping.

questions.question: What does it mean when people start a sentence with 'yeah, no'? Why do people do that?

answers.answer: It's thinking space, a verbal silence, a verbal pause, as opposed to actual silence, or just going 'hmm'. It's just a sort of quicker moving way of pausing and thinking. In the olden days they would have said 'ah' or done a contemplative chin stroke, mulling it over.

questions.question: When we get nervous, why is it that our stomach gets affected and we get butterflies, as opposed to any other part of our body?

answers.answer: The muscle that runs from your mouth all the way down your tummy and then to the small intestine is classed as a food muscle. The chemical at the neuroreceptive point is called acetylcholine and that is what pushes the food all the way down through the intestine. When the adrenaline hits those neuroreceptors, some are going to be firing off as normal and some are being swamped by adrenaline.
