So you're going to have a mismatch of the actual muscle pushing the food through and that gives you the queer feeling in your tummy. The adrenaline floods the receptors that are ordinarily responsible for peristalsis.

questions.question: Why are all planets or suns or any astral bodies spherical?

answers.answer: When stars are formed, they're attracted round by gravitational force. The spinning from the Coriolis effect creates the mass to start spinning out to the outside at the top of the fringes. But the gravity pulls it back in because of the pressure around it, which is universal. It becomes a round spherical object in the same way as a water droplet is round. So it's not stuff that's been knocked off. It's the immense force being applied to the planet that pulls it into a spherical shape. That's why asteroids, because they don't have the gravitational pull, are irregular shapes. But planets, because they're such a great pull from the gravitational forces and the spinning effect, create a perfect sphere. Like spinning when you do pottery on a wheel - everything's trying to spin out to the outer circles, but the pressure from the outside and the gravitational pull from the inside creates a perfect sphere.

questions.question: Why is there no part of the Welsh flag in the UK Union Jack?

answers.answer: The Welsh flag is not represented on the Union flag because Wales is a principality and all the others are kingdoms. When the Act of Union came about, it was the Act of Union between the kingdoms of Scotland and England (and Ireland was considered the kingdom of England). Wales is just a principality.

Wales is not represented on the Union flag because previously under Edward I, Wales was actually conquered and essentially became a part of England. When Edward I tried to conquer Scotland he wasn't able to, largely thanks to Robert the Bruce. As a result, Wales was considered a part of England and subsequently combined with the Scottish flag.

questions.question: Do animals, namely cats and dogs, get jet lag?

answers.answer: Animals don't have the same sleep pattern as humans. We have a set pattern - we sleep eight, seven, nine hours at night and are awake all day. Animals don't. They sleep at odd times. Dogs get in the basket at bedtime but some still sleep half the day round and then all night too. They don't have a fixed sleep time because they haven't got jobs. Animals haven't got the same complexity in their brains as humans. They just sleep when they think they will.

Jet lag is a result of your internal body clock not being in sync with external cues. An animal has got a different internal body clock, so they will have a different duration of sleep. Animals do have circadian rhythms but they operate differently than humans.

questions.question: In war films, why is an enemy aircraft or missile known as a 'bogey'?

answers.answer: Bogey is the NATO code word for any incoming enemy aircraft or missile. It's just a random word - code words were chosen specifically because they didn't have any relation to what they were identifying. It's a code word, it didn't have any real meaning.

An unidentified plane, as opposed to an identified one which is a bandit. It used to appear as a dot on radar screens which were green. A green dot on the radar screen looks a bit like a bogey. An unidentified aircraft is called a bogey until identified.

questions.question: What qualifies a town to give its name to its respective shire? Why do we have Bedfordshire but not Lutonshire?

answers.answer: It would have been the county town originally. The county town is where taxes were collected. It's the administrative centre of the county. The administrative centre gave its name to the shire.

questions.question: Did any British Tommy survive the whole First World War from 1914 to 1918 in the trenches?

answers.answer: Initially, the first 30,000 troops that went over (the British Expeditionary Force) got wiped out within the first three months. So of the original 30,000, none survived. Some must have been in hospital or on leave though.

questions.question: Would a baby get head rush in the womb when upside down?

answers.answer: It wouldn't work in the womb because the baby is suspended in amniotic fluid. The baby spends most of its gestation period upside down anyway.
I was a baby. [I remember from when I was a baby]

questions.question: Why don't we have a Royal Army? We have Royal Navy and Royal Air Force.

answers.answer: Because the Army, after the defeat of the Royalists in the Civil War, couldn't be called Royal, could it? They'd killed the King. There are regiments with 'Royal' in their names - Royal Fusiliers, Royal Engineers - but the British Army as a whole couldn't be Royal from that point onward.

questions.question: Did the Big Bang actually make a noise?

answers.answer: Outer space is a vacuum. There was no one there to witness the Big Bang, so there would have been no noise. The Big Bang is only a method of explaining how the expansion of the universe took place - it wasn't literally a bang as in an explosion.

Sound requires a medium - it's a compression wave where one molecule bumps into the next. The Big Bang was an expansion of space, not a conventional explosion. There was no space and no time before the Big Bang, and no medium for sound to travel through. The term 'Big Bang' was coined by Fred Hoyle as a disparaging comment.

questions.question: What's the age of consumption of alcohol on aeroplanes? Is it a universal age, or is it from the country you're coming from, or the airline, or the country of origin of the airline?
Why do flying ants only seem to appear when there's a storm brewing up?

answers.answer: Flying ants do mating flights - males and queens fly off to mate. They look for the same temperature and humidity conditions, usually before a storm, so they can mass together and mate with other colonies to reduce inbreeding. The humidity and temperature trigger their flights.

questions.question: What is brain freeze?

answers.answer: It's something to do with nerve endings in the roof of your mouth. When they get cold, blood vessels in your head dilate, and your brain interprets that as pain - hence brain freeze or ice cream headache. A way to stop it is to put your tongue on the roof of your mouth to warm it up. This explains why water doesn't cause it - milk coats the inside of the mouth differently.
Same answer my daughter gave me about two weeks ago - it's nerve endings in the roof of the mouth.

questions.question: Why do phone keypads and calculator/computer keypads have different number layouts? Phone numbers start 1-2-3 at the top, but calculators start 1-2-3 at the bottom.

answers.answer: The telephone predates calculators. Even on the old round dial, numbers were arranged 1-2-3 at the top left going down to 9 and 0 at the bottom right, with letters assigned to each number. Calculators were invented for accountants who would run their fingers up and down, so they naturally started with low numbers at the bottom. Computers just incorporated the traditional calculator structure. They reflect their separate histories.

questions.question: If you buy a stamp in Spain to send a postcard back to the UK, does the British post office get any money from that? They only do half the job.

answers.answer: It's a reciprocal agreement between all nations. When you pay for postage over here, the money goes to your postal service. But if it's going to Spain, the Spanish postal service will deliver at cost to them under this reciprocal arrangement. Otherwise the postal service wouldn't work internationally.

questions.question: What is the origin of the term nutmeg in football? When you knock the ball through someone's legs, why is it called a nutmeg?

answers.answer: Nutmeg was a very valuable trading spice centuries ago. The theory is that nut meaning testicles and meg meaning leg - in Cockney slang, 'nutmegs legs' rhyming slang for leg. When you kick the ball through someone's legs, you're kicking it through their very valuable parts.
When a nutmeg starts to ripen, the skin splits in half. It looks like a pair of legs and then you can see the actual nutmeg inside.

questions.question: Why do they call it spring rolls, not autumn rolls, winter rolls or summer rolls?

answers.answer: It might be because the vegetables that are in them come out in the spring.

questions.question: Is it libel or slander when someone on radio says something defamatory?
With a computer mouse, one of them is called a mouse, but what do you call more than one of them?

answers.answer: The plural is mouses with an apostrophe, like CDs. Mouse is actually an acronym for 'Mentally Operated User Selection Equipment' or 'Motion-Oriented User Selection Equipment' - both were developed by Xerox in the early 80s and handed over to Steve Jobs. So it's already plural, hence apostrophe S.

questions.question: Why don't books have age ratings on them?
Why is Oxfordshire shortened to Oxon instead of having a T added like Hampshire to Hants?

answers.answer: The Latin for Oxford is Oxonia, which is O-X-O-N-I-A. The abbreviation comes from two oxen.

questions.question: Is a name a word? If you can spell it, isn't it a word?

answers.answer: Yes, a name is a word. It's a noun. A word is a collection of letters that conveys meaning, and Kevin conveys Kevin-ness to everybody in Beckenham.

questions.question: What is the ringing tone you hear when making a phone call? Is it analogue or digital? Where is it held?

answers.answer: The ringtone comes from the exchange. In old automatic exchanges, a common machine on each selector bank sent out the ringtone to indicate the line was free. With digital, it's just a block of chips doing the same thing. Foreign exchanges have their own tones.

questions.question: Why is a toilet called a loo?

answers.answer: The word comes from 'gardy-loo' (G-A-R-D-Y-L-O-O), from an old dictionary. In medieval Edinburgh, people used to throw chamber pot contents out of windows, and the toilet was called the 'garderobe'. 'Gardeloo' meant 'look out for the slops' - so it was a warning before someone threw their waste out the window.

questions.question: How did cats and dogs come to be pets? Why cats and dogs specifically and not other animals?

answers.answer: It's about symbiosis and mutual benefit. The original relationship between hunter-gatherers and domesticated cats or dogs was entirely about humans getting protection and insulation from vermin and warnings, while the pets got fed and didn't have to hunt. A dog barks to warn you of intruders, a cat catches snakes and rodents.

questions.question: Why do some people always sneeze twice? Why don't we all just sneeze once?
How can Dyson claim the Airblade is the most hygienic hand dryer when you have to put your hands into a potentially dirty machine?

answers.answer: It's about speed and exposure time. The Dyson blasts everything off really quickly in a very short time, whereas traditional dryers heat up the air and spray it over your hands for a longer period, warming up and spreading any germs.

The Dyson is 99.98% bacteria-free because it's coated with silver technology - fine particles of silver in powder form mixed into the casting of the hand dryer. Even if you touch it, germs won't stick around the way they would on other surfaces. It has a lifetime guarantee.

questions.question: How far can the human eye see?

answers.answer: 7.2 billion light years. In 2008, there was a gamma ray burst visible to the naked eye for about 30 seconds that was this distance away - that's the furthest naked eye object ever seen.

questions.question: Can someone explain chemtrails? Why do some planes leave trails that stay for hours while others dissipate quickly?

answers.answer: It's basic physics - pressure, temperature, and water content determine how quickly contrails dissipate. Different planes are at different heights with different engine sizes, fuel types, and temperatures. The government is not putting secret chemicals into the atmosphere. There's no conspiracy here.

questions.question: Why when you sit on a beach is the sun always in front of you?

answers.answer: The sun is only in front of you if you're facing it. Turn around and it's behind you. You only notice it being in front because most beaches face the water and people face the water.

questions.question: Why does expensive wine taste better than cheap wine?

answers.answer: The answer is complicated - it's a journey from subjective to objective. Factors include: terroir (the land where wine is grown), quality of vines and grapes, whether grapes are hand-picked, biodynamic methods, the winemaker's expertise (expensive to employ), barrel types (steel vs French oak vs American oak), and other production variables. Ultimately it becomes somewhat subjective - most people can tell the difference between a £3 bottle and a £10-12 bottle, but once you get above £30-200, it starts to become more blurred. Like art, people have different tastes. A master winemaker's gift is to reflect what is likely to be felt by everyone tasting the wine.

questions.question: How come the mosquito transmits the malaria virus but it doesn't transmit the HIV virus?

answers.answer: Mosquitoes have two tubes - one goes to the stomach, one injects anesthetic. HIV cannot survive in the mosquito's gut because it hasn't evolved to survive like malaria has. Malaria is parasitic, not viral, so it can survive in the mosquito's gut.

questions.question: Why is the address 59 1/2 Southwark Street a half? What makes it a half?

answers.answer: They wanted to turn 56 into two buildings, so they called one of them half.

He used to work there. It's London Councils. The building is quite old, actually built after all the other buildings around it. They had 59 and 60, but built something in between the two, so they called it 59 1/2.

questions.question: Is there any other part of the body where the anatomy changes from the singular word to a plural word? The word changes completely.

answers.answer: Yes, there are. Tooth and teeth, foot and feet. You rang in with one and now you have two.

questions.question: Why do dark colours absorb more heat than light colours?

answers.answer: Black is the absence of light. Black clothes absorb all the light. White is a mixture of all frequencies of light, the whole spectrum, and it reflects all the colors. Something that's red reflects red light but absorbs all other colors. This works with infrared and other spectrums too. That's why we wear white in summer for cricket and tennis, and dark clothes in winter.

questions.caller: Owen (via Twitter - first ever Twitter Mystery Hour question)
questions.question: When a new PM moves into Number 10, are they allowed to change the decor, pictures, colours, etc.?

answers.answer: There are two answers relating to different parts of Number 10. You have the apartment where the PM and family live, and the government bits beneath that. The government bits are less alterable and controlled by committees and civil service. Inside the apartment itself, the PM can make changes. He referenced a former PM deciding the kitchen needed work.

questions.question: Why does all fake tan, product self-tan or spray tan, smell like old biscuits or popcorn?
Where does the word fortnight come from for two weeks? What is a fortnight?

answers.answer: It's just short for 14 nights - fourteen nights.

questions.question: When lightning strikes at sea, does it kill all the fish that are in proximity of the strike?

answers.answer: Yes, it'll kill the fish if they're very close. Electric eels kill fish with electricity and fishermen stun fish with electricity, but it doesn't travel too far through water. Otherwise a massive lightning storm would be followed by a biblical plague of dead fish washing up on shores. If it hits a shoal of fish, it will kill the lot.

questions.question: Why is the chess board checkered? Why is it white and black squares?

answers.answer: The black and white squares are important for draughts/checkers, not for chess. Chess was originally played on a hatched board without colors. Because the two games got packaged together in the modern world, the convention stuck for chess too. But for chess specifically, you could just have a delineated hatched board with no colors.

The queen always goes on its own color and bishops are stuck on one square - the black bishop on black squares only travels on black squares. This makes the game easier to track and prevents cheating.

questions.question: Why does the £2 coin say 'Standing on the shoulders of giants' and why is it written in English?
How did they measure the height of mountains before electronic devices like altimeters?

answers.answer: In olden days, surveyors used a device called a theodolite. They started from the sea with benchmarks at known heights above sea level. Then they set up the theodolite, measured the angle to the top and the horizontal distance, and used trigonometry (Pythagoras) to calculate the height. They worked in stages up mountains.

questions.question: Why do naval personnel wear their medals higher up on their uniform (virtually on their shoulder) while army, police, fire brigade, and RAF all wear medals on their left breast like everyone else?
What makes your voice change and go high pitch when breathing in helium gas from balloons, and why does it only last about 10 seconds?

answers.answer: The helium contracts your windpipe in a similar way to stretching a balloon opening, making the air come out contracted and squeaky

When you breathe, your larynx has a flap of tissue that vibrates at a certain frequency determining your voice pitch. Helium is six times less dense than air, so when you breathe it in, your larynx vibrates faster and your pitch goes up. The opposite gas (sulfur hexafluoride) is six times heavier and makes your voice go down in pitch.

questions.question: How did homing pigeons know where to deliver messages? How did they know to go to the right place?

answers.answer: The key word is 'homing.' Pigeons are trained to go back to their base/home. They have one home base - like a cat that comes home. You can't send a pigeon to a new base; you'd need new pigeons trained for that place.

Researchers originally thought pigeons had a magnetic compass in their brain, but they've discovered pigeons make mental maps as they fly around during training. When taken somewhere, they fly back using these mentally memorized maps.

questions.question: How are his chickens surviving 21 days sitting on eggs without eating or drinking? The food and water levels haven't been touched at all.

answers.answer: When chickens are broody, they're not laying eggs (which takes energy), so they don't need as much food and drink. The energy that would go into producing an egg a day is being conserved.

Broody hens will sit on eggs forever unless you encourage them to get up. You need to pick the chicken up, shut the hen house, keep them away from eggs for about 10-20 minutes, give them food and water, then open the house. Hens do lose weight brooding and need extra food to produce the heat for the eggs.

questions.question: Are there any major world sporting events that aren't every four years? (like World Cups, Commonwealth Games, Olympics which are all four-year cycles)

answers.answer: Darts and snooker tournaments are annual and international. Wimbledon and other tennis tournaments are annual too. However, these feature individuals from international countries rather than national teams.

questions.question: Why do we have reflexes in our knees and ankles when the doctor taps them? What's the purpose of this reflex?

answers.answer: The knee reflex is probably there because you have a muscle there, and there needs to be a way of activating the muscle that doesn't involve sending a message to the brain - going manual instead of automatic. Other muscles probably have reflexes too, but you can't access them as easily as the knee.

When you bend the knee and keep it relaxed, tapping stretches a tendon. This sends a nerve signal up to the spinal cord, which triggers the quadriceps muscle to contract, making the leg go up in the classic knee-jerk reflex. Any tendon could do this, but the knee's proximity to the skin surface makes it accessible.

questions.question: Why is a nap referred to as '40 winks'? Why not 20 or 50 winks?

answers.answer: It's just a synonym for snooze or nap. Someone decided to call it '40 winks' and it caught on, like someone named you 'Joe'.
Someone told him it's called 40 winks because 40 minutes is the perfect length for a refreshing nap.
It refers to the 40 days and nights that Jesus spent in the wilderness - a Lenten echo.

questions.question: What is the unusual smell that you smell in all health food shops?
Why do we all have national anthems? Who invented them?

answers.answer: We have national anthems for propaganda reasons - a nation wishes to increase its profile. The interesting thing is the Soviet Union didn't have a national anthem after the revolution; they used The Internationale (the anthem for all nations) because revolutionaries were internationalists. Stalin later introduced a national anthem.

questions.question: How much does it cost to make a penny?

answers.answer: It's relative to the price of metal. It costs around 0.9 of a pence to make so they make a profit. If you had 100 pennies, their weight in copper would be worth more than a pound.

questions.question: Why are Conservatives often referred to as Tories?

answers.answer: The word Tory comes from the people who lived on Tory Island off the coast of Donegal in north-west Ireland. They used to come ashore to rob and plunder - they were cops, thugs, robbers and thieves.

questions.question: Where does all the mud and aggregate from Crossrail go? Where's it all going? They must have a massive mound somewhere.

answers.answer: It goes to a nature reserve off the Essex coast called Wallasey Island near Southend. They're using the soil to create a wetland nature reserve for birds. They're adding to the island, making it bigger with all the soil from Crossrail. I used to work for TFL as a contractor.
That's absolute rubbish, James. They dig a hole and bury it.

It goes to multiple places including Rainham in Essex, up the A12, and by train. RSPB London confirmed it's sustaining wildlife and helping with flood defenses at Wallasey Island. A lot of it goes to quarries that get backfilled. I worked on Crossrail bringing muck away at night. They had 21-ton machines digging 50 foot down, stockpiling during the day, lorries taking it out at night - 19 tons at a time. It's not all going to one place.

questions.question: Why are cash registers known as tills?

answers.answer: A till is a very old term for a drawer or cupboard or shelf where you store your money at home. This developed into the business cash register being where you store money. I sell cash registers and EPOS equipment for a living.

questions.question: When were piggy banks introduced and why a pig?

answers.answer: Pig, spelled P-Y-double-G, is the name of a particular type of clay that was used to make pot in the early days. Then in the early 50s, one of the big banks picked up on the idea and made it into a pig shape. Danny in Loughton asked this question a couple of years ago and we went definitive on that.

questions.question: Why do fridges have lights but freezers don't?

answers.answer: You don't need a light in the freezer. When do you ever open your freezer in the dark? You might need a late-night snack from the fridge, but you're not going to have a late-night frozen snack.

The temperature in freezers is so low that if you put a light bulb in, the change in temperature isn't good for it. They can make bulbs that work, but it would cost about 50 quid extra on the price of the freezer. You don't open the freezer as much as the fridge either. In newer freezers they do have LEDs which are low power and low heat.

Many moons ago, fridges and freezers used to be separate. The only place you'd need a light was in the fridge because people used it from dusk or dawn when there wasn't brilliant light - back when fridges were kept in the larder. Freezers were kept in outhouses and you only went there during the day. When they put fridges and freezers together, the light in the fridge remained. You can have a light in your freezer but it's an optional extra and costs more.

questions.question: Where did the word 'strike' come from?

answers.answer: A strike is an action you take to change something. If you're a blacksmith, you hit a piece of metal with your hammer to change it. If you're a fisherman, you strike when a fish first nibbles. The action you take changes the state of something, which is why it's called a strike.

questions.question: Why would red sky in the morning suggest an oncoming storm or maelstrom? Why does red sky at night mean shepherd's delight but red sky in the morning means shepherd's warning?

answers.answer: It's air pressure. Air pressure at a certain level in the evenings speaks of tomorrow being nice. The pressure of the air filters the sunlight in a way that creates a red sky, and that suggests later in the day there'll be thunderstorms.

questions.question: Do you hear when you read? How do we actually hear our thinking process? Why do we use the word 'hear' for internal thoughts?

answers.answer: You're not hearing when you think, you're processing language. Words are being flashed across like a computer screen. The only things you can hear are sounds. You can't hear things that aren't sounds. You keep using the word 'hear' because you associate language with sound, but you're not thinking of the written word - which is also processed.

questions.question: Why do the little fish (mollies) follow my six-year-old's hand around the aquarium?

answers.answer: Fish are creatures of habit. If you stand by your pond or fish tank and feed them by hand, they get used to it and expect it. They just get used to the hand and expect feeding every time they see your hand move. (Claimed PhD in marine biology)
Yes, quite a lot of species of fish do that (give birth to baby fish rather than laying eggs).

questions.question: Is there any etiquette tradition for sharing an armrest in theatres, cinemas, on the tube, or on an aeroplane? Whose is it - the left one or the right one?

answers.answer: There is no rules, no etiquette. You're expected to get on like grown-up adults and share the armrest. His wife Judith has had complaints about this and treats people like naughty school children, telling them it's better to agree and get on. Maybe one person has it for the first half of the flight and the other for the second, or just share - one goes forward, one goes back.

questions.question: How did I manage to cut through both slices of bread in a ham sandwich but leave about half a centimetre piece of ham uncut in the middle?

answers.answer: The uncut bit of ham was effectively a scabbard for the knife, and you were still cutting the bread with the scabbard.

The bread has a lower density than the ham, so as you're trying to cut through the ham and you're not quite cutting through it, the ham is applying pressure to the bread and creating basically a part fit because of the higher pressure. It's like a scabbard of meat. (Mentioned studying science and understanding differences between materials)

questions.question: Why are all the buildings in Amsterdam made out of such small bricks?

answers.answer: The intricacy of the brickwork and smaller bricks signified how much richer you were - it was a case of ego and showing off. Smaller bricks cost more money and more time to put together. When walking down the streets of Amsterdam, people wanted others to look and go 'wow, look at that - a lot of work gone into that.' His Dutch architecture student friend studied this.

questions.question: Why is a coconut shy called a coconut shy?

answers.answer: Shire is an old English word for throw. So a coconut shy is just where you throw stuff at coconuts. (He knows the word from cricket when you have a throw at the stumps)

questions.question: Do animals' voices break in the same way as humans do? Does a dog's voice break during puberty like a human boy's voice changes?

answers.answer: Her large dog started off with a yucky bark at six months old and gradually it went yap yap woof woof and now it's really deep - coinciding with the dog being seven months old and its 'little things dropping'.

questions.question: The sun goes around (Earth around sun = a year), the moon goes around the Earth (a month), the Earth goes around on its axis (a day). So what's an hour, minute and second?

answers.answer: The Egyptians started it with the duodecimal (base 12) system. They count on their fingers using their thumb as a touch point, counting the three parts of each finger - giving 12 on one hand and 12 on the other. The Greeks through astronomy realised there were two equinoxes with equal daylight and nighttime, so subdivided into 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of night - your 24-hour day. With mechanical clocks in the 14th-15th centuries they needed finer precision, and they were measuring Earth's rotation as 360 degrees, subdivided in base 60 into minutes and seconds. (Studied as an engineer, read Scientific American)

questions.question: Why are Conservatives often referred to as Tories?
Why do they shrink wrap my cucumber but not my apples or other vegetables? If it's to keep it fresh, why not shrink wrap everything?
Why do we use the letter Z for being asleep (Zzz)? Why not another letter?

answers.answer: Z sounds like sleep - it's onomatopoeic. 'Zzz' mimics the sound of snoring.

questions.question: Why is Surrey Cricket Ground in London? The Oval is in London, not Surrey. Was it built in Surrey originally?

answers.answer: Up until the creation of the London County Council in 1889, London was only the City of London. Brixton, Clapham and areas around came under Surrey administratively. When the cricket ground was built, it was actually in Surrey.

questions.question: HB Source water is named after the Houses of Parliament and has a picture of it on the bottle. Do they have to pay royalties for using that image?

answers.answer: No. The architecture copyright would have expired years ago. You can publish Charles Dickens' books without paying royalties because he's out of copyright.

questions.question: Are professional tennis players allowed to wear sunglasses? If so, why don't they seem to wear them?

answers.answer: Yes, they're allowed. Kirsten Flipkin, a Belgian player, wears sunglasses. The reason others don't is probably depth perception - sunglasses affect how they perceive distance and depth.

questions.question: Why aren't my iron tablets magnetic? I put a magnet on one and it's not magnetic, even with a bigger magnet.

answers.answer: The iron isn't present as metal in the tablet. It's in a salt form - ferric or ferrous salt, like sulfate or chloride. Metal won't dissolve in solution, but the salt form will so it can be absorbed from the stomach. It's like asking why isn't copper sulfate magnetic.

questions.question: Why do some ants have wings?

answers.answer: So that they can fly.

Flying ants are queens. They fly off to find a new colony. The ants there either accept them or kill them. If accepted, they drag them into the colony and snip their wings off - and you've got a queen.

questions.question: What is the origin of the term 'field day'? When someone finds gossip, why would they 'have a field day' with it?
What is the biological explanation for why I go weak at the knees when I see someone climbing at heights, even sitting down?

answers.answer: It's all to do with anxiety. When your body is anxious, to prevent shutting down, blood goes to vital organs (heart, brain) and pulls away from less important parts - the arms, legs, thighs, feet. Less blood in the leg muscles makes them feel weak.

questions.question: Is boxing the only sport where a champion gets a belt rather than a trophy or cup?

answers.answer: No - American wrestling (WWF) and mixed martial arts also award belts to champions.

questions.question: Why does my cat Simba go crazy when I come home from swimming? He goes mad over anything that has been in contact with pool water, and also when we clean his litter box with cleaning products.

answers.answer: Bleach and chlorine are ammonia-based substances. Urine also contains ammonia and smells similar. When the cat smells ammonia, it's marking its territory with its scent glands (cheeks and base of head). questions.question: [Answer about handwashing hygiene]

answers.answer: Soap makes water wetter - it breaks down surface tension. Using soap means your hands will be virtually sterile regardless of whether you use a dryer or towel.

questions.question: Why don't limes have pips in them? Even my chef friend Carlos noticed this.

answers.answer: Limes do have seeds, but they're much thinner and smaller than lemon pips. The reason we don't notice them is that limes are probably picked before they're fully mature. Limes and lemons are different trees entirely, not one being an immature version of the other.

questions.question: Could a country actually change their national anthem, both lyrics and melody? How would they go about it?

answers.answer: Yes, countries can change their anthems. Germany changed theirs after World War II when the Nazi-era anthem was dropped.

questions.question: If, when a dog gets incited, can they control the wagging of their tail? Or is it just instinctive?

answers.answer: It's an involuntary but voluntary movement. At times dogs can't help it but at times it can be stopped. The dog can actually stop the wagging of their tail themselves. Dogs display their happiness and sadness in the same way - if a dog's happy it'll wag its tail. You can train a dog the same way you can train a human not to smile if they're really excited.

questions.question: How are historical sums of money updated to their modern-day equivalent?

answers.answer: It's converted through using the price of bread or milk of that time. They back-calculate using comparable products and the retail price index - comparing selling prices of things you can buy then and now.

questions.question: Why did Tyrannosaurus Rex have such small arms?

answers.answer: Because his head got so big, he would have been too heavy if he had bigger arms. He'd be out of balance and he'd be standing on his two legs.

They haven't fully evolved from the fat worm they were when they were in the sea. That's why his arms are just beginning to sprout. They've got enormous legs because he had to push himself against the waves when he was coming out of the sea.

questions.question: Why does the North Star appear not to move in the night sky at all whilst the other stars flow through the constellations?

answers.answer: Use the analogy of a spinning top - the top of the spinning top never moves position, the rest of it's spinning around.
While the Earth spins, the North Pole, as it's spinning, if you look directly up from the North Pole, it doesn't particularly spin.

The North Star is directly above our pole, and we rotate around the pole. The stars further west or east will appear to travel as you rotate around the axis of the planet. There is a faint bit of wobble, but it's generally going to always be in the same position. That's why in olden days they used it to navigate.

questions.question: Why do flies fly around in squares in my lounge, yet when I try and bat them away, they fly out of the window?

answers.answer: Their sonar, or whatever it is flies use, is reacting to the walls, so it's flying in a uniform distance from the wall at all times.

Flyers can sense air pressure and atmospheric pressure. That's how they dodge their targets. That's why fly swats have holes in them - so they can't sense the disturbance. When you swat them towards the window, they can then sense the air pressure difference outside and they know there's a source to get out of the room.

questions.question: Why do humans as a rule not eat grass?

Yes. Green leaves take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.

questions.question: Hydrogen is energy rich and can burn. Oxygen is energy rich and can burn. But H2O (water) is a different thing with no calories. When you drink water, it has zero calories. We're told that in July we're very close to the sun (that's when it's summer in England). In December we're very far away (that's winter). But New Zealand has opposite seasons - when it's summer here, it's winter there. If we're close to the sun now and it's summer for us, how can it be winter in New Zealand when they're the same distance from the sun as we are? Shouldn't the whole Earth have summer in July?

answers.answer: The Earth is always the same distance from the sun. But the axis isn't square - it's a wobble. It's a slight degree. And depending on the season, it wobbles towards the sun or away from the sun. And that's what gives you the differences. If it's wobbled towards the sun and it's hot here, it's winter on the other side of the world because that has wobbled away from the sun.

answers.answer: A generation is the average interval between the birth of a parent and the birth of their offspring. Lee heard it's around 30 years as a rule of thumb.

answers.caller: Andy from Finchley (62 years old, first time caller)
answers.answer: A generation is the lifespan from birth to death - about 50-60 years on average. When you die, your children are the next generation starting again.

questions.question: Why do we say someone has been 'hanged' rather than 'hung' when executed?

answers.answer: Suggested it might be because hanged involves death - you don't hang anything else to kill it

Hung is an adjective describing the state (like hung meat in a butcher's), while hanged is the past participle for execution. It's become a grammatical distinction where we correct people about dead humans but not about paintings.
Hanged is a judicial term - a sentence passed by authority, which is why execution is hanged. But James questioned this explanation.

questions.question: What does OK mean? What is the origin of OK?

answers.answer: Nobody knows for sure - it's one of the oldest questions
During World War I, American troops would report 'O for zero, K for killed' - zero killed meant everyone came back safely
Greek origin - 'ola kala' means all well

questions.caller: Scott from Basildon (answered about tree surgeons)
questions.question: Why are tree surgeons called that?

answers.answer: Tree surgeons cut trees in a way that doesn't damage them and allows them to keep growing. A lumberjack would just cut them down. The distinction is that tree surgeons work to keep the tree alive.

questions.question: If you gave full permission, full written consent and you die, could you be stuffed legally?

answers.answer: Steve (undertaker) told him if someone wants to get stuffed, they can do it

You cannot keep a body. A body has to be disposed of legally - burial, cremation, or burial at sea. You can employ a taxidermist or embalmer but you still have to dispose of what remains. It's a criminal offence not to dispose of the body.

questions.question: Why is it that when we get married, I'll still be mister, but my fiancée will become missy? And if we were to get divorced, she'll become miss but I'll stay mister.

answers.answer: Good old-fashioned misogyny - the notion that the woman's off the market, whereas a man is an independent entity and isn't owned by anyone

Both titles from French. Mr is from Monsieur (someone halfway to being a sir). Mrs is short for Maîtresse - when you marry, you become mistress of the household of the man. Women didn't own anything, so they were in charge of someone else's stuff. It harks back to days of women not having autonomy.

questions.question: At what age does a lamb become a sheep? When you see lambs on reservoirs they're tiny, but supermarket lamb legs are huge.

answers.caller: Dave from Barnet (friend has farm in New Zealand, father was master butcher)
answers.answer: At 12 months they become a hogget. From around 16 months they become mutton/sheep. If slaughtered between 12-16 months, it's still called lamb.

questions.question: Why is sign language different in different countries? The hand gestures should denote the word meaning, even though the word is different.

answers.answer: Sign language is the same as spoken language - it has a different structure but it's the same. Different countries speak different languages so they have different sign languages. Even in the UK, Northern signs are different from Southern signs. Words mean the same thing but are written and signed differently. In America they sign with one hand, in the UK with two hands. Different countries evolved their own systems.

questions.question: Why does asparagus make your urine smell so badly?

answers.answer: There are enzymes in asparagus that our body cannot break down. When you urinate, it has a unique smell because of those enzymes. Some people can't smell it - I can't smell it.

questions.question: How does Shazam work? It identifies a tune even when two different artists start the same way before they've even sung.

answers.answer: When a song comes out by a major record company, they run it through a machine that generates a little signature for the song. When you scan via your phone, it doesn't send the recording to Shazam - it sends just the signature of that part of the track. Then a computer algorithm matches the two together. It's called a checksum. There was a story about a famous pianist whose husband was releasing music supposedly by her, but someone with a computer saw it had exactly the same signature as someone else's recording of the same symphony - that's how they busted him for fraud.

questions.question: What's the difference between a hamburger and a beef burger?

answers.answer: A hamburger was invented in Hamburg, it's a beef burger Americanized

answers.caller: Clive from St Albans (cost accountant at Findus in the 70s)
answers.answer: Burgers legally had to contain 50% meat, beef burgers had to contain 75% beef. There was a legal requirement on those contents. A hamburger could be 50% beef and 50% filler (onions).
A hamburger is basically just served in a bun and a beef burger's not.

questions.question: What is the crystal thing on a stick that road workers hold up? There's a mirror and a little crystal-y gem on top. The tripod with a camera is on the other side of the road.

answers.answer: The mirror is reflecting a pyramid chalked on the pavement up into the lens. The guy with the stick is standing where a road junction or corner of a building is going to be - it's finite measurement for planning.

It's a theodolite. The little arrow on the mirror is for a laser. The laser comes out of the theodolite and reflects off the mirror for measurement. Every major building in Britain is set out according to sea level benchmarks - there's a primary level on a beach in the south of England and all measurements relate back to that.

questions.question: When are we going to start storing nuclear waste in space?

answers.answer: The risks are too great for the rocket blowing up before it makes it. They've thought about it but it would never happen because of the actual risk of it blowing up before it makes it to space. You'd essentially be shooting a massive nuclear weapon into space with high octane fuel.

questions.question: Does the queen or the royal family ever carry around any money? Do they ever need to use it anywhere?

answers.answer: The queen doesn't. She never carries cash. The rest of the royal family do.
The only time she carries money is on a Sunday. Apparently she carries a crisp five-pound note in the church collection plate.
Not always on plurals, but ancient Greek names ending in S only have the apostrophe at the end and Jesus. Like Xerxes.

questions.question: Why do babies cry?

answers.answer: Researchers found there's a biological reason. Breastfeeding increases this likelihood. The baby is crying in order to get upon the parents' nerves and stop them trying for another baby. It's a self-preservation technique that generations of evolution have bred into babies - their survival is enhanced if there isn't another little mouth turning up nine months hence competing for attention and food.

questions.question: Why does milk go yellow when you freeze it?

answers.answer: It's the fat and water separating in the milk when it gets frozen. The fat is yellow and as it separates, the yellow goes to the top and the white bit stays at the bottom. Milk shouldn't be frozen for over six weeks because that's when it starts to turn yellow. (Qualifications: was a home carer, older people used to freeze milk)

questions.question: Why are insects not knocked out of the sky when it rains heavily?

answers.answer: With mosquitoes they've filmed them flying around in rain and what's happening is they're rolling with the raindrops like you get taught to do if you land in a parachute or a wrestler might get hit by a raindrop. In that way they don't break the surface tension. All that force comes from a raindrop splattering but because they don't break the surface of the raindrop and they roll with it, they survive. It's as if they are almost surfing on the raindrops. (Qualifications: physicist working in defense industry as a research scientist)

questions.question: Why does the sun lighten our hair but darken our skin?

answers.answer: Melanin in skin is a chemical that responds to sunlight by making your skin darker to stop it from burning. Your hair is made of keratin which is like dead stuff with nothing in it so it just gets bleached by the sun. It's an external chemical reaction rather than an internal one.

Sunlight bleaches hair because the ultraviolet in sunlight bleaches everything it touches. It has nothing to do with what is in the hair. The UV light causes the bleaching effect. The reason skin gets darker is because melanin protects the skin by stopping the ultraviolet getting too far down into the deep. The darker the skin, the less ultraviolet penetration. (Qualifications: Professor of Robotics at Middlesex University)

questions.question: Is it possible to change one's laugh?

answers.answer: Yes, you can change how you laugh. You record yourself laughing, listen to it, use visual and auditory feedback, pick a laugh you like and then practice it that way. It's really, really hard and you have to be really motivated but it is possible. You practice it until it becomes an instinct, like how you change a lateral lisp. You probably need expert help. (Qualifications: voice/language specialist)

questions.question: What do seals drink when they're at sea? Humans can't drink seawater but seals are mammals.

answers.answer: They don't drink at times but they get most of their water content from the food they eat, which is like fish. Fish are roughly the same salt content as blood. So they get their liquid from eating fish when they're away from fresh water. If they find themselves near some fresh water occasionally, they'll have a bit of a drink. They can also eat snow sometimes. (Qualifications: loves did-you-know facts like Michael Caine)

questions.question: Why don't irons have off switches?

answers.answer: Because they're controlled by a thermostat. The thermostat will only let the iron reach the temperature you set.

Irons are a kilowatt, usually. It's a lot of power. You couldn't just have a little switch to flick. It's got to be a heavy switch like you have on the socket. There's not room in an iron for the circuitry to have all that. (Qualifications: used to sell electrical components)

questions.question: What's the difference between a pond and a lake? And if it's just size, when does a pond become a lake?

answers.answer: It's a pond if every single part of that pond can sustain life. If there's an area of that that can't sustain life (maybe because it's too deep and light can't get down or for some reason), then it's a lake. In a pond, every single piece of that body of water can sustain life. (Qualifications: goes walking around Virginia Water Lake every year and looks up facts about it)

questions.question: If there's a given distance of 100 metres, if you run it or walk it and it's raining, when would you get more wet?
Do the French use English phrases like we use French ones (je ne sais quoi, c'est la vie, raison d'être)?

answers.answer: They do not think so. They use loads of English words (le weekend, le sandwich, le parking, le chenissie for hi-fi, interview, loft etc.) but no expressions like the French ones we use. A phrase would be something like 'that's life' but they'd say c'est la vie. (Qualifications: studied in French school in Lisbon from age 3, went to university in France, lived there 5 years after university)

questions.question: Why does St. James's Park have an extra S in St. James's?

answers.answer: If it's a plural, you need the apostrophe after the S (e.g. the birds' food). But James isn't a plural - there's only one James - so it's James's (apostrophe S).

questions.question: The sugar on sour-sweet, how do they make sugar sour?

answers.answer: It is a load of citric acid, ascorbic acid, malic acid, citric acid, and the more of that you get, the more sour you go. It's just the acids, mate. Acids, plural. There's different acids. They have different intensities. They're mixed in together.

questions.question: Do dogs of a certain pedigree recognize each other? So if, for example, two Jack Russells bumped into each other, do they acknowledge that they're both Jack Russells or are they just all just dogs to one another?

answers.answer: It's not that they recognise breeds as such, but it's more that the schnauzer actually reminds him of his brothers and sisters from the litter. So he just thinks, oh, you look like my brothers and sisters. They see that and they think, oh, you look like me. You look like my brothers. So they see similarity rather than biological distinction.

questions.question: Why do they call chickenpox chickenpox?

answers.answer: We used to catch it off chickens.

In France, goosebumps is called 'chair de poule' which translates to 'chicken skin'. When you pluck the feathers out of a chicken, you're left with a little red braised dot on the chicken skin. So when you get a bad case of chickenpox, you look like you have plucked chicken skin.

questions.question: Have we ever seen the whole of the moon? Because the moon rotates the same pace as the Earth and the sun. But have we seen the other side of the moon?

answers.answer: The dark side of the moon is always facing away from the Earth. Have we seen it? No.

The Earth is currently in a locked orbit around the moon. The moon is in orbit around the Earth at the same speed that it is actually spinning on its axis, so we always see the same face of the moon. However, Apollo 11 orbited the moon so human beings aboard Apollo 11 saw the whole of the moon. There is no such thing as a dark side of the moon - all parts get light.

questions.question: I want to know why we call third world countries third world. Who are the first and the second world countries?

answers.answer: Second world was to do with socialist and pre-industrial Eastern Bloc countries like Soviet Union, China, Laos. They're still industrialized but socialist rather than capitalist. First world is capitalist, industrialized countries like America, Canada, England, most of Europe.

It goes back to the Cold War. The first world was everybody who was allied with the United States, basically in NATO. The second world was everybody who was allied to the USSR. The third world was everybody who was neutral. It's a Cold War term. It's not an economic term. It's outdated and in some respects it's a bit offensive. You're supposed to use the term developing nations now.

questions.question: Why does a paper cut hurt more than any other cut?

answers.answer: The reason why it hurts so much is because it's a shallow cut and it hasn't cut through the nerve endings. You've got nerve endings under your skin. When you cut deep, you cut through the nerve endings so the pain's short-lived. With a paper cut, you're cutting into the nerve endings and therefore the nerve endings are severed but nothing deeper. So that's why it hurts so much.

questions.question: Why are colours associated to certain things? For example, red is associated with danger and green is associated with safety, i.e. traffic lights. Why did that happen?

answers.answer: Our physiological response to a different frequency of electromagnetic radiation. Red is excitement, high passion. Fear, lust, anger. It's linked to fire originally. Some species in the animal world dress in red just to repel other animals. Green makes us more relaxed because it's like a meadow.

It's all to do with the colour wheel. The colours go around in a circle formation. Red and green are on opposite sides of the colour wheel so they stand out against each other. They offer a useful colour-based contrast. If you're quickly looking at something, you'll see red stand out and then the green will stand out more starkly than any others.

questions.question: On a normal suit jacket, what's the reason for having a few buttons, normally three buttons, on the sleeve of the jacket?

answers.answer: They used to work. You would have a working cuff on your jacket, which meant you could roll it up. The reason there are multiple buttons is that you need a certain amount of rollability space in order to be able to roll your sleeve up properly. If you don't undo your cuff on your shirt, you can't roll it up. If you undo one button on your shirt cuff, you can roll it up a bit but it gets a bit too tight around the elbow area. If you undo the second button, you can roll it all the way up to your bicep.

questions.question: Why can't I put hot food straight into the fridge? My wife always says wait until it cools down. Why can't I just put it in straight away?

answers.answer: If you put something hot in the fridge, it'll heat up the whole fridge.

You have to let food chill before you put it in the refrigerator. You have to let it cool completely at room temperature before you put it in the fridge. Otherwise, if you put it even when it's lukewarm in the fridge, the chance of it containing some sort of bacteria increases and that will give you food poisoning when you go to reheat it and eat it up.

questions.question: Why do we celebrate April Fool's Day?

answers.answer: In the 17th-18th century, the beginning of the year in this country was the 1st of April, which is why it's still the tax year. France moved the New Year to January 1st, and people who still celebrated April 1st as New Year were considered fools for failing to move with the times.

questions.question: Why do humans have an inherent capacity to lie? Is it evolutionary, or is it something that develops over time?

answers.answer: Humans cannot lie before the age of two scientifically. There was an experiment with two-year-olds and three-year-olds - none of the two-year-olds could lie, but the three-year-olds had started learning to lie to get out of things. This proves lying is a learned behaviour rather than something inherent.

questions.question: How come some animals come out of eggs and other ones are born live?
Why are they called baked beans? Because they're not baked, surely. Surely they're stewed.

answers.answer: Beans are put in cans raw, then in the factory they're put through the oven and baked so they're cooked in the can. When you get them home, all you do is heat them up. It just means cooked beans. Mr Hines called them baked beans because everyone would recognise them and it sounds better.

questions.question: Why does the time of a pendulum swing not change with the amplitude of the swing?

answers.answer: The restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position. As the pendulum displaces from equilibrium, the restoring force increases and pulls it down more. It's an exchange between kinetic energy and potential energy. The time period of the oscillation depends only on the length of the pendulum. The equation is F equals two pi root L over G where G is gravity.

With old clockwork clocks, you wind up the mechanism which runs the pendulum. You adjust the weight up and down the bar to set it to one second - this is the regulator. The pendulum is a regulator for the clock to tick once a second.

questions.question: Do bell ringers in a church have sheet music?

answers.answer: Each bell has a number. When they have a tune, they follow the numbers. Each ringer has their own bell. There's a leader who indicates to them when to ring until they've learned the code. It's written down in numbers like any music. The leader has it and memorises it or has it in front, then everyone learns their part until you learn the music and don't need it in front of you. It's the same as ordinary hand bells.

questions.question: Why do people touch their heads when they can't find wood? Where has that come from?
Why does hot water clean more effectively than cold?

answers.answer: Things dissolve more easily in hot water than cold water, particularly grease deposits in food.

The molecules in hot water are vibrating more so the technical distance between them is higher. As you increase the temperature by every 10 degrees, there's a doubling of the rate of any chemical reaction. So enzymes, surfactants and soaps will be doubling their activity and cleaning things quicker.

questions.question: Who decided the international dialing codes (like 0044 for UK, 001 for US)?
Answer to the 'touch wood' question

answers.answer: The old slang word for a piece of wood is noggin. To use a noggin is to use your head. So touching wood or touching your noggin - it's the same thing.

questions.question: Why are cowboy builders called cowboy builders?

answers.answer: When the gold rush was underway and cowboys were moving across the country, they would build their own shelters in a hotchpotch fashion with no particular expertise. They had expertise with cows but would throw up shelters in a fairly ramshackle way - ergo, cowboy builders.

questions.question: Why does February only have 28 days rather than 30?

answers.answer: Caesar wanted an extra day for July because his name was Julius, so he took a day off February and put it in July. Augustus Caesar took another day from February for August. July for Julius Caesar, August for Augustus Caesar.

questions.question: Answer about February days

answers.answer: Roman times there were only 10 months when the Gregorian calendar came around. They made it 12 months. Then they discovered a discrepancy with the amount of days in a year so it's not 365 exactly, it's point something.

questions.question: Why is the red pod on the Birmingham Eye red?

answers.answer: The red one is for private functions and weddings, you can hire it out
The orange/red one is sponsored by EDF and that's their logo

questions.question: Why are rotating tables called lazy Susans?

answers.answer: Because Susan invented it so she didn't have to walk around the table serving everybody

questions.question: Why do all French houses have shutters on the windows?

answers.answer: Someone told me it had something to do with WWII and bombing threats, but they were probably yanking my chain

They developed to keep the house cool in summer and warm in winter, now it's become part of insurance claims - if you leave your shutters open and your house is burgled in France, your insurance is invalidated

questions.question: Where did the phrase 'to offer an olive branch' come from?

answers.answer: In ancient Greece, the olive branch was a symbol of victory or peace, brides would wear one, and to offer an olive branch is to offer peace
Bible - Noah's Ark, dove sent out came back with olive branch to symbolise that the floods had abated

questions.question: How do cows produce so much milk? Are all lactating cows pregnant?

answers.answer: If you don't stop feeding the mum doesn't stop producing - that's true of all mammals
Cows need to calf once. Then as long as you keep milking them, they think it's a calf stuck in the teeth, so they keep producing milk

questions.question: If you put all the vehicles on Earth into orbit around the Earth, would the Earth still weigh the same? When you weigh the Earth, should you include stuff that's in orbit around it like the moon?
How come it never rains when it's foggy? Is it to do with air pressure or because the fog is the cloud?

answers.answer: Definitely to do with air pressure
Fog is effectively rain. It can rain while it's foggy if there are clouds above that are releasing raindrops through the fog. It's like mizzle

questions.question: Can police actually commandeer a vehicle?

answers.answer: You've seen it on The Sweeney - presumably they can
Yes, 30-odd years ago in Croydon High Street, he and a colleague commandeered a Mini to chase a stolen car - told the driver 'follow that car' and jumped in
His mum was commandeered in Dagenham 20 years ago - two cops jumped in her A-Ridge beige Volvo, told her 'floor it' and she drove to the pub at the end of Wilbur Lane

It was in the instruction book when he joined - you could commandeer a vehicle but not kick the driver out, you went with the driver who drove under police insurance. Should be used sparingly. He did it in 1959 for a burglary - just needed a lift as it was a long way to walk

questions.question: Who are the people that change the dates for Easter, Mother's Day, Father's Day, and Pancake Day? And why does Christmas stay the same?

answers.answer: The church - it's the church calendar. Easter always has to be on a Sunday, same with Mothering Sunday which is honour of the Virgin Mary feast day

Easter is stuck on top of pagan festivals - named after goddess Easterer (as in oestrogen, eggs). She transfigured into a hare who became the Easter Bunny. Easter is set on the first Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox. Christmas is fixed because it's a birthday - they've plumped for the 25th which is Yule (winter solstice). Shrove Tuesday tracks back from Easter Sunday

questions.question: Why do we have British Transport Police and normal police? Can a British Transport Police person nick me for having a blow tyre at traffic lights?

answers.answer: In the early days of policing, they were private forces with jurisdiction only within set areas. Transport Police were set up to deal with issues that crossed from one area to another - like a train travelling from A to B needs a police force to look after it

questions.question: Do magnets work in outer space?

answers.answer: Yep.

answers.caller: Annie from Dulwich (via son Charlie at Cambridge)
answers.answer: Magnets do work in space because they don't require a medium to travel through; they work perfectly in a vacuum. A magnet emits a beta flux density which is a proponent of the electromagnetic spectrum, composed of electronic and magnetic proponents angled at 90 degrees to each other and the propagation direction.

questions.question: How can airplanes possibly fly upside down?

answers.answer: You've got flaps on the wing to adjust pressure and shape. Once you're in the air, you can just flip over.

answers.caller: Paul from Waltham Abbey (Private Pilot License)
answers.answer: When the wing is inverted, as long as the pressure on the underside of the wing (which is now facing up) is lower than the air flying underneath, the plane keeps flying. High pressure underneath keeps it aloft. The flight controls become inverted - if you want to climb and you're upside down, you push forward on the stick.

questions.question: Is it more energy efficient to take two steps at a time up stairs or one step at a time?

answers.answer: It depends on the pitch of the tread, the pace of the stepper, the steepness of the steps, the energy... (admitted he couldn't fully answer)

Staircases are designed for a mean average height of the population. The most energy efficient way to get up a staircase is one step at a time, unless you're particularly tall. If you were taller, the steps would be slightly bigger for maximum efficiency.

questions.question: What exactly is a rainbow? Is it a full circle? Why do we only see half? Why did I see it upside down once?

answers.answer: Rainbows are created by sunlight hitting water droplets, splitting all wavelengths of light into constituent parts appearing as different colours. They're always curved because of how the sun projects its light. Usually you see an arc with the sun behind you and water droplets in front. If you look towards the sun with water between you and the sun, you get an annular rainbow - a full circle. What Jane saw was part of a full circular rainbow viewed from a different angle. The normal rainbow we see is part of a circle - if the ground wasn't there, you'd see the full circle.

questions.question: Where does the children's song 'The Big Ship Sails on the Alley Alley Oop' originate from, and what does 'Alley Alley Oop' mean?

answers.answer: In history class at school, she was taught that 'alley-oh' means ocean (the Atlantic Ocean). The Atlantic sank in September, referring to a boat called the Atlantic that sank in the Atlantic.

questions.question: Why are all golf buggies left-hand drive?

answers.answer: Supply and demand - most countries in the world are left-hand drive countries, they make buggies according to one fixed template.

Slow-moving golf buggies don't need right-hand drive conversion because there's no safety reason at low speeds (unlike cars). It would be ridiculous in production terms to re-engineer them when there's no need. Any company making right-hand drive buggies would be restricting their market to Britain only.

questions.question: What does eight magpies mean?

answers.answer: Five for rain, six for snow, seven for sleet, eight I don't know. (Made this up entirely)

Eight is a wish. The full verse: 'One for sorrow, two for joy, three for a girl, four for a boy, five for silver, six for gold, seven for a secret never to be told, eight to wish, nine to kiss, ten is a bird you must not miss.'

One for sorrow, two for joy, three for a girl, four for a boy, five for silver, six for gold, seven for a secret that never should be told, eight for a wish, nine for a kiss, ten for a word that must not be missed, eleven for a letter, and twelve for something better.

questions.question: What's the difference between paneer and traditional cottage cheese?

answers.answer: Paneer is Indian cheese. Beyond that, I don't know.

questions.question: Why do we always ice skate anti-clockwise around an ice rink?

answers.answer: Because everyone else is. The first person could have started clockwise and everyone would have joined in. (Made up theory about left leg being slightly shorter)
It's because our hearts are placed a little bit to the left of our centre of gravity. It's more efficient to run or skate in an anti-clockwise direction than the opposite.

questions.question: Why is it stags and hens when it should be stags and does?

answers.answer: A stag is a male turkey and a hen is a female turkey, which is why both terms are used.

questions.question: When you take your dog or cat or hamster to the vet, where do they get blood from for animal blood transfusions?

answers.answer: There was a big campaign years ago for dog blood donations. Conscientious pet owners take their pets along to donate blood just like humans do. For hamsters, blood would have to come from another hamster.
There is a programme to collect blood for dogs. They generally like to collect blood from greyhounds because their blood type is quite generic and will work for lots of other dogs.

questions.question: How do astronauts keep fit in space?

answers.answer: They have bungees, giant rubber bands for resistance training. They work against those because they're lightweight. You can do that while floating around.

questions.question: Why is there no pink in a rainbow?

answers.answer: Primary colours can't be mixed, and you can make pink by mixing red with white.

Actually you CAN see pink at the top and bottom of rainbows where the tones get lighter. That's one thing about primary colours - the ones you can't mix are red, blue and yellow, but you can mix all the other colours on either side.

questions.question: What do you call a one with 24 noughts after it?

answers.answer: A million, billion, billion, million... I wouldn't have a clue.
It's a septillion. Million, billion, trillion, quadrillion, quintillion, sextillion, septillion.
The septillion answer was the American version. In Europe, traditionally it would be a quadrillion. American billion is a thousand million, European billion is a million million.

questions.question: How were the pyramids actually built?

answers.answer: Answered with great difficulty.

Geographically, when they were building these pyramids, the ground around Egypt was all green with rivers. They would construct blocks and send them down on the river. They used astronomical alignments - the stars - to get measurements exact. They were far more advanced than we give them credit for.

It's humans, it's engineering. It's from pivots, fulcrums, pulleys. They moved 50-tonne stones up a hill using these techniques. Also the workers weren't slaves - they were quite highly skilled and even highly paid.

questions.question: Why are trees in French forests planted in neat purple lines?

answers.answer: It's the difference between a forest that's been deliberately planted by mankind to provide wood or a hunting environment (like the New Forest planted by William the Conqueror), versus one sown by nature, by the wind.

Wealthy landowners planted trees so when their daughters got married, they'd get a cabinetmaker to make furniture from these perfectly straight trees. The cabinetmaker's payment was to keep the rest of the wood. It also explains why French furniture is so fine - cabinetmakers would try to get as much thin wood as possible to have more left over.

questions.question: What's the origin of the phrase 'to pop your clogs'?

answers.answer: Presumably they didn't bury the clogs with you when you died, so they did something with them which could be loosely described as popping.
Victorian phrase meaning to sell all of your goods before you die, to pay for your funeral.

Term used by executioners - when the hanged man was brought in without laces on his shoes, when executed the muscles relax and the shoes fall off as he takes the drop. Referenced in the book 'Execution of Pierpoint' by Albert Pierpoint.

Pop was what you did when taking something to a pawnbroker (like in the song Pop Goes the Weasel). And in 19th century mills in the north of England, the last thing you'd want to do was lose your shoes because you couldn't work. So if you died or something happened to you, you'd pop your clogs.

questions.question: When was makeup invented and by who?

answers.answer: It's been around almost as long as humanity. The Egyptians had it - Cleopatra bathed in ass's milk, they put kohl on their eyes. Mesopotamians had it. It's like looking for the source of the Thames - you just saw Tower Bridge and want to find where the river began millennia ago.

Makeup has been worn since before the domestication of animals, since hunter-gatherer times. Women used red ochre to symbolise to hunters that they were ready to accept a hunter who brought the most meat home.

questions.question: Why is a third wheel/chaperone on a date called a gooseberry?

answers.answer: I'll get you an answer to that. There has to be an answer.

In the old days they used to grow strawberries in rows and gooseberries next to them (because bugs on gooseberries eat the bugs that eat strawberries). When being romantic you'd pick strawberries and take someone with you so you weren't alone. They'd pick gooseberries in the next row - close enough to keep an eye on you but not in the same row, making it romantic but chaperoned. Hence you become the gooseberry.

questions.question: Why do streets have odd numbers on one side and even on the other?

answers.answer: Someone's doing the postman - going up one side of the street and down the other. Or town planning.

questions.question: Why do things that are bad for us feel or taste really good? Like sugar - it's addictive but bad. Broccoli isn't addictive. Our body should have developed some way to make bad things not feel good.

answers.answer: If it was good for you, no one would call it an addiction. You're addicted to water. You're addicted to air. It's only called addiction when it's bad for you. It's based on pleasure.

Sugar is an evolutionary adaptive response. Somewhere in our evolutionary history we wanted to eat high sugar foods because they're highly calorific (like berries) - more energy. Heroin stimulates opioid receptors in the brain and the dopamine pathway (pleasure-reward pathway). We've moved beyond the point where sugar was necessary but our bodies haven't caught up. They still tell our brain to eat more sugar.

questions.question: What causes an itch?
How far away from a house do you have to take a mouse in order to be sure that it won't come back?

answers.answer: Indoor mice (house mice) don't survive outdoors - they die from stress or predators. They can't cope with outdoor living conditions. Taking a mouse three miles away doesn't guarantee it won't return because releasing house mice outdoors is essentially killing them anyway. The three-mile theory was just someone trying to sell a humane mousetrap.

questions.question: Is it really possible to pick a handcuff with a paperclip, as shown in Hollywood?

answers.answer: Yes, it's possible. I saw it done backstage at Manchester Youth Theatre in 1990 when someone accidentally handcuffed themselves together and it was picked with something similar.

questions.question: Why does the moon look smaller some days and bigger other days when it's full?

answers.answer: It's further away.

It's not actually distance change. When the moon is low in the sky near the horizon, we see other things in context (skyline, buildings, trees). Due to 'size constancy' in the way our brain works with depth and perception, we perceive it as bigger. When it's high up with nothing around for comparison, it looks smaller. It's a trick of the mind, not actual distance change.

questions.question: What percentage of a gold medal is actually made of gold?

answers.answer: Gold medals are predominantly silver. Only 6 grams out of the medal is actually gold.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'telling off' come from? Why is 'off' bad when telling someone off?
Is it ever not raining somewhere in the world in the whole day?

answers.answer: It rains somewhere every day. The same amount of water is in the world constantly, going from sea to sky and back. It rains in the rainforest every day. Also Manchester - it always rains at the Stockport Viaduct.

questions.question: Why do we have a 'birthday' and not a 'birth anniversary'?

answers.answer: Birthday is just shorthand for the anniversary of your birth day. The English system is actually superior because it distinguishes between a wedding anniversary and a birthday. Try singing 'happy birth anniversary' to the tune of happy birthday - you'd see the problem.

questions.question: Why do Greek people smash plates as a form of celebration?

answers.answer: It's a display of wealth - showing you have so much money you don't need to reuse plates. Posh Greek families apparently don't do it, suggesting it was more working class. By smashing plates, you're showing how well off you are.

questions.question: Why does the flavour of some liquids change with temperature?

answers.answer: Most liquids and foods contain proteins held together by delicate hydrogen bonds. When temperature goes up, these bonds break and the shape of the protein changes. The shape is what our taste buds recognise, so when they change, the taste changes. And it doesn't change back by cooling - like magnetic balls in a complicated structure thrown on the floor can't be reassembled exactly.

questions.question: Is Tourette's something peculiar to English-speaking countries, or does it happen all across the world?

answers.answer: No, it's not peculiar to English-speaking countries. A Turkish shopkeeper on Rectory Road has a severe case with pronounced tics and whistles. James questioned whether this proves it exists outside English-speaking countries since it's happening in England, but Wayne insisted the man was born in Turkey and brought it with him.

questions.question: Why are humans the only animals that cry tears when upset? What's the point of crying?

answers.caller: Pauline (Pinner) - claimed PhD in biology from Oxford
answers.answer: When you cry unhappy tears, you secrete different hormones. The hormones are in the tears - it's the body's way of getting stress hormones out of your system. That's why you feel better after crying.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'stone the crows' originate from?

answers.answer: Old cockney expression - ravens at Tower of London leaving would be catastrophic, so 'stone the crows' means an unheard-of thing would happen

answers.caller: Poppy from Reading (from George, 98, history teacher in nursing home)
answers.answer: Crows are alarmist birds - when alarmed they make noise and give away positions. People threw rocks at them to kill them and stop them making noise, hence 'stone the crows' when alarmed
During Old Navy military terms, the crow's nest was a major point. If a ship wasn't spotted and they got surprised attacked, they said 'stone the crows'

questions.question: What should we call this decade - the 2010s?

answers.answer: It's called the Twenteens - read it in a Telegraph article in 2010

questions.question: How close to the Earth does an asteroid have to come to be affected by our gravitational field?

answers.answer: It's not just about distance - it's about speed too. If it was just above Earth and wasn't moving, it would drop straight down. But moving fast means it slingshots around. Everything in space is falling - if falling towards us gets faster, if too fast enters orbit. Should comfort Elaine because it's moving very quickly and there's a lot of other stuff pulling it around

questions.question: What is the arc on the edge of the penalty box in a football pitch for?

answers.answer: It's a distance from the ball when taking a penalty - so it's a circle rather than a square. The distance from the penalty spot outer extremity is the arc. You're not allowed to stand in the arc when someone's taking a penalty

questions.question: What was the first ship to be named HMS in Her Majesty's Royal Navy?

answers.answer: Around the time of English Civil War with Charles I - the army went against him but the navy stayed loyal and became the Royal Navy. HMS would have been applied to ships at that time. Not every ship was built as HMS, they were ascribed HMS

questions.question: What happens to your Twitter account when you die?

answers.answer: Sometimes it does, sometimes it doesn't. Depends on activity. Twitter won't know you're dead - they'll only know you haven't tweeted for a while
