Friend died two years ago and his Twitter account is still online. Would assume it remains online indefinitely

questions.question: What are the origins of doing a mixtape?

answers.answer: Invention of the tape recorder - someone thought I'm going to put all my favourite songs on one tape and give it to her on Valentine's Day

questions.question: What causes the blackness and greyness in clouds?

answers.answer: It's the absence of light. Thicker clouds let less light through - like steam in a kitchen you can't see through

Clouds have density and moisture which reflects protons. Thicker the cloud, less light passes through. Like putting fabric in front of a bulb - more fabric means less light. Different density parts explain darker bits

questions.question: Has the human gestation period always been nine months since Homo sapiens began? And if yes, why hasn't it evolved shorter?
If mankind is five million years old, why has it taken so long to develop technologically and psychologically, and why only relatively recently?

answers.answer: It hasn't taken a short time - early man came on the scene about a million and a half years ago. The reason we weren't writing operas or inventing the wheel was because we had to dedicate almost all our waking hours to surviving and eating - hunting and gathering. Couldn't come back and jot up blueprints

questions.question: How did they build trenches in the First World War without getting shot?

answers.answer: It's to do with saps and sappers - engineers who dig trenches. A sap is a trench dug at 90 degrees to the main trench. You dig forward from behind your own lines, then turn sideways. You're not poking your head above the parapet. This method was used since WWI began because with mortars and catapults, you want to stay far away while putting stuff forward.

questions.question: Why does water feel colder than air at the same temperature?

answers.answer: Water has a much higher thermal conductivity than air. It will take heat away from your body much more quickly than air will. Air is quite a good insulator whereas water is quite a good conductor.

questions.question: Why are there so many sign language programs on TV after midnight?

answers.answer: Programs after midnight are usually repeats. The sign language is there for hard of hearing viewers who want to record programs and watch them later. It's a conscious decision to irritate a relatively small number of people while satisfying every hard of hearing person with the opportunity to record the program.

questions.question: What nationality would you be if born on a plane or boat in international waters? If parents have different nationalities, do you get two passports?

answers.answer: It would all depend on where the boat or plane was registered. If it was an American airplane, you'd be American.

You used to have the nationality of the airline. But people were going on aircraft pregnant to have their baby get a British passport, so they stopped it. Now it's whatever the nationality of the parents. If dual, you get both.

questions.question: Can judges ever be called up for jury service?

answers.answer: No, they can't. No qualified practising lawyer can sit on a jury. There's a ten-year cooling-off period after your practising certificate expires. The logic is that when the jury considers their verdict, the judge gives them directions, and prior legal knowledge would influence your decision.

answers.caller: Ian from Barnet (former vehicle escort manager for prisoner transportation)
answers.answer: People working in court-related jobs like prisoner transport are also disqualified from jury service for 10 years because they have too much knowledge of how courts work and could influence a jury. The spirit is that jurors should be peers with normal jobs who look at things from a normal perspective.
The law changed in 2004. Judges, barristers, and solicitors can now be called to do jury service. The Lord Chief Justice said it was unfair that they should be excluded.

questions.question: What is the origin of ships in glass bottles?

answers.answer: Similar to Scrimshaw (carving on whale bones done by sailors on long voyages). Sailors made elaborate things and used little bits of wood to make boats they put in bottles because they had bottles on the boat. Probably started when we began setting sail further afield on long voyages, around the 17th century with Francis Drake.

questions.question: Why are crisp packet colors standardized (red for ready salted, blue for salt and vinegar, green for cheese and onion)?

answers.answer: Walker's dominated the market so effectively that their color coding has been adopted by everybody else. So that if you come round someone's house and grab a blue bag, you know it's salt and vinegar and not something else.

questions.question: What happens if you don't register your baby's name within six weeks? Does the council choose one?
Why is a bundle of 26 newspapers called a 'quire'?

answers.caller: Pam from Sawbridgeworth (family in printing industry)
answers.answer: It's actually 25 sheets, not 26. It's one twentieth of a ream. The origins are from medieval manuscripts where they would have four sheets of paper folded to form eight leaves. It comes from the old French 'cuir' spelled Q-U-A-I-E-R.

questions.question: How far below your property do you actually own? Do you own the minerals under your house?

answers.answer: You own everything from the centre of the earth to the stars in the sky. But any resources that come out of it actually belong to the Crown. If you found a gold seam three foot below your cellar, that would be yours. But three hundred foot down might not be.

questions.question: Why does the Dartford Tunnel not go straight under the river? Why does it bend?

answers.answer: When the tunnels were built, we were driving around on horse-drawn carriages, and if a horse goes into a tunnel and sees a light at the other end, it has a tendency to bolt for the light.

questions.question: Do canals flood?

answers.answer: Locks control canals which all flow downwards; canals are built above water level

Canals are man-made structures with lock gate systems - top lock at highest point, bottom lock at lowest point. They have valves and channels that divert excess water to the nearest river when it rains, rather than through the lock system, so canals won't flood but rivers will.

questions.question: Why do S's in medieval texts have a little F through them in the middle of words?

answers.answer: The long F is a replacement for double S, which only happens in the middle of words because you never begin a word with it

Bob was completely wrong. The email clarifies it is the 'long S' or 'medial S' - it was never related to double S. The long S looks like a lowercase F with a little crossbar but the two letters are not otherwise related. The long medial S was used in the middle of words, while the terminal or round S was used at the end. The rule was sometimes haphazardly followed.

questions.question: Why can a microwave be made of metal and have metal trays and plates inside, but you're not allowed to put metal in the microwave to microwave food?

answers.caller: Martin (Manor Park) - Professor of Robotics at Middlesex University
answers.answer: It all depends on the size and shape of the metal. If metal reflects the microwaves, it just bounces energy off. If it absorbs them because it's a particular wavelength long, it takes in a lot of power (600-800 watts), producing current that can melt it like a fuse wire. A flat plate reflects, but a wire several wavelengths long absorbs. A plate with metal trim around it would spark because a circle acts as a good aerial.

questions.question: How could you walk around on Concorde, get up, drink champagne, feel completely normal when it's going at twice the speed of sound?

answers.answer: It's the same principle as drinking tea in a car going 70mph. The vehicle is traveling at speed but the inside isn't. You're traveling at exactly the same speed as the plane so it doesn't matter whether you're standing still or moving. Like imagine a table moving at 70mph - you'd fall off it. But when you ARE moving at that speed, you're fine.

Newton's first law - a body in motion remains in motion until a force acts upon it. When you're cruising at constant speed, there's no force on you to keep you moving. That's why you have to sit during takeoff - you need force from the chair to accelerate you. Friction keeps you in the chair, which is why you're strapped in. Once cruising, it doesn't matter what speed you're going - you can do anything. But if you brake suddenly, you can't drink tea.

questions.question: Why is it called a high street?

answers.answer: High tea, high mass, high street - perhaps high is short for highest, meaning the main street
The high street is where higher class people would have lived. It's where the main street was with the highest class of person, shops and the church or town hall.
In the past the path was raised to stop cattle getting up onto it from the street for market days. Like Upper Street in Highbury and Islington, and Angel.

questions.question: Coins have the date of manufacture on them. Why don't banknotes have a date of manufacture on them?

answers.answer: If you've got a million notes with the same date, nobody gets suspicious. But a million notes with the same serial number means someone has printed them - the serial number is for forgery prevention.
There IS a date on banknotes. Look in the middle where the yellow dots are, or either side front or back - it's the copyright date when that design was commissioned.

questions.question: In what century did human beings first start using money?
Why am I always warmer than my wife if everyone's body temperature is meant to be 37 degrees? Two of my kids are like me (hot) and two are like my wife (cold).

answers.answer: Metabolism

Body temperature is a fact measured by thermometer. But how your brain perceives the information is different for different people - this is sensory processing. Just like some people love spinning and others hate it, or some like tight cuddles and others don't - it's the same with temperature. Your sensory nervous system processes information differently. Some people perceive they're really cold, some really hot, despite having the same internal temperature. It's about pain perception and individual sensory differences.

questions.question: How do countries that don't have a royal family refer to their periods in history, like we refer to Victorian, Georgian, Edwardian, other than just using dates?

answers.answer: Maybe just the dates, numbers, or decades - the 30s, 40s, 50s

You refer to major historical events. In America: American Revolution, Pre-Depression, Depression, Prohibition, Civil War, post-Civil War, Colonial period. Now: post-Cold War, Obama era. France has Republics (First Republic, Second Republic, Third Republic). Germany has Reichs (First Reich, Second Reich, Third Reich).

questions.question: Do pigs on a farm always go back to their same little hut at night, or do they just go into one where there's room?
If I'm a misogynist (someone who hates women), what's the opposite - someone who hates men?

answers.answer: Misandrist or misandry - irrational dislike of boys or men

questions.question: What qualifications do you need to be able to do that? (become a vicar)

answers.answer: First of all, you have to have a vocation, which is the belief that God is calling you. Then you go to a national panel and they recommend you for training on the basis of nine different criteria. If you tick all the boxes, they put you forward for training and that will take two years residential or three years part-time, depending on your age and qualifications. Then you're ordained deacon first and usually ordained priest about a year later. The annual turn-down rate once you get to the final stage is about a third.

questions.question: Why do trees on the side of hills grow directly up? They don't grow out to the side. Why would they?

answers.answer: Trees grow towards the sun for photosynthesis. Photosynthesis needs sunlight so anything that does photosynthesis, like a tree or a plant or a shrub, is going to strive to reach the sun.

Trees are driven by two things. Hormones are driving them towards the sun, and there's something called the axiom of uniform stress. The tree needs the right amount of stresses in the right places. If a tree grew out of a 45-degree slope perpendicular to the ground, the tree would be unbalanced and would fall over. Therefore, the tree will bend and go upright and it will put reactionary roots on the opposite side of where it's leaning. The tree needs to be upright for stability, stability and light.

questions.question: If Scotland had their independence, would their flag be removed from the Union Jack?

answers.answer: It would revert back to how it used to look. The flag's made up of two separate acts of union. England and Wales joined with Scotland, so you had the cross of St George and the cross of St Andrew. That made up the first union flag. Then in 1800, we joined with Ireland, so the diagonal red bit is the cross of St Patrick. If the Scots leave, we remove the St Andrew's Saltire Cross. You'll have a union flag that's white with a red cross of St George and a red cross of St Patrick. If the flag came into being by certain acts of union within history, if one of those acts of union is reversed, then logically, the flag will have to change to represent that.

questions.question: Who was it who looks exactly like your daughter's mum? (splitting image vs spitting image)

answers.answer: It's spitting image. It comes from the TV programme 'Spitting Image'. The word is spitting not splitting.
Spitting image comes from the phrase 'spit and image'. You do a spit, it gives a reflection, and that's the image.

questions.question: How do they work out the mass of planetary bodies and stars?

answers.answer: I'm an A-level physics student. Basically, if you've got two stars or planets in orbit, that's called a system, and that system will have a centre of mass. So if you know the orbital speed of each body, you can work out using the distance they are away from that centre of mass using Kepler's third law of planetary motion. You can work out their masses because of the gravitational attraction between each one, and that's a physical constant. Velocity is measurable, and by combining the two, you can calculate mass.

questions.question: Who came up with the idea of a man's shirt size? Whoever decided that shirts should be measured by a man's neck?

answers.answer: Back in the day, the collar and the shirt were separate. Your collar would be bought separately from your shirt. You could wear two or three different shaped men could wear the same shirt, but they'd wear different sized collars. Because when you wear it tightly, the size of the collar really, really matters. In the 21st century, it's hard to understand because people hardly ever wear ties at all.

questions.question: Why can some people wink and some people can't?
How does a spider get a single strand of silk across really wide areas - like from a crane to a window?

answers.answer: Wind.

When the spiders release their silk into the wind, the wind actually catches hold of it and effectively works as a parachute, and they call it ballooning. It literally takes them one side of a field to the other.
The answer, my friend, is blowing in the wind. The answer is blowing in the wind.

questions.question: Do all animals burp?

answers.answer: I have a dog, and he most certainly does burp. Any animal with a gastric system and a stomach would do the same. I've seen fish blow bubbles, but whether that's a burp, I don't know.

questions.question: Why do horse heads look identical to seahorse heads? Their environments are completely different. What evolutionary mechanics made them look the same?
Can you detect a person's nationality by the way they laugh? Do different languages spawn different styles of laughter?
If you're standing on a beach looking out to sea, how far is the horizon? Do you think it'll be the same on every beach?

answers.answer: 7.2 nautical miles (which converts to approximately 6 miles). That's true everywhere, whenever there is a horizon.

Patrick was wrong. The answer is 1.25 times the square root of the height in feet of the observer. For example, at about 1,000 feet, you've got about a 30-mile range. The horizon gets further away the higher you go.

questions.question: Where does 'arm and a leg' come from? (meaning expensive)

answers.answer: It comes from medieval times when people used to have portraits painted. It used to cost extra to have the arm and leg painted. If you had a full frontal portrait, you'd need to pay for both arms and both legs. So the base price was one arm and one leg, and you paid extra for the second set.

questions.question: Is Braille the same in another language? Does it change according to the language spoken or written in the country you're residing in?

answers.answer: Braille is different in different countries. She is visually impaired and has experience with Braille.

questions.question: Why do we wake up? If you were in a dark room with no external stimulus like noise or light, what would wake you up? Is it our brain or our body?

answers.answer: During the night you're going into deep sleep. Then you will start to come out of it in the early morning. You'll get an increase in electrical activity in your brain, which will generally make you more active and more aware and bring you out of it. The fancy word is circadian rhythms. He learned this because his son suffers with epilepsy and this increased electrical activity is a trigger for his seizures in the early morning.

questions.question: Why doesn't grass grow in winter?

answers.answer: Grass doesn't grow below 5 degrees Celsius. He learned this from watching Monty Don on a gardening programme.

questions.question: How come there are pebble beaches? Is it man-made?

answers.answer: A beach is just a sandy beach but young. Cliffs break into rocks, water washes away the soil, leaving big rocks. Over thousands of years, water breaks rocks into smaller rocks, then pebbles, then eventually sand. Pebble beaches are simply beaches that haven't been weathered into sand yet.

questions.question: Why in the music world do they start counting at one, one, two, three, and then intro? And in the dancing industry, they start at five, six, seven, eight?

answers.answer: In music, the band is waiting to start up. One, two, three - not yet. Five, six, seven, eight - and then they're off, dancing when the music starts. It's the countdown to the beginning of the piece.

The one, two, three, four is the beginning of a phrase, which is why musicians say it as they come in. Five, six, seven, eight is counting the last beats of the bar before you start, to make sure you don't come in at the wrong time.

questions.question: Why do we get holiday blues? Is it a medically recognised condition? Is there a chemical explanation?

answers.answer: When you're having a good time for any reason - substances, drinking, having a good time on holiday - your brain is making lots of happy chemicals. When too many are made, the brain shuts down the amount of receptors available. Therefore, you need more the next time to achieve the same thing. So you feel depressed when you get back from somewhere brilliant. He read a book on it.

questions.question: Why do babies, before they cry, their bottom lip quivers? Does this happen on grown-ups as well?

answers.answer: Babies have undeveloped muscles and very tender, pliable skin. When crying, intense emotion causes the muscles to work hard to pull the lip down. For a baby with undeveloped muscles, just like muscles trembling during weight training, the lip quivers. Adults have more developed muscles so it doesn't happen as noticeably.

questions.question: Can dogs be bilingual? If you have commands in different languages from different owners, would it confuse the dog?

answers.answer: Dogs don't understand language - they understand sounds. Any trained dog responds to sounds, not meaning. You can train a dog to respond to any sound. The dog doesn't intellectually understand 'sit', it just associates that sound with the action. So yes, you could use 'sit' in English and 'siądź' in Polish and the dog would learn both separate sounds without confusion. The dog also responds to the melody of your voice.

questions.question: If we're adrift in the ocean, do we need to be as afraid of killer whales as we would be of sharks?
Who invented swimming?
What happens to birds when they die of natural causes? Where do they go? Why don't you ever see them fall out of the sky or fall out of a tree?

answers.answer: When birds feel poorly, they tuck themselves up in nests. If they die up there, they have flying hearses to take them to bird graveyards, which are always in trees and high up so you don't see them. Also mentioned cats running around with dinner plates during thunderstorms and birds being predated mid-flight.

Birds have a tendon in the back of their leg called the flexor tendon. When they sit down on a branch, it automatically clenches. That's why one of their toes is in reverse - three toes on the front and one on the back. They stay hooked on even after death, dangling upside down. Eventually they decompose and the tendons break down, so skeletons fall to the bottom of the tree. Scavengers - other birds, insects, beetles that bury birds - deal with them.

questions.question: How do eyelash bugs (tiny weenie bugs/follicle mites) get there? And what happens to them when we die?

answers.answer: Follicle mites are organisms that are carried in the air - they're airborne. They get on your eyelashes by landing from the air. They thrive in sebum, which is the oil that comes out of follicles. Your skin everywhere has these organisms.

questions.question: Why are things that are sad called 'the blues' and not the reds or greens? Blue sky is a lovely thing to look at, so why have I got the blues?

answers.answer: The 'blue note' is the use of a minor interval within a major key - if you're in C major, the blue note would be an E flat instead of E natural. But she didn't fully explain why it's called 'blue' specifically.

When the musical blues began in the deep south of America, prisoners who were mainly slaves had to wear blue overalls - denim. Therefore 'my man's got the blues' meant he was in prison, which meant being in trouble and sad. Then singing the blues linked to being in the blues, and getting the blues linked to both.

The blues comes from an old English term from around the 17th century - 'Blue Devils' was the nickname for hallucinations from alcohol withdrawal. A lot of the original blues musicians were alcoholics and drug addicts.

questions.question: Have the holes in toothpaste tubes got bigger to make us use more toothpaste and buy more?

answers.answer: It doesn't matter how big the hole is because you can only fit a certain amount of toothpaste on a brush. The brush heads haven't got bigger, so you can only squeeze on the same amount. Making the hole wider doesn't mean you'll use more.

questions.question: How can I get the last bit of perfume out of a spray perfume bottle?
How important do you have to be in life to be assassinated rather than murdered?

answers.answer: If you're killed for political reasons, it's an assassination. It doesn't actually have anything to do with someone being famous - it would be politically motivated, for enemies of some sort, not for personal gain or revenge.

questions.question: Why are the hairs on my head going grey, yet when I grow a beard it stays normal colour?

answers.answer: As hair gets older, it thins out. As it thins, it has a greater chance of losing colour. Also, hair on your face is more coarse than head hair, which can be very fine. So facial hair is a different type that holds colour better than thinning head hair.

questions.question: Why do insect bites itch more in the evening and at night than during the day?

answers.answer: It's to do with the level of histamine and steroid in your bloodstream. When you wake up in the morning, levels are higher. As the day goes on, levels drop. So at night your immune system responds more to the bite, trying to fix the problem, which causes more itching.

questions.question: Why do black plastic dustbin liners smell of bonfires?
How do they measure the accuracy of an atomic clock? If they built the most accurate clock ever, what do they compare it to?

answers.answer: A clock counts time by measuring a set interval between two points. Atomic clocks work by measuring radiation decay from radioactive materials like uranium - each atom decays and creates a click, and there's a constant gap between each click. Because the decay rate is constant and unaffected by external factors like heat anywhere in the universe, you can measure time incredibly accurately. As they discover heavier elements and materials with more constant decay rates, they can build more accurate clocks.

questions.question: Why is there heavy rain and light rain? What determines if rain is heavy or spitting? If a cloud is full of water, why doesn't it release it at the same rate every time?

answers.answer: In convective clouds like cumulonimbus (which produce thunderstorms), you have updrafts and downdrafts. Raindrops form in the cloud, then get carried up by updrafts where more water condenses onto them, then fall down, potentially getting carried up again repeatedly. They can grow bigger and bigger - sometimes turning into hailstones due to cold temperatures creating ice layers, or becoming very big raindrops that eventually become too heavy for any updraft and fall. In non-convective clouds like stratus (low, thick, dark clouds), there's no convection, so any water drop just falls out easily, even tiny ones, producing drizzle. Heavy rain means lots of raindrops, not necessarily bigger ones - though before thunderstorms you can get big individual raindrops that are few in number.

questions.question: Where does the term 'hard cheese' (meaning hard luck) come from?

answers.answer: If your cheese has gone stale and hard, that's bad luck

The expression first appeared in a play called 'The Tiger at Large' in a collection called 'The Acting National Drama' edited by Benjamin Webster, appearing in the 1830s. The expression involved a chap named Jed or Jem who said 'Jed or Jem, Jem, only earn a pound a week, and all they can afford is hard cheese.' So it's about being poor and only being able to afford cheap, poor quality cheese.

questions.question: If someone was stranded in space (like in the film Gravity), how long would it take for a rescue mission to be deployed? Are there any emergency space lifeboats or spaceships?

Why when a man becomes a knight does his wife automatically become Lady (like Lady Beckham), but when a woman becomes a Dame, her husband doesn't get any title? In an age of equality, why don't husbands of Dames get honoured?
Why do we feed bread to ducks? My four-year-old asked and I can't answer it. She then asked 'do they have sandwiches for lunch?'

answers.answer: Because bread is cheap, easily available, and it floats. When someone first wanted to feed ducks, they looked around their kitchen and found bread - something stale and not needed. It's still the same logic today. You wouldn't give them a tin of beans or smoked salmon; bread is the cheapest, most available option, and floating helps too.

questions.question: How do you make a word search? How are word searches constructed?

answers.answer: Using Sherlock Holmes' principle of elimination: there are only two possible ways to make a word search. Either: 1) Fill a grid completely with random letters, then search for accidental words, write them down, and set the puzzle. Or 2) Write words into a grid first, then fill gaps with random letters. The first method would mean searching through millions of random letters for accidental words - virtually impossible. Therefore, word searches are constructed by placing words in a grid first, then filling the remaining spaces with randomly generated letters.

questions.question: At what temperature does human skin start to cook? Whether in a hot bath or from sunbathing in Cyprus - when you come out looking like a lobster, at what temperature does cooking begin?
Why don't the oceans become saturated with salt over time? If rain constantly washes sodium into the sea from mountains, shouldn't the oceans be getting saltier and eventually saturated?

answers.answer: We haven't had enough years yet for saturation to occur. The oceans are so vast that the volume hasn't reached saturation point yet. Smaller bodies of water like the Dead Sea have reached higher salinity levels. There may also be a finite amount of salt that's already been washed in, or natural processes that remove salt from the ocean as well.

questions.question: Why do black bin liners smell of bonfires?

answers.answer: It's because of the make-up of the polymers - carbon, double carbon. But then all plastic bags should smell of bonfires. Perhaps it's something to do with the security or blackness of them, or when they're full of rubbish... I don't know.

questions.question: How can some people withstand holding hot stuff more than others? How can my mum pick up things that would scold most mere mortals?

answers.answer: It's just your skin getting used to it over time. Your skin gets harder to it, you get your layers used to it. It's like dealing with cold as well - postmen out in shorts in the snow because they're out all the time and feel the cold a lot less than we do. It's tolerance.

questions.question: In this enlightened day of technological scientific treatment, why is it that with a bit of fog, aircraft are grounded and delayed, yet planes can land in the dark and rain? What is the problem with fog?

answers.answer: Because they have trouble moving them around on the floor. They can fly electronically, but you can't get them on and off the runway electronically. It's the ground operations that are affected by fog.

questions.question: If you collected all the real cash in the world, all the printed money and coins, how much money would there be?

answers.answer: Less than 3% of all money ever coined is still in circulation as actual tangible currency. The rest exists digitally. You could never know for sure because currency could be buried, lost, or burnt.

questions.question: They say just before you have a heart attack, you get a sharp pain in your left arm. Why is it the left arm specifically associated with heart attacks?

answers.answer: When you're a fetus in your mum's womb, your heart is in your neck. As you develop, the heart drops down into your chest, taking with it a nerve that comes out from the spine in your neck. So as an adult, you've got a nerve that comes out from your neck, goes under your heart and then down into your arm. When you have a heart attack, it affects the nerve.
There's an artery that runs directly from the ring finger straight to the heart, which is why we wear a ring on that finger. This is also involved with heart pain and heart attacks.

questions.question: Does the sun have its own weather system?

answers.answer: Yes, the sun does have weather. There's an atmosphere around the sun with different rotational speeds at the equator and poles, creating the Coriolis effect. There's also weather caused by the magnetosphere where charged particles interact with the magnetic sphere and get force to move. The sun is on an 11-year cycle - it's more active at different points, meaning the magnetic sphere is more active, producing more solar wind.

questions.question: If all the ships and boats in all the waters of the world were taken out, would the water level decrease?

answers.answer: Six microns. According to UNCTD data, there's about 2.15 billion tonnes of ships currently at sea at any one time. A tonne of water is about a cubic metre, so 2.15 billion cubic metres divided by the surface area of the oceans (about 360 million square kilometres) equals six microns - just thicker than spider silk.

questions.question: We have a phonetic alphabet for letters (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, etc.). Is there one for numbers?

answers.answer: There isn't a separate phonetic alphabet for numbers, but there is a specific way numbers are pronounced over radio to avoid confusion. Nine is pronounced 'niner', three is 'tree'. For long numbers, you spin them out one at a time. This is part of radio operator training.

questions.question: What happens to a candle flame in zero gravity if it was in a space station? Would it be a flat disk or spherical shape?

answers.answer: The flame would be very small and circular/spherical because there's nowhere for the hot air to rise without gravity. Once it uses up all the oxygen in the surrounding area, it goes out. In space there's no up or down, so the flame goes in every direction equally.

From a physics point of view, the flame is caused by convection. If you turn a candle horizontal on Earth, the flame still goes up because of gravity. But actually, those convection forces are much greater than gravity, so it would be the same in zero gravity.
In space, a flame is spherical. The convection forces are independent of gravity.

questions.question: Why is shellfish measured as a liquid (pints) rather than by weight?

answers.answer: Many years ago before polystyrene and plastic containers, fish sellers went door to door, especially to pubs. Many customers were uneducated, couldn't read, write, or understand maths, but they understood what a pint was. It was an easy way to measure.

It goes back further to when scales were inaccurate and could be adjusted in the seller's favour. The quickest and easiest way was to serve prawns in a pint glass or pewter tankard, which had to be officially stamped and were reliable measurements.

questions.question: Do words get removed from the English dictionary? Otherwise it would become a really big book.

answers.answer: Yes, words are removed from the dictionary. I read about it in The Times - one of the words removed was 'shower bank'. Afterwards, writers like Giles Corrin used the word as often as they could to keep it alive.

questions.question: If someone donates a kidney to their brother and the brother dies during or after the operation anyway, can the donor get their kidney back?
Does anyone actually have authority over the moon? In terms of ownership? If I had the money and the means and I wanted to go and live there, would I need to ask permission from someone?

answers.answer: No one probably owns it as such.

questions.question: When you go out drinking, once you've been to the toilet once, you're forever back after every single drink. Everyone calls it breaking the seal. Is there an actual seal that gets broken in your body?

answers.answer: The body has a naturally produced hormone called ADH, standing for antidiuretic hormone. Alcohol disables that hormone in the body. The more you drink, the less the hormone's produced, which then allows your waters to pass through. It's not breaking a seal as such. It just feels like that because it's the slow effect of the alcohol.

questions.question: How do you describe colours to blind people, people born blind? How would they have done it?

answers.answer: In the film Mask, Eric Stoltz heated a stone up really hot and put it in her hands to teach her what red was. And then he put ice in her hands to teach her what blue was. Whether or not that worked or was reflective of a reality, I do not know.

A gentleman who called in who had been 100% blind since birth said colours didn't exist in his whole spectrum of life because he'd never experienced them. There is no explanation to colour because it didn't mean anything to him.

If you're totally blind and have never ever had sight, then you don't see any colour because black isn't a colour, it's an absence of colour. You can't see black unless you can see white to differentiate between the two. If you say blue to someone who is totally blind, they don't know what you mean because they know there are different shades of blue but have no concept of it.

questions.question: If you look at a bunch of birds, like swallows, they fly in funny shapes like round and up and down. They'll be joined by more birds and making the flock bigger and then eventually disappear. Why do they do that and who guides them? Is any bird in charge?

answers.answer: That's roosting.

It's an example of collective intelligence or chaos theory. Each individual bird follows a simple rule - it just follows the ones next to it that it can see out of the periphery of its vision. They fly around and other birds decide to join the party. They all start flying around together just following the ones next to them. They never create a repeating shape, which is why it's an example of chaos theory - a non-predictable shape.

questions.question: About the Big Bang Theory - do we have any idea where that spot is? The location of the bang? Where was the bang?

answers.answer: It's a bit of a misnomer because people misunderstand it. They visualise an explosion as we know it from a single point blowing up outwards. But that's not how the Big Bang happened. It literally happened everywhere at once. You can't pick out a single point in time and space and say that's where it started.

questions.question: Why do we have a dominant hand? Why aren't we ambidextrous? Why haven't we evolved to be ambidextrous?

answers.caller: June in Hoppington (archery and air rifle instructor)
answers.answer: The reason some things you do better with one hand and some with the other is to do with a dominant eye, not a dominant hand. If you hold your finger up in front of you and put it in front of a distant object, then close one eye and then the other, you'll notice that with one eye shut it stays in the same place. When you open that and shut the other one, it moves - that shows you which eye is dominant. It's which eye the message gets to the brain the quickest. So for hand-eye coordination you therefore use the hand on that side. Nobody's got two eyes that are exactly the same, nobody has perfect 20-20 vision.

questions.question: If you're in the bath and someone logs in a toaster, you'll die. If it's plugged in and you're in a swimming pool, would the same happen? How far does electricity travel in water?

answers.answer: It's Ohm's Law. It's dependent on the resistance of the water. You get electrocuted in a bath because you only have the water in the bath to create the circuit between the live and the neutral. If you put 250 volts into a swimming pool, it's different because there's more water and therefore higher resistance. If you're right next to the appliance it would be like being in the bath. But if you put the live and neutral around different sides of the swimming pool and you're in the middle, the current flow is determined by the voltage. If you haven't got enough pressure, you won't have enough current flow and therefore you won't get electrocuted. The more resistance you have, the more pressure you need to create the same current flow.

When the Costa Concordia had sunk and the lights were all fusing, you didn't see the guests and rescuers being electrocuted. The voltage and current is radiating out radially in all directions. You can look at the water as a series of parallel resistors and the voltage will drop by one over r squared, which means it drops very, very quickly. You don't have to be very far from it to not be affected by it.

questions.question: Does anyone have any legal authority over the moon? And what's the legal validity of owning a piece of moon that someone might sell you?

answers.answer: You own a piece of paper upon which is written 'this man owns a piece of the moon' but you don't actually own it. The companies selling moon rocks don't own them, it's not theirs to sell. When they plant flags, it doesn't mean one country owns it. As we venture further out there are talks of establishing a moon base. It will be an international effort. The question of which country owns it becomes redundant. It will be which species will own it - human beings as a whole. If we encounter intelligent species, then that would be a different matter.

questions.question: Why is it called a boxing ring when it's square?

answers.answer: It used to be a ring - a circle of people standing around watching a fight. When boxing evolved and became more formalised, probably after the Marquis of Queensbury brought in the Queensbury rules, the ring became a square because a square is much easier to peg out than a ring. But it was still called the ring because it used to be a ring of people.

questions.question: Are vegetarians technically allowed to eat bread? Because bread contains yeast, which is a living organism. Is it still alive after it's been baked?
How come different shades of the same colour clash? Like, why do two different blues clash when they're both blue?

answers.answer: Some colours have yellow undertones (warm) and some have blue undertones (cool). If you put a warm colour next to a cool colour, even if they're the same colour, they'll clash. I trained as a colour analysis consultant. People are also warm or cool toned, which is why some people look good in certain colours.

Colours absorb light and reflect it at different rates. That's why colours that clash are the same colour but reflecting light differently. In dim light, a black sock and a blue sock look the same colour. The brighter the light, the more the rate of absorption, the more likely colours are to clash.

questions.question: When did the Middle Ages begin and what came before?

answers.answer: You can't put an exact date on when the early ages end, but it was with the decline and fall of the Roman Empire. The Roman Empire was split into western (centred on Rome) and eastern (centred on Constantinople). I'd say by 700 AD.

The start of the early medieval period is taken to be around the fifth century AD, which coincides with when the first Anglo-Saxon kings arrived in England. Prior to that it was the Roman period. It was a gradual decline, not a sudden change. Around the turn of the fifth century, late 400s to 500s. Before the Middle Ages was the Roman period. The Middle Ages applies mainly to Europe.

questions.question: Why do stars twinkle but planets and the moon don't twinkle?

answers.answer: A star is a ball of burning gas. A planet is a lump of rock, not on fire. A star is like a candle flame and a planet is like the candle.

Stars burn pretty evenly and produce fairly even light. Stars from Earth are much further away than planets - light years away versus planets being very close. Although both look like points of light, a planet's apparent size on your retina is much greater than a star. A star is like a point, a planet is like a disk (like two ends of a drawing pin). Our atmosphere has air of different temperatures causing differing refraction. These differences affect the pointed end of the drawing pin much more than the wide end, so on a planet the differences cancel out.

Stars are not like a conventional fire - they're fusion reactors, squashing hydrogen into helium (hence Helios, the god of the sun). The points of light go through Earth's atmosphere and are deflected by various layers. In your eyes you've got rods which detect light, and the point of light gets moved from one rod to another rod so you detect it as a twinkle. It's nothing to do with disk size - that's wrong.

questions.question: What is the definition of classical music? Who decides what goes on the Classic FM chart?

answers.answer: Classical music was specifically around Mozart's time - that was the classical period. After that came the romantic period. What people call classical music is usually orchestral or chamber music, or music considered serious. If you wrote an opera now, it'd just be an opera. If you wrote a symphony now, it'd be a contemporary symphony. Unless it was composed in that specific period, it's not technically classical music. Baroque was before classical (Bach was Baroque). Beethoven onwards was romantic. Classic FM and Radio 3 decide based on what they consider serious music - written for orchestra, chamber group, or soloists.

questions.question: Why are hospital gowns designed the way they are? Why don't they open at the front or use Velcro?

answers.answer: The gowns are designed that way because most are used for people going to theatre who are under anaesthetic - it's much easier to remove a garment that doesn't go completely around the person when they can't help. Regarding Velcro: it couldn't be used because of health and hygiene reasons - the washing temperature wouldn't be hot enough to kill bacteria like blood, and it would rip the Velcro apart and melt the plastic hooks.

questions.question: Where does the term 'cold feet' come from - when someone backs out of something?
How do cows get so big and muscular eating only grass? Grass has no protein, no variety, yet cows are huge and muscular.

answers.answer: Grass has everything you need - it's just that the human stomach can't digest it. Cows have several stomachs. They eat a lot of volume and do a lot of exercise.

The grass goes into the cow's stomach and bacteria there feed on the grass. The cows don't get nutrition directly from the grass - they digest the bacteria. So they're eating meat, in a way - tiny, little microbe meats.

questions.question: Where does the word 'lukewarm' come from? What is the origin of the 'luke' part?

answers.answer: It comes from Dutch and German. The Dutch word for tepid is 'lau' and the German is 'lauwarm' meaning 'low warm'. It has nothing to do with St. Luke.

questions.question: Is there a connection between HP Sauce being called HP and the picture of the Houses of Parliament on the label? Why is the sauce named HP?

answers.answer: Originally called Garton's sauce after Fred Garton. When he found out it was being served in the Houses of Parliament, he changed the name to HP sauce. Later he sold the recipe to his vinegar supplier for about £50, who then put the Houses of Parliament logo alongside the HP logo.

questions.question: What are the origins of clapping? How did it start as a way to show approval?

answers.answer: Clapping is ape behavior that comes from our primate background. When gorillas and other apes get excited, they wave their hands about and hit things. As humans became more refined, we didn't want to hit ourselves, so we started clapping our hands together instead to show appreciation and excitement.

questions.question: Should flags fly at half-mast on Armistice Day or Remembrance Sunday?

answers.answer: No, flags don't fly at half-mast on Remembrance Sunday or Armistice Day. Half-mast is only for immediate events - like when a prime minister or sovereign dies. It's never commemorative, always reflects something that's just happened.

questions.question: What was the Battle of Karbala about and why is it being commemorated 1,374 years later?

answers.answer: The battle is about justice. Yazid was the tyrannical second Umayyad leader. Hussein, one of the grandsons of Prophet Muhammad, was invited by the people of Kufa to help overthrow Yazid. Against advice, Hussein went to Kufa but was let down by most of the Kufans. He only had 72 companions and was martyred by Yazid's army. This is specifically commemorated by the Shia community, though all Muslims agree it was a tragedy about injustice.

questions.question: Where do astronauts on space stations get their air from? How is it replenished when it runs out?

answers.answer: They take power from the solar panels and use electrolysis to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen is used for the astronauts to breathe and the hydrogen is used as fuel. They need supplies of water from Earth and the filters that remove carbon dioxide eventually wear out and need replacing, so they can't stay up there forever.

questions.question: Can you sneeze in your sleep? Can you sneeze and stay asleep?

answers.answer: Yes, you can sneeze in your sleep. The person with insomnia observed their partner making noises while sneezing in their sleep and filmed it to prove it.

questions.question: Can a noise actually knock you out or render you unconscious?

answers.answer: Yes, a really loud sound can knock you out. A very loud sound dissipates the air around it almost like an explosion. Also, high sonic frequencies can cause such extreme pain in the inner ear that the pain alone would knock you out. Like a defense mechanism - it can disorientate you and cause you to lose your footing.

questions.question: How did they measure the temperature of molten metal in the olden days before modern technology like infrared?

answers.answer: They couldn't measure it with instruments. The skill of the blacksmith or caster was in looking at the colour of the metal to judge when it was ready.

questions.question: Why do ordinary potatoes sprout within a couple of days in a vegetable rack but sweet potatoes never sprout?

answers.answer: Sweet potatoes grow from vines, not from sprouting tubers like regular potatoes. You use the actual vine that the sweet potato grows out of to replant and grow more sweet potatoes, whereas with regular potatoes you let them sprout and cut that in half to plant. They're different species - only very distantly related.

questions.question: How high do fireworks go in the sky? I went to Crystal Palace fireworks with my son and he asked me.

answers.answer: Fireworks go to around two or three hundred feet. This came from a Twitter feed of the Metropolitan Police helicopter. Because they fly between 1,500 and two and a half thousand feet, they're not affected by the fireworks. Commercial aviation flies higher than that as well.

questions.question: Who would have been the first country to implement the use of a flag? The first national flag?

answers.answer: Denmark. Chris found this answer in a pub quiz question book. He explained that Elsinore Castle, where Hamlet is set, overlooks a sound to Norway, and the Danish royal family used to charge every ship that came through that sound. He suggested the flag might have been a way of identifying ships to avoid being attacked, or a way of avoiding the charge to the Danish crown for using that bit of water.

questions.question: If an aeroplane weighs 100 tonnes laden with fuel, bags, and people, and one tonne is food, when the plane lands after everyone has eaten their meals, how much of that one tonne of food still exists?

answers.answer: They weigh exactly the same. Matter cannot be destroyed and cannot be created. Whatever matter there is in the universe now is what there was and what there will always be. If the plane was completely sealed and you burnt all the food, it would still weigh exactly the same because you haven't got rid of the matter that was there initially.

The plane would weigh less when it landed after everyone had eaten the food. There was a scientist who spent 40 years on a set of scales. 60% of what he consumed was what he experienced as weight gain. The rest went out as heat and gas. Once you've used the energy, it doesn't weigh anything.

questions.question: How do they compensate for the levels in houses on really sloped streets in old mining towns in Wales? How do architects plan to build a house on a hill?

answers.answer: The back wall is shorter than the front wall. You just need to shorten one side of the rectangle when building on a hill.

Dominic, an architect, explained: You draw a slope, put a dot at the higher part, draw a horizontal line which is your ground floor level where you enter the house. Then you continue along and drop down at the back, leaving a triangle in mid-air. The principle of cut and fill means if you draw a trapezoid, whatever you take out of the earth should ideally equal whatever you put in. You'd have a lower ground floor and could climb out of the window upstairs onto the ground behind the house. Then you cut back into the slope underneath the entry point on the high side.
You build the foundations higher at the front and lower at the back, graduating it down so that when you lay the ground floor, it's level. Some houses have stairs up to the front door.

questions.question: If you went back in time when average life expectancy was 30 or 40 years old, would people at 30 or 40 look old like they do now? Like an 80-year-old with wrinkles and grey hair?

What are the odds of twins being different colours? His friends have twins - dad is black, mum is white. One twin is black and one is white, but they look exactly the same otherwise, identical facial features.

answers.answer: If they were identical twins, they would have identical genes. Skin colour is determined by genes. So if they look the same but have different skin colour, they are not identical twins - therefore the odds are zero. They would be fraternal twins, not identical, and could look very similar just like two brothers would.

questions.question: In Durham Cathedral in the Chapel of St. Cuthbert, there's a painting on the ceiling where St. Cuthbert is wearing a cloak with swastikas around it. Why would he have swastikas on his cloak when this ceiling was painted before WWII?

answers.answer: Tony's wife Elaine is a historical expert. The swastika has been around about 4,000 years and is a sign of peace and love. It was a symbol in the Christian church before the Nazis used it. It refers to the wheel of life - the turning of life, with the four arms in a state of perpetual motion.

questions.question: Where did the phrase 'let sleeping dogs lie' come from? My dog wakes me up at 5:30 every morning demanding a walk, then sleeps all day. When I try to cuddle him, he growls. Is this where the phrase comes from?
About food on aircraft (question cut off)
Do contrails, the vapor trails behind aircraft, affect the Earth's atmosphere or create more rain?

answers.answer: Contrails are condensation trails created by heat from engines and wing vortices. They're just water vapor depending on temperatures at different heights. They don't affect anything.

Having worked in avionics and engineering for BA, I observed that when flights resumed after the Icelandic eruptions, the contrails built up so much that by midday the sky was completely overcast. The contrails do affect weather conditions.

questions.question: What causes earworms and can anyone give me a tip for how to get rid of them?

answers.answer: The science of music is fascinating. There's something about those notes working together to worm their way into your brain. The only way to get rid of it is either replacing it or not hearing it for a while so it fades away.

questions.question: How can honey be mass-produced? If honey is cheap in supermarkets, how can they produce it so cheaply when bees need nature, trees, and flowers?

answers.answer: You can mass-produce honey as long as you have enough hives and enough flowers with nectar. However, there is a limit on the months of the year - you have to shut down over winter because there are no flowers for bees to get nectar.

questions.question: Why do you need a request stop when only one bus route stops there? If you're standing at the bus stop, it's obvious you want the bus.

answers.answer: A bus stop is where buses have to stop. Regardless of how many buses go there, if there's somebody at the bus stop, they're meant to stop.
Not all buses on that route will have the same destination. Some will stop halfway across the turnaround, some will go to the full destination. So you still need to request.

questions.question: Why do cows lie down when it's raining?

answers.answer: I was always told it was to keep a bit of grass dry for when it stopped raining so they could stand on it.
That is a rubbish answer.
It's an urban myth. Studies showed cows are 50% standing and 50% sitting when it rains. There's no relationship between what they're doing and the rain - it's just where they are in the mood.

questions.question: Why don't deer ever leave Richmond Park when there are no cattle grids or gates to stop them?

answers.answer: The minor gates have cattle grids. The main traffic gates don't have them because cars come through. Deer are nervous animals and won't wait for cars then dash in behind them. They're pack animals with herd instinct, so if one leader goes out, more would follow. Their domain is inside the wall - anyone that made it out probably never returned to tell them.

questions.question: Is there a law that can stop parents from naming their child whatever they want?

answers.answer: There are no laws in this country governing what you can and can't call your child. There was a case in Scandinavia where someone wanted to name their child with numbers. David Bowie called his son Zoe (Zowie) who changed his name to Duncan when he got older.

questions.question: If someone plotted to kill the Queen, would they expect capital punishment?

answers.answer: Treason is still technically a capital offence in theory, but since the UK joined the EU, the EU required member states to abolish capital punishment. So while it was theoretically still on the books, it's effectively been abolished.
Arson in naval dockyards, piracy with violence, and high treason used to be capital offences, but since joining the EU we've had to get rid of all capital punishment.

questions.question: If identical twin females married identical twin males and each couple had a child, would the offspring be genetically the same as siblings?
Do stars revolve around other stars?

answers.answer: Yes, there are binary star systems. Our closest solar system, Alpha Centauri, is actually a binary star system with a smaller star called Proxima Centauri. All stars in our galaxy revolve around the supermassive black hole at the center.

Stars technically don't revolve around each other - they revolve around the center of gravity between them. Binary systems are two stars doing a little dance together around their common center of gravity. All stars in the Milky Way do technically orbit around the central supermassive black hole.

questions.question: Why do we have to wear white clothes when it's hot? We developed black skin to protect against the sun in hot countries, so why not black clothes?

answers.answer: The question is based on false premises. We don't have to wear white - desert dwellers are often found in black clothes. Actually, black both absorbs and reflects heat differently than white, and there's a difference between direct sunlight and ambient heat. It may not actually be cooler in white than black.

questions.question: If you buy a ticket to see a band on their 'farewell tour' or 'last ever show' and they reform 18 months, 2 years, or 10 years later, can you legally apply for a refund? Is there anything legally binding about the word 'farewell'?

answers.answer: No, there's nothing legally binding in a farewell tour. About 10 years ago, Barbara Streisand announced her final tour, did three more, and someone tried to sue the box office company but had no joy.
Richard's answer is not definitive, just something he read in the paper, but he liked the cut of his jib.

questions.question: What does the word 'para' mean? We've been arguing about this in a pub for years. Words like paramedic and parachute - what do they have in common?

answers.answer: The Greek word para means next to or beside. So a paramedic is one who comes to you rather than you going to them.
Para, as in paramedic, comes from the Greek meaning 'next to' or 'alongside'. Paralegal works alongside a professional. Parallel is two lines next to each other.
Para means next to, but it's also beyond. Paranormal is beyond normal. Paratrooper is beyond normal troops.
Parari is Latin for defend or ward off - you get this in parachute or parasol. Parasol wards off the sun, parachute defends from falling.
The word para comes from the Latin parari. In Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese, 'para' means 'stop'. A parachute stops you falling.

questions.question: Live yeast - I usually freeze it, defrost it, and it works the same as before freezing. Since it's a live organism or bacteria, how come it can be deep frozen and still survive?

answers.answer: It's something to do with bacteria. Freezing doesn't kill it - it just stops it from growing. You have to kill yeast with heat. It's like sperm and embryos being frozen for fertility treatment. It goes into stasis, biological limbo.

questions.question: Why do people take swear words as an offense? To me, words like the F-word are just very good describing words for actions and things. Who decided they would be offensive?

answers.answer: People use swear words on subjects they're frightened of. Because they're societally out of order, people get offended. Back in the Middle Ages when the church was powerful, most swearing was religious because that's what people feared.

questions.question: Why does our belly rumble? Is it psychological, a chemical reaction? Even after eating, sometimes my belly rumbles.

answers.answer: Acid. The acid in your tummy bubbles and makes the sound. It's always rumbling but echoes more when your tummy's empty so you hear it more.
It's called peristalsis - the movement of food through the alimentary canal. But what CJ means is the audible sound, which comes from overproduction of acid from the gallbladder.

Gallbladders don't produce acid - they produce bile, which isn't an acid. The noise comes from peristalsis, the squeezing of the bowel, which happens all the time. If there's no food, there's gas. When you push gas bubbles through a small opening, it makes a gurgling sound. It's called borborygmi. The gas is formed by bacteria breaking down sugars and releasing carbon dioxide, not by acid.

questions.question: After a bath or shower, why does it take longer to dry the back of your arms than the back of your legs compared to the front?

answers.answer: It's about hair. The top of your arm is hairy, the underside is hairless. Hairs hold droplets and globules, so they've done half the drying for you. On hairless skin, you just have a sheen that needs more careful drying.
It's wrong because it's harder to get to your back. Your front is easier to reach. Even on your arm, it's about accessibility.
The towel is wet while he's drying the front bit. By the time he's drying the back of his leg, the towel is already moist, so it soaks up less water.

questions.question: If you consider the time it takes for light from distant galaxies to reach the Hubble Space Telescope, is it possible that we're looking back at our own galaxy and photographing ourselves?

answers.answer: Photons propagate at the speed of light. Nothing can overtake them. The universe is expanding and there hasn't been enough time for photons to reach the limit of the universe, bounce off the boundary and come back. We could never overtake a photon with a camera to take a picture of our past.

Light leaves Earth at the speed of light and by definition nothing except light can catch up with light if it has mass. We cannot overtake light to be somewhere else looking back at our own light. Aircraft routinely overtake sound, but you cannot travel at the speed of light because as you get towards it, your mass increases exponentially. At the speed of light, your mass would be infinite and you wouldn't have enough energy. The universe is expanding at the speed of light, so any light within it can never catch up with it. We live in an open universe that will continue to expand forever.

questions.question: Is there a determined age at which the entire internal dialogue of the mind develops? Is it different from external dialogue? My bilingual nephews were taught French and English from an early age - which internal dialogue would they have developed first?

answers.answer: Whatever they spoke first is probably their dominant language. Even if there is a difference between internal and external dialogue, it's going to be just a couple of days. You can't think in words without speaking in words at some point. Some people are truly bilingual by speaking both languages from the cradle.

questions.question: When I need to use the toilet and I'm on my way home, I can hold it. But just as I pull into my driveway, suddenly I can't hold it. Why does the key in the door trigger such urgency?
How do light particles reach our eyes without being blocked or interfered with by all the other light particles bouncing around from every angle?

answers.answer: What matters is what reaches your retina. Your eye doesn't push outward into the world - light comes INTO your eye and that's what you see. The light that reaches your retina is what you perceive. The brain registers everything upside down but we turn it up.

questions.question: Why can't you buy thin sliced bread anymore? It used to exist in the 70s with Mother's Pride brand.

answers.answer: Thin sliced bread still exists. You can buy it in Budgens.
Sainsbury's own brand sells white thin sliced bread. They have medium, thick, extra thick, and thin sliced in both brown and white.
Photographs of thin sliced bread were sent via Twitter to prove it still exists.

questions.question: Why do we celebrate Jesus' birthday on the same date every year, but Easter falls on different dates each year?

answers.answer: Easter is tied to the Catholic calendar where feast days (Ash Wednesday, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, Easter Sunday) need to fall on specific days of the week, so they manipulate the ecclesiastical calendar to ensure those feasts fall on those days.

Easter is actually a pagan festival linked to the moon and the equinox. Missionary priests adopted an already existing religious festival and adapted it to Christian doctrine. The first Sunday after the spring equinox moves across the calendar each year, and that's where they stuck Easter Sunday.

questions.question: Why do men who lose hair from their head grow more hair in their ears, nose, and on their back?
How can I make my homemade cider more alcoholic? Some ciders in the supermarket are 4%, some are 7% - what do they do differently?

answers.answer: You need to add sugar for the yeast to produce alcohol. The alcohol is produced by yeast using sugar as the by-product. Yeast can be present on apple skins as wild yeast, but you should add proper brewer's yeast. The more sugar, the more alcohol you get, but too much alcohol becomes toxic to the yeast and kills it. You need a hydrometer to measure the alcohol content.

questions.question: Why is there a slidey vent thing at the top of the hose on a cylinder vacuum cleaner where it goes into the tube?

answers.answer: It's to reduce suction when needed. When you're doing worktops or delicate fabrics with strong suction, things get stuck. You open the vent to reduce the pressure so you can still vacuum but things don't get stuck.

questions.question: Why is it called the funny bone and how does it work?

answers.answer: There is a nerve that is very superficial just between the skin and the bone where the funny bone effect takes place - one of two nerves that supply the arm below the elbow. It supplies particularly the little finger and the little finger side of the middle finger. Impact causes a concussion to the nerve and you get a radiated sensation down the little finger side of the forearm involving little finger and sometimes ring finger. It's exceptional because most nerves are better protected. It's called the funny bone because of the Latin word 'humerus' which is humorous.

questions.question: What is a 49er? Why are the San Francisco 49ers called that?

answers.answer: A 49er is the nickname given to somebody who took part in the Californian gold rush in 1849. That's where they get the name, and why they wear gold in the team uniform.

questions.question: Why do you have to turn a gas cooker hob to high to light it, rather than just lighting it on low?

answers.answer: If you turn it to high first, you light it and then turn it down. If it started on low, you'd have to turn it up to light it, then turn it down again.

There's a thermocouple (a little thermopile) that needs to get hot to allow the gas to come through from the valve. You need a strong flame to hold the gas open. If you had the low position first, it wouldn't get hot enough quickly enough and probably wouldn't be in the flame.

questions.question: If Superman flew around the world backwards, would time actually go backwards?

answers.answer: No. Even if it was possible to slow down the rotation of Earth, we're traveling at the same speed as Earth with no relative velocity, so we don't feel it. But if the planet suddenly slowed down, even a small amount, we'd keep going at the same speed and it would be catastrophic - we would all die.

questions.question: Why does my phone charge faster in my car than at home when it's the same electricity?
How can you tell the difference between an indoor spider and an outdoor spider? Can a spider catch another spider in its web?

answers.answer: Each spider's web is individual to the spider who constructed it. When they weave it, they leave a trail of sticky silk that goes into little blobs. Other spiders get caught in it. A spider can catch another spider on its web, and even could catch itself if it had amnesia.

questions.question: How long is a woman's umbilical cord?

answers.answer: Midwife. Generally, they're long enough so that the baby can be delivered onto the breast without snapping. Roughly between 18 inches and two feet. Occasionally you get ones that are very short and you have to pull a bit, or really long ones.

questions.question: Is there such a thing as a homeopathic poison? If you give somebody something and they believed it would harm them, would it hurt them? For instance, if someone had a peanut allergy and you gave them something then told them there were peanuts in it, would they have the same allergic reaction?

answers.answer: Yes, you can. It's called a nocebo. The Latin translation for placebo is 'I shall please' and for nocebo is 'I shall harm.' A harmless substance that creates harmful effects in a patient that takes it because they believe it is harmful. She learned this during a sports science degree.

questions.question: When we have a half moon, how does the moon get that dead straight line down the centre of it? I understand that crescent moons have the shadow of the Earth, but where does the straight line on a half moon come from?

answers.answer: It's all about right angles. Imagine hanging a tennis ball from the ceiling with a torch at the same height shining on one side. Walk 90 degrees around and look at the tennis ball with the torch on the left. The left hemisphere will be bathed in light, the right hemisphere will not, and there'll be a straight line down the middle. When the sun is exactly 90 degrees to your line of sight to the moon, exactly half is illuminated with a straight edge.

questions.question: Who is last in line to the throne? Is it even a thing? How far do they go?

answers.answer: The actual list is infinite because you just keep going further and further back through history.
[Brief interjection] You have two lobes in your brain, two chambers in your heart... [Not a full answer]

questions.question: Why does 19 degrees indoors feel quite cool when set on a thermostat, but when you go outdoors and the weather forecast says it's 19 degrees, it feels quite warm?

answers.answer: Damp surveyor and condensation specialist. It's more to do with relative humidity than wind chill. If humidity is higher outside than indoors, you feel the temperature differently. In the UK at 33 degrees with 50% humidity, evaporation of sweat cools you. In the Amazon at 30 degrees with 90% humidity, you feel hotter because perspiration doesn't evaporate as quickly.

questions.question: Why did my avocado go brown after being left out of the fridge for just five minutes? What's the chemical reaction?

answers.answer: When you cut the fruit, enzymes are exposed to the oxygen in the atmosphere. They start to react with the oxygen and discolour. Chefs sprinkle lemon juice over fruit to prevent this.
The enzyme is polyphenol oxidase. It catalyzes reactions that make the pigments change. It reacts with oxygen and uses oxygen in the reaction to hydroxylate compounds that exist in the plant tissue.

questions.question: How long does it take for our solar system to do one orbit of the Milky Way?

answers.answer: It takes 200 million years. We're 30,000 light years from the galactic central point. This comes from Eric Idle's Galaxy Song. The galaxy bulges 16,000 light years thick in the middle but is 3,000 light years wide out by us. And since the universe is expanding, the time would change over billions of years.

questions.question: Why do humans have two of most organs (kidneys, lungs, eyes, ears, arms, legs) but only one brain and one heart? Wouldn't two hearts or two brains be advantageous?

answers.answer: The bold evolutionary answer is that at no point in human development did having two hearts provide an advantage. Either that mutation never appeared on the path of human evolution, or it appeared but provided no evolutionary advantage and so disappeared. It must have provided a disadvantage, otherwise it would have been passed on genetically. We don't use 75% of the brain we've already got, so clearly having more doesn't automatically help.

questions.question: Why do we call it a saucepan when we use it for vegetables, soup, and other things, not just sauce? Even a milk pan is called a milk saucepan. Why is the word 'sauce' constantly repeated?

answers.answer: Because you can call it what you want. If you want to call it a vegetable pan, you can. But we keep calling it saucepan so everyone knows what we're talking about. Think of sauce as a synonym for liquid. You're always cooking with liquid in it, even if it's water for vegetables.

questions.question: What do the numbers on a toaster mean? Do they relate to the heat or the amount of time your toast is in the toaster for?

answers.answer: I think I want to go to the toaster one. The toaster one, all right. It was a bit of an odd one. We haven't got an answer yet. We're running out of time. What do the numbers on a toaster mean? I don't think it's anything to do with the amount of heat. It's to do with the amount of time. So if you put it on one, it will pop up a lot quicker than when it's on six.

There's like a little bimetallic strip in there that positions it along the bimetallic strip, basically. So that's how it works, but Scott was right about what it does. Yeah, it was on its way, and it is time, and things stay warm as well, so it's not the most accurate. It's pretty crude. Yes, because that's what I said to the original questioner, is that in laboratory conditions, you'd have to let the toaster cool to the same temperature before reactivating on a different level.

questions.question: In tennis, there are various competitions. For example, the Davis Cup. Where countries will compete against one another. And the matches in those competitions are referred to as rubbers. And I wonder where that term comes from.
Why is a quad bike so called? Because quad being four and bike being two would suggest eight wheels.

answers.answer: When they were first invented, they weren't called quad bikes. They were just called quads. But bearing in mind, you sling your leg over it and ride it with a set of handlebars, the general slang became quad bike. I know this because a friend of mine used to race one, and I race a dirt bike. It's just become part of... The name has developed. But in a way, that doesn't answer the question, because when it was first invented, it should have been called a quad cycle. No, it shouldn't have been called a quad cycle, because the cycle... The cycle involves your legs, doesn't it? The cycle of your legs going round and round.

The point he was making was that you don't pedal a quad bike, so there's no cycling element to it. So you could have a quad cycle, but it would, as Lucy points out, be like a go-kart with no engine. There's no cycling involved. So a tricycle, a bicycle. You might say a motorcycle, but, frankly, you shouldn't.

Henry Ford's first four-wheeled vehicle was called the Quadricycle. Cycle's got nothing to do with pedals, it's just got to do with the wheels turning around. So the original question of why a quad bike is not called a quad cycle, or indeed a quadricicle, is just coincidence, and it actually should be.

questions.question: When I have a wash, I wash my face, wash my hands. And then dry them off in the towel. Now, presuming that having washed my face and hands, they are clean, why does the towel get dirty?

answers.answer: Because it's actually dead skin. Because that's why you have things like exfoliators to remove all the dead skin.

The one about dirty towels after a shower, I think it is the sebaceous material on the skin's surface, rather than sweat, added to desquamated cells, which rub off onto the towel. The sebaceous material oxidises to blackheads in the sebaceous glands.

questions.question: Why are radio presenters and TV hosts, TV presenters, less famous than actors, even though they occupy the same media?

answers.answer: The problem's with you, not with them. You probably walked past lots of actors, but you didn't notice, because you don't know who any of them are. You need someone like Shane Ritchie for a proper comparison with Alistair Burnett. As a Z-list celebrity, I get stopped probably once a day by people who want to say hello to me, and I've got some friends who are proper famous, and they will get stopped in some cases more and in some cases less. The nature of this job is that you know we're all friends. People think they know me, so they say, Hi, Jay.

questions.question: Does a spider's web lose its adhesive properties when wet? And if it dries out, does it then assume its stickiness again?
My daughter Nancy is ten today. We gave her a watch. And she looked at the clock on the mantelpiece and said, Daddy, why is it called a watch, not a clock? A wrist clock.

answers.answer: When I first joined the Jewish... Because, funny enough, I asked the same question. You've got to look back in the history of timepieces. You think you started with the sun dial, worked through water clocks, blah, blah, blah. Clocks, and then you'd have a carriage clock, which you'd actually have in a case, and take that round in your carriage to know the time, wherever you were. But obviously, people needed... When industrialisation and things like that started, people needed... They needed a timepiece to measure specific periods of times. Like you get a watch on a boat. So the first ones were pocket watches. You would be looking at it constantly, in a way. A pocket watch. Yes. It started with... So there's a watch you put in your pocket to carry around as a timepiece to measure specific periods of time. Not... And then, obviously, as watch and clock makers managed to make things smaller, they then produced a watch which went on the wrist, so it then was known as a wrist watch.

questions.question: Why are cats called moggies?
