answers.answer: Moggy. It's a derivation of the word mongrel. And often it's just called the mog. People say, well, I've got the mog indoors or whatever. A moggy is a cat. A cat that's not pedigree. Indeed, and they're much healthier, too. My best friend breeds Persians and I rang her up.

questions.question: How many miles above the Earth's surface does the gravitational pull start?

answers.caller: Bob (Guildford, PhD in mechanical engineering and great interest in physics and space)
answers.answer: Theoretically, assuming there's no other planetary object around, the gravity of a planet or a star extends to infinity. And beyond? And beyond. You cannot go beyond infinity. Now, the force of gravity is related just mathematically to the inverse of the square of the distance between the two objects. If the distance doubles, the force becomes a quarter. It diminishes, but it diminishes infinitely. The moon is in orbit because of the gravitational pull of the Earth extends nearly 324,000 kilometers where the moon is. So there's no point at which it starts working? No, there's no point. Theoretically, it will stop working at infinity.

There's a belt around the Earth called the Clark Belt. Yes. It's named after Arthur C. Clark, who was a great science fiction writer. And he calculated and put in books way before it was ever done how far out you'd need a satellite where it wouldn't drop back down to Earth. It's somewhere between 20,000 and 25,000 miles from... And there'd still be gravitational pull there, but not enough to drag a satellite back down to Earth. Not enough to drag it back down to Earth. The significance of the Clark Belt is that at that distance, the orbit will be geostationary. That means the satellite is going around the Earth, but it goes around the Earth once every 24 hours. So it looks down at the same spot on the planet all the time.

questions.question: Scott of the Antarctic took a gramophone with him on his expedition. And I've got a picture of the gramophone playing, and there's a husky standing in front of it, and he's got one paw raised up, his front paw, just a few inches off the ground. And I was flying a small radio-controlled plane over the park the other day, and I noticed the dog stopped. He'd done exactly the same thing. I just wondered why dogs, when they sort of pay attention to something, they lift a paw, a front paw.

answers.answer: They're getting ready to chase. Don't you think? I mean, you've got... It's a bit like a... It's better than a standing start. You've got one paw up in the air already. If you've got four paws on the ground you push off, you're going to land on your nose. I think it goes a bit deeper than that. I think it's something to do with their sort of... Something to do with their attention span, first of all. Ah, so you mean like us sticking our tongue out to concentrate? Yes, possibly.
It's a sign of stress when dogs lift their paws.

questions.question: Where does the five-day working week originate from?

answers.answer: When it became a five-day working week. My father was a Federation steward in the Transport and General Workers Union for 35 years. And I can remember in the 50s, he was duty-bound to work a six-day week or a five-and-a-half-day week. Really? A 46-hour basic working week then. And the trade union movement fought to bring the working week down, eventually from a 46 to a 44 to a 42, sorry, down to a 40. Down to a five-day week. Somewhere around late 50s, early 60s.

questions.question: Can you change your godparents?

answers.answer: I don't think, because it's a religious... I mean, you could just say, would you be my godfather? It'd be quite a sweet thing to ask someone. But I don't think it would be on any, I say, official footing.

I tried to do the same thing. Because I felt that one of them was now unsuitable to be godparent to my son. And I wanted to add a godparent as well, and I went to the vicar that had baptized my son, and I was told, absolutely, it cannot be done. Not whatsoever.

questions.question: Who made the first cake?

answers.answer: It started off in the Middle East. The ancient Egyptians baked breads and pastries with honey, milk, eggs.

questions.question: Why do men look sideways at the car going past them when women don't?

answers.answer: Women learn at a very early age not to respond to the suspicion that a man is staring at them because of men driving up and down the country staring at women. It's a sixth sense that women develop.
Women just don't care, really. We are brought up not to look at strange men looking at us in any circumstance. You don't care that you're being overtaken, usually, in the way that men do.

questions.question: Did the Big Bang take place in complete silence and complete darkness?

answers.answer: There would have been a lot of light, a heck of a lot of light, because when the Big Bang occurred, these gases were combusting and there would have been explosions all over the place.

There were no gases combusting. The Big Bang started with a point mass with 10 to the power of 78 particles - all the mass of the universe into less than the volume of a full stop. Around it was nothing - no space, no time, no nothing. The Big Bang wasn't a conventional explosion; it was nuclear physics reactions with particles changing and matter annihilating antimatter, moving out at the speed of light. The noise isn't conventional noise - it's radiation corresponding to the echo of the Big Bang at four Kelvin. If you look at static on an old TV, some of that is caused by that radiation - you can truthfully say you're looking at the echo of the Big Bang 14 billion years ago.

questions.question: When a chicken has a fertilised egg inside it, at the point the egg is still inside the chicken, is the chicken pregnant?

answers.answer: Pregnancy might only refer to mammalian gestation.

Technically, it isn't pregnant. The egg gets fertilised while inside the womb. The bird serves as a natural incubator for the egg to grow. A chicken can never be pregnant - it can only have either a fertilised or an unfertilised egg.

questions.question: Why do we pronounce some towns and cities in a foreign way? Like why does France say Londres instead of London? Why can't they just say London? Why do we say Paris instead of Paris?

answers.answer: We would have read the word before we heard it. London was Londinium before it was anything else. It's about the evolution of place names.

Different nationalities develop their own names for certain famous towns because they want to be able to pronounce them, but they can't pronounce them properly in their own national language. For example, London contains sounds that French people find very difficult - there's the 'schwa' sound in the second 'o' which doesn't exist in French, and the final 'n' would be almost silent. So they say it as it would be written in French, as a French word. Similarly, English people find it difficult to say Venezia, so they say Venice, and the French would find it very difficult to say Edinburgh.

questions.question: If you're inside a metal box with no windows, and you turn on a light bulb, then turn it off, what happens to the light photons?
Why does it get warmer in the winter when it rains, but when it rains in the summer it gets colder?

answers.answer: It has something to do with the temperature of the rain being somewhere in between the two temperatures. There's a tipping point - if the temperature into which the rain is falling is below or above a certain point, then the rain is going to have either a cooling or a warming effect.

It's all to do with cloud cover. With a clear blue sky in winter, it's normally incredibly cold, and if you get cloud cover just before the rain, that's why the temperature rises. It probably has the opposite effect in summer.

questions.question: Is there an exothermic reaction going on with one of the ingredients in a bubble bath? When you have a bubble bath, it always seems to be hotter than a normal bath, and she always needs more cold water.

answers.answer: The bubbles dissipate the heat out of the bath. The bubbles are carrying the heat out, so the bath gets cooler when it has bubbles in it.
The bubble bath provides a line of insulation, so the heat doesn't escape from the bath water. [The bubble bath keeps the heat in, similar to how clouds provide insulation.]

questions.question: Why don't we get thunder or lightning during snowstorms?

answers.answer: Thunderclouds need lots of warm moist air to form, generally over the equator or tropical regions. You're not going to have snow forming in those clouds because it'll be too warm for snow to form. The answer is the opposite - it's why you don't get thunderclouds when it's cold. Thunderclouds have lots of latent heat energy inside them, and snow can't form in that warmth.
You do get lightning and thunder in snowstorms. You just don't hear the thunder because the snow dampens it out. It's called thundersnow.

questions.question: When people from different languages impersonate other cultures, do they pick up on the same sounds? For example, if a Spanish person is doing a comedic impression of a German, would they use the same sounds as an English person doing a German impression? Would a Spanish person impersonating a German in Spanish use the same 'V for W' and 'ZZZ' sounds that English speakers use?

Does your blood actually get thicker when it's hot or cold? My Australian friend said when he left Britain and went back to Sydney, it would take a while for his blood to thin out because his blood had got thicker in England's cold weather.

answers.answer: When you dehydrate, which is obviously kind of to do with being hot, your blood thickens, which causes problems with heart palpitations and clotting. In respect to your blood thickening and thinning due to the temperature, you'd be more likely to dehydrate in hot weather, which would involve your blood thickening.

questions.question: Why is the freezer door so hard to open compared to the fridge door? I open the fridge, pour my drink, open it again to put the bottle back, go to get ice from the freezer, open it, close it, put ice in the drink, and need the arm of Arnold Schwarzenegger to open the freezer again.

answers.answer: When the door's shut, the temperature inside the freezer is freezing. When you open the door, the air from the room goes into the freezer. When you then shut the door, that warm air gets cold and the mass of it gets smaller, which causes a vacuum and the door halves stick together.

questions.question: Can people still become saints? If I go over to Syria and sort everything out, am I Saint Dave?

answers.answer: Yes, the Catholic Church effectively has the gift of sainthood in the Pope's gift. You would have to do a miracle - something that could be construed as miraculous. There are currently two Brits under consideration for sainthood: John Henry Newman and Francis Barbary. There's a process of beatification where you have to prove that a miracle has been done by their relic, and then there's quite a strict process at the Vatican.

questions.question: Why do people take their glasses off when looking through binoculars? My friend took his glasses off to look through our sea otter light. If your eyes are bad, wouldn't you leave your glasses on to see better?

answers.answer: You take your glasses off and look through binoculars because you can see clearly. Binoculars have a similar setup to lenses and refocus. The lens on your glasses focuses point to what you're seeing. When you take them off and put binoculars in front, you adjust the lens. You wouldn't want to put your glasses and stick the binoculars in front because then you actually shorten the binoculars. You can adjust binoculars for long and short distance depending on the magnification.

Most proper binoculars are fitted with special rubber cups, which are normally folded back so you don't notice them. But they are there for spectacle wearers and can be turned around so you can look through your binoculars while still wearing your spectacles. That's what the rubber cups are for. If you're astigmatic, which most people are, the focusing correction won't work, so you should keep your glasses on and use the rubber cups. If you're just ordinarily short-sighted or long-sighted, then the focusing adjustments on the binoculars can correct for that.

questions.question: Why is fat, in general (human fat, animal fat, cooking fat), so flammable? What is in fat that makes it so flammable when you set fire to it?

answers.answer: Fat is held together by hydrogen bonds. If fat is free fatty acids, they're held together with carbon with a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonds are highly malleable. The reason why fat is flammable is because the fatty acid molecules are held together by hydrogen. It's the hydrogen that goes up like a bonfire.

questions.question: Why is it that when the dishwasher is finished, everything in the dishwasher is dry, except there is always water inside non-stick pans? I think it's about the non-stick coating.
Is it true that astronauts cannot cry in space, i.e. zero gravity?

answers.answer: Astronauts in space produce tears, but the tears cannot drop from the eye because there's no gravity to take them from the eye. The tears would build up dangerously in the eyes and could eventually damage them. That's one of the reasons why Kleenex tissues were invented - to soak the tears from the eye.

questions.question: Why is it that whenever you spray a fly and it dies, it always finishes up on its back? Little legs up in the air. You never see it the way it normally walks. Always on its back. Even the picture on the fly spray can shows a fly on its back.

answers.answer: A fly is always hanging upside down the majority of the time. So when you spray it, it's top heavy and it falls on its back.

questions.question: If you had an eternal or everlasting staircase (like an escalator), and you put a slinky on it, would it go on forever?

answers.answer: On an infinite staircase, a slinky wouldn't carry on forever. The reason is about energy losses. As the slinky expands and contracts, there's internal friction between the coils, so it loses energy there. It loses more energy as heat when being stretched and shrunk. There's also air resistance as it moves down between the treads. The slinky is an inherently stable thing. You'd have to give it enough of a nudge to overcome the initial inertia.

An infinite staircase is an infinite source of gravitational potential energy. Assuming the staircase is perfectly straight and the slinky is perfect, a perfect slinky will not go on forever because slinkies have an inherent asymmetry to them. They'll go slightly off to the side.

questions.question: In theory, could you have a microwave that would make things go cold quickly? Like a kitchen microwave that could make a lump of meat from the butcher's go cold in 30 seconds? Something that sits on the worktop like a microwave.

answers.answer: Yes, you could. You could use dry ice or liquid nitrogen to freeze something at full tilt. In fact, some supermarkets used to have devices where you could put white wine in if it wasn't chilled. You could take an old microwave, chuck away all the innards, get a fire extinguisher, hook up the nozzle to the back of the microwave, stick your meat in, close the door, turn on the fire extinguisher, give it 30 seconds, and bring it out frozen solid. It's only carbon dioxide - what you're breathing out all the time.

questions.question: What is a decibel? I know it's a unit of sound, but I can't visualise it. If someone says earplugs block out 24 decibels, what does that actually mean?

answers.answer: A decibel is not actually a measurement of sound at all. It's a measurement of a ratio between either two voltages or two powers. It's logarithmic.

For every three decibels a sound level increases, it actually increases ten times. One decibel would be something virtually inaudible. Twenty decibels would probably be about the level of your TV when you watch TV at night.

Sound waves are almost identical to water waves. Loudness is dictated by how high the wave is. If you compare 10 decibels to 20 decibels, it's not twice as loud - it's 100 times louder. 30 decibels is 1,000 times louder. Zero decibels is silence. 120 decibels is an aircraft taking off. A decibel is a tenth of a bell, named after Alexander Graham Bell. It's measured by a decibel meter which works like a reverse microphone.

questions.question: Why do birds crossing a road have to swoop down in front of cars rather than maintaining their height and flying across at a safe height? Are they playing chicken or are they suicidal?

answers.answer: They use objects to disguise themselves from potential predators and to disguise themselves from potential prey. They can creep up on their prey more easily if they're going between objects or very close to objects, and they can disguise themselves from anything above that might pose a threat more easily as well.

questions.question: If steel crittle doors are that heavy, how heavy is the rest of my house in total? It's a three-bedroom detached house.
Why is it that when we're in pain, we clench our eyes shut tight and wince? It doesn't make us feel any better or take the pain away.
The earth is round, so what are the 'four corners of the earth'?

answers.answer: The phrase probably predates the discovery that the earth was spherical. It was likely coined when people believed the earth was flat.

Before the discovery of globes and before we knew the world was round, armies and navies consulted flat maps for attacks on countries. The phrase 'four corners of the earth' comes from those times. Mappa Mundi, Ptolemy, early cartographers illustrate this.

questions.question: Why is it that when you drop a milk bottle or wine bottle, it bounces first before actually smashing on the floor? Sometimes a couple of bounces before it smashes on the third one.

answers.answer: When bottles hit the ground, they hit at the bottom corner first because that's heavier. Then it bounces and lands on a weaker point - the side or somewhere that's not as thick - and that's when it smashes. Particularly applies to milk bottles and wine bottles because of their shape. I'd say 80-90% of dropped bottles bounce.

questions.question: Why does salt melt ice?

answers.answer: Salt water has a lower freezing point than water because its chemical composition is different from pure water.

questions.question: Suppose you lose something like a wedding ring, claim on the insurance and get paid out. Six months later you find the ring. Who owns it - you or the insurance company?

answers.answer: The insurance company owns it due to the principle of indemnity insurance - you can't be left in a better financial position than you were at the outset. The insurance policy has a clause called subrogation, meaning the legal rights to the ownership belong to the insurance company.

questions.question: Why do we wince when we see someone else in pain?

answers.answer: We have what are called mirror neurons. When we see somebody expressing virtually any type of emotion, our mirror neurons resonate and we experience a smaller version of the emotion they are expressing.

questions.question: My son is travelling in Vietnam and asks: if a chicken fell off a roof, would it survive? Could it fly?

answers.answer: No, chickens can't really fly. They can jump aided with their wings and get a bit of lift, perhaps to clear a six-foot fence if wings aren't clipped. But they've been bred to not fly effectively. I keep chickens and clip their wings.

questions.question: My daughter is learning grammar at school and wants to know why we say 'a teddy bear' and 'an umbrella' but 'a unicorn'. What are the rules for when to use 'a' versus 'an'?

answers.answer: It's about the phonetic sound of the letter, not the letter itself. 'U' as in unicorn sounds like 'y' (yellow), so it takes 'a' not 'an'. You don't say 'a yellow book' - you say 'a unicorn' and 'a union' for the same reason.

questions.question: Why doesn't it hurt when fingernails grow, even though it hurts when you pull them out with pliers? That's like the same physical process accelerated.

answers.answer: It happens so incrementally slowly that it just doesn't register as painful. If you ripped it out with pliers it would hurt, but the same process happening slowly doesn't hit your pain receptors.

questions.question: Why doesn't it hurt when you cut nails or pull them?

answers.answer: Nails and hair are dead material. When you cut nails you're cutting dead tissue. When you pull them you're detaching from the nail bed where there are nerves, which hurts.

questions.question: Is an apple still alive when you pick it from a tree and eat it?

answers.answer: It depends. If the apple was pollinated by a bee and has genetic material in the seed, then technically it is alive in the seed - it can germinate. If it wasn't pollinated and is sterile (cannot germinate), then it is not a living organism because it cannot survive by itself.

questions.question: Why do we say the word 'up' when we do the washing up or dress up? It doesn't really make sense. Why does it not just 'do the washing'?

answers.answer: You wash up in the sink and you put it up onto the draining board to dry (before dishwashers). For dressing up, nine times out of ten you'd dress from the bottom, starting with socks or tights.
Washing up is called washing up because washing up liquid is called washing up liquid - brands become synonymous with objects (like Hoover, Coke).
Before we had synthetic washing liquid, we used natural soaps from rivers and animal fats for washing up.

The 'up' in those expressions is merely a figure of speech relating to physical 'up' and sense of completion. Washing up means completing the task after the meal. They have the same in German. This was the up in expression.

questions.question: How tall does someone have to be not to be affected by cutting onions and the eyes?

answers.answer: There is no height because when you cut the onion the aroma goes into your nose and sets off the senses that make your eyes water. The answer is to either have running water nearby while cutting them (takes some aroma down the plug hole), put Vaseline on your nose, or be in another room. Soaking red onions in water for 20 minutes makes them less pungent.
Don't chop the ends off. Just leave the end on one end when chopping onions.

questions.question: Why is the abbreviation for pounds 'lb'?

answers.answer: It comes from Latin. 'Libra' was the Latin word for scales. 'Libra pondo' was a pound of weight. We just carried on using it and 'lb' is the abbreviation for libra.

questions.question: Why do we lose the sense of taste when we're eating something and breathe in through our nose?

answers.answer: The tubes at the back of your head - if you're breathing in or holding your nose, the aromas from your mouth don't reach your taste buds in the same way. If you're breathing in, you're blowing the aroma off the taste buds. If you're holding your nose, it's not going to reach the taste buds because there's no air at all.

questions.question: What is restless leg syndrome and is there a cure?

answers.answer: It is effectively a lack of potassium. Eating bananas will cure it - two or three bananas were enough. Mike knew this from when he was going through withdrawal as an addict and was told by his doctor.

It probably relates to iron deficiency. Anti-pigmentation and Parkinsonian drugs prescribed by GPs can be helpful. Quinine helps with cramps. It can come on late in life and is autosomal - it runs in families. There is also a link to growing pains. Very little is known about it.

questions.question: Why do men's shirts have all vertical buttonholes except the bottom one which is horizontal?

answers.answer: The upper buttonholes are vertical so they are easy to undo and do up. The bottom one is horizontal so that it doesn't accidentally come undone because that would potentially be the most embarrassing if it comes undone.

questions.question: Why do people in laboratories and hospitals wear white coats? Why can't it be brown, black, blue or whatever colour?

answers.answer: White shows dirt - it's easier to prove cleanliness. These are surgical environments where it's very important to advertise cleanliness. The white coat says 'look how clean I am.' You couldn't make that bold statement with a black or brown coat because you wouldn't be able to see stains. They change when they get dirty.

questions.question: Why do we cry when we're sad?

answers.answer: When you take the tears from someone who's sad and test them, you get a very high level of cortisol. Crying washes out the stress chemicals from the brain.

questions.question: What is the significance of the barber's pole outside barber shops? Why do they have rotating red and white stripes (and sometimes also blue)?

answers.answer: It goes back to when barbers were barber surgeons and were very primitive doctors. The red and white pole represents the blood in the bandages. You have it outside so it's immediately recognizable in case someone needs a doctor in a hurry, and this was in days before widespread literacy.

questions.question: How does a motorcycle helmet vibrate in the rain and clear water? Is it a special coating?

answers.answer: Most of the time the water just beads off as you're moving along. If it's raining heavily you can get sprays and treatments for visors but they're not great. You just wipe it with your glove when needed. Some gloves have a special spongy bit on one finger like a tiny windscreen wiper. The key is you're zipping along so water beads off, and if not you just give it a wipe with your hand.

questions.question: Apparently a banana is a herb. How can a banana be a herb?

answers.answer: I read on a Penguin bar wrapper that a banana is a herb. The banana that we eat (the yellow casing) is a fruit because it contains seeds. But the banana tree - the plant on which the banana grows - does not consist of woody tissue, therefore the banana tree is actually a herb.

questions.question: Why do estate agent boards advertise local school events? Is there a law about this? Why don't other local businesses do the same?

answers.answer: Any other business would have to hire someone to go out specifically to stick signs up, which would be a meaningful cost. But estate agents already have their sign erectors out every day driving around all of London with a list of houses where people are selling - they just add the school event signs to their existing route. So it's purely a cost efficiency reason.
Possibly related to the Town and Country Planning Act control of advertisement regulations.

questions.question: If you are cross-eyed, can you see straight out of the eye that's crossed?

answers.answer: I was born with a lazy eye - my left eye would wander inwards or outwards while I had complete control of my right eye. As I grew up I learned to choose the vision from one eye and ignore the image from the other. My brain adjusted to the defect. When judging distance (like pouring a drink), I had to concentrate on using both images for spatial awareness. The brain naturally learns which eye's image to use.

questions.question: When you take a frozen joint of meat out of the freezer and thaw it overnight, why does a pool of blood come through the apparently waterproof bag? Is it osmosis?

answers.answer: It sounds like osmosis, doesn't it?

When you freeze a bottle of liquid it expands and blows the cork off. That's what happens with the bag of meat - the liquid inside expands and creates tiny hairline fractures in the plastic. The blood seeps out through those fractures. It's not osmosis because you can't get liquid out of something sealed without a physical breach.

questions.question: How do you insure something that is priceless? If you insure the Pompeii exhibition pieces that are described as priceless, how can you put a figure on something that can't be replaced?

answers.answer: You just make up a number that represents what you'd like to get for the object against what you can afford in insurance premium. It's a negotiation. If it's lost, you get a financial settlement that helps economically but nothing can replace it culturally or artistically. Many museums don't insure their huge collections because premiums are too expensive. Museums have disaster plans for fires and floods instead. The actual value is negotiated between museum and insurer.

questions.question: In Greece they paint the bottom of trees white, in fields anywhere. I've been wondering for years. Is it something to do with insects?

answers.answer: It's lime (spelled L-I-M-E but sounds like 'asbestos') painted on the bottom metre of trees. It stops insects from climbing up into the bark and affecting the tree. It works on any tree you want to protect - olive trees, fruit trees, peach, orange, lemon trees.

questions.question: Why are there so few blue foods? Why is there not more blue food?

answers.answer: A mate at work told me that the brain doesn't allow us to eat blue food because there's nothing natural in the wild that's blue. To help lose weight, he ate off a blue plate so he'd eat less psychologically. There's also mould - blue mould is what's off - which reinforces the brain's aversion to blue food.

Naturally occurring vivid blue foods don't exist, so blue is psychologically the least appetising colour. There's no commercial reason to turn food blue. The brain has been conditioned to avoid blue foods because of mould associations.
Catering plasters are blue so they stand out on anything - this supports that blue is noticeable and distinct in food contexts.

questions.question: Whenever you see a spacewalk or moonwalk, you never see any stars in the background. The universe is full of stars but it's always pitch black. Why?

answers.answer: It's to do with the dynamic range of the camera sensor. The camera sensor has a linear response while the human eye has a logarithmic response - meaning the human eye can see multiple brightness levels at once. Cameras can't capture both the bright foreground and dim stars simultaneously. It's exactly like photographing a cloudy moon - you can either get the moon or the clouds, not both. It's a camera limitation, not a cosmic one. Wayne works as an engineer making high-spec digital cameras and does astrophotography.

questions.question: Do wasps sleep at night? Could I eat outside when they're asleep? And is the wasp repellent spray safe to use near food?

answers.answer: Wasps don't truly sleep but they do return to the nest at night when the sun goes down. They enter resting periods called quiescent periods. Once it's dark they'll be in the nest and won't fly around. You could eat your evening meal after dark without being bothered. They might be attracted to a light source they perceive as sun. Generally once they're in the nest for the night they won't come back out. I'm a pest control manager.

questions.question: Where does the term 'pitch black' come from? Is it related to bitumen or pitch used on roads?

answers.answer: Pitch is a black tar-based substance, another word for creosote essentially. So 'pitch black' means as black as pitch.

questions.question: Who pays the electricity bills for street lights, traffic lights, and other publicly used electricity? How does that work - is there a meter?

answers.answer: Street lights and traffic lights are NOT metered. The council pays a lump sum to the electricity supplier - probably dating back to the old nationalised days. It's a flat rate every year that goes up with inflation.

questions.question: A new atomic clock has been described as accurate to within one second in 300 million years. If that's the most accurate clock in the world, how can they know it's inaccurate? What are they comparing it to?

answers.answer: A second is defined by the vibrations of a cesium atom. You start your clock and count the vibrations. After a couple of days, you check how it compares. If it's three vibrations out, you multiply that up to calculate how long until a full second is lost - hence 300 million years.

questions.question: Can members of the royal family be called up for jury service?
Why does fire always burn orange? No matter what you throw on a fire - red carpet, blue carpet, wood - it burns orange. Why?

answers.answer: Every chemical in the periodic table has its own spectral line - a specific color it produces when burned. Most household items are hydrocarbons. Carbon, when burned, produces a yellow/orange flame. That's why everything burns orange - most things are ultimately made of carbon. Copper would burn green. Potassium burns purple.

questions.question: There was a story about passengers on a small aircraft who all ran to the front and tipped the plane. Would the same thing happen on a Boeing Dreamliner or jumbo jet if everyone ran to one end?

answers.answer: Yes, it could affect the balance. It's all about the centre of gravity. Even on massive planes, a small movement can adjust it. That's why airlines don't like passengers moving around too much. The pilot can adjust with trim to keep level flight, but if everyone clustered to one side, it would cause a problem.

questions.question: Why is the noise you make with your tongue called a 'raspberry'?

answers.answer: It's rhyming slang - 'raspberry tart' rhyming with the F-word. Raspberry tart = F-A-R-T.

questions.question: If you transferred a DNA strand to digital memory, how much storage would it take up?
How many cows does it take to make a pint of supermarket milk? If you buy a pint of non-organic milk, how many cows will have contributed?

answers.caller: Kevin from Wallingham (lives on a farm, former dairy farmer)
answers.answer: Guernsey cows can produce up to 36 pints a day. If a herd of 60 cows all milk goes into the same vat, one pint could theoretically contain contributions from all 60 cows. It depends on the size of the herd and the vat.

questions.question: My daughter's dog always sleeps in the car, but wakes up and jumps at the window as soon as I turn into my road - every single time. How does she know? Is it speed bumps, distance, smell?

answers.answer: It's smell - dogs recognise their own scent and the scent of home.
Dogs recognise the place through a combination of scents and sounds. They have a highly developed sense of smell.

It's the dog's awareness of YOUR anticipation. You give off chemicals when you know you're about to arrive somewhere. His dog only got excited when he stopped at his parents' house - not when driving past.
It's definitely scent - plus sounds. She has ten dogs in her car and they all start pacing and getting excited when approaching destinations and walks.

questions.question: How did people in ancient times (before Christ) refer to their years? We use B.C. for before Christ and A.D. for after, but how did the Egyptians and others date their years before our system existed?
Where does the word 'barbecue' come from, and what does it mean?

answers.answer: It's Spanish-American for 'frame made of sticks'.
It comes from the French 'de la barbecue' - when they used to put the pig on the spit, it was cooked 'de la barbecue' meaning from the barbecue (the back/bum).

questions.question: Why is it when someone's zip is undone on their trousers that someone will come up to you and say your flies are undone?

answers.answer: Flies are overlapping flaps which were held together by buttons. When they're zipped together, they're not overlapping. So it's called a buttoned fly.

questions.question: Talcum powder, the origins of that, where does that come from?

answers.answer: Talcum is a stone. You find it in the ground, you mine it, you quarry it. And then you make powder out of it.

questions.question: Why are there no instructions on toothpaste when they are on every other face wash and shampoo and shower gel?

answers.answer: The instructions on shampoo encourage you to use more than you need so you buy more. You couldn't really get away with that on toothpaste because you can never use more toothpaste than you can fit on a toothbrush.

There ARE instructions on toothpaste. Children's toothpaste says 'use a pea-sized amount', sensitive toothpaste says 'apply directly to sensitive tooth with fingertip and massage gently for one minute'. The instructions are on the tubes, not the boxes which we throw away.

questions.question: How come waves in Australia, Hawaii and America are bigger than the waves in England? I thought England is windier so wouldn't the waves be bigger here?

answers.answer: You need storms far away - like in Antarctica - hundreds of miles away. Those storms create the swell which makes the waves. In northeast England, the wind just whips up the North Sea making inconsistent waves you can't surf on. You haven't got the swell that pushes the surfboard along.

You need storms to create swell, but also the shape of the seabed matters. Good surfing areas like North Coast of Hawaii have perfectly shaped seabeds that continue the swell. That's why they built an artificial reef in Bournemouth - to reshape the seabed - though it wasn't entirely successful.

questions.question: With satellite navigation systems, is it a person who actually records the road names or turn-by-turn instructions, or is everything computer generated?

answers.answer: It's a mixture. Actors or personalities record dialogue in studios, then the computer interprets the actual street names encoded in the data and reassembles it. That's why sometimes it doesn't get pronunciation correct. If you're in the UK with purchased sat-nav like TomTom or Garmin, they've recorded voices physically. But the synthesised voice technology comes in various accents and can be programmed.

Actors go in and record dialogue. The computer then interprets the names that are encoded within the data and reads them out. That's why sometimes it doesn't get the word correct - it picks apart syllables. On brand-name sat-navs it's all generated by computer with no one recording individual street names. I work for Navtech which supplies all the data for sat-nav systems.

questions.question: Why are dusters always yellow?
Why are ladies' hairdressers called hairdressers? Why are men's places called barbers?

answers.answer: The French word for beard is 'barbe'. The bloke who cuts your beard is the 'barbeur' (barber). He would also do your hair, so a barber does both.

questions.question: If science fiction came true and there were giant spaceships and giant objects floating outside Earth's orbit, what effect would that have on Earth - our gravity, weather, orbit around the sun?
How do they drill sideways in fracking? You see the drill going down deep and then it goes off at a right angle underground. How do they do that?
Where's all the stag beetles gone? When I was a kid there were hundreds of them in June, they'd fly around about four inches long with big claws. Are they extinct?

answers.answer: They were almost extinct a few years back. They're now protected by law to try and bring the numbers back up. I saw some three weeks ago in my garden at dusk.

questions.question: Why is a south-facing garden more desirable than other gardens? I can understand more sun, but why isn't north-facing just as desirable?

answers.answer: The sun doesn't go over your house in a straight line - it curves to the south at 51 degrees latitude in the UK. That's why a south-facing garden gets sun all day while a north-facing garden is in the shadow cast by your house.

The sun rises in the east and sets in the west but it actually curves by the south because we are at 51 degrees latitude. That's why a south-facing garden will get sun all day. North-facing gardens won't get as much because your house casts shadows.

questions.question: How young can you be to die of old age? When do you shift from natural causes to old age? Is dying of old age a medical term?

answers.answer: Dying of old age isn't a medical term - something always has to pack in like your heart or lungs. The youngest they've ever had on the program who mentioned their age first was 63. I'd have said 'you're not old'. The point at which you think your age is the most interesting thing about you is when you become susceptible to dying of old age.

questions.question: How many four-fingered milk chocolate Kit Kats are made every day on planet Earth?
Why does Barry struggle to make out what is being said in modern films in a way that he doesn't in older films? Is it the actors or is there a technological explanation?

answers.answer: It's the volume being too loud. Certain cinemas like IMAX have preset volume sent directly from producers and they cannot change it. When the volume is too loud, it creates vibrations and makes the sound slightly unclear. The older films had projectionists who set the volume to suit the sound system and the cinema.

questions.question: Why is the body coated in iodine before an operation?

answers.answer: It's actually not iodine but betadine, which is a combination of iodine and povidone. It's a topical antiseptic used to stop any infection being introduced into the wound at the time of the operation. Simon is a podiatrist who has used it for 30 years on minor wounds.

questions.question: Why do Scottish juries have 15 members and English juries have 12?
Why don't dogs eat humans more, when they happily eat our dead skin, raw chicken, and other meat?

answers.answer: Because you're big and alive. Dogs like alive things like rabbits because they're not big. If you were dead, the dog would have a nibble after two days.

Dogs see humans as the alpha male or alpha female. Dogs are basically wild animals and you're head of the pack. They wouldn't dare attack you while you're alive. Even dogs not part of your family see us as being the alpha. Wolves will attack but dogs have been domesticated. John has five dogs, works at Crisis is Christmas looking after dogs, and writes for two dog magazines.

questions.question: Where were the hexagonal stones in central London that were stamped with capital city names, compass points, and distances to other places (like the signs at Land's End)?

answers.answer: They were in Leicester Square near where the old Swiss Centre used to be, in the open piazza area. They're all connected together with distances in miles and kilometres to different parts of the world. They may have been removed when Leicester Square was rebuilt a couple of years ago.

questions.question: Why are prawns that are frozen in their shells firmer and chewier than prawns that have been frozen and peeled (which are soft and mushy)?
Why can you blow air out of your eye when you hold your nose? And why is it only one eye (his right eye, and his girlfriend's right eye too)?

answers.answer: You have small drain tubes at the bottom of your eyes called tear ducts, which lead down to the back of your throat for draining away tears. When you hold your nose and blow, you're forcing air back up these tubes. Some people can do it with milk, some with smoke. The reason only one eye might work is due to resistance or a blocked duct in the other. Pat had experience with a blocked tear duct that caused his eye to water and he could feel it coming down his throat.
A friend used to do a party trick where he'd gulp milk and blow it out through both eyes.

questions.question: How come you can be sitting in the garden in blazing sunshine and within minutes after a thunderstorm, the whole garden is covered with snails? They can't move fast, so where do they come from so quickly?

answers.answer: They've been hiding under leaves, rocks, or pots. When it's wet they can move faster because moisture helps them move. They emerge from their hiding places which are probably only inches away.

questions.question: If the Queen committed a crime, would she go to prison?

answers.answer: The Queen cannot be prosecuted. In all criminal cases it's 'The Queen versus...' so you can't have the Queen versus the Queen. Her Majesty's Court Service is designed to ensure fair trials, so the case would be dismissed as not being a fair trial. In theory, the Queen can do whatever she wants with impunity. Gavin is a lawyer.

The Queen has what is called Crown immunity from prosecution. However, members of the royal family have been prosecuted in the past - the Princess Royal got speeding tickets and had her collar felt when her dog attacked another dog in Windsor Great Park. So it's specifically the Queen who has Crown immunity.

questions.question: How many snails are there in the world? How many flies are there in the world?
What is the point of vegetables? With fruit, the plant produces it because it has seeds, so when you eat it you spread the seed. But vegetables don't work that way - nothing comes out the other end.

answers.answer: Vegetables do eventually go to seed. On a farm he worked at, one carrot would produce about 100 seeds if you let them grow on. You eat them before they become overripe. That's where the expression 'going to seed' comes from - when vegetables become inedible.

questions.question: If the royal baby had been twins or triplets, how would they decide who would be king? And what if it was a caesarean section?

answers.answer: The first one to come out becomes the monarch, regardless of how. Even with a caesarean section, they would take one out first - that would be the firstborn and therefore the future monarch.

questions.question: At what point does something old become a replica from repairs? (Referenced Trigger's broom from Only Fools and Horses - the broom had the handle replaced 14 times and the head 8 times but was still considered the same broom)

answers.answer: If you started with an original, it's never going to be a replica even if there's nothing of the original left because it's a constant evolution. If you build something from scratch, then it's a replica. As long as you had one part of it, it can be classed as an original.

questions.question: Why does the Queen's head face to the right on coins but to the left on postage stamps?
How do fans work?

answers.answer: By fanning you're getting rid of hot air and replacing it with cool air
It's the chill factor - air reaches your skin at speed making it feel cooler than it really is

All fans do is blow hot air around the room. The only reason it feels cool is because of the speed that air is forced out of the fan and hits your skin - the chill factor. Same reason why when you purse your lips and increase the speed of breath, it feels cold

questions.question: What would happen if you didn't cut off a baby's umbilical cord? Would the baby die?

answers.answer: It ceases, there's nothing in it. It would just wither off and drop off, and the problem would be with the baby's belly button not being properly formed

answers.caller: Anna (Beckenham) - Mother of three, researched delayed cord clamping
answers.answer: If kept dry and clean, it will just drop off and the baby's belly button will have sealed over naturally. There's actually a movement called 'lotus birth' where they discourage cutting the cord, keeping it attached for a few days after birth, claiming benefits from extra nutrients passing from the placenta. If kept moist it can cause infection which could pass to the baby

questions.question: When did English replace French or Norman as the language of the ruling classes after the Norman Conquest?

answers.answer: The ruling class eventually realized they would have to be able to speak to the people in the language they understand

answers.caller: Brian (Boreham Wood) - Danish, been in UK a couple of years
answers.answer: The plebs never started speaking French. The aristocracy started speaking whatever language came with the rulers. But the Norman model doesn't fit because the aristocrats spoke a specifically different language from the conquered. It was Eleanor of Aquitaine who made a conscious decision to speak English. You never stopped speaking French in the sense that all those languages contributed words

By the time of 1200 and Edward I, the English aristocracy detested France. It drifted gradually. By 1230-1240, it had gone from French to English among the aristocracy. Henry V is when English was made legal in court - that's 400 years after the conquest. This is when the process was formalized

questions.question: Why do so many girls' first names end with an E sound? For example Tracy, Mary, Nancy, Hayley, Tiffany, Wendy

answers.answer: It's a term of endearment. In Greece they stick 'aki' on the end meaning little. In English we put an E on the end as a sweetness. Mary is an exception that proves the rule. People just like certain sounds more than others and in English culture the E sound has got a certain warmth
I'm not entirely confident there is an etymological or historical explanation for it. I think people just like certain sounds more than they like certain others

questions.question: Why does honeysuckle smell so strong at night but barely at all in the daytime?

answers.answer: Probably to do with the insects it's trying to attract - there must be more of them about in the evening than in the day

Honeysuckle is more perfumed in the early morning and late at night to attract moths. It's a tubular flower shape. Moths are great pollinators - they get covered in pollen and pick up much more with their brush-like bodies giving a bigger surface area. Evolutionarily you're better off attracting a moth than a bee

questions.question: Why is Lord Nelson facing the way he's facing on top of Nelson's Column?

answers.answer: He faces down the Mall

answers.caller: Paul (Mile End) - Had a very good history teacher at school
answers.answer: He's looking at the fleet of Portsmouth
He's actually facing France to make sure they're not being attacked again because of Napoleon

answers.caller: Steve (Dagenham) - Police officer for 30 years, stood on the Mall on numerous ceremonial occasions
answers.answer: If you look down the Mall, there are masts either side with models of ships on top - they're the ships of his line. He's looking at his fleet, either Portsmouth or France

answers.caller: Simon (Orpington) - Father restored and cleaned Nelson's Column 27-28 years ago
answers.answer: He definitively faces the Admiralty in Portsmouth, where his fleet would have left from. Everyone who goes up there knows this. It's the direction of his fleet origin

questions.question: Who owns the copyright to the Bible?

answers.answer: No one owns the copyright - it's too old. You could own copyright to a translation. After a certain number of years (like 100) books move out of copyright - that's why you can get Dickens for free on a Kindle. Music goes off copyright after 50 years - Cliff Richard tried to object to that

questions.question: Would a person weigh more at the centre of the Earth than on the surface?

answers.answer: I'm not sure if it's the centre of the Earth that's the origin point of gravitational pull
You would weigh considerably more at the centre of the Earth - approximately 3.5 million times more than on the surface
You would be weightless at the centre of the Earth

questions.question: Why does the monarch face left on stamps?

answers.answer: The monarch always faces left on stamps because she's placed in the top right of an envelope and looks down towards the address - it would look incongruous if her gaze was drawn away from the envelope

questions.question: Why, out of all the small domestic batteries, only one, as far as I can see, is square? That's your PP3. Why aren't they all square?
What is 2020 vision and can you have better than 2020? Because I always thought that's the best eyesight you could have.

answers.answer: 2020 vision is an indication of the distances that you can see. If you can see at 20 yards the same as someone who has perfect vision can see at 20 yards, then you have 2020 vision. Perfect vision is 20-20, but you can have 16-20 vision, meaning you can see at 16 yards what someone else sees at 20 yards. The maximum amount of vision that can be achieved is different from what is considered perfect vision.

The first part of the answer was absolutely right. If you're standing 30 yards away from something and you can read something that a person with normal vision can only see from 20 yards, then your eyesight is better than 20-20. After laser eye surgery, it's perfectly possible to have vision better than 20-20. I had LASIK in 2001 and mine was better than 20-20 when they finished.

questions.question: I'd like to know if emergency vehicle sirens are copyrighted.
Why does a bag of water with coins taped to the side of the window deter flies from coming in?

answers.answer: It's all to do with how flies' eyes work. The metal in the water and the water itself combine to catch the light and diffract it in a specific way that bombards the fly's eyeball. It can't go through the wall of light.

questions.question: Why are more batteries not square, given they'd be easier to use if they didn't roll off tables?

answers.answer: A round battery is a single-cell battery with a pole going through the middle. For ease of manufacture and for applications like torches and clocks, it's easy to have a plus and minus at one end. Square batteries tend to be multi-cells - in a PP9 you'd find two square cells of equal size and capacity totaling 12 volts. If you put round cells in a cylinder, the ones in the middle would be smaller than the ones on the outside.

questions.question: What's the law regarding sirens on private vehicles? Can civilians have sirens?

answers.answer: To drive an emergency vehicle with blue lights and sirens, you need a qualification and it has to be registered as an emergency vehicle. You can't use a siren without a blue light anytime. Ice cream vans have a different exemption. There's no central register of siren tones - manufacturers can make identical sirens for police and ambulances.

questions.question: Why is it that when you're at the British seaside, you get that wonderful salty sea air smell, but when you're on holiday abroad, you don't get that same salty sea air smell?
Why do we have silent letters in so many words? English is already the most confusing language to learn. Why does it have to be more difficult with silent letters?

answers.answer: There is no overall answer that accounts for every silent letter. Each word has a different explanation. For example, 'knife' has a silent K because it has Scandinavian origins and used to be pronounced 'kniff'. 'Vineyard' has a silent letter due to French pronunciation. Generally, silent letters come from foreign derivation - Viking language, Norman, Saxon influences. English is more mongrelized than other languages with Norman, Saxon, Scandinavian, Latin and Greek influences.

The general idea when inconsistencies in pronunciation or silent letters appear is to tell them that that's just the way it is. So many English words have derived from other languages and from ancient languages that we just have to accept that we can't correct everything to a modern way of speaking without ending up with future generations looking upon the way we speak in the way that we look upon Shakespearean English.

questions.question: When I get a pimple on my face, almost without fail, it will be mirrored on the other side of my face. Is this just me or does it happen to other people as well?

answers.answer: I get mirrored pimples as well, so it's not that rare. Possibly about 60 or 70 percent, and they'll come up a day after - one on the left cheek will come up a day after on the right cheek.

questions.question: Why does the British seaside smell different from foreign seaside?

answers.answer: It's to do with the salinity of the water, the temperature of the water, and also the sea vegetation that grows in the sea, as in seaweed around our coast. It's very similar to northern France and the coast of northern Europe. You get different types of seaweed depending on salt content and heat. In the south of England you don't get so much kelp, but you do get a lot in Scotland, so the Falklands coastline smelt a bit like the Scottish coastline. As tides go up and down and the sun dries out the seaweed, you get that smell.

questions.question: Can you confirm or correct the answer about flies and water bags?

answers.answer: I'm going to destroy it for you. It's false. Are you familiar with the TV programme, Myth Buster? They tested it quite rigorously, and they proved it was just an old wives' tale. It's completely false. It's a lie.

questions.question: Does Roberta also experience mirrored pimples?

answers.answer: Pauline asked that question. I have exactly the same issue, but never thought to ask.

questions.question: Why do non-Christian countries use the Christian calendar (Anno Domini)? Why is 2013 AD the universal dating system even for people who don't believe in Jesus?

answers.answer: Pol Pot in Cambodia announced year zero when he came to power - that's one half answer. There's also the Muslim calendar. But everyone knows what time it is because time is a constant.

Many museums and textbooks use CE (Common Era) and BCE instead of AD and BC. Not everyone follows the Christian calendar - for example, the Jewish Chronicle shows both dates: 5th July 2013 and 27th of Tamuz 5773. The Jewish calendar dates from creation, approximately 6,000 years ago, though modern orthodox Jews interpret this differently. Many non-Christian countries do follow the Christian calendar for general purposes.

questions.question: Do chefs' fingers actually get used to handling hot food over time? Or are people with less sensitive fingers naturally drawn to becoming chefs?

answers.answer: Chefs start with normal hands like everyone else. Over years of picking up hot food, they build up a tolerance. Like woodworkers who get leather hands, chefs get asbestos hands. It's not an anatomical anomaly drawing numb-fingered people to the profession.

It's true that as chefs become more experienced, their fingers become more accustomed to picking up really hot plates and bowls. It's like a calcification, callusing, or thickening of the skin on the fingertips.

questions.question: How long after the death of an American president does his family receive Secret Service protection?

answers.answer: From January this year (2013), the situation changed due to an act signed by President Obama on January 10th. The president and his wife now get security for life. If she divorces him, she loses it. Children get protection only up to age 16. All future presidents and their families get protection for life.

questions.question: Why are some counties called shires (like Yorkshire, Lincolnshire) while others aren't (like Cornwall, Dorset)? What makes those areas special enough to have that designation?

answers.answer: If you take Northamptonshire or Oxfordshire, the whole county is governed by the town with the same name (Oxford, Northampton). The county has its own independent council but is governed by the county town. This relates to county towns, not the suffix.
It goes back to the sheriff. If they had a sheriff, the area was called a Shire. It was the sheriff of the county. But Cornwall wouldn't have a sheriff because it was never Saxon-occupied.

A reeve is an Anglo-Saxon chieftain of a hundred or a group of ten sets of ten families known as tons. Groups of hundreds were shires. A leader of a shire was ergo a 'shire-reeve' (sheriff). Think of the distribution of Saxons in Britain after the fall of the Roman Empire and you get your shire locations. Cornwall was never Saxon-occupied - it was always Kernish - so it would never have had a shire appendage.

questions.question: Why do auctions call new bidders 'fresh blood'? Why call it blood at all when you could just say 'new bidder'?

answers.answer: You need to think of blood as being within a human rather than in a bucket or a bowl. It's just a figure of speech.

In fox hunting, when someone goes on the hunt for the first time and catches the fox, they get blood smeared on their faces. When they become a fully fledged member of the hunt, they get blood. Ergo, they are 'fresh blood'. So it's a new hunter tradition that became a general term for a new person.

questions.question: Is Downing Street obligated to reply to letters/communications, either legally or as a matter of courtesy?

answers.answer: There's definitely no obligation, moral or legal, to reply to every tweet or communication you send to them. They can't really reply and say 'we don't have a view or opinion.'

Margaret Thatcher used to have every letter answered. He wrote bizarre letters to her and someone answered them all. He published them in a book. But this was 30 years ago and was about letters, not emails.
It took Tony Blair's staff 10 months to reply to her letter.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'punchline' come from? Does it have anything to do with George Osborne or Mr. Punch?
What pain relief do you give a child between ages 9 and 12? Nurofen liquid is for up to age 9, Nurofen tablets are for 12 and over. What's in between?

answers.answer: Ibuprofen is actually licensed from 3 months to 12 years. There's a step-up dosage: 100mg in 5ml for younger children, then 150mg, then at age 7 you can take 200mg (10ml). Between 7 and 12, children can take tablets but over the counter it's not licensed, so you need to talk to a pharmacist. The liquid covers the gap.

questions.question: Why do certain bottles of red wine (usually Rioja) have a metal cage or mesh around them? What purpose does it serve?

answers.answer: They don't clink when packed (just guessing, made that up). It makes it seem fancier, like Chianti baskets.

It's more of a net than a cage. It was originally a tamper-proof seal to stop unscrupulous wine dealers from removing the cork of good wine and replacing it with a cheaper one. You could see if they'd tampered with the seal. It costs money so it's mainly used on quality wines like Rioja.

questions.question: Why do children's eyelids puff up when they're tired? Is it nature's way of trying to make their eyes close?
How much saliva does the average human produce per day?

answers.answer: She can't give a definitive answer because everyone makes a different amount. However, 20 years ago her esophagus ruptured, leaving her nil by mouth for nine months. Saliva still collected but was drained via a stoma in her neck covered with a colostomy bag, which she had to empty several times a day. By measuring this, she could have had a complete answer but didn't foresee the question arising.

questions.question: Why are moths so obsessed with artificial light? They fly toward my bedside lamp even though they're nocturnal. It seems nonsensical.

answers.answer: They're mistaking artificial light for the moon. Moths navigate by moonlight - they keep the light at a constant angle to fly straight. But a bedside lamp is much closer and the angle changes constantly as they fly, so they spiral in. It's not very bright of them really.

questions.question: How much saliva does the average human body produce in a day?

answers.answer: Saliva is a minimum of two to three pints a day per person. Some people produce even more, up to litres.

questions.question: Where is the duff? Why did we send pregnant women there?
Why does the Woolwich Ferry do a semi-circle when going northbound but go all weird (sideways, backwards, reverse) when going southbound?

answers.answer: They do that circuit mainly to avoid collision and wake turbulence, because they're flat-bottomed vessels so they're more susceptible to rolling and pitching than normal vessels. They also don't have normal propellers - they have a wind chime system underneath that spins and allows any vessel to move in any direction, unlike ships with rudders.

questions.question: Why do Americans eat their steak in such a strange way? They cut it with a knife, then put the fork down, transfer the fork to their knife hand and eat off the fork.

answers.answer: It was because when going back years, they used to keep one hand free to keep their hand on their gun. They would eat with a fork normally, but things demanding a knife required picking up the knife, cutting, then putting the knife down and putting the fork back in the left hand.

The early settlers only usually had one or two knives for hunting. When it came to eating meat, they would cut it up, pass the knife on to the next person, and then eat with their fork. It persisted as habit and vanity.

questions.question: Why don't male ballet dancers go right up onto their tiptoes?

answers.answer: Female dancers have shoes with a thing called a chalk (hard block) shoved up the toe end, which enables them to stand vertically on their foot and supports their toes. Men cannot wear ballet shoes with chalks because male dancers have the role of lifting and supporting the female dancers, which they can do on the balls of their feet but couldn't possibly do standing on the tips of their toes.

questions.question: Why do dogs and cats all follow the same path up and down the garden, creating a groove in the lawn?

answers.answer: It's evolution. Animals have evolved from wild animals who would patrol their territory very closely so as not to risk fighting with animals from neighbouring territory. The domesticated animals are echoing their feral patrolling behaviour.

If it's in the garden, it's geopathic ley lines. Cats love ley lines where there's underground water. Dogs hate them, so they'd go in a different direction. But she noted the caller said the dog and cat were going the same way, which would be 'a bit crackers'.

questions.question: How long are the children of US presidents protected for after the president leaves office or dies? And what about their grandchildren?

answers.answer: The incumbent president gets 24-hour security by the Secret Service for all the family. When he leaves office, he just has a close protection body officer 24 hours a day until he dies. His family don't get protection in any way, shape or form. Only the president gets protection, and the family when they're with the past president. When the past president dies, the family is on their own because there's no longer a security threat. He learned this from Bill Clinton when playing cards with him in Los Angeles.

questions.question: Can a blackbird understand a sparrow, or a pigeon understand a chaffinch? Do birds of different species understand each other?

answers.answer: Birds can communicate with each other across species. As evidence: a canary can breed with a goldfinch (called a mule), and a bullfinch can breed with a greenfinch (called a hybrid). They're variations on a similar evolutionary theme. He suggested that if different species can have children together, communication must be possible.

questions.question: Why do insects, namely ants, have such high resistance to damage? If you flick one off your hand quite powerfully, they hit the ground from quite far away and just run away.

answers.answer: Insects and other insects have exoskeletons. Their bones are on the outside.

questions.question: On bubblegum crazy rolls, there are a list of ingredients at the back. And below it, it says 'may cause an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.' Which of the ingredients or a combination of ingredients could cause an adverse effect on activity and attention in children? Also, when did they start putting these warnings on the packets?

answers.answer: The E numbers are likely the cause - specifically E-330 and E-296 which are acids. The warning relates to the long-held but not scientifically proven belief that E numbers can make children hyperactive.

questions.question: About 50 years ago, when the first Comet and Boeing 707 started flying, they flew at roughly 30,000 to 40,000 feet at 500 miles an hour. 50 years later, aircraft are still flying at 30,000 to 40,000 feet at 500 miles an hour. Why haven't they got any faster?

answers.answer: They get up to a height where they can do the optimum speed for economy. The higher they go, the faster they can go but it costs more money to get higher. They keep it at an optimum speed. If they need to make time up, they have to climb and use more fuel.

questions.question: Why are tree leaves, grass, most living plants colored green? Why is green the optimum color for photosynthesis?

answers.answer: They use infrared light to convert the sunlight and they reflect what they don't absorb. The opposite of red is green. The reason all plants are green is because they are reflecting the light that they don't need.

questions.question: Why do pigeons nod their head when they walk around? When they walk faster, the head nods even faster. When they fly, their head's done. They nod. So why, out of all the birds, does a pigeon have to nod its head when it's walking around?

answers.answer: It's because of connections in the body - the legs are attached to the head and the wings aren't.

It's because of the size and the shape of their body. If they didn't nod their heads when they walked, the motion of their walking would cause them to have quite a shaky vision. So they nod their head in time with their movement to their feet in order to keep focused on the things they're looking at.

questions.question: Why are outdoor pools always referred to as the Lido, while indoors are not? What does the word Lido mean?

answers.answer: It's the Italian word for beach.

questions.question: What's the meaning behind the tradition at a wedding of something old, something new, something borrowed and something blue?
Has there ever been a Roman Catholic Prime Minister in this country?

answers.answer: We have had a Prime Minister who is a Catholic, but he wasn't a Catholic when he was Prime Minister - Tony Blair. I'm 99% certain we haven't had a Catholic PM, but I'm not 100% certain.

questions.question: When you get into a cold car with a cold windscreen and you're breathing and there's a hot air and you get the condensation, what is it best to do? Is it best to blow cold air from your blower onto the windscreen or hot air?

answers.answer: The mist forms because of condensing air. When you get into your car and it's cold, you're breathing out warm, moist air. The warm, moist air contacts with the cold windscreen and condenses - it reduces the dew point and forms water droplets. The best thing to do is warm the screen up. By warming the screen up, you reduce the temperature difference between the moist air coming out of you and the temperature of the screen, so the water doesn't condense, so you don't get any fog.

questions.question: If the beginning of the week is Sunday, why do we disregard it and make Monday the lead day?

answers.answer: Many years ago, the Catholic religion and the Vatican changed the start of the week from Sunday to Monday. The Sabbath was shifted from Saturday to Sunday. Saturday is the last day of the week.

questions.question: Why is the alphabet determined in the order in which it is? Who determined that order? Was it to do with as language evolved?

answers.answer: The order of the letters in the alphabet is in any way meaningful or ordered. It isn't. They just had to be in some order, and that's the order they ended up in - a happy accident crossed with linguistic evolution. The alphabet must have been written before biblical times for it to be included in the Bible.

questions.question: Why do we take flowers to funerals?

answers.answer: In the 1940s, warplanes had straight wings which was the limiting factor on speed. Then in the late 40s, early 50s, they discovered that by sweeping the wings back at an angle, jet fighters could fly much closer to the speed of sound. The speed of sound is called Mach 1, which changes depending on height - at ground level it's about 750 mph, at 30,000 feet it's about 580 mph. Planes at 30,000 feet are flying at about 0.9 of Mach, very close to the speed of sound. If you make them go any faster, they break the sound barrier and a whole different bunch of aeronautical factors come into play.

questions.question: Why don't all kids have the same blood type as their mum? If a baby develops in its mum's belly and gets its blood from its mum, why don't all kids have the same blood type as their mum?

answers.answer: They have completely separate blood systems, a mother and a baby. The umbilical cord doesn't supply blood to the baby. The blood group is determined by genetics, so it's either from the father or the mother.

The different blood groups are A, B, AB, or O. It's to do with the antigen, which is just a substance on the red blood cell membrane. If you're A, B, or AB, those take precedence over O because O has no antigen. It's like Mendelian genetics. It's possible to have a blood type that neither of your parents have.

questions.question: There's a sort of statues of big cats in the area near the five-way corner where the A41 joins the A1, like pumas and the rest of them, sort of that four or five all on stilts, and I can't work out why.
What happens if all the ice in the world melts? Will we have any land left to stand on or do you think we'll be up to our neck in water?
Why can't I taste anything when we get a cold or flu?

answers.answer: If you hold your nose, your sense of taste almost entirely disappears. That's what happens when you eat something you don't like - it works.

The taste buds in the mouth are responsible for basic sweet, sour, bitter. Most of the taste that we perceive is from receptors in the nose. These receptors become inflamed and swollen and don't do their job when we have a cold. Even if you take medicine, that just eases the mucus but doesn't do much for easing the inflammation in the nostrils, so that's why we still can't taste anything.

questions.question: On the picture cards, the jacks, two of the faces are facing to the right, two of them are facing to the left. The queens, all four are facing front. The kings, three of them are facing front and one of them is facing to the left (king of diamonds). Why have they been drawn like this and what does that mean?
Why is it that only humans and dolphins are the only species that have sex for pleasure?

Lottery scratch cards with big prizes like four million pounds have been out for ages, but nobody seems to have won them. They change the reels in shops all the time. Are those four million pound tickets actually out there? If they were, they would have been won by now. So is this just force advertising?

answers.answer: I think you've got it the wrong way around. I remember a story from about six months ago about all the top prizes on a scratch card being won but they were still selling them, which got them into trouble. You only need one ticket out there at one time for the claim to be true.

questions.question: If you were in space for a long period of time, say like five years, would you age? I was watching a programme where someone was in space for 30 years and they didn't age.

answers.answer: I can't think of any reason why you wouldn't age, apart from lack of gravity so your skin wouldn't be dropping as much, perhaps. But everything else that contributes to ageing would be exactly the same.

The closer you go to light speed, the slower time goes according to Einstein's theory of special relativity. If you're going really fast like between planets, you would age slower than you would on Earth. But if you were just in space moving at a normal velocity, you would age normally. They did this on Concorde with atomic clocks and found a difference. So theoretically, for the period of time when you were travelling at top speed, you would age a little more slowly than if you'd stayed on Earth.

questions.question: When an aircraft's in trouble, he calls Mayday. But prior to that, he says Pan, Pan. What's the origin of Pan, Pan and why don't they just say Mayday straight?

answers.answer: It is derived from French. Mayday is French, and pan comes from panne (French for breakdown). It's used to indicate a mechanical breakdown. What you're effectively saying is breakdown, breakdown. Mayday means imminent danger to life. Pan-pan is an emergency where there is no expected danger to life, so a mechanical failure. There's one below that called securité, a safety message. This is used in both aviation and shipping.

questions.question: When I was younger we used to get breakfast slice, like a poor man's bacon. It was in strips like bacon but it was absolutely disgusting and lovely. Now it's just disappeared. Where is it?

answers.answer: It's been replaced by cheap bacon. Now bacon's cheap, everyone can afford it.

We had it all the time as children. My mother really liked it and it's not very nice, but my mum still buys it in Sainsbury's regularly. It's like a processed cross between a sausage and bacon, almost looks like a salami but doesn't taste like one. It's cut in round circles, vacuum-packed, and sold with things like ham and bacon. Every so often my mum resurrects it and I think oh I'll try that and it's vile.

questions.question: When a candle is lit there is no smoke, but when you blow out the candle smoke comes out. Why do you get that belch of smoke when you extinguish a candle?

answers.answer: If you blow out the flame, the wick is still hot and it allows the wax to burn but not completely. Instead of burning to carbon dioxide which is completely transparent, it burns to carbon which is soot, and that causes all the smoke.

questions.question: How do small aircraft that pull advertising banners take off and unfurl the banner, and then land again without dropping the thing? The big bar behind the plane that holds the banner would surely interfere with the landing process.

answers.answer: The aircraft goes over a grass strip next to the runway and releases the banner onto the grass. Then they swing around and land.

questions.question: Why do owners and trainers, no matter what they're wearing (suits, sports jackets, colouring ties), always wear brown hats? (like a trilby)
Why haven't we ever domesticated zebras the same way we've done with horses and ponies and donkeys?

answers.answer: The reason we don't domesticate zebras is that their bone structure means they cannot move in straight lines. They can only move in curves, which allows them to survive attacks from predators by turning on a sixpence. This doesn't work for us as a domesticated animal. Additionally, they're relatively small so they wouldn't be able to pull heavy weights. Qualifications: studied a making-of documentary for the children's film 'Racing Stripes' and has studied anatomy and physiology.

questions.question: What are the X's and S's made of metal on the side of old buildings? They have a bolt in the middle.

answers.answer: These are tie bars (or structural support bolts) that go right the way through the house. When outer walls start to sag over time with wood being part of the structure, you heat up the middle of the bolt and tighten it, which pulls the two outer walls back inwards. The facade isn't joined to the floor joists so side walls would move as the floor moves, but the bolts make sure they don't. Barry works at Hall Place in Bexley, a historic house.
