questions.question: When two people get on well, we say they 'get on like a house on fire.' But a house on fire is not a good thing - it's like saying you get on like a plane crash or boat sinking. Where did this phrase come from?

answers.answer: It's about the speed. In olden days, houses were built of wood with thatched roofs, so they'd burn incredibly fast. Saying two people 'get on like a house on fire' means they move through the stages of acquaintance or friendship very quickly. Qualifications: 'I'm old with lots of common sense and experience.'

questions.question: What is 'singing nettle' all about? (Why do stinging nettles have stings?)

answers.answer: It's about evolution and specifically mutation. At some point in the history of the stinging nettle, a mutation occurred where the plant developed a stinger. This mutation made it better for the survival of the species because plants with stingers were less likely to be eaten and more likely to replicate their genes. Grass hasn't developed this because it doesn't actually perform better if it's not eaten - grass needs to be eaten. James initially couldn't remember the word 'mutation' during the conversation and was embarrassed when hundreds of people texted to tell him.

questions.question: Why are they called moleskin trousers? At one time, were they actually made out of moles?

answers.answer: His grandad's brother was employed by gentry farmers as a mole-catcher. He would heel down the runs between molehills with big boots, wait for the mole to come along, catch it, use the moles to feed his dogs, and send the pelts to London to tailors who would make clothes from them - including collars on jackets. Moleskin is thin, durable, waterproof, and has a nice velvety feel - perfect for country shooting attire. Grandad was from Rugby area in Staffordshire.

questions.question: When a baby is in a womb upside down, how does it survive? We can't survive upside down for very long.

answers.answer: If you think of the baby in the womb as just an organ in the woman's body, the very concept of being upside down disappears because it's not breathing, not got its own blood pumping through its body - it's part of the mum. So the baby being whichever way round doesn't matter any more than whether your kidney is upright or on its side.

The fetus heart does pump blood around the fetus and placenta, so position does matter - like G-forces on a fighter pilot. The amniotic fluid acts like a G-suit: if the baby's head is lower, the pressure in the lower part of the uterus is higher, which supports the head. The amniotic fluid supports the baby as it moves around. The fetus is terribly dependent on the mother - if a pregnant mother gets injured, it's all about treating the mother because that supports the fetus. Qualifications: doctor with degree in anatomy.

questions.question: Why do people from North Kent call woodlice 'cheesy bugs' when the rest of the country calls them woodlice?

answers.answer: It's not confined to North Kent - it's also common in parts of Surrey. Back in his youth, he and his friends used to do dares involving eating insects. When you crunch a wood louse, it tastes of strong Stilton cheese. That's where the name comes from - peasant food from days of famine and poverty when people would eat wood lice. Mick has also eaten crickets in Mexico (dipped in chocolate).

questions.question: If the tide is going out on a beach in North Wales (and on the other side is roughly America), is it coming in on their side? If not, where does the water go?

answers.answer: The tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the moon (and the sun has some effect too, causing neap tides). You need to imagine it as all the water being pinched up away from the surface of the Earth - almost a magnetic pull upwards rather than a lateral pull one way or the other. So when the moon is directly above the middle of the Atlantic, someone lying on a beach in North Wales and someone on a beach in New York could both be experiencing low tide at the same time. Qualifications: learned at school.

questions.question: We have names for each finger (index, middle, ring, little) but not for our toes - we only have 'big toe' and 'little toe.' Why?

answers.answer: Toes don't really have much function except for the great toe and little toe. There's no typical classification like ring finger, index finger etc. If you start calling toes second, third, fourth, it's very easy to mix them up - for example if you're going to chop off a toe you might chop off the wrong one. David read a slightly jokey paper saying toes should be named based on the nursery rhyme - the market toe, home toe, roast beef toe, and the 'wee-wee-wee-wee-wee-wee' toe.

questions.question: Why is the bonus ball called a bonus ball if you don't get any bonus when you only get four numbers including the bonus ball?

answers.answer: The bonus ball only kicks in if you have five numbers. It's just the rules of the lottery - there's no mystery, it's just how the game works.

questions.question: Why do we have balloons when celebrating something? It's not just children's birthdays - any celebration has balloons. Why substitute balloons for something like bunting?

answers.answer: There may not be an answer to that. Why do you have cake on your birthday? Because it tastes nice. That's probably as good an answer as any.

questions.question: Who was Susan? (referring to a lazy Susan)
What is the point of police horses? I saw two on a quiet side street in a small town, trotting along. Apart from leaving poo all over the roads, what is the point?

answers.answer: At big crowds like football matches, horses are absolutely essential for crowd control. And they're up high, they can look over garden walls.
They're very big and intimidating and scary. I don't get as put off by a PCSO on a pushbike as I do as a policeman on a horse.

questions.question: Why do some birds hop and other birds walk? I don't think it's size-related but it's been troubling me for years.

answers.answer: It's just evolution. There's got to be a factor that has said it's better for me to hop than it is to walk.

The birds that walk have knee joints. The birds that don't have knee joints, don't. If you look at a chicken, a chicken has definitely got a joint between the thigh and the leg. If you look at a robin which hops, they've just got a straight bone.

questions.question: When stirring a cup of coffee for my wife, I noticed that tapping the spoon on the bottom of the mug made an increasingly high-pitched noise. When I stirred tea, it stayed the same pitch. Why does the coffee go up in pitch as I stir it but tea doesn't?

answers.answer: I have absolutely no idea, not only whether or not this is a valid question, but also what the hell the answer would be if it was.

When you add coffee granules, sugar and milk to water, the liquid achieves a certain density. The denser parts of the concoction will sink to the bottom. The more dense something is, the lower pitch it will give - like thicker guitar strings give a lower pitch because they're more dense. So the denser parts naturally sink, changing the acoustic properties as you stir and the mixture becomes more uniform.

questions.question: I've been walking in Richmond Park all my life and I've never seen a dead deer. There are deer there, so what happens to them? If a deer dies of natural causes or gets hit by a car, where does the corpse go?

answers.answer: No idea. We'll find out for you.

The Royal Parks employ two gamekeepers who drive around in Land Rovers taking care of the deer. If a deer is not feeling well, they take them to a hospital. If they're dead, they put them in the van and take them to an abattoir. They live in the parks and are on call. If the Royal Parks police find one that's been hit by a car, the gamekeepers will be there within about ten minutes. That's why you never see dead deer - the gamekeepers are doing their job very quickly.

questions.question: Why do certain things on our body grow back - like hair if we cut it, nails if we cut them - but if I lose a limb like a finger, it doesn't grow back? How does the body tell certain parts not to grow back?

answers.answer: The stuff that grows back is dead - hair and nails are made of keratin, it's dead material. But if you cut your skin, it will grow back. You're comparing apples with pears - you can't compare hair and nails to limbs because they're completely different. I don't know the answer to why we can't grow limbs back.

questions.question: Why is it called silverware in football but gold for first place in athletics?

answers.answer: I think it's just the difference between a cup and a medal. In football the cups are all silver, and no one cares who comes second or third in a football game. But I don't know why it's not called goldenware for football.

questions.question: There are eight notes in an octave, so why are there millions of tunes?

answers.answer: Think about your lottery - there's only 50 numbers on the ticket but how many different combinations are there? A tune could be 600 notes long.

As a music producer, there are 12 notes in an octave in equal-tempered scale including black keys. Each note has particular frequencies that mesh together when you make a chord, creating other frequencies. Each instrument has different harmonics and sounds. Different cultures use different scales - some Indian cultures have 20+ notes. That's why you can have so many songs.

There are 12 notes in Western music scale. Seven scales use those 12 notes. Five octaves. 12 x 7 x 5 = 420 combinations without harmonics. Then 13 chords. You can play chords in any order over five octaves in any scale starting on any root note, combining different root notes. So there's an infinite number of songs.

questions.question: What's healthier, toast or bread? My husband says there's more fibre in toast.

answers.answer: My gut instinct would say there's no difference whatsoever. You're just taking water out of it when you toast it. You're not putting anything into it.

It's healthier to eat bread plain because the act of cooking adds carcinogens. The more you toast bread, the more carcinogenic it becomes - it's been proven to cause cancers. The toast carbonates. Grilling, barbecuing, roasting - best thing is to boil food.

questions.question: What is the physical process when a man's voice breaks overnight?

answers.answer: I don't know. I know I too have not always sounded this manly.

You get an increase in testosterone. That produces a stretch in height and also in the vocal cord itself. The vocal cord gets longer, which means air flows over it differently and you get a change in pitch. It can happen overnight - testosterone acts on different parts of the body at different times.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'pass the buck' come from?

answers.answer: Passing the buck means giving something to someone else. If it's a dollar, you're giving someone else the dollar. Where buck means blame, I suppose.

It dates from the early part of the century before last, related to poker. They used to have a buck knife (a make of knife still made today) placed in front of you to show you were the banker. You'd pass the knife to someone else so they would lose the money instead of you. So you passed the buck.

questions.question: When I was fat 20 years ago and now I'm slim with a spare tyre, is the fat in that spare tyre still the same physical fat from back then?

answers.answer: The amount of fat cells you have in your body never changes. If you're born with a million fat cells, you die with a million. They just shrink and grow in size. So when you're thin you've got fat cells but they're smaller, not empty but containing less fat than when you were overweight.
Cells do regenerate. The longest time cells take to regenerate in the human body is for bone material, which is about seven years. So that fat may have similar appearance but is all new cells.

questions.question: How does an aircraft turn mechanically? The pilot turns the wheel and the plane banks - what actually happens?

answers.answer: I have no idea. You're the aviation enthusiast. I just fly in them.

When the pilot turns the wheel to the right, the ailerons (like spoilers on the wings) go upwards on the right side and downwards on the left. The aircraft spins on its axis slightly. Then he pulls back on the wheel, both ailerons equalise, the nose goes upwards, and that turns the aircraft. It's all to do with airflow over the wings - creating less lift on one side and more on the other.

The ailerons go up or down and the spoilers (on top of the wing) do the opposite. The wing dips and the pilot pulls back on the control column to stop the nose bobbing. You also use a little bit of rudder to keep it balanced. It has nothing to do with the engines - otherwise how would a glider turn?

questions.question: Why does the room/ceiling spin when you drink too much alcohol and lie down?

answers.answer: I think we've done this before - it's on the Mystery Hour Archive. It's something to do with the brain, perception is affected. But we want to know which part of the brain and how and why.

questions.question: Why is the jacket sometimes called a blazer? What's the difference between a jacket and a blazer?

answers.answer: It's definitely not a fashion thing. You'd have a blazer cut from exactly the same pattern as a sports jacket. I think it's something to do with the cloth but my five years in menswear have not provided me with an answer to that.

The blazer dates back to Nelson's navy and the captain of HMS Blazer. Crew to look smart and all look the same, so he paid for them to have blue jackets with brass buttons and they became known as blazers jackets and gradually it got shortened to blazer. School blazers would be a similar sort of garment whereas a jacket would have a pattern on it and a blazer wouldn't.

questions.question: Why can't you clench your fist when you wake up in the morning?

answers.answer: You're not trying to punch someone first thing in the morning, are you?

It's all due to blood circulation. It's how you sleep sometimes we sleep on it and you wake up and it becomes stiff. During the day, blood flows back into your hands and you can start clenching your fists again.

You have a fluid in your body called lymph, which carries white blood cells around. During the night, that evens right out across the body. During the day, muscular activity moves it around. Your hand will be very slightly swollen in the morning, which will prevent you from actually making a full fist. That's why you never shave first thing in the morning because half an hour later you need to shave again. Your actual tissue swells up slightly.

questions.question: Can sniffer dogs that smell drugs get addicted to smelling drugs?

answers.answer: The chemical the psychoactive chemicals won't be going into their bloodstream on anything like the scale they would need to be doing to build up a physical or chemical dependency, so they'd never get addicted to it. The process of smelling something doesn't increase one's chances of becoming addicted to it.
I heard about a dog in Egypt four or five years ago that got addicted because it was so good it was used all the time.

Effectively no they don't get addicted. The way that the training's done is all through a game. The dog is basically looking for the scent of the dog's nose as opposed to the item itself. The vapor that's given off from the stash is what reaches the dog's nose first as opposed to the actual substance itself. But if you didn't grab the dog quickly after it sniffed out some cannabis, it would probably eat it. It would make it very very ill but they wouldn't necessarily get addicted by it.

I have just been to a cannabis factory only this morning. I must have been to at least 100 of them and I am pleased to say I have not become addicted to cannabis but that said I am not a dog. Is it possible that Steve Stretton remembers correctly?

questions.question: Why do we brush our teeth with cold water?

answers.answer: I think it's just a tradition. We don't brush our teeth with hot water because we're putting it in our mouth. We wouldn't drink water out of the hot tap, ergo we brush our teeth with water out of the cold tap.
Because it makes the bristles on the toothbrush very soft and doesn't brush your teeth properly. My dentist told me when I was a kid.

The bristle thing is a load of waffles. With combi boilers the water feed is the same but with cylinder systems, stored hot water below 55 degrees can harbour listeria. So you can wash your face with it, but you'd be foolish to put it in your gob.

questions.question: What happens to people who die in places where it's prohibited to die? Like the Isle of Delos in Greece.

answers.answer: You can't have a prohibition of death. Otherwise everyone would go there and stay alive forever.
It's not a myth. I looked it up.
You're not allowed to die in the Houses of Parliament. They take you out, take you over to St Thomas's and pronounce you dead there. Told to me by former MP Harry Greenway.
If you die somewhere prohibited, your corpse gets carried to somewhere allowed and you will be declared dead there.

questions.question: How did the Vatican become an independent state?

answers.answer: That would be the Lateran Treaty in 1929. Prior to that, the Holy Roman Empire was huge and the Pope was in charge of huge swathes of the world. It slowly shrank through wastage and conquering until Rome was part of the Papal Sea until 1929 when the Vatican City was granted independent status by the King of Italy.

questions.question: Who looks after the internet clock? Who sets the clock that any time you do anything on the internet there's always a clock there?

answers.answer: I'm not familiar with the concept of an internet clock. That time at the bottom right is not the internet. That's my computer. You can adjust it. Is there an internet clock though?

questions.question: Why do companies insist on putting one piece of cardboard down the leg of a pair of tights when you buy them? Sometimes when you take it out, it rips the tights.

answers.answer: It increases the chance of laddering your tights before you've even got them on. There's probably something to do with packaging or them bouncing.

questions.question: Is the word 'history' based on 'his story'? My daughter was taught this at college.

answers.answer: No, it's not true. Historia is the Greek word for inquiry, asking questions. In Greek, it would be spelled iota-sigma-tau-omicron-rho-iota-alpha. There's no H in the original word. We've just added the H for ease of pronunciation. So there's no relationship to 'his'. It's a complete coincidence that English has 'his' as a possessive male pronoun and the word history begins with the same three letters.

questions.question: If your twin dies, are you still a twin? What do you call a former twin?

answers.answer: There's no word to describe a bereaved sibling, whether they are a twin or not. If your brother dies and you're not twins, there's not a word to describe your loss. But a child with no parents has a different legal status to a child with parents. A woman with a husband has a different legal status to a woman with no husband. A man with a wife has a different legal status to a man with no wife. But a brother with a brother has no different legal status to a brother with no brother.

questions.question: Why do my ears smell of cheese? My wife accuses me of eating cheese but I don't like cheese. Even after a shower, if I put my finger behind my ear, it smells of cheese.

answers.answer: No cheese - no one else smelled cheese behind their ears
There might be scent glands behind our ears

questions.question: When they removed my plaster cast with what looked like a circular saw, it didn't cut my skin even though it touched it. Why does the oscillating saw cut through plaster but not skin?

answers.answer: It oscillates at a very high frequency, between 5 and 10,000 revs a minute. However, it would cut your skin if you held it tight enough. Your skin moves as well, so it slides under the blade. But if you made your skin tight and really nailed it down, it would cut you. You feel it finish on the plaster and then you pull it away. If you felt it finish on the plaster and then pushed down harder on the skin, it would cut. It has different attachments as well.

questions.question: Why is popcorn the snack of choice in cinemas?

answers.answer: Originally cinemas sold popcorn covered in salt which was very dry, making people drink more and increasing drink sales. The markup was massive and it required minimal preparation space. Modern cinema popcorn is made in coconut oil and covered in butter.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'red tape'?

answers.answer: Barristers' chambers tie their case files together with red tape. It's literally red tape used to tie up documents.

questions.question: Where does the color go from things like washing liquid, shower gel and fabric softener when they go into water? Why doesn't black fabric softener color the water?

answers.answer: It gets diluted - put two drops of water in black fabric softener and it's still black, but put a capful in several gallons of water and it becomes diluted out of existence.
Confirmed - color just gets diluted in large amounts of water.

questions.question: If the Earth rotated the opposite way, apart from the sun rising in the west, would there be any other consequences? Would tides be affected?
Who is 'the fat lady' in 'the fat lady sings'? Is it a specific opera singer or character?

answers.answer: It's probably opera - most female opera singers are fairly well upholstered historically.

It's about US elections. The 'fat lady' is Texas, which was typically the last result to come in on election night. The 'singing' refers to the telegraph wire that used to sing when a message came in. The election ain't over until the Texan votes have been counted.
Most operas end with a soprano singing a long aria before she dies - think of La Boheme, La Traviata. They all finish in that way. That blows the election answer out of the water.

In 1933, a baseball commissioner moved the national anthem from the beginning to the end of baseball games so people would stay and exit orderly. A friend's father was an opera singer (quite fat) who used to sing the anthem at the end of games. That's where the term comes from.
It's not 'the fat lady sings' but 'the fat lady sinks' - the fat lady was the safety curtain at the front of the stage, and the show wasn't over until the curtain dropped (sank).

questions.question: How do you become a saint? What do you have to do?

answers.answer: You have to be put forward for beatification by the Vatican, then provide evidence of a miracle.
You need to provide evidence of TWO miracles - one for beatification and another before canonization.
You put someone forward to the Vatican for beatification, then after two miracles the Pope decides to canonize them.

questions.question: How far does daylight stretch? If you laid a pipeline a thousand miles straight up, would you see daylight at the other end?

answers.answer: It's the speed of light - asked what Mark thinks daylight comes from (sun)
A long, long way. The farthest we can see at night with naked eye is Andromeda Galaxy, 2,000 light years away.
Light and sound work the same way - if you heat one end of a bar, the other end stays cold. Light is absorbed by air. It depends on how bright it is.
259,200,000,000 kilometres - apparently.

Photons travel through space (near-perfect vacuum) with nothing to interact with. Once they hit a planet's atmosphere, they interact with particles and emit light you see as daylight. Once atmosphere finishes, you're in darkness. Daylight reaches as far as Earth's atmosphere - about 50km on Earth. Jupiter's atmosphere thousands of km thick, so daylight would extend thousands of km.

questions.question: If 71% of the Earth is covered with water, how much space do we have to live on? Is it 29%?

answers.answer: The water is a red herring - the question is what percentage of Earth's surface is inhabited. Britain is only 9% developed land including gardens.

questions.question: Where does the word 'ahoy' come from and why do pirates use it?

answers.answer: It's a nautical term of greeting, probably Greek or Latin in origin.

The sound 'oi' or 'hoy' travels furthest across water. 'Ahoy' combines these sounds, making it effective for nautical communication. Her father was a Russian translator in the Navy who picked this up.

questions.question: Which armrest is yours in the cinema?

answers.answer: No one knows - theoretically you'd sit on the far end and that would be right, but then someone would have two or none however you do it. The answer is the ones you can actually get your elbow on.

questions.question: On Earth, which has the most mass - all the animals, all the plants, all the sea life, or all the insects?

answers.answer: Initially said insects due to vast numbers, then changed to plants/trees based on incoming text from Kit about food chain pyramids
Explains food chain pyramid principle - plants at the bottom must outnumber everything that feeds on them, otherwise ecologies would collapse; suggests plants have the greatest mass

questions.question: How come magnets wipe computer hard disks but don't affect iPads or smartphones?

answers.answer: Explains difference between hard disks (magnetic storage with metal oxides on platters, affected by magnets) and flash drives/SD RAM (uses electrostatic charge, not affected by magnets). Qualifications: tech head

Confirms explanation - hard drives use magnetic media affected by magnetism; modern tech uses voltages/electrostatic charge sandwiched between chips like a sandwich. Qualifications: electronics designer who worked for company that developed flash technology

questions.question: What's the point of having a letterbox at the bottom of the door rather than in the middle?

answers.answer: Suggests it might protect postmen from being bitten by dogs; later says it might be aesthetics

Security reason - doors are susceptible to being kicked in; coat hangers can be pushed through letterboxes to hook up to locks. Positioning at the bottom means no lever can reach that far up to manipulate the lock. Qualifications: qualified carpenter and surveyor

questions.question: Why do the windows at the back of the car not wind down completely - there's always at least an inch left?

answers.answer: Suggests it's to stop children falling out

The wheel arch - as the window goes to the bottom corner, it would hit the door frame. Some cars like 4x4s with square doors have windows that disappear completely. Sporty coupes have more window sticking out because the door curves over the wheel arch. Qualifications: used to have a car repair business

questions.question: How much does it cost to get Tower Bridge opened for a ship to pass through?

answers.answer: It's free. You need to book in advance - 24 hours notice. Qualifications: used to be security for the bridge

questions.question: What's the origin of the phrase 'butter wouldn't melt in their mouth'?
Why do we give someone a pat on the back when they've done something good?

answers.answer: Suggests in medieval times, the back was the only part of a knight you could comfortably touch without risking injury due to armor

questions.question: Why do people tend to glance upwards when they're thinking hard about something?

answers.answer: Explains it's actually about looking left and right, not up. Left is for accessing facts/cognitive brain; right is for creativity/inventing/lying. The head follows the eyeballs, so if eyes go up slightly to left or right while thinking, head follows. Qualifications: reads books on cognitive science
Says it's a complete myth and has been proved false many times

questions.question: What's the origin of clapping to show appreciation?

answers.answer: In a performance, clapping makes an audible sound so actors can see the audience's appreciation. It's the easiest audible sound to make. Notes that in Japan, silence is the ultimate show of appreciation and respect. No qualifications

questions.question: Why can't power lines be buried underground in pipes like they've done along the canal in Camden Town?

answers.answer: Cost - burying is much more expensive than overhead lines. Also complications with gas mains, risk of hitting tube lines, and spades breaking underground cables

questions.question: Why does some people's hair come out curly and others' straight? Is there something in the scalp that makes this happen?

answers.answer: Hair follicles for curly hair are oval-shaped; for straight hair they're round-shaped
Like Play-Doh through shaped holes - the nucleus and medulla (where hair comes out) determines shape. Kidney-shaped = curly hair; round = smooth and straight. Qualifications: qualified hairdresser

questions.question: Why do we sweat when we get nervous?
I was told that a baby girl is born with all her eggs. I wondered whether those eggs could be externally fertilised, or are they too immature? When do they become viable?

answers.answer: The eggs are not viable at birth. They ripen during the woman's ovulation cycle and are released into the fallopian tube where they become viable. Viability begins at puberty once menstruation begins. Brian's wife had donated eggs and he learned about the drugs used to ripen eggs for harvest.

questions.question: The police special escort groups who do the Queen and royalty escorts, they only use whistles to get people out of the way, never sirens. Why don't they use sirens?

answers.answer: Politeness - a siren says 'get out of the way now' while a whistle says 'excuse me, please, coming through'

It's to avoid violation of regulations governing blues and twos. You can only put your siren on if you are going to the rescue at loss or harm. By using a whistle, they look official but make everyone acquiesce without violating regulations. Governed by Road Vehicle Lighting Regulation 89 and Road Construction and Vehicle Use Regulations 86.

questions.question: What is registered charity number one? What charity is registered as number one?
How do they remove Banksy's graffiti from the side of public buildings in order to sell them for huge amounts in auction rooms?

answers.answer: Depends on what it's on. If it's directly on brickwork, you can't do it without taking down the whole wall. But sometimes they take the plaster off in one piece. There have been cases where entire walls came up for sale because they're worth so much now. Banksy doesn't make any money from these sales - he sells some work of his own but his guerrilla urban artwork has never paid him.

Their restoration company (Fortress Restorations) developed a gel and technique to remove graffiti. They paint a gel on the graffiti, put a film over the top, let it mature about an hour, then peel it off with the picture intact. The gel softens the paint without destroying it, and you can then put it on a canvas. They've done this down Camden Lock where there's a copy of a Banksy.

questions.question: When listening to music, I hear commentators and critics talking about the colour of a piece of music or the colour of a performance. What is colour in music?

answers.answer: Colour is used to describe how all the instruments come together and how they play, whether it's loud or quiet. It's a description of the sounds - a way of describing variety. Light and airy sounds from higher-pitched instruments like flutes and clarinets would be 'lighter' and 'brighter', while deeper sounds from trombones and trumpets would be 'darker'.

answers.caller: Nassif (text contributor, B in Music GCSE)
answers.answer: It's related to tonality - minor scales are cold blues, major scales are warm reds. A piece in minor scale sounds sad and down, while a major scale piece sounds happy.

questions.question: Where do all the vitamins come from that get put in vitamin tablets? Do they come from a laboratory or a tree? Can you manufacture vitamins or do they have to come from natural sources?
With all the technology we have to make vehicles different colours and pimp vehicles, why are all car tyres black?

answers.answer: Tyres are black because of an additive called carbon black, which absorbs heat. When tyres get heated up from warm weather or road friction, the carbon black absorbs that heat. That's why all tyres - bike, cycle, car - are black. If you colour them, it reduces friction effectiveness and is expensive. Cars need more friction than bikes, which is why they're more standardised.

questions.question: Why do you never see left-handed violinists in orchestras?

answers.answer: Her left-handed daughter is learning violin and is being taught as a right-handed child. This is literally so they don't bash the people next to them in the orchestra.

answers.caller: Nick from Netherlands (viola player, 30 years experience)
answers.answer: Left-handed viola players do exist. He knows at least two, one who played in the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra under Simon Rattle. The instrument is bigger so it takes up more space, and string players have near-misses every day anyway. The one soloist he knows had to relearn after losing a finger on his left hand because you need slightly less fingers to play the bow.

questions.question: Every morning I wake up at 4:20 without fail. How do I stop this? It's been going on for three weeks and I can't get back to sleep. I don't have an alarm set for that time. My husband doesn't wake up. Nothing bad has happened.

answers.answer: Set your alarm for 4:15 and see what's happening outside your house at that time - could be flights, planes, or a neighbour getting up for work.
The body has an internal clock and you can condition it. She needs to program her subconscious mind to wake up at a different time.

questions.question: Why can microwave ovens heat up plates? I thought microwave energy worked on water molecules and food. How can it work on a dry plate?

answers.caller: Phil from M25 (former radio engineer with GEC Marconi)
answers.answer: Ceramics are amongst the group of materials that absorb microwave energy. Water does, but ceramics do as well. Metals behave differently - they have induced currents which cause sparking (like with gold leaf on plates). It's the same principle as stealth bombers which are painted with materials that absorb microwave energy.

questions.question: My mother always used to say if two people pour tea from the same teapot, it's a sign of ginger twins. What does this mean?

answers.answer: Tea was very expensive years and years ago. They put these things about to deter people from using the teapot... It was a way of discouraging people from helping themselves to the teapot when they were around at somebody else's house. If you picked up the teapot after the host, you'd be told you're going to have ginger twins to frighten the life out of you.

questions.question: If you feed an aspirin to a pigeon, will it actually explode?

answers.answer: I've never heard of it with an aspirin, but with baking soda - anything that gives a gas because pigeons can't pass wind. So eventually they just pop.

answers.caller: Hal (Brighton, Professor of Public Understanding of Science)
answers.answer: Bicarbonate of soda is an alkali which reacts with stomach acid and produces carbon dioxide. You would burp. Seagulls CAN burp because they regurgitate food for their young. The aspirin myth is someone confusing acid and alkali. Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid - an acid wouldn't react with stomach acid, only an alkali would. Disprin has bicarbonate of soda but aspirin doesn't.

questions.question: Tomorrow is Good Friday. Why is it called Good Friday when it clearly says anything but?

answers.answer: From Jesus's perspective it doesn't look good, but for the rest of humanity it was fairly good because he died for our sins to ensure our passage into the kingdom of heaven.

questions.question: Why don't children seem to feel the cold as much as adults?

answers.answer: Simply down to the metabolism, which decreases with age. Younger children burn their food much quicker, burning down fats, and the energy from that keeps them warmer.
The reason children feel the cold less is because they're shorter than us and so closer to the ground.

questions.question: Who was Hobson in 'Hobson's Choice'?

answers.answer: It refers to a bloke who owned a lot of horses in Oxford or Cambridge in the 18th century. He had 40 or 50 horses and when you turned up, you were given the choice of the horse in the nearest stable or nothing at all - his way of rotating horses so customers didn't overuse the best ones. In common parlance it means the appearance of a choice when there actually isn't one at all.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'gravy train'?

answers.answer: It's from a book called Blood, Iron and Steel. It's an Americanism. In the latter half of the 19th century, vast fortunes were made by railroad owners. Vanderbilt had a palace with a huge dining table with a silver miniature railway going around the outside.

questions.question: If there was no winter and it was continual summer, what would deciduous trees do? Would they lose their leaves?

answers.answer: I'm a bonsai enthusiast. The Chinese elm is sold as an indoor tree quite often. When you keep it indoors, it keeps its leaves all year round. When you leave it outside, it sheds all its leaves and it is actually a deciduous tree. So that would suggest...

If you took one to a place where it didn't have winter, it would keep its leaves all year. What it would do instead is it would randomly drop leaves after a while and keep constantly regrowing them. So it wouldn't be seasonal, it would just be constant. It responds to temperature mainly.

questions.question: Why is the orientation of the British Isles on weather maps slanted - Liverpool shown as west of Glasgow and Edinburgh - when in reality it's east of both? Why doesn't it follow latitude and longitude like maps in America?

Voyager was launched in 68/69 and has been flying through space for decades. How has it avoided being hit by asteroids? It's been through the asteroid belt and Saturn and is still sending back signals. How has it not been clobbered?
Why are some statues of famous people on horses depicted with different leg positions - some with two legs raised, some with one leg raised as if galloping, some standing still?

answers.answer: I think it's got something to do with how the person featured in the statue died. Two legs in the air means they died in battle. One leg in the air means they died from injuries sustained in battle. All four legs on the floor means they died of natural causes or old age.
That explanation is a very common conception but it's not actually true. I heard a debate about what the answer was and someone came on and said it wasn't true, but I can't remember the right answer.
I heard it on QI. It was Stephen Fry and you don't mess with him. It's an absolute myth. It's just not true at all.

questions.question: If Jupiter and Saturn are gas planets all the way through with no solid surface, would it be possible to fly straight through the middle of them with a suitable spacecraft?

answers.answer: The bigger the planet, the more pressure at the centre. Although Jupiter and Saturn may be 98-99% gas, because they're so massive, the atmosphere is so dense at the centre that it becomes physically impossible to fly through. The molecules are so packed together that it would be like flying through a solid, even though technically it's not. You'd be crushed - the craft would collapse in on itself due to the immense pressure, like a can with a vacuum inside.

questions.question: Why is Scotland Yard called Scotland Yard when it's based in London?

answers.caller: Tracy (Notting Hill) - London Blue Badge guide
answers.answer: There used to be a big palace called Whitehall Palace, which was more of a village up to the Thames. At one end where Westminster Bridge is now, there was an entrance which is still there. When the kings of Scotland came to stay or visit, their carriages went in there, and that's why it was called Scotland Yard. When the police took the area over, they kept the same name.

questions.question: Why are books released as hardback first rather than paperback? They're so much more expensive.

answers.answer: Think of it as a two-tier pricing system. The keener you are to get the book, the more you pay to get it six months ahead of everybody else. Even on Kindle, you pay more when the paper version is still in hardback.

answers.caller: Dave (Wembley) - former production executive at paperback publisher
answers.answer: In order to get the fries down on paperbacks, they have to print many, many more copies with a different method of production - a huge machine that prints from rolls of paper rather than sheets of paper. That costs a hell of a lot to set up and get running, so they have to print many more copies. Hardbacks help gauge how well the book will sell before committing to the massive paperback print runs.

questions.question: Why do hippopotamuses have pink milk?

answers.caller: Nick (Bristol) - obsessed with hippos since age 5
answers.answer: Hippos actually produce white milk but they also produce two unique acids - one called hippodoric acid (which is red) and potamusic acid (which is orange). They produce these as protection for their skin - like a suntan and antibacterial lotion. It gets into the milk by osmosis, and when the red and orange mix with the white milk, it comes out pink.

questions.question: Why can't you find a toaster where you can just make one piece of toast? You can either get two or four, and even four-slice toasters have two racks going down at the same time, effectively burning double the electricity.

answers.answer: The horrible feeling is that you might be the only man in the universe who wants one. Supply and demand.
Single-slice toasters do exist. There's a transparent single-slice toaster available.

You can buy a Dualit toaster that has three apertures but a dial on the front where you can choose how many slices you want to toast. So you can do one at a time. Dawn has one that was a wedding present.

questions.question: If my husband isn't a very good driver and I tense my body up anticipating something might happen, am I more likely to reduce injury, or could tensing up actually make things worse?

answers.answer: You're probably better off relaxed. When sleepwalkers fall, they're completely relaxed and the impact is less injurious than if they'd known they were falling and tensed up. Same with babies being dropped - they don't know they're in danger so don't get hurt as much as adults would. And drunk people fall over without tensing up. The airplane brace position helps because you're tucked in to protect your neck.

questions.question: Why does Earth have such varied climate - freezing poles and boiling deserts - while other planets like Jupiter, Mars, and the Moon (which is closer to the sun than we are) all look exactly the same? Why are we different?
Why does the back of Pepperami snacks say '150% pork'? You can't have 150% of anything, can you?

answers.answer: It's just a marketing trick - like a footballer saying they'll give 110%. It's a way of saying it's more than everything.

Actually, you were wrong. During the curing process, meat loses moisture. So if you start off with 150 grams of pork, you end up with 100 grams of finished salami. Therefore, 150% of the original ingredient goes into making 100% of the finished product.

questions.question: What do the two M's in M&M's stand for?

answers.answer: M&M stands for Mars and Murray - the two names of the guys who started the firm. M&M are the initials of the two founders, Mars and Murrie.

questions.question: Why are certain food names used as terms of endearment (like 'pickle', 'sausage', 'pumpkin') while others aren't?

answers.answer: It's probably just verbal gymnastics - some things just sound like diminutives or little sweetie compliments, and some things don't. Pumpkin might come from pumpkin pie which is practically caramel and very sweet.

questions.question: The sixth round of the FA Cup is actually the quarterfinals, but why do they call it the sixth round and not the quarterfinals when every other competition does?

answers.answer: The FA Cup sixth round still has significance because it's still played at home ground or away, whereas semi-finals and finals are played at neutral grounds. In Sweden they also call it the sixth round, and in basketball they call it 'final four' instead of semi-finals. There's no single definitive answer - it's partly tradition.

questions.question: When you buy a lucky dip lottery ticket, are the numbers pre-determined when the ticket is printed, or are they randomly generated at the moment you request them? And if you have a choice of options on instant win games, does your selection determine whether it's a winner?

answers.answer: The numbers are indeed randomly generated at the time of request. When you want a lucky dip, a request is sent through to the servers which generate a set of five or six random numbers between certain parameters.

questions.question: Where does the expression 'bully for you' come from? What is the bully?

answers.answer: It's about bullseye on a dartboard - when someone gets the best score, you say 'fully for you'. However, this was corrected.

It comes from 'bully beef' - WWI rations. It would be a good day when you were getting some bully beef for tea, so 'bully for you' meant you're getting the good rations. There's always a flavour of sour grapes around it because maybe you weren't getting any.

questions.question: Why do we get a lump in our throat when we're feeling very emotional or about to cry?

answers.answer: It's called globus hystericus - a spasm of the cricopharyngeal muscle caused when the vagus nerve (the tenth cranial nerve) is overstimulated by emotion. The 'hystericus' part indicates it's psychological. It's sometimes called globus pharyngeus. It's not linked to tear ducts - it's a separate emotional response to similar stimuli. It's a primitive reflex - we were designed as amphibians at one stage, so we have a dive reflex which closes the throat after water goes down it. This is a throwback to that.

questions.question: Is it true that there are more water molecules in a glass of water than there are glasses of water in all the oceans and seas on the planet?
What is a controlled explosion? If they blow something up, how is that any different from just setting off a bomb? What exactly is controlled about it?

answers.answer: It's a misnomer - there's no explosion at all. The explosives officer uses a remote-controlled robot with a device that fires a bolt of water at high speed into the suspect package. The speed of the bolt disrupts the device faster than it could detonate. The bang people hear is not an explosion - it's like a shotgun being fired to fire this device off. They use portable x-ray machines to see what's inside, then point 'the stick' at the control mechanism of the detonator. The water jet can go through suitcases and even metal boxes. Only for 14-inch thick concrete bunkers do they have to do it manually with the big suit.

questions.question: The brain cells grow and die - if you could transplant your brain into a new body (clone your body and transfer your brain), could you live forever? How many times can brain cells rejuvenate before the brain says enough's enough?
Why is a can of corned beef the shape that it is? Nothing else comes in that shape - thinner at the top, fatter at the bottom. Why is it diagonal?

answers.answer: The shape is to do with viscosity and atmospheric pressure. You undo the big end of the tin, punch a hole in the middle, then the small end at the top - and it slides out in a block. The tapering makes it easier to get out. Once you release the atmospheric pressure by punching a hole, the pressure equalises and you can easily overcome the atmospheric pressure keeping it in the tin. It's like a sandcastle on the beach.

questions.caller: Simon (Camberwell) - asking on behalf of Paul
questions.question: My friend has eight radiators in his house. He turns seven of them off and only has one on. Why isn't his heating bill seven times cheaper?

answers.answer: All radiators are plumbed in parallel, not series. In parallel, you can turn radiators on or off individually without shutting down the system. If it were series, turning one off would shut the whole system down. With parallel plumbing and thermostatic valves, you can shut down individual radiators and save money, but not seven times as much because the boiler still has to heat the same water.

questions.question: When men lose their hair, why does it fall out symmetrically (like a monk's halo from a central bald spot) rather than in irregular random clumps?
The gas giants Jupiter and Saturn don't have solid surfaces. If you had a suitable spaceship, could you actually fly straight through the middle of them?

questions.caller: James (host) - extra questions from the recap
questions.question: Is it possible to tickle someone to death?
Why do you set a fan oven to a lower temperature than a non-fan oven? I put a thermometer in and it reads the same temperature.

answers.answer: The fan oven has to be set lower because moving air cooks things much quicker than still air. It's the opposite effect of a wind chill factor. The circulating warm air cooks more effectively than the stationary air, so you can set it a little lower and achieve the same cooking result.

questions.question: If penguins mate for life, how long do they wait after their partner disappears before mating with another penguin?
Why do I get allergies from white wine but not red wine? Someone told me it's due to sulfites in the sterilisation process for the bottles, so why wouldn't the same apply to red wine?

answers.answer: Sodium metabisulfite, which is used to sterilise wine and get rid of yeast, is slightly sulfurous. If you leave it in open air or at room temperature, after a while it will all evaporate and you won't taste it. White wine is chilled, red wine is not. The colder temperature of white wine means the sulfites don't evaporate as readily, so more are present when you drink it.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'best foot forward' come from? And why would one foot be better than the other?

answers.answer: It comes from the Masonic ritual when a person is initiated into a lodge. As they move into the lodge, they're asked to step off with their left foot and are told this is their best foot. When asked why, the answer is simply 'because it is.'

It's actually a military term about which foot you leave from when you start marching. The leading foot became the 'best foot.' It may have become the Freemasons' terminology, but before that it was because it was the first step you took when you marched.

questions.question: Why is the Isle of Dogs called the Isle of Dogs?

answers.answer: King Henry VIII used to keep his hunting dogs in that area.

Edward III was the first king to keep his greyhounds in that area and it became a monarchic tradition subsequently. There's also a Ben Jonson play that predates Henry VIII's reign which name-checks the Isle of Dogs.

questions.question: Where was Gene Pitney when he was 24 hours from Tulsa?

answers.answer: Gene Pitney didn't write the song himself. It was 'The Brokeback Act' written by someone else. Tulsa was chosen because it's roughly in the middle of America, so if you're driving overnight you can pretty much be anywhere in America and be 24 hours from Tulsa. Tulsa is in Oklahoma, not Kansas.

questions.question: When I take a plastic bottle of fizzy drink out of the fridge and unscrew the cap, the bottle gets really cold. Why does this happen?

answers.answer: When gas expands, it cools. When gas compresses, it heats up. This is basic schoolboy physics from about 60 years ago. If you take a valve off a bicycle tyre, the air that comes out gets cold. When you pump a tyre up, the pump gets hot - that's endothermic. The same principle applies to the expanding gas in the fizzy drink bottle.

questions.question: How far east do you have to go before the wind changes from east to west? How does it know when to turn?

answers.answer: The wind doesn't turn around. An east wind or a west wind is defined by where it's coming from, not where you are. It doesn't matter where you go all the way around the world - if it's coming from the east, it's an east wind. The direction is defined by the person experiencing it, wherever they are.

questions.question: Why do gas fires need a flue but gas cookers don't? You can leave an oven on for hours without getting carbon monoxide poisoning.

answers.answer: A gas cooker doesn't burn nearly as much gas as a typical gas fire. Most gas fires are flued to the outside - same as a boiler. But a gas hob doesn't burn enough gas to affect the people in the house. If you left it on for weeks, you might have a problem, but it's not designed to run that long. You work out the area of air in the room relative to the kilowatts the fire burns and assess whether it needs a vent.

questions.question: Why do so many convenience shops call themselves 'Food & Wine' specifically? Why not 'Food & Drink' or 'Groceries'?

answers.answer: The name signals to passing shoppers that not only can you buy food there, but they've got an alcohol licence as well. 'Food and drink' might suggest soft drinks. 'Food and sundries' doesn't tell you anything specific. 'Food and wine' announces they have an alcohol licence, which makes a big difference to whether you'll pop in. I have a friend who owns a shop called Central Food and Wine.

questions.question: Why do they say 'the camera adds ten pounds'? Where did that specific number come from?
Why do we scratch our heads when we're thinking about something?
Why do we say 'do you fancy a bit of how's your father?' Where does that phrase come from?

answers.answer: It's from an old British farce where a young guy is courting a young girl in a parlour, and he knows her father is eavesdropping. So every time she tries to make a move on him, he goes 'oh, how's your father, by the way? Is he well? Is he keeping well?'

questions.question: Why is Mayday used as a distress call? Why not help?

answers.answer: Mayday comes from French 'm'aidez' meaning help me.

questions.question: Why do professional athletes wear different coloured shoes on each foot?

answers.answer: It's just a way of selling more trainers. Footballers wear neon pink boots and if you're enamoured of a player, you'd go out and buy those boots. Then you buy different coloured pairs.

They're actually two different colours split down the middle. When you're running, you see the outside of one shoe and the inside of the other, so they look like two different colours. It's just fashion and looking nice.

questions.question: What is the difference between an electric under-blanket and an electric over-blanket, apart from the obvious where they go? Why does it say 'must not be used as an over-blanket'?

answers.answer: The electric blanket has two kinds of insulation - electrical to keep you from getting shocked, and thermal to keep heat distributed inside the blanket. A cheap blanket would have very little thermal insulation, and if used as an over-blanket, the thermostat would try to get the wires to heat up and all the heat would escape into the room. The wires would get hotter and hotter and eventually the electrical insulation would start to melt. Whereas if you cover it with an overblanket, that traps the heat in and the thermostat shuts the current off before the wires get too hot.

questions.question: Children's illness chicken pox - why is the pox named after a chicken? We don't catch it off chickens.

answers.answer: The reason it's called chicken pox is when you run your hand over the child's skin, it feels just like a plucked chicken. It's the same as goosebumps.

questions.question: Why are lords called by their surname (Lord Sugar) and knights are called by their first name (Sir Alan)?
On a large commercial jet, when it comes into land, the wheels are stationary before it hits the deck. Why don't they spin the wheels up to match the landing speed?

answers.answer: If the wheels were spinning around, it would take more time to stop the plane. Spinning wheel equals speed. If the wheel's spinning around, it makes you go faster.

When the wheels are stationary, they create more friction and slow the airplane down. Also, if wheels were spinning via a mechanism, one wheel might spin faster than the other and could tear the aircraft apart. And there's the weight factor - any mechanism to spin wheels adds weight which costs money.

questions.question: Why do window cleaners use ladders that are narrow at the top, as opposed to conventional ladders which one would have thought would have greater stability?

answers.answer: So there's less chance of putting the top of the ladder through a window. With a conventional ladder, there are two points of contact with the area you need to reach. If you reduce that to one point of contact, you automatically increase the area you can reach from the top of the ladder, facilitating cleaning of more windows more effectively.
The window cleaner's ladder sets on three points instead of four, making it less likely to wobble and safer. Three points of contact with solid surfaces are easier to achieve than four points.

The narrow top allows you to pitch them against the corner of a bay window and reach both the right and left windows without moving the ladder. You climb up once for one window, and the same ladder position reaches the other. It works for bays and any smaller gaps you couldn't get a conventional ladder into.

questions.question: Why can't you get British bacon in the US?
Is there a tip pool for the Ballboys and Ballgirls at Wimbledon? Do the multi-millionaire players put money in for a tip for the volunteers from local schools?

answers.answer: They get a tip. The players have a whip round for the Ballboys, Ballgirls and staff who work in the players' lunch canteen. You get a cheque at Christmas - about 50 quid, 30 quid as a Christmas bonus, accrued over the year.

My daughter did the Wimbledon Championships a couple of years ago. They do get paid but not from the players. They get paid by the All England Lawn Tennis Club - about 200 pounds for the two weeks. No tips from the players.

questions.question: When a bowler bowls six balls and the batsman fails to get a run, they refer to it as 'he bowled a maiden over.' Why?

answers.answer: A maiden is a synonym for virgin, meaning unblemished. An over is six balls. So a maiden over means you've bowled six balls unblemished - no runs scored. The double meaning with sweeping a woman off her feet is a coincidence.

questions.question: Why is it when you make a pancake, it only browns in certain spots? It never browns all the way around, even though it's made of the same thing.

answers.answer: The air as it heats rises and takes some of the batter away from the hot surface of the pan, leaving only points of contact where the pancake batter is still in closest contact with the pan. Those points brown into what you see as brown spots.

questions.question: Why does soap sting your eyes, but not any other part of your body? What's actually in soap that is causing that stinging?

answers.answer: Carbolic acid.

Soap has a very high pH. The eyes have a very low pH tolerance. The eyes are alkaline and the soap is acidic. It's a chemical reaction between the two. Baby soap has very low pH which is why it doesn't sting.
Alkaline is the high pH and acid is the low pH. It's the clash of the two that explains why soap stings your eyes.

questions.question: Why does Saturn have rings around it and no other planet has?

answers.answer: The rings are made up of particles of various sizes, from things you can't see to larger almost asteroids. They settled into orbit based on their sizes due to gravitational pull. Lots of little bits of gravel go around Saturn and there's so much of it that it creates the ring - it's multiple rings, maybe a few hundred rings. It's like gravel jigsaws.

questions.question: Why is it easier to get to sleep on your side?

answers.answer: It might be to do with breathing. You only really snore when you're on your back. Maybe it's the fetal position when we're in the womb.

The fetal position or sleeping on your side is because the human body is used to that position. It's a position of comfort and a position of being safe. It happens in all mammals. It's more emotional than physical - a physical, emotional memory.

questions.question: Sometimes when you touch somebody, you get an energy/electric shock. What causes it?

answers.answer: It's static electricity. They've got electricity on them, they're conducting electricity. They're like a battery full of static electricity because they've got rubber shoes on or been on a nylon carpet. You come along and connect the battery and the electricity flows into you.

You're earthing your body which has static electricity in it. You're the battery, not the other person. It could also be the other person discharging to you. You can get a little spark which is induced EMF (electromotive force). The direction of the induced EMF is such that it tends to oppose the change producing it. When you separate contacts of a switch, there's a spark before it completely separates, opposing that change. The change when touching someone is from not touching to touching, and it's opposing that, so you get the little spark.

questions.question: What are the 11 secret herbs and spices found in KFC?

answers.answer: They're a secret. If someone told you it wouldn't be a secret. KFC aren't allowed to tell you.

In the mid-90s, KFC went from a privately owned company to a franchise and changed from Kentucky Fried Chicken to KFC. Two people on the board know one half of the ingredients each, but neither knows what the other person knows. One person knows one half, another person knows another half. The information is kept in a safe that lawyers have access to. Even for KFC internally, no one knows all the ingredients.

questions.question: Why don't planes disrupt clouds in any way, shape or form?
In Switzerland where they speak four languages (Italian, French, German, Romansh), when they have a football team and the manager wants to talk to them, what language do they speak?

answers.answer: French is the dominant language, the lingua franca. German speakers can also speak French, so French would be the mainstream language.

Actually, German is the predominant language in Switzerland - about 60-30 percent breakdown. Only three cantons speak French. The football team will almost certainly be coached in German. In French-speaking Swiss schools, they learn German like we learn French in England.

questions.question: Why do umbrellas have a point or spike on the end?

answers.answer: The spike protects the umbrella material. A hard button on top means when you use it as a walking stick or to stab a Russian spy, you won't damage the cloth. You need a long bit so none of the cloth comes into contact with the pavement. It's tradition now because lightweight rubber stoppers didn't exist when umbrellas were popularized in the 17th century.

questions.question: If there is a number before infinity, what is it?

answers.answer: Infinity minus one. Infinity isn't a number in the sense, it's more of an idea. The only way you could ever say on paper what was before infinity would be to take one off infinity.

questions.question: Why is horse meat just called horse meat? Is there another name for it?

answers.answer: It's the Normans. Before the Norman invasion in 1066, peasants ate simple English-named food. Nobles ate fancy food with French names like beurre (beef) and porc (pork). When the Normans arrived, they brought their fancy French names. We never got a French name for horse because it was never considered fancy enough to deserve a French name.
We get poultry from the French word poulet for chicken. Cheval is French for horse, but it's not used as a meat name. There are no other names for horse meat.

questions.question: What is the origin of the phrase 'to fly off the handle'?

answers.answer: Thinking of trying to crank something up and getting so fast and furious that the handle flies off.

It's from medieval swordsmanship. A sword has a big piece of metal that goes into the handle, held in place by wooden pegs. If those pegs break while swinging the sword, the sword will come flying out the handle at great speed and could impale someone - that's 'flying off the handle'.
It might actually be about an axe head flying off a loose handle rather than a sword. Thomas C. Halliburton's 'The Attaché', published in 1843, is the first known usage of that phrase.

questions.question: When they colorize black and white films like 'World War II in Colour', how do they know what all the colors are?

answers.answer: They color each frame by hand individually. That's why it's so rare and expensive to colorize old films. For colors they don't know for certain, they make educated guesses - like uniforms being khaki. They check some things historically from archives and then just take a punt. For things like what color a girl's dress was, they just use whatever colors they had lying around.

questions.question: Why do newspapers print test blocks of each color on every copy when nobody checks each page?

answers.answer: He had no idea - said it was a technological question rather than journalistic.

They are color density blocks. When printing, you measure them with a machine called a densitometer which reflects light. If there's too much ink of one color, it affects the color balance. In the old days, they measured against a swatch. They take out a sheet regularly to make sure the color balance is right. Modern printing uses computer control.

questions.question: How do they colorize black and white films - do they color each frame by hand?

answers.answer: Yes, they color each frame by hand. There are 726,000 frames in 'World War II in Colour'. They don't know the colors for sure - they just guess and once they've made a decision, they stick to it.

questions.question: Why do we have a full English breakfast but we don't have a full English dinner or full English lunch?

answers.answer: It's because the ingredients are always the same sort of things and it was invented in England. You get an Ulster Fry in Northern Ireland which is exactly the same but with soda bread and potato bread.

questions.question: About cows - if you had a cow in a field and you never milked it, what would happen to the others?

answers.answer: Cows, like all mammals including humans, don't produce milk all the time. You first have to produce offspring, then milk production starts. As long as you continue suckling with a mechanical effect, it continues to stimulate milk production. So you can breastfeed for a week, three months, six months, or five years - if you continue, the milk continues. If you stop abruptly, you can get mastitis, but generally cows and humans will just stop producing milk.

questions.question: Why don't we have a traditional English lunch like other countries have?

answers.answer: We don't have a traditional English lunch because we have roast beef for our dinner, but we never have done a traditional lunch, whereas other countries do.

questions.question: Crossings. Puffin, pelican, toucan. What's that about? Zebra. Zebra crossing. Obvious. Understandable. Easy. Black and white. Stripe on, stripe off. Stripe on, stripe off. Cannot work out the other three. I'm in the process of learning to drive and these have come up and I cannot fathom it.

answers.answer: Pedestrian or pelican crossings, puffing and tooting crossings? Pelican, it's pedestrian light controlled. They're basically the ones with the yellow box you press the button. Puffing is pedestrian user-friendly. So they've got cameras on the top that either face the county amount of cars that go through or where people stand on either side of the road to change the lights accordingly. And toucan, or toucan, is two can cross. So it would be a pedestrian and cyclist. Usually near parks and stuff like that. And so probably the, well, whichever one came first, probably the pelican. They managed to find a seabird-based nickname for the new ones when they came along.

questions.question: I have given up cakes and chocolates for Lent. But I missed the pancakes day because I was away and I was saying to the guys at work, are pancakes considered cakes? The question may be in the answer. The answer may be in the question pancakes. It went all the way to the European Union at one point whether or not a Jaffa cake was a cake or a biscuit. Exactly, that's what I said. But if a pancake's not a cake, what is it?

answers.answer: Pancakes are not cakes.

Biscuits get softer if left out. Cakes get harder if left out. Ipso facto, Jaffa cakes get harder, and therefore they were termed as biscuits, and therefore didn't attract the VAT. Biscuits tend to be hygroscopic and absorb water, and cakes tend to lose water because they dry out. So I think if you left a pancake out, especially the traditional UK pancake, which doesn't rise, I suspect that would get harder. Pancake needs a genus. Maybe an order, rather than a genus. I think in order, it's a genus. It needs an order all of its own.

questions.question: I've just spent a week away in Bulgaria. Most European countries use the same alphabet, bar a few little accents and flicks. The Bulgarians, it's completely different. Same as the Greeks and the Russians. Is it derived from somewhere like that? Because I know it's close to Greece.

answers.answer: You're describing the Cyrillic script. Which is all to do with the schism in the Catholic Church that unfolded at some point around the 10th or 11th century. And half of the Christians went to Rome and stayed with Latin, and half of the Christians went to Constantinople and went with the Cyrillic... It was Saints Cyril and Methodius. Methodius took... I told you it was going to fall apart! But it is to do with religion and that other business.

In Western Europe, so in England, France, Spain, we use a Latin alphabet. And in Eastern Europe, the Cyrillic languages, the Cyrillic script, for example, in Russia and so on, are based on the Greek alphabet. It's just the evolution of language, basically. If you have a look at the German language and the alphabet they use in Germany, it's actually halfway in between the two. You have a Latin foundation, but you have a lot of other sort of linguistic, like the characters, like the esset in German, that's actually coming from Greek. If you look at religion as well... Cyril was a Greek Orthodox missionary, and when he was taking the Bible to various Balkan countries which had no written language, only a spoken language, he had to invent a new script, which he based on the Greek, but with different characters, to express the sounds that were particular to those languages. In Western Europe, because we got conquered by the Romans, the foundation originates from Roman Catholicism, and we use Latin.

The boundary of the Eastern and Western Roman empires fell in exactly that part of Europe. When Constantine set up the new Eastern capital in Constantinople, Latin was still the common language, but over time, the influence of Greek culture, in the East, and the wish to differentiate, led to the adoption of the Greek language. Therefore, where the boundary between East and West occurred, so you've got the appearance of the different alphabets in each side of the boundary. Because Cyril was a Greek Orthodox missionary and took his language and adapted it for the Slavonic and Balkan countries subsequently.

questions.question: Do animals have accents? So if you've got a dog that's been born and lived in Scotland all its life, will its bark be any different to another dog that's been born and lived in London all its life? Or do birds sing with a different accent in different parts of the country?

answers.answer: I think they do, you know, but I'm going to need someone to... I think birds sing differently according to where they are in the country.
They do. Yes, I once met a Scottish cow who said, Occi the moo.

Primarily in London pigeons, they always seem to go, hoo-hoo-hoo, hoo-hoo-hoo. On a recent trip to Hungary, I noticed all the pigeons go, hoo-hoo-hoo, and they all do it differently. It was definitely three tones, but definitely arranged differently. They were definitely different. And they all do it.

questions.question: Why are apartments called apartments when they're all squashed together? As in, they're not apart?

answers.answer: They're flat. Flats are when they're... They haven't gone upstairs... And the apartments are in one building, but they're apart. So it's about a building with the same door, but there's dwellings in it that are apart. You wouldn't need a new name if you had a different door for every dwelling, because they wouldn't all be in one building. So it's about an apartment is in a building with a shared door, but is apart from the other dwellings in that building.

questions.question: I enjoy the fruit a pear. The delicious yummy fruit. I like a pear. I like a bit of cheese I find goes well with a pear. So having agreed that a pear is a delicious yummy fruit, why is it when something goes wrong, we say it's gone pear shaped?

answers.answer: Because the shape of a pear is not always desirable, particularly in the context of glass blowing. It comes from the glass blowing. If you're blowing your glass and you want to get a nice bowl shape, which is the basis of most glass vessels, if something goes wrong in the blowing process, I have to be careful how I phrase this, if something goes wrong in the blowing process, the lump of glass at the bottom of your pipe goes pear shaped. Ergo, when things go wrong, they go pear shaped.

questions.question: I'd like to know why is it always brandy being given when somebody feels ill? Why not anything else? Why is there always brandy?
Why is a club sandwich called a club sandwich?

answers.answer: I'm 98% sure, 99% sure, it's named after the club in which it was invented in New York. And rather like the Earl of Sandwich, which created the idea of a sandwich in the first place when he was playing cards and sent for a piece of meat between two bits of bread while it's saving getting up. There was a club in New York, and I can't remember which one. It might have been the Knickerbocker Club, I forget which, that invented the club sandwich. And so ever since then it's been a club sandwich.

questions.question: A friend and I were talking about this the other day. As you go east or west from GMT, you either gain or lose hours. And I think when you get to the international date line on the other side, there's a 24 hour difference. If you cross west, you lose 24 hours, and east you gain or vice versa. If you were able to circumnavigate the globe in under 24 hours, would that mean that you could gain days or lose days, depending on which direction you're going?

answers.answer: I think time travel is about the speed of light. Speed of light's about 6 or 7 million miles per hour. You already do, don't you? I mean, you already go back because of time zones, or am I missing the question again? I think you may. The thing is you don't ever carry on going all the way around to a full... So if you could circumnavigate the whole globe in less than 24 hours, would you go back in time? Theoretically, yes.

It's convenience time and it's not a question. Elapsed time is what we all experience as we move from one place to another. And you can't have a day in the same place. Or two days in the same place. So there has to be the international date line which skirts as far as possible through all of... The line is slightly annoying.

questions.question: Why is a tank top called a tank top? Because it's got absolutely nothing to do with the military. Bullets don't bounce off it.

answers.answer: It does come from the military. Tank tops. It comes from the First World War on the first original tanks. They were riveted plates, leapt over, and when the bullet would strike the edge of the tank, the spray would go inside of the bullet with the fragment, and the droplets would spray onto the occupants and the drivers and the crew. So they developed a thing called the tank top, which was made in leather, which actually started to go completely over the head and right the way down the shoulders. And then your helmet was on top of that, and you wore goggles as well. Why would it not cover the arms? Because your arms were covered anyway, which your jerkins and your normal uniform. But so was your chest. This stopped the droplets of the molten metal falling down your neck. Not commanders. All staff. All staff in a tank.

questions.question: Why is everyone apologising? What makes small babies small?

answers.answer: Well, I think it's the fact that they're not as big as you think they are. I met my first cousin once removed at eight weeks old the other week, and I was holding him, and he smiled at me, and I thought, well, he doesn't know what's funny, does he? He didn't smile at you, David. What was he doing? No, he wasn't doing anything else. It was wind. We checked. It was wind. Everybody thinks that they've got this amazing, they're like baby whisperers. They're like baby whisperers. It was wind. It's the first time they picked up a baby. Oh, my God, he's smiling! He's just letting one go.

questions.question: Monoblock tap in a bathroom. When you turn it on and the cold comes out, it makes a certain noise. When you turn the hot on, when the water coming out of the tap is still cold, it will make the same noise. But when the water gets hot, it makes a different noise. Why?

answers.answer: Hot water expands, which is correct. Everything expands when you heat it, pretty much, doesn't it? The hot water is coming through. It's just that the temperature's changed. But the hotter it is... No, the pressure will be affected by the heat. Hot water, it takes up more room than cold water. And there may even be some steam involved. So as it comes out of the pipes, it gets faster. Ergo, the sound... the point of emission changes.

The cold water is coming from your main feed outside, which has very high pressure. The hot water has to be heated somehow, like your boiler or whatever method you've got. And that's where the pressure drops. The reason is expansion. Hot water and cold water are two different densities.

questions.question: We were watching rugby at the weekend, and I was just wondering, why is it that rugby players don't have their names on the back of their T-shirts, but football players do?

answers.answer: Football players are too stupid to remember their own names, Laura. And rugby players who have had good educations and paid attention at school, they're intelligent enough not only to remember their own names, but also to sort of get A-levels and degrees and things.
