questions.question: Why could I see the moon at 10am this morning in a crisp blue sky?

answers.answer: This happens regularly throughout the month depending on the time of year. It relates to how the moon orbits Earth while Earth orbits the Sun. The moon doesn't have its own light - it reflects sunlight. Certain times of the month, when the moon has gone around Earth to a certain degree, sunlight still shines on parts of the moon. When the sun is up, the moon is typically on the other side of the planet, but sometimes it's just coming around the corner. The light still bounces off some parts of the moon. You'll notice you won't necessarily see a full moon during the day - sometimes you'll see three quarters of it but not all.

questions.question: Why is it called a landing? We have a landing at the top of the stairs between the bedrooms.

answers.answer: It's a landing stage, like a pontoon in a river. It's where you stop and regroup and then carry on again.

It's because you take a flight of stairs to get to the landing. You get on the landing first to get to the other side. Also, if you fall out of the loft, it's somewhere to land - it's quite a hard landing but it is.

questions.question: If cows and goats and sheep eat only grass, how come they produce so much fat in their milk and cholesterol? If I ate grass, I wouldn't get fat.

answers.answer: Their digestion is far more efficient than ours. They've got more than one stomach. In one of the stomachs, the green food is broken down by bacteria, and the energy they derive is mostly the waste product of the bacteria rather than the food they're eating. They give off enormous amounts of sugar. The bacteria feeds upon the stuff in the stomach, and the cow feeds upon the waste products of the bacteria.

questions.question: The skin on the outside of your body is identical to the skin on the inside of your mouth. When you slice the skin on the outside of your body, it bleeds. When you slice the skin on the inside of your mouth, it blisters. Why?

answers.answer: In your mouth, it's not a blister, it's a scab. And the same on your skin. It's just fairly instantaneous. Your mouth isn't bleeding persistently. That's evolution. Because you'd lose too much blood through your mouth. It's a lot more inconvenient to have blood in your mouth than it is to have blood on your knee.

questions.question: What language do referees speak during a match? For example, England and Brazil. If the referee doesn't speak English or Portuguese, what language does he speak so everybody can understand each other?

answers.answer: I think it's probably English, don't you?

questions.question: Boxes of eggs in the supermarket are kept on the centre aisle, not refrigerated. Yet the box says keep refrigerated. What is so special in the supermarket that they can be kept unrefrigerated, yet we have to keep them in the fridge?

answers.answer: I think the answer will be contained within the difference between a sell-by date and a use-by date. You're not going to buy eggs fresh in a supermarket that have been hanging around for two weeks. But they're going to hang around for two weeks in your house, so you may as well refrigerate them to reduce the possibility of them going off.

You don't have to keep eggs refrigerated. A lot of stores don't keep them refrigerated because they're self-dispositive. They're self-sterile. So the shell keeps the egg sterile from outside influences, bacteria, etc. The instruction to refrigerate is to cover themselves in terms of health and safety.

questions.question: My dog is really clever - she sits, rolls, everything. But why can't she suck through a straw?

answers.answer: Your dog doesn't want to suck through a straw. That is actually the answer. Which is why I'm taking this.

Puppies can clearly suckle from their mother, otherwise they'd start off dead. But the physiognomy - the shape of the face and the oral motor physiology - changes when adulthood comes. They lose the ability to form a lip seal. The snout grows and they don't need to do it anymore, so they lose the ability roughly around the time they don't need to do it anymore. It's evolution.

questions.question: If you've got a lump of cheddar cheese and you melt it, does the fat intake increase?

answers.answer: When you melt cheese, the fat splits from the protein and the other stuff in the cheese - which is why you see curds and whey or oil. The fat that was already in the cheese just separates. The chemical constituency is identical. The physics has changed slightly in the way they're combined - they just separate. The calorie count would be identical. The chemical analysis would be identical. They're just mixed up differently, like a milkshake.

questions.question: Why do we need to earth electricity? How do we earth something? How do astronauts earth their spaceship?

answers.answer: The spaceship doesn't need earthing because it's not running on 230 volts AC - it's running on DC. Most things in your house run on 12 volt internally, but 230 volts is used because it's the cheapest, most efficient way to transmit electricity to your house, and that needs earthing. A boat doesn't need earthing because it's sat in water, which is the best conductor of electricity. When earthing a system, you drive a six-foot steel spike into the ground and ground it to that.

questions.question: Why do we only have crosswords, especially cryptic ones, in the English language? Do other papers like Le Figaro have crosswords?

answers.answer: Most definitely other languages have really difficult crossword puzzles. I know for at least two other languages in Europe that have them - Danish and German. They do the really cryptic ones that a Brit would never have any idea how to solve unless they were fluent in German or Danish.

questions.question: These colour catching sheets that people put in their washing machines - how do they work? They look like pieces of paper but I want to know how they actually work.

answers.answer: I haven't got the slightest idea what you're talking about. I don't do the washing in my house.
The colour catcher sheet will be red but the rest of the clothes... you've got different temperatures at which different materials absorb dye.

questions.question: Why can't you get back bacon in America? I've never been able to get it. Always that streaky stuff.
Why do coins have dates on? My seven-year-old son asked me this the other day, and I don't know why.
Why does the academic year start in September and finish in July, as opposed to starting in January like the calendar year?

answers.answer: Because they needed children to be free during the summer to help picking the harvest - peas, potatoes, etc. The academic year is geared around end-of-year exams, after which comes the big rest. They didn't want a six-week holiday in the middle of the school year.

questions.question: Why are the rubber bands around bunches of asparagus purple?

answers.answer: It's to differentiate between different grades or qualities of asparagus. A green rubber band, a red rubber band - different colors show different qualities so it can be clearly identified on your plate so you're not chewing it.

questions.question: Why have humans evolved such big brains if scientists say we only use 20 or 25% of our brain?

answers.answer: It's not true that we only use 20% of our brain. Different bits of our brains are specialized for different jobs, so we don't use all of our brain at all times, but the idea that we have mysterious untapped potential is just a myth. She never found any research evidence to support this idea at all.
Humans developed big unused brains from evolution from when we were different species. As we are no longer doing those activities, new activities create new brain material.

questions.question: Why do boxers win belts instead of trophies like in other sports?

answers.answer: Back in the olden days, when boxing gloves were really thick with leather, the laces used to get really tight around their wrists, so they'd never give them a trophy after the fight. They'd always put the belt round their waist because you couldn't pick a trophy up with gloves on.

The difference between belts and trophies is that belts came about as a much more prestigious way of honouring professional boxers. Amateur boxers get trophies and cups, they don't get belts. Professionals, if you're a world champion professional, you get a belt.

questions.question: Why does the lowercase letter G in old-fashioned type fonts look almost like a number 8, when nobody actually writes it like that?
What is the highest a bird can fly?

answers.answer: The highest flying birds are geese, especially Canada geese. They average 9,000-10,000 feet but have been seen up to about 35,000-40,000 feet. They fly over 1,000 miles a day. These are the birds that caused the engine strike on the Hudson River.

Cranes that migrate across the Himalayas in summer. In a David Attenborough-type documentary, they followed these cranes flying at heights in excess of Mount Everest and Kinchinjunga. They circle for 5-6 hours waiting for an updraft to take them over the mountains - around 30,000+ feet.

questions.question: Why does American English drop the silent vowels that appear in British English spelling (colour/color, honour/honor)?

answers.answer: It has to do with migration from England to America and the Mayflower - Americans wrote more phonetically because literacy levels were lower at the time, so people wrote down what words sounded like.

It was actually a very deliberate change to American spelling by Noah Webster and others - Americans decided to simplify their spelling. Theodore Roosevelt may have had something to do with it (early 20th century). This made it easier to learn, especially for immigrants who weren't English speakers.

questions.question: Why is the roof of a ship's bridge house called 'Monkey Island'?

answers.answer: On smaller ships like trawlers and whalers, you have a tall mast and send crew members up there to scout for whales or fish. You climb like a monkey to get there, ergo 'Monkey Island'. These days radar systems are up there but they still free-climb.

questions.question: Why don't cat's eyes light up on roads anymore? When she was a child she thought there was a little man under the road holding lights up.

answers.answer: Cat's eyes never actually lit up - they reflected light. Headlight technology has advanced so you don't need them as much. On motorways there are still different colors: amber for central reservation, white for lane lines, green for exits, red for motorway entries, blue for service stations.

questions.question: Why are the pedestrian railings staggered at halfway points on roads, so you have to turn left or right before crossing the rest of the way?

answers.answer: It's a pedestrian calming measure to slow people down so they don't dash across when lights are about to change. You only cross half the road at a time. The railings force you to pause and redirect.

questions.question: Did dinosaurs have genitalia in the way that we would recognise them now? What did they look like?

answers.answer: Yes, dinosaurs had reproductive organs. Different types had different setups - some were egg-layers, some had live babies. Lizards and snakes have two reproductive organs called hemipenes (males only) and only use one at a time as backup. Tortoises, crocodiles, and alligators have one. Reptiles are the closest living relatives to dinosaurs.

questions.question: Why can't you get green olives on pizza? Why don't pizza restaurants offer green olives?
If the Prime Minister woke up one day and decided he didn't like the colour of the front door of 10 Downing Street, is he allowed to change it?

answers.answer: Number 10 is a listed building. Mrs Cameron or any other prime minister's wife couldn't change it without permission from the Prime Minister. It's at least Grade 2, probably Grade 1. Grade 1 means they've got to have permission for everything.

questions.question: When you sign off from a letter or maybe a Christmas card, a birthday card, who decided that a kiss would be represented by an X?

answers.answer: From Mr Evans my history teacher - documentation in the Middle Ages most of us couldn't actually read or write, 98% of us couldn't. So when we had to do any signature, it was denoted with an X because they couldn't even sign their name, and then they kissed it in good faith. You put an X to mark your name and then you kissed the document as a sort of pledge.

questions.question: What happens if you commit a crime and end up in prison and you're claustrophobic?

answers.answer: Every time a prisoner gets taken into a prison, they're always assessed on arrival. There's always a doctor and a healthcare professional to see if there are any difficulties that a particular prisoner has. For that first night, there will always be somebody monitoring a new arrival. If there is an issue of claustrophobia or any other illness, the individual will almost certainly be transferred to a healthcare unit. Most prisons have got healthcare units. If there was a defined condition of claustrophobia, it would be a doctor or a psychiatrist that would be able to identify whether that exists or not, and whether the bloke's trying to pull a fast one. Assuming it's not and it's identified, then he would almost certainly be taken into an inpatient unit. Some prisons with inpatient healthcare units have got four-bed or six-bed bays like in hospitals. That whole area would be locked up and secure but it wouldn't feel oppressive. (David is the chair of an independent monitoring board looking at standards in one of Her Majesty's jails.)

questions.question: I've just recently moved home, and the central locking on my car doesn't work when my car's parked on my driveway. It'll work everywhere else - at the shops, at work. But it doesn't work when I'm parked on the new driveway.

answers.answer: We had it with one of our customers - every time he brought it into the garage it would work, it was perfect, but he said it wouldn't work at home. We thought he was a bit of a nutcase, but it turned out he had a remote doorbell, like one of these wireless doorbells. And it was interfering with the signal on the central locking when he pressed it outside his front door.

questions.question: I've got my new iPhone 5. Given that it does practically everything my laptop does, why don't I need to put antivirus on it?

answers.answer: One of the reasons they can't get viruses is the apps themselves. When you download an app, they go through the Apple screening process so they make sure there's no malicious code in the actual software. The software applications themselves are what they call sandbox, whereby the application doesn't have the authority to access other areas of the system files on the phone.

I agree with Anwar except for one point - he's right about the native applications, but there is always a danger when you're using your browser that there is some malicious code that isn't covered by Apple's pretty rigorous screening process.

Because Apple's iOS is Unix-based, there are viruses for Unix systems, but since Windows is still the ubiquitous operating system, there's more return for the hacker writing a virus. It is possible to get a virus on your Mac or iPhone. It's just incredibly rare. Market forces.

questions.question: Hair colours - we have black, brown, grey, white, but why are they not yellow and orange? Why do we call them blonde and ginger instead of yellow and orange?
When they talk about plant, as in plant hire, as in machinery, where does that term come from? Where does that word come into JCBs and big diggers?

answers.answer: When we refer to plants, we're normally referring to it as air conditioning units. What happened was initially we started referring to it as an air conditioning unit, and then it went on to other kind of mechanical things that we would put to support buildings. Then it went into the machinery. Initially air conditioning units because of purifying the air within offices. Before that, in offices, we used to increase the amount of plants that we would put in the offices to purify the air. When they started putting units in, they used to substitute for plants. And that's basically it.
I'm an architect and that's one of the things that came up in my lectures back when I was at university.

questions.question: Why is it that the price of baby food and baby milk powder is exactly the same price throughout all the supermarkets? There's never any differentiation at all. Even though there's competition between supermarkets, there's no competition on baby milk.

answers.answer: By law, shops are not allowed to put any promotions or anything like that on baby milks. So that explains why you won't get one going cheaper than another. They're not allowed to undercut. They're not allowed to do a buy one get one free. They're not allowed to do anything. They're not even allowed to put a label under the milk saying it's a really good price. The reason is that people shouldn't be encouraged to bottle feed in preference to breastfeed. Follow-on milks can have a reduction, but not the stuff that is an essential for the bottle-feeding baby. I would guess that a lot of the price is set by the actual formula manufacturer.

questions.question: My deaf dog barks and whimpers in his sleep and wakes himself up. Can he hear himself? Can he take himself by surprise if he sleep-barks?

answers.answer: If his ears don't work, he can't hear in the conventional sense, but he is capable of surprising himself by making that noise because if he sleep-barks, he will essentially vibrate. Evelyn Glennie, the profoundly deaf percussionist, responds to vibration somewhere other than her eardrums. She can feel the music. So the dog will feel the vibration when he barks in his sleep.

questions.question: Widow's peak - why is it called that? Can you explain what it actually is?

answers.answer: When Queen Victoria was widowed, she made a business out of being a widow. She adopted a headdress which had a peak at the front. If you look at coins at the time, you'll see that there is a headdress that has a peak. She stopped wearing her tiaras. She went into court mourning and the hairstyle looks like the hat. So it's called a widow's peak. There's a peak over the forehead. I got it from Elizabeth Longford's biography of Queen Victoria.

questions.question: When someone's titanium knee replacement gets cremated, what happens to the titanium? Does it come out in the ashes? Is there a market for second-hand titanium?

answers.answer: Dad had two knees and two hips. They tried to take him out before they cremated him. They send them back for recycling - to the hospital, to the scrap metal merchant.

That can't burn in a cremator goes into a consecrated plot of land in a crematorium after the funeral, and the family are just given the cremulated bones, which form the ashes. You'd bury the knee - any artificial joint. The only exception is pacemakers, which have to be removed prior to cremation.

questions.question: Why can't you have alcohol patches like nicotine patches, or chocolate patches? If they can do it for nicotine, why can't they do it for alcohol or chocolate?

answers.answer: I think the answer is to do with ritual. The physical ritual of lighting up and inhaling is part of psychological dependency.

Your alcohol patch idea might possibly work with a tiny number of chronic alcoholics. The reason it hasn't been made is because there wouldn't be enough money in it. Your nicotine patch works for every single smoker trying to give up, so there's money in it. Most people who ever drink don't want to give it up.

questions.question: How does an ice spike form in my birdbath? There's nothing dripping into it, it's not under anything, and it's about 10 inches long at about a 30-degree angle.

answers.answer: James tried to find answers but was initially uncertain.

The water freezes gradually. As the top surface freezes, everything expands. You get a crack in the centre that opens. Due to the expanding water underneath, the water pours out of that crack and freezes on the outside, creating a small tube. It keeps rising and forming a tube until it's cold enough at the top to seal it off. It happens when it's not cold enough to freeze all the water quickly enough before the tube can form.

questions.question: Why is it that when we do a pound sign, we put the pound sign first, and every other symbol that I can possibly think of - like 20 pence, we write 20 and put the P after - why is it with money we always put the sign first and say it the opposite way round?

answers.answer: If you put the pound sign after the pound, where would you put the pence? Like if you've got £4.50, that's why it's currency.
It's because those are imperial measurements and not metric. If you're young you probably don't know how many ounces there are in a pound.

If you've got 1,000 pounds and you put the pound sign after, you could put something in front of the 1,000 like a nine and make it 91,000. It goes back to accountancy and ledgers. It stops people from adding numbers on the end. The pound and decimal point act as brackets - it's very hard to get anything into the bracket.

questions.question: What happens to ants when it rains? Do all these ants drown or do they survive? Water gets into the cracks in the pavement where they live.

answers.answer: I imagine you're talking about an ant's nest which has got a tiny entrance. So the answer will be you might get a little bit of water right in the entrance, but if an ant can squeeze through it, it's not going to flood. The nest will be underneath - they've dug out the nest underneath the paving slabs.

When ants make their nest, they burrow down into the soil and then come back on themselves towards the surface in an S-bend and then go back down again, creating an airlock. When it rains, the water goes into the airlock but it won't go any further into the nest. The ants scurry down into the nest as quick as they can. It will gather in the S-bend and then once it dries it can then come back out again. In torrential rain over long periods, it could overburden the S-bend.

questions.question: Do spiders feel the cold? I saw a spider on its web in freezing cold weather.

answers.answer: Spiders are cold-blooded. Cold-blooded creatures don't feel the cold, do they? Isn't that the whole point of being cold-blooded?

They do feel the cold. In September, October, November, they try to get into your house to seek shelter. What they do is if they're on the outside and it's particularly cold, they slow themselves right down. Sometimes they will get frozen to death if they don't get into the correct temperature zone. During the day once it gets warmer, they will speed up. As their temperature rises, the spider will get warmer and become more active.

questions.question: Scientists recently discovered atoms were not solid. If you look up a picture of an atom on Google, all you see is neatly packed little balls. If they're not solid, what are those balls?
Why is a fridge or a freezer less efficient to run when it's iced up? If it's already frozen, it's already down at the temperature required to freeze.

answers.answer: It doesn't reach that temperature and then stay there. It will warm up slightly and then that kicks in the bimetallic strip on the thermostat and it starts freezing again. If it's full of ice, it's melting and refreezing in incremental stages much more often than it would in an empty freezer. So every time it turns off and on, it uses a bit of electricity. Ergo, a frosted-up freezer uses more energy than a clean one.

questions.question: Every time I clean my toilet with bleach and leave it for a while, the water level seems to drop. Is this just me?

answers.answer: This is all about the S-bend. The same would happen if you poured water in. You pour it in and it fills up and then it slowly sinks down again as the S-bend empties or fills.

It's down to water pressure. You've got to have the same water pressure on both sides of the S-bend. Because bleach is denser than water, you pour it down one end and to equalise the pressure, it pushes out the water from your side out the other side of the S-bend. The bleach remains on this side of the S-bend - kind of like osmosis.

It's nothing to do with water pressure because in a toilet you've got an airlock the other side of the bend so there's an air gap. The actual answer is that chlorine is a bleach compound. Bleach is the active ingredient which is a gas. When you put it in the toilet, the bleach evaporates out into the atmosphere having done its cleaning, so the mass is less.

questions.question: My seven-year-old son asked me what time it is on the moon if it's three o'clock in the afternoon on Earth. I couldn't explain it.
Jack provided an answer to Kareem's question about atoms

answers.answer: That's how they're modelled but he's not seeing them, he's seeing a representation. It's just to make it intuitive. What we call solid is actually like millions and millions of atoms all bonded together. It's like a magnet - if you have two magnets they repel each other. If you're touching a table, you have electrons in your finger and electrons on the table, they repel each other and that gives us the illusion of solidness. Atoms are mostly just nothing - 99% empty space.

questions.question: Is the first leaf that falls off the tree in autumn the first leaf to grow back in spring?
Why is it called bric-a-brac? I was at my local village hall and they were selling bric-a-brac - all those bits and bobs on the table.

questions.caller: Donna (Harrow) - question from her son Cameron
questions.question: If I stand near the border of a country and fire a gun across the border, and it kills somebody in the other country, in which country is the crime committed?

answers.answer: In a way, the answer is both. Initially, the country where the bullet injured the other person would punish you, but as a citizen of your own country, if the punishment for that crime is higher there, they have the right to punish you further. You're not absolved of crimes just because you're in another country.

questions.question: Why are Catholic religious people known as being left-footed?

answers.answer: I think it's just because they were in a minority.

questions.question: Why do lots of men refer to women as birds when birds are both male and female?

answers.answer: It comes from the borough of Southwark in South London in medieval times. It was where all the brothels were situated because it was outside the city of London. The brothels were called stews and were all licensed by the Bishop of Winchester. All the prostitutes that worked in the stews were called either Winchester geese or wagtails. A common euphemism that if you were bitten by a wagtail meant you caught the syphilis. And that's actually where we get the word birds from.

questions.question: When you open envelopes in the dark, a certain kind of envelope, as you pull the sticky bit apart, emits a tiny, almost phosphorescent blue glow. Why does this happen?

answers.answer: The glue is designed to flash when it's first opened so that you can tell if your envelope has been tampered with and the contents have been pre-read. It's any of a number of glues that will discharge static electricity when it's first pulled apart.

questions.question: If you touch the top left-hand corner of your phone screen and you have Twitter there, but then you swipe to the next screen and you've got a different app like Crazy Wings or Tiny Wings in the exact same top left corner, how does the phone know that the same touch point has changed from one app to another?

answers.answer: If you just simply touch your screen and don't move your thumb, it executes dozens of lines of code which are telling your operating system that the user is touching the screen. If you swipe left, swipe right, up or down, it tells the software to change the view to this particular view. When you touch a section, it executes that application which is placed there. Think of it as a cube - you're focusing on different sections of the cube and each face of the cube has different buttons on it. When you swipe to the left, you're effectively rotating the cube. You've told the operating system that you've swiped to a different face. The other view still exists, it's just that you as the user can't see it.

questions.question: Why did the various Apostles never have surnames or family names, considering they were the founder members of the Christian religion?

answers.answer: They didn't have surnames. They didn't need them. If you go back two thousand years to Palestine, you knew people by their origin or occupation. Matthew from Nazareth, Mark, Luke the Scribe, John, Judas from Iscariot - that's all you needed to distinguish between people. You can't just invent them a thousand years later.

questions.question: In TV and film production, when they want to add visual images, they always use a green screen. What is it about green that makes it special? Could it work if it was any other colour?
Why is the cabinet called the cabinet?
What would happen to the display on a portable sat-nav if you took it on a plane at 30,000 feet? Would it still show all the roads below?

answers.answer: It would be out of range of the triangulation point, so you wouldn't see anything.

I saw a video on YouTube with a guy actually opening a sat-nav on an aeroplane. It's just everything that you see when it's in your car. You can actually see the arrow which was on the screen showing the position of the plane and you could see all the roads that the plane was flying over on the sat-nav.

questions.question: The world revolves in 24 hours. Why does it take 20-22 hours to fly to Australia? Why can't you just fly into the sky in a balloon, stay still, wait 12 hours, and come back down in Australia?

answers.answer: The Earth revolves together with its atmosphere, and the planes fly in the atmosphere. It would be technically possible, but not economical, just to fly very, very high out of the atmosphere into space. And then the Earth wouldn't be pushing the atmosphere along with it.

questions.question: Why is a green screen green?

answers.answer: The green screen is used to segregate colour from the foreground and the background. If you've got a weatherman, he stands in front of a green or blue screen and he can't wear green or blue because the programme is inserted into the background. It's green and blue because there's no colour in the human face that can be misconstrued as green or blue. You couldn't have red because people have got red faces. Couldn't have black because people have got black faces. Couldn't have purple because people have purplish tinges to their complexions.

questions.question: What is the difference between gammon and ham?

answers.answer: The difference is the way it's brined, cured, and cooked. A ham is cut from the carcass and then treated, whereas gammon is meat that is cut from the carcass after being treated. It's about what happened to it before purchase.
A ham is a cooked gammon. A gammon by itself is cured, and when you cook it, it becomes a ham.

Gammon is an uncooked piece of bacon. A gammon is a cut of meat - gammon is the leg. When it's cooked, it becomes ham. When you go into a butcher's, you probably asked for ham or gammon and they probably said cooked or uncooked.

questions.question: What is it in our spittle that creates that demisting effect when we spit on a diving mask and wipe it around?

answers.answer: It might be the salt in saliva. The salt on the inside lowers the temperature at which steam forms.
There's something in our human saliva like a demister.

The saliva is used to clean the mask inside before you dive. When you've spat at it and rubbed it into the lens, you then rinse it off with water. The thin layer left on the lens makes it harder for condensation to penetrate.
Saliva has naturally occurring wetting agents in it, and that makes the little droplets of water stick together so you get a flat film of water rather than little droplets that obscure vision.

questions.question: Why does my hair and nails seem to grow longer on one side than the other? Specifically, my right side of hair seems to grow faster than my left side, and my toenails on my right foot seem to grow faster than on my left foot.

answers.answer: The hair growth difference is due to the way she brushes her hair towards the right parting. The fingernails grow faster on the left hand because she uses her right hand all the time, wearing down the nails more.

questions.question: What makes one get a bending sensation from eating horseradish, wasabi, or mustard?

answers.answer: The plant has evolved over the years to be unappetizing to potential consumers by being hot and burny, to stop animals eating it. But humans as a species have evolved to quite enjoy the burning sensation.

questions.question: Do you use more battery power if you make a call, or do you use less battery power if you're receiving a call?

answers.answer: When you receive a call, you're also transmitting because you're answering the person who's called you. So the power exchange is identical whether you're making or receiving.

With duplex transmissions (which is what we have now), both parties can talk and listen at the same time - both transmitting and receiving simultaneously - so it takes exactly the same amount of power. However, with simplex transmission (like old police radios), you push the button to talk and the other person can't talk while you're doing that.

questions.question: Why do we say 'excuse my French' after swearing?

answers.answer: After the Norman Conquest, the aristocracy in this country would speak French. The French imported curses with them. You had two types of swearing - Anglo-Saxon swearing (bodily function type swearing) and French swearing (religious blasphemy, like 'Sacrebleu' or 'Mon Dieu'). Over the years as the French and Saxon peoples merged, Gallic blasphemy became synonymous with any swear word. So now if you swear, you say 'excuse my French', whereas a thousand years ago you would have sworn in French.

questions.question: Why do we call a 123-dart checkout a 'Shanghai'? (60-20-40, treble 20, single 20, double top)

answers.answer: I don't know. I really don't know.

questions.question: Will leap years eventually have to be taken away because in a thousand years' time we would have jumped ahead of ourselves and it would be summer when it should be winter?

answers.answer: Leap years exist because the orbit of the Earth around the Sun is not exactly 365 days. A year is 365 and a quarter days, roughly. Every four years, you accommodate by sticking an extra day on. The leap year system keeps us in alignment with the seasons.

questions.question: Why do we clink glasses when we say cheers?

answers.answer: It goes back to Victorian times when people were closing business deals. There was a lot of rivalry between different people doing deals, but they used to congratulate each other. To ensure the rival didn't poison your drink, they used to tip a little bit of each other's drink into each other's glass - so you'd have to clink glasses, swap a little bit. If you were trying to poison me, you'd now poison yourself. Then the trust just evolved into clinking glasses.

questions.question: What is a 'tog' in duvets?

answers.answer: TOG stands for Thermal Overall Grade. It's a trademark for the suitability of duvets for different seasons. It's about insulation qualities, not thickness or weight. The higher the rating, the warmer the duvet and better suited for winter; the lower the rating, better suited for summer.

questions.question: How do sandbags work to stop flooding? Water goes straight through sand, so how can sandbags possibly work?

answers.answer: If you pack sand tightly together so the particles are all touching, it's more water-resistant than when it's loose with gaps between particles. A sandbag is very tightly packed sand that provides a temporary barrier against flood water. It takes a lot longer for tightly packed sand to saturate than loose sand. Until it saturates, water can't get through. It won't work forever, but provides temporary respite while waiting for water levels to go down.

questions.question: Where does the tradition of cutting a dead tree and decorating it in our living rooms for Christmas start? Is the tradition of bringing a dead tree into our homes rather than dancing round one in the town square?

answers.answer: The reason why we bring them in around Christmas is because the pagans during Saturnalia, which is a celebration held around the same time as Christmas, they would bring in fir trees as an act of sympathetic magic, and they'd bring the fir trees into their home to ward off bad spirits.

questions.question: What note does Big Ben chime at and is it dependent upon atmospheric weather conditions?

answers.answer: The temperature differential wouldn't affect solid metal with a melting point of several thousand degrees.

It's in the key of A. No, it shouldn't do, because that bell is quite a big bell. That's why it's called Big Ben. It's one of the biggest bells in that tower. The bell is tuned by making the mouth bigger or smaller when the iron is warm enough to bend. Big Ben had a kind of piston inside the bell which springs into action when the bell is chimed.

questions.question: If the future king or queen adopted a child, would that child still be allowed to be heir to the throne?

answers.answer: I have an inkling from memory that an adopted child couldn't be monarch, but I could be wrong.

questions.question: Why do people absolutely reek so offensively the next day after having lots of garlic, yet the night before if they had garlic bread they don't smell terrible?

answers.answer: You can smell the decaying garlic that's stuck on their skin.

Garlic has a very high concentration of sulfurous compounds, and when that mixes with the bacteria in your mouth, eventually you get very strong bad breath. Sulfurous compounds are responsible for most bad smells. Parsley has a counter effect upon that. When chopping garlic, if you take out the greeny core in the middle, that must be where a lot more sulfurous compounds have gathered as the garlic ripens. They gather more in the core and work their way out. If you take that out before cooking, you get a nicer flavor and you don't get quite a pungent aftermath.

questions.question: Why do we always close our left eye when we want to focus on something, like looking down the barrel of a gun, and if you hold your finger up and close your right eye, your finger is no longer in line?

answers.answer: Our brain processes two separate messages from each eye and combines them to give us a field of vision. When you want to focus on something very specifically, you need to reduce your field of vision by half to just one lens, so you close one eye. If you were left-handed, you'd do it the other way around.

We have an eye that's dominant just like we have a dominant hand. When you hold your finger up and close one eye and the thing behind the finger moves, that tells you which is your dominant eye. You should close the less dominant eye. The reason it's dominant is because the message from that eye gets to the brain quicker.

questions.question: Why is it called a round of toast? If you ordered two pieces of toast, you say two rounds of toast. Why do we say a round of toast and why do we say a round of drinks?
Why do Afro-Caribbean people have Afro hair, as in very tight, curly hair? Why is it confined to people of colour?

answers.answer: There must be an evolutionary reason.

Afro hair is heat-resistant and protects their heads from the sun. Africa is very hot. Hair has six layers of skin. The new hair grows up looking for light. As it grows through the offset layers, it slightly fractures and splinters, making it curly. But as you know, none of us are purebreds. We're all intermixed.

questions.question: Why is your salary also known as wages?

answers.answer: Wages is based on an hourly rate. If you're in a job that pays by the hour, like a bus driver, you get paid a wage. Other jobs where someone works in an office on a set fee regardless of hours worked is a salary. Wages used to be based on a weekly wage.

It goes back to medieval times when you had people called wage earners. They used to journey around the country and earn their money as they went, like tinkers. It was two words - wage earners. Wage was to do with the way, W-A-Y, and the journey. They were the itinerant workers way back hundreds of years ago.

questions.question: At National Lottery rehearsals, do they use blank balls or do they use numbered balls?

answers.answer: They have numbers on them. They use about three or four rehearsals with the full numbers on them. They use the same balls in rehearsal as in the real draw.

questions.question: Where did the saying from cold turkey come from?

answers.answer: Cold turkey is Boxing Day. The day after the party when you've got all that cold meat left over.
When someone had been in rehab, they said the skin could be a description of what your skin looks like during chemical withdrawal. But why pick a turkey and not a chicken?

questions.question: When grooming nasal hair, occasionally there's a rogue hair that looks like a spider's leg, about three or four times thicker than any other hairs. Why does this happen? Is it always in the same nostril?

answers.answer: The answer might be age. When you get older, your nose is going to be full of those babies.

questions.question: If I wear my coat indoors, does it mean it will be less effective when I step outside into the cold?

answers.answer: If you wear your coat indoors, you're acclimatised to it. So when you walk outside, you don't really feel the benefit as if you were to put it on when you were outside. But it doesn't mean you're worse off health-wise - you just won't feel as comfortable as you would if you put the coat on to address the increase in cold. If you used to walk out without your jacket, you'd be freezing and then feel the benefit of putting your coat on. Whereas if you walk out with your coat on, you're already acclimatised, you're still going to feel the cold but not any worse than if you hadn't worn it at all.

I disagree. If you put your coat on inside in a warm environment, you've got that layer of insulation already heated up. And when you walk outside, you've already got that heat wrapped around you. So not only would you be the same or worse off, you'd be actively better off for wearing your coat indoors than if you put it on outside.

questions.question: Why is it called a 'tattoo' when referring to the Edinburgh Tattoo or military tattoo? Where does the origin come from?

answers.answer: It comes from a Dutch word dating back to the time of William of Orange. It means the sound of the drum used to call troops together. Before barracks, troops were billeted in various places, so drummers would beat out a tattoo to call all the troops to come together in the morning or evening before being sent to their allotted billets. There's a link between pubs and soldiers - all the soldiers would be in the pub, and 'Do, den, tap, to' means 'turn off the tap'. So publicans would turn off the taps and all the soldiers would return to barracks. That became corrupted into 'tattoo'. It has no link whatsoever with body art tattoos - it's a complete verbal coincidence.

questions.question: Why do we remember things leading up to an accident but not remember anything after the accident? Why do we lose those memories?
What's the explanation for 'tying the knot' with regards to a wedding? Where does that phrase come from?

answers.answer: At some point they tied knots at wedding ceremonies - it's probably symbolic.

It dates back to colonial India when the British ruled. When Indians get married, before taking the seven sacred steps around the fire, the woman and the man are tied together with a scarf that drapes them, then they take the seven steps and are married. So it has to do with that tradition.

In the Anglican Church, after the vows, the couples join their hands together and the priest wraps his stole around their joined hands, saying 'Those whom God has joined together, let no man put asunder.' This involves a symbolic knot.

questions.question: In France they are guilty until proven innocent. Has there been any research to find out which system is fairer - innocent until proven guilty or guilty until proven innocent?

answers.answer: The British model is innocent until proven guilty - the burden of proof literally lies with the prosecution. You have to prove beyond reasonable doubt that you did it. The European model, not just French, is the opposite - the burden of proof lies with the defence. You have to prove beyond reasonable doubt that you didn't do it. There's no way of establishing definitively which is fairer because you'd need everyone to admit they'd lied after being found guilty, which is never going to happen.

questions.question: How do smartphone touchscreens work? Is it electrical, completing a circuit, or magnetism?

answers.answer: I used to play trivia machines in pubs - early examples of touchscreens. Sometimes they wouldn't register your finger, especially when I was about to win the jackpot. Sometimes licking your finger made it work better.

The human body creates an electrical impulse and there's a circuit underneath the screen. When you touch the screen, it completes that circuit. The first touchscreen was invented at CERN in the 1970s because computers weren't advanced enough to physically flick all the switches at once, so someone invented a touchscreen to bring all those switches in front of him at the touch of a button. Water is a good conductor of electricity, which is why licking your finger sometimes helped with old touchscreens.

questions.question: Why are there 60 seconds in a minute? Wouldn't it have made more sense to go up to 100?
Is there a genetic or inbuilt gene that means all boys will be taller than their mother?

answers.answer: I don't think there's any genetic guarantee. All we need is someone whose son is shorter than them to disprove this theory. Your 12-year-old is at your chin already, so he's not far off surpassing you.

When you first have a baby, they give you a book where there's an equation using the dad's height and the mum's height to work out an approximate height the child might be. It's not exact because there are other factors like nutrition, recessive genes, and tall uncles. Most sons are bigger than their dads. But it's not guaranteed - if there's a shorter recessive gene in the family, the son could be shorter than his mum.

questions.question: How long does it physically take to print a million pounds at the Royal Mint?
Barn owls hunt exclusively at night and are stealth hunters that can't be seen or heard. So why are they white? Shouldn't they be dark if they're hunting at night?
[Follow-up on the 60 seconds question]

answers.answer: The previous answer was about divisibility, but the origin goes back to the ancient Egyptians who used to count using their thumb. You count the pads on your fingers - three pads on each of four fingers, which gives you 12. That's where the base-12 system originated, leading to 60 seconds in a minute (five 12s).

questions.question: Is there a maximum height for a basketball player if you wanted to play?

answers.answer: No, there is no restriction on the height of a basketball player. Yao Ming, the tallest basketball player, was 7 foot 11. The reason someone nearly 9 foot tall wouldn't automatically be a brilliant basketball player is because of the three-second rule - you cannot stand in the area under the basket for longer than three seconds.

questions.question: When you hear of stars dying, why has that not affected any of the major constellation stars? The stars that make up the major constellations, like Orion's Belt and so forth, how have none of them stars ever died?

answers.answer: Stars die every few million years, so in the space of an average human life, we're not going to be in a position to track that.

Stars live for billions of years, and the whole lifetime of mankind is only a couple of hundred thousand years, so you're just not going to catch the big ones. However, it does happen - about a thousand years ago, a star went supernova, and it was recorded by the Chinese, and we now see it as a nebula.

questions.question: Why do we call mincemeat mincemeat when there's no mince in it? We know the mincemeat inside mince pies.

answers.answer: Back long ago, before you had freezers, you had to kill off a load of your herd of animals at the end of the season because you couldn't afford to feed them. You couldn't freeze the meat, so you would cut the meat into strips and layer fruit and meat. The fruit juices would keep the meat fresh. Towards Christmas time, you'd have a wooden chest full of fruit with not much meat left, and because you didn't throw anything away, you ate the mincemeat which had got the fruit juices in it. That's why when you open a jar of mincemeat, it's got suet in it - all the flavors of the meat and the fruit.

questions.question: Why do we only teach our children till the 12th times table and not further on? 15th, 16th times table?

answers.answer: We learned the 12 times table because there were 12 pennies in a shilling (old currency) and 12 inches in a foot. You needed the multiplication of the 12s for quick calculations involving money or measurements.

questions.question: How could we see things in slow motion? Through our actual eyes? Would you have to slow down the speed of light?

answers.answer: That would create different space-time continuums, which is not possible according to all the rules of physics.

The perception of time slows down for humans in dangerous situations - like when your mind goes into overdrive processing information. The human eye is capable of processing around 25 frames per second, and in extreme situations, it may process faster, making it seem like time is slowing down for one person while others perceive things normally.

questions.question: Can a hair from a dog get implanted in a human arm and continue to grow?

answers.answer: Suggested the caller was gullible and someone was having fun at her expense.

As a doctor (now psychiatrist), explained that once a hair has left the body, it needs a hair follicle to grow, which is inside the skin. Even if it landed follicle-first in a pore, it wouldn't be attached to the blood supply it needs. It would be dead tissue. The ginger fellow was probably messing with her, unless he genuinely believed it.

questions.question: Can the internet ever be turned off? Could we wake up one morning and everyone try to go online and then it's gone?

answers.answer: The internet was created by the US military and American academia to provide communications following a nuclear war. If part of it got destroyed, it could bypass the broken part and communicate through other means. The World Wide Web is just a graphical interface on top of the internet. If you turned off every computer in the world, the internet would still exist in some form - it's the physical infrastructure of wires. It would just be inaccessible.

questions.question: Can birds fly backwards?

answers.answer: Initially dismissed the question and was preparing to give her a coating for asking a stupid question.
Hummingbirds can fly backwards - they hover and then back out.

questions.question: Can an animal procreate with another animal of a different species? Like a dog have offspring with a cat, or could a human have some sort of offspring with another animal?

answers.answer: Lions can breed with tigers (ligers), but they're from the same cat family. They can graft an ear onto a rat's back, so it might be scientifically possible in a laboratory.

Different species can't successfully produce young because they have different numbers of chromosomes in their sperm and eggs, so they don't have perfect pairs to match up during fertilisation. Things that are really close genetically, like lions and tigers, have the same number of chromosomes even though they're different animals. You couldn't do this in a laboratory - you'd end up with chromosomes that weren't joined and paired, so you wouldn't produce a being.

questions.question: What happens to the turkeys that Barack Obama will pardon on Thanksgiving? Do they go to a farm at the White House or get killed later?
Why do carrots and parsnips keep very crispy for 4-5 days if kept in water in a container in the fridge, but go rubbery in two days if kept in the fridge without water or in a vegetable rack?

answers.answer: Suggested it might be osmosis - water passing into the carrot.
Confirmed it was osmosis with the carrots and parsnips.

questions.question: What was a snod, or what is a snod? (about Snodland village named after something)

answers.answer: There is no official reason for the name being Snodland, but theory and history say it's because there's a Saxon called Snod, or Mr Snod. Mr Snod is buried on Snodland Hill. That's why.

questions.question: Why do we say lieutenant and the Americans say lieutenant (with the F sound)?

answers.answer: Lieutenant is a French word. It literally means left in place. So the second in command would be called the lieutenant second in place. The French don't pronounce it with an F. But in the best traditions of British military, we decided to keep that pronunciation. I was in the RAF whilst at university and we had lectures on this very subject.

The word loo is the same as when you have a loo day or something like that. It's a French word for place. But the old French was l'oeuf. L'oeuf tenant. And we've stayed with it. And the Americans have gone with it, reading it as it were, phonetically.

questions.question: Do short-sighted people become better sighted as they grow old?

answers.answer: No, it doesn't get better. Long-sightedness and short-sightedness are two completely different conditions. Short-sightedness means you need something for the distance. Long-sightedness is caused by the lens deterioration with age. Someone who's short-sighted, for example a minus two in the distance, the reading addition might be a plus two, which makes it zero. So they just don't need glasses for reading. But minus two is still minus two for the distance. You could have both. One isn't going to cure the other.

questions.question: Who invented the game It, or Tig, or Tag?
When does a brook become a stream and a stream become a river?

answers.answer: You can step over a brook, you can jump over a stream, but you have to swim a river. And if you get up to sea, you need a boat.

questions.question: Why don't surgeons bleed when cutting flesh during operations?

answers.caller: John from Acton (used to make surgical diathermies)
answers.answer: The surgeon is using a device known as surgical diathermy. This produces radiofrequency current which goes through the patient's body. It's so fast, he can't feel it, but it does fry the meat that you're cutting through. Consequently it doesn't bleed. It's also very sterile because nothing can exist in that sort of temperature. It cauterizes the wound as you make the wound.
Something called diathermy. You have a strong electrical current passing through a blade which basically burns off the blood vessels as you're going through. It cauterizes.

questions.question: Do colourblind people have to purchase a colour TV licence?

answers.answer: I don't think black and white licence exists anymore. When you switched over from analog to digital, you need a telly to plug in a digital box. Black and white tellies are quite old. Colour's been in since 1968 or 69. You can't buy black and white TV licences anymore. If you're colourblind, you can still see colours, but they're not the right colours, so you would still have to have a colour licence.
You can get black and white television licences for £49.50. You still can. Some people will have really old black and white tellies and they only want a black and white TV licence.

questions.question: How do saltwater fish, sharks and things, drink? Or do they need to drink? How do they cope with the salt?
Why is it when you eat something sour, it makes your cheek contract and you pull a face?
Why do pushbikes have their sprockets and gears on the right-hand side of the bike?

answers.answer: It keeps the chain taut. If it was on the other side, it wouldn't happen. Because you do the big push with your right foot, not with your left foot. On a motorbike, you don't have to do any pushing at all.

questions.question: Why isn't there technology to record smell, like we record sound and video?
Why are telephone boxes outside Fortnum & Mason black?

answers.answer: The phone box itself was sold off to big corporate companies for their own advertising. BT or the General Post Office as was sold off some of the phone boxes to corporate companies. They then took over the running of the internals and externals and were allowed to paint them their own advertising colours.

questions.question: Why can't I buy just magenta, yellow and cyan paint instead of hundreds of colours, since printers can make a million colours from just those three plus black?
What does the expression mealy-mouthed mean?

answers.answer: It's someone who's not brave enough to say what they mean, or honestly say what they mean. Beating around the bush.

Mealy-mouthed actually means softly spoken, as if you have meal in your mouth. It began as a descriptive of diction and evolved to describe talking in a way where you're not actually saying what you really mean. Like talking with your mouth full means you can't really understand what someone is saying.

questions.question: What happens to the crusts of loaves that are used in the ready-made sandwich industry?

answers.answer: They probably get put in a big blender and sold as breadcrumbs or something. If you buy cheap sandwiches from supermarkets, sometimes you get a crust.

questions.question: How do communion wafers get made so perfectly round?

answers.answer: They're made with a cutter from big sheets of what is essentially rice paper on a production line. Before being blessed by the priest, they're just bread - like biscuits being cut with cookie cutters.

questions.question: Why do girls curtsy but boys bow?

answers.answer: Theo later gave an answer about bowing being a sign of respect and showing you're not afraid. James noted it might have something to do with clothes/dresses vs trousers but wasn't sure.

Bowing is a way to show when you first meet somebody that it's a sign of respect and a sign that you're not afraid of the men. In the civilized world, we don't fear that. By bowing your head, you're showing you're sure of yourself.

Historically women curtsied so their headdresses or tiaras wouldn't fall off their heads, which is why gentlemen remove their hats when bowing. Men could bow because their wigs were long and came down the front either side of the face and would stay on if they bent forward.

questions.question: Why do you get sleep in your eyes when sleeping at night but not when sleeping during the day, even for the same amount of time?

answers.answer: It's about how much your eyes move while you're sleeping. If your eyes are moving a lot, they'll keep the fluid moving and you won't get the crystallized deposits. (He later retracted this answer, admitting he had no qualifications.)

questions.question: When animals bare their teeth it's hostile, but when humans bare our teeth it's a smile. Why? Are we the only species that smile?

answers.answer: It might be part of human evolution that the smile is deliberately designed to disarm someone we approach. Maybe showing we're not hostile. Humans are more emotionally evolved than animals - if a lion could smile, it could lull prey into a false sense of security before attacking.

questions.question: Where do women wear the poppy flower - left or right? And where does the Queen wear it?
What is a dry riser?

answers.answer: A dry riser is a pipe with an inlet at ground level that goes all the way up a tower block with outlets on every floor that have caps on. When there's a fire, the fire engine plugs its hose into the inlet at ground level, water shoots up to the floor where the fire is, and firemen plug their hose into the outlet on that floor to fight the fire. It's dry because it's not charged with water until it's needed.

questions.question: At 1800 revs per minute the turbo comes on in my van. What is the most economical speed to drive at - with the turbo on or off?

answers.caller: James (Essex, cab driver with 23 years experience)
answers.answer: Every car advertisement puts the urban cycle in brackets at 56 mph as the most economical. Much faster than that, even in top gear, your turbo kicks in and sucks a lot more air into the engine, therefore burning more fuel. You burn 30% more fuel between 50 and 70 mph.

questions.question: Where does the word 'gringo' come from?

answers.answer: In Mexico and Texas when it was Mexican territory, Mexican soldiers wanted the American soldiers to go away. The American soldiers wore green uniforms. So the Mexicans said 'green go' in English - go away. That evolved into 'gringo'. In the Dominican Republic, gringo actually means free range - polo gringo is free range chicken. It's not rude at all - it's actually friendly.

questions.question: When somebody dies and their body gets embalmed, what happens to that blood?
Why does the moon look silver in the sky and not yellow, given that the sun looks yellow?
Why do some stars twinkle and some stars don't?

answers.answer: Stars that don't twinkle are planets. It's all to do with the way light hits the atmosphere. The planets are closer to Earth so the effect is less noticeable. Out of the atmosphere, you won't see stars twinkle - it's the Earth's atmosphere that causes the twinkling.
(Phone line was very poor - difficult to understand) Something about pulsars and stars falling apart.
Every star is a ball of gas, and each dying star twinkles at a different time because that's the activity we can see.

questions.question: Why are the people doing sign language on TV always on at 4 or 5 in the morning, not at 6pm or 10pm? Do they think deaf people sit up all night waiting for the news?

answers.answer: There's scientific evidence that the more hard of hearing you are, the less sleep you need. They tape the news and set their machines to record it so they can watch it when they get up.

questions.question: Why was 18 holes chosen as the number of holes to be played in a golf turn and a golf match?

answers.answer: When the first golf courses were being constructed, it was decided that no one would really want to play more than 18 holes.

In the 1800s, St. Andrews had 22 holes and the governing body decided to shorten it to 18 holes. Because St. Andrews was thebenchmark of the time, the Americans followed suit, and that's how you get 18 holes. There are also theories that 18 shots in a bottle of Scotch is why they made it 18 holes.

questions.question: Why does a mobile-to-mobile call end when one party hangs up, but a mobile-to-landline call continues running after the landline hangs up? The mobile caller still has to pay for the ongoing call.

answers.answer: On the mobile network, there's greater revenue if it works like that - the call continues until the mobile caller also ends it.

questions.question: What is the origin of the term 'goody two-shoes'?

answers.answer: It's from a children's book called 'The History of Little Goody Two-shoes', written and published by John Newbery in 1765.

questions.question: What came first - salsa music, salsa dancing, or salsa the food?

answers.answer: Salsa is Spanish for sauce, so the sauce came first. The salsa dance was called that because it's a mixture of Spanish, African rhythms, all sorts of different instruments - similar to how salsa sauce mixes tomatoes, herbs and various ingredients together. It's a conglomerate of different things put together.

questions.question: Why is a woman with dubious morals known as a tart?

answers.answer: A tart has an open top - everything is on display. A pie has hidden depths. You have to cut into it to find out what it's got to offer. A tart, it's all there right in front of you.

questions.question: Do all fruit and vegetables we have in the world always exist? When did they first appear? Are they still evolving?

answers.answer: Fruit and vegetables do evolve, particularly fruits. They throw what are known as sports - where something slightly different grows on the same tree. A nectarine is a sport that grew on a peach tree. The same thing happens with apples - Russets are a sport. Natural mutations occur and then growers take advantage of superior variations.

questions.question: When you buy a size 12 pair of shoes, what are they measured in? It's not inches, centimetres, or feet.

answers.answer: They're measured in barley corns. It's an old Anglo-Saxon measurement. Ten barley corns made an old inch. Three barley corns used to make the yinch - an old inch. It's been standardised since then to around eight and a half millimetres.

questions.question: Why do moths come out at night but butterflies don't?
What does a surgeon do mid-operation if he needs to go to the toilet?
Why do we say 'take soup' and 'take tea' but not 'take lunch' or 'take dinner'?

answers.answer: It's just a grammatical abbreviation. We use 'take' for things that are optional. When sitting down for a meal, soup would often be an optional extra - 'Is sir taking soup? Actually no, I'll go straight to the main course.' It's an abbreviated form of 'partaking.'

questions.question: How do worms breathe so deep in the soil when there's no air down there?
What is the meaning of 'arms' in pub names like the Fisherman's Arms and the Blacksmith's Arms? It's not about coats of arms.
How do doctors know when the body is 'full' during a blood transfusion? When do they stop putting blood in?

answers.answer: They use catheterization to monitor output. The kidneys filter blood efficiently - if there's too much fluid, it gets filtered out quickly. You need about nine litres running around normally, and if you give ten, you just pee it all out. Blood pressure and urine output are monitored to know when you're 'full'.

questions.question: A shark's tail moves side to side (vertical), while a dolphin's tail moves up and down (horizontal). Which is more efficient? If a shark and dolphin raced, who would win?

answers.answer: It's about physiology and breathing. Dolphins and mammals that need to breach the surface for air have vertical tails - the up-and-down motion helps them surface. Fish with gills use sideways motion to help water travel through gills. In a race, the dolphin would probably have the better start (Usain Bolt), but the shark might overtake with more endurance (Mo Farah). The dolphin is very powerful as one long muscle, but the shark is heavier and has more torque.

questions.question: Why are movie credits printed in that weird, tall, squashed-up script? It's like Star Wars text. Why not just print it in standard font like the rest of the poster?

answers.answer: It's called 'title treatment'. It's contractually required that the director's name must be a certain percentage of the cap height. The elongated script font allows more letters vertically in a small sideways space.

questions.question: Where does golf terminology come from? Eagle, birdie, bogey - what's the origin?

answers.answer: Birdie came from American professional golfers in the 30s or 40s. When one played a good shot, the other said it was a 'bird of a shot' because it flew from club to green. Eagle and albatross are also American expressions, not Scottish. Bogey comes from the tune 'Colonel Bogey' which was whistled by Kenneth Oldsford when playing golf in Scotland before it was adapted. The four count comes from being the loudest sound you can exhale in one gasp.

questions.question: Why don't we hear about things disappearing in the Bermuda Triangle anymore? Does it still exist?

answers.answer: The phenomenon was caused by massive releases of methane gas from the seabed, which destabilised buoyancy in the water and stalled aircraft engines by taking oxygen out of the air. The geological activity that released the gas has stopped, so the phenomenon has expired even though the triangle itself still exists.

questions.question: How do wildlife programmes know there are 27 million birds on a lake or 27 million wildebeest crossing the Serengeti? Who counts? How can they possibly know?

answers.answer: The principle is based on population density sampling. If you know how many animals are in one square mile, and you know the total area covered (e.g., 30 square miles for wildebeest), you multiply up to estimate the total. It's an extrapolation from a sampled percentile.

questions.question: Do radio broadcasts and TV programmes actually get beamed out into space? How far do they go? Do they dissipate or degrade?

answers.answer: Signals do dissipate. You need a lot of power to reach far - megawatts - to bounce signals off the moon or distant planets. The waves keep traveling but without a receiver/transponder to pick them up and amplify them, they just idle out. An alien would need a responder to understand what's coming through.

questions.question: Why are they called 'spring tides' when they happen in autumn? Does it have anything to do with the season spring?

answers.answer: Spring tides have nothing to do with the season. They happen monthly after every full moon. The term refers to forward momentum, like something 'springing' forward - it's the highest tide it can be. You'll also get a neap tide when there's no moon.

questions.question: Why can you project any colour onto a surface except black? Why can't you project black?

answers.answer: Black isn't really a colour - it's the absence of light. You can't make the absence of light out of light.

questions.question: How do you make water? My five-year-old daughter asked this and I didn't know the answer.

answers.answer: Burn hydrogen in the air - it combines with oxygen and creates water. You could burn any hydrocarbon and get water, energy, and carbon dioxide.

Complete combustion of anything produces water and carbon dioxide. So out of a car exhaust pipe, you're literally getting water - H2O comes out with CO2. The easiest way to explain to a five-year-old: when you burn something that has hydrogen in it, the hydrogen joins with oxygen from the air and makes water.

questions.question: What was Crystal Palace called before the exhibition was built there?

answers.answer: It was known as Norwood. There's still a West Norwood and Upper Norwood. They did try to rebrand the area as 'Norwood Heights' but it didn't take off.

questions.question: Why is the sea salty when all the rivers are fresh and run to the sea? Why doesn't the salt go back up the rivers?

answers.answer: Salt was originally in rocks. Water has been washing it out of rocks and carrying it down to the sea for thousands of years. When seawater evaporates, the salt stays behind, so it accumulates in the oceans. When water goes back up into the sky as rain, the salt doesn't evaporate with it. So rainfall into reservoirs, streams and rivers is fresh, and all the salt stays in the sea.

questions.question: How do guide dogs know where to take their owners? If you're going to the grocers down a high street, how does the dog know where it's going?

answers.answer: A guide dog works in straight lines. When you first have your dog, you learn the regular routes. After a while, the dog gets to know familiar destinations. They walk in straight lines, sit at curbs, and the owner gives commands: forward, left, right, stop, stay. The dog is in control of the person but only goes on command. Some routes become familiar through repetition.

questions.question: Where does the phrase 'raining cats and dogs' come from?

answers.answer: The expression comes from early England when drainage wasn't good. When it rained heavily, cats and dogs used to float around. They also used to sleep on top of houses, so they would fall down when heavy rain came. People with umbrellas would say it's raining cats and dogs because that's how heavy the rain is - animals falling off roofs.

In the Middle Ages, households had open ceilings where you could see the roof rafters. They kept cats and dogs for rodent problems. The animals slept in the rafters because it was warm near the cooking fire. When cooking smoke was heavy or blocking the chimney, the smoke would irritate the animals in the rafters, making them jump down. That's where the saying comes from - literally cats and dogs falling from the ceiling.

questions.question: Why can't light be stored? You can store electrical energy in a phone, chemical energy, kinetic energy in a spring. Why can't you capture and store light?

answers.answer: Light is made up of particles called photons. When photons come into contact with any particle down to an atom, they transmit the energy they're carrying into that atom. Theoretically, if you contained light in a perfectly reflective box (which is impossible in the practical world), it could be contained and would keep bouncing from reflective surface to reflective surface. But practically, as soon as anything comes into the photon's way, it transmits that energy into the next particle. That's why you can't stop or store light.

questions.question: How do spiders build webs so quickly? How do they span across doorways? And why don't they break when you fire a hosepipe at them, but you can break them with just a flick of your finger?

answers.answer: When you brush a spider web with your hand, it sticks to you and you pull away. With a jet of water, the spider web is elasticated - it reacts the same way as when you cushion a football with your foot. It stretches and absorbs the impact rather than breaking.

questions.question: If you're underwater and you come across a shark, apparently you're supposed to scream at it. If you scream underwater, would your bubbles carry your scream to the surface where people above could hear it?

answers.answer: No, the bubbles won't carry your scream to the surface.

Sound can travel through water - water is more dense than air so sound actually travels better through water than through air (that's why you can hear a train before it arrives at a platform). But it won't be trapped in a bubble - the sound leaves the bubble and travels through the water. You would hear someone underwater if they were loud enough, but it wouldn't come out in a bubble.

Sound definitely travels through water - otherwise whales and dolphins would never be able to communicate. My five-year-old son regularly dunks himself underwater in the bath and screams, and it's very audible even when I'm downstairs. The sound travels through the water to the surface.

questions.question: If a Premier League footballer scores 30 goals in a season but 5 are own goals, does that still count as his total goal score? Would he get the Golden Boot ahead of someone who scored 30 legitimate goals?
What is the oldest company in the world?

answers.answer: There's a company in Japan called Congo Gummy (or Gummy, to rhyme with Brummie). They were established in AD 578 and were in construction. My grandson had to do a project on construction companies and this came up.

There's a company called Bilgin that makes cymbals for drum sets, called Zildjian. It's well over 2,000 years old and originated in Greek (which would explain the name). It was founded during the Ottoman Empire in the 17th century.

questions.question: Why does beer stay liquid in the freezer but freeze solid the moment you take the cap off?

answers.answer: It's due to pressure. When beer is in the bottle, it's under pressure. When the cap is released, pressure reduces and therefore the beer freezes. It's the same analogy as water boiling at a lower temperature on a mountain.

Water, when it freezes, needs a nucleation point - something like dirt or a bubble for the crystal to seed off. The inside of a beer bottle is completely sterile with no dirt and no bubbles because the CO2 is kept in solution under pressure. It's cold enough to freeze but won't because there's nothing for the crystal to seed off. When you take the lid off, bubbles appear instantly, providing nucleation sites, and it freezes instantly.

questions.question: I suffer with cold hands all year round, even in summer. But when I wear nail polish, my hands are warm. Why?
Where do the particles come from in the Hadron Collider? When they collide particles, do they get them from atoms? And if so, where are they? Are they in the air floating about?

Forty years ago he was told that turning off a fluorescent light bulb uses equivalent power to about five hours of leaving it on. Should he turn it off if he's going back in the kitchen within three or four hours?

answers.answer: A fluorescent tube works on the hot cathode principle. You have a strip of mercury and a gas (possibly argon) in the tube. You need a big bolt of electricity to heat up the mercury to fire the gas. There's a starter which is effectively a capacitor. If he's got the original capacitor from 40 years ago, then yes, it probably does use a lot of power and might be inefficient. But modern starters don't use much power at all. With modern fluorescent tubes, you should just turn them on and off with gay abandon. If he has the old type, anything over about 20 minutes of being away and it's worth turning off. They don't use that much power either way.

questions.question: If you drink a can of Coke and then swallow a Mentos mint, is the same thing going to happen as if you drop a Mentos mint into a Coke bottle?

answers.answer: The chemistry might be the same. But you'd have to swallow the mint whole, which is just weird, and it'd probably get stuck on the way down.

Mythbusters tested this. They put a pig stomach on a rig, filled it up with Coke, and dropped a Mentos in. It didn't explode. The reason is that all the carbon dioxide in the liquid shoots out of the liquid when you drop the mint into it for chemical reasons. But the simple act of pouring it out of the bottle into anything else, be it a human stomach or a pig stomach, removes the concentration of carbon dioxide needed to affect any form of explosion.

questions.question: Why does porridge stick to a nonstick pan?

answers.answer: Porridge has a flour consistency in it. When you put it in the pan, that's why it sticks. The milk may not be enough to counteract it.

questions.question: (Answer to Beverly's question) Where do the particles come from in the Hadron Collider?
Why do geese fly in a V formation?

answers.answer: It's aerodynamics - same reason cyclists tuck in behind each other to get into the slipstream. They use less energy and take it in turns to be at the front to conserve energy over long journeys.

They benefit from the slipstream - a bit of aerodynamic hydroplaning from the wing which disturbs the air so they fly in quieter air. They also check-navigate each other during long migrations.
