There's a device the size of an iPhone costing about £200 that reads the bills. It raises the material to create one dot, three dots, or five dots depending on the note. He works for an optician. South Africa has dots printed on notes already.

questions.question: Why does hair go darker when wet?

answers.answer: Hair under a microscope looks like a pine cone when dry. When wet, those scales lie flat, so instead of reflecting light you get a uniform colour spectrum. It's lighter when dry because of internal reflection.

questions.question: Where does talcum powder come from geographically? Is it mined?

answers.answer: Main ingredient is hydrated magnesium, sourced mainly from Australia or around China/Asia. It's just chemistry - zinc oxide and other ingredients. He was R&D scientist for The Body Shop in Littlehampton.

China Clay (kaolin) from Cornwall mining villages - decomposed granite. It's used in talcum powder, toothpaste, pottery, fine paper. Blasted out with monitor hoses. China Clay Museum in Cornwall shows talcum powder as a by-product.

questions.question: Has there ever been a Travel Update during Business Hour (Mon-Fri) with absolutely nothing to report?

answers.answer: Yes, she has reported nothing, usually on bank holiday Monday mornings. During business hours there's always roadworks.

questions.question: How can a camping fridge that burns gas actually make things cold?

answers.answer: Absorption fridges are silent (no compressor). The gas burner heats the bottom of a self-contained cooling unit filled with a mixture of hydrogen and other chemicals. The liquid boils, goes through the cooling unit, draws heat away from the fridge area creating coldness, then drops back down and reheats - a self-contained system using chemical reactions and boiling points as catalyst. Opposite of exothermic reaction.

questions.question: Where is talcum quarried? Is there a town of Talc?
Why is cheese yellow?
Why does water go down the plug hole in opposite directions in the northern and southern hemisphere, and does it go straight down at the equator?

answers.answer: Yes, at the equator the water goes straight down without rotating

questions.question: In crime dramas, why are unidentified bodies called John or Jane Doe?

answers.answer: John Doe started as DOE - Dead On Entry (or DOA - Dead On Arrival depending on region). Jane was added as the female equivalent

questions.question: Why are zippers on men's trousers called flies? Why aren't women's zippers called flies?

answers.answer: It's because of the two wings - it might relate to codpiece days when women didn't wear them
Fly is a type of needlework fitting - a flap over buttons or a zip. It's used on men's and women's clothing including skirts and blouses

questions.question: Why does a cut stop hurting the moment you put a plaster on it?

answers.answer: When you cut or burn yourself, you expose nerve endings. What causes pain is the flow of air over those nerve endings. The plaster stops the air flow, hence no pain. Same reason people put cling film on burns.

questions.question: Why do they call frozen water that falls on the ground black ice?

answers.answer: It's only black because it's the colour of the tarmac beneath, making it invisible to drivers, hence more dangerous than visible white ice

questions.question: What is the aircraft that flies over South London every afternoon, making a distinctive zigzag pattern at about 2,500 feet?

answers.answer: It's a surveillance aircraft - a twin-screw PA-31 Piper. They use infrared cameras to spot cable theft from railway lines. The caller is a Stansted air traffic controller and has seen it land there.

questions.question: Why does your head go shiny where you lose hair, but your forehead stays matte when you've never had hair there?

answers.answer: The follicles are still alive and producing sebum (sebatic fluid), which makes the scalp shiny. Forehead doesn't have hair follicles, just skin pores, so stays matte.

questions.question: Where did the original currencies of Eurozone countries go when the Euro was introduced?

answers.answer: Old banknotes were burned and coins melted down. You can still find old Drachmas and Francs in junk shops.

questions.question: Why are there no 3p, 4p, 7p coins?

answers.answer: We simply don't need them. With 1p, 2p, 5p coins you can make any amount. Having 50p and £1 coins is easier than carrying 50 or 100 of the smaller ones. It's a decimal system based on 1, 2, 5 intervals.

questions.question: Why do military drummers rest their drumsticks just below their nose when not playing?

answers.answer: It's showmanship - a stylistic flourish. He is the commanding officer of Gateshead Squadron Air Cadets and runs their squadron band.

questions.question: During Trooping the Colour, are the guards' machine guns actually loaded?

answers.answer: Never. The only thing in the magazine is a penny so it makes a good sound when they do the drill. The reason is if you drop a weapon it might go off.

questions.question: The European Space Agency is building a telescope that can look back 40 billion years to the creation of the universe. How does a telescope look back in time?

answers.answer: Light takes time to travel. The sun's light takes 8 minutes to reach us - we see it as it was 8 minutes ago. The further away something is, the longer its light has taken to reach us, so we're seeing it further back in time. That's the speed of light - 186,000 miles per second.

questions.question: How do football commentators instantly know how many kilometres a player has run during a match?

answers.answer: There's a chip in the player's boot - advanced pedometer technology that measures distance, speed, and power. Her father-in-law was assistant Australian football coach and worked with this technology.

questions.question: What is the little plastic insert in the neck of spirit bottles for?

answers.answer: To slow down the pouring rate - so you can pour properly without drowning yourself

It's called a Guara pourer. While it does slow the pour, the main purpose is to prevent bootlegging - it stops people refilling bottles with cheap spirits and selling them as premium brands. It's a one-way valve.

questions.question: Why do people in Madeira leave a bottle of water leaning against car tires?

answers.answer: To stop dogs urinating on the tyres. Dogs won't foul where there's fresh water - it's an evolutionary thing. People used to do this on front lawns too.

questions.question: Do sinks really drain in opposite directions in the northern and southern hemisphere due to the Coriolis effect?

answers.answer: At sink size, it's a complete myth. The Coriolis effect is real but so small it only works on large things like tornadoes. Sinks have imperfections that override it. In perfect lab conditions at the equator, water would go straight down.

questions.question: Is there any other country which has a national anthem centred on a person like ours rather than honour and allegiance to their country?

answers.answer: Probably dictatorships like Turkmenistan - Turkmenbashi changed days of the week to reflect his mother's name. Also North Korea.
Poland. Their anthem mentions General Dąbrowski, who brought Polish forces from Italy to Poland. He's credited as one of the architects of modern Poland.

questions.question: What happens to the things that are confiscated by the police from criminals - cash, vehicles, counterfeit goods? Does it pay for the operation, go to government, pay for police?

answers.answer: I honestly don't know. The money from ill-gotten gains... what happens to the Bill-gotten gains?

Most of it goes to the Treasury. But police can apply to get some back because they put in the hard work. It might boost their own budget - they could hire extra officers, have a Christmas party, or buy a new Black Mariah. Cash gets put into interest-bearing accounts.

questions.question: Where does the 'circus' come into it for Piccadilly Circus, Oxford Circus, Ludgate Circus? Why aren't they called circles?

answers.answer: It's Latin. A bit of Latin goes a long way. Bread and circuses.
It just means a junction of roads, from Latin. At Piccadilly Circus all the roads come to one point. In Roman times, the circus would be at the most central point in the transport structure.

questions.question: Where does the first bee/wasp come from each year? If they hatch in nests/hives each year, where have they been all winter?

answers.answer: They hibernate. My mum had a nest in her loft during wintertime.

At the end of the year, bees produce queens or virgin queens and males. The virgin queen goes through winter hibernating while pregnant, then makes a nest in the spring. The male bees die. She starts the nest off and as she gets more workers, they take over. The queen lives for the season.

questions.question: When you change money to go abroad, how is the exchange rate worked out? Why is a pound worth $1.50 one minute and $1.60 the next?

answers.answer: It's like a share price. Reserves like gold go up and down. Currencies change when you compare them to each other. It's a reflection of the economic strength of the country that holds the currency. The Euro would be worth more if Greece weren't in it.

questions.question: How come we can hold our breath but we can't hold our hearing?

answers.answer: Because you've got ears on the side of your head, not lungs. What on earth might someone say the reason why you can't hold your hearing like you can hold your breath?

In your lungs or throat you have valves or an epiglottis at the top of your windpipe. When you hold your breath, the muscles around your epiglottis constrict so you can hold your breath with your mouth and nose open. Your ears are just open orifices. The epiglottis is something like a lid.

It's about survival. There's a survival imperative for being able to hold your breath when you're immersed in water. There's no survival imperative for shutting off your hearing - in fact, just the reverse. It's more important to keep hearing even when you sleep.

questions.question: How come during summer flying insects like bees aren't beaten to the ground with rain?

answers.answer: The really tiny ones ride on raindrops, almost inside them. The bigger ones like bees stay out of the way. You don't see a massive bee swimming across a rainstorm.

questions.question: Why do pigeons have such mashed-up feet - toes missing or whole feet missing? Is it electric cables, rats chewing, or dissolved by their own excrement?

answers.answer: Businesses put acid on the high parts of their buildings. When pigeons land, their feet dissolve. It's to keep them off the buildings. My friend used to be a height access specialist and had to get rid of the leftover feet and stuff. It's out of reach - only birds can land there.

questions.question: How do they concentrate orange juice?

answers.answer: They just take the water out by boiling it. It does slightly change the taste. They do it for ease of storage and pasteurisation to make it last. They ship frozen concentrate and re-dilute it at the other end so they're not shipping water from the orange tree to the breakfast table.

questions.question: In Victorian mugshots of criminals, why are they photographed with hands clasped against their chests? Even lady criminals do it.

answers.answer: It's to identify any deformities or fingers missing. It's another means of identification, to show if a particular criminal is missing his left ring finger, for example. Like tattoos and other identifying marks. In the days before sophisticated forensics, this was useful for police.

questions.question: What sort of bird might have laid an egg in my hanging basket and gone away and deserted it?

answers.answer: Foxes or squirrels bury eggs in strange places. They pick up fallen eggs and bury them for later. Colin found it under foliage, not actually buried underground, so it could have been stashed there.

It's most likely a collared dove's egg. They sometimes lay eggs in weird places, almost as if they were dying to lay an egg and just drop it anywhere. If it'd been a blue tit or great tit, the eggs would be speckly; if a song thrush, they'd be blue and smaller. Collared doves are suburban birds, nest all year round, and make very flimsy nests in weird places.

questions.question: Why, when you jump off small heights of a couple to three feet, why do you shout Geronimo?

answers.answer: Geronimo was a warlike and fierce Native American chief. During WWII, a US Marine colonel decided that if his men shouted 'Geronimo!' as they jumped out of aeroplanes, it would work as a war cry and pump them up. It became a war cry from a war chief adopted by the Marines.

questions.question: Where does the term 'pulling my leg' come from?

answers.answer: It goes back to when people were being hung. To make sure they were dead, they used to grab their legs so they weren't pulling a fast one - giving a tug on their legs to ensure the job was done. If you were still alive, hanging onto your legs would finish you off. So the person pulling the leg was making sure the other person was telling the truth.

questions.question: Do sheep have to be shorn every year?

answers.answer: Yes, they must be shorn every year for infection control. If you have a farm or keep sheep with wool that grows for industrial purposes, you have a legal requirement to shear them every year.

questions.question: Why is it when you put salt on a slug that it melts?

answers.answer: It's called osmotic pressure. When you sprinkle salt, you're creating a situation where the fluids from the slug's skin flow to the salty area, thereby dehydrating the slug and it dies.

questions.question: When you're in a bath, how come only your feet and hands go wrinkly and not the rest of your body?

answers.answer: Because that's where the skin is thickest. The stuff that comes into constant contact with other things is where you'll have the thickest skin, like pads on an animal's paw. This will be answered with the slug question - it's a biological/chemical reaction involving similar principles.

questions.question: When someone says they can smell the rain, what is it that they can actually smell?

answers.answer: You're not actually smelling the rain. When rain is nearby and reaching you, it's releasing chemicals and surfactants mainly trapped on buildings and roads - that's what you're smelling. You won't smell rain once it's actually raining. In summer it smells stronger because drier periods trap more of these chemicals.

questions.question: What is the atomic structure of a shadow?

answers.answer: A shadow doesn't have an atomic structure. It has no physical substance - it's simply the absence of light.

questions.question: Why is it when you put a shell to your ear, you can hear the ocean?

answers.answer: It's sound waves bouncing off a surface which causes vibration in your ears, making you think you can hear the sea. It's just one noise confusing you. When you cup your ear, sound waves bounce off the surface of the shell back into you - it's like white noise. It would happen with any cup or shell. It's about vibration and sound.

questions.question: Why have supermarkets changed from cardboard trays for cans to unrecyclable plastic wrapping?

answers.answer: Plastic is cheaper. There's no law in place about recycling and environmentally friendly packaging, so they've worked out they can do it more cheaply with shrink-wrapped plastic.

questions.question: When a big star implodes and leaves a black hole, how can the black hole have the same mass as the original star but have the same gravitational pull that sucks things in?

answers.answer: It's Einstein's theory. Imagine the universe as a sheet, and when you put something on it, a beach ball might weigh the same as a marble but the beach ball will sit on the sheet while the marble will push the sheet down. The further down it is, the more gravity it has. When the star implodes, it takes up less space, so there's more mass per square centimetre, which is why light is trapped even though it's got the same mass.

questions.question: Where does all the water come from when you cry tears? Some people cry for an hour - where does it all come from?

answers.answer: Tears come from tear ducts. The water comes from your body with salt in it.
It's the opposite of osmosis. There are glands called the lachrymal glands, or tear ducts, which extract water from the bloodstream using energy to push water through a membrane - active transport.

questions.question: Why do weather forecasters give you the temperature that it's going to be in the shade and not in direct sunlight?

answers.answer: Because if you leave something in sunlight, it would keep getting hotter and hotter. It would just keep cooking. The shade temperature is the actual air temperature.

questions.question: Why do even really skinny women have bingo wings?

answers.answer: It's a tricep muscle.

questions.question: Is the human race the only beings that commit suicide, or do any other animals suffer depression and actually go through with it?

answers.answer: Bees commit suicide by stinging themselves. If they're injured and won't make it back to the hive, they curl their tail round and inject themselves with the poison.

Upland geese in the Falklands mate for life, and if either side of the partnership dies, the other will just sit next to the corpse and die. They won't move. You can be fined by the local magistrate's court if you kill one of the geese without a licence.

questions.question: Does the word jubilee only refer to royal celebrations like silver and golden jubilees? Is it exclusively related to royalty?

answers.answer: Jubilee is a very ancient word coming from 'yobel', a ram's horn blown by the Israelites every 50 years to mark the anniversary of releasing Hebrew slaves. It applies to any major anniversary - Roman Catholic Church has jubilee years at 25th, 50th, 60th anniversaries including ordination anniversaries.

questions.question: Why do people say GOP when writing about the Republican Party but never say it out loud? Why is it only used in print?
Why is the Queen never called the Queen of Britain, given that Wales, Scotland and Ireland are all included in the term Britain?

answers.answer: She isn't the Queen of England - she's the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It became verbal tradition from the Act of Union when Queen Anne was the last monarch to be just Queen of England before the union with Wales and Scotland.

questions.question: Why aren't there any jokes on ice lolly sticks anymore?
What are those silvery aluminium-looking things at Bond Street tube station that look like cameras but aren't cameras?

answers.answer: They're subsidence monitors for the Crossrail project. They send out a beam to orange mirror discs around the tunnels and check the reflections to monitor if the station is shifting. Daniel is a service operator for the Underground and has been briefed on them.

questions.question: What is faster, a thought or a lightning bolt?

answers.answer: It depends where you start from. The lightning bolt discharge itself is instantaneous - a million to one speed. But a thought runs to the thousandth of a second because you've got to get the electrical charge plus the chemicals at the end of the neuron. However, if you start from when the lightning begins in the cloud, that build-up takes hours. So it depends on your starting point.

questions.question: Why do you get a continuous reflection of yourself when you look at two mirrors facing each other? Why does it go on forever?
Where does the expression 'Fanny Fanacapan' come from?

answers.answer: From Gracie Fields, the music hall star. It was a slightly derogatory term for someone who didn't get on with things, someone hanging around, dawdling and daydreaming. She'd say it in a hurry-up fashion to get them to move on. It was one of her stage characters in music hall shows.

questions.question: What is a phenacotan?

answers.answer: Spike Milligan wrote a poem called 'Fred Phenacotan'. Spike wrote back to explain that phenacotan is a Lancashire term meaning a little deer (D-E-A-R), specifically a term of endearment from a mother to a daughter. Gracie Fields was also from Lancashire.

questions.question: How far is the total distance of the coast of England, Wales and Scotland if you walked all the way around?

answers.answer: You will never get an answer because it's always changing. If you look at the houses that are falling into the sea and the way the waves weather the coastline, you will never get a true reading. If you look at Humber, where you've got the spit, the silt moves down further the coastline so it makes it wider in one area, smaller in the other area. The coastline is always changing due to weathering, tides and variables.

questions.question: When Man City won the Premiership on Sunday, they raised the cup. But only three minutes prior everyone thought Man United had won. What would they have raised? Are there two trophies?

answers.answer: Before the finals were played, they did say on national TV that there were going to be two cups, one at each ground. One of them has to be the cup, the one you get to keep. One of them is just a spare cup.

His son was a ball boy at Arsenal and said they have a helicopter, and they will fly it while they're setting up the bit in the centre of the pitch. If it's Southampton and Sunderland that are both in with a shout on the last day next season, they might have to get a faster helicopter.

questions.question: Why can't you have your cake and eat it? What's the point in having a cake if you can't eat it?

answers.answer: Think of it as money. You can't have your cake and eat it means if you eat it, you haven't got it anymore. You might want to keep it because you might want to eat it at a later date. Two nice states of affairs: the pleasant prospect of eating a delicious cake and the pleasant prospect of having a delicious cake in the cupboard at home. They're both pleasant, but you can't do both with the same money or the same cake.

questions.question: If you and I travel by plane somewhere far, we get jet lag. Migratory birds fly over. Do they suffer jet lag?

answers.answer: Birds can't get jet lag. The reason is because of logic. A bird couldn't get from New York to London even if they were going that way in seven hours. It would take them weeks, probably. So they have a sort of incremental adjustment of the body clock. By the time they arrived in Hendon, they would have already adjusted to the time in the Northern Hemisphere or the Western Hemisphere. So there's no way birds could get jet lag. Unless the bird was on a plane.

questions.caller: Roy (in studio - question from friend via email)
questions.question: Why does a wooden spoon placed over a pan of boiling water stop it from boiling over?

answers.answer: The wooden spoon is a living thing and it absorbs all the steam. Therefore, the steam can't accumulate to create the heat to make it boil over. It doesn't work on oil because there's no steam - it's not water so it won't be absorbable by wood.

Wood, on the molecular level, is quite rough. It bursts the bubbles, which are very thin, like one micron thin. If the foundation bubbles have been burst, you can't build any bubbles on top of them. A boiling over pan is bubble upon bubble upon bubble. If your foundation bubbles have been burst, therefore it will not overflow.

questions.question: Why are Londoners called Cockneys?

answers.answer: It comes from Cocaigne (C-O-C-A-I-G-N-E), which was an early name for what is now the east end of London, in the sort of environs of Bow. Cocaigne was a sort of mythical area where everything was wonderful and perfect, like a sort of utopia, and it became applied to that quarter of London by Londoners.

questions.question: What is the point of cutting the cake at a wedding reception? What is the symbolic meaning?

answers.answer: It goes back to being a representation of the unity, the new unity of the husband and wife. It's shown by them doing their first act together as such, and that is cutting the cake together. It's their first job as man and wife.

questions.question: Why shouldn't you cut the nose off the cheese? How has that come about?

answers.answer: When a cheese is made and manufactured, and it's in a sort of barrel shape like a Stilton, they mature at different levels through the depth of the cheese over time. Like rings on a tree, each one's a flavour thing. If you chop the nose off, then you're depriving other people of that whole symphony of flavour - the most mature bit of the cheese probably. With a very hard cheese like cheddar, there's not going to be that much difference from the middle to the rind, but you're still going to get a softer, mellower, nuttier cheese in the middle than at the outside.

questions.question: Can you watch 3D TV if you've got one eye?

answers.answer: Yes, it's definitely true. When watching 3D with glasses on, if you close one eye, it stops being 3D. Jones the Engineer said you wouldn't be able to pinpoint them as easily if you had one eye.

If you shut one eye and look at an object a little way away and line your finger up with an edge of that object, then shut the other eye and the place on the object has moved considerably. The further away the object, the more that shift. That is depth. It needs two eyes to be judged, and 3D is all about depth.

We have an interocular distance of approximately 65 millimetres. Things around about over 30 metres away don't really perceive any further depth, but things far in front of us are perceived as depth and they cause our eyes to diverge or converge accordingly. You can't see 3D with one eye. There is an eye-brain system that kind of thinks neurophysiologically that we can perceive 3D even if we can't see it.

I've only got vision in one eye, James, and it is true. 3D doesn't work for me. I remember when I was small and everyone was wearing all those daft glasses in the cinema, I wondered what all the fuss was about.

questions.question: If you have a cup in your hand, fill it to the brim with water, and walk in a straight line without looking down at it, you're less likely to spill any. And if you were to look down at it, you'd then find you're toppling it and it's going all over the place. Why does this happen?

answers.answer: It's a scenario called negative suggestion. Your brain is focusing so much on not doing something, as when you're looking at the cup of water, that it almost overloads your brain with information. You then inevitably, without a shadow of a doubt, are going to either spill it, or fall off the tightrope, or whatever it is that you may be doing. By thinking about it going wrong, it is more likely to go wrong.

questions.question: Who decided that pink is a girl's colour and blue is a boy's colour?
Will the police officers who are demonstrating today be policed by their colleagues and go around breaking up McDonald's and shops? Will they be kettled?

answers.answer: The 20,000 coppers on the streets are off-duty. Any organised public protest will involve a police presence. They only get kettled if they misbehave.

questions.question: When the premiership footballers finish their match, what happens to their kit?

answers.answer: They get a massive stock at the beginning of the season. Every squad member from 1 to 40 gets their numbers and names individually on shirts. Some players like to keep their shirts throughout the season so they'll wash and wear them. At the end of the season, remaining stock goes to the scholars (under-17s) for their following season or gets given to charity.

On match day they take at least three shirts per player - one for the first half, one for the second half, and one for medical emergencies (like nosebleeds or ripped sleeves). The kit man collects all the kit, takes it back to the club, launders and presses it. During Alan Pardew's reign at Newcastle, they had a similar system.

questions.question: Why does pressing the car alarm key fob against your head make it work when you're outside the normal range?

answers.answer: Your body acts like an aerial or transmitter. When you put the transmitter against the body, the body acts like an amplifier. It amplifies the RF (radio frequency) signal going towards the car. The fluid in your body transmits and amplifies the signal.

questions.question: Why does the Olympic torch never go out?

answers.answer: It never goes out from the moment it's lit in Greece. There is a keeper of the flame. The flame is transported in a brass lamp to the UK. The torches are lit from that flame. It's a relay of flame, and each torch on each leg of the journey is lit from that original flame. It covers the whole of the United Kingdom including Ireland.

questions.question: Where does the term 'Rosas' come from to describe police?
In business, people talk about sister companies and parent companies - where's the brother company?
Why is the jingle 'Greensleeves' so popular with ice cream vans?

answers.answer: Possibly because there's no royalties to play as it could be in public domain. Also it's a very recognisable tune that's simple to play. Nursery rhymes are popular too for the same reasons.

questions.question: Why are slugs selective? Why do they shred to pieces some plants and ignore others?
Why can you never get tinned spaghetti on toast anywhere? You only get beans on toast, tomatoes on toast, mushrooms on toast, eggs on toast, cheese on toast.

answers.answer: If you overcook spaghetti, it turns to slush. It's a manufactured product rather than a grown product. Things like beans, tomatoes, mushrooms keep their form on a hot plate or in a bain marie. If you heat spaghetti and keep it hot, you end up with floury, tomatoey soup which is disgusting.

Macro doesn't sell humongous tubs of spaghetti but does sell the big tubs of beans. Bookers does sell large tins of spaghetti. But the fact that they don't sell them as readily is because they don't get used in catering - they'll turn to slush.

questions.question: How can a farmer know that an egg is fertilised but at the same time have some eggs that he isn't sure about?

answers.answer: You shine a torchlight through the whole egg. If it's been incubated for a little bit, you can see a little chicken growing inside. So the eggs she has might not be at that point yet where you could tell. If the farmer hasn't checked them, he wouldn't know. The other possibility is the farmer's ripped her off.

questions.question: What do Chinese burns have to do with China or Chinese people?

answers.answer: It comes from martial arts. When an opponent is thrown and you've grabbed them by the wrist and throw them, they often get burns called in passing a Chinese burn. They can also get burns when dragged along the floor on the mat. It's also called an Indian burn in America.

questions.question: Who owns the moon?
What happened to the Unilever statues that were on top of the Unilever building on Blackfriars Bridge?
What does 'freedom of the city' actually mean and what does that person get?

answers.answer: It depends on the city. You get a key - which would have been to the city gates back when they had them, but now it's mostly symbolical. You might also be allowed to drive your sheep down the high street, or practice archery on the green. It's not like a Merlin pass - you can't go into a restaurant and get a free meal. It's not negotiable.
